title: One interest rate, three inflation realities. Why Europe’s price shock is so uneven
description: Finland, Germany and Lithuania share the euro and the ECB’s 2.50% deposit rate, but with September inflation at 2.7%, 3.3% and 6.1% respectively, they show how one policy meets different price realities.
content: Three countries share one currency and one central bank rate, yet their inflation rates differ by more than twofold.In September, annual inflation was 2.7% in Finland, 3.3% in Germany and 6.1% in Lithuania, according to Eurostat’s harmonised index (HICP), published in October. The euro-area average was 3.8%. All three face the same European Central Bank (ECB) deposit rate of 2.50%.An energy shock felt unevenlyThe common thread is energy. Eurostat data show energy prices across the euro area rose 18.9% in September, adding 1.71 percentage points to inflation, almost half the headline figure. Excluding energy, euro-area inflation was 2.3%.How that shock plays out depends on a country’s energy mix, tax choices and the strength of its domestic economy.Lithuania: energy, taxes and wagesLithuania sits at the top of the range, and food is not the reason. Eurostat figures show food, alcohol and tobacco inflation at 0.5%, while energy prices jumped 33.0% and services inflation reached 6.9%.The International Monetary Fund (IMF) attributes the surge to elevated energy prices amid continued import dependence, strong domestic demand and higher excise duties. Policy added to the pressure. From January, Lithuania raised the VAT on residential heating, hot water and firewood from 9% to 21%. The government’s draft budget estimated that the heating change alone would add 0.5 percentage points to inflation.Pressure has spread beyond fuel and heating. Eurostat data put Lithuania’s core inflation, excluding energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, at 3.9%. The Bank of Lithuania expects average wages to rise 9.4% in 2026, and the European Commission links services inflation to strong pay growth and an 11.1% rise in the minimum wage.Higher wages may leave many workers better off on average. But pensioners, benefit recipients and low-income households with large energy bills are more exposed. There is also a second-round risk. Labour-intensive service businesses can pass higher wages into prices, keeping inflation elevated after the energy shock fades.Finland: cushioned and sluggishEurostat figures show Finland faced a similar energy shock, with energy inflation at 13.1%, yet headline inflation stayed at 2.7%. The European Commission says Finland’s relatively low reliance on fossil fuels softened the blow. Statistics Finland found that cheaper electricity and owner-occupied housing costs restrained its national consumer price index, even as petrol, diesel and heating oil pushed it up.Domestic price pressure is weak. According to Eurostat, core inflation was 1.4% and services inflation 1.7%. The Bank of Finland forecasts 10.4% unemployment in 2026, while the Commission expects GDP growth of 0.8%. Statistics Finland reports nominal earnings rose 3.5% year on year in the third quarter, or 1.2% in real terms.That combination helps explain why another rate rise may seem overly restrictive from Helsinki.Germany: a spike concentrated in fuelGermany falls in the middle. Eurostat data show energy inflation at 13.4% and core inflation at 2.5%. Germany’s statistics office, Destatis, found motor fuels up 37.1% and heating oil up 74.9% in the national index. Excluding those two items, inflation was 1.8%.Wage pressure is moderate. Negotiated wages rose 2.9% year on year in August, and the Bundesbank projects the same average for 2026. Eurostat puts services inflation at 2.8%.Policy also muddies the picture. Existing federal measures lowered electricity, gas and district-heating prices, and a new fuel-tax cut took effect on 1 October, so it is not included in September’s figures. National interventions can shift measured inflation monthly without changing the underlying European shock.What a single rate meansThe ECB raised its deposit rate from 2.25% to 2.50% in September, arguing that the Middle East conflict was keeping inflation above target and that the full effects of the energy shock had yet to emerge.Subtracting national headline inflation from the ECB rate gives a rough real-rate proxy: minus 0.2% in Finland, minus 0.8% in Germany and minus 3.6% in Lithuania. This simple calculation based on ECB and Eurostat figures is not a true measure, since households and firms act on expected inflation and face different borrowing costs.The policy tensions differ by country. Finland’s weak growth and high unemployment argue against tightening. In Germany, the rate is easier to defend given core inflation of 2.5%, but September’s acceleration was driven almost entirely by fuel and heating oil. In Lithuania, the rate looks loose against 6.1% inflation, though higher rates cannot reverse a VAT increase or lower imported fuel prices. They work by weakening demand and curbing second-round effects.Transmission also varies. ECB research finds that policy works faster and more strongly where variable-rate debt and household leverage are more common, and Lithuania is among the countries relying on variable-rate mortgages with short reset periods.Yet a recent study covering 2000 to 2025 suggests output and inflation responses to monetary policy are less uneven than often assumed, as some structural differences offset each other.Sources: Eurostat, ECB, IMF, European Commission, Bank of Lithuania, Bank of Finland, Statistics Finland, Destatis, Bundesbank.

title: Meta shares jump 5% as AI investments fuel revenue growth
description: Meta Platforms said Wednesday that its third-quarter profit jumped more than threefold, as the social media giant's revenue climbed sharply, adding to confidence that the firm's AI spending is improving the business.
content: Meta shares rose about 5% in after-hours trading on Wednesday, as the tech company delivered strong growth and said its AI investments were paying off.Meta’s core advertising business delivered a strong quarter, with the company reporting a 26% increase in total revenue to $64.6 billion, helped by AI recommendations, more ads being shown and rising ad prices.And investors are eyeing promising new businesses around Muse, the personal artificial intelligence agent the company launched in September. CEO Mark Zuckerberg said Meta’s Muse agent could eventually generate more revenue per user than apps like Instagram and Facebook.According to Zuckerberg, the future Muse business model is expected to include subscriptions, ads, e-commerce tools and other features. Zuckerberg added that more than 10 million people in the US and Canada have set up accounts for Muse."The launch of Muse, Meta's AI model, aims to fuel that next growth development and early signs look promising," Ben Barringer, head of technology research at Quilter Cheviot, said.The 10 million Muse users, with much of the activity focused on shopping and travel, spend an average of around $200 per purchase through the agent. "Meta wants to scale this to one billion users globally and get to profitability quicker than the company would usually do, underscoring their confidence in Muse and its capabilities," added Barringer.The CEO noted that Muse requires significant computing power to run, but that the company expects to improve its cost efficiency by more than 10 times in the next year, "which will enable it to be profitable once the revenue lines are at scale."The parent company of Facebook and Instagram reported net income of $9.86 billion, or $3.83 per share, for the July-September period. That's up from a profit of $2.71 billion, or $1.05 per share, in the same period a year earlier, when earnings were hit by a large one-off tax charge."We hit major milestones this quarter toward delivering personal superintelligence for everyone — including launching Muse and Muse Wonder, our first frontier model," said CEO Mark Zuckerberg in a statement. "Our investments are paying off, the core business is strong, and we're seeing velocity across the board."Meta said the number of daily active people using its "family of apps" — Facebook, Messenger, Instagram and WhatsApp — grew 3% from a year earlier to an average of 3.64 billion in September.However, Meta’s quarterly free cash flow turned negative for the first time since 2012 due to intense spending on artificial intelligence.The company has been spending aggressively to build out its artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities, and investors are looking for signs that the investments are paying off.Meta raised the lower end of its estimate for 2026 capital expenditures and now anticipates spending will range from $135 billion to $145 billion, compared with an earlier estimate of $130 billion to $145 billion.The firm didn't provide an estimate for spending next year but noted that it expects to continue investing aggressively to support its core and AI businesses.For the current quarter, Meta is forecasting revenue in the range of $73 billion to $76 billion, the midpoint of which is higher than the $73.65 billion analysts are expecting."All in all, though, Meta's core business remains strong, and with Muse being scaled up at pace, you can see a solid runway for future growth too," Barringer said.Legal costs take a bite from earningsMeta reported its earnings just hours after another financial penalty was announced in a case in New Mexico.A judge ruled that Meta must pay $25 billion to New Mexico after a jury found last month that the social media giant had deceived users about data privacy in a case related to the Cambridge Analytica scandal."We continue to monitor active legal and regulatory matters that could significantly impact our business and financial results," CFO Susan Li said on a call with analysts.Meta still faces "a number of youth-related trials scheduled in the coming months in the United States," Li continued.Meta’s third-quarter profits took a hit from a settlement worth up to $18.59 billion over social media’s effects on teen mental health.In August, Meta reached the settlement with 48 US states and agreed to take steps to keep children under 13 off Instagram and Facebook and teens aged 13 to 17 in age-appropriate accounts.Excluding the impact of a $9.89 billion charge related to this agreement, the company's third-quarter earnings would have been $7.40 per share, Meta said.New shares could help fund Zuckerberg's billionaire tax billAlso Wednesday, Meta announced that its board had approved the creation of a new class of publicly listed, nonvoting Class C common stock, effective in January. The move is intended in part to boost the company's ability to raise capital for AI infrastructure investments."Meta plans to issue nonvoting shares to fund AI investments without diluting CEO Mark Zuckerberg's control," said Andrew Rocco, stock strategist at Zacks Investment Research."It mirrors what Google has done too, as the hyperscalers look for various streams of investment to help fund their capex plans," Barringer said.The new share structure could also help keep the founder and chief executive in California.In a securities filing, Meta said Zuckerberg's voting power "could drop to approximately 53 percent or lower" if he has to sell a significant portion of his voting shares to pay increased taxes.That is a possibility due to a controversial tax on billionaire wealth, Proposition 40, that California voters will decide on in November.Existing shareholders will be given one new Class C share for every Class A or Class B share they already own — meaning Zuckerberg will also receive nonvoting shares and could eventually sell them to pay the new tax without diluting his voting power.

title: Russian strikes kill 7 in Ukraine after US envoy meets Putin
description: Ukraine's air force posted a warning in the early hours of "more ballistic missiles towards Kyiv" and instructed residents to stay in shelters.
content: Russia and Ukraine traded attacks overnight, with seven killed on the Ukrainian side, authorities said on Thursday, despite renewed diplomatic efforts involving the United States.The attacks came shortly after US envoy Steve Witkoff met Russian president Vladimir Putin in Saint Petersburg for talks on ending the war.In Ukraine, authorities say those killed include a man in Sumy, a woman in Kharkiv, three people in Zaporizhzhia and two in Donetsk.In the capital, Kyiv, the mayor Vitali Klitschko posted on social media that strikes had wounded 15 people in the capital, eight of whom had been taken to hospital.In another post that strikes had damaged metro infrastructure at the Pivdenny Bridge, which officials said had restricted traffic between parts of the city.Ukraine's Airforce had posted warnings on Telegram throughout the early hours of "ballistic missiles towards Kyiv" and reports of fighter jets, and instructed residents to stay in shelters.On Thursday morning, the airforce said it had shot down an 181 Russian UAVs overnight, adding there were still strike drones in the air.In Russia, the mayor of Moscow Sergei Sobyanin said that two people had been wounded during mostly-intercepted barrages of 630 drones headed towards the region, 163 of which were approaching the capital city. Elsewhere, the governor of Tula said air defences destroyed 70 drones, while Lipetsk’s governor reported one man wounded.US talks with RussiaPresident Donald Trump said following the meeting with Putin and Witkoff, the two sides were “maybe now the closest we’ve been” to ending the conflict, although no breakthrough was announced.The Kremlin said it was “in principle” willing to resume trilateral talks involving Russia, Ukraine and the US, potentially in mid-November after the US midterm elections.Ukraine has also backed renewed trilateral negotiations, with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy saying Kyiv wanted a meeting as soon as possible.Witkoff described his talks with Putin as “constructive”, while acknowledging that “important work” remained.Following the talks, Russia agreed to release US citizen Stephen Hubbard, a retired teacher convicted by Russia of fighting as a mercenary for Ukraine, allegations he has denied.Trump has delayed further sanctions on Russia, saying doing so had helped secure Hubbard’s release.Trump also struck a fresh agreement with Russia to sell diesel, aimed at reducing fuel prices that have risen during the wider Middle East conflict, a move that has drawn criticism from Kyiv and several European governments.

title: Europe Today: France under fire as Macron faces backlash, Putin opens door to Ukraine peace talks
description: France prepares for another weekend of protests as Macron faces criticism over his Gulf tour. Meanwhile, Putin signals readiness for Ukraine peace talks after meeting Steve Witkoff, and Hungary detains former central bank governor György Matolcsy over suspected fraud.
content: On today's show:Méabh Mc Mahon speaks to Stanislas Gaudon of the Alliance Police union about preparations for another weekend of protests in France, as police warn they are underresourced and unprepared to deal with further unrest.Maia de la Baume reports on French President Emmanuel Macron's Gulf tour, where he is seeking to secure oil and diesel supplies amid rising fuel prices and growing unrest at home. We ask why he chose to travel now and how the protests are affecting his presidency.French Socialist MEP Jean-Marc Germain joins us from Strasbourg to discuss France's deepening political crisis, Macron's increasingly isolated position and whether the unrest could have wider consequences for the European Union.Sasha Vakulina, Euronews' Ukraine correspondent, analyses US envoy Steve Witkoff's meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg, following talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and European leaders in Oslo. We ask whether a new round of peace negotiations is any closer and whether Kyiv is signalling a willingness to compromise.Finnish MEP Pekka Toveri from the European People's Party, a former army general and chair of the EU-Ukraine Committee, discusses whether Putin's peace offer can be trusted and whether Europe can sustain its support for Ukraine.When and where to watch Europe Today?You can join Euronews’ chief anchor Méabh Mc Mahon and our EU editor Maria Tadeo live on TV and Euronews' website as well as digital platforms (YouTube, Facebook, X, and Instagram), every weekday at 8 am Brussels time.In just 20 minutes, our new format brings you the day's key events plus crucial analysis of all the stories shaping the EU and beyond. It's also available as a newsletter and podcast.

title: ‘This used to be paradise’: How intensive farming is destroying Europeans’ favourite swimming spots
description: 'Green sludge' is appearing on Europe's shorelines as warming waters, sewage and agricultural runoff fuel the growth of toxic algae.
content: “I remember our beautiful beach before the pollution,” says Brittany resident Jean Hascoet, who leads the local campaign group Baie de Douarnenez Environnement. “Now, with thousands of pigs near our town, everything is different.”Across France and Spain, Europe’s shorelines are being choked by toxic algal blooms. Scientists are clear on the cause: decades of chemicals leaching into waterways. Poorly handled human sewage, as well as fertilisers and excess manure from ever-expanding factory farms, are to blame.Seas warmed by climate change are further fuelling the rapid growth of the algae which disrupts delicate ecosystems, killing off fish and plant life. Some types can also cause nausea, vomiting and rashes in humans – prompting hundreds of swimming bans across the continent this summer.Climate investigations outlet DeSmog visited some of the worst impacted spots in Europe, speaking to fishers, swimmers and business owners whose livelihoods and wellbeing depend on healthy waters.‘Spain’s sacrificial zone’: Farming threatens a protected lagoon “You’ll never see me swimming in that water again,” Fina says. The 84-year-old from Murcia lives with her husband on the beachfront at Los Urrutias, on the west coast of Spain’s Mar Menor, Europe’s largest saltwater lagoon. Rotting seaweed piles up on the shore, giving off a foul stench. “This used to be paradise. The sea was teeming with seahorses,” Fina says. The last decade has seen a sharp increase in sea life-choking algae in Mar Menor – a hotspot for Spanish and international tourists. Despite being granted ‘legal personhood’ by the Spanish government in 2022, giving it rights to protection and restoration, the lagoon remains under stress from agricultural runoff.Cyanobacteria, also known as blue-green algae, is reliant on nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphorus to grow. Intensive farming in the Mar Menor region provides a ready supply of nutrient-rich manure, slurry and fertiliser runoff. Studies estimate agriculture is responsible for around 85 per cent of the nutrients entering the lagoon, with urban sources making up the rest.“The land can’t accommodate it all,” says Pedro Luengo, a biologist and spokesperson for the campaign group Ecologistas en Acción in Murcia. “We’re a sacrificial zone.”Even to the east of the lagoon, furthest from the farmland, local authorities must work hard to preserve an artificial paradise for tourists. In the first three months of 2026, they collected more than 4,000 tonnes of algae from Mar Menor’s shores and nearby water – roughly the weight of 1,000 elephants.But it hasn’t shielded those who rely on the lagoon for their livelihood.“We used to catch far more gilt-head seabream and prawns. Now the catch is much smaller,” says Rubén Albaladejo, a fisherman from Lo Pagán. “The Mar Menor is a drain into which everyone dumps their rubbish and waste.” Rising water temperatures are further hindering the reproductive ability of these species: “We’ve reached 30 degrees – something we’ve never seen before,” says Albaladejo.Scientists warned in August that human-caused climate change added around 2°C to peak Mediterranean sea temperatures and around 1.4°C in Western European seas, according to World Weather Attribution. The Mediterranean averaged a record 27.07°C in July.Spain’s environment ministry is funding eight projects with more than €11.5 million to cut livestock pollution, including new ways of treating pig slurry and moving sheep to open pasture. They are part of a €675 million national programme to recover the lagoon, but by the end of 2025 only about 16 per cent of that budget had been spent.‘The Lough is dead’: Fishers in Northern Ireland face their worst ever yearTwo thousand kilometres away in Northern Ireland, Declan Coney has also seen Lough Neagh – the UK’s largest lake – devastated by blue-green algae every summer since 2023. “Fishing was instilled in me – generation after generation,” Coney says. But “this year has been the worst ever for fishing. The Lough is dead.”Trout and eel numbers have fallen in recent years, in part due to the oxygen-depleting algae whose weight forces Coney’s fishing nets shut, so fish can’t swim inside. Since the 2000s, the lough has been besieged by invasive zebra mussels. By hogging phytoplankton, these mussels deprive other species of a vital food source, as well as attaching to fishing nets and ripping them. “There’s no money [in fishing],” says Coney, who has been working on the lake since 1975. “It’s not a livelihood anymore.”As in Spain, Lough Neagh’s algal blooms are the result of decades of nutrient pollution. Northern Ireland’s livestock sector has grown rapidly, supported by government expansion plans since 2013: poultry numbers have risen by a third, and pigs by 74 per cent. Earlier this year, nonprofit Watershed Investigations and UK newspaper The Guardian found evidence of cattle, pig and human faeces in samples of water from the lough, which spans nearly 400 square kilometres and provides 40 per cent of Northern Ireland’s drinking water. Regulations aimed at improving Lough Neagh’s water quality, including reducing phosphorus and nitrogen levels in animal feed, and limiting manure application, need to be strengthened and better implemented, a report by the Office for Environmental Protection concluded in April. It notes positive investment and efforts from farmers but says more on-farm support and oversight is needed.Mary O’Hagan lives on the north-west of the lake. During the COVID-19 pandemic, she set up a wild swimming group, and found that the cold water had huge benefits – from improving mental health to relieving chronic pain. “In my 30s, I didn’t have much of a life, I wasn’t looking after myself. Swimming in Lough Neagh changed my life completely,” O’Hagan says. “We had a community.”But after the second year of the blooms, she felt forced to shut the swimming group down. “It was like Armageddon. To see the shores covered as far as the eye can see in pea green sludge was horrendous,” she says. “I couldn’t in all good conscience organise swims where people would be exposed to bacteria, algae, or god knows what else.” Blue-green algae can cause vomiting, diarrhoea and skin irritation.‘More animals than people’: Manure run-off poisons Brittany’s beaches Brittany, in northwest France, faces its own deadly battle: sea lettuce algae has been linked to as many as six fatalities on the region’s beaches since the 1980s. When it breaks down, it can produce hydrogen sulphide – a lethal gas that smells like rotten eggs – which can cause blocked airways and fluid to build up in the lungs if inhaled in large quantities. Locals here are vocal about their suspicions of the cause. Near the tourist town of Saint-Brieuc, one resident has scribbled “les cochons” – the pigs – across an official sign warning about the danger and symptoms of inhaling toxic gas from the algae. “We have many more animals than people,” says environmental author Yves-Marie Le Lay, who wears a protective mask at his local beach when algae growth reaches dangerous levels. Although Brittany’s peninsula covers just five per cent of France’s surface, its 6.8 million pigs account for 58 per cent of the country’s total population. “We have a manure problem, it all ends up in the rivers.” France’s national audit court, the Cour des comptes, found in 2021 that more than 90 per cent of the nitrogen in the affected bays comes from agriculture.Environmental activist Fabrice Hamon is uneasy about the coming months. On his local beach, Plage de Penfoul, E. coli forced a partial swimming ban in 2025. This summer’s drought now means that harmful excess nutrients have built up in the soil of nearby fields treated with manure.“Right now there’s a build-up of bacteria in the fields,” Hamon says. “All it takes is a heavy downpour and, bingo. It’s a slow-acting poison: little by little, ecosystems are being degraded by the build-up of pollution linked to intensive farming.”Hamon is working on a system to monitor for the bacteria in around 20 rivers that flow onto local beaches, so that tourists and local beachgoers can check for warnings through an app called La Météo Bacterio.Elsewhere in Europe, citizens can report the presence of blue-green algae through the Bloomin’ Algae app by the UK Centre for Ecology & Hydrology. The app is available in the UK, Belgium, Greece, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Norway.‘The sea was dead’: Baltic blooms flourish in record heatCitizen science projects like Hamon’s could become vital in the battle against pollution in Europe’s waterways.In northern Germany, volunteers led by the Schleswig-Holstein branch of the environmental nonprofit Bund für Umwelt und Naturschutz Deutschland (BUND) are collecting water samples twice a month from local rivers to help pinpoint sources of pollution and help cut nutrient runoff into the Baltic Sea.Jürgen Leicher, the group’s deputy chairman, has been sailing these waters for 40 years, and says this year’s algal blooms are the worst he’s ever seen. Temperatures in Germany broke records for three consecutive days in June, reaching almost 42°C. Satellite images of the Baltic in August show vast algal blooms swirling towards the coast. Algae grows quicker and lasts longer in warm waters, as higher temperatures allow it to digest and reproduce at a faster rate. “You feel really afraid when you sail for hundreds of miles through a yellow-brown dirty sea,” says Leicher. “All the way through this algae, the sea was dead. You see no birds, no mammals, no fish. It’s so empty.”Isabel Seeger, marine conservation expert at Deutsche Umwelthilfe, says the source of the problem is clear: “Our current agricultural system, which is reliant on high fertiliser consumption and manure from mass livestock farming, is the biggest cause of eutrophication in the Baltic Sea.”The intergovernmental body HELCOM estimates that agriculture accounts for up to 90 per cent of nitrogen and up to 80 per cent of phosphorus in diffuse nutrient run-off into the Baltic.Despite decades of intergovernmental efforts to reduce nutrient pollution, such as placing strict limits on agricultural fertiliser inputs, the Baltic is struggling to recover from the environmental damage combined with rising temperatures.Each year, when algae dies it sinks to the seabed, taking large amounts of phosphorus with it. That phosphorus is released back into the ocean in future years – a dangerous feedback loop that gains speed as the sea warms.Ultimately, though, scientists say that nutrient pollution must be slashed to limit the recurrent harmful algae growth – and that means transforming agricultural practices. “The science is clear on what needs to be done,” says Professor Friedhelm Taube from Kiel University (CAU), who spent 12 years advising Germany’s Ministry of Agriculture. Governments should support farmers to use less nitrates-heavy fertiliser; plant catch crops like grass clover that absorb some of the excess nutrients from soils before they run into rivers, lakes and the sea; and reduce the number of animals farmed to one livestock unit per hectare – a technical term that translates to just one dairy cow or roughly three pigs – on limited land, he says.For campaigners in Murcia, the choice is just as stark: “Either we wreck the Mar Menor or we transform the agricultural model,” says Luengo.Additional research by Joey Grostern

title: Kenichi Yoda, Princess of Asturias laureate: "Ghibli is closely tied to its time"
description: The new president of the legendary Japanese studio argues that beauty must be sought even when portraying horrors such as war. In Oviedo, Yoda, Ghibli’s public face, says they will continue to explore contemporary themes and concerns, just as their founders did.
author_name: Javier Iniguez De Onzono, Maria Muñoz Morillo
content: A former reporter for Japanese newspaper Yomiuri Shimbun, where at the start of his career he covered stories on the Ghibli animation studios, it is highly unlikely that Kenichi Yoda (1974) could have imagined he would one day go on to lead the very company he specialised in during his time as a culture journalist.His rise to the summit of this legendary temple of cinematic anime came on 22 June, when he took over the presidency from Hiroyuki Fukuda. His interview with Euronews takes place 48 hours before he accepts, on behalf of his studio, the 2026 Princess of Asturias Award for Communication and Humanities.The ideas of two of its creators, the late Isao Takahata and his partner Hayao Miyazaki, together with the work of the roughly 200 people employed by the company, remain one of the main gateways into Japanese culture for millions of people around the globe.That was the case with "Marco" and "Heidi" in Spain. The anime series were broadcast between the dying days of Francoism and the Transition, at a time when Ghibli had not even been dreamt up by the pair of film-makers who met in a trade union while both were working at the Toei Doga studio in the 1960s. Those series were probably, with the exception of milestones such as the films of Akira Kurosawa, the first contact an entire generation of Spaniards had with the Land of the Rising Sun.Yoda laughs when asked whether they see themselves as an instrument of Japanese soft power. "I think each work exists only because its directors and animators poured so much care into it. It makes us very happy that, as a result, people all over the world watch them. But we do not do it for the sake of diplomacy," says the president.Ghibli and the terrible beauty of warIn 2026 it is impossible not to ask Yoda about one of the themes that recurs most frequently in the studio's scripts, alongside environmental protection, friendship and the strength of its female characters: armed conflict.Takahata, a communist sympathiser, was an outspoken defender of Article 9 of the Japanese Constitution and a convinced pacifist, while Miyazaki was steeped in war from childhood: his family's company manufactured parts for military aircraft on the fascist side during the Second World War.Both bear witness to this fixation in such animated classics as "Grave of the Fireflies", through "Princess Mononoke" or "Howl's Moving Castle", and up to "The Wind Rises". In today's Japan, which is allocating unprecedented shares of its GDP to its Self-Defence Forces and whose Defence White Paper has been driven by the far-right politician Sanae Takaichi, is it still possible to make pacifist films?Yoda deftly sidesteps the question. "How to portray war is a very important issue for Studio Ghibli. Of course, it is better if there are no wars. But what I find admirable about Miyazaki as a director is that he has also been fascinated by the weapons used in war, and by fighter planes, by their beauty as objects, as forms. Of course, he has not the slightest sympathy for war. But there is in him a feeling he cannot resist: the allure of those things as objects. And that is, in a way, something very human," he argues.We also ask him about one of the studio's most quoted lines, uttered by the lead in "Porco Rosso" (1992), when in a cinema he declares that he would rather be a pig than a fascist. Would a line like that get through a contemporary script meeting, whether at Ghibli or another studio? Once again, the executive opts to duck the issue: he says he is very pleased that one of Emmanuel Macron's favourite films (recalling a remark made during an official visit to Japan) is "Porco", as the interviewee points out.The question of artificial intelligence also hangs over the Covadonga room at the Hotel Reconquista, where laureates of the Princess of Asturias Foundation traditionally stay. It arises in connection with the famous viral clip of Miyazaki (source in Spanish) from 2016, in which he brutally deflates two developers from another company as they try to sell the genius a kind of proto-AI to use in his drawings. "It is an insult to life itself," he tells them."Ten years on, in every single interview I am asked what Studio Ghibli thinks about AI," Yoda says with a sigh. "It is very difficult to predict how it will develop, and I think we are all living with that uncertainty. But if there is one thing we can say right now, and I say this in a personal capacity as well, it is this. Imagine two restaurants: one where the food is made by an AI and another where it is made by people. I would undoubtedly choose the latter."His team signal that it is time to wrap up the interview, but the former journalist says he wants to make one last point. "Listening to your questions, I realised that Ghibli is very closely tied to its own era (...) Every day we debate what the studio can do in this day and age and about the kind of era we are living in. In that sense, I feel we are creating something with a sense of proportion," he argues."There is great honesty in the way we approach artistic creation," he continues. "This is not a business plan: it is about thinking seriously about how the studio responds to its own time. That is what the studio's day-to-day work is now. And it has probably always been that way." The coming decade will show whether, after the generational handover from Miyazaki, still active at 85, the iconic studio manages to maintain its creative independence and ideals, after enchanting millions of children and adults far beyond the Japanese islands.

title: A fraught push for peace, and a race to fund Ukraine
description: Good morning. It’s Mared Gwyn with your Thursday newsletter. Today: the fraught push to revive peace talks between Ukraine and Russia, cash for Kyiv becomes intertwined in talks on the next EU budget, and Argentina’s Milei reignites a war of words with Spain’s Sánchez.
content: Back to square one?: After Wednesday’s meeting between Vladimir Putin and US envoy Steve Witkoff in St Petersburg, the Kremlin says Russia is "in principle" ready to resume trilateral negotiations with Ukraine and the US in mid-November, with Abu Dhabi emerging as a possible venue, my colleague Sasha Vakulina reports.But we have been here before. Moscow has repeatedly entertained negotiations without softening its maximalist demands, Sasha writes. This time appears no different: Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov has suggested that proposals Witkoff brought from his talks with Zelenskyy and European leaders in Oslo offered little Russia considered useful.Witkoff, meanwhile, called Putin a "humanitarian" following the release of an American detainee. A reminder: The Russian president is wanted by the International Criminal Court over the alleged unlawful deportation and transfer of at least 20,000 Ukrainian children. A separate summit involving Trump, Putin and China's Xi Jinping is also under consideration, potentially to discuss Ukraine's future without Kyiv at the table. Whether it will take place, or how it relates to the proposed peace talks, remains unclear.Zelenskyy told Fox News last night that Ukraine could accept a ceasefire along the current front lines without recognising Russian sovereignty over occupied territory — a position Kyiv has articulated before.Despite the diplomatic flurry, the fundamental positions have so far barely shifted.Stubb’s role: Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said on Wednesday that Russia could welcome Finnish President Alexander Stubb’s involvement in peace negotiations, provided he avoids simply “parroting” Europe’s position on Ukraine.Stubb took a leading role in this week’s talks in Oslo along with his Norwegian counterpart, and has been among the names floated as a potential EU envoy to future peace talks. But the Kremlin now seems to be dictating the terms under which Stubb can take part in the talks before they even start.Trump accused of taking sides: Meanwhile, former US Army lieutenant General Ben Hodges told my colleague Shona Murray that President Donald Trump is taking Russia’s side and deliberately undermining Ukraine's ability to defend itself against Russia."He was never going to support Ukraine, and was going to take the Russian side, the signs were all there," Hodges tells Euronews, adding that he does not “trust” the US administration. More.Explosive mix: At the same time, the fight over the next EU budget is becoming rapidly intertwined with the search for additional support for Ukraine, Jorge Liboreiro writes.Next month’s extraordinary EU summit, originally planned to advance the budget talks, has been extended to two days from 26-27 November to incorporate Ukraine. The stakes are fast rising. The change of agenda follows President Zelenskyy’s request for an additional €70 billion in military and financial support for 2027. EU leaders have agreed to address the massive shortfall, but Brussels is urging other allies, such as the UK, Canada, Norway, Australia and Japan, to increase their donations so the bloc isn’t left bearing the brunt.The next step is for the European Commission to determine how much of the €70 billion the EU will have to fill. The calculation will then help design options to raise the money. As we told you earlier this week, joint debt seems like the likeliest avenue, even if it’s costly amid sky-high borrowing costs.Costa’s move: ahead of the special summit, European Council President António Costa will present a new compromise on the EU budget. The political process has barely moved, as leaders remain split in opposing camps (“Frugals” vs “Friends of Cohesion”). “For Europe’s stability, we must approve our next long-term budget by the end of this year,” Costa said yesterday, in a new appeal to member states.Costa’s compromise will pay close attention to the so-called new own resources, the EU-wide taxes meant to bring additional revenue to the budget. Luca Bertuzzi breaks down some of the options on the table.EU diplomats are split on whether the EU budget and funding for Ukraine should be addressed as one package. The spectre of next year’s French presidential election also looms over the debate. “The fact is that these are the most pressing issues for the remainder of the year, definitely,” one diplomat said.Weidel’s plan: Meanwhile, the leader of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) Alice Weidel presented her plan to radically reform the EU during a visit to the European Parliament in Strasbourg on Wednesday. Emboldened by a major victory in Saxony-Anhalt's regional election last September, the AfD is currently topping the national polls."Our aim is to assume government responsibility after the next federal elections,” Weidel said. My colleague Vincenzo Genovese breaks down Weidel’s plan, and compares it to the one unveiled by France’s Marine Le Pen in Brussels last week. Milei reignites war of words with Sánchez as Spanish PM declares himself ‘leftie and proud’Javier Milei let it be known he had arrived in Madrid on Wednesday.The Argentine libertarian launched a tirade against Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez as he began a visit to the Spanish capital. Milei, who has blamed socialism for Argentina’s economic malaise and cultural decline, accused Sánchez of acting like a dictator.His visit comes amid a highly polarising political campaign ahead of the 29 November election, with Sánchez positioning himself as the last bastion against what he calls the ultra-right and a coalition of reactionary forces, including Milei.At a breakfast event, the Argentine president called Sánchez a “shameless dictator” and suggested the Spanish prime minister was fuelling an “invasion” in Ceuta, the Spanish enclave that saw a mass border breach from neighbouring Morocco in July."The socialists would rather reign in hell than serve in heaven. That is why they encourage the invasion. Every immigrant is a vote. If the price to pay is the destruction of the country, they are more than willing to pay it,” he said.Christina Thykjaer and Maria Tadeo have more analysis.More from our newsroomsEU prosecutors raid far-right group's offices in €4 million funds scandal. The European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) raided the offices of the far-right Patriots for Europe (PfE) group in Brussels and Strasbourg on Wednesday as part of an investigation into the alleged misuse of millions of euros in EU funds. The searches are linked to an investigation into the former Identity and Democracy (ID) group, which included France’s National Rally, led by Marine Le Pen and Italy’s Lega, led by Matteo Salvini. Vincenzo Genovese has the story.EU journalism prize awards investigation into human rights abuse at Italy’s migrant centres in Albania. An investigation highlighting human rights violations at Italy’s controversial migrant centres in Albania won the European Parliament’s Daphne Caruana Galizia Prize for journalism on Wednesday. The report is titled "Cuffed, caged, cast away: this is Europe’s ‘innovative solution’ for unwanted migrants" and questions the legality of the centres, which have become a source of inspiration for European migration policy. Vincenzo has more.In apparent swipe at Trump, Macron slams 'stupid comments' by foreign leaders on France protests. France's President Emmanuel Macron has criticised world leaders who he said were campaigning for upcoming elections "at France's expense" with "unacceptable and even stupid comments" about the country's riots last weekend. Estelle Nilsson-Julien has more.Europe weighs energy-saving measures as Middle East crisis deepens. EU governments could ask households and businesses to cut their energy use as the war in the Middle East drives up prices and threatens oil and gas supplies, according to a document seen by Euronews. Marta Pacheco has the details.We’re also keeping an eye onEuropean Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos attends the Berlin Process Leaders' Summit in Montenegro.European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa meet with the President of Vietnam Tô Lâm.That’s it for today. Sasha Vakulina, Jorge Liboreiro, Luca Bertuzzi and Vincenzo Genovese contributed to this newsletter.

title: Tesla's profit drops as it explores a possible merger with Musk's other public company, SpaceX
description: Tesla reported a decline in third-quarter profit, but generated more cash than analysts expected, leaving investors with a mixed picture as it explores a possible merger with Elon Musk's other big company, SpaceX.
content: Tesla reported lower third-quarter profits on Wednesday as Elon Musk's electric vehicle maker ramped up spending on artificial intelligence, robotics and autonomous transport.The electric vehicle maker reported third-quarter net income attributable to shareholders of $787 million (€701 million), or 22 cents per share, down 43% from the year-earlier period. Besides marginally lower car sales, Tesla saw a drop in revenues from regulatory credits and energy generation and storage.Revenue was essentially flat at $28 billion (€24.9 billion), falling slightly short of the company-compiled average analyst forecast of $28.3 billion.Excluding certain items, though, earnings per share of 48 cents beat Wall Street analyst expectations by 3 cents.One standout for the quarter was Tesla's $1.5 billion (€1.3 billion) in free cash flow, a measure of cash generated after subtracting investments needed to keep the business running.Given heavy spending on artificial intelligence, analysts had expected Tesla would report it had burned through cash, not generated it. However, free cash flow was still down 62% from a year earlier."It seems Tesla is taking a more capital-efficient approach, delaying longer-term projects to be able to self-fund their AI growth," said Morningstar analyst Seth Goldstein, calling the unexpected positive cash flow the big surprise of the quarter.Tesla is rolling back its annual spending forecastThe company also reported more than doubling capital spending from a year earlier to $4.7 billion (€4.2 billion) for the quarter, but analysts had expected a far bigger increase.Tesla cut its full-year 2026 capital spending forecast to about $20 billion (€17.8 billion), from more than $25 billion (€22.3 billion). Chief financial officer Vaibhav Taneja said the company was managing its spending efficiently and planned to fund it mainly through operating cash flow.Besides robotaxis and AI, Tesla is investing heavily in Musk's "Optimus" humanoid robots as well as developing Terafab, a chip manufacturing project in Austin, with SpaceX.On the positive side, Tesla reported strong demand for its paid driver-assistance software, with more than 75% of new vehicles delivered in North America including a paid subscription sign-up.The company calls the feature Full Self-Driving (Supervised) in North America. Despite its name, the software requires active driver supervision and does not make the vehicle autonomous.Tesla's automotive gross margin, excluding regulatory credits, also improved. For the three months through September, it reached 18.1%, up from 15.4% a year earlier.Tesla had previously reported delivering 486,532 vehicles last quarter, a rise from 480,126 in the prior three months, but down 2% from a year earlier.The modest rise in deliveries from the previous quarter did not translate into higher net profit.Musk said Tesla was aiming to produce about five million vehicles a year by around 2030, compared with approximately 1.65 million produced in 2025."After many years of sort of grind and things being fairly flat, I think we're now headed for a lot of fun and significant growth," Musk said.The company has faced questions about the rollout of its robotaxi business, which has fallen short of Musk's earlier ambitions.In Texas, where Tesla has focused its robotaxi launch, more than 800 Tesla vehicles are registered for autonomous service, according to FSD Database.Tesla shares were down 3.2% in after-hours trading after climbing 3.6% during the regular trading session.SpaceX merger talks add to questions over Tesla's futureQuestions about Tesla's future loomed larger with talk of the potential SpaceX tie-up. The companies have a combined stock market value of about $3.5 trillion (€3.1 trillion).In a SpaceX conference call after that company reported earnings on Tuesday, Musk said both companies had formed special committees of independent directors to explore a possible merger. He said no terms had been agreed and there was no guarantee of a deal.Merger speculation and SpaceX's strong results helped lift shares in both companies on Wednesday. Forbes estimated Musk's wealth at $1.013 trillion (€902 billion) at 10.30am New York time, putting him briefly back above the trillion-dollar mark.Musk said the two companies could gain from working together on AI software, chip design, robotics and satellite infrastructure, including space-based computing.Musk declined to discuss the possible merger further on Tesla's conference call.

title: Drinking tea could lower your risk of stroke, but only if it’s not too hot
description: Drinking tea three or more times a week is linked to an 11% lower risk of vascular disease, such as stroke or heart attack, a new study suggests. However, burning hot tea was linked to the opposite effect: a 16% increase in vascular disease risk.
content: Regular tea drinking is linked to a lower risk of vascular diseases such as stroke, coronary heart disease and heart attack, according to a new study. Tea is made by steeping the processed leaves of Camellia sinensis, an evergreen shrub native to East Asia. All varieties —including white, green, oolong, black and pu-erh— come from this single plant, with their distinct flavours determined by how much they oxidise. The beverage is a regular part of the diet in many cultures. From the English breakfast to Chinese tea ceremonies, it is present in the daily lives of millions of people worldwide. Tea’s bioactive compounds, including polyphenols and flavonoids, have antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and endothelial-protective properties that preserve the inner lining of blood vessels and maintain healthy circulation, all of which can help prevent vascular diseases, according to a study published in the Journal of Internal Medicine. Researchers followed nearly 500,000 Chinese people for an average of nine years, recording their tea consumption and any diseases that developed during that period. They found that those who drink tea regularly three or more times a week showed 11.2% lower overall risk of vascular disease. The strongest association was for ischaemic stroke with a 36.6% reduction, followed by cerebrovascular disease at 19.1%.The protective associations varied substantially depending on how the tea was prepared and consumed, the researchers found. Among participants, the median intake was between two and three cups a day; however, the lowest associated risk was in those who consumed six to eight cups daily. Black tea showed the strongest and most consistent association with vascular diseases, followed by green tea. Researchers attribute this to the fermentation-derived compounds, such as theaflavins, which have anti-inflammatory and lipid-regulating properties. The temperature and strength of the brew also made a difference. Researchers found that the best combination was moderately strong and non-scalding tea. Surprisingly, burning hot tea was linked to the opposite effect: a 16% increase in vascular disease risk. Very hot drinks have previously also been associated with a greater likelihood of oesophageal cancer. Tea is not a silver bullet The protective association of habitual tea consumption was consistent across most demographic subgroups but was significantly stronger in individuals with obesity, the researchers noted. Despite these results, the authors warn that drinking tea alone does not protect against cardiovascular disease and that it should form part of a broader healthy lifestyle and complement established prevention strategies. “This was an observational study and other differences in people’s diets and lifestyles could help explain the findings,” said Dell Stanford, senior dietitian at the British Heart Foundation who did not participate in the study, adding that the results don’t prove “that a daily cuppa protects your heart.” Cardiovascular disease remains the leading cause of illness and mortality in the European Union, accounting for one in three of all deaths and affecting an estimated 62 million people.

title: Canada unveils $6.2bn plan to shield manufacturers as Trump trade tariffs bite
description: Prime Minister Mark Carney said the Trump tariffs make both US and Canadian industries weaker and reduce choice for households in both countries.
content: Canada has announced a $6.2 billion (€5.7 billion) package to protect its steel and auto industries from US tariffs, as Prime Minister Mark Carney warned that Washington has permanently altered a trade relationship built over decades.Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford jointly unveiled the plan on Wednesday, directing $3.7 billion (€3.4 billion) to steelmakers and $1.8 billion (€1.65 billion) to automakers over five years, with $1.1 billion (€1 billion) of the auto funding coming from the federal government in Ottawa.The announcement came the same day US-owned Cleveland-Cliffs confirmed layoffs at its Hamilton, Ontario, plant, underlining the human cost of the trade dispute.“US tariffs have upended a trade bargain that’s existed for decades,” Carney said. “They’ve raised costs for American families while putting Ontario workers and businesses at a disadvantage.”The damage to the auto sector is already visible in the trade figures, as Canadian auto exports to the US have fallen more than 10 percent, while US exports to Canada have dropped more than 20 percent, a decline Carney said hurts both sides of the border.“Tariffs make both our industries weaker and reduce choice for our families,” he stressed.Carney confirmed he spoke at length with President Trump on Wednesday, covering trade, Iran and the Middle East.He signalled no breakthrough but said Canada remains ready to negotiate. Talks collapsed in August after Trump imposed 50% tariffs on around $20 billion (€18.4 billion) in Canadian goods, prompting Canadian retaliation.For his part, Ford was direct about what the dispute has done to bilateral ties. “No matter what happens in the midterms, no matter who sits in the White House, we’re not going back to the way things were,” he said.US embassy accuses Canada of meddling in midtermsCarney has set a target of doubling Canadian exports to non-US markets within a decade, acknowledging that an integrated North American auto industry may no longer be Washington’s priority.“Their approach has changed,” he said. “So must ours.”Meanwhile, the day took a sharper diplomatic turn when the US Embassy issued a statement accusing Canadian politicians of seeking to influence next month’s American midterm elections.The embassy named Industry Minister Mélanie Joly for discussing retaliatory tariffs targeting Republican states and Ford for running a US television ad featuring former President Ronald Reagan criticising tariffs, the ad that prompted Trump to walk away from trade talks in October 2025.Both leaders rejected the allegations. So did independent analysts.“The implicit assumption that Canada could significantly alter the outcome of the midterms is absurd,” said Daniel Béland, political science professor at McGill University.

title: Residences, shower spas and private lofts: The most luxurious airline experiences ranked
description: Think luxury travel is all about the seat? A new ranking of the ‘most outrageous’ luxury airline experiences has found that not all perks begin at takeoff…
content: What can money buy when you’re travelling in the sky at 40,000 feet?Beyond the hefty price tag that comes with first-class fares, AirAdvisor has scoured the world’s major international airlines to rank the “most outrageous” individual experiences on offer both in-flight and before takeoff.The company created a longlist of the "extraordinary premium amenities" currently on offer by airlines and assessed experiences that could only be independently verified through official airline or airport sources.AirAdvisor’s ranking of the top 10 most outrageous airline luxuries in 2026 excluded private aviation, discontinued amenities, concepts not yet available to the public as well as standard offerings, like lounge access, amenity kits and conventional lie-flat seats.“Premium air travel has become an arms race," said Anton Radchenko, Founder and CEO of AirAdvisor.“A lie-flat seat is no longer enough to stand out: airlines are now competing with bedrooms, showers, private lounges and spaces designed for couples or groups.“What is striking is how scarce many of these experiences remain – often limited to one aircraft type or only a handful of routes.”The 10 most outrageous airline luxuries in 2026The research scored qualifying luxury experiences out of 100 across five criteria: extravagance, which had a weight of 35%; rarity 25%; privacy and exclusivity 20%; access scarcity 10%; and beyond-the-seat experience 10%, which looks at offerings such as showers, spas or private apartment-style space.Here’s how the top 10 experiences ranked:1. Etihad Airways’ The Residence – 98/100: Three-room apartment in the sky2. Emirates’ A380 Shower Spa – 91/100: Shower at 40,000 feet3. SWISS’ First Grand Suite – 88/100: Private loft in the sky for up to three people4. Air France’s La Première – 85/100: Private 45 m² suite before boarding the flight5. Singapore Airlines’ Suites – 82/100: Cabin class with a separate seat and double bed6. Lufthansa’s Allegris Suite Plus – 80/100: Two-person first class suite that becomes a double bed7. Japan Airlines’ A350-1000 First – 78/100: 1.23m-wide suite with a minibar and 43-inch screen8. Emirates’ A380 Onboard Lounge – 76/100: Cocktail bar at 40,000 feet9. Qatar Airways’ Al Safwa First Lounge – 72/100: Thermal jacuzzi before boarding10. Virgin Atlantic’s Retreat Suite – 68/100: Business class suite where four people can dine togetherAirAdvisor only considered a maximum of two experiences per airline to avoid the ranking being dominated by a single carrier. The research was also based on information from September 2026.An apartment, shower and ‘loft’ in the air?The top spot was awarded to The Residence experience by Etihad Airways, which offers travellers a three-room suite to relax in even before they've reached their destination.It features a private bedroom, ensuite shower facility and separate living room. Meanwhile, before boarding, travellers can also benefit from home or hotel check-in, chauffeur transfers and a personalised welcome when they get to the airport."The Residence achieved near-maximum marks for extravagance, rarity, privacy and the extent to which it goes beyond a conventional airline seat," AirAdvisor said in its report.Emirates’ A380 Shower Spa comes in second, and is exclusively available to first class flyers. While in the sky, passengers can access a dedicated shower room with a vanity area, changing space and heated flooring.Rounding off the top three is an experience from a European carrier: SWISS’ First Grand Suite.Unveiled in 2025 and launched in 2026, this product offers a heightened level of privacy: combining two adjoining first class suites, including the aisle, to create a fully secluded space on long-haul flights. The private area can function as a bedroom, office or meeting room for up to three travellers.

title: Marine Le Pen vs Alice Weidel: How the far right wants to reshape the EU
description: AfD leader Alice Weidel unveiled her EU vision in Strasbourg a week after Marine Le Pen did the same in Brussels. Both parties seek to reshape the bloc around national sovereignty but differ on fiscal policy, energy and the extent of reform.
content: Neither party now advocates leaving the EU. Instead, both want to reshape it into an alliance of sovereign states, with weaker institutions and reduced powers.If they come to power, their plans could undermine the Franco-German partnership that has long driven European integration and reshape the future of the EU.Alternative for Germany (AfD) leader Alice Weidel unveiled her “New Deal for Europe” at a press conference in the European Parliament on Wednesday, a week after France’s Marine Le Pen presented her own vision at the upscale The Hotel in Brussels.Both leaders are in strong electoral positions. After a major victory in Saxony-Anhalt's regional election last September, Weidel's AFD party is on track to lead a German State for the first time in history, and is currently leading the polls at the national level. "Our aim is to assume government responsibility after the next federal elections", Weidel said in Strasbourg.In France, a recent Ifop poll puts Le Pen at 34% to 38% of the vote in the first round of France's 2027 presidential election, despite the recent wave of protests across the country.Both parties oppose continued funding for Ukraine, criticise the EU’s regulatory burden, reject deeper integration and want to curb the powers of EU institutions.But they differ on fiscal policy, energy and how far their countries should break from common rules. The AfD goes further, proposing opt-outs that would allow Germany to bypass certain EU policies.Euronews examines the RN and AfD’s plans for Europe, highlighting the key differences and similarities between two of the continent’s leading far-right parties.No more money to UkraineBoth leaders agree on ending financial support for Ukraine’s resistance to Russia’s war of aggression.At her press conference last week, Le Pen argued that France’s strained public finances could no longer sustain aid to Kyiv and called for the lifting of EU sanctions against Russia.“We obviously agreed to maintain a whole series of mechanisms to train their soldiers, to train their army, to provide them, including aid in terms of equipment, but we can no longer finance Ukraine, so this funding will stop,” she said.Weidel said on Wednesday she wants a peace treaty and called for a “reasonable diplomatic approach,” which takes into account the “security interests of Ukraine and Russia.”In a recent interview with The Economist, she argued that Ukraine had already lost the war and pledged to end Germany’s support for Kyiv.Fiscal policy: the sharpest divideThe most significant difference lies in their approach to fiscal policy.Le Pen wants to harmonise taxes on tobacco, alcohol and large companies at EU level to prevent fiscal dumping across Europe. She also suggested that the European Central Bank (ECB) revise its mandate to give more weight to economic growth, rather than focusing on price stability."As I have always believed, the ECB must rethink its course of action. It is essential that it take into account employment, growth, and innovation, given that the monetary easing policies pursued between 2010 and 2022 were not targeted at future investments," she said last week.The AfD, by contrast, opposes any transfer of fiscal sovereignty to supranational institutions and claims that the ECB must strictly confine itself to its original price-stability mandate."There is a ban on the ECB, the European Central Bank, financing state debt. And what is the ECB doing? It's financing state debt", Weidel said.Both parties, however, firmly oppose common EU debt and want to cut their countries’ contributions to the EU budget. Le Pen aims to cap France’s net contribution at €5 billion a year. Neither Weidel nor the AfD’s New Deal for Europe paper specifies a figure, instead emphasising the need to “end Germany’s role as paymaster.”Energy: EU carbon border tax vs freedom to use coalOn energy and climate policy, both parties criticise the EU Green Deal and support nuclear power, but differ in their approaches.Le Pen rejected the “climate-sceptic” label for her party, backed an EU carbon border tax and proposed tying member states’ contributions to the EU budget to their carbon emissions, thereby incentivising the transition to clean energy.“The further a country deviates from the [Paris agreement] targets, the more it should have to contribute,” she said.The AfD paper instead stresses total freedom to choose the national energy mix, meaning Germany must be free to use nuclear power, coal, gas and renewable energy according to the needs of its economy."Now we rely completely on an ideological energy transition of wind and solar power. We see this development also throughout Europe, through the implementation of the Green Deal, the building energy law, and above all the ban on combustion engines. This is a blatant disruption of the free market economy," she said.Le Pen targets the Commission; AfD seeks to weaken Parliament tooBoth parties want the European Commission to be stripped of powers and reduced to a “secretariat at the service of countries”, as Le Pen put it.“The Commission wants to be a State, we don’t want it,” she said, rejecting any EU executive ambitions on security, diplomacy and intelligence. She also wants to abolish the European Committee of the Regions and the European Economic and Social Committee, two advisory bodies representing local authorities and social interests.Weidel has a similar position. "We don't want a Commission that is not elected to intrude and disturb your private life and [Member States] decision making [process]," she said.The AfD goes a step further, questioning the legitimacy of the European Parliament and advocating a Europe centred on sovereign nation-states.One of the most far-reaching proposals in the New Deal for Europe states: “The EP should no longer be elected directly, but instead be composed of delegates appointed by national parliaments.”Different strategies for changeLe Pen envisages reshaping the EU following elections in Spain, France, Italy and Poland, where far-right parties are expected to win or make significant gains.Poland’s Law and Justice party could return to power, while Spain’s Vox could join the government alongside the Popular Party. In France, Marine Le Pen could become the country’s first far-right president."This will be our shared undertaking for the years and, the decades to come. [...] It will not simply consist of undoing what has been very badly done over the past 30 years on the European stage," she said, claiming the new "Europe of nations" will feature EU institutions not exercising any authority over the member states.The AfD, by contrast, identifies 2029 as the pivotal year for EU reform, when the European elections could deliver a “patriotic right-wing majority in the European Parliament.”The party also floats disruptive national options should its planned reform of the EU fail. These include making extensive use of opt-outs for Germany in areas such as free movement, defence, taxation, social policy and migration."If Schengen [system] is over and it doesn't work, we need to get out of Schengen and protect our borders," Weidel said, pointing to challenges to free movement amid episodes such as the large-scale arrival of irregular migrants in Ceuta last July.The opt-out on migration would mean that Germany "will no longer participate in any European distribution mechanisms [of migrants] or asylum quotas,” disrupting the bloc's Migration Pact. Berlin currently holds the biggest solidarity quota in the EU and is in charge of relocating 4,555 asylum seekers from frontline member states in 2026.AFD leaves the door open for EU exitIf far-reaching reforms to the EU’s structure prove unattainable, the AfD’s plan states that "the German people should then decide for themselves," a formulation that could be interpreted as an implicit reference to a referendum on EU membership as a last resort, although Weidel did not raise this possibility at her press conference.Le Pen, once a strong advocate of France leaving the EU, has gradually abandoned the idea, shifting towards a strategy of radically reforming the bloc from within during her 2022 presidential campaign.Dave Sinardet, a Belgian political scientist who specialises in far-right parties, considers EU withdrawal an unrealistic scenario.“Most radical right parties have evolved their position towards the EU in the last years,” he told Euronews, adding that after Brexit no political force is seriously considering leaving the Union.“On this, AfD is really moving in the same direction that RN has already moved in the past. They are abandoning the ideas as Le Pen abandoned Frexit,” he said.

title: El Salvador launches military operation in Haiti to free four kidnapped aviation technicians
description: Bukele warned that failure to free the men who have been missing since Sunday’s attack on an armoured vehicle would trigger a far more powerful operation.
content: El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele announced Wednesday that he had launched a military operation to rescue four Salvadoran aviation technicians kidnapped by gangs in Haiti, warning of a far more forceful response if they are not returned alive and unharmed.The four men have been missing since Sunday, when gangs opened fire on an armoured vehicle in the Santo area of Croix-des-Bouquets, on the outskirts of Port-au-Prince. The technicians fled the burning vehicle and have not been seen since, marking the first major attack on the international gang suppression force since it began operating in Haiti.Addressing Haitian gang leaders directly, Bukele issued a stark ultimatum.“Today’s attack is nothing compared to what is coming if they do not release the four hostages alive. And do not take our words as empty threats,” he wrote on X, sharing a video of armoured vehicles with shattered windows moving through smoke.He added that if the men were returned safely, “everything will go back to the way it was before the kidnapping” but stopped short of specifying whether any further action would involve Salvadoran, Haitian or international forces.Bukele stressed that El Salvador’s mission in Haiti is strictly non-combat. The four men are aviation technicians whose primary role is to carry out medical evacuations, he said, adding that the Salvadoran contingent “consists only of pilots and technical personnel, not to wage war.”Haiti declares rescue an “absolute priority”Haiti’s government responded Wednesday evening, saying the abduction of the technicians was an “absolute priority.”A meeting was held at the prime minister’s office to assess ongoing operations and coordinate with the Gang Repression Force, according to a government statement.“All necessary resources are being mobilised to achieve this goal,” the statement said. It was not immediately clear whether Haitian authorities had confirmed that the four men are still alive. A spokesperson for the gang suppression force did not respond to requests for comment.The attack underscores the scale of the challenge facing international forces in Haiti, where gangs are estimated to control around 70 percent of Port-au-Prince. The country is also preparing for its first general election in more than a decade.El Salvador is one of several countries, including Chad, Jamaica and Guatemala, contributing to the multinational gang suppression force, which has more than 2,000 troops on the ground.The UN originally approved up to 5,550 security personnel and more than 50 civilian staff for the mission in 2025. The force received at least a six-month extension through March 2027 from the UN Security Council.In early October, El Salvador passed a law extending its own participation in the force for a year, also broadening its mandate beyond medical evacuations to allow the deployment of civilian and military personnel according to the mission’s broader needs.

title: Disappointed after meeting, French unions call for 5 November action
description: Trade unions, unanimously disappointed after their meeting with the government, are calling for a large mobilisation on 5 November. The CGT's general secretary is urging workers to "generalise the strike".
content: Union leaders who met Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu at the Matignon on Wednesday left the nearly two-and-a-half-hour meeting disappointed.According to Sophie Binet, head of the General Confederation of Labour (CGT), Sébastien Lecornu did not announce "any measures" to respond to the multiple protests. There was "no consideration of our demands", she lamented.The CGT, which took part in the 17 October demonstrations that degenerated into riots and looting in several cities over the weekend, will once again take to the streets on Saturday for the "act II" of the cost-of-living mobilisation announced by a "yellow vest" coordination.For the unions, the central objective remains the mobilisation launched by almost all of them among private- and public-sector employees for 5 November. "The time has come to move the mobilisation up a gear; from that date strike action must take over", said Sophie Binet.By then, the secretary-general of the French Democratic Confederation of Labour (CFDT, the country’s largest union), Marylise Léon, expects "social responses" to workers’ expectations.According to the president of the French Confederation of Christian Workers (CFTC), Cyril Chabanier, the government has nonetheless "opened the door" to "a discussion" on raising the minimum wage. On this issue, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has called for things to "move quickly".At Matignon, the unions also regretted that secondary school and student organisations had not been invited to the meeting.They are expected to be received again on Monday by the education minister. Édouard Geffray has promised initial measures to respond to the demands expressed on the platform set up by the government. Secondary school pupils have been mobilised for several weeks, with the support of university students, calling for more resources for education, improvements to the state of school buildings, replacement for absent teachers and the scrapping of the Parcoursup platform which handles tertiary education access and is seen as deeply flawed.On a Middle East tour, Emmanuel Macron calls for "firmness"Speaking from Qatar, Emmanuel Macron called for "firmness" towards those responsible for the violence and on Thursday convened a meeting with the intelligence services to examine the failings of 17 October. The president, however, made no announcements on the many demands voiced by the protesters, including on purchasing power or funding for schools and universities.Emmanuel Macron, who then travelled on to Saudi Arabia where he was received by crown prince and de facto ruler Mohammed bin Salman, said the French would get a "fair return" from this tour, notably on diesel prices.On Wednesday, several political figures from across the spectrum again condemned what they see as a failure of those in power. Édouard Philippe, the Horizons presidential candidate, criticised Emmanuel Macron’s decision to maintain his trip to the Gulf. Former head of state François Hollande, for his part, attacked a government he considers weak. Marine Le Pen, the National Rally candidate for the presidential election, targeted what she called the "waning power".Several curfews renewedIn Paris, the police prefecture has imposed a new curfew in certain areas for the night from Wednesday to Thursday.The decrees "ban the presence of adults and minors alike in the areas around Place de la République and the Les Halles district from 11 pm today until 6 am tomorrow", the police prefecture said on X.In Lyon, the Rhône prefecture has decided to renew the curfew and the ban on gatherings, extending the measures that were in force on the previous two nights in Lyon. The curfew runs from 11 pm to 6 am, two hours later than the previous ones, which started at 9 pm.Around 2,500 people in police custody and 174 jailedDuring a visit to Marseille, which saw violent clashes at the weekend and where the town hall was vandalised, justice minister Gérald Darmanin reported 2,500 people taken into police custody following the violence and the looting of numerous shops during the 17 October mobilisation.Of these, 917 people have been brought before prosecutors with charges to be tried in immediate appearances. The minister, who pledged that justice would be firm, said this figure had doubled, or even tripled.In Paris, of the 557 people taken into custody after the violence and looting in the capital, 300 appeared before a magistrate by midday on Wednesday. On Tuesday evening, Paris prosecutor Laure Beccuau said that none had claimed a motive "of whatever political nature", even as the government accuses "the ultra-left" of being largely behind the violence.The strategy for maintaining public order has also been called into question for several weeks. The Defender of Rights announced on Tuesday that it had received 46 complaints since the start of the secondary school students’ movement, more than ten of which concern incidents from the weekend. At the same time, the IGPN, the police internal affairs body, has been tasked with at least six investigations relating to those two days.

title: Pope Leo XIV post-op results show no further treatment required as tumour was localised
description: The pontiff needs no further treatment, his doctors said, eight days after an hour-and-a-half operation on his right lung.
content: Final histological tests and molecular biology analyses carried out on tissue removed during Pope Leo XIV’s surgery have confirmed the presence of a localised pulmonary adenocarcinoma.A subsequent oncological assessment has determined that no further therapy is necessary.The update was given by the Pope’s doctors, Dr Luigi Carbone and Prof Stefano Margaritora, as they reported on the pontiff’s postoperative progress.The examinations confirmed that the disease had not spread beyond the lung. In light of these results and the specialist evaluation, no additional oncological treatment has been deemed necessary.It was the Pope himself who, during the Angelus prayer on 11 October, revealed that he had a nodule in his right lung. He was then admitted to hospital and underwent surgery on 13 October, in an operation lasting around an hour and a half.

title: Aberfan: King Charles marks Welsh mining disaster that killed a generation of children
description: Survivors shared their memories with the royal party, six decades after an official verdict, a raid on donations and a fight over the tips that followed.
content: King Charles III has led tributes to the people of Aberfan on the 60th anniversary of the disaster, in which 116 children and 28 adults died when a colliery spoil tip collapsed onto Pantglas Junior School in Wales in 21 October 1966.The King, Queen Camilla and the Prince of Wales met survivors in the Welsh village. The King and Prince William laid wreaths at the memorial garden, and the Queen placed a posy."We have heard stories of heartbreak, but also of heroism," the King said. "We have heard of the most agonising grief, but also of the most inspiring grace."Coal bosses had been warned of the danger beforehand, yet no one was prosecuted or lost their job.What happened at Aberfan?Aberfan is a small coal-mining village in the valleys of south Wales, in the United Kingdom. For decades, waste from the local colliery had been dumped in huge heaps, known as tips, on the hillside above the houses.These tips had moved before - the heap of coal waste had slid in 1944 and again in 1963, but the warning signs were not acted on.On the morning of Friday 21 October 1966, one of the tips gave way. Shortly after 9.15am, over 100,000 cubic metres of sodden waste poured down the mountain and onto the village school, just as lessons were starting.The last child to be found alive was pulled out at 11:00 that morning.The scale of the loss is still hard to grasp. The disaster claimed the lives of 144 people, 116 of them children, and an entire generation of the village was all but wiped out. Within days, the UK Parliament ordered an official inquiry.What did the inquiry find?On 26 October 1966, the UK government minister for Wales appointed a tribunal led by senior judge Lord Justice Edmund Davies. It heard evidence first in nearby Merthyr Tydfil and then in the Welsh capital, Cardiff.Its verdict, published in August 1967, was unequivocal - "Blame for the disaster rests upon the National Coal Board," the state-owned body that ran Britain’s coal industry.
