As a result of the inquiry, information about every one of the board’s tips was gathered for the first time.People across Britain and around the world sent money to help the grieving village, and the disaster fund grew to £1.75m (€2.08m).What happened to the money donated?In 1968, UK Prime Minister Harold Wilson’s government forced the disaster fund to give up £150,000 (€178,000) to pay for removing the remaining coal waste heaps above Aberfan, even though those tips belonged to the National Coal Board.The village had to wait almost three decades for the money to be returned. Ron Davies, the UK government’s minister for Wales, repaid it in 1997, and the Welsh Government later gave Aberfan charities a further £2m.The fund made equal payments to every bereaved family. The UK's Charity Commission tried to block these payments as it wanted the trustees to be satisfied that each parent had been "close" to the child who died. The trustees defied the Commission and paid the families anyway.The fund was attempting to support families because the National Coal Board was paying them very little. The board raised its compensation offer from £50 to £500 (€596) per bereaved family.Sixty years later, organisations across Wales were invited to observe a minute’s silence at 9.15am on Wednesday, the moment the tip collapsed.

title: Lithuania seizes major synthetic drugs lab run by Dutch national
description: Police recover more than 500kg of methamphetamine and 300kg of amphetamine in a three-day operation targeting a suspected international supply network.
content: Lithuanian authorities have uncovered one of the largest synthetic drugs laboratories in the Baltics, seizing hundreds of kilograms of drugs and thousands of litres of chemical precursors at a site near Vilnius allegedly run by a Dutch national of Turkish origin. “[Drugs] were being produced on an almost industrial scale,” Saulius Briginas, Deputy Chief of the Lithuanian Criminal Police Bureau, told journalists during a press briefing on Wednesday. Investigators believe the Dutch citizen organised the laboratory's work and coordinated its illegal activities alongside three other members who were all Lithuanian nationals.Preliminary figures indicate that police recovered more than 3,000 litres of BMK, a chemical precursor used in the production of amphetamines; more than 500kg of methamphetamine; more than 300kg of amphetamine; and around 4.5kg of the synthetic cathinone 3-CMC. This amounts to over 4 million single doses, Briginas said.“On the wholesale illicit market, the drugs would be worth more than €2 million,” he said. “At street level, the value could be ten times higher.” Such figures, Lithuanian authorities believe, indicate that the drugs could not have been intended solely for the Lithuanian market. Instead, the operation was geared towards markets across Europe, with the Netherlands, Germany, Belgium and the Czech Republic among the countries to which the drugs may have been destined.The investigation also uncovered the industrial-scale procurement of chemicals needed to manufacture synthetic drugs. The group sourced laboratory equipment and chemical substances from China, India and several European countries, while also purchasing some uncontrolled substances from specialist suppliers in Lithuania.Police found 380 cylinders of hydrogen originating from China at the laboratory. Hydrogen is used in the manufacture of synthetic drugs, while sulphuric acid was reportedly purchased in quantities of one tonne per transaction. The operation extended beyond the laboratory itself. Police intercepted a shipment intended for the Czech Republic after finding 17kg of amphetamine crystals in two plastic containers inside cargo handled by a Lithuanian logistics company.Under Lithuanian law, offences involving the illegal production, possession and smuggling of particularly large quantities of narcotic or psychotropic substances can carry prison sentences of up to 18 years.

title: Colombia seizes 7.6 tonnes of Netherlands-bound cocaine at Cartagena port
description: Separately, two Dutch nationals wanted by prosecutors in the Netherlands have been arrested in Colombia.
content: Colombian police have seized 7.6 tonnes of cocaine bound for the Netherlands at the port of Cartagena, President Abelardo de la Espriella announced on Tuesday."The National Police has just achieved the largest cocaine seizure in the port of Cartagena in the last 10 years," he wrote on X.According to Colombia's National Police, the drugs were hidden in powdered panela, an unrefined cane sugar, and were found by its anti-narcotics directorate in an operation coordinated with the US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA).De la Espriella said security forces had seized 132 tonnes of cocaine, worth around $6.1 billion, in his government's first 75 days."There is no truce against narco-terrorism! Every dose we prevent from reaching the streets saves lives, and every dollar we take from them weakens their criminal structures," he added.Separately, the Dutch Public Prosecution Service (OM) confirmed to the Dutch newspaper AD that two Dutch nationals had been arrested in Colombia at its request.Colombian prosecutors named them as Ronny and Ulrich. Neither authority has linked the arrests to the seizure. According to the EU Drugs Agency, 330 tonnes of cocaine were seized in the EU in 2024, down from 419 tonnes in 2023.

title: Thélyson Orélien row: publisher says AI used to write 'C'était ça ou mourir'
description: The Quebec author has been at the centre of a controversy for weeks. On Wednesday, his Canadian publisher Les Éditions du Boréal admitted that AI was indeed used to write his latest novel.
content: The case has been shaking the French-language publishing world for weeks. On Wednesday 21 October, the Canadian publisher Les Éditions du Boréal announced via a press release (source in French) that Thélyson Orélien had indeed used artificial intelligence (AI) to write his novel "C'était ça ou mourir", contrary to what he had previously claimed."New information, confirmed in recent days, indicates that artificial intelligence was used in the writing process (of the novel), even though the author had assured us, on several occasions, that he had never resorted to it in creating his book", the publisher said in a statement on Wednesday."As a result, Boréal will not reprint the novel and will not publish any further books by Thélyson Orélien."This announcement comes just a week after the publisher had said it was backing the author, insisting it had no evidence that would make it possible to establish with certainty that AI had been used.In the face of mounting doubts, and after Thélyson Orélien "announced that he would not provide any further material", the publisher says it has "commissioned an in-depth external analysis" of "all the working versions of the novel"."We still do not know to what extent AI was used in the creation of "C'était ça ou mourir", and we will probably never have a definitive answer on that point" but "for us, the fundamental issue is the relationship of trust between authors and publishers", the publishing house added.The controversy was sparked by accusations from the X account "Balance ton Claude", which claimed to have identified extensive use of AI in the novel. The affair has since shaken the sector and, for weeks, fuelled questions about the future of the writing profession.

title: Milei reignites war of words with Sánchez as Spanish PM declares himself ‘leftie and proud’
description: Javier Milei has reignited his war of words with Pedro Sánchez during a visit to Madrid, as the Spanish prime minister declared himself “leftie and proud”.
content: Javier Milei let it be known he had arrived in Madrid.The Argentine libertarian launched a tirade against Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez as he began a visit to the Spanish capital. Milei, who has blamed socialism for Argentina’s economic malaise and cultural decline, accused Sánchez of acting like a dictator.His visit comes amid a highly polarising political campaign ahead of the 29 November election, with Sánchez positioning himself as the last bastion against what he calls the ultra-right and a coalition of reactionary forces, including Milei.At a breakfast event, the Argentine president called Sánchez a “shameless dictator” and suggested the Spanish prime minister was fuelling an “invasion” in Ceuta, the Spanish enclave that saw a mass border breach from neighbouring Morocco in July."The socialists would rather reign in hell than serve in heaven. That is why they encourage the invasion. Every immigrant is a vote. If the price to pay is the destruction of the country, they are more than willing to pay it,” he said.While more than 70,000 migrants crossed illegally into Ceuta, the vast majority returned to Morocco within 48 hours. Some 7,000 remain, although they would not be eligible to vote.Milei, known for his chainsaw economics and sweeping cuts to public spending, saw his verbal acrobatics reach a crescendo as the day progressed.He urged Spanish voters to oust the Socialist government “a patadas” — literally, “by kicking them out” — if necessary.Milei and Sánchez have clashed in the past and see each other as polar opposites.In 2024, during a visit to Madrid, Milei called Sánchez’s wife, Begoña Gómez, “corrupt”. Gómez is under investigation and faces trial, but denies any wrongdoing.The remarks triggered a diplomatic spat between Buenos Aires and Madrid, prompting Spain to recall its ambassador over what it described as “unacceptable” remarks.With the campaign underway, Sánchez got ahead of the attacks from his Argentine counterpart, tweeting that he was “leftie — and proud” before the visit. He also shared a screenshot showing his iPhone playing “Fanático” (fanatic) by Lali Espósito, an Argentine singer and outspoken critic of Milei.While Spanish sources described Milei’s latest comments as completely out of place, his attacks may play into the hands of Sánchez, who faces an uphill battle ahead of the November election.Chainsaw politicsSánchez is running an aggressive campaign, positioning himself as the only candidate able to “safeguard the social rights” of the majority.He has also warned that a government led by the mainstream conservative Partido Popular (PP) and far-right Vox would undo years of progress. The PP is leading in the polls, with several opinion surveys suggesting the two parties could secure a governing majority.At a rally, Sánchez told supporters that "a chainsaw cannot build anything, it destroys" and suggested PP-Vox would do the same. "If there's a lesson from Milei's visit, it's that they will do to Spain what Milei is unfortunately doing to Argentina."Chainsaw, or la motosierra, is a campaign slogan used by Milei to describe budget cuts.For the Spanish Socialists, the aim is to dominate the progressive camp by rallying all forces to its left. But that alone would not guarantee a return to government, as Spain’s parliamentary system requires sufficient support in parliament to form a government.“If raising pensions, increasing the minimum wage or defending the right to abortion makes me a leftie, then I am a leftie,” the Spanish prime minister said, concluding: “Yes, I am a leftie, and proud of it.”Sánchez also replaced his picture on social media with an image bearing the slogan “Leftie and proud” against a red background.As Milei landed in Madrid, a banner appeared outside the PSOE’s headquarters on Calle Ferraz, the party’s historic base in the Spanish capital.It read: “The lefties, men and women, welcome you to Spain.”Milei, polarising to the right tooWith the general election only weeks away, PP leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo, who has cultivated an image of a moderate conservative, did not meet Milei.The two men have never been photographed together.Milei did, however, meet Madrid regional president Isabel Díaz Ayuso, a trailblazer on the right whose political style is far more combative.For Feijóo, Milei's visit represents a delicate balancing act, as he seeks to project a more institutional, statesmanlike image.To govern in Spain, Feijóo will most likely have to enter a formal coalition with Vox.While the two parties have forged alliances at regional level, they have yet to do so nationally. Vox’s group in the European Parliament, Patriots for Europe, is seen by Feijóo’s European political family, the European People’s Party (EPP), as lying outside the pro-European consensus.Asked by reporters whether his visit to Madrid had put anyone in an awkward position, Milei rejected the premise, telling journalists: “That’s a view held by people who are intellectually limited, which is your case.”

title: EasyJet is covering the cost of a baby’s first passport for customers in the UK
description: Parents can get a £66.50 (€79.40) discount on easyJet holidays if travelling with an infant under the age of two.
content: There are plenty of milestones in the first two years of life. Baby’s first smile, baby’s first words, baby’s first steps… but what about baby’s first holiday?According to a new survey of 2,000 British parents who have taken their little ones abroad at least once before the age of five, 82% agreed that it was a landmark family moment, while more than half called it “one of their proudest parenting milestones”.Now, easyJet is making it a little cheaper for those looking to head away with their sprogs as the airline group is offering to pay for the cost of a child’s passport in the UK.The £66.50 (€79.40) discount on easyJet holidays is available for one child under the age of 18 months per booking. You’ll need to book before 26 November, for travel before 31 October 2028. Infants will need to be under two years old at the time of travel.While the thought of travelling abroad with kids that young may be daunting, 48% of those polled said it was easier than they’d expected, and 87% would do it again.According to easyJet holidays data, there has been a 10% increase in infants travelling this year compared to 2025, even though there are still two months left of the year.“Travel has a unique way of bringing families together, and a baby's very first holiday is often one of those moments parents remember for years to come,” Stuart Wright, customer director at easyJet holidays, said.“By covering the cost of a baby's first passport, we're helping more families start making those memories that little bit sooner.”Flying with kids under the age of twoMost airlines will allow infants under the age of two to travel for free on their parents’ lap. Many carriers – notably not easyJet, for the sake of this article – also offer bassinets that attach to the bulkhead wall in front of you that your little one can sleep in during the flight.In the UK, child passports are valid for five years. Much like when applying for an adult passport, you’ll need to submit two identical photos of your child alongside various documents like the birth certificate, and your British passport to confirm your claim to British nationality. Kids under the age of five don’t need to have a neutral expression or be looking directly at the camera for the photo; babies under the age of one don’t even need to have their eyes open.You’ll need a countersignatory who can confirm your child’s identity. This person will need to have known you for at least two years, work in or be retired from a “recognised profession” such as a teacher or a social worker, live in the UK, and have a valid British or Irish passport themselves.All the exact details about how to apply are on the UK government website.

title: Palantir says NATO AI system has no ‘kill switch’ after Starlink disruptions in Ukraine
description: The American software firm says it cannot shut off NATO AI systems amid European fears of dependence on US tech following disruptions to Ukraine’s Starshield access.
content: US software company Palantir has sought to reassure European allies that its military AI system used by NATO has no “kill switch”.Palantir’s executive vice president for the UK and Europe, Louis Mosley, told Reuters on Wednesday that neither the company nor the US could switch off the Maven Smart System AI platform used by NATO’s military headquarters and several European armed forces.“What we have seen in the news over the past few days around Starlink is extremely concerning,” Mosley said in an interview in Brussels.“But as concerns Palantir, I can provide categorical reassurance that where customers have bought our software, they are in full operational control of that software,” he said.“There are no kill switches. There’s no ability for Palantir or the US government to reach in and switch it off.”It follows recent disruptions to Ukraine’s Starlink and Starshield services, which raised alarm over the reliance on US tech firms.On 13 October, Kyiv accused Washington of deliberately slowing Starshield, the SpaceX-operated military communications system that Ukrainian forces depend on at the front, as well as SpaceX’s civilian satellite network Starlink.Reports later emerged that the White House had ordered Elon Musk’s SpaceX to limit Ukraine’s access to Starshield, the military-grade version of the Starlink satellite network.Musk defended himself on X, and claimed that the “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS.”To which US President Donald Trump replied, saying, “it wasn’t me, and I don’t think it was Elon. I don’t know if it was anybody. From what I understand, it’s the same as it’s always been.”The lack of clarity over who was responsible for the decision is one concern. But for European leaders, the prospect of the Trump administration using US technology that Europe has become so reliant upon as political leverage against its allies is even more alarming.Palantir’s Maven systemNATO currently uses Palantir’s Maven system, which relies on AI to process large volumes of battlefield data from satellites, radar, drones and other sensors to speed up decision-making.Palantir won a €480 million tender with NATO in 2025 to supply Maven to the alliance. It has since been deployed at NATO’s Allied Command Operations at the Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe (SHAPE), and in June this year it achieved “full technical operational capability”.Some European NATO members, including France and Germany, have opted out of Maven, alarmed at the possibility of a private company having so much control over battlefield operations.“Allowing industry personnel access to national German datasets is out of the question," German Vice Admiral Thomas Daum said earlier this year.France has meanwhile developed its own service, Arcadia, in an effort to build its own defence data ecosystem and maintain technological sovereignty.

title: Barclays to cut 5,000 jobs as it turns to AI to improve efficiency
description: British bank Barclays said on Thursday it would cut around 5,000 jobs, or roughly 5% of its global workforce, by the end of 2026 as it turns to AI and other technology to streamline operations and improve efficiency.
content: Barclays shares edged lower in London after the bank said on Thursday it would cut around 5,000 jobs, including around 1,000 already cut in the first half of the year.The announcement came alongside an earnings update that showed Barclays’ net profit grew 13% in the third quarter, helped by surging income in its equities division.Barclays said in an earnings presentation that it was implementing “organisational simplification and technology change efficiency driven by AI”.About 60% of the job cuts affect support functions, including developers, as AI makes staff more productive, according to the bank.Will Howlett, a financial analyst at Quilter Cheviot, said the announcement illustrates "just how significantly AI and automation could reshape the banking industry over the next few years"."Banks have spent heavily on technology for years, but we are increasingly reaching the point where that investment translates into fewer people being required to run the business," he said, adding that "Barclays expects its efficiency measures to deliver more than £1.1 billion (€1.31bn) of savings, which should help bring down costs and improve profitability."The bank’s profit attributable to shareholders rose to £1.65 billion (€1.97 billion) in the third quarter from £1.46 billion (€1.74 billion) in the July–September period a year earlier.Barclays chief executive C. S. Venkatakrishnan said he was pleased with the bank’s operational and financial momentum, and said the investment bank division “delivered strong equities performance”.Income from equities jumped 47% year-on-year, while total group income for the quarter climbed 3% to £7.37 billion (€8.79 billion)."The investment bank was weaker, particularly in fixed income trading, but Barclays remains on track against its longer-term targets," said Howlett. He added that "the question is increasingly whether Barclays can turn technological investment and a smaller workforce into sustainably lower costs without compromising growth." If it can, he said, "there is still considerable scope for improved returns.”The bank also announced a £500 million (€596 million) share buyback.The AI “announcement comes as the company failed to match expectations with its third-quarter performance — with the unveiling of a healthy share buyback failing to entirely ease investors’ disappointment”, noted AJ Bell investment director Russ Mould.He added that while costs increased across the wider group, there are two "major clouds over the business".“The first being a widely expected increase in tax on the sector in next week’s (UK) budget and the other being a reported probe into possible misrepresentation of risks in its private credit portfolio,” Mould said.According to the FT, the Bank of England was examining claims that Barclays had understated risks linked to financing for private credit funds. The concern is whether Barclays made these exposures look less risky in its books, allowing it to hold less capital to cover potential losses.Barclays has said its private credit exposure is treated in line with accounting and regulatory capital requirements.

title: EU Parliament awards Sakharov Prize to ICC in rebuke of US sanctions
description: The European Parliament awards the Sakharov Prize to the International Criminal Court in a show of support after the US imposed sanctions on the institution.
content: The European Parliament on Thursday awarded the International Criminal Court (ICC) the Sakharov Prize for Freedom of Thought, signalling opposition to US sanctions threatening the court’s work.The annual prize recognises individuals and organisations defending human rights and fundamental freedoms. Past laureates include South African leader Nelson Mandela and Russian opposition figure Alexei Navalny.US President Donald Trump’s administration announced sanctions against the ICC on 9 October, following repeated criticism of its arrest warrant for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and its investigation into the conduct of US troops in Afghanistan.“This is a message of hope and resistance sent to Donald Trump. We will not abandon the rule of law and international justice. We will stand with the ICC for as long as it takes,” said French MEP Chloé Ridel, who nominated the court.Parliament’s political group leaders chose the ICC over two other shortlisted candidates: Tanzanian lawyer Tundu Lissu, who faces political persecution, and Iranian sisters Taraneh and Romina Rahimi, nominated on behalf of those persecuted by Iran’s authorities.The Socialists and Democrats (S&D) group put forward the ICC and its officials, with other political groups eventually backing the nomination. The decision surprised some insiders, who had expected Lissu to win.Last week, MEPs from across the political spectrum urged European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to protect the Netherlands-based court from US sanctions.They called for the use of “all instruments at our disposal”, particularly the EU’s Blocking Statute, which shields European companies and individuals from the effects of certain foreign sanctions.EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas described the threat of sanctions against the ICC as “not acceptable” on 9 October, reaffirming the bloc’s commitment to international law. The EU has yet to take concrete action.

title: Six European destinations included in ‘Best of the World’ selection for 2027
description: National Geographic has curated its list of 25 must-visit places for 2027, with six destinations in Europe making the cut, including the Tricity area in Poland and Vestland in Norway.
content: National Geographic has unveiled its list of the 25 destinations around the world that travellers should add to their 2027 itineraries, with six being in Europe.First launched in 2012, its “Best of the World” selection has showcased where to go if you have “a sense of adventure, a fascination with the past”, or seeking the “simple pleasure of wandering unfamiliar city streets”.Vestland in Norway was among the European destinations to make the cut. Here, travellers will find “epic fjord adventures and wellness-led travel” in one of Europe’s “most breathtaking landscapes”, the magazine said.Vestland’s sheer scale of natural wonder was also highlighted. “Wherever you go, big wildness awaits”, including sky-high cliffs, turquoise waters and cascading waterfalls.Poland’s Tricity area, which combines three adjacent cities – Gdańsk, Gdynia and Sopot – also made the list along with German city Leipzig.For a musical getaway, Leipzig is recommended for its grand opera, orchestral halls and jazz clubs. The city is set to expand its existing 5.3km-long Music Trail, a route that takes visitors to numerous key historical sites, with a second 7.2km loop.Also making the list is Normandy in France, especially as the region is set to host "Millenium 2027: European Year of the Normans". The celebration marks the 1,000th anniversary of William the Conqueror’s birth. Throughout 2027, more than 1,000 events will take place, including concerts, medieval feasts and theatrical street performances.Along Spain’s northern coast, Santander will welcome the opening of two world-class art museums in 2027. The region of Cantabria is “often overlooked”, the magazine said, but its capital city is “poised to change that”. Next year an outpost of the Museo Reina Sofia will open in the city and the Museum of Prehistory and Archaeology will move to a new home.For quiet trails and dark night skies, Dumfries and Galloway in Scotland is a must-visit – especially for stargazers. Next summer, the Scottish Dark Sky Observatory is set to open amid the “rippling hills” of the Galloway and Southern Ayrshire UNESCO Biosphere.Best of the world beyond EuropeGlobally, National Geographic called on travellers to “join the biggest celebration of Afro-Brazilian culture in one of South America’s most historic cities”. For the first time in decades, Salvador in Brazil will host the Salvador Carnival immediately after the Festa de Iemanjá – which is the biggest festival of the Candomblé religion.In Africa, Malawi is described as the continent’s “best-kept secret” that offers “thrilling nature experiences without the crowds”, especially as the classic safari circuit continues to grow in popularity. Thanks to government initiatives and work by conservation organisations, travellers can see the “big five” – lions, leopards, elephants, rhinos and African buffalo – in Malawi’s top wildlife regions, including Liwonde National Park and Majete Wildlife Reserve.Other destinations to make the selection include Luxor in Egypt, Chengdu in China, Maya Ka’an in Mexico, and the Pacific Coast Highway in California, United States.National Geographic’s ‘Best of the World’ list for 2027Vestland, Norway Penang, Malaysia Luxor, Egypt Madison, Wisconsin, USA Puerto Rico Dumfries and Galloway, Scotland, UK Niigata Prefecture, Japan Chengdu, China Pacific Coast Highway, California, USA Jaipur, India Grenada Salvador, Brazil Cape Froward National Park, Chile Santander, Spain Normandy, France The Ozarks, USA Halifax, Nova Scotia, Canada Armenia Melbourne, Australia Leipzig, Germany Baltimore, Maryland, USA Malawi Maya Ka’an, Mexico Tricity (Gdańsk, Sopot and Gdynia), Poland Kuélap, PeruPoland on the international tourism mapThe tricity area of Gdańsk, Gdynia and Sopot were included on the National Geographic list. It joins the group of Polish destinations previously distinguished by the magazine: Białowieża Forest in 2019 and Łódź in 2022.Crucially, the accolade underlines that Poland's Baltic coast has far more to offer than sandy beaches and a traditional summer holiday.Together the three cities form a region where coastal landscapes blend with historical heritage, culture and a modern way of life.The authors of the list encourage people to explore the region with the invitation: "Discover revitalised waterfronts and bold Baltic flavours in three seaside cities that are coming into their own."Three cities, three different storiesGdańsk draws visitors with its landmarks and centuries-old port history. Among the most important sights are Long Market (Długi Targ), the medieval Crane, the Museum of the Second World War and the European Solidarity Centre. The former Gdańsk Shipyard grounds also attract particular attention.Significantly, the industrial spaces are being given new functions and are becoming venues for meetings, artistic events and a vibrant food scene.Gdańsk's mayor Aleksandra Dulkiewicz stressed the importance of the distinction for the local community at the press conference."Gdańsk is a city of freedom, solidarity and openness,” she said. “A place where history meets modernity and everyone can find something for themselves. This accolade belongs to the residents of Gdańsk, who every day create the unique atmosphere of our city.”Sopot stands above all for its spa traditions, seaside atmosphere and closeness to nature.The city invites visitors to stroll along the beach and hike through the Tricity Landscape Park. Its attractions can be discovered outside the peak summer season as well.Sopot's mayor Magdalena Czarzyńska-Jachim noted at the press conference: "Experts from all over the world have recognised the resort's exceptional atmosphere and the quality of our tourist offer, which Sopot's entrepreneurs work on every day in cooperation with the Sopot Tourism Organisation."Gdynia, meanwhile, is distinguished by its modernist architecture and a history linked to the development of Poland's maritime economy.The city, whose dynamic expansion began in the interwar period, became a symbol of Poland's renewed ambitions on the Baltic.It is worth emphasising that in 2026 Gdynia's Modernist Centre was added to the UNESCO World Heritage List.Gdynia's mayor Aleksandra Kosiorek drew attention to the special timing of the accolade."This distinction has particular significance for us in the year of the centenary of Gdynia being granted city status,” she said. “A hundred years ago Gdynia was a symbol of a bold look to the future and today it once again shows that it is an open, dynamic and inspiring city. We are pleased that its history and present day have been recognised by one of the world's most recognisable travel publications.”Gastronomy and events all year roundLocal cuisine also plays an important role in the National Geographic recommendation. Tricity chefs use regional products, draw inspiration from Kashubian traditions and give classic dishes a contemporary twist.Fish from the Baltic are another key element of the offer.The region also attracts visitors with its cultural and sporting events. Gdańsk hosts St Dominic's Fair and the Shakespeare Festival, while Sopot organises a literary festival.In turn, in 2027 Gdynia will host the main multi-class regattas as part of the Sailing World Championships. Kolosy, the National Meeting of Travellers, Sailors and Mountaineers, is also planned there.An additional advantage is the ability to travel conveniently between the three cities without a car. Thanks to this, a single trip can combine sightseeing historic monuments, relaxing by the sea and exploring modernist architecture.

title: Prix Pascal: New French literature prize launched for books co-written with AI
description: A new literary award has just been launched and aims to recognise work written in collaboration with AI. Its timing is problematic, to say the least.
content: A new prize for AI-written books has launched this week in France, and the timing couldn't be worse.The Prix Pascal de Littérature IA comes after weeks of controversy over the use of AI by finalists for a number of literary prizes, including the Prix Goncourt, France's most prestigious literary prize.Since September, the French literary world has been rocked by the Thélyson Orélien affair, triggered by allegations of extensive use of AI in the Canadian-Haitian author’s novel, "C’était ça ou mourir".Yesterday, Orélien's Canadian publisher confirmed that AI had indeed been used in the writer’s book and dropped the author. Orélien continues to deny the allegations and spoke to Libération journalist Rachid Laïreche, telling him that he drew on external souces for historical research.“I said that I wrote the book; it’s not as if AI wrote it,” he insists. “Just as when translating languages, I used tools,” adding that he “didn’t expect any of this”.Now, the Prix Pascal is openly encouraging the use of AI – whilst insisting on its website that the prize "is not a technology competition"."AI is already present in writing workshops, in manuscripts and in bookshops, often unnoticed," states the website. "The Pascal Prize asks the question aloud: what constitutes a work of literature when the author and the machine collaborate?"Entrants must submit a manuscript, as well as a technical dossier specifying the algorithmic assistance used. All major language models are allowed, including ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and LLaMA.“Whilst others hunt down AI using conflicting detection tools, the Prix Pascal asks authors to declare its use: no proselytising, no lawsuits – transparency as the basis for debate and collective intelligence,” say the award’s organisers.“The prize is open to anyone who writes in French, anywhere in the French-speaking world, regardless of nationality or place of residence, and without the need for a publisher,” state its founders Philippe Rodriguez, Albin Serviant and Gilles Mentré - all technology entrepreneurs. Rodriguez is a founding partner at the mergers and acquisitions advisory firm Avolta; Serviant is the former chair of the LGBTQ+ magazine Têtu; and Mentré teaches at Harvard and the University of Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne.“The jury is looking for an unpublished work that is useful or thought-provoking,” they added.A call for entries was launched yesterday, and the composition of the "jury of five prominent figures" is due to be revealed at the end of the month. The winner of the 2026 prize will be announced in mid-December. No prize money is at stake, although assistance with publication will be provided.Considering French law neither regulates nor prohibits the use of AI to write a literary work, the prize remains legitimate. However, it has been launched at a time when creatives are speaking out against the use of AI and demanding regulations and safeguards be put in place.The new prize is named after French mathematician and philosopher Blaise Pascal, with the Prix Pascal website stressing that Pascal "is the only Western thinker to have been both a pioneer of mechanical devices and a master of language."His quotation "À mesure qu'on a plus d'esprit, on trouve qu'il y a plus d'hommes originaux" is also cited - "The more wit one has, the more one realises there are original people."What are the odds the celebrated polymath and author of "Pensées" is spinning in his grave right now?

title: France confirms first human case of Shamonda virus, previously found only in animals
description: French authorities have confirmed the first known human case of Shamonda virus, which mainly affects cattle, in a patient in Lyon who died in early October, adding that there is no health risk to the general population.
content: French authorities have confirmed an infection with the Shamonda virus in a patient in Lyon who died in early October, marking the first time the virus has been reported in a human. Until now, the Shamonda virus was considered not to be transmissible to humans. This case is the first documented and reported detection of the virus in a human. “This is therefore an exceptional case involving a severely immunocompromised patient,” the authorities said. The Shamonda virus was detected in Europe for the first time this summer. It belongs to a group of viruses transmitted by biting insects called midges, and until now it has affected mostly cattle, considered the main hosts among infected animal species. Sporadic infections in small ruminants and horses were also reported in France this summer. The infected patient was a severely immunocompromised patient and had been receiving treatment for a serious illness at the Hospices Civils de Lyon, the French Agriculture Ministry said in a statement. According to the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC), the specific midge species involved in transmission in this case is still unknown. French authorities say that the hypothesis is that the patient was infected through an insect bite, specifically from a tiny fly, Culicoides midge, in eastern France.“According to investigations carried out so far, the brain complications observed in the immunocompromised patient before their death were very likely linked to the Shamonda virus infection,” the Ministry said. “Based on current knowledge of the virus, no health risk to the general population has been identified to date”.Clinical, laboratory and epidemiological investigations are still ongoing to determine whether the virus caused or contributed to the patient’s death and how the infection was acquired, together with the World Health Organization (WHO) and the ECDC.In infected adult cattle, the main symptoms are fever, lethargy and diarrhoea. In dairy cows, a significant drop in milk production may also be observed, according to Sciensano, Belgium’s national public health institute.Shamonda virus was first detected in Nigeria in the mid-1960s and has since been reported sporadically in cattle in West, East and southern Africa and in Japan. This summer, it was detected for the first time in Western Europe, with cases reported in Austria, Belgium, France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland, as well as Jersey island.This story has been updated to include a comment from the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC).

title: Refusing to cross, unable to escape: Seafarers recount Hormuz dangers to Euronews
description: Euronews spoke to a crew member of a cargo vessel anchored off Pakistan for weeks and an Iranian maritime manager about dangers in the vital waterway — where traffic has fallen 90% since the war began and at least 95 seafarers in commercial roles have died.
content: The Al Ruwais, a 314-metre liquefied natural gas carrier flying a Bahamian flag, has been sitting adrift off the coast of Pakistan for weeks.Fearing for its safety, its 34-member crew does not want to test the waters and attempt to cross the Strait of Hormuz, despite demands from the ship's owners."What strikes me as strange is that this company is willing to risk the ship just to pass through the Strait of Hormuz," an electrician aboard the UAE-owned vessel told Euronews."If it were up to the company, we'd go through, but for that to happen, the entire crew would have to agree. And they don't. I am waiting to leave by boat for Pakistan, where I will board another vessel."Under maritime regulations, the right to refuse transit into a designated warlike area is individual, meaning that one sailor objecting is enough to stop a vessel from moving into a danger zone.On ships whose crews do agree to cross, companies have offered captains up to $100,000 (€89,000) per month plus $50,000 (€44,500) risk bonuses, while ordinary crew wages have risen four to six times."On other ships, they give as much as $10,000 (€8,900), but not everyone gets the same amount, and it depends a lot on the position and base salary," the sailor aboard Al Ruwais told Euronews."It's only fair that everyone gets the same amount, otherwise, it would mean that the captain's life is worth more than that of the deckhand."No passage is safe, sailors sayA vital waterway for the world's energy trade, the Straight of Hormuz has been under two concurrent naval blockades since the outbreak of the Iran war following US-Israeli strikes in late February.The southern corridor near Oman is patrolled by US forces, while the northern route passes through Iranian-controlled waters. The IRGC Navy has stated that vessels transiting routes it considers unauthorised face what it described as "punitive action".Traffic through the strait has collapsed as a result. More than 125 vessels passed daily before the war. That figure has fallen to fewer than 10 to 12, a drop of more than 90%, according to ship-tracking firm Kpler.Drone attacks, sea mines and strikes from unknown projectiles have driven the decline, with UK Maritime Trade Operations recording multiple incidents involving fires, sinkings and power failures aboard tankers and LNG carriers.Ships that do attempt the crossing have taken to turning off satellite AIS transponders, extinguishing running lights at night and shutting down radio equipment to avoid detection.The dangers are somewhat different for Iranian sailors. Hamed, a 50-year-old former captain who now runs a maritime management company in Iran, told Euronews that since March of last year the war has resulted in the deaths of some 95 seafarers in commercial, fishing, passenger, tugboat and offshore platform support roles.Military vessels have suffered heavy damage and ships undergoing repairs in Bandar Abbas have been struck, he said, although precise casualty figures have not been officially released."Nearly 60% of our ships are sanctioned and forbidden from calling at foreign ports such as India, Pakistan, the UAE, Oman, Kuwait, and Iraq," Hamed said. "Even Pakistan's maritime borders, where Iranian vessels used to travel, have now been closed to us."Around 40% of southern Iranian seafarers have refused sea assignments, he said, with many shifting to the Caspian Sea to handle increased grain imports from the north. Wages in the south have been raised by 30 to 100%.Sailors now earn between 50 and 80 million tomans (€165 to €265) per month, and captains between $1,200 and $4,000 (€1,100 to €3,700).US forces have boarded Iranian commercial vessels roughly 15 times since the war began, Hamed said, arriving by helicopter and speedboat to inspect cargo for explosives, with no guarantees of their safety.“The US has provided no safe-passage guarantees for Iranian commercial ships," Hamed said. "Every week we witness aerial or naval drone attacks on Iranian vessels."He estimated that roughly 35,000 Iranian seafarers across approximately 2,000 vessels continue operating in southern waters to deliver wheat, corn and medicine to ordinary Iranians.If the situation deteriorates further, he warned, authorities could be forced to declare a complete shutdown and evacuate coastal facilities.

title: Websites go dark after AI exposes major programming language security flaw
description: Government agencies and companies around the world shut down websites Wednesday after two critical flaws came to light involving PHP, a programming language that is the basis for a large share of the internet.
content: Critical security flaws have been discovered in PHP, a widely used programming language that helps power around 70% of the world’s websites.Developers released emergency fixes on Wednesday, while cybersecurity authorities urged organisations to update affected systems immediately or take them offline until they could be secured.The warning prompted governments, companies and major online services in several countries to temporarily shut down websites and other systems as a precaution.The vulnerabilities were uncovered with the help of artificial intelligence. Security firm Calif identified one of the flaws in August during an OpenAI-funded audit of PHP, while Google-owned cybersecurity company Wiz independently discovered and reported both vulnerabilities. OpenAI said its GPT-5.6 Sol model was used in the Calif research.The PHP security team rated both vulnerabilities 9.2 out of 10 for severity. Details were meant to remain confidential while developers prepared fixes, but information about the flaws emerged publicly before the planned release, intensifying the race to secure vulnerable systems.Security researchers initially reported little evidence of widespread exploitation before the vulnerabilities became public. However, attempted attacks have since been detected, increasing concern that unpatched systems could be targeted.Websites and services taken offlineThe Wikimedia Foundation, which operates Wikipedia, said it deliberately took a number of supporting services offline while security updates were installed and warned users that some disruption could occur.Amazon Threat Intelligence also detected attempts to exploit the vulnerabilities, including activity before their public disclosure. Security researchers have since reported attempts to target vulnerable systems in the wild.Several European governments have also taken precautionary action.France’s Interior Ministry temporarily took prefecture websites offline while updates were applied, while Germany’s federal IT provider ITZBund shut down several government websites. German officials said the move was precautionary and that no security incidents had been identified.Government and public-service websites were also taken offline in countries including the Netherlands and Finland, as authorities worked to secure their systems.In the UK, the National Cyber Security Centre urged organisations running PHP to identify vulnerable systems, monitor them for suspicious activity and install security updates as soon as possible.

title: Peru scraps advance reservations for tickets to visit Machu Picchu
description: The new system also means that only named tickets are available for purchase, so you’ll need to make sure your ID matches to explore the 15th-century Inca site.
content: One of the New 7 Wonders of the World, Machu Picchu is a bucket list destination for many travellers.And if you’re planning a trip there soon, we have good news, as securing a ticket is now much easier.That’s because Peru’s Ministry of Culture has scrapped advance reservation tickets to the UNESCO World Heritage Site.Instead, travellers will now have just 15 minutes to complete their purchase on the official ticketing website, Tu Boleto, before the reservation is dismissed and returned to circulation.The new system also means that only named tickets are available for purchase, so your ID must match your ticket if you want to enter Machu Picchu.The change was made to make sure that the “availability shown on the platform corresponds to tickets that can actually be purchased by the public”, according to the Ministry of Culture.The new ticketing system has been introduced as a trial run initially, and the 15-minute time limit for purchase may be increased or decreased after this period.There has been no update to the strict limit on the number of visitors to the Machu Picchu citadel, which is set at 5,600 during the high season and 4,500 during the low season. The Inca Trail network is also capped at 750 visitors per day.There are 1,000 tickets available for purchase at the DDC-Cusco of Machupicchu Pueblo ticket office daily, with these available to use the day after purchase.Getting to Machu PicchuEuropeans who want to visit the 15th-century Inca site will need to fly to Peru’s capital Lima before taking a domestic flight to Cusco.From there, you can take a train or bus to Aguas Calientes (Machu Picchu Town), before hiking or taking another bus up to the citadel.There are direct flights to Lima from Madrid, Barcelona, Paris and Amsterdam.

title: Italy and Spain to end border checks, easing tensions after Ceuta migrant row
description: Italy and Spain agree to end temporary border checks, easing tensions following the Ceuta crisis.
content: Italy and Spain have agreed to permanently lift temporary border checks, ending the suspension of Schengen rules between the two countries.The decision follows a phone call between interior ministers Matteo Piantedosi and Fernando Grande-Marlaska. Last week, Prime Ministers Giorgia Meloni and Pedro Sánchez signalled their intention to end the checks on the sidelines of the European Council.In identical statements, the two governments said the decision followed a careful assessment of the situation and that the current suspensions would not be extended.The move will be accompanied by increased information-sharing to ensure security across the Schengen area, according to Spanish and Italian interior ministry sources.The announcement puts an end to a political saga that had triggered unprecedented politival tensions between Madrid and Rome, after Meloni announced immediate checks following the massive border breach in Spain's autonomous city of Ceuta in July.More than 70,000 people crossed illegally into the enclave from Morocco.On 1 August, Rome temporarily reintroduced border checks with Spain, suspending Schengen rules and screening travellers at ports and airports. The Italian Interior Ministry said the targeted checks focused mainly on non-EU nationals to strengthen border security and prevent potential terrorist threats.Italy and Spain do not share a land border, while Ceuta lies outside the Schengen area, meaning free movement rules do not apply there.The move sparked diplomatic tensions with Madrid. Spanish Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares called it “absurd” and “a disgrace”. A week later, Spain introduced reciprocal checks on travellers arriving from Italy.An agreement between the two interior ministers, alongside alternative cooperation measures, will allow the bilateral checks to be phased out.

title: World’s largest wealth fund posts $30bn loss as rising rates hit bonds
description: Norway's sovereign wealth fund ended the third quarter with a $30 billion (€26.4 billion) loss, as falling bond prices weighed on its overall performance.
content: Norway's sovereign wealth fund, the world's largest with assets of around €2.1 trillion, reported an investment loss of 278 billion kroner (€26.4 billion) on Thursday, as it was weighed down by higher interest rates.Norges Bank Investment Management (NBIM), which manages the fund, reported a negative return of 3.5% on its fixed income investments, which account for just over one quarter of its portfolio. Around 70% of these investments are in government bonds.The third quarter saw a global bond sell-off, with government bond yields rising to levels not seen since the financial crisis, amid growing concerns over mounting government debt in the US and the EU.This was accompanied by central banks, including the US Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank, raising key interest rates as inflation rose in the US and the eurozone."The fund’s return was close to flat, ending slightly negative as rising interest rates led to weaker results on our fixed-income investments," the fund's deputy CEO Trond Grande said in a statement.Rising market interest rates generally push down the price of existing bonds, as newly issued bonds offer more attractive rates.The fund's overall investment return was −0.5%, while its investments in company shares yielded a gain of 0.5%, with large differences between sectors."Energy companies rose the most, while interest-rate-sensitive sectors such as utilities and real estate fell,” said Grande.At the end of September, the fund was worth 22,014 billion kroner (€2.09 trillion), with 72.1% invested in shares and 25.8% in bonds. The rest was held in unlisted real estate and renewable energy infrastructure.Real estate investments brought a 0.4% return, and unlisted renewable energy infrastructure investments yielded 7.5%.Including currency movements and new money added, the fund’s total value fell by 670 billion kroner (€63.6 billion) during the quarter.

title: Italy's truckers' protests leave supermarket shelves empty and airports without fuel
description: Italy's government has warned of criminal penalties for truck drivers blocking roads in protest over soaring fuel prices, as authorities move to clear demonstrations disrupting transport and deliveries in the country's south.
content: Italian authorities are stepping up efforts to dismantle roadblocks set up by protesting truck drivers in southern Italy, warning that those responsible could face criminal charges and even prison sentences.The protests, fuelled by anger over rising diesel prices and mounting transport costs, have prompted police intervention and raised concerns about disruptions to supply chains.Business Minister Adolfo Urso said on Wednesday that authorities were identifying those involved in the blockades and preparing to remove them."Preventing only lorries from passing while allowing cars through still amounts to a roadblock, with criminal consequences, including possible prison sentences," Urso told parliament.According to government figures, police have identified 1,339 people, reported 71 to the authorities and issued 242 administrative fines.The Interior Ministry has also ordered police escorts for trucks to keep goods moving, including 500 vehicles in the southern region of Campania alone.Fuel costs at the heart of the disputeThe unrest comes amid growing pressure on the Italian government to tackle rising fuel prices, which have hit transport companies, farmers and fishing businesses particularly hard.Lawmakers are discussing a proposal to introduce a flexible cap on petrol and diesel prices, including fuel supplied directly to commercial operators outside traditional filling stations.The measure is being considered as part of a broader fuel decree that has already passed the Senate and is now before the lower house of parliament.The government says it is working to ease the financial burden on the transport sector, with Urso announcing plans to release more than €1 billion in support.That includes €434.8 million already allocated to compensate hauliers for higher diesel costs and approximately €590 million to help companies modernise their vehicle fleets.But despite the promised financial relief, protests continue in parts of southern Italy, leaving the government facing the twin challenge of containing fuel costs and preventing further disruption to the movement of goods.Supermarket shelves empty as truckers' protests disrupt food suppliesThe truck drivers' protests are beginning to take a toll on everyday life in southern Italy, with supermarket shelves running empty, fresh produce going to waste and concerns growing over disruptions to essential services.Roadblocks have prevented deliveries from reaching shops and distribution centres, leaving perishable goods, including fruit and milk, stranded at production sites."We need to unblock Italy so that our entrepreneurs are able to sell their goods and our citizens are able to buy them," Agriculture Minister Francesco Lollobrigida said on Wednesday.He also questioned the motives of some protest organisers, suggesting that the backgrounds of certain individuals deserved closer scrutiny.Southern Italian cities warn of growing crisisThe mayors of Naples and Bari have urged the government to intervene urgently, warning that continued disruption could bring their cities to a standstill."The situation in the cities of southern Italy remains extremely critical and risks worsening further as the hours pass," Naples Mayor Gaetano Manfredi and Bari Mayor Vito Leccese said in a joint statement.They warned that food deliveries were failing to reach distribution centres, leaving supermarket shelves increasingly empty.Waste collection and public transport services are also being affected, raising fears of rubbish piling up in the streets.The mayors called on Transport Minister Matteo Salvini to bring forward talks scheduled for the 27th, arguing that cities could not afford to wait.Airports run out of fuel as motorway blockades spreadThe disruption has extended beyond roads and supermarkets, with two airports in southern Italy reporting shortages of aviation fuel.Crotone and Reggio Calabria airports, both in the Calabria region, have been left without fuel for aircraft, according to official aviation notices.Airlines and flight crews have been advised to arrange refuelling at other airports to ensure they can complete their journeys. Operations at Lamezia Terme airport remain unaffected.Meanwhile, fresh roadblocks in the Campania region have caused major traffic disruption, including temporary closures on sections of the A1 Milan-Naples and A30 Caserta-Salerno motorways.Queues stretching several kilometres formed as demonstrators blocked key junctions, disrupting one of southern Italy's main transport corridors.Transport industry calls for blockades to endItaly's main road haulage associations have joined calls for the government to clear the roadblocks, warning that the protests are now damaging the very industry they were intended to defend.Following talks with Transport Minister Matteo Salvini, industry representatives urged Interior Minister Matteo Piantedosi to intervene.They argued that continued disruption was no longer justified after the government agreed to provide financial support to transport companies struggling with rising fuel costs.Salvini said more than €1 billion had been made available to the sector, including approximately €480 million to offset higher fuel prices and more than €500 million to support fleet modernisation.More than 32,000 applications for fuel-related financial assistance have already been submitted.The government says payments are beginning, but with blockades continuing and essential supplies under pressure, authorities face growing demands to restore normal transport operations across southern Italy.

title: Macron holds emergency security meeting as France braces for fresh wave of protests
description: Two days before a new day of protests, Emmanuel Macron is bringing intelligence services together at the Élysée after the 17 October security failure. In the afternoon, political parties and the mayors of major cities will be received at Matignon.
content: Crisis meetings are multiplying at the highest level of the state this Thursday, two days ahead of a feared "Act II" of the social mobilisation, after the violence and looting committed on the margins of demonstrations against the high cost of living last weekend in France.With several city centres under curfew for the third night in a row and new gatherings already banned today, Emmanuel Macron is this morning chairing a security council bringing together the prime minister, the relevant ministers and "all the intelligence services".Scheduled for 10 a.m., the meeting is intended to take stock of the "intelligence, anticipation and security arrangements" for the coming weeks, but also to review the "failures that led to last weekend's events", according to the Elysée.Emmanuel Macron will speak at the end of the council.The French authorities have acknowledged a failure of the intelligence services, which largely underestimated the scale of the 17 October mobilisation. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez had expected to see around 200,000 people in the streets, compared with 550,000 to 800,000 participants counted. Nearly 60,000 members of the security forces were deployed across the country on Saturday, without managing to prevent the acts of vandalism committed on the fringes of the marches, images of which travelled around the world.The security arrangements planned for the new mobilisation on Saturday 24 October will be reinforced by the presence of soldiers from the Sentinelle force and elite units of the police and gendarmerie, such as RAID, GIGN and the BRI.Junior interior minister Jean-Didier Berger announced on BFMTV a "20%" increase in law enforcement numbers compared with 17 October.Matignon to meet parties, with several heavyweights staying awayIn the afternoon, consultations will continue at Matignon. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu will receive representatives of the political forces present in parliament, notably to discuss a possible "change" in the doctrine of public-order policing."Together with the interior minister, I want to talk to them about the police. We are told that the police kill or the police injure. And for the past two days we have been hearing: 'What are the police doing?' It is a very French kind of politico-media schizophrenia", he wrote in a letter sent to political parties and cited by several media outlets.Security at presidential campaign rallies is also expected to be on the agenda for this meeting.In a sign of mistrust towards the executive, several candidates in the 2027 presidential election will give the meeting a miss: Marine Le Pen and Jordan Bardella of the National Rally, as well as former prime minister Édouard Philippe, will be absent.By contrast, Green party leader Marine Tondelier, Socialist primary winner Raphaël Glucksmann and the Republicans' president, Bruno Retailleau, have confirmed they will attend.LFI vows to "wreck" the meetingLa France insoumise and the government have been trading barbs since the violence on 17 October, each blaming the other for the chaos. The government accuses the radical left movement of "fanning the flames" of the anger expressed in the streets, while LFI denounces the authorities' strategy of "letting things rot", accusing them of failing to respond politically to demands it considers legitimate, particularly those of secondary school students.Jean-Luc Mélenchon will be represented at Matignon by LFI coordinator Manuel Bompard. But on Tuesday, speaking to supporters in response to the prime minister's letter, the movement's leader set the tone: "We're going to go, we're going to wreck your meeting!"The LFI founder was responding in particular to the passage in which Sébastien Lecornu states that "no disagreement, no anger, no political ambition can justify resorting to violence"."Are you going to make us sign a certificate? Is that what you want? Do you really think we are going to do that? Of course not!" retorted Jean-Luc Mélenchon.A few hours before the meeting, Manuel Bompard wrote that he would go to Matignon to ask for "apologies", "explanations" and "political answers to the mobilisation of the French people".Mayors of Paris, Lyon and Marseille demand answers from the stateThe consultations will not be limited to the parties. The mayors of Paris, Lyon and Marseille, three major cities particularly affected by last weekend's violence, will also be received.The Green mayor of Lyon, Grégory Doucet, is going there "with the aim of obtaining explanations about the chain of events that led the state to fail to anticipate Saturday's events properly", his team told Euronews.At the start of the week, the three mayors, Grégory Doucet, Emmanuel Grégoire and Benoît Payan, had already complained, in a joint op-ed published in Libération, of the "feeling that whole swathes" of their cities, although "used" to popular expression, had been "left without protection".The three left-wing mayors called for the creation of an "independent commission on the public-order strategy deployed that day", as well as the establishment of an "exceptional national solidarity fund" to finance repairs to the damage.

title: EU planned to scrap clock changes. Why are they still happening?
description: This Sunday the clocks will be turned back again, even though the EU Parliament set abolition in motion at the end of 2019. Why?
content: Changing the clocks twice a year has long been unpopular across Europe. In a 2018 EU-wide consultation, 84% of respondents supported ending the seasonal time change, reflecting widespread frustration with the practice.The following year, the European Parliament overwhelmingly backed a European Commission proposal to abolish the twice-yearly clock change.Yet years later, Europeans are still moving their clocks forward in spring and back in autumn. The proposal has remained stalled, with EU member states unable to agree on how to implement the change. The COVID-19 pandemic and Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine also pushed the issue down the political agenda.On Sunday morning the time change takes placeTraditionally, the clocks go back in autumn on the last Sunday in October. In the night from 24 to 25 October 2026 the clocks will be set back from 3 a.m. to 2 a.m. This means that those who do not work at night can sleep for an extra hour. It will then get light earlier in the morning and dark earlier in the evening.With the change at the end of October, Central European Summer Time (CEST) comes to an end and most of Europe returns to Central European Time (CET), commonly referred to as winter time. Portugal and the United Kingdom also change their clocks, but in both countries it is one hour earlier than in most of continental Europe.In the United States, daylight saving time does not end until 1 November.According to the travel portal Reisereporter, clocks are not changed in Morocco, Thailand, Japan, Argentina or South Africa.West Germany and other EU states followed France’s lead in 1980 in order to harmonise the time. In 1976, the government in Paris had introduced summer time in response to the oil crisis, with the aim of saving energy. That justification is now widely seen as outdated. Most recently, even the leap second has already been scrapped.EU Council blocks end of clock changesIn 2019 the European Parliament voted by 410 to 192 in favour of abolishing the clock change, which was originally meant to take effect from 2021. But a final law has been held up because the EU member states have not given their approval.To this day, the countries have not been able to agree on whether summer time or winter time should apply permanently. Because different regimes could cause economic and organisational problems, implementation is still on hold pending a joint solution. It is therefore unlikely that the system will be scrapped in the near future.

title: Did Slow Horses' season finale cliffhanger give us a major James Bond casting clue?
description: The sixth season of the hit TV show Slow Horses has come to an end, and with it a cliffhanger that could have major casting implications when it comes to the identity of the next James Bond...
content: Warning: Spoilers for Season 6 of Slow Horses.The latest season of Apple TV's Slow Horses has come to an end, and left audiences with an almighty cliffhanger that seems perfectly almost too perfectly timed when it comes to a certain casting decision... Based on the novels by Mick Herron, the British thriller spy series follows the best of the worst: Slough House's unit of disgraced MI5 agents, who work under the sweary supervision of Jackson Lamb (Gary Oldman). The season finale of the show's sixth season aired yesterday and with it came an unexpected turn for one of the show's main cast, River Cartwright, played by Jack Lowden. The season has been a bloody one, with the death count racking up as the Slow Horses have been targeted by a Russian hit squad, leading to the deaths of fan favourites Struan Loy (Paul Higgins), JK Coe (Tom Brooke) and Emma Flyte (Ruth Bradley). However, the most shocking demise was kept for last, as season regular River was apparently killed off in a shocking last-minute twist. After surviving assassination attempts throughout the season, River is seen in his grandfather's house about to reunite with his love interest Sid (Olivia Cooke). As he sets up a bottle of wine and two glasses, he suddenly collapses having apparently been posioned by residue on his hands from a crow bar he moved seconds before. Struggling to breathe, he calls out Sid's name and the screen fades to black.Did they kill off one of the show's main stars, who has been a Slough House mainstay since Season 1 in 2022? Maybe... Those who kept watching for the sneak-peak trailer of Season 7 noticed Lowden's absence and heard Standish (Saskia Reeves) asking Lamb about River, with Lamb sarcastically replying: "I got a postcard. ‘Weather’s lovely in the afterlife. Sunset’s to die for. Love and hugs’”. Seems final enough, although those familiar with Mick Herron's novels know that River survives his Novichok poisoning, so it’s entirely possible that the character will show up in upcoming seasons. However, the possible demise of River seems rather convenient considering the upcoming casting announcement of the new James Bond...Lowden is currently one of the favourites to take over from Daniel Craig as 007, alongside Callum Turner, Jack Barton and Jacob Elordi. If this is it for River in Slow Horses after six seasons, that means the Scottish actor is contractually open and with a free schedule to take on the role of Bond.This is pure conjecture but the timing does seem rather fortuitous, especially since Bond 26 producer Amy Pascal recently shared that "the end of the year is a good bet" when it comes to the timing of the new actor's announcement. “I would say the end of the year is a good bet,” said Pascal. “We are being really, really methodical. Having worked with Barbara Broccoli at the studio, I mean, Daniel Craig is a hard act to follow. And it’s got to be something really different that is stirring and exciting and different.” Then there was the apparent "leak" in August, when Richard Osman, British TV presenter and author of the best-selling Thursday Murder Club mystery novels, shared on his The Rest Is Entertainment podcast that he had insider knowledge suggesting that Lowden was "strongly considered" to be the next Bond.Lowden is best known for playing River Cartwright in Slow Horses but has been seen on the big screen in Christopher Nolan's Dunkirk, Mary Queen of Scots (2018) and Benediction (2021). He will appear later this year as Mr Darcy in Netflix's new adaptation of "Pride and Prejudice". Earlier this year, Euronews Culture reported that the official casting for Bond was underway and that Lowden would be an ideal candidate for the 007 mantle. We wrote regarding Lowden: " Spy credentials? Check. Charisma levels? Suit him up. Pre-existing rapport with the casting director? Done. Married to Saoirse Ronan who has previously expressed an interest in being cast as a Bond villain? Make this happen." So, from MI5 reject to MI6's top agent? Not long to find out. Bond 26 will be directed by Canadian filmmaker and four-time Oscar nominee Denis Villeneuve and is being written by Peaky Blinders creator Steven Knight. Production is expected to kick off in 2027, with a release planned for 2028. Slow Horses will return for a seventh series, expected to arrive in autumn 2027.

title: Riots in France: tourism sector fears drop in foreign visitors
description: Images of the riots in France, broadcast worldwide, are already slowing hotel bookings, and tourism professionals fear ongoing violence will further deter foreign visitors.
content: Images of the riots in France, broadcast around the world, are alarming tourism professionals. The first consequences are already being felt in hotel bookings, and those in the sector fear the situation will worsen if the violence continues."This surge in violence in city centres, in Nice, Paris and Lyon, is catastrophic", laments Christelle Cassagne, head of ADN Tourisme, a federation that brings together France's institutional tourism bodies."When you book a hotel for a week, it is not to stay shut away in your room", she adds.Tourists hesitant to go ahead with their stayIn Paris, the closure of the Louvre museum on Monday because of a student gathering at its entrance also frustrated many tourists who had come to discover the famous museum.In this tense climate, some travellers are reconsidering their stay in the capital.According to MKG Consulting, the first effects are already visible, with Parisian hotels reporting a slowdown in bookings for the next six weeks.In the space of just 24 hours, between 19 and 20 October, their lead over the same period in 2025 narrowed significantly, dropping from 1 to 0.2 percentage points for stays scheduled from 20 to 29 October, and from 3.5 to 1.9 points for those from 20 to 25 October.Fear of fresh riots weighs on tourismAccording to Didier Arino, director of the consultancy Protourisme, the scale of the repercussions will depend mainly on whether the unrest continues. A single day of riots in Paris is thought to have triggered the cancellation of around 1% of bookings for the month, still a relatively limited impact."The further customers travel, the more sensitive they are to security risks, and the greater the consequences", he points out.The United States, China and Germany are among the countries that have issued warnings to their nationals planning to travel to France.These advisories could particularly weigh on arrivals of American and Asian tourists, whose spending is generally higher than that of European visitors."If this lasts for two weeks, it is not very serious. But if it continues for several months, it will be catastrophic", warns Laurent Abitbol, chairman of the management board of the Selectour travel agency network.

title: EU journalism prize awards investigation into human rights abuse at Italy’s migrant centres in Albania
description: An investigation published by Dutch platform De Correspondent on the controversial Italy-Albania migration deal, now seen as a model for deportation hubs outside the EU, has won the Daphne Caruana Galizia Prize.
content: An investigation highlighting human rights violations at the controversial migrant centres Italy established in Albania won the European Parliament’s Daphne Caruana Galizia Prize for journalism on Wednesday.The investigation, published by Dutch outlet De Correspondent in January 2026, explored two centres in Shëngjin and Gjadër built to accommodate asylum seekers rescued at sea while Italian authorities reviewed their applications.The report is titled "Cuffed, caged, cast away: this is Europe’s ‘innovative solution’ for unwanted migrants". It puts into question the legality of the centres, opened in 2024, which have become a model for European migration policy, as several countries seek to establish return hubs for migrants outside the EU.Following repeated legal setbacks, Giorgia Meloni’s government repurposed the centres in March 2025 to detain irregular migrants already in Italy ahead of their deportation to their countries of origin.The report documented violations of fundamental rights and European law in the treatment of migrants and their transfer to the centres, issuing a warning on the new EU policy on migration.Access denied, FOI requests ignoredFive EU countries seek to establish similar return hubs in Africa by 2027, following the adoption of a controversial EU law that provides a legal framework for such arrangements, legalizing the transfer of irregular migrants to countries they have no connection to.“The deal is a blueprint for how to erode human rights, undermine the European rule of law, and normalize far-right views on migration,” reads the prize-winning report.Maite Vermeulen and Giacomo Zandonini, the authors of the report published in January 2026, also estimate that around €259 million was spent on the facilities over their first two years of operation, during which 256 people were detained — equivalent to approximately €1 million per person.“It is a big PR operation, more than a policy that would actually expedite returns [of migrants],” Vermeulen told Euronews, considering that the Italian approach is neither cheaper nor more effective, and does not deter irregular arrivals.She argued that other EU countries could not follow the Italian model without breaching human rights. “That is a story we tell ourselves to make [return hubs] acceptable or palatable,” she told Euronews.The investigation also denounces the “smokescreen” put in place by the Italian authorities to hide the details of the deal. Journalists were denied access, freedom of information requests often went unanswered, staff at the centres signed strict non-disclosure agreements, and contracts were not made public.The jury for the prize is composed of journalists from all EU member states.

title: Kremlin open to new Ukraine peace talks as Russia frees US teacher Stephen Hubbard
description: Moscow says Putin, Trump and Xi will meet in Shenzhen next month after "constructive" talks with US envoy Steve Witkoff, while a US diesel deal easing sanctions on Russia has angered Kyiv and European capitals.
content: Russia is willing to return to three-way negotiations with the United States and Ukraine on ending the war, the Kremlin said on Wednesday after Vladimir Putin hosted US envoy Steve Witkoff in Saint Petersburg. However, it complained that recent Ukrainian and European proposals lacked "substance".The talks, which lasted more than three hours in Putin's home city, coincided with the release of Stephen Hubbard, a retired American teacher jailed in Russia for allegedly fighting as a mercenary for Ukraine. Witkoff announced the release during the meeting.The Kremlin also said preparations were under way for a summit in the Chinese city of Shenzhen next month between Putin, US President Donald Trump and China's Xi Jinping, describing it as "the first such meeting in history."Witkoff said talks were "constructive" but that "important work" remained, as the Kremlin downplayed new Ukrainian and European approaches to ending the conflict."Discussions were constructive, and will continue with trilateral talks between the United States, Russia, and Ukraine at the technical level," Witkoff said on social media."While there is still important work left to do, President Trump remains committed to seeing this war end."The US envoy, who has made several unsuccessful trips to Russia in pursuit of a settlement, arrived in Saint Petersburg a day after what he called a "productive" meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Norway.He told Putin he saw "some degree of momentum" in the US-led talks.Diesel deal angers Kyiv and EuropeWitkoff also told Putin that Washington was "grateful" for a recent diesel deal, under which US sanctions on Moscow were eased to allow Russian fuel to flow to the United States.The arrangement has provoked outrage in Ukraine and across Europe. It is widely seen as an attempt to bring down fuel prices for American consumers ahead of next month's midterm elections, which are expected to be difficult for Trump's Republican Party.The deal is one of several steps by the Trump administration seen as favourable to Moscow, at a time of growing tension between Washington and Kyiv.Witkoff said the US was interested in further "business and economic cooperation" with Russia once the war ends.
