"We even talk about it now openly with the Ukrainians to give them some sort of sense about what the possibilities will be when this whole conflict is over," he said.Hubbard freed without prisoner swapHubbard was first imprisoned by Russia in 2022 on charges that Hostage Aid Worldwide, a hostage advocacy group, has called bogus. He was sentenced to nearly seven years in prison following a closed-door trial in 2024.Russian prosecutors accused him of joining the Ukrainian military after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022 and fighting alongside Ukrainian forces until his capture two months later.The Biden administration had classified Hubbard as wrongfully detained.He is the second American released by Russia in roughly two months, following the release in August of former US Marine Robert Gilman, who had been seriously ill and was jailed on contested charges of assaulting a police officer.His release coincided with Witkoff's visit and came as Trump has taken several steps favourable to Moscow, amid growing tensions between Washington and Kyiv.In an open letter to Trump published by Hostage Aid Worldwide in August, Hubbard's sister, Patricia Hubbard Fox, praised the president but also claimed her brother had endured "constant beatings, torture and starvation" while in detention.

title: Zelenskyy backs freezing front line as first step towards Ukraine ceasefire
description: The Ukrainian leader insists Kyiv must have a seat at any negotiations and wants security guarantees from Washington and European allies, as a row over slowed SpaceX satellite services rumbles on.
content: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that halting the fighting along the current front line is the most realistic route to ending the war with Russia, opening the way to ceasefire talks."Right now we have to freeze, and I think this is (the) real way to end this war. We call it ceasefire... freeze and stop," Zelenskyy told US broadcaster Fox News's "Fox and Friends" programme on Wednesday. He was asked whether he would accept a deal that fixed the front along its current lines.His comments came as US special envoy Steve Witkoff held talks with Vladimir Putin in Saint Petersburg.Zelenskyy said Ukraine was willing to negotiate in any format, but insisted that Kyiv must be directly involved."I always said that we are open to negotiate in any format, any topics. But don't speak about us without us, please."He also stressed that any agreement must come with security guarantees from Ukraine's partners, including the United States and European allies. Such guarantees, he said, would mean Ukrainians are not "afraid... that occupation will come back, aggression will come back, killings will come back."Satellite rowThe interview came days after Kyiv accused Washington of deliberately slowing Starshield, the SpaceX-operated military communications system that Ukrainian forces depend on at the front. Ukraine also uses Starlink, SpaceX's civilian satellite network.Zelenskyy said both services remained "still limited", but added: "Secretary (of State Marco Rubio) told me that he will work with his team on this to unblock this."The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday that SpaceX owner Elon Musk had personally ordered the cut in Starshield services. Musk had previously suggested that any restrictions would have come from Trump, a claim the US president has denied.

title: Qatar in Motion | Made in Qatar: Local brands with global ambitions
description: This episode of Qatar in Motion explores how local talent is driving economic diversification. We reveal how innovation, enterprise and ideas are being proudly made in Qatar and finding its way to the global stage.
content: We meet the entrepreneurs behind a new generation of homegrown businesses redefining what ‘Made in Qatar’ means. From Mazzraty’s locally produced dairy and poultry products, to Raw Middle East’s plant-based food movement, we explore how innovation, sustainability and ambition are driving Qatar’s economic diversification, and turning local ideas into global impact. We also meet JTA International Investment, which is quietly showing how Qatar is investing and scaling global businesses and helping them reach new markets.

title: African health ministers to hold Ebola crisis talks as Nigeria confirms first case
description: African health ministers will hold crisis talks on Ebola as Nigeria becomes the fourth country to confirm a case. The patient is now in isolation, while her contacts, including her spouse, a Swiss national, are being monitored.
content: The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) has called for urgent action to contain the growing Ebola outbreak and is convening African health ministers to coordinate the response, as Nigeria becomes the latest country to confirm a case.The outbreak began in Congo and has so far also spread to Kenya and Uganda; the latter said it has no cases at the moment. Such geographic spread across Central, Eastern and Western Africa demands urgent, coordinated action, Africa CDC said. “Ebola is crossing borders. Our response must move faster, with stronger coordination, greater solidarity and decisive political leadership,” said Jean Kaseya, director general of Africa CDC in a press release. “We have the expertise and the capacity on this continent. We must mobilise them together to stop this outbreak and save lives,” he added. On Tuesday, Nigeria reported its first case, linked to a traveller from Uganda who arrived there earlier this month. Uganda, which declared itself Ebola-free in July after recording 20 cases, has denied claims that Nigeria’s first case originated there. “Travel through Uganda does not establish that infection occurred here. The location of exposure remains under investigation,” the ministry said in a statement on X. The ministry insisted Uganda has “no confirmed active Ebola cases."Nigerian authorities said they were tracing 44 contacts.The patient, who entered Nigeria on 5 October, was initially treated for malaria but failed to recover, arousing suspicion among the attending physicians, Odianosen Ehiakhamen, an assistant director at the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control, local media reported. The patient is now in isolation and receiving medical care. Ehiakhamen said the contacts are mostly healthcare workers, along with the patient’s spouse, a Swiss national. Ebola is highly contagious and spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person, including blood and vomit, or via contact with contaminated materials and surfaces, such as bedding and clothing. Congo is experiencing its deadliest outbreak, with at least 4,000 deaths since May and 9,552 confirmed cases.The outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, for which no licensed vaccine or specific treatment exists, although trials are underway in Congo. The risk of importation into Europe from the outbreak areas remains very low, according to the European Center for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC).“While sporadic importations cannot be excluded, the probability of multiple independent importations is very low, even in a pessimistic scenario whereby incidence continues to rise in the affected regions,” the Center wrote on its website.

title: Poland’s abortion reforms would leave it among the EU’s most restrictive, even if signed into law
description: Poland’s parliament, Sejm, has voted to ease some of the country’s abortion restrictions, but the changes would leave its laws among the most restrictive in the European Union — and face an uphill battle to become law.
content: On Tuesday, 20 October, the Sejm, the lower house of Poland’s parliament, passed amendments to the Criminal Code that would ease some penalties for people helping women access abortion care and restore access to abortion in cases of severe foetal abnormalities. The vote marks a tentative step towards fulfilling Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s coalition pledge to restore reproductive rights, made nearly three years ago. But even if the legislation survives a likely presidential veto, it would fall well short of the coalition’s promise.The changes would not introduce abortion on request up to 12 weeks of pregnancy, a pledge made by Tusk’s Civic Coalition during the election campaign. Their passage into law is also uncertain: President Karol Nawrocki, who took office in 2025, has previously said that he would not support legislation easing abortion restrictions. Under current law, anyone who terminates a pregnancy with a woman’s consent can face up to three years in prison. The same penalty applies to people who assist a woman in obtaining an abortion or encourage her to have one. The proposed bill, backed by 217 parliamentarians, with 213 voting against and three abstaining, would exempt doctors, nurses and midwives from criminal liability when an abortion results from a medically necessary procedure intended to protect a pregnant woman’s health or life. “It's time to end the punishment of all those who love, worry, and respect our choices,” Katarzyna Kotula, the government’s equality commissioner and a lawmaker from the Left, said on X. Another bill, passed with 233 votes in favour, 203 against and one abstention, would again permit abortion in cases of severe and irreversible foetal abnormalities or an incurable condition threatening the foetus’s life. It would overturn the effect of a 2020 ruling by Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal, which found abortion on the grounds of severe and irreversible foetal abnormalities unconstitutional. ‘Incremental step forward’Seeing these changes become law remains a challenge. Even if it passes the Senate, it will need Nawrocki’s signature. The president is aligned with the opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party, which oversaw a tightening of abortion restrictions five years ago. Overriding a presidential veto would require a three-fifths majority in the Sejm, a threshold Tusk’s coalition does not have.Despite that, such an “incremental step forward” shouldn't be understated “as it's the first time in many years now that there's been movement in the Polish Parliament,” Leah Hoctor, Senior Regional Director for Europe at the Center for Reproductive Rights, told Euronews. A similar attempt was unsuccessful in July 2024, after failing to secure the required majority.However, even if the amendments become law, Poland would remain one of only two EU countries, alongside Malta, where abortion on request in early pregnancy is not legal.“The legal changes that these bills represent are so narrow in scope that for most women who need abortion care, that care will remain illegal,” Hoctor said, adding that women would still be forced to travel to access care. That would leave Poland out of step with much of Europe, where abortion on request in early pregnancy is legal in most countries and several governments have moved to reduce barriers to care and remove criminal penalties. “Poland is an outlier in the European context,” she said. "Globally, Poland and the US are two of only four countries in the last 30 years to have removed a ground for legal abortion from their laws," she added.Abortion in Poland is allowed when pregnancy threatens a woman's health or life or results from a criminal act, including rape or incest. Such a near-total abortion ban has been criticised by international human rights bodies. The European Court of Human Rights has ruled against the country in several cases involving barriers to abortion access, while in 2024, following a three-year inquiry, the United Nations Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women found that Poland’s abortion laws had resulted in grave and systematic violations of women’s rights and called for comprehensive legal reform.

title: Roaming roots: Artist Gulnur Mukazhanova explores her nomadic heritage at Frieze London
description: Presented in collaboration with Turkish Airlines, artist Gulnur Mukazhanova brought her ongoing Bosağa textile series to Frieze London 2026.
content: What can a piece of fabric tell us about where we come from, where we have been and where we are going?At this year's Frieze London, considered one of the world's most influential contemporary art fairs, Kazakh-born, Berlin-based artist Gulnur Mukazhanova explored these questions through a series of textile artworks that brought together centuries of cultural history.Presented in collaboration with Turkish Airlines, Bosağa: Journeys Across Cultures and Time features a triptych from her ongoing Bosağa series which she began in 2021. The title comes from a word shared by Kazakh and other Turkic languages, meaning “threshold” - a point of passage between places, cultures or even different states of being.At the heart of the works is felt - a material deeply rooted in the nomadic traditions of Central Asia. Traditionally used to construct yurts, felt provided shelter for generations of the artist's ancestors as they travelled across vast landscapes.Mukazhanova combines handmade felt with fragments of vibrant fabric collected during her travels across Asia. Rather than sewing or gluing these pieces together, she pins them into place, creating a feeling of fragility and reflecting the idea that things don’t have to be permanent.Her work also draws inspiration from the tuskiiz, a traditional Kazakh embroidered wall hanging often rich in symbolism and associated with protection. Her research into 14th-century Italian art also informed the series, particularly the richly decorated carpets that travelled from Asia to Europe along the Silk Road.

title: Brussels goes back to the drawing board on Europe-wide taxes
description: European Council President António Costa has taken over the negotiations on the bloc's next long-term budget, with one of the biggest question marks being how he will resolve the challenge of new EU-wide taxes.
content: European Council President António Costa is scrambling to find new EU-wide taxes to fund the bloc's next long-term budget after last week's inconclusive summit left leaders deadlocked over how much they are willing to pay.With national governments reluctant to increase their contributions, Costa is exploring ways to raise money directly for Brussels, from taxes on large companies and digital services to levies on tobacco, carbon emissions and online gambling. And with negotiations entering a critical phase, no option appears to be off the table.“To reach an agreement, we need to keep national contributions at a reasonable level, while preserving our ambition and the means to deliver on our common priorities. For this to be possible, it is fundamental to consolidate the work on the new own resources,” Costa said at a press conference following last week's European Council summit.Throughout his tour of the capitals, Costa returned again and again to the same point: EU-wide taxes are essential to square the circle between strained national budgets and the bloc’s emerging priorities.EU leaders failed to bridge their differences over the budget last week, leaving Costa to steer the next stage of negotiations.During his tour of European capitals, he repeatedly stressed that new EU revenue sources – known in Brussels as own resources – are essential to reconcile strained national finances with the bloc's growing spending ambitions.“We had three tests for new own resources. One, that they command unanimity. Two, that they can deliver substantial funds. And three, that they’d be ready, by the 1st of January, 2028,” Thomas Byrne, Ireland’s Minister of State for European Affairs, said when presenting when presenting the country's budget compromise.The Irish proposal nonetheless drew criticism from all sides, including the European Parliament, whose ideas for new taxes on digital services, online gambling and crypto assets could raise up to €25bn a year.“It is clear that the presidency refused to take any decision on the revenue side, proposing only minor adjustments. We are especially very disappointed that none of Parliament’s proposals were taken on board, despite having received positive feedback from many member states,” said MEP Danuše Nerudová (Czechia/EPP).Indeed, the Irish compromise kept the Corporate Resource for Europe (CORE), one of the most contested proposals among member states, which argue that taxing companies runs counter to the EU’s competitiveness agenda.The Commission has defended the proposal, stressing that CORE would only hit large companies with a net annual turnover above €100m, and that the contribution would normally be lower than the bonuses paid to their senior executives.But the Commission is now examining whether CORE could be combined with a digital levy, another controversial proposal that risks provoking Washington because most of the world's biggest technology companies are American.Under the emerging idea, the tax would no longer target a specific sector. Instead, the threshold would be set high enough to ensure that it fell mainly on large foreign companies, whether American or Asian.Such a compromise could become increasingly important as other potential revenue sources run into opposition.One proposal would divert 30% of revenues from the EU's Emissions Trading System (ETS), which charges major polluters for their carbon emissions, into the EU budget.Poland has been particularly vocal against sending ETS revenues to Brussels. The issue has become so politically charged at home that Warsaw may struggle to accept it as it heads towards elections next year.The Irish compromise also kept the Tobacco Excise Duty Own Resource (TEDOR), which would see member states pay the EU a 15% call rate on the excise duty on tobacco products. Governments fear it could fuel the black market and lead to a drop in quality.Luxembourg is particularly opposed. Though small, the Grand Duchy is a net contributor that seldom objects to the Commission’s budget proposals, so it may have significant political capital to spend against TEDOR.Other proposals have attracted broader support. The least controversial is a revenue source linked to the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), which puts a carbon price on certain imports, including steel and cement, to ensure foreign producers face costs comparable to their EU competitors.A tax based on the amount of electronic waste each EU country produces is also largely uncontroversial, with most open issues technical in nature.Parliament’s proposed tax on online gambling, however, has met strong opposition from Malta, home to most of the EU’s betting websites.Another parliamentary proposal, a tax on capital gains from crypto assets, is widely seen as extremely difficult to implement, with highly uncertain yields given the market’s volatility.Greece has also proposed coordinating national 6G spectrum auctions to finance the EU budget. But member states have long resisted harmonising spectrum allocation, which has traditionally brought in significant national revenue.“Now is the moment to evaluate the situation and assess the best way forward. We do not exclude taking on board any proposals,” an EU official with direct knowledge of the matter told Euronews on condition of anonymity.“We will need to modulate the own resources to better distribute their impact on the member states,” the official added.

title: Eurozone government debt climbs to 88.8% of GDP as Italy closes in on Greece
description: Government debt in the eurozone rose to 88.8% of GDP in the second quarter of 2026, with Italy closing in on Greece, the most indebted member state, and France's debt climbing to 119.1% as its borrowing costs topped 5%.
content: Public debt across the 21 countries of the eurozone reached 88.8% of their combined economic output between April and June, up from 87.3% a year earlier, the EU's statistics office, Eurostat, said on Wednesday.Italy's debt ratio is now less than one percentage point below Greece's, while France's has climbed to 119.1% as its borrowing costs rose above 5%.The debt-to-GDP ratio compares what governments owe with the size of their economies. Under EU rules, debt should not exceed 60% of GDP, and annual budget deficits should not exceed 3%.Across the wider EU, government debt rose to 82.9% of GDP in the second quarter, from 81.4% a year earlier. In cash terms, eurozone governments owed some €14.4 trillion.Full-year figures, also published on Wednesday, show EU debt rose to 81.5% of GDP in 2025 from 80.3% in 2024, while the bloc's budget deficit held at 3.1%, just above the EU's 3% limit.EU debt has stayed above 80% of GDP since the COVID-19 pandemic, when it peaked at 89.5% in 2020.For the eurozone, Eurostat's headline full-year figures still cover the 20 countries that used the euro last year, as Bulgaria joined on 1 January 2026. Their debt rose to 87.7% of GDP from 86.6%.Eurostat also expressed a reservation about the quality of Bulgaria’s 2025 data on how it records spending by its road infrastructure agency.Germany, the bloc's largest economy, saw its debt ratio rise to 62.8% from 61.4% as its deficit widened to 2.9%.Deficits are also increasing again this year. Adjusted for seasonal swings, the combined deficit of eurozone governments edged up to 3.3% of GDP in the second quarter from 3.2% in the first, while the figure for EU governments rose to 3.5% from 3.1%.Last year, 12 member states had debt above the EU’s 60% ceiling, and 11 ran deficits of 3% or more.Italy closes in on Greece while France's debt and yields climbGreece remained the most indebted EU country at 140.8% of GDP in the second quarter, but Italy was just behind at 139.9%.Greece's ratio has fallen by 11.2 percentage points in a year as the country runs budget surpluses, while Italy's rose by 1.3 percentage points in the second quarter alone.In 2022, Greece's debt stood at 177.8% of GDP, against 138.4% for Italy.France has the third-highest debt-to-GDP ratio, at 119.1%, up 3.7 percentage points in a year, one of the steepest rises in the bloc. Debt also remained above 100% of GDP in Belgium and Spain, at 110.2% and 101.4%, respectively.Estonia had the lowest ratio, at 26.1%, followed by Denmark and Luxembourg, while Poland recorded the sharpest increase in its debt ratio, up 6.7 percentage points from a year earlier.The figures landed on the same day the yield on France's 10-year government bond rose above 5% for the first time since 2002, as investors demanded more to hold French debt.France's deficit was 5.1% of GDP last year, the fourth-largest in the EU after Romania, Poland and Belgium.A divided French parliament is debating the 2027 budget, which aims to bring the deficit down to 5% of GDP, while Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu lacks a majority to pass his spending cuts.Ratings agency Moody’s is due to review France’s credit rating on Friday, with most economists expecting a downgrade that could push its borrowing costs higher still.

title: Macron calls for extreme caution in Gulf, secures critical gas deal in Qatar state visit
description: French president concludes his state visit by reinforcing the strategic partnership with Qatar. He declares his Gulf tour objectives achieved after securing a crucial gas deal with Qatar as he seeks to lower tensions over living costs in France.
content: French President Emmanuel Macron issued a stern warning on Wednesday in Doha about the Gulf's fragile security situation, urging “extreme caution” to avoid escalating tensions that could reignite conflict, after talks with Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani.At the end of his two-day state visit to Qatar, Macron told the media that “no one can ignore that we are in a period that despite everything can lead to tensions: elections in Israel, the midterm elections in the United States, and so during this time efforts and initiatives must be doubled to avoid that these tensions don’t result in a resumption of conflict.”The French president said he discussed at length Qatar’s mediation efforts with Sheikh Tamim and that “in the next hours or days we will have Iran’s answer,” on the ongoing negotiations with the United States at a time when “there is a lot of uncertainty and measures taken by one side and the other that I would not comment on. “Hailing France’s relationship with Qatar as “partners in trust who helped the security and stability” of the region, Macron said he was “very cautious because no one can tell how the situation will evolve in the next days and weeks.”Macron said that the two leaders also discussed ways to secure the transit of ships through the blocked Strait of Hormuz, with the “biggest difficulty now being the cost of transport multiplied by 10 because of too few ships come for transit as they are not insured.”France and the Gulf countries are working on a mechanism to address this reality, on “diversification in infrastructure” and ultimately on reducing the dependence on Hormuz, the French president said.Macron says France secured gas from QatarMacron announced that he had secured a gas agreement with Qatar which would cover France’s needs for the winter period and which will contribute to lowering fuel and transport costs, “reducing pressure on prices from November” and “avoiding difficulties.”"We secured the equivalent of two terawatt-hours per month of LNG for the winter period, which was important for us and which will allow us to move forward," the French president told the media.“Our objectives are achieved because we received guarantees on volumes where we had pre-existing uncertainties and all these agreements reassure us for the months to come, to have better conditions for our citizens and to avoid the shortfalls which were predicted by certain (energy) operators,” he added as he sought to lower prices of energy following violent protests over the rising living costs in France.He explained that France’s energy priority needs were diesel, which he secured in the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain, and then gas, which he obtained in Qatar, as “guaranteed volumes on which we depend, which posed a risk for the next months.”Macron was accompanied on his Gulf tour by French business leaders including the chief executives of France's largest energy companies, TotalEnergies and Engie. TotalEnergies already has substantial interests in Qatar, including a partnership with QatarEnergy in the North Field East LNG expansion project, one of the world's largest.France secured commitments for an additional 200,000 tonnes of diesel per month from the UAE and Bahrain amid soaring fuel prices.France to expand defence ties with QatarFrance and Qatar hailed their defence partnership during Macron’s state visit, as France was one of Qatar's main defenders during the Iran war.Emphasising how “the partnership showed its strength” during the war, Macron announced new agreements to continue supplying Qatar with the new 5th-generation Rafale fighter jets, along with radars, air-defence systems, and armoured vehicles.Macron said that “all the countries in the region are looking for more autonomy and to develop their own capacity for defence.”Qatar’s Rafale fighter jets escorted Macron’s plane on his arrival in Doha on Tuesday, both as part of the state visit honours, but also to showcase the defence cooperation between the two countries.After departing from Qatar, which the Elysee announced as the last country to visit during his Gulf tour, Macron made a surprise stop in Saudi Arabia in a show of support for Riyadh’s efforts to combat the Houthis in Yemen.During his visit to Doha, he said that France has been working with Saudi Arabia in a “defensive capacity” to secure global energy supplies disrupted by the conflict with the Houthis.Developing France-Qatar relationsQatar’s emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al-Thani praised the “fruitful” talks with Macron during the first state visit by a French president to Doha.In a post on X, Sheikh Tamim said that the two leaders “explored ways to strengthen our strategic partnership and expand areas of cooperation between our two countries, alongside exchanging views on the most prominent regional and international issues”.“We take pride in the progress our relations have achieved and in our shared commitment to entrenching security and stability while serving the mutual interests of our two peoples,” he added.Qatar’s foreign ministry hailed the visit as “historic” as it “confirmed a strong strategic partnership and the will to strengthen cooperation and coordination on regional and international issues.”Qatar’s Ambassador to France Sheikh Ali bin Jassim Al Thani said both countries sought to expand cooperation in investment, energy, defence, education, healthcare, and technology, including artificial intelligence, digital transformation, and cybersecurity, according to Qatar’s News Agency.More than 665 French companies operate in Qatar, while bilateral trade in goods between the two countries reached around 6.39 billion riyals in 2025, according to Qatar News Agency.

title: In apparent swipe at Trump, Macron slams 'stupid comments' by foreign leaders on France protests
description: Speaking in Doha on Wednesday, Macron called out leaders for instrumentalising unrest in France for their own political gain, following riots which occurred across the country over the weekend.
content: France's President Emmanuel Macron has criticised world leaders who he said were campaigning for upcoming elections "at France's expense" with "unacceptable and even stupid comments" about the country's riots last weekend.In an apparent swipe at US President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, he stated "there are people who campaign at France's expense — leaders who are in campaign mode, whether here in the region or on the other side of the Atlantic," he commented.Although many protesters marched peacefully during mass demonstrations across France over the weekend, widespread looting and clashes with police overshadowed protests organised by trade unions, the Yellow Vest movement and students.Speaking from Doha during a visit to Qatar, Macron denied allegations that foreign interference contributed to these events. He called out "subsequent foreign manipulation of information, which led to equally unacceptable and stupid comments from many people, including foreign leaders."He criticised leaders who shared fake AI videos generated by artificial intelligence. "We have people who explained that we had been invaded by hordes of migrants and Islamists", he said.Donald Trump is currently in campaigning mode for the US midterms and has sought to turn French protests — the majority of which were peaceful, ahead of violence which erupted on 17 October — into an opportunity to highlight the perceived threats of immigration and what he claims is the decline of Western civilisation.Trump claimed that France was "under siege, looted and set ablaze by migrants, jihadists and communists" on Monday. He has framed the unrest to suggest that the same fate awaits America if the Democrats win.Macron told reporters that France already faced domestic issues and that the situation did not need to be inflamed further, stating "in these moments, we see who loves France and who doesn't."Emergency measures in place ahead of fresh protestsMacron also announced that he would convene an emergency meeting with ministers and intelligence officials on Thursday to obtain a "detailed account" of the events of 17 October. France's government has already recognised losing control of the events of the situation that day.He stressed that a "roadmap" had been laid out on Monday morning, including curfews and restrictions on mass gatherings, which will remain in place ahead of new protests set to take place on 24 October."People who want to reek disorder in city centres on Saturday, will be prevented."He also underlined the importance of dialogue with unions and political forces, in order for all actors to take responsibility."There have been too many ambiguous situations. There were too many instances where it was argued that there was legitimate violence. However, there is no such thing as legitimate violence.""The beginning of violence is a justification for what follows. In a democracy, nothing justifies violence," he said.Macron’s state trip to Qatar is part of his three-day trip to the Gulf region, aimed at securing France's energy supplies, amid a major cost-of-living crisis, which has driven unrest across the country.On Tuesday he announced that the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain had pledged to deliver a combined additional 200,000 tonnes of diesel per month to France.

title: Airbnb bans check-out chores like stripping the bed or taking the bins out
description: Hosts can no longer ask guests to do anything that would take “significant effort or time, or would typically be performed by a cleaner”.
content: A common complaint around staying at an Airbnb is the dreaded check-out chores, like stripping the bed linen or taking the bins out.But now the short-term rental service has updated its rules to prevent hosts from including such tasks in their house rules.According to its community policy update, guests can’t be asked to do things that require “significant effort or time, or would typically be performed by a cleaner”.As an example, hosts can’t ask you to wash and put away dishes, but they can ask you to put used tableware in the sink.In a statement shared with Euronews Travel, Airbnb said: “House rules help guests understand what hosts expect, but we've heard from our community that they can be confusing, onerous and hard to manage.“So we've redesigned them to make them easier to discover and clearer to set, alongside a new policy that keeps requests reasonable, with no surprises.”Airbnb’s house rules updatesAs part of the update, house rules are now shared on the listing page, in the trips tab, and in reservation reminders.There are seven standard house rules hosts can share, which cover check-in and check-out times, the number of approved guests, smoking, approval for pets, designated quiet hours, and commercial film and photography.Hosts will also be able to add “reasonable” requests, and these can be updated at any time. Airbnb will flag any requests that do not fall in line with the new policy, and the host will need to remove them, or make an appeal.The cleaning fee should only cover a standard tidy up between guests, and hosts are not allowed to charge guests for not doing something listed in the checkout tasks.

title: Feeding Our Tomorrow: how India’s women-led, sustainable farming is reaching Europe
description: India showcases sustainable, tech-driven farming and women’s empowerment at SIAL Paris 2026, as a new EU-India trade deal reshapes food ties.
content: At SIAL Paris 2026, the India Trade Promotion Organisation put sustainable agriculture, women’s empowerment and a changing relationship with Europe at the heart of India’s food story.When Jawed Ashraf took to the stage at the opening of SIAL Paris 2026, in the presence of French Minister Anne Genevard and an international audience, he described an agricultural revolution taking place across India. Led by small farmers, he said, it rests on diversity, resilience, sustainability and greater self-sufficiency. These themes defined the India pavilion, which carried a simple title: “Feeding Our Tomorrow”.As Chairman of the India Trade Promotion Organisation (ITPO), Ashraf led India’s presence as Partner Country at the exhibition, held at Paris Nord Villepinte from 17 to 21 October 2026. He knows the French capital well: he was India’s ambassador to France and Monaco from 2020 to 2024 and received the Commander de la Légion d’honneur for his service. More than 140 Indian exporters joined the pavilion, with live culinary masterclasses and a programme on plant protein, women-led agriculture and rice exports.A farm sector built on sustainabilityAshraf described a shift towards more sustainable, climate-resilient farming, with less chemical use and better traceability. Drones, sensors, artificial intelligence and the Internet of Things (IoT) help farmers manage water, fertilisers and crop protection more efficiently, a growing advantage as extreme weather puts pressure on food production.The stakes are global. Feeding a growing population amid climate pressure, trade disruption and inflation will demand change. India already produces grains, fruit, vegetables, dairy, meat and seafood for roughly one sixth of humanity, and Ashraf sees that capacity, paired with more sustainable methods, as part of the answer.2026: the year of the woman farmerThe UN has designated 2026 the International Year of the Woman Farmer, and Ashraf used the occasion to highlight the role women play in India’s agricultural transformation. Many farmer/producer organisations are founded and run by women, raising household incomes and giving women greater independence and influence in their communities.One of those women travelled to Paris. Priyanka Rhushikesh Mohite, from Nashik in Maharashtra, is a certified agricultural drone pilot. Her husband, an agricultural adviser, heard about a Government of India scheme training rural women to operate drones, the Namo Drone Didi Scheme. She applied, won a place and completed a month of training in Pune. She has flown since August 2024.The practical gains are striking. Her drone sprays nano fertilisers and spreads seeds. Watering an acre once took a full day and around 200 litres of water. With the drone, she says, it takes seven to eight minutes and 10 litres.Yet technology is only part of her story. “I am a simple housewife,” she says. Becoming a pilot has given her an identity of her own, respect in her community and the chance to encourage other women to follow. Before 2024, she could never have imagined travelling to Paris, and she thanked ITPO for the opportunity.A trade deal with wider reachA free trade agreement (FTA) reduces or removes customs duties on many traded goods and sets rules to ease cross-border commerce. The EU-India FTA was concluded in January 2026 and is expected to be signed by the end of the year. It builds on India’s arrangements with the UK and the European Free Trade Association, which have opened further opportunities for Indian food products through zero or reduced tariffs.Ashraf believes the benefits could reach farmers and small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs), provided they meet market requirements and reach European buyers. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has called the agreement the “mother of all deals”. Ashraf sees a partnership between economies representing around two billion people, with democracy and the rule of law as shared foundations.Its reach extends well beyond food. According to Ashraf, India’s exports to Europe have grown by more than 100% in a decade, led by electronics, machinery, electrical goods and mobile phones. Future cooperation could span artificial intelligence, advanced manufacturing equipment for data centres, clean energy, green mobility, biopharmaceuticals and critical minerals, alongside digital technology, defence, education and science. Energy security is a shared concern, and he sees nuclear power as one area for closer work.He says trade between India and Europe has nearly doubled in a decade and that European investment in India has risen from 80 billion to 140 billion in four years. In France, bilateral goods trade stood at around €13.6 billion in 2025-26, and 38 CAC 40 companies operate in India.“An FTA is an enabler,” Ashraf says. Exporters and trade agencies must now turn it into business.From commodities to brandsFor food exporters, that means thinking beyond volume and price. Ashraf wants more Indian products to build a recognisable presence in Europe, which requires understanding European standards, strengthening logistics and creating products that stand out on the shelf. At SIAL the emphasis was on packaged, ready-to-eat and premium foods, backed by traceability and geographical indication tags for products tied to particular places, such as Naga chilli and Mithila makhana, the edible seeds of the fox nut plant.ITPO is also considering offices in several European cities, with Frankfurt, Paris, Milan and Rotterdam among the options. Taking flightPriyanka Rhushikesh Mohite’s journey to become a drone pilot is one example of what that change can look like. Her drone is a practical tool for farming. It has also given her a profession, a public voice and a reason to imagine new possibilities for other women in her community.For India, the challenge now is to turn that kind of progress into something more widespread, while building a stronger presence for its food producers in European markets.

title: This country aims to attract €18B in cleaner energy investment
description: Kazakhstan aims to mobilise €18 billion in investment in cleaner energy through its just energy transition platform, QaJET, with support from the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD).
content: The initiative targets renewable power and grid upgrades while addressing the impact on workers and coal-dependent communities.Fossil fuels still supply around 85% of Kazakhstan’s electricity, according to LowCarbonPower. The country wants to expand renewable power, but that will also require upgrades to its electricity networks and support for workers in regions that depend on coal.To help finance that shift, Kazakhstan aims to attract $20bn (€17.4bn) through QaJET, its just energy transition platform. Backed by the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), the initiative brings together public and private investment.The platform is already operational and is due to be officially launched at COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, in November.It supports Kazakhstan’s goal of carbon neutrality by 2060 and its commitment to cut net greenhouse gas emissions by up to 25% by 2030 compared with 1990 levels, subject to international support.Kazakhstan’s Just Energy Transition platform QaJETAccording to the platform’s investment breakdown, around half of the funding, approximately €8.7bn, is intended to support 10 GW of new renewable energy capacity by 2035.A further quarter, around €4.35bn, is earmarked for integrating renewables into the power system and improving its reliability. The remaining quarter will support electrification in transport, industry and small and medium-sized enterprises, alongside upgrades to electricity networks and smart energy systems.The platform is expected to reduce annual greenhouse gas emissions by more than 20 million tonnes, equivalent to around 7% of Kazakhstan’s energy-related emissions.Projects already in the pipelineQaJET already includes projects worth more than €1bn, including a major wind farm in the Zhambyl region and an electricity infrastructure upgrade in Almaty.The Mirny wind farm, scheduled to enter operation in 2028, will have a capacity of 1 GW and include 150 turbines, alongside a battery energy storage system with a capacity of 600 MWh.The project, developed by TotalEnergies and its Kazakh partners, is expected to generate around 4 TWh of renewable electricity annually. Its output will be sold to Kazakhstan’s state-owned Financial Settlement Centre for Renewable Energy under a 25-year agreement.The project is expected to avoid up to 3.5 million tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions a year.The second project focuses on modernising electricity distribution infrastructure in Almaty and the surrounding region. The EBRD is providing a loan of up to 102 bn tenge (€194m) to Alatau Zharyk Company, which serves around 50,000 commercial customers in Almaty and the surrounding region.The funding will help the company install automated metering and remote-control equipment and upgrade its low- and medium-voltage distribution networks.Investment opportunitiesBeyond the projects already in the pipeline, Kazakhstan faces the challenge of modernising its existing energy infrastructure and preparing workers for the transition.“We are a carbon-dependent country, with large combined heat and power plants and power stations. These facilities and the energy networks need to be modernised. Workers in the energy sector also need to be retrained as part of the energy transition,” said Saule Sabieva, Climate Policy Director at the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources.The government is seeking support from international partners, including the European Union, the United Kingdom, the Green Climate Fund, the Global Environment Facility and the Climate Investment Funds.Ensuring a just energy transitionMoving away from coal also presents social and economic challenges, particularly in regions where employment and local economies depend heavily on conventional energy production.Before major changes are made, QaJET’s partners are expected to assess the regions most exposed to the risks of decarbonisation and identify ways to ensure people have access to new economic opportunities.“We are expecting these findings. After that, we will be able to assess our major infrastructure projects and calculate their costs for inclusion in the project portfolio,” Sabieva said.She identified Karaganda, North Kazakhstan and East Kazakhstan regions as likely to face some of the greatest challenges.More broadly, she said, the difficulties would affect regions where electricity is generated by large combined heat and power plants and major power stations.Attracting renewable energy investmentThe EBRD says Kazakhstan has many of the prerequisites for expanding renewable energy, including strong natural resources and a government seeking to improve the regulatory environment.“Kazakhstan is blessed with the natural resources needed for renewable energy projects,” said Yerlan Ramazanov, the EBRD’s Deputy Head of Kazakhstan and Regional Head of Energy.He pointed to regulatory changes, competitive auctions and long-term power purchase agreements as factors helping to attract investors.These agreements provide greater predictability for developers and help lenders assess the risks associated with renewable energy projects.Referring to the electricity buyer, Ramazanov said, “Over 11 years of experience, I would say that the agreements are being honoured and the off-taker is paying in full and on time.”Renewable energy auction tariffs have also fallen since the system was introduced in 2018. Kazakhstan is developing domestic expertise, with local companies increasingly involved in building and operating renewable energy projects.Remaining barriersDespite progress, several obstacles remain. Ramazanov highlighted limitations in grid capacity and stability, as well as the challenge of balancing electricity supply as more renewable energy comes online.The EBRD is already working with officials to develop the regulatory framework for battery storage and pumped-storage projects.For investors, stable rules and a clear long-term outlook are essential. QaJET’s target of adding 10 GW of renewable energy capacity by 2035 could help provide that direction, setting out the scale of Kazakhstan’s ambitions.With its renewable energy ambitions, growing project pipeline under QaJET and support from the EBRD, Kazakhstan is working to create new opportunities for investors to build a cleaner, more resilient energy system.

title: Angolan-Portuguese singer IAMDDB accuses Israel of stealing her identity in AI video
description: Angolan-Portuguese artist IAMDDB has condemned the unauthorised use of her likeness in an AI-generated propaganda video shared by Israel's official social media accounts. The Manchester-based singer accuses the government of using her image without permission.
content: Angolan-Portuguese rapper and singer IAMDDB has accused Israel's government-run social media account of "stealing" her identity in an AI-generated propaganda video. The now-deleted clip was shared across Israel's official social media profiles and featured a woman bearing a striking resemblance to the Manchester-based musician, reciting lyrics such as: "Colonisers? Say the name. Jews from Judea, it's in the damn name, same Hebrew letters, same culture, same prayers remain." According to the Manchester Evening News, the AI-generated video was created by Israeli-born, New Jersey-based video director Eyal Be, and was captioned: "'GO BACK WHERE YOU CAME FROM!' We did". Activist Rafael Shimunov noticed the similarity, uncovering a press shot of IAMDDB during a photoshoot she did for a 2018 Crack profile, wearing a near-identical outfit as the woman in the clip.Shimunov wrote X: "There is nothing more funny than Israel stealing the identity of a British Angolan-Portuguese singer to create a fake Israeli in an AI video about indigeneity. Her name is IAMDDB." IAMDDB – whose real name is Diana Adelaide Rocha De Brito - responded to the clip on X, writing: "Hiya yeah so - why did you steal my identity for something I 100% did not consent to?"Now, in an official statement, she wrote: "It has come to my attention that AI-generated visuals resembling me have been used in a video shared by the official Israeli government account. I want to make it absolutely clear that I did not authorise, approve, participate in or consent to my image being used in this video. I have no involvement in its creation or its message." She added: "I have always approached my music and my art from a place of love, freedom, humanity and connection. I do not support genocide, the killing of innocent people, or the suffering of women, children or families. My heart is with every innocent person experiencing loss, displacement and violence, especially the Palestinian people who have endured unimaginable suffering."IAMDDB said that she'd performed in Israel in the past, before "the awareness or understanding of the situation that I have today". She said: "Had I understood then what I understand now, I would have made a different decision. That performance should not be taken as an endorsement of any government's actions, past or present." She also raised concern about the use of AI: "I am taking advice and exploring the appropriate steps to protect my image, my work and my rights." "I stand for humanity. I stand against the killing and suffering of all innocent people. And I stand for every artist's right to decide what their name, face and work are associated with. My image is mine. My voice is mine. My values are mine. Free Palestine."

title: God Save The Queens: New exhibition celebrates the women of punk and 50 years of She Punk history
description: There’s no denying the boys made a lot of noise. But foundationally, punk is female. A new exhibition opening in London celebrates the women of punk and to mark 50 years of She Punk, Euronews Culture picks five essential 70s female punk albums that every self-respecting fan should own.
content: Most people will tell you that punk rock kicked off in New York in 1976 when four rascals from Queens released their self-titled debut and gave the world the first punk anthem - 'Blitzkrieg Bop'. The Ramones' hugely influential debut album celebrates its 50th anniversary this year, with many honouring punk's supposed Year Zero. However, Joey, Johnny, Dee Dee and Tommy didn't come out of nowhere, with several artists like The Stooges, The Velvet Underground and the New York Dolls considered as the music genre's forebearers – the artists who were punk, ie: rejected overproduction and mainstream arena rock, before the movement had a name.Both a music genre and major cultural phenomenon leading to a subversive subculture expressing rebellion and an anti-establishment spirit through music, fashion and socio-political statements, the word 'punk' usually conjures certain names... Ramones, Dead Kennedys, Sex Pistols, The Clash, Gang of Four, The Damned, Bad Brains, Buzzcocks, Misfits, Black Flag, The Cramps... The list goes on and there’s no denying the boys made a lot of noise. But foundationally, punk as music, punk as an anarchist mindset, punk as a counter-cultural ideology, is female. Fearless artists like Patti Smith, Siouxsie Sioux, Nina Hagen, Poly Styrene, Viv Albertine, Debbie Harry, Linda Lunch and Poison Ivy shaped the punk movement in the 70s and were the driving force of a genre that was in fact a revolution. They shattered conventions, pushed boundaries, and tore down the expectations thrusted upon them. And one exhibition knows it. This Friday marks the opening of "Up Yours! God Save The Queens" - a new multidisciplinary exhibition at London's Museum of Youth Culture which honours "50 years of She Punk!" Curated by Lauren Estelle Jones, Celeste Bell and Vivien Goldman, "Up Yours! God Save The Queens" brings together rare archival material, unseen photography and contemporary artworks. The exhibit prioritises and celebrates the women who shaped punk culture and shows that the genre should never be reduced to just four rapscallions in Converse or a few safety pins on your jacket.Because female punk artists and female-led bands have often slipped beneath the radar of certain (not all) music fans, Euronews Culture has put together a by no means exhaustive list of five essential 70s female punk albums that every self-respecting punk fan should own. These are the albums from the trailblazers who paved the way for every female musician and female led-band that came after them, from Bikini Kill, Hole, L7 and PJ Harvey to Le Tigre, Sleater-Kinney, Yeah Yeah Yeahs and Amyl and the Sniffers. Patti Smith - ‘Horses’ (1975)Patti Smith’s debut album redefined the New York punk scene before it even had a name. A regular at Manhattan’s legendary venue CBGB, Smith's dreams of becoming a poet led her to the city's vibrant world of underground literature, art and music. 'Horses' established her as the “godmother of punk”; it's an eclectic and commanding declaration of artistic freedom, merging Beat lyricism with brash rock passion and the minimalist aesthetic of then-formative punk. Songs like 'Free Money' and 'Break It Up' are classics, as is her radical reworking of Them's 'Gloria'. Then there's 'Land', the 9-minute masterpiece which showed that Smith wasn't just a part of forming the punk movement; she was carving out a new space for female artists around the world. (On a side note, when are the Nobel Foundation going to give her the Nobel for Literature?)Blondie - ‘Blondie’ (1976)Debbie Harry was another CBGB regular alongside Patti Smith, and she too helped shape the New York scene. Her striking bleached-blond look was part of the visual language of punk, and even if Blondie leaned more towards new wave and pop sensibilities and found more mainstream success (especially with their 1978 classic 'Parallel Lines'), the band's first record had an unmistakable punk DIY energy to it. Kicking off with 'X Offender' (originally titled 'Sex Offender' but renamed because radio stations wouldn't play a song with such a provocative title), the album is a bold, foot-stomping gem which brought pop out of the 60s and shoved it into the 70s with a snarl.X-Ray Spex - ‘Germfree Adolescents’ (1978)Poly Styrene, the founder of UK band X-Ray Spex, is recognized as the first multiracial frontwoman of a punk band. She wore braces, made her Day-Glo rags, and sang anti-consumerist lyrics, upending every expectation of what a frontwoman could be. The band's debut album tackled feminism, identity politics, consumer society and not giving a shit about other people's opinions. As she screeches in the anthem 'Art-I-Ficial': “I am a poseur and I don’t care! I like to make people stare!” The album's highlight can be found on the reissue with the empowerment single 'Oh Bondage Up Yours!', with the chant "Some people think little girls should be seen and not heard, but I think 'Oh bondage, up yours! One, two, three, four!”. It became the prototypic British punk rallying cry but also a feminist statement that influenced many punk acts, including the 90s riot grrrl movement.The Slits - ‘Cut’ (1979)Another British gem, this time from the trio The Slits, who are not to be underestimated in how they too defined punk as feminist. The band boasted an unpolished style which fused punk rock, art pop and elements of dub and reggae, challenging both the music industry and societal norms. Their 1979 debut album is a defiant and raw collection of anarchic hits like the self-determination anthem 'Instant Hit' (later sampled by Lauryn Hill), 'Shoplifting', 'Newtown', and the classic 'Typical Girls' - a protest against female stereotypes. “Typical girls get upset too quickly / Typical girls can't control themselves / Typical girls are so confusing," incants singer Ari Up, before asking the question: "Who invented the typical girl?" The Slits defied preconceptions through humour, verve and a 'fuck you' spirit. Much like X-Ray Spex, their music would go on to influence countless other musicians and movements like riot grrrl and fourth-wave feminist punk music of the 2010s.The Raincoats - ‘The Raincoats’ (1979)Since the "Up Yours! God Save The Queens" exhibition is in London, we're sticking to the UK for our last pick. The first full-length album from the British foursome The Raincoats is perhaps best known for the ramshackle, off-kilter cover of the Kinks' hit song 'Lola', but the rest of the album is a ragged racket to treasure. It's dissonant, odd, features plenty of violins (courtesy of Vicky Aspinall), and is completely captivating. Bolstered by Ana da Silva and Gina Birch's vocals, as well as ex-Slits member Palmolive's drumwork, the anything-goes spirit present throughout the album is at the very heart of punk. The band used their songs to call out the establishment and address societal ills like rape culture and misogyny. If you're looking for a copy, seek out the 1993 reissue, which includes the single 'Fairytale in the Supermarket', and also check out their 1977 song 'No One’s Little Girl' (only released in 1982), featuring the lyrics: "I'm no one's little girl, oh no, I'm not / I'm not gonna be, cause I don't wanna be / I never shall be on your family tree..." "Up Yours! God Save The Queens" opens on Friday 23 October at the Museum of Youth Culture in London and lasts until 22 November.

title: Polish teenager, 16, suspected of plotting massacre as police uncover weapons arsenal at home
description: A 16-year-old suspected of plotting a massacre has been detained by police in Warsaw, Poland. Investigators believe the teenager was preparing to kill multiple people. Officers searching his home discovered what they described as "an entire arsenal of dangerous items".
content: Acting on intelligence about the alleged plot, officers tracked down the teenager's home in Warsaw, where they discovered a stockpile of weapons and other dangerous items."The 16-year-old had a bulletproof vest and a gas launcher. At the scene, an investigation team carried out an inspection with a forensic technician present," the police reported.Forensic experts examined the scene, while officers secured what they described as an "entire arsenal of dangerous items" as part of the investigation.Teenager in a special centreThe 16-year-old was detained. "After carrying out the necessary procedures with his participation, the officers brought him before the family court," the officer stressed.The teenager, "by decision of the family court, was placed for three months in a regional juvenile educational centre.""Officers also handed over the collected evidence in order to initiate explanatory proceedings and to consider applying an isolation measure to the minor," Sulowska summed up.

title: Ryanair CEO predicts biggest airfare rise in European history
description: Ryanair boss Michael O’Leary predicts European airfares could rise by up to 20% in 2027 as higher fuel costs, taxes and reduced capacity put pressure on airlines.
content: CEO Michael O'Leary told Euronews that airfares would rise significantly in 2027 because of higher fuel costs. He also criticised European environmental taxes for adding to airlines’ costs.The chief of Europe’s biggest budget airline expects airfares to go up by as much as 20% in 2027 across Europe, as airlines are hit by higher jet fuel costs while the Iran war continues to drive up oil prices.According to O'Leary, airlines are largely unhedged against higher jet fuel prices from April 2027.Jet fuel prices in Europe and the CIS averaged $207.61 a barrel in the week ending 16 October, up almost 128% from a year earlier, according to the International Air Transport Association’s (IATA) monitor.Many European airlines, including Ryanair, had strong hedge positions through 2026, O’Leary said, but their protection is much more limited from April 2027. He told Euronews that Ryanair had locked in fuel at about $67 a barrel this year, but he added, “our oil price will double” next year.Speaking at a press conference in Brussels on Tuesday 20 October, he said: "You're going to see airfares rise next year in Europe, I think by 10, 15, maybe 20%. You're going to see the biggest increase in airfares, I would say, in history in Europe for the next 12 months."“We’re 85% unhedged next year, and most of the other European airlines are in a similar position,” he said.Higher jet fuel prices have squeezed margins for airlines without hedging protection.Prices of crude oil and refined products, including jet fuel, rose rapidly following the outbreak of the Iran war and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Brent crude futures, the international benchmark, traded at $109.86 on Wednesday near a five-month high.According to O'Leary, on top of the higher fuel costs, there will be fewer seats available in 2027 as a result of bankruptcies and takeovers in the European aviation market.O'Leary was in Brussels to announce a major cut to the company’s operations in Belgium ahead of an increase in the country’s aviation tax from €2 to €7 in January 2027.Ryanair is cutting 20 routes and 1.1 million seats from its Belgian winter schedule, blaming the tax rise. The airline said it was moving six aircraft to lower-cost European markets.

title: What does Lufthansa gain from its €1.2 billion TAP Air Portugal deal and when?
description: Lufthansa expects about €450 million a year in synergies from buying up to 49.9% of TAP Air Portugal for €1.2 billion, but Portugal’s continued control, lengthy regulatory reviews and the slow progress of its ITA Airways deal suggest the gains could take years to arrive.
content: Lufthansa's €1.2 billion winning bid for up to 49.9% of TAP Air Portugal could bring the German group around €450 million in yearly savings and extra revenue.However, the Portuguese state's grip on the airline, drawn-out competition reviews and delays in integrating Italy's ITA Airways into the group indicate the benefits may be slow to materialise.That is the conclusion of a report published on Tuesday by Gimme Credit, an independent corporate bond research firm.Portugal's government picked Lufthansa's offer last week over a rival bid from Franco-Dutch group Air France-KLM.The deal still needs final negotiations, approval from Portugal's cabinet and clearance from the European Commission, with completion pencilled in for 2028.Lufthansa will pay €1.025 billion for 44.9%, it said, rising to up to €1.2 billion for 49.9% if it also buys shares first offered to TAP's employees, representing up to 5% of the airline, and pays a so-called ticking fee, which accrues until the deal closes.The Portuguese state will keep 50.1%, but Lufthansa will get to name TAP's CEO, while the government will hold a majority on the board.Lufthansa's offer valued TAP about 16% higher than Air France-KLM's and was entirely in cash, while its rival offered a mix of cash and shares."Lufthansa has gone a long way to secure its winning bid," Gimme Credit noted, while Lufthansa CEO Carsten Spohr called TAP "a strong and profitable airline".TAP stayed in the black for a fourth straight year in 2025, but its net profit shrank to €4.1 million, hit by a one-off tax adjustment, and it lost €99.2 million in the first half of 2026 as fuel costs surged.Lufthansa's management believes the synergies will come from commercial activities, better network connections, joint purchasing and cargo, according to Gimme Credit's director of European research, Cedric Rimaud.The big prize is TAP's network to Brazil and the rest of Latin America, along with traffic between Europe and Portugal, and between southern Europe and North America.Spohr said the deal would "sustainably strengthen our [Lufthansa's] position in the South Atlantic market".Management expects traffic on those routes to grow by about 2% to 3% for Latin America and 6% to 7% for the others between 2025 and 2030, Rimaud said.TAP holds 24% of seat capacity between Europe and Brazil, second only to Latin American group LATAM, according to aviation data firm OAG.With TAP, Lufthansa’s airlines would hold 36%.TAP also flies only Airbus jets, which make up most of Lufthansa's fleet, "bringing some natural economies of scale between the two airlines," Rimaud said, as some spending on engineering, training and maintenance can be pooled.A long road to 2030Lufthansa has promised to grow TAP's fleet to 117 aircraft by 2035 and invest €500 million in Portugal, the government said.The firm has also pledged to keep TAP as a standalone airline, which, along with the state's control, "will limit the ability to rationalise operations across the whole group,” Rimaud explained.Lufthansa expects TAP to join its transatlantic joint venture with United Airlines and Air Canada, in which the partners coordinate schedules and share revenue. It made a similar promise when it bought into ITA Airways in January 2025.ITA is still waiting for the US Department of Transportation's approval, and its first jointly coordinated flight across the Atlantic is not due until summer 2027.EU competition officials will also examine the joint venture, and Rimaud sees "revenues from this integration unlikely before 2030".Growth at TAP's Lisbon hub is capped too, as the airport is full and a replacement will not open before 2034, according to OAG.Lufthansa can pay for TAP from its own cash, and Gimme Credit does not expect "a significant uptick in Lufthansa's leverage". TAP's own debt poses little threat either, with no significant repayment due until its bonds mature in 2029.Gimme Credit expects Lufthansa to seek to buy the rest of TAP by 2028, after Portugal launched a process for the airline's full privatisation. It kept its "sell" recommendation on Lufthansa's bonds, noting a yield of 5.52%, against 6.9% on Air France debt.While it expects TAP to join the transatlantic venture eventually, Gimme Credit sees that happening "over a longer time horizon than what management promises".

title: The 50 Best Restaurants 2026: 20 restaurants in Europe included on extended 51-100 list
description: Ahead of next month’s 50 Best Restaurants announcement in Lima, Peru, an extended list has been unveiled for 2026 with 20 European eateries included.
content: Just weeks before The 50 Best Restaurants 2026 selection is announced in Peru’s capital Lima, an extended list covering positions 51-100 has also been unveiled – with 20 European restaurants featured. The extended list features restaurants from 36 cities across six continents, after votes by more than 1,100 international restaurant experts including chefs, food writers and culinary specialists. Europe is the most represented region with 20 restaurants across 11 countries making the cut, followed by 17 from Asia, six from North America, three from South America, two from Africa and two from the Middle East. At No.51, Uliassi in Senigallia, Italy, is Europe’s highest-ranking restaurant on the extended list.Belgium, France, Germany and Spain each have three restaurants featured, giving them the joint-largest European representation. In Belgium, The Jane in Antwerp ranks No.63, followed by Willem Hiele in Oudenburg at No.66 and Eliane in Brussels at No.86. France’s entries are Arpège (No.67) and Septime (No.81) in Paris, alongside Le Doyenné in Saint-Vrain (No.84). Germany’s three representatives are all in Berlin: Nobelhart & Schmutzig (No.76), Coda (No.82) and Tim Raue (No.85). The three Spanish restaurants on the list are Cocina Hermanos Torres in Barcelona (No.69), Txispa in Atxondo (No.80), and Aponiente in El Puerto de Santa María (No.100).The UK has two London restaurants, Kol (No.70) and The Ledbury (No.83), which returns to the extended list for the first time since 2019. Elsewhere, Denmark’s Koan in Copenhagen takes No.57, Sweden’s Frantzén in Stockholm No.58, Slovenia’s Hiša Franko in Kobarid No.60, Portugal’s Belcanto in Lisbon No.75 and Türkiye’s Neolokal in Istanbul No.94.The full 50 Best Restaurants 2026 ranking will be announced on 4 November at a gala ceremony in Lima, Peru. title: Europe weighs energy-saving measures as Middle East crisis deepens
description: EU Energy Ministers will consider demand cuts if the Strait of Hormuz remains closed in the months ahead, according to a document seen by Euronews.
content: EU governments could ask households and businesses to cut their energy use as the war in the Middle East drives up prices and threatens oil and gas supplies, according to a document seen by Euronews.Energy ministers will discuss possible EU-wide measures to reduce consumption when they meet on 29 October, amid growing fears that disruption to supplies through the Strait of Hormuz could persist for months.The proposal to consider demand cuts comes from Ireland, which currently holds the rotating presidency of the Council of the EU and is chairing negotiations between member states.Gas prices have surged by 140% since the US and Israel launched their war against Iran, while Brent crude was trading at $110 a barrel on Wednesday. Even if the conflict ends, its impact on oil markets could last for months, while the consequences for gas supplies could be felt for years, the Irish presidency warns.EU officials have so far identified energy prices as the biggest ripple effect coming from the Middle East, even if Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen has urged EU capitals in September, for the second time, to consider energy demand cuts.The EU's gas transmission operators recently warned that the bloc could face a gas shortfall of 12% to 15% of demand if a severe cold snap hits this winter. Storage levels are at 74% as of 20 October, according to data from the industry body Gas Infrastructure Europe, their lowest since 2011.Nearly eight months after military attacks led to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a key chokepoint accounting for 20% of the world's oil and gas transit, diesel and jet fuel are particularly exposed to price and potential supply disruptions.EU weighs demand cutsWith the European Commission running out of options to cushion the impact of the crisis, ministers will consider whether reducing consumption should become part of the EU's response, alongside emergency stock releases and financial support."What are the lessons learned from EU coordination in responding to energy impacts as a result of the Middle East Conflict, and how should the EU prepare for a scenario in which the Strait of Hormuz remains partially or fully closed in the months ahead? What, if any, demand reduction measures should be considered at EU level?," reads the Council document.The Council document does not propose specific energy cuts or establish that ministers have agreed to them. But it sets the stage to assess how far EU capitals are willing to go in managing consumption if supply disruptions persist.The debate signals a growing recognition that the EU can't guarantee energy security through imports and emergency stock releases alone if a major supply route remains blocked.French President Emmanuel Macron secured diesel from Gulf countries on Tuesday after Saudi Arabia offered additional spot crude cargoes for delivery to Europe from late October to mid-November. The move followed the G7 agreement to release more emergency oil stocks, under pressure from Washington.Meanwhile, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said it is ready to coordinate more emergency oil releases by member countries if they wish to do so in order to counter rising prices.Spain confirmed it would release 4.4 million barrels of strategic oil stocks during October, as part of its existing emergency commitment.More car-free Sundays?Shortly after the US-Israeli military attacks against Iran, the Paris-based IEA also announced a 10-point plan for countries to cut oil use, including "Car-free Sundays", a practice widely used during the energy crisis in the 1970s.Other measures could range from voluntary appeals to households and businesses to save energy to targeted restrictions on consumption by particular sectors, depending on the severity of the crisis.However, any EU-wide initiative would raise questions over who should bear the burden, whether industry should face restrictions and how to protect vulnerable households without further damaging the bloc's competitiveness.The central question for ministers is whether demand reduction should be coordinated at EU level or left to national governments.A common approach could help prevent countries from competing for scarce supplies, but EU governments face different levels of exposure to gas shortages, different electricity prices and different industrial needs.A proposal from the Commission tabled at the 15-16 October Council summit to aggregate energy demand at the EU level is also currently on the table for capitals to assess. The goal is for Brussels to coordinate energy demand and distribute it to EU countries based on their needs.

title: UK approves drilling at controversial North Sea gas field despite environmental concerns
description: The Shell Group, one of the project's co-developers, predicts the field can produce around 6.5% of the UK’s gas production at its peak.
content: The UK government on Wednesday announced plans to start drilling in a controversial North Sea gas field.The decision was welcomed by energy groups but criticised by environmentalists, who warned of higher carbon emissions. The Jackdaw field lies 240 kilometres east of Aberdeen, Scotland.However, the government argued that the project could strengthen the UK's energy security as the war in Iran drives up energy prices."At a time when people are really struggling, it's right that we look in a responsible way at maximising the existing energy reserves we have in Britain that could help," Labour Prime Minister Andy Burnham said."We're committed to moving towards renewable energy and reaching net zero by 2050. But even on our ambitious climate path, we'll still require oil and gas as part of our energy needs for decades to come."Critics also argue that the move will do little to lower electricity bills for UK households, as oil and gas prices are set by global markets.A Scottish court ruled last year that previous approvals for Jackdaw and Rosebank, another North Sea oil and gas project, were unlawful after failing to account for their indirect carbon emissions.The government has yet to decide whether to approve Rosebank, which is believed to hold the UK's largest untapped oil reserves.Zack Polanski, leader of the left-wing Green Party, called the decision "climate vandalism", while Greenpeace said the approval showed "the toxic grip fossil fuel lobbyists still hold over our energy policy"."True pragmatism means severing our reliance on expensive oil and gas that leaves British households broke, supercharges extreme weather, and leaves our energy security at the mercy of petrostates," said Ami McCarthy, head of politics at Greenpeace UK.

title: Trump tells companies to pay 'dividend' to communities to make data centres popular
description: The US President made the comments on his social media platform Truth Social on Wednesday, encouraging companies to strike deals with local communities to make data centre developments more popular.
content: US President Donald Trump has suggested that companies building data centres should pay a “dividend” to the communities where they are based to make them more appealing to local residents.With companies around the world racing to deploy AI infrastructure, there has been a widespread backlash against new projects due to the substantial water and energy requirements of these sites and the impact they have on the local environment, energy prices and water scarcity.The US President said that he had been “watching data centers very closely” and that he had “come to a very strong conclusion” over the matter, namely that highly unpopular data center projects become “extremely popular” once a financial deal is struck to address locals’ concerns.On energy, Trump stated that he had personally mandated that data centres must "make their own electricity and give or sell any excess back to the local community, or grid” to offset energy price increases, believing that if they do so, there “could be a substantial decrease”.In 2026 alone, at least 47 large-scale projects have been delayed and more than 1000 local communities across the US have formally proposed or sought moratoria, zoning caps or strict environmental limits on incoming AI infrastructure, according to financial site Investing Live.Yet there are no signs of developments slowing down. Investing Live’s analysts say US AI infrastructure spending is projected to exceed $10 trillion (€8.9tn) between 2025 and 2032, around 3.6% of the country’s GDP per year.While some data centre projects have gone ahead once agreements, now referred to as “Community Benefits Agreements” or CBAs, have been struck with local authorities, this hasn’t necessarily resulted in shifting public opinion.Earlier this summer, Meta struck a deal with Texas governor Greg Abbott over a controversial data centre project in El Paso, Texas, funded by investment giant BlackRock.What started as a $1.5 billion (€1.3bn) investment in 2023 and blew up to a $14 billion (€12.5bn) mega-campus project, resulting in widespread public backlash and prompting authorities to consider scrapping the project. In June, the local council voted 5-3 against cancelling the deal.The governor then reached a deal establishing a number of guardrails to protect the local community, including paying making Meta pay for their electrical infrastructure, reuse their own water and promise to “eliminate reliance on outdated taxpayer-funded incentives”.Meta has since commented on the deal, but not on the specifics set out by the governor, with critics including Democratic nominee for governor of Texas Gina Hinojosa, who argues that the agreement does not set out any binding conditions on the tech company.
