Meta expects construction to finish in two years.In September, the first fully executed CBA for a data centre project in the US was signed by the Lancaster City Council in Pennsylvania for a $6-10 billion (€5.3-€8.9bn) cloud computing and AI complex — the Lancaster AI Hub.It included a number of measures aimed at supporting the local community such as a $10 million (€8.9 mn) economic development fund, another $10 million (€8.9 mn) fund for sustainable development and clean energy, $250,000 (€222,500) planning fund and $10 million (€8.9 mn) worth of credit to protect the city should the default on its environmental and financial promises.And this October, developer Digital Realty won initial public approval for a project in De Soto, Kansas, for a new 280-acre data centre campus by bypassing local rules and paying citizens directly.The company is offering locals $1000 (€890) in utility and property tax credits for 10 years, as part of an overall $20 million (€17.8mn) investment that they argue will provide recurring tax revenue, create jobs and deliver other economics benefits to residents.Close to home in Europe, so-called "Cash for Communities” approaches have taken off.In Ireland this October, one of Europe’s largest data centre clusters, OpenAI has said future data centres could come with cash for local communities to address citizen concerns over their impact.The country, however, already has strict requirements for data centres including a mandate that they must provide electricity into the grid.Germany also has strict reciprocity requirements, especially in relation to energy use. In major hubs such as Dietzenbach, where Google is building a multi-billion euro campus, developers must first secure energy infrastructure deals to feed excess heat generated by data centres back into the grid to lower local residents’ utility bills.

title: Trump is taking Russia's side against Ukraine, former US general tells Euronews
description: Former US Army lieutenant General Ben Hodges warns that Washington’s approach is weakening Ukraine’s defences, while former US ambassador to NATO Kurt Volker urges Europe to prepare for a future with less American support.
content: Retired US Army Lieutenant General Ben Hodges has accused President Donald Trump of deliberately undermining Ukraine's ability to defend itself against Russia, saying the administration's actions were "entirely predictable"."He was never going to support Ukraine, and was going to take the Russian side, the signs were all there," Hodges tells Euronews. "I do not trust this administration to be honest about what they are doing with Russia for or against Ukraine," he said an interview from his home in Frankfurt. "What he has done to Ukraine was entirely predictable."Hodges believes recent US decisions restricting Ukraine's defences and its ability to respond to Russian bombardments are designed to pressure Kyiv into surrendering territory in exchange for an end to the war."This has been the goal of the Administration from the beginning, when US Secretary of State Rubio said in the first weeks of being in Office that Ukraine was going to have to give up some land in order to end the war, as if this was a Manhattan real estate deal," he said.In recent days, US President Trump has demanded Ukraine stop targeting Russian diesel refineries as part of its military response to the Kremlin's full-scale invasion. The Ukrainian government said they would agree to it if Russia likewise stopped targeting Ukrainian energy infrastructure. The Kremlin refused. Trump has also waived new bipartisan sanctions on Russia just days before they were due to take effect. The measures, part of the so-called Lindsey Graham Act, named after the late Republican senator, included tariffs on major buyers of Russian oil.Since then, Ukraine have been unable to access the Starlink satellite system owned by Elon Musk but controlled by the US. The Ukrainian military use it to intercept jet-powered drones, often Iranian origin Shahed drones. Ukrainian President Zelenskyy says the army's access is restricted after speeds exceeding 161 km/h meaning the can no longer intercept these deadly drones. Speaking to journalists in Brussels last week, Zelenskyy described the situation as "painful", pointing to the lives lost as a result of the restrictions.Trump has also called for elections in Ukraine, and for Zelenskyy to be replaced.He has blamed Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries for rising diesel prices, despite a surge in energy prices following US and Israeli attacks on Iran in February.The resulting disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway through which roughly a fifth of global oil supplies normally pass, has added to pressure on energy markets.Washington has also come under scrutiny over the delivery of Patriot air defence interceptors to Ukraine which have been funded by European countries.Under NATO’s Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL), European allies and Canada purchase US-made weapons and interceptors for Ukraine.However, global shortages of Patriot systems have complicated efforts to replenish Kyiv’s defences, with US stockpiles under pressure from as a result of military operations in Iran.A NATO official told Euronews that PURL deliveries were continuing but declined to comment specifically on Patriot shipments.Hodges is pessimistic about the prospect of a breakthrough between Washington and Kyiv, arguing that the impasse reflects a deliberate policy choice.“There isn't a hope in hell the administration is providing Patriot [defence systems],” he added.“They're even preventing other countries from delivering such systems to Kyiv,” Hodges told Euronews.Zelenskyy has also said that the delivery of Patriot interceptors is being delayed, despite the systems’ importance in defending against certain Russian missile attacks.“Right now, a new missile package is still awaiting Mr Hegseth's signature,” Zelenskyy said on Tuesday.European partners are also awaiting US approval to transfer Patriot interceptors from their own stocks to Ukraine, Zelenskyy said in an interview with an Italian newspaper."The Administration's actions with Patriot interceptors and intelligence are all intended to pressure Ukraine into accepting a terrible outcome by which Ukraine would have to agree to allowing Russia to keep what it has taken and perhaps even more," said Hodges. “The horrific thing about what Trump is doing is that it's got real-world life-and-death impact for Ukrainians,” said Kurt Volker, a former US ambassador to NATO who served during Trump's first administration.Europe urged to take tougher line on RussiaBoth Hodges and Volker argue that European countries must respond more decisively to Russia’s hybrid aggression.They warn that if Russian President Vladimir Putin believes Washington is on Moscow’s side, the Kremlin could be emboldened to intensify its attacks.NATO countries have faced a range of so-called grey-zone incidents, including drone incursions, sabotage and arson. However, European governments have been reticent in formally attributing responsibility to Moscow. Germany and Estonia are among the countries that have only recently blamed Russia for specific incidents.Hodges argues that European governments must each time recognise Russia as the aggressor and impose consequences for attacks.He suggested European countries seize Russian shadow-fleet vessels operating in the Black Sea in response to such incidents. He also called for an end to issuing visas to Russian citizens entering the EU and urged European governments to reconsider the use of frozen Russian assets to support Ukraine.Europe needs to tell Russia "every time we have an incident, we will seize a shadow fleet vessel out on the Black Sea," said Hodges."And how in the hell are Russians still getting visas to move around Europe," he asked.While several EU governments agree Russian frozen assets could serve both as compensation for damage caused by the war, and as a penalty for Russian war crimes and aggression, the Belgian government continues to oppose moves to use the assets without sufficient guarantees against the financial and legal risks.Around €180 billion is kept in Euroclear, a Belgian repository, which amounts to the vast majority of the approximately €220 billion.Hodges says Belgium's refusal to budge on the issue is "unacceptable.""It's unacceptable the country that hosts NATO and the EU is so unwilling to unlock the door to one of the best things we can do to support Ukraine," he said.Volker, who also served as the US special envoy for Ukraine during Trump's first administration, said Europe needed to develop a “Plan B” for its security as Washington's relationship with Moscow shifts.For decades, Europe's security architecture has relied heavily on the United States. Volker said a new agreement involving European countries and other allies, modelled on the Coalition of the Willing, might be needed to defend the continent.Europe must “start pushing back on hybrid attacks otherwise one of these will lead to major escalation”, Volker said, warning that Putin could be emboldened by his relationship with Trump.European governments should also make clear that any aircraft or drone entering NATO airspace unlawfully would be intercepted, Volker said.He added that Russia should be held responsible if civilian casualties result from such incidents.

title: No kids invited: A new travel package offers a child-free flight and adults-only cruise
description: JetBlue Vacations has teamed up with Virgin Voyages for a four-night trip on board Brilliant Lady which includes a dedicated adults-only flight from New York.
content: Anyone who has had a relaxing pool day disturbed by screaming kids will have dreamt of a completely child-free holiday.And while there are many adults-only resorts out there, you can’t escape young ones on the journey – or you couldn’t until now.That’s because JetBlue Vacations and Virgin Voyages have teamed up for “Do Not Disturb”, an adults-only holiday that includes a dedicated kid-free JetBlue flight and a Virgin Voyages sailing.Taking place from 4-8 March 2027, the four-night package includes round-trip flights from New York's JFK to Fort Lauderdale/Hollywood International in Florida.The itinerary includes stops in Key West as well as Virgin Voyages' Beach Club at Bimini in the Bahamas. “We love creating vacations for all kinds of travellers, including families, but we also know there are moments when adults are looking for a different kind of getaway,” Jamie Perry, president of Paisly, JetBlue’s travel website, said.“With Do Not Disturb, we wanted that feeling of truly switching off to start well before you step onto the ship. “From the flight to the transfer to the cruise itself, we’ve thought about the entire journey so our customers can simply show up, settle in and enjoy some uninterrupted time away.”What to expect on boardGuests will be sailing on the relatively new vessel, Brilliant Lady, which has just 60 cabins on board.First launched in 2025, there are more than 20 restaurants and bars on board, including Spanish eatery Rojo by Razzle Dazzle, Mexican spot Pink Agave and Korean barbecue Gunbae.Aside from making your way through the food options, guests can head to the spa, relax by the rooftop pool, or enjoy live entertainment across the cruise ships’ various venues.

title: Former Hungarian central bank chief György Matolcsy detained in financial fraud probe
description: The investigation follows scrutiny of the central bank's foundations, which managed more than €1 billion in public funds. Matolcsy has denied wrongdoing.
content: Former Hungarian central bank governor György Matolcsy was detained on Wednesday morning and taken to the Central Chief Prosecution Office for Investigations.A longtime associate of former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, Matolcsy led the National Bank of Hungary (MNB) for 12 years until 2025."My client is suspected of the felony of financial fraud causing significant financial loss and the misdemeanour of using a forged private document," Matolcsy's lawyer, Pál Bátki, told Hungarian newspaper Telex.Bátki said his client's questioning had not yet begun but was expected to take place later that morning.In a statement issued on Wednesday, the prosecution office said it was conducting coordinated operations at several locations as part of an investigation into suspected breach of trust causing particularly significant financial loss.Prosecutors said they expected to release further details early in the evening, once the initial investigative steps had been completed.Being detained for questioning does not mean Matolcsy has been remanded in pre-trial custody. It remains unclear whether he will be allowed to leave after questioning. If he is formally named as a suspect, a court may decide whether to order his pre-trial detention.Matolcsy was questioned as a suspect in a separate case in September over alleged abuse of office involving pressure on Erste Bank Hungary, part of Austria's Erste Group. He denied the allegations and was allowed to leave after questioning.Investigation into central bank foundationsThe current leadership of the MNB and Hungary's State Audit Office have both filed criminal complaints concerning the central bank's foundations.Optima Investment, the asset manager of the Pallas Athéné foundations established by the MNB under Matolcsy in 2014 and merged in 2019, managed almost 500 billion forints (more than €1 billion) in public funds.The State Audit Office identified an opaque network of companies and investments, serious management failings and suspected criminal offences.The merged foundation, PADME, and Optima subsequently faced severe financial difficulties. Hungarian media have also reported links between the investment network and associates of Matolcsy's son, Ádám.Matolcsy has previously denied allegations concerning the management of the central bank foundations' funds.On 26 May 2026, Hungary's parliament adopted a resolution to establish an inquiry committee into alleged abuses at the central bank.Investigators have also been examining suspected breach of trust involving the foundations and the renovation of the MNB's headquarters, alongside a separate money laundering investigation.In May 2026, authorities said they had seized cash and securities worth 91.8 billion forints.

title: More Russians are settling in the EU with each year of war in Ukraine
description: Eurostat data show 876,600 Russian nationals held valid EU residence permits at the end of 2025, with Germany, Spain and Estonia hosting the largest communities.
content: The number of Russian citizens legally residing in the EU has grown by 105,000 since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022, reaching 876,600 by the end of 2025, an analysis of Eurostat data shows.The figure represents a 13.6% rise from the 771,800 Russians holding valid temporary or permanent residence permits across EU member states in 2021. Germany hosts the largest community, with 218,000 residents, followed by Spain (116,800) and Estonia (78,400).Southern Europe has seen the sharpest growth: Spain issued residence permits to 44,400 Russian nationals over the period, France 13,700, while Cyprus and Portugal saw their Russian-born populations increase 2.5 and 3.5 times, respectively.Several EU states have moved in the opposite direction. Latvia, Estonia and the Czech Republic have recorded the largest drops in Russian residents, driven by tough migration policies and, in the Baltic states, security concerns over large Russian-speaking communities.Significant communities have also formed outside the EU. In Serbia the Russian population rose from roughly 5,000 before the invasion to 61,900 by the end of 2025. By spring of this year, Kazakhstan had absorbed more than 107,000 Russian migrants, while Armenia and Georgia hosted 43,500 and 70,000, respectively.Turkey drew large numbers in the immediate post-invasion period but later tightened residency rules. By June, valid Russian permits there had fallen to 75,900, half the 2023 peak.Researchers tracking emigration patterns have identified at least four distinct waves since February 2022. The most recent, running from this spring, has been sparked by renewed claims of impending mobilisation for Moscow's all-out war in Ukraine."Everyone now understands that they have no future in Russia. There is no image of the future, no understanding of what will happen in six months or a year," said Anastasia Burakova, a lawyer and founder of Kovcheg, a legal assistance project for Russians abroad. "What is more, there are risks linked to mobilisation and conscription, which people feel very personally."'Now I have nothing and I feel free'Ivan, 19, left Russia this spring to avoid conscription and now works in construction in Yerevan, posting videos on YouTube. A year earlier he had been a mobile phone store manager."I thought: this is it, this is life, everything is going the way it should," he said in a YouTube video. "Now I'm sitting on a bench in Yerevan, with no title and no steady job. My wife is next to me. Back then I was a manager and felt trapped. Now I have nothing, and I feel free."Surveys by independent researchers show the Russian emigrees include predominantly young couples, often without children, with both partners under 36.They tend to have high levels of education and are concentrated in professions either vulnerable to political repression — journalists, human rights workers, political analysts — or in high international demand, particularly IT, engineering and academia. Around 20% of those who left do not hold university degrees. Some 18% are studying or plan to study abroad.They fall into three broad groups: those who have settled and expect to remain abroad long-term, those who have already moved once and are preparing to relocate again, and those still in Russia who intend to leave within six months.The economic impact on host countries has been visible yet uneven. In Armenia and Georgia, the sudden influx of people and capital contributed to GDP growth of between 9% and 9.4% at its peak between 2022 and 2024, according to analysis published by the CASE Center research institute.Average Russian household incomes in Serbia ran to around €3,500 per month against a local average of €900. In Georgia the figures were €3,300 against €650. The effect has since moderated as host economies adapted, with growth settling back to 5–7% annually.Rather than competing for local jobs, most Russian migrants have worked remotely or set up their own businesses.In IT, up to 41% have maintained income from foreign clients, while in the media sector around 21% have done so, channelling money into host economies through taxes and everyday spending.Meanwhile, Russian authorities and independent researchers have documented some returns, but the scale remains disputed.The independent OutRush sociological project estimated that no more than 8% of emigrants had returned to Russia by summer 2024, with around 5% more intending to do so.The Institute of Applied Economic Research at RANEPA, a state-linked academic institution, put the overall return rate from the 2022–2023 wave at roughly 10%.Estimates from consulting firms and recruitment agencies are considerably higher, ranging from 16% among IT workers to 40–45% of those who left at the peak.Commonly cited reasons for returning include difficulty finding work, legal status problems and the closure of relocated Russian businesses.Russia's own official resettlement programme recorded a historic low in 2025, drawing only 26,700 people into the country.Euronews could not independently verify Russian government data.

title: Hansel and Gretel in the mountains: parents abandon sons in Germany
description: In South Tyrol, parents on a hike let their sons climb alone to a mountain hut. They turn back, but the hut is closed and the children are left to fend for themselves at 2,300 metres.
content: Like a grim fairy tale gone wrong: in South Tyrol, the mountain rescue service had to save two German brothers from distress in the mountains in the middle of the night. The boys, aged 13 and 16, had been abandoned by their own parents and ended up stranded at more than 2,300 metres in front of a locked mountain refuge.The family had set off on the hike together in Toblach. After a few hours, however, the parents turned back and simply let their sons continue alone. The plan was for the teenagers to spend the night at the Bonnerhütte, as the parents believed they were experienced enough. Yet no one had checked the opening times in advance. The traditional hut, built in 1897 by the Bonn section of the Alpine Club, had already closed for the season a week earlier.The emergency call finally came in at around 1 a.m. The boys were out in the cold with nowhere to take shelter after climbing more than 1,000 metres in altitude. Mountain rescuers brought the brothers to safety and took them to hospital. According to the Pustertal mountain rescue service, the teenagers were inadequately dressed and severely hypothermic; one of the boys was vomiting. They have since been discharged from hospital. The rescuers spoke of "great carelessness" and stressed that such irresponsible behaviour is thankfully rare.The story is chillingly reminiscent of the fairy tale Hansel and Gretel by Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm, first published in 1812. Only this time, the children were not abandoned in a forest, but on the icy heights of South Tyrol.

title: A stunning Alpine retreat will open at the foot of the Dolomites this winter
description: Le Graal Cortina will have just 30 rooms, including 13 suites, when it opens in Cortina d'Ampezzo.
content: The Dolomites are a bucket list destination for many, offering spectacular views no matter the season.But if you’ve booked a trip for this winter and haven’t sorted your hotel yet, we might just have a new option for you.Le Graal Cortina is set to open later this year within a reimagined 1920s palazzo. Boasting just 30 rooms, including 13 suites, the boutique property in Cortina d'Ampezzo might just be the chicest new stay in town.Designed by Italian architect Achille Salvagni, you can expect deep woods, warm velvets and plenty of light in the space that puts the mountains at the core of the experience.What to expect at Le Graal CortinaThe property offers direct access to the region’s iconic ski terrain and Cortina’s historic centre.After a day on the slopes or hiking the trails, you can relax at Le Graal Spa, which comes complete with an indoor pool, sauna, hammam, cryotherapy chamber and treatment rooms.Dining is also at the heart of the experience, with three restaurants and bars to choose from.At Le Monsù, you can expect a classic fine dining experience, with the name coming from the Sicilian version of the French Monsieur Le Chef, the head chefs at aristocratic residences.For a more informal experience, you can book a table at all-day dining spot Le Café, which is envisioned as a blend between a café, a bistrot, and a pâtisserie, offering Sicilian dishes with a contemporary twist.If you’re after a nightcap, you can swing by Le Graal Bar. The American bar has its own take on classics like the negroni or a spritz, and you can also order canapés and pastries.Other new openings in the DolomitesLe Graal Cortina certainly isn’t the only new opening this winter.In early December, The First Cortina by The Pavilions Hotels & Resorts will also open its doors in Cortina d’Ampezzo.The 76-key property will be home to a spa as well as several restaurants, including celeb hotspot Zuma.Next year, the historic Hotel Cristallo in Alta Badia will reopen under the Mandarin Oriental brand following extensive renovations.It will have 83 rooms, including 30 suites, as well as a number of restaurants and bars as well as the brand’s iconic spa.

title: Italy deploys 500 troops to Milan under new security decree following violent clashes
description: Meloni said nearly 200 police officers had been injured and 330 people detained, around half of whom she said were of "foreign origin".
content: Italy approved the deployment of an additional 500 troops to Milan on Tuesday following violent clashes at protests over the rising cost of living.Demonstrations turned violent over the weekend in several Italian cities, including Milan, Turin and Bologna. Protesters clashed with police, while shops were looted and property damaged.However, the cabinet stopped short of granting soldiers additional policing powers, reportedly following opposition from President Sergio Mattarella.The deployment forms part of the government's new Public Security Decree, which introduces tougher measures targeting violent protests and juvenile crime."Destroying and stealing is not protest, it is crime, and the state's response must be firm," Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said in a video posted on X after the cabinet meeting.What does Italy's new security decree include?The decree presumes that minors aged 14 to 18 can be held criminally responsible unless proven otherwise. Under the Rocco Code, the opposite applies: a minor's ability to understand their actions and their consequences must be established.It also extends the use of "delayed arrests" to minors and allows judges to impose precautionary measures on those over 16, even if these disrupt ongoing educational programmes.Another provision creates a new offence of "violent participation in public demonstrations", targeting people in groups of more than five who unlawfully use potentially harmful objects in a way that poses a concrete danger.The Justice Ministry has also extended the use of delayed arrests under Article 382-bis of the Code of Criminal Procedure to offences including devastation and looting, attacks on public utility facilities, violent participation in demonstrations and group-related property damage.The decree also makes prosecution automatic in all cases involving injuries inflicted on judicial police or public security officers. Currently, such offences are prosecuted automatically only in aggravated cases.Justice Minister Carlo Nordio said people who organise groups for violent demonstrations, including through social media, could face four to 12 years in prison under a new offence.

title: US envoy in Russia for  Putin talks after 'positive' Zelenskyy meeting
description: Moscow says it is prepared to consider economic proposals from Washington but will not make political concessions, while the Kremlin insists that a lasting settlement on Russia's terms, rather than a temporary energy ceasefire, remains its objective.
content: Russia has ruled out making political concessions to Washington ahead of talks between President Vladimir Putin and US envoy Steve Witkoff, signalling that Moscow remains unwilling to soften its maximalist negotiating position despite renewed American efforts to end the war in Ukraine.Witkoff arrived in Saint Petersburg to meet Vladimir Putin, following what US Secretary of State Marco Rubio described as "positive" talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Oslo on Tuesday.Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Moscow would examine proposals brought by Witkoff and Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, but made clear that any economic or financial benefits would not be accompanied by political concessions."We'll see what they propose. If they offer something that benefits us economically and financially, then why not?" Lavrov said, according to remarks reported by Russian media."But this must be done without any political concessions on our part," he added, stressing that Russia should rely on itself rather than expect favourable treatment from Washington.His comments underscore the difficulties facing the latest diplomatic initiative, which comes after Trump reached a diesel agreement with Putin and criticised the impact of Ukrainian strikes on Russia's energy sector on global fuel prices.Lavrov also cautioned against expecting a fundamental change in US-Russian relations under Trump, describing the United States as "at best a competitor" and warning that future American administrations could reverse any economic concessions.Kremlin rejects energy ceasefireThe Kremlin, meanwhile, reiterated its opposition to any temporary halt in attacks on energy infrastructure, despite Trump's earlier announcement of an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine."Nothing has changed. We need peace, not a ceasefire," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Wednesday.The statement comes as Russia continues its attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure ahead of winter, raising further questions about the prospects for a limited agreement to protect power facilities.Peskov also acknowledged that a comprehensive settlement could not be reached without Ukraine's participation, even as Moscow prepares to discuss the latest proposals directly with Washington."Of course, it is impossible to fully resolve the Ukrainian issue without someone from Kyiv being present," he said, adding that someone in the Ukrainian leadership would have to take what he described as a responsible decision.The Kremlin spokesman also cast doubt on the contribution Finnish President Alexander Stubb could make to the diplomatic process, suggesting that merely repeating the broader European position on Ukraine would do little to advance negotiations.Stubb took part in Tuesday's talks in Oslo alongside Zelenskyy, Witkoff and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, with discussions focusing on proposals for ending the war and possible security guarantees for Ukraine.'Time to make a deal'The latest diplomatic push comes amid deepening tensions between Kyiv and Washington, following Trump's criticism of Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure and reports of delays in US-made Patriot interceptor missile deliveries already paid for by European countries.Following his meeting with Witkoff, Zelenskyy thanked Washington for resuming intelligence-sharing on incoming Russian strikes, describing early warnings of ballistic missile attacks as essential to protecting civilians."We are thankful that intelligence works," Zelenskyy told reporters in Oslo, calling the warnings "very, very important for our people, for children, adults, civilians".Trump, meanwhile, renewed his calls for Ukraine to reach an agreement with Russia, telling reporters at the White House on Tuesday that Kyiv needed to "make a deal".Zelenskyy has insisted that Ukraine must be directly involved in any negotiations determining its future."If there are issues about Ukraine, our future, it can be acceptable only when we are at the table of negotiations," he said on Tuesday.

title: El Niño tracker: How the weather phenomenon is wreaking havoc around the world this week
description: El Niño is combining with climate change to drive extreme weather conditions around the globe.
content: From starving cattle in parched El Salvador to a "terrifying" threat to the world's coral reefs, this year's exceptionally strong El Niño is being felt across the globe.The natural weather phenomenon occurs when sea temperatures in the Eastern Pacific Ocean become unusually warm, which happens roughly every two to seven years.Previous El Niño events have contributed towards record-breaking heat, fuelling long-standing droughts, flash floods and deadly wildfires across the globe.While most El Niño events increase global average temperatures by around 0.2°C – enough to trigger extreme weather across the Global South – it is a fraction of the additional human-caused warming from climate change.Here is how this year's so-called 'Super El Niño' is playing out around the world.El Niño threatens coral reefs and forestsThis year's El Niño adds "a terrifying level of additional risk" for the world's coral reefs, according to David Obura, chair of the UN's expert nature panel.Corals are highly sensitive to heat, and climate change is already making bleaching events more frequent and intense.The fourth global bleaching event and this year's El Niño have put corals in even greater jeopardy.Obura led a major reassessment of coral health, published in the science journal Nature, that found reef-building species had deteriorated sharply since the last global census in 2008, with 44 per cent threatened with extinction.Forests are also at risk. Global deforestation slowed last year, according to the independent Forest Declaration Assessment, but the gains are unlikely to last as conditions worsen in Central Africa and El Niño raises fire risks across the tropics.Livestock suffer as drought strikes El SalvadorDrought fuelled by El Niño is wreaking havoc across Central America's Dry Corridor, which stretches from Mexico to Panama.In El Salvador, where August temperatures were 4.3°C above normal, livestock are suffering the impacts."Imagine how thin this little animal is! Why? Because of a lack of grass," says Antonio Aguilar, a 54-year-old rancher, pointing to a cow reduced to skin and bones at a livestock market in Sensuntepeque.The El Niño, expected to peak by year's end, is unfolding amid accelerating human-caused warming, which amplifies its effects. A warmer atmosphere dries out soil, deepening drought, and holds more moisture, making rains more extreme.Heavy rain closes Iguazu FallsExtreme downpours fuelled by El Niño caused the Iguazu River to flow at six times the normal rate last week. Park authorities in Argentina responded by closing tourist trails, including the walkway to the Devil’s Throat, the largest and most dramatic of the Iguazu Falls' cascades.South America, the southern US, East Africa and Central Asia have all experienced heightened flood risks during previous El Niño events.In Argentina's northeast, tthe Paraná River rose to a dangerous 4.7 metres on 15 October, prompting evacuations in nearby towns. Flooding has also forced thousands from their homes in Paraguay and Uruguay.Global poverty risks stoked by extreme weatherUN development chief Alexander De Croo warns that El Niño, combined with surging energy costs and higher interest rates, could push millions into poverty as the vulnerable are hit by crisis after crisis.In particular, severe drought linked to El Niño is affecting more than half of Sudan – where conflict is already fuelling famine – causing localised crop failures and depriving households of food and income.Many staple imports, such as maize and beans, could also put Europe's food security at risk, according to the IHE Delft Institute for Water Education in the Netherlands.While El Niño is out of our control, human-caused warming can be minimised by cutting emissions. De Croo urges private investors to recognise both the "economic cost" of climate change and the "business case" for tackling it.Sri Lanka's central bank warns that El Niño could undermine the island's fragile recovery from its worst economic crisis in decades, with torrential rains forecast through December and prolonged drought early next year.Will this year's El Niño be record-breaking?How this El Niño ranks depends on how it is measured, and agencies' differing methods make direct comparisons difficult.Britain's Met Office calls it "unprecedented" and Japan's weather agency calls it the strongest ever observed, but US forecasters have not declared a record – yet.The strongest El Niño year in NOAA's dataset is 1982. The agency says the current event will likely surpass it."By any measure, we are looking at a very strong El Niño," says climate scientist Emily Becker of the University of Miami. She adds that only once it is over will scientists know "where it fits in the context of history".Because climate change is warming oceans everywhere, the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) now measures how warm or cool the east-central Pacific is compared with the rest of the tropical ocean. That difference is what drives global weather impacts.How do a few degrees of warming in the Pacific exert so much influence?Under NOAA's updated index, a 2.5°C anomaly in a key Pacific region relative to the rest of the tropical ocean, sustained over three months, would make for the most intense El Niño on record.That might not sound like much, but the El Niño-Southern Oscillation is the leading natural driver of year-to-year climate variability.Shifts in where the ocean releases heat into the atmosphere ripple across global weather, leaving some regions cooler and wetter and others hotter and drier. These effects are known as "teleconnections".But while El Niños, and their opposite number La Niñas, when the equatorial Pacific is colder than normal, load the dice toward certain outcomes, they do not guarantee them.

title: Europe’s pensions rank among the world’s best – but how secure are they?
description: A new ranking of 55 retirement income systems reveals how Europe’s pension systems compare, with concerns over the long-term sustainability of benefits in some of the continent’s largest economies.
content: The Netherlands offers the best pension system in the world, according to the Marsh CFA Institute Global Pension Index (MCGPI).The top-ranking country received a score of 85.8 out of 100, followed by Denmark at 84.1 and Iceland at 84.0. They are the only European systems awarded the best grade. Singapore, Israel and Australia complete this category, which includes the best pension systems globally.The index compared 55 retirement income systems, covering 66% of the global population.They measured each system against three major sub-indices, which assess the adequacy of retirement income, whether systems can keep delivering and the strength of their governance and safeguards.Against these individual priorities, the ranking changes substantially: Kuwait scores highest for adequacy, Denmark leads on sustainability, and Finland tops the integrity sub-index, according to the Global Pension Index.To lead the overall ranking, a pension system needs to combine good benefits with long-term sustainability and a high level of integrity.That combination earned the Netherlands the top spot in 2026 for the fourth year running.The report calls it a “robust retirement income system,” with a state pension providing a reliable income floor, with additional workplace pensions covering most employees. A large pool of invested pension assets helps guarantee future payments. The system has strong regulation, governance, and member protection, which build confidence, the report said.The Netherlands is currently reforming its pension system. It is moving from promised benefits, usually linked to salary and years worked, towards individual pension pots based more directly on contributions and investment returns.The reforms come as low interest rates have made promised payments harder to fund, while funding rules sometimes delayed increases to keep pace with inflation. Workplace pensions were also less suited to people who changed jobs frequently or became self-employed.The transition is expected to be completed by 2028.European pension systems comparedThe index compares 19 European countries, including Turkey.Following the Netherlands, Denmark and Iceland, the next best pension systems are in Sweden, Finland and Norway, followed by Switzerland, the UK, France, Ireland, Belgium, Germany, Portugal and Croatia. These countries received B+ or B grades, indicating systems with sound structures and many good features, but also areas for improvement.Countries in the next two categories, C+ and C, include Spain, Poland, Italy and Austria, with systems that have some good features, but also major risks or shortcomings that could undermine their efficacy or sustainability. These categories include the US and mainland China, the world's two largest economies.Several major European systems provide good benefits but face serious challenges with long-term funding.European countries with the most long-term vulnerabilities include Austria, Italy and Spain.The contrast is particularly sharp in Spain. The EU’s fourth-largest economy scored 83 for adequacy, indicating strong retirement benefits and resources, but just 33 for sustainability.France, the EU’s second-largest economy, scored 85 for adequacy but only 49.3 for sustainability.In Europe, Turkey is at the bottom of the overall ranking with the lowest score for resources and funding among the European countries assessed. Its sustainability score is also among the lowest.The report noted that the world’s retirement income systems face mounting pressure. People are expected to live longer on average, but declining fertility rates mean that fewer people are entering the workforce to finance their pensions. Graham Pearce, global defined benefit segment leader at Marsh, told Euronews Business that “one of the key challenges for unfunded pension systems is that the number of retirees relative to workers is expected to increase significantly over the coming decades”.In these systems, today’s workers’ contributions help pay today’s retirees, rather than being invested to pay their own future pensions.European central bank leaders have also sounded the alarm about the long-term prospects of pension systems in Europe’s largest economies.Bundesbank president Joachim Nagel told Handelsblatt in May 2026 that linking Germany’s retirement age to life expectancy after 2031 could help. He called the country’s new private pension scheme, due in early 2027, “an important step towards a stronger funded pension pillar”, but warned it would not be enough to tackle long-term sustainability problems.Speaking to Le Figaro that month, François Villeroy de Galhau, then Banque de France governor, warned that financing public spending through deficits shifted costs to younger generations. “We are transferring the burden of debt and pensions to our children,” he said.In September 2026, the European Commission called for supplementary saving alongside public pensions, warning of growing pressure on public budgets and the risk that “too many people will face a sharp drop in income when they retire”.Adapting systems to a longer, more flexible retirementTo future-proof pension systems, including those in Europe, without raising retirement ages or reducing benefits, governments will need to raise additional revenue to fund a growing number of retirees.According to Pearce, “This could be achieved through higher taxes or social security contributions, or by enabling and incentivising those who are willing and able to work longer to do so, which would also generate additional tax revenue”.The report predicts that pension systems that clarify their objectives, strengthen funding and build flexibility into their system today can become some of the best pension systems in the future.The report suggests that pension systems can be made more sustainable by increasing private pension coverage for employees and the self-employed, improving the governance and transparency of private pension plans, raising the retirement age to reflect increasing healthy life expectancy, and helping more people work at older ages so they can save more for retirement.It also recommends encouraging higher levels of private saving and introducing measures to help reduce the gender pension gap and gaps affecting minority groups.According to Pearce, younger workers should not necessarily expect less generous public pensions over the next 10–20 years. However, he said building up invested retirement savings alongside state pensions would be needed to make systems more sustainable.He also expects greater use of auto-enrolment schemes to supplement public pensions. These automatically sign workers up for a pension scheme, usually with the option to opt out. Contributions are taken from their pay, often topped up by their employer, and invested to provide income alongside their state pension.Commenting on countries such as France and Spain, which score highly for adequacy but poorly for sustainability, Pearce warned that “without action to improve the sustainability of public pension systems, such as raising retirement ages or introducing an element of pre-funding at an early stage [investing money now to help pay future pensions], governments may eventually face difficult decisions as existing arrangements become unaffordable.”These decisions could include reducing pension benefits, he added. “Taking action now can help preserve the retirement expectations of today's workers while avoiding passing an excessive financial burden on to future generations,” he said.

title: Attacked owner of looted Paris shop: '10 years of work destroyed, I have not slept in three days'
description: Originally from Bangladesh, Hassan arrived in France in 2010. After spending years working in hospitality, he managed to save enough to open his own business. In the aftermath of the weekend riots in Paris, his shop has been left completely destroyed.
content: Hassan recalls breaking down in tears, after he was forced to abandon his tech and courrier shop, located on a main street off the Place de la République in Paris, to rioters who ransacked his premises over the weekend."They attacked me physically and threatened to break a wine bottle on my head. I was forced to abandon my business", he told Euronews.Originally from Bangladesh, the father of three arrived in France in 2010. He spent years working in hospitality, before he saved enough to open a shop with his associate in 2016."About 10 years ago, we built this place up gradually, bit by bit," he said."This was once my workspace, but now there's nothing there. I have not slept since it all happened", he lamented from behind the counter where he would normally welcome clients.As he awaits insurance assessments, Hassan is unable to clear up the destruction, leaving him surrounded by the physical aftermath of the weekend's violence. Smashed phones, empty delivery parcels and glass line his shop floor. He must also still pay rent, bills and his employees.His shop is located in one of the areas of Paris which was the hardest hit by violence on 17 October. Although many protestors marched peacefully, in many areas they were hijacked by violence, as looters raided and destroyed businesses, from small firms to major enterprises.'How is this possible?'Following advice from the French authorities, Hassan locked up his shop for the afternoon on Saturday. Hours later, when he logged into his security camera app on his phone, he froze in disbelief."I saw around 30 people in the shop. I thought, how is this possible?"He decided to rush back to his business, but the police initially refused to grant him access to the perimeter around his shop, due to the ongoing intense levels of violence and rioting.When he begged police to let him through and showed them images of his shop being destroyed in real time, they accepted.But when he arrived on site, he realised he was utterly helpless, with no police in sight.Euronews separately obtained footage of looters breaking into the adjacent apartment building, where one of the shop entrances is located. Neighbours begged them to stop, but were unable to, as they also feared for their own safety."There was a mix of young girls and boys. Some looked 15 years old. There was a constant stream, once a group had finished stealing, a new one would arrive."The looters stole phones, tech, as well as parcels. Some remained outside, as individuals handed each other goods through the smashed storefront. The storeroom in the basement was also ransacked.'We just want to make a living and do our job'A local courrier worker who had delivered many of the stolen packages told Euronews he had seen some businesses in an even worse state."We just want to make a living and do our job with honesty. Others want to destroy everything."Across the road, an Intermarché, one of France's biggest supermarket chains, has been closed since it was plundered over the weekend. Workers have spent days cleaning up the shop, picking up pieces of glass and restocking shelves.Some hard-left activists have condemned damages to small businesses, while expressing greater tolerance for looting major supermarkets and companies, which they regard as symbols of capitalism.But for the postal worker interviewed by Euronews, this logic does not hold, "it's not justifiable. It's the same, it's all destroyed."Following the looting, local worker Noam set up a crowdfunder page for Hassan, which has already attracted thousands in donations."We know Hassan because he helps us with deliveries and other tasks regularly. He's someone we're used to working with. We are trying to help as much as we can, because there is a huge amount of work to be done, but we want to get through all of this with a community spirit."Riots which followed largely peaceful protestsThe French government has launched emergency financial aid and structural relief programs to support impacted shops. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said on Monday that businesses hit by the unrest would be able to put staff on activité partielle, France’s state-funded furlough scheme, from Tuesday.The weekend's violence followed four weeks of largely peaceful student protests against deteriorating conditions in French schools.Throughout the movement, human rights organisations have accused law enforcement of using excessive force against protesters. Much of the criticism focuses on rubber-bullet launchers, known in France as LBDs, and stun grenades, which critics blame for serious injuries to protesters.On Saturday, trade unions, the yellow vest movement and students participated in major demonstrations across the country. Although most protestors marched peaceful, rioters overshadowed this, as they carried out mass looting and clashed with the police.France has since instated a curfew in many parts of the country and significantly increased security measures ahead of upcoming protests on 24 October. The government has also announced the deployment of military forces, alongside the police in order to maintain public order.

title: Trump’s embrace of Putin roils Europe, but not enough to break with the US
description: Donald Trump's embrace of Vladimir Putin has driven a wedge between the transatlantic allies. But for all their outrage, Europeans are not yet ready to break away from the United States and go their own way.
content: The rift between Europe and the United States over Russia's war on Ukraine has plunged to a new depth as Donald Trump doubles down on his embrace of Vladimir Putin, jolting an alliance that was already treading on thin ice.Over just two striking weeks, the US president has struck a diesel deal with his Russian counterpart, eased economic sanctions on Moscow, called for new elections in Ukraine and dismissed the legitimacy of its president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, whom Trump said was "more difficult to deal with" than Putin.Zelenskyy, increasingly defiant, has denounced the diesel deal as a "historic mistake" and cautioned that other US-Russian agreements related to gas flows, banking, chemicals and the immobilised assets would be next in line.Ukraine has identified sudden limits on the use of the Starlink satellite technology and US-made weapons deliveries."I believe steps have been taken to convince Ukraine to capitulate," Zelenskyy told Bloomberg in remarks that revived the long-running dread that Trump and Putin would conspire to thrash out a backroom deal that ends in Kyiv's surrender.Moscow's pitch for a trilateral meeting with Putin, Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping further fuelled those fears."I would do it. Not so much for Ukraine, because Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine," Trump said when asked about the trilateral.The rapid succession of events has caught Europeans off guard, who, after previous setbacks, believed they had learned to navigate Trump’s unilateral style of diplomacy.Once again, they find themselves blindsided and undercut by a close ally that is willing to make overtures to Russia without demanding a single concession in return."We want to leave no doubt about our position towards Ukraine, and at the same time, we know that the Americans have other interests," German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said last week at the end of a two-day summit in Brussels.In a swipe at Trump, French President Emmanuel Macron denounced the "ambiguities" of some leaders and warned: "Capitulation is weakness. Weakness is danger."Italy's Giorgia Meloni deplored the diesel deal as a "very risky choice" that legitimises Moscow and weakens sanctions. Denmark's Mette Frederiksen lamented that "we, the Western alliance, are in a worse position now than we were a few days ago".On Tuesday, High Representative Kaja Kallas upped the ante and explicitly accused the US of pushing Ukraine to "surrender on Putin's terms".Conscious couplingYet despite the criticism and widespread indignation, Europe remains unwilling and perhaps unprepared to break away from Trump and pursue an independent course.Brussels, Berlin, Paris and London still prefer to maintain an active, even if precarious, channel with Washington to influence its thinking as much as possible, as shown in their participation in the latest round of US-led peace talks in Miami and later in Oslo."Europe will live with the consequences, and that's why we need to see a more unified Europe at the table," Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said.For Kyiv, the European presence has become indispensable to offset the White House's Russian-friendly slant. Zelenskyy has repeatedly encouraged Europe to develop a parallel channel with Russia, but Moscow has shown no interest.Though Trump's latest actions prove the European push has been limited at best, the thinking remains unchanged: the seat at the table must be preserved at all costs."We have to move forward, because we also know cooperation with the US is essential for Ukraine to fight its war. Everybody knows the volumes that are part of the diesel deal are low," a senior diplomat said, speaking on condition of anonymity."So keep calm and carry on. Deplore and continue. But no over-dramatisation either. That's in none of our interests."Some officials find reassurance in the belief that Trump’s rapprochement with Putin is largely motivated by a desire to deflect responsibility for high fuel prices ahead of next month's midterm elections, in which opinion polls show his Republican Party will lose.Trump claims that Ukraine's successful strikes on Russia's oil refineries are to blame, but energy experts agree his war on Iran is the chief culprit of the oil market turmoil."We have dialogue, and we'll continue to have dialogue. It has taken us to positive results in what our interests are concerned," a senior official said. "This is the best way."Yet there is a growing recognition that Europe and the US have fundamentally diverged in their approaches to Russia, with differences that may prove impossible to reconcile.Europe, for now, bets on sanctions to cripple the war machine, long-term decoupling to avoid vulnerable dependencies and strict diplomatic isolation. Although some far-right and far-left parties question this logic, the strategy is widely shared.The US, by contrast, is dangling economic incentives for Russia to engage in the peace negotiations. These reportedly involve an early partial release of sovereign assets and the resumption of gas flows to Europe, both of which Europe has already rejected. Deals related to Lukoil and nuclear technology are also said to be in the works.European officials contend the American approach is flawed because it ignores Putin's fixation with territorial conquest, the core reason why he launched the invasion. No deal, however lucrative, can replace Ukraine's annihilation in Putin's mind, they say.Washington's invitation to Putin for the G20 summit in Florida, which a dozen European leaders are scheduled to attend, is another sign of glaring discrepancy.As Trump moves closer to Putin, the ideological gap between the two sides of the Atlantic is unlikely to narrow any time soon. If anything, it could deepen even further, raising serious questions about what might happen when the peace process reaches the endgame and allies are called to make joint decisions of exceptional significance.Maria Shagina, a senior fellow at the International Institute for Strategic Studies, says the White House's actions are designed to pressure Europe into relinquishing its pressure front and accommodating the US stance on Russia."The more fundamental question is whether Europe can sustain an independent sanctions strategy over the longer term. The EU and the UK retain considerable economic leverage over Russia, but can they translate that leverage into effective and sustained pressure on Moscow without US participation?" Shagina told Euronews."The challenge is not simply whether Europe possesses sufficient economic power, but whether it has the political will, institutional capacity and strategic coherence to deploy that power independently of Washington, something that until now has been inconceivable."

title: AI and digital transformation reshape aviation, but safety remains non-negotiable
description: At the World Aviation Festival in Lisbon, Hitit CEO Nevra Onursal Karaağaç and digital transformation lead Aras Kubilay urged gradual modernisation of airline systems and warned of the risks of adopting AI without a clear strategy.
content: Artificial intelligence and digital transformation are opening up new possibilities for commercial aviation, from personalising the passenger experience to forecasting operational disruption. But the modernisation of a highly regulated sector demands changes that go far beyond technology, argue two executives from Hitit, a Turkish provider of technology solutions for the aviation industry, in an interview with Euronews during the World Aviation Festival (source in Portuguese), in Lisbon. For Aras Kubilay, who is responsible for industry engagement and business development at Hitit (source in Portuguese), aviation is facing a structural shift in the way it manages its digital systems. The challenge is to modernise the infrastructure underpinning day-to-day operations without compromising flight continuity and passenger satisfaction. "Airlines are extremely complex businesses and they operate continuously, 24 hours a day, seven days a week," he said. That means they cannot simply shut down operations for several days to replace their core IT systems. The scale of the challenge becomes even clearer when set against the pace of digital transformation. According to Kubilay, airlines are well aware that they need to change, but many still struggle to take the first steps. He cited survey data collected from industry executives last year: 72% regarded digital transformation as crucial. This year, he said that during the WAF he had heard estimates that the share has risen above 90%, although he stressed that he does not have an updated official figure. Even so, only 27% of airlines are thought to have taken concrete action. "If we do not move in this direction in the next two to three years, we could face problems," he warned. Instead of attempting to replace an entire infrastructure in one go, Kubilay advocates a phased approach, allowing carriers to pinpoint specific issues and roll out incremental improvements. "You do not start with a major overhaul all at once. You replace parts as needed and then, if the results are positive, you keep going in that direction," he explained.Where is AI adding value in aviation? Artificial intelligence sits at the heart of this transformation, but its use needs to be tied to concrete objectives. In Kubilay's view, airlines must first decide whether they want to increase revenues, cut costs or improve the customer experience before launching new projects. "If they say they are going to do everything at once, simply by adding an AI label, they will spend money and nothing will happen", he cautioned. Hitit says it already embeds AI tools in different components of its solutions, including cost accounting, reporting and the management of operational disruption. Nevra Onursal Karaağaç, the company's CEO, explained that these applications can make users' work easier, allowing them, for example, to obtain reports by submitting written requests, without having to manually enter multiple parameters. The technology can also help to anticipate weather-related problems affecting flights. Kubilay described a model that combines physical characteristics of runways, their orientation to the wind and weather patterns to predict situations in which a flight may have to be rescheduled. With that information, airlines can anticipate potential delays or reroutings, instead of reacting only once a disruption has already occurred. Despite these possibilities, he warned of the risks of relying blindly on AI systems, especially in customer service. Without naming the airline, he referred to a case where an artificial intelligence system is said to have allowed refunds above the amount paid and changes to flights that should not have been authorised. "In such a sensitive and complex sector as air transport, it may be necessary to think twice," he noted. Safety, he stressed, must not be sacrificed in the name of convenience. Systems need to be configured with clear rules and limits on what they can do, with appropriate control mechanisms remaining in place. Karaağaç also emphasised that developing technology for aviation requires more than programming skills. "You need to understand the aviation world itself," she said, arguing for collaboration between industry consultants, business analysts and development teams.The spread of artificial intelligence is also changing the way passengers search for and purchase flights. For Kubilay, this shift could be an opportunity for airlines to regain control over their relationship with customers, in a market where flight comparison sites and digital intermediaries tend to make price and schedule the central factors in travellers' decisions. As AI assistants become more widespread, passengers may start to search for trips through conversational queries, specifying not only their destination but also the purpose of their journey or their preferences. That information and context could help airlines put forward more relevant offers, instead of presenting a long list of undifferentiated options. "If they do not control customer engagement, it is very easy to swap one airline for another," he argued. Kubilay believes personalisation can benefit both passengers, who will save time finding what they are looking for, and airlines, which will be able to offer products better tailored to each person's needs. Even so, the transformation should preserve the familiarity of these digital platforms. When systems are modernised, the aim should not be to force passengers to learn how to use apps and platforms all over again. "Ideally, people should not be able to tell that anything has changed. The only things they should notice are that everything works better and has become simpler," he explained.A future without check-in? One change that Kubilay sees as feasible in the coming years is the elimination of check-in as a distinct step in air travel. He recalled that the process dates back to the era of paper tickets, when part of the document had to be torn off to confirm its use. Despite digitalisation, some of those practices remain embedded in today's systems."We want to abolish check-in completely. You buy your ticket, go to the plane and that is it," he explained. Bringing that vision to life will, however, depend on the co-operation of the entire industry. Verifying passengers' identity, border controls and security requirements involve different entities and cannot be solved by a single company in isolation. Kubilay highlighted an initiative developed using standards set by the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) and promoted by the International Air Transport Association (IATA), called Digital Travel Credentials (DTC), which aims to facilitate the use of digital identity credentials. The goal is to cut down on the need for passengers to repeatedly present and validate the same information throughout their journey. According to him, an IATA study found that, on a typical trip, passengers have to provide the same information seven times. "We have to show our ID when we make the booking, when we check in baggage, when we board the plane, when we go through customs. Then again when we land. Why can I not do this just once and the authorities communicate among themselves?" he asked. Any reduction in these steps will nonetheless have to respect security requirements. Kubilay explained that digital credentials can be verified through digital signatures and confirmation of their authenticity by the issuing authorities. The aim is to simplify travel without compromising the safety of passengers and operations. Hitit seeks to consolidate international expansion Founded in 1994 by two women, Hitit started out developing passenger loyalty solutions and progressively expanded its activity to core reservation systems, ticketing, check-in and other airline operations. The company now develops solutions covering a range of operational needs, including schedule planning, operations control, accounting, cargo and travel agency systems. According to Karaağaç, Hitit worked with 17 airlines in 2018 and, in 2026, provides services to nearly 70 carriers. The most recent public figures cited by the Turkish firm's CEO point to 68 airlines in 47 countries, with its solutions used at more than 900 airports. "Although our roots are in Turkey and the company was founded in Turkey, we are already a global business," Nevra Karaağaç underlined. Hitit became a company listed on the Istanbul stock exchange in 2022. For Karaağaç, international expansion will continue to be based on close relationships with airlines and the ability to adapt to their needs. Kubilay, for his part, argues that the future of aviation technology will depend on more interoperable systems that allow airlines to combine solutions from different providers without being locked into a single partner. Operators should avoid situations in which they lose control of their own data or find themselves unable to switch provider. "Technology must be compatible with the future," he cautioned, explaining that companies need flexibility to adapt to changes they cannot yet foresee. Looking ahead to the next five years, Kubilay expects digital transformation, the modernisation of commercial systems and the adoption of AI to reach a sufficiently broad scale to become the industry norm, while maintaining safety, operational continuity and passenger trust, even if the sector's most ambitious goals are not achieved within the original deadlines.

title: 'This is possible': Emissions must fall by 18% in next 4 years to limit worst impacts of global warming
description: “Every additional fraction of a degree and additional year of warming above 1.5°C increases climate impacts and risks, such as the deadly floods, heatwaves and wildfires that have plagued many nations this year”.
content: The world is moving in the right direction towards relying less on fossil fuels and more on renewable energy, thereby cutting the planet-warming emissions that are causing more frequent and intense extreme weather all over Europe.But we must move much faster and invest far more in cutting carbon emissions, according to a major new report released today by the United Nations Environment Programme.The report lays bare the chasm between rhetoric and action when it comes to tackling global warming, and the challenge facing political leaders at November's COP31 climate summit.Global commitments to cut planet-heating emissions are falling far short of the climate goals set out in the Paris Agreement and put the world on course for 2.6C warming this century. But there is still hope.The report looks at a ‘lowest possible’ 1.5°C overshoot scenario, in which peak warming is limited to 1.7-1.8°C.To get onto this pathway, global greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions would have to be cut by 18 per cent by 2030, 45 per cent by 2035 and 69 per cent by 2040, relative to 2025 levels. Large-scale removals of CO2 from the atmosphere will be required to return to or below 1.5°C.Current policies will lead us to 2.8C of warmingEven if countries deliver their latest climate pledges in full, global temperatures could still rise 2.6C above pre-industrial levels by 2100, says the annual Emissions Gap Report.That would blow past the historic goal agreed in Paris: keeping warming well below 2C while striving for a safer 1.5C. Any chance of keeping to 1.5C had been "lost" due to decades of insufficient climate action, the report says."The world can no longer avoid overshooting the 1.5 degree limit, and the consequences are already devastating," says UN chief Antonio Guterres in a statement to launch the closely-watched report."Deadly floods, brutal heatwaves, raging wildfires, lost lives, crippled economies, deepening inequalities, and those least responsible are suffering first and worst."Overall, global greenhouse gas emissions in 2025 were broadly on a par with record levels in 2024, with the difference between the two years too small to call, the report says.Carbon emissions just from burning coal, oil and gas - the main driver of climate change - rose slightly in 2025 compared to the previous year.Guterres says deep and immediate cuts were needed to protect humanity from worsening impacts but instead "emissions remain at record levels. And national climate plans and current policies fall dangerously short".Sticking just with current policies would see warming hit 2.8C, the report says.Exceeding 1.5C is now inevitableScientists warn that every additional fraction of a degree above 1.5C increases extreme weather events and the likelihood of irreversible changes to the planet, from dying coral reefs to melting permafrost.The world has already warmed roughly 1.4C relative to pre-industrial times and crossing 1.5C is expected in a matter of years.The G20 accounts for three-quarters of global emissions but Guterres says "all countries, especially the big emitters, must do more" to stop heating the planet.This latest UNEP warming outlook is worse than last year's due to the formal withdrawal of the United States from the Paris accord and upward revisions of historical emissions, says report co-author Anne Olhoff.Emissions growth slowed down among the G20 but the US was a "major exception", it added.Among the world's top-six emitters, preliminary data for 2025 showed emissions increases in the US, Indonesia and China and decreases in India, Russia and the European Union.But in terms of magnitude, the US increase of 133 megatons of CO2 equivalent "far exceeded" that of any other country, driven by higher electricity demand and a rebound of coal power generation.The next-largest increase was recorded in Turkey, which is hosting the UN climate summit in Antalya from 9-20 November.The US is the world's second-largest polluter, behind China. US President Donald Trump has called climate change a hoax and rolled back clean energy policies while boosting fossil fuel production.UNEP executive secretary Inger Andersen told reporters that no country was shielded from climate change and impacts were being felt "on every nation on the planet, including the US".Less coal and lower methane emissionsThe report details a scenario with a 50 per cent chance of bringing global warming back down to 1.5C by 2100.To get there, warming must peak around 1.8C by 2050 and vast amounts of carbon dioxide would have to be removed from the atmosphere to bring temperatures down further.Electricity generation from coal would need to fall by at least 75 per cent in 2035 relative to 2025 and be effectively phased out globally by 2040.Methane emissions would need to be at least 25 per cent lower than 2025 levels by 2035 and at least 40 per cent lower by 2040."The main takeaway is simple - governments need to get on with enacting policies that cut fossil fuel use as soon as possible," says Bill Hare, CEO of global policy institute Climate Analytics.Some climate-vulnerable developing nations have accused bigger emitters of abandoning the Paris goals and a showdown over the 1.5C target is expected at COP31."This is a historic failure of political leadership. The science has been clear for decades, but governments have chosen delay over action. The consequences will be measured in lives lost, not just degrees of warming," says Mohamed Adow, director of Kenya-based think tank Power Shift Africa.Guterres agreed there was a climate "leadership gap" but said overshooting 1.5C "is not surrender".

title: Netflix shares drop on slowing engagement and revenue growth
description: Netflix shares fell after its latest earnings failed to cheer investors as the streaming giant faces mounting competition and reportedly plans to cut around 1,000 jobs.
content: Netflix stock dropped more than 5% on Tuesday after its quarterly earnings release failed to ease investor concerns about a slowdown in viewer engagement and revenue growth."We know there’s some investor concern about our view hours growth," the company said in a letter to investors, referring to how the company measures engagement, and added that it was "confident" it could accelerate that growth.The California-based streaming giant has struggled to meet investor expectations for several quarters as it faces competition from other streamers, gaming and sports.Netflix "has underperformed significantly over the last 6-12 months" and investors are concerned "about soft engagement trends, decelerating revenue growth, a slower margin expansion outlook, and most recently content executive leadership changes," John Belton, a portfolio manager at Gabelli Funds, told AFP in a statement.In its third quarter ending in September, Netflix recorded $12.87 billion (€11.09bn) in revenue and $3.7 billion (€3.19bn) in net income, above investor expectations, according to FactSet.It did not provide overall figures for subscriber view hours in the quarter, but noted that in India the metric increased 24% compared to the same period last year.In July, Netflix said subscribers spent 97 billion hours watching content in the first half of the year, a 2% increase over the first half of 2025.It stopped reporting subscriber numbers in the first half of 2025.But the company touted growth outside the US while acknowledging challenges stateside."We do need better execution in the US. Our content around the world is largely working," co-CEO Ted Sarandos told investors on an analyst call on Tuesday, highlighting engagement, subscribers, revenue and profits across Latin America, Europe and Asia."The US is also working. It's just not growing as fast as it could or as fast as we'd like," Sarandos continued.Job cutsThe company will also reportedly cut around 6% of its workforce, or 1,000 jobs, according to media reports.Among them were seven high-level employees in charge of television deals and content, The Hollywood Reporter reported last week.The company also recently replaced chief content officer Bela Bajaria, who oversaw popular shows including Stranger Things, Bridgerton and Squid Game, in addition to pushing the company's live entertainment strategy, according to CNBC.Netflix appointed former Disney executive Peter Rice as its new content chief."Peter Rice understands talent relations, and in a competitive market, creative talent have choices of where they want to work," Sarandos said on the call on Tuesday.Diverse formatsCompetition from other streamers has forced Netflix to work harder to attract and retain both paid and ad-supported members.The company has increasingly dipped into live sports — with agreements to stream major events like the Olympics and World Cup — in addition to gaming and shorter-form content. The NFL and WWE are also on board to stream live events.In the US, it reached 7.8% of streaming television viewers in July compared to YouTube's 14.2%, a record for the Google-owned site, according to media analytics firm Nielsen.The World Cup lifted overall television viewership in July, according to Nielsen."It's really important to remember, roughly 95% of our spend and nearly all of our revenue is focused on that core, where we see a long runway for future growth," Sarandos said on Tuesday's call, emphasising its commitment to traditional television and film content.The company also missed expectations on advertising revenue growth."We are currently a bit behind our aggressive target for the year. We're still growing" on advertising, nonetheless, co-CEO Greg Peters said on the call."We see the benefits when we continue to roll out other products like new ad formats, which help with our growth," Peters added.

title: What is Spain’s DANA weather phenomenon and is climate change making it worse?
description: A DANA caused the deadly flooding in Valencia in 2024 which killed 200 people.
content: A storm in eastern Spain has killed five people and left cars and streets submerged in water, and the DANA weather system is behind it.Storm Adam dumped 700 litres of rain per square metre in just 24 hours in some areas of the Valencia region. Floodwaters swept away parked cars, submerged roads and cut off residents, some of whom had to be airlifted to safety by emergency crews.The coastal resort of Oliva was one of the areas worst hit by Sunday night’s storms. A 79-year-old woman was found dead in her home, while a man suffered a fatal heart attack at a local campsite. The third victim was a man who drowned while swimming at a beach in Sagunto. Firefighters in neighbouring Catalonia also reported the death of a woman who fell into a rain-swollen stream.Storm Adam is reminiscent of the sudden downpours that devastated Valencia in 2024, when some areas saw a year’s worth of rain in just 24 hours. 200 people lost their lives, making it one of the worst flood-related disasters in Europe since the late-1960s and the worst in Spain for many decades.The government came under heavy criticism for the lack of warnings to the public about what was to come. Thankfully they appear to have learnt their lesson: warnings were sent to mobile phones before Storm Adam hit, urging people to avoid travelling, stay away from rivers and ravines, and seek shelter on higher ground or on the upper floors of buildings.The 2024 storm introduced many Europeans to a weather phenomenon that often hits Spain: DANA. What is it and is it becoming more deadly as the climate warms up?What is a DANA? DANA stands for ‘Depresión Aislada en Niveles Altos’. It’s not easy to translate into English but it essentially means periods of heavy rain, stormy weather and a sudden drop in temperatures. The bigger the temperature difference, the bigger the storm. This is why the worst DANAs are usually at the end of summer in September and October, and are more likely to happen in parts of southern and eastern Spain.Put simply a DANA is a very intense wind current that forms when it breaks away from a polar jet, a sort of pocket of cold air surrounded by warmer air that can move around and cause extreme weather. It’s the meeting of hot and cold air fronts causing extreme weather.Southeastern Spain is particularly vulnerable to DANAs because it’s where the Atlantic and Mediterranean meet, meaning that cold air fronts can meet warm air fronts at certain times of year.
