It’s also an area where mountains favour the formation of storm clouds and therefore rainfall.DANA is increasingly used in everyday language in SpainSome Spanish people now use the term DANA to refer to a big storm, but this hasn’t always been the case.For many years Spaniards have used the phrase ‘gota fría’, literally meaning ‘cold drop’, The Local Spain explains. But as technology has advanced, and it has become easier to predict and understand the weather, meteorologists say that DANA is a more useful term because it’s more specific. On its website, Spain’s meteorological agency Aemet explains that: “The term gota frìa is a relatively old concept and has been superseded over the years. New ways of understanding tropospheric processes and new observational tools have made us revise and redefine the ideas linked to these isolated pockets of cold air at higher levels.“We believe that the concept of DANA, which we associate with the Anglo-Saxon term ‘cut-off low’, is more accurate and realistic than that of gota fría. As the concept of a gota fría is not very precise and incomplete, it is understood that it should be replaced by a more modern one.”Is climate change making DANAs worse?The Valencia floods in 2024 made worldwide news, with many shocked by the scale of loss and devastation in a wealthy European country. Much analysis followed, with climate scientists asking what role global warming played. It was confirmed that a DANA was to blame and that global warming very likely made it worse. “No doubt about it, these explosive downpours were intensified by climate change,” Dr Friederike Otto, lead of World Weather Attribution at the Centre for Environmental Policy, Imperial College London, said in 2024.The floods were caused by a ‘cut-off low pressure storm system’ that had migrated from an unusually wavy, stalled jet stream. This system then got stuck over the region, pouring down a year’s worth of rain in eight hours.Unusually warm sea surface temperatures, made much more likely by human-caused climate change, and our warming atmosphere, however, directly impact how much rain these storms can hold. The ground in many parts of eastern and southern Spain had also been left less able to effectively absorb rainwater following severe drought.A rapid partial analysis done by Dr Otto’s group of international scientists suggested that human-caused climate change made Spain’s rainfall around 12 per cent heavier. It also found that the weather event the region experienced was twice as likely.Though it isn’t a full, detailed attribution study, they said climate change is the most likely explanation for the extreme downpours.“With every fraction of a degree of fossil fuel warming, the atmosphere can hold more moisture, leading to heavier bursts of rainfall. These deadly floods are yet another reminder of how dangerous climate change has already become at just 1.3°C of warming,” Otto adds.

title: Elon Musk backs SpaceX-Tesla merger as rocket firm turns profit
description: Elon Musk has signalled his support for a potential merger between SpaceX and Tesla, as SpaceX reported a sharp rise in revenue and its first quarterly profit since going public.
content: Elon Musk said on Tuesday that he would back a merger of SpaceX and Tesla, as his rocket and AI company reported its first quarterly profit since going public, driven by deals to rent out computing power to AI firms.Asked about a possible tie-up on a call with analysts, Musk said he felt he was “tap dancing through a minefield”, but that a combination would be “a good idea”.Shares in SpaceX shot up nearly 5% in after-hours trading following the comments.Musk said special committees of independent directors at both SpaceX and Tesla had been established to study the idea at the request of shareholders.He added that he could not take part in their talks because he had a conflict of interest.Musk is chief executive of both companies and also serves as chairman and chief technology officer of SpaceX.He owned 48.4% of SpaceX as of 30 June, according to a regulatory filing, and controls more than 82% of its voting power through shares carrying enhanced voting rights.He holds about 20% of Tesla.The committees have not agreed on the terms of any deal, and there is no guarantee they will, Musk said, cautioning that it would be overstating the position to treat a merger as a certainty.Any deal would need the backing of a majority of all Tesla shares, not just those voted, which Musk called “quite a high hurdle”.He said the two companies could benefit from working together on AI software, chip design, robotics and space-based computing.His remarks came after SpaceX posted net income of $4.4 billion (€3.8bn) for the July–September period, compared with a loss of $1.1 billion (€0.95bn) a year earlier.Revenue jumped 161% to $14.6 billion (€12.6bn). The quarterly results follow a bumpy start on Wall Street.SpaceX began trading on the Nasdaq on 12 June after an IPO priced at $135 a share that raised about $85.7 billion (€73.9bn).Its first earnings report as a listed company showed second-quarter revenue of $7.8 billion (€6.7bn) and a net loss of $541 million (€466m).The AI division, which SpaceX now calls “Super Intelligence”, drove the turnaround. Super Intelligence is US President Donald Trump's preferred term for AI.The unit's revenue rose more than ninefold from a year earlier to $7.6 billion (€6.6bn), overtaking the Starlink satellite internet business as the company's largest source of sales.Cloud computingSpaceX credited new cloud services agreements, wider adoption of its Grok chatbot and its acquisition of Cursor, an artificial intelligence coding start-up.SpaceX's cloud customers include Anthropic, which agreed in May to pay nearly $45 billion (€38.8bn) over three years for computing power at SpaceX's Colossus data centres.Google signed on in June, agreeing to pay $920 million (€793m) a month from October through June 2029.The AI unit reported an operating profit of $431 million (€371m), compared with a loss of $1.7 billion (€1.5bn) a year earlier.As with other AI companies, spending remains heavy.SpaceX invested $19.6 billion (€16.9bn) in the quarter, of which $16.4 billion (€14.1bn) was invested in AI, bringing capital spending for the first nine months of the year to $48 billion (€41.4bn).Its computing capacity reached 1.7 gigawatts, up from 0.6 gigawatts a year earlier.Musk said he was “fairly confident” that SpaceX could bring an additional 10 gigawatts of computing capacity online in 2027.That would come on top of the approximately 2.5 to 3.0 gigawatts it expects to have running by the end of this year.He added that power, cooling and electrical equipment were “somewhat of a limiting factor”.Revenue at the Starlink satellite internet unit grew 69% to $5.2 billion (€4.5bn), and consumer subscribers reached 13.6 million.Average monthly revenue per consumer, however, fell to $69 (€59) from $83 (€72) a year earlier.SpaceX also completed the first revenue-generating flight of Starship, the giant rocket central to Musk's Mars ambitions and to deploying satellites at scale.The flight carried 26 next-generation Starlink satellites into orbit.

title: Alberta’s “no” to separation gives Carney a boost as Trump pressure unites Canadians
description: Roughly three in four voters rejected starting a path toward separation, as Trump’s trade war and annexation threats push Canadians closer together.
content: Voters in Alberta, Canada’s oil-rich province, on Tuesday overwhelmingly chose to remain in the country, giving Prime Minister Mark Carney a boost in his push for national unity as US President Donald Trump’s trade war and annexation threats rally Canadians around their flag.With about 90% of voting areas counted, 75% backed staying in Canada, according to unofficial results from Elections Alberta.“Don’t mess with Canada. President Trump is watching this,” said Thomas Lukaszuk, a former Alberta deputy premier who led the Forever Canadian campaign against separation.The referendum was not a direct vote on independence. A “yes” result would have set Alberta on a path toward a later vote on leaving Canada.Carney: “A great result for Canada”“It’s a great result for Canada that Albertans have chosen unity,” Carney told reporters in Ottawa before a Cabinet meeting on Tuesday.He argued that the quarter of voters who supported starting the separation process did not all necessarily want independence. In his view, only a smaller “hard core” favours leaving. Some voters have said they backed the question to send Ottawa a message rather than to break away.Carney said he spoke with Alberta Premier Danielle Smith on Tuesday morning about the results and about closer federal-provincial cooperation, including on immigration.Some voters said they backed the separation question without wanting Alberta to leave. Edmonton voter Shawn Campbell said he voted to begin the process to send a message: “It sends a message to Ottawa that Albertans are not happy.”Others criticised the vote itself. Dave Malka, 59, of Edmonton, objected to spending money on a “referendum on a referendum” rather than on healthcare. With Trump threatening Canada, he said, “It seems to be happening at the absolute worst time when we should be united. Instead, we’re fighting among ourselves.”If you need to cut for length, drop Malka’s healthcare point and keep only the Campbell quote. If you’re running long-form, the full section is fine, and you can restore Khowaja.Alberta premier rules out another referendumIn a televised address Tuesday night, Smith welcomed the outcome and promised not to call another separation referendum while she is premier.“Yesterday, Albertans voted overwhelmingly in favour of remaining a province of Canada,” Smith said. “The voter turnout was historic and a powerful testimony of the passion Albertans feel for our country and our province.”She said Alberta would keep pushing Ottawa for more provincial autonomy, but that disputes would be resolved through Canada’s political and legal institutions, not through separation.Thomas Lukaszuk, a former Alberta deputy premier who led the Forever Canadian campaign against separation, told supporters: “Don’t mess with Canada. President Trump is watching this.”Separatists concede defeat, but not the causeMeanwhile, Alberta separatist organiser David Parker acknowledged the scale of the loss.“Independence feels far away, and we should not pretend this was not a defeat,” he wrote on social media.Still, separatist leaders insisted they would carry on. At a referendum-night gathering at an Edmonton restaurant, the crowd fell silent as the results came in.“We’re not going anywhere,” said Jeff Rath of the Alberta Prosperity Project. “We’ve dominated the conversation in the last year. We’ve been educating Albertans on the benefits of independence, and we’re going to continue moving forward.”Rath had said before the vote that he would be thrilled with 30% support. He also said he wanted Smith removed as leader of the United Conservative Party (UCP) and believed the party could splinter, possibly producing a new pro-independence party.From fringe cause to lasting movementAlberta is home to the world’s fourth-largest proven oil reserves. It is cowboy country and a conservative stronghold, with a political culture that has long had more in common with the American West than with much of Canada. Resentment toward the federal government in Ottawa runs deep, but it has not traditionally translated into broad support for independence.Former Premier Jason Kenney noted that separatist parties historically drew only 1% or 2% of the vote. He said anger over COVID-19 restrictions helped mobilise activists who later embraced the separatist cause.Trump’s trade war and his threats to make Canada the 51st U.S. state have helped Carney build support in Alberta, a province where Liberal prime ministers have historically been unpopular.

title: 'Time to make a deal,' Trump tells Zelenskyy as he complains US has got 'nothing back' from Ukraine
description: Trump's comments came shortly after Zelenskyy met with a US delegation headed by special envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo.
content: US President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that he wanted his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelenskyy to "make a deal" with Russia as he complained that the United States had received "nothing back" for its support for Kyiv.Speaking to the media in the White House, Trump said: "We want Zelenskyy to make a deal. He can make a deal.""He could have made a deal two years ago when we had our little chat in the Oval Office," he continued, seemingly referencing the pair's heated exchange during a meeting in early 2025. "He's going to have to want to make a deal, because I don't think his people are going to stand for it any longer."Zelenskyy and Trump have endured a volatile relationship since the US president began his second term in January last year, but it has soured further in recent weeks after Trump struck a diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin and criticised the impact of Ukrainian strikes on Russia's energy sector on global fuel prices.On Tuesday, Trump - who is gearing up for key midterm elections to determine the make-up of Congress for his final two years in office - seemed to pin the blame for the ongoing war on Zelenskyy, repeatedly saying he had had the opportunity to make a deal and that the US had got nothing in return for its help "except grief, death," and "tremendous monetary loss.""We have given tremendous amounts to Ukraine; we've got nothing back. Other than high diesel," Trump added. "The American taxpayers are tired of it.""It's time to make a deal," he said.Zelenskyy's Oslo talksTrump's comments came shortly after Zelenskyy met with a US delegation headed by special envoy Steve Witkoff, who is scheduled to travel to Russia for a meeting with Putin on Wednesday.Following the talks in Oslo, which also involved Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, Zelenskyy had appeared relatively positive, telling journalists he had recently held a constructive call with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and calling for a trilateral meeting with Trump and Putin.Zelenskyy also addressed reported restrictions on US intelligence sharing during a press conference with the Nordic leaders, saying he was "thankful" that "intelligence works now.""I'm speaking about early warning, what is very important for our people, for children, adults, civilians, because we can hear when ballistic is coming," he said.In a post on social media later in the evening, Zelenskyy added: "It was constructive because all of us want peace – Ukraine, Europe, the United States. And we will see what happens tomorrow."

title: Investment summit: German government strikes AI deal with Nvidia
description: At the "Invest in Germany" summit in Berlin, the federal government, despite early negative headlines, secured a partnership with AI firm Nvidia and new investment from Amazon.
content: Shortly before the investment summit in Berlin, Nvidia boss Jensen Huang delivered a sharp slap in the face to Germany. He said it pains him to see how far this economically advanced country has fallen behind. And the 63-year-old CEO of the world's most valuable company gave what he sees as left-behind Germany some blunt advice: "Just get to work!" ("Just get on with your work!")Yet Jensen Huang evidently still believes in Germany, because at a fireside chat with Chancellor Friedrich Merz, a crucial AI deal was agreed, according to media reports. As first reported by Handelsblatt, the federal government intends to contribute a nine-figure sum in euros to the cooperation.The combination of German engineering expertise and cutting-edge AI technology is expected to give Germany's economic base lasting strength, Merz and Huang stressed.In total, the chancellor said, the investment summit in Berlin produced commitments worth 800 billion euros up to 2028. Some 200 company bosses gathered for the meeting.Amazon to invest 16 billion euros in GermanyAnother US corporation, internet giant Amazon, plans to invest around 16 billion euros in Germany in 2027, as was also announced at the investment summit in Berlin. A third of the money is to be channelled into expanding data centres for Amazon's cloud provider AWS.According to Amazon, around 3,000 employees already work in Germany for its cloud services subsidiary AWS. The planned 4.8 billion euros for AWS in Germany will be invested primarily in the Frankfurt am Main area.Businesses urged to make their data available to AINvidia says it invested almost a billion dollars in Germany in 2025. The US corporation, headquartered in California, holds stakes in numerous German start-ups and companies. Huang repeatedly stresses that data must be seen as a national resource, which should not be exported but used to build a "national intelligence".Around a dozen German companies are expected to take part in the project with Nvidia, which is being supported by the federal government, including Siemens, Audi and AI start-up Black Forest Labs from Freiburg im Breisgau. Nvidia is already working with Siemens in Erlangen on device production.Chancellor Merz called on companies in Germany to open up their industrial data to artificial intelligence, in order to safeguard the competitiveness of sectors such as the car industry. Maintaining Germany's industrial base is, the CDU leader argued, a crucial advantage over other economies.Did Friedrich Merz manage to convince leather-jacket fan Jensen Huang with his comments about traditional German virtues?In Berlin the chancellor actually declared: "Germans are considered hard-working, go to bed early and get up before sunrise. (...) On holiday we are the first on the beach and lay out our towels even before breakfast. And when we agree on delivery dates, we stick to them."Most recently, the outlook for the German economy has brightened somewhat. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) now expects growth of 1.3 percent in Germany in 2026, after previously forecasting just 0.7 percent. Whether a further upswing will materialise thanks to investments by US tech giants remains to be seen.

title: France's Macron begins state visit to Qatar as part of wider Gulf tour
description: Qatar welcomed the French president with full state honours on his arrival in Doha as the two countries are strengthening their strategic ties. Facing protests at home, Macron is seeking energy deals with Gulf partners to help ease fuel prices in France, but also contributing to regional stability.
content: Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani welcomed French President Emmanuel Macron with full state honours, including cannon salvos and a cavalry procession, as he began his two-day state visit to the Gulf nation on Tuesday.After the official welcome ceremony, the two leaders met at Lusail Palace to discuss strengthening strategic ties between France and Qatar, including energy security, defence and regional stability, as well as investments and cooperation in multiple fields.Macron was received at Hamad International Airport by Qatar’s Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of State for Defence Affairs, Sheikh Saoud bin Abdulrahman bin Hassan Al Thani, after fighter jets escorted his plane on arrival as part of the state visit honours, followed by a state motorcade procession through Doha towards Lusail.Macron's state visit to Qatar concludes his regional Gulf tour to develop strategic partnerships also with the United Arab Emirates, Kuwait and Bahrain, where the French leader secured pledges of additional energy supplies from Gulf partners.The tour has already produced commitments for additional diesel. The French presidency said France had secured pledges for an extra 200,000 tonnes a month from the UAE and Bahrain, around 100,000 tonnes from each.Including supplies from Saudi Arabia, the commitments totalled 295,000 tonnes a month, equivalent to just over 10% of French consumption, the Élysée said.In a speech to the French nation on Sunday after a weekend of violent protests that engulfed France, Macron said he would travel to the Gulf countries to secure France’s energy supplies and to address the grievances over fuel prices and the cost of living, while his government worked with fuel distributors to ensure those efforts translated into lower prices for consumers.Energy security and regional tiesMacron is accompanied by French business leaders including the chief executives of France's largest energy companies, TotalEnergies and Engie. TotalEnergies already has substantial interests in Qatar, including a partnership with QatarEnergy in the North Field East LNG expansion project, one of the world's largest.Qatar’s foreign ministry said Tuesday’s talks would be followed by a strategic dialogue on Wednesday to discuss "many regional matters of mutual concern,” covering energy, the economy, investment and defence.Speaking at a briefing in Doha, the ministry’s director of media and communication, Ibrahim bin Sultan Al Hashmi, described France as a friend and ally and underlined its position during the ongoing regional crisis.France was among Qatar's main defenders during the Iran war, securing the Gulf country's air defence with fighter jets and other capabilities and is now seeking to develop additional defence ties.The visit also builds on wider investment ties. During the Emir’s 2024 state visit to France, Qatar pledged €10 billion in investment across sectors including energy transition, artificial intelligence, aerospace, and healthcare.

title: Power outage hits Google Cloud services disrupting UK banks
description: A power outage at a Google Cloud data centre in London caused serious network disruptions to its services Tuesday, the US tech giant said. The issue has since been "mitigated" for "most" customers, it added later.
content: A power outage at a Google Cloud data centre near London caused serious failures to services on Tuesday, the US technology giant said, as several UK banks reported widespread disruptions.Google said in a service update that its Cloud services suffered an outage "due to a power event."The company has since announced that the issue had been "mitigated" for "most" customers, with a "very small number" still experiencing issues.Services for the digital bank Revolut, including withdrawals from ATMs, bank transfers and bank card top-ups, were disrupted, which a source close to the matter attributed to the Google Cloud failures.UK lenders Lloyds and HSBC also confirmed customers were facing issues with their banking services.Google said the incident began at 0608 GMT on Tuesday."Multiple Google Cloud services are experiencing elevated errors and intermittent network failures in europe-west2 region," Google said in an earlier update, referring to its London data centre.Internet service tracker Downdetector indicated that hundreds of reports had been made of problems affecting other businesses, including the property website Rightmove and the Royal Mail postal service.Lloyds said it was aware "some customers are having issues with our app and online banking".HSBC confirmed that customers were experiencing "difficulties accessing our services" and said that it would "monitor the situation, which is also affecting other organisations".A Revolut spokesperson said the bank was "working to fix the issue since it was identified" and offered its apologies "to anyone affected and for any inconvenience caused"."We can confirm that all our customers' money and data are safe," the spokesperson added in a statement.

title: Qatar revamped its entire defence system in six hours, intelligence chief reveals
description: At Doha’s Global Security Forum, Qatar’s head of intelligence revealed how the war with Iran forced the Gulf country to urgently redeploy its defensive assets, while the US ambassador to Turkey offered new insights into a fundamental shift in Washington's presence in the Middle East.
content: In a rare public appearance, Qatar’s head of the Intelligence and Security Authority Brigadier General Khalid Mohammed Al-Nuaimi revealed how Qatar took the dramatic decision to redeploy its entire defensive systems in just six hours to counter Iran's war threats.Addressing the Global Security Forum in Doha on Tuesday, Al-Nuaimi said the redeployment was “unprecedented and successful”, based on eight months of adapting Qatar’s forces, defence capabilities, and military doctrine, which had been built for a totally different threat landscape.⁠ ⁠When asked about Qatar’s response to countering drones during the war, Qatar’s head of Intelligence replied that the six-hour overhaul was based on fast-moving changes to Qatar’s defence systems, both at concept level, but also in the allocation of defence assets.“We adapted. we redeployed and we did it within six hours,” Al-Nuaimi revealed, adding that “we were caught off guard, yet we adapted rapidly, out of sheer necessity.”Also during the Global Security Forum, Qatar’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Dr Majed al-Ansari said the Qatar-mediated US-Iran negotiations “are ongoing and we are seeing engagement from both parties.”“The fact that we are not hearing about it is a good sign that we are doing our job properly,” the Qatari diplomat added amid the rising tensions and concerns that the Iran war may restart.Washington's fundamental shift in the Middle EastIn addressing those worrying concerns, US ambassador to Turkey and Special Presidential Envoy for Syria and Iraq Tom Barrack told the forum that "America wants a peace deal” which would be based on “ceasefire in the straits” as well as a focus on “easing the pain on the Iranian people”."Prosperity is the only answer," Barrack underlined as a way out of the current standoff, adding that "we don’t need a reboot" of the previous US-Iran peace memorandum.He identified the obstacle to a deal as a “lack of trust.”“What has happened from the beginning of these discussions and negotiations is a lack of trust," Barrack explained, which comes down to the fact that the "IRGC does not trust the US. And the US does not trust IRGC."The US envoy said he did not know if the Iran war was a mistake but admitted that it had “unintended consequences” and that US President Donald Trump is a "no forever wars president."Barrack told the forum in Qatar that the US will not leave the Middle East, even if in the region “what everybody is saying: OK, I cannot rely on America to solve all my problems,” explaining that “the bargain is not to control, but to not leave. We are not leaving.”"America is the guarantor to the world for the last 80 years and it is no longer there," the US diplomat said, explaining that "what is happening in this administration is not an abandonment, it is a message for realignment."The US envoy appeared to contradict one of the US administration’s declared goals in launching the Iran war, which was regime change in Tehran.Barrack spoke broadly about how the US pursued 23 regime changes across the Middle East and concluded that "every time we try and intervene, change the person or the regime, it seems to have been a mistake."Instead, he said, the US’ goal is to "bring everybody, put them in a tent, give them coffee, put the guns and daggers on the table, and let’s figure something else out," through “patience, presence, dialogue."In this context, the top US diplomat also commented on the escalating tensions between Israel and Turkey, saying that "my belief is Israel is way too smart to actually pick a real fight with Turkey. I don’t think Israel wants that, I know Turkey does not want that."'Houthis are here to stay,' former MI6 chief saysMeanwhile at the forum, Qatar’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Dr al-Ansari also reiterated his country’s position on Yemen that alongside the other Gulf nations “Qatar is supporting our brothers in Saudi Arabia in defending their sovereignty against this attack.”Also commenting on the Yemen war, the former head of the UK’s foreign intelligence agency MI6 Sir John Sawers told the Doha Global Security Forum that “the Houthis are here to stay."They are not going to be defeated, and they are going to remain in control of a large part of Yemen for the foreseeable future," Sawers said."The Houthis have got their own national Yemen agenda," he explained, adding that the group "exposed the limited options that Saudi Arabia has in terms of dealing with" them over the last 10 years, as their efforts "to sustain an alternative government (in Yemen) have not been successful over the last 10 years."

title: Why is the European Union turning up the heat on the Arctic?
description: The EU’s revamped Arctic strategy puts security at its core, citing growing Russian and Chinese activity in the region. It focuses on ramping up European security capabilities, military mobility with NATO, icebreakers, satellite surveillance, and a maritime security hub.
content: The European Union presented its revamped Arctic strategy on Tuesday, spelling out how much the region has grown in importance for the bloc’s geopolitical priorities, particularly in areas such as security, energy, trade and connectivity.Melting ice caused by climate change has long been turning the Arctic into a new arena for geopolitical competition, as new trade routes open, natural resources become accessible and military deployments become increasingly feasible.“Since our previous Arctic strategy in 2021, we face a much harsher security environment. The Arctic is no longer insulated from the world’s geopolitical tensions. Our updated Arctic strategy reflects this new reality by putting security firmly at its core,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said at the press conference presenting the initiative.In a major shift from the previous strategy, Brussels now recognises that “multilateral cooperation remains indispensable, but it can no longer be the sole foundation of the European Union’s Arctic approach.”In other words, the bloc no longer sees the Arctic merely as a place to promote cooperation. It treats it as part of Europe’s strategic neighbourhood, where cooperation with partners must go hand in hand with the ability to protect its own interests.Security and defenceThe strategy sets out a new political framework for regional policy, the Northern Neighbourhood. It brings together strategic partners such as Norway, Iceland, Canada, the UK and the US, with regular summits planned to discuss common issues.Last November, the European Parliament already adopted an Arctic recommendation calling for a more security-oriented EU policy and closer EU-NATO cooperation, with particular attention to Russian military expansion and scrutiny of Chinese strategic activity.“Moscow has reopened Soviet-era bases and is testing new weapons in the region,” Kallas said. “China’s strategic ambitions in the High North are also growing. Beijing’s investments in ports, minerals and critical infrastructure need careful scrutiny.”Yet while recognised as a partner, Washington has itself been a key factor in the EU’s recalibration, notably after US President Donald Trump’s stated ambition to annex Greenland, which later led to an agreement with Denmark and Greenland.“When we see that sovereignty, territorial integrity and the rules that have underpinned stability in the region can no longer be taken for granted. We have to act and change our strategic posture and, together with like-minded partners, stand up to these values,” Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said at the press conference.In response to the deteriorating security landscape, the strategy vows to strengthen the EU’s strategic capabilities, notably by expanding its icebreaker fleet and launching a pilot project on satellite-based surveillance.Cooperation with NATO is meant to improve the logistics of military mobility, focusing on “rapid large-scale deployment of troops in and across the Arctic, when needed, as well as the reinforcement of west-east transport links in the European Arctic and to the Baltic Sea.”Trade routesOpening Arctic trade routes would give the EU a shorter alternative for reaching Asian markets, bypassing chokepoints such as the Suez Canal and the Red Sea.Russia, meanwhile, has invested in infrastructure along the Northern Sea Route, which runs along its Arctic coast, while China promotes its “Polar Silk Road” as part of its broader connectivity ambitions.The Russian and Chinese presence is seen as a potential threat to the sovereign rights of countries in the region and could escalate tensions, prompting the EU to commit “to ensure that freedom of navigation is preserved on all trade routes.”To that end, the EU plans to develop a maritime security hub with partner countries. It would facilitate information sharing on issues such as tracking Russia’s shadow fleet, detecting illegal fishing and marine pollution, and strengthening situational awareness.Brussels also pledges to enforce the safety and environmental standards of the Polar Code, a binding international regulatory framework, using tools such as inspections to ensure a level playing field for vessels transiting the region.The strategy also envisages a foresight study on Arctic shipping routes to anticipate traffic flows, emerging maritime corridors and fleet requirements.Energy securityCommission officials made clear that Brussels does not intend to change its 2021 position: the bloc will not drill for hydrocarbons in the Arctic nor will it buy oil and gas from new developments in the region."The EU’s position on drilling in the Arctic remains the same, and it’s very clear: oil, coal and gas must stay in the ground," Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen said.Brussels argued that new drilling would neither meet the bloc's energy-security needs nor offer a convincing economic case. Still, the mention of a moratorium, strongly opposed by Norway even if non-binding, was softened from the final version,“Even if there were to be development, exploration, and even drilling activities in the Arctic, it will take several years up to a decade easily to get that out of the ground,” one Commission official said, arguing that the bloc would not need those resources by then.Conversely, the Commission wants to develop the Arctic’s potential for renewable energy, including wind, hydropower, geothermal power and renewable hydrogen. But EU officials acknowledged that producing clean energy is only part of the challenge.Electricity must either be used locally or connected to markets capable of absorbing it; hence, the strategy points to stronger electricity connections between Finland and Sweden.The Aurora power line, inaugurated in January 2026, is already linking the two countries’ electricity grids, with further work envisaged to deepen electricity-market integration and ease grid bottlenecks.Connectivity infrastructureConnectivity is another major pillar of the EU’s Arctic policy. The bloc has been trying to diversify its subsea cable infrastructure and avoid single points of failure through the Far North Fibre, which would link Europe, Greenland and Canada to east Asian countries.This network is meant to bring high-speed broadband to remote indigenous towns and also serve as a vital redundant data route for mainland Europe, ensuring more secure data sharing and telecommunications.Critical infrastructure has also become a prime target in a hybrid campaign that Russia has been escalating in recent weeks, including attacks on submarine infrastructure such as undersea cables.According to Reuters, a joint NATO operation last month disrupted a Russian exercise testing new deep-sea submarine capabilities designed to disable undersea cables, with the aim of cutting the connection between mainland Norway and the Svalbard archipelago.The strategy therefore plans an Arctic cable hub to protect and support the repair of submarine cables in the North Atlantic and Arctic, following the model used in the Mediterranean and the Baltic Sea.Brussels is fast-tracking Rail Nordica — a massive engineering project to migrate northern Finland's railway network to the standardised pan-European track gauge.Critical raw materialsThe Arctic in general, and Greenland in particular, holds deposits of minerals considered critical for Europe’s clean-energy transition, batteries and defence industry, including rare earths, graphite and lithium.Critical raw materials projects are under way in Norway, Finland and Sweden, which benefit from facilitated conditions such as access to finance and faster permitting because of their strategic relevance.At the same time, “the EU will continue to advocate against deep-sea mining until the scientific gaps on deep-sea ecosystems are properly filled, until it can be demonstrated that no harmful effects arise from deep-sea mining,” the strategy reads.

title: Kaja Kallas accuses the US of pushing Ukraine to 'surrender on Putin's terms'
description: "American negotiators have been trying to push Ukraine into surrender for almost two years," Kaja Kallas said amid rising EU-US tensions.
content: High Representative Kaja Kallas has sharply accused the United States of pressuring Ukraine to capitulate on terms exclusively favourable to Russian President Vladimir Putin, just as a new round of peace talks unfolded in Oslo, Norway."American negotiators have been trying to push Ukraine into surrender for already almost two years, one and a half years now," she told the European Parliament on Tuesday."Why Ukraine hasn't surrendered on Putin's terms is because Europe has been supporting Ukraine."Kallas also argued that European presence was necessary at the negotiating table to "balance" the positions embraced by the White House, which have become increasingly tilted to Moscow's interests.Relations between the US and Europe have worsened since US President Donald Trump struck a diesel supply deal with Putin and eased sanctions until April 2027 without obtaining any Russian concessions in return.Trump has called for new elections in Ukraine, which are barred during wartime, and complained that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was "more difficult to deal with" than Putin. Zelenskyy, in turn, said he feels betrayed by Trump."I believe steps have been taken to convince Ukraine to capitulate," Zelenskyy told Bloomberg in a recent interview.Kallas raised the alarm about the latest developments as she addressed the Parliament in Strasbourg, where several MEPs complained Europe lacked a peace strategy."That is not true," Kallas said, referring to a document she had presented to EU capitals with demands that Europe should expect Moscow to fulfil in a future settlement."If Russia is presenting their maximalist demands and requests, we should put our maximum demands on the table to balance these negotiations, and also to send a clear message to Russia that for all of those things that they are interested in – lifting sanctions – Europe needs to be around that table because they are European decisions.""We are not giving these things up for free because it is not only peace that could be there, but it's also that this peace is long-lasting and just," she added.Kallas accused Russia of endangering the security of the Black Sea with its armed blockade, weaponising food supplies and trying to trigger a global famine. Romania and Bulgaria have recently reported Russian drone strikes off their territorial waters.The High Representative also censured Moscow for refusing an energy ceasefire and ramping up its bombing campaign against Ukraine ahead of the winter season."Ukraine wants peace more than anybody because they have been under bombardment for already four years now, and the fifth year is going on," she said."And Europe wants peace. It is not right to say that we don't want peace. The only one who doesn't want peace is Russia. Let's be very clear-eyed about this."Kallas has been among Europe's loudest critics of Trump's turn to Moscow. Last week, she told Euronews the diesel deal was a gift to Putin.Brussels insists that despite growing disagreements, engagement with the US should continue to influence the peace process and defend Ukraine's interests.Senior officials from the European Commission, NATO, Germany, France, the United Kingdom and Poland flew to Oslo on Tuesday to take part in the latest round of talks.

title: How Turkey and Uzbekistan are preparing their cities for a changing climate
description: From Turkey’s push to make its cities and energy systems more resilient to a new city rising outside Tashkent, planners are changing how urban areas are built, powered and adapted to environmental pressures.
content: Cities are home to more than half of the world's population, concentrating people and infrastructure in places increasingly exposed to heat, flooding, drought and other climate-related pressures.In Turkey, resilience is being built into both the fabric of cities and the energy that powers them, from housing and infrastructure to the tracking of renewable electricity. In Uzbekistan, planners are working at two different scales: designing New Tashkent largely from the ground up while adapting the existing capital to a changing climate.Building resilience into Turkish citiesThe earthquakes that struck southern Turkey in February 2023 damaged or destroyed hundreds of thousands of homes and displaced millions of people. Reconstruction has since extended beyond housing to municipal infrastructure and essential services.Yasir Yılmaz, General Manager of Turkish property developer Emlak Konut, says large-scale rebuilding has extended beyond housing to wastewater infrastructure, streams and transport networks.“While rebuilding the cities and 450,000 homes, we've restored every city complete with its infrastructure and social amenities,” Yılmaz said, adding that special attention was also paid to the climate resilience of the buildings.Resilience also depends on the energy that powers those cities.EPİAŞ, Turkey’s energy market operator, runs the Renewable Energy Guarantees of Origin system, known as YEK-G. Its electronic certificates show that a corresponding amount of electricity was generated from renewable sources, with each certificate representing one megawatt-hour.The voluntary system uses blockchain technology to record information about renewable electricity from generation to consumption.Mustafa Aydin, Vice President of Energy Exchange Istanbul, points to electric vehicles as one application.“With the YEK-G certification system, we can prove that the electricity produced by renewable energy plants actually reaches consumption,” he said. Electricity used for charging can be matched with generation from solar, wind and hydropower.For Chris Mensah, Special Advisor to the Climate High-Level Champion, physical infrastructure and technology are only part of preparing cities for environmental risks.“The responsibility is not about whether it is the obligation of one or the other, but creating awareness, knowledge and teaching right from the beginning,” he said.Mensah argues that climate education should begin early, with schools helping people understand the risks their cities may face.Starting with a blank canvasMore than 3,000 kilometres away, a city is taking shape on the eastern edge of Uzbekistan's capital.Construction of New Tashkent began in 2023. While large parts remain building sites, the master plan provides for 2,000 hectares of green space and another 500 hectares of parks. Several major facilities, including a trigeneration plant and electrical substation, were commissioned in October 2026.Building a city from scratch allows decisions about water, vegetation and energy to be incorporated before residents arrive.That is particularly important for greenery. Trees can provide shade during Uzbekistan's hot summers, but maintaining vegetation creates its own demand for water.Saidazim Sharipov, Adviser to the Director for Urban Planning Projects at the New Tashkent Directorate, says species are being selected with local conditions in mind.“Particular attention has been given to trees that can withstand dry conditions and require less water,” Sharipov said. “Drip irrigation systems are being used to reduce water consumption.”The approach extends beyond irrigation. Sharipov says wastewater is due to be treated for reuse as technical water and for landscaping, while buildings are expected to collect rainwater or reuse treated wastewater on their grounds.Water requirements have also influenced the landscape. Planners are using locally adapted shrubs that require less irrigation than lawns, while canal beds have been lined to limit seepage, according to Sharipov.Heating and cooling a new cityNew Tashkent's energy infrastructure is being assembled while construction continues.Sharaf Rajabov, Deputy Director of the New Tashkent Directorate, says rooftop solar panels are being incorporated into projects across the development.The trigeneration plant, part of a group of new infrastructure projects in the city, is intended to provide heating and cooling through a centralised network.“In summer, the system provides hot water as well as chilled water for cooling homes. In winter, steam produced by the boiler plant is used to provide heating,” said Asiltürk Çakmak, the project's General Engineer.Some infrastructure is operating, while other elements remain under construction or at the planning stage. With much of New Tashkent yet to be occupied, many of these systems have not yet operated under the demands of a fully populated city.Finding space in the existing capitalThe situation is different inside Tashkent, where existing streets, buildings and neighbourhoods leave less freedom to redesign the urban landscape.More than 1.35 million trees and shrubs were planted across the capital between 2022 and 2026, according to Uzbekistan's ecology authorities. Further green belts are planned, including new areas in Bektemir district and along the Chirchiq River corridor.A new project in Bektemir shows what that process looks like on the ground.In spring 2026, a green belt covering 4.23 hectares was established there, according to Bekjon Egamov, Chief Specialist at the Tashkent City Department of Ecology. It contains 1,415 ornamental trees, watered using drip irrigation to reduce water use.Unlike New Tashkent, where green space can be planned before neighbourhoods are built, projects such as Bektemir have to find room for it within a city that is already there.

title: Uzbekistan expands transport links and eases travel rules to turn its tourism boom into economic gains
description: As international visitor numbers grow, Uzbekistan is introducing financial incentives for tourism businesses, expanding air and rail connections, and easing travel requirements. The reforms aim to attract investment, increase tourism revenue and create new economic opportunities across the country.
content: Uzbekistan welcomed a record 11.7 million international visitors in 2025, according to the National Statistics Committee, as the country continued to expand its tourism industry. UN Tourism data shows that international arrivals rose by 37% in the first quarter of 2026 compared with the same period in 2025, placing Uzbekistan among the world's five fastest-growing tourism destinations.The expansion is also reflected in the sector's economic performance. During the first seven months of 2026, the country received more than 7.7 million foreign visitors, an increase of 22.6% year on year. Tourism services exports, meaning earnings from services provided to international visitors, reached nearly €3.5 bn, according to the Tourism Committee.Behind these figures is a broader effort to strengthen tourism's contribution to the economy through financial incentives, improved transport connections, visa liberalisation and investment in visitor infrastructure.Financial incentives and tourism investmentFinancial support is becoming an important part of Uzbekistan's tourism strategy, with measures designed to encourage airlines to open new routes and help local businesses attract international visitors.Under measures announced for the 2026 Open Tourism Season, qualifying airlines opening new routes were offered subsidies of €89 for each foreign tourist brought into the country, alongside a 20% discount on airport services. Tour operators were also offered up to €4,460 for every 1,000 international visitors attracted from eligible overseas markets.Separate incentives support qualifying charter flights and selected tourism start-ups, while investment in accommodation continues to expand. New facilities added more than 22,000 beds across the country during the first seven months of 2026.The measures aim to stimulate private-sector activity and encourage businesses to develop new tourism markets, although their longer-term impact will depend on whether the additional demand becomes commercially sustainable.Expanding air and rail connectivitySamarkand International Airport offers an example of how infrastructure investment is supporting the sector's expansion.According to Dmitry Martynenko, the airport's Commercial Director, passenger traffic has tripled since 2022, supported by a new terminal, an open-skies policy and efforts to attract international airlines.In 2025, the airport handled a record 1.5 million passengers, around 10% more than the previous year. A total of 24 airlines operated flights to 30 destinations."We are now actively developing flights to China. We are also working on opening routes to Southeast Asia," Martynenko told Euronews.The airport has also introduced automated baggage handling systems, digital passenger services and a capsule hotel, reflecting efforts to improve the traveller experience and expand commercial services.Rail investment is another part of the country's transport strategy. The new Jaloliddin Manguberdi train has reduced the Tashkent–Khiva journey from 14 hours to seven and a half, making one of Uzbekistan's main historical destinations more accessible."Today, we are providing high-speed rail services to more than ten cities in Uzbekistan, and we plan to expand this network year by year," said Hikmatulla Rahmetov, First Deputy Chairman of Uzbekistan Railways.He added that one planned project is a dedicated high-speed passenger railway connecting Tashkent and Samarkand, designed for trains travelling at speeds of up to 300 km/h.Improved transport connections could encourage tourists to visit more destinations, supporting hotels, restaurants and other businesses beyond the main transport hubs.Visa reforms and new tourism marketsAlongside infrastructure development, Uzbekistan has been easing entry requirements and expanding international promotion.Citizens of more than 90 countries can enter without a visa for varying periods, while electronic visas are available to eligible travellers from other markets.The Tourism Committee is also promoting Uzbekistan through international exhibitions, roadshows and digital platforms, including Expedia and Trip.com.According to Oybek Hakimov, Adviser to the Chairman of the Tourism Committee on Strategic Planning and Information Analysis, the introduction of a reciprocal 30-day visa-free regime with China has been accompanied by substantial growth in visitor numbers."By the end of 2025, the number of tourists from China had increased more than sixfold compared with 2023," Hakimov said.The authorities are also seeking to diversify tourism beyond established Silk Road destinations. More than 50 tourism villages and neighbourhoods have been developed, alongside new mountain resorts and regional attractions.These initiatives could help distribute tourism spending more widely, creating opportunities for local accommodation providers, guides, craftspeople and small businesses.Improving services for international visitorsAs visitor numbers rise, service quality is becoming another important factor in the industry's competitiveness.For Romanian tourist Cezar Marksteiner-Ungureanu, who was visiting Uzbekistan for the first time, the experience challenged some of his expectations."I felt all the time very secure. I think security is my last problem in Uzbekistan," he told Euronews.However, he also pointed to shortcomings in the information available at some museums, highlighting areas where visitor services could improve.South Korean visitor Gown Yong Won was impressed by Khiva's preserved historical architecture and local hospitality."I've visited many historical sites in Europe and elsewhere, but I think this is the first time I've seen an entire city preserved as a historical site like this," he said.Turning growth into economic valueUzbekistan's tourism development strategy for 2026–2030 sets targets of attracting 20 million international visitors annually, increasing tourism's contribution to 7% of GDP and raising tourism services exports to $6 billion.Achieving these ambitions will depend on more than increasing arrival numbers. The economic impact will also be shaped by how long visitors stay, how much they spend and how effectively local businesses benefit.While financial incentives and infrastructure investment may help attract new visitors, maintaining growth will require commercially sustainable transport connections, competitive services and a wider range of tourism products.

title: Lionel Messi sparks euphoria in Oviedo ahead of Princess of Asturias award ceremony
description: The Argentinian footballer has arrived in Spain's Oviedo region with his wife Antonela Roccuzzo, greeting hundreds of fans awaiting him. This Friday he will receive the 2026 Princess of Asturias Award for Sports.
content: Leo Messi has landed in Oviedo, where on Friday night he will receive the 2026 Princess of Asturias Award for Sports, one of Spain's most prestigious prizes.The Argentine footballer arrived in the Asturian capital on Thursday, where hundreds of fans were waiting to welcome him. His visit has generated huge excitement far beyond his supporters.Messi reached the city at around 13:00, accompanied by his wife, Antonela Roccuzzo. He was greeted there by the director of the Princess of Asturias Foundation, Teresa Sanjurjo, to applause and the sound of bagpipes. The Inter Miami player also spent a few minutes with his fans, signing shirts and photographs.The anticipation surrounding his visit has also been evident in the programme of events scheduled ahead of the ceremony. Tickets for Messi’s meeting with young people and schoolchildren at Oviedo’s Palacio de los Deportes sold out in barely 13 minutes. The awards ceremony will take place this Friday at the Teatro Campoamor.The Argentine, who has collected 47 titles over the course of his career, has been honoured with the 2026 Princess of Asturias Award for Sports (source in Spanish) in recognition both of his sporting achievements and of his commitment to children.The jury has praised his talent, his career and his charitable work to improve disadvantaged children’s access to education and healthcare.

title: Volvo Cars announces 2,500 job cuts as it swings to quarterly loss
description: Chinese ownership has not shielded Volvo Cars from competition in China, as the Geely-owned carmaker steps up its turnaround efforts amid pressure from local rivals, US tariffs and the removal of EV incentives.
content: Sweden-based carmaker Volvo Cars said on Friday it would cut about 2,500 jobs worldwide, as US tariffs and strong competition from local brands in China pushed it into a third-quarter loss.The company, majority-owned by Chinese group Geely, reported revenue of 66.9 billion kronor (€6bn) for the third quarter, down nearly 23% from the same period last year.It swung to a net loss of 5.7 billion kronor (€513mn) for the quarter from a net profit of 4.5 billion kronor (€405mn) a year earlier."We continue to operate in a very tough environment with strong external challenges: de-globalisation, hypercompetition and climate change," chief executive Håkan Samuelsson said in a statement.In response, the company announced an additional 5-billion-kronor (€450mn) savings plan, on top of its earlier cost-cutting programmes. It said the new measures would lead to about 2,000 job cuts in Sweden and 500 more elsewhere, by ending consultant contracts, through natural attrition and through targeted exit packages for employees.The company expects the full financial effects of these measures by the end of 2027.The company, which had bet heavily on electric vehicles, said the removal of consumer incentives for fully electric cars and plug-in hybrids in the United States under President Donald Trump had also hit its margins.In 2024, Volvo Cars dropped a plan to sell only fully electric cars by 2030."We are convinced that we have the right long-term strategy addressing these challenges. However, in the short term, with severely challenged volumes, we need to reinforce our turnaround plan with additional decisive actions, lowering our break-even point and improving cash flows to make us more resilient," Samuelsson said.Struggling along with other European carmakers in the face of a difficult global landscape, Volvo Cars last year announced an 18-billion-kronor (€1.62bn) cost-cutting plan. That plan included around 3,000 job cuts worldwide.The company said in September that Škoda Auto CEO Klaus Zellmer would replace Samuelsson no later than 1 October 2027.

title: Albanian opposition and ruling party lawmakers scuffle in parliament over student protest tensions
description: The clashes broke out after parliamentary leadership rejected opposition demands to debate ten days of student demonstrations that have gripped the capital Tirana.
content: Lawmakers in Albania's parliament clashed on Thursday as opposition members of parliament attempted to disrupt a session, while the assembly continued voting on legislation amid tensions in the country.The clashes broke out after parliamentary leadership rejected opposition demands to debate ten days of student demonstrations that have gripped the capital Tirana.Opposition MPs held up photographs of students injured by police during previous protests and blocked the parliamentary podium, while the assembly pressed ahead with voting on legislation amid the chaos.For nearly two weeks now, demonstrators have clashed repeatedly with police in the city centre, hurling rocks, flares, firebombs and fireworks. Officers have responded with batons, water cannons and tear gas.On Thursday, large crowds of students gathered at the parliament's entrances as the protests entered their tenth consecutive day.What the students wantHigh school and university students are demanding lower tuition fees, greater state investment in education and an end to corruption in the education system.They have since joined a broader anti-government movement calling for the resignation of Socialist Prime Minister Edi Rama. Rama has, however, vowed to resist.“A wave of stones, an attempt to overthrow the government and change those in power through the imposition of violence, something that will never be allowed to happen, in any form or for any reason,” he said after meeting teachers and school representatives on Tuesday.The Albanian prime minister argued that legitimate grievances were being exploited by those deliberately inciting violence.The student protests follow months of demonstrations organised by the Flamingo movement, which emerged in opposition to a major luxury tourism development on Albania’s southern Adriatic coast linked to an investment firm founded by Jared Kushner, son-in-law of US President Donald Trump.Interestingly, Albania is not alone. Governments across Europe are facing street pressure over rising fuel costs, deteriorating public services, underfunded schools and a deepening housing crisis.France and Italy have seen similar protests, while tent camps have sprung up in Spain and Portugal over unaffordable housing. Demonstrations were also planned in Greece this week.

title: Less product, same price: what is supermarket ‘shrinkflation’?
description: From chocolate bars to toothpaste, everyday products are getting smaller while prices stay the same. Known as “shrinkflation,” this is making groceries increasingly expensive for Europeans, who end up paying the same for less.
content: ‘Shrinkflation’ happens when manufacturers reduce the weight, volume or quantity of their products while keeping prices unchanged. “[Shoppers] purchase the same product in the same packaging, but will buy less for the same price,” said Loïc de Hults, a senior associate at law firm CMS Belgium. The practice is not new, but has become more common in Europe since the 2022 inflation surge. In 2019, a French syrup maker reduced its bottles from 750ml to 600ml, with consumer group Foodwatch later reporting a price increase of more than 37% per litre. In Germany, a brand reduced its chocolate bars from 100g to 90g, prompting a court ruling against the company in May 2026. Another one also introduced smaller 75g chocolate bars in 2026, compared to its usual 100g format. According to a 2025 European Commission report, 74% of consumers have noticed products getting smaller without becoming cheaper. The reason is rising production costs. “Some manufacturers have been looking at reducing the packaging and the quantities to maintain prices, instead of increasing them,” said Christel Delberghe, director general of EuroCommerce, which represents European retailers and wholesalers. “Cost increases are being passed on through the chain overall,” added Leena Whittaker, EuroCommerce's director of competitiveness. “If the costs of energy, inputs, production, and processing increase [...], prices will go up.” Consumer groups are calling for tougher rules, and countries including France and Austria have introduced measures requiring supermarkets to flag smaller products. But the EU has no specific law against shrinkflation, relying instead on broader rules against misleading business practices. Same packaging, less product Manufacturers have several ways to reduce product sizes, from leaving empty space in bags to using thicker packaging or raised bottoms. The strategy plays on a psychological blind spot: reductions of just 5% to 7% can go unnoticed. Some companies also advertise a “new recipe” or “improved quality” without drawing attention to changes in quantity. Shoppers should watch for changes in net weight, fewer items in multipacks or unusually large packaging compared to what's inside. Checking the price per kilogram or litre on supermarket shelf labels also helps compare products. Should there be laws against shrinkflation? Food and non-alcoholic drink prices across the EU rose by roughly 33% between 2021 and 2025. But the EU has not introduced rules specifically targeting shrinkflation; EU law requires food packaging to display net quantity, and supermarkets to show prices per kilogram or litre. The Unfair Commercial Practices Directive only bans ‘misleading practices’. De Hults believes these EU laws already offer some protection. “There is already a general prohibition of misleading practice. And in in Germany, for instance, the court of [Hamburg] considered that reducing the volume of a product and keeping the same packaging without correctly informing the consumer is a misleading practice. So, this is already covered by European law,” he said. Still, he acknowledged that shoppers may not immediately notice when a familiar product gets smaller: “If it's something that [they're] buying weekly, the first time that they will buy the new product, they will obviously not notice unless they're really reading all the labelling on the products,” he said. The issue reached the European Parliament. On 15 July 2025, its Internal Market and Consumer Protection Committee held a public hearing where lawmakers examined how practices like shrinkflation and dynamic pricing affect shoppers, leading to a question to the Commission about whether existing consumer laws were enough to tackle shrinkflation. The Commission defended current rules, pointing to mandatory weight labels and unit prices as ways for consumers to identify price increases. It said national authorities must enforce the law and promised to continue monitoring the market. National regulations? In March 2025, the Commission opened proceedings against Italy after it introduced rules for manufacturers to put warning labels on products that had shrunk. Brussels argued that these labels could create barriers to trade between EU countries and suggested notices on supermarket shelves instead. Other European countries have their own rules. Since July 2024, French supermarkets larger than 400 square metres must warn shoppers when products shrink but their price per kilogram or litre increases. Stores must show the old and new quantities, along with the price increase, for two months, or risk fines of up to €15,000. Austria introduced similar rules in April 2026, requiring larger supermarkets and health and beauty shops to flag products that shrink while their unit price rises by at least 3%. Romania also introduced mandatory notices in 2024, while Belgium has discussed similar legislation but has yet to adopt specific rules. Competition between supermarket chains also affects how much shoppers pay, as retailers compete on prices and negotiate with suppliers. Differences between countries are not always what shoppers might expect: Eurostat figures for 2024 put food prices 18% above the EU average in France, compared with 7% in Belgium. De Hults warned that different national rules could complicate matters for manufacturers selling products across Europe: “If we are speaking about packaging, it has to be regulated at EU level. Otherwise, it will be too complicated for the manufacturers,” he said. Common EU rules would help companies understand what they can and cannot do, particularly as more countries introduce their own requirements: “Specific rules at EU level would be good just so that everybody knows what they can do in every country”, he added. EuroCommerce, however, believes the existing legislation is enough. “Adding yet another layer of regulation will not necessarily change much in relation to consumers, but it will certainly add some more regulatory burdens, and cost, and reporting obligations, and uncertainty on the retailers,” said Delberghe.

title: EU-Canada 'love story' needs more than warm words, senior MEP warns
description: European Parliament’s point man on Canada, Tobias Cremer, told Euronews that the planned “associate membership” should include an institutional framework formalising closer ties between the EU and Canada.
content: The EU must turn its offer of “associate membership” to Canada into a meaningful partnership that goes well beyond trade, Tobias Cremer, the European Parliament's standing rapporteur on Canada, told Euronews.European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen invited Canada to become the EU's first “associate member” in September, but gave little indication of what the unprecedented status would mean in practice.The offer comes as geopolitical upheaval draws Brussels and Ottawa closer together. Canada is embroiled in a trade war with its traditional US ally, while the EU is struggling to keep Washington on its side over Ukraine.The two sides are due to meet at a summit in Montreal at the end of next week, with agreements expected in several areas, including critical raw materials and digital cooperation.“For the last couple of months, we've been great, Canada and Europe, at writing each other love letters and saying how much we really want to work together,” said Cremer, a German socialist MEP. “But I think now is really the time to start to get serious and turn that love story into concrete commitments.”He added that “associate membership” must mean the “closest possible partnership that the EU can offer to a non-European country and since Canada is probably the most European of non-European countries that should be very close.”Beyond trade dealsCremer insisted that the relationship must amount to more than “a trade deal ‘plus’”.“There must be a new quality to the relation.”He called for a “pragmatic approach,” involving sectoral agreements covering trade, defence, digital cooperation, the Arctic and students, but also going further.“We should go a step further and start embedding all of these great initiatives into something more enduring, into a common institutional framework of coordination and cooperation.”Cremer suggested that Canada could participate “as an observer” in the Council of the EU, where national ministers meet, and called for the creation of a formal parliamentary partnership assembly.Such a body could follow the model of the existing EU-UK Parliamentary Partnership Assembly, which brings together 35 members from each side twice a year for sessions that can focus on specific policy areas.Regarding the UK, however, the MEP described it as a European country for which, “if it wishes so,” the ambition “should not be associate membership, but full membership.”His comments came as UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham recently floated the idea of rejoining the EU, with polls showing that a majority of Britons want to return to the bloc.But Cremer also argued for closer cooperation not only with the UK and Canada, but also with countries such as Australia and South Korea.“I think it is of our interest to bring all of these actors together and say 'hold on, actually the majority of the world wants to play 21st century politics which is focused on collective security, on shared interests, on mutual respect rather than might is right.'”

title: 'It's terrifying': Ukraine and Europe on edge as Trump sides with Putin
description: Trump’s pivot towards Putin has reignited fears that Washington is pushing Ukraine towards capitulation, regardless of the consequences. Alarmed, Europeans are scrambling to get the peace talks back on track.
content: Ukraine and its European allies have long suspected Donald Trump had a soft spot for Vladimir Putin.Now, they are discovering it goes far beyond anything they imagined.In a shell-shocking sequence of events, the US president aligned himself with his Russian counterpart, struck a diesel deal, moved to ease years of sanctions and appeared to sidestep punitive legislation he had signed just one month earlier.His broadsides against Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, a recurring feature of life at the White House, took on a new bitterness.The Kremlin, long betting that the Western front would eventually crumble, seized the opening to dangle further joint ventures and float a trilateral summit between Putin, Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping. For Russia, whose economy is showing signs of strain, such a meeting would confer the great-power status Putin has long craved.Trump says he is on board.Meanwhile, in Ukraine, sudden restrictions on Starlink, the satellite technology controlled by Trump's close ally Elon Musk, and unexplained delays in US-made weapons deliveries have fuelled fears that Washington is undermining Kyiv to Moscow's advantage."American negotiators have been trying to push Ukraine into surrender for almost two years," EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas told the European Parliament earlier this week, in strikingly undiplomatic terms."Why Ukraine hasn't surrendered on Putin's terms is because Europe has been supporting Ukraine."Speaking off the cuff, Kallas gave voice to fears that have haunted Ukraine and its European allies since Trump's re-election — and that are now coming into sharper focus: that, in his relentless pursuit of a grand deal worthy of a Nobel Peace Prize nomination, Trump could be prepared to sell Ukraine out."Nobody can quite understand Trump fascination with Putin. He elevates Putin to a point far beyond what he's entitled to - I mean Russia has an economy the size of Italy," a senior European official told Euronews."This is all very disturbing. It's terrifying that you send two property dealers into a negotiation with Putin, where they decide they want to divide up a country."The remark was a reference to US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, both of whom, like Trump, made their fortunes in real estate.The pair have caused consternation across Europe over reports that they have floated proposals to release frozen Russian assets and resume Russian gas supplies to Europe as incentives in peace talks. European governments have rejected both ideas.Witkoff came under widespread fire this week after describing Putin as a "humanitarian". Hours later, Russia launched 21 ballistic missiles at Kyiv, three carrying cluster-munition warheads designed to maximise casualties and damage among civilians."The US keeps trying to lure Putin with lucrative deals if he can just get the Ukraine problem out of the way. But Putin is already one of the richest men in the world. What he wants is to establish a greater Russia," the official added."For Europe, we are simply not built to operate in this kind of ruthless transactional environment."Another official, also speaking on condition of anonymity, said it was "worrying and frustrating" to hear Trump's pro-Russian tirades, which have been linked to mounting political pressure ahead of next month's midterm elections.Republicans risk losing control of both the House and the Senate as voters grow disillusioned with Trump and inflation bites amid high energy prices.Trump has sought to deflect blame by pointing to Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries, even as energy experts identify his war on Iran as the main driver of disruption in global oil markets."Until the midterms, it's hard to draw any firm conclusions from his statements. It feels like we need to hold our nerve until then," the second official said."That's obviously much harder for Ukraine in practice. Still, I don't get the sense that they're on the verge of collapse."A Democratic victory would constrain Trump's domestic agenda, but its impact on his foreign policy is less clear. As his latest moves demonstrate, the president has considerable latitude to reshape the American position on the world stage.Trump's disdain for Europe and affinity for Russia long predate the current electoral cycle."There's a clear feeling around the table that it is even more important to support Ukraine," a senior European diplomat said."Some optimists hope things will improve after the midterms, but I doubt it."Trump vs ZelenskyyUS pressure on Ukraine has been mounting for at least a year.In November 2025, a US-backed 28-point peace proposal, reportedly drafted in Moscow before being submitted to Washington, called for Ukraine to cede territory, limit the size of its armed forces and permanently renounce NATO membership.European governments quickly closed ranks, seeking to revise the proposals they warned would leave Ukraine vulnerable to renewed Russian aggression.Since then, the divide has widened beyond the terms of a potential peace deal to the military capabilities Ukraine needs to defend itself.Kyiv has accused Washington of delaying deliveries of Patriot interceptor missiles funded by European allies, interrupting intelligence-sharing on incoming Russian ballistic missiles and restricting access to satellite communications.Ukrainian officials believe the measures are intended to pressure President Volodymyr Zelenskyy into accepting a deal more favourable to Moscow.The White House has denied imposing restrictions for political reasons. US officials have also denied claims that Witkoff and Kushner, the special envoys, threatened to withdraw military and intelligence support unless Kyiv made concessions.The stakes are potentially fatal. Patriot interceptors are among Ukraine's key defences against Russian ballistic missiles, while US intelligence provides crucial early warning of incoming attacks. The early-warning system has since been restored."Without America, things would be much harder for us," Zelenskyy told US senators.In mid-September, Ukrainian government sources told Euronews that Washington would not grant Kyiv a licence to manufacture Patriot interceptors, effectively shutting down Ukraine's ambitions to produce the technology domestically.This came despite Trump's earlier public promises to grant Ukraine a production licence. Zelenskyy later said the US president had approved the move, although no final licensing agreement had been officially confirmed.The dispute highlights a broader vulnerability for Kyiv: its continued dependence on Washington for both weapons deliveries and the ability to manufacture critical military technology.Pressure has also extended to Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil refineries, which have reduced Moscow's export capacity and hit its war revenues.Trump has demanded that Kyiv halt the attacks. Zelenskyy initially refused, arguing that the strikes represented one of Ukraine's strongest sources of leverage.As tensions with Trump escalated, however, he offered to suspend refinery strikes for 30 days in exchange for additional Patriot interceptors to protect Ukrainian cities from Russian ballistic missile attacks.No Patriot interceptors were delivered.In parallel, Trump has stepped up his personal attacks on Ukraine’s president, urging Kyiv to hold new elections and appoint "someone else" to negotiate with Moscow. Ukraine’s constitution prohibits elections during wartime.The contrast is particularly striking when it comes to political legitimacy.In March 2024, the US government under President Joe Biden rejected Russia’s presidential election as neither free nor fair, citing the exclusion of genuine political opposition and voting in occupied Ukrainian territories.Yet Trump has not called for new elections in Russia or demanded a change of leadership in Moscow. Instead, he has invited Putin to attend the G20 summit in December, another overture that has caused alarm.Trump appears uninterested in demanding concessions from Russia, shifting the burden instead onto Ukraine, which he sees as the weaker party. Washington has even eased sanctions on Russian diesel without securing any change in Moscow's behaviour."Let's face it: one guy is looking for cash, and the other is looking for glory," another senior diplomat said, dismissing Trump's approach to lure Putin with economic partnerships as "futile" because the two have ultimately competing aims.Europeans are aghast, but not yet ready to break away.After months of dealing with Trump's outbursts — over tariffs, Greenland, the ICC, Big Tech and other flashpoints — European leaders have adjusted their approach to the mercurial president. Not every Truth Social post warrants a public response, officials privately say.The strategy remains threefold: support Ukraine, pressure Russia and engage with the US — all at once. Europe must preserve its seat at the negotiating table to influence Washington's thinking as much as possible, even if it means enduring pain and swallowing its pride.This week offered a case in point.Just as tensions between Trump and Zelenskyy threatened to spiral, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb hastily organised a new round of peace talks in Oslo before Witkoff flew to Moscow."We fully understand that there has been a lot of noise in the public space," Stubb said, in a not-so-subtle reference to the row."In my experience, peace requires patience. But unfortunately, war does not wait."

title: Dream prize, everyday reality: why a German is selling his Haribo island
