description: A private island, a log cabin and Canada next door: in 2005, Bavarian Matthias R. won this unusual prize. Twenty years on, he wants to sell, as wild land needs upkeep and it is a long way to travel for a short holiday.
content: Some people win a gift basket, Matthias R. won an island. In a Haribo competition, the man from Kahl am Main in Lower Franconia became the owner of a private retreat in Canada in 2005. Now the chapter of island ownership is about to end: the plot is being offered for 348,000 Canadian dollars, the equivalent of around 220,000 euros.Gummy bears thrown in with the grand prizeThere is a reason why the story sounds like an especially generous advertising stunt. Haribo launched the promotion in April 2005 with everything that helps sell the dream of dropping out: a private island in Nova Scotia, a wooden house, the first flight there and a canoe complete with fishing gear. Haribo's famous Gold Bears were supposed to take care of the initial supplies, even though in nutritional terms they are clearly not suitable for a long-term life in the wilderness.Thomas Gottschalk was also part of the package, at least in the campaign. As Haribo's advertising partner at the time, he was, according to the company, supposed to help build the wooden house and promote the prize draw on television. The dream of getting away from it all was pushed with considerable effort: no fewer than 15 million promotional stickers were planned for the bags of sweets.A paradise with a composting toiletThe current sales listing advertises the property under the name "Back Lake Islands". It is located in the eastern Canadian province of Nova Scotia, in Shelburne County. According to the estate agent, the property covers around 6.5 hectares and the sale also includes adjacent wetlands.The marketing copy reads: "Escape everyday life to your own private island paradise – just 30 minutes from the shops and amenities of Shelburne. A short boat ride from the shore takes you to your personal retreat, where you can enjoy lakeside living for at least three seasons of the year. The adjoining marshland, which also forms part of the island property, invites you to extensive exploratory tours in a unique natural environment."The plot features a log cabin with two bedrooms and a bathroom. According to the listing, two small boats, a jetty, a shed and a generator are also included. As for leisure activities, the agent recommends swimming, canoeing, fishing and hiking.The fixtures are clearly more suited to a nature holiday than a luxury resort: solar panels provide electricity, a pump draws water from the lake and there is a composting toilet for calls of nature.You cannot wish the distance awayThe owner's parents tended the property for years and put a great deal of work into it, reports the Bild newspaper. The journey there now takes around ten hours in total, and these days they no longer embark on the long trip. On top of that come ongoing expenses: the report speaks of around 2,500 euros in annual property tax, in addition to flights and car hire.The dream of a private island with gummy bears thrown in was a gift; the work that came with it was free of charge. But perhaps an adventurer will now be found for whom this lonely island is simply perfect.

title: A Budapest reset, and a scramble to get Ukraine peace talks back on track
description: Good morning. I’m Mared Gwyn. In this Friday edition: Ursula von der Leyen is set to become a headline act at Hungary’s 1956 revolution commemoration, and Europeans grapple with Trump’s “terrifying” Ukraine approach.
content: Brussels-Budapest reset: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa will join a commemoration of the 70th anniversary of Hungary’s 1956 anti-Soviet uprising in Budapest today, with von der Leyen expected to deliver a speech in parliament alongside Prime Minister Péter Magyar. It’s arguably one of the clearest signals yet of the new chapter in EU-Hungary relations, our Hungarian correspondent Sándor Zsiros writes this morning.Major turning point: The thaw in relations between Brussels and Budapest comes after years of acrimony under Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s predecessor, Viktor Orbán – with von der Leyen’s speech likely to capture a moment of change, Sándor reports.In the past, von der Leyen was portrayed on billboards in Hungary as a public enemy. She is set to address the same parliament where just a few months ago Orbán lashed out at the EU.The commemoration is the first big international event for Magyar since he took office in May. He had extended an invitation to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, as first reported by Euronews, but the Ukrainian leader is unlikely to attend. Diplomatic ties between Ukraine and Hungary have improved dramatically since Magyar’s election in April. Yet, Budapest surprised EU diplomats earlier this week by blocking the next steps in Ukraine’s EU accession talks, despite Kyiv meeting its previous demands.French President Emmanuel Macron was also set to take part, but cancelled the trip in the wake of riots in France. Moldovan President Maia Sandu and Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze are both expected to attend.Ukraine latest: Meanwhile, Vladimir Putin has offered another remarkable explanation of Russia's war against Ukraine: Moscow doesn't want to fight its neighbour. It is Ukraine, apparently, that insists on fighting Russia.The Russian president also declared that Russians and Ukrainians are effectively "one people" – an argument Moscow has repeatedly invoked to justify its invasion and occupation of Ukrainian territory – and expressed confidence that the two countries could reach an agreement, provided it served Russia's imperialist interests, my colleague Sasha Vakulina writes.And what if Ukraine doesn't agree?: "Well, then it will be otherwise," Putin said, promising that Russia would achieve all the "objectives" of its all-out war against Ukraine.Meanwhile, Zelenskyy is awaiting a briefing from US envoy Steve Witkoff on Friday, followed by further consultations between Ukrainian, American and European teams. As diplomacy hangs in the balance, Moscow continues to pound Ukraine. Overnight on Thursday, Russia launched ballistic missiles carrying cluster warheads at Kyiv, targeting the historic city centre and damaging monastery buildings, homes, shops and cafés.Maximum alarm: Meanwhile, Europe continues to grapple with Donald Trump’s embrace of Vladimir Putin, which has revived long-gestating fears that the two presidents will secretly thrash out a deal that ends in Ukraine’s capitulation. Moscow’s pitch for a summit between Trump, Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping has further fuelled the impression that Europe’s security architecture is hanging by a thread, my colleague Jorge Liboreiro reports this morning.“It’s very disturbing. It’s terrifying,” a senior official said. “We’re simply not built to operate in this kind of ruthless transactional environment.”Jorge Liboreiro, Sasha Vakulina and Shona Murray have this must-read story depicting a continent on edge. Chin up: Despite the alarming circumstances, European officials insist that engagement with the Trump administration must continue to ensure the European point of view is reflected in the peace process. For Ukraine, European presence is fundamental to counter Washington’s transactional approach.Russia has indicated it’s prepared to resume trilateral talks at the technical level with the US and Ukraine in mid-November. Brussels hopes the format can expand into multilateral talks to include European representatives as well, although it’s far from guaranteed that Moscow would agree. PHP security flaw: Why websites across Europe went dark and what it means for youAI models have uncovered what OpenAI calls "one of the most impactful" security bugs in recent memory, hidden in PHP, a programming language that quietly powers most of the internet. It’s sent organisations worldwide scrambling to shut down websites before hackers can exploit them.The bugs sat undetected in PHP’s code for more than a decade. It took cutting-edge AI models from OpenAI and Google to turn a long-suspected weakness into a working attack — and now the race is on to close the door.The Dutch government pulled its DigiD digital identity system, the Overheid.nl government portal and the website of the lower house of parliament, with the Port of Rotterdam, hospitals and the country’s five largest political parties following suit.Even the Dutch National Cyber Security Centre took its own site down.Finland’s state IT provider Valtori switched off government web services wholesale “as a precautionary measure,” France’s Interior Ministry put local administration sites into maintenance mode and Germany’s federal IT service ITZBund took down several portals.CERT-EU, the cybersecurity service for the EU institutions, went further than most, telling any organisation unable to patch immediately to take its websites offline rather than risk being hacked.The European Commission, ENISA, CERT-EU, Europol and the EU’s network of national cyber response teams also issued a joint statement urging organisations to act immediately, prioritising systems exposed to the internet.Una Hajdari has more.More from our newsroomsEU Parliament awards Sakharov Prize to ICC in rebuke of US sanctions. The European Parliament has awarded the Sakharov Prize to the International Criminal Court in a show of support after the US imposed sanctions on the court. The abstention of the far-right Patriots for Europe group was decisive in breaking the deadlock over the final choice. Vincenzo Genovese has the details.Italy and Spain to end border checks, easing tensions after Ceuta migrant row. Rome and Madrid have agreed to end temporary border checks, in a sign of de-escalation after weeks of tension over the Ceuta migrant crisis. The decision follows a phone call between the countries’ interior ministers, after prime ministers Giorgia Meloni and Pedro Sánchez signalled their intention to end the checks in Brussels last week. Fortunato Pinto has the story.Gulf nations brace for possible return to all-out war between US and Iran. The volatility around the Israeli and US midterm elections is fueling fears of renewed US-Israeli strikes on Iran in a short and intensive military campaign to push Tehran into concessions, with Iran vowing a devastating response against the Gulf nations. Peter Barabas and the Euronews Doha bureau have more.We’re also keeping an eye onEU trade ministers gather for informal talks in Dublin, IrelandHungary holds a commemoration of the 70th anniversary of the Hungarian Revolution of 1956. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa to attend.That’s it for today. Jorge Liboreiro, Sándor Zsiros, Sasha Vakulina and Vincenzo Genovese contributed to this newsletter.

title: Could lab-made gold crash prices like diamonds? US start-up says it turned mercury into gold
description: Little-known San Francisco start-up Marathon Fusion says it has turned mercury into stable gold at ten times the rate of CERN's record, raising a question that has haunted the diamond trade: could lab-made gold one day sink the price of the mined metal?
content: Marathon Fusion, a small fusion energy company in San Francisco, announced on Wednesday that it had transmuted, or converted, mercury into stable gold last month, beating a record set by CERN tenfold. The Geneva-based organisation runs the world's largest particle physics laboratory.The claim, which has not been independently verified, revives an alchemist's dream and a market fear that lab-made gold could do to bullion what lab-grown precious stones did to diamonds.Founded in 2023 by Kyle Schiller and Adam Rutkowski, a former SpaceX engineer, Marathon develops fuel systems for future fusion power plants, which aim to generate electricity by fusing atoms together, as the sun does.It lists the US Department of Energy as a partner on its website and won a 2023 award from ARPA-E, the department's agency for high-risk energy research.Its backers include Breakthrough Energy, the climate technology network founded by Bill Gates, and Anglo American, the mining group that owns De Beers, the world's leading natural diamond company behind the "A diamond is forever" slogan.In its announcement, the company said it had turned "mercury into real, stable gold, beating CERN's record by a factor of 10".In 2025, CERN said its Large Hadron Collider (LHC), the world's most powerful particle accelerator, had created about 29 picograms, or 29 trillionths of a gram, of gold during its 2015–2018 run. That amounted to around 86 billion gold nuclei, or atomic cores, which existed for only a tiny fraction of a second before being destroyed in collisions with accelerator equipment.Marathon's method fires neutrons from fusion reactions at mercury, turning it into an unstable isotope, or form of the metal, that decays into gold.It also claims to have broken a 40-year-old Soviet record with its plasma centrifuge, a machine that spins electrically charged gas at high speed to separate isotopes used in fusion fuel.It says it is now building a reactor in San Francisco to achieve record power density, meaning the most power produced for its size.The gold claim has not been independently verified, and the material available does not establish how much gold was produced or at what cost.What happened to diamonds?Lab-grown diamonds are chemically identical to mined stones.Although specialists can tell them apart, factories churned them out and sold them for a fraction of the price.Wholesale prices for lab-grown stones fell 90% to 95% from their 2015 levels, diamond industry analyst Paul Zimnisky said last year, while competition from lab-grown stones also weighed on mined diamond prices.De Beers launched its own lab-grown brand, Lightbox, in 2018 at $800 (€712) a carat. However, it shut it down in 2025 to focus on natural diamonds.De Beers made an underlying loss of $511 million (€455mn) in 2025, and Anglo American is in talks to sell its 85% stake for about $1 billion (€890mn) to a group led by former De Beers boss Gareth Penny, according to Bloomberg, citing people familiar with the matter.Swiss luxury group Richemont, which owns Cartier, and US jeweller Signet, which owns Kay and Zales, are reportedly also in talks to join the group.Why gold is differentGold is a far bigger market.Mines produced 3,672 tonnes in 2025, and about 222,600 tonnes have been mined throughout history, according to the World Gold Council.Central banks also hold it in their reserves as a safe store of value, and many have been buying heavily in recent years, including those of China and Poland.Gold traded at $4,062 (€3,617) an ounce on Thursday, more than 27% below its record high of $5,598 (€4,985) in January.Marathon's own 2025 study estimated that a fusion plant could make about 5 tonnes of gold a year per gigawatt of electricity, roughly the output of a large nuclear reactor.On that basis, 100 such plants would add an estimated 500 tonnes a year, roughly 14% of last year's mine output.However, no fusion plant yet sells electricity, and the first commercial ones are still years away. The gold could also contain radioactive isotopes and might need to be stored for up to 18 years before it could be sold, the company has said.There are currently no public plans to attempt to produce and commercialise the product, but unlike lab-grown diamonds, transmuted gold, once its radioactivity fades, would be impossible to tell apart from the mined kind.

title: Europe Today: France braces for fresh protests as EU leaders seek Hungary reset
description: France is bracing for another weekend of protests after last week’s demonstrations turned violent, as the government faces pressure to restore order. Meanwhile, EU leaders visit Hungary amid hopes of a reset in relations, while Serbia’s snap election puts President Aleksandar Vučić under pressure.
content: On today's show:Sándor Zsíros, Euronews' Hungarian EU correspondent, examines the significance of European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa visiting Budapest to mark the 70th anniversary of Hungary's 1956 uprising against Soviet rule. The visit, hosted by Prime Minister Péter Magyar, signals a potential reset in relations between Hungary and the EU after years of tensions under Viktor Orbán.Estelle Nilsson-Julien reports live from Paris as France prepares for another round of mass demonstrations on Saturday. Following last weekend's violence and looting, the government has announced heightened security measures, while protesters remain determined to take to the streets.Alice de Brito, vice president of France's main student union UNEF, joins us to discuss why students are protesting, the challenges they face and whether the upcoming presidential election offers hope for change.Polish Deputy Interior Minister Maciej Duszczyk speaks to us about the growing divisions between EU leaders over migration following the unrest in France. We discuss Emmanuel Macron’s response to foreign leaders commenting on France’s protests, Poland’s demands for tougher migration rules and the tensions between Donald Tusk and Pedro Sánchez over the EU’s Migration Pact.Berta López Domènech, analyst at the European Policy Centre, examines Serbia’s upcoming snap parliamentary election, where a student-led movement hopes to challenge President Aleksandar Vučić after two years of demonstrations. With concerns mounting over electoral irregularities and the country’s democratic direction, we ask whether the opposition can bring political change.When and where to watch Europe Today?You can join Euronews’ chief anchor Méabh Mc Mahon and our EU editor Maria Tadeo live on TV and Euronews' website as well as digital platforms (YouTube, Facebook, X, and Instagram), every weekday at 8 am Brussels time.In just 20 minutes, our new format brings you the day's key events plus crucial analysis of all the stories shaping the EU and beyond. It's also available as a newsletter and podcast.

title: Oil prices climb above $113 as AI sell-off rattles stocks and investors buy bonds
description: Rising energy prices added to inflation concerns as doubts over AI spending hit tech stocks; investors sought safety in US bonds, and France’s borrowing costs remained above 5%.
content: Asian shares were mostly lower on Friday after the latest sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks weighed on markets around the world, giving the benchmark S&P 500 its worst day since July.Oil prices were hovering at their highest levels since May on worries about the war with Iran, with Brent crude trading at $113.73 per barrel early Friday, up 0.5% after a 4% jump in the previous session. Brent settled at $113.17 on Thursday. US benchmark West Texas Intermediate crude rose 0.6% to $100.08 per barrel.Oil rallied on Thursday as deadly attacks in Saudi Arabia fuelled concerns that a full-scale regional conflict could further choke off global energy supplies.On top of the risk premium, soaring shipping costs are adding to the cost of delivering oil.By mid-October, the cost of shipping crude from the Middle East Gulf to Asia on a large tanker had climbed to over $37 per barrel, more than five times its level before the war began, according to MarketWatch.Gas prices jumped, too. November futures for the European benchmark, Dutch TTF, traded above €90 per megawatt-hour on Thursday.Concerns about AI build-out hit stock marketsOn Thursday, in the US, the S&P 500 fell 1.2%, while the Nasdaq composite tumbled 2.6%. The weakness in tech stocks was so overwhelming that it masked strength elsewhere in the US market, where the majority of stocks actually rose. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added less than 0.1%.AI-related stocks have been swinging on worries that their boom may be under threat because of how expensive it has become to borrow money to build data centres and buy more AI chips. Investors fear share prices shot too high during a years-long frenzy, even though companies in the industry continue to report growth.Meta Platforms, which is pushing its Muse AI agent, lost 7% after reporting stronger revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected, though its profit fell short. The company behind Facebook and Instagram also said it would introduce a new class of non-voting shares, giving it another way to fund AI investments and other expenses while preserving existing shareholders’ voting power.Tesla fell 3.1% after reporting third-quarter profit above analysts’ expectations, though its revenue was weaker than forecast.The global sell-off in AI stocks knocked Nvidia down 4.4%. Because the chip giant is the largest company on Wall Street by market value, movements in its stock carry more weight in the S&P 500 than any other, and it was the single biggest drag on the index.CoreWeave, which has borrowed money to buy Nvidia’s AI chips and rent out access to them through its cloud services, has been particularly shaky in recent weeks because of worries about its debt. It dropped 10.1%.Technology stocks face fresh tests next week when Microsoft, Amazon and Alphabet report their earnings. The Federal Reserve’s next interest rate decision is also due next week, on Wednesday, 28 October.Bond market worriesBond market worriesWorries about big government debt loads and strained budgets are hanging over many developed economies. Protests across France have raised pressure on the government to increase spending, which could add further to its debt.France's 10-year government bond yield stood at around 5.07% late Thursday, compared with Germany’s 3.34%, putting the gap at about 173 basis points. Italy’s 10-year yield was around 4.61%.Debt and inflation fears had helped drive a major global bond sell-off, pushing US Treasury yields to their highest levels in decades.But US yields fell sharply on Thursday as investors bought US government bonds in search of something safer to own as AI stocks tumbled.The yield on the 10-year Treasury tumbled to 4.97% from 5.13% late Wednesday and from more than 5.30% earlier this month. The 16-basis-point daily fall was a sharp move for the benchmark yield.Thursday’s drop in yields came even as another report suggested the US economy may be doing better than economists expected. New applications for unemployment benefits fell by 6,000 to 194,000 last week, their lowest level since July, suggesting layoffs remained low.Investors will also watch Friday’s preliminary business activity surveys for the eurozone, the UK and the US for signs of how higher energy prices and borrowing costs are affecting growth.In other dealings early Friday, the US dollar rose to 156.93 Japanese yen from 156.77 yen. The euro was unchanged at $1.1215. Sterling traded at $1.3391.Gold futures fell nearly 1% to $4,020.20 an ounce.

title: Europe just had its deadliest summer. Which country was hit the hardest by extreme heat?
description: Europe faced its ‘worst summer on record’ for heat deaths – with climate change responsible for two-thirds.
content: Europe’s sweltering summer is estimated to have claimed more than 50,000 lives in urban areas, making it the “worst on record”, according to a new report.Researchers are clear on the cause: climate change – primarily from the burning of fossil fuels – was responsible for about two-thirds of these excess heat deaths.The figure far outstrips the previous highest figures of about 29,000 deaths in the summer of 2022 and 28,000 in 2003 across the area modelled.It’s a testament to the extreme heat faced by the world’s fastest-warming continent between June and August this year. A succession of heatwaves saw temperatures in Western Europe soar 2.9°C above the 1991-2020 average – even rising by as much as 12°C on some days – often hitting countries that are neither used to nor prepared for such highs.“These numbers are a stark reminder that our hotter, more extreme summers are having an increasingly severe impact on public health,” says study co-author Dr Clair Barnes, an extreme weather and climate change researcher at Imperial College London. “Behind these statistics are real people whose lives were lost and real families who grieve for them.”Nearly one-third of deaths estimated occurred during the particularly intense heatwave between 17 June and 1 July, when temperatures were on average 5.3°C above the norm.How were summer heat deaths estimated?The study used modelling to estimate the number of heat-related excess deaths during summers dating back to the start of the century. “The true burden of mortality, in fact, due to heat is not directly observed or measured,” says study co-author Dr Malcolm Mistry, assistant professor in climate and geospatial modelling at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine (LSHTM).“Heat is therefore often commonly referred to as a ‘silent killer’, with the death toll underreported in several regions globally.”The scientists used temperature records and modelling based on the historical relationship between heat and mortality to estimate the number of casualties in summer 2026. They took geographic and environmental features, socioeconomic factors, availability of health services, and age-specific temperature-mortality links into account.The modelling was applied to 854 urban areas across the EU, UK, Norway and Switzerland – areas that make up around 40 per cent of the population of the 30 countries studied. A separate attribution study covering the summers of 2000 to 2025 was used for comparison, with results for these years proving broadly consistent with official statistics released by national health authorities. Many European countries are yet to release final figures for summer 2026.Researchers then compared the actual temperatures with those that would have been expected without warming from climate change to estimate the additional deaths caused.Overall, 65 per cent of heat-related excess deaths – or around 32,000 – in summer 2026 were attributed to human-induced climate change. Earlier in the century it was estimated to be responsible for about 40 per cent of heat-related deaths.“It is yet another reminder both of the imperative of rolling out targeted interventions to protect those who are most vulnerable to this increasingly extreme heat, and of the growing need to rapidly transition away from fossil fuels to slow the pace of change and limit future warming,” says Dr Barnes.Who is most at risk from extreme heat?Vulnerable people are most exposed to the dangers of extreme heat, including those suffering from disease; elderly or very young people; and those unable to move away from the heat – either for physical or socioeconomic reasons.In the summer 2026 study, people aged 85 and over accounted for roughly half of the estimated deaths. But younger adults were also affected: there were an estimated 800 excess deaths among people aged between 20 and 44, and a total of around 6,000 people under the age of 65.The researchers also found geographical variations, with Southern Europe experiencing significantly more deaths linked to high temperatures than Northern Europe.This is primarily due to the higher temperatures faced by countries further south, although other vulnerabilities also came into play. “For example, factors such as increased air pollution levels, limited green space infrastructure, accessibility to health systems and heat alerts,” explains study co-author Dr Garyfallos Konstantinoudis, assistant professor at ICL’s Grantham Institute.Europe’s unprecedented summer: Which country was worst hit?The public health risks of Europe’s scorching summer were immense, with several governments issuing heat warnings and real-time estimates of heat-related mortality.According to the summer 2026 report, Italy is estimated to have suffered the highest number of heat-related excess deaths: a total of 13,303. Next was France at 7,268, followed by Spain at 6,824.Traditionally-cooler countries also struggled in the heat, which was made more dangerous by infrastructure designed for a different climate and citizens unaccustomed to such highs.Germany faced an estimated 6,340 excess deaths and the UK 4,354.“In the UK, the summer is historically the quietest time for our health service. This summer, however, saw demand and strain that was akin to a really bad winter virus season,” says Andrew Hartle, Professor of Practice of Anaesthesia at Imperial College Healthcare. The accuracy of the modelling means it has the potential to allow health services to prepare for extreme events before they hit.Besides cutting greenhouse gas emissions to limit future warming, cities can invest in adding green-blue spaces, which come with the cobenefits of reducing temperatures and improving air quality. Northern and Western Europe should look to the south for solutions that are already well established, the study’s authors say. These include investing in climate shelters; retrofitting buildings to better withstand the heat, such as by adding external shades or blinds; and promoting behavioural changes like checking in on vulnerable neighbours, not going out in the midday sun, taking heat advisory warnings seriously, seeking shade, and drinking plenty of water.

title: Drones, AI and cybersecurity on display as Milipol Qatar brings together firms from 33 countries
description: Around 280 companies from 33 countries gathered at Milipol Qatar, displaying drones, robots and AI systems. Exhibitors discussed changing security needs, while officials examined how to protect essential services and respond to cyberattacks and emergencies.
content: Security companies from 33 countries gathered in Doha this week for Milipol Qatar, displaying drones, robots and AI systems as the country reviews its defences following the Iran war.The three-day exhibition, which ended Thursday, covered equipment for policing, emergency response and industrial safety, along with discussions on cybersecurity and protecting essential services.Alexandros Lakatamitis, general manager of West Bay Petroleum, which brought drones to the exhibition, said government and industry customers were taking security more seriously.“The security bubble that we’ve enjoyed for so long is no longer there,” he told Euronews.Lakatamitis, who grew up in Qatar, said security had become a more pressing consideration across government and business, including among the customers his company speaks to daily.Around 280 companies participated in the exhibition at the Doha Exhibition and Convention Center, according to Major Khalid Saadon Al-Kuwari, a member of the Milipol organising committee. About 70% came from outside Qatar.Major Al-Kuwari said the event brought together “solutions for whatever challenges that different governments and different countries are facing”.He said it gave governments an opportunity to examine systems already tested in other countries and consider how they could be used at home.The exhibition took place during a week of security discussions in Doha.On Monday, Qatar’s Defence Minister Saoud bin Abdulrahman Al Thani said the country was drawing on lessons from the Iran war to improve protection against ballistic missiles, drones and cyberattacks.He also outlined plans for a local defence production hub and closer cooperation with regional and international partners.Sending machines into dangerOn the exhibition floor, companies also presented equipment intended for civilian emergencies and hazardous industrial work.Lakatamitis described how drones could search large areas for missing people. Photographs collected during a flight can be analysed by software to identify possible signs of a person, helping rescuers decide where to concentrate their efforts, he said.He also pointed to industrial inspections, where a drone fitted with gas-detection equipment could investigate a suspected leak without sending someone into a potentially dangerous location.Those applications were part of a broader discussion about using AI in security. The second Doha International Conference on AI & Security ran alongside Milipol, with sessions on responsible AI use, autonomous systems and the protection of critical infrastructure.At a cybersecurity seminar on Thursday, officials discussed how to keep essential services operating during an attack.Khalid Al Nasr, assistant director of the information security department at Qatar’s National Cyber Security Agency, said the response needed to extend beyond restoring IT infrastructure to ensuring vital government services continued or were restored within an acceptable timeframe.At the discussion, Al Nasr called for cybersecurity to be incorporated into disaster recovery and crisis management plans, with clear responsibilities to reduce confusion during an incident.The exhibition also saw fresh international security agreements. Qatar and France signed a cooperation plan between their interior ministries covering 2027–2030, aimed at strengthening coordination and exchanges of expertise.A joint statement following French President Emmanuel Macron’s visit to Doha said the expanded partnership covered homeland security and civil protection.On Thursday, Qatar's Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani launched the sixth Watan exercise during a visit to Milipol. The exercise brings together security, military, and civilian agencies to rehearse emergency responses.

title: Québec, Kyoto and Wachau Valley: These are the world’s best places to visit for autumn foliage
description: The top spot went to Québec City, with only one European destination making the cut.
content: With leaf-peeping season peaking, there’s never been a better time to head out to admire the golden colours.And now the question of where to go has been answered thanks to a new study.By looking at things like broadleaf density, daily autumn sunshine hours, local tour options and rising searches, IgluCruise has evaluated 40 popular destinations to come up with a top 10 list of autumn colour spots.Surprisingly, New England didn’t claim the number one spot. Instead that accolade went to Québec City in Canada thanks to its tree density, the number of excursions you can book there, and the rise in searches.Second place went to Kyoto in Japan. Momijigari, or going leaf-peeping, is a big deal here. Every year, the Japan Meteorological Corporation (JMC) releases forecasts for the best time to see the red maple trees and the yellow gingko trees.In 2026, the best date to see Kyoto’s red leaves is 11 December, while the gingko tree leaves will turn yellow around 27 November.Third place went to Burlington in Vermont. The US dominated the list, with four destinations making the cut overall: Portland, Maine (fourth); Jackson, New Hampshire (fifth); and Bar Harbor, Maine (seventh).Canada also had a strong showing, with two other cities making the cut – Halifax, Nova Scotia (ninth) and Saguenay, Québec (10th).Japan also had a second city in the top 10, Hiroshima in eighth place.The best European destination for autumn coloursOnly one European destination made the top 10: Wachau Valley in Austria, which was sixth on the ranking.Located around an hour by train from the capital Vienna, the Wachau Valley is a popular spot for river cruising as the Danube flows through here.The valley, which is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, is known for its vineyards, and after a day of leaf-peeping you can unwind in one of its many traditional wine taverns.The top 10 destinations for autumn colours Québec City, Québec, CanadaKyoto, JapanBurlington, Vermont, USAPortland, Maine, USAJackson, New Hampshire, USAWachau Valley, AustriaBar Harbor, Maine, USAHiroshima, JapanHalifax, Nova Scotia, CanadaSaguenay, Québec, Canada

title: Major emitters fall short on climate action despite health pledges in their climate plans
description: Governments claim to protect public health while failing to tackle fossil fuel dependence, as new research by the Global Climate and Health Alliance exposes a gap between climate rhetoric and action.
content: The European Union and other major emitters are paying lip service to the health impacts of climate change while failing to match their rhetoric with sufficiently ambitious emissions cuts, according to a recent analysis of 132 countries’ climate commitments by the Global Climate and Health Alliance, a coalition of NGOs.Unlike most countries, the EU submits a single joint nationally determined contribution (NDC) under the Paris Agreement, covering the bloc and its 27 member states.The Global Climate and Health Alliance’s Scorecard assesses how well countries integrate health into their national climate plans across eight categories, including climate-related health impacts, air pollution, healthcare sector action, health co-benefits, just transition, governance, financing and implementation. While the EU, Indonesia, South Africa, Türkiye, Canada and the UAE score higher for health, this is not matched by the emissions reductions needed to protect populations. “Hypocrisy is a perfect word for that,” Jess Beagley of the Global Climate and Health Alliance told Euronews, arguing that governments cannot claim to prioritise health without addressing the fossil fuel dependence driving global warming and pollution.“We can’t pay lip service to health unless we are taking action on health,” she said.The alliance’s 2026 Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) Scorecard placed the EU 12th, with 19 of the 20 highest-scoring countries coming from low- and middle-income economies. Colombia topped the ranking with 29 points out of 32, followed by Nigeria with 25 and Cambodia with 24.Among the high-emitting economies receiving mid-range health scores, the EU was the only one whose climate plan included a specific target for reducing air pollution, according to the assessment. This concerns the phase-out of hydrofluorocarbons by 2050.However, none of the countries in this group included specific targets for black carbon, nitrous oxide or ozone, pollutants that contribute to global warming and can damage human health.For Beagley, the contradiction is clear: fossil fuels drive climate change while also causing harm through air, water and soil pollution, with consequences ranging from respiratory illnesses to cancer and neurological disorders.Healthcare systems are left dealing with the consequences of decisions made across the wider economy, she said.“The healthcare [sector] is really on the front line,” Beagley said. “The burden that falls is the end result of a wider climate action that has been taken or not taken.”Rich countries under pressureThe health consequences are already being felt worldwide following the recent events. The figures cited in the report include more than 1,400 deaths and over 6,600 people missing in Nepal, eight million children at risk of hunger in Eastern and Southern Africa and tens of thousands of deaths associated with European heatwaves.“If this year doesn’t change the way that we’re taking action on climate and health,” she said, “then it’s pure wilful denialism and an abandonment of the populations that government should be protecting.”Beagley argued that wealthy countries with high historical emissions must cut pollution faster and help finance climate action in developing economies.“It really should be on the richest and highest emitting countries in the world that have profited from fossil fuel-driven development over decades and decades,” she said. “Those countries should be reducing their emissions furthest and fastest.”For the EU, that means cutting its own emissions while providing financial support to countries in the Global South to implement their climate commitments under the Paris Agreement.The alliance also highlighted gaps in policymaking, with Beagley saying health ministries were closely involved in developing national climate plans in only 15% of countries covered by the analysis.Without their involvement, governments risk overlooking the health consequences of decisions on energy, transport and industry.COP31, approaching in November, will be a chance to showcase whether the mounting health impacts of extreme weather would finally translate into more ambitious policies.

title: Magnitude 7 earthquake strikes Tibet killing at least 16 people and destroying hundreds of homes
description: It was the most powerful earthquake to strike the region in five years, according to Chinese media.
content: A powerful magnitude 7 earthquake has struck China’s Tibet region, killing at least 16 people, injuring 54 and collapsing hundreds of homes in and around the northern city of Nagqu, official media reported.The quake hit at 10:33 p.m. local time on Thursday, with its epicentre 191 kilometres east-northeast of Nagqu in a sparsely populated, high-altitude area of northern Tibet, according to the US Geological Survey.It was the most powerful earthquake to strike the region in five years, China’s state broadcaster CCTV said.At least 339 homes and 20 livestock sheds collapsed, according to the Nagqu media office.Chinese President Xi Jinping called for all-out efforts in rescue and medical relief operations.Thus far, more than 1,600 people have been deployed for search and rescue operations, with emergency supplies including 1,000 prefabricated housing units, 3,000 tents, folding beds, flashlights and winter clothing delivered to the area.Aftershocks, rockfalls and disruptionThe USGS recorded at least seven aftershocks ranging in magnitude from 4.3 to 5.2, all at a depth of 10 kilometres. The main quake struck at a depth of 18 kilometres.Rockfalls triggered by the earthquake forced authorities to close a section of National Highway 317 to all but emergency, rescue and official vehicles while crews worked to clear debris. Local railway authorities halted train services through the affected area as a precaution.China’s state news agency Xinhua reported that communication has been cut in some areas hit by the quake.Intermittent snow is forecast across the earthquake zone over the next three days, complicating rescue efforts.Nagqu lies more than 300 kilometres north of Lhasa, Tibet’s capital.

title: Four Italian activists held during West Bank olive harvest amidst rising settler violence
description: Italy's Foreign Ministry is seeking information on the detention of several Italian activists in a West Bank village as they accompanied Palestinian olive farmers.
content: The clampdown on international volunteers working to defend the Palestinian olive pickers targeted another group on Thursday, which included four Italian women, stopped by the Israeli Defence Forces.Their detention was made public by the Italian Foreign Ministry, which announced that it had requested clarification from Israel. The Italian women were stopped in the village of al-Bweib, south of Hebron, after news emerged yesterday of a similar measure taken against other international activists, among them two fellow Italians, Manuel and Alberto Tartarotti, later expelled from the country."As soon as they were informed of what had happened, the Italian Embassy in Tel Aviv and the Consulate General of Italy in Jerusalem got in touch with the Israeli authorities, requesting urgent clarification about the circumstances of the detention and about the situation of the Italian nationals.The Foreign Ministry has so far obtained confirmation that the Italian women are being held at a police station", the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said, confirming the presence of four Italian citizens in the group of international activists detained today.Failure of 'seeking prior approval'Yesterday, a large-scale IDF operation led to the stopping and detention of around 90 volunteers, including Democratic candidate for the United States Congress Brad Lander, who was later released together with dozens of other activists under strict restrictions on their movements.This year's olive harvest has been marked by violence between Israeli settlers and Palestinian villagers, with the latter attempting to gather their crops and the former attempting to steal them.The Israeli military said the farmers and volunteers had failed to seek prior approval for the harvest and were detained “due to the security risk posed by conducting an uncoordinated harvest near an Israeli community.”It later added that it viewed “the arrival of dozens of activists as an act intended solely to provoke, which undermines the harvesting process.”In recent weeks there has been a surge in attacks carried out by groups of extremist settlers, culminating last weekend in the wounding of a photojournalist working for the Wall Street Journal and in an assault on several European diplomatic vehicles.

title: Thousands protest in Poland over stalled abortion law reforms
description: Since 1993, Poland has allowed abortion only in cases of severe foetal abnormalities, risks to the mother's health or life, or pregnancies resulting from rape or incest.
content: Thousands of people took to the streets of Warsaw and more than 20 other Polish cities on Thursday to demand abortion rights, marking the sixth anniversary of a near-total abortion ban introduced following a ruling by Poland's highest court.The demonstrations were held under the slogan "Red card for abortion". Participants carried red cards and banners opposing the current abortion laws, with slogans including "Abortion ban kills women" and "Women's hell continues".The protests came just days after parliament approved two bills aimed at easing abortion restrictions in the predominantly Catholic country. However, both measures are expected to face a veto from conservative President Karol Nawrocki.People accuse Prime Minister Donald Tusk's liberal government of failing to deliver on its promise to reform the country's strict abortion laws.Zofia Marcinek of the Warsaw-based reproductive rights group Abortion Dream Team described the legislation as a series of "token gestures" rather than a genuine attempt at reform, arguing that the government was aware the bills were unlikely to survive a presidential veto.She accused the government of trying to win back women's support ahead of next year's parliamentary election by appearing to take action on abortion rights.What the two abortion bills proposePoland's parliament voted on Tuesday to ease the country's strict abortion laws, which are among the most restrictive in the European Union.The first bill, proposed by Tusk's Civic Coalition (KO) and the Left, would partially decriminalise abortion and remove criminal penalties for assisting someone in obtaining one, an offence currently punishable by up to three years in prison.The second bill, introduced by the more conservative coalition partners Poland 2050 and the Polish Peasants' Party (PSL), would overturn the effects of a 2020 Constitutional Tribunal ruling that banned abortion in cases of severe foetal abnormalities.The first bill passed with 217 votes in favour, 213 against and three abstentions, while the second was approved by 233 votes to 203, with one abstention.Where the protests took placeAlongside full decriminalisation, protesters are demanding access to legal abortion up to the 12th week of pregnancy, full access to the "morning-after" pill, and action by local authorities to disperse illegal protests held outside hospitals in Warsaw and Gdańsk and the AboTak clinic in Warsaw.Demonstrations took place in 26 Polish cities as well as in London. Organisers announced another protest for Sunday.

title: Spanish and Portuguese unions discuss joint general strike
description: Several Spanish trade unions have already called a general strike for 11 November, but the leader of Spain's biggest union CCOO says a joint strike with Portuguese unions is now being considered.
content: Portuguese and Spanish trade unions are in talks over a possible "Iberian general strike", Unai Sordo, secretary-general of Comisiones Obreras (CCOO), said on Thursday in an interview with the programme "Los Desayunos" produced by Spanish broadcaster RTVE and the EFE news agency.According to Sordo, Portuguese unions are considering calling a general strike on 11 November, the same day as a planned walkout in Spain involving the country's two main trade union confederations, CCOO and the General Workers' Union (UGT).The aim, Sordo explained, is to organise an "Iberian general strike", although he stressed that the plan depends on a decision by Portuguese trade unions.'Saramago strike'"It is up to the Portuguese to decide whether, in the end, we join forces in a mobilisation across the Iberian Peninsula that would also be historic", the CCOO secretary-general said.Sordo also caustically referred to José Saramago, the Portuguese Literature Nobel laureate, who spent nearly two decades living in Lanzarote in the Canary Islands and maintained close ties with progressive movements."If they hold [the strike] in Portugal, we are going to call it the Saramago strike", Sordo concluded.The general strike in Spain on 11 November has been planned for several weeks and is scheduled to take place 18 days before snap elections called by Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, after parliament rejected government measures aimed at tackling the housing crisis.Both countries have seen protests over housing affordability and the rising cost of living. Inspired by demonstrations that began in Madrid's Puerta del Sol square in late September, thousands of protesters camped overnight in central areas of Portuguese cities, including Porto and Lisbon.Demonstrators in both countries are demanding decent, affordable housing, with many arguing that having a job is no longer enough to afford rent in major cities.

title: Judge orders Trump to sit for a deposition in his BBC defamation lawsuit by December 11
description: The BBC has accused Trump of seeking to postpone his deposition until January 2027.
content: A federal judge on Thursday ordered US President Donald Trump to sit for a deposition by 11 December in his $10 billion (€8.6 billion) defamation lawsuit against the BBC.The order by US Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett came after the BBC's lawyers accused Trump of delaying his appearance.Trump could face sanctions, including the possible dismissal of his lawsuit, if he fails to comply, unless the discovery period is extended beyond 18 December.Charles Tobin, an attorney representing the BBC, said that with two months left in the discovery period, “we still haven’t been able to depose the plaintiff.”Tobin said Trump had initially agreed to be deposed on 16 October but cancelled, citing a “matter of national importance.” However, the president was campaigning in Georgia that day, according to the lawyer.“He was participating in party politics and prioritized that over sitting for the deposition,” Tobin said.Trump filed a lawsuit against the BBC in December 2025, accusing the British broadcaster of defamation and deceptive and unfair trade practices over a documentary titled “Trump: A Second Chance.”The 33-page lawsuit accused the broadcaster of presenting a “false, defamatory, deceptive, disparaging, inflammatory, and malicious depiction of President Trump,” describing it as “a brazen attempt to interfere in and influence” the 2024 US presidential election.The BBC admitted to editing together parts of Trump's 6 January 2021 speech, making it appear he had encouraged violence at the US Capitol. The broadcaster apologised, and two senior executives resigned, but it denied defamation.

title: MEPs call for Yemen's Houthis to be added to EU terrorist list
description: A non-binding European Parliament resolution urges a freeze on all the Yemeni group's funds, as the EU struggles to counter the threat to civilian maritime traffic in the Red Sea.
content: The European Parliament on Thursday approved a resolution calling for Yemen's Houthis to be added to the EU’s list of terrorist organisations.The call follows an escalation in recent weeks of attacks on Saudi Arabia by the Iran-backed group, which prompted the UK to pledge defensive missions to protect Riyadh, while the EU struggles to increase its naval presence in the Red Sea to shield commercial vessels from possible attacks.The non-binding text, adopted by a large majority of MEPs in a show of hands, urged the freezing of all funds and economic resources belonging to the Houthis and their facilitators.Inclusion on the EU terrorist list mainly entails financial restrictions — freezing all bank accounts and property held in EU countries, and banning EU individuals and companies from financing the listed group.The final decision rests with the EU member states, which must approve any new listing unanimously.The European Parliament justified its request by condemning the Houthi naval blockade of Saudi Arabia and their attacks on energy infrastructure and commercial shipping in the Red Sea and the Bab el-Mandeb strait, which are severely disrupting maritime traffic and driving up energy prices in the region.The resolution describes the attacks as flagrant violations of international law, stressing that many Yemeni civilians have been killed and displaced, and that the country’s humanitarian crisis has deepened since the latest attacks.The group formally known as Ansar Allah, which has been at war with the internationally recognised government of Yemen since 2014, launched a blitz offensive along the Red Sea coast in July to take control of the vital waterway crucial to the world's energy and cargo shipping.A counteroffensive by the Saudi-led coalition saw much of the gains made by the Houthis reversed, but the group still poses a threat to international vessels traversing the strait that links Europe and Asia.The Houthis have pledged safe passage to all ships bar those linked to Saudi Arabia, while continuing their attacks against energy infrastructure and airports across the neighbouring kingdom.MEPs also stressed the crucial role of Aspides, the EU naval mission in the Red Sea, and urged member states to provide additional naval and air assets.The mission currently has three ships from Italy and Greece, with two more pledged by Belgium and the Netherlands. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas has said at least 10 are needed.

title: Families of missing Azerbaijanis call for support from European institutions
description: Families of more than 4,000 Azerbaijanis still missing since the first Karabakh war brought their demand for answers to the EU institutions, hoping that the peace process between Armenia and Azerbaijan, after decades of suffering on both sides, could finally clarify the fate of their relatives.
content: Azerbaijani families of missing persons demanded support from EU institutions in Brussels during their demonstrations this week in front of the European Parliament and European Commission headquarters, as they continue to seek the truth about the fate of over 4,000 loved ones still missing since the first Karabakh war.Organised by the Garabagh Missing Families Public Union, the families asked for help in their quest to establish the fate of their relatives, which include children, women and elderly people, who remain missing since the first war that ended in 1994, urging the EU institutions to pressure Armenia into disclosing archive information and the locations of mass graves.With 32 mass graves recently discovered in Karabakh, the families have emphasised that their right to know the truth after 30 years requires international attention. They said the group had not received international recognition or aid to help find their relatives.The families said that Armenia has not disclosed any information about the missing persons, but they hoped that the peace process between Armenia and Azerbaijan can now shed light on the fate of their loved ones and achieve closure.The rally participants wore white jackets, each with a picture of their loved one, their date of birth and a question mark, symbolising their unknown fate."My husband Azad Jabbarov went missing in Khojaly and for 34 years we know nothing about him," said Farida Jabbarova, a participant at the rally."And here, I represent him and more than 4,000 people who went missing and require justice for them and to receive information."The demonstration displayed personal items of those missing, including passports, photos and clothes.According to Konul Behbudova, head of the Garabagh Missing Families Public Union, 328 missing persons were identified with DNA examinations and the remains of 273 victims were handed over to their families, but the fate of thousands is still unknown."These territories are contaminated with mines and unexploded ordinance, that's why it's difficult to find them," Behbudova said."Our goal is to find the places were these people were buried and find any information about their fate, to get their remains and be able to burry them and to have a place in the cemetery to visit them," Jabbarova said.The plight of the Azerbaijani families is now part of the wider peace process and reconciliation between Armenia and Azerbaijan after decades of tragic wars over Karabakh which brought immense suffering to both nations, with thousands of casualties and refugees on both sides.Armenia said that hundreds of Armenians are also missing following the Karabakh wars and has also sought answers about their fate as well.

title: Police find 74 migrants in overcrowded conditions in Ceuta, arrest suspected exploitation ring leader
description: The National Police has found 74 migrants crammed into a house in Ceuta's Príncipe district, including 10 unaccompanied minors, and arrested a man on suspicion of labour exploitation, assault and facilitating irregular immigration.
content: Spanish National Police reported on Thursday that the located 74 irregular migrants last Tuesday, living in overcrowded, precarious conditions, including ten unaccompanied minors, at a property in the El Príncipe neighbourhood of Ceuta.The operation led to the arrest of a local resident, who is allegedly the leader of a criminal organisation involved in facilitating irregular migration and other criminal activities.The intervention forms part of an investigation into suspected offences related to facilitating irregular immigration, violations of workers' rights, bodily harm and the labour exploitation of minors.Police enquiries have uncovered indications that some of the minors housed in the property may have suffered physical assaults, including injuries caused by dog bites. Investigators are also seeking to determine whether both minors and adults were subjected to labour exploitation and forced to carry out various tasks, with their vulnerability being exploited.Large police deployment in the El Príncipe neighbourhoodThe operation required a significant police deployment because of the complexity of the area where the property was located and the potential danger posed by the organisation under investigation. According to the National Police, several of its members have extensive criminal records.Inside the property, officers found 54 men, ten women and ten unaccompanied foreign minors. The detainee is suspected of offences involving the facilitation of irregular immigration, violations of workers' rights, causing injury to a minor and the labour exploitation of minors.Police step up operations after migrant camps cleared in CeutaThe operation comes against a backdrop of increased police activity in Ceuta, following the clearance of the settlements on Benítez beach and El Trampolín. The dismantling of these camps is thought to have led some of the migrants who had been living there to move to other parts of the city, including the El Príncipe neighbourhood.In response to this situation, the National Police are maintaining surveillance and operational deployments both around and inside the neighbourhood.The operation also targets the logistical infrastructure of the organisation under investigation, which allegedly housed large numbers of people while preparing to arrange their irregular transfer to mainland Spain.The investigation was conducted in coordination with various police units along the Andalusian coast and central services, in collaboration with the public prosecutor's office to combat migrant smuggling.

title: Meloni government approves aid for transport, farming and fishing sectors amid intense pressure from truckers
description: On Thursday, Giorgia Meloni's government approved the aid bill after truckers staged a protest against the spiralling cost-of-living crisis and high fuel prices. The protests have brought many critical sectors and services, including food deliveries, to a standstill.
content: The Italian Council of Ministers has approved a decree-law providing urgent support for the road haulage, agriculture and fisheries sectors, in response to protests - largely by truckers - against the soaring cost-of-living crisis and rising fuel prices.In the early hours of Thursday, before the decree was approved, truckers in Sicily and Calabria had suspended their operations - including the hauling of foodstuffs as part of their protest efforts.Officials in Italy said that the strikes had halted the production of the famed buffalo mozzarella, causing an estimated 3 million-euro loss in just 24 hours as the milk cannot reach dairies in the Naples region and the finished cheese cannot reach customers.Many have begun to gradually resume deliveries of foodstuffs after the decree was signed into law on Thursday, but the wider protest has not stopped and has grown to incorporate more ports in the country's south, with many vessels still refusing to return to work due to the high price of diesel.The decree allocates €60 million to cover fuel costs in the agricultural sector. These funds are due to "arrive very quickly through Agea", according to Agriculture Minister Francesco Lollobrigida.'The governmnent listens'The money will be used to purchase approximately 121 million litres of fuel, "with a contribution of up to 45 cents"."After a first intervention that covered the initial part of the year, this measure runs until 15 October, compensating the companies that have bought agricultural fuel," added Lollobrigida,The Agriculture Ministry is expected to set out the procedures and deadlines for submitting the documents proving the supply of petrol or diesel in the coming days, and will make direct payment of the subsidy to beneficiaries within thirty days of receiving the paperwork.The contribution will be paid by crediting the beneficiaries' bank accounts."Agreement with the road haulage associations, funds already being paid out and new measures for farmers and fishermen approved today by the Council of Ministers," wrote Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni in a post on X."The government listens to those who demonstrate peacefully and works to provide concrete responses," she added.Meloni detailed that she has asked Interior Minister Piantedosi to "accept the request coming from the haulage, farming and retail associations to guarantee free movement, the supply of goods to businesses and therefore to citizens, while also preventing speculation on prices that would otherwise be inevitable".Dismantling of blockades still plannedBut tensions continue to remain high between the government and protesters, who are refusing to back away from their demands.Deputy Minister for Infrastructure and Transport Edoardo Rixi said at a press conference that imposing a back-to-work order on the blockades has been requested to ensure essential public services return, which are seriously at risk due to schools resorting to remote teaching and fuel shortages in some areas such as Campania.Rixi reiterated the importance of constructive dialogue, while confirming the intention to move ahead with dismantling the blockades in the South if the talks break down."The back-to-work order and other measures are the last tools we want to deploy before clearing the protests," he said."We cannot allow supermarkets in Naples to be empty indefinitely or people to have to walk because filling stations have no petrol. In the next few hours we will take a decision in the light of the answers that are given."

title: Beyond five-star luxury: What's next for hospitality in Qatar?
description: Qatar has no shortage of luxury hotels and restaurants. Now the focus is on experiences and technology that give visitors a reason to come back.
content: Qatar has spent the past decade expanding its hospitality industry, with new luxury hotels, restaurants and a growing number of international visitors. But attracting tourists is only part of the challenge. How do you give them a reason to return?In this episode of CULT, Aadel Haleem visits Hospitality Qatar 2026, where 120 companies are showcasing the latest developments in the industry, from food and equipment to technology.Hotel operators explain why travellers increasingly want more than just a comfortable room, what surprises first-time visitors and how Qatar is attracting guests from new international markets.We also meet Spanish businesses exploring opportunities in Qatar, including a Barcelona-based technology company working with Visit Qatar to help tourists discover lesser-known attractions through rewards and incentives.With more than five million international visitors in 2025, the focus is shifting towards creating experiences that make people want to come back.

title: Germany arrests Ukrainian national on suspicion of spying for Russia
description: A Ukrainian national has been arrested on suspicion of spying for Russia. According to federal prosecutors, he allegedly gathered defence-related information.
content: A Ukrainian national was arrested in Brandenburg on Thursday on suspicion of spying for Russia, the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office in Karlsruhe has announced.The suspect is alleged to have used contacts within the European defence industry to obtain sensitive information. According to the Federal Prosecutor General's Office, Vadym Y. had been in contact with a Russian intelligence service via an intermediary since at least July 2025.In connection with the war between Russia and Ukraine, he is said to have obtained militarily relevant information for the service from within Germany. This included, among other things, information on the production of armoured vehicles, ammunition and explosives, as well as personnel and military facilities at sites used to secure NATO's eastern flank.While some of the information was publicly accessible, the suspect is said to have deliberately obtained other details by approaching individuals working in the European defence industry.Investigation for acting as an intelligence agentThe Federal Public Prosecutor's Office is responsible for cases that affect Germany's national security and involve suspected espionage on behalf of a foreign power.The case comes at a time when German security authorities are issuing increasingly stark warnings about suspected Russian espionage and sabotage activities.Other suspected espionage cases in GermanyAs recently as April 2026, Euronews reported on the arrest of a man in Berlin who is alleged to have passed information on Germany's military support for Ukraine, defence companies and military convoys to a Russian intelligence service. Potential targets for sabotage operations are also said to have been involved.Another case concerns a 53-year-old Ukrainian from Attendorn in North Rhine-Westphalia. According to a ruling by the Federal Court of Justice made public in October, he is accused of having monitored another Ukrainian in a refugee shelter on behalf of Russia's domestic intelligence service FSB and of having passed on information about that person's contacts via Telegram. In this case, charges have now been brought for acting as an intelligence agent.The cases differ in their specific allegations. However, they illustrate that investigations by German authorities cover both the gathering of military information and the surveillance of individuals who might be of interest to Russia.Presumption of innocence appliesIn the current case in Brandenburg, the investigation is still ongoing. The precise background to the alleged gathering of information and any possible additional accomplices remain to be established. Until a final conviction is reached, the presumption of innocence applies to the accused.

title: Russia strikes Kyiv with three cluster-warhead ballistic missiles, Zelenskyy says
description: The latest Russian bombardment of Ukraine's capital came just hours after US envoy Steve Witkoff met Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg, underscoring the stark contrast between Washington's renewed diplomatic efforts and Moscow's continuing attacks on Ukrainian cities.
content: Russian forces struck Kyiv overnight with three ballistic missiles carrying cluster warheads designed to inflict maximum casualties across densely populated areas, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed on Thursday.One of the missiles struck Pechersk, the Ukrainian capital's historic centre, hitting an area between the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra and the Holy Presentation Monastery, damaging religious buildings, homes, shops, cafés and other civilian infrastructure.The missiles were designed to detonate in the air as they approached their targets, dispersing explosive submunitions across an area 400 metres in diameter, Zelenskyy said.Serhii Beskrestnov, Ukraine's presidential adviser known by his callsign "Flash", earlier identified one of the missiles as an Iskander equipped with a K5 cluster warhead.At least two dead and dozens injured"This warhead detonates above the ground and is used specifically for inflicting maximum harm to people and equipment over an area of 400 by 400 metres," Beskrestnov said, adding that its 58 bomblets explode in the air.Zelenskyy accused Moscow of deliberately targeting civilians in Kyiv's historic centre, insisting that the choice of both weapon and location was intentional."This is another extraordinarily revealing strike – revealing because it was no accident. The choice of weapon was deliberate, the choice of target area was deliberate, and so was the intent to inflict as much loss and damage on civilians as possible," he said."There was no military target nearby, not even in theory, and the weapon was designed to cause widespread destruction."The strike was part of a large-scale Russian aerial assault on the Ukrainian capital and surrounding region overnight on 21–22 October.At least two people were killed and 34 others injured, including five children, across the affected areas, according to Zelenskyy.The bombardment came in several waves, with ballistic missiles and drones striking residential neighbourhoods, transport facilities and medical infrastructure across the capital.Kyiv authorities reported damage in the Holosiivskyi, Obolonskyi, Pecherskyi, Sviatoshynskyi and Dniprovskyi districts.Ukraine's Air Force said Russia had launched 210 drones, including 110 jet-powered variants, alongside Iskander-M, S-400, Zircon and Onyx missiles.Ukrainian air defences intercepted or suppressed 181 drones, including 87 jet-powered variants, while strikes were recorded at 32 locations and falling debris at another eight.Zelenskyy said Russia had fired 21 missiles in total during three waves of ballistic strikes on Kyiv.The attacks continued throughout Thursday, with further strikes reported in Kharkiv, Dnipro, Marhanets, Mykolaiv and Kherson, as well as several other regions. In Kharkiv, a commuter train was hit, according to the Ukrainian president.Zelenskyy said Russia had carried out more than 170 strikes against critical energy facilities since 11 October, despite Ukrainian air defences intercepting significant numbers of drones and some missiles.He warned that Ukrainian intelligence identified Russian priorities for further attacks in the coming weeks, accusing Moscow of exploiting delays in Western air defence supplies."Russia is clearly taking advantage of the slowdown in air defence supplies from our partners," he said, calling for the accelerated delivery of military assistance already approved by Ukraine's allies.The overnight bombardment came just hours after US special envoy Steve Witkoff met Russian President Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg as Washington sought to revive negotiations to end the war.During the visit, Witkoff described Putin as a "humanitarian", despite the Russian president being wanted by the International Criminal Court over the alleged unlawful deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children.Zelenskyy said on Wednesday that Ukraine was ready to accept literally any form of truce, on any aspect of the war, that Russia would be willing to agree to.But following the latest attacks, the Ukrainian president questioned Moscow's willingness to pursue peace."Russia has not changed the way it wages this war, and it is taking no steps that would signal a genuine desire to end it," he said.

title: EIB to double climate funding to €30bn as extreme weather costs soar
description: The European Investment Bank's €30 billion for climate financing reflects a shift from climate mitigation to economic protection -- and comes a week before the European Commission is due to present its own climate resilience plan.
content: The European Investment Bank (EIB) plans to double its financing for climate adaptation to at least €30 billion by 2030, as Europe steps up efforts to protect infrastructure, water supplies and agriculture from the growing economic toll of extreme weather.“Climate adaptation is a no-brainer,” EIB President Nadia Calviño said, arguing that every euro invested in prevention saves €10 in damage and repairs.Wildfires, floods and heatwaves caused an estimated €43 billion in economic losses across the European Union in the summer of 2025, according to a joint study by the European Central Bank (ECB) and the University of Mannheim. The study projects that the cumulative economic impact could reach €126 billion by 2029.More than 600,000 hectares have burned across the EU this year, more than twice the long-term average over the past two decades, with temperatures registering their highest across Europe in June alone.European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced a European heatwave plan during her inaugural State of the Union speech in September, after a dramatic summer that saw at least 35,000 excess deaths linked to heatwaves.From cutting emissions to limiting the damageThe EIB's €30 billion financing announced on Thursday marks a renewed emphasis on preparing for the consequences of climate change, alongside efforts to cut greenhouse gas emissions.The EIB, which sometimes brands itself as Europe's climate bank, explicitly recognised that investment is not keeping pace with growing climate adaptation needs."While understanding of physical climate risks has grown significantly in recent years, adaptation investment remains constrained by limited project pipelines, capacity gaps and financing barriers," the EIB's second climate adaptation plan says."Accelerating adaptation will require stronger project preparation, better technical capacity and greater mobilisation of public and private capital."The financing plan targets investment in energy networks, public buildings, water systems and farming, while helping EU companies bring climate adaptation technologies to market.The financing package will combine loans, guarantees and advisory support, with a focus on making adaptation projects easier to identify and finance, including for smaller businesses. The EIB will also develop tools to help public authorities and companies assess local climate risks.The initiative gives climate policy a direct economic and competitiveness dimension, as governments face the prospect of mounting costs from droughts, floods, heatwaves and wildfires. It also positions the EU's lending arm as a tool for mobilising investment in resilience technologies.However, the announcement leaves open how the €30 billion will be distributed between countries and sectors and how much additional private investment the plan is expected to attract.Rummaging for moneyEU countries are already struggling with little fiscal space, with talks on the next multi-annual budget going sour at the latest gathering of EU leaders on 15-16 October.However, Climate Action Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra recently acknowledged the tight fiscal situation but maintained that upfront investment is cheaper than repeatedly paying for climate damage."All evidence shows that making the upfront investments is way cheaper than just being hit by fire, being hit by floods and then paying for the damage. That's just way more costly," Hoekstra said.The Commission's EU climate resilience framework is expected next week and it should bring more clarity on the Climate Insurance Alliance, also touted by von der Leyen during her September inaugural speech.Paul Fox, senior research and advocacy officer at the watchdog Finance Watch, said that insurance is key to a functioning economy and cutting off the most exposed regions is becoming a market failure that the EU must address."Postal services reach communities across Europe not because every location is profitable, but because they provide a service people need. Natural hazard insurance should be guaranteed on the same principle. It gives people the security to build their lives and the confidence to invest in the future," said Fox.

title: Beyond oil: The Sectors shaping this country’s economic future
description: Azerbaijan is seeking to diversify its economy through manufacturing, agriculture, logistics, tourism and renewable energy, while attracting new international investment.
content: Reducing dependence on oil remains a key part of Azerbaijan’s economic strategy, with growth opportunities spanning manufacturing, agriculture, logistics, tourism and renewable energy. Industrial zones and new business initiatives are helping expand production and exports, while digital transformation is opening further opportunities.Speaking on Business Horizons, Yasin Jalilov, Deputy Director of Azerbaijan Business Development Fund (ABDF) highlighted economic stability and diversification as advantages for investors, pointing to sectors such as agro-food processing, green energy and pharmaceuticals.ADBF aims to simplify access to support for entrepreneurs. Meanwhile, sales at Sumgait Chemical Industrial Park exceeded €572 million in the first half of 2025, including nearly €283 million in exports. Agricultural and agro-industrial exports also rose by almost 23% between January and July 2026.

title: Gulf nations brace for possible return to all-out war between US and Iran
description: The volatility around the Israeli and US midterm elections is fueling fears of renewed US-Israeli strikes on Iran in a short and intensive military campaign to push Tehran into concessions, with Iran vowing a devastating response against the Gulf nations.
content: The Gulf countries and the wider Middle East are bracing for a possible resumption of hostilities in the Iran war amid multiple simultaneous warnings and media reports of increasing intensity and detail, coupled with a massive US military build-up in the Gulf and Israeli and Iranian armies placed on high alert, raising fears of an imminent escalation with devastating consequences for the region.Against the backdrop of growing speculation over the last weeks that the US and Israel may launch a new attack against Iran before or after the mid-term elections in the US and next week’s
