elections in Israel, a new US Department of State travel alert issued on Wednesday evening was relayed by news agencies and wider media as an urgent signal as to the imminence of war restarting, with the Gulf nations bearing the brunt of a potentially larger conflict.The US Department of State announced that it ordered non-essential US government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia as “the hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly beyond that immediate area.”Several news outlets reported that families of embassy staff in the United Arab Emirates, Jordan, Qatar, and Bahrain were also ordered to leave, quoting multiple diplomatic sources.US Department of State spokesperson Tommy Pigott said these reports were “inaccurate."“The US Department of State issued an ordered departure for non-emergency U.S. government employees and their family members in Saudi Arabia only,” as a result of the growing Houthi attacks, Pigott said in a post on X.The US Saudi warning follows a Middle East-wide red alert issued by Washington on Monday to US citizens in 12 countries across the Middle East, warning their citizens in Israel, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Lebanon, Jordan, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, the UAE, Yemen and Iran, citing risks of potential attacks on US interests.War vs electionsWith days before Israel’s close elections in which prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu could lose power, and ahead of next month’s US midterm elections in which war-linked high prices have sparked voter anger, there are growing concerns and speculations that US-Israeli attacks on Iran could resume.The US has been rebuilding a massive strike force in the Gulf by sending more military assets to the region, including a third aircraft carrier and thousands of troops, to join the largest US naval and air force in the Middle East since the invasion of Iraq in 2003.Iran has been warning for weeks that it has reorganised its defence capabilities and that any attack would be matched with what they called a devastating response against US interests and civilian infrastructure across the region, which would be far worse than their previous attacks on the Gulf nations and longer in time too.Iranian officials and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) are preparing for war, having declared their “100% certainty” that the US and Israel will attack them again.According to reports in Iran, Tehran activated its so-called Mosaic Defence doctrine by which Iran would operate in a decentralised way, by giving local commanders a list of targets to keep fighting even if the central command is destroyed.In parallel with the US Department of State alert on Wednesday, the New York Times and other media reported that the US and Israel have developed specific plans for new strikes on Iran after the US midterm elections.US President Donald Trump declared recently that any considerations for a new attack on Iran would be made after the US midterm elections. According to the New York Times report, which quoted US officials, targets would likely include Iran’s energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities, and arsenals of missiles and drones, with the objective of pushing Iran into a deal to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu earlier this week on an unannounced trip in Israel to discuss “the threats in the region.” Speaking at an IDF officer graduation ceremony on Wednesday night, Netanyahu said that the Tehran regime has to be finally overthrown.The Israeli premier justified this by stating that Iran's Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei "decided to follow in his father's footsteps (to attempt) once again to develop the bombs of death."’The younger Khamenei, who has been selected as the new supreme leader following his father Ali Khamenei's killing in the US-Israeli strikes on Tehran in the opening salvo of the war on 28 February, is yet to be seen in public amid continued reports questioning his health condition.Earlier this week, US media reported that dozens of Israeli fighter jets and refuelling aircraft reportedly flew towards the Iranian border before turning back, calling the sorties a military exercise and a "show of force," according to the Times of Israel newspaper.According to media reports, US officials have questioned Israel's fighter jet deployment, believing the purpose of the exercise was to test Iranian air defence units and provoke them to open fire.In parallel, Israeli media reported that Israeli security officials warned the government that an attack on Iran could be perceived as political interference in the election next week.Israel’s opposition leader Yair Lapid told the Israeli media that “based on the information available to me, there is absolutely no reason to attack Iran or anywhere else before the elections.” Calls for extreme caution amid uncertaintyMeanwhile on Thursday, seven oil tankers caught fire or were damaged in the Strait of Hormuz after being hit by Iran or striking naval mines, Tehran said, a markedly high number as tensions wind upward over concerns about a return to all-out war.Iran still asserts control over the waterway, a central point of leverage in any talks with the US over the war. During his state visit to Qatar, French President Emmanuel Macron issued a stern warning on Wednesday about the Gulf's fragile security situation, urging “extreme caution” to avoid escalating tensions that could reignite conflict, after talks with Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani.Macron told the media that he was “very cautious because no one can tell how the situation will evolve in the next days and weeks.""No one can ignore that we are in a period that despite everything can lead to tensions: elections in Israel, the midterm elections in the United States, and so during this time efforts and initiatives must be doubled to avoid that these tensions don’t result in a resumption of conflict,” the French president explained."There is a lot of uncertainty and measures taken by one side and the other that I would not comment on."Nevertheless, the US-Iran exchanges continue through international mediators, with Qatar and Pakistan leading the efforts to find a diplomatic breakthrough.The US has previously applied pressure and threats on Iran to push for concessions and reach a deal. A return to all-out war would again endanger civilians throughout the region and complicate global deliveries of oil, natural gas and related products like fertiliser from the region and likely bring another spike in energy prices around the world.

title: MEPs side with industry in vote to delay methane rules
description: EU lawmakers say their position balances climate ambitions with easing supplies – at a time of turmoil in energy security.
content: European Parliament lawmakers on Thursday rejected a European Commission proposal to delay the EU's methane rules by one year, instead backing a three-year postponement until 2031.The move highlights growing divisions over how far the EU should go in softening environmental regulations as governments struggle with high energy prices, supply disruptions and concerns about industrial competitiveness.The EU's methane regulation requires companies importing fossil fuels to show that their suppliers outside the bloc meet equivalent standards for monitoring, reporting and verifying methane emissions.Parliament President Roberta Metsola described the vote as "strengthening Europe’s energy security" amid uncertainty in global energy markets."The Parliament swiftly voted in favour of postponing certain obligations under the EU Methane Regulation, giving energy companies more time to prepare for the new rules. A more realistic timeline, effective implementation and continued progress on cutting emissions," Metsola wrote on X.The Commission proposed a one-year delay following pressure from the oil and gas industry and several EU countries, recently joined by France. They have cited concerns over energy security and high prices amid continued disruption to key shipping routes in the Middle East.But the centre-right European People's Party (EPP) pushed for a vote on delaying the EU's methane rules, amid a breakdown in political negotiations on Wednesday, according to three parliamentary sources.Virgil Popescu, an EPP MEP and former Romanian energy minister, said on 20 October that he would seek a three-year postponement of certain obligations, citing the difficulties facing domestic oil and gas producers, including those operating older wells.Centre-right secures longer delaySocial Democrats and Liberals backed the Commission's one-year delay, while the Greens and the Left called on the EU executive to reject its proposal and stick to the 2029 timeline.Jutta Paulus, a Greens/EFA MEP and lead negotiator on the methane regulation, accused the Commission of bowing to pressure from the oil and gas industry."The call by Conservatives and the Far-Right to postpone the methane regulation by three years is an absolute scandal. Once again, Conservatives and the far right are pursuing policies that undermine climate action and serve the interests of the fossil fuel industry," Paulus reacted on Thursday.Under the EPP-backed proposal, the Commission would also assess in mid-2029 whether further changes were needed if energy companies continued to face compliance difficulties or concerns over security of supply persisted."The European Parliament has backed our proposal for a targeted three-year postponement, providing greater legal certainty, allowing verification systems to become fully operational and ensuring equal treatment of EU producers and importers," said Greek EPP MEP Dimitris Tsiodras.EPP group spokesman on industry and energy Christian Ehler had described the Commission's one-year delay as "far from sufficient". He said the EPP and at least 15 EU countries have been calling for a three-year delay."This is not about increasing or permitting further methane emissions, it is about security of supply and lower energy prices," Ehler said.The legislation is being considered under an urgent procedure, with the aim of bringing the changes into force before the end of the year.Methane rules under pressureEU member states adopted methane rules in May 2024, introducing the bloc’s first framework for measuring, reporting and verifying methane emissions in the energy sector as part of efforts to curb one of the most potent greenhouse gases. Failure to honour such requests for data incurs penalties.However, the Commission proposed in July waiving penalties linked to the bloc's methane rules for three years to appease industry fears and pressure from the US, the EU's largest liquefied natural gas (LNG) supplier.A longer postponement could carry a political cost for the EU's climate ambitions. Extending the timetable would give suppliers more time, but could also weaken the incentive to invest in emissions monitoring and leak reduction.Environmentalists argued that delaying the application of the methane rules won't address supply or pricing concerns."It is global supply shocks and Europe's dependence on fossil fuels that are driving current market pressures," the independent platform European Civil Society Observatory on Methane said in a statement.The group estimates that implementing the regulation fully and on schedule could generate around €704 billion in climate, health and economic benefits, against regulatory costs of €49 billion.It also argues that the measures could prevent an estimated 155,000 premature deaths worldwide by 2030.Flora Witkowski, gas policy coordinator at Climate Action Network (CAN), said the EU is responsible for the harm caused by dirty fossil gas extraction and imports.“Today’s vote by the EU Parliament to delay the EU methane regulation only serves the interest of the fossil fuel industry, not people. It will only facilitate Europe’s dependence on fossil fuels and prolong the energy price crisis, while costing an additional €185bn in damages and derailing efforts to mitigate the climate crisis.

title: Digital bank Revolut suffers worldwide outage: Everything you need to know
description: Revolut's app and services became inaccessible to millions of users on Tuesday. The issue, which appeared to be linked to a power outage at a Google Cloud data centre near London, has now been "fixed" and services have been "restored," the company said.
content: Online banking app Revolut said an issue causing major disruption for millions of users on Tuesday had been "fixed.""Due to a recent Google Cloud outage, customers may have experienced temporary service disruption on the Revolut app today," the company said on Tuesday evening. "The issue has now been fixed, and services are now restored."Reports first emerged this morning of users being unable to access their money or use their bank cards after a system failure, with cards reportedly declining when trying to make payments, while others received an error message as they tried to log in to check their accounts.Following widespread reports on social media, the company put out a statement to reassure its customers that it was working to resolve the issue and that their financial assets were intact.“We are currently experiencing a service disruption affecting multiple services. We can confirm that all our customers’ money and data are safe,” Revolut said in a statement.“We’ve been working to fix the issue since it was identified this morning and apologise to anyone affected and for any inconvenience caused.”The issue appeared to be linked to a power outage at a Google Cloud data centre near London that caused serious failures to services on Tuesday.Google said in a service update that its Cloud services suffered an outage "due to a power event." Several other UK banks also reported disruption.Google has since announced that the issue had been "mitigated" for "most" customers, with a "very small number" still experiencing issues.Millions of customers affectedMillions of Revolut users were left unable to access their funds or make payments using their cards on Tuesday as the problem persisted.Complaints came from across the world, with users in the UK, Ireland, France, Spain, Japan and other countries all reporting disruption. It is unclear if the outage is affecting every Revolut user.Revolut is Europe’s most valuable startup, currently worth $121.1 billion, making it more valuable than traditional European banking giants like Barclays, Lloyds and Santander.Revolut says it has more than 80 million retail customers and is currently growing at roughly a million new users every 17 days, putting it on course to cross the 100 million customer threshold by mid-2027.The online bank took off thanks to its many benefits when travelling abroad, including competitive exchange rates, fee-free spending, global access to ATM cash withdrawals without fees, with higher tier memberships offering medical insurance, airport lounge access and trip delay coverage.Revolut users can also make instant transfers free of charge to one another as well as international transfers quickly with low upfront fees.The UK-based startup’s largest markets are in the UK (13 million), Spain (6 million) and France (5 million).More than 750,000 companies also use the Revolut Business service.

title: PHP security flaw: Why websites across Europe went dark and what it means for you
description: AI models uncovered what OpenAI calls "one of the most impactful" security bugs in recent memory, hidden in PHP for more than a decade. From a Pokémon sleep tracker to the Dutch parliament, websites went dark worldwide to stay ahead of hackers.
content: Artificial intelligence has exposed two critical security flaws in PHP, a programming language that quietly powers most of the internet, sending organisations worldwide scrambling to shut down websites before hackers can exploit them.The bugs sat undetected in PHP’s code for more than a decade. It took cutting-edge AI models from OpenAI and Google to turn a long-suspected weakness into a working attack — and now the race is on to close the door.As AI’s fast-advancing capabilities fuel concern over a new era of cyberattacks, here is what you need to know.Europe reactsThe Netherlands pulled its DigiD digital identity system, the Overheid.nl government portal and the website of the lower house of parliament, with the Port of Rotterdam, hospitals and the country’s five largest political parties following suit.Even the Dutch National Cyber Security Centre took its own site down.Finland’s state IT provider Valtori switched off government web services wholesale “as a precautionary measure,” France’s Interior Ministry put local administration sites into maintenance mode and Germany’s federal IT service ITZBund took down several portals.CERT-EU, the cybersecurity service for the EU institutions, went further than most, telling any organisation unable to patch immediately to take its websites offline rather than risk being hacked.The European Commission, ENISA, CERT-EU, Europol and the EU’s network of national cyber response teams also issued a joint statement urging organisations to act immediately, prioritising systems exposed to the internet.What is PHP and why does it matter?Created in the early 1990s, PHP is a name that originally stood for Personal Home Page and is the code that runs behind the scenes on roughly seven in 10 websites, according to security firm Wiz Research, which calls it “a backbone of the web”.While languages such as HTML handle what you see on a page, PHP handles what you do not, such as checking logins, processing payments, serving up content.It underpins WordPress, Drupal and Joomla, the platforms behind everything from personal blogs to online shops and government portals.That reach is what turns two bugs into a global event. Wiz said every PHP version released in the past decade is affected by at least one of the flaws, and that even a bare-bones “Hello World” page on an unpatched server could be vulnerable.A fix was released on Wednesday, with the PHP Foundation telling tech departments around the world that “if you run PHP, it is imperative that you update now.”Patched versions are PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35. Anything older no longer receives official updates and should be treated as exposed unless a vendor has backported the fix, the European Union’s cybersecurity emergency response team (CERT-EU) warned in an advisory.The result has been a wave of apps and websites going dark, from the Paris police website to a Pokémon sleep tracker, as developers patch their underlying code. Government sites across Europe were among those pulled offline as a precaution.How did AI find the flaws?Both vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and rated 9.2 out of 10 for severity, sit in the parts of PHP that nearly every request touches, namely memory management and error handling.If a web request hits PHP’s memory limit at exactly the wrong moment, the software can be tricked into running an attacker’s code without any login.The PHP Foundation admits its own developers first spotted signs of the problem in 2024, during an external audit.A theoretical exploit was sketched out, but with no concrete route to an attack and a tiny core team weighing the trade-offs of a fix, work stalled and restarted for months. The foundation called the delay “a structural failure”.Then AI got involved. In August, security firm Calif, working on an OpenAI-funded audit of PHP’s source code and using OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol model, reported a fully working remote attack with the same root cause.OpenAI independently flagged the same issue the same day. Wiz followed with further attack vectors two weeks later, using its own Wiz Atlas tool alongside Google’s Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-5.6 Sol.“With frontier AI models and the right tools, a single researcher completed in a week what previously would have taken a world-class team months of work,” Wiz researchers wrote.OpenAI called the discovery “one of the most impactful vulnerabilities in recent memory,” adding that it “marks a new phase, where AI can find security bugs with internet-scale impact”.The findings were kept under wraps while a fix was developed.Then, on Tuesday afternoon, the two CVE identifiers leaked onto online forums and social media.PHP brought its release forward by a day, and Calif mistakenly published — then deleted — a video showing its proof of concept working against several targets, the PHP Foundation said. Copies spread quickly.“The trouble with tools like AI is that the moment all the information’s out there, people can weaponise it very, very quickly,” Steve Kerrison, senior lecturer in cybersecurity at the Singapore campus of James Cook University, told AFP.“That’s why everybody’s acting with such urgency to respond to this issue.”Have sites already been hacked?Not necessarily. “Taking websites offline does not necessarily mean they have been hacked. It can be a responsible measure to protect systems while security updates are applied,” said Dimitrios Salampasis of Australia’s Swinburne University of Technology.The PHP Foundation said its security team inspected the proof-of-concept code circulating after the leak and found no functional exploit at the time of release.“The evidence that security researchers are seeing is that nobody was actively performing attacks using the techniques available,” Kerrison said.The picture is shifting, however. Web infrastructure firm Cloudflare said on Wednesday it had observed attack traffic aimed at its customers, and CERT-EU warned that the public circulation of technical details raises the likelihood that attackers are already probing the flaws.Larger institutions, from government agencies to news outlets, should be able to patch relatively quickly. Others may be left exposed for far longer.“There are sites, systems and people out there who will have no idea about this and still won’t for days, weeks and months,” Kerrison warned.That could include user-run blogs and small business sites, which hackers could hijack to spread computer viruses, send spam or host malicious content.Could there be other consequences?Any data breach could come back to haunt customers long after the patch, if their personal information is harvested for phishing attacks — where someone is tricked into handing over a password or payment details.The tangled, interlinked nature of online systems also means the risk does not end when you update your own server. Many sites rely on third-party services that may themselves run PHP.If those third parties are slow to patch, “then even though you patched yourself ... you’re still unsecure,” said Rahat Masood, senior lecturer in cybersecurity at the University of New South Wales in Sydney.PHP is not the whole story, Kerrison added. Strong cybersecurity means several layers of defence, so that one broken lock does not open every door.The PHP Foundation, for its part, is using the episode to make a pointed plea. The language runs government services, banks and online stores worldwide, yet its security still rests on a small group of foundation-funded developers and volunteers.Tools can now find bugs faster than ever, it said, but deciding how to fix them without breaking the web takes experienced engineers.

title: Why Elon Musk wants to merge Tesla and SpaceX before Trump leaves office
description: Elon Musk has opened the door to merging Tesla and SpaceX into a $3.5 trillion (€3.1tn) giant, the latest step in years of folding his companies into one another, with a deal reportedly aimed at closing before US President Donald Trump leaves the White House.
content: The world's richest man confirmed this week that Tesla and SpaceX are exploring a merger. Together, the companies are worth about $3.5 trillion (€3.1tn), making it potentially the biggest merger ever.It would cap a string of deals tying Elon Musk's businesses together, and the goal is to complete it while Donald Trump is still the US president, according to Bloomberg, citing people familiar with the matter.A merger between Tesla and SpaceX would be the latest chapter in a story that began a decade ago, when Musk started stitching his companies together.In 2016, Tesla bought SolarCity, a solar panel installer run by his cousins, a deal that was only upheld by a Delaware court after years of litigation.In March 2025, his AI start-up xAI swallowed X, the social network formerly known as Twitter, which Musk acquired for $44 billion (€39.1bn) in 2022.In February this year, SpaceX absorbed xAI, in a deal that valued the rocket maker at $1 trillion (€890bn) and the AI firm at $250 billion (€222bn), ahead of SpaceX's initial public offering (IPO).Four months later, SpaceX listed on the Nasdaq, raising $85.7 billion (€76.3bn) in the biggest stock market debut in history.Seen together, the deals look like part of a long-running plan to fold Musk's businesses into one publicly traded group. Musk himself spoke of "more and more overlap" between Tesla and SpaceX on an earnings call in July.On Tuesday, Musk told analysts on SpaceX's earnings call that both companies had set up committees of independent board members to study a merger. He called it "a good idea", while admitting he felt he was "tap dancing through a minefield".Why one companyMusk argues that AI will decide where both companies go next.They are already jointly developing Terafab, an AI chip factory in Texas, while Tesla's driverless cars and Optimus humanoid robots could benefit from the computing power SpaceX is racing to build, including planned data centres in orbit.The numbers also fit.SpaceX posted its first quarterly profit since listing, earning $4.4 billion (€3.9bn) as revenue jumped 161%, but its capital spending reached $19.6 billion (€17.4bn) in the quarter, mostly on AI.By contrast, a day later, Tesla reported that its net profit fell 43% to $787 million (€700mn) on flat revenue of $28 billion (€24.9bn), as deliveries slipped 2%. In a combined company, SpaceX's surging revenue could help offset Tesla's figures.Merging the businesses would also allow Musk to run all their operations under one roof, moving engineers and resources between the companies without disclosures or lawsuits over related-party deals.Control is another potential benefit.Musk owns about 48% of SpaceX and holds more than 80% of its votes through special shares, but only about 20% of Tesla. Since 2024, Musk has said he is uncomfortable turning Tesla into an AI and robotics leader without at least 25% of the votes.A merger could also make him richer, as his Tesla pay package treats many of its performance goals as achieved if certain types of mergers go through.Racing the political clockReportedly, the aim is to announce a merger deal in the first half of 2027 and complete it before US President Donald Trump's term ends in January 2029, according to Bloomberg, citing people familiar with the matter.Completing the deal while Trump is in office could give it a friendlier political reception, although it would still face regulatory and shareholder scrutiny.Musk, who led Trump's cost-cutting drive in 2025 before a public falling-out, has since made up with the US president and returned to the administration.He has also become the biggest known donor supporting Republican candidates in next month's US midterm elections, giving more than $276 million (€245mn) since July, according to a spokesperson for America PAC, Musk's conservative super PAC.A Democratic win could bring tougher scrutiny of SpaceX's federal contracts and Tesla's self-driving software.SpaceX itself warned in its listing documents that a shift in power in Congress could have a "material and adverse impact on our growth and competitive position".The committees have yet to agree on terms, and any deal would need the backing of more than half of all Tesla shares, which Musk called "quite a high hurdle". He cautioned that a merger was not certain.Tesla shareholders meet on 3 December.

title: Europe’s EV boom has saved these 6 oil-importing countries almost €2 billion since start of Iran war
description: “Every EV on the road reduces exposure to volatile oil markets, and as fleets grow – so does the protection against future supply shocks.”
content: Electric car fleets have cushioned the spiralling costs of oil imports following the war on Iran and subsequent energy crisis.Brent crude, which is used as the worldwide benchmark for oil prices, rose to near $100 (around €89) a barrel on 22 October – the highest in five weeks as concern grows over potential escalation in the Middle East. On February 27, the day before the US-Israel war on Iran broke out, Brent crude traded at $67(€59.63) per barrel, around 32 per cent lower than today’s prices.The rising costs have been largely attributed to Iran’s stranglehold on the Strait of Hormuz, a 167km shipping route that usually carries around one-fifth of the world’s daily oil and seaborne liquefied natural gas (LNG) supplies.At the same time, global sales of electrical vehicles (EVs) have surged by 11 per cent year-on-year, while combustion engine vehicles fell by six per cent in the first eight months of 2026.How EVs are saving Europe billionsA new analysis by energy think tank Ember found that the EV boom has displaced an estimated 200 million barrels of crude oil, worth $20 billion (€17.82 billion) between March and August 2026The study, which covers 56 countries that together account for more than 90 per cent of EV sales and more than 80 per cent of all car sales globally, found that China accounted for the largest share of these savings. The country’s electrified fleet, which consists of around 44 million EVs, has saved $14 billion (€12.48 billion) worth of crude oil. EU Member States were responsible for a further $3.1 billion (€2.76 billion) of the crude oil displaced by EVs between March and August 2026. Germany and France represent the largest share in savings at around $760 million and $560 million (€677 million and €499 million), respectively. However, when comparing oil displacement to each country’s oil consumption, Denmark emerged as Europe’s clear frontrunner. As of August 2026, the country’s current EV fleet has displaced 6.4 million barrels of oil per year, equivalent to 13 per cent of the country’s oil consumption in 2025. Elsewhere in Europe, the UK’s EV fleet displaced around $790 million (€704 million) of crude oil in the six months since the start of the fossil fuel crisis. For context, the UK imported £21.5 billion (€25.64 billion) of crude oil in the 12 months to the end of August 2026, according to the UK governmentSix European countries (Denmark, France, Germany, the Netherlands, Sweden and the UK) have together saved almost €2 billion by lowering oil-imports.EVs reduce ‘exposure to volatile oil markets’“The countries that invested in EVs before this crisis are now better protected and a growing number are following,” says Euan Graham, a senior energy analyst at Ember. “Every EV on the road reduces exposure to volatile oil markets, and as fleets grow – so does the protection against future supply shocks.”Graham adds that the global shift to EVs goes beyond cutting emissions, providing countries with improved “energy security and economic resilience” amid political instability.Are EVs better for the environment?The environmental pay-off on EVs depends on how the battery was made and whether it is charged using clean electricity or fossil fuels.A 2020 report by NGO Transport & Environment found that EVs outperform diesel and petrol cars in all scenarios, even on carbon-intensive grids such as Poland, where they are about 30 per cent cleaner than conventional vehicles.In the best case scenario, where an EV runs on clean electricity with a battery produced with clean electricity, EVs are already about five times cleaner than conventional equivalents.Ahead of the COP31 UN climate summit, co-host Türkiye has unveiled its “defining priority” to raise the global share of energy demand by electricity to 35 per cent, up from around 20 per cent, by 2035.Experts are concerned that the pledge could allow governments to count expanded gas-fired generation as progress towards electrification targets – a move they say will “seriously undermine climate goals”.“Let’s not let electrification become the Trojan horse of our times, used to hide new fossil fuel consumption rather than promote renewable energy,” says Claire Smith of campaign coalition Beyond Fossil Fuels.

title: Super tanker ablaze after striking mine in Strait of Hormuz, IRGC says
description: The IRGC navy accused the tanker of having turned off its positioning and radar systems in an effort to evade detection.
content: A super tanker has caught fire after striking a sea mine in the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Saturday.In a statement shared via Iranian state media, the IRGC's navy said a tanker carrying more than two million barrels of oil struck a mine whilst "attempting to pass through an unauthorised route" in the Strait, causing a "massive explosion" and a "fierce fire." It is unclear exactly where the incident took place.Iran's Fars news agency posted a video appearing to show the vessel ablaze.The IRGC navy accused the tanker of having turned off its positioning and radar systems in an effort to evade detection."The Strait of Hormuz is closed, and the consequence of defying Iranian regulations in the Strait of Hormuz is burning in the fire of trust in the terrorist US army," the IRGC navy added in its statement.The Strait of Hormuz is a crucial gas and oil transit chokepoint that has been at the heart of tensions between Washington and Tehran since the Iran war broke out in late February.Iran effectively cut off the passage, which usually carries around 25% of the world’s seaborne oil trade, following US and Israeli strikes on the country, prompting the US to impose a naval blockade on Iranian ports.The US military has repeatedly pushed back on claims that the IRGC has control of the Strait, saying commercial vessels have continued to transit the region "despite unwarranted IRGC aggression."Admiral Brad Cooper, the commander of US Central Command (CENTCOM), said in an update on Friday that US forces were working with regional allies and partners in the shipping industry to help protect vessels navigating the Strait."Let me be clear, the Strait of Hormuz is controlled by the United States and our regional partners, not Iran," he said. "It remains open for business."

title: EU prosecutors raid far-right group's offices in €4 million funds scandal
description: The searches are linked to an probe into the alleged misuse of more than €4 million by the now-defunct Identity and Democracy group, whose debts Patriots for Europe could be forced to repay.
content: The European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) raided the offices of the far-right Patriots for Europe (PfE) group in Brussels and Strasbourg on Wednesday as part of an investigation into the alleged misuse of millions of euros in EU funds.The searches at the European Parliament’s two main seats are linked to an investigation into the former Identity and Democracy (ID) group, the Parliament confirmed to Euronews.PfE, which includes France’s National Rally, led by Marine Le Pen; Italy’s The League, led by Matteo Salvini; and Hungary’s Fidesz, led by Viktor Orbán, could be ordered to repay more than €4 million allegedly misspent by its predecessor.“It would appear that these searches are linked to the complaint lodged against the Identity and Democracy group, which dissolved in 2024,” the PfE group said in a statement, insisting that it has no “legal continuity” with ID and is therefore “not involved in the ongoing investigation”.Neither the EPPO nor the Parliament has released further details about the searches.The Parliament “cooperates with relevant authorities” and “does not have any additional comment,” its press service said.Jean-Paul Garraud, an MEP who leads the National Rally delegation in the Parliament, wrote on X that the searches targeted “the offices of former ID staff members”.The anti-graft body has been investigating since last July the alleged misappropriation of EU funds by ID between 2019 and 2024. The group brought together MEPs from far-right parties such as France’s National Rally, Italy’s Lega and the Alternative for Germany (AfD).ID dissolved after the 2024 European elections, and many of its parties went on to form PfE, which also includes newcomers Spain’s Vox and Hungary's Fidesz.An opinion approved by the Parliament’s Committee on Budgetary Control (CONT) last September argued that EU funds wrongly spent by ID during the previous term should be repaid by PfE once the investigation is closed.Under the Parliament’s rules, a political group is treated as “the successor” of a dissolved one, and therefore liable for any remaining debt, if certain conditions are met.These include “a decisive share of the former group’s members moved together into the new formation”, “premises, IT systems, bank accounts or other assets passed to the new structure”, and “the new name and public messaging presenting the entity as the direct heir of the dissolved group, or following so closely in time that the rebranding appears designed mainly to shed liabilities.”

title: EU should revive talks on broader China trade deal, top MEP says
description: As EU lawmakers prepare to visit Beijing, the European Parliament's trade chief is calling for a broader agreement that could revive elements of a frozen investment pact and address unfair Chinese trade practices across multiple industries.
content: The European Union should seek a broad trade agreement with China, potentially including investment, rather than continue negotiating over individual sectors, a senior European Parliament lawmaker said on Wednesday.Bernd Lange, the German Socialist who chairs the Parliament's Trade Committee, made the call ahead of a visit to Beijing next week by 12 MEPs, as Brussels and China seek to ease mounting trade tensions.The two sides reached a deal on hybrid cars on 9 October, but the EU views it as insufficient to address a trade imbalance that sees the bloc run a deficit of around €1 billion a day with China.Brussels and Beijing previously negotiated a Comprehensive Agreement on Investment (CAI), but the European Parliament froze its ratification in 2021 after China imposed retaliatory sanctions in response to EU measures over human rights abuses.“It is necessary to have a more comprehensive agreement,” Lange told reporters. “I'm also in favour to have an agreement quite soon. Negotiation forever make no sense.”Lange added that the discussion should include investments. Speaking of the CAI, he also said: “Perhaps it's useful to have a look at that, specifically regarding the investment part.”Beyond cars, a wider threat to industryEarlier this month, the European Commission announced a deal under which China agreed to halve its hybrid car exports to the EU over the next four years.Under the agreement, the EU will introduce country-specific quotas allowing 350,000 Chinese hybrid cars onto the European market annually, with a fixed annual adjustment rate of 6%.The deal was presented by the Commission as a "first phase" of the negotiation which will continue on a technical level until next political talks scheduled for March 2027.But French liberal MEP Pascal Canfin, who will join Lange on the trip, warned that the EU needs to look beyond individual industries. He argued that the Commission's negotiations on behalf of the 27 member states should address broader unfair trade practices that threaten European manufacturers across multiple sectors.“We are open for negotiation, sector per sector, but at the same time, we look at things that it is not a sectorial threat,” Canfin said. “It's the risk of horizontal unfair practices that would have a very detrimental impact on our industries.”During their visit to China from 27 to 29 October, EU lawmakers will meet representatives of the Chinese Ministry of commerce and members of the National People’s Congress. They are also expected to hold meetings with high-tech business representatives in Hangzhou.Lange highlighted other issues that should be covered by a future agreement with Beijing, including Chinese export restrictions — Beijing imposes strict licensing requirements on EU businesses seeking to export rare earths, essential to European industry — unfair subsidies in the chemicals and machinery sectors, and a 20% price surcharge on EU bids in public procurement.The EU is walking a tightrope in its relations with Beijing, pushing for dialogue while simultaneously enforcing trade defence measures to protect its industry.Last week, EU leaders gave the Commission a political mandate to introduce unilateral quotas to protect the chemicals and machinery sectors, given the urgency of the threats posed by Chinese competition.However, some member states, such as Spain, favour a softer approach towards Beijing, keen to secure Chinese investment.

title: No evidence foreign powers sparked Europe’s riots, but they exploited them
description: There is so far no evidence that foreign powers caused Europe’s riots, only that they exploited them, despite politicians blaming online manipulation for them. Brussels has refused to act, citing a lack of evidence.
content: There is no conclusive evidence that foreign powers fuelled riots in France, Italy and other European countries through social media, although some have exploited the unrest to push their own narratives.The European Commission has faced pressure to act against suspected disinformation campaigns by countries such as Russia, but has so far held back, citing a lack of evidence.“There is no evidence of foreign interference in the events that took place. However, there has been foreign manipulation of information in the aftermath; that much is true,” French President Emmanuel Macron told reporters on the sidelines of his visit to Qatar.“But there are many people who have sought to exploit the situation. There are people campaigning at France’s expense,” he said.The distinction matters. Other European officials have gone further, blaming foreign powers for the unrest that has gripped cities in France, Italy, Belgium and Spain.Italian Defence Minister Guido Crosetto said at a conference on Tuesday that the riots in Milan were “the result of what I call a ‘hybrid war’ that someone is waging in our nations by resorting to unconventional tools such as TikTok, social media, YouTube”.French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot made a more limited claim at an OECD-hosted conference last week. “A few days ago, the high school student protests in France were themselves exploited by hostile narratives emanating from Russia, China, Iran, and the MAGA community. We see them, we denounce them, and we respond,” he said.National regulators, including France’s Arcom and Italy’s AGCOM, have extensive powers to tackle potential disinformation operations under the Digital Services Act (DSA). They work closely with the Commission, with their most recent meeting taking place on Tuesday.However, while regulators have urged the Commission to launch a formal investigation, the EU executive says there is insufficient evidence to justify one.“We don’t have any information or definitive confirmation that foreign information manipulation is behind the events in France and elsewhere,” an EU official with direct knowledge of the matter told Euronews on condition of anonymity.The disagreement highlights a gap between the accusations made publicly by some national politicians and the evidence available to the authorities.“The situation is unfolding at national level, and the Commission is definitely ready to assist and support the national authorities,” Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said. “Let the French authorities carry out their work first. We are ready to assist where we can.”The DSA also provides for a crisis response mechanism that can be activated in the event of a serious threat to public security or public health in the EU. This would give the Commission emergency powers over online platforms.So far, however, there has been no move to activate it.Meanwhile, law enforcement authorities have asked online platforms to provide information to help identify those involved in vandalism and looting.In France, looters have attempted to sell stolen goods on the second-hand marketplace Vinted, prompting police to ask the platform for help identifying those responsible."We are actively collaborating with law enforcement and the French authorities, and we continually adapt our processes to detect and counter emerging risks and malicious behaviour," a Vinted spokesperson told Euronews.There is evidence that Russia-linked disinformation networks, including those behind Operation Overload and Doppelgänger, have seized on the violence to amplify their online campaigns.However, unlike during the Ceuta migration crisis this summer, when extensive evidence showed that thousands of people had been mobilised by false information circulated online, the protests in France, Italy and elsewhere appear, so far, to have been exploited by foreign actors rather than driven by them.

title: Dialogue in the dark: David Bowie meets Nina Simone at Steve McQueen's exhibition at Guggenheim Bilbao
description: Steve McQueen’s exhibition “66–76–26” at Guggenheim Bilbao Museum is a sound sculpture with no image. It is a link between the decades, the emotion of love and understanding, and it also stars David Bowie and Nina Simone.
content: When you enter the room it is dark. Only a few light spots, fluffy carpet and an amazing sound. One corner belongs to Nina Simone. She sings acapella, separated from her daughter’s friend, David Bowie, who responds to her with the same words of the same song from another corner.It is almost like listening to your own family as we all know Simone and Bowie’s voices so well. They share something special with visitors. Two voices, one emotion. Love. But this duet never happened. Be present and receiveThe Oscar-winning filmmaker and artist Steve McQueen heard Wild is the Wind for the first time 30 years ago. The song was written by composer Dmitri Tiomkin and lyricist Ned Washington for the 1957 film of the same name. Later, it was taken to another register entirely by Nina Simone in 1966 and then a decade later, David Bowie paid tribute to her version. What McQueen appreciated the most in those two performances is the pure yearning – the want, the need, the must. Knowing the lyrics are so important to the artist, visitors don't need to be familiar with either the song, Simone, Bowie or McQueen at all to enjoy the exhibition, according to its curator, Lekha Hileman: “This is an exhibition that’s very experiential. It's about feeling, it's about being present," she told Euronews Culture. "It's about slowing down and just receiving something. So in that way, it's very universal.”As McQueen said, the viewer is the other voice in the work. How David met NinaSteve McQueen was inspired not only by the song, but by the way it had so many new lives thanks to the next generations of artists. He likes the story about how Bowie met Simone in 1975.“[Nina Simone’s] daughter wanted to go to David Bowie's concert, so she dragged her mother to take her, and they met afterwards. I think [that] Bowie version is almost homage to Nina. There's a certain kind of imitation of her voice, but then it goes somewhere,” said McQueen.The original version was a Johnny Mathis song, sang in 1957, which was nothing like Nina Simone’s.“She took that song and took it to another stratosphere. So by putting these two versions together, it's complimentary," said McQueen. "They're both singing A major. And it's one of those things where I just felt that by putting those two things together, these two stones, it makes fire. And I know for sure they would be extraordinary, happy with this collaboration, with this duet.”Tension and loveThe title “66–76–26” refers to the years in which Simone and Bowie respectively recorded the song, as well as to the year of the exhibition at Guggenheim Bilbao itself.Both recordings, in 1966 and 1976, came out in moments of political tension. The work invites reflection not only on the song’s enduring power but also on the social and political conditions through which these recordings have travelled. Created during periods marked by upheaval, uncertainty, and transformation – the civil rights movement, Vietnam, Watergate – the performances speak with particular force to the present moment. “Particularly now things seem very turbulent. And I think when things are very turbulent, the things that you hold on to are the things which are precious to you, which is love," said McQueen. "And again, I know it sounds sort of corny, but it's important because that's the basis of us all in one way, shape, form or the other."That's what we crave and that's what we need. So to come back to some kind of understanding of love is important, at least for me,” explained McQueen.Between work in cinema and the galleryThe plan of having Steve McQueen at Guggenheim Bilbao Museum began six years ago and the exhibition opened on the 9th of October, on his 57th birthday.Perhaps best known for his work as a filmmaker, McQueen won an Oscar, a Golden Globe and a BAFTA for his movie 12 Years a Slave. He also won several plaudits for Hunger including the Caméra d’Or at the Cannes Film Festival.But prior to those landmark works, McQueen made his name as a pioneering contemporary artist, who represented Great Britain at the Venice Biennale and has had shows at the Tate museums in London among others. In parallel with the exhibition, the Guggenheim Bilbao will present a film programme dedicated to McQueen’s cinematic work, offering audiences an opportunity to consider the relationship between his work in cinema and the gallery.“66–76–26” highlights the concerns that have long animated his artistic practice: perception, embodiment, memory, duration, and the capacity of art to create spaces for reflection and encounter.Steve McQueen's sound installation "66-76-26" at Guggenheim Bilbao Museum is open until 13 February 2027.

title: Skyrocketing windmills: The world’s tallest wind power plant is going to dwarf the Eiffel tower
description: The world’s tallest wind turbine is currently under construction in eastern Germany; it will rise 365 metres above ground level. This makes it taller than the Eiffel Tower. The technical masterpiece is due to be operational this autumn. Hans von der Brelie was granted access to visit the site.
content: Smalltown Klettwitz lies at the very heart of Germany’s Lusatia region. Lignite used to be mined here for decades. The bucket-wheel excavators have left gaping scars across the landscape.But the country is reaching a turning point: Germany is now getting serious about ending coal burning. And Klettwitz is transforming into a frontrunner in the countrys race to handle the climate crisis in a more sustainable way.Solar and wind farms now stand on the spoil heaps of the former opencast mine, as far as the eye can see. Among these, one steel structure in particular catches the eye - the GICON high-altitude wind power plant. It is still under construction but already outgrowing the neighbouring giant windmills.It is a big dayIt is a big day for the GICON team: Europe’s biggest and most powerful crane, a yellow monster machine, is lifting a tower segment weighing many tonnes into place. Up there, some 160 metres above ground level, climbers are putting the pieces together.GICON employs some of Germany’s finest engineers. The company was founded by Jochen Großmann. Why is the GICON team building such a massive structure in the first place? Euronews wants to know.Why so high, Professor Großmann?“Because the wind blows stronger and more steadily the further I get from the Earth’s surface,” Großmann explains on site, while a team of high-altitude climbers is moving up and down the steel struts spiderman-style. “That’s why wind turbines have become taller and taller – because there’s so much wind up there that they generate more than double the output of the turbines standing here in the surrounding area.”Future wind farms should have ‘two storeys’Großmann’s idea: future wind farms should have ‘two storeys’ so that the wind can be ‘harvested’ twice – once at the bottom and once at the top. “Retrofitting existing wind farms with taller windmills alongside regular ones give us two tiers of high-altitude windmills, and allows us to triple the yield from the same area,” Großmann estimates.An incredible amount of potentialGICON plans to erect 100 high-altitude windmills by the early 2030s, then the objective is to scale it up to 1,000 plants in a few years’ time. GICON could become a global player, “the opportunity is there”, Großmann tells Euronews.“All the wind farms in Germany would offer the potential for 4,000 additional high-altitude wind turbines,” the GICON-CEO stresses, “Simply by retrofitting existing wind farms. That’s an incredible amount of potential. This also applies to African countries. We’ve had enquiries from Asia. The Chinese are asking about it. I think there’s huge international potential here.”

title: UK inflation jumps more than expected fuelling rate hike expectations
description: Britain's annual inflation rate accelerated by more than expected in September, rising to 3.5% on surging fuel prices. This comes a week before the UK government presents its autumn budget and as UK public sector net debt tops £3 trillion.
content: Annual consumer price inflation in the UK rose to 3.5% in September 2026, its highest since October 2025, from 3.1% in August, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said.The higher-than-expected reading comes one week before the Labour government presents its annual budget on 28 October, which is expected to address cost-of-living pressures.The rise was largely driven by fuel price increases. Average diesel prices in September reached their highest level since July 2022, as the US-Iran war sent petrol and diesel prices soaring.Transport, particularly motor fuels, made the largest upward contribution to the change in annual inflation, the ONS said. Transport prices rose by 6.6% year-on-year, up from the previous month’s 4.6%.Annual services inflation accelerated to 3.7%. Housing and household services and communication costs rose by 5.3% and 5.8% year-on-year, respectively. Food inflation was unchanged at 1.3%.Core CPI inflation increased to 2.8% from 2.6%. Compared with August, consumer prices rose 0.4%, following a 0.5% increase. “The energy price cap rose slightly in October, with households braced for an even larger hike early next year," said Danni Hewson, AJ Bell head of financial analysis. He added that expectations are influenced by rising service costs, as well as the significant increase in the price of raw materials that businesses use to produce, on top of the jump in the cost of transporting those goods."The knowledge that funding our lives is only going to get harder in the coming months will impact consumer confidence," Hewson said.The Bank of England is widely expected to raise interest rates at its next meeting on 5 November, which could be the first such move since 2023. This could follow increases by the European Central Bank and the US Federal Reserve amid renewed inflation pressures."Market expectation of a November increase is now nearing 100%, with more than a 50% chance that a second hike will follow before the end of the year,” Hewson said.The UK central bank's current benchmark rate is 3.75%, against an inflation target of 2%.UK borrowing rises as public debt surpasses £3 trillionIn a separate release, the ONS said that public borrowing was nearly £25 billion (€29.8 billion) in September 2026.UK public sector net borrowing totalled £24.5bn (€29.2bn) in September, £1.8bn (€2.1bn) more than a year earlier, surpassing market expectations.The higher borrowing comes as "spending, including higher debt interest costs, increased more than government income, partly reflecting the impacts of inflation", the ONS said.This comes as a recent global bond sell-off has driven up bond yields, making borrowing more expensive for leading economies including the US, France, Germany and the UK. UK 10-year gilt yields were just below 5.4% at the end of September, having reached a 19-year high earlier that month.Meanwhile, UK government borrowing between April and September 2026 reached £97.8bn (€116.5bn), slightly below the same period last year and the equivalent of 3.1% of gross domestic product (GDP). The amount was still £6bn (€7.1bn) more than the Office for Budget Responsibility's forecast.Public sector net debt at the end of September 2026 was provisionally estimated to have exceeded £3 trillion (€3.57 trillion) for the first time. However, as a proportion of the economy, debt was lower than a year earlier, the ONS said.Debt stood at 94% of GDP, down from 94.7% a year earlier.

title: New Beatles attraction ‘to rival Graceland' coming to Liverpool in 2028
description: The new 9,290-square-metre site in the heart of Liverpool has been compared to Graceland and Dollywood and will repurpose the iconic St Johns Beacon into a viewing tower.
content: 2028 is going to be a big year for the Fab Four.Not only will Sam Mendes’ The Beatles: A Four-Film Cinematic Event hit cinema screens in April, but a huge immersive fan experience will open in Liverpool - one to rival Graceland and Dollywood.Apple Corps have announced plans for a “spectacular” new Liverpool home for the long-running attraction The Beatles Story, which will be moving in 2028 from its current home in Liverpool’s Albert Dock to a brand-new site that was formerly St Johns Market in St Johns Shopping Centre, directly opposite Liverpool Lime Street station.The new iteration of Liverpool’s The Beatles Story is billed as a “multi-hour experience” and will be more than four times its current size. Set across a new 9,290-square-metre site in the heart of the city, the iconic St Johns Beacon will house a ‘Yellow Submarine’-themed 360-degree panoramic viewing experience over the city.The Beatles Story promises to use “immersive technology, original artefacts and spectacular reconstructed sets to bring the Beatles’ extraordinary story to life” - as well as recreated settings from the group’s history.Fans will get to go on a journey “through the world that created The Beatles, from the streets of post-war Liverpool, through their formative years in Hamburg and the explosion of Beatlemania, to the heights of their international fame”.Sets and props from Mendes' movies will create versions of Liverpool’s Cavern Club, where the band got its start; the famous Abbey Road studios in London; and Shea Stadium, the site of their legendary 1965 performance."I find it incredible and humbling that people are still interested in our story and it’s very exciting to me that The Beatles Story and The Beacon are being transformed in such an exciting way in the heart of Liverpool city,” said Paul McCartney.“I love Liverpool. It’s part of who I am, it’s part of who The Beatles are. If you’d told us this was going to happen when we were hanging out and getting started we’d never have believed it. The extraordinary plans the Apple Corps team have shown me for The Beatles Story take me right back to that journey, from Liverpool to the world and back home again."He added: “It couldn’t have happened without Liverpool and I can’t wait for people to be able to step into our story and share the experience.”Prime Minister Andy Burnham added that the development marked “the kind of ambition I want to see more of across Britain: backing the things our great cities do best and turning that global reputation into jobs, opportunity and growth”.“But the best legacy we can give The Beatles is to make sure theirs isn’t the last great British success story to begin this way,” Burnham added. “Talent exists in every part of our country; opportunity still doesn’t. I want the next generation of young artists, wherever they grow up, to believe there is a route from their bedroom, rehearsal room or local venue to the very top of the world. The fact that this project will help open those doors makes it even more special.”Apple Corps’ CEO Tom Greene promised that The Beatles Story would be “a world class destination” and compared it to Graceland or Dollywood, while Liverpool City Region Mayor Steve Rotheram shared how money raised from this “pilgrimage” would also be paying back into the local grassroots.“Every ticket sold will go towards ensuring that the band’s extraordinary story is kept alive and passed on to generations still to come, helping the next generation of Liverpool artists start writing stories of their own,” said Rotherham. “That feels very Liverpool: fiercely proud of where we’ve come from but always looking to what comes next.”The new iteration of The Beatles Story will open in 2028. Sam Mendes' four films are slated for a simultaneous release in April 2028. They will star Paul Mescal as Paul McCartney, Harris Dickinson as John Lennon, Joseph Quinn as George Harrison, and Barry Keoghan as Ringo Starr.

title: New Romanian prime minister Luca Niculescu and cabinet members sworn in
description: Independent diplomat Luca Niculescu wins parliamentary backing for a minority government, but analysts warn the calm may not last.
content: Romania on Tuesday swore in a new cabinet following a vote that ended a months-long political impasse.Prime Minister Luca Niculescu, an independent diplomat, won 280 votes in favour of his proposed cabinet, with 58 against. He plans to start work immediately, with a large budget deficit at the top of his agenda.President Nicușor Dan nominated Niculescu, 55, a diplomat and former journalist, on 5 October, the president’s fourth pick for the job, after three earlier nominees failed to form a government.Niculescu was widely expected to succeed after securing pledges of support for a minority government from the Social Democrats and other parties. He has reportedly reached a deal with several parties for six months of backing while a longer-term agreement is negotiated.Speaking in Parliament after the vote, he thanked lawmakers for trusting his cabinet.“I present a governing programme, a team, and a commitment to work toward several clear objectives,” he said. “And I want to tell the Romanian people, from the very start, what kind of government this will be. A government that brings funds and investments into the country.”The political crisis gripped Romania since MayThe political crisis has gripped Romania since May, when then-Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan was ousted in a no-confidence motion. The motion was filed jointly by the Social Democratic Party, which had been part of his governing coalition, and the Alliance for the Unity of Romanians party. Bolojan’s government had pursued strict austerity measures.Bolojan took office in 2025 with the aim of ending one of Romania’s worst political crises since the end of communism and of reducing a massive budget deficit.Romania has faced a long stretch of instability since the annulment of a presidential election in December 2024. The country has also struggled with rampant inflation and a technical recession. Last year, it recorded one of the highest budget deficits in the European Union.Tuesday’s vote came weeks after lawmakers rejected a cabinet proposed by Dan’s third pick, Siegfried Muresan. That failure prolonged the crisis and raised the prospect of early elections, at a time of regional security concerns linked to Russia’s war in neighbouring Ukraine. Romania is a member of both NATO and the EU.Experts warn that tensions could flare again soon. Niculescu’s support rests on a six-month arrangement with several parties, and a longer-term deal has yet to be agreed.

title: Greece tourism: August 2026 arrivals up 2.6%, with foreign visitors leading growth
description: Arrivals reached 7.43 million and overnight stays 34.69 million, with short-stay rentals up 5.2%, compared with just 1.5% for hotels and campsites.
content: Tourist traffic in Greece moved on an upward trajectory in August 2026, with arrivals and overnight stays in hotels, campsites and rented rooms increasing compared with the same month in 2025.However, behind the overall positive picture, significant differences emerge both between Greek and foreign visitors and between the different types of accommodation.According to provisional data from the Hellenic Statistical Authority (ELSTAT), total arrivals reached 7,429,931, up 2.6%, while overnight stays amounted to 34,685,695, posting a 2.1% increase. The rise in arrivals was therefore 0.5 percentage points higher than the corresponding growth in overnight stays.Foreign visitors drive the increaseForeign tourists played a decisive role, accounting for 76.7% of all arrivals and 84% of overnight stays. Greek residents, by contrast, represented 23.3% of arrivals and 16% of overnight stays.The gap is particularly evident in overnight stays: the share of foreign visitors was 68 percentage points higher than that of Greeks. The figures highlight the stronger contribution of international demand to the overall activity of accommodation establishments.In terms of annual change, arrivals of foreign visitors increased by 2.9%, compared with 1.7% for Greek residents, a difference of 1.2 percentage points. Similarly, overnight stays by foreigners rose by 2.3%, against 1.2% for Greeks, widening the gap to 1.1 percentage points.Rented rooms grow more rapidlyThe sharpest increase in tourist activity was recorded in collective short-stay accommodation, that is, rented rooms. Arrivals there rose by 5.2%, outpacing by 3.7 percentage points the 1.5% increase observed in hotels and campsites.The difference was even more pronounced in overnight stays. In rented rooms, overnight stays climbed by 4.6%, compared with just 1.1% in hotels and campsites – a gap of 3.5 percentage points.This picture shows that, in terms of percentage change, short-stay accommodation moved significantly faster than the category of hotels and campsites.Foreign and Greek visitors across accommodation typesIn hotels and campsites, arrivals of foreign visitors increased by 1.9%, while those of Greek residents rose by 0.5%, a difference of 1.4 percentage points. For overnight stays, the corresponding rise was 1.2% for foreigners and 0.8% for Greeks, narrowing the gap to just 0.4 points.In rented rooms, by contrast, the increases were clearly higher. Arrivals of foreign visitors went up by 5.5%, against 4.2% for Greek residents, while overnight stays grew by 5.1% and 2.2% respectively. As a result, the gap between foreign and Greek visitors reached 1.3 percentage points in arrivals and 2.9 points in overnight stays.Foreign visitors stay for longerThe average length of stay in August remained at 4.7 days, unchanged compared with August 2025. Nonetheless, the difference between the two categories of visitors is noteworthy.Foreign tourists stayed on average 5.1 days, while Greek residents stayed 3.2 days. This is a gap of 1.9 days, as the average stay of foreigners was roughly 59% longer than that of Greeks.The same pattern is observed both in hotels and campsites and in rented rooms: in the former, the average stay of foreign visitors was 5.1 days, compared with 3.2 days for Greeks, while in the latter it stood at 5.2 and 3.3 days respectively.ELSTAT’s figures for August 2026 confirm an increase in tourist traffic, with clearly faster growth in rented rooms and a stronger contribution from foreign visitors. At the same time, the rise in arrivals outpaced that in overnight stays, while the average length of stay remained unchanged.

title: A chilled stay: Europe’s coolest ice, snow and igloo hotels to visit this winter
description: If you’re planning a winter escape, why not embrace the cold and check into an ice, snow or igloo hotel? From seasonal ‘properties’ in Swedish and Finnish Lapland to a year-round icy stay in Norway, here are five places in Europe for a cool getaway.
content: This winter, the coolest holiday destinations may just be where the temperature barely hovers above freezing.In Europe, there are various ice, snow and igloo hotels which offer guests the charm of a winter fairy tale: icy accommodation set against the Northern Lights in a snow-covered escape.But the experience begins long before check-in. Many seasonal hotels rely on ice harvested from nearby rivers and lakes, while others use fresh snow to preserve a year-round frozen retreat.Here are some of Europe's coolest "properties" to keep on your radar this winter season and beyond.Snowhotel 365, Bjørnevatn, NorwayLocated at Snow Resort Kirkenes in northern Norway, Snowhotel 365 offers guests a unique experience with each room being hand-carved by international ice sculptors – so no two rooms are alike.Although indoor temperatures hover around -4C, each room comes with a thermal sleeping bag and access to the property’s heated lounge, sauna and showers. As an all-inclusive Arctic adventure, each stay also includes breakfast and a three-course dinner.Here, the winter fun doesn’t have to end when the weather takes a warmer turn. Guests can check in year-round, even in the middle of summer.Each year, 30 tonnes of ice and fresh snow are used to preserve and renew the property. Over time, as the snow turns into solid ice, the hotel's walls, ceilings, and sculptures develop new textures and shapes.ICEHOTEL, Jukkasjärvi, Swedish LaplandEach winter, as the Torne River freezes, artists and sculptors from around the world gather to mould ICEHOTEL anew.For five months of the year, starting in December, guests can check into its temporary rooms or art suites before it melts back into the river again.Temperatures in the ice rooms hover around -5C, however, each room is kitted out with reindeer hide blankets and sleeping bags to keep guests warm. Meanwhile, the art suites are individually designed with a selection of artists bringing their creativity to life.ICEHOTEL also offers a range of dining concepts, including an “ice menu” where dishes are served on plates made of ice from the river.Arctic SnowHotel, Rovaniemi, Finnish LaplandIn Rovaniemi, the capital of Finnish Lapland, the winter season from 15 December until the end of March sees the grounds blanketed by snow, with rivers and lakes freezing. It also means the Arctic SnowHotel opens its doors for guests to stay the night.Since 2008, a “new hotel” of ice and snow has been moulded each year at this popular attraction, where 20 rooms can host as many as 70 guests.Guests can choose from a double suite that sleeps two, all the way up to a family room that sleeps up to six guests.The cool experiences also continue at the Ice Restaurant, where meals are served on an ice plate. While the Ice Chapel offers an unforgettable setting for those seeking a space for spirituality.Arctic SnowHotel also has a resident “Northern Lights Watcher”, who keeps an eye on the skies and ensures no guest misses the magical display of the auroras.Sorrisniva Igloo Hotel, Alta, NorwayAlta in Norway is home to Sorrisniva – the world’s northernmost igloo hotel.Harvesting ice from the Sierravannet mountain lake, it takes 250 tonnes of ice and 7,000 cubic metres of snow to build the igloo hotel each year under a special theme.After being rebuilt, guests are welcome to stay from 20 December to the end of March, with rooms and suites to choose from. With no two seasons ever being the same, each winter, ice sculptors turn the suites into their canvas – designing the furniture and room’s ice sculptures.For adventure travellers, snowmobiling across the Finnmark plateau, chasing the Northern Lights, snowshoeing and husky sledging are among the itinerary of activities to try.Iglu-Dorf Zermatt, SwitzerlandIn the Swiss Alps, Iglu-Dorf Zermatt is rebuilt each winter at 2,700 metres on the ski slopes above the car-free resort.At this remote mountain location, guests can stay in hand-carved igloos linked by snow corridors, from 19 December to 4 April, with the igloos’ temperature remaining around freezing point.During the daytime, the outdoor terrace is a shared dining space that serves Swiss cheese fondue, alongside a selection of other snacks and hot and cold beverages.Beyond Zermatt, overnight stays are also possible across other Swiss igloo villages, including Davos and Gstaad, as well as further afield in the German Iglu-Dorf on the Zugspitze and in Kühtai near Innsbruck in Austria.

title: Severe weather in southern France: one dead near Marseille, one missing in Corsica
description: In Haute-Corse, a person went missing in Ghisonaccia on Tuesday evening; another was found dead in Saint-Mitre-les-Remparts in the Bouches-du-Rhône.
content: Cars swept away, neighbourhoods and homes flooded: a new bout of severe weather has lashed south-eastern France, moving from Occitanie towards Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur. The heavy rain, which began on Monday, was easing in intensity by around midday on Tuesday.On Tuesday 20 October, a 75-year-old was found dead in Istres, in the Bouches-du-Rhône department, after being swept away by floodwaters in the commune of Saint-Mitre-les-Remparts. A helicopter had been deployed in an attempt to locate the missing person.In Haute-Corse, one person is missing in Ghisonaccia, the prefecture announced. Two people were on board a 4x4 when it was carried away by the Fium'orbu river. One managed to escape through the window, but the other is being searched for by rescue teams.North of Solenzara (Corse-du-Sud), almost 400 millimetres of rain have been recorded since the start of the episode, "and 191 millimetres in a single hour" at the airport, Météo-France said.In Istres, around fifty kilometres west of Marseille, evacuations also took place. Residents affected by the flooding were moved to a sports hall, local authorities said.The heavy rainfall that began on Monday triggered major flooding from the Hérault department through to Bouches-du-Rhône and made it necessary to bring dozens of people to safety.In Hérault, the town of Lunel was hit by intense rain and thunderstorms, according to the fire service. Around fifteen people were taken in by the municipality in a reception centre. Images on social media show cars submerged up to their windows as rising water levels filled the streets.In Nîmes, where traffic was extremely difficult on Tuesday morning and the A9 motorway was closed for several hours, the situation was gradually returning to normal by midday and municipal facilities, shut since Monday afternoon, were reopening. Train services to and from the city were still disrupted.Some sections of motorways around Marseille were partially flooded and slip roads were closed. In the city, tram services were suspended on Tuesday morning.This Mediterranean weather episode is linked to a cold low-pressure system named Adam, which has brought torrential rain and flooding to Spain, where at least four people have lost their lives.

title: IRGC mines set tankers ablaze as Tehran threatens expanded attacks
description: Iran’s foreign ministry further warned Washington it would retaliate against any strike, and an IRGC spokesperson threatened to target undersea internet cables in the Gulf in another escalation of the ongoing war of words between Tehran and Washington.
content: Iran's IRGC said two oil tankers struck mines the elite paramilitary had laid in the Strait of Hormuz, setting both vessels ablaze, as Tehran threatened further attacks on shipping and cutting undersea cables while promising to unveil new weapons in its arsenal.The IRGC said in a statement that the tankers tried to use what Iran unilaterally designates an unauthorised route through the strait's southern section, near the Omani coast."With the explosion of mines laid by the IRGC Navy in the illegal passage south of the Strait of Hormuz, two offending tankers were set on fire and brought to a standstill," the IRGC statement said. Neither vessel was named nor was the precise location disclosed.Tehran has no recognised authority under international maritime law to restrict or authorise passage through the Strait of Hormuz, which is subject to the right of transit passage under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea.The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported on Tuesday that it had received an account of "an incident between an oil tanker and military forces" on Monday, some 121 nautical miles east of the Omani city of Duqm. UKMTO reported no damage or casualties and did not identify the vessel.The IRGC also claimed that their air defence system had shot down a US MQ-9 drone over the strait on Monday night. A US official, speaking to US media outlets, dismissed the claim as untrue.Some Iranian domestic outlets, including the state-affiliated Fars agency, reported that a US airstrike hit a naval base in Konarak in Sistan and Baluchistan province on Monday, wounding two military personnel and targeting an air defence installation. Washington has not commented on the report.IRGC spokesperson Hossein Mojabi threatened on Monday to target undersea internet cables in the Gulf and the strait, saying "new weapons will be unveiled" with the aim of, in his words, removing US military presence from the region.'We do not leave any blow unanswered'Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said Tehran would retaliate against any US attack."In practice we have shown that we absolutely do not leave any blow unanswered," he said in response to reports that Washington had urged Iran to hold back in the event of a strike on Kuh Kalang."A US attack on Kuh Kalang and Iran not responding is fantasy and empty talk," Baghaei said.The IRGC-affiliated Tasnim news agency quoted an unnamed Iranian security source as saying uncertainty over decision-making authority in Washington was complicating negotiations, naming Vice President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Trump administration negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner as figures whose respective roles remained unclear to Iranian officials.Arsenio Dominguez, secretary-general of the International Maritime Organisation, said about 6,000 seafarers have been stranded in the strait since the war began. He criticised shipowners for continuing to send crews into the area.US media have previously reported that the Pentagon was deploying the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group and the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit to the Middle East, adding approximately 10,000 sailors and Marines to the region by the end of November. Washington has not confirmed the deployment.Roughly one-fifth of the world's oil passed through the Strait of Hormuz before the war that began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February. Both Tehran and Washington have implemented blockades in the strait, while Iran has repeatedly targeted cargo vessels using the southern section of the waterway.

title: France vows 'massive' security operation involving military forces for expected weekend protests
description: Some military forces from Operation Sentinelle will be deployed to free up police and gendarmes for the expected demonstrations, French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said.
