content: French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said on Tuesday that a "massive" security operation would be in place during further expected protests on Saturday after cost-of-living demonstrations turned violent across France over the weekend.Speaking to parliament on Tuesday, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez also announced plans to deploy military forces from Operation Sentinelle to free up police and gendarmes for the expected demonstrations.Nuñez said their mission would be "to replace internal security forces mainly on static guarding duties" in order to "free up police officers and gendarmes to carry out public-order missions."Operation Sentinelle, launched in January 2015, has 10,000 soldiers deployed across France to defend against potential terrorist attacks.Troops are usually stationed outside sites deemed sensitive, such as places of worship, schools, tourist locations, railway stations and airports. Sentinelle soldiers have previously deployed at events such as the Paris 2024 Olympics and the Paralympic Games.Nuñez added that the aim on Saturday would be for security forces to operate with increased "responsiveness and mobility" in order to deal with "scattered" and "extremely mobile" groups.The interior minister said he was also "considering the possibility of banning demonstrations that have not been declared and that could lead to public disorder."Demonstrations declared to the prefecture, as is required, could also be affected, but only where "the organiser or the security team do not give us reason to believe that the demonstration will not get out of hand."With regard to demonstrations that do not pose a risk to public order, Nuñez said it was "essential to prioritise routes away from public buildings and high streets," as well as to "step up intelligence-gathering efforts in order to identify as accurately as possible the number of participants, particularly the most radical ones, so that security measures can be adapted accordingly."The minister also promised to show "resolve," adding: "We will be there."

title: Italy to respond to Milan clashes and looting ‘with great firmness’, foreign minister says
description: From preventive detention to bans on gatherings: proposed measures and new powers for troops deployed in Milan
content: Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani has vowed that the government would respond to recent clashes and looting in Milan "with great firmness" as he announced that 500 military personnel would be deployed to the city's streets."Five hundred military personnel, who will also be granted judicial police powers, will be deployed to help ensure security and carry out robust preventive measures," Tajani said on Tuesday on the sidelines of the Welfare Italia Forum in Rome.Protests that have gripped France in recent weeks spilled over into Italy over the weekend, as cost-of-living demonstrations descended into violence and brought clashes with police in cities including Milan, Turin and Bologna."Furthermore, a series of regulatory and legal decisions will be introduced to make it more difficult for minors to engage in criminal activity," Tajani announced.New government measures being considered include the extension of preventive detention to up to 24 hours, including for those under 18; allowing delayed arrests for property damage committed by groups; and a ban on gatherings for individuals deemed a threat to public order.The package could also include new offences and harsher penalties for acts of violence during demonstrations.The troop deployment will reinforce a security operation already in place in Milan, with soldiers to guard key locations and help maintain order in public areas.Preventive detention of up to 24 hoursOne of the main proposals is to extend the maximum period of preventive detention from 12 to 24 hours and allow it to be applied to minors, where the legal conditions are met.Preventive detention is not a conviction and does not necessarily mean an offence has already been committed.It is a preventive measure that can be used when specific conditions are met and there are concrete grounds to believe someone poses a threat to public order.Its use, particularly in the case of minors, must comply with the safeguards provided by law.Gang crime and finesThe proposals could also toughen penalties for vandalism committed by groups.One option under consideration is a specific offence of aggravated damage committed by a group, carrying harsher penalties when several people act together to damage public or private property.A security bill already under debate in the Senate sets out provisions on damage committed by at least five people, with prison sentences of up to five years and fines of up to €15,000.The government could bring forward or revise some of these provisions in the new decree.Another measure is arrest in flagrante delicto on a deferred basis, which allows suspects to be arrested later on the basis of evidence such as photographs and video footage, even if they were not caught in the act.The government is considering extending its use to group damage to strengthen action against those involved in acts of destruction.The League is also calling for mandatory arrests for acts of devastation during demonstrations and for deferred arrests to be permitted within 48 hours.Some of these measures are already provided for under current law. The scope of any changes, and the offences they would cover, remains to be seen.Ban on gatheringsOther measures under consideration include tightening restrictions on gatherings, potentially extending their use beyond political demonstrations to prevent group violence.The measures could target people already known to the authorities for violence, assaults or property damage, including incidents linked to brawls and the so-called mala movida (rowdy nightlife), where legal conditions are met.The government is also considering strengthening the questore’s formal warning, issued by the public security authority to people deemed a threat and urging them to comply with the law. The aim would be to make existing preventive powers more effective.Tighter rules on roadblocks and assaults on public officials are also being considered. According to reports, one option is to crack down on those who organise or participate in organised violence during protests, potentially through a specific offence relating to criminal association. The details remain to be confirmed in the final text.Juvenile justice and penalties for parentsThe package could also include measures to strengthen the juvenile justice system. Members of the governing coalition have called for more staff at juvenile courts and additional places in detention facilities to speed up proceedings and the implementation of judicial measures.Another proposal would tighten administrative penalties for parents whose children are involved in certain violent incidents.Existing legislation already provides for penalties in some cases, so any new provisions would need to clarify what additional obligations or consequences would apply.There has also been discussion of making it harder for young foreign nationals convicted of serious crimes to obtain Italian citizenship.The proposal, backed by members of the League during parliamentary debate, does not appear to be among the measures confirmed for inclusion in the forthcoming decree.

title: Could your neighbourhood impact your dementia risk? Study says yes
description: People living in areas surrounded by greenery may have a lower risk of dementia, according to a new study.
content: Having more green space close to home was linked to a 20% lower risk of developing dementia in a new study by Stockholm University and the Karolinska Institute in Sweden.“This highlights the immediate environmental surroundings of the home as an important piece in creating conditions that support brain health and healthy ageing," says Cecilia Stenfors, research leader and co-first author of the study. The study, published in the journal Alzheimer's & Dementia, included nearly 3,000 participants who were followed for 16 years. The researchers mapped the amount of vegetation around participants’ homes. They also tracked their cognitive health and the development of dementia over time.They found that living closer to green space seemed to have a protective effect against dementia. The association was strongest for greenery in the area closest to the home, within 100 metres, and weakened as the distance from home to green zones grew. How does this protection work? The authors pointed to several reasons why dementia risk may be affected by green space. These range from direct factors such as stress relief to the facilitation of health-related behaviours, including better sleep, physical activity, and social stimulation and cohesion. “Natural environments and greenery can support psychological restoration, reduce stress and enhance feelings of well-being,” said Stenfors. Green spaces may also support health indirectly by shielding people from hazardous environmental exposures such as traffic noise, air pollution and extreme heat, the authors wrote. Considering brain health in urban planning In 2025, an estimated 9 million people were living with dementia in the European Union, and that figure is projected to grow to over 14 million by 2050. According to the authors, this growing number highlights the need for new strategies such as sustainable urban planning that supports brain health. “Brain health needs to be considered when we plan and develop our cities and residential environments,” said Stenfors. “Greenspace around our homes can be a shared resource for public health, climate adaptation and biodiversity,” she added. To achieve this, it is important both to protect existing vegetation and to create green environments that are accessible and usable for people with different needs and abilities, the authors noted. The environment’s impact on brain health has been gaining more attention in recent years. “The direct environment, but also the broader environment in terms of housing organisation, has an impact on your sleep and overall also on your brain health,” neurologist Ulf Kallweit, who is also a co-chair of the environmental influences task force at the European Academy of Neurology, told Euronews Health.

title: Von der Leyen, Costa head to Budapest in sign of EU-Hungary thaw
description: Ursula von der Leyen and António Costa will join Hungarian PM Péter Magyar in Budapest on Friday to mark 70 years since the 1956 uprising, signalling a reset in EU-Hungary ties after Viktor Orbán’s years in power.
content: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa will travel to Budapest on Friday to mark the 70th anniversary of Hungary’s 1956 anti-Soviet uprising.French President Emmanuel Macron will not attend the ceremony, the French embassy in Budapest announced, contradicting a statement last week by Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar.The event marks a major thaw in relations between Brussels and Budapest after years of acrimony under his predecessor, Viktor Orbán.It will be von der Leyen’s first visit to Hungary since 2024, when she attended a European Political Community summit in Budapest.Under Orbán, Hungary repeatedly blocked EU initiatives to support Ukraine, opposed financial and military assistance to Kyiv and maintained close ties with Russian President Vladimir Putin.But since Magyar’s Tisza Party swept to power in April, the new government has pledged to bring Hungary back into the European mainstream and settle its longstanding disputes with Brussels.In a sharp break with Orbán’s policies, Magyar’s government has identified Russia as a security threat and approved the opening of four negotiating clusters in Ukraine’s EU accession talks.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has also been invited to the commemoration, but Magyar said he is unlikely to attend. The Hungarian prime minister has said he invited all European leaders except Putin. The full list of participants has not yet been released.On 23 October 1956, Hungarian students took to the streets to protest against Soviet occupation. The demonstrations quickly grew into a popular uprising, which the Red Army later crushed. Zelenskyy’s presence would have drawn parallels with Ukraine’s defence against Russia’s full-scale invasion.The commemoration could also allow European leaders to signal their support for Magyar after the Orbán era and to speak up against Russia's war in Ukraine.This article has been updated with news of French President Emmanuel Macron not taking part at the event.

title: EU Parliament leaders set for re-election despite cracks in centrist alliance
description: Manfred Weber, Iratxe García Pérez and Valérie Hayer are expected to be re-elected unopposed, even as growing tensions threaten the centrist alliance supporting Ursula von der Leyen.
content: The three political groups underpinning the European Parliament's centrist majority are set to re-elect their leaders on Tuesday, with little prospect of surprises despite growing tensions within their alliance.The European People's Party (EPP), the Socialists and Democrats (S&D) and the liberal Renew Europe group will hold internal leadership elections in Strasbourg on 20 October, with the outcomes all but a foregone conclusion.The EPP is expected to re-elect German Manfred Weber, who has led the group since 2014 and faces no challengers. “He has an iron grip on the group. No one would even think of trying to topple him,” a senior MEP told Euronews.The main contest will be for the group's vice-presidencies, with 12 candidates vying for 10 seats. All current vice-presidents seeking re-election are expected to retain their positions, while outgoing Portuguese MEP Lídia Pereira is likely to be replaced by Hungary's Eszter Lakos.There is little prospect of a contest among the Socialists either. Spanish MEP Iratxe García Pérez is set to be re-elected unopposed, extending her tenure and making her the longest-serving leader in the group's history.Renew Europe chair Valérie Hayer is also the sole candidate to lead the liberal group. The French MEP, who belongs to Emmanuel Macron’s political camp, is expected to be elected by acclamation, with overwhelming support, a source within the group told Euronews.A challenger could still enter the race at the last minute, before the vote, triggering a ballot election.Once re-elected, Weber, García Pérez and Hayer are expected to discuss the future of the centrist alliance supporting European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen for the remainder of the parliamentary term.The informal coalition agreement currently underpinning that alliance has come under repeated strain in the last year, as the EPP has increasingly relied on a right-wing majority, joining forces with the European Conservatives and Reformists (ECR) and far-right groups on key migration and climate files.

title: Ukraine needs another €70 billion, but where will the EU find the money?
description: The EU is searching for another €70 billion to sustain Ukraine's war effort in 2027, but rising borrowing costs and divisions over the Russian assets leave Brussels with few easy options.
content: The European Union is scrambling to find an additional €70 billion for Ukraine next year, after Russia's escalating assault on the country and its economy rendered the bloc's existing financial support plans insufficient.At the end of a two-day summit last week, EU leaders heard directly from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy about the scale of the shortfall."The war will cost €155 billion next year. And we need at least €70 billion more from you: for defence, for weapons, and for our resilience. This is a realistic amount. And I ask you to find this support. It will help us hold Russia back," he said.According to Zelenskyy, the extra injection of cash will help Ukraine ramp up domestic production of its cutting-edge drones to stop Russia's advances on the battlefield, disrupt its supply chains and undercut its war apparatus."We really need at least €70 billion additionally for next year," he added.The appeal struck a chord. EU leaders tasked the European Commission with exploring ways to plug the gap, which is considerably larger than Brussels had anticipated.Until now, the bloc based its support on the €90 billion loan that leaders signed off last December. The loan was designed to cover two-thirds of Ukraine's financial and military needs for 2026 and 2027 combined, with other allies covering the remaining third.Crucially, the Commission devised the loan assuming that the war would end sometime in 2026. Instead, Moscow has intensified its offensive, including daytime attacks aimed at crippling Ukraine's already fragile economy.Kyiv has spent weeks warning that it will need an additional $32.6 billion to support its budget and $45 billion for its armed forces next year – a combined $78 billion, or approximately €70 billion.Brussels initially declined to comment on the staggering figure. But after several rounds of technical discussions, it has accepted the estimate and concluded that the money must be found if Ukraine is to sustain its war effort.The €70 billion would come on top of the €45 billion the EU plans to disburse under its existing loan, as well as several billion euros from other programmes.Faced with a swelling bill, Brussels has been quick to stress that the €70 billion will be a "joint effort" with other allies, such as the UK, Norway, Canada and Japan."We always said that we cannot walk this alone. We cannot do this all alone. Therefore, our partners in general must step up," a Commission spokesperson said."They have to come forward with pledges, and they have to deliver on those commitments. This is very important."It is not yet clear how much of the €70 billion the EU will provide, given that the previous split of two-thirds vs one-third has not worked out as planned. Nor is it clear how quickly Kyiv will need the money. What is clear is that the options for raising such a vast sum at short notice are severely limited.Adding to the pressure, the high-stakes negotiations will unfold in parallel with the bitter fight over the next long-term budget and the lead-up to the French presidential election, where frontrunner Marine Le Pen has vowed to end all aid to Ukraine.Tapping the marketsRaising fresh joint EU debt on the financial markets, as Brussels is already doing for the €90 billion loan, currently appears the most likely option, according to diplomats and officials. The Commission could increase the existing credit facility, effectively extending the current financing arrangement.The bloc, with its stable AAA credit rating, has become an in-demand bond issuer since the COVID-19 pandemic, with its auctions often oversubscribed. Mario Draghi, the former Italian Prime Minister and ECB President, has called for large-scale borrowing.The financial landscape, however, has sharply deteriorated since December, when leaders signed off on the loan. Borrowing costs have soared worldwide in response to surging oil prices, rising public debt and strong demand for AI spending.European countries have been hit particularly hard, especially those already heavily indebted. Belgium is now borrowing at rates comparable to Greece, while France is paying more than Italy.This makes the prospect of fresh debt politically sensitive, even difficult, as it would add to the mounting pile of interest payments.Yield on the bloc's 10-year bond has risen from 2.8% in January to 3.44% in September – a significant increase, although less pronounced than in many other markets."This is a dynamic that affects all insurers around the world, and our relative position importantly has not deteriorated," the Commission spokesperson said."We remain an extremely competitive issuer."If joint borrowing emerges as the main option, several countries are expected to opt out.Hungary, Slovakia and the Czech Republic are already exempted from the €90 billion loan. At last week's summit, Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico said he and his Hungarian counterpart, Péter Magyar, had agreed to maintain the policy."If they (other countries) want to provide a loan to Ukraine, they can do so, but at least two countries are indicating at this point that we will not participate in this financial mechanism," Fico said. "We show solidarity in other ways."Another country likely to sit it out is Bulgaria, whose new prime minister, Rumen Radev, has repeatedly criticised the bloc's military assistance to Ukraine.Tapping assetsIn recent weeks, several countries have floated an alternative avenue to equip Ukraine with long-lasting financial firepower: the immobilised assets of the Russian Central Bank, worth a massive €210 billion across the bloc's territory.Sweden, the Netherlands, Spain and Poland revived the debate in August. The Nordics, the Baltics, Germany and Ireland have since expressed support.These are the same countries that last year pushed the hardest to channel the assets into a zero-interest credit for Ukraine. For the most part, they are the largest bilateral donors to Ukraine and see the assets as a way to ensure genuine burden-sharing.The project failed when it bumped into Belgium's fierce resistance, which holds €185 billion of these assets in Euroclear, a depository in central Brussels.Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever warned that using the assets would amount to confiscation and have catastrophic consequences for the country. He demanded the total mutualisation of risks and uncapped guarantees against all possible liabilities.Leaders recoiled at the prospect of bailing out Belgium's banking system and, at the last minute, opted for joint debt to set up the €90 billion loan.Despite that setback, supporters of using the Russian assets have not abandoned the idea. Ukraine has consistently brought the topic into the conversation.Zelenskyy said that if Europe does not use them, Russia would seek to retrieve them. (The US has reportedly pitched a plan to partially release the assets as an incentive for Russia to engage in the peace talks, but Europeans shot it down.)"The main priority is that Russia doesn't have the opportunity to influence later on the discussion on these assets, because we know very clearly they want to bring these assets back," Zelenskyy said last week. "It's one of Russia's aims."De Wever remains firmly opposed. During the summit, the Belgian premier, on his own initiative, took the floor to tell his peers that his objections remained unchanged, Euronews understands. He argued the money should be kept firmly locked in until the end of the war to prevent external meddling by Moscow or Washington.The message was received. Officials and diplomats left the summit with the impression that the assets had little chance of succeeding this time around.The failure of last year's proposal remains fresh in their minds. France and Italy, whose support would be crucial, are still considered reluctant to use the assets.Belgium's position is even more entrenched. It opposes not only tapping the sovereign funds but also transferring them from Euroclear to an EU-owned custodian, a legal workaround that some have promoted to break the impasse."The issue will be coming up over and over. Eventually it may find a resolution. I don't think short-term it's going to be on the agenda, like this month or the next one," Katarína Mathernová, the EU ambassador to Ukraine, told Euronews."While the assets remain frozen and they are in Europe and under our regime and now under European jurisdiction, they certainly are for the leaders to discuss in the future. And I think that will happen, but not in the short term."

title: New four-lane bridge between China and North Korea opens after a decade of delay
description: The new bridge's opening comes about a month after North Korea and Russia opened a road bridge as part of their efforts to cement relations.
content: A new four-lane road bridge linking China and North Korea finally opened on Thursday, 12 years late, enabling the Asian giant and its isolated nuclear-armed neighbour to substantially step up cross-border trade.China is North Korea's largest trading partner and a vital diplomatic and political backer, although relations have not always been smooth with the ruling Kim dynasty.Hundreds of people gathered on Thursday in the northern Chinese border town of Dandong, taking selfies in front of the 3,026-metre New Yalu River vehicle bridge before it opened.Trucks bearing the nations' flags began moving in both directions late in the morning, with some of the North Korean vehicles decorated with flowers."It's great," one woman who came to watch told the AFP news agency in the town dotted with Chinese as well as Korean shops and restaurants, where residents were relieved the bridge had finally open."It's already been over 10 years. It's certainly going to be good for business," she said, without wishing to be named, accompanied by her friend and her dog."I hope the standard of living in North Korea can rise to the level we have here," Dandong local Yu Shuyan, who before the pandemic had visited North Korea, said.Chinese Premier Li Qiang said that the bridge symbolised Beijing's friendship with Pyongyang and that relations were "entering a new stage and opening a new chapter"."Thanks to the joint efforts of both sides, the successful opening of the bridge will not only strongly boost economic and trade cooperation between the two countries but will also further facilitate people-to-people exchanges and tighten the bonds of affection between the two peoples," Li said by video link at the opening ceremony. China’s Xinhua News Agency reported.The structure was completed in 2014, but its opening was delayed due to a lack of connecting roads and customs facilities on the North Korean side, South Korea's Yonhap News Agency reported.North Korea also sealed its borders during the COVID-19 pandemic, and train journeys between the East Asian neighbours only restarted in March after a six-year halt.The new bridge is not the only border crossing between the two countries.But the new structure will supersede the "extremely narrow" rail-and-road Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge downstream on the Yalu River, said Lim Eul-chul, a North Korea expert at Kyungnam University."Previously, transporting heavy cargo such as industrial machinery, raw materials, construction materials and energy-related supplies required extreme caution because of safety concerns surrounding the ageing bridge," Lim told AFP."The new crossing will make such shipments much easier and more efficient," he said, calling it a "groundbreaking development" that will substantially increase cargo traffic.Russia-North Korea bridgeThe new bridge's launch came about a month after North Korea and Russia opened a road bridge as part of their efforts to cement relations.Experts say Chinese officials likely felt uneasy about its opening.China has long been North Korea’s biggest trading partner and economic pipeline. But in recent years, North Korean leader Kim Jong-un has prioritised Moscow, sending thousands of troops and conventional weapons to support Russian President Vladimir Putin’s war in Ukraine, apparently in exchange for military and economic assistance.But Kim has recently drawn closer to China with the apparent intent to improve his country's economy and build a front against the United States.China, for its part, wants to restore its unique influence over North Korea. Last year, about 98% of North Korea’s external trade was with China.North Korea has not yet resumed issuing tourism visas to Chinese citizens, who once made up the bulk of its overseas visitors.South Korea's unification ministry said that Seoul is "closely monitoring" the situation regarding the new bridge.

title: Airbnb introduces weather protection that will pay out if it rains too much on your holiday
description: The optional insurance add-on, available in 10 European countries, will mean you get daily payouts if downpours threaten to ruin your trip.
content: With the clocks set to go back this weekend, dark, miserable nights are drawing in for most of us.Our only hope for escape (aside from the seasonal depression-busting daylight lamps) is an actual escape for a spot of winter sun.Imagine you go all that way in search of Vitamin D and to swim in the sea only for it to rain the entire time. Heartbreaking.It would undoubtedly feel like a waste of money (why didn’t I just stay at home?) – but this new announcement from Airbnb could lessen the blow somewhat.The holiday home rental company is now offering optional weather protection insurance that will payout travellers on days it rains during their trip.“Rain can cast a shadow over a trip guests have been looking forward to, but it shouldn't define it,” Justin Brouse, Airbnb’s director for strategic partnerships, AirCover and insurance, said.“We're excited to work with Chubb to introduce weather protection, so guests can get value back when it rains spending less time dealing with a disruption and more time enjoying their trip.”How Airbnb’s weather protection worksAirbnb guests who live in Austria, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, Ireland, the Netherlands, Poland, Spain or Sweden will have the option to add on weather protection when booking.The policy covers both domestic and international trips, although it isn’t available for trips in every country.Underwritten by Chubb, the policy will have a daily payout of between €50 and €1,000 if there is rain of at least 1.5 mm in an hour between 8 am and 8 pm at your Airbnb stay’s location for the minimum number of hours shown in your insurance policy. The number of hours, and payout, will vary from country to country.The rain monitoring is automatic and is taken from sources such as NASA, the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), so you won’t need to submit evidence for a claim, you’ll just be notified if you can make one.Other options for weather-related insuranceFounded in 2022, WeatherPromise also offers insurance that covers your trip if it rains.Working on a similar premise, the policy will payout automatically if it rains more than the specified amount agreed upon.All you need to do is enter the hotel address where you are staying, the dates of the trip, and the covered amount, i.e. the cost of the trip.

title: Are Hungary and the EU friends again? The Ring in Budapest
description: The Ring visits Budapest to ask whether Prime Minister Péter Magyar has reset Hungary’s ties with the EU. After April’s landslide, Brussels agreed to release €16.4bn in blocked funds, but several issues remain unresolved.
content: The Ring, Euronews' weekly debate show, travels to Budapest to find out how Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar is resetting relations with the EU after years of tension under the previous government led by Viktor Orbán.Magyar, who won a landslide victory in April’s parliamentary election, has been warmly welcomed by Brussels. In May, he reached a deal with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on the release of €16.4 billion in funds blocked over longstanding rule-of-law and corruption concerns.Hungary has also lifted its veto on opening EU accession negotiation clusters for Ukraine.However, some issues remain unresolved, including migration and the rights of sexual minorities.So, has Magyar delivered on his promise to bring Hungary back to the heart of the EU?In the Budapest edition of The Ring, Tibor Navracsics, a former minister in Orbán’s government and a former EU commissioner, and István Szent-Iványi, a foreign policy expert and former ambassador, debate the question.

title: Neanderthal remains dating back 46,000 years identified in Abauntz cave, Navarra
description: Six bone fragments from Abauntz cave in Navarre belong to a 46,000-year-old male Neanderthal; DNA and radiocarbon dating reveal the last Neanderthals of the western Pyrenees.
content: An international team has identified the first Neanderthal remains in Navarre. They are six bone fragments recovered during previous campaigns in the Abauntz cave which, according to the analyses, belonged to a man who lived around 46,000 years ago.The discovery was presented on Monday (19 October) at an event led by the president of the Government of Navarre, María Chivite.The assemblage includes three metacarpal bones and a middle phalanx from the right hand of an adult individual. These are joined by two other fragments that have been identified as human through protein analysis. Genetic studies confirm that the remains come from a male Neanderthal.Some of the bones preserve carnivore bite marks; those traces offer clues about what happened to the body after the individual’s death and how the bones ended up inside the cave.The fossils were found in an archaeological context with stone tools and animal remains, some showing signs of having been processed and eaten by the human groups that occupied the cavity. That context helps to situate Neanderthal presence at Abauntz and to understand what activities were carried out there.A Neanderthal in Navarre that fills a gap in the western PyreneesUntil now, there were no fossils that could directly confirm that Neanderthals passed through this area."For the first time we have human remains that allow us to directly identify the presence of Neanderthals in Navarre," explains Andion Arteaga, who co-directs the project, in a press release issued by the team.The date matters. Forty-six thousand years ago Neanderthals were still living in different parts of Europe. A few millennia later, around 40,000 years ago, the species disappeared from the continent, in a period also marked by the expansion of Homo sapiens.The location of Abauntz adds further interest, as the cave lies in a natural corridor connecting the Iberian Peninsula with the rest of Europe, making it a good place to study mobility and possible contacts between human groups on both sides of the Pyrenees.Ancient DNA and direct datingRecovering ancient DNA from remains tens of thousands of years old is not common. Genetic material degrades over time and its preservation depends on the conditions in which the fossils have remained.The team has combined palaeoproteomics, genetic analyses and radiocarbon dating to identify the bones, determine the individual’s sex and establish their chronology precisely. This work is being carried out together with the University of Vienna and the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Leipzig. The clearest precedent is El Sidrón, in Asturias, where genetics has shed light on kinship, social organisation and the evolutionary history of Neanderthals."Being able to recover ancient DNA and obtain direct dates for the fossils is particularly significant," stresses Mikel Arlegi, also co-director of the project.Genetic analyses are ongoing and could provide more information about the evolutionary history and demographic dynamics of these populations.The research originated at the Institut Català de Paleoecologia Humana i Evolució Social (Iphes-Cerca), based in Tarragona, which remains involved through Lucía López-Polín, Andreu Ollé and Aitor Burguet. The project is co-directed by Arteaga, from the Centre for New Technologies at the University of Warsaw and associated with Iphes-Cerca, and Arlegi, a postdoctoral researcher at the Musée de l'Homme in Paris.The team brings together more than 25 specialists from different disciplines and institutions, including the National Centre for Research on Human Evolution (CENIEH) and the Institute of Archaeology of Mérida (IAM, CSIC–Government of Extremadura).The project is supported by the Government of Navarre, through the Directorate-General for Culture–Príncipe de Viana Institution, by the Council of the Ultzama Valley, the Arraitz-Orkin local council and the Palarq Foundation. Members of the team taking part in the new excavation campaign, which is still under way in the cave, also attended the presentation event.

title: Mastering the ‘Schengen shuffle’: How to make sure you don’t break the 90 in 180 days rule
description: Non-EU citizens can easily work out how many days they have left to travel within the EU via the Entry/Exit System (EES) website.
content: As a Brit who voted Remain, I yearn for the pre-Brexit days when the only thing limiting my time travelling around the continent was the amount of money in my bank account.Alas. No point dwelling on the past – unless Andy Burnham wants to go ‘all the way’ and rejoin? Please, and thank you. Or someone with an EU passport wants to get down on one knee…For citizens of third countries, the maximum stay within the Schengen Area is 90 days within any 180-day period, and as someone who travels within the EU frequently, tracking my days has become a bit of an obsession.I’m not the only one, either – there’s a whole group of people attempting the “Schengen shuffle”, aka alternating between Schengen and non-Schengen countries to stay within the rules without leaving Europe.There’s an easy way to keep an eye on your limit, but first, let’s cover the rules. What you need to know about the EU’s ‘short stays’ rulesAs previously mentioned, “short stays” allow non-EU citizens to spend up to 90 days within a 180-day period within the Schengen Area.Taking it back to basics, the Schengen Area covers 29 countries: 25 of the 27 EU member states (Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, Croatia, Czechia, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, Netherlands, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain and Sweden), and four non-EU countries (Iceland, Norway, Switzerland and Liechtenstein).In case you were wondering, the two EU member states that aren’t in the Schengen Area are Cyprus and Ireland.While citizens from some countries, such as China, Indonesia, India and the Philippines, require visas when entering the Schengen Area, those from countries such as the UK, the US, Australia and New Zealand do not. You can find the full lists on the EU law website here.How to check how many days you have left within the Schengen AreaThe 90 days within a 180-day period doesn’t “reset” every six months, but instead operates on a rolling basis. That means you’ll need to look back at the past 180 days and count how many you’ve spent within the Schengen Area, and that you’ll gain back days as time progresses.The EU’s much-maligned Entry/Exit System (EES) was introduced last year (and fully enforced from April) to allow for the automatic detection of overstayers.You could keep track of your 90 days manually, but you can also check how long you can stay on the EES website here.You’ll need to input your passport details, put in the intended dates of your next trip, and which country you’re visiting. The website will then tell you your remaining days upon entry, and upon exit. Easy peasy.The penalties for those who overstay vary from country to country. Some countries, like Germany, could fine you up to €3,000, while others could ban you from re-entry for a few months, or even several years.You’ll also likely face stricter border controls the next time you attempt to enter the Schengen Area, and you may be refused entry.

title: Europe Today: Blame continues in France, Russia kills two children in Kharkiv
description: Blame in France over protests continues as Sébastien Lecornu accuses the ultra-left of orchestrating the unrest. In Kharkiv, two children are among the victims of a Russian strike on a park as Putin reportedly floats a summit without Kyiv. And we interview with Ryanair CEO Michael O’Leary.
content: On today's show:Estelle Nilsson-Julien reports from Paris, where the political blame game continues over who is responsible for the weekend’s unrest. French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has accused the “ultra-left movement” of seeking to “orchestrate deep unrest” in the run-up to next year’s presidential election.We hear from Audelia Sitbon, a pharmacist near Place de la République in Paris. Last Saturday, rioters smashed their way into her shop, looted her stock and set it ablaze. Left with empty shelves, shattered glass and worries about how to support her three children, she shared her story with Euronews’s Valérie Gauriat.We speak to Patrick Molinoz, mayor of Venarey-les-Laumes, as French retailers now face hundreds of millions of euros in damage. Shops of all kinds, from small boutiques to luxury stores on the high street, were targeted by thieves and vandals.We speak to Ryanair CEO Michael O’Leary for the view from industry on Europe’s wave of protests, as people also take to the streets of Spain, Portugal and Italy.Sasha Vakulina reports on the latest developments in Ukraine’s war, where two children were among the victims of a Russian drone strike on a park in Kharkiv yesterday. It comes as Vladimir Putin has reportedly proposed a summit with Trump and China’s Xi Jinping next month to discuss ending the war, potentially without Kyiv at the table.When and where to watch Europe Today?You can join Euronews’ anchors Méabh Mc Mahon and Stefan Grobe live on TV and Euronews' website, as well as digital platforms (YouTube, Facebook, X, and Instagram), every weekday at 8 am Brussels time.In just 20 minutes, we bring you the day's key events plus crucial analysis of all the stories shaping the EU and beyond. Also available as a newsletter and podcast.

title: German mortgage rates climb to highest since 2009 as Iran war stokes inflation fears
description: Mortgages in Germany are now at their most expensive since 2009, with the average rate on ten-year loans nearing 4.5%, according to broker Interhyp, as inflation fears stoked by the Iran war push up borrowing costs.
content: Getting a loan to buy a house in Germany now costs more than at any time since the 2009 financial crisis, as worries that the Iran war will keep inflation high and drive up interest rates, Munich-based mortgage broker Interhyp said.The typical rate on a ten-year loan is now close to 4.5% which is above the previous peak of just over 4.4% reached at the end of 2023, according to the broker.The average rate on ten-year mortgages has climbed from 3.9% as recently as May, Interhyp CEO Jörg Utecht stated, citing data.Interhyp’s latest survey of lenders, published on 15 October, put the ten-year average at about 4.4% but it continues to rise. However, most banks polled expect rates to hold steady over the next two months, while 60% see them falling over six to 12 months and 40% expect further rises.Both Interhyp’s figures and data on home loans to households from the Bundesbank, Germany’s central bank, show borrowing costs have not been this high since the 2009 financial crisis.Data from the European Central Bank (ECB) also confirmed how quickly borrowing costs have swung.The average German mortgage rate jumped from 1.48% in early 2022 to 4.15% at the end of 2023, eased to 3.57% in early 2025 and climbed back to 3.91% in the second quarter of this year, before the latest jump.War and the ECBUtecht blamed the latest rise mainly on the Iran war and the inflation fears it has fuelled.To keep prices in check, the ECB has raised interest rates twice this year, lifting its key deposit rate to 2.5%.For an average home loan, the recent increase adds almost €200 to monthly repayments, Utecht said, adding that some customers had become more hesitant.He also explained rates would only come down significantly once the conflict is resolved for good, which he saw little sign of so far.Despite the increase in borrowing costs, "German house prices continue to edge higher," Dutch bank ING said in an analysis last month, arguing that the housing market’s weakness was showing up everywhere except in prices.Prices rose 0.6% year on year in the second quarter of this year, according to the federal statistics office Destatis, leaving them more than 5% above their 2024 low but still 8.2% short of their 2022 high.Meanwhile, new mortgage lending was down more than 1.5% between January and July.ING said "the chronic lack of housing supply has prevented a more pronounced correction in prices", adding that residential construction "remains subdued".It also warned that "a meaningful rebound in housing demand appears unlikely in the near term".Borrowers will next look to the ECB, which announces its next interest rate decision on 29 October.

title: Turkmenistan summits focus on regional cooperation and Caspian Sea crisis
description: Leaders from across Eurasia gathered in Turkmenistan for three summits focused on strengthening regional trade, transport connectivity and economic cooperation, while addressing the growing environmental crisis facing the Caspian Sea.
content: Ten presidents gathered in Avaza on Turkmenistan's Caspian coast on Thursday and Friday for three simultaneous summits on regional security, economic integration, and a rapidly shrinking sea that leaders warned has become as much an economic crisis as an environmental one.The gatherings — the eighth Consultative Meeting of the Heads of State of Central Asia, the CIS Council of Heads of State and the first Caspian Ecological Forum — brought together leaders of post-Soviet states as the region marks 35 years of independence.Azerbaijan attended the Central Asian consultative meeting as a full member for the first time, having been admitted at the previous summit in late 2025.President Ilham Aliyev thanked Turkmenistan's leadership for supporting the accession and said Azerbaijan's trade with Central Asian countries had grown by more than 50% over the past year. Baku will chair the format in 2027.Regional trade among participating states reached approximately €11.6 billion last year, around 8% of their combined total, according to figures cited at the summit. Leaders set a target of raising it to at least €17 billion.Host President Serdar Berdimuhamedov opened the meeting by calling for deeper cooperation, saying the six states' mutual trust was sufficient to accomplish "all the tasks outlined."Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev offered the group's most pointed assessment of its track record. Since 2018, he said, more than 200 initiatives had been put forward but only a fraction carried out."I believe that the effectiveness of our work should be determined not so much by the number of proposals and initiatives as by their practical value and results," Tokayev said.Leaders also discussed transport, including the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route and the East-West and North-South corridors, as ways to connect the region with international markets.Tokayev said construction of the Aral-Caspian highway, which began in August and will run more than 1,500 kilometres, would cut the road route from China to Europe by roughly 1,000 kilometres and reduce transit delivery times to three days.World Bank projections cited at the summit put Caspian Sea freight traffic at a potential fourfold increase by 2040 if planned infrastructure is built.Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev proposed an Infrastructure Development Council to coordinate cross-border projects, describing the region as a potential "key land route for global trade" but warning that roads and railways alone would not be sufficient.Other proposals included a joint low-carbon energy strategy, coordinated water and pollution management, expanded collaboration on critical minerals and connecting national data centres to support artificial intelligence development. A joint statement was signed at the close of the meeting.CIS: Long-term strategy proposedThe CIS Council of Heads of State met in Avaza as the organisation marked its 35th anniversary.Tokayev called on member states to agree a development strategy through 2035 and answer a fundamental question: "how do we envision the Commonwealth in the long term, and what place should it occupy within the rapidly changing geopolitical architecture of Eurasia?"He also proposed a CIS+ format to expand the organisation's engagement beyond its current membership.Mirziyoyev called for closer industrial cooperation, fewer trade barriers and better transport connections, arguing the group should move "from the simple exchange of goods to the joint creation of full-fledged value chains."He proposed linking special economic zones and industrial parks across CIS countries, mutually recognising product conformity certificates, and expanding access to public procurement markets.Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian attended as a special guest. Uzbekistan assumed the CIS chairmanship, with the next heads-of-state meeting scheduled for October 2027 in Bukhara.Leaders backed Turkmenistan's proposal to designate 2029 as the Commonwealth's Year of Transport Connectivity.Caspian Sea decline raises further concernsThe first Caspian Ecological Forum, proposed by Berdimuhamedov at the UN General Assembly in 2023, was convened to address what participating leaders described as a crisis that has moved well beyond the environmental sphere.The sea's surface area has shrunk by more than 16,000 square kilometres since 2000, with the coastline retreating by tens of kilometres in some areas as reduced river inflows, rising temperatures and human activity press on the ecosystem. The Caspian seal population has fallen from an estimated one million to around 270,000 over the past century."This is no longer an environmental crisis, but an economic crisis with dangerous consequences," Pezeshkian said. The retreating coastline threatens shipping and port infrastructure, fisheries, energy installations and coastal communities.Tokayev proposed a shared digital platform to monitor water levels, coastline changes, biodiversity, pollution, and river inflows, along with a joint portfolio of restoration projects.He pointed to Kazakhstan's partial recovery of the North Aral Sea — its surface area has grown by 36%, improving water quality and fish stocks — as evidence that coordinated action can deliver results.Kazakhstan has also proposed establishing a UN Water organisation to coordinate international efforts on water security.

title: At least five killed and thousands evacuated as Storm Adam batters eastern Spain
description: Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez will visit Valencia on Tuesday to see the impact of the storm.
content: The DANA weather system Storm Adam began to ease on Tuesday after leaving at least five people dead and causing severe flooding in eastern Spain. In the Valencia region, the Civil Guard evacuated more than 2,100 people and rescued almost 500 since the start of the storm, according to the latest update released by the force.Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez will visit Valencia on Tuesday to see the impact of the storm. The visit is scheduled for around 12:30, after which the premier is expected to speak to the media.The Valencian town of Oliva is among the worst affected, with rainfall of 600 litres per square metre in 24 hours. Around 600 people received assistance at the municipal centre and 400 spent the night there from Monday into Tuesday.Emergency operations have deployed more than 1,300 Civil Guard officers, with helicopters, boats and specialised units for water and mountain rescues.Although the rain has lost intensity in the Valencia region and stay-at-home orders have been lifted, the State Meteorological Agency (Aemet) is keeping warnings in place in nine provinces on Tuesday, with particular attention to the rainfall forecast in Catalonia and the Balearic Islands.Historic rainfall of more than 700 litres per square metreAemet has described the rainfall as exceptional in the Valencian counties of La Safor and Marina Alta, where some of the largest rain accumulations in recent decades have been recorded.In L'Atzúvia in Alicante province, 713 litres per square metre fell during the episode, while Pego registered 632 litres in 36 hours, 430 of them in just six hours.The intensity of the rain caused the rivers Girona and Vernisa and the Beniopa ravine to overflow, as well as flooding in numerous municipalities.According to RTVE, the episode ranks among the most intense ever recorded in Spain, behind the historic rainfall in Oliva in 1987, when 817 litres per square metre fell in 24 hours, and the rains from the 2024 DANA, with 772 litres in Turís.In Oliva, the streets were left completely under water and many residents had to take refuge on the upper floors of their homes or climb onto rooftops as they waited for rescue teams to arrive.The severe flooding forced the Generalitat Valenciana to temporarily lock down 145 municipalities in Valencia and Alicante on Monday. Authorities urged people to avoid travelling and seek shelter on upper floors because of the risk of further surges. The restrictions were gradually lifted in the afternoon.The storm also caused road closures, transport disruption and the suspension of classes for more than 100,000 pupils.Balearic Islands and Catalonia also sufferedThe storm has also hit the Balearic Islands, particularly Ibiza and Formentera, where the rain has caused torrents to burst their banks, flooding and numerous road closures.In Ibiza, more than 130 incidents have been recorded, including fallen trees and problems accessing the airport, where standing water forced some operations to be suspended.In Formentera, up to 203 litres per square metre were recorded in 24 hours. The UME has also been deployed on the islands to help with emergency work and remove the accumulated water. The Balearic government suspended classes in Mallorca, Ibiza and Formentera on Monday, a precautionary measure affecting around 160,000 students.In Catalonia, the heaviest rain shifted towards the provinces of Barcelona, Girona and Tarragona on Monday afternoon, after Aemet issued warnings for heavy and persistent rainfall.Mobile phone alerts, key to the response to the stormThe Generalitat Valenciana has used the ES-Alert system to send warnings directly to the mobile phones of citizens in areas threatened by the rain.The first messages were sent over the weekend, before the storm reached maximum intensity, and were repeated on Monday as the flood risk increased.The alerts urged people to avoid travelling, stay away from rivers and ravines and seek shelter on higher ground or on the upper floors of buildings.The rollout of these warnings marks a difference from the handling of the October 2024 DANA, when delays in emergency communications were the subject of fierce criticism.

title: Oil prices top $110 as traders weigh Middle East supply risks
description: The price of Brent crude remained at a five-month high as uncertainty over when energy supplies will return to normal amid the war with Iran keeps oil inflated.
content: Oil prices continued to trade around a five-month high on Tuesday morning, as traders weighed the risk of further Iranian attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, amid relatively strong flows of crude oil from the Persian Gulf.International benchmark Brent crude futures traded at around $110 a barrel ahead of the European markets opening, while US benchmark WTI crude traded above $104 a barrel for delivery next month.According to ING's commodities strategists, the high prices despite strong flows "suggest the market is pricing in a significant risk premium, given the situation's volatility". There is no sign for now that the risk premium is about to erode.The strategists added that record tanker freight rates are adding to costs. The US is considering allowing the sale of sanctioned tankers, enabling them to return to the legitimate market, boost shipping capacity and reduce oil delivery costs. However, they noted that it remains unclear how much capacity this would add or how quickly it could bring any relief to prices.US Energy Secretary Chris Wright told Fox News that crude flows from the Gulf have recovered to about 80% of their pre-war level. However, supplies of refined products face greater constraints.Meanwhile, Asian LNG spot prices rose to $30.4 per million British thermal units on Monday, the highest since December 2022, Bloomberg reported, citing traders. This comes as UK Maritime Trade Operations reported that an LNG tanker came under fire from a small boat off Yemen on Saturday, fuelling further concerns about the safety of energy shipments in the region.European gas prices were also trading near their highest levels in years. Dutch TTF natural gas futures for delivery next month were just below €88 per megawatt-hour on Tuesday morning, easing somewhat from above €89 just before 6am, according to ICE data.Stock markets in the redEuropean stock markets opened with slight losses on Tuesday, after coming under pressure on Monday, when French stocks and bonds led the declines. Protests in France weighed on market sentiment, putting the spotlight on the unsustainable finances of Europe's second-largest economy.In London, the FTSE 100 lost 0.2% at the open, as did the CAC 40 in Paris, while the DAX in Frankfurt lost more than 0.4%.In the UK, investor sentiment was slightly supported by reports that Chancellor John Healey will not raise capital gains tax in next week’s Budget. The tax rate is currently 18% for basic-rate taxpayers and 24% for higher-rate taxpayers, compared with income tax rates of 20% to 45%.Additionally, the UK labour market proved to be more resilient than expected. The unemployment rate fell to 4.7% in the three months to August, from 4.9%. The number of payrolled employees in the UK increased by 13,000, the biggest rise in a year. The stronger figures could give the Bank of England more room to hold its key interest rate steady as it tackles inflation.In Asia, tech firms led heavy losses as investors brushed off a rebound on Wall Street amid growing fears about the AI investment boom ahead of key earnings releases.The Nikkei 225 in Tokyo dropped 1.3% as Kioxia shed nearly 2% and tech investor SoftBank plunged more than 5%. The Shanghai Composite index recovered to close 0.1% higher. In Hong Kong, the benchmark index lost 1.1%, while South Korea's Kospi lost more than 3.7% by the time European markets opened.South Korean AI infrastructure company Elice fell as much as 33% on its Kosdaq debut, amid concerns about borrowing costs, competition and the long-term returns on AI spending.Taiwan's TSMC was also in the red, though the country's Taiex inched higher.There were also losses in Sydney, Singapore, Wellington and Manila.The selling came despite a positive day on Wall Street, where the Nasdaq was pushed solidly higher by gains in Amazon, Microsoft and Nvidia.Focus is now on company earnings, with SpaceX, Meta and Tesla due to report this week.Since markets hit record highs in June, investors have increasingly questioned whether tech companies are worth their high valuations — and when, if ever, their huge spending on AI will pay off.Rising interest rates have also raised concerns about heavily indebted firms, as higher borrowing costs put pressure on their finances.In the bond market, US, German and French 10-year government bond yields eased slightly, with the US yield at around 5.123%, France's at 4.903% and Germany's at around 3.439% right after the European opening.In currency trading, the US dollar inched down to 158.45 Japanese yen from 158.46 yen. The euro traded at $1.1225, little changed from $1.1227.Gold prices were slightly lower when European stock markets opened, trading at around $4,152.80 an ounce.

title: With 29 designated Cittaslow cities, Türkiye is leading the way in slow travel
description: The Cittaslow’ initiative has been highlighting the lesser-known burgs around the world which celebrate local food, culture and history. Türkiye is the proud owner of 29 such towns, all offering unfettered access to myriad aspects of Turkish culture.
content: The hustle of a big, sprawling city can be intoxicating; they’re often a hub of noise, unfamiliar scents and eye-opening events. And while big cities can be great places to start when visiting a new destination, it’s sometimes in a location’s quieter, more remote, regions where its long-held traditions still thrive, and local cuisine is still a staple, not a novelty. Enter Cittaslow, an initiative established in Italy in 1999 designed to shine a light on the ‘slower’ – but still special – towns and villages keeping a country’s culture alive.Of the 310 currently registered Cittaslow towns in the world, Türkiye has an impressive 29, all possessing distinctive aspects of Turkish way of life, from organic food markets and ancient ruins to sweeping plateaus and swathes of agricultural land.From coastal fishing villages to mountaintop towns, here are some of Türkiye’s most enigmatic ‘slow cities’ slow travellers should check out. The Aegean coastlines’s laidback locales Peppered along the iridescent Aegean coast are some of Türkiye’s most striking Cittaslows. Seferihisar, for example, was selected for its beautiful tangerine orchards and wealth of organic markets. It was Türkiye’s first ‘slow city’ and today, its agricultural heritage remains a major source of income. Visitors can expect to see citrus fruit orchards and grapevine-laced hills, as well as meticulously curated olive groves and lush green fields bursting with vegetables. Plus, since you’re never far from a slice of ancient history in Türkiye, they’ll also find the ruins of the ancient city of Teos just a few kilometres from Seferihisar city centre. This area serves as a key gateway to the Teos Vineyard Route, where local viticulture flourishes among thousand-year-old olive trees. For those looking to explore further, it also forms a vital part of the Ionian Route, a trekking path that connects the cultural heritage of the ancient Ionian League through breathtaking Aegean landscapes. A little to the south, tucked into the crevice of the Gulf of Gökova, is Akyaka, a Cittaslow famed for its serene beauty and unique architectural style. Buildings here were inspired by Muğla’s 18th-century Ottoman-era designs and revamped through Turkish architect Nail Çakırhan’s discerning eye, furnishing them with distinctive wooden shutters, balconies and often double staircases.The town’s position near the Azmak River, a crystal-clear channel winding through the Gökova Plain, is a protected area, offering a bucolic setting for nature-lovers who can enjoy boat rides along the eucalyptus-banked waters, go bird-watching or simply bask in the peace bestowed by a stroll through the idyllic landscape. With over 500 islands surrounding Türkiye, that ‘island’ lifestyle is always close by. Gökçeada sits off the very Western tip of the Turkish mainland and is the country's largest island. It’s also Türkiye largest island.Northern Türkiye’s Black Sea abodes Türkiye’s other coastline is one spattered with high mountains, sweeping hillsides and tumbling rivers. On the eastern edge of the Black Sea, close to the Georgian border, sits Şavşat, an idyllic town flanked by the peaks of the Karçal Mountains.Inhabited today by a mix of Georgian and Turkish peoples, the town is a contradiction of historical remnants and the lush foliage of the Artvin region. On the one hand, the ruins of a castle believed to have been built in the 9th century make for eerie exploration, while on the other, wandering through the conifer, chestnut, rhododendrons and fir trees which cluster the hillsides is a supremely peaceful experience. It’s particularly picturesque in the autumn, when the landscape transforms into rolling sheets of golden leaves. Flying under the radar, in the middle of Türkiye’s Black Sea coastline, is the ‘happiest place’ in the country. Gerze was founded in 1400 BCE and declared a Cittaslow nearly 4,000 years later, in 2017. As a town, it's a near-pastiche of quaintness: toy shops sell hand-carved toys, a Friday farmers’ market shares produce from all across the region and Gerze’s legacy as a fishing town is ever on display thanks to an abundance of fresh seafood for sale.The outskirts of the town are equally enticing: the Çeçe Sultan Tomb, once an important place of pilgrimage, lies just 15 kilometres from the city centre, while the surrounding hillsides prove a popular paragliding spot for those prepared to hike the 400-metre heights of Yelken Tepe (they’ll be rewarded with a 15-kilometre flight route – the longest in Türkiye). The Black Sea’s Cittaslows don’t stop there, however. On the western tip of the coastline, the once capital of the ancient Thracian tribe, Vize, is filled with ruins and architecture from its colourful military history. The remains of 6th century pipes that used to form an ancient water supply route that carried water towards İstanbul, a Roman theatre and the walls of a fortress built around 72 BCE are just the beginning of the cultural wonders to uncover. The serene shores of Türkiye’s lakesides While Türkiye’s dramatic coastlines attract many, there are slow traveller treasures to be found inland too. Some of the country’s most beautiful lakes (Türkiye boasts more than 300) can be found between the Anatolian plateau and the Mediterranean coast. Eğirdir Lake is the fourth largest in the country, and abutted by Eğirdir town, which huddles on the water’s southern shores. It’s a popular stopping point for those making their way to Cappadocia, but is a far cry from the hustle and bustle of a big city. The land surrounding the lake’s green-blue waters are furnished with apple orchards and shaded by mountains to the southwest and the islands of Can Ada and Yeşil Ada on the horizon to the northeast.Today, the ‘ada’s are connected to the mainland by a causeway, and well worth a visit. Settlements on Yesil Ada (Turkish for ‘green island’) date back to the Eastern Roman era, but are more noticeable for their Rum architectural flourishes.A wander around Eğirdir town itself reveals the crumbling remains of a castle thought to have been built by the Lydians then modified by the Romans, Eastern Roman and Seljuks, a small mosque – Hızırbey Camii – and a variety of local restaurants specialising in freshwater delicacies. Diners can sample lake bass, eel, lobster and carp all while looking out at a blissful lakeside vista. Boat trips, paddleboarding and a wade in the bracing waters of the Halk Plajı (the public beach) are also great ways to take in the town. We’d be remiss not to mention Türkiye's largest lake, Lake Van. Sporting a total area of 3,755km2 , its shorelines are vast, meaning there’s plenty of room for yet another Cittaslow: Ahlat. Not only does this burg boast simply glorious views, but it retains myriad remnants from across its history. There are oodles of historic sites to pore over here, including Neolithic caves and thousands of engraved tombstones at the Ahlat Seljuk Cemetery, believed to be the largest Turkish-Islamic cemetery in the world.

title: Trump says he is ready to meet Putin and Xi in China
description: Trump also renewed his criticism of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy saying it was "time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine."
content: US President Donald Trump said Monday he is willing to sit down with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in China next month, confirming media reports that the three leaders could meet on the sidelines of an Asia-Pacific summit in Shenzhen.Trump said such a summit would centre on denuclearisation but might also touch on the war in Ukraine.Asked by reporters whether he would join Putin and Xi to discuss Ukraine, Trump downplayed that as the main draw. “I would do it, not so much for Ukraine, because Russia, frankly, has been fine with Ukraine. They haven’t been doing much,” he said. “We would have it to talk about nuclear weapons and denuclearisation.”Pressed on whether Ukraine would come up at a meeting with the two leaders, Trump said he would do “whatever I can do to end the war".Beijing says it has no details while Kyiv insists on involvementEarlier, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said, "Given that all three heads of state might potentially attend a summit in China, the topic of such a hypothetical meeting has indeed been mentioned."The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) group holds a summit in the Chinese city of Shenzhen on 18-19 November. China, Russia and the United States are all members.But Peskov added that "no substantive proposals or agreements, neither regarding the meeting itself nor its potential agenda and content, have been discussed or put forward by anyone".China's foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said she had no information about a possible meeting while Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha bristled at the suggestion of a meeting without Kyiv."A trilateral meeting between the leaders of Russia, China and the US would do only the opposite: encourage Putin to continue this war," he said.Putin, he insisted on social media, was "not a global leader; he is a war criminal".The Kremlin's Peskov said that "a final settlement is impossible without the participation of someone from Kyiv who is prepared to take on the responsibility".But Putin has repeatedly ruled out meeting Zelenskyy until after a final peace deal is ready and has repeatedly questioned Zelenskyy's authority to sign a deal following the expiry of his five-year term under martial law.Trump, who has renewed his swipes at Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in recent days, on Monday said it was “time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine.”"Zelenskyy doesn't know what he's talking about," Trump said when asked about the Ukrainian's comments. "To be honest, I think it's time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine."

title: Pop culture iconography as protest: Why has the One Piece skull been adopted by French protesters?
description: Pop culture as expression of revolt: Gen Z have adopted a symbol from a popular manga for their protest movements. Here’s why the One Piece flag has become a recognised symbol of revolt during French protests - and beyond.
content: When young people challenge the establishment, they often adopt fictional works or popular culture iconography in their protests, with some images and symbols becoming unlikely rallying cries.Amid the banners, placards and slogans seen on the streets of France, a black flag with a smiling skull wearing a straw hat frequently pops up. The pirate emblem immediately speaks to fans of the manga series One Piece: it’s the "Jolly Roger", one of the most recognizable logos in pop culture. The iconography was already present during last year’s September protests in France, and it has re-emerged during the ongoing student protests and street demonstrations across France – as well as in Belgium, Italy and Greece.But how has the One Piece pirate flag become a country and continent-spanning symbol against repression and government corruption?A bit of background first. For those of you who aren’t familiar with One Piece, it’s a popular Japanese manga created by Eiichiro Oda. In a nutshell, it follows the adventures of the Straw Hat Pirates, who stand up for those oppressed by repressive rulers and authoritarian corruption – a fight against tyranny under their flag, the “Jolly Roger”. First published in 1997 – the year which coincidentally marks the first year of Gen Z births – the manga has become a worldwide phenomenon, selling more than 500 million copies and being translated into 40 languages. It holds the Guinness World Record for the most copies published in the same comic book series by a single author, and has spawned an animated TV series, a live-action Netflix show, as well as several films.In France, the show is extremely popular and its volumes are bestsellers.Over the years, the flag of the grinning skull has been seen at protests in Nepal, Indonesia, the Philippines, Morocco, Italy, the UK, and has been omnipresent during the protests rocking France in the past few weeks.Whether the One Piece image is seen at student protests, rallies against police brutality, protests on government social media bans, or at pro-Palestine demonstrations, the common visual denominator reflects how the manga symbol has resonated with Gen Z, who have adopted it as their symbol for defiance and ultimately, hope. It is hardly an unexpected symbol, as it stands for freedom and resistance against oppression for the source material’s ragtag rebels. And now IRL, speaking to disaffected youth and Gen Z aching to be heard.The fictional world making its way into the real one represents a useful transfer as narratives and their values are not limited to borders or causes, thereby creating a global sense of unification and a shared language of solidarity. It’s also an advantageous transferral, as transforming fictional touchstones into real-world emblems of defiance means these symbols are harder to suppress by governments who still seek to maintain an anti-authoritarian appearance.The use of the Jolly Roger once again reveals that culture and politics are inextricably intertwined - especially for young activists and a digitally-savvy generation who use social media to communicate their thoughts and fears through cultural references.There’s plenty of precedence, as the Jolly Roger flag isn't the only pop culture symbol to have been used in protests over the years. Here’s a look five instances of cultural touchstones used as political expression in the last 15 years. V for Vendetta Inspired by 2005’s V for Vendetta, the international hacktivist group Anonymous started using the movie’s iconic Guy Fawkes mask to conceal their identities during protests. The mask became widespread in 2011 during the “Occupy” movement, and has lasted as a face-of-dissent symbol, taking aim at corrupt systems and governments. As V states: "People should not be afraid of their governments – governments should be afraid of their people.” The Hunger Games The series of YA books by Suzanne Collins and the subsequent films starring Jennifer Lawrence contain several symbols of resistance, from the Mockingjay pin to the three-finger salute. This silent gesture of defiance was used by the character Katniss Everdeen as a way to show her solidarity with the oppressed, and it has since been seen in protests from 2014 onwards, from anti-military coup demonstrations in Thailand to Hong Kong’s protest for universal suffrage. The Handmaid’s Tale In 2017 and 2018, women across the US wore scarlet cloaks and white bonnets from Margaret Atwood’s “The Handmaid’s Tale", as a response to anti-abortion legislation and policies threatening female reproductive rights. In the dystopian book and TV series, the handmaids are made to wear the uniform under the law of Gilead, the dystopian country in which fertile women are forced into childbearing servitude. The costume frequently reappears in women’s rights demonstrations worldwide - from Argentina’s 2018 demonstrations for abortion rights, to the 2019 protests against US President Trump’s visits to the UK. The JokerIn the aftermath of civil war, Lebanese protestors demonstrating against the government’s new austerity measures in 2019 adopted the likeness of the Clown Prince of Crime, with many taking inspiration from Joaquin Phoenix’s face paint in Joker. It’s a get-up that is recognised worldwide, one which grants anonymity to demonstrators and in the case of Lebanese protestors, allowed their strife to gain heightened visibility. The Joker also stands as a symbol of rebellion, embodying a disregard for societal norms and conventions. As such, the use of the clown face signifies a reminder to embrace irreverence towards the established order, making it a popular emblem in protests worldwide. Pepe the FrogThe alt-right, MAGA and Trump himself, who tweeted a meme of Pepe during the 2016 US presidential election, adopted the green frog as a way to appeal to the youth. American cartoonist Matt Furie created the image in 2005 and was furious at how his creation had been co-opted in such a hateful way. Before killing off the character in a 2017 comic, he wrote an essay for TIME in 2016 in which he said: “It’s completely insane that Pepe has been labelled a symbol of hate, and that racists and anti-Semites are using a once peaceful frog-dude from my comic book as an icon of hate.” Despite Pepe being used by the alt-right in the West, it was re-appropriated and reclaimed by Hong Kong protestors in pro-democracy demonstrations in 2019.

title: EU summit: Leaders meet to tackle energy prices, spar over budget and rally behind Ukraine
description: The two-day summit of EU leaders comes with a packed agenda topped by energy prices, the long-term budget and Russia's war on Ukraine. Hybrid warfare, enlargement and migration will also feature prominently.
content: Spiralling energy prices, the EU's long-term budget and support for Ukraine in the wake of Donald Trump's latest overture to Vladimir Putin will dominate the conversation as the leaders gather for a two-day summit in Brussels.Enlargement, hybrid warfare, economic stagnation, rising borrowing costs, trade imbalances and irregular migration will also feature in the talks.The meeting will start early on Thursday with a hotly anticipated discussion on energy prices, which hostilities in the Middle East have sent skyrocketing. Oil remains above $100 per barrel despite a coordinated G7 release, while gas trades at its highest level since winter 2022, with underground storage running below average.The market shockwaves have rattled EU leaders, who are under mounting pressure to deliver tangible relief for households and industries, especially as temperatures cool down and the heating season begins.Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis have led the charge, asking Brussels to relax the bloc's fiscal rules to allow governments to finance "temporary and targeted measures" to cushion the energy crunch.Other countries, however, worry that excessive flexibility will promote fossil fuel consumption and discourage investments in the green transition.Meanwhile, six member states (Austria, Germany, Italy, Poland, Portugal and Spain) have proposed an EU-wide windfall tax to capture excess profits from energy companies amid high prices. But the idea remains divisive and has not gained enough traction.Energy will be followed by another pressing economic challenge: China.With a €1 billion trade deficit every day, Brussels threw down the gauntlet by imposing a deadline on Beijing to deliver "tangible results" by October at the latest.Those results emerged last week in Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič's trip to Beijing, where he secured preliminary concessions on hybrid and plug-in hybrid cars, rare earths and permanent magnets, and market access for European companies."We're satisfied with the results, but for us, it's only a first step because imbalances are not specific to one sector – there are across the board," a senior diplomat said, cautioning implementation will be key to show whether Beijing is serious."Why is China agreeing to something that China has never agreed before? (Because) they're starting to realise they're killing their customers. We're not naïve."The concessions avert, for now, an all-out trade war.
