Leaders are expected to call on the Commission to continue "results-oriented dialogue" with China and "urgently enhance" trade tools to retaliate if needed, according to the draft conclusions seen by Euronews.In a sign of exasperation, Germany and France have pitched a "kill switch" to cut off China's access to the EU market if the deficit remains unsustainable.Money talks, but does anyone listen?The summit's most contentious moment will arrive on Thursday afternoon when the next seven-year EU budget is put on the table. The wrangle will take place against the backdrop of steep borrowing costs, particularly alarming in France.European Council President António Costa has appealed to member states to move away from their red lines and reach an agreement by the end of the year so that the complex legislative work can be fully completed before January 2028.Ireland, the country holding the rotating presidency, has tabled a proposal that cuts the original draft by €141 billion. But the knife mostly spares agriculture and cohesion funds and falls instead on research, technology, climate action, security and foreign policy.The Irish "nego-box" has made everyone unhappy.The so-called "frugals" (Austria, Denmark, Finland, the Netherlands, Sweden and Germany) say the cuts need to go much deeper and across the board. The 17 "Friends of Cohesion" say the opposite, that the cuts have gone far too deep. The European Commission warns its vision of a modernised, flexible budget is in real danger.On top of that, nobody agrees which EU-wide taxes should be approved to collect additional revenue for the common pot.The clash of opinions and the unwillingness to compromise bode ill for Costa's ambition to have a unanimous deal in December. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's shock decision to call snap elections adds yet another layer of uncertainty."I don't think there will be blood on the wall, but it's important in these sorts of negotiations that leaders feel where the contradictions are," another senior diplomat said. "We are not in a hurry. We need a good deal. We don’t feel any time pressure."The first day will end with a strategic debate on how to prepare the 27-strong bloc for the admission of new member states and reform its internal decision-making. Montenegro, the frontrunner in the accession race, aims to close all chapters this year.Backing Zelenskyy, rebuking TrumpFriday will be dedicated to Ukraine in the presence of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.The peace talks took a dramatic turn after US President Donald Trump blindsided Europeans by cutting a deal with his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, to bring tens of thousands of Russian diesel into the US market. Washington issued a sanctions waiver until April 2027 to enable what would until now have been a forbidden sale.The news jolted Europeans and prompted a scramble to close ranks and rally behind Ukraine to control the fallout from a unilateral, uncoordinated decision that has revived memories from the Trump-Zelenskyy showdown in the White House.Although the diesel deal is likely to have a limited impact on the prices at the pump, which Trump wants to lower ahead of the midterm elections, there is greater concern over the diplomatic implications of providing relief to Russia at a time when it escalates its attacks to decimate the Ukrainian economy ahead of the winter.The summit's conclusions have been changed to add a rebuke: "The European Council regrets the United States' decision to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian diesel."Trump has spent the last few days calling on Zelenskyy to stop attacks on Russia's oil refineries and abide by his energy ceasefire. Zelenskyy says he is ready for the truce as long as Russia complies, but Russia keeps bombing Ukraine's power facilities.Europeans are reluctant to endorse Trump's petition because the long-range strikes are Kyiv's greatest leverage over Moscow. Giving it up would further tilt the war."It's not the first time that we're going through divergences with the US in what the Ukraine war is concerned, but I would disagree with the idea that we're ignored," a senior EU official said."We have seen that dialogue with the US doesn't always lead to full agreement in the way the EU and the US see things, but it's always better than not having dialogue," the official added. "This is what needs to continue to be done. It's the normal thing."The last item on the summit will be a strategic debate on migration poised to pit Sánchez against the Meloni-led majority in the room. In the aftermath of the Ceuta border crisis, Italy introduced border checks with Spain, and Spain retaliated in kind.The checks, which are conducted randomly at airports, last to this day.

title: France's riot damage doubles: How will businesses pay for the destruction?
description: At least 3,000 French shops were hit over the weekend. Insurers say they are mobilised, but lost trade may not be covered. Here is who pays the riot bill.
content: The number of shops damaged during France's weekend riots has reached at least 3,000, twice the figure reported just a day earlier.Yet insurers, who are expected to pick up much of the bill, still have no estimate of what the destruction will cost them.France Assureurs, the country's insurance federation, told Euronews that its members were "fully mobilised to support affected policyholders".It could not provide an initial estimate of losses or say how many claims had been already filed.Its crisis team is now working with public authorities across France following what the federation described as "extremely violent events".French markets underperform as damage bill risesOn Sunday, Carrefour chief executive Alexandre Bompard, who also chairs the FCD retail federation, estimated that around 1,500 shops had been affected.He put the industry's losses at several hundred million euros.By Monday, the government's count had reached 3,000.Carrefour alone reported damage at 50 stores, including 20 that had been looted.Financial markets were also under pressure on Monday. France's CAC 40 closed 1.1% lower, underperforming the broader Euro STOXX 600, down 0.9%.Carrefour shares lost 2.2%, while luxury group LVMH fell 1.8%. A Louis Vuitton boutique in Marseille was among the stores broken into over the weekend.Insurance stocks declined too. AXA shed 1.3% and reinsurer SCOR lost 0.9% in Paris. In Milan, Generali fell 2.3% and Unipol dropped 3.2%.French government bonds also came under selling pressure on Monday.The yield on the country's 10-year bonds rose by around eight basis points to 4.94%. Germany's equivalent yield increased by less than four basis points.That widened the difference between French and German borrowing costs to approximately 148 basis points.What the 2023 riots tell us about the costFrance has a recent benchmark for what a weekend like this can cost.The riots that swept the country in June and July 2023 resulted in €793 million in insured losses, France Assureurs told Euronews.Insurers handled around 17,000 claims, averaging roughly €46,600 each.Two-thirds of the total, about €523 million, went on shops and business premises. A quarter, close to €200 million, went to local authorities whose town halls, schools and buses had been attacked.Cars made up the remaining 7%.Even those figures did not capture the full extent of the destruction.A subsequent French Senate inquiry estimated property damage at closer to €1 billion. Some losses had never been declared, while others were only partly covered by insurance.The comparison is particularly relevant now because the number of shops affected appears to be higher.CCI France counted around 2,500 vandalised businesses during the 2023 unrest. This weekend's government tally has already exceeded that figure.France's new riot insurance scheme is not readyFrance sought to address the insurance problems exposed by the 2023 riots in its 2026 budget law.The legislation makes riot damage cover compulsory in certain property insurance policies and creates a national fund to help insurers absorb major losses.Insurers would finance the fund through contributions of up to 1.5% of relevant premiums, while the state would provide guarantees of up to €4 billion a year.But the scheme has yet to take effect. It still needs European Commission approval and a government implementing decree.For businesses hit by this weekend's violence, that means compensation will depend on their existing insurance contracts.Insurance may cover the damage, but what about lost sales?Most French policies for shops and buildings include “riot and civil commotion” cover, according to France Assureurs.That usually pays for fire, theft, vandalism and smashed shopfronts. It also tends to cover the plywood boards and security guards a gutted store needs in the days afterwards.Lost trade is where many shopkeepers will come up short.Compensation for a full or partial closure depends on optional business interruption cover.It pays on lost gross profit, not lost sales, and normally only when physical damage covered by the policy forced the shop to shut.Some contracts go further and pay out even if the premises were untouched. That applies only “in the circumstances expressly specified in the policy”, the federation said.Policyholders generally have five days to notify their insurer, and filing a police complaint is a prerequisite for some types of cover.The state’s share of the billPrime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said on Monday that businesses hit by the unrest would be able to put staff on activité partielle, France’s state-funded furlough scheme, from Tuesday.He also asked local officials to impose targeted curfews, and said a state of emergency would follow “if necessary”.President Emmanuel Macron refused the resignation of Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez, as the number of arrests passed 2,400.Every euro of support lands on a budget expected to post a deficit of 5.4% of GDP this year, with public debt at 119% of GDP.And while the final bill for the riots is still unknown, one thing is becoming clear: the cost will extend well beyond the shops that were attacked.

title: France presses resale platforms to remove 'stolen' goods after unrest
description: France's digital minister on Monday urged online resale platforms to remove listings for "stolen items" following Saturday's looting and summoned representatives of companies including Vinted and eBay for talks.
content: Six months before France elects a successor to President Emmanuel Macron, the country was rocked over the weekend by some of its worst street violence in years, with thousands of shops damaged, many looted. The unrest came after weeks of student demonstrations demanding better conditions in schools.More than 3,000 businesses suffered damage, according to the authorities. Since Sunday, screenshots have circulated on social media showing online resale listings for items allegedly stolen during the weekend unrest."Stolen items from this weekend are being offered for sale on certain platforms," digital minister Anne Le Henanff said on X."We expect these platforms to remove the listings in question without delay," she said.She convened representatives of six platforms for a meeting in the presence of interior and justice ministry officials."They will also be required to cooperate closely with state authorities so that those reselling stolen goods can be prosecuted," Le Henanff added.According to the French commerce ministry, representatives of Vinted, Amazon, eBay, Leboncoin, Meta and TikTok as well as French online retail association Fevad were invited for talks.Contacted by AFP, Vinted said it applied a policy of "zero tolerance" in such cases and was cooperating "actively with law enforcement and the French authorities"."Since this weekend, our teams have acted immediately to identify and remove listings that may involve stolen goods, and we have strengthened monitoring of suspicious listings," the Vilnius-based second-hand platform said, without specifying the scale of the problem.eBay said it was "not in a position to confirm an increase in listings that may be linked to thefts committed over the weekend".The online auction platform said it used "proactive technological tools" to detect the sale of stolen goods.

title: At least 14 killed and seven injured in landslide at illegal gold mine in Colombia
description: Armed groups in Narino, an illegal mining hotspot on the border with Ecuador, control the clandestine gold trade as well as trafficking drugs and engaging in extortion.
content: A landslide at an illegal gold mine in southwestern Colombia killed 14 people and injured seven, a regional official said on Monday.Armed groups in Narino, an illegal mining hotspot on the border with Ecuador, control the clandestine gold trade as well as trafficking drugs and engaging in extortion.Videos shared on social media show people and a backhoe evacuating bodies from the mine to a canoe on a nearby river.Narino's Peace and Security Secretary Alex Gonzalez gave the revised death toll to the Caracol television channel, adding that the search for survivors had ended.Rescue teams struggled to reach the site due to the difficult terrain and the presence of criminal groups, the governor's office said."Communities have no other economic alternatives than these extremely risky activities. Traditional small-scale mining has practically disappeared," a source from the office told the AFP news agency.Mine accidents in Colombia are frequent, particularly at unregulated sites.Locals in the municipality where the mine collapsed on Monday have reported selective killings carried out by armed groups over suspicions of collaboration with security forces and rival organizations, or of stealing gold.

title: ‘Albertans chose Canada’: Carney hails vote to reject referendum
description: Separatist leaders vow to fight on, warning the province’s governing party could split over the issue.
content: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has welcomed Alberta’s decisive rejection of a move towards independence, saying the province had chosen national unity at a time of mounting pressure from Washington."On October 19, Albertans made a clear choice. They chose unity, to build together, and to take care of each other. Above all, Albertans chose Canada," Carney said in a statement on Tuesday.With more than one million votes counted, 77 per cent backed remaining in Canada, according to unofficial results from Elections Alberta.Monday’s vote was not a direct ballot on independence. A win for the separatists would instead have set the western province on a path towards a binding referendum on leaving Canada.The result is a boost for Carney, who grew up in Alberta and had urged a decisive outcome as US President Donald Trump wages a trade war against Canada and threatens to make it the 51st US state.Alberta, a conservative stronghold with the world’s fourth-largest proven oil reserves, has long resented the federal government in Ottawa, largely over the management of its oil industry. Premier Danielle Smith has accused Carney’s predecessor, Justin Trudeau, of trying to curb oil production to advance his climate agenda.Separatist parties once won only 1 or 2 per cent of the vote, but anger over COVID-19 restrictions helped energise the movement.Smith opposes independence but called the referendum under pressure from separatists within her United Conservative Party."Albertans have voted for a stronger Alberta in a united Canada," she posted on social media.The separatist campaign drew interest from Trump’s allies. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent described Alberta as a natural partner for the United States, and billionaire Elon Musk posted on X that the province should separate. Separatist leaders also met officials at the US State Department.Thomas Lukaszuk, a former deputy premier who led the Forever Canadian campaign against separation, told supporters: "We are a solid country that’s united from coast to coast to coast."Separatists insist their cause is not finished. Jeffrey Rath, a leader of the Alberta Prosperity Project, said the push for independence would continue."We’ve learned a lot of lessons from this fight," he said.

title: Inflation squeeze pushes Europeans onto the streets. Can the EU help?
description: Euro-area inflation climbed to 3.8%, its highest in recent months, and Europeans are taking to the streets to demand relief from soaring energy, food and housing costs. Watch the video.
content: Euro-area inflation climbed to 3.8% in September, up from 3.2% in August, according to Eurostat’s flash estimate. Energy prices rose 18.8% year on year, with Lithuania (6.1%), Bulgaria (5.6%) and Spain (5%) recording the highest rates.Protests followed across the continent. Unions marched in Brussels and Paris, students camped outside Greece’s parliament, and thousands rallied in Lisbon and Porto over rents. In Spain, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called a snap election for November 29 after Congress rejected two housing decrees.Brussels says it is coordinating oil stock releases and urging targeted aid instead of blanket subsidies, after governments spent €17.9 billion cushioning bills this year.But the EU does not set prices, rents or tuition fees. National governments largely control those levers, and pressure to deliver keeps rising. Can the EU help citizens deal with inflation?

title: Planning a Christmas getaway? Here’s where flights and hotels could cost less
description: From the best days to fly to the destinations seeing price drops on hotels, this is where you should be headed for Christmas in 2026, according to a new KAYAK study.
content: Looking to get away this Christmas, but don’t want to spend an arm and a leg to do so?Not to worry, because KAYAK has released its Christmas travel trends covering the cheapest destinations to fly to from France, Germany and the UK, plus where hotel prices are falling.Based on flight and hotel searches made between 1 April and 1 September for travel between 19 December 2026 and 9 January 2027, compared to the same period last year, the results might surprise you.Here’s what you need to know to save some serious cash.The cheapest destinations to fly to this ChristmasThe cheapest destinations to fly differ by country, with France seeing return flights to Milan from €126, to Brussels from €153, to Venice or Berlin from €161, and to London from €169.As for Germany, Milan is also a winner, with an average return price of €116, as is Rome (from €169), Vienna (from €170), Paris (from €190) and London (from €192).For Brits, the cheapest return flights can be found to Dublin (from £127 / €151), Barcelona (from £131 / €155), Milan (from £142 / €169) and Prague or Madrid (from £143 / €170).Hotel destinations that are getting cheaperShockingly, Rovaniemi in Finnish Lapland, better known as the home of Santa Claus, has seen a 22% drop in accommodation prices compared to last year, with an average of €275 per night.Other cities in Europe you can visit for less include Istanbul, with prices down 12% to an average of €76 per night, Paris (-5%, €140 average per night), Adeje in Spain (-8%, €235 average per night) and York in the UK (-8%, £96/€114 average per night).Further afield, Thailand could be an option, with Koh Samui prices down 21% to an average of €115 per night and Bangkok prices down 20% to €76 per night. Tokyo prices are down 19%, to €110 per night, while Singapore prices are down 13%, to €164 per night.Bucket list destination the Maldives is down 10%, to €916 per night, while classic Christmas city New York is down 11% to €273.In the Caribbean, prices in Fort-de-France, the capital of Martinique, are down 10% to €123 per night.When to travel and when to bookIn general, the best time to book international flights is around 15-30 days ahead of your travels, according to Expedia data revealed earlier this year.The same is true for Christmas flights from Germany, with decreases seen in December, while those in France will have to play flight price chicken and wait until the week before Christmas.In the UK, flights should typically wait until six weeks before the big day.As for when you should fly, for French and British travellers 23 December is the cheapest day, while for Germans, it’s 21 December, according to the KAYAK data.If you’re staying at home for Christmas but want to delay the January blues, consider flying on New Year’s Eve, which is the cheapest day to fly out across all three countries.As for booking hotels, France has a similar timeline compared to flights, with domestic accommodation rates around 18% lower than in October the week before Christmas. Internationally, though, rates are around 7% lower from late November to December.In Germany, the two weeks before Christmas offer rates 9% lower compared to peaks in mid-November, while in the UK, waiting until the fortnight before 25 December can save you 16% internationally and 20% domestically.The cheapest check-in date for France both domestically and abroad is 21 December, while those in Germany can check in on Christmas Day domestically for the best rates, or 21 December abroad.Brits will want to check in on 22 December if staying in the UK, or 23 December if heading elsewhere.Winter sun, without the hefty price tagThe cheapest destinations in general are closer to home, but if the long, winter nights have you down, you’ll need to look long-haul to get a good dose of Vitamin D.For French travellers, flight prices to Casablanca and Rabat in Morocco are down 19%, as well as 12% to Agadir. Fares to Koh Samui are also down 17%, or you could head to Sri Lanka for 11% less compared to 2025.Germans can get to Lima in Peru for 29% less than last year, to Cairo for 18% less, and to Port Louis in Mauritius for 14% less, while both Cancún in Mexico and Marrakech in Morocco are down 8%.Finally, Brits can get their fix in Agadir, Morocco, with flights down 26%, or in Kingston or Montego Bay, Jamaica, with prices down 21% and 18% respectively.

title: Albanian PM Rama accuses anti-government protesters of crossing 'red line' amid violent demonstrations
description: The European Commission released a statement condemning the violence in Albania on Sunday, saying it had "no place in a democratic society" and that the response "must remain within the law and proportionate."
content: Edi Rama has accused some of those taking part in anti-government protests in Albania as having crossed a "red line" as demonstrations continued across the country on Monday.Anti-government "Flamingo" protests have been ongoing in Albania for months amid calls for Rama to resign as prime minister, but clashes ramped up early last week as a student movement calling for action over high tuition fees launched fresh demonstrations."Protests are a right, whereas violence is a crime, and this red line will be drawn firmly at this critical stage of our democratic development," Rama wrote in a post on social media on Monday."The rioters must and will bear the legal and financial consequences of their blindness," he continued, whilst also urging protesters to "distance themselves" from rioters."I and the governing majority are ready for dialogue with anyone except the rioters and political parties that do not distance themselves from violence," Rama added.Violent clashes with police in recent days have seen protesters set buildings alight, hurl molotov cocktails, and shoot fireworks at officers, who have responded with rubber bullets, water cannons, and tear gas.Hundreds of people, including police officers, have reportedly been injured in the violence."We will continue our movement until Rama resigns. We are not criminals, we want social peace and better living conditions in our country," Leka Sina, a 22-year-old student, told the AFP news agency."Violence is not a solution, but the government also needs to reflect deeply to understand this revolt," Sina added.Rama has sought to pin the blame for the unrest on foreign influence.The European Commission released a statement condemning the violence in Albania on Sunday, saying it had "no place in a democratic society" and that the response "must remain within the law and proportionate.""Freedom of assembly and expression are fundamental rights and core European values, to be respected and exercised peacefully," the Commission said in its statement. "In a candidate country firmly committed to the EU accession process and making important progress on its EU path, grievances should be handled through constructive dialogue and in a peaceful manner."

title: France's traditional smoked sausage under threat – but is Brussels really to blame?
description: Political parties across Brittany are up in arms over the French government's failure to defend andouille de Guémené, a traditional sausage suspected of posing a cancer risk.
content: Anyone who has tried andouille de Guémené knows it is not easily forgotten. Served in a crêpe with sautéed onions, the traditional Breton smoked pork sausage has a devoted following. When I told my French editor I was writing about it, she immediately exclaimed: “L’andouille de Guémené? J’adore!”But her enthusiasm faded when I explained that the speciality from western France was caught in a regulatory dispute that could threaten its very existence.The problem lies in EU rules limiting levels of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), potentially carcinogenic compounds produced during smoking. Andouille de Guémené is traditionally smoked over beechwood, a process that leaves soot on its surface and increases its PAH content.The sausage's distinctive flavour depends on this centuries-old method, leaving producers caught between preserving tradition and complying with food safety rules.A sausage under threatIn the town of Guémené-sur-Scorff, Benoît Rivalan, owner of the century-old Maison de l’Andouille, fears French authorities could shut down his business over the EU's limit of 12 micrograms for certain PAHs."We are on their radar," he told Euronews, despite having introduced a special technique to reduce contamination.“We employ a protective sleeve. It’s like a compression stocking: we put one over each andouille during the smoking process, and it captures 80% of the PAHs while preserving the flavor.”But Rivalan warns that being forced to adopt further measures could undermine the traditional production method, which relies on smoking over a wood fire.The story of Brussels bureaucrats threatening a beloved Breton speciality has gained traction in recent weeks among France's EU-sceptic far right.But is Brussels really to blame? The reality is more complicated.EU rules allow member states to request exemptions, something the French authorities have never done.Paul Leguernic, a right-wing local councillor and knight of the Brotherhood of Guémené Andouille Tasters, is furious.The gastronomic association, founded in 1994, campaigns to protect the traditional sausage from industrial imitations.“Successive French governments have refused to apply for an exemption for French smoked products,” Leguernic told Euronews, adding that it was easy to blame Brussels when the real issue lies in how Paris has implemented the EU regulation.For years, producers tested their sausages without the skin to demonstrate compliance with EU limits. But the French Agriculture Ministry subsequently required them to test the entire sausage, arguing that consumers also eat the skin.The results were dramatic."We went from levels ranging between 6 and 8 micrograms to levels of between 120 and 150 micrograms of PAHs," Rivalan said.Pressure mounts on ParisLeguernic accused the French authorities of interpreting the European rules too strictly."The French authorities adopted an overly zealous interpretation of the European regulation, as the soot generated during the smoking process settles on the skin rather than penetrating the product itself."He also criticised their refusal to accept a label advising consumers to limit their consumption of the skin.Loïg Chesnais-Girard, the left-wing president of Brittany’s regional council, wrote to the French government on 28 September, urging it to submit a request for an exemption to Brussels. Last week, all the region’s political parties, except the Greens, adopted a resolution backing the calls made to Paris."Consumer food safety must remain an absolute priority, but regulations must also be able to take into account the specific characteristics of traditional production methods and the very limited health risks associated with consuming such a product," the resolution reads. Several EU countries have already secured exemptions for traditional smoked meats, including Ireland, Croatia, Cyprus, Spain, Poland and Portugal. Finland and Sweden have also obtained derogations for products smoked over smouldering wood or other plant materials.“It’s crystal clear: France has failed to do its job when it comes to smoked andouille,” Socialist senator Simon Uzenat told Euronews. “It has failed to make the voices of these regions heard.”A European Commission spokesperson confirmed to Euronews that Paris had not yet requested such a derogation, unlike 10 other EU countries. “France can still request one.”The derogations apply to smoked meats whose production methods cannot be modified without significantly altering the flavour of the products. “If maximum levels were applied, such traditionally smoked products would disappear from the market resulting in the closure of many small and medium size enterprises,” the EU regulation reads.Rivalan has cut production by 30%, reducing his workforce in anticipation of a possible closure."If the authorities order us to shut down, we’d rather have to lay off 14 people than the 19 we used to employ."For now, the future of andouille de Guémené remains uncertain. Whether the traditional sausage survives in its current form may depend less on Brussels than on the willingness of the French government to seek an exemption already available under EU law.

title: US allegedly holding up delivery of Patriot air defence missiles, Zelenskyy says
description: Relations between Kyiv and Washington have soured over military aid and intelligence sharing, with Zelenskyy saying that Ukraine received no warning of Russian missile strikes that targeted energy facilities in the capital region.
content: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused the United States of deliberately delaying the delivery of interceptor missiles to his war-torn country ahead of reported talks with a top US envoy on Tuesday.Relations between Kyiv and Washington have soured over military aid and intelligence sharing, with Zelenskyy saying on Monday that Ukraine received no early warning of powerful Russian missile strikes that targeted energy facilities in the capital region.US-led diplomatic efforts to end Europe's deadliest conflict since World War II have stalled in recent months, as Washington has shifted focus towards the war with Iran.Zelenskyy told US senators on Monday that "the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles" already paid for by European countries and that the shipment was waiting for US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth's signature.He said several European countries were ready to transfer Patriot interceptor missiles from their own stockpiles but were still awaiting US approval."The missiles are ready and they could already be in Ukraine," Zelenskyy said. "But unfortunately, there is still no approval."The United States has denied making any changes to intelligence sharing with Ukraine.Trump has also denied ordering a reduction in speeds on the US government-owned and -controlled Starshield network after Elon Musk, whose company SpaceX developed it, said the order could only have come from the White House.Strained relationsA public rift erupted between Trump and Zelenskyy when the US leader partially lifted sanctions to strike a diesel-supply deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin.Trump also slammed Zelenskyy as a warmonger for Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries."Zelenskyy doesn't know what he's talking about," Trump said on Monday in another attack on his Ukrainian counterpart."To be honest, I think it's time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine."Trump said he was ready to meet Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping in China next month to discuss denuclearisation, adding that talks could also cover the Ukraine war, fuelling fears in Kyiv that it was being sidelined.Kremlin spokesman Dmitri Peskov confirmed earlier that "the topic of such a hypothetical has indeed been mentioned", when asked about a Wall Street Journal report on Sunday that Trump, Putin and Xi could meet.Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said that such a meeting would "only encourage Putin to continue this war".News outlet Axios reported that White House envoy Steve Witkoff was travelling to Oslo on Tuesday to meet Zelenskyy and European leaders and then to Russia to meet Putin.Russian strikesZelenskyy also spoke to Pope Leo XIV on Monday, according to the Vatican, days after the Catholic leader held a similar call with Putin.The Vatican said the pope had urged both sides to allow for the flow of aid into the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky and to let civilians leave.Russia's latest strikes again hit Ukrainian energy facilities and infrastructure across the country, knocking out power to more than 500,000 people and forcing emergency repairs to the battered grid."Once again, there was no early warning from our partners," Zelenskyy said, as he catalogued the damage, deaths and injuries.A strike near the northeastern city of Kharkiv killed six people, including three children, authorities said.US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, on a visit to Uzbekistan on Monday, denied that intelligence sharing had been withdrawn with Ukraine and backed Trump's call for Zelenskyy to focus on ending the conflict.

title: Researchers use ChatGPT-style technology to predict stroke risk from a person’s DNA
description: A new AI tool that identifies genetic risk factors for stroke could open the door to more personalised prevention and treatment.
content: Researchers have developed an AI model that analyses a person’s DNA to catch genetic risk factors for stroke — the second leading cause of death worldwide.A team at the University of Technology Sydney (UTS) has identified specific genes that show a higher predisposition to ischaemic stroke — the most common type of stroke, in which a blood clot blocks blood flow to the brain. “When someone has a stroke, particularly at a young age, they often want to know whether other family members are also at risk,” said Kairui Guo, the study’s corresponding author. “These new AI tools will provide the ability to better help families understand that risk.”Genetics account for roughly 38% of an individual's stroke risk, according to previous research.“Traditionally, in thinking about stroke risk, genetics hasn’t been a main consideration; however, this study highlights the significant impact of genetic factors,” said Guo, adding that processing that much data at an individual level to provide a personalised assessment would be impossible without AI. To improve stroke risk prediction, the team created a new AI model based on transformers — the same technology that underpins large language models such as ChatGPT — and trained it on genetic variations to identify links to ischaemic stroke. The model identified 18 genetic variants associated with ischaemic stroke. It pointed to key genes, such as EDEM2 (active in the brain cortex) and KANK2 (in whole blood), as major contributors to stroke predisposition.The team tested the model on two major medical datasets, which together included more than 40,000 people. It successfully categorised individuals into low, medium and high genetic risk groups. Over time, individuals placed in the high-risk group were 21% more likely to suffer a first-time ischaemic stroke compared with those in the low-risk group. Until now, scientists have estimated genetic risk using polygenic risk scores (PRS) — a statistical tool that estimates a person’s genetic risk of developing a disease, based on the combined effects of many genetic variations. However, this method overlooks how different genetic variations interact with one another or how their specific positions along the DNA sequence affect overall risk.Towards more personalised medicineThe new model could pave the way for future personalised and targeted treatments. “AI can be used to find associations between human genes and disease, and build personalised risk assessments, to help prevent a potentially life-changing or fatal event,” said Jie Lu, director of the Australian Artificial Intelligence Institute.Lu said the next step is a multimodal AI tool that can combine a genetic risk assessment with other types of data, including health and lifestyle surveys, scans and imaging, to better assess stroke risk. “Genetics are only one part of stroke risk. The ability to combine a genetic score with clinical and lifestyle information, including established risk factors such as blood pressure, age, atrial fibrillation, type 2 diabetes and cholesterol, could enhance monitoring and prevention,” said Lu.

title: Japan launches unprecedented mission to bring back samples from Mars' moon Phobos
description: NASA has landed nine spacecraft on Mars over the past 50 years, and China touched down in 2021, but no one has returned samples from Mars, let alone its moons.
content: Japan has launched a spacecraft on a first-of-its-kind journey to Mars, where it will try to land on the planet’s moon Phobos and bring a piece of it back to Earth.The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency, which is leading the effort, launched the spacecraft before dawn on Tuesday from the main spaceport on Tanegashima Island, with officials declaring success an hour later, when the spacecraft separated as planned from the rocket’s upper stage.Flight controllers burst into applause, shaking hands and embracing each other.Five space agencies are backing the five-year mission, which will put a robotic sample collector and a small rover on Phobos, the larger and nearer of Mars’ two tiny moons.A first for Mars and its moonsThe $578 million mission, known as MMX for Martian Moon Exploration, centres on a 5-tonne spacecraft expected to reach Mars by late next summer. It will match Phobos’ tight orbit before releasing Idefix, a French-German rover named after the white terrier in the Asterix comics.No bigger than a microwave oven, Idefix will drop onto Phobos on its own, bouncing for several minutes before stopping in the moon’s extremely low gravity.“There’s a lot of adrenaline and a lot of excitement and a lot of wow,” said NASA astrophysicist Tom Statler, who is involved in the project.NASA has landed nine spacecraft on Mars over the past 50 years, and China touched down in 2021, but no one has ever ventured onto Phobos or its companion, Deimos, and no one has returned samples from Mars, let alone its moons. If successful, dust, soil and rock from Phobos will reach Earth in 2031.Analysts believe Japan has an edge, having already completed two asteroid sample returns.Phobos is a lumpy, potato-shaped rock about 22 kilometres across. Studying it could explain how Mars’ moons, and possibly moons elsewhere, formed.What happens after Idefix the rover lands?The four-wheeled rover is designed to right itself if it lands upside down. All bets are off, though, if it sinks into soft soil or gets wedged between rocks, said the French Space Agency’s Julien Baroukh. Once the rover’s solar panels are deployed, the vehicle can no longer right itself, he added, which is why it will move at a glacial 1 millimetre per second (0.04 inches per second).Idefix will serve as a “scout for safety,” according to Baroukh, as it prowls around Phobos for 100 days. Japanese flight controllers want to avoid powdery soil and rough terrain when the mothership — a four-legged stationary lander — descends to the surface to gather samples in late 2028 or 2029.The lander will spend just two hours on Phobos, drilling and vacuuming up at least 10 grams (one-third of an ounce) of material before launching back into space. It will then study Deimos during a series of flybys, leave the Martian neighbourhood in 2030 and hurry back to Earth to deliver the samples in the Australian desert in 2031.It is a treacherous undertaking, with wreckage littering the path. The moons’ names are hardly comforting: Phobos is Greek for 'fear', and Deimos means 'dread'. They are the twin sons of Ares, the god of war, known as Mars in Roman mythology.Scientists hope to learn how Mars’ two moons formedRussia failed in all three of its Phobos attempts, as well as in many other Mars endeavours. In its only other Mars mission, Japan failed to get a spacecraft into orbit around the red planet. Even NASA has had its share of flops in the quest to answer the burning question: did life ever exist on Mars?By studying the moons, scientists hope to learn whether Phobos and Deimos formed in the aftermath of an ancient collision between Mars and a battering space rock. The moons might also be stray asteroids that were captured by Mars’ gravity.Either way, scientists expect to find traces of Mars on Phobos, making the samples an irresistible two-for-one that should help demystify how planets and moons form, and perhaps even the recipe for life. The findings will help shape future Mars missions, including crewed ones, said Lindsay Hays, NASA’s acting planetary science director.“It is a once-in-a-lifetime chance. We are part of the first sample return mission from the Martian system,” said Markus Grebenstein, the German Space Agency’s rover chief.Japan is not alone in seeking the scientific riches in the Martian system’s rocks and dirt. China plans to launch its own Mars sample return mission in 2028. NASA, meanwhile, is still debating how to retrieve the more than 30 sample tubes collected by its Perseverance rover, the new champion of off-Earth driving.Japan and China could end up neck and neck in returning samples from the Martian system, as both are targeting 2031.Japan is investing $350 million (€308 million) in this mission. NASA is contributing $87 million (€77 million), the French Space Agency about $68 million (€60 million), the German Space Agency about $56 million (€49 million) and the European Space Agency some $17 million (€15 million).

title: Egyptian cucumber farmer helps archaeologists find giant Ramses II statue fragments
description: A farmer’s discovery has led to the remains of two colossal royal statues and ancient inscriptions in Egypt’s Nile Delta. Archaeologists have identified one as Ramses II and are investigating how the finds fit into the area’s history.
content: An Egyptian farmer growing cucumbers on his land has helped archaeologists find the remains of two colossal royal statues, including a head of Ramses II measuring 1.6 metres tall.Khaled Khalil came across a stone bearing ancient carvings on land in front of his home in Behbeit el-Hagar, a village in the Nile Delta’s Gharbia governorate, and alerted antiquities officials.Officials examined the stone before an Egyptian team from the Supreme Council of Antiquities began a rescue excavation, according to the Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities.Egyptian news outlet Youm7 reported that Khalil had been growing his crop in a greenhouse on the plot and had not expected to find such a large ancient statue.“See? Cucumbers bring antiquities,” Gharbia governor Alaa Abdel Moaty joked during a visit to the farmer’s home last week, according to the newspaper.What archaeologists foundThe newly discovered head depicts Ramses II wearing the double crown of Upper and Lower Egypt. Archaeologists also found part of the statue’s back pillar bearing his Horus name, one of the pharaoh’s formal royal names.Hisham el-Leithy, secretary-general of the Supreme Council of Antiquities, said the head’s proportions suggested the complete statue could originally have stood about 8.5 metres tall, including its base.The surviving section of the second statue measures about 2.4 metres. Its legs and base are missing, but the face remains well preserved. It wears the royal nemes headdress, part of which is also missing.Archaeologists think it may depict Ramses II because its facial features resemble those of the first head, although that identification has yet to be confirmed.A separate pink granite block, about 1.3 metres long, carries hieroglyphic inscriptions including the titles “King of Upper and Lower Egypt” and “Son of Ra”.Ramses II ruled Egypt for more than six decades, from around 1279 to 1213 BC, during the 19th Dynasty. Colossal statues of the pharaoh still stand at Abu Simbel, one of the best-known monuments of his reign.Behbeit el-Hagar is known for the ruins of a large temple dedicated to the goddess Isis. Excavations and studies are continuing to establish how the newly found pieces relate to one another and to the surrounding site.Tourism and Antiquities Minister Sherif Fathy visited Khalil to thank him for reporting the find. The farmer and his wife were awarded a trip to perform Umrah, the Muslim pilgrimage to Mecca that can be undertaken throughout the year.During the visit, Khalil also asked the governor to help cover the remaining cost of an ambulance for the village. Residents had already raised part of the money, he said, according to local media.

title: These are Europe’s cosiest cities to travel to this autumn, according to a new ranking
description: From Bruges’ fairytale streets to Lisbon’s sun-soaked cafés, these European cities are perfect for a cosy autumn escape.
content: As temperatures drop and autumn settles in, it’s the ideal time to explore European cities which seem made for cosy escapes. Think winding cobbled streets, historic cafés and canals lined with colourful leaves. Now, a new study of Reddit discussions has revealed the continent’s cosiest destinations for autumn 2026, with Bruges taking the top spot. Amsterdam and Prague follow closely, but the ranking also features some surprising destinations you might not expect – like sunny Lisbon and Athens.The study, by UK-based holiday home letting agency Big House Experience, looked at cities within continental Europe (and outside of the UK), and analysed Reddit discussions before ranking the destinations according to the number of upvotes they received. These are the cities to visit to feel the snuggest as it gets chillier and the “-ber” months continue. Which European cities are the cosiest?Picture a cosy city, and Bruges will probably come straight to mind, with its cobblestone streets, fairytale-esque medieval architecture and picturesque canals. It’s little surprise, then, that the Belgian city topped this ranking, with more than 15,000 upvotes across relevant Reddit content.World-famous for its historic buildings and, of course, chocolate shops and quaint cafés, Bruges is the ideal spot for a truly cosy trip. Be sure to wander through the winding streets, which have a real old-world feel, or duck inside a comfy eaterie for a Belgian hot chocolate. Following closely behind Bruges is Amsterdam, which got 14,477 upvotes. Over the border from Belgium, the Dutch capital boasts historic canal houses, independent coffee shops and tree-lined waterways, which turn beautiful shades of red and orange come autumn. While Amsterdam is a great city to visit year-round, it’s especially cosy in the chillier months, when hearty dishes are on the menu. Don’t miss the chance to try poffertjes, either. These fluffy, miniature puffy pancakes are served hot with a melting pat of butter and a dusting of powdered sugar and make the perfect autumn treat. Next up in the ranking are Prague and Kraków, with Reddit upvote scores of 11,098 and 10,117, respectively. Both of these Central European cities are well known for their historic architecture and atmospheric – and, yes, cosy – old towns, which are home to countless spots for visitors to warm up and wind down after a busy day’s exploring. In fifth place on the list is a city which may come as a surprise to some: Athens. The Greek capital is usually thought of as a sunny destination and isn’t on many people’s “cosy city break” list, but it did get 9,243 upvotes on Reddit. Athens proves that cosy doesn’t have to mean cold, with sun-drenched streets, traditional tavernas, tucked-away cafés and lively neighbourhoods offering a welcoming atmosphere throughout the autumn.It’s followed in the ranking by another famously sunny city: Lisbon, which got 3,243 upvotes. Lisbon’s tiled streets, historic trams and pastel-coloured buildings give it plenty of charm, while neighbourhood cafés, cosy wine bars and mild autumn temperatures make it ideal for a seasonal escape.If you’re not a fan of the cold, but love feeling snug, both Lisbon and Athens offer a milder autumn escape, with cosy cafés and atmospheric streets to enjoy without the chill that sets in across much of Europe.In seventh place, it’s back to chillier climes with Copenhagen. The Danish capital got 2,850 upvotes thanks, in part, to the fact it embraces the country’s concept of hygge, which centres around creating a warm, comfortable and inviting atmosphere, which is easy to find all around the city. Salzburg and Utrecht complete the ranking, with 2,397 and 1,040 upvotes respectively. Austrian city Salzburg pairs mountain views and properly crisp weather with traditional coffee houses, while Utrecht in the Netherlands offers a quieter city break – and a great alternative to Amsterdam – with leafy canals, historic streets and independent cafés.The cosiest cities in continental EuropeBruges, Belgium Amsterdam, The NetherlandsPrague, CzechiaKraków, PolandAthens, GreeceLisbon, PortugalCopenhagen, DenmarkSalzburg, AustriaUtrecht, The Netherlands

title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang warns Germany is falling behind in AI race
description: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Huang are set to unveil a joint AI pact intended to speed up the integration of AI products across German industry.
content: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang warned that Germany is falling behind in the artificial intelligence race as he spoke to members of the media in London last week.Despite its strong potential and wealth of talent, Huang believes progress in Europe is being blocked by too much hesitation and analysis and has called on policymakers to be quicker to put AI into practice.In response to concerns about the country's technological competitiveness, the German government has been planning closer cooperation with the US company.At the Invest in Germany investment summit in Berlin this week, Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Huang are set to unveil a joint AI pact intended to speed up the integration of AI products across German industry.The German government is preparing to commit hundreds of millions of Euros to the initiative.Alongside start-up Black Forest Labs, around 10 established German companies including Siemens and Audi are expected to take part.The partnership builds on the Sovereign Open Source Foundation Models initiative, an alliance dedicated to developing powerful open-source AI systems.The funding is to be used primarily to buy computing capacity in Deutsche Telekom's Industrial AI Cloud, which is equipped with Nvidia's latest Blackwell hardware.The government hopes the investment will make Germany a more attractive destination for innovation and technological development.On Tuesday, senior international executives, investors and government officials at the Invest in Germany summit will discuss new investment in Germany, focusing on artificial intelligence, energy and infrastructure, as well as the competitiveness of the German economy.

title: 'We are here to help them,' says major trade union on joining students for nationwide protests
description: Two separate major protests – one led by trade unions, the other by students – were initially slated to take place in Paris on Saturday. Eyewitnesses say the protests have converged into one massive demonstration demanding government remedies to the ongoing crises.
content: Members of the yellow vest movement and trade unions staged major protests across France on Saturday over rising fuel pricing and a spiralling cost-of-living crisis, which was also joined by a separate student-led protest demanding an increase in funding for schools.Speaking to Euronews, Karl Ghazi, a representative of the Paris branch of the General Confederation of Labour (CGT), one of France's largest trade unions, revealed that the protest was arranged in part to support the student-led mass protests which have rocked the country in recent weeks, demanding the government revamp the education system, increase in school funding and access to resources as well as modernise classrooms and institutions.“We are here to help them, because we have more experience,” said the representative. “We can keep things calm if there are issues with police or such.”Originally, two major protests were set to run parallel in the French capital, Paris, each with their own set of asks, though the demands share a lot of overlap.A protest, organised by the yellow vests, was meant to start from the Place de la Republique, with Place de Clichy pegged as the end destination.The student-led protest, which shares the start point, was meant to march towards Nation with another group marching towards Place de la Concorde.When protests started however, around 2 pm local time, the protests seemed to converge into one large mass demonstration at Place de la Republique, prompting security personnel to deploy in large numbers. French media outlets say thousands of people swarmed the popular Parisian square.“We all have common demands, whether it’s students, high schoolers, the 'Yellow Vests,' or the trade unions — we are fighting for better public services, more resources, a better quality of life, better wages, and so on,” said Ghazi, speaking to Euronews’ correspondent in Paris.“There is less and less money in the public coffers. I don’t know exactly what they should be doing at the Élysée, or which laws they ought to be pushing, but I do know that when I go to the hospital, the resources just aren’t there anymore,” said Damien, a 22-year-old construction worker who travelled from Troyes to participate in the protests in Paris, and member of the yellow vests movement.“We need to redistribute wealth, so that we can ensure everyone can make it to the end of the month without struggling. We need to ensure our children have access to a decent education. We need to hear the demands of 80% of the population, rather than dismissing them as isolated movements,” said Jessica – another yellow vest protester – to Euronews.“Instead of continuing to say that these are isolated incidents, I believe that they are actually taking this path because they have seen us become exhausted by previous movements,” she added.The protests, according to eyewitnesses were largely peaceful. In many places – seen by our correspondents – protesters could be seen chanting peacefully and playing musical instruments. But, they quickly turned violent as masked protesters scuffled with riot control units.Heavy clashes were reported at Place de la Republique between demonstrators and police forces. Dozens of people were arrested and protesters reported tear gas and water cannons being deployed to disperse the masses.French presidential hopeful, far-right candidate Marine Le Pen, quickly labelled the rioters as elements of the far-left, who she accused of “poisoning” the spirit of the protests.“Loot, ransack, destroy, attack law enforcement: the rioters have once again poisoned the October 17 demonstrations in defence of purchasing power,” wrote Le Pen in a post on X.“Legitimate social demands have once again been held hostage by the far left and the speeches of Jean-Luc Mélenchon's deputies, who, by legitimizing violence, viewing order as oppression and disorder as a right, seek to plunge the country into chaos.”“We will free them from Macronist toxic policies and protect them from the violence of the far left,” she added.Beyond Paris, protests took part in several other major cities, including the country’s second largest, Marseille and Lyon.Local officials in Marseille say several people were arrested after protesters managed to breach the city’s town hall after ramming the doors with security barriers.The town hall in the city of Grenoble also faced similar incidents where protesters were able to briefly break-in. Local officials there reported some damage in the building after police forces were able to contain the situation.In Lyon, protesters set fire to a tourism office. The attack occurred in a central square where groups of hooded youths were throwing projectiles and fireworks mortars at the police, who responded with tear gas, dispersal grenades and a water cannon.The protests follow four weeks of student demonstrations over a range of issues, including teacher absences, overcrowded classrooms, and outdated facilities.The rising cost of fuel, caused by the US-Israeli war on Iran and the subsequent closure of the strategic Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world’s oil typically flows, have spiralled an already bad cost-of-living crisis, causing widespread discontent across the country.Protesters accuse the government of not doing enough to intervene in the ongoing crises and of mismanaging public funds. They have vowed to continue protesting until their demands are met.

title: Rubio puts Trans-Caspian trade and critical minerals at centre of Central Asia talks
description: The US and five Central Asian governments backed closer transport and industrial cooperation at a C5+1 meeting in Samarkand. Rubio also held bilateral talks, while Uzbekistan signed the Artemis Accords.
content: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the foreign ministers of five Central Asian countries agreed to deepen cooperation on transport, critical minerals and security at a C5+1 meeting in Samarkand on Monday.The talks brought together the United States, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan. In a joint statement, they backed investment in the Trans-Caspian trade route, closer industrial cooperation and simpler customs procedures.A trade route to EuropeThe Trans-Caspian route, also known as the Middle Corridor, connects Central Asia with European markets through the Caspian Sea, the South Caucasus and Turkey, bypassing Russia."We're going to enhance the infrastructure of the Trans Caspian trade route and give our partners more ways to reach American and Central Asian markets," Rubio said.Washington also wants to diversify supplies of critical minerals used in energy technologies and advanced manufacturing. The six governments identified mineral processing, energy cooperation and cybersecurity among their priorities, but the joint statement gave no figures for new infrastructure funding.Uzbek Foreign Minister Bakhtiyor Saidov proposed cooperation extending from mineral exploration to processing and local industrial clusters. He also called for closer links between the C5+1 diplomatic forum and the B5+1 business platform to involve companies in identifying projects.The US push comes as the five Central Asian states maintain extensive economic ties with Russia and China. Speaking separately to Euronews in Samarkand, Rubio said Washington was seeking competition, not exclusivity."This is not about coming here to say, stop talking to somebody else or stop working with some other country," he told Euronews.Bilateral talks with the five ministersRubio also held separate meetings with each of his Central Asian counterparts.Kazakhstan's Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tileuberdi discussed trade, energy, critical minerals and technology with Rubio. Kazakhstan's Foreign Ministry said the US Secretary of State expressed interest in visiting the country after the G20 summit in Miami in December, although no date was announced.The US State Department said they also discussed Kazakhstan's commitment to join the Abraham Accords, a US-backed framework for normalising relations with Israel.Rubio also met Kyrgyzstan's Foreign Minister Jeenbek Kulubaev to discuss bilateral cooperation. Tajik Foreign Minister Sirojiddin Muhriddin raised trade, investment and regional security, according to his ministry.Rubio held talks with Turkmenistan's Rashid Meredov, with the two countries preparing another round of political consultations in Ashgabat in November.Uzbekistan and the US held the first session of their Enhanced Strategic Partnership Dialogue, covering trade, energy, technology and security. Following the talks, Foreign Minister Saidov signed the Artemis Accords in Rubio's presence, making Uzbekistan the 77th country to join the international framework for peaceful space exploration.

title: Dutch PM Rob Jetten and partner expecting child via surrogate mother: 'Someone very special is on the way'
description: "Being a surrogate mother feels like a very special way to help make our dear friends’ dream come true," Lisa, the surrogate mother, was quoted as saying.
content: Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten and his partner, Argentine field hockey player Nicolás Keenan, are expecting their first child, the couple announced on Monday."Someone very special is on the way. See you in 2027, little one," they wrote in a post on Instagram."There are no words big enough to thank our eggdonor, our surrogate mum Lisa and both their families. None of this would be possible without you," they added.Jetten's party, D66, has also released a statement, saying the pregnancy was made possible thanks to a couple they are friends with who already have children of their own."The surrogate mother is Dutch, as is the egg donor," the statement continued. "This is not a case of commercial surrogacy. The surrogate mother and the egg donor are acquaintances of Jetten and Keenan. They are delighted to be able to help fulfil the two fathers-to-be’s dream of having a child in this way."Jetten and Keenan announced their engagement in November 2024."Being a surrogate mother feels like a very special way to help make our dear friends’ dream come true," Lisa, the surrogate mother, was also quoted as saying.Jetten was born in Veghel in the southern Netherlands in 1987 and grew up in nearby Uden. He went on to study at the Nijmegen School of Management before beginning his career at ProRail, which is responsible for maintaining railway infrastructure in the Netherlands.He became a Member of the House of Representatives for D66 in 2017 and later worked as the minister for climate and energy policy under former Dutch PM Mark Rutte, who is now NATO secretary general.

title: Norway to extend proposed under-16 social media ban to online games and messaging apps
description: Online games and messaging services were initially expected to receive broad exemptions, but the government has now decided to assess platforms based on their potential risks to children.
content: Norway is set to introduce a social media ban for children under 16, with the government announcing on Monday that it is finalising legislation to be submitted to parliament by the end of the year.The proposed restrictions will also cover potentially harmful online games and messaging services, beyond conventional social media platforms, the government said in a statement.TikTok, Snapchat and Roblox, a popular online gaming platform where users can create and play games while interacting with others, would likely fall under the proposed law."Children's safety must come first," said Lene Vågslid, Norway's minister for children and families, adding that the legislation was nearly complete.The restrictions aim to protect children from harmful content, addictive features, illegal advertising and unwanted contact from strangers.Online games and messaging services were initially expected to receive broad exemptions, but the government has now decided to assess platforms based on their potential risks to children.This means services considered harmless, such as messaging apps used for school communication, could remain accessible.Vågslid said the government was also safeguarding children's "right to participate," although Monday's announcement did not explain how this would be ensured under the proposed restrictions.Technology companies would be responsible for verifying users' ages, with systems required to comply with European data protection rules.Norway's centre-left Labour government published a draft bill in 2025 proposing a minimum social media age of 15 before revising the threshold to 16 in April this year. The legislation has since undergone public consultation in Norway and the European Economic Area (EEA).Social media restrictions in EuropeNorway joins a growing number of European countries moving to restrict children's access to social media amid concerns about online safety and addiction.Denmark has adopted similar restrictions, while Spain is pursuing a ban for pupils under 16.In September, France attempted to ban social media for children under 15, but its Constitutional Council struck it down over freedom of expression concerns.At the European Union level, the European Commission proposed the EU Kids Act in September, which would also introduce age-based restrictions on social media, online games and other digital services.

title: France launches ‘massive’ law enforcement operation after weekend looting, PM says
description: Lecornu said nearly 200 investigators would analyse footage from the weekend to identify suspects in the Paris region alone after businesses were destroyed and looted after protests turned violent on Saturday.
content: French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu announced on Monday a “massive” law enforcement operation following widespread rioting and looting across the country over the weekend.Major cost-of-living protests turned violent on Saturday, with demonstrators clashing with police in several cities. Buildings and vehicles were set alight, while masked individuals smashed shop windows and looted stores.Unrest continued in Paris on Sunday, as masked youths erected barricades and police charged crowds and fired tear gas, a Euronews journalist on the ground reported.“We have decided on several things,” Lecornu told reporters on Monday. “The first, of course, is a particularly significant and large-scale criminal justice response.”“The second wave of legal action is the one that will be carried out in a more deliberate, methodical manner,” he added, noting that footage circulating on social media showed many alleged looters had not covered their faces.“And so, we now have a very significant, massive law enforcement operation getting underway today,” he said.Lecornu added that nearly 200 investigators from the Paris Police Prefecture would analyse images and footage from the weekend to identify suspects in the Paris region alone.The Paris police prefect said on Monday that a task force would be set up to review all available footage from CCTV systems, shop security cameras and social media.Hundreds of police officers, gendarmes and firefighters were injured during the weekend’s violence in France, authorities said, with around 2,400 people arrested.Lecornu said he had also asked regional authorities to impose “localised and partial curfews” on Monday evening to prevent further rioting and looting.The announcement came after French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said police had “lost control” in some cities during the unrest.President Emmanuel Macron warned that those responsible for the destruction “must pay” for their actions.“Those who looted must pay back; those who sought to bring down the Republic will be held to account,” he said in a televised address to the nation on Sunday evening.

title: Mental health at work starts by breaking the taboo, EU agency says
description: Nearly half of European workers face mental health risks on the job, yet the subject remains taboo.
content: Health and safety is the backbone of working life. However, as workplaces and working practices evolve, new challenges emerge while old ones remain unsolved. Against a backdrop of staff shortages and ageing populations, Europe’s workforce is battling poor mental health; however, the issue is still not being recognised at workplaces, William Cockburn, EU-OSHA executive director, told Euronews. “Whether we're asking employers or workers, they identify a reluctance to speak openly about mental health issues as the … main obstacle to actually taking action,” he said.Many EU employees say their jobs are hurting their mental health. Nearly half of workers (45%) face risks to their mental health on the job, according to the European Agency for Safety and Health at Work (EU-OSHA). “We see psychosocial risks at the workplace, for example, long working hours, highly intense work, emotionally demanding tasks … and we link that to increased impact on workers’ health,” Cockburn said. Around 44% of workers report severe time pressure or overload. According to the European Trade Union Institute (ETUI), work-related depression costs the EU more than €100 billion a year, when absenteeism, reduced productivity, and healthcare and wider social costs are combined. Despite the burden these conditions place on employers, Cockburn said a reluctance to talk and persistent stigma among workers are slowing action. So, what can be done about it?For Cockburn, mental health issues “need to be addressed like physical health issues at work”.The approach, he noted, is to assess the risks first and then adapt whatever is needed to minimise harm.“We identify hazards like long working hours, like adverse relationships at work … to an extreme you can go to bullying and harassment, violence or threats of violence,” he added. Workers should be part of the conversationWhile many see mental health as a personal issue, Esther Lynch, general secretary of the European Trade Union Confederation (ETUC), argues that prevention should focus on the workplace rather than on the individual affected. “We don't wait until people have a finger chopped off before we put guardrails in place,” Lynch said. “We do a risk assessment and say what's the risk associated with the way this work is carried out and then we put the guardrails in place”. To achieve this, experts agree, workers must be part of the conversation. Yet only 45% say they are consulted about the stressful aspects of their jobs, according to EU-OSHA. “Worker participation is a legal obligation under European law, but it's also a key success factor for successful interventions in health and safety at work,” said Cockburn. This week, the EU-OSHA launched the Healthy Workplaces campaign, an initiative to help employers prevent, assess and manage psychosocial risks at work. One of its aims is to overcome this reluctance to speak about mental health struggles. “When we invest in building and keeping healthy working environments, we improve not only people's well-being, we reduce sick leave and staff turnover; we improve performance, and we don't put pressure on our health systems,” said Roxana Mînzatu, executive vice-president for social rights and jobs, at the campaign’s launch on Tuesday. “It’s a win-win for everyone.” This story has been updated to clarify that the Healthy Workplaces campaign was launched by the European Agency for Safety and Health at Work.

title: Ebola: Kenya confirms eighth case as DRC outbreak reaches new province
description: Kenya has confirmed an eighth Ebola case, while the outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo continues to spread to new areas.
content: Kenyan authorities have detected an eighth case of Ebola in the country after another person tested positive while in quarantine, a health ministry official said on Sunday. The latest case is a 49-year-old man who had attended to the first Ebola patient. He showed symptoms including fever, high temperature, headaches and muscle pain and had been quarantined after probable exposure to the virus. "Today we tested 38 persons; one turned positive," said Health Ministry chief Patrick Amoth, adding that the man had been in quarantine since 9 October.Kenya reported its first-ever Ebola death on 5 October when a man who had been living in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) died after returning to Kenya. The other seven cases are relatives of the first patient or health workers who treated him; Amoth said they were in a stable condition.The ministry said 128 contacts of the first patient remain in quarantine. The country remains open, with no restrictions on travel, trade or public gatherings, as advised by the World Health Organization (WHO). However, the country is stepping up work on Ebola surveillance and community awareness. The neighbouring Tanzania has tightened border screening and introduced mandatory health declarations and 21-day monitoring for travellers arriving from high-risk countries.The outbreak reaches eighth province in CongoMeanwhile, the outbreak continues to grow in the DRC and has reached an eighth province. Two new cases, including one death, have been reported over the last weekend in previously unaffected Nord-Ubangi, which borders the Central African Republic. Nord-Ubangi lies between Sud-Ubangi and Bas-Uele, the last two provinces the disease had reached, where recurring armed violence has forced thousands to flee and seek refuge in nearby Congolese communities. Authorities have reported 9,455 cases and 4,561 deaths so far in what has become the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history. “We see pockets of Ebola generally going down, but unfortunately geographically it’s spreading out,” WHO Regional Director for Africa Mohamed Yakub Janabi told The Associated Press. Janabi said one of the biggest challenges has been persuading infected people to seek medical care, adding that some deaths occur in communities outside health centres.The outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, for which no licensed vaccines or specific treatments are available, although trials are under way in the DRC.

title: From 'Werwulf' to a 1930s Batman: Key takeways from Robert Eggers masterclass at Lumière
description: A world exclusive for 'Werwulf', talk of Lily-Rose Depp's eyes, and the enduring horror of Ridley Scott's 'Alien'... Director Robert Eggers treats audiences at Lyon's Lumière Film Festival.
content: A guest of honour at this year’s Lumière Film Festival was American director Robert Eggers, the mastermind behind gothic folklore horror gems like The VVitch, The Lighthouse and Nosferatu.Prior to the upcoming release of his new film, Werwulf, a werewolf horror film set in 14th-century England starring Nosferatu alum Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Lily-Rose Depp and Willem Dafoe, the director sat down with the Lyon audience to discuss the dark and instantly recognisable worlds he has created on screen.Sadly, there was no time for any questions on the director’s upcoming project - an adaptation of Shakespeare's "Romeo And Juliet" – and very little space given to the audience so they could ask questions. This is a recurring issue at the Lumière Festival and a shame, since the only two questions afforded to the attendees of Eggers’ masterclass were excellent.Still, the Lumière audience was treated to nothing short of a world exclusive: the first screening of the beginning of Werwulf, which was prefaced by Eggers saying that the grading process is complex and that he was still working out some of the kinks in the lab.Warning: Mild spoilers for the opening scenes of Werwulf.The film starts with a howl in the dark, followed by the first (and not last, as Eggers confirmed) transformation. There’s vomit, there’s screaming, there’s writhing, there’s bone crunching. Safe to say that this is Eggers – as is his custom - taking mythical authenticity seriously and delivering something that goes beyond the sudden eruption of face fur... It’s significantly more visceral than any other body horror transformation we’ve seen in previous werewolf movies. The audience barely got to glimpse the creature’s final form, but did witness the consequences. In this case, a lot of dead livestock. This was followed by a bloodied figure (Taylor-Johnson), back in human form, who knocks on a door and is greeted by a disfigured woman (Depp) in a... shall we say unique way, which suggests that Eggers will be tackling the knotty interspace where violence, animality and sexuality co-exist.Take it from us: we’re in for a treat once Eggers' latest horror film is released and if you liked Nosferatu, chances are you'll get a kick out of this. Werwulf comes out next year, on 1 January in the UK and the following week in mainland Europe. Before we get more nightmares under a full moon, here are the key takeaways from Robert Eggers’ masterclass.On what he’s watching... “All my favourite directors are dead and I rewatch films often – I watch Jack Clayton’s The Innocents once a year, and there are a lot of films I often revisit. In fact, I have a hard time keeping up with what’s in cinemas sometimes, because I’m always chipping away at a list of old films which generally have to do with research for what I’m currently working on.”On the importance of silent cinema... “I love silent cinema. Everybody knows the story that when sound cinema began, there was a dip in people using images to tell stories and it became all about dialogue. Of course, there are exceptions to the rule. Fritz Lang immediately knew how to do it. I think that I’ve succeeded in Werwulf in making a film where you can turn off the sound and still understand the story. The images are telling the story. Werwulf is also in Middle English, archaic English, but for English speaking audiences who don’t have the benefit of subtitles, you don’t really need to understand anything anyone says to understand the story. I was watching 12 Angry Men last night and it’s great – it's a dialogue-driven film and it’s cinema. But I’m more interested in telling stories with images.”On the recurring image of women’s eyes in his films... “Eyes are the window to the soul... And Anya (Taylor-Joy – The VVitch) and Lily-Rose (Depp – Nosferatu) have big eyes, so that helps! It can be a frustrating discipline for the actors at times... In The Odyssey, Christopher Nolan shoots with IMAX cameras, which are so big that actors can’t see each other, and they devised a mirror system so that actors can see each other. But I always put a little piece of tape near the lense, so actors often have to look at the camera... I always like tight eyelines... Watch Elem Klimov’s Come And See, and you realise why it’s a good idea to do that!On why the past is such an inspiration compared to the modern world... “I get enough of the kitchen sink in my own kitchen! It’s always a mirror to society but if the mirror is too close, I feel like the film can be working too hard to say something. By trying to make a film that is timeless and of the time... It’s impossible. Of course, I don’t live in a vacuum, and if I was making a period movie for purely a period audience, or a Viking movie for a Viking audience, that would be a problem! But in endeavouring to go into not only the verisimilitude of the physical world of the period but also the interior world of the period, I think we may be able to more easily see who are today and where we’re going.”On the use of specific languages... “Language is always very specific in all of my films and I like the way language informs how you think. Language isn’t perfect and it can’t really express everything.
