When you learn other languages, you learn different ways to think. ‘Oh, in Germany, they have a word for that concept I struggle to describe...’.”On the common setting of night in his films... “I hate night shoots! The older I get, the more it’s difficult! But if you’re making a vampire movie or a werewolf movie, you don’t have a choice. You know, I don’t like the end of Nosferatu, because it doesn’t really work. The monster, the actual vampire, has power in the darkness. But also, when you don’t see the monster, the monster has power. Like in Ridley Scott’s Alien. When you shine a bright light on the monster, it’s killing the illusion – because then you’re seeing Bill Skarsgård in makeup.” On what a Batman film directed by Robert Eggers would look like... “There’s an internet rumour that I was doing a black-and-white, 1930s Batman as a detective movie... There are only so many movies you can make in a lifetime, so I wouldn’t make a comic book movie. But if I could make an infinite amount, that sounds like it could be fun! A 1930s Rolls Royce Batmobile, anyone?”On creating a new monster from scratch, one which isn’t inspired by past myth or folklore...“I’m not very creative! I read something that I haven’t seen and I do that! There is a part of me that feels this connection with the past and the urge to preserve it. For example, witches becoming hares is something common in British and Celtic folklore, but in America that idea was totally lost.”On defining what a monster is... “It’s always a reflection of us. (...) What is the trauma that doesn’t die? (...) There are many modern horror directors that I admire, but the touchstone for a creature is still for me Alien, 1979. The (H.R.) Giger design – it’s a phallus with a vagina... It’s us. And also, it has no eyes, and this gives it power. This is often the problem with werewolf movies – it's that the eyes of the werewolf aren’t right and you understand that it’s someone in a suit. With Alien, the creature is cold, which gives it more threat.”Werwulf is out on 25 December in the US and Canada, and early January 2027 in European cinemas.

title: US issues rare Middle East red alert warning to its citizens in the region
description: Washington has taken the rare measure to issue a red alert to US citizens in 12 countries across the Middle East, citing risks of potential attacks on US interests.
content: US embassies across the entire Middle East issued identical security alerts on Monday, warning their citizens in Israel, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Lebanon, Jordan, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, the UAE, Yemen and Iran to exercise heightened vigilance.The alerts warn all US citizens of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures and travel disruptions due to the risk of military escalation linked to Yemen’s Houthis and Iran.The warning covering 12 countries states that “the hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly beyond that immediate area” and to “develop contingency plans in advance.”“Iran and groups supportive of Iran may target other US interests overseas or at locations associated with the United States and Americans throughout the world, including US businesses and other institutions,” the alert said.In Saudi Arabia, the embassy warned of a “complex security environment,” as “Iranian-supported Houthis have engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions.”The alert also states that “Iran and groups supportive of Iran may target other U.S. interests overseas or at locations associated with the United States and Americans throughout the world, including US businesses and other institutions.”In Qatar, the US embassy urged its citizens on Sunday to monitor official alerts and local media, avoid demonstrations and large gatherings, and follow instructions from local authorities.⁠Qatar Airways announced on Monday that it will suspend its Saudi-bound flights to and from Riyadh and Dammam until 24 October and reduce flights to Jeddah from seven to four per day.

title: Did an ancient Egyptian god inspire the Oscar statuette? A 2,700-year-old bronze offers a clue
description: A 2,700-year-old Egyptian statuette of the god Ptah, which recently sold at Frieze Masters in London, may hold a clue to the origin story of the Oscar statuette.
content: Could the iconic design of one of Hollywood’s most coveted awards owe a debt to an ancient Egyptian god?A 2,700-year-old bronze figure of Ptah, the Egyptian creator god and master architect, has drawn attention at Frieze Masters in London, where an antiquities dealer has uncovered a possible link between the sculpture and the design of the Oscar statuette.The figure was once owned by newspaper magnate William Randolph Hearst, a friend of Cedric Gibbons, the art director who designed the Oscar statuette in 1928.Antiquities dealer Rupert Wace says he discovered the connection while researching the object's provenance ahead of the fair. "We found out that this particular piece was with (Randolph) Hearst and the chap who designed the Oscar called Cedric Gibbons was a frequent visitor and friend of Hearst's, and would have visited him both in Saint Simeon in California and his place in New York where he had a specific Egyptian collection room."Cedric Gibbons, who died in 1960, never confirmed directly what inspired his famous design - but the similarities are striking to see, and he was in the right place at the right time"The whole thing is supposition in a sense. We put two and two together and either made four or five. We can't prove it. It's uncannily similar and was in the right place with the right people at the right time for it to be more than just a coincidence," explains Wace.And even if its Hollywood connection remains a mystery, the statuette still remains a significant and fascinating piece of ancient Egyptian art. It dates back to the late period of ancient Egypt, shortly before it was conquered by the Achaemenid Persian Empire."Without the history, this piece would still be fantastic. It's a very fine bronze. It's got a very good history, collecting history. So the extra Hollywood angle is the cherry on the cake," says Wace.The statuette was sold on the opening day of Frieze Masters for an undisclosed sum.Frieze Masters 2026 ran from 14 to 18 October in Regent's Park London, hosting an estimated 60,000 people.

title: Start Crying Your Heart Out: Why Liam Gallagher is wrong about Fontaines D.C.
description: Liam Gallagher says Fontaines D.C. “are not good enough” to open for Oasis on their upcoming ‘Live ’27’ tour... Give us a break.
content: Liam Gallagher says a lot of things, but his latest take couldn’t be more misjudged.Oasis’ Live ’27 Tour was announced last month after plenty of speculation and following the Britpop band’s highly successful Live ‘25 Tour. Due to frenzied demand, the upcoming tour – which includes dates across mainland Europe - has been expanded to 42 dates, which are now all sold out.So far, only Richard Ashcroft has been confirmed as support for their forthcoming shows, and we know of one act who won’t be joining them... The gobby Oasis frontman has said that the Irish band Fontaines D.C. are “not good enough” to open for his band on their upcoming Live ‘27 Tour, adding that they “don’t have any tunes”.With all due respect to Gallagher, the self-proclaimed “Godlike rasta icon legend biblical omnipresent prophet” (as per his X handle), his comment is a steaming pile of proverbial.First things first, Fontaines D.C. are arguably the greatest act currently recording and gigging. Bold statement, but consider the evidence...Since their 2019 debut ‘Dogrel’, Grian Chatten and his post-punk lot have been going from strength to strength at a borderline unprecedented pace. In the space of only eight years, they’ve released five albums, with each record outdoing their previous output, showing a band unwilling to rest on their laurels and pushing their sound forward.Their third album, 2022’s ‘Skinty Fia’, felt like the band peaked, wrapping a three-album run that would leave most modern groups green with envy. But then came 2024’s ‘Romance’, a record we described in our Best Albums of the Year list as “a consecration” and confirmation that they are, without a shadow of a doubt, “one of the most consistently exciting modern bands around”.This was confirmed with their recent live shows, as the band not only delivered the goods on stage but showed that they were also unafraid to stand up for what they believe in – unlike some saccharine, first-dance-at-the-twee-wedding singers. Surely they couldn’t top ‘Romance’ and were due an inevitable dip... But once again, Fontaines D.C. have exceeded all expectations with the release of their fifth LP last Friday (16 October). ‘Dopamine Chamber’ is a doomy, gloomy, and cinematic(-y) record that cements them as the best band of their generation. They’ve embraced a synthier direction, with many tracks like lead single ‘Marianne’ and album standout ‘Mimesis’ recalling Depeche Mode. Another reference point throughout is The Cure, as the riffs on ‘Happy For You’ and ‘You Miss Me’ sound reminiscent of Robert Smith’s playbook.Beyond these touchpoints, to the band’s great credit, 'Dopamine Chamber' never feels like it's leaning on the past for inspiration and always sounds like a Fontaines effort. Chatten’s show-stopping lyricism and vocals once again prove he’s a spellbinding frontman – one who invites the listener on the latest album to find power in confronting the darkness at the heart of the bleak times we live in, rather than seek refuge in blind optimism.All to say that ‘Dopamine Chamber’ is an astonishing effort, one not far from masterpiece status, and Liam Gallagher would do well to actually listen to the tunes Fontaines D.C. have in their arsenal before slagging them off. No modern band has achieved their level of quality output, and when you consider that five-for-five track record compared to Oasis’ discography, it’s hard to not reach the conclusion that Gallagher’s recent take is, frankly, terminal.No one is denying that Oasis was at the heart of the Britpop movement and contributed to defining a 90s sound for a generation. However, their output pales compared to that of Fontaines D.C.’s. Granted, ‘Definitely Maybe’ (one record deemed overrated in the good Euronews Culture parish) and ‘(What’s The Story) Morning Glory?’ are considered classics, but Oasis haven’t released a cohesive album since 1998's ‘The Masterplan’. Their last effort to date, ‘Dig Out Your Soul’ (2008), left much to be desired, and there are seemingly no concrete plans to return to the studio anytime soon. Just touring the hits.There's nothing wrong with that, and this isn’t a bid to pit one band against the other; rather, recognising that respect needs to be paid. So what gives with Gallagher’s comments? Maybe they’re due to a 2024 interview with Studio Brussel, in which Fontaines’ guitarist Carlos O’Connell said he “couldn’t give a shit” about the Oasis reunion. At the time, bassist Conor Deegan III added: “I’m not excited about it either, to be honest. I feel like we get caught in the last era – like the ’10s – and into such a nostalgic thing that we’re forgetting to make new things.”This prompted Gallagher to respond: “Fuck them little spunkbubbles I’ve seen better dressed ROADIES.” Sure thing, Liam. But beyond comments that feel they’re from an overgrown toddler throwing a hissy fit, those “spunkbubbles” are consistently proving they’re the future. They certainly don’t rely exclusively on nostalgia to sell tickets. ‘Dopamine Chamber’ only goes to show that Oasis would be lucky to have a band of Fontaines’ caliber as an opening act. As you were.'Dopamine Chamber' is out now.

title: This 19th-century Portuguese farmhouse in the Algarve is being transformed into a wellness retreat
description: Shanti-Som Algarve will offer six different programmes focusing on things like detoxing, relaxation, and burnout recovery.
content: Wellness retreats have been soaring in popularity over the past few years, with resorts making use of increasingly fancy tools to kickstart your health journey (hyperbaric chambers or cryotherapy, anyone?).But that’s certainly not the only way to do things, as proven by Shanti-Som, the wellness retreat brand that first opened its doors in Marbella in 2011.Now set to open a second resort in Portugal in February 2027, Shanti-Som Algarve will offer six structured programmes focused on different goals, with the aim that the healthy habits you learn are simple enough to keep up with long after you leave.The new 22-room retreat, which is just a 20-minute drive away from Faro Airport, is set within a restored 19th-century farmhouse surrounded by four hectares of orange and almond orchards.“We see Shanti-Som as a hybrid of a holiday, a private wellness club and a gym,” hotel manager Ophélie Acaris said. “You can switch off completely and be looked after, but you also leave with real, practical ways to feel stronger, healthier and happier. “Whether someone comes for better sleep, more strength, a reset or simply time away from everyday demands, the experience is shaped around what they need.”What to expect at Shanti-Som AlgarveGuests can choose from six programmes: relaxation, yoga, pilates, detox, strength and fitness, and burnout and nervous system recovery, with the latter two being exclusive to Shanti-Som Algarve.Strength and fitness is aimed at those who are looking to focus on longevity, bone density and muscle strength as they are getting older, and includes one-on-one training sessions, reformer Pilates, guided hikes and a full health check with a nutritional consultation.As for burnout and nervous system recovery, guests will instead spend their days doing breathwork, guided meditations, sound healing and hot-cold contrast therapy, alongside life coaching sessions.Unsurprisingly, the property has an impressive wellness area, complete with an infinity pool, sauna, hammam, ice bath and gym, plus private treatment rooms for massages or facials.Each of the retreats are full-board, and you can book in for as long, or as little time, as you need.Outside of the resort, Shanti-Som Algarve is close to beaches like Praia da Falésia and Praia da Marinha, as well as Ria Formosa lagoon.

title: Body horror and 'Becoming America': The best things to do, hear, see or watch in Europe this week
description: Chris Pratt returns for season 2 of Prime's gritty Reacher follow-up, 'The Terminal List', while Tom Rhys Harries brings body horror to the DC Universe in 'Clayface'. Here's what to look out for this week.
content: It's a big week for DC Universe fans as Clayface hits cinemas — but an even bigger week for those needing an extra hour of sleep.The clocks fall back this Sunday, so it's officially time to pull out your chunkiest knitwear, pour something pumpkin spiced, and embrace the darker days by burrowing under the covers with an 8-part crime thriller on Prime.Of course, if you're not ready to go full hibernation mode yet, this week also sees plenty of new exhibitions opening across the continent. Notable highlights include an exploration of North America's early history at London's Science Museum, and German painter Conny Maier's imaginary paradise at Munich's Pinakothek der Moderne.As an added bonus, don't forget to check out our Lumière Film Festival content. Although the event has now ended in Lyon, our resident film critic David Mouriquand has been busy publishing highlights and interviews with acclaimed filmmakers like Todd Haynes and Tsui Hark — so even if you missed out, you can at least feel like you were there!Until next time — here's what's coming up.Exhibitions and eventsBecoming America: How Science Shaped a NationWhen: 23 October 2026 — 25 April 2027Where: Science Museum (London, United Kingdom) The Declaration of Independence was signed 250 years ago, marking the birth of a country that would go on to become one of the world's most powerful, influential — and divisive. The Science Museum marks this through a fascinating look at how science and technology shaped North America's early developments, spanning four decades of its history up to the 1790s, when George Washington was elected as the first US president. There are more than a hundred rare objects on display, including a first print of the Declaration of Independence and a map by Benjamin Franklin that charted the Atlantic Gulf Stream. Find out more here.Conny Maier: Searching for Paradise When: 21 October 2026 — 17 January 2027Where: Pinakothek der Moderne (Munich, Germany)German painter Conny Maier, who previously won the Deutsche Bank Artist of the Year award in 2021, has transformed the Pinakothek der Moderne museum into an eery and enchanting purgatory. From pastel pink florals to flaming woodland, her bold and evocative canvasses create an immersive atmosphere that carries visitors between paradise and apocalypse; drawing on medieval art, Expressionism and more to expose non-human worlds — and our collective fragility. Find out more here.Bonus highlight: The fifth edition of Art Basel Paris, a vast and vibrant annual contemporary art fair, takes place from 23 - 25 October 2026 at the Grand Palais. Movies Clayface Where: Cinemas When: 23 October The DC Universe's new 'Gods and Monsters' chapter continues with an origin story for one of Batman's most famous foes: Clayface. Tom Rhys Harries stars as Matt Hagen, an actor who undergoes experimental facial reconstruction surgery after being left disfigured by a mob boss. Written by Mike Flanagan (best known for his Stephen King adaptations), the movie leans heavily into its body horror elements as Hagen finds himself mutating into a clay-like form while his grip on reality also begins to crumble.Bonus highlight: A poorly young girl is gifted a companion robot (Jenna Ortega) in Taika Waititi's adaptation of Kazuo Ishiguro's best-selling book, Klara and the Sun. Out from 23 October in most parts of Europe.TV series The Terminal List Where: Prime Video When: 21 October For those stuck in a post-Reacher streaming slump, Prime's got another gritty action show to fill the void. Based on Jack Carr's popular series of novels, The Terminal List follows US Navy SEAL James Reece (Chris Pratt) as he sets out to avenge the deaths of his platoon — uncovering dark governmental secrets along the way. In this second series, Reece's grief, anger, and desire for redemption has grown even stronger after the murder of his family, leading him across the world on a violent mission for answers and justice.Bonus highlight: The third season of Netflix comedy Nobody Wants This, starring Kristen Bell and Adam Brody as a couple facing complicated cultural challenges, streams from 22 October. MusicJohn Legend: MuseWhen: 23 October American singer and pianist John Legend is back with a new blend of soul-soothing gospel, hip-hop and Afrobeats — this time in collaboration with Pharrell Williams. Recorded at Pharrell's studio within the Louis Vuitton HQ in Paris, 'Muse' features 16 tracks that explore faith, devotion and intimacy through experimental new sounds; the album acting like a form of reconnection and rebirth for two longterm friends.Bonus highlights: The fifth album from British singer-songwriter Michael Kiwanuka, FUDGE is a passion-fuelled swell of psychedelic soul — released on 23 October 2026.

title: How a $5 billion ‘Gas Ring’ could strengthen Central Asia’s energy security
description: A proposed $5bn (€4.45bn) gas network could help five Central Asian countries share supplies and meet winter demand. The ‘Gas Ring’ would link new and existing pipelines, but funding and agreements between governments remain to be finalised.
content: The Central Asia Gas Ring would connect Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan through more than 3,000 kilometres of new and upgraded pipelines.The proposal was discussed at the second Central Asia Oil and Gas Forum in Tashkent.Kazakh energy expert Askar Ismailov first presented the idea at the forum's inaugural edition in 2025.He estimates the core infrastructure would cost $5bn (€4.46bn), including $2bn (€1.78bn) for new construction and $3bn (€2.68bn) for modernisation and digitalisation. The proposed network could carry around 20bn cubic metres of gas annually, he says.How five countries could benefit from a shared gas networkThe proposal reflects differences in gas resources, infrastructure and demand across Central Asia. Turkmenistan, with substantial reserves, could gain additional regional customers, while other countries could obtain more supply options.Ismailov now advises the Geneva-based Global Gas Centre, a non-profit organisation bringing together gas industry executives and experts, which is actively involved in advancing the proposal.“The Gas Ring project is a very interesting one because it will enhance the security of supply of all these countries,” the centre's executive director, Valérie Ducrot, told Euronews.Uzbekistan is both a major producer and consumer of gas, with demand rising during the winter. Kazakhstan also produces gas, but much of its resource base is in the west, away from major population centres.Kyrgyzstan relies on imported gas, while Tajikistan generates most of its electricity from hydropower but also imports gas. Tajikistan imported 126.4m cubic metres from Uzbekistan in the first half of 2026, according to its energy ministry.The countries already trade gas across borders. The proposed ring would build on those connections, adding sections and upgrading existing pipelines to enable more flexible flows.“When Uzbekistan or some other Central Asian countries like Kyrgyzstan or Tajikistan demand more gas during winter time, we can do it in reverse mode,” said Assylbek Jakiyev, chairman of PetroCouncil Kazakhstan, an oil and gas industry association.He was describing the potential for reverse flows, rather than an agreed operating arrangement.From proposal to investmentIsmailov said Uzbekistan's national oil and gas company, Uzbekneftegaz, had expressed interest after preliminary talks.He also said the Global Gas Centre had signed a memorandum of understanding in May with authorities in Karakalpakstan, an autonomous republic within Uzbekistan.He reported discussions with prospective investors from China and the Middle East.Beyond funding, the project would require agreements on supply volumes, transit rules and the operation of interconnected pipelines, including which sections could carry gas in both directions.No final financing structure, agreement among all five national governments or construction timetable has been publicly announced. The projected cost and capacity remain estimates from the proposal's backers.Uzbekistan expands exploration as gas output declinesUzbekistan is seeking to strengthen domestic production alongside regional connections. Large industrial enterprises produced 24.2bn cubic metres of natural gas in January–August 2026, down 16.3% year on year, according to national statistics.At an October review, Uzbek authorities reported that five new gas-condensate fields had been discovered this year and 80 wells had been drilled between January and September, with a further 40 planned for the final quarter.“Natural gas remains a cornerstone of Uzbekistan’s energy system,” Denis Borodenok of UNG Overseas, a wholly owned Uzbekneftegaz subsidiary and co-organiser of the Tashkent forum, said.The government is also pursuing deeper exploration in the Ustyurt region and measures to improve output from existing fields.Domestic drilling and cross-border connections address different aspects of energy security: increasing production and making supplies easier to distribute.Wider energy links with Azerbaijan and EuropeThe Tashkent forum also discussed opportunities to strengthen energy links between Central Asia, Azerbaijan and European markets.Assylbek Jakiyev of PetroCouncil Kazakhstan said closer cooperation with Azerbaijan and the EU could help Central Asian producers expand hydrocarbon exports.Some partnerships are already taking shape. Azerbaijan's SOCAR, Britain's BP and Uzbekneftegaz are partners in an oil and gas exploration project in Uzbekistan's Ustyurt region.Azerbaijan also supplies natural gas to EU countries through the Southern Gas Corridor. Deliveries reached 12.5bn cubic metres in 2025, according to the European Commission. The EU and Azerbaijan reaffirmed their wider energy partnership in March 2026.

title: Looting and buildings ablaze: France's violent Saturday protests in 10 pictures
description: Addressing the protests in a post on social media on Saturday evening, French President Emmanuel Macron said there was "no place for violence" in France.
content: Cost-of-living protests descended into violence across parts of France on Saturday as demonstrators clashed with police officers and set buildings and vehicles alight.More than half a million people are thought to have joined the demonstrations, including 110,000 in the French capital, Paris. Violence also broke out in cities such as Lyon, Marseille, Bordeaux, Rennes, Strasbourg, Grenoble, Nice, Toulouse, and Limoges, where the town hall was almost completely destroyed in a fierce blaze.French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said on Sunday that more than 500 police officers, gendarmes, and firefighters were injured during the protests, with 1,800 people arrested.Euronews has put together 10 of the most dramatic images from the day.

title: Tee off in Europe’s most underrated golf holiday destinations
description: If you’re looking to book a European golfing holiday away from the traditional hotspots, then pack your clubs and head to underrated destinations like Varna on Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast, Gimsøya in Norway or Costa Navarino in Greece.
content: Golf has long been one of the biggest drivers of the sports travel sector and in Europe there are stunning options for golfing getaways right across the continent. Aside from picking which club to use, golfers face another tough choice: where to go in Europe for a golf holiday, especially when seeking somewhere under the radar and away from the traditional hotspots.According to Golfbreaks, UK Google search interest in “golf package holiday” increased 750% year on year, while interest in “quiet golf courses” rose almost 140% over three months. The Google Trends figures were current to September 2026. In response to the demand, the golf travel operator’s experts have selected seven destinations they consider "underrated", supported by internal booking data comparing 2026 with the equivalent period in 2025.Varna in Bulgaria leads the list, while Portugal features twice, alongside destinations in Spain, Norway, France and Greece."Golf is steeped in tradition, and course quality is often judged by history and reputation," said Cameron Ritchie, Head of Product - Europe at Golfbreaks. "But some of Europe's most rewarding experiences can be found away from the established resorts. “Choosing a less conventional destination often means quieter courses, better value for money and a more authentic experience, while still enjoying championship-quality golf in spectacular surroundings."Underrated golf destinations in EuropeVarna, BulgariaComporta and Tróia Peninsula, PortugalNorth-east Majorca, SpainGimsøya, NorwayBiarritz, FranceTavira, PortugalCosta Navarino, GreeceThe top golf courses to playVarna, BulgariaBulgaria is often overlooked, but golfers are "starting to discover its excellent-value courses and hotels", with Golfbreaks reporting a 173% rise in demand in 2025, and a further 47% in 2026 to date. The area around Varna, on Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast, is picked out as an underrated golf destination and Thracian Cliffs Golf & Beach Resort is the headline attraction, with sea views from every hole. Other options where golfers can stay and play include BlackSeaRama Golf & Villas and Lighthouse Golf & Spa Resort.Comporta and Tróia Peninsula, PortugalThe Tróia Peninsula and Comporta are better known for surfing than golfing, but demand is up 85% year-on-year, according to Golfbreaks data. Golfers can tackle the Dunas and Torre championship courses at Terras da Comporta, alongside the Robert Trent Jones-designed Tróia Golf Club. Beaches and the Sado Estuary add appeal between rounds. North-east Majorca, SpainAway from Palma and the island’s south-western resorts, Club de Golf Son Servera offers tree-lined fairways and water hazards. It is also Majorca's only private members' club but still welcomes visitors. Capdepera Golf Club brings mountain scenery and Mediterranean views, while Club de Golf Alcanada is another option. When not playing 18 holes, golfers can explore beaches and traditional towns in Majorca’s north-east.Gimsøya, NorwayAbove the Arctic Circle, Lofoten Links Golf Club offers the chance to play beneath the midnight sun during summer. Its coastal layout winds through dunes and rugged terrain, framed by sea and mountain views. Lofoten Links Lodges provides a nearby base for visiting golfers.Biarritz, FranceOne of the oldest golf courses in France, Golf de Biarritz le Phare combines a long history with fast greens and challenging bunkers. At the nearby Golf d’Arcangues, rolling terrain and Pyrenees views welcome players, while Golf de Seignosse expands the regional choice.Tavira, PortugalThe charming town of Tavira in the eastern Algarve is often overshadowed by Vilamoura and Albufeira. Nearby playing options include Quinta da Ria Golf Club, overlooking the Ria Formosa Natural Park, and neighbouring Quinta de Cima, with undulating fairways and water hazards. Monte Rei Golf Resort adds a Jack Nicklaus Signature course to the options around Tavira.Costa Navarino, GreeceGolf in Greece has “long flown under the radar”, said Golfbreaks, but that’s “starting to change” with a 140% rise in demand for Costa Navarino. Its four golf courses include The Dunes and The Bay, plus the International Olympic Academy Course and The Hills Course. The latter two were designed by José María Olazábal and opened in 2022, adding further variety to this golf destination in Greece’s Peloponnese.

title: Smashing pumpkins: Annual squash festival draws thousands to Brussels castle
description: Organisers in Belgium expect 50,000 visitors at a pumpkin festival that will celebrate the wonderous ways of using the big vegetable.
content: Some call them pumpkins, for others they're simply squashes, or jack o'lanterns when carved creatively, however you dice or slice them - pumpkins have taken over a castle near Brussels, Groot-Bijgaarden, for its annual pumpkin festival.Sourced from across Belgium and as far away as Portugal and Germany, the pumpkins come in all shapes and sizes — including a giant weighing 772 kilograms.The festival offers more than a display of the autumn harvest. Visitors can try their hand at pumpkin carving ahead of Halloween, while some of the largest pumpkins have been turned into makeshift kayaks.Despite a difficult harvest following a hot summer, the event continues to draw families and pumpkin enthusiasts for a celebration of autumn, with organisers expecting around 50,000 visitors this year.

title: Data centres are the new front line and Europe’s AI factories should slow down, says UN adviser
description: Data centres have become prime military targets and the drone strikes in Ukraine should force Europe to rethink where it builds its AI infrastructure, one expert says.
content: Data centres in Ukraine, Russia and the Middle East have become crucial targets in conflict that can temporarily bring down a country’s economy and public facilities such as banks and hospitals. Russia has struck data centres in Kyiv and Ukrainian drones hit back at multiple data centres in Russia in recent weeks, in attacks Kyiv has described as aimed at places that provide revenue streams for Moscow’s war machine.The military targeting of data centres should prompt Europe to rethink where it builds its AI infrastructure, said Mehdi Paryavi, an adviser to the United Nations and founder of the International Data Center Authority (IDCA) think tank.“When you hit enough important targets, you can take down the entire economy,” he told Euronews Next. As societies digitise, taking down a data centre can mean “paralysing the functions of military, healthcare and finance”.Data centres are the physical facilities where a company can house its servers and data. They are also crucial to artificial intelligence as they supply the massive amounts of energy it needs.They become especially important in warfare as Ukraine uses AI for drone targeting as well as other military uses. The new target on data centres should make countries consider more where they build them, Paryavi said, but he argued the industry’s long-standing advice to choose sites carefully and keep their locations quiet may no longer be enough. “Maybe you need iron domes, maybe you need to build them underground, or you need to build bunkers,” he said without getting to specifics due to national security reasons. But “the days that you would just build data centres in random locations are over,” he said.He also acknowledged that no country has a solid answer to how to do that without slowing the race to build AI capacity.A European hub Asked whether the strikes will make European governments rethink their plans for AI gigafactories, a type of data centre, Paryavi said: “100%”.When asked about Europe’s plans for data centres, a spokesperson from the European Commission told Euronews Next that it launched a tender to establish up to seven AI gigafactories across Europe. “The call is still open. Once closed, the proposals will be evaluated and then the award decisions will be taken,” it added. The call will close on November 12. However, there was no specific comment about whether the targeting of data centres in warfare would change any data centre plans. The economic cost to data centre damage can also be astronomical and “almost irreversible” to replace for many countries, including Europe, said Paryavi.Data centres can cost up to $25 billion each and take up to three years to build. “Europe cannot afford to finance hundreds of billions of dollars of assets and then somebody takes them out,” Paryavi said. “I project that the whole thing [the building of data centres] has to slow down.”He urged European states to act as a bloc, saying no single country could do it alone, as combined with the security risks are global energy shortfalls as well as a lack of trained workers. Rather than having scattered data centres, he advised building them in concentrated areas so you could build an iron dome to protect them. “Building data centres and digital hubs is the only way a nation or a hub or data centre companies can secure themselves,” he said.

title: The world’s best countries to live in for 2026 – and six of the top 10 are in Europe
description: Monaco topped the ranking thanks to its high quality of life and infrastructure, with Andorra hot on its heels in second place.
content: Been dreaming of a life abroad, but haven’t decided on where to go yet? Then you might just want to take a look at this new ranking.Produced by Nomad Capitalist, the Nomad Lifestyle Index evaluated 63 destinations against five pillars: Nature and climate; tax; residence and access; safety and freedom; and quality of life and infrastructure.Within these pillars, the ranking looked at things like air quality, extreme weather risk, routes to legal residence and citizenship, the Global Peace Index, life expectancy, cost of living and broadband speed, among others.After crunching the numbers, the top 10 is filled with European countries, including the number one spot: Monaco.Every destination was given a score out of 100 for each of the five pillars, which were then used to calculate an overall score.The three top destinations – Monaco, Andorra and the United Arab Emirates – were separated by just 0.74 points.The best places to live in EuropeMonaco claimed the top spot as it was the only country to receive a perfect 100 score under the quality of life and infrastructure pillar, but it also ranked highly for its safety and freedom score.In second place, Andorra leads in the safety and freedom pillar while also having the fourth-best nature score, with the cleanest air of any European country included in the Nomad Lifestyle Index. It was pipped to the top spot because of its route to citizenship, which takes 20 years of residence and requires a language and history test.Malta took fourth place, with praise for its strong passport and route to naturalisation within five years. It also ranked highly in the nature pillar, but was held back by its tax score and quality of life and infrastructure rating.Portugal, a long-time favourite of digital nomads, came fifth, ranking highly for its safety and freedom, residence and access, and tax scores, but was let down by its nature score as it is exposed to extreme weather conditions as a result of climate change.Cyprus placed sixth, coming second in the residence and access pillar, with a strong passport and seven years to naturalisation. Its quality of life and infrastructure score held it back, as well as the air quality.Rounding out the top 10 is Switzerland, which performed well in the safety and freedom pillar.The top 10 destinations to live around the globeMonaco – 73.89Andorra – 73.68United Arab Emirates –73.15Malta – 72.11Portugal – 70.09Cyprus – 68.42Singapore – 67.12Cayman Islands – 66.50New Zealand – 66.43Switzerland – 65.44

title: Lisbon airport taxis: Fixed fares aim to end 'tourist trap'
description: Since Thursday, passengers landing at Lisbon airport who want to take a taxi can now rely on a fixed price for their trip.
content: Over the past few years, there have been many reports from tourists about excessive prices, scams and even drivers refusing to take passengers from Lisbon airport.Faced with problems affecting both foreign visitors and locals, a protocol was signed last September to set fixed fares for taxi journeys.Several complaints on social media describe allegedly tampered taximeters, mileage being diverted and cases in which taxi drivers will only accept cash payments.Back in August, Josien Nation, a Dutch citizen living in Portugal, described the situation as a "tourist trap". In a video posted on the Facebook page Nations Without Borders, she said that "not all taxi drivers are 'crooks'", but that some try to negotiate the fare before setting off and then make the trip with the meter switched off, a practice expressly banned in Portugal.In another account, posted in a Reddit group, a passenger says that on a journey from Lisbon airport to Rossio he was charged 18.50 euros, even though the meter showed 13 euros. According to the post, the driver justified the difference with an additional luggage fee. He also refused to let the passenger pay by card.Most of these accounts come from tourists or foreign nationals living in Portugal who are allegedly treated as tourists. However, there are also testimonies from residents who use the service, such as a Portuguese man who shared his experience on the same platform."The last time I arrived in Lisbon, after a trip, I got into a taxi and immediately got back out again," he began. "The driver said he didn't take card payments. I asked him how much the journey from the airport to my home might cost, as I had some cash with me, but he replied that the price depended on a series of factors, such as traffic and how long the journey would take, among other nonsense."Other users also say that some taxi drivers take less direct routes to reach their destination, in an attempt to make the journey longer and thus justify overcharging.To prevent many of these situations, a fixed-fare mechanism came into force on Thursday, under which everyone will pay the same for trips to certain areas. Anyone travelling to areas within the so‑called "zone 1" (see image below) will pay 16 euros during the daytime, from 7:00 to 22:00, and 20 euros at night, from 22:00 to 7:00.For trips to "zone 2", a daytime journey costs 19 euros and rises to 23 euros at night. These fares also apply at weekends and on public holidays.Destinations not covered by the scheme will continue to be charged using the meter.The fares include luggage, removing the additional fee of 1.60 euros that used to be charged for bags exceeding 55x35x20 centimetres.Carlos Silva, president of the Portuguese Taxi Federation (FPT), explained in comments to Portuguese news agency Lusa that the system will only be fully operational from November and that a price still needs to be set for areas outside the capital, such as Moscavide, Sacavém and Prior Velho.He believes "it is not fair for someone to pay 16 euros to Parque das Nações and, if the destination is a little further on but already in another municipality, Loures, and so close to the airport, for the service then to be paid according to the meter".'Tourist prices'Reactions to the new price list were quick to appear on social media, with many people branding the fares far too high and pointing to short journeys, such as trips from the airport to the parish of Alvalade or to Parque das Nações, both little more than two kilometres away.An Instagram user says she usually takes a taxi to Oriente station, in Parque das Nações, and used to pay between 7.50 and 10 euros. "And now a fixed fare at such a high rate, why?", she asks. Among the comments, some argue that alternative transport platforms, such as TVDE services, will be the main beneficiaries of the new fares.Some accuse the authorities of setting "tourist prices" or "rubber-stamping" the high fares and practices of many taxi drivers. "They are going to legalise what some have already been doing for years: turning off the meter," reads one comment.Others, meanwhile, recognise the need for fixed prices in the name of transparency. "Having already seen this system in other countries, having the fares per destination set in advance without depending on the meter is actually useful," writes one user on Reddit.The possibility of using public transport, such as the metro and the bus, is also mentioned in the comments, although users point to obstacles such as "large, heavy suitcases" or "travelling with children".Protocol goes beyond faresThe new fares, which came into force on Thursday, will cover all taxi drivers in this first phase, even those not yet accredited to operate at the airport taxi rank. "Accreditation will also start to be carried out on Thursday," the official explained.Carlos Silva also believes that these new rules could attract more drivers and ensure more taxis are available at the airport rank. "We know that many do not stop at the airport for various reasons, but that they are considering doing so if there are rules, because at the moment they do not feel comfortable. Fixed prices may be more advantageous, offsetting the time they might have to wait", he said.If you arrive at Lisbon airport today, you can already expect these prices on taxi services. However, information panels are still missing in the arrivals area and outside, displaying this information so that it is visible to everyone. Transparency is one of the pillars of this new regulation, along with "improving the quality of the service and protecting users".The protocol on fixed-price journeys, signed in September by Lisbon City Council, ANA - Aeroportos de Portugal, the Lisbon Tourism Association (ATL), the FPT (Portuguese Taxi Federation) and ANTRAL - National Association of Road Transport in Light Vehicles, also lays down other rules, such as the "non-refusal of services" by taxi drivers.Taxi drivers are also obliged to accept vouchers and electronic payments, meaning the payment terminal must be operational.PSP inspections confirmed need for regulationThe tightening of measures, even though they will only be fully implemented at the start of next month, also follows a major inspection operation by the Public Security Police (PSP) at the arrivals area of Humberto Delgado Airport in Lisbon at the end of August, during which 67 offences related to taxi activity were detected.In a statement, Lisbon Metropolitan Command (COMETLIS) said that around 100 taxis were inspected at the site, resulting in 32 offences for "incorrect positioning of the taximeter", out of a total of 67.Among the offences detected, eight related to lack of a CMT (Taxi Driver Certificate), six to lack of mandatory documents, six to fire extinguishers past their expiry date, three to lack of vehicle inspection and three to "lack of Group 2 on the taxi driver's licence" (the mandatory driving licence certification for taxi drivers).Two offences were also recorded for a taximeter past its validity period, two for taxis in poor condition, one for failure to use restraint systems, one for lack of insurance, one for driving under the influence of alcohol and one for parking in a private car park.The PSP also issued two warnings to present documents and complied with two requests for external action that were pending against one of the drivers.Joana Mourão Carvalho contributed to the writing of this article.

title: At least 19 injured as minibus collides with train near Channel Tunnel
description: The prefecture of Pas-de-Calais confirmed that "no deaths are to be reported at this stage and no lives are in danger".
content: A collision between a minibus and a shuttle train at the Eurotunnel site in northern France left 19 people injured on Thursday evening, local authorities said.Two people were hospitalised with serious but not life-threatening injuries, while 17 others sustained minor injuries. The minibus driver was among those hurt.The minibus carrying truck drivers was heading toward the tunnel entrance when it veered off course and struck the side of the shuttle train transporting vehicles through the busy Channel Tunnel between France and England. Authorities confirmed that the vehicle did not overturn."An accident involving a minibus transporting heavy goods vehicle drivers who were about to board a Le Shuttle shuttle occurred this evening, at the loading platform of the Eurotunnel site," the Pas-de-Calais prefecture wrote on X.The crash has occurred at the tunnel entrance in the town of Coquelles, near Calais.The minibus driver was a Eurotunnel employee, while the victims were all men of different nationalities, according to local authorities.The sub-prefect of Calais, Agathe Cury, said a judicial investigation had been opened, adding that it was the first accident of its kind at a Eurotunnel loading platform.About 200 emergency responders, including ambulances, helicopters and police officers, were deployed to the scene.Vehicle shuttle service through the tunnel was suspended for 90 minutes before gradually resuming late in the evening, authorities said. Eurostar passenger trains and freight services were unaffected.The tunnel, which opened in 1994, carried 3.4 million vehicles last year, along with millions of Eurostar passengers.

title: Iconic New York hotel The Plaza set to close for four years for restoration works
description: Having first opened on Fifth Avenue in 1907, The Plaza Hotel has been a New York City landmark for more than a century.
content: The Plaza Hotel has been a landmark on New York City’s Fifth Avenue for more than a century, instantly recognisable thanks to its iconic façade.Now that façade is getting a facelift, with works set to take at least four years to complete. The hotel will close its doors in January 2027.In a statement, The Plaza Hotel management said: “The undertaking reflects the complexity of maintaining a property of such architectural and historical significance, with careful consideration given to preservation requirements and the building’s long-term care, as well as the safety of our guests, employees, and the wider community.“The scope and complexity of the façade works require detailed planning and coordination with relevant stakeholders, alongside adherence to applicable historic preservation requirements.”The Plaza Hotel has been recognised as one of the Historic Hotels of America, one of just 288 properties selected by the National Trust for Historic Preservation.The history of The Plaza HotelThe Plaza Hotel, which is styled after a French Renaissance chateau, first opened in 1907 and quickly became an icon – it even featured in The Great Gatsby and was the setting for the Eloise series of books.Outside of the world of books, The Plaza Hotel has been shown on the silver screen numerous times, with films shot here including Home Alone 2: Lost in New York (which has a cameo from Donald Trump, who owned the hotel at the time), Crocodile Dundee and Sleepless in Seattle.Since the beginning, The Plaza Hotel has been a hub for celebrities, with famous past guests including The Beatles, Liza Minnelli and Frank Lloyd Wright.Afternoon tea at The Palm Court is a must for many New York City tourists, so if you’ve been putting off a trip, you might just want to book your flight ASAP or you’ll miss your chance for nearly half a decade.

title: Why you should visit Sigulda, the autumn capital of Latvia
description: The banks of the Gauja River are transformed into a sea of orange during the cooler months.
content: New England is synonymous with autumn, but while there’s too much orange in the White House, many of us will be looking elsewhere for our leaf-peeping fix.Thankfully, there’s somewhere with plenty of golden hues much closer to home: Sigulda.Regarded as Latvia’s autumn capital, the town is just over an hour away from the capital Riga by train and boasts an abundance of trees that turn shades of yellow, orange and red when there’s a chill in the air.Best of all, you’ll likely have the scenery all to yourself as you won’t find any tourist crowds here – other than those who read Euronews Travel’s autumn bucket list, which included Sigulda as a must-visit.I first visited Sigulda last summer, and made it my mission to return in the autumn to see it for myself, which is exactly what I did earlier this month.Here’s what you should do while you’re there.What to do in SiguldaWhile the town itself is very pretty in autumn, the best scenery can be found around the Gauja River, which you can cross via cable car.The seven-minute ride passes over the Gauja Valley, and along the way you’ll spot several castles.After passing to the other side of the river, you can take a short walk through the woods to Gutman's Cave.The largest cave in the Baltics, the walls are covered in carvings from lovers who have visited here over the centuries.The cave is associated with the legend of the “rose of Turaida”, a girl named Maija who was abandoned during the Swedish-Polish war and grew up in Turaida Castle (more on that in a moment).Maija fell for the castle’s gardener, Victor Heil, and the pair would meet in the cave. Unfortunately, army deserter Jakubowsky also fell for Maija, and lured her to the cave by pretending to be Victor before murdering her after she tricked him into attacking her by saying she had a magic scarf that would protect her from all injuries.From Gutman’s Cave, it’s another short walk to Turaida Castle. From the top of the main tower, you’ll have views all around, with each window offering a vista prettier than the last.The castle itself dates back to 1214, and you’ll be able to learn about its history through several exhibitions on site, while the gardens are home to numerous sculptures from Indulis Ranka.There are a number of castles scattered around Sigulda, including the New Castle, which is home to several creative businesses which occupy the old manor buildings.Here, you can buy your very own Sigulda walking stick, with the patterned cane serving as a symbol of the town.Sigulda is seen as the gateway into Gauja National Park, so there are plenty of hiking trails where you can put your walking stick to good use. Your best source for trails is Enter Gauja, the official tourism website for the region.Another popular town to visit within the Gauja region is Cēsis, which is home to a medieval castle dating back to the 13th century.How to get thereBoth Sigulda and Cēsis are accessible by train, which takes around an hour and 10 minutes from Riga for the former and an hour and 20 minutes for the latter.You can grab a ticket in the station, or book through the Vivi website.If you don’t want to walk, there are buses from Sigulda to Turaida Castle, but they run just once per hour, so you may be left waiting a while. Tickets can be bought directly from the driver with cash or card.

title: Kenya records second Ebola case as outbreak in Congo keeps growing
description: Kenya has confirmed its second Ebola case, a close relative of the country’s first victim, as the outbreak in Congo continues to grow.
content: Kenya has recorded its second case of Ebola, the health ministry said on Wednesday, adding there was "no evidence" of any large-scale transmission of the virus.The country reported its first-ever Ebola death last week after a man who had been living in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) died after returning to Kenya. The second patient is a close relative of the deceased, the ministry confirmed. The epicentre of the outbreak is Congo’s Ituri Province, but Uganda and Kenya have also reported cases. "The Ministry of Health confirms a second case of Ebola," it said in a statement, adding the 39-year-old man was a close family member of the first victim and already in quarantine and being monitored when the virus was detected. These are the first two cases of Ebola ever reported in the country, including all the previous outbreaks.The patient was isolated "as soon as he developed fever, fatigue and joint pains", the ministry said, before being tested and found positive for the virus.It emphasised that such early detection "limits the chance of passing the virus to others", and that "there is no evidence of spread in the wider community".The ministry said it had traced 113 of the 128 people the patient identified as close contacts. Kenya's first victim was a national, who fell ill around a month ago and had been treated in the DRC, before travelling overland to the Ugandan capital, Kampala, and flying into Nairobi on 3 October.He was hospitalised in Nairobi, but later died on 5 October, according to Health Minister Aden Duale.Cases grow further in CongoMore than 4,000 people have died in Congo since the country declared the outbreak in May. Public health authorities have confirmed over 9,000 cases and 899 patients are hospitalised in isolation as of 13 October. The most affected province is Ituri, where 6,734 cases, including 3,177 deaths, have been reported. As cases in Congo continue to rise, the European Center for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) warns that the outbreak remains a public health emergency of international concern and the response is particularly challenging in remote and hard-to-reach areas.The WHO also noted that contact follow-up is “a major operational pressure” and has fallen below the targets in recent weeks. The current outbreak is caused by Bundibugyo virus, for which no licensed vaccines or specific treatments are currently available. Frontline workers in Congo are being vaccinated with Ervebo — the only licensed Ebola vaccine targeting other strains.The vaccine was “highly effective” against Ebola Zaire virus in the past, but it is not yet known whether it can provide “meaningful protection” against Bundibugyo disease, which is still spreading in the DRC, the United Nations said in a press release. The risk of importation into Europe from the outbreak areas remains very low, according to the ECDC.“While sporadic importations cannot be excluded, the probability of multiple independent importations is very low, even in a pessimistic scenario whereby incidence continues to rise in the affected regions,” the agency wrote on its website.

title: AI in healthcare: from fighting epidemics to family doctors
description: A situation report in an hour instead of a day: in Africa's fight against Ebola, AI shows how it can bolster healthcare, in Germany too. But experts warn of opaque systems and unresolved risks.
content: Since May, teams on the ground in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) have been fighting the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus. Every day, so-called health workers knock on doors and offer advice. They record recoveries and deaths and refer people with suspicious symptoms to medical facilities.The knowledge of these health workers, whose notebooks reflect the condition of entire communities, has been digitised, according to a report by the AI company Anthropic.Who has fallen ill? Who did the person have contact with, and where were they staying before they knew they were infected? To evaluate the answers and reports, Anthropic's Claude model was used. Among those involved in the study were CEPI, the WHO Regional Office for Africa and the national biomedical research institute INRB.AI helps to assess the spread of epidemics more quickly"A situation report is now produced within an hour instead of taking an entire working day," explains Marie Roseline Darnycka Belizaire, Director for Emergency Preparedness and Response at the World Health Organization (WHO) Regional Office for Africa. Artificial intelligence can help to assess the spread of epidemics more quickly and to target medical assistance more precisely, the WHO deputy director said on stage at the World Health Summit.While analysing the data, potential outbreak hotspots were identified and preparations made, such as getting stocks of medical supplies to key hubs or high-risk areas.That can be decisive in an emergency. The earlier health authorities respond to a potential outbreak, the better they can prepare and organise care. AI is intended to help process information from different sources more quickly and support decision-making by those in charge.This positive example of how artificial intelligence can be used in healthcare illustrates a level at which AI can be deployed with relatively little risk. Experts, however, see far more possibilities for the future use of artificial intelligence.The technology could improve diagnoses, relieve medical staff of administrative tasks and help to deploy scarce resources more strategically. At the same time, it raises fundamental questions: how reliable are the results? Can medical professionals understand how an AI arrives at a decision? And do patients really benefit?AI as a support for overstretched healthcare staffDemand for healthcare is growing worldwide. At the same time, many places lack staff, time and equipment. For Thomas Zapata, Director of the WHO Academy in Lyon, this is a key starting point for the use of artificial intelligence."We have to think about a paradox we are currently facing. We have more health professionals worldwide than ever before, and we have unprecedented technologies at our disposal," Zapata said in a panel discussion at the World Health Summit. Yet, he added, there is still an enormous shortage of healthcare workers. "Demand for health services keeps on rising."He sees AI as a way to narrow that gap. It is crucial, however, not to see it as an end in itself, but as a tool to be integrated into existing health systems."AI is an enabler, a means to an end. At the moment we are very fascinated by technology and AI, but I think we need to place it in the right context within the health system," warns Zapata. In his view, artificial intelligence fits in two areas. On the one hand, AI could change the way care is organised; on the other, training and continuing education for health workers must adapt to the new possibilities.Ultimately, AI can of course help to reduce workloads, streamline administrative tasks, improve clinical decision-making and enhance diagnostic processes. For him, it is particularly important that the technology frees up time for what cannot and should not easily be automated: caring for patients.Above all, the Ebola crisis in the Democratic Republic of Congo has shown that trust in local health systems is lacking.That gives doctors more time for their patientsAutomated processes can make a particular difference where healthcare staff work under intense time pressure. Cecilia Mbaca, Senior Technical Adviser for Health and Emergencies at the aid organisation CARE, knows these challenges from more than 15 years on the front line.For her, three questions are crucial: can AI support clinical decision-making? Can it take over repetitive tasks? And does it help to tailor care more closely to the individual needs of patients?"If AI does this work very well, that leaves more time for the personal aspects of care, so that we can ask questions, listen, examine patients and refer them on to the next level of care," explains Cecilliah Mbaka, Senior Technical Adviser for Health and Emergencies at the aid organisation CARE as well.She herself spent more than 15 years working on the front line, with little support, limited resources and a heavy workload.In epidemics in particular, it is not just about medical data. Trust within the population also plays an important role. People must be able to trust that they will be protected and properly cared for in a health facility. In affected communities, this trust can be decisive in whether people seek medical help in time.It is estimated that around 50% of deaths in villages in the DRC occur outside medical facilities, according to epidemiologist Maximilian Gertler. The local health system is under pressure and was not prepared for the Ebola outbreak. Thousands of protective suits are needed every day to shield nursing staff from contamination. Germany recently increased its aid by 21 million euros.AI can therefore support the organisation of care. On its own, however, it cannot ensure that people trust medical facilities. As AI experts themselves criticise, the path leading to a diagnosis is still often opaque.The transparency problem: how does AI arrive at its diagnosis?Modern AI systems can analyse large volumes of data and detect patterns that humans might miss. Yet in many cases it remains unclear exactly how they reach their results.Thomas Thesen, Professor of Medical Education and Informatics at the Geisel School of Medicine at Dartmouth University in the United States, describes the problem like this: "They are extremely good at recognising patterns, but they are really bad at explaining to us what those patterns actually are." Chatbots and large language models such as Claude or ChatGPT have what he calls an explanation problem. In this respect, artificial intelligence remains a black box.This so-called black-box problem is particularly relevant in the healthcare sector. When a system provides a diagnosis or treatment recommendation, medical professionals need to be able to judge whether it makes sense in the specific case. A result on its own is not always enough; the path leading to it also has to be traceable."That is the problem of explainability. They cannot explain in human-understandable language how they arrive at these conditions."This black-box issue concerns not only transparency but also responsibility: who is liable if an AI provides a wrong recommendation? That is why, for Mbaka, it is crucial that AI does not simply spit out results, but genuinely supports decision-making.Expert: AI must not replace learning in trainingArtificial intelligence can also help in training medical professionals, for instance by making information more accessible or assisting with repetitive tasks. But when it comes to learning itself, Thesen, the professor of medical education and informatics, also sees risks.He points to a study that compared searching for information via conventional search engines with using an AI chatbot. The students who used the chatbot ended up with more superficial knowledge that was less firmly anchored."These so-called desirable difficulties are actually very important for the learning process. And if you outsource all the cognitive work of learning to a chatbot – which may be highly efficient – you do not actually learn anything."Anyone who needs to retain knowledge in the long term should not, in his view, let an AI take over every mental step. Especially in medicine, it can be crucial to make the right decisions even when technological support is not available.Thesen therefore also recommends using AI primarily where it reduces workload. Where the aim is to understand knowledge and retain it in the long term, independent learning must continue to have its place.

title: Rooms with a view: The highest hotel in France just opened in the Pyrenees
description: Featuring 16 double rooms with panoramic views, the Hôtellerie des Laquets is connected to Pic du Midi via a private cable car.
content: There are rooms with a view, and then there’s this: The highest hotel in France, located some 2,620 metres above sea level.Found in the French Pyrenees, the Hôtellerie des Laquets was originally built between 1930 and 1933.Having been closed for more than 30 years, the renovated property reopened its doors to guests in late September.The original hotel building has been kept, with furnishings paying homage to Pyrenean alpine culture, while the new wing is pure minimalist Nordic chic.Featuring 16 double rooms, all of which offer panoramic views, you can reach the hotel by taking a cable car from La Mongie to the summit of the Pic du Midi, before taking a private cable car down to the property below.The views aren’t the only thing set to impress, either, as the hotel’s restaurant will feature a menu from chef Stéphane Tournié, who earned a Michelin star at Les Jardins de l'Opéra in Toulouse.Hôtellerie des Laquets overtakes Refuge de Solaise, which lies at 2,551 metres above sea level in the Alps, for the title of France's highest hotel.The highest hotel in Europe overall is Glacier Hotel Grawand, is 3,212 metres above sea level in Val Senales in South Tyrol, Italy.What to expect at Hôtellerie des LaquetsThe Hôtellerie des Laquets is located within the Pic du Midi International Dark Sky Reserve, meaning it’s a brilliant option for stargazing, with unobstructed views of the Milky Ways sans light pollution.At the summit, you can learn all about the science behind the observatory at Espace Expériences du Pic du Midi, before heading to the planetarium for an immersive show ahead of the real show that evening.Pic du Midi is also home to a 12m-long footbridge that juts out into the mountainscape, offering fantastic photo opportunities.From December this year, the hotel’s spa area will open, complete with sauna and steam rooms.

title: Can a European Security Council help the EU fight Russia’s hybrid attacks?
description: The EU wants a faster political response to sabotage, cyberattacks and drone incursions. Experts say the proposed Security Council could help, but only partly.
content: Sabotage, arson, cyberattacks, disinformation, and drones in restricted airspace. Russia’s hybrid campaign against Europe no longer looks like isolated incidents. The EU is now rethinking its response.In September, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the hybrid threats facing Europe are “less and less hybrid and less and less threats”. Her State of the Union address introduced a new idea, the European Security Council.From resilience to deterrenceFor Ionela Ciolan, a research officer at the Wilfried Martens Centre for European Studies, the challenge is clear. Russian hybrid warfare today, she says, means the “weaponisation of everything,” from attacks on critical infrastructure and election interference to targeted arson and the instrumentalisation of energy.The EU’s response has so far leaned on resilience and coordination. Its Hybrid Toolbox, activated in June 2024, bundles cyber, sanctions, diplomatic, and support measures. It created a dedicated Russia hybrid sanctions regime, with first listings in December 2024, and rapid response teams, first deployed in Moldova in 2025.Analysts now see a shift. Faster public attribution to Russia, more talk of imposing costs on Moscow, and viewing incidents as parts of one campaign. Parliament adopted a report in September calling for a more proactive approach by 470 votes to 129.Gaps remain, sanctions need unanimity, intelligence is fragmented between capitals, and there is no consensus on when sabotage merits a collective military response.What is on the tableThe proposal has three linked parts: a standing leaders’ forum, an Emergency Security Protocol, and a funding instrument for shared capabilities such as air defence. The protocol is the most relevant for hybrid threats. Von der Leyen described it as Europe’s answer to NATO’s Article 4, letting any member state convene all 27 governments when it feels its security is threatened.The Commission is reportedly considering inviting partners such as the UK, Norway, Ukraine, and Canada. No formal legislative proposal has been tabled, and no legal basis, voting system, budget, or launch date has been agreed.Luigi Scazzieri, a senior policy analyst at the EU Institute for Security Studies, is blunt about what it would be. In von der Leyen’s version, the Council is essentially a dedicated European Council meeting with invited partners. “This is not a decision-making body per se,” he says.That means it cannot cut through the disagreements that slow EU responses. Scazzieri argues its worth lies elsewhere: “The key value […] is not necessarily speed, but it’s more the cross-policy coherence.” He says it would help the EU think more strategically about its toolbox, from sanctions to spending, while NATO keeps collective defence.Critics, he acknowledges, will say Europe already has plenty of forums, including the European Political Community.The threshold problemThe harder question is when a hybrid attack becomes graver. Ciolan points to the EU’s mutual assistance clause, Article 42.7, and the debate over operationalising it for hybrid attacks.“A cyberattack that shuts down hospitals or sabotage that disables a power grid could have consequences comparable to a conventional military attack,” she says. Moscow, she adds, thrives on the grey area: “Russia exploits ambiguity to complicate attribution and delay a collective response.”Her conclusion is that Europe needs common rules: “Europeans therefore need a shared framework for assessing these attacks, and must be able to respond to hostile actions even when they remain below the threshold of armed aggression.”In her view, a Security Council and an Emergency Security Protocol could help member states “move more quickly from national reactions to a common European response, bringing together military and non-military instruments.” The decision to invoke Article 42.7 would stay with the state under attack.A hedge against Washington?Steven Blockmans, deputy director at the International Centre for Defence and Security in Tallinn, says the idea was revived by doubts about US commitment to NATO’s Article 5. The concept dates back to a 2018 proposal by Angela Merkel and Emmanuel Macron. He sees a Council as a fallback if the North Atlantic Council were blocked, whether by Washington or another ally. He links its new momentum to the Greenland crisis and says Defence Commissioner Andrius Kubilius has pushed the idea for more than a year.Blockmans argues the body would need teeth to be credible. “It would boost the legitimacy of a European Security Council if its governance had decision-making procedures,” he says, giving national parliaments a democratic backstop and linking it to NATO-compatible command structures and a dedicated budget.That, he says, is an ideal that would take years of treaty drafting. But if the situation demands it, “an informal construct could well be created tomorrow, if push comes to shove.”So is the European Security Council a tool against hybrid attacks? From what we know so far, only partly. As proposed, it would improve coordination and give leaders a regular space to discuss security with partners. The Emergency Security Protocol could provide an earlier political entry point for incidents below the armed attack threshold. But experts agree that the underlying obstacles lie in national politics.

title: Entire Swedish reality show season lost weeks before premiere amid disputed AI claims
description: The project could not be restored, wiping out hundreds of days of work, according to Swedish newspaper Aftonbladet.
content: An AI agent reportedly deleted an entire edited season of a Swedish reality show just five weeks before its planned premiere, forcing the broadcaster to postpone its release until next year.Swedish newspaper Aftonbladet, citing unnamed sources, reported that the production company behind a reality show named The Challenge Sverige had given an AI agent access to its server, where it deleted the completed season.The project could not be restored, wiping out hundreds of days of work, according to the report.Swedish commercial broadcaster TV4 confirmed to Aftonbladet that a “technical failure” had caused the loss, pushing the planned 22 November premiere back to 2027.Its news division initially repeated the newspaper’s account of AI involvement, but in an update on Wednesday afternoon, TV4’s head of programmes Mia Lindqvist denied that an AI agent was responsible, saying “that is not true”.Adapted from the American show The Challenge, the series is billed by TV4 as the world’s toughest reality contest, combining physical challenges, mental endurance and strategic alliances.How can AI agents go wrong?Although the Swedish TV channel has rejected the AI explanation in this case, other incidents have exposed the risks of systems that can act on users’ behalf.AI agents use software tools to carry out tasks, such as drafting and sending emails, rather than simply generating responses. Depending on their permissions, they can make changes to real files, websites and computer systems.Problems can arise when a system misunderstands instructions, misjudges an action’s consequences or works around an obstacle instead of stopping.In a report published on Friday, Anthropic said models given impossible tasks could pursue “unintended and sometimes misaligned strategies to achieve their goals”.In July, its Claude Haiku 4.5 model submitted fabricated information about an unsolved homicide to the US police website while performing example tasks. TV4 said all the original footage of the show remains available but the season must be edited again from scratch.

title: Expedia unveils its 2027 destinations of the year – and only two are in Europe
description: Just 10 cities and regions made the cut, with South Lake Tahoe in California topping the list ahead of Hyogo in Japan and Punta del Este in Uruguay.
content: South Lake Tahoe in California has just been named Expedia’s 2027 Destination of the Year, with searches up 195% compared to 2025.North America’s largest alpine lake offers skiing in the winter and kayaking or paddleboarding come summer, making it a perfect year-round destination.The 10 destinations chosen by the group in its Unpack ’27 trends report span North America, South America, Asia and Australasia – with only two in Europe.Hyogo in Japan claimed second place, with searches up 95%. The prefecture, which is “one of Japan’s most unsung destinations with coastline, mountains and castles in one stretch”, was also identified as deserving of Expedia’s Smart Travel Health Check.Introduced last year, the check identifies places managing tourism responsibly while offering rich experiences.Third place went to Punta del Este, Uruguay’s glamorous coastal city which saw a 65% surge in searches, while fourth place went to Sedona in Arizona, which was praised for its yoga retreats, hiking opportunities and world-class spas.Rounding out the top five was Busan, the port city on South Korea’s southeast coast, best known for its beaches and film festival (and, of course, the zombie movie Train to Busan).Trending destinations in Europe Perugia in Italy came out seventh overall, with searches up 35% compared to last year.The capital of Umbria, visitors flock here year-round for its 14th-century hilltop city centre filled with historic sights, but the jazz and chocolate festivals are also a big draw.The only other European destination to make the cut was Chichester in the UK, with searches up 30%.Located on the West Sussex coast, Chichester is known for its Roman ruins, with a city walls trail looping the historic city.From here, you can take a stroll through South Downs National Park, feel the sand between your toes at West Wittering Beach or take a trip to Arundel Castle.Expedia’s 2027 Destinations of the YearSouth Lake Tahoe, California, US (+195%)Hyogo, Japan (+95%)Punta del Este, Uruguay (+65%)Sedona, Arizona, US (+55%)Busan, South Korea (+50%)Holbox, Mexico (+45%)Perugia, Italy (+35%)The Tweed, New South Wales, Australia (+35%)Niagara-on-the-Lake, Canada (+35%)Chichester, UK (+30%)

title: Tsui Hark at Lumière Festival: ‘We don't know where the future will bring us’
description: "We all know that the thing about humanity is that we always fear being replaced by something." Euronews Culture sits down with legendary Hong Kong filmmaker Tsui Hark during this year's Lumière Film Festival.
content: Anyone who is a fan of Hong Kong cinema and martial arts films will immediately recognise the name Tsui Hark.He is one of the key figures in Hong Kong’s New Wave, responsible for reinventing the martial arts genre. As a writer, producer and director, he boosted the careers of many like Chow Yun-fat, Jet Lee and even John Woo. And until last year with the box office success of Ne Zha 2, the 75-year-old director’s film The Battle at Lake Changjin was the highest-grossing Chinese film of all time.Four of his films - the period romantic comedy Shanghai Blues (1984), the groundbreaking action-comedy Peking Opera Blues (1986), the martial arts epic Once Upon a Time in China (1991) and the action thriller Time And Tide (2000) - are being honoured and screened at this year’s Lumière Film Festival.Euronews Culture sat down with the legendary filmmaker after the Lumière ceremony during which directors are celebrated with a golden plaque on Rue du Premier Film, beside the Institut Lumière, to talk about the festival, his work, and the challenges we face.Euronews Culture: How does it feel having your plaque on the Lumière wall now?Tsui Hark: I feel very dreamy, as a matter of fact! (Laughs) You know, I suddenly realized that I’ve come to the place where motion pictures started, at their beginning. I never thought that I would come to a place like this, where you suddenly go back to the original motion picture. It becomes a very surreal thing. You come to a place where your career was started by someone that you don't know, but they [the Lumière brothers] are the source of your creativity and everything. I feel very blessed, being given the task of making movies.During your stay at the festival, several of your films are being screened, including restored versions of Shanghai Blues and Peking Opera Blues. How does it feel seeing these films on a big screen once more? It’s strange with the films I've made 40 years ago! (Laughs) For me, it's like it's very far, far away, and suddenly they come back again. It makes you feel like the time never passed. You go to a theater showing your film that you made 40 years ago, and people still like it.
