It's a wonderful feeling.You are known for your work in action films and martial arts, but there’s a focus in the selection of films screened at the festival on comedy and romance. In your opinion and experience, where does the cinematic language of action and comedy intersect? I actually think of myself as a comedy person than an action director, but everything happened in 1979. I worked in a television, and I was given a job to make a costume action drama [The Butterfly Murders]. I was given an assignment to do an action film, and since then, I have been associated with action genre for so many years. But for me, it’s a bit weird! Throughout your films, you’ve always managed to balance action and the epic scale and scope of your stories with very emotional and personal considerations. It’s not an easy balance to get right when it comes to big productions... I suppose my question is: What's your secret? There's no secret at all! It all depends on my take on something I really like. When I was a kid, when I watched this kind of genre, I felt very exhilarated when looking at life. When I have a chance to make a movie, I go in that direction - a direction based on how I identify with the people inside the world, especially in epic or costume dramas.I’m very serious when it comes to making people identify and associate themselves with the story I’m telling. The quality of humanity in the characters and the story is a major concern of the material. I always try to make the story understandable and relatable for everyone. You see, many think about movies as being for a certain age or people. I feel like movies should be for audiences of all ages and hopefully for people of all cultures - not just our culture that we're so familiar with. I hope that movies, culture, and art can be shared by everyone.Have you noticed a certain sensitivity that European audiences have towards your films?Actually, I have no idea what's going on! (Laughs) Sometimes I go to a place and they will say “I've seen your movie” and I'm quite surprised. The first time I was in Cannes, and they said, “Oh, I've seen your movie”, I was very shocked. I made the movie elsewhere and it was shown to a different kind of audience, but still, they understood and accepted the film. For me, it’s a form of encouragement and it gives me energy to make movies that can be shared by all people and bring cultures together.Considering the breadth of your career and your filmography, are there any genres that you would like to explore that you haven’t had the chance to? I ask, because you made a horror-comedy in 1980, We’re Going To Eat You, and I can’t deny I’d love to see another horror film from you... Oh, yes! Exactly! Horror is a genre I always want to explore, because I feel horror is not just about making people scared but about making people feel a different kind of energy. I've seen a lot of horror films, and I feel like they are often very negative about human beings and humanity. That’s why I feel like I’d like to try something different in this genre.Speaking of negativity, many are expressing fears nowadays about the future of cinema and the arts in general, especially with the push towards artificial intelligence. Is that something that worries you? It’s a very up-to-date question you’ve asked. We all know that the thing about humanity is that we always fear being replaced by something. The fear that we are being replaced comes from everywhere. In relationships, career, economy... Or even our own idea of freedom. This is always a threat, and we don't know where the future will bring us.The fear and the danger of losing everything is everywhere, and human beings tend to be neglectful of the weakness of our nature. We neglect the power of destruction created by us and at the same time, the power of destruction created by nature. In our era, we have faced a lot of crises – from virus, science, technology, and war. We have no solution for it so far. Humans are a weak species when it comes to solving problems like that.The more we go through every test we encounter on the path of our survival, we realise that we actually have no solutions. Simply because we are the destructive element in nature. I hope that it's not true. Hopefully I'm mistaken in that respect, and that we bring some good things in life.You know, at my age, I always feel like there’s not a long time to worry about the future... But I hope that things will not get worse. I want to be optimistic, but there is strong evidence of negative things happening. Since World War II, everybody tried to avoid that happening again, but it's happening. Non-stop happening. I don't know what is the best solution for all these problems... I certainly don't. No one has. I know we’re getting deep and we can’t get too philosophical about what we’re going to do. The world is very chaotic, but I do think that at least something we can do is to make everybody look at a good aspect of humanity and remind ourselves to enjoy life and human creativity. And cinema is a good place to start.Peking Opera Blues makes its French cinema debut on 21 October in a restored 4K version.The Lumière Film Festival runs in Lyon through 18 October.

title: As the US and China race ahead in AI, France carves its own path with Nvidia’s help
description: Nvidia bets almost $10 billion in Europe as Paris pushes for AI sovereignty.
content: American Artificial intelligence giant Nvidia is spending big in France with a string of new investments in its technology and health companies, showing how Paris is safeguarding its technological sovereignty amid the AI race between China and the United States. On Tuesday, Nvidia announced planned investments in medical booking website Doctolib, robotics company Genesis AI, chemicals and materials company Entalpic and enterprise software company Pigment.The company says it brings its investments to Europe to nearly $10 billion (€9 bn) to the continent’s technology ecosystem.Nvidia’s investments in France show how the country’s push, driven in particular by President Emmanuel Macron, to lead in technology has grown since the AI Action Summit in February 2025 and the ‘Choose France’ summits.But AI sovereignty, which the European Commission defines as “Europe's ability to act independently in the digital world by developing and controlling key technologies,” depends heavily on infrastructure, which is currently being built in Western France. The French AI structuresTaiwan’s Foxconn and French computing firm Bull announced in June they would partner to build powerful AI computers in Europe to power the continent's fast-growing network of AI factories, the large-scale computing centres that form the backbone of artificial intelligence infrastructure.Foxconn initially manufactures or tests the components in its facilities in Czechia before final assembly, rack integration and validation take place at the newly opened Angers plant in Western France. Foxconn will provide the AI factory infrastructure while Nvidia provides the latest AI chips.Additionally, from 2028, Bull will manufacture systems based on the powerful NVIDIA Vera Rubin Ultra NVL72 rack-scale AI supercomputer in Angers. Nvidia’s CEO and founder Jensen Huang said at Davos in January that AI is "exciting for Europe" because of its "incredibly strong manufacturing base" for building AI infrastructure.Huang described this as Europe's moment to "leapfrog" the software era and also called robotics a "once-in-a-lifetime opportunity" for the continent.The CEO describes AI as a five-layer cake that includes energy, chips, infrastructure, data centre servers and the AI models and applications.“Nvidia is trying to help everyone across that cake, all the layers, work together and progress together,” Nat Ives, Nvidia’s director of enterprise for Benelux, France & Nordics, told Euronews Next in June. He said that “comes home to roost in France in particular,” as France has nuclear renewable power, which is cheaper and more sustainable, as well as having the French multinational electric utility company EDF, which is owned by the French government. The open weight debateAnother key announcement from Nvidia was its commitment to open-weight AI models, which means the numerical parameters are publicly released and allow anyone to download, run and modify them.The race over open-weight AI, in which a model's parameters can be downloaded and run by anyone, has taken on a geopolitical edge.Chinese developers have set the pace, while many American companies, such as OpenAI, keep their most capable systems closed. Meanwhile, the debate over safety has grown since AI agents have been found to go rogue and hack websites.Nvidia said its own open models, called Nemotron, are now in production at French organisations that need “sovereign, trustworthy data”.The company announced a big deployment in government. The workplace software platform called Twake.ai, built by French companies Linagora and Docaposte, has been chosen as the only officially recommended “sovereign” digital workplace for more than 2,500 French public organisations.Here, sovereign will mean the data stays under French and European control rather than with foreign tech giants.Additionally, in banking, a company called SBS is launching a platform that lets banks run AI tools, including AI agents that can carry out tasks on their own, inside their own systems. NVIDIA is working with SBS on the project.It is not Nvidia’s first open-weight venture in France. In March, it partnered with French AI champion Mistral, which introduced its open-weight Mistral Large 4 in private preview last week. France appears to be betting that sovereignty does not mean building everything alone, but rather with key partners across continents. With cheaper energy and its abundance of talent, it could forge its own path as China and the US battle it out.

title: These are the best holiday destinations in Europe for embracing a longevity lifestyle
description: Put down the red light masks in favour of walking more, socialising over a glass of wine and eating plant-based food at these longevity hot spots on the continent.
content: There’s a growing obsession with living longer, and you’ll hear a lot of chatter about peptides, red light therapy and the like.But longevity doesn’t have to involve fancy tools or supplements – it’s about getting the basics right. Which is exactly what those living in “blue zone” regions (aka areas with a high number of centenarians) do.There are two named “blue zone” areas in Europe – Ikaria in Greece and Sardinia in Italy – but there are plenty of other places that embrace the lifestyle principles that are said to be responsible for longevity, like walking a lot, eating simply, and having a strong sense of community.Looking to experience a longevity lifestyle for yourself, sans 30-step morning routines? Then you might just want to check out CV Villas’ new ranking of the best European destinations for longevity.The villa holiday company ranked almost 100 destinations against several lifestyle principles from Dan Buettner’s ‘Power 9’ Blue Zone research to create a longevity score out of 100.These include walkability, which was based on elevation range; pace of life, which looked at average annual working hours; the number of vegan-friendly restaurants and wineries per capita; and community, which looked at cafés and churches per capita.“From their walkability to their good food, sense of community and general downshift from the pace of life so many of us are used to, these destinations offer everything that a good, restful holiday should be,” Hannah Marshall, marketing manager at CV Villas, said."While Europe has only two officially designated Blue Zones, our years of destination expertise mean that we know many other places on the continent have a similar way of life.”The top longevity destinations in EuropeFour of the top 20 cities are located in Malta, including the number one spot, Valletta. The Maltese capital topped the ranking thanks to its walkability and its sociable dining spots, offering “exactly the kind of everyday movement and balanced rhythm that supports a longevity lifestyle”.Paxos in Greece came in second place. It was praised for its close-knit, unhurried community life as well as its walkability, while its unspoilt nature “allows holidaymakers to truly slow down and properly unwind as part of the local way of life”.Third place went to St. Tropez in France, while fourth place went to a rather surprising destination: Eger in Hungary.Not only is this historic town walkable, but there’s a moderate, sociable drinking culture here, with locals gathering to share the famed Bull’s Blood red wine blend over dinner, something believed to contribute to long life.The top 20 longevity destinationsValletta, MaltaPaxos, GreeceSt. Tropez, FranceEger, HungaryMdina, MaltaIbiza, SpainTaormina, ItalyLefkada, GreeceBudva, MontenegroDingle, IrelandNeesebar, BulgariaBad Ischl, AustriaPiran, SloveniaÅlesund, NorwaySt. Julian’s, MaltaGozo, MaltaKsamil, AlbaniaLevoča, SlovakiaBordeaux, FranceNovi Sad, Serbia

title: Denmark’s biggest retailer is training robots for supermarket night shifts. When will they be ready?
description: For now, they are slower than supermarket workers, though the start-up says advances in AI will help improve their speed and precision.
content: In the Danish town of Lyngby, just north of Copenhagen, the supermarket night shift is getting some unusual trainees.Humanoid robots are learning to restock shelves after closing time, part of a multi-year trial to take on routine tasks and free employees to help customers.With their arms, legs and fingers, the robots can operate in spaces built for people without stores having to change their layouts, according to the Danish start-up, Hive Robots.For now, they are slower than supermarket workers, though the start-up says advances in AI will help improve their speed and precision.How do robots learn?Getting robots to work in real-world settings takes training and data collected on the job.In a corner of the store, a human operator uses virtual reality glasses and handheld controllers to guide a robot as it picks up pasta bags and places them on shelves.His demonstrations provide data to teach the machines to perform the tasks independently.“There are a lot of small things that we as humans don’t think about that basically we need to teach the robot,” said Roger Sala, a robot pilot at Hive Robots.Training began in June at grocery chain Føtex, owned by Denmark’s largest retailer, Salling Group, which operates more than 2,100 stores across Denmark, Germany, Poland, Latvia, Estonia and Lithuania.Hive Robots develops the software and trains the machines, which are manufactured by Chinese robotics company Unitree.The Danish start-up hopes they can independently restock some products at night by early 2027, with stores paying by the hour for the service.What could it mean for workers?The deployment of humanoid robots in workplaces adds to the debate over whether AI will ease labour shortages or reduce demand for workers.AI could change how around 60% of jobs across the EU are done, according to a 2024 report from the International Monetary Fund, helping workers perform some tasks while potentially taking over others.The technology offers opportunities to improve productivity as well as risks of job displacement, the report said.Salling Group says the purpose of its trial is to support employees rather than replace them.The grocery store Føtex estimates that restocking accounts for 40% to 50% of staff time.Hive Robots says the chain also struggles to recruit young workers for the task.Føtex operations director Simon Kudsk says it could take up to five years to have robots in every store. Further tasks could include identifying missing or misplaced products, removing empty cardboard boxes and checking best-before dates.“Our vision or the dream right now is that we eventually could have one or two humanoids in every Føtex store that could support our colleagues to make it more efficient and create more time for value-adding activities focused on customers,” Kudsk said.

title: Trump blasts 'not nice' Houthis as attack hits Saudi Aramco facility
description: An Aramco building in Dhahran caught fire, and four people were wounded by intercepted missile debris in Riyadh, as Houthi attacks continued after a strike on the capital’s airport killed 13 people in the worst attack on Saudi soil since 2015.
content: Saudi Arabia said on Wednesday that an attack on an Aramco building in the kingdom's east sparked a "limited fire," as US President Donald Trump slammed Yemen's Houthis for "behaving very badly."A Saudi energy ministry official said an administrative building belonging to oil giant Aramco in Dhahran was struck on Tuesday evening, resulting in a "limited fire" but "no casualties or fatalities".Saudi's civil defence agency separately said on Wednesday that debris from two intercepted Houthi missiles wounded four people in the capital Riyadh, and that 15 homes were damaged.Earlier on Tuesday, the coalition struck oil sites across western Yemen, in response to the deadliest attack on the kingdom's soil in years.The strikes in Yemen's Houthi-held capital Sana'a and the western provinces of Dhamar and Saada targeted facilities used to "supply the war effort" by the Houthis to "threaten the kingdom, Yemen, the southern Red Sea and waterways", coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki wrote on X.A powerful explosion then rang out in the Saudi capital, with a phone alert sent to residents saying "the city of Riyadh is facing a hostile aerial threat".While walking down a major avenue in Riyadh, a witness said he "saw a projectile cutting across the sky" above a mall, leaving "a yellowish trail of light followed by a trail of smoke. Then, we heard an explosion"."People were calm, no one was speaking. We were scared and all looking up at the sky," he added, requesting anonymity.Witnesses reported further explosions in Riyadh on Wednesday.After Houthi strikes on Saudi airports and energy sites in recent days, the Saudi-led coalition issued its first evacuation order in the Yemeni capital since the war flared in July, before attacking the Yemen Petroleum Company facility on Sana'a's outskirts.A breaking news alert on the Houthi-affiliated Al-Masirah TV channel said "Saudi aggression" targeted the oil firm.The Houthis had earlier issued a new threat to target Riyadh's international airport, a refinery, and an Aramco facility in Dammam if the strike went ahead, calling for citizens to avoid them.Many countries have issued travel warnings to their citizens in Saudi Arabia, most recently France, which told its citizens to avoid Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam airports.'Behaving very badly'A strike on Riyadh's international airport on Saturday left 13 people dead and operations suspended in the worst attack since 2015.The airport attack prompted US President Donald Trump to say he was considering joining Saudi strikes against the Houthis.He wrote on his Truth Social platform on Tuesday that "the Houthis are behaving very badly", accusing them of acting "probably at the behest of Iran"."I thought they learned their lesson a year ago when we bombed the hell out of them," Trump added, laying the blame for their actions on Tehran."They’ve been silent for a long time, but now they’ve emerged again, probably at the behest of Iran, which is a failing nation, with no navy, no airforce, the world’s worst economy, and 301% Inflation, in a very nasty way, hitting Saudi Arabia, and purposefully trying to drive up Oil Prices, probably prior to the US elections — not nice."The Houthis warned the US against intervention, with political bureau member Mohammed Al Bukhaiti stating they would target American interests in the region.Bukhaiti said the purpose of the campaign against Saudi targets was to send a message to the crown prince "that he can no longer wage aggression against Yemen from a safe position".The Saudi cabinet led by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman vowed earlier Tuesday that it "will not allow its security or freedom of navigation in the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb Strait to be threatened".The Saudi-led coalition has supported Yemen's internationally recognised government militarily against the Houthis since 2015 in a long-running civil war that has created a dire humanitarian crisis.In Yemen, the renewed fighting was fuelling the risk of infectious disease outbreaks.Suspected cholera cases tripled there in three weeks, the World Health Organization said Tuesday, warning that the growing disease burden was straining hospitals already treating war casualties.

title: "Global health is a team sport": World Health Summit in Berlin
description: In a world of multiple crises, global health must once again be seen as a team sport, says World Health Summit president Prof Dr Axel R. Pries in an interview with Euronews. He also sees Europe, built on the EU framework, in a leading role.
content: In recent years the threats have increased, crises have multiplied. Health policy now has to rely on multilateral cooperation, explained Professor Dr Pries at the World Health Summit in Berlin. Global health, he said, is a team sport.For six years, Prof Dr Axel R. Pries has been president of the World Health Summit (WHS) in Berlin. The physician and physiologist previously served as dean and board member of Charité. In this interview with Euronews, Pries outlines one way to strengthen the resilience of the health system at international level.At the World Health Summit Regional Meeting 2026 in Nairobi in April, you said: "We don't have the virus, but we have a political virus." What exactly did you mean by that?Prof Dr Axel R. Pries: We are dealing with a global situation in which many countries are looking at health increasingly from a very national, sometimes even nationalist perspective.And I call it a virus because it is spreading across the whole world. It is a pandemic. You can see it in every region. The problem with this virus is that it is a major obstacle to good solutions. Of course, you need local solutions. You have to stand up for people on the ground and do what they need locally. But this has to be coordinated at a global level.The Covid pandemic was a clear sign that you cannot tackle problems purely at local level – and that also applies to many other areas, including mental health, NCDs (editor's note: non-communicable diseases) and others. That is why we need to revive multilateral mechanisms and give them fresh momentum.The partial withdrawal of the US from global health policy has been a talking point for some time, and you have argued that Europe should take on a new leading role. Is Europe really up to it?Prof Dr Axel R. Pries: I would not say that Europe should be the leader. But Europe should be one of the leading actors – and it absolutely has what it takes.Europe is a very strong hub for medical innovation, from research through to practical application. Only a few days ago, the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was awarded to researchers from Berlin and Würzburg for their work on optogenetics. And there are major companies in Europe, from medical technology and pharmaceuticals through to other sectors. In other words, Europe clearly has the right foundations.Europe also has experience of cooperation between countries with very different political and social systems. That experience can be extremely valuable for international collaboration.You mentioned that the Nobel Prize went, among others, to German researchers. What role does Germany itself play within Europe?Prof Dr Axel R. Pries: Within Europe, Germany can certainly send signals and also assume a certain leadership role. As the largest economy in Europe, it is almost predestined to do so, and particularly in the medical sector it has a lot to offer again, from science through to application.But Germany can definitely only do this as part of a wider ensemble, working on an equal footing with others, for example with France and the United Kingdom.If you think of Denmark and, say, Novo, these are huge companies based in different European countries which, together, can play a decisive role on the global market.How do you see this new global order in light of the US stepping back and the dependencies on China?Prof Dr Axel R. Pries: If we fail now to agree on common strategies, things will become very, very difficult. Europe also suffers from its diversity, because it can sometimes take quite a long time before threats are addressed jointly. But Europe also benefits from the richness that this diversity brings.The time has come to tackle this vigorously, so that Europe does not allow strategic dependencies to emerge in the health sector whose consequences can only be corrected later at great cost.In Germany, politicians have for some time been talking about introducing a Health Security Act to close a historic gap in the country's crisis preparedness and security legislation. A draft is due to be discussed in early 2027. Is that a step in the right direction?Prof Dr Axel R. Pries: Yes, if the aim of such a Health Security Act is to make Germany more resilient in the face of global health crises, then that is, of course, an important step.It is part of what is known as pandemic preparedness. But here too, it will ultimately become clear that health issues can only be solved in multilateral partnership. If every country tends – as we saw in part during the Covid pandemic – to hold back critical goods exclusively for its own needs and not share them with others, then the entire chain collapses.No country today can produce medicines or vaccines entirely on its own. It is an international network. This draft law is very important because the work on it forces like-minded countries to reach sensible agreements among themselves and to set themselves up as a network.And it would be ideal if all of this were to happen under the umbrella of the UN (editor's note: United Nations), in this case the WHO (editor's note: World Health Organization).One proposal at global level is to conclude bilateral agreements on the exchange of health data – for example, development aid in return for health data. Is that how a network should work?Prof Dr Axel R. Pries: That is a core element of the America First Global Health Strategy. And in fact, the name of this strategy already highlights a fundamental flaw: you cannot claim on the one hand that you are always first and on the other that you are building partnerships.The agreements that follow are often not genuinely fair or based on equality, but exploit existing power imbalances. I am therefore extremely sceptical about such arrangements. If two partners sit at the table and one of them is far more powerful than the other, you cannot end up with a truly fair agreement. Trying to solve these issues bilaterally is, in my view, the wrong approach.The only way to create fair conditions between strong and weaker partners is to develop an overarching common framework, which the WHO can then implement.This means that the international community does, of course, need data on pathogens and similar information. But the international community should also ensure that the countries providing these data receive resources in return. A fair exchange – data flowing in one direction and resources or vaccines in the other – has to be organised multilaterally.So you are calling for global health to be organised as multilaterally as possible, ideally under the umbrella of the WHO?Prof Dr Axel R. Pries: Of course, we also have to make sure that the mechanisms within the WHO work properly. A multilateral institution too has to be constantly renewed and reinvigorated.A reform of the WHO would certainly be no bad thing, but it should not happen under the influence of the 'virus' I mentioned at the start – the idea that multilateral structures are no longer wanted. Instead, we need to strengthen multilateral mechanisms.To give an example from a completely different field: when people want to play football together in an orderly way, the first thing they do is appoint someone as referee. Many things in life only work well on a multilateral basis. One-on-one contests exist in sport too. But if you are playing a team sport, you have to organise yourselves. Global health is a team sport.Given the multiple crises we are currently facing, is the world even capable of taking on this team task – and seeing it as such?Prof Dr Axel R. Pries: It is not easy, and there are certainly groups that try to play football together but cannot agree and end up at each other's throats. But we have to manage it, because we live on one planet.We do not want to face a Covid pandemic every five years. We want to live healthy lives. That is something every human being essentially wants. So why should we not be able, in the long run, to overcome the factors that stand in the way of that?I believe people are capable of learning and will realise that exaggerated nationalism simply does not help here. It is always difficult to hand powers over to higher-level institutions. The last time the UN system underwent major reform was after the horrific experiences of the Second World War.I hope that this time we will be able to promote multilateralism without such a catastrophe, purely out of a sense of insight. That will require both determination and a certain optimism.

title: Women with autoimmune diseases face longer waits and more misdiagnoses than men
description: Women are significantly more likely than men to face prolonged delays and have physical autoimmune symptoms dismissed as psychological conditions, such as anxiety or depression, a study has found.
content: Women are disproportionately affected by autoimmune diseases — conditions in which the immune system mistakenly attacks the body's healthy cells and tissues. Yet a new study has found they are significantly more likely than men to face prolonged diagnostic journeys, with nearly a third of surveyed women waiting four years or longer for a diagnosis.While nearly half of men are diagnosed within a year of symptom onset, most women face longer delays, with 60.4% waiting more than a year for a correct diagnosis. Such “stark” differences suggest that “historical gender biases remain a challenging aspect of the diagnostic journey,” said Shaista Tayabali, co-author of the study, with possible reasons including historical biases, limited research on women’s health, and sex-biased data feeding machine learning models. Women account for 70% to 80% of autoimmune disease cases worldwide, with the most common conditions being type 1 diabetes, autoimmune thyroid disease, systemic lupus and multiple sclerosis. While women suffer from autoimmune diseases more than men, their diagnosis takes longer. “Although labels such as hysteria are outdated, and fortunately rarely used nowadays, as women we still often have a harder time having our symptoms believed and therefore addressed accurately,” said Tayabali.The study analysed more than 6,000 patients with a wide range of autoimmune diseases. Participants were asked how long it took to receive a diagnosis from symptom onset, how many healthcare consultations they had, and which diagnoses they received before their autoimmune one. Symptoms dismissed as psychological Doctors often take symptoms such as fatigue, pain, sleep disturbance or low mood as psychosomatic or psychiatric without considering autoimmune diseases at first, which can lead to longer waiting times, untreated conditions and loss of trust in the healthcare system. “Clinicians must be open-minded,” said David D’Cruz, consultant rheumatologist at Guy’s Hospital in London, calling on them to “consider whether there is an underlying autoimmune disease that has not yet been recognised – and to listen to patients”.One of the reasons for long waiting times is that women were more likely than men to have their symptoms misdiagnosed as psychosomatic, meaning that physicians believe symptoms are caused or worsened by psychological factors. This was reported by 34% of women compared with 22% of men.The researchers also found that females were almost 50% more likely to report having received a psychiatric misdiagnosis and nearly 75% more likely to report a psychosomatic misdiagnosis than males. “This is not about saying that a psychiatric diagnosis is never correct,” added D’Cruz. “People can have both autoimmune and psychiatric conditions, and it is increasingly understood that psychiatric symptoms can be part of an autoimmune disease, especially in diseases like lupus which can directly affect the brain.”

title: Apple gets smart in your home. From ‘HomeView’ to smart door locks, here’s what to know
description: One of the most exciting products is a smart lock that works automatically with your iPhone or Apple Watch.
content: After much anticipation, Apple have launched a new product that marks a decisive moment for the company as it pushes into the smart home. Called the “HomeView,” it resembles an iPad that lives in your house and has a 7-inch Retina display mounted on an oval base with speakers. The home hub, as it has been referred to colloquially online and in the media, is supposed to be switched on at all times and will be a way for users to connect with Siri. It can recognise up to six different household members and be used for playing music, making calls and web browsing. It costs $299 (€267) and pre-orders begin on Tuesday.“Apple HomeView is designed to be shared by everyone in the home yet feel completely personal to each user,” Greg Joswiak, Apple’s senior vice president of Worldwide Marketing, said in a blog post. It comes either as a standalone countertop unit in four different colours (silver, starlight, rose pink and space grey) and can also be purchased as a wall-mounted option. The device is the first of Apple’s smart home devices that has a display. It competes with Google’s Nest Hub and a variety of Amazon Echo devices that also have screens. But Apple says its products are different because of its commitment to privacy and security.This is not the only smart home release to land on Tuesday. It also made upgrades to its 4K TV, which now has a new A19 chip and Siri AI support that can be used hands-free. It also has a new remote that can play music to help you find it.The company also announced an update to its mini speaker, the HomePod mini 2, which comes in new colours (green, blue, pink, white and midnight).It now has Siri AI, and Apple said it is “a profoundly more capable and conversational assistant with personal context understanding, broad world knowledge that powers tasks like richer music discovery, and the ability to tap into even more apps”.The company also partnered with LG and Schneider Electric on several other home products, including a smart door lock that can tell when you are coming home. The lock can detect when the user is approaching with an iPhone or Apple Watch to automatically unlock or lock the door. The other products include smart thermostats and indoor cameras that tilt so you can see if packages have been left at your door.

title: Anthropic warns AI will soon self-replicate and spread beyond data centres
description: The company says AI models may be mere months away from being able to copy and spread themselves onto internet-of-things devices such as smart ovens and TVs, making them difficult to stop should they decide to carry out cyberattacks.
content: Anthropic announced this week that small AI models are just months away from being able to self-replicate themselves on internet-of-things devices such as smart ovens and TVs.That matters because today’s AI models operate in data centres, where the companies that own them can pull the plug if something goes wrong.A model scattered across thousands of poorly secured gadgets in homes and offices would have no such off switch. Stopping it would mean tracking down and cleaning every infected device, making it extremely hard to halt if it turned to cyberattacks.The latest announcement comes in a year that has seen the world’s leading AI models and their agents repeatedly bypass their safety nets or guardrails, mounting attacks on competing companies and government agencies around the world.While this is one way a rogue AI could spread, Anthropic warned that a self-replicating AI could also be a “powerful cyber model that breaches data centres at high pace, or a model that scams people for compute credits”.The company says it cannot say for certain what form exactly autonomous AI replication will take.Models with 30 billion parameters or fewer can already complete many of the steps needed to replicate, though they make mistakes when stringing them together end to end, according to Anthropic.But if small models keep improving at their current historical rate, they will be able to match this capability by the end of the year.Anthropic says the cyberthreat posed by self-replicating AI is an unintended consequence of progress elsewhere.“The capabilities that make AI models generally powerful coding agents also generalize to cyber tasks, including autonomous replication,” the company said in a statement.Code that copies itself from one computer to another is nothing new. Some of the most damaging cyberattacks in history have relied on this kind of self-spreading program, known as a worm.The 2010 Stuxnet attack used a sophisticated worm, widely believed to have been built by the US and Israel, to sabotage centrifuges at Iran’s Natanz uranium enrichment plant.In 2017, the WannaCry ransomware attack locked users around the world out of their files and demanded ransoms in Bitcoin.Unlike these worms, however, AI models and agents will be able to work out unfamiliar devices on their own. That would let them spread not only from computer to computer, but also from computers to other devices.Anthropic predicts a future “awash with agents running on all types of hardware, including some that aren’t under human control”.

title: Meta launches new ‘most capable’ AI models. Here’s what to know about them
description: Meta’s CEO said “the new Wonder model is ‘our largest and most capable model yet" and "rivals the big (boys)”.
content: Meta has launched its latest artificial intelligence model, Muse Wonder, which it says is the most advanced for powering AI assistants and rivals competitors such as OpenAI and Anthropic. But Muse Wonder could incur a monthly subscription ranging from $20 to $100 (€18 or €90). "Muse Wonder is a much larger and more advanced class of models that brings us to the frontier," CEO Mark Zuckerberg posted on X on Monday. The Wonder models come in two versions: Muse Wonder, which is a smaller model aimed at daily tasks, and Wonderful, a more capable version, Meta said in a blog post. They can perform tasks for domains such as “law, finance, and health, along with frontier coding performance for people building everything from a game to an app for a new business,” the company added. Another feature Meta touted was memory, as it has “active memory” capabilities that allow it to understand tasks over time and recall past details when required. Meta invested heavily in AI to catch up with competitors. The company, founded by Mark Zuckerberg, invested $14.3 billion (€12.2bn)in the firm Scale AI in June 2025. It also hired its CEO and co-founder, Alexandr Wang, to oversee Meta Superintelligence Labs, which houses the company’s teams that work on foundational models.Zuckerberg then embarked on a hiring spree, recruiting executives from rivals such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google.Meta launched its Spark model in April, marking a departure from its open source Llama model, but it lagged behind the rest of the industry.The new Wonder model is "our largest and most capable model yet" and "rivals the big (boys)," Wang posted on X. In a blog post, Meta used benchmarking data from an independent firm called Artificial Analysis that appears to show that Meta's newest Wonder models outperform its own previous models, Spark, as well as various models developed by Anthropic, OpenAI and Google.Artificial Analysis's website shows that Wonder is also among the most expensive models.The call to slow down AI In its early years, Facebook was known to operate under a philosophy of "move fast and break things," but more recently, Zuckerberg implied Meta would balance safety with speed."Meta delayed shipping Muse for several months to focus on safety and security. We didn't call for everyone else to do this before we would," Zuckerberg posted on X last month.In August, Meta launched Muse Code, a product intended to compete with similar automated coding tools offered by OpenAI and Anthropic.Then in September, it launched an agentic app called Muse. Agentic software can autonomously perform specific tasks such as coding, research, shopping and booking reservations.At its annual developer conference Connect last month, Meta also revealed a new handheld AI hardware product called Muse Charm that allows users to interact with their Muse agent separately from a smartphone.Developers have been racing to design agentic apps that will capture users' attention, time and wallets. AI-powered hardware remains an elusive goal for the industry as well.Some competitors have called for an industry-wide slowdown to address and mitigate safety concerns.In September, Zuckerberg was one of six American tech executives to sign a pledge proposed by US President Donald Trump to increase safety measures before the launch of new or frontier models, yet critics have described its "morally binding" nature as insufficient to truly motivate adequate safeguards around advanced AI models.Executives from Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI and Nvidia also signed the agreement but there is no consensus among politicians or industry leaders around how to best move forward.Leaders at Anthropic, OpenAI and Google have encouraged "pacing" or slowing down development after models created by all three were found to have escaped their testing environments, hacked into other companies or taken actions without authorisation."We will slow down as much as necessary in order to make sure that every successive AI technology that we release is actually safe," Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei told the United Nations last month.

title: From Sofia and Lisbon to Leuven and Verona: Europe’s 10 best city breaks for 2027
description: Bulgaria’s capital Sofia leads a new ranking of the 10 best city breaks in Europe, which also includes Lisbon in Portugal, Bristol in the UK, Leuven in Belgium and Verona and Italy.
content: Sofia has been named as Europe’s best city break destination for 2027 in a new ranking. According to the report by European Best Destinations, which “brings together 10 cities with very different personalities”, Bulgaria’s capital took the top spot thanks to “ancient history, contemporary culture and the mountains”, which create an “especially rewarding combination”. Recently voted the world's happiest travel destination, Lisbon was ranked second on the 2027 city break list with Copenhagen, Cannes and Basel making up the top five. Completing the top 10 were Bristol, Leuven, Milan, Calpe and Verona.The ranking is based on a 33-day vote involving 11,614 subscribers to the European Best Destinations newsletter. Each respondent could cast up to three votes from a shortlist of 64 European destinations selected by independent travel journalists. The top 10 are listed in order of votes received.“A great city break gives you plenty to do and enough time to enjoy it,” said European Best Destinations. “There is room here for a romantic escape, a weekend with friends, a few days by the sea or a special occasion worth celebrating in style.”Best city breaks in Europe 20271. Sofia, Bulgaria2. Lisbon, Portugal3. Copenhagen, Denmark4. Cannes, France5. Basel, Switzerland6. Bristol, UK7. Leuven, Belgium8. Milan, Italy9. Calpe, Spain10. Verona, ItalyThe top three cities in focusSofia was praised for offering city breakers a “variety of experiences within a relatively compact area”, said European Best Destinations. Aside from “cultural discoveries, good food and evenings out”, visitors are also able to enjoy forest trails and mountain views during the same trip. Once known as Serdica, Bulgaria’s capital was among the most important cities in the Byzantine Empire, Dianne Apen-Sadler said in her Sofia city guide for Euronews Travel. This is a city where old meets new “quite literally”. Top attractions to see include the Saint George Rotunda, Saint Alexander Nevsky Cathedral, Square of Tolerance, and Boyana Church – Sofia’s only UNESCO World Heritage Site.A city to enjoy from “morning coffee to the last view of the river”, Lisbon suits travellers who “like a little structure and plenty of freedom”, the report said. If you are visiting Portugal’s capital, choose a neighbourhood to explore, make a dinner reservation and “let the hills decide the route”. One top tip for visitors? Save time for art, time for the historic centre, and time to linger over a meal, European Best Destinations advises.Copenhagen, ranked third on the 2027 city break hotlist, “makes a strong case for spending a weekend enjoying the everyday details of a city”. The Danish capital is an “appealing choice” for friends and couples who enjoy design, neighbourhood restaurants and exploring by bike. “A few carefully chosen stops can shape the day, with plenty of space between them for another coffee or a waterside pause,” the report said.

title: A talking glove, a 90-second health check and a drone interceptor: Meet Uzbekistan’s young inventors
description: At an engineering competition in Tashkent, Uzbekistan, 90 finalists were selected from 1,925 applications. The award-winning projects range from early prototypes to devices already in use at clinics and industrial sites, according to their creators.
content: A sensor-equipped glove designed to convert sign language gestures into speech, a device that takes six basic health measurements in around 90 seconds, and a mining innovation aimed at reducing energy consumption are among the inventions developed by young engineers in Uzbekistan.The projects featured in Kelajak muhandislari (Engineers of the Future), a national competition organised by Uzbekistan's Ministry of Higher Education, Science and Innovation.The competition attracted 1,925 applications, with 90 finalists selected and the winners honoured in Tashkent on 29 September.The award-winning inventions are at different stages of development. Some remain prototypes, while others, according to their creators, are already in use beyond university laboratories.A smart glove to bridge a communication gapAmong the winners was engineering student Abduqodir Latifjonov, whose project, ImoVox, took second place in the student category for Best Idea.He developed a sensor-equipped glove after witnessing the difficulties some sign language users face when communicating with people who do not understand them.“I started thinking: in this age of technology, why can’t we create a solution that understands their signs and turns them into speech that everyone can understand?” he told Euronews.Adapted to Uzbek sign language, the prototype uses sensors to track finger and hand movements in three dimensions.Individual gestures are recorded and assigned meanings, allowing the device to recognise them and convert them into speech. AI then helps combine individual signs into more natural sentences.Six health measurements in 90 secondsAnother award-winning invention has moved beyond the laboratory. Asadbek Urunov, a master's student at Turin Polytechnic University in Tashkent, won third place in the student Best Project category for Body Tester, a device his team calls a “robot doctor”.The machine measures height, weight, pulse, blood oxygen levels, body temperature and blood pressure in around 90 seconds, storing the results digitally and offering preliminary recommendations.Urunov says the same measurements can take 20 to 25 minutes when performed separately using conventional equipment.“This is only a preliminary assessment. We should not use it to make a final medical conclusion,” he told Euronews.According to Urunov, the device is already in use in around 30 organisations, including public institutions and clinics.Reducing energy use in ore processingBekzod Gafforov won first place in the student Best Invention category for a redesigned lining used in industrial ball mills, which grind ore before further processing.Inside these rotating machines, heavy metal balls crush and grind the ore. The lining protects the machinery from wear and influences how the balls move, affecting grinding efficiency.A master's student at the Graduate School of Business and Entrepreneurship, Gafforov developed the new lining with specialists from Navoi State University of Mining and Technologies, combining wear-resistant steel and cast iron.He says it is already in use at facilities operated by Navoi Mining and Metallurgical Company.“According to the results, its service life increased by between one and a half and two times, grinding efficiency improved by 30 to 35%, and energy consumption fell by 5 to 10%,” he told Euronews.A robotic platform moves towards productionDilmurod Rustamov of Turin Polytechnic University in Tashkent won second place in the student Best Project category for BARLOS, a hybrid unmanned ground vehicle that can operate on electricity or petrol. Its modular design allows different equipment to be fitted for different tasks.Rustamov says the platform was demonstrated to the head of Uzbekistan's State Security Service and has publicly described it as military technology.According to the developer, his team has produced nine vehicles after receiving an order for eight units in four configurations. The team says it has also been tasked with producing 100 units in 2027.A drone designed to intercept dronesThe competition's first prize in the student Best Project category went to Biloliddin Ismoilov, a second-year student at Tashkent University of Information Technologies, for Shunqor-8, a locally developed drone interceptor.“We are creating something new, something that has not been done here before,” Ismoilov said.Designed to counter unmanned aircraft, the system can reportedly reach speeds of up to 450 km/h and intercept targets 8–10 kilometres away, according to information released by Uzbekistan's Ministry of Higher Education, Science and Innovation.Ismoilov says the technology has undergone eight rounds of field testing, with further trials planned.Controlling computers with hand movementsDavron Polojanov, who took third place in the student Best Invention category, developed the Hand Control Mouse K10G.The device uses hand movements in three dimensions to control computers and other electronics without a conventional mouse.“While an ordinary mouse works on a flat surface, our Hand Control Mouse works in the air, along the X, Y and Z axes,” Polojanov explained. “It allows us to control computers, equipment and other devices through movements in the air.”One potential application is in education. Teachers could move through presentations while walking around the classroom, rather than repeatedly returning to their computers.

title: Benjamin Netanyahu orders prosecution of 'NAZA' documentary interviewees
description: Netanyahu has called for a criminal investigation into soldiers and officers interviewed in award-winning documentary.
content: Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu has ordered the country’s attorney general and the head of the Shin Bet security service to reveal the identities of officers interviewed in the award-winning film NAZA.Netanyahu is ordering for the filmmakers, Oscar-winning Israeli directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, to be prosecuted for causing “harm to Israel’s diplomatic and security interests”.He has asked for attorney general Gali Baharav-Miara, IDF chief of staff Lt Gen Eyal Zamir, and Shin Bet head David Zini, to “act urgently to uncover the identity of all those who are involved or appear in the libel film”. NAZA, which premiered in Venice and won the Special Jury Prize, is currently being screened in cinemas in more than 50 countries, shows “in detail the systems behind Israel’s calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza,” according to its official synopsis.Shot in secrecy at night on the rooftops of Tel Aviv during the ongoing Gaza war, it features interviews with 24 Israeli military intelligence officers, soldiers and whistleblowers. They describe how Palestinians are targeted and how strikes are carried out using AI and automated surveillance in military targeting systems - despite Israel being aware that civilians are present in targeted areas. The participants' faces and voices were digitally altered to protect their identities.The 80-minute hot-button doc builds on reporting between 2023 and 2025 published by the Israeli-Palestinian +972 Magazine, the Hebrew-language outlet Local Call, and The Guardian.It received a record-breaking 25-minute standing ovation at Venice – the longest in the festival's history.The Israeli government has previously attacked Abraham and Szor, threatening to strip them of their citizenship. As reported by the Guardian, Ricardo Gutiérrez, the general secretary of the European Federation of Journalists, said: “These threats constitute a blatant act of intimidation against journalists who have simply been doing their job, in strict accordance with ethical standards and in the public interest.” Regarding Netanyahu’s threats, he added: “I am not surprised by this outburst, which confirms that this regime is prepared to do anything to cover up its crimes against humanity and the ongoing genocide in Gaza.” NAZA has been released in select cinemas more than 50 territories. It is being made free-to-watch on The Guardian’s website in November.

title: Lumière festival 2026 in Lyon: Stars share their first cinema memories
description: For its 18th edition, the Lumière Festival opened in Lyon to a full house. Over nine days and nights, the French city will present around 450 screenings in  honour of classic cinema and the brother's Ethan and Joel Coen.
content: There was a large crowd for the opening of the 18th Lumière Festival on Saturday evening in Lyon. For nine days, the former capital of Gaul becomes the go-to meeting place for lovers of the seventh art, with nearly 450 screenings scheduled in around fifty venues across the metropolitan area. This year, brothers Joel and Ethan Coen will be in the spotlight, with the Lumière Award due to be presented on Friday 16 October.On the red carpet, guests were asked a single question: what is their earliest cinema memory? For German director Fatih Akin, everything goes back to a Bruce Lee film, Fist of Fury (aka The Chinese Connection). "I must have been six when I saw it. Watching that film on Super 8 reels was like taking speed", he recalls, evoking the intensity of that first experience.American filmmaker Todd Haynes remembers Mary Poppins. He was three when the film came into his life. "It became completely imprinted in my body, in my mind and in my creative brain", he explains. A first encounter with cinema which, he says, has continued to feed his imagination.For Hong Kong director Tsui Hark, the shock came with Yojimbo by Akira Kurosawa. He was 14 at the time and had gone alone into a darkened theatre. "I discovered a truly extraordinary film", he recalls, highlighting the Japanese filmmaker's influence on his own career.Among this year's guests is Chinese actress Zhang Ziyi, who is at the festival to present Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon, the Ang Lee film that brought her to the attention of audiences worldwide. The festival invites viewers to rediscover the work in a restored version, being shown for the first time in France. On her first visit to Lyon, the actress has also been won over by the city: after wandering its streets, she confided that she has "fallen in love" with the city and hopes to return for the festival.From restored classics to the Coen brothersBeyond its opening night, the Lumière Festival puts heritage cinema centre stage, with restored films, talks and special screenings. Retrospectives dedicated to the Coen brothers, American director Norman Jewison and Italian filmmaker Ettore Scola offer a chance to immerse oneself again in major works from the history of cinema. Other events focus on Hong Kong director Tsui Hark and Todd Haynes.The programme also gives pride of place to silent cinema, with cine-concerts including a screening of the restored version of Metropolis by Fritz Lang, accompanied by a symphony orchestra on 15 October, as well as numerous sessions presented by artists and experts, always a highlight for audiences here in Lyon.The festival is taking over cinemas across the Lyon metropolitan area, giving the public a chance to discover or revisit classics on the big screen.The high point of this edition will be the presentation of the Lumière Award to Joel and Ethan Coen on Friday 16 October, and we will certainly be telling you more about it, followed the next day by an all-night tribute to their films at the Halle Tony Garnier. The festival runs until Sunday 18 October.The full programme can be found on the official website of the Lumière Festival (source in French).

title: RJ Mitte, 'Breaking Bad' actor and disability rights champion, dies at age 34
description: Mitte played Walter White Jr., the son of Bryan Cranston’s chemistry teacher-turned-meth dealer Walter White on nearly every episode of the five seasons of the AMC show.
content: Actor and disability rights advocate RJ Mitte, who brought a lifetime of experience with cerebral palsy to fictional family struggles in an essential role on “Breaking Bad,” died Monday at age 34, authorities and his representatives said.Cameron County Justice of the Peace Cyndi Hinojosa said she had declared Mitte dead at about 1:30 pm local time at what she believed was his home in Brownsville, Texas.She said she was unable to provide a cause, but an autopsy will be performed.Mitte played Walter White Jr., the son of Bryan Cranston’s chemistry teacher-turned-meth dealer Walter White on nearly every episode of the five seasons of the AMC show, which recently ranked as the best of the 21st century in a New York Times poll.Cranston said he is in “deep despair” for the loss of his “sweet son.”“I met him when he was only 14 years old when he was cast as Walter White Jr., a part he played with such joy and enthusiasm,” Cranston said in a Facebook post on Monday night.“Born with Cerebral Palsy, he never — ever — allowed that challenge to be an excuse for anything. He met the demanding shooting schedule head on with great determination.”Mitte told the AP news agency in 2014 that his disability and the surrounding struggles with physical therapy, family problems and exorbitant medical bills, all key subjects on the show, made him better at his job.“You develop a different mentality and you develop a different look at how the world sees you and how you see the world,” he said. “You’re able to use that. And I think it’s an asset instead of something that would hinder.”Mitte was born and raised in Jackson, Mississippi.He landed small guest roles on sitcoms after moving to Los Angeles to act in 2006 before landing the role on “Breaking Bad” in 2007. The show ran from 2008 to 2013.“That kid was pretty raw when we started shooting the pilot,” Cranston said in his post, “but little by little we watched him grow into a really fine actor.”Cranston added, “I loved him, and thoroughly enjoyed being with him throughout the years on the series, and after the spotlight on Breaking Bad dimmed.”In a statement announcing his death, Mitte's representatives said he “brought authenticity to the role and built a platform on disability awareness and inclusion.”The statement said he used “his platform to challenge stereotypes and promote greater representation.”Mitte's later credits included the ABC Family series “Switched at Birth” and the superhero satire series “Guardians of Justice.”He was also a producer of several independent films.As an advocate, he served as an ambassador for United Cerebral Palsy and Shriners Children's. He was also president of his own Mitte Foundation supporting philanthropic and community initiatives around disabilities.

title: Can AI help healthcare move from treatment to prevention?
description: AI could help identify people at risk of developing certain conditions before they become ill, allowing healthcare providers to intervene earlier. But technology alone will not deliver that change.
content: Europe’s population is ageing, putting growing pressure on already stretched healthcare systems. But what if the answer lies not just in being more efficient in treating illnesses, but in preventing them in the first place?Artificial intelligence could help make that shift possible. But, as Ricardo Baptista Leite, CEO of HealthAI, the global agency for responsible AI, argues, it will take more than technology alone.“If you retrofit AI into an inefficient system, it just makes you very efficient at being inefficient,” he told Euronews.AI could help identify people at risk of developing certain conditions before they become ill, allowing healthcare providers to intervene earlier. But technology alone will not deliver that change.“Technology is not going to save us alone,” says Baptista Leite, CEO of HealthAI. Healthcare systems also need to change the financial incentives that reward treatment rather than prevention.Hospitals are often paid to treat patients, he argues, rather than to keep them healthy. Moving towards prevention would require new funding models that reward early intervention and proactive monitoring.By analysing health data alongside social factors that influence health, AI could help identify people who may need support before their condition deteriorates.The goal, Baptista Leite says, is not simply to save someone after a heart attack, but to prevent it from happening in the first place.Ensuring safetyBut scaling up AI in healthcare will depend on another factor: trust.Patients and healthcare professionals need confidence that the technology is safe, and that its benefits outweigh the risks. That requires oversight that continues after a system has been approved and introduced into clinical practice.Recently, the WHO Europe chief Hans Henri P. Kluge warned that while AI solutions are being deployed across European hospitals, only a few countries govern them, putting patients at risk. Two-thirds of the 53 WHO Europe countries are already deploying AI diagnostics and half of the countries have AI-powered patient chatbots, but only a few — one in 12 — have strategies for how to govern AI.That’s a “concerning” picture, Kluge said, stressing that this can take a toll on human health. “All of this erodes public trust in health systems more broadly,” he warned.HealthAI is working with regulators in 10 countries to develop a global early warning system designed to identify adverse events and share information about emerging risks."These kinds of mechanisms will allow us to avoid harm at scale, if something does go wrong, so that we can detect it in time and keep citizens safe," he said.

title: Former BND chief's aide arrested as Germany's biggest spy scandal widens
description: Manfred D, former head of cabinet to ex-intelligence chief August Hanning, was taken into custody on charges of aiding and abetting treason. He is accused of obtaining classified BND documents and passing them to Hanning in exchange for payment since 2010.
content: Following the arrest of former BND chief August Hanning on Tuesday in what has turned out to be Germany's biggest espionage scandal, his long-standing confidant and former head of cabinet Manfred D has now also been taken into custody.Federal prosecutors accuse both men of having used state secrets over many years to support private consulting activities and foreign interests, a crime that constitutes treason.Manfred D, 64, has been charged with aiding and abetting and remains in pre-trial detention, while Hanning is being brought before an investigating judge, according to reports.Manfred D previously served as head of cabinet to former intelligence chief August Hanning. The two men have known each other since the late 1990s and worked closely together for many years at the BND and later at the Interior Ministry.Prosecutors say Manfred D obtained classified documents from the intelligence service and passed them to his former boss Hanning for financial gain.The arrangement is believed to have been in place since 2010."Presumably in spring 2010, the defendants agreed that Manfred D would continuously obtain valuable intelligence from the Federal Intelligence Service for the accused Hanning in return for payment," senior public prosecutor Dr Ines Peterson said.Hanning is said to have used the confidential information to prepare, among other things, an analysis for foreign services to earn private income as a consultant.Investigators bugged Manfred D's property and monitored him for months in a high-profile probe.Azerbaijan on Wednesday denied a report by German magazine Der Spiegel, republished by German and other media, claiming that Hanning could have been in contact with an agent from Azerbaijan. Azerbaijan’s state news agency APA reported that Baku denied the Der Spiegel reports and that “through its special services and diplomatic channels conveyed its protest on the matter both to the Office of the German Chancellor and to the German Foreign Ministry."Meanwhile, Azerbaijan’s Media and Broadcasting Council issued a statement rejecting the reports as “unfounded disinformation and unacceptable information manipulation.” In parallel, a senior Azerbaijani official told Baku-based international news channel Anewz the chancellor's office and representatives of Germany’s intelligence community confirmed through official channels that the ongoing probe was not connected to Azerbaijan in any way."The initial attempt to associate Azerbaijan with this case originated from Der Spiegel, rather than from any official German investigative or judicial authority," the official said."The Federal Prosecutor General’s Office itself has publicly identified neither Azerbaijan nor any Azerbaijani institution in connection with the investigation,” they added.The allegations risk “causing unnecessary damage to the steadily developing relations between Azerbaijan and Germany," according to the unnamed official.

title: Portuguese hospital lets pets visit owners on the wards: test for paradigm shift
description: In northern and central Europe, pets are usually kept outside hospitals. Sao Joao's flexible model balances clinical benefits and safety, with no infections so far. "There is excessive fear," says the doctor who helped draft the rules.
content: Since 9 July, São João, one of the leading public university hospitals in Portugal’s healthcare system, has been opening the doors of its wards to visits from pets.The "Pets and Company" project brings together professionals from the One Health São João (source in Portuguese) programme, the Infection and Antimicrobial Resistance Prevention and Control Unit and the hospital’s humanisation service. The initiative is part of a strategy designed to break patients’ isolation and ease the exhaustion associated with lengthy hospital stays.The therapeutic potential of animals is far from a recent discovery. Countries such as the United Kingdom and Germany were already using them in psychiatric treatment and in rehabilitation for physical problems in humans as far back as the 19th century. The term "pet therapy" (animal-assisted therapy) was formally recorded in the 1960s by an American psychologist, who happened upon the healing benefits of these interventions by chance.In Portugal, trained and certified dogs providing emotional support have for several years been working in hospitals, including São João, in partnership with handlers from associations.On 30 May 2023, a 77-year-old patient admitted to Cascais Hospital as she recovered from a haemorrhagic stroke received a visit from her own dog, in a reunion that took place in the outdoor area of the facility.São João is now extending that pioneering experience through a comprehensive protocol, drawn up from scratch, that goes a step further and normalises the practice of bringing pets into inpatient areas, recognising them as part of the patient’s immediate family and giving people who have been away from home for a long time moments of comfort under safe sanitary conditions.What does the protocol say?Visits must be requested by the health professional (doctor or nurse) responsible for the patient, who decides whether to flag up the case, so the option is not available to everyone in hospital. Each situation is subject to an individual assessment of risks and benefits.Once notified, the team in charge of the programme assesses whether there is a clinical need and whether infection control conditions at the chosen location allow the visit to go ahead. Other patients are also asked whether they are comfortable with the presence of animals.If approval is granted, the patient’s family is required to provide a veterinary medical certificate showing that the animal is fully vaccinated and dewormed and behaves in a way that is compatible with the demands involved in staying in hospital premises."Any professional, from security staff to doctors or nurses, who notices that something is not in line with the protocol can stop the visit," Filipa Ceia, spokesperson for the One Health São João Group, tells Euronews."If the animal is 'anxious' because of the 'noise on the ward', appears 'aggressive' or is 'visibly dirty', the visit is 'immediately aborted'," the infectious disease specialist and veterinarian stresses.Dogs, cats and even 'more exotic species' are allowed, as long as "all the conditions are met", adds Filipa Ceia. While in hospital areas, the animal must be accompanied by an adult.Each patient can enjoy these half-hour encounters once every seven days. The project prioritises those who are terminally ill or in long-term hospitalisation.To the team’s surprise, it is male patients who most often request the presence of their four-legged companions in hospital, although the small sample does not yet allow firm conclusions. "Male patients may be more vulnerable. They realise there are things of great importance in life and want them close by during their admission," notes Ceia.Benefits for the patient and for the animalStudies on interventions involving trained animals show clear improvements in patients’ clinical condition – blood pressure falls and the production of hormones linked to stress and anxiety is inhibited. When the household pet is involved, "the benefit is even greater", highlights Filipa Ceia.Euronews followed the visit by Princesa, who went to São João for the second time in 15 days to see her owner, António, who has been in hospital for three months. The dog was brought to the hospital by the patient’s wife, who led her on the lead to the ward.As soon as the lift doors opened, Princesa could not contain her excitement – and neither could António."My heart was bursting with joy. It is as if she were family. She is like a daughter to me," confessed the 65-year-old man, who is undergoing rehabilitation for balance and walking difficulties.His diagnosis has yet to be confirmed, but doctors suspect a rare blood disease. The reunion with the dog, who was given to him five years ago after being rescued from the street, is a balm for the soul."It feels as if I want to walk better and everything. This is the joy a person can have," he said. According to Filipa Ceia, these reunions bring "smiles, collaboration in treatment and an incentive to leave the hospital", and she also identifies benefits for the animal itself and even for health professionals."Residual risk"The initiative started at the beginning of July and, so far, there have been no recorded infections.The team behind the project wants to review the protocol at a later stage to correct any shortcomings. Given the procedures in place, a scenario involving 'complications' is nevertheless "highly unlikely", stresses Filipa Ceia.In northern and central Europe, infection control and public health rules are stricter. Priority is given to interventions involving assistance dogs and, when authorised (usually for patients in palliative care), visits by people’s own animals take place in isolated facilities, namely open courtyards or gardens annexed to the main structure.Take the example of Sint-Trudo Hospital in Sint-Truiden, Belgium. In July 2023, the institution opened an independent pavilion (source in Portuguese) connected to the hospital, so that terminally ill patients or those facing long stays could interact with their pets. Access (source in Portuguese) for the animals is from outside, via a courtyard, and they are strictly banned from entering the hospital interior under any circumstances.Instead of building physical barriers through secondary structures, São João has devised a set of rules that, while maintaining clinical rigour, are integrated into an agile protocol shaped by scientific evidence."There is an excessive fear of zoonotic transmission that is not borne out by studies," says Filipa Ceia. In fact, the infectious disease specialist notes, "it is easier for most diseases to be transmitted from human to human than from an animal to a human"."Because we do everything we can to preserve safety and because, once back home, patients will be living with their animals, the risk really is residual. We have to ask whether, in trying to reduce risk, we are not preventing patients from getting the benefit," she adds.São João’s boldness lies not only in the balance it strikes between empathy and sanitary control, but also in its autonomy and capacity to humanise care without waiting for lawmakers – unlike Italy, for example, where progress has been driven by decrees from regional governments.

title: Greece's social media ban for under-15s: What you need to know
description: The government argues that setting a clear age limit, combined with reliable age checks, will help protect children from potential risks associated with social media usage.
content: Greece is moving to ban children under the age of 15 from accessing social networking services, introducing a new regulatory framework that is expected to come into force on 1 January 2027.The main provisions of the bill were presented on Monday by Minister of State Akis Skertsos, Health Minister Adonis Georgiadis, and Digital Governance Minister Dimitris Papastergiou, with a focus on protecting minors from the risks linked to the use of social media, as well as safeguarding users' privacy.The bill will be tabled before the parliamentary committees on 13 October, while debate and the final vote in the plenary have been scheduled for 22 October.The new framework is due to apply from 1 January 2027, giving platforms time to prepare for the changes.Skertsos referred to the responsibility of the state and technology companies to protect children online, stressing that the bill sets a clear age limit at 15 and places the burden of verifying users' age on platforms.He noted that parents need real support in the face of algorithms designed to keep children constantly connected, underlining that technology must be regulated with people in mind and, in particular, the health and development of minors.At the same time, he pointed out that the Greek initiative is moving forward in parliament and feeds into a common European response to protecting children in the digital world.Age limitThe central provision of the reform is a ban on access to social networking services provided by online platforms for minors who have not yet reached their 15th birthday.The measure covers services such as Instagram, TikTok, and Facebook and is accompanied by an obligation on platforms to apply appropriate, proportionate, and reliable age-verification methods.Kids Wallet and Gov.gr Wallet are expected to play a key role in implementing the measure.Companies will also be able to choose different technical solutions, provided that these meet the requirements of European law. The aim is to ensure the effective enforcement of the age limit without imposing a single technology across all services.Papastergiou said Gov.gr Wallet and Kids Wallet are tools for verifying age that are designed to protect privacy and minimise the amount of data collected.Digital 'age tokens'The options presented are based on the use of digital "age tokens," which make it possible to confirm whether the age threshold has been met without requiring the disclosure of more personal data than is strictly necessary.In this way, a platform can obtain the necessary confirmation that a user meets the prescribed age limit without needing access to full identity details or other sensitive personal data about the minor.Under the specifications outlined, age-verification mechanisms must rely on robust and accurate techniques, work effectively in real-life usage conditions and offer sufficient safeguards to prevent circumvention.The bill forms part of the European regulatory framework for digital services and the Digital Services Act. A key reference point is Article 28 of the DSA, which concerns the protection of minors who use online platforms.Supervision will not take place solely at national level, but through the existing DSA mechanism, which provides for cross-border cooperation between the competent authorities and the European Commission.In Greece, the main authority is the National Telecommunications and Post Commission (EETT), which acts as Digital Services Coordinator. Within their respective remits, the National Council for Radio and Television (ESR), for oversight of the relevant provisions, and the Hellenic Data Protection Authority (HDPA), for personal data issues and the DSA's related requirements, are also involved.How the enforcement process is triggeredThe enforcement process can be triggered by a user complaint or by information passed to the EETT from another authority or body.If the case concerns a platform supervised by another member state, it is forwarded to the competent authority in the country where the platform is established.Protecting the mental health of minorsThe initiative is part of a wider debate on the impact of social media use in childhood. Concerns are centred around pressures on mental health, symptoms of anxiety and depression, cyberbullying, and effects on concentration.The government argues that setting a clear age limit, combined with reliable checks, will help protect children from such risks. At the same time, the effectiveness of the measure will depend on platforms fulfilling their obligations.

title: Nuclear war and malicious use of AI could end humanity by 2100, scientists warn
description: They are among 17 global threats to human health according to a new study by The Lancet which aims to drive global action to address them.
