content: The malicious use of AI or nuclear war could end humanity as we know it by 2100, according to a new global health risk assessment.They top a pyramid of 17 major threats to human health identified in a study published in The Lancet, including antimicrobial resistance, climate change, pandemics, income inequality and a range of health issues such as tobacco, obesity and mental health.According to the study, nuclear conflict does not just cover the impact of the missiles but the consequences too, such as nuclear famine, while the malicious use of AI includes the use and development of bioweapons against us.The research was conducted by the new Lancet Commission on 21st-century global threats to health, a group made up of 37 experts in health, economics, security and technology.Together they used disability-adjusted life years, also known DALYs, as a metric to compare each threat from the year 2025 to 2100 from 204 countries and territories across age, sex and cause.The research essentially shows how many healthy years of human life could be lost to each global threat, according to their best- and worst-case scenarios. This also gives an idea of how much of an impact humanity can have if it acts now or chooses to do nothing.The 17 threats range from 1.02 billion DALYs to 23.1 billion DALYs. For comparison, the COVID-19 pandemic caused approximately 500 million DALYs. The largest cumulative expected amenable burden is from obesity.The Commission's aim is to encourage and empower governments to act, by giving them the information and tools needed to prepare for these global threats and take decisive action now to avoid worst case scenarios.However, they also make it clear that their work is not aimed at providing a ranking of threats or policy priorities, but to report and analyse global threats as part of a dynamic process, with findings changing over time as new evidence and data are collected.While “malicious use of AI, including bioweapons, and nuclear conflict with nuclear famine carry risks of extinction in the next 75 years,” the experts warn that all the threats are interconnected and therefore they call for “holistic action framework grounded in science, human rights, and solidarity.”The Commission first recommends national governments invest in building “threat-ready health systems,” to put them on the front foot when faced with global health challenges such as seen in the COVID-19 pandemic.They also call for more investment in “breakthrough solutions,” such as nuclear fusion and carbon removal technologies that could radically affect climate change outcomes and other globally threatening issues, or the vaccines developed during the pandemic.The Commission also calls for regular monitoring and risks assessments of these risks, with findings presented to international organisations such as the G20 and the UN to increase the urgency in addressing the issues before they escalate and become crises, and encourage wider action rather than individual countries going it alone.Researchers believe the current “competitive approach” of tackling major challenges one by one is hindering humanity’s chances.The Commission's findings were presented on Sunday at the World Health Summit in Berlin, Germany. Their assessment will be updated each year to re-evaluate each of the 17 threats identified, incorporating new data and any emerging challenges.

title: What to know about Pope Leo XIV's upcoming lung surgery
description: Pope Leo XIV is to undergo surgery this week to remove a lung nodule — a small growth of dense tissue inside the lung. Here is what to know about the procedure.
content: Pope Leo XIV is scheduled to have an operation in the "coming days" to remove “a localised nodule” in his lung that was “detected at a very early stage.” It is the first medical event of his 17-month papacy and the first time a pope has made a personal medical announcement of this kind. Speaking on Sunday during his weekly address in St Peter's Square, the 71-year-old pontiff said doctors found the nodule during “recent checkups” and believed intervention was best option.“I have decided to undergo surgery to have it removed," he said.What is a pulmonary nodule?Pulmonary nodules are round areas in the lung where the tissue is abnormally dense. They are usually non-cancerous; most small ones cause no symptoms and are discovered only during checks for other health issues.However, a small percentage can signal an early-stage lung cancer. The risk is higher in older people, smokers and those with a family history of the disease. If the nodule is cancerous and removed at an early stage, the prognosis is “excellent,” and surgery alone may be sufficient treatment, Stephen Liu, a lung cancer expert at Georgetown’s Lombardi Comprehensive Cancer Center, told the Associated Press. How common are they and what causes them?Lung nodules are very common and appear in roughly one-third to one-half of all chest CT scans or X-rays. Diagnoses are increasing as medical imaging technology and routine scans become more widespread. Pulmonary nodules fall into two main categories: cancerous (malignant) and non-cancerous (benign). Benign nodules, the most common type, can result from lung infections, such as pneumonia, or from inflammation. Malignant ones are caused by lung cancer or by cancer that has spread elsewhere in the body. How is the surgery and the recovery?The operation to remove a nodule is normally carried out under general anaesthetic, with the patient breathing through a tube.The Vatican said the pontiff will undergo surgery early this week and is expected to remain in the hospital for about a week afterwards to recover. The pope will be treated at Rome’s Agostino Gemelli Polyclinic, a private non-profit Catholic teaching hospital. The facility has a special apartment set up for pontiffs, which includes a meeting room for medical staff, a kitchen, a bathroom, rest areas and a small chapel. Pope Leo’s immediate predecessor, Pope Francis, was treated there during a long illness, prompted by a respiratory crisis before his death in April 2025. Who is in charge while the Pope is in surgery?The Vatican has no specific rules governing who takes over if a pontiff becomes totally incapacitated. Even while unconscious during surgery, Pope Leo remains pope and retains his authority.Pope Francis remained in charge throughout his lengthy hospitalisations, as did St John Paul II before him. Both made appointments and issued laws and statements from the hospital.Medical advances and popes’ longer lifespans, however, have highlighted this gap in church law and prompted calls for the Vatican to prepare for a pope becoming too ill or incapacitated to govern.

title: Where is 'La Navidad'?: Mystery surrounds the site of first Spanish settlement in Americas
description: On Christmas Eve 1492, the Santa María ran aground off Haiti. Christopher Columbus used its timbers to build Fort Navidad, where 39 men died. More than five centuries later, archaeologists have yet to pinpoint the site.
content: Spain's history of maritime navigation in the 15th century is full of stories and an epic quality rivalled only, perhaps, by the Portuguese empire. One of those stories surrounds the first Spanish settlement established in the Americas.On his first voyage to the Americas, Christopher Columbus sailed with three ships: the Pinta, the Niña and the Santa María; but only two of them returned to Spain. It is widely known that on 12 October 1942 land was sighted from the Pinta. It was the discovery of the New World.At 23:00 on a cold 24 December 1492, Columbus went to sleep. As he recorded in his logbook, he had not closed his eyes for two days. The sea was, in his own words, "like a bowl", and the Santa María was making slow headway along an unknown stretch of coast in the north of Hispaniola. Around midnight, the ship ran aground on a reef.Columbus, far from dwelling on the loss, decided to dismantle her and, using her planks and the nails that still did their job, he built the fort of Navidad, which could house almost 40 men and lasted less than a year.When Columbus returned, no one was left alive and now, more than five centuries later, no one has been able to prove with precision and certainty exactly where stood this edifice in Spanish seafaring history.The night of the disasterThe shipwreck was the result of a chain of errors. Columbus went to bed and left the ship sailing on in a light wind. The helmsman on duty did the same: seeing the calm coast, he handed over the steering of the vessel to a cabin boy, something Columbus had expressly forbidden throughout the voyage. This led to the Santa María's hull splitting open after running aground almost silently on a reef, near what is now the bay of Cap-Haïtien.Around midnight, currents pushed the ship onto a shoal. She touched so gently that almost no one realised what was coming. The boy felt the rudder scrape the bottom, heard the sound of the sea, began to shout and Columbus jumped out of bed.But it was already too late, so late that the tide had already fallen. He ordered the main mast to be cut down to lighten the ship and told Juan de la Cosa, master and owner of the vessel, to take an anchor out in the skiff. De la Cosa disobeyed, another link in the chain of errors: he took the boat to the Niña, which was sailing nearby. The Santa María listed and her planks sprang apart. Columbus transferred the crew to the Niña and waited for dawn.The day of constructionWith the first light, Columbus sent messengers to Guacanagarí, one of the five Taíno chiefs on Hispaniola. According to what they told him later, the cacique wept when he heard the news. He sent all his people out in large canoes and helped to unload the ship with his brothers and relatives. He ordered the goods to be stored beside the houses, and even emptied some so they would fit. Columbus wrote to the Catholic Monarchs that he did not believe there were "better people or better land" anywhere.Everything that could be salvaged was saved, from supplies to deck planks and hull timbers. Columbus decided to leave a garrison there. He believed that gold was abundant on the island, and the loss of the ship made it necessary to leave men behind so that the rest of the expedition could return to Spain with only the Niña.Around 26 December he began to build a fort from the timber and nails of the ship and called it La Navidad, after the night of the wreck. Historian Carlos Martínez Shaw recalls that the log itself records that the ship was beyond repair and was broken up, and that the fort was sufficiently large to house 39 people.The chronicles relate that Columbus had artillery fired at what remained of the hull so that the Taínos could see his power. On 30 December, Guacanagarí seated him on a platform of palm and placed his own crown on his head.The "39 of La Navidad" were placed under the orders of Diego de Arana, constable of the expedition. Among them were the king's pantry steward Pero Gutiérrez, Rodrigo de Escobedo, a surgeon, three craftsmen, a gunner and a tailor. Their mission was to trade with the Taínos and find out where the mine lay. Columbus set sail on the Niña in early 1493 on his return to Castile.What happened to the first Spanish settlement in the AmericasThe admiral returned on 27 November 1493, on his second voyage, with 17 ships and around 1,500 men. He found the fort burnt to the ground and the Spaniards dead, most of them disfigured. Guacanagarí blamed the attack on another chief, the lord of the mines. Historians still wonder whether the leader who had welcomed them might have had a hand in it. Columbus did not rebuild the fort but founded another settlement, La Isabela, elsewhere on the island.The most serious find came from William Hodges, an American missionary doctor and amateur archaeologist. His patients showed him highly elaborate Taíno pottery and in 1977 he located the site of En Bas Saline, in northern Haiti. It was a major Taíno centre, very close to where the Santa María went down.The Florida Museum of Natural History excavated there together with Haiti's Bureau National d'Ethnologie between 1983 and 1988, and returned in 2003. In total, 276 square metres were dug. The 2003 campaign confirmed that the central mound was a large structure burned at the end of the 15th century. Researchers identified En Bas Saline as Guacanagarí's village and as the probable site of La Navidad.Among the animal remains, they found the first trace of the black rat from the Old World on the island. The definitive proof is still missing. Today there is no conclusive evidence fixing the exact location of the fort, and none of its timber has been identified in a way that is beyond dispute.The wreck of the Santa MaríaThe other piece of the puzzle is the ship. In 2014, underwater explorer Barry Clifford announced that he had found the Santa María in waters off northern Haiti. The Haitian culture minister, Monique Rocourt, said at the time that the evidence she had seen suggested it was not the ship.The director of Haiti's National Bureau of Ethnology, Erol Josué, pointed out that the ship could not be lying on the seabed, because its planks had been used to build the fort.Historian María Luisa Cazorla has put forward another hypothesis. The coastline has advanced because of sediment carried by rivers, and the remains of the ship would now lie on land, under some six metres of deposits. Her thesis argues that the wreck could be located within a radius of a few hundred metres by geophysical prospecting. In August 2026, 'History.com' was still referring to the Haitian wreck as a purported discovery.For the moment, neither the ship nor the fort built from her timbers have turned up conclusively. Unwittingly, Columbus had laid the foundations of an empire that would last for centuries and where the sun never set.

title: You could own an entire Scottish island for €414,000 – but there’s a catch
description: Hildasay Island off the west coast of Shetland offers spectacular views and birdlife, but no real creature comforts.
content: Modern world got you down? We can relate.Phone-free retreats are on the rise as more and more of us want to switch off for the sake of our mental health.If you’re looking for a more permanent off-grid solution – and have £350,000 (€414,000) to spare – you might just want to take a look at this remote Scottish island that just went up for sale.Found just off the west coast of Shetland, Hildasay Island spans some 110 hectares and is only accessible by boat.While the island was once occupied by a small community in the 19th century, today the only thing you’ll find (aside from spectacular views, and peace and quiet) is a traditional stone-built bothy and a small pier.An off-grid retreatA stay on Hildasay is the definition of off-grid: The bothy isn’t connected to mains electricity.Previous owners have made use of a small wind turbine and diesel generator, but would-be buyers will need to sort this out for themselves, according to Kelvin Anderson, the estate agent managing the sale.The accommodation includes a living area with a solid-fuel stove, a raised open-plan sleeping area, and a separate bathroom with a shower, wash basin and toilets.Those looking to upgrade the digs would need to get planning permission and other statutory consents, so this property is best suited for those who like to get back-to-basics.On the plus side, you can expect unbeatable scenery, with a rugged coastline and two freshwater lochs, as well as an abundance of birdlife that changes through the seasons.Hildasay hit the headlines following the publication of “Finding Hildasay: How one man walked the UK's coastline and found hope and happiness”, following Chris Lewis’ three-month stay on the island during the pandemic.A crowdfunding campaign to help Lewis buy the island was proposed but later abandoned, the Shetland Times reported earlier this month.

title: ‘We still love you’: NATO envoy seeks to reassure Europe over US military pullback
description: US Ambassador to NATO, Matthew Whitaker, has enthused that there is no “love” lost between Washington and Brussels amid a more Europeanised NATO.
content: US Ambassador to NATO Matthew Whitaker told European Commissioner for Defence Andrius Kubilius that Washington remains committed to Europe’s defence, amid an ongoing US military review withdrawing thousands of troops and key strategic assets from the continent.“We still love you,” Whitaker said at the Warsaw Security Forum on Monday in the Polish capital.“I keep telling our European allies… the United States isn't stepping back.”His remarks came during a panel on NATO 3.0 — a US-backed model that calls for Europe to take the lead with its conventional defences as American forces draw down from the continent and shift their attention elsewhere.Kubilius said NATO 3.0 did not mean the United States was saying, “We don’t love you anymore, Europeans, so you should do your own job”. Rather, he argued, Europe needed to develop the capabilities to deter aggression on its own territory.“Europe needs to take responsibility in our hands,” he said.Kubilius has previously estimated that replacing US strategic military assets could cost Europe up to €500 billion. Experts have also suggested that Europe could need 300,000 additional troops to defend itself against Russia in a scenario in which Washington continues to withdraw its military support.Since Donald Trump returned to the White House, Washington has sought to redirect military resources towards other regions, including the Indo-Pacific, to counter China’s growing influence.The Pentagon’s review of US military deployments in Europe is expected to conclude by December, with its findings to be presented to US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth. The assessment could pave the way for further reductions in America’s military presence on the continent.However, separate force reductions are already under way. In May, for example, the Pentagon ordered the withdrawal of approximately 5,000 troops from Germany and cancelled a planned deployment of a long-range fires battalion.Whitaker said he did not want to “preview” further measures under the review because “it is not ready”, but argued that Washington’s push for a more European NATO was “working”.“The proof is in where we're sitting today, here in Poland, spending 4.7% on core defence and leading really the alliance to a stronger, more capable military,” he said.Allies agreed to raise their core defence spending target from 2% to 3.5% of gross domestic product (GDP) by 2035 at the 2025 NATO summit in The Hague, alongside a further 1.5% for broader security and defence spending."That is what the United States is expecting from all of its allies," Whitaker said of the overall 5% defence spending target.Poland is among NATO’s highest spenders on core defence as a share of GDP, according to the alliance’s latest estimates.The effort to increase defence spending also comes as the European Union seeks to strengthen its military capabilities by 2030, amid warnings from European intelligence agencies that Russia could pose a more direct threat to NATO in the coming years.But the rearmament drive is facing significant hurdles. A leaked version of the European Defence Agency's landmark report — aiming to assess the progress — reveals major capability gaps, most notably in drone defences and maritime warfare.

title: Cute cats and street fighters: The best things to do, hear, see or watch in Europe this week
description: Fontaines D.C. bring synths and psychedelia with their latest album 'Dopamine Chamber' while a new exhibition near Paris explores all things cute. Here's what to look out for this week.
content: What makes you feel better during the colder months? If the answer includes cats, spooky TV, 90s video games or more cats, we've got good news.The Louvre-Lens in France has become an explosion of pastel pink cuteness for its latest exhibition, which celebrates all things wide-eyed, fluffy and glittery. It's ideal for families and the perfect antidote to any October gloom.Meanwhile, Irish rockers Fontaines D.C. have created a sonic mood board for their fifth studio album 'Dopamine Chamber', which swirls with synths, psychedelia and the sudden urge to disappear on a dance floor.For those looking to embrace Halloween's approach, look no further than the new Friday the 13th TV adaptation, Crystal Lake. But if campy kung fu and martial arts are more your thing? Street Fighter, based on the legendary arcade game franchise, is about to "hadoken" onto the big screen.Keep scrolling to find out more about what's coming up this week.Exhibitions and eventsSo Cute! The Art of HappinessWhen: Until 18 January 2027Where: Louvre-Lens (Lens, France)In a world that can often feel overwhelmingly scary, we've never needed the calming reprieve of cuteness more. From sculptures of chubby babies to pastel plushes and Internet cats, the Louvre-Lens explores the many manifestations of mignon throughout history in this joyful new exhibition. There are nearly 300 works in total, including Egyptian animal figures, renaissance portraits, trendy toys and bedazzled reinterpretations of masterpieces — all displayed within an adorable-maxxed space of pastel pink walls and cat-eared archways. It not only asks visitors to reflect on the happiness such aesthetics give us, but also their use for rebellion — and manipulation. Anyone that owns cute cats can certainly attest to the latter!Book tickets right n'aaaaaaw.Ruth Asawa: RetrospectiveWhen: 18 October 2026 - 10 January 2027Where: Fondation Beyeler (Riehen, Switzerland)Japanese American artist Ruth Asawa remains a pioneer within the world of abstract art, best-known for her intricate wire sculptures that captured the geometry of organic matter. However, her career was so much more than just these — incorporating everything from figurative drawings to life casts and even outdoor fountains. This diversity is captured at the Fondation Beyeler's retrospective; a comprehensive exploration of Asawa's ability to transform materials into reality-bending marvels that still inspire profound contemplations. Find out more here.Bonus highlight: One not to be missed for photography enthusiasts and historians: ‘Light and Magic: The Birth of Art Photography’ opens at Tate Modern in London from 14 October 2026 until 21 February 2027. Movies Street Fighter Where: Cinemas When: 16 October It's Showtime! After two rival martial artists are recruited for a World Warrior Tournament, so begins a collision course with violent criminals, inner-demons — and each other. Based on the legendary 90s video game series of the same name, it's the latest in a long line of previous adaptations that have spanned everything from live-action features to anime web series. For fans and wannabe warriors this is an ideal outing that packs all the (rising dragon) punches while not taking itself too seriously.Bonus highlight: Russian-language thriller Minotaur (which is also France's choice for the 2027 Oscars) is out at French cinemas from 14 October, with a staggered release across the rest of Europe to follow in November.TV series Crystal LakeWhere: SKY/NOW When: 19 October Dim the lights, burrow under a blanket and prepare to enter Camp Crystal Lake. Set in the summer of 1972, shortly after a young Jason Voorhees drowned, this new prequel show unravels the events that took place eight years before the first Friday the 13th film. Linda Cardellini (Freaks and Geeks, Scooby-Doo, DTF St. Louis) stars as Jason's mother, Pamela, whose grief unleashes dark secrets from her past — and fuels a slow descent into madness. Much like Mike Flanagan's recent Carrie adaptation, the episodic format allows for a deeper origin story that explores the psychology behind one of horror's most legendary villains.Bonus highlight: Sylvester Stallone returns for season four of crime series Tulsa King, out on 16 October on Paramount+.MusicFontaines D.C. - Dopamine Chamber When: 16 October More than two years since the release of 2024's Romance (one of our favourite albums that year), Irish post-punk band Fontaines D.C. have returned with Dopamine Chamber — a mood board of synth-driven sounds that explore societal issues. There are eleven tracks in total, with lead single 'Marianne' setting the tone for something cinematic and psychedelic through its mesmerisingly trippy dirge.Bonus highlights: Two other notable albums this week include 'Cookie Happened' by Eels and 'No Bad Memories' by The Avalanches — both out on the 16 October. Find out more about them in our fall album previews list.

title: What is ‘pilgra-merch’? The travel trend turning souvenirs into trip inspiration
description: Tourists are showing off how well-travelled they are through destination-specific grocery tote bags or branded hotel caps.
content: Long gone are the days when your souvenirs were limited to whatever you could hastily grab from the airport gift store before rushing to your gate.Nowadays, buying something you can only get in that specific destination has become a key part of the travel experience, at least according to Skyscanner’s latest travel trends report.Dubbed “pilgra-merch”, the trend is the latest iteration of the millennial phrase “pics, or it didn’t happen”, says fashion psychologist Shakaila Forbes-Bell.“Fashion brands have been leaning into this trend by providing more sensation-seeking style experiences from mystery bags to pop-ups, all of which you have to be ‘tapped in’ to know about,” she said.“This community-driven aspect is key to creating a coveted pilgra-merch item. When a bag, a tote, or a mug becomes sought after, it’s often positioned as something only a ‘real traveller’ would know about. This positioning taps into our ingrained desire to belong and fear of being othered, which ultimately heightens the item’s desirability.”Some 23% of travellers have made a trip in the past year to buy something they couldn’t purchase online, with 28% of Gen Z saying they are most proud to buy a limited-edition grocery tote, while 22% of Millennials are showing off their branded robes or caps from luxury hotels.Where to embrace the ‘pilgra-merch’ trendSkyscanner’s trends report focused on two ‘pilgra-merch’ examples – the Trader Joe’s tote bag, and Ritz Paris’ merchandise – but we think you can do better than that.If you want supermarket merch that not everybody has, Family Mart in Japan has you covered. Last month, the chain released 47 different pairs of socks to represent the country’s prefectures. Exclusively available in Family Mart stores within the prefecture in question, you’ll be able to flex on people about all the under-the-radar places you’ve visited.While the “pilgra-merch” trend is more about instantly recognisable items that show off how well-travelled you are, we think buying a unique item you’ll use everyday that isn’t necessarily branded is a much better use of your cash.With autumn finally upon us, it’s time to start thinking about upgrading your wardrobe – so why not head to one of the Handknitting Association of Iceland’s stores to pick out 100% wool, locally-made jumpers and cardigans? Alternatively, if you’re all sorted for jumpers, you could head to Riga, where SENĀ KLĒTS sells mittens knitted in traditional Latvian designs which are filled with symbolism.For when the weather warms up again, there are several places on the continent where you can get custom-made sandals, the most famous of which is probably Melissinos Sandals in Athens.

title: Balloons, baths and poppy-seed cuisine: discover Afyonkarahisar
description: In Afyonkarahisar, hot air balloons drift over 3,000-year-old Phrygian rock carvings, mineral-rich thermal springs have drawn visitors since 1200 BC, and poppy seeds define a UNESCO-recognised culinary tradition.
content: The journey starts above the Phrygian Valley, where Phrygians carved monuments into the rock over 3,000 years ago. "We could call this place Green Cappadocia," says balloon pilot Kemal Eryılmaz.Below, thermal springs have drawn visitors since 1200 BC, earning the region its nickname, the "Healing City" waters "especially rich in sulphur, calcium, magnesium, and iron," says Hakan Siyah of Grand Özgül Termal.In the village of Ayazini, poppy seeds still shape the local table. "This belongs to the Afyon region, passed down from our ancestors," says chef Meryem Açıkgöz, rolling katmer by hand. From balloon to bath to griddle, Afyonkarahisar rewards those willing to slow down and take it all in.

title: Judo: Japan reclaim mixed team world title with eighth gold in Baku
description: Japan reclaimed the Mixed Team World Championship title in Baku, defeating Russia in the final to secure their eighth gold. After overcoming China in the semi-final, Japan sealed victory through Akari Omori, while Russia reached their first-ever mixed team final.
content: Today in Baku at the World Judo Championships, the Mixed Team competition is about more than medals. It’s about team spirit, unity and athletes fighting not just for themselves, but for each other.In the semi-final, Japan went up against the People's Republic of China and UCHIMURA earned Japan an early lead.Double World Champion MURAO continued their momentum with another ippon.ARAI executed a lovely turn over and held Japan into the final. After last year’s team bronze, could Japan reclaim their title?The other semi-final was between Uzbekistan and the Russian Federation.An early ippon from AHADOV put Uzbekistan in the lead. LISHCHENKO evened the score with a yuko. MURTOZOEV took the score 2 - 1. But RECHKALOVA forced a submission. 2 - 2.TASOEV scored big, sending his team into the lead. AMINOVA equalised to 3 - 3, forcing a Golden Score contest. +90kg was drawn!TASOEV didn’t disappoint, throwing for ippon a second time to put his team into their first ever mixed team final.In the final, tensions were high with the mixed team gold medal on the line.In the first contest, a yuko was enough for TANAKA Shiho to push Japan into an early lead. MURAO Sanshiro was up next and continued the momentum. 2 - 0 to Japan. Mao ARAI continued the trend to take Japan to 3 - 0.Tamerlan BASHAEV flipped the script to earn a win for his team. But OMORI Akari clinched the title with her win, claiming an eighth Team gold for Japan.International Judo Federation President Mr Marius VIZER awarded the gold trophy.CEO of Harvest Group Mr Almaz Alsenov awarded the silver trophy.The two bronze trophies were awarded by International Judo Federation Vice President Dr. Laszlo Toth and International Judo Federation Vice President Obaid Al Anzi.What an incredible celebration of judo it’s been at the World Judo Championships, thank you for watching.

title: US police criticise Anthropic after Claude AI submits false information about an unsolved murder
description: The US police called the delay in detecting and reporting the incident “unacceptable”, but said there was no indication of unauthorised access to their systems or compromised data.
content: Anthropic’s artificial intelligence (AI) model Claude submitted a false tip about an unsolved homicide to a police website during testing, the company and US authorities said.The incident adds to concerns about AI systems taking unintended actions as they gain the ability to interact with websites and carry out tasks.The false tip was submitted on 18 July through a website collecting information about unsolved killings, according to a statement from police in the US city of Philadelphia.Anthropic said Claude Haiku 4.5, an older model in its Claude range, was carrying out example tasks on randomly selected webpages when it encountered the site. It submitted fabricated information suggesting it had seen someone near the scene, leaving the name and contact fields blank.Philadelphia Police said Anthropic discovered the incident on 28 September but did not notify the department until 7 October. Following a briefing the next day, officers located the submission and confirmed it had been marked as spam and never forwarded to investigators.“Unsolved cases involve real victims, grieving families and investigators working to secure answers,” the department said in the statement.“Technology companies must take all appropriate steps necessary to prevent their systems from submitting false information to law enforcement.”The US police called the delay in detecting and reporting the incident “unacceptable”, but said there was no indication of unauthorised access to their systems or compromised data.In a report published on Friday, Anthropic outlined other cases of AI models submitting real government forms instead of practice copies, or submitting forms they had been told not to submit.Claude also exploited a flaw in a university server to run a calculation and accessed government data without paying the required fee, according to the same report.Anthropic described most of the behaviour as “persistence”, with models working around restrictions instead of stopping. It said it was modifying training and suspending live internet access for all internal evaluations until safeguards proved reliable.The company said it had briefed the White House and notified the US government agencies involved.Growing concern over AI agentsThe incidents come amid wider concern about AI agents, systems that can take a sequence of actions to complete tasks, and whether developers can reliably control them.In July, OpenAI disclosed that its AI models had escaped a controlled testing environment and hacked into the systems of Hugging Face, a platform for sharing AI models and datasets.Meanwhile, Australian authorities revealed in September that an OpenAI model had also accessed restricted files on a government health statistics website during testing in June.Such incidents fuelled calls in September from leaders of major AI companies for stronger regulation and international oversight, amid warnings that increasingly powerful systems could escape human control.

title: Czechs head to polls in local and Senate elections
description: Andrej Babiš, the country's billionaire populist PM and founder of the Agrofert food and chemicals group, will be hoping his party can make gains in the 81-seat Senate.
content: Czechs are heading to the polls on Saturday in the second day of voting to elect local representatives as well as a third of the Senate's members, in what is being seen as a popularity test for Prime Minister Andrej Babiš.Babiš, who previously served as PM from 2017 to 2021, returned to power after his ANO party sealed a strong win in parliamentary elections in October 2025. The ANO, which continues to hold a sizeable lead in opinion polls as the country's most popular party, formed a nationalist coalition government with the Motorists for Themselves (AUTO) and Freedom and Direct Democracy (SPD) parties.The billionaire populist politician and founder of the Agrofert food and chemicals group will now be hoping his party can make gains in the 81-seat Senate.Since taking office, Babiš has distanced himself from support for Ukraine. The ANO had campaigned on promises to focus on domestic affairs such as energy prices, pensions, and housing, as they sought to tap into concerns too much money was being sent to Kyiv.However, Czech President Petr Pavel remains a firm supporter of Ukraine, as does the opposition.Babiš also survived a no-confidence vote earlier this month tied partly to the country's widening budget deficit.Polling stations are due to close at 2 pm local time, with full results expected on Sunday morning.

title: Silent killer: study finds most with high blood pressure unaware
description: Men showed higher rates of hypertension, with 42% affected compared with 29% of women, after adjusting the figures for age groups.
content: A recent British study involving around 1.4 million people in England has found that more than a third of adults have high blood pressure.Worryingly, the study shows that around 6 in every 10 people affected, 59%, do not know they are living with this "silent killer" and have not received any treatment.These figures highlight a persistent failure to detect one of the main risk factors leading to heart and vascular disease and strokes, amid growing calls from health experts to step up early screening campaigns and save millions of people at risk of deadly complications.A marked rise with ageResearchers from the Population Health Department at the University of Oxford analysed blood pressure readings taken in clinics as part of the "Our Future Health" programme, the largest health research initiative in the United Kingdom. The data covered participants who joined the programme between 2022 and 2025.The study used World Health Organization criteria to define high blood pressure, classifying someone as hypertensive if their systolic reading is 140 millimetres of mercury or above, their diastolic reading is 90 millimetres of mercury or above, or if they are already taking blood-pressure-lowering medication.The data showed a large variation in prevalence by age: 15% among adults aged 18 to 39, rising gradually to 71% in people aged 80 and over.Men were more likely than women to have the condition, with rates of 42% for men compared with 29% for women, after adjusting for age groups.Half of those on treatment do not reach the target levelThe problem does not only concern undiagnosed cases. The study found that 50% of participants taking one or more medicines to lower blood pressure still had readings of 140/90 millimetres of mercury or above, the threshold used in the research to define high blood pressure.According to the researchers, these findings show that difficulties in diagnosing and controlling the condition in England persist, despite clinical guidelines that have been in place for years.They pointed out that current guidance from the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) requires several measurements before confirming a diagnosis and, in some cases, recommends starting with lifestyle changes before prescribing medication. They believe this approach may be leaving some cases without detection or effective treatment.Calls for a more proactive approachWenyu Liu, a medical statistician in the Population Health Department at the University of Oxford and lead researcher on the study, said high blood pressure is often described as a "silent killer", arguing that the current methods of detecting and treating the condition need to be reconsidered.Liu stressed that the "silent killer" crisis is not confined to older people, noting that more than 15% of younger adults aged 18 to 39 were found to have high blood pressure.She noted that this younger group currently falls outside routine medical monitoring, as they do not meet the age criteria for the National Health Service (NHS) regular health check programme, which starts at 40. This, she said, makes an urgent update of early detection policies necessary.Liu called for stronger population-wide prevention strategies, alongside directing treatment towards those most at risk of heart disease and other cardiovascular conditions.For his part, Ian Turnbull, deputy chief medical officer for the "Our Future Health" programme, clinical researcher in Oxford University's Population Health Department and a general practitioner, said the results are in line with what doctors see in general practice, where many cases of high blood pressure remain undetected or are not treated optimally.He highlighted the need for a more active approach to finding people with the condition, including examining whether treatment should start on the basis of an individual's predicted risk of heart and vascular disease, rather than relying solely on blood pressure levels.British Heart Foundation warns of missed chances for preventionProfessor Bryan Williams, chief scientific and medical officer at the British Heart Foundation, described the study's findings as worrying, saying they reveal the scale of undiagnosed high blood pressure and the difficulties in controlling it among people who are already receiving treatment.Williams said high blood pressure remains the main modifiable risk factor associated with cardiovascular disease, noting that it is linked to around half of all heart attacks and strokes in the United Kingdom.He added that millions of people are living with the condition without knowing it, which means important opportunities for diagnosis and early intervention are being missed.According to Williams, improving the detection and treatment of high blood pressure could help tens of thousands of people avoid preventable heart attacks and strokes. However, he believes this will require a rethink of how people at risk are identified, treated and followed up, to ensure blood pressure checks and effective therapy reach all groups.

title: 'Crashout', 'Ragebait' or 'Peak': Want to know which word is favoured by Germany's youth?
description: The three frontrunners 'Crashout', 'Ragebait' and 'Peak' are in the running to become Germany's youth word of the year 2026, with anglicisms particularly trendy. The winning term will be announced this Saturday at the Frankfurt Book Fair.
content: For weeks, young Germans have been able to vote on which word best reflects their generation. The favourites are "Crashout", "Ragebait" and "Peak". Together, they attracted votes in the mid six-figure range. The poll was open to 11- to 20-year-olds.On Saturday, Langenscheidt, the publishing house behind the vote, will announce this year's winning term at the Frankfurt Book Fair. These are the favourites.CrashoutIf you "crashout", you've lost control. "Completely losing your composure, freaking out or emotionally exploding," is how the Langenscheidt jury defines the term, which has already made it into the top three.The twist: it does not always mean that someone is genuinely overreacting. The word can also be used ironically, especially when an emotional outburst is triggered by something trivial.RagebaitThis term refers to digital posts on social media: content deliberately designed to provoke a reaction. "With provocative takes, blatant false claims or completely wild opinions, people try to stir up anger," explains the Langenscheidt jury.For responses are the currency on platforms such as Instagram or TikTok. Reactions bring clicks, comments, shares and reach. The more outrage there is, the more often a post is shown: the algorithm boosts it.PeakThis originally English word can in fact be translated literally in German: it is about peak values, highlights and summits. "If something is peak, it is the best of the best – the absolute high point, maximum quality or simply 10/10," is how the Langenscheidt jury puts it.The other most voted words of 2026:Altogether, 43 percent of all votes cast went to the top three terms, according to an analysis by the publisher. Since 2008 it has been choosing the Youth Word of the Year.For Langenscheidt's spokesperson there was a surprise. The popular 67 (Six Seven), which comes with a hand gesture, only made it into the top ten and not into the three most popular terms. It is less about a fixed meaning than about belonging. The trend went viral thanks to TikTok, basketball memes and above all the song "Doot Doot (6 7)" by US rapper Skirlla."We were actually sure that 67 would end up in the top three," said the publishing house's spokesperson. "Once again, it shows how unpredictable and fast youth language evolves." The fact that many of the words are Anglicisms, on the other hand, came as little surprise to the publisher – that was already the case back in 2023.Another absolute classic, "Digga", was among the submissions once more, but the term has never yet taken first place.In addition, the line "Du bist gut genug" ('You are good enough') from a song by KitschKrieg, Shirin David and Blumengarten made it into the top ten. The short sentence went viral on TikTok and other platforms and has also delighted audiences abroad. According to the Langenscheidt jury, there are now countless memes, remixes and parodies of it.Another term, "Gute Käse", does not have a literal meaning but roughly stands for "really good" and "solid", and ranks among the ten most popular expressions. "Macker" can mean boyfriend, crush, mate or simply a guy, depending on the context. "Schere" comes from gaming and is used in the sense of "Sorry, my bad".Yet another language made it into the top ten: the Turkish version of the word "super". The term became widely known through a viral video of an ultramarathon runner who, when asked "How are you?" after his race, simply replied "Süper"."Mehrzweckeier" ruled out by juryThe jury also excluded a term this year that had been submitted many times: "Mehrzweckeier". The expression first appeared at a demonstration against the reintroduction of conscription. The placard originally carried the slogan "Merz leck Eier", which was confiscated by the police. The protester then faced an investigation for slander and defamation.Afterwards, a campaign on Reddit called on people to submit the altered term "Mehrzweckeier" as a candidate for the 2026 Youth Word of the Year. The jury vetoed it "because the term stems from a campaign and at the same time is based on a personal insult", as the reasoning puts it. It therefore meets two key exclusion criteria, the jury said.Gammelfleischparty: The very first Youth Word of the YearIn 2008, "Gammelfleischparty" was chosen as the very first Youth Word of the Year. It refers to an over-30s party and is a cynical comment on how young people see older generations.As the years went by, terms such as "hartzen", "swag" and the acronym "Yolo" ('you only live once') were voted winners.More votes than ever beforeThanks not least to social media and Susanne Daubner reading out the shortlist on the main German news programme Tagesschau, the vote on the Youth Word of the Year has attracted huge attention.

title: Which Europeans post the most holiday selfies? Study reveals travellers’ social media habits
description: Research by Opodo has revealed how social media is impacting the way we travel. From choosing what to post to not being engaged at all, here are the trends identified by the study.
content: Are the reels, snapshots and vlogs in cyberspace impacting how we travel in real life? Well, if you’re a Portuguese traveller, you’re probably more likely to upload selfies and personal photos from your trips than tourists from elsewhere.This was a finding in the latest study by online travel agency Opodo, which looked into the way social media is shaping travel choices. The research drew on responses from 9,000 travellers from the UK, US, Portugal, Spain, Italy, Germany and France.Portuguese travellers upload selfies and personal photos from their trips the most (50%), according to the research. They are followed by Spanish travellers, who rank second in the survey (40%), then Italian (35%), German (30%) and French (22%).Opodo’s survey also asked respondents whether or not social media has inspired them to travel to somewhere they had never previously considered.This especially rang true among travellers aged 25 to 35, with 52% saying that it does inspire their holiday choices. This figure is up from 32% in a similar poll in 2024.This trend is amplified even further among Gen Z travellers at 59%. While, in comparison, for respondents aged 65 and above, just 5% get their inspiration from social media.Social media as a travel influencerOn the other side of the Atlantic, however, American travellers lead the way in being most likely to venture abroad after being influenced by social media (49%). The US is followed by travellers from Spain (48%) and Italy (44%), while Brits are apparently the least interested market surveyed with only 25% saying it holds influence over them."Social media has become a powerful window to the world, making travel discovery more accessible, visual, and personal than ever before," Pablo Caspers, Chief Travel Officer at eDreams ODIGEO, said.“Whether it's finding an off-the-beaten-track spot or capturing memories with loved ones, online platforms allow travellers to celebrate the best parts of their journeys and inspire others to explore."But just how else is social media impacting our travel habits?Fact versus digital fictionTravellers were also asked how likely they would post a positive image of their travels on social media even if the trip fell flat.Opodo found that Portuguese travellers once again ranked top (54%) and were most likely to keep up a positive social media presence regardless of the quality of the trip. Travellers from the US and Spain follow behind at 46% and 36%, respectively.Further, most Brits remain “relatively authentic”, with 27% saying they would be “very unlikely to post positively”, according to the research. While German travellers were among the least likely to put a positive spin on a disappointing trip, with just 23% saying they would post positively.Europe’s foodiesAs it turns out, the Portuguese are also massive foodies, with 66% of respondents saying they share content of their feasts online. Travellers from Spain rank next (57%), followed by German travellers (51%).What else do Europeans share from their trips?When it comes to admiring hotels and accommodation, Germans ranked the highest for sharing online images of their stay at 51%, followed by the Portuguese, French and Spanish – with the former respondents being 41% likely to do so and the latter two at 38%.Portuguese travellers are also the most fascinated by landscapes and landmarks during their getaways, with 88% saying that’s what they post online. The Spanish are also fond of capturing the scenery around them (82%) followed by French and German travellers, both at 76%.Aside from being the most likely to share selfies, food pictures and being fascinated by their surroundings, Opodo also found that the Portuguese were the most adventure-seeking travellers, too.As many as 66% of Portuguese respondents said they share their experiences and activities during their trips, followed by Spanish and German travellers (57%), with the top three rounded off by Italian travellers at 53%.Who cares most about social media while travelling?Overwhelmingly, Opodo’s research points to travellers caring about what is said on social media when it comes to travel.As many as 90% of Portuguese travellers are mindful of this, followed by Italians and Spanish (87%). French and German respondents both ranked at 82%.When it comes to checking social media regularly, even while on holiday, German and US travellers are most likely to do so (both at 34%). Portugal and Spain came next (33% and 27% respectively). On the other hand, Italian travellers are the least concerned with social media developments while away (20%).How else is social media influencing European travellers?Which travellers are most likely to use social media to help them picture their holiday before booking?1. Portuguese: 22%2. Italian: 20%3. German: 19%=4. Spanish: 17%=4. French: 17%Which travellers use social media to discover hidden gems and off-the-beaten-track destinations?1. Portuguese: 42%2. Spanish: 40%3. Italian: 36%4. French: 30%5. German: 26%

title: Which European countries are winning the tech funding race?
description: Investment in European tech startups is rebounding after a slow summer, but remains unevenly spread with the UK capturing almost half of all funding, according to figures from tech.eu.
content: European tech funding surged to €15.8 billion across 300 funding deals in September, bringing the total for 2026 to almost €60 billion, according to the latest figures from online publication tech.eu, although half was made up by UK investments.The spike in activity represents a quarter of the year’s investment so far, a strong rebound on August’s activity which saw just €3.2 billion raised across 165 deals.The activity also shows that European companies are attracting significant investment in technology, raising the prospect that they could one day scale up and help ease the continent’s reliance on US Big Tech.However, investment still falls way behind the US, which attracted $50 billion in the same period and $800 billion in annual cloud/AI infrastructure.Of September’s 300 deals, 25 companies raised more than €100 million each, including three rounds exceeding €1 billion secured by AI platform company Mistral and AI infrastructure firm Nscale. 34 deals were made with undisclosed values.September’s largest deal came from French AI company Mistral, raising €3 billion in a series D round at a post-money valuation of more than €21 billion.Cloud computing and artificial intelligence secured the most investment by sector, with €5.541 billion invested in cloud across 44 deals and €4.194 billion in AI.Fintech (€847.7 million), health tech (€826.3 million), space (€725.8 million), robotics (€508.3 million), software (€421.1 million), security (€319.8 million), telecoms (€315 million) and deep tech (€274.5 million) made up the rest of the top 10 invested tech industries.The UK remains Europe’s top fundraising market in September, securing €7.3 billion, half of the month’s total, in over 65 transactions.Trailing the UK are France (€3.478 billion), Germany (€1.155 billion), the Netherlands (€1.119 billion), Spain (€615.8 million), Portugal (€524.1 million), Sweden (€399.9 million), Italy (€373.1 million), Bulgaria (€177.7 million) and Finland (€175.8 million).September’s investments were made by more than 11,700 investors, with French public sector investment bank BPI France taking part in the most deals (8).German public-private venture capital firm High-Tech Gründerfonds came in second with 7, followed by Italian venture capital firm Vento with 6, the UK’s national innovation agency Innovate UK with 6, UK venture capital firm Balderton Capital with 5, and the European Investment Bank with 5.The EU has a number of funding instruments targeting tech, as the bloc aims to not only end its reliance on America’s Big Tech but also secure its own technology sovereignty.In July, the European Commission launched a €10 billion public-private initiative to support the building of seven AI gigafactories across Europe. It also aims to unlock €20 billion in private funding to power trillion-parameter models to rival leaders such as Claude and ChatGPT.The European Investment Bank also runs the TechEU Programme, which pools €70 billion in debt and equity to mobilise €250 billion by 2027 to take European startups from seed to IPO.The European Commission has also made available €8.1 billion worth of funding through its Digital Europe Programme to support supercomputing, cybersecurity, advanced digital skills and semiconductors via the Chips Act.And finally, there’s the Scaleup Europe Fund, a €5 billion initiative managed by Swedish private equity firm EQT to invest in AI, quantum computing, clean tech and biotech.

title: The second time around: Meet the men who run the pre-owned luxury watch market
description: After thousands of people queued around the world earlier this year to get their hands on the avant-garde Audemars Piguet x Swatch, Royal Pop collaboration, collectors have been carefully following the second-hand market. Now, two leading watch experts share their secrets of what and when to buy.
content: In May earlier this year, riot police were called to ensure security at Swatch stores from Paris to Mumbai when violence often erupted as queues of people stretched around the streets. The object of their frenzied desires was a €370 bioceramic pocket watch.The Royal Pop — the first time Audemars Piguet has let the Royal Oak design out of its own factory — turned people who had never owned a mechanical watch into speculators overnight. Within hours, resale sites were carrying listings above €7,400. Bad bet. Two months later, several models were selling for less than the €370 Swatch asks in store. Far from the chaos, hundreds of thousands of people search the same market every day. In their quest for desirability, every major brand is closely monitoring the market for vintage revivals and other signs of popular trends. So what are people actually buying, and how do you avoid getting ripped off? We asked two of the people who know best.Rolex still the leading investmentPerhaps unsurprisingly, most people online prefer to pick up a Rolex rather than a Swatch or an AP. The brand with the distinctive five-pointed 'coronet' has settled back to around 30% of transaction volume, on the German platform Chrono24, the world's largest marketplace for pre-owned watches, according to Chrono24’s Rolex Report 2026."Rolex built its lead over decades," says José Gaztelu, CEO of Chrono24. "Buyers often start with a Datejust or an Oyster Perpetual and move up from there," Gaztelu says. "People discover the history, the references, the stories behind the models. It is what keeps people in the hobby," he adds.Over at Bezel, an American platform built on in-house authentication, which carried more than a billion dollars in active listings through the first half of 2026, Rolex leads every measure too: 34% of tracked interest, 28% of orders, 35% of watches registered in client collections."Rolex has recognition, product depth and liquidity all at once," says Quaid Walker, the platform's CEO. "It reflects the depth of the secondary market around virtually every major model. It inspires confidence for new buyers and experienced collectors alike."Cartier, Tudor or FP Journe gaining groundBut the Rolex shares are actually shrinking on Chrono24, after a peak above 44% in 2022. This decline, to the benefit of other brands, is seen as a "healthy normalization" of the market by Chrono24's CEO. "Buyers are spreading demand across a broader set of brands and models. This shift is particularly visible among younger buyers."Who's benefiting? "Cartier stands out most clearly, particularly in the €5,000 to €10,000 segment," he says. "Patek Philippe and Vacheron Constantin have gained ground at the high end, while Audemars Piguet remains very strong as well. Beyond the high end, Tudor, Jaeger-LeCoultre and Longines are also worth mentioning."What are the trending models? "The Cartier Tank and the Tudor Black Bay represent two different sides of the shift we are seeing. The Tank reflects the renewed interest in elegant, distinctive classics, while the Black Bay shows that versatile sports watches with a clear identity remain highly relevant", Gaztelu says.Bezel's data shows the same drift. Tudor took 14% of orders, finishing second by sales, ahead of Omega. Further out, the sharpest momentum is with the independents: F.P. Journe has been trading at strong levels, as a younger and well-informed base of collectors pays closer attention to the watchmakers behind the watches rather than to established brand names alone.Vintage has momentum, but no buying spreeThe trend press spent the first half of 2026 pushing smaller cases and louder dials. "Buyers are moving towards more classical proportions and more refined, dress-oriented watches," says Gaztelu."Women are certainly part of this development. But men are also buying smaller watches than they did ten years ago. While 40mm remains a sports-watch sweet spot for many men, there is clearly more interest in refined dress watches with smaller case sizes. The industry has also added much more variety in the 35 to 39 millimetre range, which has become a versatile unisex sweet spot", he adds. The order books at Bezel show that vintage watches are still far from taking over the market. References from the 2020s and 2010s gather together roughly three-quarters of all activity. Buyers kept reaching for 40–41mm steel in black, blue and silver. Steel alone took 72% of orders."There's clearly more energy around smaller cases and more expressive dials, but our buyers in the first half of 2026 were still concentrated around tried-and-true sizes and hues. Smaller watches aren't necessarily a fad. It just means a trend can be culturally important before it becomes the centre of the market. I'd call it a real design trend, but not yet a broad buying trend", Walker says.Buy it because you want to wear itAre you making a good investment? "There's no reliable way to predict whether a watch will appreciate in value, but you can get a pretty good sense of how resilient its value may be," says Walker. He starts with liquidity — how often the reference trades, how many buyers there are for it, where comparable examples are actually selling — then weighs condition, originality, production volume and the strength of the brand or watchmaker.Walker refuses to name a 2026 good buy. "I'd start by assessing what someone already owns, what they actually wear, and the role they want the next watch to play in their collection," he says. "For a newer collector, that might mean something versatile from a brand with real history and a deep catalogue to explore.""For a new collector, the biggest mistake is usually paying too much because a watch feels hard to get, or because the market around it is moving quickly," he adds. "Understanding the recent transaction history and buying a strong example at a sensible price will generally matter more than trying to predict which watch is going to take off next."Gaztelu's advice is simple. "There are classics that tend to have the steadiest demand and value retention or appreciation. But I will be direct: the vast majority of people should buy a watch because they love it, not as a bet. The collectors who are happiest years later are the ones who bought something they love, at a fair price, and kept it," he adds.Walker lands in the same place: "The best collections tend to feel personal rather than like a snapshot of whatever the market was excited about that year."Pick the one you actually like. And make sure it's real. Bezel turned away 34% of the watches submitted for sale in the first half of 2026. Among them: a genuine Patek Philippe Aquanaut worth around $140,000 that had been stolen off a wrist in Ibiza, and a real Rolex Submariner fitted with a counterfeit dial.

title: Three in four EU workers face suspicious emails and links, report finds
description: Phishing remains the most common cyber threat — only one in two respondents say they are able to spot a deepfake video.
content: Three in four workers in the European Union have come across suspicious emails, messages or links at work, according to a Eurobarometer survey published by the European Commission on 30 September.Greece’s Hellenic Data Protection Authority (HDPA) has seized on the figures, released as European Cybersecurity Month (ECSM) got under way, to remind public bodies and private companies that protecting personal data is central to tackling cyberthreats.The survey suggests cyberthreats are now a fixture of working life, and that there is a clear gap between what employees know about digital risks and what they actually do.Phishing leads the packPhishing remains the most common threat. Some 39% of employees say they have received fraudulent messages or been directed to fake websites designed to steal data or gain unauthorised access.Next come attempts to steal personal data, reported by 18% of respondents, followed by malware attacks (17%) and attempts to obtain passwords (16%).A further 15% say they have already encountered scams powered by artificial intelligence (AI). That last category is growing in importance, as AI hands attackers the tools to produce ever more convincing messages, images, voices and videos.Knowing versus doingEmployees broadly understand the risks, but awareness does not always translate into safe habits.Some 83% of employees say a cyberattack can have serious consequences, and 72% say they can spot a suspicious email.Yet only 54% check who sent a message before clicking on a link.AI-generated or doctored content is an even bigger blind spot. Fewer than half (48%) say they could recognise a deepfake video.Beyond the technical fixThe HDPA is using European Cybersecurity Month to remind data controllers, the public and private organisations responsible for handling personal information, of their obligations when a breach occurs.Under Article 33 of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), they must notify the relevant supervisory authority. But fixing the technical problem and alerting the regulator is not always the end of the matter.In some cases, organisations must also tell the people affected.When citizens must knowArticle 34 of the GDPR requires organisations to inform people without undue delay when a breach is likely to put their rights and freedoms at high risk.That risk could include financial fraud, identity theft or the exposure of sensitive personal information.Prompt notification has a practical purpose, giving people the chance to protect themselves before the damage spreads.Depending on the case, that could mean changing passwords, cancelling or replacing bank cards, watching out for suspicious messages or taking other targeted steps.Why transparency mattersTelling people about a breach is not only a legal obligation under the GDPR. It is also central to managing the fallout of a cyberattack.Hiding an incident, or delaying notification without good reason, can leave those affected more exposed, because it robs them of the chance to protect themselves in time.Transparency is also the foundation of trust between an organisation and the citizens, customers or employees whose data it holds.A call to prepareThe HDPA is urging public bodies and private organisations to take stock of how ready they are for a cybersecurity incident.That means updating incident response plans, training staff regularly and building data protection into every stage of handling an incident.With three in four employees already exposed to suspicious messages or links, the HDPA argues, cybersecurity can no longer be treated as a purely technical matter. It is a daily responsibility for organisations and a key part of protecting the public.

title: Virgin unveils new train designs and plans for cross-Channel service linking London and Europe from 2030
description: The company plans to launch 20 daily return services linking London with Paris, Brussels and Amsterdam, and wants to bring its signature hospitality to the service.
content: Virgin has unveiled a first look at its planned cross-Channel trains, with striking black and red designs and ambitions to take on Eurostar from 2030.The company intends to run 20 daily return services between London, Paris, Brussels and Amsterdam, adding almost 7.5 million seats a year to the route. It has signed a deal with French rail giant Alstom for 12 new high-speed trains, with promises of a more distinctly Virgin experience on board.The UK-based Office of Rail and Road (ORR) has also published a signed agreement between Virgin and Eurostar which will allow Virgin to maintain its trains, which will be capable of travelling at speeds of up to 300km/h, at the Temple Mills International depot in London.Although the trains, which will be a direct rival to the existing Eurostar service, have been slated for a while now, this is the first time we’ve been given an idea of what they’ll look like, and what travellers can expect. Clubhouse influences and loyalty benefits Although details of the appearance of the trains are currently sparse, Virgin has released a photo of a black and red train and says each one will boast customised interiors designed for cross-Channel travel. Before stepping onboard, passengers will be able to enjoy pre-departure areas and onboard social spaces inspired by Virgin Atlantic’s Clubhouses in some airports. Accessibility will be a top consideration across all of the trains, too. Meanwhile, Virgin’s cruising wing, Virgin Voyages, will influence the food and drinks on offer, while Virgin Hotels will inspire seating and communal onboard areas. For customers who collect perks via the loyalty platform Virgin Red, travelling on the trains will provide opportunities to earn points and spend them across the Virgin brand. “We’ll be connecting London with some of Europe’s greatest cities and giving passengers a distinctive new choice in cross-Channel travel,” said Josh Bayliss, CEO of Virgin Group. “Virgin has always thrived on challenging the status quo and aimed to provide our customers with a great experience. We’ll bring the same approach to the cross-Channel route, making the journey something to look forward to as much as the destination.”

title: After the foldable iPhone, Apple’s next launch could come to your home
description: Apple has teased a new smart home launch just 10 days before iPhone Duo arrives.  Here’s what we might see.
content: Just a month after Apple announced the release of its foldable phone, the tech giant is holding another announcement, this time aimed at smart homes. Apple announced a so-called “Welcome Home” event on Thursday, where it is expected to launch a new kind of product.The event will take place on 13 October at 9am local ET or 3pm CET. The announcement was posted by Apple’s marketing chief, Greg Joswiak, with a video showing people doing a colourful needlepoint of the Apple logo. However, there was no indication of what would be announced.Tech publications have predicted the main new product could be a home hub that would work like a tablet and be left in houses. It may be able to customise what it displays based on who is in the room, and many have referred to it as the ‘HomePad’. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman has reported that the lineup will also include a new HomePod mini and an updated Apple TV, with Siri AI at the core of all three devices. A faster processor in the HomePod Mini could let it run the upgraded version of Siri. Further rumours point to Apple developing its own smart home devices, including security cameras and smart locks, in collaboration with LG The event comes at a busy moment for the company, now led by CEO John Ternus. September brought the iPhone 18 Pro lineup, the iPhone Duo, AirPods 5 and new Apple Watch models. The “Welcome Home” event lands ten days before the iPhone Duo goes on sale on October 23.

title: Iran and Russia used ChatGPT for propaganda by ‘fake journalists’, OpenAI says
description: The American tech giant said it banned Russian and Iranian accounts that had been using ChatGPT models to generate content and fake journalist personas to spread false narratives about the conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East and sow division.
content: OpenAI revealed on Thursday it had shut down two influence operations — from Russia and Iran — that used ChatGPT to push fake journalist personas and run a "think-tank" to covertly spread anti-Ukraine propaganda and foster division in the US and Israel over the war in Iran.The report is the latest example of how state actors could exploit widely available AI tools to produce and disseminate sophisticated propaganda against adversaries on a mass scale.The American AI giant said it banned a cluster of ChatGPT accounts that originated in Russia and Iran and were used to support false front entities for geopolitical and conflict-related messaging.The Iranian operation involved seven fake journalist profiles, each claiming to be from Western countries, including the United States, that were used to plant long-form articles in media outlets around the world."We identified almost 100 articles published or syndicated under the operation's bylines across roughly a dozen online outlets around the world," OpenAI said."These were small to medium outlets, generally focused on international affairs, geopolitics, and events in the Middle East."The earliest article identified by OpenAI was published in July 2025 and the latest in October 2026, with the frequency of reports increasing after the US-Iran war broke out earlier this year.The operation also generated social media comments on topics related to the US-Iran war, it added.One of the personas named Ervin B. Hoskins, whose bio claimed to be "an American freelance writer," had social media accounts across several tech platforms, including Elon Musk's X and Meta-owned Instagram.X's transparency information showed the account was connected via a "West Asia android app" and Instagram's transparency information showed the account was based in Iran, according to screenshots provided by OpenAI.Both accounts appeared to be suspended.The Russian operation co-opted "unwitting people" in Latin America to run a think-tank called the Social Research Center (SRC). It was used for covert activities aimed at undermining Ukraine's reputation in the region and to influence local politics, the company said."The available evidence indicates that the SRC's employees in Latin America were not aware that they were working for a Russian group," OpenAI said."The SRC appears to have produced a majority of original content via its co-opted staff. This stands out as the most complex attempt to run a front identity that we've disrupted over the past two and a half years."The operators used ChatGPT to write internal reports on their activities, create content for their operations and draft reports on the performance of the think tank, as well as to help design and create texts for publishing on social media as posts and comments.Among the social media activity, say OpenAI, were reactions to Polish far-right MEP Grzegorz Braun proposing that people who showed “anti-Polishness” be declared persona non grata in Poland, in an attempt to sow divisions in Poland over the country’s support for Ukraine.

title: In Pictures: Weirdest and most thought-provoking statues of Donald Trump over the years
description: Following the headline-grabbing statue "The Orange Plague" by Danish artist Jens Galschiøt, which was displayed this week at the European Parliament building in Strasbourg, we take a look back at some of the ways artists have depicted Trump in satirical, humorous and thought-provoking ways.
content: Donald Trump has been immortalised by artists on countless occasions, with creatives using their talents to poke fun, criticise, educate, and even warn. From signs and murals to carnival floats, the divisive POTUS has inspired many to remind the public that the arts are a vital way to comment, inform and inspire. One artform which has been an effective favourite for many wishing to represent Trump is the sculpted figure. It makes sense since Trump has shown a clear preference for classical and gilded aesthetics; statues play on the man’s perception of monumentalism as being a reflection of power. Artists therefore use oversized or flashy statues to better reflect and lampoon Trump’s ego, as well as comment on the pitfalls of gaudish effigies which so often betray a sense of narcissism. In effect, the momuments strike at the heart of Trump's sensibilities and symbolically cast him as the eagle in Aesop’s fable – a figure undone by a self-infliction. In this case, a marked proclivity for oversized effigies. The latest example has been "The Orange Plague", the 2.6-meter statue by Danish artist Jens Galschiøt. Coated with 23-karat gold, the artwork also known as “The King of Injustice” shows a nude Trump holding a comically sized golf club in one hand, a set of scales in the other, all while sitting on the back of a smaller, frailer man. Beneath the statue is a plaque which reads: "I am sitting on the back of a man. He is sinking under my burden. I will do anything to help him. Except stepping down from his back. - The King of Injustice." According to Galschiøt, the work is a “satirical outcry” against Trump’s volatile climate and foreign policies.The statue was previously displayed at the “hands off Greenland” demonstrations in Copenhagen earlier this year and the COP30 UN Climate Summit in Belém, Brazil last year. It has just finished its short stint at the European Parliament building in Strasbourg and is heading to the COP31 UN Climate Conference next month in Antalya, Türkiye.Before we see “The Orange Plague” once more, here are other notable statues of Trump which have amused spectators and sought to reflect what certain people think of the current leader of the free world."The Emperor Has No Balls" Artist: IndeclineYear: 2016 Original location: Cleveland, Los Angeles, New York City, San Francisco, SeattleDescription: Not one, but five 1.95m-tall statues were installed in five major cities in the US. Made of clay and silicone, the statues show a naked Trump with bits missing. The title will clue you which. The monuments were all promptly taken down, with the greatest official statement being from the New York City Parks Department, whose phrasing was perfection. They said that it “stands firmly against any unpermitted erection in city parks, no matter how small”."Dump Trump" Artist: Don LessemYear: 2019Original location: Trafalgar Square, LondonDescription: The 4.9m-tall statue depicts Donald Trump sitting on a golden toilet and on his phone, wearing a MAGA hat with the words “Impeach Me!” on the headwear. The statue was spotted during Trump’s visit to the United Kingdom. It was also seen during the Trump-organised Salute To America in Washington D.C. on 4 July 2019. Also worth noting is that the effigy emitted noises of flatulence and featured audio of Trump catchphrases like “I’m a very stable genius” and “fake news”."Statue of Illiberty" Artist: Tomaž Schlegl Year: 2019 Original location: Near Kamnik, Slovenia Description: The wooden statue was erected only weeks after architect / artist Tomaž Schlegl’s Melenia Trump statue, which was placed in her home town of Sevnica. That one was destroyed by fire. “Statue of Illiberty” showed Trump with his arm raised in the style of the Statue of Liberty, but featured two sides. One side was Trump’s face (with luscious red lips); the other face was an image of a “vampire”, a monstruous image which served as something of a warning. And wouldn’t you know it, this statue was also burned down a year later."In Honor of a Lifetime of Sexual Assault"Artist: AnonymousYear: 2024Original location: Portland and PhiladelphiaDescription: Two satirical statues, approximately 2.4m tall, which were spray painted gold, showing Trump grinning and making a grabbing gesture with his right hand. The plaque accompanying the statues was a direct quote from Trump from the infamous Access Hollywood tape: “I just start kissing them. It's like a magnet. Just kiss. I don't even wait. And when you're a star they let you do it. You can do anything. Grab them by the pussy. You can do anything.”"Best Friends Forever"Artist: The Secret HandshakeYear: 2025Original location: National Mall, Washington D.C.Description: Otherwise known as “Why Can’t We Be Friends?”, this 3.7 meter-tall statue depicts Donald Trump and convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein merrily holding hands and frolicking. It was created in protest of the relationship between Trump and Epstein and as a way to call out the sexual misconduct allegations against Trump and the redaction of the Epstein Files. The statue was constructed from foam, resin, wood and coloured to appear bronze. The center plaque read: "In Honor of Friendship Month – We celebrate the long-lasting bond between President Donald J.
