Trump and his “closest friend” Jeffrey Epstein.” It was dismantled by the US Park Police within 24 hours of installation but "Best Friends Forever" was temporarily reinstalled at various other locations in Washington D.C."King of the World"Artist: The Secret HandshakeYear: 2026Original location: National Mall, Washington D.C.Description: The 3.6m statue was seen this year as a companion piece to "Best Friends Forever", as it also depicts Trump and Epstein. This time, the anonymous artists belonging to The Secret Handshake mimicked the Jack and Rose pose from Titanic. The plaque accompanying it read: "The tragic love story between Jack and Rose was built on luxurious travel, raucous parties, and secret nude sketches. This monument honors the bond between Donald Trump and Jeffrey Epstein, a friendship seemingly built on luxurious travel, raucous parties, and secret nude sketches."

title: Frozen testicular tissue transplanted in bid to restore fertility after chemotherapy
description: Protecting fertility is a major challenge for young men undergoing aggressive treatments such as chemotherapy. Freezing their own testicular tissue before such treatments could help.
content: A young patient in Edinburgh has undergone a pioneering procedure, receiving a transplant of his own testicular tissue, frozen before he began chemotherapy, in a development that could pave the way for male fertility preservation, a first such procedure in the UK and second worldwide.“This is a big step towards helping boys facing treatments that damage their fertility to have children of their own,” said Rod Mitchell, professor of developmental endocrinology at the University of Edinburgh’s Institute for Regeneration and Repair.The 19-year-old received a bone marrow transplant in 2023 to treat a serious blood disorder. Before starting treatment, he had testicular tissue removed and frozen because the high-dose chemotherapy could permanently damage the cells needed to produce sperm.Three years later, tests showed that the patient had no sperm in his semen. In August 2026, doctors implanted some of his previously frozen testicular tissue back into his body in the hope that it would begin to produce sperm, the University of Edinburgh said in a press release.“Fertility is something I’ve struggled with personally for a long time. I’ve always wanted to have children of my own but at some point, I found myself starting to slowly accept that that might never be possible for me,” the patient said after the transplant. “Having this procedure has given me genuine hope for the future.”In the next eight months, doctors will remove and examine some of the transplanted tissue to determine whether sperm have been produced. Why freezing tissue Protecting fertility is a major challenge for young men undergoing aggressive treatments such as chemotherapy. Semen freezing is an established option for adolescents and young men. It is not available to prepubertal boys, however, because they do not yet produce semen, leaving them with no means of preserving their fertility.Storing testicular tissue could offer an alternative. It contains spermatogonial stem cells, which produce sperm from puberty onwards. Doctors hope that tissue frozen before treatment can later be returned to the patient and allow sperm production.The Edinburgh testicular project was established in 2015 with the support of Children with Cancer UK. Since then, more than 1,200 patients in the United Kingdom and more than 3,100 worldwide have now had testicular tissue stored for potential future clinical use. “We are beginning to see some of these young men return to explore their fertility options. This study offers real hope for future fertility in boys facing cancer treatment,” Mitchell added. Experimental phases The trial procedure in Edinburgh is the first of its kind in the UK and only the second reported worldwide. The first reported transplant of frozen testicular tissue took place in Belgium in January 2025. In that case, the cryopreserved tissue was reintroduced into an infertile man who had undergone chemotherapy in childhood, after 16 years in storage. The researchers wrote in the preliminary results of the study that dormant stem cells within the transplanted tissue revived and began producing sperm cells, a process known as spermatogenesis.When researchers evaluated the tissue a year after surgery, they confirmed that the sperm cells had developed fully.

title: French authorities arrests at least five people over €9 million theft from Renoir Museum
description: The suspects are believed to include the two alleged burglars, who reportedly broke into the museum at dawn by cutting through a fence.
content: After a major manhunt, at least five people have been arrested in France in connection with the theft of four artworks from the Renoir Museum on 8 September.The two suspected burglars are believed to be among those arrested.French newspaper Nice-Matin, which first reported the arrests, said the suspects could be linked to an organised criminal gang.The theft took place at dawn on 8 September, when a group of thieves described as "well-equipped" and "well-informed" broke into the museum through its gardens, according to the town’s mayor, Bryan Masson.They sliced through a fence and entered the museum through the ground floor by smashing a window, and then cut the clips securing the artwork frames with an electric saw, Masson said in remarks carried out by local broadcaster Ici Azur.According to Masson, the pair were "spotted thanks to the town's video surveillance cameras". Initial reports estimated the stolen haul to be worth up to €9 million euros.In a written statement obtained by the AP news agency, two of the stolen works were found left in the museum garden as the thieves fled from police who had been alerted by the alarm. But the two others - Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano (1910), and Young Woman at the Well (1886) - are still missing.The Renoir Museum, located between Cannes and Nice, is the Mediterranean coastal town most famous attraction. Open since 1960, it was the painter's last home before his death in 1919 from pulmonary congestion when he was 78-years old.

title: Scientific study reveals scariest horror movie – with one 2026 title breaking heart rate record
description: The ranking was determined by a study monitoring audience's heart rates and BPM increases while watching horror films.
content: Halloween is creeping up and many of you will be wondering: “What should I be watching to get in the mood for the big night?” Well, if you're sticking to rigorous scientific research, we can reveal what the scariest films are – with no accounting for taste or your tolerance for jump scares.The Science of Scare Project, now in its seventh year, tracks the pulses of hundreds of volunteers, who watch hours of English-language horror movies whilst fitted with heart rate monitors.Their scientific study establishes a Scare Score system, which combines both heart rate (measured in beats per minute - BPM) and heart rate variability (HRV - measured in milliseconds), which measures the time in between each beat of your heart. Peak heart rate is also taken into consideration, with the highest point proving to be a valuable indicator and leading to an overall ranking of the scariest horror movies. Scroll down for the Top 20 scariest films according to the study. This year, 15 new contenders, including breakout hits Obsession and Backrooms, challenged horror favourites, while not yet cracking the Top 20. A24's paranormal podcast horror film Undertone is scientifically the scariest movie of 2026 and took the overall position of 33 in the rankings.Most notably for this year’s study, Resident Evil broke a jump-scare record held by the film which has remained at the Number 1 spot for the last four years - with Zach Cregger‘s 2026 release recording a heart rate peak of 134 BPM.For general reference, a normal resting heart rate for both adult women and men typically falls between 60 and 100 beats per minute (healthiest being between 70 and 80).However, the top spot still belongs to Scott Derrickson’s 2012 supernatural horror film Sinister.The film raised viewers’ average heart rate by 34%, from 64 to 86 BPM, with its most terrifying moment reaching 131 BPM. Its combination of sudden shocks and lingering dread earned it a Scare Score of 96/100.Here’s the list of the 20 scariest horror movies according to the study: Sinister Host Skinamarink Insidious The Conjuring Hereditary Smile 2 Smile The Exorcism of Emily Rose Talk To Me Hell House LLC The Conjuring 2 It Follows The Dark and the Wicked The Descent Paranormal Activity The Babadook A Quiet Place 2 The Autopsy of Jane Doe Insidious 2 Check out the full rankings and methodology in detail here. As we’ve previously noted when it comes to the Science of Scare’s findings, the results are largely dominated by modern horror films which employ jump scares. It tracks considering the methodology is centred around heartbeats; however, many dreadheads and gorehounds consider the ubiquitous cattle-prod tactic to be cheap and an overused ploy to illicit easy frights. They’re great for a quick adrenaline rush, but many would argue that the jump scare startles rather than actually scares. Do heart rate modulations necessarily equate to a film being the scariest? It's a valuable metric, but not necessarily synonymous with films that manage to burrow under your skin and set up camp. Those are the long-term scariest.Still, if the Science of Scare’s study gets people watching the very underrated The Autopsy of Jane Doe, who are we to grumble?

title: Italy probes gaming giant Activision Blizzard over in-game spending by children
description: Italy’s antitrust authority is investigating whether monetisation practices in Call of Duty Mobile and Diablo Immortal amount to a “widespread infringement” of EU consumer protection rules, particularly in relation to children.
content: Italy’s antitrust authorities have launched an investigation into Microsoft-owned gaming company Activision Blizzard amid claims it has used predatory game monetisation such as “loot boxes” and pay-to-progress designs in its popular mobile games Diablo Immortal and Call of Duty Mobile to target and exploit children and other players.Italy, supported by consumer protection authorities in Norway and Denmark, is first seeking to find if the games company’s practices constituted a “widespread infringement” of EU consumer protection rules following player and public backlash in recent years.Activision Blizzard is known worldwide for genre-defining game series Call of Duty, Warcraft, StarCraft and Diablo, among others, and was bought by the big tech company in 2023 for $75.4 billion (€67.29bn)Should the company be found in breach of the Italian Consumer Code it could face fines of up to 4% of its annual turnover in each of the affected countries, according to the European consumer law framework.Italy’s investigation is part of a wider EU coordination launched at the end of September by the European Commission’s Consumer Protection Cooperation (CPC) Network, with actions set to launch across the EU with the aim of strengthening the protection of gamers’ rights targeting nine video games companies.The CPC Network is coordinating action against Activision Blizzard UK Limited, Crytek GmbH, InnoGames GmbH, King.com Limited, Mojang AB, Plarium Europe S.à.r.l., PLR Worldwide Sales Limited, Riot Games Limited, Supercell Oy and Ubisoft EMEA SAS.Italy’s investigation is the first step of this EU-wide approach.Chief among the Italian authorities’ concerns is how the company’s practices have targeted children who are more at risk of gaming addiction and unable to understand or keep track of how much they are spending, especially as the company relies on virtual currencies paid for with real money to make purchases of in-game items, benefits and features.Authorities highlighted the “lack of transparency and fairness in the use of virtual currencies” within the games, said the Authority in a statement.The move is part of a wider drive at European and global level against tech companies over concerns their platforms’ and games’ designs negatively harm young people’s mental health, following a spate of suicides.Just last month, the European Commission unveiled a proposal to protect children online known as the EU Kids Act, which aims to introduce a requirement for digital service providers to first prove that their platforms are “safe by design” and age-appropriate before children can use them.The proposal specifically targets video games, including a ban on loot boxes — virtual mystery packages containing random items such as equipment and cosmetic gear — for children, as well as a requirement to clearly display real currency costs for in-game purchases and purchase alerts.The proposal also aims to curb addictive behavior in children including banning “streak” mechanics that require players to login regularly or even daily as well as notifications encouraging children to resume or keep playing longer than they want.The EU-wide action follows an open dialogue launched by the CPC Network with the video games industry last year, which the organisation diplomatically saying that it “did not bring satisfactory results,” especially in addressing monetisation and virtual currencies practices.Parallel to these actions, the Commission is expected to present an EU Digital Fairness Act later this year, with measures including banning “dark patterns” (manipulative designs and false urgency), unfair personalization practices and subscription traps.“Roughly half of Europeans play video games… With that reach comes responsibility. The industry must ensure that its games do not expose players — especially children — to harmful or unfair practices,” said Michael McGrath the EU’s consumer protection commissioner.“The game must be fair, and the rules must be respected. National authorities, with the support of the Commission, will make sure they are enforced,” he added.Many gamers have also complained over the years over what they see as pay-to-win mechanics being employed more frequently by video game publishers.These mechanics reward players who have spent more money in game, giving them an unfair advantage over players who have not despite them being more skilled.This reduces the game to a battle of bank accounts rather than skill or merit. Games companies have often defended this decision by saying their games are free to play, and that paying is optional.In a July 2022 interview with the Los Angeles Times, the former head of Blizzard Entertainment Mike Ybarra defended their gaming business model saying the company “gives a free Diablo experience to hundreds of millions of people, where they can literally do 99.5% of everything in the game".He also claimed the vast majority of players had not spent any money and that players could complete the game without paying.

title: The funniest animal photos of 2026: Nikon Comedy Wildlife Awards finalists revealed
description: This year’s competition attracted more than 10,000 entries from 112 countries - a record for the awards.
content: From crocodiles channelling their inner Elvis Presley to a handstanding leopard and orangutans apparently flipping the bird, the finalists for the 2026 Nikon Comedy Wildlife Awards are finally here.This year’s shortlist is packed with 40 Individual Finalists, three U16 Category Finalists, four Portfolio Category Finalists and nine Video Category Finalists. More than 10,000 entries were submitted from 112 countries – the highest number in the Awards’ history.Tom Sullam, co-founder of the Comedy Wildlife Photography Awards, says: “The Comedy Wildlife Photography Awards started very gently, somewhere out on the vast plains of the Serengeti. What began as a small effort to raise awareness of wildlife conservation has grown into something far bigger than we ever imagined."He added: "The competition is now truly global, and a decade or so on, we want to make it even bigger, funnier, and more far-reaching than ever. We use humour to get people to feel empathy towards wildlife, and it's that empathy that creates behavioural change for the better.”The winners will be announced on 8 December at a awards evening in London, followed by a free exhibition showcasing the 2026 finalists from 9 to 13 December at Gallery@Oxo.Until then, take a paws and enjoy some of our personal favourite finalists of the year.

title: Graphene opens new way to detect brain damage after stroke
description: An international team of scientists involving Spain's CSIC has developed graphene sensors that pinpoint the brain regions most vulnerable after a stroke, tested in mice, opening the door to preventing further damage and improving treatment.
content: An international team of scientists has developed a graphene-based technology that makes it possible to monitor brain activity and identify the areas at greatest risk of sustaining additional damage after a stroke. The breakthrough, tested in mice, could help drive the development of more precise treatments for stroke.The research, published in the scientific journal "Brain (source in Spanish)", involved the participation of Spain's National Research Council (CSIC), the University of Manchester, the Catalan Institute of Nanoscience and Nanotechnology (ICN2) and the German company Multi Channel Systems.When a person suffers an ischaemic stroke, a blockage interrupts the blood flow to part of the brain. However, the lesions can continue to spread because of waves of disturbed electrical activity, known as spreading cortical depolarisations, which move through the affected brain tissue.Until now, accurately detecting these signals has been a challenge, as conventional technologies struggle to record the extremely slow electrical changes that occur during this process.Graphene helps identify the brain's most vulnerable areasUsing high-sensitivity graphene sensors placed on the brains of mice, the researchers succeeded in recording these electrical waves with an unprecedented level of detail. The results showed that the characteristics of the signals made it possible to distinguish between relatively healthy brain tissue, tissue at risk and tissue that had already suffered severe damage.The scientists also found that these signals could anticipate the blood-flow response. While in healthier areas it increased to support recovery, in vulnerable regions it could fall even further, worsening the injury.The team also discovered that a low dose of ketamine, a drug already used in medicine, reduced the duration of the harmful electrical waves, improved the blood-flow response and reduced the extent of brain damage in animal models. These findings point to a possible neuroprotective effect of ketamine after a stroke, although it has not yet been shown to offer the same benefits in humans.A potential tool to improve treatments"In broad terms, the study shows how cutting-edge technologies can not only improve the way brain activity is measured, but also reveal new and important information about how brain lesions develop and how they might be treated", explains Rob Wykes, a researcher at the University of Manchester.For his part, Anton Guimerà-Brunet, a CSIC researcher at the Institute of Microelectronics of Barcelona, stresses that recording low-frequency brain activity is still a challenge for current technologies. "We have been developing our graphene-based technology for years, with our first results published in 2018, and the challenge has been to standardise and refine it for use in relevant preclinical studies", he says.The breakthrough is part of a scientific collaboration launched years ago between institutions in Spain and the United Kingdom to develop graphene devices capable of recording brain signals.Although the technology is still at the preclinical research stage, the scientists believe that in future it could make it possible to monitor in real time the condition of brain tissue during a stroke, identify patients at greatest risk of additional injury and contribute to the development of new treatments.

title: From barbershops to nature courses: How community-driven campaigns are rethinking men’s mental health
description: As waiting lists for mental health care continue to grow, community-driven campaigns across Europe have been finding unique ways to support men in particular.
content: At a small barbershop in Brixton, south London, men’s lives are being transformed. Not just through a new haircut or fresh beard trim — but by opening up about their mental health. “People confide in barbers and often share things that perhaps they wouldn't with their partners or friends,” Ben Theophanous, owner and co-founder of Curfew Grooming, told Euronews Health. “The relationship is often strong, but there is an element of superficiality that provides a unique platform for sharing feelings,” he added. Curfew Grooming is one of more than 100 barbershops across the United Kingdom to receive Mental Health First Aid (MHFA) training through the 12th Man Campaign — a community-driven initiative founded in 2013 by mental health nurse Nick Little and his late friend Oz Osborne. The campaign takes its name from the football term for a team’s fans and provides support for men by normalising talking about mental health in everyday spaces.These spaces include barbershops and tattoo studios — places where there’s already a one-on-one dynamic. Employees who volunteer take an online course, which guides them through how to spot signs that a customer might be struggling; how to ask meaningful questions and how to direct them to the right resources if needed. “We're just handing the responsibility to men in society to look out for their friends and their family. To recognise mental health more in their lives and to talk about it,” Nick Little told Euronews Health. Nearly 1 in 7 people around the world are living with a mental health condition, but men are still less likely than women to reach out for help — and three times more likely to die by suicide, according to the Office of National Statistics.Those who are looking for professional help encounter another issue: long waiting times. For example In the UK, people were eight times more likely to wait for over 18 months for mental health treatment on the National Health Service than those waiting for physical health treatments, according to data analysed by the charity Rethink in 2025. Increasingly, community-led initiatives are stepping in as a way to fill these gaps in the system — not to replace professional services, but to put more preventative measures in place before people reach crisis. “Let's put trust in society and invest in our community businesses, because that's the front line,” Little said. Engaging men with nature Similar community-based and male-focused initiatives are happening all across Europe. In Denmark, many of these have used the Vildmandsprojektet (Wild Man) project as a blueprint; a 9- to 12-week nature-based rehabilitation program for men in crisis. Co-founded by nature psychologist Simon Høegmark in 2014, its development was partly inspired by Høegmark’s own personal experiences with mental health. Over a decade ago, he travelled to Norway to hike and regain his “footing.”“After several days of heavy thoughts, I reached the summit of a mountain overlooking Lysefjord. For a brief moment, the thought of jumping crossed my mind,” he recalled. But as quickly as these thoughts took over, the views of Lysefjord became awash with light — and something inside Simon shifted. “The sun broke through the clouds, illuminating the entire landscape. I experienced a moment of self-forgetfulness, a sense of connection, and a love for life,” Høegmark told Euronews Health. While the experience did not immediately resolve his psychological crisis, it allowed the beauty of nature to take over — its stillness settling the thoughts in his head and replacing them with a sense of hope. “I saw my situation more clearly. I decided to investigate why encountering nature can affect people so profoundly, and how nature can be professionally utilised as a framework for recovery and rehabilitation,” he said. After launching the Vildmandsprojektet project in 2014, Høegmark conducted many studies alongside a team of researchers to monitor its effects. One such study involved 114 men, who showed significant improvements in their physical and mental quality of life, as well as a reduction in self-perceived stress symptoms after taking the course.“These improvements were evident immediately after the course and — on several measures — six months later,” Høegmark said, also noting a lasting sense of community even after the courses had ended. “This serves as a vital bridge between a time-limited public program and everyday life, where habits and relationships need to endure,” he added. The project ran from 2014 for a period of over eight years, during which time around 700 men participated in its courses. Since then, its Nature, Body, Mind, and Community (NBMC) method has been adopted by more than 50 Danish municipalities and adapted for both men and women. While Høegmark cautions that Vildmandsprojektet was never intended to replace psychiatric treatment, it has proved itself to be an accessible format for men that might otherwise be reluctant to engage with mental health services. “My professional interpretation is that [the NBMC method] can strengthen participants' sense of agency and ownership regarding their own wellbeing,” said Høegmark. “However, the method must be used as a supplement within a cohesive health service framework that includes clear referral pathways should a participant require more specialised care,” he said.The growing importance of community-driven careAlongside local initiatives, nationwide healthcare systems have also begun looking into community-driven care as a tool to alleviate wait times. One example of this is social prescribing, which the NHS has been offering as a way to connect patients with activity groups. These can include gardening, walking, art and crafting clubs — anything that encourages reconnection with the outside world.“The reason I'm so in favour of this more community-driven style of support is that the format can be more relevant to everyday life, more aligned with people's hobbies and things that they normally would do anyway,” Stella Chan, a professor of evidence-based psychological therapies at the University of Reading in England, tells Euronews Health. “It's less stigmatising and also easier to assess,” she added, which can in turn help ease resistance. While some have argued that social prescribing is not enough — and avoids addressing more serious underlying societal issues like economic inequality — research suggests it’s become an important way to bridge medical and non-medical support. “Mental ill-health and mental disorders are among our major global health challenges, and we need both robust treatment and far more prevention,” Høegmark said.

title: Barcelona team develops AI that detects ageing in blood stem cells
description: ChromAgeNet has decoded chromatin architecture, the 3D organisation of DNA in the nucleus, distinguishing young from aged blood stem cells and opening new paths for cell rejuvenation.
content: Ageing gradually undermines the body's ability to regenerate, severely affecting the production of blood cells. In this race against the biological clock, analysing changes in blood stem cells is crucial to opening the door to interventions that can slow their decline and restore their original function.A scientific team in Barcelona has developed ChromAgeNet, an artificial intelligence tool that detects ageing in blood stem cells by analysing the three-dimensional structure of their DNA.Published in the journal "Aging Cell", the research, led by Maria Carolina Florian (IDIBELL) and Paula Petrone (BSC-CNS/ISGlobal), shows that the organisation of chromatin contains information that makes it possible to distinguish cells from young and aged mice.A bridge between biomedicine and supercomputingTo train the model, the researchers applied convolutional neural networks to 3D images of the nuclei of mouse stem cells (source in Spanish). ChromAgeNet uses neural networks to decipher how DNA ages. AI makes it possible to detect subtle structural variations that are imperceptible to the human eye.One of the main concerns when using neural networks in biomedicine is not knowing what they base their decisions on. ChromAgeNet overcomes that barrier by offering an explainable AI (XAI) system.The tool managed, on average, to correctly classify around 68% of cells as coming from young or aged mice using images obtained with DAPI, a standard, low-cost stain.In addition, ChromAgeNet stands out as an explainable AI, allowing researchers to investigate which image features contribute to its predictions. These analyses highlighted, among other regions, changes at the periphery of the nucleus associated with ageing.The analyses showed that chromatin is compact and organised at the edges of the nuclei of young cells, while in aged cells it appears dispersed. As a proof of concept, the tool assesses how certain epigenetic drugs (source in Spanish) induce changes in chromatin organisation that are consistent with patterns more akin to those observed in young cells. This showcases the potential of the tool for screening treatments that could regenerate blood tissue and strengthen the immune system. The code and the image database are already available to the international scientific community.Collaboration with AI research teamsAs for the practical applications of this research, Dr Maria Carolina Florian, principal investigator at the Bellvitge Biomedical Research Institute (IDIBELL), explains to Euronews: "Currently, we have developed a tool that works as a proof of concept in murine haematopoietic stem cells. We are now working to optimise it and adapt it to human stem cells, with the hope of using it to evaluate new drugs that can act on nuclear architecture and be used to rejuvenate aged stem cells."Maria Carolina Florian tells Euronews that this work "has found the ideal ground to become a real tool thanks to the expertise of Dr Paula Petrone (BSC and ISGlobal). We plan to continue developing it and expand it for use with human stem cells. In addition, we are applying for further EU funding and seeking to establish links with other scientists in Europe who are interested in the practical application of our work."For her part, Paula Petrone believes that this research "shows that a deep-learning algorithm can tell apart young and aged stem cells by analysing images of cell nuclei stained with a low-cost substance called DAPI."3D maps and open code to rejuvenate cellular architectureThe internal map of the cell nucleus reveals a distinctive signature: in youth, chromatin is tightly entrenched at the edges of the nucleus; with age, that architecture falls apart. Identifying these patterns could help to study the decline of blood stem cells and to assess potential strategies capable of regenerating haematopoietic tissue and triggering changes throughout the body.To demonstrate the practical potential of the algorithm, the team designed a proof of concept: they applied the tool to aged cells exposed to various epigenetic drugs. The goal was to determine whether the molecules were able to produce changes in chromatin organisation consistent with a more youthful state.To accelerate new discoveries, the team has released the tool's code and a public database of 3D images of stem cells, with the aim of finding drugs that reinforce the immune system and quality of life in old age.Numerous international studies underpin the evidence for the fundamental role of the immune system in the ageing of the body, as Maria Carolina Florian points out: "In our laboratory, we have contributed by demonstrating the possibility of stimulating and rejuvenating aged haematopoietic stem cells to improve not only immune system function, but also life expectancy and the health of the organism as a whole."Long-term promise, caution for now: the science behind ChromAgeNet calls for prudenceThe new ChromAgeNet tool will help to understand the basic molecular mechanisms involved in the ageing of haematopoietic stem cells, which could become targets for therapies to rejuvenate them. "We hope to deepen our knowledge, consolidate our findings and identify new tools and drugs to improve the function of aged haematopoietic stem cells," Florian concludes."In future, this technique could be used to screen new drugs with rejuvenating potential. By treating aged cells with different candidate compounds, AI could use image analysis to identify those that induce changes consistent with a more youthful state," Paula Petrone tells Euronews.For Dr Petrone, "Extending life expectancy is not as important as extending healthy life expectancy. The discovery of new drugs with rejuvenating potential could help, for example, to improve ageing of the immune system and thereby support healthier ageing."The researcher nevertheless stresses to Euronews the need for caution: "We must be very careful not to overestimate our results. These new technologies take years to be developed, validated and eventually reach the clinic. Our research is just one small contribution to the study of how we age and to the search for strategies that can support healthy ageing."

title: Astronaut Sophie Adenot returns to Earth after record space mission
description: Sophie Adenot left the International Space Station on Wednesday after an eight-month stay, the longest by a European astronaut, and splashed down on Thursday at around 5.30 pm with three fellow crew members.
content: Sophie Adenot spent 235 days 400 kilometres above the Earth. After a day-long journey, the French astronaut splashed down on Thursday 8 October at 5:35 p.m. (French time), together with three other members of the International Space Station crew, in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of San Diego, California.The final minutes of the flight brought intense sensations for the Frenchwoman, Russian cosmonaut Andrei Fediaiev and the two Americans Jessica Meir and Jack Hathaway: a high-speed plunge through the atmosphere, then a slowdown under powerful parachutes, all while communications were cut.After exiting the spacecraft and undergoing a brief medical check-up, the four astronauts will be flown back to dry land in the United States, first to Naval Air Station North Island in San Diego, then on to NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas.A medical team from the European Space Agency (ESA) will then take charge of Sophie Adenot during the long return flight to Cologne, in Germany. There, the astronaut will be reunited with her loved ones and will begin a recovery programme lasting several weeks.Thirty years after Claudie Haigneré, Sophie Adenot became in February the second Frenchwoman to cross the Karman line, the internationally recognised boundary between the atmosphere and outer space. She also became the first French woman to venture into the vacuum of space, during three spacewalks on 18 and 25 August and 1 September.With 237 days spent in space, the eleventh French astronaut now holds the record for the longest European spaceflight. The previous record-holder, Italian astronaut Luca Parmitano, spent 201 days in orbit in 2019–2020.

title: The disease that once ravaged Europe still exists: could plague return to Spain?
description: The death of a scientist in Russia has reignited fears of plague. Spain has seen no local cases for decades, yet the disease persists elsewhere. How real is the risk in Europe?
content: Plague, one of the deadliest diseases in history, has once again made headlines in recent days following the death of a scientist in Irkutsk, in Siberia. The woman died from pneumonia of unknown origin, which raised suspicions of a possible pneumonic plague infection.However, the Russian authorities have stated that no cases of plague have been confirmed in the region and that tests carried out on the deceased woman’s contacts have come back negative. The World Health Organization (WHO) has requested additional information to clarify what happened and has offered its support to the Russian authorities.Although no cases of routine transmission of this disease have been recorded in Europe for decades, the bacterium that causes it remains present in different parts of the world and continues to cause human infections every year.Does plague currently exist in Spain and Europe?Plague is not currently circulating routinely in Spain or in the rest of Europe. According to the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC), the disease has been absent from the continent for more than 50 years.This does not mean, however, that the bacterium has been eradicated from the planet. Plague is caused by Yersinia pestis, a microorganism that lives naturally in certain populations of small mammals, especially rodents, and in the fleas that infest them.The bacterium can be transmitted to humans through the bites of infected fleas, contact with tissues or body fluids from infected animals and, in the case of pneumonic plague, via respiratory particles from sick people.Therefore, although the current risk for the Spanish and European population is very low, the disease can still appear wherever there are animal reservoirs of the bacterium.Is there a risk of plague in Spain? What the Health Ministry saysSpain has gone decades without registering locally acquired cases of plague, but it maintains active epidemiological surveillance of the disease. In April 2026 the Public Health Commission updated the national protocol, revising case definitions, the epidemiological characteristics of the infection and the information that must be collected in the event of possible infections.This update, which predates the incident in Siberia, adds to the early-warning mechanisms already in place in Spain. For its part, the European Union examined the Russian case on 7 October, although international health authorities are still awaiting information that could clarify the cause of the researcher’s death.Where does plague still occur in the world?According to the WHO, plague remains endemic in several countries in Africa, Asia and the Americas. Between 2019 and 2025, most of the human cases reported to the organisation were concentrated in Madagascar and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. In Madagascar, for example, cases of bubonic plague are recorded virtually every year during the epidemic season, which usually runs from September to April.The disease also appears sporadically in regions of Asia and the Americas. In the United States, an average of around seven human cases are reported each year, mainly in rural areas in the west of the country.The persistence of the bacterium in wild animals explains why it is so difficult to eliminate the disease completely, even when human cases are rare.What is the difference between bubonic and pneumonic plague?Plague can present in three main forms: bubonic, pneumonic and septicaemic. Bubonic plague is the most common and usually occurs after the bite of an infected flea. It causes fever, general malaise and painful swelling of the lymph nodes, known as buboes.Pneumonic plague affects the lungs and is particularly dangerous because it can be transmitted from person to person via respiratory particles. Without treatment, it can progress rapidly and prove fatal. Septicaemic plague, meanwhile, occurs when the bacterium multiplies in the bloodstream and can lead to a severe, generalised infection.Unlike what happened during the great epidemics of the past, plague can now be treated with antibiotics. However, early diagnosis is essential to avoid serious complications and reduce the risk of death.What risk does the Siberia case pose for Europe?The suspected case of pneumonic plague in Siberia has prompted European health authorities to monitor the situation closely. The European Commission included the Russian incident on the agenda of its Health Security Committee meeting on 7 October, while the ECDC pointed out that there was no evidence of secondary cases or sustained person-to-person transmission.The WHO has also concluded that the risk to the European region is very low. Although the disease has not been eradicated worldwide, its presence on other continents does not mean that Europe is facing a new epidemic.Epidemiological surveillance, early detection of cases and treatment with antibiotics are crucial tools to prevent its spread. Plague still exists, but today’s health situation is very different from the one that allowed the Black Death to devastate Europe in the 14th century.

title: Scientists in Austria and China create the world’s first nuclear clocks. Here’s why it matters
description: The new nuclear clocks measure time by using lasers to make subatomic particles.
content: Scientists have invented the world’s first nuclear clocks that they say could unlock the fundamentals of physics. The two devices are the newest atomic clocks, which measure time by monitoring light by using transitions occurring inside the atomic nucleus, involving protons and neutrons. Atomic clocks have been used to keep precise measures of time and were first created in 1949 and, despite the name, do not use nuclear fusion or fission. The world's best clocks have relied on electrons jumping between energy levels in atoms but the discovery has shown that the reference for a clock can come from the nucleus itself. The research teams from China’s Tsinghua University and other institutions in the country and Austria’s TU Wien reported their breakthroughs separately in two papers published in Nature on Wednesday. The clock uses thorium-229, a rare atom whose nucleus can switch energy states using ultraviolet light from a laser. It is the only nucleus known to work this way.The team built a laser that makes ultraviolet light at 148.4 nanometres and aimed it at small calcium fluoride crystals containing thorium-229.The key finding was that the nuclear clocks worked. The laser stayed locked to the thorium-229 nucleus and kept steady time, reaching a precision of about one part in a quadrillion (10⁻¹⁵) over the test period. While precise timekeeping is vital for everyday technologies such as satellite navigation and telecommunications, nuclear clocks could make these systems more preciseThey could also be important in fundamental physics, the paper reads, however, it does not specify the exact use cases.

title: Kazakhstan seeks to build an AI-powered economy and manufacturing sector
description: Kazakhstan wants artificial intelligence to become more than a digital tool: the country is seeking to make it a new engine of economic growth, from universities and factories to energy and infrastructure.
content: Chatbots alone will not build a true AI economy. The real shift comes when artificial intelligence truly becomes part of how people earn a living, how companies make things and how governments make decisions."People should start to recognise that AI is not a toy. AI is not chatbots," Lee Kai-fu, founder and CEO of 01.AI and chairman of Sinovation Ventures, told Euronews in the Kazakh capital, Astana."AI needs to become the tool with which people make a living. Then, and only then, does this become a people's digital economy."That leap from a conventional economy to an AI-driven one ran through the AI & Digital Bridge forum, which brought government officials, tech companies, investors and experts to Astana.For Kazakhstan, the ambition is to use AI not merely to modernise existing industries but also to help the country reform its manufacturing industry and move further up the value chain.“The true value of AI lies in augmenting human capabilities,” President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said during the third meeting of the Artificial Intelligence Development Council, held alongside the forum.“Competition is no longer limited to natural resources, capital, and markets; it now extends to the speed at which production efficiency can be improved,” Tokayev said.The country's IT sector is already expanding abroad. IT service exports exceeded €860 million last year, while Kazakh digital solutions are now used in more than 100 countries.Digital Development Minister Zhaslan Madiyev said Kazakhstan was developing all five layers of the AI economy, from energy infrastructure, chips and cloud platforms to language models and applications.“We see the greatest potential for Kazakhstan in applied AI: in creating and scaling solutions that increase the efficiency of the economy and business, as well as the quality of people’s daily lives,” Madiyev said.The potential market is significant. Madiyev cited estimates putting the global addressable AI market at more than €43 trillion.AI and the factory floorThe 2026 UN Industrial Development Report identifies AI as one of the five transformative megatrends reshaping the global economy.For Kazakhstan, this matters because the country is trying to reduce its dependence on raw materials and increase the share of higher-value-added production.In the first eight months of this year, industrial production reached almost €90 billion, while manufacturing grew by 8.4% year-on-year, according to Tokayev.But maintaining that growth will require more than increasing production volumes.“To sustain high rates of economic growth, we must increase labor productivity, modernise the industrial base, and expand the production of high-value-added goods,” Tokayev said.AI could help companies achieve that by allowing engineers to make more accurate decisions, automating processes and giving managers real-time information about production.At the AI Development Council meeting, Tokayev instructed the government to identify companies for comprehensive AI transformation, accelerate the transition from pilot projects to commercial applications, develop industrial databases and reduce risks for investors.Building the people behind the technologyBut AI infrastructure alone will not create an AI economy. Kazakhstan also needs people capable of developing and using it.Lee Kai-Fu argues that fears about AI destroying jobs miss a more important shift: workers who learn to use AI effectively could gain an advantage over those who do not.“People are always wondering how can I get a job? AI is taking my job. That is not so, because it is you who knows how to use AI that can make the most money,” he said.That philosophy is already being incorporated into Kazakhstan's education system.The forum saw the launch of Qazaq AI Research University (QAIRU), the country's first specialised research university focused on artificial intelligence and the first AI-enabled university in Central Asia.“Qazaq AI Research University is set to become not only a center for training highly qualified specialists but also a leading hub for applied research. Its entire research program must be directly aligned with the practical needs of economic development,” Tokayev said.The university started operating on 1 September with 528 bachelor's and master's students. Its programmes cover machine learning, physical AI, industrial AI and smart systems, AI systems engineering and security, intelligent unmanned aerial systems and digital law.Students also use AI throughout their education, including for coursework, lectures, scheduling and tracking their progress.The infrastructure challengeKazakhstan's ambitions, however, face challenges that extend well beyond education.Research by the MIT Kuo Sharper Center for Prosperity and Entrepreneurship (MIT KSC) assessed AI readiness in four Central Asian countries and Azerbaijan, looking at regulation, infrastructure, human capital, academic programmes and private-sector adoption. Researchers interviewed 650 startups and 130 companies.The region has strong political support for AI, but access to critical infrastructure remains a constraint.“We see that Central Asia rapidly building its own infrastructure for AI. We see a strong political will backed with funding in AI, both infrastructure and academic programs. But at the same time, we see some major constraints, like access to microchips,” said Shamil Ibragimov, MIT KSC Director of Research.Electricity could become another bottleneck as demand for data centres grows.“One of the major constraints is a deficit of electricity in the region. Most countries in the region are facing the dilemma of choosing how to use power capacity, do you build more data centres or do you focus on the general audience?”The issue illustrates the physical side of the AI race. Algorithms may be digital, but they depend on chips, data centres, cloud infrastructure and large amounts of reliable electricity.From forum to economic transformationThe scale of AI & Digital Bridge reflects Kazakhstan's growing focus on the sector. The forum attracted around 25,000 visitors, 300 speakers and almost 200 startups and IT companies, with 62 memorandums and agreements signed.The event was part of the AI Month programme, running from September 23 to October 23, and included the AI & Digital Bridge Awards 2026 and the final of the Astana Hub Battle. Four startups won €21,500 each, while other participating companies secured funding of up to €170,000.But the forum's real significance lies beyond the deals and announcements.Kazakhstan is trying to turn AI from a technology sector into an economic infrastructure — one that can raise productivity, strengthen manufacturing, create new businesses and change how people work.Whether that strategy succeeds will depend less on how many AI projects the country launches than on whether those technologies make their way into factories, businesses, universities and everyday life.

title: Two-thirds of young Europeans suffered childhood trauma, with lasting life impact, WHO finds
description: Two-thirds of European children experienced trauma that ‘follows them into the classroom, job market and their relationships’.
content: More than two-thirds of young people in Europe have experienced childhood adversity ranging from domestic violence to the death of a parent, exposing them to poorer mental health and quality of life years later, according to a new report from the World Health Organization Regional Office for Europe. More than one in five young adults reported experiencing four or more adverse childhood experiences.“When a child grows up around violence or a household in crisis, we shouldn't be surprised that it follows them into the classroom, job market and their relationships years later,” said Natasha Azzopardi-Muscat, director of health systems at the WHO/Europe.She added that the extent of the problem is often overlooked and the consequences expand to several aspects of people's lives. “This isn't a mental health issue in isolation. It's a social and economic one, and it needs every sector at the table, not just health services,” said Azzopardi-Muscat. The report surveyed more than 26,000 young adults aged 18 to 30 across Europe between November 2025 and January 2026. It measured exposure to nine forms of adversity, such as physical, emotional or sexual abuse, physical neglect, household substance use, household mental illness, parental separation or death, and witnessing domestic violence during their childhood.“The findings are remarkably consistent. Adverse childhood experiences are at the root of poorer health, social and economic outcomes among young adults across Europe,” said Mark Bellis, from Liverpool John Moores University and academic lead for the study.The most common experiences were parental separation or death, witnessing domestic violence or suffering emotional abuse. Exposure to chronic stress in early childhood, which can be caused by these adverse experiences, disrupts brain development, impairs emotional regulation and alters physiological stress response systems, the report noted. Young adults reporting four or more adverse experiences suffered significantly higher rates of physical pain or discomfort, difficulties with everyday activities like work or study, impaired mobility and self-care difficulties. Among those who reported exposure to four or more adverse experiences, 76.3% felt they had needed professional mental health support in the previous year, compared with 36.7% of those who reported none. However, young people most exposed to harmful experiences were also more likely to report that they had not received the mental health support they felt they needed, the report warned. Breaking the cycle Without effective prevention and early intervention, harmful experiences tend to recur across generations, the authors warned. Adults affected by childhood adversity face higher risks of raising their own children in conditions marked by financial stress, domestic violence, and parental mental ill health. Despite this stark picture, the report noted that even those exposed to more adverse experiences could still achieve positive outcomes. The good news, Bellis said, is that adverse childhood experiences can be prevented and their impacts reduced. “With support from policymakers, investment in safer and more nurturing childhoods will help deliver healthier populations, stronger communities and a more prosperous future for Europe,” he added.

title: Tallinn Airport lets driverless shuttles run close to airplanes, opening the way to wider airport automation
description: Euronews Next exclusive: A driverless shuttle now carries aircraft workers and spare parts at Tallinn Airport, with no safety agents on board.
content: Autonomous cars and shuttles are no longer rare on city streets, but airports with their extraordinary safety rules are a different matter.At Tallinn Airport, Estonian company Auve Tech is now running its MiCa shuttles on routes passing close to parked aircraft — for the first time, without a safety operator on board. It is a step the company hopes will make driverless transport pay for itself and perhaps spread to other airports.The Tallinn shuttles serve Magnetic MRO, an aircraft maintenance firm with hangars on opposite sides of the airfield. They move workers, tools and spare parts between the sites throughout the day.Getting here took years. Auve Tech began testing their tech at the airport in 2023, and the commercial service started in 2025, first with a required safety operator on board. Taking that person out was the hard part."When conducting a drive inside the airport, that's a whole other story. You have so many layers of safety rules that you have to comply with," Deivis Sepp, Fleet Operations Lead at Auve Tech, told Euronews Next. "That's why getting the permit is kind of a miracle."Sepp said the airport's safety board has been reviewing the shuttles' performance data every week throughout the test period."Terabytes and terabytes of data have been gathered," Sepp told Euronews Next. "They are not giving us the permit like, 'Hey, just go ahead and do your thing, do the innovation.' It doesn't work like that."How MiCa worksMiCa is a small electric shuttle that Auve Tech unveiled in October 2022. It is designed for last-mile transport in pre-mapped areas, and it carries up to eight passengers. MiCa is rated Level 4 for self-driving — meaning it can drive itself without a human at the wheel, but only within defined conditions, such as a mapped route.To ”see” its surroundings, the shuttle uses ten cameras and seven laser-based sensors, which give it a 360-degree view. It does not roam freely between the planes — it follows a fixed route with rules built in and reacts immediately to any potential obstacle."It will see enough ahead to make a decision," Sepp told Euronews Next. "We are at a cross section, looking from one place to another, and if it's safe to move, it will go."The shuttle also reacts to small hazards. Euronews' reporter had to grab a handrail when the shuttle braked hard midway through the ride, apparently for a bird crossing its route.“Small birds are flying around here, and it detects everything near it," Sepp told Euronews Next. "So of course safety comes first for us."Humans are still part of the system, but from a distance. The vehicle makes its own decisions, and a remote operator in a tele-monitoring room watches over it."The vehicle decides what to do, whether to do it and when to do it," Sepp told Euronews Next. "But if some glitch happens, it will ask permission from the tele-monitoring operator."Making the sums add upFor Auve Tech, removing the on-board operator is a crucial economic step. Taavi Rõivas, Chairman of the Supervisory Board and a former Estonian prime minister, said a safety operator on board "doesn't make much sense commercially"."Regulatory needs are there to still have a human in the loop, but one human can supervise or remotely monitor several vehicles," Rõivas told Euronews Next.He put the break-even point at around three vehicles per remote operator."If you look at three vehicles at the same time, see what they're doing, and if necessary give some minor guidance, then we can match the price of human-driven vehicles," Rõivas told Euronews Next."Once we can roll out this service in this way, I believe the scaling of autonomous vehicle transportation will be very, very rapid."Their main client already sees the benefit in cost and reliability. Risto Mäeots, CEO of Magnetic Group, said his company drives "almost 50,000 kilometres every year" between its hangars. Before the shuttles, they had to only use human drivers, which sometimes brought problems of their own."We faced a lot of reliability issues. For example, people can get sick, and there was staff turnover," Mäeots told Euronews Next. "It turned out to be a big challenge."He described transport as a cost centre for a maintenance business, not a source of revenue. He also said the company, which competes with much larger aviation players, has to be inventive to survive."We half-joke that we don't have a right to exist because we are a small company against major aviation players," Mäeots told Euronews Next. "So for us to exist, we have to really think out of the box.""We thought it was going to be predominantly used by people, but now we see an equally important part is spare parts being delivered between the hangars," Mäeots told Euronews Next. Bulky items still travel by conventional vehicles because of the size limits.Auve Tech now wants to take the model elsewhere. Rõivas said the immediate target is the large number of last-mile shuttle services running in closed environments, such as corporate campuses, where regulators find it easier to allow vehicles without safety operators."Globally there are hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of last-mile shuttle services, only in closed environments," Rõivas told Euronews Next. "We see that we can either match the price or outperform the price of the current service."Interest is coming from Europe, Japan, Abu Dhabi and the US, he said. Other airports’ representatives are visiting Tallinn "pretty much one airport per week" to see the service working. Some consider carrying VIP passengers or move people between gates in such shuttles."We are expecting to have, very soon, announcements that much bigger airports than Tallinn will have a similar service up and running," Rõivas told Euronews Next.Sepp is confident about the direction. "I believe within the next 10 years, autonomous transportation solutions inside the airport will be a common thing to see," he told Euronews Next.

title: The 'death' of back-office jobs: Office work in the AI storm
description: From insurance payouts to banking, AI is taking over tasks that once took hours or days of human work — which office jobs are first in line for automation?
content: Two years ago, processing a health insurance claim at one of Greece's largest insurance companies took on average 14 days. Medical opinions, test results, invoices and policy details all had to be checked and cross-referenced before payment was given the green light.Today, the processing time has been cut to around one minute and the compensation is paid out the following day.Driving this change is AI Flows, an artificial intelligence tool for document processing and workflow automation developed by the Greek company Archeiothiki. The system handles around 1,500 claims a day, "reads" the documents, extracts the necessary information and cross-checks it against the policy and the insurance company's rules.Above all, though, it enables something that was previously practically impossible: checking 100% of cases rather than just a sample. This makes it possible to spot potential fraud that would otherwise have gone unnoticed.The example of the Greek insurer offers a snapshot of a much broader transformation unfolding in offices across Europe.From 16 hours to a few minutesIn banking, similar technology is used to assess the ESG (environmental, social governance) criteria of companies seeking finance.The process involves around 300 questions. To verify the answers, staff must hunt for data in company reports running to hundreds of pages, ranging from the ratio of men to women to information on environmental performance and corporate policies.This check used to require about 16 hours of human labour. Now, an AI system can search for the necessary information even in reports running to 400 or 500 pages, identify the relevant passages and process them in a fraction of the time.The final assessment of ESG criteria influences the interest rate at which the company will be financed.Jobs on the frontlineArcheiothiki currently applies AI Flows to around 100 different workflows for ten clients, mainly banks, insurance companies and businesses in the healthcare sector.But what is happening in Greece is far from unique.Office roles that have traditionally formed the back office of companies are among those most exposed to the new generation of artificial intelligence.According to the report "Generative AI and Jobs: A Refined Global Index of Occupational Exposure", published in May 2025 by the International Labour Organization (ILO) and the Polish research institute NASK, administrative and clerical occupations remain the category of jobs most exposed to generative AI.Among the most exposed roles are data entry clerks, staff involved in accounting and bookkeeping, and administrative secretaries. In high-income economies, roughly one in three jobs shows some degree of exposure to generative AI.Artificial intelligence has already entered European workplaces on a large scale. According to the study "Digital Monitoring, Algorithmic Management and the Platformisation of Work in Europe" by the Joint Research Centre of the European Commission, published in October 2025, 30% of workers in the EU already use AI tools in their jobs. Use is particularly high in office work.The transition also has a clear gender dimension. More recent ILO research shows that occupations where women are in the majority are almost twice as likely to be exposed to generative AI as those where men predominate: 29% compared with 16%.One key reason is the greater presence of women in administrative, clerical and support roles."I will not hide it. There are jobs that are lost too," was the response of Archeiothiki executives when asked about this by Euronews.The picture they sketch, however, is more complex. In many cases, automation is not used simply to carry out the same volume of work with fewer people. It allows companies to take on tasks that were previously practically impossible to perform at this scale.One client, for instance, had around 50 people working on a single process and still built up a year-long backlog. In other cases, where only a sample of cases could previously be checked, now the entire set can be examined.This aligns broadly with the ILO's assessment. The organisation warns that the "exposure" of a job to artificial intelligence does not necessarily mean that role will disappear. Few occupations consist solely of tasks that can currently be fully automated. For this reason, the most likely outcome for now is the transformation of jobs rather than their complete replacement.The next data reservoir: the public sectorIn Greece, the next major field may lie in the millions of documents that have already been digitised in the public sector.According to Archeiothiki's chief executive, Andreas Papadakis, the company has carried out around 15% of the relevant digitisation projects for the state.The problem is that much of this new digital archive remains effectively "blind". Physical documents were turned into digital files and given basic metadata so they could be searched. Their content, however, was not necessarily converted into structured data that can be analysed and put to use.The first stage of digitisation was to turn mountains of paper into digital files. The next stage is already under way.AI systems are no longer confined to reading and recording documents, but can extract information, cross-check it and execute entire workflows.This shifts automation away from repetitive data-entry tasks to a much larger portion of the traditional back office.

title: Rebranded Jaguar unveils its first electric sportscar: The Type 01EV
description: Hailed as the most technologically advanced and powerful Jaguar in the company’s history, it premiered in New York today, targeting a younger, wealthier and mostly American customer base.
content: Luxury car manufacturer Jaguar unveiled its first new model since its controversial rebrand two years ago at a flashy New York launch party attended by actress and new company ambassador Florence Pugh, in a bid to win over younger, richer and mostly American audience.The luxury four-door GT Type01EV is Jaguar’s first foray in the electric vehicle (EV) market. Its ultra-modern, brutalist, sharp-edged design is a massive shift from its previously quintessential British elegance.The radical design is an attempt by Jaguar’s hierarchy to shake off its previously antiquated albeit storied legacy that started as being a car for racing enthusiasts to one for the posh elite. They now have a newer, younger and richer demographic in their crosshairs.Jaguar says the new model is the first production from its new Jaguar Electric Architecture (JEA), a dedicated platform for the next generation of Jaguar modes, as the company embraces its original motto “Copy Nothing” to create a vehicle they feel is unique.It’s also gigantic.Coming in at 5.2 metres long and 2 metres wide, it is longer than most SUVs and too long for most European carparks.That makes it something of an awkward fit for Europe, where narrow roads are already struggling with the weight and size of today's monstrous vehicles. It would be far more at home on America's vast, endless highways.But that has not stopped SUV numbers from exploding on EU roads in recent years.The Type01EV is very low to the ground for its size, standing at only 1.4 metres tall, making it a particularly sleek looking vehicle.It weighs in at a huge 2700 kilograms, significantly heavier than its competitors such as the Porsche Taycan Turbo GT (2,200kg) and a little more than the Mercedes-Benz EQS (2,585 kg) which shares a similar length.The Type 01EV’s three motors and battery are extraordinary too. Not only are they powerful, clocking in 1030 horsepower and taking it from 0 to 100 kph in 3.2 seconds, it boasts an impressive 450-mile (720km) range, way above most of its rivals, with only the Porsche Taycan marginally more powerful.The battery also charges at 350kw, allowing it to charge 200 miles (321km) of range in just 13 minutes and go from 10% to 80% charge in just 22 minutes, making it even more appealing to drivers wishing to make the switch to an electric vehicle.But it won’t be for everyone.Base models will start at around €167,470 in Europe, with bespoke specifications and customisations taking it up to €185,470.Jaguar’s rebranded new car does retain a sense of Britishness though, with the Type01EV designed, engineered and built in the UK, according to their website.Orders are scheduled to open in early 2027, with the first delivers in Europe expected in the second half of 2027.Jaguar is a British and global car icon known for models such as the Jaguar E-Type driven by Frank Sinatra, Steve McQueen and described by Enzo Ferrari as “the most beautiful car ever made”.Before its rebrand in 2024, the company was facing a severe, multi-year identity and financial crisis caused by a failing business strategy that relied on an aging core audience and failed to win over younger consumers.Jaguar was making cars that were not common enough to compete with BMW and Mercedes nor exclusive or “cool” enough to compete with Porsche or Bentley.The car company took the plunge with a radical rebrand in 2024, releasing an advert that featured no car at all. Instead, models in brightly coloured clothing spouted slogans such as “live vivid”, “delete ordinary” and “be the jag you are”.The campaign was criticised by many including political figures such as Donald Trump and Nigel Farage for “going woke,” with Elon Musk asking on social media platform X, “Do you sell cars?”Jaguar defended the ad campaign, telling Sky News at the time that the company wanted “to be bold and disruptive".The new model’s launch comes as parent company Jaguar Land Rover recovers from a cyberattack that forced the company to halt production last year. One month later, the company announced it would cut 4,000 jobs as part of a major cost-cutting drive.Today’s unveiling is the culmination of a years-long strategy to reposition the car manufacturer.

title: Denmark introduces bill to protect people’s faces and voices from deepfakes
description: The bill follows a broad political agreement reached in June 2025 but would still allow satire, parody and political or social criticism unless it constitutes misinformation posing serious dangers to others.
content: Denmark is due to introduce a bill on Thursday that would ban the sharing of realistic deepfakes of people’s faces and voices without their consent.The proposed amendment to Denmark’s copyright law would protect ordinary people as well as artists, including against digital imitations of their performances.Deepfakes are images, videos or audio generated or manipulated using artificial intelligence (AI) to make someone appear to say or do something they did not. They can be used to spread false information or humiliate those depicted.“With artificial intelligence, you can create manipulated videos and images with just a few clicks and share them on social media,” wrote Zenia Stampe, Denmark’s culture minister, in a statement.“One of the main goals of the bill is to get the tech giants to take down manipulated content quickly, so that it causes the least possible harm.”The bill follows a broad political agreement reached in June 2025 by then-culture minister Jakob Engel-Schmidt under the previous government to protect people against unauthorised digital imitations.It includes exceptions for satire, parody, caricature and criticism of power and society, although these would not cover misinformation posing specified serious dangers to others’ rights, essential interests, life or property.The minister hopes the law will take effect at the start of 2027.Denmark’s move comes as countries around the world grapple with the rapid rise of AI.EU countries bound by the bloc’s directive on violence against women must implement it by 14 June 2027. It requires them to criminalise creating sexually explicit manipulated material and subsequently making it publicly accessible without the depicted person’s consent, where this is likely to cause serious harm.Denmark is not bound by the directive because of its opt-out from EU justice and home affairs rules.France already prohibits sharing AI-generated images or audio depicting someone without their consent when the artificial nature of the content is not obvious or expressly disclosed.Separate rules prohibit sharing sexual deepfakes without consent, regardless of labelling.In the United Kingdom, creating or requesting non-consensual intimate deepfakes became a criminal offence in England and Wales in February. Sharing such images can carry a prison sentence of up to two years.

title: Women in this Sardinian village live exceptionally long. Researchers are asking why
description: Researchers say Bolotana, a town of just a bit more than 2,000 inhabitants in Sardinia, may join Japan’s Okinawa and Greece’s Ikaria among the world's longevity hotspots.
content: Women in Bolotana, a small town on the Italian island of Sardinia, can expect to live to 91 years — more than two years longer than the Italian national average, according to a new study.Women in this village are also three times more likely to reach 100 years old than women living elsewhere in Italy. Researchers estimated that 13.8% of women in Bolotana who reach age 70 will live to 100, compared with approximately 3.5% of women in Italy and 3.6% of women in the United States. “We think this is the longest-lived female population in the world, or close to it,” said S. Jay Olshansky, from the University of Illinois Chicago School of Public Health. Among international benchmarks, Bolotana women ranked second only to Hong Kong for both remaining life expectancy at age 70 and survival to age 100. Bolotana first attracted attention because of its unusual concentration of centenarians. In 2024, six people aged 100 or older were living in the village, a prevalence roughly 11 times higher than that of the United States, according to the researchers’ estimates. The study, published in the journal Frontiers in Aging, analysed demographic records from the village, which has about 2,300 residents and found a favourable pattern of survival among older adults between 2021 and 2025, particularly women. The study documented 38 centenarians among 3,060 people born in Bolotana between 1900 and 1925.The findings suggest the community could represent a new “blue zone” — regions where people have unusually long lives, and where there is a disproportionately high concentration of nonagenarians and centenarians. While the study confirms that something unusual is happening in Bolotana, it doesn’t determine the exact causes behind this phenomenon. However, the authors highlight several factors that may play a role, including dietary patterns, genetics, physical activity, family support and social cohesion. Most food is grown locally, including olive oil rich in healthy fats. Families often live close together, and social isolation is rare. “You’ve got this close-knit community where people take care of each other,” Olshansky added. “Movement is largely done by walking, not by driving.” Other blue zonesEstablishing blue zones has been contentious and challenging, as it requires extensive record-keeping. “What makes Bolotana extraordinary is that it has an incredible historical record that allows us to definitively evaluate ages at birth and death,” Olshansky said. “The municipal and baptismal records date back centuries and allowed us to independently verify ages.” Other blue zones that have been singled out and confirmed by researchers include Okinawa, Japan, the Nicoya Peninsula in Costa Rica and Ikaria in Greece. A fourth blue zone has also been identified in Sardinia, located across six villages in the east-central part of the island, in a region called Ogliastra.

title: Menopause drug Lenzetto to return to Spanish pharmacies in November
description: Hungarian pharma company Gedeon Richter has told Euronews it expects to resume supply of its menopause treatment in Spain from mid-November, but warns global limits may stop it from meeting demand in 2027.
content: Lenzetto, one of the most widely used hormone treatments to relieve menopausal symptoms, will once again be available in Spanish pharmacies from the second half of November, its manufacturer Gedeon Richter has confirmed to Euronews."We expect the product to be available in pharmacies from the second half of November," the pharmaceutical company said in response to questions from Euronews. Gedeon Richter says it will do "everything possible" to guarantee stable production for the rest of this year and in 2027, although it acknowledges that worldwide supply constraints may prevent it from fully covering current demand.The company traces the origin of the current shortage of the medicine in Spain to a sharp rise in demand for menopause hormone treatments in Europe. In an email, the company explained that growth has been far higher than expected and that both manufacturing capacity and the supply of the device used to administer Lenzetto, the applicator, could not keep pace with the surge in demand.Gedeon Richter stresses that the situation is temporary and "is not related to any problem with the quality or safety of the medicine". The issue, according to the company, is simply that high demand has outstripped its production capacity.To increase the availability of its medicine, the laboratory says it is making full use of its current production capacity and working to expand both the number of suppliers and its manufacturing options. It is also trying to improve the supply of applicators and increase their production capacity, among other measures.These plans include a new plant and a new production line. In Romania, Gedeon Richter has also launched a dedicated investment project to strengthen its manufacturing capacity. The company warns, however, that expanding pharmaceutical production takes time because of quality controls.The company also acknowledges that the measures adopted will not resolve the situation overnight. It says it is working so that the changes can improve supply as quickly as possible.A problem affecting other marketsThe shortage of Lenzetto is not limited to Spain. Gedeon Richter confirms that there is currently a global shortage of the medicine, although the severity of the problems varies between markets depending on local demand, forecasting capacity and logistical possibilities.The situation has for months made it difficult to obtain some hormone treatments used to relieve menopausal symptoms. The lack of Lenzetto forced patients and healthcare professionals to turn to other forms of estradiol, which eventually generated a domino effect on some of the alternative treatments.The European Medicines Agency (EMA) has also identified the Lenzetto shortage and is studying possible coordinated measures at the European level. In Spain, the Spanish Agency of Medicines and Medical Devices (AEMPS) has likewise recorded supply problems affecting other medicines, such as Evopad, Estradot and Bijuva."The supply problem started in April with Lenzetto and has subsequently affected other transdermal hormone therapies such as patches and gels," AEMPS said in a statement (source in Spanish) published in early October.
