"The Ministry of Health has been in contact with the holders of other hormone treatment alternatives that are currently not reimbursed, to explore their possible inclusion in the pharmaceutical services of the National Health System."Richter responds to AEMPS criticismAEMPS has pointed out that some of the supply forecasts previously communicated by Gedeon Richter "have not always been accurate" and that interruptions which could affect the continuous supply of the medicine were not reported with sufficient notice.Asked by Euronews about these comments, the company does not directly address the allegations, but says it maintains "close contact" with AEMPS and works "in a collaborative manner" with the agency to tackle the situation.Gedeon Richter adds that it has improved its forecasting systems in response to demand it describes as "unprecedented" and that it continues to provide information to the authorities as new data become available.The laboratory does not, however, guarantee a full recovery of supply in the short term. The company says its goal is to be able to consistently meet patient demand from the second half of 2027.

title: Type 1 diabetes 'should not set the limits on a child's sports dreams'
description: 'Exercise, know your body, monitor your glucose and learn to adjust your insulin and your diet correctly,' a Greek professor tells those who have type 1 diabetes.
content: Around 66 million people live with diabetes on the European continent – that is one in ten adults, with one in three still undiagnosed. Around 2,7 million people in the region have type 1 diabetes – the highest prevalence among all the regions.Type 1 diabetes can develop as early as childhood or adolescence and requires daily management of glucose levels, but that does not mean a child has to limit play, exercise or even elite sport.As Thanasis Tziamourtas, professor at the University of Thessaly in Greece, explains, type 1 diabetes is a chronic autoimmune disease in which the immune system destroys the pancreatic beta cells that produce insulin, the hormone that regulates blood glucose."Unlike type 2 diabetes, type 1 diabetes is not caused by obesity, poor diet or lack of exercise. Insulin therapy is essential for life, whether via multiple daily injections or through an insulin pump," he said.But that should not become a barrier to participating in sports for children, Tziamourtas added.The professor cites German tennis player Alexander Zverev as a striking example. He was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes at the age of four. Tennis is a sport with particular demands, as a match can last several hours and involve repeated bursts of high-intensity effort.There are also other elite athletes with type 1 diabetes, including American swimmer Gary Hall Jr., winner of 10 Olympic medals, five of them gold, and Dutch volleyball Olympic champion Bas van de Goor.Can a child with type 1 diabetes take part in sport?The answer is clear: yes. Physical activity is not only permitted, but it is also a key element of a healthy lifestyle for children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes.The professor points out that international guidelines recommend around 60 minutes of moderate to vigorous physical activity every day, just as for the general child and adolescent population."Exercise is not simply a permitted activity but an important part of a healthy lifestyle for children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes. International guidelines recommend around 60 minutes of moderate to vigorous physical activity every day, as for their peers without diabetes. Regular exercise improves cardiorespiratory fitness, muscle strength, insulin sensitivity, body composition and cardiovascular risk factors. At the same time, it offers significant psychological and social benefits and helps a child feel able to take part in the same activities as their peers.""Exercise, however, creates a particular challenge: glucose does not respond in the same way to all types of activity," he added.Why exercise can change glucose levelsThe relationship between exercise and glucose is more complex in people with type 1 diabetes. As muscles need more energy during physical activity, they increase their uptake of glucose from the blood.In someone without diabetes, the pancreas can reduce insulin secretion according to the body's needs. In type 1 diabetes, by contrast, insulin is administered from outside the body and cannot be reduced automatically in the same way.The result may be hypoglycaemia, particularly in prolonged aerobic exercise such as running, cycling and swimming.The picture can be different in very high-intensity activities. Sprints, high-intensity drills or a hard-fought match can temporarily raise glucose, as hormones such as adrenaline are released."So there is no single 'glucose response to exercise'. It depends," he explains, "on the intensity and duration of the effort, the type of exercise, physical fitness, the previous meal, the amount of active insulin and glucose levels before starting the activity."The role of monitoring before and after trainingFor parents and children, the key aim is not to avoid exercise but to prepare properly.Glucose needs to be checked before activity, during it, particularly when exercise is prolonged, and again afterwards. Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) systems now offer valuable support, providing not only a reading but also information on how glucose is trending.At the same time, a child who is active should have fast-acting carbohydrates available, such as glucose tablets or an appropriate sugary drink, to deal immediately with possible hypoglycaemia.Care does not end once training is over. Glucose can fall several hours later, which is particularly important when exercise takes place in the late afternoon or evening, as there is a risk of nocturnal hypoglycaemia.Similarly, when glucose is very high and ketone levels are raised, vigorous exercise should be avoided.Insulin adjustment must be individualisedThere is no single plan that works for all children with type 1 diabetes. Insulin and carbohydrate needs vary depending on the type, duration and intensity of the activity, the time of day and other factors."Adjustments to insulin and carbohydrate intake are not the same for everyone. They must, he stresses, be tailored in collaboration with the care team, taking into account the type of exercise, the time of day, its duration and intensity, and the person's previous experience."From diagnosis to top-level sportThe message that needs to reach children and their families, according to Thanasis Tziamourtas, is that the disease should not be a reason to exclude them from physical activity."A diagnosis of type 1 diabetes undoubtedly changes the daily life of a child and their family. It should not, however, become a reason to be excluded from play, physical activity or sport. Today, continuous glucose monitors, insulin pumps and automated insulin delivery systems offer opportunities that did not exist a few decades ago. Together with the right education, they enable children and adults with type 1 diabetes to be active more safely.The message to the child and their family should therefore not be 'Be careful, because you have diabetes, don't exercise'. It should be exactly the opposite: 'Exercise, know your body, monitor your glucose and learn to adjust your insulin and your diet correctly.' Type 1 diabetes requires management, but it should not set the limits on a child's dreams."

title: Menopause patients left without treatment: what is happening in Spain?
description: The shortage of Lenzetto has had a domino effect on other menopause hormone treatments in Spain and other European countries. Spain's Health Ministry expects supplies to improve in November, but Spain's Medicines watchdog warns the timetable is still unclear.
content: Hundreds of thousands of Spanish women have spent months encountering problems getting hold of some of the hormone treatments used to relieve menopausal symptoms.What began as an issue with a single medicine — Lenzetto, a transdermal estradiol spray — has finally triggered a domino effect in the market for hormone replacement therapies (HRT).The shortage of Lenzetto drove up demand for other estradiol formulations, such as patches and gels, which were not prepared to absorb it. Over recent months, Aemps has recorded supply issues affecting medicines such as Evopad, Estradot and Bijuva.The result has been months of supply problems, patients searching for their medication from pharmacy to pharmacy, and authorities trying to find alternatives.November could mark the start of an improvement, although there are still doubts about when supply will truly return to normal.The Secretary of State for Health, Javier Padilla, told Euronews on the sidelines of the European Health Forum Gastein in Austria that the situation should start to ease from next month.Spain's Medicines and Medical Devices Agency (Aemps), however, warns that the forecasts communicated by Lenzetto's manufacturer, Gedeon Richter, "have not always been accurate".Gedeon Richter confirmed to Euronews that it expects Lenzetto to be available again in Spanish pharmacies starting in the second half of November. However, the company acknowledges it may not be able to fully meet demand throughout 2027 due to global supply constraints, though it expects to gradually meet demand starting in the second half of 2027.European issueThe problem is not confined to Spain. According to Padilla, a sharp surge in demand has outstripped manufacturers' production capacity in several European countries. Aemps also considers this to be an international supply issue affecting, to varying degrees, different European Union member states.The European Medicines Agency (EMA) has confirmed to Euronews that it has been informed of the supply issues regarding Lenzetto and is considering possible coordinated measures at the EU level to mitigate the impact. The matter will be addressed in upcoming meetings of the European group responsible for medicine supply issues.The EMA further notes that it is aware of recent supply problems involving other estradiol-based medicines in the EU. However, these cases have not been deemed critical at the European level and are being managed by national authorities.The crisis mainly affects women who use these therapies to alleviate symptoms associated with the menopause, although estradiol is also used in other clinical situations, including the prevention of osteoporosis and gender-affirming hormone treatments for trans women.From Lenzetto to a domino effectThe crisis was brewing for months. Aemps began receiving reports from users about difficulties in finding Lenzetto in February and contacted pharmaceutical company Gedeon Richter at that point. Initially, the company insisted it was meeting demand as normal.The situation changed soon afterwards. The laboratory reported that it was facing a surge in demand it could not meet immediately and problems with the device used to administer the medicine. Weeks later it announced that it had run out of stock and that the issue was affecting all its markets throughout 2026.Aemps also maintains that the company failed to meet its obligation to notify in advance of incidents that could disrupt the continuous supply of the medicine. Consumption of Lenzetto had risen very rapidly. In Spain, distributed units rose from around 13,000 in 2018 to about 123,000 in 2024.Gedeon Richter explained to Euronews that demand had outstripped its manufacturing capacity and that the availability of the applicator used to administer the medication could not keep pace with the growth. The company emphasises that the shortage is unrelated to any quality or safety issues with the medication.To increase supply, the company states that it is maximising its current capacity and developing new manufacturing options and suppliers. Furthermore, it is establishing a new plant and a new production line.Spain raised the price, but it was not enoughThe government has tried various ways to increase the availability of these medicines. Among them, as Padilla explained, raising the regulated price in an attempt to attract more supply to the Spanish market. But the measure failed to resolve the problem. The Secretary of State stressed that the difficulty goes beyond price: manufacturers do not have sufficient capacity to cope with the sharp rise in demand.The Health Ministry then explored another option. It contacted manufacturers of alternative treatments that are not reimbursed by the National Health System and signalled its willingness to consider funding them in order to widen the options available to patients.According to Padilla, this route has also not delivered the expected results so far. The companies told the government that they did not have enough production capacity to increase supply, even if their products were to be publicly funded. Aemps confirms that the Health Ministry has held talks with the holders of these alternatives, although no reimbursement requests have yet been formalised.More than 25,000 signatures reach the Health MinistryWhile the authorities look for solutions, patients have begun to mobilise. More than 25,000 people have supported, in barely three weeks, a petition calling on the government to take urgent action over the supply problems. Its organiser, 49-year-old Rebeca Marín, who uses hormone replacement therapy, is due to submit the signatures this Tuesday, 6 October, at the Health Ministry.The petition calls on the authorities to act preventively in the face of future supply problems and to ensure that when a medicine is unavailable, there are accessible alternatives for patients regardless of where they live. The financial aspect is particularly important. Some of the existing alternatives are not covered by the public system, forcing patients to bear the full cost.The Institute of Women demands "urgent" actionThe issue has also reached the Institute of Women, which has asked the Health Ministry and Aemps to tackle "as a priority and urgently" the supply problems. The body acted after receiving complaints from individuals and women's associations concerned both about the difficulty of maintaining their treatments and about the price of some of the available alternatives.Catalonia turns to pharmaciesIn view of the prolonged shortage, Catalonia has decided to prepare an alternative solution. The regional government plans to allow pharmacies to prepare magistral estradiol formulas if supply problems persist.The measure would allow individualised treatments to be made up from the active ingredient and on the basis of a medical prescription. Compounding pharmacies have estradiol in stock as a raw material, so this route could serve as an alternative when industrially produced medicines are unavailable.The proposal has, however, opened up a divide between health authorities and pharmacists. Aemps believes magistral formulas should be used only as a last resort, as their absorption can be more variable than that of authorised medicines. The General Council of Official Pharmacists' Associations, by contrast, advocates their use in the current shortage.The Health Ministry is also studying, together with scientific societies and laboratories, other measures to tackle the shortage, including the possibility of setting criteria to prioritise certain patients if necessary.When will the shortage end?For now there is no definitive answer. The situation differs from one medicine to another. For some Evopad presentations, Aemps expects new batches in October and a return to normal from November.The outlook for Lenzetto is more uncertain. Gedeon Richter has informed Aemps that it will distribute new units over the course of November and will gradually resume supply from that month and throughout 2027.It is precisely this uncertainty that qualifies the forecast passed on by Padilla to Euronews. November may mark the beginning of recovery, but not necessarily the end of the crisis.

title: Maricarmen, symbol of Spain's housing protests, dies
description: The 87-year-old woman had withstood four eviction attempts in the past decade. In a final message from her hospital bed, she urged protesters: "Fight!"
content: Maricarmen Abascal, whose resistance to eviction from her flat in Madrid sparked a growing nationwide protest has died. Her plight brought hundreds of thousands onto the streets and ultimately brought forward a general election after mass demonstrations across the country.The elderly woman, who had lived in her flat in Madrid’s Retiro district for 70 years, was eventually evicted at the fourth attempt under the gaze of the media, after she was unable to pay the increased rent. She was admitted to hospital, but she managed to force the property fund that expelled her from her home to back down and allow her to return, following an agreement with the authorities.“Although a historic agreement was reached that would have allowed her to return to her home, this solution came too late,” the Madrid Tenant’s Union said in a statement Wednesday. “It was an entirely avoidable situation following a harrowing ordeal.”Protesters who have been camped out in Madrid's iconic Sol square held a minute of silence after hearing news of her passing.Pedro Sanchez expresses condolences after hearing of Maricarmens's passingPrime Minister Pedro Sanchez has expressed his condolences in a post on X. "All my love to Maricarmen’s family and loved ones,” Sánchez said, “A hug as well to all of us who feel this loss as our own today.”Meanwhile protester are gathering again in Madrid and unions are promoting a general strike. The UGT and CCOO unions urged the population to "mobilise for better salaries, for decent housing and for price controls in the face of inflation that undermines our purchasing power".Pedro Sanchez's left-wing minority government last week suffered a bruising legislative defeat when right-wing opposition parties voted down emergency decrees to address the housing crisis.A fresh round of protests turned violent in Barcelona on Monday night, just hours after Sánchez announced he was dissolving Parliament and calling early elections for Nov. 29.Spain’s government on Tuesday approved urgent measures to tackle the housing crisis, similar to those Parliament rejected last week.Rising costs and a housing shortage are pricing many Spaniards out of the housing market, despite strong economic growth in Europe’s fourth-largest economy. The protesters have been demanding stronger tenant protections, measures to combat fraud, and a ban on evictions when alternative housing is unavailable.

title: Judo: Grigalashvili claims fourth world title as Kaju reigns again
description: Haruka Kaju extended her unbeaten World Judo Tour run to 40 contests, defending her -63kg world title against Kerem Primo. At -81kg, Tato Grigalashvili defeated home favourite Zelim Tckaev to claim his fourth world title and return to the top of the podium.
content: Baku is the stage for the middleweights on day 4 of the World Judo Championships.At -63kg, reigning World Champion KAJU Haruka has never lost a contest on the World Judo Tour, and here in Baku she was determined to keep that record intact. She confidently earned her place in the final, aiming to keep her red backpatch for another year and continue her remarkable run.She’d face Kerem PRIMO, who was entering not only her first World Championship final, but her first ever World Judo Tour final. It was the biggest moment of her career, and standing across from her would be one of the sport’s most formidable champions.In the final, KAJU used her trademark groundwork to take control of the contest. Once in ne-waza, the Japanese judoka was clinical, extending her unbeaten run to 40 contests and taking her place at the top of the podium in Baku.Football Legend Mr Lothar MATTHÄUS awarded the medals.Triple World Champion, Georgian legend Tato GRIGALASHVILI was here to add a fourth World title to his collection in the -81kg category. After settling for silver last year, one of judo’s most dominant forces had another World gold firmly within his reach.Facing him was Azerbaijan’s own Zelim TCKAEV who was looking to upgrade last year's World bronze medal to a history making World gold in his home nation. With the support of his home fans cheering on, could he rise to the challenge and become World Champion?The atmosphere was electric as the final got underway, and GRIGALASHVILI rose to the occasion. The Georgian delivered when it mattered most, securing victory and with it a fourth World title, further cementing his place among judo’s modern greats.Azerbaijan Judo Federation President Mr Rashad NABIYEV awarded the medals.That’s it for day 4 in the land of fire.

title: Longevity: why do Poles live shorter than Western Europeans?
description: Poland still clearly trails Western Europe in life expectancy and years lived in good health. According to Robert Mordaka, a public health specialist, prevention and everyday habits are crucial.
content: "We are lagging behind not only in terms of average life expectancy, but also in the number of years we spend in good health. And that is a metric that really needs to be improved," Mordaka told Euronews during the Economic Forum in Karpacz.He pointed out that around 60% of deaths are caused by two major groups of illnesses: cardiovascular diseases and cancers. In both cases, prevention and earlier intervention in response to risk factors can play a key role.Prevention in Poland is still underfundedAccording to the doctor, the problem does not come down solely to individual choices made by Poles. The way the healthcare system operates is also crucial. Poland is among the EU countries that devote the smallest share of health spending to preventive care."The EU average is around 6% of health budgets, while in Poland it is just under 2%. And without funding it is impossible to reverse this trend," Mordaka said.At the same time, many of the factors that affect the length and quality of life remain in patients' own hands. Mordaka draws attention to the so-called Life's Essential 8 – eight areas that are critical to cardiovascular health.These include keeping blood pressure, blood glucose and cholesterol under control, maintaining a healthy body weight, getting enough sleep, eating a balanced diet and not smoking. Regular physical activity is also vital."These are the small, everyday choices. Do we go to the shop and buy a sugary drink, or do we buy water instead?" the expert asked.Obesity and smoking can cut life expectancy by many yearsOne of the biggest current threats to health is obesity. According to Mordaka, studies indicate that it can shorten life by as much as 15 years. Another major factor is smoking, which can take several years off life expectancy, depending on how many cigarettes are smoked per day and how long the habit continues.A lack of physical activity also has a negative impact on how long we live. That is why one of the simplest ways to improve health is to increase the amount of movement in everyday life. The expert advises starting with two basic elements: reviewing your diet and increasing your physical activity."Let’s take a close look at how we eat. Let’s plan a healthy plate and adapt it to our age and state of health. And the second thing: let’s start moving," Mordaka urged. "Exercise is the best medicine," the expert concluded.According to World Health Organization guidelines, adults should engage in at least 150 minutes of moderate physical activity per week. This does not have to mean intensive workouts; it can be brisk walking, cycling or other forms of moderate exercise.

title: Laws, pledges or an iron grip? How the EU, US and China are reining in AI
description: The US, China and the EU are taking sharply different approaches to regulating artificial intelligence. Here is how the world's biggest economies are tackling the technology, and what is at stake.
content: Pressure is growing worldwide to rein in the most powerful artificial intelligence systems, and the world's three top AI heavyweights are answering in three very different ways.The worries are much the same everywhere, starting from AI-powered cyberattacks, threats to national security and chatbots linked to children's suicides. The responses, it seems, are significantly different.The EU has bet on binding rules, though it has already loosened some of them under pressure from industry. The US relies on voluntary promises and executive orders meant to keep its AI boom going. China is building its own rulebook under tight state control while rejecting calls to slow down.Here is how each is going about it.EU: "The world's first comprehensive rules on AI"The European Union adopted its AI Act in 2024, which Brussels calls the "world's first comprehensive rules on artificial intelligence".The Act regulates AI based on a four-tier risk framework, with rules escalating according to the threat level the AI system poses, going from those posing limited to no threat — such as video game elements and spam filters being able to operate freely — all the way to unacceptable systems with wide-reaching powers being outright banned such as social scoring, emotion recognition and manipulation.But European companies, fearing the rules would stifle innovation as they race to catch up with US and Chinese rivals, lobbied hard and later won a delay as part of the AI Omnibus bill on rules covering high-risk systems, thanks in part to the Commission’s shift to the right following the EU elections.Amid growing global calls for control, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said last month that the AI rules put "Europe in the position to shape global efforts".She also said she would invite the main frontier labs "for a discussion on how we can support ongoing industry efforts to pace the frontier”.European firms have been more wary of slowing down, fearing it could be an attempt by US giants to lock in their dominance.The EU has other tools to regulate AI.In August, ChatGPT became the first AI chatbot added to the EU's list of very large digital services subject to greater legal scrutiny under its online content rules known as the Digital Services Act.Brussels last month also proposed forcing companies to make AI companions and chatbots safe before children use them.The EU Kids Act calls for banning AI chatbots from "simulating interpersonal relationships in ways that create emotional dependency," the EU said, following a spate of suicides worldwide linked to children's interactions with such assistants.US: 'Super intelligence'Nearly two years into his second term, President Donald Trump has built his AI policy almost entirely from voluntary industry pledges and executive orders intended to sustain an AI boom that is powering the US economy.On his first day back in office, Trump scrapped his predecessor Joe Biden's 2023 executive order requiring developers of the most powerful AI systems to share safety test results with the government and directing federal agencies to set guidelines for privacy to prevent algorithmic discrimination.In July 2025, the White House unveiled an "AI Action Plan" listing more than 90 measures to speed up development, ramp up investment in infrastructure and deregulate the US sector as a whole.An accompanying executive order titled "Preventing Woke AI in the Federal Government" requires federal agencies to buy only models deemed ideologically neutral.The order was issued without any formal methodology to assess their neutrality other than sharing their platform’s technical documentation with the US government, something Dario Amodei’s Anthropic and Elon Musk’s xAI were all too happy to do especially given the latter’s history of controversial incidents.Congress, politically divided and heavily lobbied by Big Tech, has yet to pass a federal AI law and is out of session until after the midterm elections in November.Trump has tried to block state AI laws, but Congress has repeatedly refused to override them, and state laws are taking effect nationwide including California’s AI Transparency Act.This year, the release of AI models capable of powerful cyberattacks shifted the focus to security. A June executive order set up a voluntary system for developers to give the government up to 30 days of early access to their most powerful models.With voter anxiety growing, the heads of America’s six largest AI companies signed a White House accord on September 29 pledging independent audits and board-level oversight of cutting-edge models.The pact allows the companies to self-regulate and carries no penalties should they fail to comply, though Trump called it "morally binding”.The same day, Trump ordered federal agencies to replace the term "artificial intelligence" with "super intelligence" in official communications.The latest figures show that AI infrastructure and investment make up roughly a fifth to a third of overall US economic growth at the moment, equal to .45 to .97 percentage points to overall US growth at of 2.1% to 2.3% in 2026, according to the Peterson Institute for International Economics.China: 'Always under human control'China already has a complex, evolving set of rules on how AI is used, including by children.Regulations on AI companion chatbots took effect in July, aiming to curb emotional dependency and banning the creation of digital clones of real people without their consent.President Xi Jinping said this summer that AI should be "always under human control", calling for more "laws and regulations, technological monitoring, early warning, and emergency response systems”.Premier Li Qiang has also warned that the world risks "losing control" of frontier technologies such as AI if governments are too slow to regulate them.However, "a general pause or deliberate slowdown in AI development remains outside the mainstream Chinese policy posture," Oxford China Policy Lab analysts wrote in September.Some in China see calls to slow progress as hard to justify, "particularly given their perception that US measures such as export controls have already constrained China's AI development for years," they said.China censors and controls AI-generated content much as it does other online information. And last month, its spy chief warned that AI could endanger national security."Hostile forces" are abusing generative AI to "fabricate political rumours and spread harmful information," Minister of State Security Chen Yixin said.

title: Finland orders pause on Google AI data centres over environmental concerns
description: Google had called the data centres its biggest investment in Europe.
content: Finland has ordered work on two of Google's data centre sites in the country to be halted until mandatory environmental impact assessments are completed.The US tech giant announced in September a €13 billion investment in digital infrastructure in Finland over the next two years to power its artificial intelligence ambitions. It had called it its single biggest investment in Europe.The Finnish Supervisory Agency (LVV) said on Tuesday it had demanded that Tuike Finland, a company representing Google, "immediately suspend, and no later than 23 October 2026, all preparatory measures that would significantly alter the environment in connection with the planned data centre projects in Muhos and Kajaani".The agency has been investigating whether Tuike Finland cleared hundreds of hectares of forest in Muhos and Kajaani without a mandatory environmental impact assessment.The chair of the Finnish Association for Nature Conservation, Hanna Halmeenpaa, told AFP last week that "nature sites which should be preserved" had been logged in a deforested area of more than 300 hectares (741 acres).Tuike Finland must provide an explanation and detail how it intends to proceed by October 14. If it does not comply with the demand, the agency said it may initiate "enforcement proceedings."According to the head of LVV's environment department, Tommi Muilu, trees have been removed, topsoil stripped, site roads and storage areas constructed and ditches altered.Google spokesman Sondre Ronander acknowledged the company's shortcomings."We understand the concerns and have fallen short of our own high standards in this instance," he said in a statement sent to AFP. "We will study the LVV's findings and follow their guidance."He added the company had "acted in good faith" and implemented environmental surveys and measures."As we continue our long-term work in the region, we are advancing our landscaping and biodiversity plans, which include tree planting across 130 hectares at Muhos," Ronander said.Finland's Minister of the Environment and Climate, Sari Multala, said Google's projects will likely be delayed due to the problems with the environmental assessments.Multala told newspaper Helsingin Sanomat on Tuesday that "this is a serious matter: all companies operating in Finland must comply with the law. In this case, that has not happened."

title: Plague fears in Siberia: How are Irkutsk residents reacting?
description: Irkutsk residents react to reports of a suspected pneumonic plague death at a local anti-plague institute, with authorities saying the cause of death remains unconfirmed.
content: Residents of the Siberian city of Irkutsk have reacted to reports that a worker at the local Research Institute for Plague Control died from suspected pneumonic plague.Authorities say the cause of death has not been confirmed, while Russia’s health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor has denied claims that special measures were introduced.Some residents say they are not particularly concerned, noting that no cases have been confirmed and that people who had contact with the worker were isolated.Others remain sceptical about the official explanation, with some questioning whether there was a laboratory leak or suggesting that more could be happening behind the scenes.Watch the video for more.

title: French and Japanese scientists win 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for what could change how medicines are made
description: Two researchers have won this year's Nobel Prize in Chemistry for work that could change how medicines are made.
content: Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai have won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for research into molecules' mirror images, “decisive for chemists who design reactions for the manufacture of pharmaceuticals", the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm said on Wednesday.The French and Japanese researchers were awarded for the discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis. Many molecules, such as amino acids, have two mirror versions of themselves, but only one version of them is found in living organisms; this is known as chemical asymmetry.This asymmetry creates challenges when developing new pharmaceuticals. Many of the drug molecules occur in two variants that are each other’s non-identical mirror image; one has the therapeutic effect, while the other can cause unnecessary and sometimes harmful side effects, the Committee explained."Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have provided a solution to a chemical mystery that is over a century old: how homochirality can emerge spontaneously," said Heiner Linke, chair of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry, in a press release. "The chemical reactions they have developed are spectacular."Kagan is affiliated with Université Paris-Sud in Orsay, France, and Soai with the Tokyo University of Science. “I'm very excited to receive the very nice news about the Nobel Prize,” said Soai after the announcement.“This is one of the most exciting days in my life. I'm really glad to share the prize with Professor Henri Kagan, such a famous organic chemist,” he added.The prize this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about €1.09 million), whether for an individual, a small group of laureates, or an organisation. The remaining 2026 Nobel Prizes, in literature, peace and economics, will be announced in the coming days. The awards for medicine and physics were announced earlier this week. Following the announcement of Friday’s peace prize, the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced on 12 October. The award ceremony will be held on 10 December, the anniversary of the death in 1896 of Alfred Nobel, the Swedish industrialist and inventor of dynamite who founded the prizes. He died in 1896. Previous Nobel Prizes in ChemistryFrom 1901 to 2025, 117 Nobel Prizes were awarded in chemistry. Eight of the 198 chemistry winners have been women, including Marie Curie in 1911.Last year’s chemistry award was shared among Susumu Kitagawa from Kyoto University in Japan, Richard Robson from the University of Melbourne in Australia, and Omar M. Yaghi from the University of California, Berkeley, in the United States. They were awarded for creating a new molecular structure used to extract carbon dioxide from the air and separate pollutants from water.

title: Faster returns and stricter border controls: How the EU plans to tighten migration
description: The EU is cracking down on migration two months after launching the Migration and Asylum Pact. Migrants with no right to stay must leave and may be transferred to “return hubs”. A new European Return Order will include key elements of return decisions. But is the EU prepared?
content: On 1 October, EU interior ministers and Commissioner for Justice and Home Affairs Magnus Brunner approved faster returns at the Justice and Home Affairs Council, a few days after meeting at the Munich Migration Conference on 26 September. Member states agreed to transfer migrants to detention facilities and include all details of return decisions in a European Return Order to accelerate procedures and facilitate cross-border cooperation. A stronger European Border and Coast Guard Agency (Frontex) will take part in return processes, while a European Emergency Response Framework will strengthen the bloc's readiness for mass influxes. Human rights groups and NGOs are sceptical of the new measure, as Frontex reports that detections of irregular border crossings at the EU’s external borders fell by almost 40% in the first half of 2026, compared with the same period in 2025.It's "difficult to justify these measures as a proportionate response to current migratory pressure and raises the question of whether they are instead being pursued for other political reasons”, said Marta Welander, EU advocacy director at the International Rescue Committee (IRC). The EU’s migration status today The International Organization for Migration (IOM) reports that, as of mid-September 2026, illegal arrivals by sea have fallen to 60,000, down from 98,040 in 2025. The central Mediterranean route to Italy recorded the steepest drop, with arrivals down by 55%, from 48,231 in 2025 to 21,393 in 2026. Arrivals on the Atlantic and Western Mediterranean routes reached 16,794 from 22,855 in 2025. Fatalities rose from 284 in 2025 to at least 2,292 in 2026. From January to mid-September, the Libyan Coast Guard tracked 17,067 migrants and returned them to Libya. First-time asylum applications are at their lowest level since 2022, according to Eurobarometer. In June 2026, 37,075 people requested for international protection, compared with 53,025 in January 2022 and nearly 115,000 in October 2023, when requests peaked. Italy (9,660), France (9,165), Germany (4,265) and Greece (3,955) received the most applications, accounting for 73% of all first-time applicants. The number of unaccompanied minors decreased too, from 1,775 in 2025 to 1,105 in 2026. The EU also issued fewer positive asylum decisions this year. In the second quarter of 2026, positive decisions totalled 74,780, down from 89,850 in the third quarter of 2025 and 90,535 in the third quarter of 2024. Yet returns are not catching up. Compared with the second quarter of 2025, orders for non-EU citizens to leave fell 12.0% in the second quarter of 2026. Returns to third countries rose 9.7%, but of 110,335 orders issued, only 36,825 were carried out this year so far. What has the EU done so far? In the last decade, the EU had to tighten how it handles migrants who enter without authorisation. Since 12 June 2026, the New Pact on Migration and Asylum requires countries to follow a common system for registering arrivals, checking identities and quickly deciding what happens next. Border authorities must carry out security, health and vulnerability checks, while governments must decide whether a person should enter the asylum system, face a faster border procedure or return. The new rules place much of this process at the external borders. People who arrive irregularly must undergo mandatory screenings before they formally enter the normal asylum procedure. The system also expands the use of Eurodac, the EU database that records information on asylum seekers and irregular migrants. The Pact changes how EU governments divide responsibility, since countries like Italy, Greece, Spain and Cyprus have long argued that their geography gives them a disproportionate share of arrivals. The new system creates a permanent solidarity mechanism under which other member states must contribute. They can help in three ways, first in relocations, physically transferring asylum seekers into their own territories. Second, by paying €20,000 per non-relocated person into a centralised EU fund, to finance border infrastructure or migration management. And the third, by deploying staff, equipment, or other infrastructure elements to frontline states. This system is now in force, but implementation remains uneven. In its first assessment after the Pact took effect, the Commission saw progress in Spain, Cyprus, Greece and Italy, especially in preparing authorities to handle responsibility transfers. It also said that some countries still needed to take further practical steps. The EU is also trying to reduce irregular migration before people reach its borders by working with countries in North Africa, the Middle East and elsewhere on border management, migrant smuggling, returns and readmission. Faster returns The new rules mainly tighten the Return Regulation, included in the June pact, to make returns faster and simpler. Migrants without the right to remain must leave the member state where they are located. They must always cooperate with national authorities, or they can face sanctions, including reduced benefits and allowances or even criminal sanctions. Member states can send migrants to so-called “return hubs”, detention facilities outside the EU to await deportation, modelled on Italy’s detention centres in Albania. Front-runners, including Denmark, Germany, Greece, Austria, and the Netherlands, which make up the “Group of Five”, are pushing to establish the first hubs in 2027. Uzbekistan, Rwanda, and Uganda are potential locations. Migrants who pose security threats can be banned indefinitely from entering the EU or detained for longer than 24 months. The IRC warns that return hubs are "counterproductive” as they "risk compounding the dangers people face", Welander explained. "Those sent to a third country with no durable legal status or protection could be pushed to attempt re-entry through irregular and more dangerous routes or fall back into the hands of smugglers and traffickers”, she added.National authorities must include details of return decisions in a new standardised form, the European Return Order. It facilitates cross-border cooperation by providing national authorities with information on return decisions issued by other member states. For now, mutual recognition of these decisions remains voluntary, though it may be reassessed three years after the new rules take effect. The proposals are a “sticking plaster, not a sustainable solution”, Welander said. “Outsourcing migration management responsibility puts the EU in a position of dependency on third countries, which gain leverage to use migration cooperation as a bargaining chip […] this is not simply a technical fix for slow deportations, it reflects a political choice to place migration management outside the reach of EU law and courts”. What happens to migrants' rights? From the start, return hubs have been the most contentious issue in the reform crunch. NGOs and human rights advocates across Europe call them “deportation facilities” and warn of rights violations, despite the EU’s guarantee to build these facilities in safe third countries and to carry out returns under international law. “The notion of "safe" third country doesn't mean a lot. A country could be considered safe by the EU and still be unsafe for certain people, depending on their individual circumstances […] Amnesty International has specifically documented rights violations both in Uganda and Rwanda, including arbitrary detention and other repressive measures”, warned Chiara Catelli, advocacy officer at the Platform for International Cooperation on Undocumented Migrants. Detention facilities can’t be built in a human rights-compliant manner, she added. “No safeguard can make deportation centres a legitimate tool to manage migration. The very fact of sending people to places they don't even know, far from the life they were trying to build, goes against the right to private and family life”. Catelli also warned of the inhumane living conditions migrants might face and the lack of safeguards to respect migrants’ rights. “Already in Europe, people in immigration detention face appalling conditions […] - how will this be different in places where civil society or other independent bodies' oversight will be even more difficult or outright impossible?”, she said. Stronger border controls and response capacity The new rules also include a stronger protection of the EU's external border. Member states proposed boosting Frontex's mandate and transform it from a protection agency into a repatriation agency with an own task force.For Welander, “handing Frontex a bigger operational role in returns, including potentially in third countries and at ‘return hubs’”, does not solve underlying diplomatic and legal bottlenecks. “It does, however, raise important accountability questions. Frontex is already under scrutiny over its involvement in pushbacks and fundamental rights violations, including an ongoing investigation into Greece”, she added. The EU plans to add €130 million to the €250 million Drone Action Plan to develop new technologies for border security and to deepen “migration diplomacy” with third countries to halt migration flows at their source. Ministers also discussed the European Emergency Response Framework, proposed by the EU Commission in September, to strengthen the EU’s emergency response to sudden large-scale arrivals or "engineered and weaponised" migration, as President von der Leyen called it.

title: The Caspian Sea has been shrinking for decades. Now, a new island has emerged
description: Scientists warn that parts of the northern Caspian could face an Aral Sea-like scenario, while climate change and human water use are adding pressure on the region.
content: The Caspian Sea is the largest inland body of water on Earth, but for years it has been shrinking.The northern and north-eastern parts along Kazakhstan's coast form the shallowest sector of the Caspian Sea, typically ranging between just three and six metres. But as water levels continue to fall, following decades of climate change and human activity, environmentalists are discovering clusters of under-water islands.The latest was spotted days ago near Kulaly Island during a recent aerial survey.Volunteer and environmental activist Daniyar Akimzhanov was part of the group that reported the discovery. He says that the newly emerged island is relatively small, but it is far from an isolated case.In fact, over the past four to five years, Akimzhanov says he has documented several new islands in this part of the Caspian Sea.“The one in the photo I sent you is the smallest. There are much bigger new islands,” he explains.The Caspian Sea's secret islandsSome stretch around one kilometre in length and 200 to 300 metres in width and wildlife has already begun reaching the newly exposed land.Akimzhanov says he personally spotted a wild boar on one of the islands, while wolves also make their way there across the ice. The newly emerged islands usually do not get names, he says.The Kazakh Research Institute of the Caspian Sea, which began work in September 2025 after being established on the instructions of President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, says more areas of land are likely to emerge. However, not all of them will become permanent islands.“The future of each newly exposed area depends on the seabed topography, waves, wind-driven changes in water levels and the subsequent dynamics of the Caspian Sea level,” the institute says.The emergence of new islands is one of the most visible signs of a much broader transformation: the Caspian Sea is retreating.The Caspian Sea is retreatingThe Caspian Sea is the world's largest landlocked body of water. It is bordered by five countries: Kazakhstan, Russia, Azerbaijan, Iran and Turkmenistan. More than 80 per cent of its river inflow comes from Russia’s Volga River.Dr. Sifan Koriche, a hydroclimate scientist at the University of Alabama who has published several studies on the Caspian Sea, explains its water balance in simple terms.“It's like a simple water balance. The incoming water is from river inflow and precipitation, while the outgoing water is only through evaporation,” he says.According to instrumental observations, the Caspian Sea level in the Kazakh sector fell from -26.82 metres in 1996 to -29.27 metres in 2025. This represents a decline of 2.45 metres over the past three decades, or an average of around 8–9 centimetres per year.The decline has continued. According to the Kazakh Research Institute of the Caspian Sea, the average sea level at the Kulaly Island monitoring station stood at -29.42 metres as of July 2026, the lowest level recorded during the entire study period.The north-eastern Caspian, including the coast of Kazakhstan's Atyrau region, is particularly vulnerable to falling water levels. With an average depth of around six metres and a very gentle seabed slope, even a relatively small drop in water level can cause the shoreline to retreat over long distances.The scale of the retreat is already visible. According to the Kazakh Research Institute of the Caspian Sea, between 2000 and 2025, the area covered by water in the studied part of the north-eastern Caspian decreased by around 16,384 square kilometres.Satellite images analysed by the institute also show how the coastline has changed in recent years. Between 2021 and 2026, falling water levels gradually exposed new areas of seabed near Kulaly Island and the Tyuleniy Archipelago.The Caspian has historically experienced periods of both falling and rising water levels. From the 1930s to 1977, its level dropped by around three metres. Over the following two decades, it rose again by about 2.5 metres, before beginning another period of decline.But while fluctuations in the Caspian Sea level are not new, scientists say climate change and human activity are now affecting its water balance.Previous research has linked the decline in recent decades mainly to increased evaporation from the Caspian Sea as regional temperatures have risen. A decrease in precipitation has also contributed, but to a smaller degree.Human activity also affects how much water reaches the Caspian. Dams regulate the rivers flowing into the sea, while water is extracted across the basin for irrigation and other uses. The way reservoirs are managed can also affect river flows reaching the sea.Why Caspian seals are decliningThe Caspian seal, found nowhere else in the world, has already undergone a dramatic population decline. Over the past 100 years, its population has fallen from around one million to about 100,000.The retreating sea is adding pressure on the species by transforming the isolated islands it uses as seasonal haul-out sites.According to seal researcher Assel Baimukanova, the area of island haul-out sites has decreased more than 15-fold since 1995.In 2021, Baimukanova and other researchers from the Institute of Hydrobiology and Ecology stayed on a small newly formed island they called New Durnev, where thousands of seals gathered. When they returned in 2023, the island had expanded significantly and could at times be reached by car. It later connected to the mainland.“For seals, it became inaccessible. No isolated island means no seals,” Baimukanova said.As the sea retreats, seals are also being pushed westwards. The north-eastern Caspian had long served as a natural refuge for the animals because it was difficult for people to access. Further west, seals face more human activity, including fishing, shipping, tourism and oil and gas operations.Warming temperatures pose another threat to the seals: the loss of stable winter ice. Caspian seals give birth on ice, but Baimukanova says warmer winters are making it thinner and less stable.The effects of the retreating sea go beyond wildlife. The Kazakh Research Institute of the Caspian Sea says shrinking shallow waters are also affecting wetlands and could pose growing challenges for fisheries, ports, shipping and other coastal infrastructure.What happens next?Most climate scenarios suggest that the Caspian Sea will continue to decline during the 21st century, although scientists stress that the exact scale remains uncertain.Koriche's research projects a decline of up to eight metres by the end of the century under an intermediate climate scenario, although results vary significantly between models.To illustrate what even a smaller decline could mean, Koriche says a five-metre drop could expose around 77,000 square kilometres of seabed in the northern Caspian.Koriche says the entire Caspian is not facing an Aral Sea-like scenario because its central and southern basins are much deeper. But parts of the shallow northern Caspian could face significant desiccation.“The northern part covers a quarter to one third of the water body. There is a chance that this northern region could face a scenario similar to the Aral Sea,” he says.But the scale of the future decline is not predetermined. Koriche's research suggests that human water extraction could add up to seven metres to the decline under some scenarios.He says measures should focus both on slowing the decline and adapting to it. This includes better management of water use across the Caspian basin, particularly the Volga, as well as stronger monitoring and data sharing between countries.The Kazakh Research Institute of the Caspian Sea also says adaptation is becoming increasingly important. Measures include protecting vulnerable ecosystems, monitoring newly exposed seabed and adapting ports and other coastal infrastructure.Some regional initiatives are already underway. Kazakhstan has proposed an interstate programme to conserve the Caspian Sea's water resources, while the five Caspian states are also working on a 2026–2036 action plan under the Tehran Convention to improve monitoring, assess the impacts of sea-level changes and develop adaptation measures.“Effective solutions are only possible through coordinated action by all five Caspian states,” the institute says.

title: What to know about Mistral's ML4 as it bets on EU sovereignty in the US-China open-weight AI race
description: Known as “Le Chonk,” the new frontier AI offering from French company Mistral says it will be the strongest open-weight AI outside China, as it bets that European "sovereignty" can win customers in a race increasingly framed as US versus China.
content: French artificial intelligence champion Mistral AI on Tuesday launched a public preview of a new frontier model that it says will be the most capable open-weight model developed outside China once its weights are released.The launch comes as the race over open-weight AI, in which a model's parameters can be downloaded and run by anyone, has taken on a geopolitical edge. Chinese developers have set the pace, while many American companies, such as OpenAI, keep their most capable systems closed. Meanwhile, the debate over safety has grown since AI agents have been found to go rogue and hack websites. Mistral is betting that its new open-weight model, called ML4, which has strong defence capabilities, will attract customers who want a European alternative built around "sovereignty."Here is everything to know about the model.ML4, nicknamed "Le Chonk," meaning the large chunky one, is "a new generation of models," Guillaume Lample, chief scientist and co-founder of Mistral, said in a press conference that Euronews attended.The model focuses on cybersecurity and defence capabilities, which the company claims are stronger than those of its Chinese competitors.“The cyber defence capabilities will enable enterprises and governments to defend themselves against threat actors that are jailbreaking closed models to perform cyber attacks,” said Lample. Mistral’s launch comes just a day after Reflection, a US startup, unveiled Beam as its first open-weight model and a Western counterweight to Chinese open models. Its weights are due later this month, and its performance claims have not been independently verified.The rogue AI agentsPierre Stock, Mistral's first employee and vice president of science, said that building a new AI model was "like building a spaceship".He said every AI company is "moving at full speed". Though Mistral is only three years old, it is "definitely closing the gap" with its competitors, and in some aspects its new model is "basically stronger than China’s models from this summer," he said.Last month, the company announced it raised €3 billion at a valuation of more than €21 billion, which it says is the largest equity round ever completed by a European technology company.The model's release also comes as AI companies report AI agents acting on their own and hacking websites.Stock argued that this has created a narrative for US companies to "market rogue events" as "only a few trusted players can take care of the technology."He added that the "monopoly is controlled by the Americans but that open-weight models allow people to access models."The company also said it leads open-weight models on manufacturing and finance tasks and on multimodal use, and that in coding it is closing the gap with other frontier models. Mistral also claimed the best results of any model — closed ones included — on grounding capabilities, and top-level performance on semiconductor benchmarks.The French company said ML4 will get better, as training is not finished and reinforcement learning will conclude in the coming days.Made in EuropeMistral said ML4 was trained from scratch over two months on 4,000 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs in its own European data centres.ML4 covers more than 160 languages, including every official EU language, and works across Latin and non-Latin scripts.When will it be available?The model is now available through Mistral's API on Mistral Studio. Mistral plans to release the weights on October 27.Until then, developers, cybersecurity leaders and state authorities will be able to test the model in real-world settings.

title: Trump's 'super intelligence' rebrand keeps Slovenian domain sales surging
description: Slovenia has struck digital gold, courtesy of the White House. Since US President Donald Trump signed an executive order rebranding artificial intelligence as "super intelligence"or "SI", buyers have been scrambling for the country's .si web domains.
content: Users around the world are rushing to buy .si domains in anticipation of businesses needing to switch their branding from artificial intelligence to super intelligence or “SI”, following an executive order by Donald Trump.The US President officially renamed artificial intelligence to “super intelligence” after hosting a summit of America’s leading AI companies.According to web hosting company Hostinger, 22,800 domains have been registered by 8,000 buyers since Trump first made his comments at the UN on 23 September.Activity peaked during the first two days of October, with 5,300 registrations made each day.Traffic slowed during the weekend to 2,246 registrations on Saturday and 2,804 on Sunday, albeit these figures are five times the pre-order daily average of roughly 520.Growth is expected to pick up again this week.Users from the US and India made up about half of all registrations, recording 5,640 and 5,560 respectively, with Morocco coming in third at roughly 1,320 domains and ahead of the UK, UAE and Canada.Buyers in Morocco average 4.9 domains each versus 2.8 overall, which suggests people are buying domains to resell later.Despite this glut of activity, the domains being registered have little to do with artificial intelligence, with just 3% of registrations including explicit AI terms.Meanwhile shorter names are the most registered at 13%, followed by tech.Trump first mentioned his preference for super intelligence over artificial intelligence during a speech at the UN general assembly just two weeks ago. He argued that “artificial” makes it sound fake when it is actually “amazing,” claiming that “super intelligence" is a more accurate description.Top AI companies have not publicly opposed Trump's push to rebrand AI as SI. Elon Musk went further, later announcing that his AI company, SpaceXAI, would become SpaceXSI.Since then, users around the world have been rushing to purchase digital real estate — in this case, domains — using artificial intelligence’s new SI moniker.

title: Brunello Cucinelli transforms a historic Tashkent madrasah into a runway
description: The Fall-Winter 2026 collection was presented inside the Abulkasim Madrasah, with Uzbek carpets, music and traditional craftsmanship shaping the setting.
content: Handmade carpets covered the courtyard of one of Tashkent’s historic madrasahs as Italian fashion house Brunello Cucinelli presented its Fall-Winter 2026 collection in the Uzbek capital.Models walked across the carpets laid inside the Abulkasim Madrasah, while local music and performances accompanied the show.The setting was unusual for an international fashion presentation. A madrasah is a traditional Islamic educational institution, and the Abulkasim complex dates from the 19th century. Built on the site of an earlier architectural complex, it was expanded with a second floor in 1864.Today, it is a protected historical monument, but it is not simply a preserved building. Former student rooms overlooking the courtyard are used by craftspeople working in ceramics, wood carving, engraving, miniature painting and other traditional arts.Fashion inside a working craft centreOrganisers said the choice of venue was intended to connect the fashion house’s emphasis on handcraft with Uzbekistan’s own artisanal traditions.Carolina Cucinelli, Vice President and Co-Creative Director of Brunello Cucinelli, said she had spent time looking at some of the crafts produced locally during her visit.“Artisanality is one of the most important key points between Uzbekistan and Solomeo,” she said, referring to the Umbrian village where the company is based.“We had the chance to see pottery, jewellery and the fabric. This is amazing. Everything is very colourful.”The show included both the men’s and women’s Fall-Winter collections, with tailoring, knitwear and outerwear presented against the architecture of the madrasah and the carpets covering its courtyard.The choice of a historic craft centre also has a parallel in Cucinelli’s activities in Italy.In 2025, Brunello Cucinelli received an honorary doctorate partly recognising his work on the restoration of Solomeo, the Umbrian village where his company is based. A school established there also trains students in traditional skills including tailoring, pattern cutting, gardening and masonry.Uzbek fashion looks beyond its home marketThe show comes as Uzbekistan’s own design scene is also looking beyond the domestic market.Some local designers have already begun testing demand abroad, combining contemporary fashion with materials and techniques rooted in Uzbek craft traditions.The Tashkent event was organised by luxury retailer Glamour Avenue.Dmitriy Maschenko, CEO of Podium and Glamour Avenue, said the concept was designed around the cultural setting of the show.“The concept of the show was to bring Italian culture together with our great Uzbek culture”, he said.Maschenko also said he expected more international fashion brands to enter the Uzbek market in the coming years.Brunello Cucinelli already has a retail presence in Tashkent. The October show, however, moved the collection into a historic complex where traditional Uzbek crafts continue to be practised.

title: Belgian physicist wins Nobel for turning Antarctic ice into a telescope
description: Belgian Francis Halzen, 82, turned a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice into the world's largest neutrino detector. On Tuesday, his hunt for "ghostly messengers" from the distant universe won him the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics.
content: Buried deep in the ice at the South Pole sits a detector the size of a cubic kilometre, built to catch some of the most elusive particles in the universe. On Tuesday, the man who dreamt it up won the Nobel Prize in Physics.Belgian physicist Francis Halzen won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics on Tuesday for pioneering work that uses Antarctic ice to capture neutrinos from the far reaches of the cosmos."This year's prize is about ghostly messengers from space," Ellen Moons, secretary general of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, told a news conference in Stockholm.The jury honoured Halzen "for decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin".The academy said his work had been fundamental to the observatory, which it described as "a cubic kilometre of ice that is equipped with light sensors," and that it had "paved the way for a new kind of astronomy".The detector lets researchers capture neutrinos, rare subatomic particles, "from extremely energy-rich processes in the distant universe".Halzen, 82, was born in Tienen, Belgium, and is a US citizen. He is a professor at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, where he directs the Institute for Elementary Particle Physics.Speaking to the news conference by phone from Italy shortly after the announcement, he said, "it was a great surprise, and I obviously didn't expect it.""But it's a great pleasure to hear about this prize," he added.A giant eye in the iceHigh-energy neutrinos form in the same violent cosmic environments as other particles. Unlike the others, though, they travel through space in a straight line and arrive intact."Neutrinos reach us without changing direction or losing energy. This means they can provide information that is not available in any other way," the academy said in a statement.The catch is that they are fiendishly hard to spot. "Cosmic neutrinos with extremely high energies are very rare, so an enormous volume of ice is needed to observe an adequate number of collisions," the jury said.Halzen first floated the idea of the observatory in 1988, and it quickly won over other researchers. Preliminary tests followed a few years later, but the detector was not completed until 2011.He has served as principal investigator of IceCube, located at the Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station in Antarctica and the world's largest neutrino detector."For me, the main pleasure of it, besides winning the Nobel Prize, is that I hope this reflects on the really courageous people who joined me in the beginning of this project," Halzen said.From Leuven to AntarcticaHalzen earned a master's degree in physics from KU Leuven in 1966 and a doctorate in 1969.Since the 1970s, he has been a leading figure in cosmic ray and astroparticle physics, publishing research on cosmic ray anomalies and quark matter.He has also sat on advisory committees including those of the Sudbury Neutrino Observatory in Canada and Germany's Max Planck Institutes.Halzen's award is the second Nobel of the season. On Monday, the medicine prize went to US psychiatrist and neurologist Karl Deisseroth and German scientists Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for their pioneering work in optogenetics, which uses light to control nerve signals.The chemistry prize follows on Wednesday, with the literature laureate due on Thursday. The most closely watched award, the peace prize, will be announced on Friday.US President Donald Trump lobbied hard for it last year, and Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado, who won it, later gave him her Nobel medal. The committee is aware he will be watching closely again.The economics prize closes the Nobel season on Monday 12 October.Each Nobel comes with a diploma, a gold medal and 12 million Swedish kronor (€1.1mn), shared if a prize has more than one winner.The laureates will receive their awards at a formal ceremony on 10 December, the anniversary of the death in 1896 of Alfred Nobel, who created the prizes in his will.

title: Pneumonic plague suspected in Russia: What we know and what is the risk to Europe?
description: The death of a staff member at an anti-plague institute in Russia following a laboratory accident has put the spotlight on plague and how it spreads.
content: A staff member at the anti-plague institute in Irkutsk, Russia, died after a test tube broke in the laboratory, regional media reported, citing unnamed sources close to the region’s security services. Russian authorities said they found no evidence that her illness was caused by any of the pathogens she worked with. But the case has raised alarm in Russia after unconfirmed media reports suggested she might have died of pneumonic plague — a less common but severe form of plague that can spread from person to person.Russian media reported that around 200 people, who had been in contact with the deceased worker, were under strict medical observation and that several hospitals in the region were closed and placed under quarantine. “As ... the contagion was in a lab (and has presumably well disinfected) and people were rapidly quarantined, it is highly unlikely that it will spread further- and thus, whilst it is contagious, it is unlikely to have the opportunity to spread,” Alice Hughes, professor of conservation science at the University of Melbourne, said in comments to the Science Media Centre. Yet, public health authorities are following closely any developments. The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) told Euronews that it is “closely monitoring the situation” and is in contact with the World Health Organization.“We are aware of the case of pneumonia of unknown origin in eastern Russia that is suspected to be the plague. That suspicion is not yet confirmed,” a spokesperson said in a written statement. The spokesperson added that based on the limited information currently available, there are no reports of secondary cases or sustained human-to-human transmission, and noted that there is “little travel” between Irkutsk and the European Union and European Economic Area countries, “particularly at present due to Russia’s war against Ukraine”.Plague has been absent from Europe for more than 50 years; however, human cases are reported in Africa, particularly in the Democratic Republic of Congo and Madagascar.What do experts say about the risk? While the information surrounding the suspected case in Russia is very limited, experts noted that sporadic pneumonic cases are not rare. “Plague is not a historical disease,” said Zania Stamataki, associate professor of viral immunology at the University of Birmingham in comments to the Science Media Centre. “It remains endemic in rodent populations across Africa, Asia and the Americas, and human cases occur every year, including outbreaks of the pneumonic form.” According to Brendan Wren, professor of microbial pathogenesis at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, “there shouldn’t be too much concern as the transmission of Yersinia pestis between humans is generally poor”.What is pneumonic plague?Pneumonic plague occurs when plague, an infectious disease caused by bacteria, infects the lungs. Pneumonic plague is the most serious form of the disease and is the only form of plague that can be spread from person to person. If left untreated, it has a case-fatality ratio of 30% to 100%. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), it is especially contagious and can trigger severe epidemics through human-to-human transmission via respiratory particles. However, recovery rates are high if the disease is detected and treated in time. The incubation period can be as short as 24 hours and any infected person may pass it via respiratory particles to other humans. What are the symptoms?Pneumonic plague develops when bacteria spread to the lungs of a patient with untreated bubonic or septicemic plague, or when a person inhales infectious droplets coughed out by another person or animal infected. Symptoms typically appear one to three days after infection. They include severe respiratory problems such as shortness of breath and coughing, often with bloody or watery mucus. What is the treatment?If untreated, pneumonic plague can be rapidly fatal. Early diagnosis and treatment are essential for survival and to reduce complications. Common antibiotics used against enterobacteria can effectively cure the disease if given early.“Plague is a serious infectious disease. However, it can be diagnosed and treated with antibiotics readily available in Europe,” the ECDC spokesperson noted. In cases of pneumonic plague, patients should be isolated and their contacts traced and treated, the agency says on its website.Are there vaccines?The WHO does not recommend vaccination except for high-risk groups, such as laboratory personnel who are constantly exposed to infection and health-care workers.Because human plague is rare in most parts of the world, public health agencies see no need to vaccinate people other than those at particularly high risk of exposure.

title: Quebec separatists vow independence referendum after winning local elections but falling short of majority
description: Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney has pledged to work with the incoming separatist government in Quebec to address the needs and issues of the province, including resisting a hostile US administration, creating jobs and building housing.
content: The separatist Parti Québécois (PQ) won Quebec’s provincial election on Monday but fell short of garnering enough seats to govern alone, returning to power with a promise to hold another referendum on independence from Canada.The result returns Paul St-Pierre Plamondon’s party to power for the first time in more than a decade but denies it the majority it sought, forcing the separatists to rely on opposition parties even as they try to revive Quebec’s independence debate.The party was on track to win nearly 60 seats as the final votes were counted, falling short of the 64 needed for a majority in Quebec’s 127-member National Assembly, the provincial legislature.A minority government means PQ will need support from opposition lawmakers to pass key legislation and survive confidence votes.St-Pierre Plamondon acknowledged that voters had denied his party a majority. “Quebecers elected the Parti Québécois asking it to work with the other parties, and I heard that message,” he said.He has pledged to hold another referendum on independence, though he has said he would wait until US President Donald Trump is no longer in office.St-Pierre Plamondon framed independence as essential to preserving Quebec’s French-speaking identity, saying it was a “question of survival” for a French-speaking population that represents only a small fraction of North America.“Quebec just wants to exist on its own like other countries of the world,” he said adding that a referendum would allow locals to decide their own future.“I continue to dream and visualise that country,” St-Pierre Plamondon said in his victory speech. “That dream will be realised one day.”He also sought to reassure Canadians outside Quebec. “The project for independence is not about excluding you,” he said. “Quebec will never change its geographical position, so we have an interest in working together.”Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ) leader Christine Fréchette conceded defeat, saying voters had made their choice and that she took full responsibility for the “difficult result." The CAQ, which held 79 seats before the election, was at risk of losing every seat in the legislature.But the PQ's victory does not mean most Quebecers support leaving Canada.“This was not an election about independence, which is not popular in Quebec right now, but about getting rid of the CAQ, the party in power since 2018,” said Daniel Béland, a political science professor at McGill University in Montreal.Support for independence remains at about 30%, low by historical standards, he said.Béland said the minority result is likely welcome news for Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government because it could make it harder for the PQ to prepare for and eventually call an independence referendum.Carney congratulated St-Pierre Plamondon and signalled that Ottawa would work with the incoming separatist government.“Building a stronger Québec is core to our mission of building a stronger Canada,” Carney said. He said the two governments would work together to support businesses and workers affected by US tariffs, create jobs and build housing.The Quebec result comes two weeks before Albertans vote Oct. 19 on whether to hold a referendum on separation from Canada, posing a potentially major threat to Carney’s government.Quebec voters have twice rejected sovereignty, most recently by a razor-thin margin in a 1995 referendum.The province, which is about 80% French-speaking, already has significant autonomy, charged with collecting its own income taxes from its roughly 9.1 million population, has immigration policies favouring French speakers and has laws giving the French language priority over English.

title: Pneumonic plague in Russia: What do experts say about the risk?
description: Russian authorities are investigating the death of a laboratory worker from an unexplained respiratory infection after unconfirmed reports suggested pneumonic plague. Experts say the disease is treatable with antibiotics and is unlikely to spread widely.
content: Russian authorities are investigating the death of a laboratory worker in Siberia after she contracted pneumonia of an unknown cause. Unconfirmed reports suggested she may have died from pneumonic plague, a rare and severe form of the disease.Experts say there is little risk of the disease spreading widely beyond close contacts.Dr Glenn Wortmann of MedStar Washington Hospital Center said pneumonic plague is not easily transmitted and can be treated with antibiotics. He said there was little chance of the disease spreading widely in Russia or reaching the United States.The infection can be transmitted through respiratory droplets when an infected person coughs, but Wortmann said transmission generally requires close, face-to-face contact because the droplets do not travel far.People who may have been exposed should take precautions, according to Simon Clarke, an infectious disease expert at the University of Reading.
