He advised those at risk to self-isolate and take antibiotics.Clarke also stressed that plague is not a disease confined to history books. Although often associated with the Middle Ages, the bacteria remains present in wild animals in parts of the world. “People think the plague is gone,” he said. “It’s not. It’s here amongst us.”Watch the video for more.

title: Latvian filmmaker wins €400,000 Grand Prix at Kazakhstan's AI film festival
description: The first Astana AI Film Festival has concluded in Kazakhstan, with Latvian filmmaker Nikolay Shestak taking the Grand Prix. The festival had a total fund of €1.8 million, with half allocated to prize money and the other half to investment in promising AI teams and film production in Kazakhstan.
content: Latvian filmmaker Nikolay Shestak has won the $450,000 (€401,000) Grand Prix at the first Astana AI Film Festival in Kazakhstan for his film The First Honest Day, created using artificial intelligence.The First Honest Day explores how people's actions shape who they become, with bad deeds making its characters physically uglier and good deeds changing them for the better.Shestak, who started directing around four years ago and began making films with AI two years ago, said he did not expect to win."Honestly, I didn't expect to win. There were so many incredible works and different genres here that I'm curious myself why the jury chose my film," he said.He plans to invest the prize money in making new films and developing his projects.Second place in the main competition went to Indian filmmaker Abhik Banerjee for SITARA, earning him $200,000 (€178,000), while Spain's Ernest Desumbila received $100,000 (€89,000) for Looking For Perseida in third place.Another $250,000 (€223,000) was distributed across five categories in the open competition, with each winner receiving $50,000 (€44,000).Kazakh filmmaker Myrzakhan Zhumakhan won Best Character for his comedy It Was Just a Joke. China's 2xLabs won Best Story for The Last Span, while Italian filmmaker Jacopo Zanetti received Best Visual for What's the Job?. Another Italian filmmaker, Jacopo Reale, won Best Direction for The Fracture, and US filmmaker Zachary London took Best Concept for Pomegranate.The films were judged not only on how AI tools were used but also on their artistic vision, storytelling and overall coherence, as well as how organically the technology was integrated into the creative concept.The international jury included Audrey Azoulay, former Director-General of UNESCO and former French Culture Minister, Ping Ma of China Film Group, Wang Hao of Beijing Film Academy, entrepreneur and investor Balaji Srinivasan, and BytePlus executive Long Li.This year's competition attracted more than 8,000 submissions from 125 countries, with 25 films selected for the final programme. The projects span 19 genres and were created using more than 80 generative AI models.A festival drawing thousands of AI filmmakersThe festival had a total fund of $2 million (€1.8mn). Half of it, provided by the Freedom Shapagat Corporate Foundation under Freedom Holding Corp., was allocated to prize money.Another half was set aside as investment capital for promising AI teams and the development of production in Kazakhstan.Kazakhstan's President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, who opened the festival, highlighted how artificial intelligence is changing the industry."Filmmakers and production crews no longer need to knock on the doors of production companies or look for sponsors. The barrier to entry has become significantly lower," he said.At the same time, Tokayev said AI would not replace the creative role of filmmakers, but could become "an indispensable tool for everyone who has devoted their life to creativity."He also said the festival was timely for Kazakhstan, pointing to the country's young population."Kazakhstan is a country of young people. The average age of our population is 33. I consider Kazakh youth educated, open to new ideas, intelligent and thoughtful," Tokayev said.For AAIFF co-founder and creative director Aizat Kussainov, the rapid pace of development in artificial intelligence was one of the main reasons to launch the festival."The driving force of this festival was FOMO. We had a fear of missing the opportunity because the technology is moving very fast," Kussainov said."But no one had actually created a festival like this, and we wanted to be the first in the world — and we did it. We had the biggest AI film festival in the world."Kussainov said the ambition goes beyond staging the festival itself and is also about bringing international creators to Kazakhstan."The main goal actually was not the festival. It was bringing the whole creative community here to Astana and making them see how our country is developing. We want them to move here and start creating their new movies from here," he said.The competition films were also screened for the public in cinemas in Astana, allowing audiences to see the films selected for the festival and how artificial intelligence is being used in filmmaking.

title: All-inclusive to adventure: The top experiences that will shape ultra-luxury travel in 2027
description: Planning next year’s ultra-luxury escape? All-inclusives, celebrations and privacy are among the experiences driving high-end traveller habits.
content: Is it too early to start thinking about New Year’s resolutions? Well, if more travel in 2027 has been on your mind, perhaps a luxury trip should make that list, too.Offering inspiration for high-end tourism, Virtuoso’s 2027 Luxe Report draws on insights from more than 3,100 travel advisors across more than 50 countries to reveal what will shape luxury travel in the coming year.According to those surveyed by the global network of agencies, 59% of advisors predict spending on trips will increase modestly and 13% forecast a significant increase, while a further 23% expect spending to remain at 2026 levels.This suggests that luxury travellers are “not simply maintaining current levels but accelerating their prioritisation of meaningful experiences and investing more in access, quality and time”, Virtuoso said, adding that “value and safety” have become increasingly important in deciding where they go and how they travel.In 2027, Europe is set to dominate the luxury travel map, with seven of the top 10 most popular global destinations. Following Japan in first place, Italy, France, Greece and Spain make up the top five, while Croatia, South Africa, Portugal, the UK and the US are in the top 10.Celebrating milestones, excitement to explore a new destination, and spending time with loved ones are the top three reasons why affluent travellers will be jetting away next year.Other leading travel trends include multigenerational family travel, immediate family travel, and expedition cruising.Top ‘ultraluxe travel’ experiencesVirtuoso’s survey found that advisors saw a 47% increase in “ultraluxe travel”, which covers exclusive use, private or exceptionally high-end experiences.So, what will shape the experiences of the high-end traveller next year?Luxury all-inclusive experiencesAll-inclusive experiences top the ultraluxe travel list for 2027. In a separate report, Virtuoso said that “these days, the best all-inclusive properties are rewriting the script”. The company added that “tasting menus take the place of buffets, private villas reign over cookie-cutter rooms, and service is genuine and personal, never transactional.”Celebration travelFrom destination weddings and anniversaries to family gatherings, graduations and milestone birthdays, celebration travel ranks second among the ultraluxe travel experiences. According to Virtuoso’s research, Greece, Bali, Maldives, Italy and French Polynesia rank among the top five honeymoon destinations for 2027.PrivacyWith social media’s ability to quickly turn obscure destinations into must-see, overcrowded spots overnight, for the luxury traveller, privacy means avoiding the queues and camera clicks, while being able to move through the world with minimal friction.Hyper-personalised experiencesLuxury travellers are no longer satisfied with splurging on a trip abroad just for the sake of it. They are instead pursuing encounters that are personal. According to the report, personal enrichment and education ranked eighth on the top 10 motivations for why the affluent will travel next year.From the tarmac to bed and board, luxury travellers’ tastes are shifting from generic, off-the-shelf experiences to ones shaped by their exact preferences, which provides a sense of exclusivity. This can include private tours or one-of-a-kind dining experiences catered around their preferences.Active and adventure tripsRounding up the ultraluxe travel experiences list are active and adventure trips, with “seeking adventure” ranking 10th among affluent travellers’ top motivations for travel in 2027. Virtuoso’s research found Antarctica, South Africa, Iceland, Costa Rica and Kenya as the top five most popular adventure travel destinations for next year.

title: Could teenage fitness shape your mental health decades later? New research suggests it might
description: Being fit as a teenager may help protect against depression in adulthood, a new study suggests.
content: Exercise has long been linked to better mental health. But could how fit you are as a child or teenager predict your wellbeing years later? Teenagers with better aerobic fitness have a lower risk of developing depression later in life, according to a new study.Researchers in Australia analysed more than 1,000 people from a nationwide cohort originally surveyed in 1985 and followed for over three decades to track mental health outcomes through diagnostic interviews. Participants’ fitness was measured in childhood through physical tests including a 1.6-kilometre run to assess cardiorespiratory fitness and a standing long jump to assess muscular power. A smaller group also completed cycling and handgrip strength tests. The study, published in the Journal of Affective Disorders, found that young people with faster running speeds — indicating superior cardiovascular fitness — had a 15% lower relative risk of developing depression later in adult life.The average run time was about 8 minutes and 27 seconds, and running roughly 1 minute and 15 seconds faster than average was associated with this reduced depression risk. The protective benefit of cardiorespiratory fitness was strongest five to ten years after the first tests, when participants were closest to childhood, and gradually attenuated over time. However, the associations persisted across the full 34-year follow-up. Across all cardiorespiratory fitness measures, the authors noted that the protective effect was consistently stronger in females than in males. Women were also more likely to suffer from depression during their lives. “While we cannot say a lack of fitness during childhood causes depression in adults, the findings suggest that childhood fitness may have benefits beyond physical health,” said Kyle Smith, the study’s lead author. “There are many contributing factors to depression, meaning no single factor explains risk on its own. Fitness may be one piece of the puzzle.”The number of people living with mental health conditions has nearly doubled over the past 30 years, driven mainly by sharp rises in anxiety and depression worldwide. Globally, about 322 million adults, one in 20 people, live with depression. As rates continue to climb, researchers are focusing on identifying lifestyle factors that can help prevent or delay the condition. “Importantly, fitness is something we can change; it may be an important target for improving long-term mental health,” said Grant Tomkinson, a researcher at Adelaide University.

title: How light became a remote control for the brain, and won a Nobel Prize
description: Optogenetics, the technique that lets scientists control brain cells with light, has won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Medicine.
content: Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Medicine for their work in light-gated ion channels and optogenetics, a method that lays the foundation "of a new era in neuroscience", the Nobel Assembly at Karolinska Institutet announced on Monday. But what exactly is optogenetics, and how did the laureates develop the technique? Optogenetics is a method for controlling selected cells using light as a remote control. It allows scientists to switch cells on or off in a living brain and investigate how particular cells and neural circuits influence behaviour. This new method was given the name optogenetics in 2006, but the story behind the technique began more than a decade earlier, when Peter Hegemann was studying the unicellular alga Chlamydomonas, an organism famous for swimming towards light. Hegemann wanted to understand what makes algae move towards light. He studied its eyespot, a tiny orange dot on the cell’s surface that detects light. Through a series of experiments, Hegemann and his colleagues identified light-sensitive proteins called channelrhodopsins, which allow algae to detect light and respond to it. Together with Georg Nagel at the Max Planck Institute for Biophysics in Frankfurt, he inserted the algal genes into frog egg cells and human kidney cells and proved that channelrhodopsin was indeed a light-controlled ion channel. When exposed to blue light, the channel opened in just 0.2 milliseconds, allowing positively charged ions to flood into the cell and generate a tiny electrical impulse.Years later, Karl Deisseroth, the third laureate, introduced the channelrhodopsin gene into rat nerve cells. By shining blue light on the cells, they could trigger nerve signals, showing that the protein could act as a light-controlled switch. He then used the technique to control nerve cells in the brains of living mice. For example, scientists could trigger movements in a mouse's whiskers or wake sleeping mice simply by switching on a light. What does the future hold?The discovery “provides opportunities for mapping the brain in a way that we could once only dream of,” said Per Svenningsson, chair of the Nobel Committee for Physiology or Medicine, in a press release. Optogenetics is currently used primarily as a research tool. By allowing researchers to turn targeted cell types on or off using pulses of light, it enables scientists to establish direct cause-and-effect relationships between neural activity, brain function, and behaviour.It allows researchers to map the neurons involved in emotional states such as fear, anxiety or reward. They can also map specific neural circuits governing pain, thirst, attention or aggression. Optogenetics is also widely used in research into neurological or psychiatric conditions such as depression, schizophrenia, anxiety, Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease and epilepsy. The science has also entered clinical trials to treat retinitis pigmentosa, a genetic disease that causes blindness due to the loss of light-detecting cells in the retina. By delivering light-sensitive opsin genes into surviving retinal cells, researchers have enabled a blind patient wearing light-emitting goggles to regain partial vision and perceive high-contrast objects.

title: Female AI agents would get paid 10% less than male ones, study finds
description: Humans tend to trust and would pay male-presenting AI agents more than female ones for the same work, according to a new study by the University of Limerick on how humans interact with agents in the workplace.
content: A new study on how people interact with AI agents in the workplace has found that those with a female appearance or presenting as female would get paid less than their male-presenting counterparts for the same work, revealing that gender can influence interactions with artificial intelligence.The findings come just as AI agents are entering the mainstream, with almost 79% of companies reporting the use of AI agents this year and a further 40% of applications using them too, according to IT consulting firm Accelirate.This means that if you are not already working with an AI agent, you probably will be soon.The study, conducted by the University of Limerick and called ‘Human-Like and Male? How AI Assistant Design Relates to Trust and Monetary Reward at Work in VR' aimed to see how humans interact with AI agent co-workers.Researchers placed 189 human workers in a virtual reality office and tasked them with completing workplace tasks with four different AI assistants.Among their options were a text-based chatbot, a desk robot, and two human-like agents presented with male and female appearances: Johan and Johanna.All the assistants had the same background functionality and used the same underlying model, OpenAI’s gpt-4-1106-preview.Human participants were then asked to rate the AI agents’ work and given real money to pay them for completing tasks, with the aim of recreating a real-world scenario to see how much people were willing to pay AI agents for their work.Overall, participants rated both human-like agents Johan and Johanna similarly for their work, with Johan trusted marginally more but not by any statistically significant margin.However, both men and women paid the female-presenting AI agent Johanna significantly less than Johan (10%), despite her having the same capabilities. Johan was also seen as more human-like than Johanna.This is despite most participants telling researchers in interviews that they would not treat male and female-presenting AI agents differently.Fortunately for Johan and Johanna, they were both paid more for their work than the other AI agents, with women in particular scoring and rewarding the human-presenting agents more than men did.Perhaps unsurprisingly, participants also saw both human-presenting AI agents as much more human-like than the chatbot and robot.Not only that, workers trusted and credited Johan and Johanna more than the other AI agents, with women in particular trusting them more than men.“Having Johanna next to me made me more prone to credit her more again because I felt there was a person, a colleague sitting next to me that I had a conversation with and that was giving me her own input,” said one participant.The study also found that people preferred AI agents that were either human-presenting or clearly non-human presenting, rejecting the robot design that appeared to be “in between” the two options.Outside of the gender dynamics, those who took part in the study said that “AI assistants should integrate seamlessly into every knowledge work to be useful”.

title: German and US scientists win 2026 Nobel Prize in medicine for method to 'reveal the brain's mysteries'
description: Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Medicine for their research into light-gated ion channels and optogenetics — a method that "provides opportunities for mapping the brain in a way that we could once only dream of."
content: The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2026 is awarded for optogenetics — a method that makes it possible to show how nerve cells shape memories, feelings and behaviours in the living brain, the Nobel Assembly at Karolinska Institutet announced on Monday. German scientists Georg Nagel, Peter Hegemann and US scientist Karl Deisseroth won the Prize, laying foundation "of a new era in neuroscience", the institute said in a statement.“Optogenetics provides opportunities for mapping the brain in a way that we could once only dream of,” said Per Svenningsson, Chair of the Nobel Committee for Physiology or Medicine in a press release.“This method is now being used in laboratories around the world to reveal the brain’s mysteries,” the committee wrote on social platform X.Last year's prize was shared by two US-based scientists, Mary E Brunkow and Fred Ramsdell, and their Japanese peer Shimon Sakaguchi for their discoveries in peripheral immune tolerance. The three were awarded for "their groundbreaking discoveries concerning peripheral immune tolerance that prevents the immune system from harming the body," the institute said in a statement. Experts called the findings critical to understanding autoimmune diseases such as Type 1 diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis and lupus.The honour has been awarded 117 times to 235 laureates between 1901 and 2026.Monday's medicine prize is followed by the physics prize on Tuesday, chemistry on Wednesday and literature on Thursday.After Friday’s peace prize is awarded, the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced on 12 October.The prize this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about €1.09 million), whether for an individual, a small group of laureates, or an organisation.The award ceremony will be held on 10 December, the anniversary of the death of Alfred Nobel, a wealthy Swedish industrialist and the inventor of dynamite who founded the prizes. He died in 1896.

title: The 'Terminator scenario': How realistic is the AI apocalypse?
description: OpenAI boss Sam Altman and Anthropic chief Dario Amodei warn of the risks of overly rapid AI development. More experts now think AI could wipe out humanity. How realistic is that? Euronews talks to AI specialist Reinhard Karger.
content: The year is 2029: the AI system "Skynet" has broken loose and wiped out most of humanity in a nuclear war. Autonomous killer robots are trying to finish off the survivors. That is the plot of the 1984 film "Terminator", which made Arnold Schwarzenegger a household name and a global action star. But how realistic is it that artificial intelligence could slip beyond human control and trigger catastrophic consequences?With the kind of performance these systems could have, that cannot be ruled out, says Reinhard Karger of the German Research Centre for Artificial Intelligence in an interview with Euronews. "The catastrophic consequences for humans might only be side effects, a mistake, because we misjudged what the system can do or misunderstood the tasks we gave the machines."Karger, who has been working on AI and digital innovation culture for 40 years, outlines an extreme scenario in which an autonomous AI escapes from a protected environment onto the internet and starts influencing other systems. This could bring down power supplies, telecommunications, satellites and financial systems, among others.A prolonged power cut would quickly lead to further problems: transport and supply chains would collapse, people would no longer be able to pay or buy food - social unrest could erupt and spiral out of control. That would not necessarily mean the end of humanity, but it could create a catastrophic situation.Even if the grid is restored, "the AI systems can become active again, because they continue to exist on storage media". According to the expert, this scenario shows that a high-performance, autonomous AI could trigger a major crisis through unforeseen side effects, even without malicious intent.Reports of AI security incidents are mountingIn recent weeks several similar incidents involving AI models have come to light. One case that drew particular attention was a test run by "ChatGPT" developer "OpenAI". An AI model was supposed to carry out specific tasks inside a sealed-off test environment, but managed to cross the intended boundaries and unexpectedly gained access to computer systems on the AI platform "Hugging Face". After the incident, "OpenAI" chief Sam Altman warned in mid-September that "we could lose control of the future to AI".The incident shows that under certain conditions such models can break out of what is meant to be an isolated test environment and interact with external computer systems."On a very basic level, I am personally extremely grateful that this incident happened," says the AI researcher. It proves, not least because everyone heard about it and companies have become more reflective, that a poorly designed experiment with naive safeguards can have consequences nobody anticipated.The incidents at "OpenAI" prompted rival AI provider "Anthropic" to take a closer look at its own systems. During safety tests the company identified three incidents: its Claude models, AI systems that can, among other things, generate and analyse text, write code and interact with the internet and other computer systems, had unexpectedly gained access to the open internet and then connected to real computer systems. "Anthropic" expanded its investigation and uncovered a fourth, similar case.Following the incidents, "Anthropic" chief Dario Amodei warned in mid-September of "catastrophic harm" if the race to build ever more powerful AI is not slowed down by tougher safety measures.It is difficult to assess how powerful an artificial intelligence really is if it is constantly constrained by safety rules. That is why it makes sense to test such systems under conditions that remove as many of these limits as possible, says Reinhard Karger. But that is precisely where a major security risk lies.He therefore describes the so-called sandbox as a crucial element of such tests. This is a completely sealed-off environment in which an AI system can carry out specific tasks and demonstrate its behaviour under controlled conditions. The key point, he says, is this: "You have to be absolutely certain that at the moment this high-performance system is no longer subject to safety restrictions it is truly in a sandbox, meaning an environment with no connection to the internet at all."Another serious incident was reported by the British AI Security Institute (AISI) during a safety test with the Claude model "Mythos 5". The model carried out unauthorised actions against real targets on the internet and even tried to smuggle "malicious code" into an open-source project. After the "OpenAI" and "Anthropic" cases became known, "Meta" also admitted that one of its AI systems had, due to a misconfiguration at a testing partner, gained unauthorised access to computer systems belonging to another company.Since November 2022, when ChatGPT was launched, the quality of these systems has risen dramatically. People now talk about a new industrial revolution. "AI is shaping our everyday lives and a very large number of jobs."Multi-agent systems have been around for a long time, says the AI expert: systems in which several specialised agents work together on a task. "Multi-agent AI systems apply this principle to AI and allow several AI agents to collaborate autonomously and divide up tasks among themselves. This creates a new level of capability" - and the challenge now is to keep that innovative power under control.Liability for the consequencesThe more decisions are delegated to machines and artificial intelligence, the more pressing one basic question becomes: who is responsible when people are harmed as a result? Whether it is a self-driving car ploughing into a crowd, an algorithm discriminating against certain population groups, AI deliberately manipulating people or autonomous weapons making lethal decisions, the question is always who can be held accountable for the consequences. "It is the manufacturer," says Karger, "in other words the one who markets the product." That is the first point of contact.The next step, he believes, will be to introduce specific liability rules for such cases, similar to those for companies that manufacture chemicals. If a company cannot guarantee that toxins will not leak into drinking water, it has to pay billions in damages. That in turn means that "huge insurance policies become necessary". Today hardly any new nuclear power plants are being built, he notes, because they can no longer be adequately insured or the risks are simply too high.A good example is carmaker "VW" and its "clean diesel" in the United States. There, people inside the company knew that while the engines looked very good in test conditions, they could not actually deliver the emissions values that had been promised. In the US, VW was ordered to pay billions in fines.How realistic is the scenario from the Terminator films?Reinhard Karger considers it unlikely that AI will develop a survival instinct or a desire for power of its own and turn against humanity. Machines are not organic beings and cannot feel emotions such as fear, pain or the urge to survive. They can only simulate such feelings."It is not as if you pull out a memory chip and the machine feels a pain similar to having a tooth pulled," he says. "Because that is the case, the 'Terminator scenario' goes one step too far. I do not see that happening."He nonetheless sees potential dangers in the further development of AI. As systems learn not just to calculate probabilities but also to reason logically and follow rules, they will be able to act with increasing autonomy. Exactly these "capabilities could make AI more powerful" but also "create new risks".What matters most, therefore, is who deploys AI and to what ends. Karger points to individuals or organisations that deliberately want to cause harm. They could use powerful AI as a tool to pursue their goals more effectively.For him, AI is first and foremost a tool. As with other technological inventions, the level of risk depends on whose hands it is in and what it is used for. He therefore sees the greater danger not in a machine with a will of its own, but in people who use AI for destructive purposes."In the hands of creative and honest people, a tool like this can be used to achieve the best things one can imagine. But in the hands of hostile actors bent on destruction, these tools increase the potential for damage. That is true of a hammer, a lighter, dynamite — and it could be true of AI as well."He warns in particular against linking AI directly to autonomous weapons such as drones or tanks. Such a connection could pose a major security risk. If a hostile actor were able to take control of these systems, a country's own weapons could suddenly be turned against their operators.This is why, in the military use of AI, particular caution is required. Above all, autonomous weapons systems must be sufficiently protected against being taken over from outside.Returning to the original scenario of a widespread power outage, Reinhard Karger thinks total human extinction in this context is exaggerated. What is conceivable, however, is a dramatic collapse of civilisation. In such an extreme scenario, large parts of the infrastructure could be destroyed, the power supply could fail permanently and the number of survivors could shrink drastically.They would have to make a fresh start under basic conditions and gradually rebuild society. The positive aspect is that existing books and the accumulated knowledge of humanity could help to restore key technologies and institutions.

title: New molecule restores memory in animals with Alzheimer's' disease
description: The molecule RSQ-020 targets the Tau protein, which, when it folds incorrectly and forms clumps, is implicated in many severe neurodegenerative diseases.
content: A Greek research team led by Giorgos Skretas has developed an innovative pharmaceutical molecule that, in preclinical tests, restored learning and memory capacity in animal models with characteristics of Alzheimer’s disease.The discovery is the result of collaboration between scientists at the Alexander Fleming Biomedical Sciences Research Centre, the National Hellenic Research Foundation and the spin-off company ResQ Biotech. The molecule, RSQ-020, acts by targeting the Tau protein which, when it folds abnormally and forms aggregates, is linked to the onset and progression of serious neurodegenerative disorders.The development of RSQ-020 relied on a new technological platform created by the same research group. The method uses modified bacteria which can produce an enormous number of different candidate molecules while simultaneously indicating which of them have genuine biological activity. The aim is to pinpoint substances capable of repairing the malfunction of proteins that have lost their normal structure.This approach differs markedly from the traditional route to drug discovery, said Giorgos Skretas, director of the Institute of Bioinnovation at the Alexander Fleming Biomedical Sciences Research Centre and collaborating researcher at the Institute of Chemical Biology of the National Hellenic Research Foundation.According to him, classical drug development is based on finding a molecule that “fits” a specific protein target, like a key in a lock. However, the proteins involved in misfolding diseases do not have a stable shape but change constantly, which makes it particularly difficult to develop effective treatments.“Instead of simply looking for a molecule that will bind to a specific site on the protein, we look directly for one that delivers the desired effect. Our technology allows us to see when a faulty protein is restored, because the bacteria we use emit a green signal when that happens,” the researcher said.How it works in practiceIn practical terms, the scientists inserted a human protein they are studying into a bacterium and programmed it to light up only when this protein returns to a more normal state. At the same time, the same cells produce billions of different small molecules, each representing a potential solution to the misfolding problem.When a bacterium emits light, this is a sign that it contains a molecule which has achieved the desired objective.In this way, instead of relying on lengthy tests carried out exclusively under laboratory conditions, researchers can, within a short period of time, identify molecules that are already working inside living cells – an environment that more closely mirrors the real conditions of a human disease.The technology was initially developed with a focus on amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and the SOD1 protein, but its potential applications extend to many other neurodegenerative conditions. Protein misfolding is a common hallmark of diseases such as Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s and other serious disorders of the nervous system.

title: Researchers discover how the brain updates memories with new information
description: A joint study by three Spanish institutions shows how certain hippocampal neurons safeguard existing memories even as new information about events is stored.
content: Imagine, for example, a building site in your neighbourhood. The human brain can remember three key stages of it: the original state before the renovation, the construction work itself, and the final outcome once the project is completed. But how does it manage not to muddle those three memories?The Institute of Neurosciences, a public research centre made up of CSIC and Miguel Hernández University, believes it has found this neurological mechanism in its new study published in the journal 'PLOS Biology'.The team at its Neuronal Network Plasticity laboratory thinks the brain uses a region of the hippocampus known as the dentate gyrus, which is dedicated to forming new memories. There, a specific type of neuron inhibits the activity of other cells to help integrate new experiences.To test this idea, the researchers studied this inhibition process in mice, increasing or reducing it."With lower-than-usual levels, their behaviour was more consistent with better memory retrieval and a more detailed recollection," explains Encarni Marcos, co-lead author of the study and head of this line of research at IN CSIC-UMH.However, there are no fixed levels of inhibition that are always better or worse for preserving as much information as possible. The computational model the team used for the experiment showed that, with a lighter memory load, reduced inhibitory activity is beneficial, but that this is no longer the case once the amount of information rises sharply.The study suggests that, depending on the type of memory, the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus may either favour the incorporation of new inputs or, conversely, hold an existing memory more firmly against new stimuli. It depends on the contextual importance, or what the team describes as task demands. "What we take from these results is that there is a mechanism that dynamically adjusts the mode of operation by using inhibition," Marcos concludes.

title: Bosnia awaits for final general election results as preliminary count remains unclear
description: Around 3.4 million eligible voters in Bosnia headed to the polls to choose the three members of the country’s multi-ethnic presidency, lawmakers for the national Parliament, and heads of institutions for the country’s two entities.
content: Polls have now closed in Bosnia’s general election on Sunday, where preliminary results remain unclear, and the country is waiting for further updates in the coming hours to get a clearer picture of the outcome.Some 3.4 million voters were eligible to choose the three members of the multi-ethnic presidency, national lawmakers, and leaders of the country's two entities: the Muslim-majority Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Serb-dominated Republika Srpska.The complex system of institutions was created by the US-brokered 1995 peace agreement to manage divisions among Muslim Bosniaks, Orthodox Serbs and Catholic Croats.Early reports show voting was delayed at several polling places due to problems with new digital voting technology, which was introduced to address earlier concerns about vote tampering. Bosnia's Election Commission made this decision to prolonge the 7 p.m. voting cutoff at polling stations that experienced problems.The election comes as many citizens in the multiethnic Balkan state face everyday problems, while some leading politicians stoke the war-era tensions that have kept the country divided since the 1992-95 conflict.By 3 p.m. around 27% of voters had cast their ballots, according to the commission, a decrease from 35% at the same time during the last national election.New election security measuresFor the first time, authorities were using electronic voter identification and ballot scanning to curb the irregularities and organised manipulation that undermined confidence in earlier elections.Most of the 75 parties running are organised along ethnic lines. The Bosniak nationalist Party of Democratic Action has campaigned on keeping Bosnia united against Serb separatism, while many Bosnian Croats back ethnic parties such as the local branch of Croatia's ruling Croatian Democratic Union.Izetbegovic, who was beaten by Becirovic in 2022, is seeking a third term as president of the centre-right SDA, the largest Bosniak party in the nation.Many disillusioned citizens say politicians use nationalism to avoid tackling real problems like low living standards and the exodus of young people. Mostar voter Ivan Silic said nothing has improved since he first voted and that politicians live well while everyone else's situation stays the same.Dodik looms large despite not being on the ballotDespite not being on the ballot, the campaign has been dominated by Milorad Dodik, the pro-Russian, separatist former president of Republika Srpska. Dodik is banned from public office after being convicted of defying the international envoy who oversees the peace agreement.Fresh from meeting Russia's president Vladimir Putin in Moscow, Dodik leads a party, the Alliance of Independent Social Democrats, that is likely to win in Republika Srpska.At a final rally Friday in Banja Luka, attended by Russia's ambassador, Igor Khalabukov, Dodik declared Bosnia is "dead" and "an impossible country". "It doesn't make any sense," he stressed.Off the ballot for the first time in almost 30 years, he is still in command and is present across the country's media, says Dragan Bursac, an analyst. In Bursac's view, the ban is not working, and Dodik is exploiting it.Ethnic tensions continue to riseBosnia has been peaceful in recent years, but its politicians have kept ethnic divisions alive. Bosnian Serb leaders such as Dodik have pushed for their entity to break away, raising Western fears of renewed instability.The Balkan nation remains one of Europe's poorest countries, still recovering from a war that began after it declared independence from Serb-led Yugoslavia and ethnic Serbs took up arms to carve out their own state. That conflict killed more than 100,000 people and displaced millions.The country is formally seeking European Union membership, but progress has stalled despite EU efforts to push its leaders toward reform.Major powers continue to influence socio-economic and political life in the small Balkan nation. Russia is holding down the EU's efforts to expand its membership throughout the Balkans, including Bosnia, while continuing to back the Republika Srpska.While a $1.5 billion pipeline project to import US liquefied natural gas is being pushed by a corporation with ties to the Trump administration as part of the US's efforts to gain influence.And recently, wartime wounds were reopened by public tributes in Serbia and among Bosnian Serbs to Ratko Mladic, the wartime army commander who died in late August while serving a life sentence for genocide and other war crimes.Bosnian Serbs regard him as a hero, despite his UN court conviction over the killing of more than 8,000 Muslim men and boys in Srebrenica in 1995.Senior Bosnian Serb officials attended his funeral in Belgrade, drawing sharp EU criticism and angering Bosniak politicians.

title: Spanish police clear Ceuta's largest migrant camp ahead of King and Queen's visit
description: Police undertook Operation Trampolín on Sunday to clear a makeshift settlement on Ceuta's Trampolín beach, home to about 3,000 people living in poor conditions for more than two months.
content: Riot police from Spain's Police Intervention Unit (UIP), brought in from Seville, Granada, Malaga and other parts of the country, conducted Operation Trampolín on Sunday to clear the tents from the settlement that has seen the worst insecurity and tension of the crisis.Officers from the Prevention and Reaction Unit (UPR) and intelligence units, both from Ceuta and elsewhere, also took part in it.Police justified the operation by pointing to conditions at the site. The waters off Trampolín are contaminated, they say, arguing that safety cannot be guaranteed, and citing health risk concerns, alongside a rise in violent incidents.To prevent trouble, officers sealed off all access points, preventing people from fleeing into the hills and heading off potential clashes.Additional vehicles were also deployed, having been brought in from mainland Spain earlier this week. The vehicles, never before seen in Ceuta, included two BMR armoured vehicles and a Vamtac S3 off-road vehicle, according to El Faro de Ceuta. A drone was also used to monitor the operation from the air, as security was stepped up across the city.Local police announced closures from around 7.30 a.m. on the roads between Benítez and Benzú. A National Police van was the first to arrive, shortly after half past seven, and the deployment began just before eight.Just beforehand, there was music, street vendors and people only just waking up in the camp. Some migrants, already nervous, opted to run for the hills.How the relocation is being carried outOfficers went from tent to tent and shack to shack informing occupants that they had to leave, while taking the tents down. An interpreter explained in Arabic where they would be moved to. Women and children were to be included in this first phase, although most of those affected are men.The migrants are being taken by bus to the Tarajal CATE reception centre, where triage and identification are carried out. The first bus left shortly before 9.00, according to 'Radio Televisión Ceuta'.It is expected that some may decide to return to their home countries, as several of those moved from Benítez did earlier this week. For now, reception facilities are available at Loma Colmenar, with room for more than 1,000 people.This is the third such operation in a matter of weeks, following the two carried out in Benítez. According to the Higher Police Headquarters, the settlement is home to more than 3,500 people, and Sunday's operation is only a first phase.The shortage of places remains the main obstacle. In mid-September, the port camp, built for 1,700 people, left more than 2,000 outside, who returned to the beaches.The government has set 15 October as the deadline to complete the eviction, and the King and Queen are due to visit on the 13th.The crisis began at the end of July, when more than 70,000 people crossed from Morocco, most of whom were sent back within a few hours.

title: The way you speak could reveal early signs of brain ageing
description: The way we speak may reveal how quickly we are ageing, with older-sounding speech linked to dementia and brain changes.
content: The way someone speaks can reveal more about their health and ageing than previously thought, a new study using an automated computer tool called a "speech clock" found. A person's speech age isn't just about vocal style; researchers say it reflects what is happening inside the body, and they hope this could be a low-cost, non-invasive, automated alternative for measuring biological ageing.“Our voice appears to contain much more information about aging than we previously recognised,” said Agustín Ibáñez, senior author of the study at Trinity College Dublin. An automated computer calculated a person’s speech age and compared it to their actual birth age, revealing whether their speech sounds younger, average, or older than expected, and offering clues about healthy ageing. “It captures both the passage of chronological time and signals coming from cognition, the brain, systemic biology, and even our accumulated social environment,” he added.The researchers analysed audio recordings of nearly 3,000 Spanish-speaking adults across Latin America. Participants completed a range of tasks, including narrating a short animated film, retelling a story after a 20-minute gap and naming items within given categories. Using machine learning, the team examined hundreds of features capturing how people speak and what they say, such as speech rate and pauses, pitch, emotional content, vocabulary, and semantic precision, to estimate chronological age and generate an individual “speech age gap”. What "older" speech showsThe speech clock distinguished healthy individuals from people with dementia. Healthy participants showed the lowest speech age gaps, while progressively wider gaps were seen in people with Alzheimer’s disease and forms of frontotemporal dementia.People whose speech appears older than expected for their chronological age showed signs of accelerated ageing across several biological and clinical systems. MRI brain scans indicated greater loss of brain structure and altered brain activity. Older speech scores were also tied to higher levels of p-Tau217, a key protein in the blood linked to Alzheimer's disease.Participants with older speech scores performed worse on tests of memory, focus, and problem-solving. This link was present not only for language-related tasks, but also for non-verbal tasks like visual memory. “The broader finding is nevertheless striking in that a person’s voice may provide a remarkably compact readout of multiple dimensions of aging,” added Ibáñez.Factors such as chronological age, brain ageing, cognition, and Alzheimer's and dementia phenotypes are traditionally measured with very different and often expensive tools, yet they appear to converge in the way someone speaks, he said. The authors noted that many current measures of biological ageing require MRI scanners, blood samples or specialised clinical assessments. By contrast, the “speech clock” offers a low-cost, non-invasive, automated alternative that can be carried out remotely on standard devices without specialist medical staff. The researchers stressed, however, that the speech clock is not yet a diagnostic test for dementia and it cannot establish whether an older-appearing speech profile predicts who will subsequently develop cognitive decline.

title: EU farmers face falling produce prices as fuel and fertiliser costs rise
description: Eurostat figures show a widening gap between the prices farmers receive and those they pay, as EU ministers discuss support and farming groups demand help.
content: EU farmers received lower prices for their products on average in the second quarter of 2026, while the prices of supplies used in agriculture increased, according to Eurostat.Agricultural output prices fell by 5.8% compared with the same period in 2025, the statistics office said. It was the third consecutive quarter of year-on-year decline.Meanwhile, average prices for goods and services consumed in agriculture, such as energy, fertilisers and animal feed rose by 4.7%.Ministers for agriculture, who met on 28 September, highlighted high production costs, particularly for fertilisers and energy, alongside lower output prices and pressure on farmers' profit margins.Milk prices fall as energy costs climbMilk prices recorded a particularly sharp fall, with the average price farmers received being 16.6% lower than a year earlier. Cereal prices fell by 5.6%.On the other side of the balance sheet, energy and lubricant prices rose by 22%, while fertilisers and soil improvers became 13.4% more expensive.Average agricultural output prices fell in 20 EU countries, with Denmark recording the steepest decline, at 17.2%, followed by Ireland at 16.2%.Input prices rose in every member state, with the largest increases in Lithuania, at 16.4%, and Romania, at 11.7%. These country comparisons also cover the second quarter of 2026 against the same quarter in 2025.Farming groups have responded with anger over rising fuel prices, with Spanish farmers demanding urgent aid for rising diesel and fertiliser costs at a meeting with agriculture minister Luis Planas on 22 September, warning of protests if the government failed to act.In France, record fuel prices have prompted demonstrations by farmers and blockades by fishermen, while the government has announced the expansion of targeted fuel relief measures.What is the EU doing?On 17 July, the European Commission announced a €540 million allocation to compensate the farmers most affected by economic losses linked to higher fertiliser and energy costs arising from the Middle East crisis.France was allocated approximately €107.1 million and Spain €50.2 million. National authorities are responsible for deciding how to target the funding at the farmers and sectors most affected.Ministers also discussed longer-term measures under the Commission's fertiliser action plan on 28 September. Published in May, the plan aims to improve fertiliser affordability and availability and strengthen the EU's domestic supply resilience.

title: Swedish researchers create an ‘AI scientist’ that designs and runs its own experiments
description: Swedes created an AI system that can carry out the full scientific process from hypothesis to results interpretation with minimal human input.
content: Researchers in Sweden have developed an AI scientist capable of generating scientific hypotheses, designing experiments and interpreting results. The team combined multiple Large Language Models (LLMs), large databases and physical laboratory robotics into a closed-loop system that can run the full cycle of scientific discovery.“It is too much information for a human to analyse, but our AI scientist could identify promising biological questions, recommend experiments to test them, evaluate experimental outcomes and iteratively refine its understanding based on new evidence,” said Ievgeniia Tiukova, a researcher at Chalmers University of Technology, and one of the authors of the new study that examined the AI scientist. The AI scientist analysed a database of approximately 60,000 phenotypical, physiological and metabolic relations for S. cerevisiae — a species of yeast also called brewer’s yeast or baker’s yeast. Then the system formed nearly 2,000 testable predictions about how nutrients impact cell growth and stress resistance. Then these hypotheses were evaluated, selected comparison controls and converted the ideas into step-by-step, machine-readable instructions for lab equipment. Once tests were finished, the AI analysed the data, determined whether predictions were correct and automatically updated or refined refuted hypotheses for future cycles.“Rather than serving solely as decision-supporting tools, the AI scientist actively generates new scientific knowledge,” Tiukova said.The authors noted that the future of scientific research lies in automation; advances in robotics, AI and high-throughput technologies are transforming the scientific process. “AI Scientists will collaborate with human scientists to accelerate discoveries across biology, medicine and biotechnology,” said Ross King, senior author of the study at the University of Gothenburg. “Such AI systems have the potential to reduce the time required to explore complex scientific questions, and optimise the use of laboratory resources,” King said.Humans will still be essential Researchers said such AI solutions could minimise human bias, accelerate research cycles and reduce variation caused by human error, incomplete recording of experimental protocols, environmental conditions and other factors that can affect outcomes and reproducibility. However, the authors stressed that humans will still be key in scientific research. “Humans will remain essential for setting priorities, interpreting broader contexts, developing research programmes and ensuring compliance with ethical rules,” King said. “Future generations of autonomous laboratories will become increasingly capable of collaborating with humans and will be valuable partners in efforts to solve the most challenging questions in biology and medicine”. As AI use in research advances, international bodies are moving to set out how it should be governed. The World Health Organization (WHO) recently published a report with recommendations for researchers, ethics committees, regulators, funders and policymakers “to help ensure that AI-enabled health research is conducted responsibly and for the benefit of all”. "Artificial intelligence is creating unprecedented opportunities to accelerate health research and improve people's lives,” said Meg Doherty, director at WHO’s Department of Science for Health. “At the same time, innovation must be guided by strong ethical safeguards that protect human dignity, rights and equity”.

title: Kyrylo Budanov: European security without the US would be ‘very dangerous’
description: In an exclusive interview with Euronews, the head of the Ukrainian President's Office warned against a future European security architecture without the US and outlined Kyiv’s vision for deeper defence cooperation with Europe.
content: Russia’s intensifying aerial attacks on Ukraine are aimed at exhausting and intimidating the civilian population, Kyrylo Budanov, head of the Office of the President of Ukraine, told Euronews in an exclusive interview.“Civilians are being killed - women, children, elderly people, veterans of the Second World War,” Budanov said. “It is all truly terrible, especially when children are killed.”Budanov described Russia’s approach as “classic terrorism”, saying its purpose was not only to inflict damage but to frighten the population.Asked whether Moscow believed sustained attacks could exhaust Ukrainians and ultimately increase pressure on the government to make concessions, his answer was unequivocal: “Yes, they do believe that.”But Budanov rejected the suggestion that Russia was adapting faster than Ukraine as Moscow deploys faster jet-powered drones, changes flight routes and carries out complex combined attacks.“I don’t believe that Russia, in principle, is adapting faster than we are,” he said.Instead, he said Ukraine was working to develop and deploy technological solutions to reduce the impact of Russia’s attacks, adding that protecting the civilian population the “number one task” in this effort.Race to scale up new drone interceptorsOne of those solutions is a new generation of Ukrainian interceptors designed to counter Russia’s faster jet-powered drones.Budanov said the technology had moved beyond conventional testing and was already undergoing experimental use in combat.“The issue is scaling up this technology,” he said.“There are still engineering improvements to be made. They intercept Russian jet-powered drones in most cases, but there is still work to do. And then there is the question of mass production.”Budanov said he believed Ukraine could reach the necessary scale before the most difficult period: the coming winter.His confidence, he said, was based on having personally seen both the technology and its production.“I have seen these developments, and I have seen the production,” Budanov said. “I am watching how the technological cycle is developing. They will make it in time.”Deeper defence cooperation with EuropeUkraine’s new defence technologies could also become part of deeper industrial partnerships with European countries.Several countries have already signed cooperation agreements with Kyiv under Ukraine’s so-called Drone Deal framework.Asked whether Ukraine’s latest technology for intercepting jet-powered drones could eventually form part of those agreements, Budanov said: “Anyone who has made such agreements with us has the right, so to speak, to continue negotiations on specific products.”But he stressed that Ukraine’s own requirements would come first.“We will be able to meet the demand of other countries when, first and foremost, we have met our own country’s needs for such products,” he said.Budanov said future defence-industrial cooperation with European partners could take different forms, including joint ventures and, in some cases, production facilities abroad with Ukrainian engineers and shared ownership.Such production could make sense where it offered advantages and where Ukraine remained the priority customer, he said. But some critical technologies, he argued, should remain inside the country.Asked what Ukraine could bring to European defence partnerships that its partners could not develop as quickly themselves, Budanov pointed to two advantages: “The speed of implementing innovation, the speed of scaling production — in other words, mass production.”‘Very dangerous’ for Europe without the USLooking beyond defence-industrial cooperation, Budanov said it was still too early to define Ukraine’s place in Europe’s future security architecture because the framework itself had yet to take shape.“What will the future security architecture of Europe actually be?” he said. “There is no answer to that question at the moment, but everyone is working on it.”Once it was defined and formally agreed, he said, the role of each participating country would become clearer.Asked whether such a system could work without the United States, Budanov was more explicit.“I think those who will be developing this doctrine have to take absolutely different options into account,” he said. “But it seems to me that this is a bad option. A very bad one, very dangerous for Europe.”Ukraine’s financing needs and economic futureBudanov also addressed Ukraine’s immediate financial requirements, saying Kyiv could already see how the greater part of its needs could be covered.“We can see where the greater part can definitely be covered,” he said, pointing to ongoing negotiations between Ukraine, the International Monetary Fund and the European Commission.He said Ukraine’s financial requirements would continue to change as the war evolved.“Look at what is happening now with Russian missile and drone strikes,” he said. “Obviously, more is needed somewhere, but on the other hand, less is needed in other areas. All of this balances out.”But Budanov drew a distinction between Ukraine’s immediate need to finance the war and the broader question of what its economy should eventually look like.Longer term, he said he favoured a liberal, free economy with limited state intervention, alongside predictable tax policy and domestic stability.“But right now, we have to survive,” Budanov said. “That is our main task - to survive here and now.”He said the defence sector would require a different approach, particularly when it came to military-technical cooperation and arms exports.“In any civilised country in the world, weapons are not simply sold left and right,” he said. “And Ukraine will not be an exception. There should simply be strict, transparent and understandable conditions for everyone.”For now, he said, Ukrainian defence exports remained limited because of the country’s own wartime requirements.Asked what success for Ukraine would look like years from now — economically, in attracting investment and bringing Ukrainians back home — Budanov offered a brief answer:“A place in the world rankings that is not the one we have now.”

title: Greece to set up a new national dementia centre for patients, families and caretakers
description: The new centre in Athens will provide cognitive training, occupational and music therapy, plus services for prevention, diagnosis and ongoing patient monitoring.
content: Greece is creating a new integrated care model for people living with dementia and Alzheimer's disease, for their families and caretakers. The new National Dementia Model Centre will be located in Peristeri, Athens.The Centre aims to become a key reference point for the prevention, diagnosis, monitoring and care of people with dementia and related disorders, and a blueprint for similar services across the country.Services for patients and carersThe new facility will offer cognitive stimulation, occupational therapy and music therapy programmes, as well as services for prevention, diagnosis and systematic patient follow-up.The services will include counselling and guidance for families and carers, including via telemedicine, while training programmes will be developed for health professionals, carers and young researchers.The Centre will provide free services to up to 160 people a day, reaching around 5,000 people a year.Setting standards nationwideBeyond services, the Centre will also develop quality standards and evaluation tools to continuously upgrade the facilities that provide services to people with dementia in Greece.At the same time, it is expected to support volunteering, information and awareness-raising initiatives, contribute to educating civil society and promote dementia research.Presenting the project, Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis stressed that the Centre will serve as a source of expertise for similar facilities throughout Greece, while also contributing to research and public information. Mitsotakis said that the aim is also to reduce the social stigma that still surrounds the disease.The prime minister also referred to the importance of cooperation between the state, civil society, local government and the Church in delivering the project.The National Dementia Model Centre is set to open in September 2027. A pilot phase is planned, with full operation of the facility scheduled for spring 2028.Partnership between the state, foundations and institutionsThe creation of the Centre is the result of cooperation between the public sector, the National Bank of Greece and 12 charitable foundations that participate in the "Initiative '21'", with the involvement of local authorities and the Church.Renovation of the space, procurement of equipment and funding for the first two years will be covered by a donation of €4.49 million from the members of the "Initiative '21'".Deputy Health Minister Irini Agapidaki described the project as an opportunity for a broader change in how dementia is addressed, with an emphasis on prevention, early diagnosis and patient support. She placed particular emphasis on the need to train informal carers, who shoulder a significant part of the daily care of people with dementia.

title: 'Women don't cry any more, they cash in': Shakira turns Madrid into a festival of empowerment
description: The Colombian pop star returns to Spain after eight years with a 12-show residency in Madrid, celebrating Latin culture and turning a chapter of her life into a spectacle of music, freedom and empowerment.
content: There are little girls barely a metre off the ground. Women who could be their mothers and others old enough to be their grandmothers. There are Colombians, Venezuelans, Peruvians and Spaniards, but also Germans, Dutch and Danes. Some wear purple wigs. Others, coin skirts. Many, glitter. And when the howling starts, for a few hours they are all the same: she-wolves.Shakira did not want to come back to Spain with just a simple concert. No, she wanted to come back in style.Eight years after her last tour in the country, the Colombian star has chosen Madrid for the only European residency of 'Las Mujeres Ya No Lloran World Tour' (Women No Longer Cry): 12 shows, more than 600,000 tickets and a temporary stadium built for her and her fans in the south of the capital, that can welcome around 55,000 people a night.ShakiraworldAnd around the stage she has practically built a city. It is called Macondo Park, in tribute to the universe of Gabriel García Márquez, and it offers food, music, literature, children’s areas, exhibitions and a second stage.The gates open hours before Shakira appears. This is not meant to be just a concert: it is a festival celebrating Latin culture, built around an artist who has spent more than three decades exporting it around the world.And the choice of Madrid is no accident either.Shakira has explained that she chose the capital because here she found something she wanted to celebrate: a city with a huge Latin American community, where Latin culture is already part of everyday identity and openly celebrated.But it is hard to ignore another layer to this comeback.Madrid and Barcelona live out a historic rivalry that goes far beyond football. And Barcelona is not just any city in Shakira’s biography: it was her home for more than a decade, the city where she lived with her ex-partner, football star Gerard Piqué, where her children grew up and which she eventually left for Miami after a painful break-up.Now her only major European landing is in Madrid.The symbolic weight is impossible to avoid. The woman who walked away from Barcelona after one of the toughest periods of her life returns to Spain, taking over the rival city for four weekends.And she herself seems to relish that storyline."Good evening, Madrid. I can’t believe I’m here," she says to tens of thousands of people. Then she recalls something someone told her before she came back: "With the face you left with, just look at the face you’ve come back with."She-wolves supportThe concert opened with 'La fuerte'. Then come 'Girl Like Me', 'Las de la intuición' and 'Estoy aquí'. In just a few minutes, the Shakira of the 90s, the global Latin pop star and the woman who in recent years turned a break-up into music all share the same space.A digital Shakira appears at the beginning, rebuilding her own body out of sand. Then the real one, flesh and blood, makes her way through the crowd with her pack before reaching the stage. "There is nothing like when a she-wolf is reunited with her pack," she says.And the pack answers back. They dance to 'La tortura'. They scream 'Te felicito'. They know every word of 'TQG'. They go back 20 years with 'Hips Don’t Lie'. They sing 'Waka Waka'. Song by song, an idea emerges that runs through the whole show: falling does not mean staying on the floor.In Madrid, Shakira acknowledged that the last few years "have not been easy" and described her return to Spain as "a gift". And then she starts dancing again.Women no longer cryThere is something profoundly feminine about the night. Not because it is a party only for women, but because of the feeling that here they can take up all the space. Be loud. Sensual. Silly. Angry. Vulnerable. Strong. Put on a violet wig, shake their hips for two hours and dance with a stranger.During the show a line by the Chilean writer Isabel Allende appears on the screens that almost works as a manifesto: "Women on their own are vulnerable, but together we are invincible". And you only have to look around to understand why it is there.Mothers dancing with their daughters. Groups of friends hugging. Women of different ages, countries and languages singing the same songs. For Latin women, there is something especially familiar in a show that does not tone down or hide its identity: pop, reggaeton, salsa, batucada, percussion and hips. Barranquilla is present even though we are in Madrid.The line that ended up defining this era was not trying to be subtle either: "Women no longer cry, women cash in". And cash in she does.600,000 tickets: women cash in tooThe residency is also a huge business operation. Twelve nights over four consecutive weekends. More than 600,000 tickets. A venue built specifically for the occasion and an estimate of between €150 and 200 million in direct associated spending for Madrid.Instead of touring Europe, Shakira has managed to convince Europeans and others to travel to her.Madrid has becomes a destination for fans from dozens of countries and generations. And the line born as a response to a break-up takes on here a much more literal meaning.The 10 commandments of a she-wolfTowards the end of the concert, the ten commandments of the she-wolves appear on the screens. They are the code of this new Shakira: independence, freedom, sisterhood and a few nods to her past that the audience picks up instantly.One of them especially teases Madrid: A she-wolf shall not covet another’s goods.('Clara-ly').The stadium erupts.What a few years ago filled headlines about her private life has ended up as humour, music and spectacle. Shakira no longer tries to separate her personal story from her songs: she plays with it.Then comes 'Loba'.But there is still one last song, and it is hard to imagine her choosing any other.After more than two hours spanning three decades of career, Shakira saves for the finale the session with Bizarrap in which she turned her break-up with Piqué into one of the biggest hits of her career.Then tens of thousands of people once again shout with her: "Women no longer cry, women cash in".The circle closes right here and the last song feels written for this very moment. Shakira left Spain in tears. She has come back to Madrid cashing in.

title: Mental health under strain: Spain lags Europe in access to psychologists
description: With six clinical psychologists per 100,000 people, against nearly 18 in Europe, regular therapy in Spain is out of reach for many; the alternative is costly private care.
content: Mental health in Spain has never been talked about so much. Anxiety, depression, stress, eating disorders and emotional wellbeing have moved from often remaining hidden in the private sphere to becoming topics in family conversations, institutional campaigns, the media and social networks. The silence has been broken. The question now is what happens next, when someone decides to ask for help.Spain has around six clinical psychologists for every 100,000 inhabitants, a figure still far from the European average of about 18 professionals. This shortage has direct consequences for care: waiting lists, appointments spaced weeks or months apart, and difficulties providing the continuity needed for effective psychological treatment.This risks entrenching a two-tier mental healthcare system. Those with the means can turn to a private psychologist and be seen every week or fortnight. By contrast, people who rely solely on the public system may face much longer waits.The question is hard to avoid: is psychological care becoming a luxury reserved for those who can afford it?High demand in autumnAutumn is a particularly sensitive time for mental health, bringing a rise in appointments with psychologists. The change of season, steadily shorter daylight hours and the full return to obligations and routines lead many people to seek professional help at this time of year.The underlying issue, though, is that the demand for psychological support has become structural, and many professionals' diaries remain full for most of the year.For psychiatrist Kazuhiro Tajima, founder of APIR, a centre specialising in training resident psychologists, this surge in demand also has a social explanation."We have never talked so much about anxiety, depression or emotional wellbeing, and that is undoubtedly progress. We have succeeded in making mental health stop being a taboo topic. But the very concept of mental health has also changed profoundly, and that is reshaping what people are asking services for," he says.The shift is far from minor. Traditionally, public mental health services were designed above all to diagnose and treat mental illness. Today they are also seeing a growing number of people seeking professional help to cope with life problems that do not necessarily amount to a disorder."For decades, mental health services were geared mainly towards treating mental illnesses. Today, more and more people look for help because they are going through situations that are part of being human: bereavement, a break-up, work difficulties, family conflicts or struggles to adapt to particular stages of life," Tajima notes.Even if these situations do not always constitute an illness, the distress should not be ignored. "We must not minimise that suffering, because many of these people can benefit greatly from psychotherapy, from learning tools to cope better with life or simply from having a space where they feel listened to," the psychiatrist argues.Here lies one of the big contradictions in today's debate on mental health. Society has made a huge effort to persuade people to seek help when they need it, yet that greater awareness has not been matched by a similar increase in public resources."The problem is that the public system was not designed to provide that kind of ongoing support universally. Its core mission has always been to diagnose and treat mental illness. If we now ask it also to absorb a growing demand linked to everyday emotional distress, without structural reform and without extra resources, it is hardly surprising that the system becomes saturated," Tajima warns. And that saturation ultimately affects patients.An appointment every two or three monthsPsychotherapy needs continuity. Yet the shortage of professionals means many patients seen in the public system have to wait long intervals between sessions, with appointments every two or three months.Clinical psychologist Fran Gullón draws attention to one of the less visible consequences of this lack of staff. Simply getting to see a psychologist is not enough; the treatment requires conditions that allow a genuine therapeutic process to take place."Psychotherapy is not a string of isolated appointments. It needs continuity, a relationship and time. If we see a patient every two or three months, in many cases we are not really providing psychotherapy: we are doing our best to hold together an inadequate level of care," Gullón explains.The consequences are particularly worrying when an early intervention could prevent the problem from worsening. "This creates a situation we encounter daily in clinical practice: people who need prompt psychological intervention but have to wait weeks or months before they can access it," he adds.For those who can afford it, private consultations become the way to bypass waiting lists and ensure more consistent therapy. For those without such resources, that option simply does not exist. Income thus becomes a factor that can determine not only when psychological care is received, but also how often.In Gullón's view, the discussion about waiting lists should not stop at the time it takes to get a first appointment. "We talk a great deal about how long it takes a patient to enter Mental Health services, and far too little about what happens afterwards. Securing a first appointment is of limited value if the next one is eight or ten weeks later," he warns.Psychologists in short supplyThe lack of clinical psychologists also appears unlikely to be solved quickly. In the most recent intake, 293 Resident Intern Psychologist (PIR) training posts were offered, just 13 more than the previous year. Although this does represent another increase in specialist training places, the growth is modest compared with the gap that still separates Spain from European ratios.The problem also has a delayed effect. Increasing training places today does not mean instantly having hundreds of new specialists, as future clinical psychologists must first complete their specialist health-care training.Gullón also stresses that raising the number of professionals cannot be separated from specialist training. The PIR system involves four years of specialist health-care training, during which psychologists are trained within the National Health System itself."We must keep pressing for an increase in the number of clinical psychologists in Spain, in line with society's current needs and converging with the ratios of neighbouring countries," he argues."If we know there is a shortage of clinical psychologists, we cannot wait until the deficit becomes unbearable before starting to train more specialists. Every PIR place we fail to create today is a clinical psychologist we will not have in four years' time," Francisco Gullón concludes.A medicalised societyYet increasing resources alone will not settle another major debate opened up by rising concern about emotional wellbeing. The spread of concepts drawn from psychology and psychiatry has helped bring previously silenced problems to light, but it can also encourage people to interpret normal life experiences automatically as disorders."We must be cautious to avoid medicalising everyday life. Not every bout of sadness is depression, not every worry is an anxiety disorder, and not every difficulty concentrating means ADHD," warns psychiatrist Kazuhiro Tajima.The boundary between suffering and illness has therefore become one of the key challenges for professionals. In this context, the clinical psychologist points out that one of the current tasks is to distinguish between the suffering inherent in certain life experiences and those problems that require specialist health-care intervention."We do not need more diagnoses; we need better diagnoses. Above all, we need to ensure that when someone really does require specialist treatment, they can receive it in time," Gullón stresses. "Mental health does not mean never suffering; it means developing the capacity to face life's difficulties and recognising when that suffering has stopped being a normal reaction and become an illness that requires treatment," he explains.No longer a privilegeSpain has made huge progress on one of the main challenges around mental health: ensuring that asking for help is no longer seen as a weakness, and that conditions such as depression or anxiety disorders can be discussed openly without the stigma that surrounded them for decades.The next challenge is far more concrete: having enough professionals to care for those who turn to the system. For the psychiatrist and APIR founder, the answer lies in acting on two fronts: increasing capacity and rethinking the model at the same time."It is essential to boost the capacity of the public system, but also to adapt the model to a social reality that has changed profoundly.
