Only then will people who genuinely need specialised psychological care be able to receive it at the right moment."Psychologist Francisco Gullón agrees that real progress will come when social awareness is matched by care capacity. "We have achieved something tremendously important: people have lost their fear of asking for help. Now we have to make sure that asking for help actually leads somewhere." In his view, "mental health cannot depend on your postcode or your bank balance. If psychotherapy is indicated, being able to receive it as often as necessary should be determined by clinical criteria, not by money."There is a contradiction that is becoming harder and harder to ignore: citizens are urged to seek help when they need it, but when they finally do so they discover that seeing a psychologist may depend on how much money is in their bank account.

title: France's far-right National Rally gains ground in Senate and forms group for first time
description: RN presidential candidate Marine Le Pen hailed a "historic victory" after the results were announced.
content: France's far-right National Rally (RN) party and its allies secured a record 14 seats in the right-wing dominated Senate in polls on Sunday, effectively quadrupling its number in the 348-seat chamber just months before a presidential election.RN presidential candidate Marine Le Pen hailed a "historic victory" after the results were announced.Local elected officials vote for new senators for half the upper chamber every three years, each to serve a six-year term.The far-right party entered the Senate for the first time with two seats in 2014, when it was known as the National Front, and won three seats in 2023.Le Pen is eyeing her best chance yet at power in elections next year when centrist President Emmanuel Macron steps down."This is a historic victory, and a major milestone with the formation for the first time of a group in the Senate," she said on X.Nine RN senators were elected on Sunday, according to an AFP tally of results, on top of the three who won seats in 2023.A further two were elected from RN ally Eric Ciotti's Union of the Right for the Republic (UDR) party.RN president Jordan Bardella said the party's senators would form a group with UDR allies.Ciotti quit the right-wing Republicans (LR) party in 2024 after calling for an alliance with the far right.The upper chamber's LR president of more than a decade, 77-year-old Gerard Larcher, is expected to be re-elected next week.The right, centre and left-wing Socialists looked set to remain the three major forces in the upper house, according to initial results.The hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) party won its first-ever seat.Le Pen's anti-immigration party emerged as the single largest party in the lower-house National Assembly after Macron called snap polls in 2024, though it fell well short of a majority.

title: Deep mining for memories: Greece opens digital archive to preserve Serifos ironworks history
description: "The Living History of the Serifos Mines", a project by the Friends of Serifos funded by Cycladic Identity, has created a digital archive of Greek mineworkers' history and memories.
content: Serifos is one of the most beautiful islands in the Cyclades. Behind its major tourism development lies a history that most people know nothing about. The island was an important mining centre as far back as antiquity. Its subsoil is rich mainly in haematite and magnetite, with the result that to this day half of Serifos is perforated with galleries and shafts after many years of mining.In the south-west, mainly at Mega Livadi and Koutalas, visitors can still see rusted rails, machinery, tools, wagons and loading piers. These are the visible traces of the intensive mining activity that shaped the island until the mid-20th century.In more recent times, iron ore extraction began in 1870 and became more systematic from 1885 onwards. Annual production often reached 200,000 tonnes. Mining was not only a livelihood for locals; many others arrived from different parts of Greece to work on the island.In 1963, the mines closed for good, forcing most workers to migrate and change profession. The mining sites were abandoned. Their story, however, remains deeply etched in the soul and identity of the islanders.To highlight and preserve these memories, the Friends of Serifos Association launched the project "The living history of the mines of Serifos", with the support of the Cycladic Identity initiative of the Museum of Cycladic Art. The research, interviews and documentation of material lasted a year. The result is a journey into the past, a moving exploration of residents' memories and the history of the mines, captured in a printed and a digital album.Digital undergroundThe digital archive (source in Greek) contains more than 250 photographs, rare documents, press clippings from the period and 10 first-hand testimonies by miners and their descendants who are still alive. This was deemed necessary because for decades the history of the Serifos mines survived mainly through the oral accounts of those who had lived and worked there.As generations pass, these testimonies had to be recorded before they disappeared forever. At the same time, information panels with QR codes were installed at the mining sites, allowing visitors to read the miners' interviews on the spot.Earlier this month, the Friends of the Cultural Heritage and Environment of Serifos Association presented the project to local residents, organised a round-table discussion with miners and their descendants, and held a guided tour of the mining sites at Mega Livadi, led by Thodoris G. Livanios.Katerina Papathoma, Vice-President of the Friends of Serifos Association, was the Programme Manager. Although she is not originally from the island, she has been living here for years and has grown deeply attached to it."The aim of the Friends of Serifos Association is twofold. First, to save and preserve this living history of the mines of Serifos. This was done through recordings and live interviews given to us by the miners and their descendants on the island. The second aim is that we want to share this story. The fact is that even we who live here in Serifos do not really know this history," explained Papathoma."I realised this when all the material was brought together and I saw that many aspects of this place's history are completely unknown. So first we ourselves have to learn, to answer questions we may have and to understand what happened with the mines."The second reason is to have a structured body of information so we can pass it on to young people. It is the young who will very soon be called on to deal with Serifos's issues. They need to know these places in order to become attached to them and, if possible, to protect them."Miners' strifeSerifos was the largest mining centre in Greece after Lavrio. The mines at Mega Livadi are a listed historic site. This was where the bloody miners' strike of 1916 took place. They demanded the introduction of the eight-hour working day and more dignified working conditions from their employers, the German company Grohmann.The uprising was universal. It was driven by starvation wages, punishing working hours, appalling living conditions and the total lack of safety measures, which often led to deaths and crippling injuries.The strike ended in bloodshed, during which four strikers lost their lives (Th. Kouzoupis, M. Zoilis, M. Mitrofanis, I. Protopappas) and two members of the gendarmerie were also killed (Ch. Chrysanthou and I. Triantafyllou). Konstantinos Speras (1893–1943) was the leading figure in the strike. Born in Serifos, he became a key figure in Greece's workers' and trade union movement.The Municipality of Serifos has for several years been trying to turn the area at Mega Livadi into an open-air mining museum that will showcase the history of the mines, the area's unique identity and offer a different kind of development for this abandoned region.Konstantinos Revintis, The mayor of Serifos, spoke to Euronews at the site of the strike: "We are standing in the historic place where the miners' strike for the first eight-hour working day and for better working conditions took place, on 21 August 1916. It is a historic site that we want to highlight by creating here an open-air mining museum that will tell the story without a voice, simply through traces."Everything that still exists here must be restored. We have formed several partnerships with various bodies of recognised standing that have the necessary technical and management expertise, such as the National Technical University of Athens, the University of the Aegean, the Hellenic Society for the Environment and Cultural Heritage, Europa Nostra, the World Monuments Fund, the World Monuments Watch and other organisations. The Mega Livadi Association is a local body that shows particular sensitivity on this issue."And of course, we as the Municipality are playing the leading role. If the Ministry of Culture can support us, that would be ideal, as well as the Ministry of Finance, because we are in a coastal zone here," said Revintis. "Our aim is to complete this project and return the site to public use so that people can visit it and so it can become an attraction, both for permanent residents and for visitors."The project "The living history of the mines of Serifos" was funded by Cycladic Identity, an important initiative run by the Museum of Cycladic Art since 2022.Its goal is to safeguard the intangible cultural heritage that has shaped the island's history over the centuries. To date, the museum has supported 26 projects in total on 15 Cycladic islands and will soon announce ten more for 2027:"The Cycladic Identity initiative is essentially our concrete way of saying thank you to the islands. In practice, we support organisations active on the Cycladic islands in the fields of culture, biodiversity and intangible cultural heritage," explained Theano Agalloglou, Project Manager of the Cycladic Identity initiative at the Museum of Cycladic Art."We want to engage as many residents as possible. We want them to feel proud of their unique cultural and natural heritage, but also to raise their awareness. We believe it is extremely important that the oral testimonies of the miners, or 'Metalliotes' as they were called on the island, are documented, digitised and preserved as a legacy for the new generation," added Agalloglou.The project and the album were presented at the Theatre of the Serifos Association in Chora. There, former miners and descendants of mining families shared their stories and memories with the audience.The testimony of Andreas Livanios (Katsafouris)"I went to work in the mines around 1956–57. I was still a child. I went because at that time everyone, the whole of Serifos, worked in the mines. The mine meant great hardship, because those from Mega Livadi and Koutalas lived nearby. I am from Kallitsos, in the north. To leave home and reach Mega Livadi, it took us three hours on foot. We had to get up at 2 in the morning, get ready and leave at about twenty to three so that we would be at the worksite at ten to six or a quarter to six. If we arrived at one minute past six, we were sent to the office and lost the day's pay."It was exhausting because it was night and there was no road. We walked without light, in the cold and rain, along a path through the fields. I worked on compressors that pumped air. I went in the morning because these compressors ran on dynamite. I would put a small stick of dynamite inside, tap the detonator with a hammer and the machine would start up."What was left from the mines was only damage and hardship. They have eaten away all the guts of Serifos. There are galleries in the mountains where, if you go in, you get lost. Even now, when I think about it, I can hardly breathe. All the wealth left this place. Nothing was left for the island, which could have become a little Paris if the resources had been used properly."The testimony of Alexandros Livanios"On both my mother's and my father's side, they were miners. My mother's father survived, although he was very seriously injured. He spent a couple of years in hospital but pulled through. He survived and even kept all his limbs, but for two years he had lost his mind. My other grandfather on my father's side, Alexandros Klaos, was killed. His body is still inside a mine at Aspros Kavos. My father never met his own father. My grandmother was pregnant with him when her husband was killed. There is no mining family in Serifos that does not have either someone injured or someone dead."The mines were both a blessing and a curse for the island. They kept people here, because mining was the main occupation and farming was a sideline. These people worked from night to night in the mines. Only Sundays were left for them to go and work their fields. Usually it was the woman who replaced the man because he was tied up with work. If you think that he had to leave from Chora and walk two hours to Mega Livadi, he had to get up in the middle of the night and return again at night."The school at Mega Livadi had 150 children when I was a pupil there. Gradually it was deserted and became a necropolis. In winter there are almost no residents at all. After the mines closed, there was both internal and external migration. I went to sea. I started out as a lathe operator and then went into the maritime sector because the pay was better, much better."The testimony of Thodoris G. Livanios"I am an amateur researcher and folklorist. I have recorded dozens of people who worked in the mines and are unfortunately no longer with us, including people who experienced the 1916 strike. These are unique testimonies that I keep in my archive."We are children of miners, children of workers. We are descendants of the victims, not of the German exploiters. I have countless memories, because I experienced a lot in the mines both as a child and later through recording powerful testimonies that, unfortunately, have not yet been fully used. I have made several documentaries, television and radio programmes, and I have documented the popular culture of Serifos."Serifos is an empty shell. It was exploited by the Grohmanns and the successive employers who extracted the ore, drank the workers' sweat, drank the workers' blood and, in the end, left them unpaid."

title: Ukrainian suspect arrested after fatal stabbing at Polish abbey
description: A knife attack at a Catholic abbey in Poland left one person dead and four others injured. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy condemned the attack as a "horrific crime" and called for the perpetrator to be held accountable.
content: A Ukrainian man was arrested on Thursday after a knife attack at a Catholic abbey in southeastern Poland left one person dead and four others injured.Police said the 31-year-old suspect attacked four men and a woman at the 17th-century abbey in Jarosław, around 30 kilometres from the Ukrainian border.The attack took place at approximately 9:30 am, when police received reports of a stabbing.Polish media identified the person killed as a priest. Police confirmed the death to AFP but did not verify the victim's identity.Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the "murderer" would be "punished with the full severity of Polish law."Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński also addressed the attack in a post on X."Tragic events in Jarosław. A Ukrainian citizen was immediately detained by the police after an attack on five people. The services are investigating the motives and circumstances of the incident," he wrote.According to prosecutors, the suspect had entered Poland from Germany and was travelling towards the Ukrainian border. Instead, he went to the abbey, where he allegedly took a knife from the kitchen and attacked clergy members and worshippers.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy condemned the attack, describing it as a "horrific crime.""The perpetrator of this evil must bear full responsibility in accordance with the law," he said."We are shaken by this evil," Zelenskyy added. "Justice must be done."Local newspaper Gazeta Jarosławska published photographs showing fire engines and police vehicles outside the monastery, with its entrance cordoned off.

title: Chinese goods transshipment haunts Trump-Xi meeting: Nine Latin American countries flagged by the White House
description: The White House named nine Latin American nations among 40 flagged for transhipping Chinese goods, before the Trump–Xi summit in Washington as the issue is likely to be discussed during the meeting on Thursday.
content: On Thursday, Chinese President Xi Jinping will meet US President Donald Trump again, this time at the White House, four months after the two last saw each other in Beijing.The meeting comes with a backdrop that weighs particularly heavily on Latin America.In August, the White House published a report on trade transshipment, the shipment of Chinese goods through third countries to avoid tariffs, which flags more than 40 economies as risk points.Nine of them in Latin America or the Caribbean including Mexico, Brazil, Argentina, Chile, Colombia, Peru, Panama, Costa Rica and the Dominican Republic.The "great transshipment scam": What the US report saysThe document is titled "The Great Transshipment Scam: Rise, Scope, and Costs" and was signed on 13 August by the White House Office of Trade and Manufacturing Policy, headed by Peter Navarro, Trump's chief adviser on trade and manufacturing.It runs to 25 pages, with a Trojan horse made of containers on the cover.The mechanism it describes is a familiar one: relabelling, repackaging, re-invoicing, minor assembly work and false declarations of origin, all supported by free zones, bonded warehouses and logistics hubs where there is no real transformation of the product.The report does not provide a single headline figure, but instead compares five independent estimates of the money lost, two from US official bodies and three from private firms, which the White House itself warns are neither additive nor directly comparable with one another, because each one uses a different methodology and covers a different universe of products.Goldman Sachs offers the most conservative estimate. It puts the loss at $40 billion (€35bn) a year, the lowest figure, based on an econometric model using 2023 data and focused solely on the re-export channel.The White House Council of Economic Advisers puts the range between $34.2 billion (€29.7bn) and $89.6 billion (€78bn), with $60 billion (€52.2bn) as the midpoint, by cross-checking tariff codes country by country.The private AI supply-chain intelligence firm Exiger puts the figure at $75 billion (€65.3bn), a number the report adopts as its central case for the rest of its calculations on jobs, GDP and lost revenue.The Department of Commerce offers a broader reading with a simple method, calculating an upper ceiling of $109 billion (€94.91bn), although with a stricter cross-check of exact shipments via Mexico, India and Vietnam it cuts this to $67 billion (€58.3bn).Altana, another supply-chain intelligence company, sets the upper limit at $303 billion (€263.8bn), the widest and least tightly defined of the five estimates.On that base of €65.3 billion, Exiger's, the report calculates an annual loss of between €16.5 and €22.6 billion in tariff revenue, to which it adds 450,000 jobs displaced and up to 150 billion less in GDP.The fact that five sources arrive at such disparate figures is not a contradiction but a reflection of what each of them measures and how granular their data are. At one end of the spectrum is Goldman Sachs, which isolates one very specific channel, goods that are rerouted specifically to dodge the China tariff, and measures it with final 2023 data; hence the lowest number.At the opposite end is Altana, which does not analyse products one by one but relationships between factories: it tracks which facility produces what, through which intermediary and to which destination, and counts as potential transshipment any suspect route, including goods that do undergo a real transformation in the intermediate country. This breadth of criteria is what pushes its estimate up to 303 billion.That combination of reasonable breadth and on-the-ground verification at factory level is what leads the White House to adopt Exiger's figure as its "central case" for the rest of the report, jobs, GDP, lost revenue, instead of choosing either the highest or the lowest of the five.To put these figures in context, the White House compares them with items in the federal budget itself: €21.7 billion is almost the same as the budget request the Space Force has made for 2026 (€23bn) and exceeds that of US Customs itself which is (€20bn).The report also provides evidence from enforcement on the ground: comparing the 526 days before and after Trump's inauguration, shipments with irregularities detected by Customs rose by 245%, from 93,744 to 323,677, and the additional revenue associated with those irregularities increased by 169%, from 8.36 to €22.4 billion.The legal basis for tightening these controls is executive order 14411, "Strengthening Customs Enforcement" (Fortalecimiento de la fiscalización aduanera), which Trump signed on 3 June 2026 and which grants Customs more tools on importers' liability, bonds, ownership transparency and penalties.On that basis the "Detective Border" is being built, the artificial-intelligence system that Customs is already testing to cross-check shipping routes, ownership histories and declared production capacity.Nine Latin American countries among the 40 singled outWashington divides the 40 countries into three tiers according to their role in the network. In the first, that of "diversified scale leaders", Mexico appears alongside Canada, the European Union, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Israel.In the second, with deeper production integration with China, are Brazil together with Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, Turkey and Vietnam. The third tier, that of "smaller opportunistic targets", groups Argentina, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Panama, Peru and the Dominican Republic, along with Singapore, Switzerland, the United Arab Emirates and other small economies.The report also includes a map of "Latin American corridors", Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia and Peru, defined as diversion routes between the Pacific and the Atlantic that combine bonded warehousing with regional assembly.The White House itself stresses, however, that appearing on the list does not amount to a formal accusation of fraud: it acknowledges that the increase in exports from these countries to the US does not in itself prove that illegal transshipment is taking place.Mexico was the first to react. President Claudia Sheinbaum rejected the allegation on the very Friday the report came out: "We have shown the United States that there is no triangulation scheme", she said at her morning press conference, explaining that a large share of the goods arriving in Mexico gain real added value before being re-exported, within the law. Her government is in direct contact with the Department of Commerce and with the US trade representative, Jamieson Greer.In Santo Domingo, the Ministry of Industry, Trade and MSMEs also moved to defend the transparency of its foreign trade, stressing that the report imposes no sanctions or restrictions and that the reference to the Dominican Republic reflects its free zones and port infrastructure, not any irregular operation that has been detected.Several of the countries named had already made moves before the report, gestures that now take on a different meaning: Mexico imposed tariffs of up to 50% on Chinese cars in December, ahead of the review of the USMCA, and Colombia set a 35% tariff in March on steel imports from countries without a trade agreement, with China as the main party affected.The tug-of-war with CK Hutchison and ChinaNo case illustrates the tension better than Panama's. On 29 January, Panama's Supreme Court declared unconstitutional the concession, in force since 1997, that allowed Panama Ports Company, a subsidiary of Hong Kong's CK Hutchison, to operate the ports of Balboa and Cristóbal at both ends of the canal.The lawsuit was brought by the Office of the Comptroller General, which alleged contractual irregularities and an accumulated tax debt close to $1.2 billion (€1bn).The ruling came in the middle of negotiations, already stalled at that point, on the sale of those ports to a consortium led by BlackRock for $22.8 billion (€19.8bn), a deal that Beijing had asked to handle "with caution".The US Congress hailed the decision as a defeat for China in the canal; Panama took effective control of the terminals on 23 February, and China responded by freezing talks on new projects in the country and summoning the Panamanian ambassador.President José Raúl Mulino said that Panama would not be pressured by Beijing. Months later, the country appears in the lowest tier of the transshipment report, but with symbolic weight that outweighs any trade figure.What is at stake for the region in the 24 September meetingAccording to the official agenda for the Washington meeting, they will discuss issues such as the Strait of Hormuz, financial sanctions on Iran, the global tariff war and controls on artificial intelligence.On the question of the global tariff war in particular, Latin America will gain prominence "on the board", as foreign-policy analysts describe it: China overtook the European Union years ago as Latin America's second-largest trading partner, and in several countries it is already ahead of the United States in terms of trade volume.The Peruvian port of Chancay, financed with Chinese capital, had already featured in analysis ahead of May's summit in Beijing as a source of concern for Washington, which sees it as an infrastructure with potential dual use, civilian and military, in the South Pacific.Neither Brookings nor most analysts expect that 24 September will produce signed agreements on transshipment: the consensus, several say, is that the day will be more about photos than commitments, although the tightening of customs controls that began in August will continue regardless of what happens at the White House that day.

title: 'I'm done with medical abuse': actor Arnaud Denis dies by euthanasia in Belgium
description: The French actor and director had been in unbearable pain since a polypropylene prosthesis was fitted in 2023 after a right groin hernia. Aged 43, he was euthanised this Tuesday in Namur, Belgium.
content: Actor and director Arnaud Denis, left severely disabled after the insertion of an anti-hernia implant, chose to end his life by euthanasia in Belgium on Tuesday at the age of 43 to put a stop to his suffering, his lawyer Philippe Courtois told AFP."The decision taken by Arnaud Denis was made in consultation with three doctors in Namur. His body could no longer carry him. He had lost control of it. Arnaud Denis’s death is the consequence of the intense pain he had been enduring for many months," he added.Best known for his productions of Choderlos de Laclos' Les Liaisons Dangereuses and Molière's Les Femmes Savantes, Denis had been suffering since a polypropylene mesh implant was fitted on 17 July 2023 after a right groin hernia.The operation triggered numerous side effects, which eventually drove him to have the implant removed in the United States in April 2024.The actor was diagnosed with myalgic encephalomyelitis, in the context of ASIA syndrome (an inflammatory reaction linked to exposure to an adjuvant). The implant is thought to have caused persistent inflammation and disrupted his immune system."I can no longer leave my home, I have no social life, I have no life at all. I no longer have anything that constitutes the dignity of a man’s life. And it is getting worse and worse. I live like a cancer patient in the terminal phase. The doctors have nothing left to offer me," he confided in early 2026 to the regional daily Dauphiné Libéré (source in French).'A man knows deep down when he is doomed'On 5 January 2026, Denis lodged a complaint with the Public Health Division of the Paris public prosecutor’s office for "unintentional injuries", but it was dropped at the end of August "for lack of sufficiently established offence".Seeing no other way than euthanasia to end his suffering, the actor said at the beginning of the year: "A man knows deep down inside when he is doomed." On 18 March, he was admitted to a palliative care unit in a Belgian hospital, pending approval of his euthanasia request.His lawyer condemned what he called "a silent public health scandal", arguing that "thousands of patients" are "exposed to high-risk implants, without clear information or informed consent, suffering serious medical complications, most of them irreversible"."Medtronic has acknowledged in a letter sent to Mr Arnaud Denis that implanting parietal reinforcement devices may be the cause of chronic and acute post-operative pain, an unwanted effect mentioned in the instructions for use of the Dextile device intended for healthcare professionals. Yet these instructions are intended for healthcare professionals and not for patients, who receive no information," Philippe Courtois pointed out.Denis set up a collective called "French victims of hernia prostheses", which has gathered hundreds of testimonies on social media from people who have suffered adverse effects linked to anti-hernia implants.

title: How fake Naxos potatoes and modern ambitions are threatening the future of a world-renowned crop
description: Historic Naxos potatoes hold protected status, but young people on the island no longer want to be farmers.
content: Naxos is the largest island in the Cyclades and its eponymous variety of potatoes has been grown here since the late 18th century. Sold all over Europe, the crop is an important part of the local economy. Sowing and harvesting takes place twice a year with the second time happening every September. Euronews went to meet Naxos potato farmers and learn more about a crop under threat.We meet Stelios Vathrakokoilis, one of the biggest potato growers on Naxos and President of the Galanado Agricultural Cooperative, and ask him what makes the island’s potatoes so special. "First of all, we have abundant sunshine almost all year round," he says. "Second, we have the sea all around us, at a distance of three to four kilometres. Third, we use cow manure on our fields, as much as we judge necessary, and the fourth and most important factor is that our subsoil lacks certain elements. That element is calcium. If, in these areas, you grow tomatoes or vegetables without adding fertilisers, they will start rotting on the back side of the fruit. That means a lack of calcium. Potatoes are not bothered by this. So it is the absence of calcium from our soils that gives the potato about 80 per cent of its distinctive flavour."Young people don't want to farm potatoes anymoreIn the 1980s, annual production of Naxos potatoes reached 15,000 tonnes. Every member of a family worked on the crop. Families today are smaller and children follow other career paths. Some 300 families on the Cycladic island are involved in potato farming today and production has dropped to a mere 5,000 tonnes.What is a fake Naxos potato?In 2010, the Naxos potato was granted protected status. This means that potatoes must be given the seal of approval before being able to be sold under the Naxos potato label.Farmer Stelios Vathrakokoilis explains that some package up potatoes as Naxos when they are, in fact, inferior varieties."We started marketing Naxos potatoes first through the AB Vassilopoulos supermarket chain. A year later, Sklavenitis came in very strongly, followed by all the chains, so that all this product was going straight onto supermarket shelves.""But even there, some fraud takes place. I don’t know who, but certain people buy potatoes from other regions, even other continents, especially Egypt. They take them into their packing plants, package them and sell them as Naxos potatoes.""This happens even more in the street markets. If you walk into a market with 20 or 30 stalls, you will see all of them claiming to sell Naxos potatoes. They are not from Naxos. Out of forty stalls, perhaps one or two sell the real thing. Everyone calls their potatoes Naxos because the price is higher and the taste better. The upshot is that consumers can find genuine Naxos potatoes in 99 per cent of cases only on supermarket shelves. Only there will they find them."Water and labour shortages threaten the future of Naxos potatoesThe shortage of labour has become acute in recent years and is a serious concern for farmers - it is very difficult to find workers with the legal right to work.Water shortages are also an issue. More residents and tourists on the island along with prolonged drought means water resources are spread much more thin.Farmers have to buy expensive water from the municipality, supplied from desalination plants.Farmer Stelios Vathrakokoilis is sounding the alarm for the future, seeing production shrink and problems multiply:"The basic precondition for having production is manpower. A second point, and what I see when I look ahead over the next five to ten years, is that we will be searching with binoculars to find a farmer, not only on Naxos but across Greece.""It makes no sense for one 'stremma' of land to leave €1,500 in a Dutch farmer’s pocket, €1,200 for an Israeli farmer and €50 for a Greek farmer. It can not go on like this! Clearly we are doing something wrong. We are still using traditional methods, techniques from decades ago, and we are not moving towards something different, such as hydroponics or similar systems, with smaller areas, better working conditions and more income.""What I see is that in 5–10 years there will be no Greek farmers left anywhere in the country. And I think this is broadly a European issue as well, as we can see from the protests farmers are staging in France and Germany.""It is not sustainable to pay €2.5 per litre for diesel fuel, to have fertiliser prices through the roof, seed prices through the roof and monthly wages of around €2,500. If you try to farm under these conditions, you will end up completely in the red," stresses Stelios Vathrakokoilis.The local farmers union is trying to helpThis year the Union of Agricultural Cooperatives of Naxos marks a century of activity. It stands by the producers and works to solve the many challenges facing the island’s agricultural and livestock sectors. The Union’s goal is to support both the product and the people who grow it:"Naxos potatoes are not just another product. They are the history of the place, its production, its economy. They are the wealth of the farmer and the livestock breeder," Dimitris Kapounis, President of the Union of Agricultural Cooperatives of Naxos, tells Euronews."Potatoes arrived on Naxos before the time of Kapodistrias, so you can see the passion, the love, the genuine cultivation of the land in this chapter we call Naxos potatoes," he says.Every year the island hosts a major festival celebrating the potato. The 17th Potato Festival was held on 12 September at the port of Naxos. The centenary of the founding of the Union of Agricultural Cooperatives of Naxos was celebrated at the same time.More than 3,000 people took part in the event in Nikiforos Mandilaras Square, alongside local organisations and representatives of the farming community. Residents and visitors sampled different recipes in which Naxos potatoes took centre stage, and enjoyed performances by musicians and dance groups.

title: The keg is tapped: Munich springs to life as Oktoberfest returns
description: Munich is once again in its own special “state of emergency”: for 16 days, the Theresienwiese becomes a mix of a traditional Bavarian costume catwalk, funfair, beer garden and open-air stage, as Bavaria’s capital celebrates the return of Oktoberfest.
content: By late morning, it was clear: the Wiesn was back. Decorated horse-drawn carriages, brass bands and festival hosts made their way towards the Theresienwiese, while growing crowds gathered around the fairground. Munich had dressed up for the occasion, and apparently nobody intended to worry about details such as calories, footwear or the weather forecast – not least because Bavaria was enjoying glorious sunshine and temperatures just above 20 degrees Celsius.The Theresienwiese was already filling up earlier in the day. At around 10:35 a.m., the traditional procession of the Wiesn landlords got under way. Around 1,000 participants, including festival hosts, showmen, musicians and waiting staff, made their way through central Munich to the Theresienwiese in decorated carriages and horse-drawn wagons.Beer only after the keg is tappedThe festival tents had already opened at 9 a.m., initially serving non-alcoholic drinks and light snacks. Beer could only be served after the official tapping of the first keg. The fairground rides also started operating only afterwards.The big moment finally came at exactly noon in the Schottenhamel festival tent. Munich’s new mayor, Dominik Krause, took the mallet and, for the first time in his term of office, tapped the first keg. After the traditional “O’zapft is!” and the twelve cannon shots fired from the Bavaria, the monumental bronze statue and landmark of the Free State of Bavaria, it was clear: there was no turning back. The beer could flow.As the first one-litre stein made its way to Bavarian Minister-President Markus Söder, the most important question of the day on the Theresienwiese was probably already being asked: Where can we still find a seat?Millions of visitors expectedThe Wiesn is one of the largest folk festivals in the world and attracts millions of visitors from Germany and abroad every year. According to Bavarian public broadcaster BR, around 6.5 million people attended the last Oktoberfest.This year, a Maß of beer costs between €14.80 and €15.90, depending on the tent, meaning visitors once again have to dig a little deeper into their pockets. A large pretzel at the Wiesn costs around €5 to €6.For getting to the festival, the city recommends using public transport. The Theresienwiese can be reached via several U-Bahn and S-Bahn stations. Anyone travelling by car should be prepared for an extremely difficult search for a parking space around the fairground.

title: Monet time: French Renaissance painter's rarely seen 'Iris' set to break sale record
description: A total of 28 works from the Schlumberger collection are being sold at Sotheby's France. Valued at more than €40 million, they include four paintings by Claude Monet, pieces by Paul Cézanne and Gustave Moreau, and a sculpture by Camille Claudel.
content: Between €22 and 30 million, the highest estimate ever placed on a painting sold in France. That is what a buyer could spend to obtain 'Iris' by Claude Monet.On 22 October, Sotheby's auction house will be offering the rarely seen work by the French Renaissance master for sale, alongside other works from the Schlumberger family's private collection.A monumental painting created by Monet at the end of his life, the canvas is, according to curators, in remarkable condition. "It has no varnish, it is on its original canvas and has never been restored. They are exactly as Monet painted them 100 years ago," explains Thomas Bompard, co-director of the Modern and Contemporary Department at Sotheby's France. Canvases preserved in the Schlumberger living roomEvery detail counts. Varnish alters the chromatic tones of a painting, according to art historian Marianne Mathieu.But restoration could damage the texture of the paint on the canvas. "Late Monet is a Monet who works the material. So to truly discover and understand him, that material has to be preserved. And we still have these thick impastos."Hung in a Schlumberger family sitting room for a century, 'Iris', like 'Weeping Willow', also up for sale and valued at between nine and ten million euros, has never been moved.Above all, it has never been seen in colour by the general public. It was acquired by Jeanne Schlumberger (1889-1983), "a brilliant art collector", from the painter's family through "the visionary gallerist" Katia Granoff, according to Thomas Bompard, without going through an auction room."Many people knew the story, or at least knew of the existence of this collection; people whispered that these were the finest Monets in Paris, but very few had actually seen them. That is also what is fuelling today's excitement," he notes.A collection valued at €40 millionAnother factor that has pushed prices higher is the centenary of the death of the Impressionist artist, who died on 5 December 1926. Two exhibitions on the painter's life open in Paris at the end of September: "Monet, Painting Time" and "Stories of Landscapes, from Monet to Hockney".In all, 28 works are up for auction at Sotheby's, in a sale expected to raise more than €40 million. Among them are four Monets, as well as a sculpture by Camille Claudel and several paintings by Gustave Moreau.Also being sold on this occasion is a wall composition of three works by Paul Cézanne. "La Ferme", the central painting, is "the largest work by the artist ever to be offered at auction" and is estimated at between €600,000 and €800,000.The three paintings have been designated as "national treasures", a measure intended to give the state 30 months in which to arrange a possible acquisition.

title: A loaf of luxury: Could a $60 Austrian rye bread become a New York status symbol?
description: Give us this day, our daily bread. Or, combine New York's sky-high prices with a touch of Austrian artisan baking, served up in minimalist Soho chic, and you get a rye luxury loaf that sells for $60.
content: If New York is famous for bagels and sky-high prices, Austria, much like Germany, is renowned for its love of bread. Now the two worlds have collided thanks to a family-run bakery from Graz that's baking its rye sourdough loaf in the heart of Soho. Presented in sleek minimalist style, it's priced at $60 a loaf, that's roughly €52.The new bakery "Rye" on Lafayette Street is deliberately focusing on a single product: an organic rye loaf weighing around 1.5 kilogram, made with natural sourdough and no yeast.But if you can't or don't want to have a whole loaf you can order smaller portions or topped slices of bread, for example with chocolate spread, caviar or butter. The bread is baked in a two-tonne oven which, according to the owners, was specially imported from Germany.Behind the concept is the Auer family from Graz, which in Austria runs more than 40 branches of the store.The choice of rye bread as a flagship product is no coincidence: Austria has long been regarded as a rye nation; nowhere else in Europe does this grain make up such a large share of bread production.Founder Martin Auer explained his motivation in a dpa dispatch: they "can 'hardly wait'" to share their enthusiasm for natural sourdough bread with New Yorkers. The advantages of the loaf, he says, are its intense flavour, how long it stays fresh and how easy it is to digest.Bread is in any case regarded by the German Nutrition Society and the World Health Organization as an important part of a balanced diet, chiefly because of its high fibre content, which has been shown to reduce the risk of heart attack and bowel cancer.According to the company, the recipe goes back decades: Auer senior is said to have learnt the method from a farmer on an alpine pasture and later brought it back to Graz.For a few dollars more: Should a loaf of bread cost that much?The long tradition comes at a price. Martin Auer himself appears unfazed by the criticism but says he can understand it. His argument: New York is one of the most expensive cities in the world.He told the Deutsche Presse-Agentur: "This is one of the most expensive cities in the entire world, and one of the most expensive streets in this most expensive of cities. People should take a look at what a flat costs here." On top of that, all the ingredients for the bread have to be imported.The production process itself also drives up the price: natural sourdough, unlike fast-rising yeast bread, sometimes needs several days to mature, during which microorganisms slowly acidify and aerate the dough. That ties up staff, time and space in the bakery and makes sourdough bread inherently more expensive than industrially manufactured goods.Even so, "Rye" is an outlier by New York standards as well: a standard loaf of bread in the city usually costs only a few dollars, and traditionally baked sourdough bread is available in many places for between $10 and $20.What the bread costs per kiloIf you work out the loaf price per kilogram, the "Rye" bread comes in at about $40, or around €34 euros per kilogram. For comparison: in Germany, customers pay on average just over €5 per kilogram of bread at the bakery, and just over €3 in the supermarket.Even Berlin's organic bakery chain "Zeit für Brot", known for its stylish shop design and loyal fan base, prices its best-selling house loaf at around €9-10 per kilogram. That is clearly above the national average, but still only a quarter of what is being charged in Soho.Mixed reactionsThe price of the bread has become a talking point online. Critics see a staple food that is being turned into a luxury item for the well-off. One baker wrote in a comment that the price was "completely detached from reality", especially at a time when there is so much debate about the sustainability and accessibility of food. Other users have called the amount outrageous, even by New York standards.But there is also support. Some commentators are simply pleased to see a loaf without a long list of ingredients and made with unbleached flour, and point out that good artisanal baked goods in New York often cost €20-30 anyway. Others refer to the location in Soho, an area largely inhabited by wealthy residents, and consider the price understandable in that context.Between outrage and enthusiasm, at least one thing is certain: the loaf from Graz hardly leaves anyone indifferent.

title: Fishing waste from as far away as US and Canada washes up on Portuguese beaches
description: Lobster-fishing plastics have drifted across the Atlantic and washed up on Faial and Pico islands, over 3,000 km away. The oldest item dates back to 1983.
content: Since 2010, researchers at the University of the Azores have been monitoring waste brought in from the sea, until they began noticing the same objects appearing again and again."We started to realise that these items, which at first we did not know where they came from, had certain numbers on them. And when we started to find quite a lot, we began trying to look up what they actually meant," explains Christopher Pham, researcher and head of the marine litter research group at the University of the Azores.It turned out that the objects were coming from the lobster fishery, a sector with significant economic weight along the North American Atlantic coast. They also realised that the numbers printed on some of these plastics were mandatory tags that make it possible to identify their origin and date.That is how a study involving scientists and volunteers began."We asked local people and colleagues that if they went to the beach and managed to find these items, they should bring them back," says Christopher Pham. "We had at least ten people who were very interested and kept sending us material every month."Between 2017 and 2025, they found more than 1,500 items on the beaches of Faial and Pico.These two islands are part of the Portuguese archipelago of the Azores, located in the middle of the Atlantic Ocean, about 1,600 km from mainland Europe.Waste travels more than 3,000 kmThese items are objects or fragments of objects that are placed in the sea to catch lobster, such as corners and clips from the pots (cage-like traps), funnels or tags.The tags with legible inscriptions had their origin in the United States (63%) and Canada (37%). Within the United States, the tags referred mainly to the state of Maine (80%) and Massachusetts (11%). The tags from Canada refer to the province of Newfoundland and Labrador.The study, published this summer, says it is an example 'of how an isolated oceanic archipelago is directly exposed to plastic waste from a coastal fishery that operates more than 3,000 km away'.For waste to make the journey across the ocean from the North American coast to these Atlantic islands is not exactly a surprise to the researchers; it is more a confirmation. This movement of debris had already been suggested by models showing the behaviour of currents, winds and waves."We know there is that direct link and it was to be expected that we would receive particles from this part of the Atlantic, because the currents really circulate clockwise, from west to east," says Christopher Pham, explaining that this study validates those models.And although this study is limited to the islands of Pico and Faial, this waste can travel much further, even all the way to mainland Europe."These lobster-fishing items are also quite frequent along the Portuguese coast and even in England and Ireland," adds the researcher.More than 40 years in natureThe researchers were also able to determine the age of part of this waste because among it there are tags stamped with the year of registration.Most of the tags are between 7 and 13 years old. The most recent dates from 2023 and the oldest from 1983, meaning it was put into the sea more than 40 years ago. This shows that these plastics can reach the Azores in just two years and then remain in the environment for many decades without breaking up."Most of the items entered the sea many years ago. That is also significant because it shows that plastic has enormous persistence in the environment", says Pham."It is very likely that, if we keep looking, we will find things that are perhaps even older. Because these tags are made from very high-quality plastic."Access to this information was possible because this industry in North America requires this material to be tagged, even though the rules differ between the United States and Canada, for example in terms of the information provided and how long the tags remain valid.More waste on Azores beachesLobster fishing is the most economically important fishing activity in the United States and Canada. In 2020, lobster exports from the two countries were worth around 1.74 billion euros.Estimates suggest that every year three million pots (traps) are deployed off the coast of the United States and two million off Canada to catch these crustaceans.But lobster fishing is not the only source of pollution on Azores beaches. There is other fishing-related waste on these beaches in the middle of the Atlantic, but it is less common and cannot be traced back to its source."We found trawl nets, but a trawl net can be used in Greenland or in Brazil. In those cases we no longer know where it comes from," explains Cristopher Pham."Sometimes we manage to find some pots that are typical of octopus fishing, but these traps are used from Spain all the way to Morocco; they are not as specific as in the case of lobster."Other types of waste also wash up on these beaches, and they can come from anywhere."We almost never know the precise geographic location. Sometimes we have Chinese bottles, but we do not know if they come from China. They probably come from a Chinese ship that was offshore and threw the bottle into the sea," says Christopher.Besides bottles, there are also cigarette butts, shoe soles and lighters. But the most common waste consists of small pieces of plastic, "a 2-centimetre white piece of plastic", fragments of an unrecognisable object."All these towns that are dumping huge amounts of plastic into streams," says Christopher Pham. "With sunlight and the action of the sea, it starts to fragment and then you get that soup of fragments that entered the sea many years ago but are no longer recognisable in their original form."Tackling the problem at sourceOnly by knowing where these objects come from can we take measures at the source to solve the problem. That is why labelling fishing gear, as happens in the lobster industry, is so important.The Food and Agriculture Organisation of the United Nations (FAO) has issued recommendations that gear used in fishing should be identifiable. The scientists at the University of the Azores stress how important it is to adopt this practice.The team behind this study also has specific recommendations for the fishing industry in North America. These include better management of gear, incentives to hand in old material and the creation of collection points.For these researchers, the next step is to carry out a more systematic analysis, in terms of the density and volume of waste from lobster fishing."To try to understand whether this is increasing or decreasing and what proportion it represents in the overall picture of plastic pollution – what contribution these items make," explains Christopher Pham.But they believe the most important work has already been done: alerting the authorities in the United States and Canada, so that they act."It is important that you take action to reduce this flow of plastic into the sea, because people who have nothing to do with the pollution are becoming victims," Christopher Pham concludes.

title: Catherine Ringer, iconic singer of French rockers Les Rita Mitsouko, dies aged 68
description: The iconic singer of the French duo Les Rita Mitsouko has died from a sudden, aggressive form of cancer.
content: A voice, a style, an energy and a freedom that left their mark on several generations. Catherine Ringer, singer and co-founder of French pop rock group Les Rita Mitsouko, has died at the age of 68.Her children announced her death to AFP, saying she had been taken by "a fast-acting cancer" on 14 September 2026.Ringer was born in Suresnes in 1957. Her father, Sam Ringer, an Ashkenazi Jew born in Poland, had been deported to several concentration camps. Catherine Ringer recounted his story in the song 'C'était un homme', on the album 'Cool Frénésie'.In 1979, she met Fred Chichin, and from their artistic and personal encounter came one of the most original duos in French music. Les Rita Mitsouko would quickly create a world apart, blending rock, pop, funk, electro and chanson.Critical and commercial success arrived in the mid-1980s with the song 'Marcia Baïla', which became emblematic of the French scene. The band then reeled off a string of hits, including 'Andy', 'C'est comme ça' and 'Les Histoires d'A'.Their music, their videos and their offbeat aesthetic turned Les Rita Mitsouko into a phenomenon that far exceeded the usual boundaries of rock.In November 2007, the death of Fred Chichin, also taken by cancer at just 53, could have brought the adventure to an end. Instead, Catherine Ringer chose to keep their repertoire alive. She pursued a solo career and regularly returned to the stage with the songs of Les Rita Mitsouko.Still active in 2026, she had notably performed in Paris last February. She was due to continue championing on stage the body of work born from her collaboration with Fred Chichin.With her death, French music loses a unique figure. Catherine Ringer remains inseparable from Les Rita Mitsouko, but also from her very own way of taking to the stage: free, provocative, original and widely loved by audiences.

title: Will Seat disappear? Government confident as Volkswagen weighs brand's future
description: The government says it is confident Seat will continue after Volkswagen kept several options open for the brand beyond 2030, adding no decision has yet been made on its future.
content: Seat's future is once again at the heart of the debate over the transformation of Spain's automotive industry. The government has closed ranks in defence of the historic brand after the Volkswagen group acknowledged that its continued existence beyond 2030 is under review.First Vice-President and Economy Minister Carlos Cuerpo said this week that the government will make "every effort necessary" to keep Seat, a brand he described as "traditionally Spanish".The government's stance comes after SEAT S.A. clarified its future plans in response to reports of a possible disappearance of the brand. The company has confirmed it will press ahead with the launches and updates already scheduled, including mild-hybrid versions of the Ibiza and Arona planned for 2027.However, the brand's future after the current product cycle remains undecided. The company acknowledges that regulation, the cost of electrification and the investment needed to develop a new generation of electric vehicles are making it "increasingly complex" to continue investing in the brand."Several scenarios remain possible beyond 2030," the company says (source in Spanish), which stresses that "no decision has yet been taken". The brand's continuation will depend, among other factors, on how regulation evolves, consumer demand and market conditions."A solid future" for SEAT S.A.The company is also keen to distinguish between the future of the Seat brand and that of SEAT S.A., the company that encompasses Seat and Cupra and whose main industrial site is in Martorell, near Barcelona.Volkswagen maintains that SEAT S.A. has a "solid future" within the group and plans to strengthen its industrial role, while Cupra will remain the company's main driver of growth and profitability.The group is also sticking to its commitment to electrification in Spain. Volkswagen and SEAT S.A., together with the partners in the Future: Fast Forward project, announced in 2022 an investment of 10 billion euros to drive electrification, including the transformation of the Martorell plant to produce urban electric vehicles.Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez described Seat in June as an "iconic brand in Spain" (source in Spanish) and as a "fundamental" element of both the industrial ecosystem and the country's identity during a visit to Martorell.

title: Rubio calls on Cubans seeking change to form 'discrete partnership' with CIA
description: The Trump administration has repeatedly stated that its goal is to bring about a change in Havana's leadership, with President Donald Trump himself having claimed the country is "ready to fall."
content: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has urged Cubans seeking change in the country to form a "discrete partnership" with the CIA, the US' foreign intelligence service.In a post on social media, Rubio said "now is the time" for those looking to "create positive change" in Cuba to act."The disappointment of failed promises, corruption, and the privileged lives of only a few; seize this opportunity to create the change you desire through a discrete partnership with the CIA," he wrote.The Trump administration has repeatedly stated that its goal is to bring about a change in Havana's leadership, with President Donald Trump himself having claimed the country is "ready to fall."In January, Trump ramped up pressure on Cuba after announcing an oil blockade of the island nation following a US military operation to capture former Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro."Cuba lived, for many years, on large amounts of oil and money from Venezuela," Trump wrote in a post on his Truth Social account at the time."There will be no more oil or money going to Cuba - zero!" he continued, adding: "I strongly suggest they make a deal, before it is too late."Speaking to reporters in September, Trump appeared confident that he could come to an arrangement with Cuba."I would say that Cuba and us will make a deal," he said. "I don't think we'll need the military."The CIA has shared tips for Cubans looking to work with the agency, advising people not to not use a device or internet connection linked to their identity or place of work and to "remove all software, apps and programmes from the device you are using to contact us."It asks people wanting to get in touch to share their base location, job title, and "type or level of access you have to information of interest to our organisation."

title: US designates helium as critical material as Europe faces supply squeeze
description: The US has declared helium a critical material as war in the Middle East and export curbs by Russia and China squeeze global supplies of a gas vital to chipmaking, leaving Europe scrambling to secure its share.
content: The United States designated helium as a critical material on Friday, citing its essential role in semiconductor manufacturing and energy production, as well as growing concerns over disruptions to global supplies.The move by the US Department of Energy will make additional federal funding available to helium producers and bring the material under closer government monitoring.Helium is mainly extracted as a byproduct of natural gas processing. The US is the world's largest producer of both natural gas and helium, with Qatar and Russia also among the leading helium producers.Helium exports from Qatar have been severely disrupted by Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz amid its war with Israel and the US. Iranian strikes on Qatari infrastructure have further affected supplies, while Russia introduced temporary export restrictions in April to protect its domestic market.US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said the Trump administration was seeking to reduce dependence on foreign sources of critical materials, boost domestic manufacturing, support American jobs and strengthen economic and national security.“President Trump is bringing back America’s manufacturing industry, and that means making sure we have the materials needed to build things in America again,” Wright said in a statement.Europe faces mounting pressure on helium suppliesWhile the US is seeking to strengthen domestic production, Europe has faced growing difficulties securing helium supplies, compounded by China's decision in July to impose a temporary export ban on the gas.Although China is not a major helium producer, it has served as a transit hub for Russian supplies reaching Europe, according to a July report by the Financial Times.The EU banned direct imports of Russian helium in 2024, but some supplies reportedly continued to reach European markets through China.

title: UN chief race enters decisive phase as new contender arrives
description: UAE’s star diplomat Lana Nusseibeh has entered the race for the UN secretary-general position, challenging front-runner Rebeca Grynspan at a decisive time for the global organisation's future. The UN chief race could now lead to the first ever female secretary-general.
content: As the race to elect the next UN Secretary-General enters its final phase, former Costa Rican Vice President Rebeca Grynspan retains a challenging lead, but a new contender is emerging, as UAE Minister of State Lana Nusseibeh announced her candidacy this week.The growing excitement around the race is also fueled by the prospect of a female UN secretary-general, something that has never happened in the UN's more than 80-year history.As part of a complex election process, an informal straw poll of officials in the deciding United Nations Security Council last week gave Grynspan a narrow lead over her closest competitors: Guyana’s former Foreign Minister Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett and Argentina’s International Atomic Energy Agency Director-General Rafael Grossi.But after receiving two opposing votes the race has been relaunched allowing new candidates to participate.The winner needs at least nine votes from the 15-member UN Security Council without opposition from any of the five permanent members — the US, the UK, France, China and Russia — and they have until the end of December to choose the successor to current UN chief Antonio Gutteres, before the UN General Assembly confirms the appointment.Campaigning alongside Grynspan, Grossi and Rodrigues-Birkett are former Ecuadorian Foreign Minister Maria Fernanda Espinosa, former Senegalese President Macky Sall, former UN Under-Secretary-General Olara Otunnu of Uganda, and Ecuadorian diplomat Ivonne A-Baki.UAE’s Nusseibeh announced as fresh contender Senior UAE diplomat and UAE Minister of State Lana Nusseibeh energised the race when her nomination was announced this week, known for her versatility in “quiet diplomacy” in the campaign for peace and for creating space for wider political settlements. Launching her candidacy, Nusseibeh said, “I have spent much of my professional life working in and around the United Nations, and I have seen first-hand what determined diplomacy can achieve - countries with profound differences finding common ground, and agreement where people said agreement was impossible.”In her vision statement, she puts peace and security at the core while also promising to deliver across the board on development and human rights, as well as reform the organisation around focus and results. "I am standing to be secretary-general because I believe this is a moment to act with greater urgency: to act earlier, bring people together across difference, and drive the work forward until it produces concrete results," she said.“I wish to offer myself to this office as I would serve it: speaking frankly with every government and answering to none.”A highly regarded diplomat who grew up between Abu Dhabi and the UK in a family of well-known political figures, Nusseibeh previously served as the UAE ambassador to the UN and is credited with elevating the UAE's profile during that time.Nusseibeh, 48, who led the UAE’s successful bid for a Security Council seat, said that several countries approached her during the last UN General Assembly and urged her to stand.“It's recognised today that we need someone who offers generational change for the organisation,” she said. During the country’s 2022 to 2023 term, Nusseibeh secured the adoption of Resolution 2720, which opened the way for humanitarian aid deliveries into Gaza. A Hebrew speaker, she said she secured support for the resolution by arranging visits from Council members to the Rafah border crossing. If she succeeds, Nusseibeh would become the first woman to lead the United Nations since its establishment in 1945, the first of Palestinian descent, and the second Secretary-General from the Arabic-speaking world after Egypt's Boutros Boutros-Ghali.“I think ⁠it would be great if the next secretary-general is a woman, but I am not running because I am a woman, I am running because I am stubbornly optimistic about the future of the United Nations and I believe we need someone who is relentless in the pursuit of diplomacy to open doors,” Nusseibeh said on Wednesday.Grynspan holds a challenging leadCosta Rica's former Vice President Rebeca Grynspan, 70, was born to Jewish parents who fled Poland before World War II, and she has built a Jewish family ever since. She lost her grandparents in the Holocaust after they decided to remain in Poland. In a May interview with Euronews, Grynspan said, “I know exactly what wars take away from you and what peace allows you to do.” “I am a generation that have lived in peace. I have never experienced war directly. But millions of people in the world today live in war zones, in conflict. And that is why I am running, because I know the difference, what peace and opportunity can do for you and your family,” she told Euronews.Currently Secretary-General of the UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD), Grynspan said she agreed with US President Donald Trump’s “constructive” criticism that “the UN has great potential, but it's not living up to that potential,” and that a reformed UN can make a difference.Grynspan told Euronews how she believes that in our multipolar world “the choice is if we will have multipolarity with multilateralism that bears the promise of prosperity and cooperation, or if we will have multipolarity without multilateralism that will lead us to fragmentation into a world that will be more unstable, more prone to conflict, and less prosper.” “So we need to create again these spaces. For the convergence of divergent interests,” she added.On the other hand, she also hailed the “amazing things that are happening in the world: you look at technology and you look at the digital world, the artificial intelligence, what is happening in medicine and in science.”“You see those breakthroughs that you can bring to the people on the ground, to the millions of people that have right now no opportunity, that live in poverty, in absolute destitution or in hunger.““And you know that the world is developing really the capacity, the possibility for everybody to have a dignified life. That will depend on us. It will depend on our choices,” Grynspan explained in an interview for Euronews.She said that the UN election race was “not like a business-as-usual type of election.”“Conflicts in the world are going up. Trust between the countries, but also in the multilateral system, is going down. And time is running out," Grynspan told Euronews as she presented the vision of her candidacy to become the new UN secretary-general."So this is a moment in which we have to raise to the challenge to bring cooperation, solidarity, the principles of the UN Charter again into the center of the agenda,” she concluded.

title: Ukraine hits Russian data centres in blow to Moscow's AI capabilities
description: Drones hit three Yandex facilities, a Sber centre and a VKontakte server farm across five Russian regions, causing persistent failures in payments, navigation and cloud services. Experts say restoring the infrastructure could take months or years.
content: Ukrainian drones struck five data centres belonging to Russia's largest technology companies in October, causing widespread failures in cloud services, payment systems and navigation apps nationwide.The Ukrainian armed forces hit three Yandex facilities: in Sasovo in the Ryazan region on 7 October, in Kaluga on 9 October, and in Vladimir on 11 October.On 14 October a Sber data centre in Balakovo in the Saratov region was struck, and on 18 October a VKontakte data centre in the Leningrad region near St Petersburg came under attack.Yandex, Sber and VKontakte together run much of Russia's consumer internet infrastructure, from taxi apps and card payment processing to cloud storage and messaging.None of the companies has disclosed the scale of the damage. Russians have reported persistent difficulties paying for goods, ordering taxis, using navigation services and accessing cloud storage.Experts say restoring the infrastructure could take months or years, and the strikes have set back Russia's artificial intelligence development, Mikhail Klimarev, head of the Internet Protection Society, told AP.Russia continues to target Ukraine's IT sectorThe attacks come as Russia has itself been systematically targeting Ukrainian data centres this autumn.On 19 October a Russian strike completely destroyed one of the largest facilities of the Ukrainian operator Datagroup in Kyiv, which was declared beyond repair.The following day a Russian attack damaged Kyiv's GigaCenter. Russia hit several other Ukrainian data centres in September and October.An earlier Russian strike on a Kyiv data centre in July disrupted internet access, mobile communications and television across the city.Moscow has targeted Ukraine's IT systems since day one of Russia's full-scale invasion: cruise missiles struck a government server facility on 24 February 2022, and a Russian missile hit the National Data Backup Centre in central Kyiv on 1 March.Ukraine has since moved most of its data to servers in European countries, limiting the impact of subsequent attacks.Russian data centres are more vulnerable than Ukrainian ones, analysts say. Under legislation designed to create a so-called "sovereign internet," Russia requires companies to store all data on servers inside the country. That concentration makes the facilities easier to target."Russia's problem is that it has to provide air defence over a vast territory, and it does not have enough resources for that," said Nick Reiners, senior geo-technology analyst at Eurasia Group."Since all the infrastructure and all the data are located inside Russia, it is relatively easier to disable them." Why air defence systems were not protecting Russian data centres, or failed to do so, has not been explained.Sensitive to fireAnalysts describe the facilities as soft targets: vast halls filled with servers, power equipment and cooling systems where even a small explosive charge can cause serious damage.Satellite imagery of the struck Yandex facilities shows fires that may have destroyed microchips and other fragile components."After such a strike it is hard to expect anything to have survived: data-centre equipment is fragile, demanding and expensive. Soot from fires is extremely harmful to electronics," Klimarev told AP.The damage to Yandex is particularly significant for Russia's AI ambitions. The company's three supercomputers, used to develop AI models, rank among the world's top 500. The most powerful, housed in the Sasovo facility, once ranked 19th globally but has since fallen below the top 100."Ukrainian drone strikes will probably delay the development of Russian artificial intelligence even further," Connor Martin of the Council on Foreign Relations said. Before the strikes, Russia was already several years behind the US and China.Restoring the hardware will be complicated by Western sanctions and the global chip shortage. Yandex's supercomputers run on Nvidia A100 processors, which Russia cannot legally import.Klimarev said the strikes may carry an unintended consequence for Russian internet policy."Paradoxically, the attacks on data centres have saved the Russian internet from isolation, because companies will now be forced to move their computing resources, most likely to Europe," he said."It is quite likely that many Russian companies are now studying the European market in search of opportunities to rent computing capacity," Klimarev said. He added that Russian authorities might ease their attempts to tighten internet controls to limit the economic damage.Infrastructure for malign purposesMoscow has for years actively used its IT sector for spying on its users, as well as conduct malign hybrid operations elsewhere.Under Russia’s SORM legislation, all domestic internet companies including Yandex, VKontakte and Sber are legally required to install FSB backdoors giving the security services access to user data and communications.These data centres are integrated into Russia’s surveillance apparatus, not purely commercial infrastructure.VKontakte specifically has been extensively used for state-sponsored propaganda and recruitment. Ukraine banned it in 2017 partly on those grounds.The Kremlin has demonstrably used AI tools in its disinformation operations, such as rewriting real news articles with pro-Kremlin slants and fabricated claims, publishing them across dozens of sites designed to mimic legitimate international outlets, including Euronews.It has also used AI-generated video and audio to fabricate statements attributed to Western officials. AI-cloned voices impersonating European politicians have also circulated, though some were detected before they spread widely.More recently, it has flooded the internet with repetitive pro-Kremlin content to skew what AI chatbots retrieve and eventually how they are trained. NewsGuard stress tests found chatbots repeated false claims in roughly a third of responses when prompted adversarially.Researchers at the Carnegie Endowment have however stated that training-data poisoning is slow, heavily filtered and increasingly countered by behavioural rules built into newer models.EU sanctions prohibit the supply of IT services, software and cloud capacity to Russian companies.Firms seeking to circumvent the restrictions have used intermediaries, anonymous hosting providers or foreign corporate structures. Brussels has been tightening enforcement of those rules.

title: Trapped miner in coal mine in Turkey confirmed dead, bringing death toll to three
description: Three miners were killed and five injured, two of them seriously, in an explosion at a privately owned mine in northern Turkey.
content: The miner who had been trapped following an explosion at a coal mine in northwestern Turkey has also been confirmed dead, local authorities reported, bringing the death toll to three.The explosion at the mine in the town of Gelik was caused by a "firedamp," or flammable gas, local authorities said.Five others were injured, two of whom are in serious condition."Eight people were in the tunnel, seven were rescued. Unfortunately, two of our miners died after being taken to hospital," said Zonguldak governor Osman Hacibektasoglu.A rescue operation had been underway to reach one person trapped in the mine, who has now been confirmed dead.Two of the rescued miners suffered burns and were in serious condition. One of the critically injured miners had been transferred to Ankara and preparations are under way to transfer the second miner."One of the miners is still inside the mine. We have made contact with him and are trying to get him out," the governor added.The blast occurred at around 10 in the morning. After an emergency call, teams from the Disaster and Emergency Management Authority (AFAD), as well as medical and fire crews, were dispatched to the site.According to local newspaper Pusula, the explosion took place at a private mine owned by Demir Madencilik. An investigation has been opened to determine the exact cause of the blast.Mine accidents are not uncommon in Turkey. Earlier this month, five people were killed in a coal mine collapse in Soma, Manisa in western Turkey.The independent monitoring group, Worker Health and Work Safety Assembly, or ISIG, reported that 1,267 miners were killed in workplace accidents between 2013 and 2025, mostly from incidents of cave-ins and suffocation.

title: From education to cancer care: Global summit calls for better support for children
description: Experts interviewed by Euronews explained why improving children's lives requires more than simply expanding access to essential services.
content: With 412 million children living in extreme poverty, a global summit in Uzbekistan has called for greater investment in children's healthcare, education and protection, alongside closer coordination between services that often operate separately.This was at the core of the Samarkand Declaration, adopted on Thursday at the end of a two-day gathering attended by representatives from more than 100 countries.The declaration calls for stronger social protection systems, nationally determined targets and regular reporting on the quality and effectiveness of services for children.According to UNICEF, two-thirds of the child-related UN Sustainable Development Goal indicators it monitors are off track, raising concerns about progress towards the 2030 targets.Why access to services is not enoughProviding access to essential services does not necessarily guarantee children receive the care and support they need, summit participants said."We should invest not sector by sector, but we should complement each other and this will give a better result for the children," UNICEF Regional Director Édouard Beigbeder told Euronews.Beigbeder also highlighted the importance of
