investing in social workers and healthcare professionals, rather than focusing exclusively on infrastructure.Uzbekistan's First Lady Ziroat Mirziyoyeva, who received the WHO Director-General's Award 2026 for her contribution to childhood cancer care, also called for closer cooperation between services."Let us integrate medical, social and psychological support so that parents do not have to go from one institution to another in search of assistance," she told the summit.Turkey's First Lady Emine Erdoğan questioned whether conventional indicators adequately reflect children's experiences."However, going to school does not always mean receiving a quality education, not being hungry does not mean being properly nourished, and not being subjected to violence does not mean being loved and valued," she said.Protecting children from violence means services need to work together, particularly when victims require medical treatment, psychological support, social assistance and legal protection.Global Head of Child Protection at Save the Children International Rebecca Smith told Euronews that children face violence at home, in conflict zones and increasingly online.She stressed the importance of ensuring that survivors can seek support without facing stigma.Uzbekistan presents its approach to integrated careUzbekistan used the summit to show how different services can be brought together to support children and families.“Because for a parent, a child is not the future. A child is the present,” Shahnoza Mirziyoyeva, First Deputy Director of Uzbekistan's Social Protection Agency, told the summit.In an address to participants, President Shavkat Mirziyoyev emphasised that children's wellbeing should be measured by their quality of life today, not their future economic contribution.According to figures presented by Mirziyoyev, preschool enrolment has increased from 27.7% to 78%, while the number of inclusive schools has risen fivefold over the past two years.Visiting First Ladies also attended the opening of the new Imkon rehabilitation centre in Samarkand, which combines preschool education with medical, psychological and educational support for children with disabilities.The facility can accommodate 150 children and provide outpatient rehabilitation services to up to 100 children aged three to 18 each month.Lebanon's First Lady Nehmat Aoun, who visited the centre, told Euronews that countries should learn from one another's experiences to improve children's education, care and protection.Childhood cancer exposes global inequalitiesThe importance of coordinated healthcare becomes particularly evident in childhood cancer, where a child's chances of survival differ dramatically depending on where they live.A parallel international congress in Samarkand examined inequalities in early diagnosis, specialist treatment and access to essential medicines.According to the World Health Organization, around 400,000 children and adolescents develop cancer worldwide each year. High-income countries cure more than 80%, compared with fewer than 30% in many low- and middle-income countries.Carlos Rodriguez-Galindo, Executive Vice President of St. Jude Children's Research Hospital, told Euronews that delayed or missed diagnoses are among the main obstacles."The only way to address childhood cancer is by a comprehensive package," he said.Such an approach requires earlier diagnosis, specialist care, reliable access to medicines and continued support for children and families.The WHO has set a global target of at least 60% survival for children with cancer by 2030.The congress also announced the creation of a Global Network to support children with serious and life-threatening illnesses, including cancer.Bringing together first ladies and spouses of heads of state, the initiative aims to strengthen international partnerships and improve access to care.Uzbekistan's first lady will chair the network for two years. Mirziyoyeva also proposed an international mechanism to improve children's access to essential medicines.An exhibition titled "The World Through a Child's Eyes" presented initiatives connecting healthcare, education, social protection and family support.

title: Oil spill hits UAE beaches as tanker attacks multiply near Hormuz
description: The UAE’s Ministry of Climate Change said teams were deployed to contain a spill affecting Umm Al Quwain’s beaches, days after a tanker was struck by a projectile off the UAE coast, causing a fire.
content: The United Arab Emirates reported an oil spill from a tanker off its coast on Friday, as numerous vessels in Gulf waters came under attack in the ongoing Iran war.The authorities "detected a tanker oil spill affecting Umm Al Quwain's beaches," the Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said in a statement, referring to an emirate north of Dubai.It said "teams immediately began containment, cordoning, clean-up and remediation... to limit environmental impacts", adding that the emirate's beaches had been closed.Many residents in the country's north have reported unusual oil-like smells on social media in recent days, including in northern districts of Dubai.Frequent attacks on ships have been reported in recent weeks near the Strait of Hormuz, control of which remains at the heart of the war between Iran and the US.The maritime security agency UKMTO reported on 9 October that a vessel had been hit by a projectile off the UAE coast, causing a fire that was later brought under control.According to maritime security company Vanguard, the vessel was the oil tanker GEM NO.2, sailing under the Panamanian flag.Roughly one-fifth of the world's oil passed through the Strait of Hormuz before the war that began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February. Both Tehran and Washington have implemented blockades in the strait, while Iran has repeatedly targeted cargo vessels using the southern section of the waterway.Earlier this week, Iran's IRGC said in a statement that it targets tankers trying to use what Tehran unilaterally designates as an unauthorised route through the strait's southern section, near the Omani coast.Tehran has no recognised authority under international maritime law to restrict or authorise passage through Hormuz, which is subject to the right of transit passage under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea.The UAE lies close to the Strait of Hormuz, just 40-50 nautical miles from the waterway's narrowest point.

title: Flash floods swamp southeast Australia as record October rainfall forces school closures
description: A television reporter abandoned his shoes and glasses and dived into rising floodwaters to save a driver whose car was sinking fast in Morayfield, Queensland.
content: Torrential rain has triggered flash flooding across southeast Queensland, Australia, breaking multiple October rainfall records, stranding drivers, forcing school closures and prompting hundreds of emergency calls over two days.The deluge began on Thursday with a water treatment plant near Moreton Bay, north of Brisbane, recording more than 250 millimetres of rain in 24 hours.Some locations received nearly 180 millimetres in just three hours. Beerburrum recorded its wettest October day on record, while Toowoomba experienced its heaviest October rainfall in 29 years.Flooded roads damaged infrastructure, disrupted electricity supplies and forced 14 schools to close.Authorities urged residents in parts of Caboolture and Burpengary to prepare to evacuate as a fresh wave of rain struck southeast Queensland on Friday, compounding the damage.Reporter jumps into floodwater to rescue trapped driverOne of the most dramatic moments of the crisis unfolded in Morayfield on Thursday, when Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC) reporter Will Murray and a bystander jumped into floodwaters to rescue a driver trapped in a rapidly sinking car.Murray told the ABC that the vehicle began to float and sink within seconds of driving into the flooded road, leaving no time to wait for emergency services.“My colleague and I sort of started to watch him sink further into the water and thought, ‘well, we don’t have time to wait,’” Murray said.“So I threw off my shoes, gave my glasses to my colleague and jumped in and started swimming. And thankfully somebody nearby jumped in with me to give me a hand.”The pair initially tried to break the car’s rear windscreen but were forced to move to the side of the vehicle. What Murray saw through the back window made the urgency clear.“Couldn’t get that door open. Got up onto the ute tray, looked through the back window and you could see that the water was up sort of shoulder level, sort of towards chin level, just terrifying and angling down,” he said.They eventually managed to open a door and pull the driver to safety. No injuries were reported.Authorities had already issued flood warnings across the area.At least eight weather stations recorded more than 300 millimetres of rainfall between Wednesday and Friday morning, more than three times the volume originally forecast by the Bureau of Meteorology.Wet conditions are expected to persist into the weekend, with forecasters warning of another peak on Monday and a cold front potentially shifting the weather pattern later in the week.Parts of New South Wales are now also in the path of the storm system.

title: France bolsters security as businesses fear renewed unrest during Saturday protests
description: A massive security operation has been deployed across France for major protests on Saturday. Businesses across the country remain tense following violence which overshadowed peaceful demonstrations last weekend.
content: Some 70,000 law enforcement officers are set be deployed across France on Saturday, while the Louvre and several other major Paris museums will be closed as authorities seek to prevent renewed violence during protests.Last weekend, peaceful demonstrations were overshadowed by violence and unrest. Masked individuals looted shops and intimidated business owners, stormed public buildings, smashed store windows, and clashed with police forces.Demonstrators plan to take to the streets once again on Saturday to denounce the cost-of-living crisis, while students are still protesting against what they view as inadequate conditions in schools. Students, members of the CGT labour union and activists from the “yellow vest” movement are set to join.French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said some 70,000 police officers and gendarmes would be deployed, along with helicopters, armoured vehicles and water cannons. In addition, elite police units will help secure public buildings like city halls in a “highly mobile” security operation, he said.“There have been numerous calls from radical far-left groups on social media to commit acts of violence and vandalism. There have also been renewed calls for looting, with those messages clearly being spread by rioters," Nuñez said at a news conference.“We will be absolutely uncompromising" with those involved in violence, he added, warning that police will have a “very firm approach to making arrests, and there will be legal consequences.”Anger after authorities change approved Paris protest routeWhile some protests have been banned for security reasons in several cities, including Lyon, Nice and Montpellier, marches are expected in many other places including in Paris and Marseille. Authorities have also diverted some protest routes away from shopping streets and public buildings to limit damage.Police in Paris had initially approved a protest march between Bastille and Nation squares in the east of the capital but overturned the decision on Friday, instead proposing a route between Porte d’Italie and Porte de Vincennes along the city's southeastern edge.Local businesses near the newly approved protest route have expressed concerns that they were caught off guard and implement the necessary precautionary measures.The move has also prompted pushback from unions who contested the decision and vowed to march anyway in a joint press release shared on Friday."Once again, the authorities are seeking to disrupt the marches and impose unrealistic deadlines on the organisations for reorganising. Such tactics are becoming increasingly common throughout the country," Jean-Luc Mélenchon, leader of the hard-left France Unbowed party wrote in a post on X, while also calling for people to follow unions' instructions.Marine Tondelier, the head of the Green party, added: "These last-minute route changes will scatter the demonstrators. This is highly problematic and dangerous, given the lessons of last weekend."Landmark Paris sites including the Louvre, the Musée d'Orsay, the Picasso museum, along with the Grand Palais will close their doors on Saturday.Art Basel, one of the world's most prestigious contemporary art fairs, opened to the public Friday — but only for the day, with the threat of unrest prompting organisers to cancel the weekend program."This decision has not been taken lightly, and the safety of everyone involved in the fair remains our utmost priority," organisers said in a statement Thursday.Businesses on edge ahead of protestsThe manager of a supermarket in central Paris, which was looted last weekend told Euronews on condition of anonymity that his entire team remained on edge ahead of Saturday's protests, despite bolstered security measures.He said that his shop would remain open during the morning and that he would "assess the situation" later in the day."We have a metal shutter and we've added some plywood, but we know that these metal shutters took about a minute and a half for protestors to break through. The same goes for our electronic door. So, unless we implement security like banks have, there's really no way to stop them. Last weekend they arrived in huge groups, used bricks, it was incredibly violent."When teenagers ransacked his supermarket last Saturday, overwhelmed police forces were unable to intervene. The next day, when the looting resumed, law enforcement made it to the scene, pushing back gangs of violent teenagers.Many of the staff remain traumatised, "we've worked so hard to ensure we managed to clean and restock. But, frankly, I haven't had a proper rest in about 13 days. Everyone on our team"Frankly, I haven't had a proper rest in about 13 days. We're all under a lot of pressure. Everyone on our team is feeling it. There's a palpable tension, and we're trying to manage it, but to keep everyone calm and prevent any major incidents from occurring. Unfortunately, there's a risk that something bad will happen, and we need to prevent that from happening."Anti far-right protest plannedA demonstration in the city of Orléans, located south of Paris, will also take place on Saturday.About 50 organisations have called for a protest against the far right on the sidelines of the two-day congress of Marine Le Pen’s nationalist, anti-immigration party ahead of next spring’s presidential election. Organisers include labor unions, left-wing political parties, student organisations and anti-racism groups.Hugues Moutouh, the prefect of the Loiret region, said that 20,000 to 30,000 demonstrators from across the country were expected.Le Pen, whom opinion polls place as the front-runner in next year’s election, accused left-wing organisations and political parties of trying to “disrupt a political party’s democratic congress,” on public news broadcaster FranceInfo.Still, she said she had “no concerns” about security because the government had “recognised the need for measures allowing the congress to proceed safely.”

title: Winter time or summer time? What the science says about the best option for health
description: Permanent standard time would be better for health, experts say, while once again we are to change our clocks over the weekend.
content: This weekend, many countries will move their clocks one hour back to return to winter, or “standard,” time — the one more closely aligned with the sun — after months of the summer schedule. Clock changes happen twice a year and although there have been multiple attempts to end them, every spring and autumn the clocks still shift by an hour.The seasonal time change was brought in to save energy during the First World War and was revived in many countries in the 1970s.Researchers now warn, however, about the health impacts, especially of the spring change.Yet deciding whether to keep the practice is only the first step.“Ending the clock change solves one problem, but it creates another decision: which time should we live on year-round?” said Raymond Lam, professor of psychiatry at the University of British Columbia and lead author of a recently published analysis on the health effects of daylight saving time. While eliminating clock changes resolves short-term disruption, the permanent system chosen determines chronic, long-term public health outcomes, the authors wrote. “The health evidence points to standard time, largely because morning light matters for our body clocks, sleep, and mood.” Both choices have pros and cons: permanent daylight saving time keeps evenings lighter, which may support recreation, social activity, commuting and some economic activity. However, it also pushes sunrise an hour later, leaving more people waking, travelling to school and commuting to work in darkness during the winter. “Our biological clocks need morning light to stay synchronized with the 24-hour day,” said Ralph Mistlberger, professor of psychology at Simon Fraser University in Canada. “Permanent daylight saving time moves that light an hour later just when winter mornings are already darkest.” Permanent standard time preserves earlier winter dawns, which naturally align with human circadian rhythms by providing essential morning light to synchronise the biological clock.Morning exposure to light helps compensate for the biological clock's natural tendency to lag, reducing sleepiness and supporting alertness, sleep quality and mood, the analysis noted.The analysis identifies standard time or winter time as the best option for health. “Time policy is a public health policy,” said Alexandra Choi, medical health officer with Vancouver Coastal Health. “If governments choose permanent daylight saving time, they should plan for the consequences before the first winter — from safer morning travel and flexible start times to monitoring sleep, mental health, and injuries.”

title: Debt: Moody's spares France, "a brief respite", not a "vote of confidence"
description: Despite downgrade consensus, the agency kept France's sovereign rating unchanged, a short-lived relief, say economists, warning of a debt time bomb and worsening political and social tensions.
content: An unexpected piece of good news: Moody's has left France's sovereign debt rating untouched. Although markets had widely expected a downgrade, the New York-based agency on Friday evening maintained its assessment at Aa3 with a negative outlook.France's ten-year borrowing rate (OAT) has soared this week, while the country is under strain after the riots of 17 October, which have added to investor unease. Moody's nevertheless justified its stance in a statement, explaining that "the Aa3 rating is based on the assumption that a 2027 budget reducing the deficit will be adopted, while funding costs and social tensions will moderate somewhat over the coming months".As soon as the announcement was made, the government rushed to hail the decision. Economy Minister Roland Lescure was the first to react. He sees in it "recognition of the strength of our economy and the credibility of the budget" presented by the government. In his view, the goal of adopting by the end of the year a "responsible" budget that brings the deficit down to 5% is "non-negotiable".In a more defensive tone, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu welcomed on X the fact that Moody's decision "confounds the doom-laden forecasts of many 'experts'" (his quotation marks) "and of those who speculate on French debt".According to the head of government, the ongoing budget debate in the National Assembly "shows our creditors that there is a way forward".He also highlighted a measure which, in his view, reflects the seriousness of current economic policy: "With the release of 10 million barrels of diesel we will have an impact on pump prices from 1 November, without playing fast and loose with the public finances"."A welcome surprise"A tougher stance from Moody's had nonetheless appeared inevitable. Speaking to Euronews a few hours before the verdict, Théophile Legrand, rates strategist at Natixis, even saw it as the "central" scenario. He stressed, however, that a downgrade would have been "largely" anticipated by the markets and that its announcement might therefore "not on its own trigger a pronounced reaction".The decision ultimately taken is "a welcome short-term surprise for the government and the markets", notes the Natixis expert, following the announcement, from the corporate and investment banking arm of the BPCE group.This relative leniency should not, however, be interpreted as a vote of confidence in the trajectory of the public finances, he warns. Moody's "indeed maintains a negative outlook, which means that the risk of a downgrade remains fully present".The 24 October protests, "a test for the government"The second act of the protests, scheduled for this Saturday, will be closely watched by investors. "The mobilisation expected this weekend will be a test for the government, particularly its ability to manage the situation" after the unrest on 17 October, says Théophile Legrand.And even if the chaos seen last week is avoided, it would be more of a respite than a real relief. "The most worrying signal is the persistence of a climate of political uncertainty, likely to maintain pressure on French bonds", the economist points out."The excesses observed during the protests have certainly poured fuel on the fire", agrees Jérémie Peloso, chief Europe strategist at BCA Research. "However, it is above all the political deadlock, the glaring lack of budgetary ambition, both from the current government and from the various presidential candidates, and the deterioration of the public finances that are igniting the bond market," he laments in a comment to Euronews."French government debt has become a real pariah"It had not happened since 2002. This Wednesday, France's 10-year borrowing rate broke through the 5.1% mark, compared with 3.2% before the start of the war between the United States and Iran, a level that was already regarded as high."This bond rout is obviously having negative consequences for the French economy", recalls Jérémie Peloso, who speaks of repercussions "particularly painful" for property, as access to credit is becoming ever more difficult."The market for French government debt has become a genuine pariah", argues the economist. "The reason is simple and has been known to all for years: French public finances are on an unsustainable path." Added to this, he continues, are the return of inflation against the backdrop of war in the Middle East, "anaemic" French growth and expectations of increases in the ECB's key interest rates.Jérémie Peloso does not rule out that, in the short term and given the scale of the rise in yields in recent days, there could be "an opportunistic return of buyers to OATs, in a 'buy the dip' logic." In his view, this movement could be supported by the losses recorded on equity markets, "likely to trigger switches into bonds, traditionally seen as safe-haven assets".This week, several French shares stumbled on the stock market. Carrefour's share price fell by more than 13%, after the group put the cost of the 17 October looting at between 80 and 200 million euros. In the luxury sector, Kering plunged 16% and Hermès 7%, against a backdrop of weaker quarterly results and shops trashed on the fringes of the protests, an additional vulnerability that is worrying investors.Even so, investors turning to bonds "must not lose sight of the fact that French debt remains a genuine time bomb", insists Jérémie Peloso. "All the more so as an explosive presidential election is looming in less than six months," he adds."Ultimately, the most worrying issue remains the glaring lack of political will to tackle budgetary imbalances seriously", the expert says, stressing that "none of the major parties" seems ready to accept the political cost of drastic savings."As long as this reality does not change, investors will find it very hard to regain confidence in French debt.""A crisis of confidence specific to France"For Jérôme Mathis, economics professor at Paris-Dauphine University and author of the blog "Finance at the heart of our lives" (source in French), the most worrying signal is not the absolute level of interest rates but the growing spread with Germany."The recent underperformance of French bonds compared with German Bunds primarily reflects a crisis of confidence specific to France", he believes."The United States is also borrowing at rates close to 5%, which shows that high rates are not in themselves an anomaly. By contrast, when Germany remains close to 3.4% while France exceeds 5.1%, it means investors are demanding a risk premium that is specifically French."According to the expert, for a long time French OATs were seen as almost equivalent to German Bunds. "That assumption no longer holds today. It is the clearest sign of a loss of budgetary and political credibility, and probably the most serious warning sent to France since the European sovereign debt crisis," he says.With secondary school pupils and yellow vest protesters mobilising, investors now fear that "any serious attempt to restore the public finances will run into strong social and political opposition," Jérôme Mathis notes.The budget battle in Parliament is growing fiercer by the day. On Friday, Public Accounts and Civil Service Minister David Amiel railed against what he called the "fourth dimension" in the National Assembly."Billions are raining down and savings are mechanically wiped out to applause", he complained, "even as interest rates soar."The minister particularly deplored the fact that the social security deficit has "worsened by more than 5 billion" since the start of the examination of the bill, singling out in particular the National Rally.Jérôme Mathis recalls that markets have already shown their sensitivity to "political scenarios liable to call into question the state's financial commitments."During the 2022 presidential campaign, Jean-Luc Mélenchon's rise in the polls coincided, he says, with "a surge in questions about the future of French debt", linked to his plan to cancel part of it."And we now find the same combination": the prospect of a second round pitting Marine Le Pen against Jean-Luc Mélenchon and the continued presence of the LFI candidate's proposal to cancel the share of public debt held by the European Central Bank, or to turn it into perpetual, zero-interest debt.

title: Arrest made after major fire breaks out at Hitler's 'Eagle's Nest' mountain retreat in Bavaria
description: The building, completed in 1938, was designed to be used as a retreat for Nazi officials, although it was rarely used by Hitler himself.
content: One person has been arrested after a major fire broke out at Adolf Hitler's mountain retreat in the German state of Bavaria.According to Bavarian police, the blaze at the alpine resort - known as the "Eagle's Nest" in English or "Kehlsteinhaus" in German - began on Friday evening.A fire alarm was raised at around 9:15 pm, with firefighters able to see flames "clearly visible" as they approached the site, finding it "fully ablaze" on arrival, police said."The fire service’s extensive fire-fighting operations are still ongoing. So far, no people have been found inside the Kehlsteinhaus – at this stage, no one has been injured as a result of the fire," a statement from the force read."Shortly after the fire broke out, a suspect came to the attention of the investigators. This person has been taken into custody. Whether the individual is connected to the fire is currently the subject of the criminal investigation," it added.The building, completed in 1938, was designed to be used as a retreat for Nazi officials, although it was rarely used by Hitler himself.This is a developing story. Please check back here for details.

title: YouTube, AI and neurodivergent representation: How Gen Z and Gen Alpha are redefining modern storytelling
description: Gen Z and Gen Alpha still want better on-screen representation — but also aren't as against AI storytelling as you might expect, according to the 2026 Teens and Screens report.
content: In an era of entertainment that's dominated by nostalgia, younger generations are redefining storytelling through YouTube, TikTok, and even artificial intelligence (AI), according to the 2026 Teens and Screens report.Conducted by the Center for Scholars & Storytellers (CSS) at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), the report began five years ago as a way to analyse the media habits of more than 1,500 Americans aged 10-24.Its latest findings highlight how much contemporary storytelling has diversified, with Gen Alpha and Gen Z finding just as much value in unconventional media formats like 30-second videos to feature-length films.The majority of the survey's respondents (72.9%) chose YouTube as their favourite medium for storytelling, while nearly 4 in 5 said that short-form videos can tell a story too, with TikTok (64.2%) scoring highest among social media platforms.TV shows (70.3%), movies (70.2%) and video games (68.5%) all followed closely behind, with respondents choosing the cinema as their favourite weekend activity for the third year in a row.This mirrors recent findings across Europe, with 50% of cinemagoers in the UK under 35-years-old according to the Cinema Advertising Association. Meanwhile, CineEurope reports that 47% of young people now discover films through TikTok.More 'relatable' charactersDespite younger audiences being a major target demographic for the entertainment industry, their actual experiences and desires are still frequently unheard or misunderstood.A recurring theme is their desire to see more relatable stories, with 55% of those surveyed wanting to see more neurodivergent characters on screen — a number that increased among LGBTQIA+ youth.Only 22.7% of respondents felt that current media portrayals of neurodivergence “ring true to real life” most of the time. One such portrayal that received huge backlash in 2021 was Sia's directorial debut Music, in which Maddie Ziegler, a neurotypical actress, played a nonverbal autistic woman.The adolescents and young adults also said they wanted to see more “hopeful, uplifting stories with people beating the odds,” “friendships and social groups,” and “people with lives like mine.”This continues the findings of previous reports that young people want less sex on screen and more platonic relationships, with 52% saying they believe that romantic relationships in media are more central to the lives of fictional characters than they are in real life.“The call for greater neurodivergent and friendship representation is just some examples we found of the broader demand for more diverse and authentic portrayals,” said study co-author Stephanie Rivas-Lara.Opinions on AIFrom fake actors to social media slop, AI has rapidly taken over the media landscape and become a major source of contention among younger viewers.Despite this, the survey's respondents seem more curious than worried about the technology, with 28.2% saying they were “fascinated" and 25.6% “excited". On the other hand, 22% said they felt "doomed" and 10.1% were "scared".Opinions on AI were most positive among the youngest respondents, aged 10-13, with 44.2% describing programmes about AI as "fascinating".The future of entertainmentWhile cinema attendance massively declined during the pandemic, there's been a steady increase in the years since as young people strive to escape their phone screens, find communities, and reconnect with the outside world.Recent blockbuster hits like Backrooms and Obsession, which were directed by YouTube creators, also prove that younger audiences are craving more original stories that utilise internet formats and lore; reflecting the digital worlds they have grown up in.“The gatekeepers have changed, and young people themselves are deciding what they want to watch and what they want to see more of in the content they choose,” said Yalda T. Uhls, founder and CEO of CSS and adjunct professor in UCLA’s psychology department.“Industry leaders should ‘tune in’ to young people as well as the experts who have positive youth development and their well-being in mind,” Uhls added.“This year’s report clearly illustrates that this is the key to creating quality content that wins over today’s youth.”

title: Booking an electric flight in Europe is only 10 years away, says influential Dutch researcher
description: Aeroplane manufacturers should be forced to pivot to electric as car companies have, says influential Dutch researcher Maarten Steinbuch.
author_name: Ruth Wright, Hans Von der Brelie
content: The Netherlands is pushing the world towards electric flight faster than most European countries. One of the world’s first battery-powered passenger planes is being built by Dutch start-up Elysian Aircraft. Development is well underway: “There will be six engines. And we have folding wingtips, so that we fit into the current gates’ infrastructure of the airports, because the wings are very large,” explains co-founder Daniel Jacobson. Cutting fossil fuel emissions is the most pressing challenge facing the world, and aviation is a big contributor. “By being able to transport 90 passengers for initially 800 kilometres and eventually 1,000 kilometres you can reduce emissions to zero, from half the world’s flights,” Jacobson says. “That is a very large amount of flight activity in the world. And you reduce total emissions from aerospace by 20 per cent.” Should the European Union be backing electric air travel? What can e-planes learn from EVs? When will ordinary passengers be able to fly in an electric plane? Euronews Earth sat down with Maarten Steinbuch, a renowned Professor of Mechanical Engineering at Eindhoven University of Technology, to get his expert view of the future of electric flight.We can’t leave it to the airlines to cut their own emissions Aviation contributes six per cent to global heating, when CO2 as well as other emissions are taken into account. In wealthy countries, aviation is responsible for a much larger share, according to data seen by campaign group Stay Grounded.The aviation industry is, of course, aware of its impact and has made promises to cut emissions. The International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), the UN agency responsible for regulating international aviation, adopted the goal of “carbon neutral growth from 2020”. However, CO2 emissions from international aviation have increased since 2020, as the goal focuses on offsetting the sector’s CO2 emissions rather than committing to real emissions reductions.Climate Action Tracker rates the ICAO’s goal of carbon neutral growth from 2020 levels as “Highly insufficient”.The European Commission, Professor Steinbuch says, is focused on helping “current aviation” to “become as sustainable as possible”. But rather than helping current planes to reduce the emissions they create, the Commission should be supporting a pivot to zero emissions planes – electric ones. “There is not enough attention yet to have a revolution in airspace electrification. So, it’s more an evolution and not yet a revolution.”Could electric planes become as common as EVs?Electric vehicles have been adopted across Europe, faster than many people predicted. Sales grew year-on-year from 2020 to 2025, with one in four cars sold worldwide in 2025 being electric, according to the International Energy Agency. As a result, about five per cent of the global car stock is now electrified, displacing 1.2 million barrels of oil per day in 2025.This shift did not happen by magic but because car companies were put under pressure through government policy. “I have seen, in the electrification of passenger cars, that being strict on dates when manufacturers of cars effectively should have a sufficient number of models of electric cars available really helped,” says Professor Steinbuch. He believes that if similar requirements were made of aeroplane manufacturers, we could see real change. “We need legislation saying that part of a fleet could be electrified in this or that year. Push that also with legislation.”The European Commission also needs to speed up how quickly new aeroplane designs are certified. Safety must be the “first, second and third” priority, of course, but “it could help if the European Commission would put a little bit more effort in, so that those processes could be accelerated and giving space for scale-ups to build up both on the infrastructure for electrification of airflights, but also for the manufacturing and the startups who make new planes.”When will electric flights be available to us all?Seeing the owners of low-cost airlines become influential millionaires, it can be difficult to imagine aviation losing its grip on the market. But Professor Steinbuch says there are plenty of reasons to be optimistic that electric flights will be common in the not too distant future – and there’s one key component.“It’s not a dream, it is very real and the most important part of development is the batteries. Batteries are the key thing. All over the world billions of euros and dollars are spent in development. Why? Because everybody knows that batteries are the Holy Grail for the transition both in mobility as well as in energy.”Batteries are so crucial because they power electric planes, and how long they last determines how far they can fly. “If solid-state batteries with double the capacity – up to 500 watt-hours per kilogram – come onto the market, electric flying will attract the interest of far more people. And this point will come soon.”How soon? “I think in 2032 or so, within six years, we might see the first 500 km range airplanes for cargo and for passengers, at five seats, so that's a very small scale – but still it will be a start for specialised purposes.” Three years later, in 2035, “we could see nine-seaters, maybe 20-seaters, flying with a range of 500 kilometres. 80- or 90-seaters will be more close to 2040, even maybe beyond.”

title: Grocery prices across Europe: Where is food most expensive and why?
description: Grocery prices vary widely across Europe. Bread can cost more than three times as much in one country as in another. Euronews Business takes a closer look at the differences and what drives them.
content: Food takes a sizeable share of household budgets across Europe, but the cost of filling a shopping basket varies widely from country to country. In the EU, food and non-alcoholic beverages account for 13.6% of household spending, compared with 23.6% for housing and utility bills, according to Eurostat.Which countries are the most expensive for groceries, and what drives these differences?According to mid-2026 data from Numbeo, a crowdsourced cost-of-living database, the grocery index ranges from 57.2 in Moldova to 189.2 in Switzerland, with the EU average set at 100. This means groceries are 89.2% more expensive than the EU average in Switzerland, while they are 42.8% cheaper in Moldova.To illustrate the gap, a basket costing €100 at average EU prices would cost €189.20 in Switzerland and €57.20 in Moldova, based on the index.Numbeo’s index takes New York as the base at 100. Euronews Business converted the index to use the EU average as 100.Which are the most expensive countries?Three of the five most expensive countries are Nordic. Iceland (183.6) ranks second, followed by Norway (154.4), Luxembourg (134.9) and Denmark (128.4). The other Nordic countries are also above the EU average: Finland (119.7) and Sweden (116.6).Among five of Europe’s major economies, France is the most expensive for groceries, at 27.5% above the EU average. Spain (89.7) is the only one below the average. The UK (111.9), Germany (111.6) and Italy (110.2) are above it, with similar price levels.Austria (124.5), Ireland (122), Belgium (117.6) and the Netherlands (116.4) are also among the more expensive countries, all above the EU average.Cheapest EU country: Groceries in Romania cost a third lessWithin the EU, Romania (66.7) is the cheapest country for groceries, with prices 33.3% below the EU average.More broadly, groceries are cheaper in Eastern European and Balkan countries, including EU candidates. For example, the index is 59.8 in North Macedonia, 67.9 in Bosnia and Herzegovina and 68.8 in Serbia.Turkey (82.1) is more expensive than several EU members, although it remains below the EU average. Turkey also has the highest food inflation in Europe.Lower prices do not mean greater affordabilityIlaria Benedetti, an associate professor at the University of Tuscia, pointed out that while food prices are lower than the EU average in some countries, households spend a larger share of their budget on food. For example, groceries are cheaper in Romania, but households spend 23.1% of their budgets on food and non-alcoholic drinks. This share is also above 20% in Bulgaria.“Lower prices do not necessarily mean greater affordability,” Prof. Jeremiás Máté Balogh from Corvinus University told Euronews Business.Pointing to differences in wages and purchasing power, he emphasised that groceries can be cheaper in absolute terms but less affordable relative to what people earn after tax.An 18-item grocery basket costs €69.84 in the EUNumbeo lists 19 items in its “Markets” category. Euronews Business collected the prices of these items in October 2026. Adding together the listed prices of 18 items, with each counted once rather than weighted, gives an average EU basket cost of €69.84.Cigarettes are excluded from the Euronews calculation because prices vary substantially and the share of smokers differs across countries.As with the index, the grocery basket is most expensive in Switzerland at €137.90, while Moldova is the cheapest at €41.10.The basket also costs more than €100 in Norway (€116.10). Other expensive countries include Luxembourg (€99), Austria (€88.10) and Denmark (€87.70).France is still the most expensive among the five major economies compared. The basket costs €87.40 in France, compared with just €63 in Spain. These groceries cost €80 in Italy, €75.20 in Germany and €69.10 in the UK.The 18 grocery items can be bought for less than €50 in North Macedonia (€43.90), Kosovo (€45.50), Romania (€45.90), Georgia (€46.90), Poland (€49.60), Serbia (€49.70), Montenegro (€49.80) and Bosnia and Herzegovina (€49.80).However, these rankings are based on nominal prices. When purchasing power is taken into account, the gap narrows. The rankings may also change slightly when the basket is weighted.The role of energy prices and labour costs“Labour costs have likely become one of the most persistent drivers of grocery prices across Europe, but energy costs remain an important factor,” Balogh said. He noted that higher energy, fuel, and transportation costs continue to affect agricultural production, food processing, and distribution. Benedetti said that energy is the main driver of recent rises in food prices, particularly fuel this time. She added that, since the strikes on Iran at the end of February, the average price of diesel in the EU had risen from €1.59 per litre on 23 February to €2.24 on 28 September, the highest level since records began in 2005.“Diesel moves the whole food chain, from tractors to the lorries that supply supermarkets,” she told Euronews Business.She also pointed out that when inflation slows, prices do not necessarily fall. If inflation remains positive, they keep rising, only more slowly, from a higher level.Why does bread cost more than three times as much in Denmark as in Bulgaria?“The price of food in a shop is only partly the cost of the food itself,” Benedetti said.“It also includes wages, energy, rents, transport and taxes, which are much higher in richer countries.”She noted that a 500g loaf of fresh white bread costs €3.18 in Denmark and €1.02 in Bulgaria — more than three times as much, according to Numbeo. A dozen eggs, a more standardised product, costs €4.52 in Denmark and €2.69 in Estonia, less than twice as much.Balogh explained that differences in grocery prices across European countries reflect a combination of factors, including wages, land and labour costs, retail market structure, taxation, exchange rates, logistics and transportation costs, agricultural productivity and consumer preferences.

title: Sun, sand and snorkelling: A week in the Maldives on two stunning resort islands
description: On the turquoise blue waters and sandy shores of the Maldives, Fakhriya M. Suleiman explored two resort islands. Here’s her week’s itinerary filled with snorkelling, dining experiences and a bit of R&R.
content: Up until recently, when I pictured a trip to the Maldives, I only imagined villas over turquoise blue waters and barefoot luxury on sandy shores. In October, I had the chance to see beyond the picture-postcard image with a visit to two island retreats on the Indian Ocean archipelago.My week-long stay began with a brief arrival to the bustling capital, Malé, before hopping in a speedboat to the first stop on my trip: OBLU Nature Helengeli by SENTIDO.On the compact island of Helengeli, I stayed in a lagoon villa complete with a private pool that spills onto the vast Indian Ocean. A highlight of my stay was the open-air bathroom designed to bring the tropical outdoors indoors, while still maintaining privacy.After three nights on Helengeli, I was whisked away on a speedboat to the island of Sangeli. Upon my arrival to the resort, OBLU Select Sangeli, I was given a traditional Maldivian “maruhabaa” welcome, with coconut leaf origami necklace placed around my neck as a “boduberu” drum procession played in the background.My water villa also had a private infinity pool and direct access to the lagoon. The distinctive touch, however, was the room’s glass floor panel that offered a glimpse of the waters below.From the comfort of my room, I could peer into the water and watch the occasional sea creature swim by.House reef snorkelling and dolphin encountersThere’s always a first time for everything, and having never snorkelled before, I wasn’t quite sure what I’d find within the islands’ house reefs. Across both stays, access to the house reefs is a mere walk or swim away.Donning my snorkel mask, flippers and trusty life jacket, I met the islands’ deep sea residents, including spotting sea turtles, eagle rays and stingrays and an array of reef fish, including a mellow puffer fish.My sea encounters were not limited to daylight hours, either.As the sky formed sunset-orange hues, I boarded a traditional wooden dhoni for a cruise along the atoll’s blue waters. Here, I saw a pod of spinner dolphins, with some putting on an acrobatic display of leaps and twirls above the water.Fresh sea catches, coconuts and lots of tunaIf snorkelling was the highlight of my week, then eating my way through the islands came a very close second, especially with the variety of buffet and à la carte concepts to choose from.I sampled the popular Maldivian breakfast dish, “mas huni”, simply meaning fish and coconut. Typically served alongside local flatbreads like a faratta or roshi, the protein-filled breakfast combines tuna chunks with finely grated coconut, alongside zesty lime and onions and topped with chilli flakes to taste.Speaking of which, tuna lovers are certainly spoiled for choice at the resorts, with offerings from tuna dumplings to smoked and spiced chunks of tuna.The archipelago’s palate is also heavily influenced by other south Asian cuisines, including flavours from India and Sri Lanka. My favourite sweet treat came from Raga Route in the form of a gulab jamun cheesecake, which was so tasty, my sweet tooth goaded me to order seconds.My week ended with an Indian Ocean gala dinner at the Courtyard eatery on Sangeli. The gathering can be considered as a Maldivian "Malaafai", which are feasts shared among friends and families.During the dinner, there were live cooking stations for guests to choose from samosa, papdi or aloo tiki chaat as well as quickly sample a morsel of panipuri. The buffet featured popular rice dishes, including biryani and a cart serving Indian faloodas.Rest and relaxationAfter snorkelling, swimming in my private pool and strolling in the sand, it was only right that a spa treatment (actually, two…) made it onto my itinerary.On Helengeli, I sauntered to the ELE|NA Ayur facility and opted for the “relax and unwind” treatment, which focused on my back and included a mini foot massage. I was able to enjoy my massage in the outdoor treatment area, where the aroma of the applied hot coconut oil was accompanied by birdsong and the quiet ripple of koi fish in the nearby pond.I also visited ELE|NA Ayur on Sangeli, but this time, the focus was my skin. The treatment was designed to detoxify, regulate excess oils and give me that sought-after island glow. Before my facial had even started, I was presented a tray with a turmeric, honey and brown sugar shot, along with a refreshing cold towel infused in fragrant lemongrass oil.In the treatment room, a gentle vitamin C cleanser was applied, followed by a cucumber mist and a citrusy yoghurt-based exfoliant to finish.What to know before you go and getting thereEU citizens, as with all foreign nationals travelling to the Maldives, must complete the free digital self traveller declaration, "IMUGA", at least 96 hours before arriving to the Indian Ocean archipelago. After approval, tourists are then granted a visa on arrival for a stay up to 30 days.Guests staying at OBLU Nature Helengeli and OBLU Select Sangeli must also check in online via the apps prior to arrival.When arriving at Velana International Airport, the main international airport in the Maldives, resort representatives guide you to the speedboat annex to continue the journey by sea, or, if catching a seaplane, there’s a dedicated terminal with a fleet of 11 seaplanes that fly to four islands.Fakhriya M. Suleiman was hosted by OBLU Nature Helengeli by SENTIDO and OBLU Select Sangeli. Both resorts are part of the Colours of Oblu collection in the Atmosphere Core portfolio.

title: Princess and prizewinners champion hope against 'darker times' at Princess of Asturias Awards
description: The heiress to the throne quoted Paul Valéry through a Studio Ghibli character – "The wind rises, we must try to live!" – to conclude a strongly political speech about combating contemporary disillusionment, a theme echoed in several of the other winners' speeches.
content: "And they saw nothing / No future at all / Yet I was free". "They saw nothing, no future at all, but I was free".Performing the revolutionary spoken-word poetry with which she launched her artistic career, poet Patti Smith captured the spirit of the speeches at the 46th Princess of Asturias Awards as she sang 'Wing'. In the song, which pays tribute to the Spain that honoured her on Friday at the Campoamor Theatre in Oviedo, she pokes fun at the mistaken notion that human beings can survive without one another, while also championing personal freedom.She was not the only laureate (although she was certainly the one who received the loudest cheers from the audience, with that warmth also evident on the streets of Oviedo in recent days) to underline the importance of collectivity alongside the defence of individuality, as humanity enters an uncertain second quarter of the century.The president of the Princess of Asturias Foundation chose to open the awards ceremony by quoting Meryl Streep, one of the most memorable laureates of recent years thanks to her unbridled enthusiasm when she found herself surrounded by Asturian pipers: the ceremony was described as "the echo of the voices of many of our heroes of the 20th century and of this young century of ours".Christina Koch challenged stereotypes about engineers with a carefully crafted speech designed to connect instantly with the audience ("The first time I came to Spain, I wept openly in the middle of the street"). Her selection as the recipient of the Princess of Asturias Award for Concord was a call to seek unity among members of "a species capable of coming together", one that is connected by "the search for affection".Raised in a household headed by a staunch supporter of Brexit, British historian Timothy Garton Ash prompted one of the evening's few spontaneous rounds of applause when he twice referred to Britain as an inseparable part of the Old Continent.Nor was this the only political gesture by the committed Europeanist: in a forceful defence of the freedoms won through academia, journalism and the law, Garton Ash explicitly mentioned the International Criminal Court, which has been fiercely attacked by the Trump administration and whose judges have been sanctioned by the United States."No AI will ever be able to replicate the emotion stirred by your work", the princess said of Julian Barnes, the Literature laureate. He opened the series of speeches with a reference to one of the most renowned Spanish painters. "When you look at Velázquez you realise that everything has already been said; most writers and artists have at some point in their lives had insights as instructive as his." Rosalía put it more simply a few years ago: "It's all been invented".King Felipe VI was even more explicit than his daughter when discussing AI. "We live in a world in which Artificial Intelligence sometimes seems to us, because it is so efficient and immediate, more reliable than human intelligence. Our laureates dismantle that impression: their achievements, lived and worked for down to the marrow, show that only through effort and perseverance can talent turn its potential into tangible, lasting realities".An appraisal of democracy by the monarchThe King also referred to the upcoming Spanish general elections. "In a mature society like ours, the practice of democracy also takes time. It is not exhausted in a single election, like the one we will soon experience, when citizens will once again bear the very great responsibility of defining the political direction of our country".He sent a clear message to citizens and their political representatives. "Democracy requires daily commitment, civic and demanding, and care for its forms and institutions, so that we can continue to guarantee our coexistence, to foster that search for the common good which, as far as possible, meets and balances the legitimate interests of all citizens", Felipe VI said.Towards the end of the ceremony, the heiress to the throne chose to quote one of the most moving lines associated with the Communication and Humanities laureate, Studio Ghibli, represented by its president, Kenichi Yoda. The protagonist of one of its films, quoting Paul Valéry, enthusiastically proclaims : "The wind rises, we must try to live!". Both she and the laureates seem to agree on the spirit of the era ahead and how best to face it.

title: Jihadists reportedly urge attacks during protests in Portugal and Spain
description: Spanish newspaper El País has obtained what it identifies as an Interior Ministry report detailing calls for attacks on police officers and protesters during weeks-long demonstrations in several European countries.
content: Spanish authorities have reportedly detected calls from jihadist groups to attack police officers and demonstrators during protests taking place in several European countries, including Portugal.Portugal's Internal Security System (SSI) says it is "closely monitoring" the alert: "The Secretary-General of the Internal Security System is closely monitoring the situation referred to [jihadist calls for attacks on police officers and demonstrators] within her remit and in constant liaison with the relevant authorities," the SSI said in a response to the main Portuguese news agency Lusa.According El País, the Spanish Interior Ministry reportedly identified messages on a website allegedly linked to the Islamic State (IS) group, urging attacks on police officers and demonstrators during protests that have been going on for several weeks in European countries including Portugal, Spain, France and Italy.The demonstrations peaked last weekend amid a wave of violence in France, where buildings such as Limoges City Hall and the Lyon tourism office were set on fire and largely destroyed. Italy also saw violent incidents, including arson attacks, particularly in Milan.In Portugal and Spain, the daily protests and "camp-outs" in the squares of some of the largest cities, notably Lisbon, Porto and Madrid, have been largely driven by the cost of living and the housing crisis.The Spanish daily says it has seen an internal document from the Cybersecurity Coordination Office containing messages encouraging militants to take advantage of mass demonstrations and street clashes to carry out attacks.According to El País, the way the protests are organised, with those in France alone estimated to have brought together more than 800,000 people last weekend, offers "a rare opportunity to attack them" and means that the police "become easy prey when there are skirmishes with demonstrators".The jihadists are also said to have provided practical advice on how to carry out the attacks, calling for "martyrdom" through suicide bombings or vehicle-ramming attacks.

title: Macron denounces deadly shooting near Paris as 'racist terrorist attack'
description: One of the wounded, who is of North African origin, is reportedly in 'critical condition.'
content: A gunman opened fire from his car in a Paris suburb on Friday, killing one person and injuring five others, including a 12-year-old girl shot eight times.French President Emmanuel Macron visited Trappes, southwest of Paris, and condemned the shooting as a "racist terrorist attack". Authorities suspect the attacker targeted people of foreign origin.This was a "racist, terrorist attack", said the Elysee presidential palace.French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez visited the two affected towns, describing the shooting as "clearly a terrorist crime".The man was "firing at random, wanting to cause a bloodbath" as he drove through the southwestern working-class towns of Trappes and neighbouring La Verrière, Trappes mayor Ali Rabeh said.The suspect, 39, was arrested in nearby Coignières, according to a source familiar with the case. Police found a submachine gun and tear-gas grenades in his possession, a police source said.Prosecutors said they had opened an investigation for "murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise".Most of the victims were of foreign origin, and prosecutors are investigating whether they were targeted because of their "real or supposed race, ethnicity, nationality or religion".Rabeh said the man was firing sporadically from his car and that the person killed was "of African origin".According to the mayor, one of those injured is "in critical condition" and "is of North African origin".It was "objectively a racist, probably Islamophobic attack," Rabeh added, calling for national unity as the toll rose from an earlier count of four wounded."Very serious events have just taken place in Trappes," French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu wrote on X. The prime minister said that "all the resources of the security forces and the judicial authorities are fully mobilised." He added that "the national anti-terrorism prosecutor’s office has announced it is monitoring the situation.""I offer my sincere condolences to the family and loved ones of the person who died, and my full support to the other victims," the mayor of Trappes wrote on Instagram. "An investigation is under way to determine the exact circumstances of these events and the motives of the gunman," he added, saying the town would set up a psychological support unit in the coming hours.

title: E9X: The battery-powered plane with 90 passengers on board and a range of 1,000 kilometres
description: Flying without kerosene is no longer just a dream, with pilots being trained to fly electric planes in the Netherlands. Before long, these battery-powered planes could be carrying 90 passengers and flying distances of up to 1,000 kilometres.
content: Johannes, Peter and Floris are thrilled. The pilots are carrying out the first test flights for the scaled E9X demonstrator. It’s a world premiere — and if all goes to plan, their electric model plane could soon become a big passenger aircraft.After a soft landing, the aircraft is still in one piece — and now the real adventure can begin: analysing the flight data in the Elysian Aircraft laboratory, which sits beside Amsterdam’s Schiphol Airport.Over the next two decades, the global number of air passengers could double. This is bad news for the global climate, so the young Dutch start-up Elysian is working on a solution.The world’s first battery-powered passenger aircraftDaniel Jacobson is one of the founders of Elysian Aircraft. With ten million euros in start-up capital, his team now aims to develop one of the world’s first big, battery-powered passenger aircrafts.“The design pretty much stands”, Jacobson tells Euronews in his workshop. “There will be 6 engines. And we have folding wingtips, so that we fit into the current gates’ infrastructure of the airports, because the wings are very large. We are talking about more than 50 metres.”Battery-packed wingsJacobson shows Euronews the first full-scale model of the innovative wing. The battery packs are integrated into the wing’s structure. To give a better idea of the scale, there are roughly 40 battery packs across the entire wing, each pack weighing around 1000 kg.“Yes, we are an obese plane”, the Elysian manager admits. Yet he smiles confidently: “We are always on a diet, trying to reduce weight. How can you use different materials, how can you combine things, how you do thermo-management. And it’s also IP (intellectual property) that we are generating here.” There are no further details — it’s top secret at this stage.Battery-wings — a revolutionary idea, and the key to success. The co-founder and co-CEO of Elysian Aircraft sounds rather proud: “There was really this consensus in the academic world and in the industry that flying electrically with a large aircraft would never be possible. We have disproven that with our research on our design.”Reducing global aerospace emissionsBut what are the benefits? “By being able to transport 90 passengers for initially 800 kilometres and eventually 1000 kilometres you can reduce emissions to zero, from half the world’s flights”, Jacobson says. “That is a very large amount of flight activity in the world. And you reduce total emissions from aerospace by 20%.” The E9X is due to be operational by 2034. Europe is doing rather well in the race for the future of aviation, Jacobson believes. “But comparing it to the US or even China, we should fund start-ups and innovation much more aggressively when we want to keep our advantage”, the top manager urges with regard to the EU. Pilots prepare for electric take-offWe stop at the small regional airport of Teuge. Here, flying on electricity is already a reality. The E-Flight Academy trains pilots from several airlines in an environmentally friendly way at a low altitude. Co-founder Merlijn van Vliet takes Euronews on a ride in a small 2-seater: “In this aircraft we have two batteries with 11 kilowatt-hours each. So, in total we have 22 kilowatt-hours on board. We can fly 45 to 50 minutes with them and still have ten minutes of reserve capacity.”We follow the banks of a river through green meadows where Dutch cows are grazing. “We are now flying towards the old city centre of Deventer. They don’t hear us. So, we can fly wherever we want and they don’t hear us on the ground”, Merlijn beams. What is his vision for the future? “In ten years, this will grow big and we will fly electric with 40 or 60 passengers — or even more.”Charging infrastructureJurjen de Jong is a pioneer. He is developing a European charging infrastructure for electric aircraft.“We will expand from the Netherlands to the Nordic States, to France, to Germany and Switzerland”, the co-founder of NRG2fly tells Euronews. “And then we will have a fully-fledged network of low-emission, low-noise electric mobility and that is really what we’re going for”. Airports are surrounded by huge car parks. Solar panels, tens of thousands of electric cars and stationary energy storage systems could be connected to form a network — “the inter-net of energy”, as Jurjen calls it.Teuge airport is testing the scaled concept. “We have 500 solar panels on the rooftop”, Jurjen explains, “their energy is stored in a battery. So basically, we have a whole energy hub which is providing energy instead of taking energy from the grid.”NRG2fly co-founder Jurjen de Jong has a broader vision too: “My dream is to have all regional electric planes powered by the sun. And then we can leave a better world for me, my children and everybody.”

title: Italy preparing with elite troops and drone surveillance for 24 October protests
description: On 24 October Rome will be locked down with 1,500 officers, Milan with 1,800 police and soldiers.
content: Nationwide protests against the rising cost of living are expected in Italy and France on Saturday 24 October. Authorities and business owners fear a repeat of what happened on 17 and 18 October, when hundreds of people were involved in violent incidents targeting shops and law enforcement.Protests are planned in several Italian cities, including Milan, Bologna, Genoa, Turin, Rome and Florence. According to "Mappa della rivolta", a website that collates protest initiatives, more than 30 mobilisations are scheduled, ranging from marches and sit-ins to assemblies and strikes.The capital will be under tight security for the occasion. Rome's police headquarters has drawn up a security plan to manage both notified demonstrations and spontaneous rallies announced online. In addition to the usual units deployed to handle protests, drones from the State Police's 1st Flight Department and aircraft from the Carabinieri will also be used. In all, around 1,500 officers will be deployed, with checks stretching from city squares to railway stations.Tactical advice on how to deal with police clashes on social mediaRome's Cybersecurity Centre is also operational, monitoring posts and activities on social media in coordination with Digos, the specialized operational division of the Italian State Police.The digital dimension is making it harder to manage the protests. On Telegram, TikTok and Instagram, guides on how to prepare for clashes are circulating. Advice ranges from bringing water, painkillers and vinegar to lessen the effects of tear gas, to guidance on what to wear and how to behave if disorder breaks out.In Milan, there will be around one thousand police officers and Carabinieri, 300 municipal officers and 500 soldiers deployed following the latest government security decree. Here too, drones will be used to monitor the marches. Authorised demonstrations will take place away from the Duomo, while protests are banned in the Garibaldi and Porta Venezia districts.In Turin, a demonstration is expected that has been organised by activists from the antagonista scene linked to the former Askatasuna social centre, together with members of the 17 October Movement and students. Marches are due to start at 2 p.m. in Piazza Arbarello.Following the unrest on 17 October, on Friday Digos carried out searches targeting around 100 people, 51 of whom were minors. Operations took place in several cities, including Bari, Bergamo, Florence, Genoa and Verona.

title: Meghan Markle 'distressed' by child abuse image allegations against father
description: Markle has been estranged from her father since 2018, when he was caught staging paparazzi photos in the run-up to her wedding to Harry.
content: Prince Harry's wife, Meghan Markle, said on Friday she was "deeply distressed" by allegations that her father possessed child abuse images, adding that she had previously prevented him from having contact with her children over other "troubling and disturbing" allegations."I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed," Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, said in the statement.The Sun, Daily Mail and Telegraph reported that the images were allegedly found among the belongings of Meghan's estranged father, Thomas Markle, at his former home in the Philippines. He denies the allegations.Philippine authorities are investigating the allegations, the country's justice undersecretary said on Friday, according to Reuters.Not the first 'troubling and disturbing allegations'"Our Anti-Trafficking and Anti-OSAEC (online sexual abuse and exploitation of children) task ‌force in Cebu is currently investigating the matter," Nicholas Ty, Philippine justice undersecretary, told Reuters.Thomas Markle, who reportedly now lives in a rehabilitation centre in Florida, denied the allegations, telling the Daily Mail they were "sick lies" that had left him "shocked" and "hurt".Following the reports, Meghan said she had seen a letter in 2018 sent to London's Metropolitan Police and its Royalty and Specialist Protection unit containing similar allegations."It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated," she said in a statement.The duchess, who has two children, added she hoped it could "now be understood that, despite certain media publications' distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them".Prince Harry and Meghan stepped back from royal duties and left Britain in 2020 amid tensions with the royal family. They unexpectedly returned to the UK with their children in August 2026.

title: Bayern Munich manager Vincent Kompany hospitalised after collapse during training
description: A few weeks ago, sporting director Max Eberl said that Kompany, who reportedly needed help climbing stairs, had been struggling with both a viral infection and a hip injury.
content: Bayern Munich manager Vincent Kompany was taken to hospital by ambulance on Friday after collapsing at the club's training ground.He reportedly collapsed after observing a training session involving Bayern's reserve team at the Sabener Strasse facility in Munich."Vincent Kompany had to seek medical treatment on Friday after collapsing during training for FC Bayern's amateurs," a statement from the Bundesliga club read.Emergency services were called to the scene, with German newspaper Bild reporting that a rescue helicopter also landed at the training complex.Last week, it was reported that Kompany was suffering from a viral infection affecting his legs, raising doubts over his availability for Wednesday's Champions League match against Arsenal.However, he returned to the dugout for the match and had only resumed training duties a few days before Friday's incident.A former captain of the Belgian national team, Kompany started his managerial career six years ago and has been with Bayern since May 2024.

title: A year ahead of the ‘wrecking ball’: Scientists find new clue to predict when El Niño will strike
description: Predicting El Niño a year in advance could help communities and decision makers better prepare for the weather phenomenon's impact.
content: This year’s El Niño could be “literally off the monitoring charts” as the UN weather agency warns its impacts will extend into 2027.The natural weather phenomenon, which typically occurs every two to seven years, is still intensifying in the Pacific – driving extreme weather across Central America’s Dry Corridor, which stretches from Mexico to Panama, and threatening coral reefs and forests.“The current El Niño event could be unprecedented in strength,” Celeste Saulo, secretary-general of the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), told reporters in Geneva earlier this week. "This will have far-reaching consequences for weather patterns across the world.”Tom Fletcher, the UN’s under-secretary-general for humanitarian affairs, described El Niño as a “wrecking ball” of extreme heat, drought and flooding, warning it would bring “massive humanitarian consequences”.But communities and decision-makers may soon be able to better prepare for the wrath of El Niño – and its cooler counterpart La Niña – thanks to a new breakthrough. Can we predict future El Niños?Researchers from CSIRO, Australia’s national science agency, and the University of Melbourne have just identified the conditions that make it possible to predict some El Niño and La Niña events up to a year in advance. El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) events like El Niño and La Niña typically peak around December and can usually be forecast with confidence around six months in advance. Predicting them earlier has long been a challenge. But after analysing more than 7,500 historical ENSO forecasts from climate models developed in nine countries, scientists found that knowing whether the Pacific is in an El Niño, La Niña or neutral state when a forecast is started can provide valuable clues about how reliable a forecast is likely to be 12 months later. The study, published in the journal Science Advances, found that forecasts initiated during La Niña conditions consistently performed well even when predicting ENSO events a year ahead, while forecasts beginning from neutral conditions were far less reliable. Co-author Dr Mandy Freund from the University of Melbourne and researcher with the Australian Research Council Centre of Excellence for 21st Century Weather, says that the findings provide a new way to assess confidence in long-range climate forecasts. “We’ve known for some time that the starting conditions affect how well model forecasts perform, but our study really shows how drastic those differences in performance can be,” explains Lead author Dr Nandini Ramesh.“The exciting thing about our results is that we can use that information. We can identify which forecasts deserve greater confidence and potentially warn the public about El Niño events much earlier.” The breakthrough could help improve how early warnings are communicated. However, Dr Ramesh, a senior research scientist at CSIRO, says the team is still a “few steps away” from applying the findings to the models used by forecasting agencies. “But these results hold promise for being able to communicate early warnings for future events,” she adds.How can the world prepare for El Niño?El Niño is a natural phenomenon, meaning it can’t be stopped. However, wide forecasts will give countries longer to prepare. “The key is to manage water and prepare for the changes in where and when rainfall occurs,” says Davide Faranda, research director at France’s National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS).For example, Faranda explains, governments can store and distribute water more carefully, better control how reservoirs and underground water are used, adjust farming schedules and irrigation practices, and prepare communities for droughts or floods.Farmers can also reduce their losses by changing planting dates, irrigating at cooler times of day, storing water ahead of droughts and taking steps to protect their crops and livestock from extreme heat.Tackling climate change could help limit future damage too. While El Niño events can increase global average temperatures by around 0.2°C – enough to trigger widespread destruction – the burning of fossil fuels has added considerably more heat into the atmosphere. El Niño’s impacts are therefore compounded by an already warming world. It’s why 2025 was the third warmest year on record – hotter than the El Niño year of 2016 – despite the naturally forming cool drag of a La Niña event.“We cannot eliminate El Niño through climate mitigation,” Faranda says, “but we can reduce the extent to which climate change makes its consequences more severe.”

title: Romania and EU accuse Russia of new drone attack as ship capsizes in Black Sea
description: A massive search and rescue operation is underway off the Romanian coast in the Black Sea following a new drone attack on a commercial ship that both the European Commission and Romania call as another Russian escalation.
content: A commercial ship was hit by a drone off the Romanian coast on Friday morning, killing one sailor, with three others missing and nine rescued as the vessel caught fire and capsized, in an incident that Romania's President Nicușor Dan called "a new example of the tragic consequences of Russia's aggression against Ukraine."The Romanian coast guard led a massive search and rescue operation 13 nautical miles east of Romania's largest port Constanta looking for the missing sailors, but adverse weather and reduced visibility prevented a helicopter rescue, Romanian authorities told Euronews Romania.Romania's Naval Authority said the vessel, identified as the Comoros Islands-flagged Khoryv, sent a distress signal after the drone strike around 10 am local time (9 am CET).It sustained "major damage and capsized, with an imminent risk of sinking," according to the Romanian Naval Authority.The ship's crew consisted of 10 Ukrainian citizens and three Azerbaijani nationals.
