The Romanian Ministry of Interior said that “10 were recovered by another commercial vessel in the area, nine alive and one deceased, while three others are still missing,” according to Euronews Romania.Dan said in a statement that "this attack is a new example of the tragic consequences of Russia's aggression against Ukraine," indicating that Romania has determined that the attack originated from Russia."It is time for Russia to take seriously the peace initiatives of the United States and Europe, to accept the ceasefire proposals, and to end the war," Romania's president said.Romania's Prime Minister Luca Niculescu said that "what happened today, once again, in the Black Sea outside Romania's territorial waters, is unacceptable and a flagrant violation of international law and specifically of freedom of navigation, a result of Russia's escalation."Niculescu announced that "we will continue our efforts with our allies and coordination with Bulgaria and Turkey to ensure freedom of navigation and maritime security."In a later statement, Romania's prime minister said that he had "an in-depth phone conversation" with Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi in which he "reaffirmed Romania’s steadfast solidarity with Ukraine in defending its sovereignty and territorial integrity, as well as our continued support."He said the two leaders "agreed to strengthen our joint projects in the fields of drones, infrastructure, logistics and energy to enhance regional connectivity and security.""Our strategic partnership provides the framework for continued close coordination, including on the protection of the rights of persons belonging to the Romanian minority in Ukraine, which remains high on our agenda.""The Romanian government remains committed to supporting Ukraine’s accession to the EU," Romania's new prime minister said, outlining his position as he has just been sworn into office.The attack took place right outside Romania's territorial waters. The country's new Defence Minister Ștefan Radu Oprea said the army can intervene only when the drones enter Romania's airspace.Both European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa condemned the attack, declaring that they stand in "full solidarity" with Romania.Von der Leyen said she was "deeply alarmed by yet another Russian escalation in the Black Sea.""These reckless attacks target innocent lives and openly defy international law," she said in a statement."My thoughts are with the family and loved ones of the sailor that was killed. And with the families of the three crew members still missing. My gratitude goes to the rescue teams working tirelessly to find them."Offering condolences to the victims families, Costa said that "the EU stands in full solidarity with Romania following this morning’s attack on a vessel off its coast.""Attacks off the coasts of EU Member States in the Black Sea are increasing as a consequence of Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine. Such attacks are unacceptable and must stop," the EU Council president said."The EU is united in its opposition to Russia’s illegal war of aggression against Ukraine and its escalating hybrid campaigns," Costa added.This is the latest drone attack incident in the Black Sea off Romania and Bulgaria's coasts, on NATO's eastern flank, after a series of similar attacks over the last weeks which resulted in casualties and ships' destruction.Romania and Bulgaria have requested NATO's support for surveillance and control systems as well as response capabilities against drone attacks in the Black Sea.Niculescu said that "our country is set to benefit from additional equipment following Romania's efforts at the NATO allied level. "EU's High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas told the European Parliament on Tuesday that suspected Russian drone strikes on civilian shipping in the Black Sea are piling further pressure on global food supplies.The EU's foreign policy chief said vessels had come under attack six times in 10 days, describing it as "a dangerous and unacceptable escalation".Kallas accused the Kremlin of trying to choke off Ukraine’s income while Russian troops make little progress on the battlefield.Follow Euronews Romania for continuous breaking news coverage of this developing story.

title: First human case of cattle virus Shamonda: How worried should Europe be? EU agency explains
description: The first human case of Shamonda virus, confirmed in France, poses no wider threat to Europeans, the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) told Euronews.
content: Europe’s public health authorities need to be aware of the first human case of Shamonda virus confirmed in France, but not “panic,” the ECDC told Euronews, as investigations into the patient’s death continue. French authorities confirmed on Thursday a Shamonda virus infection in a patient in Lyon who died in early October, marking the first time the virus, previously seen only in animals, mainly cattle, has been reported in a human. “This is a very special case,” Tamás Bakonyi, principal expert on vector-borne and zoonotic diseases and one health-related issues at the ECDC, told Euronews.The affected patient had leukaemia and was “severely immunocompromised,” making it easier for the virus to infect the person. “The whole process of viral infections or other kinds of infections are behaving differently in those [immunocompromised] individuals than in healthy people,” Bakonyi said. While it cannot be excluded that the virus can spread to other humans, “it does not mean that now we should be concerned, that we should be in panic,” he said, adding that there is limited evidence of a broader threat.“The studies [in France] indicated that it was a quite long period that the patient had already been carrying the virus and then developed encephalitis and died,” Bakonyi said. The Shamonda virus belongs to a group of viruses transmitted by biting insects called midges. The virus was first detected in Nigeria in the mid-1960s and has since been reported sporadically in cattle in West, East and southern Africa and in Japan. This summer it was also detected in Western Europe. Cases were reported in Austria, Belgium, France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland, as well as the island of Jersey. Investigations are ongoing Although it had never been reported in humans before, Bakonyi said that experts and public health institutes in European countries had already been looking into whether the virus can cause infections in humans. “This is an alert, but we have seen this,” Bakonyi said, adding that millions of people have lived in an environment where the virus is present and it has never been reported as a problem.“It cannot be excluded that it also propagates in other humans, so that is the alerting part and that is why now there are ongoing investigations to clarify every aspect,” he said. Those include clinical, laboratory and epidemiological investigations to determine whether the virus caused or contributed to the patient’s death and how the infection was acquired.Some of these studies include testing for antibodies in people who may have been exposed to the virus, such as veterinarians and farmers, to see if they have been infected even without developing symptoms. The case underlines how closely animal and human health are linked. That’s why ECDC together with European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) are taking one health approach — working together in the fields of animal and human health they have begun gathering scientific data and other relevant information, including input from experts across different countries, to inform its risk assessment.

title: EU trade Chief seeks to rebalance EU-China trade as Brussels weighs tougher measures
description: The European Commission hopes to curb Chinese imports in additional sectors in upcoming talks with Beijing while exploring new trade defence measures, though the move risks triggering retaliatory action from China.
content: EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič said on Friday that the EU was walking a tightrope in negotiations with Beijing, weighing conventional trade measures against broader political considerations.After several months of negotiations, Brussels and Beijing reached a deal on 9 October to curb imports of hybrid cars from China. However, the agreement is unlikely to significantly narrow the EU’s record trade deficit with China, which has reached €1 billion a day, a gap the European Commission is seeking to reduce.“There are whole sectors under threat; each head of states and government is concerned that there might be potential heavy losses of the jobs,” Šefčovič said on Friday, after a meeting of the 27 trade ministers in Ireland.He added: “We have to proceed not only with the traditional trade techniques, but also with a very political approach, how to balance the trade between between China and the European Union.”A new round of discussions is taking place at a technical level with Beijing until the end of the year, with political negotiation scheduled for January and March 2027.But given the urgency, EU leaders gave the European Commission a political mandate last week to work on a “kill switch” tool that would allow Europeans to cut off China's access to their market to counter economic distortions.Under the October deal, the EU will introduce country-specific quotas allowing 350,000 Chinese hybrid cars onto the European market annually over four years, with a fixed annual adjustment rate of 6%.Striking a deal on new sectorsThe Commission aims to extend the agreement to other sectors, but EU officials warn that progress will also depend on Beijing’s response to the EU executive’s efforts to strengthen its trade defence tools.The Commission is set to present a new instrument on 9 October aimed at encouraging EU companies to diversify their suppliers of strategic products to reduce their dependence on China.It also hopes to present a proposal for the so-called “kill switch” that same week and ahead of the December summit of EU leaders. Pushed by France and Germany earlier this month, it would allow the Commission to adopt radical measures against Beijing in the event of economic pressure on the EU market.Another unilateral EU trade defence measure targeting Chinese chemicals and industrial machinery could also come in December, with the risk of prompting Chinese countermeasures.According to the latest Chinese customs data, China's exports to the EU have continued to surge, rising by 25% over the past year.

title: EU vies to expand role in Ukraine-Russia peace talks to influence US thinking
description: Brussels wants to turn the next round of trilateral peace talks betwen Ukraine, Russia and the US into a multilateral format with European representation.
content: The European Union is seeking a greater role in peace talks to end Russia’s war on Ukraine, potentially including direct contact with Moscow.The United States wants to resume trilateral talks at the technical level in November, after its midterm elections. Ukraine says it welcomes any format at any time, while Russia has said it is “ready in principle”.The peace process stalled in February after the US launched its war on Iran, shifting much of its diplomatic focus to the Middle East.Brussels sees a possible resumption of talks as an opportunity to move from a trilateral to a multilateral format, bringing European representatives to the table and giving the EU a chance to influence Washington's thinking, which has recently shifted sharply in Moscow’s favour, setting off alarm bells.Europeans, however, have a track record of being blindsided, dismissed and even ignored by their American counterparts, so there is no guarantee of success.“Now, there is an expectation that there will be a multilateral-level discussion with representatives at senior official level, and the EU will be present at these talks,” European Commission deputy chief spokesperson Arianna Podestà said on Friday.“We have always worked to have Ukraine in a position of strength, and we have always worked for a just and lasting peace for Ukraine. We’re doing so on every occasion.”Podestà said the EU should be represented jointly by the European Commission, the bloc’s executive arm, and the European Council, which represents member states.Asked whether this could involve European officials meeting Russian representatives face to face, she left the door open.“At this stage, I wouldn’t have further details to provide. The expectation is that there would be a joint Commission-Council representation that would attend the meetings,” she said. “Beyond that, I don’t have other elements to share.”Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov did not immediately oppose European participation, as Moscow has done in the past, but stressed that the next round of talks under preparation would remain trilateral.“Nothing can be ruled out a priori,” Peskov said.“But these talks we are discussing, which are scheduled for the first half of November in Abu Dhabi, will take place in a trilateral format.”A seat for two?It remains unclear whether both EU institutions will have a place at the table.The last rounds of talks involving Ukraine, Europe and the US, first in Miami and later in Oslo, included only Bjoern Seibert, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s powerful chief of cabinet.Pedro Lourtie, chief of cabinet to European Council President António Costa, was not invited.National security advisers from Germany, France and the UK — the so-called E3 — and NATO attended the Miami talks. In Oslo, Italy took France’s place.Discussions focused on security guarantees for Ukraine, sanctions against Russia and post-war recovery. After the Oslo talks, US special envoy Steve Witkoff met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Saint Petersburg for nearly three hours.The Kremlin later dismissed Witkoff’s proposals as offering “little of real value” towards ending the war, while signalling its readiness to resume technical-level talks.EU officials and diplomats say Moscow has yet to show signs of abandoning its maximalist demands or engaging meaningfully in the peace process. But with the stakes so high, they argue, Europe cannot afford to sit on the sidelines.US President Donald Trump’s decision to strike a diesel supply deal with Putin and ease long-standing sanctions on Russia has alarmed European capitals, reinforcing their view that the EU’s presence at the table is essential as a counterweight to Washington.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, whom Trump has repeatedly criticised, has urged European leaders to establish their own diplomatic channel with Moscow.Earlier this year, Costa quietly opened a line of communication with Russia, but the initiative failed to yield results and was put on hold.The idea of appointing a special envoy was discussed again by EU leaders at last week’s summit. No consensus candidate emerged, but Finnish President Alexander Stubb has returned to the conversation after co-hosting the latest round of talks in Oslo.Moscow later said it could accept Stubb as an intermediary, provided he did not “parrot” the European position — a condition unlikely to sit well with the Finnish president, a staunch supporter of Ukraine.

title: CICA members look to turn regional dialogue into action
description: The Conference on Interaction and Confidence-Building Measures in Asia (CICA) brought together member states to discuss regional security, economic cooperation and shared challenges, with a focus on strengthening the organisation's role and turning dialogue into practical action.
content: For more than three decades, the Conference on Interaction and Confidence-Building Measures in Asia (CICA) has provided a platform for dialogue among countries with different political and economic priorities. Its 28 members are now looking at ways to strengthen cooperation on regional security, economic development and emerging challenges.Under Azerbaijan's chairmanship, which began in 2024, discussions have focused on strengthening the organisation's institutional framework and making cooperation more practical. Migration, climate change and artificial intelligence were among the issues raised, alongside finance, education and business. As CICA enters a new phase, attention is turning to how member states can translate discussions into lasting cooperation.

title: Melania Trump secures ceasefire in Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, White House says
description: The agreement, due to take effect on 29 October, is intended to allow humanitarian aid and civilian evacuations in a city where residents have endured years of Russian occupation, severe food shortages and dangerous attempts to escape.
content: US First Lady Melania Trump has secured an agreement between Russia and Ukraine to temporarily halt military operations in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, the White House announced on Friday. The intent is to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and evacuate civilians trapped near the front line.The localised ceasefire is scheduled to begin on 29 October, with both sides agreeing to suspend military action in the southern Ukrainian city and establish a designated safe passage for residents wishing to leave, according to the White House.Oleshky lies on the Russian-occupied eastern bank of the Dnipro River, opposite the Ukrainian-controlled city of Kherson. Before Russia's full-scale invasion, it had approximately 24,000 residents. According to White House estimates, only 1,700 to 2,000 remain, including around 50 children.The announcement comes amid a deepening humanitarian crisis in Oleshky, where residents face severe shortages of food, clean water and medicine, while attempts to escape have exposed civilians to mines and drone attacks.Speaking exclusively to Euronews on 13 October, Tetiana Hasanenko, head of the Oleshky city military administration, described a city devastated by more than four years of Russian occupation."The city is practically destroyed," she said. "There is almost no building that has not been damaged."Hasanenko estimated that around 2,000 people remained in Oleshky, including 35 children who, she said, were unable to leave.She described residents surviving on a single meal a day, sometimes consisting of only a few spoonfuls of grain, while others had resorted to eating weeds.Melania Trump's role in the agreementAccording to the White House, the First Lady and her representative worked directly with Russian and Ukrainian leaders to negotiate the terms of the humanitarian pause, including its timing, technical procedures and implementation.Melania Trump initiated discussions with both sides, acting in what the White House described as the formal role of "Exclusive Intermediary"."The situation in Oleshky is dire. Oleshky is a front-line war city on the brink of disaster," she said.The First Lady described the remaining population as predominantly elderly residents in urgent need of medical attention and basic supplies, with limited electricity, mined roads and continuing military attacks complicating humanitarian access.She argued that her intervention had been essential to securing the agreement and making aid deliveries and evacuations possible.Under the proposed arrangements, civilian representatives from Ukraine and Russia will visit residents in their homes to assess their needs and coordinate assistance.Those wishing to leave will be offered transportation to their preferred destination, with Melania Trump saying she expected some to choose Ukraine and others Russia.The First Lady also said she had secured the participation of an impartial American media organisation to accompany and document the operation, although the White House did not identify the organisation.The statement did not specify how long the ceasefire would last or provide detailed security guarantees for those involved in the humanitarian operation.A 25-kilometre 'road of death'Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since the first days of Moscow's full-scale invasion in February 2022. The city was further devastated by flooding following the destruction of the Kakhovka dam in June 2023, which submerged large parts of the area and damaged already fragile infrastructure.In her exclusive interview with Euronews, Hasanenko described how residents attempting to flee had been forced to walk approximately 25 kilometres towards the village of Radianske, crossing heavily mined territory exposed to drone attacks.Many were already physically weakened by hunger, she said, while some who managed to escape subsequently returned with food for children and elderly relatives unable to make the journey themselves.Hasanenko said people had been killed by mines along the route, with some bodies left unrecovered."This road really is a road of death," she said.She also accused Russian forces of targeting food deliveries and punishing residents suspected of receiving assistance from Ukrainian troops.Euronews has been unable to independently verify conditions inside Oleshky, which remains under Russian occupation and inaccessible to independent journalists.A humanitarian operation in occupied territoryThe White House said the initiative originated during a private discussion at Melania Trump's Fostering the Future Together event in New York, held during the 81st United Nations General Assembly.Both countries then assigned teams to coordinate the arrangements, including demining, according to the White House.The agreement, if implemented, could provide a rare opportunity to reach civilians who have spent years largely cut off from regular humanitarian assistance.But with Oleshky remaining under Russian military control, questions remain over how safe access will be guaranteed, how the suspension of hostilities will be monitored and whether residents will be able to leave freely for their chosen destinations.

title: Wind-powered snow sleds and coral recovery hope: Positive environmental stories from 2026
description: Eco anxiety is very real, so we share this year's most uplifting stories to prove there’s hope for our climate.
content: With powerful nations rolling back climate protections and temperatures soaring ever closer to dangerous thresholds, it's hard not to feel worried about the state of the planet.As green journalists, climate anxiety, climate doom and even environmental existential dread are a daily presence.These terms all describe the negative feelings, such as stress, fear, anger and grief, that confront us when the reality of a warming Earth hits home. With almost daily stories of destruction and loss of life due to extreme weather, it’s impossible to escape the impacts of climate change.Rather than being paralysed by helplessness, though, experts suggest that we channel these feelings into action.At Euronews Earth, we know we play a key role in combatting climate doom. While it’s our job to be truthful and accurate in our reporting and not downplay or greenwash the realities, we also want to remind you that there is always hope.This is why, for the past four years, we’ve kept a roundup of positive environmental news. Every year we cover hundreds of good news stories, from eco-innovations and green breakthroughs to climate wins and feel-good reports on nature.Here are this year's top positive stories so far - including the small and local, the silly that made us smile - and the enormous and potentially world-changing.If you came across a great, positive story that we haven't covered, please reach out to us on Instagram or X to share your ideas.Positive environmental stories from October 2026Europe’s EV boom has saved these 6 oil-importing countries almost €2 billion since start of Iran warElectric car fleets have cushioned the spiralling costs of oil imports following the war on Iran and subsequent energy crisis.Amazon deforestation hits record low in BrazilDeforestation in the Amazon rainforest has fallen to its lowest level since records began in 1988, Brazil's government has announced.‘Every sunny surface’ is being put to work. Europeans transforming their homes with solar drivewaysEuropeans are transforming their driveways and patios into mini solar farms, bringing the continent closer to a “cheaper, more secure” energy system.Bleached corals recover in record time after touching healthy clonesIn the lab, bleached corals recovered within just seven weeks of being put in brief contact with healthy corals.A kite-powered snow sled designed in Spain is gliding across Antarctica in world-firstExplorer Ramón Larramendi will lead an 80-day, 3,400 km South Pole expedition in a kite-powered vehicle that can travel up to 80kph.Europe’s sponge cities are turning rain from waste into a valuable resourceThe EU is creating a ‘Sponge Facility’ to help implement nature-based projects that aim to make cities less prone to droughts and floods.From tigers to turtles: The conservation success stories that prove there’s still hope for wildlifeBiodiversity continues to be degraded at an “alarming pace” – but experts insist there are still grounds for hope.‘Europe is ending its addiction to a toxic, costly drug’: Heat pump sales soar as electricity taxes fallHeat pump sales in European homes rose by 11 per cent in the first half of 2026, following a surge in gas prices linked to the Iran war.Huge victory for Spain as two cities crowned greenest in the EU. Which countries missed out?Zaragoza has been named European Green Capital 2028. The city received the first-place prize for its "strong governance and long-term commitment, helping the city respond successfully to growing climate challenges".‘It’s given my mental health a massive boost’: Why everyone should hone their bushcraft skillsIf you’re not a military green-clad survivalist or a forest-bathing wellness enthusiast, you might feel “a little bit lost” in the great outdoors, says bushcraft instructor and conservationist Jim Todd.It’s a problem the brightly coloured Bushcraft Bus – the mobile home of wilderness and nature education – aims to solve.Positive environmental stories from September 2026‘A gold mine’: How old EV batteries could help prevent Europe from wasting solar and wind energyRetired electric vehicle (EV) batteries could transform Europe’s outdated energy grid – preventing billions of euros wasted on electricity annually.‘Sunlight salary’: Exactly how much solar panels knock off your energy bills – even under grey skiesBritain may be famous for grey skies and rainy days, but its sunshine could still help residents shave more than €1,000 a year off household electricity bills.Fat Bear Week returns as Alaska's biggest bears compete for the crownSixteen bears are competing in this year's tournament, with last year's winner, Chunk, officially known as Bear 32, hoping to defend his title. Chunk reportedly weighed 544 kilograms when he won last year's contest.New Zealanders pick robin brought back from near-extinction as Bird of the YearDespite only 350 remaining, the bird received 26,000 votes, with a record one in every 50 New Zealanders taking part in this year’s competition.Argentina’s first solar train runs on batteries charged by the Andean sunThe Tren Solar de la Quebrada can run nearly double its current length on solar power alone.‘World’s largest untapped energy source’: How waste heat could help Europe end its reliance on gasCapturing and reusing waste heat could be the next “breakthrough” in Europe’s energy security and competitiveness – helping sever its reliance on gas.Barcelona has a bold plan to protect its vulnerable coastline – and it could be prize-winningBarcelona has been announced as a finalist for The Earthshot Prize in the Revive Our Oceans category. The Spanish city is pouring €150 million into restoring one of Europe’s most intensively used urban coastlines.'Remarkable': Scientists discover new wild cat species for first time in 100 yearsThe Tilcayo tiger cat is a small feline with a spotted, leopard-like coat, and was first identified in the mountainous Yang's region near La Paz, the capital of Bolivia.‘Recovery becomes self-propelling’: Five positive tipping points that can save the worldLandmark new research from The Earthshot Prize and the University of Exeter has revealed 51 solutions that can trigger “rapid and transformative change” to repair the planet over the next five years.‘Incredible progress’: Inside the €682bn drive to turn the Mediterranean into a renewable powerhouseMore than 552 GW of utility-scale solar and wind projects have been announced, or are already under development, across the Mediterranean.From tiny houses to skis: This Swedish company is finding creative uses for retired wind turbinesSince introducing a landfill ban on blades, nacelle covers and nose cones in 2021, Swedish company Vattenfall has come up with some creative ways to repurpose hard-to-recycle materials from wind power.Inside the world’s first solar ambulance transforming remote healthcare even when the sun goes downThe world’s first solar-powered ambulance has officially taken to the road, in what has been described as an “important first step towards the future of sustainable healthcare”.How ‘solar bonds’ could cut your energy bills without upfront installation costsPublished by the Common Wealth thinktank, the report, titled A Right to the Sun, proposes a universal Solar Bond scheme under which all households with a suitable roof would be eligible to access solar panels without credit checks or other eligibility requirements that are usually associated with conventional loans.'We have to contribute to nature': Meet the communities 'marrying glaciers' to bring new water to lifeIn the Pakistan-administered Gilgit-Baltistan – an autonomous territory in the wider disputed Kashmir region – communities are turning to the Indigenous practice of glacier grafting, known locally as Gang Khswa, to combat water scarcity and adapt in the face of climate change.Solar outpaces coal for the first time in China: How does Europe compare?China's solar energy capacity has surpassed that of coal-fired power for the first time ever."As of the end of July this year, China's installed solar power capacity reached 1.286 billion kilowatts," China's National Energy Administration (NEA) said.Positive environmental stories from August 2026'They wrote little letters': How kids in Portugal are making money off their neighbours' plastic wasteSisters Ariela and Alice had already been using Portugal's bottle return scheme to earn money but since June they have upped the ante: now, instead of just returning their own bottles, they are asking their neighbours' for their empty plastic bottles and making money off those too.Balloons take years to decompose: UK researchers invent ‘Bioloon’ as nature-friendly alternativeA UK PhD student may have found the solution to a global problem – the deadly risk that discarded balloons pose to wildlife.Powered by sunshine: London fruit and veg market now home to the city’s largest rooftop solar projectOne of the UK’s largest fruit, vegetable and flower markets, New Spitalfields stocks London restaurants with green goodness every day. Now it’s got a green power source of its own: London’s largest rooftop solar installation.Record-breaking investment in renewables could cement Canada as new clean energy superpowerCanadian officials have announced plans for "the largest clean energy investment in North American history."Athens' former airport is transforming into one of Europe's largest urban green spacesWith more than 30,000 trees and around three million shrubs covering 70 per cent of its area in greenery, The Ellinikon Park in Elliniko, Greece, will transform a former airport into one of the largest urban green spaces in Europe.3,700 years young: Portugal is home to hundreds of ancient olive trees that outlive many generationsIn Portugal there are hundreds of trees estimated to be at least 2,000 years old, particularly olive trees, which over the years have been certified by the University of Trás-os-Montes and Alto Douro (UTAD)From the Hundred Horse Chestnut to the ancient olive tree: Where to see Italy's oldest treesItaly's Agriculture Ministry has updated the national list of monumental trees with 82 new entries.Harvesting rainwater from rooftops could cut the number of heatwave days and reduce air con relianceRooftop rainwater could be a secret weapon in tackling extreme heat, following Europe’s blistering summer.New research from The University of Manchester in the UK modelled a system that stores rainwater harvested from rooftops and automatically sprays it onto buildings during hot weather.The beetle that hears fire: Why it is so valuable to scienceThe black pine jewel beetle is drawn to forest fires. This seeming paradox actually aids woodland recovery and inspires new early wildfire detection tech.Human hair used as protective barrier in oceansA new environmental initiative is using human hair to help protect the oceans, building barriers from donated locks to shield parts of Brazil's coastline from oil spill pollution.‘An underused tool’: How regenerative farmers are shielding Spanish land from wildfiresEurope’s regenerative farmers are providing vital wildfire protection – but they need more support.A Japanese inventor is turning soil into a source of electricity72-year-old inventor Satoshi Nakagawa says he has pioneered "micropower collection (MPC)" – a way to source tiny dribbles of electrical current from everything from wine to French bread.Solar power was Portugal's main source of electricity in July – a first for the countryLast month, renewable sources accounted for 53 per cent of consumption, with solar providing 19 per cent of that energy, followed by hydro, wind and biomass.Short-haul electric flights could be a European reality in less than four yearsEuropean travellers could take electric flights on some of the continent’s most popular routes by the early 2030s, thanks to rapid advancements in tech.Can bison help prevent forest fires in an increasingly threatened Spain?As Spain faces a wave of wildfires, a study led by Rewilding Spain explores whether European bison could curb undergrowth and make forests more fire-resilient.First tiger released into the wild in Kazakhstan 70 years after Turan tiger extinctionMore than 70 years after tigers disappeared from Kazakhstan, a female Amur tiger named Umit has been released into the wild. The release is part of a programme to restore the species to its historic range in Central Asia.Wind and solar overtake fossil fuels in GermanyGermany is likely to wean itself off polluting coal “much sooner” than originally planned, after hitting a major milestone in its clean energy transition.Solar car parks could cut electricity bills by €32,00 a yearEurope’s car parks could be turned into mini solar farms to slash electricity bills and bolster decarbonisation targets.“Car parks can generate electricity without taking up additional land, which is an important consideration given the planning challenges that ground-mounted solar can encounter,” Rob Stait of Alight, one of Europe’s leading solar developers, tells Euronews Earth.Positive environmental stories from July 2026How beavers are quietly tackling Europe’s raging wildfires and helping burnt landscapes recoverBeavers build dams, dig channels and transform small streams into broad wetland areas. This helps keep plants lush and green, even throughout long periods of drought.It means when a wildfire ignites, the green vegetation near the beaver ponds will be much harder to burn compared to dried-out areas.There are only four certified 'therapeutic forests' in the world: One is now in PortugalThe Bussaco National Forest has become the first certified Therapeutic Forest in the Iberian Peninsula, joining an exclusive group of just four sites worldwide.‘Major victory’: Sweden plans to ban forever chemicals in everyday products ahead of EUSweden has announced plans to ban ‘forever chemicals’ in consumer products as early as 2028.“This is a major victory for human health and for the Swedish environment,” the Minister for Climate and the Environment, Romina Pourmokhtari, said in a statement released on 23 July.Amazon forest fires fell to all-time low in 2025Forest fires in the Brazilian Amazon fell to a historic low in 2025 after peaking the previous year, according to a new report.Deforestation in the world’s largest rainforest also eased off last year, the report from environmental monitoring network MapBiomas says, which drastically reduces the amount of fuel available to start fires.Orange lips and a froglike roar: New monkey discovered after 18-year search in Congo rainforestAlmost two decades after an unusual monkey was first sighted in the treetops above a Congo rainforest, an international team of researchers has described it as a new species.‘Excellent profit’: Meet the Bavarian hop farmer securing his harvest and income with solar 'hats'Climate change, heat and dry farmland are hitting Bavaria’s key crop. Could solar panels save it? One German farmer is exploring how agrivoltaics can combat heat-related drought impacts and produce renewable energy for the farmSweeping victory for Europe as 15 nations top climate scoreboardEurope has dominated new global sustainability rankings, but experts warn that all nations are “still far from critical goals” to tackle climate change.The Environmental Performance Index (EPI) – produced by researchers at Yale and Columbia University – is released every two years and ranks countries from around the globe on their commitment to sustainability.Solar generated record 25% of EU power in June with Germany, Spain and Poland leading the raceFor the first month ever, solar power provided a quarter of the EU’s electricity this June.Solar generated a record 52 TWh of EU electricity in June 2026, making up 25 per cent of monthly generation for the bloc. This beat solar’s previous monthly high of 47 TWh (23 per cent) in May 2026.Cooling your home and lessening eco-anxiety: What are the hidden benefits of rooftop solar panels?Solar has been described as a “shining star” of the EU’s energy transition, helping to shelter households from the crippling cost of fossil fuels.But aside from lowering our energy bills and weaning Europe away from polluting oil and gas – adding rooftop solar panels to your home comes with a host of hidden benefits.Italy could be the next country to build a solar railway after Switzerland’s successful trialEurope’s infrastructure is embracing the renewables boom, with one company determined to transform the continent’s railway lines into mini solar farms.Last year, Swiss start-up Sun-Ways unveiled the world’s first-ever solar railway after rolling out 100 metres of photovoltaic (PV) panels in between active tracks in Buttes, a village in the Val-de-Travers district.Denmark, Portugal, Lithuania lead the way as EU share of electricity from renewables hits 46%The EU’s share of electricity generated from renewables continues to grow, new Eurostat data reveals.In the first quarter of 2026, it reached 45.5 per cent of the total electricity generated. This is up from 42.7 per cent in the same period in 2025.Pigeons, frogs and beetles gather in Milan City Hall to debate the rights of urban animalsHumans wearing animal masks gathered at Milan City Hall for the first Parliament of Living Species this month. Their goal was to convince policymakers to consider the creatures they represented when making decisions about what to build and where in Italy’s second biggest city.Air quality is improving across Europe as report finds ‘steady decrease’ in major pollutantsEurope’s air quality is getting better, despite “persistent pollution episodes” threatening to halt progress.The EU’s Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) says in its latest report that while some parts of the continent are still experiencing issues with local air pollution the overall outlook “remains encouraging”.'The storks were here before me': Pensioners live side-by-side with storks in this Croatian villageIn the Croatian village of Cigoc, storks are not just visitors – they are residents. Each spring, white storks return from Africa to nest on the rooftops of the village's traditional wooden houses, in such numbers that they regularly outnumber the people who live there.Positive environmental stories from June 2026Europe’s heat pumps replace Middle East gas imports twice over. Which country is leading the way?Heat pump sales have soared across Europe, cushioning households from the crippling costs of gas amid the war on Iran.According to a new analysis from the European Heat Pump Association (EHPA), the continent’s heat pumps provide as much heat as the liquified natural gas (LNG) carried by more than 200 tankers.Europeans are making the most of cheap solar panels – by creating green garden fencesSolar fences are gaining ground in Europe, as households continue to invest in renewables amid the war on Iran.Glow-in-the-dark plants warn of crop pestsA team of Spanish researchers has created plants that glow in the dark and change colour when infected, allowing early detection of crop pests and diseases with ordinary cameras.Solar-powered fridges are boosting farmers’ incomes by 50% while cutting food wasteSolar-powered, off-grid cold rooms, warehouses and cooling hubs allow farmers and traders to preserve perishable goods without relying on expensive and unreliable electricity grids. This shift is gaining momentum across Kenya, Nigeria, Ethiopia, Rwanda and South Africa.Spain’s renewables revolution is paying off: Electricity bills are lower despite energy crisisSpain’s electricity bills have fallen while many other countries have seen a rise since the energy crisis caused by the outbreak of the Iran war.New analysis shows that households have each saved €10 per month on their electricity bills since the Hormuz strait was effectively closed in March. Thanks to the country’s commitment to the clean energy transition, renewables have reduced the influence of fossil fuels on the electricity price by 75 per cent since 2019.France adds 157,000 hectares of protected forestFrance has created seven new biological reserves and expanded two existing ones. Together, they safeguard an additional 157,000 hectares of forest as it works toward placing 10 per cent of its land under ‘strong protection’ by 2030.‘Coal power has lost its status’: Solar power outstrips coal in US despite Trump's attacksEven as President Donald Trump boosts coal over clean energy, solar power is hitting new milestones in the US and remains the leading source of new power.Positive environmental stories from May 2026‘Even a five-year-old can do it’: Collecting river water samples helps map life on 10% of EarthCombatting wildlife decline, eDNA technology is turning simple water and soil samples into a global biodiversity map.Clean energy saved EU €51 billion in 2025 by cutting fossil fuel imports - as solar leads the wayEurope made huge energy cost savings in 2025 thanks to reducing its dependence on polluting fossil fuels by driving investment in renewables.Using wind and solar to generate power meant significantly less reliance on imported oil and gas, according to energy think tank Ember.From fur to data: How eDNA is revolutionising wildlife monitoring in AfricaScientists in Rwanda's misty Volcanoes National Park are turning to a new tool to protect endangered mountain gorillas and golden monkeys: environmental DNA.Known as eDNA, the technology identifies species using genetic traces – fur, faeces – left in soil and water, eliminating the need for researchers to physically locate the animals.Pee for the planet: How football fans are tackling Sweden’s fertiliser problem using urineEleda Stadion, home of Malmö FF, opened its doors – and its toilets – on 24 May to an initiative aiming to gather 1,000 litres of human urine.The goal? millenia-old purification technique could be the cure for Europe’s microplastic-riddled drinking water.In a recent study, seeds from the ‘miracle’ moringa tree were found to match or outperform their chemical counterpart in filtering out aged PVC microplastics – one of the most harmful plastic types for human health.Solar and wind outpace coal as energy crisis fails to spark fossil fuel revivalA predicted ‘coal comeback’ due to the Iran war energy crisis has not materialised, according to a report by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA).Total fossil fuel power generation fell by one per cent compared with the previous year, with gas-fired generation falling by four per cent.Hungary election promises renewable energy investment and foreign factory crackdownsHungary’s ecosystem.‘Clean power everywhere’: How space-based solar could help us go beyond net zero targetsOnce considered a dystopian fantasy, space-based solar could soon transform the renewable energy power sources as early as 2040'Ridiculous' plan developed at Florida zoo saves wild rhino's eyesight in AfricaAnimal behaviourists from Florida travelled to Africa in August to help an endangered white rhino with a life-threatening, parasitic eye infection.They developed a plan based on lessons learned at Palm Beach Zoo, where animals are taught to voluntarily participate in their own care."The rhinos are just thriving now and they feel really, really confident that this solved their problem,” says Angi Lacinak, co-founder of Precision Behavior.Quiet, comfortable and low emissions: the project has been declared a resounding success by the Swedish Transport Administration following an evaluation of its pilot route.Return of Sardinia’s griffon vultures hailed as one of Italy’s greatest conservation success storiesSardinia's griffon vultures were on the brink of extinction at the beginning of 2010.The population of the birds had been plummeting due to indirect poisoning, including from pesticides and chemicals ingested by animals they fed on.But today, the Italian island is home to more than 500 individuals, making it one of Italy’s most impressive conservation success stories.An ‘Uber on rails’: French company adapts vans to train tracks to revive abandoned networksFrance has thousands of kilometres of disused railway tracks which are too costly to renovate Ferromobiles using the lines.Portugal tops EU leaderboard as over 80% of electricity in January came from renewablesAccording to the Portuguese Association for Renewable Energies (APREN), a staggering 80.7 per cent of the country's electricity generated in January 2026 came from renewable energy.It marks the best record in nine months, since Portugal suffered a mass blackout that triggered nationwide chaos, and bumps the country up to second in Europe overall. Non-EU Norway came first, with 96.3 per cent renewable electricity production last month, while Denmark dropped to third place with 78.8 per cent.‘Hot sand for a cooler climate’: Has Finland finally found a solution to industrial heat emissions?Finland is harnessing the unexpected power of sand to decarbonise industrial heat – a major “blind spot” in global emissions.Industrial heat production is one of the largest and hardest-to-solve sources of carbon emissions, accounting for around one fifth of the world’s total energy consumption.Are air fryers secretly improving indoor air quality?Air fryers often use less electricity compared to conventional ovens, meaning they’re a great way to keep energy bills low in the face of spiralling costs.Now, new research says air fryers may be better for indoor air quality too - with one key condition.Positive environmental stories from January 2026‘Off the fossil fuel rollercoaster’: 10 European countries pledge €9.5bn for North Sea wind projectsAlmost a dozen countries have rallied together to get off the “fossil fuel rollercoaster” and transform the wind energy sector.Belgium, Denmark, France, Germany, Iceland, Ireland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Norway and the UK have signed the Hamburg Declaration – a landmark commitment to deliver 100GW of joint offshore wind projects across shared North Sea waters by 2050. This is enough electricity to power around 143 million homes.Can a ‘sustainable’ fungicide save France’s vineyards from climate-driven disease?Winemakers have been offered a glimmer of hope after France banned fungicides heavily relied on to protect their harvest from mildew and mould.Sean Smith, CEO of Eden Research, a tech company based in the UK, has come up with a “viable and sustainable” alternative to copper-pesticides.Solar and wind overtake fossil fuels in the EU for the first timeWind and solar generated more EU electricity than fossil fuels for the first time in 2025, marking a “major milestone” in the transition to clean power.‘Historic’ High Seas Treaty comes into forceThe much anticipated High Seas Treaty has come into force, marking a “historic milestone” for global ocean conservation.Covering almost half of the planet’s surface, the High Seas lie beyond national borders and form part of the global commons. Meet the scientist determined to change thatAn “invisible” key to tackling the climate crisis has taken centre stage after evolutionary biologist Dr Toby Kiers was named the winner of the 2026 Tyler Prize for Environmental Achievement.The Laureate, which is often touted as the ‘Nobel Prize’ for the climate, recognises “outstanding” scientific work in environmental science, health and energy that benefits humanity. Here’s what will changeFrance’s ban on "forever chemicals" came into force on 1 January following mounting concern over the adverse health impacts of these persistent pollutants.The landmark bill was passed on 20 February 2025, with more than 140,000 citizens calling on their MPs to support the ban.

title: Late invitations and spats leave Hungary’s 1956 commemoration with ‘modest’ guest list
description: Hungarian PM Péter Magyar had hoped to host top leaders in Budapest for the 70th anniversary of the 1956 revolution. But last-minute invitations and spats with Paris and Kyiv kept Macron, Tusk and Zelenskyy away, leaving only EU chiefs Ursula von der Leyen and António Costa attending.
content: Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar sought to bring European leaders to Budapest for a major commemoration of the 70th anniversary of the 1956 revolution.In the end, only European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa are attending on behalf of the EU leadership.Late invitations and diplomatic tensions contributed to the absence of key figures, including French President Emmanuel Macron, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.Magyar had planned a major international commemoration on 23 October to mark the anti-Soviet uprising, saying the day after his landslide election victory that he wanted to welcome some of the world’s most senior leaders to Budapest.“We really hope that on the 70th anniversary of the 1956 revolution, on October 23, when we will welcome world leaders here, either the US Secretary of State, the Vice President, or the President will be able to visit here,” Magyar told reporters on 13 April.In June, Magyar personally invited Macron in Paris, extending similar invitations to Tusk in Warsaw, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.Around 40 countries sent delegations to Budapest, though most EU member states were represented by ministers or parliamentary speakers rather than heads of government. Moldovan President Maia Sandu and Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze also travelled to the Hungarian capital.“It was a mistake that they set expectations so high,” István Szent-Iványi, a foreign affairs expert and former diplomat, told Euronews.“Europe and its individual member states are struggling with a thousand problems, and they didn’t feel that it would be worth coming,” he said.Euronews reached out to the Hungarian government but had not received a response by the time of publication.Late invitationsSources close to the Hungarian government, speaking on condition of anonymity, said said the ceremony was complicated by delays in sending official invitations, many of which were not dispatched until September, when leaders’ schedules were already full.Tusk had already scheduled a trip to India, while Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni had planned a visit to Kuwait.One source said the government had acted in good faith but that communication between the prime minister’s office and the foreign ministry had been poor.“We will do better in the future,” the source added.Remarks irk Paris and KyivMagyar’s comments linking riots in France to migration may have contributed to Macron’s decision not to attend.“Seeing this senseless destruction and unjustified violence, perhaps it is now clear to everyone why Hungary takes the toughest possible stance on migration,” Magyar wrote in a social media post last Sunday, drawing criticism in Hungary and France.The following day, the French embassy in Budapest announced that Macron would not attend, adding that his visit had never been confirmed by France.On Wednesday, Macron criticised what he called “stupid comments” by foreign leaders linking migration to the unrest. Besides Magyar, US President Donald Trump and Tusk had made similar remarks.“We’ve had people claiming that we were invaded by hordes of migrants and Islamists, which is completely false,” Macron said. “The fact is that all those speaking ill of our country right now are people who don’t love our country. And those people irritate me.”Magyar has also faced criticism over his invitation to Zelenskyy, as Euronews first reported last week.At the EU summit in Brussels, Zelenskyy expressed openness to visiting Budapest, but Magyar downplayed the possibility just days later. Zelenskyy’s adviser Dmytro Lytvyn also pushed back against the remarks.Ukraine is represented at today’s commemoration by its parliamentary speaker. The Ukrainian president’s office said the visit was arranged independently and was not intended to replace Zelenskyy’s attendance.Dániel Hegedűs, deputy director of the Institut für Europäische Politik, said Magyar’s public comments had not helped the commemoration.“Those social media appearances can be interpreted as interference in French domestic politics, and obviously did not facilitate Macron’s visit,” he said.He added that Magyar’s response to Zelenskyy’s invitation, saying everyone had been invited, “sends the message to the partners that whether they come or not is not a strategic issue”.Georgian prime minister’s presence stirs controversyThe guest list also includes Irakli Kobakhidze, Georgia’s controversial prime minister. suppression of dissent.Brussels has criticised Kobakhidze’s Georgian Dream party for its close ties to Russia, its role in derailing Georgia’s EU integration path and its crackdown on dissent.“We know it’s a pro-Russian oppressive regime, so it doesn’t really belong here, in the vicinity of a memorial to the 1956 revolution. But they say here that it’s protocol, everyone was invited, and he said he would come,” Szent-Iványi said.This week, Georgia’s Constitutional Court began hearings on a request by the governing party to ban five pro-Western parties.Von der Leyen and Costa attendVon der Leyen and Costa are the most senior EU figures attending, signalling Brussels’ support for Magyar’s pro-European policies following the end of Viktor Orbán’s tenure."Six months ago the people of Hungary voted for a new chapter. To turn the page on years of division, of trust eroded, freedoms rolled back, prosperity undermined" von der Leyen said in Budapest.Von der Leyen and Costa had initially been expected to miss the commemoration due to an EU-Gulf Cooperation Council meeting scheduled for Saturday in Riyadh. Its postponement last week cleared the way for both to attend in Budapest.Szent-Iványi said that leading European missing the ceremony does not mean that they are turning their backs on Magyar.“This is a modest list of participants; that’s a fact. But I think the presence of von der Leyen confirmed the message that this election meant Hungary returning to Europe”.

title: France's bond drama takes centre stage ahead of ECB rate decision
description: The European Central Bank is expected to hold rates next week as France's bond sell-off tightens borrowing conditions across the eurozone, while ECB President Christine Lagarde has made clear that the first steps to tackle French debt woes must come from Paris, not Frankfurt.
content: When the European Central Bank (ECB) meets next Thursday, it is widely expected to leave interest rates unchanged, partly because rising government bond yields are already pushing up borrowing costs across the eurozone.ECB President Christine Lagarde has played down hopes of a rescue, saying the solution to France's debt problems lies at home.The yield on France's 10-year government bond traded above 5% on Friday after rising to that level on Wednesday for the first time since 2002. The gap with German 10-year bonds, the eurozone's safest debt, was above 170 basis points.Meanwhile, the 30-year yield was at 5.5%, and the gap with German 30-year bonds was even wider at 184 basis points.On Thursday, the cost of France's five-year credit default swaps, contracts that insure investors against a government default, also climbed above 100 basis points for the first time since October 2012, when the eurozone was going through its sovereign debt crisis.Lawmakers remain split over next year's budget, which includes €43 billion in spending cuts and additional revenue measures that the government has no majority to push through.Ratings agency Moody's, which rates France Aa3, its fourth-highest grade, with a negative outlook, delivers its verdict on Friday evening, and a downgrade is widely expected. A one-notch cut to A1 would put France's rating at the equivalent level to those assigned by S&P and Fitch.Civil unrest is adding to investors' concerns.More protests are expected this weekend, and Paris police prefect Patrice Faure has advised business owners in a letter to hire private security.French trade unions, unanimously disappointed after meeting Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu on Wednesday, have called for a large mobilisation on 5 November.Sophie Binet, head of the CGT, one of France's biggest unions, urged workers to "generalise the strike".Bonds doing the ECB's jobThe case for another rate hike is still there.The ECB has raised rates twice this year, lifting its deposit rate to 2.5%, and eurozone inflation jumped to 3.8% in September, driven by energy prices.Yet German yields have climbed so much since September that their effect on growth and inflation roughly matches a 25 basis point hike, Carsten Brzeski, global head of macro at Dutch bank ING, estimated in an investor note on Thursday."For France, it’s closer to a 50 basis point hike," Brzeski wrote, adding that "the bond market has taken over the ECB's job".Brzeski expects the ECB to wait for new staff forecasts in December before deciding on its next hike.ECB President Christine Lagarde told the European Parliament on 28 September that long-term rates "have risen notably, which will slow growth".Could the ECB intervene?ECB officials have played down the possibility of intervening to lower France's borrowing costs, but have stopped short of ruling it out.The central bank bought government bonds during the eurozone debt crisis to stabilise markets and ensure its rate decisions continued to feed through to the economy.Speaking on the sidelines of the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank in Bangkok last week, Lagarde said that "there are particular circumstances that lead to some countries being more affected, France being a case in point.""The primary and first solution lies at home in France. And it has to do with fiscal policies," the ECB president added.Banque de France governor Emmanuel Moulin went further last Friday, saying the conditions for ECB intervention were not met at that time because there was no financial fragmentation in the eurozone.However, both officials spoke before France’s 10-year borrowing costs rose above 5%.If the ECB decides to intervene in the French bond market, one option could be the Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI), which was created in 2022 and has never been used.The TPI lets the ECB buy the debt of countries whose borrowing costs climb in ways it judges unjustified by their economic fundamentals and threaten the transmission of monetary policy across the eurozone.For a country to be eligible, it needs to meet several criteria, including following EU fiscal rules and keeping its debt on a sustainable path.France is nursing a debt-to-GDP ratio of 119.1%, and the current budget negotiations offer little prospect of a quick reduction in the deficit, which is necessary to put the debt on a sustainable path.Meanwhile, the government expects its debt-servicing costs to rise by more than €10 billion in 2027 compared with this year."The bar for activating the ECB's bond-buying programme remains high," Brzeski wrote in a separate investor note last week.He added that, for France, that would at least mean passing its full budget. Acting too early could be "interpreted as monetary financing of the debt of a country unwilling to follow the rules," he warned.The ECB's other emergency tool, Outright Monetary Transactions (OMT), was created in 2012 at the height of the eurozone debt crisis to allow unlimited purchases of a struggling country's short-term bonds.However, it is only available to governments that first sign up to a bailout programme from the eurozone's rescue fund, the European Stability Mechanism.Instead, Brzeski expects the ECB to quietly pause the reduction of its bond holdings, reinvesting maturing debt flexibly as it did during the COVID-19 pandemic.Should turmoil spread to other eurozone bond markets, Brzeski sees TPI as a last resort. If France continued to fall short of EU fiscal rules, "the ECB might even consider purchasing bonds from almost all eurozone countries, except for France," he said.For now, Brzeski sees next week’s rate meeting as "uneventful on action but clearly not on words".

title: A rhythmic gymnast’s journey from childhood dream to national pride
description: Azada reflects on her first international competition, representing Azerbaijan and her ambition to become a strong senior gymnast.
content: For 15-year-old Azada Atakishiyeva, rhythmic gymnastics has become much more than a sport. What began in early childhood grew into a passion that has shaped her life and ambitions. She took part in her first international competition in Georgia at just five years old, marking the beginning of a journey built on dedication and hard work. Representing Azerbaijan abroad and hearing the national anthem at competitions remain among her most meaningful experiences. Now, Azada is working towards her dream of becoming a strong senior gymnast and making her country proud.

title: Belgium boosts heating-oil aid for vulnerable households as energy prices rise
description: Belgium is stepping up targeted aid to shield vulnerable households from soaring energy costs, but the limited support may fall short as prices rise.
content: Belgium will set aside €15 million to increase heating-oil subsidies for vulnerable households this winter as rising fuel prices squeeze household budgets.The temporary measure will cover heating-oil deliveries made between 1 December 2026 and 28 February 2027, Federal Energy Minister Mathieu Bihet announced on Friday.The existing allowance will rise progressively with prices, from a maximum of €0.20 per litre to €0.50 when heating oil reaches €1.775 per litre or more.The move comes amid persistent disruption in the Middle East, which has fuelled energy-market volatility. Brent crude was trading at $114 a barrel on Friday, up from $70 before the US-Israeli war with Iran.The additional support is targeted at eligible households facing higher heating costs, rather than consumers as a whole."Heating one's home should never become a luxury. When the price of heating oil rises sharply, it is the most vulnerable households that feel the impact most severely," Bihet said."We are temporarily increasing support to help them get through the winter with greater peace of mind and protect their purchasing power."Although heating oil is being phased out, it remains an important source of residential heating in some EU countries, including Cyprus and Ireland. In Belgium, it accounts for around 35% of residential space heating, second only to natural gas.Consumption is particularly high in rural areas and older buildings, especially in Wallonia, where nearly half of households rely on heating oil because they lack access to the gas grid.Across the EU, heating oil accounts for about 14% of residential space-heating energy, with roughly one in six heating systems running on oil, according to Odyssee-Mure, a tool supporting the evaluation of energy-efficiency policies.At the current Belgian price of €1.62 per litre, a delivery of 1,500 litres costs €2,430. The existing maximum subsidy of €300 covers only a fraction of the bill.Under the reinforced scheme, the allowance would rise to €487, bringing the household's net cost down to €1,943.The support is limited to households meeting the existing eligibility criteria for the Social Heating Fund; it is not available to everyone who uses heating oil.Federal Energy Minister Mathieu Bihet advised applicants to check their eligibility and the application procedure with their local public social welfare centre, known as the CPAS in French or OCMW in Dutch.The government has allocated €7.5 million to the Social Heating Fund to finance the increased heating allowance, with a further €7.5 million earmarked for the Gas and Electricity Fund. Support under the latter scheme is also distributed through public social welfare centres, subject to eligibility criteria.The measures offer short-term relief but are limited by their budget and eligibility requirements, leaving many households facing higher energy bills without additional support.Bihet said the increase was intended to protect the purchasing power of families most exposed to rising heating costs.The government has not said whether further measures will be introduced if prices rise beyond the levels covered by the scheme.

title: First Russian diesel shipment is heading to US under Trump-Putin deal
description: The shipment, carrying about 40,000 tonnes of diesel, follows a deal that temporarily eased US sanctions on Russian diesel as Trump seeks to lower fuel prices.
content: A tanker carrying Russian diesel is en route to New York after US President Donald Trump announced a deal with Moscow in early October, according to data from the maritime tracking firm Kpler.The Malta-flagged tanker Agioi Fanendes loaded about 40,000 tonnes of ultra-low sulphur diesel, roughly 300,000 barrels, at Russia’s Baltic port of Primorsk.The tanker is signalling New York as its destination, with an estimated arrival date of 7 November, according to Kpler. That would be four days after the US midterm elections.Separate shipping data from LSEG also put the cargo at 40,000 tonnes.If delivered as indicated, it would be the first Russian diesel or gasoil cargo shipped to the United States tracked by Kpler since July 2023, and the first diesel shipment from Primorsk to New York since January 2022.The buyer and seller were not immediately known.On Wednesday, Russian news agencies quoted Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak, who oversees energy policy, as saying the first shipment of Russian diesel bound for the United States would depart the following day. He said more shipments would follow as Russian and US companies worked out contracts for the deliveries.On 9 October, Trump announced an agreement between Washington and Moscow for the delivery of Russian diesel to the US and global markets, temporarily easing US sanctions on Russian diesel. Russia also agreed to lift its own ban on diesel exports.Trump said Russia would immediately supply 300,000 tonnes, followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and 1 million tonnes “immediately thereafter”.The measure was seen as an attempt to lower fuel prices for American consumers ahead of the US midterm elections. It drew sharp criticism from Ukraine and its allies, including members of Trump's Republican Party.The move also comes after Russian diesel exports had shifted mainly to Brazil, Turkey and African countries following the EU’s embargo on Russian petroleum products in February 2023.

title: Tributes paid to actor Tom Skerritt as star of Alien and Top Gun dies aged 93
description: Tom Skerritt, a Hollywood veteran actor, known for iconic roles in Alien and Top Gun, has died aged 93 of natural causes, according to a statement released by his family.
content: Tributes have been paid to the Hollywood veteran actor Tom Skerritt, best known for his starring roles in Alien and Top Gun, who's died aged 93.His family revealed he died on Wednesday from natural causes.“While the world knew Tom through his remarkable acting career, we knew him for his humor, curiosity, wisdom, generosity and the love he brought into our lives," the family said in a statement. "He cared deeply about imagination, creativity, storytelling, service, veterans, the natural world and helping others find and share their own voices.”On screen, Skerritt was the embodiment of a solid, wry authority figure, whether as a flight instructor in Top Gun, a tough-but-fair sheriff on TV's Picket Fences or the doomed captain of Alien.He was twice nominated for an Emmy — both for Picket Fences, winning outstanding lead actor in a drama series in 1993.Other career highlights include playing the patient husband of Shirley MacLaine in Turning Point, Sally Field’s husband in Steel Magnolias and a scheming opportunist who stands in the way of Jodie Foster’s attempt to communicate with extra-terrestrial life in Contact.Julia Roberts, who played as his daughter in Steel Magnolias, posted a picture of the pair describing Skerritt as "a shining light of a gentle man. RIP", followed by a broken heart emoji.Skerritt's first film role came in 1962's War Hunt, a Korean War movie which also marked the debut of Robert Redford, Sydney Pollack and Francis Ford Coppola.Redford, who died last year, became a lifelong friend. “There was such a deep connection we made with each other that it matured into a level-headed friendship,” Redford told the Seattle Times in 2007. “His values were close to mine, and he kept his integrity.Talking about himself in 1997, Skerritt told the Seattle Post-Intelligencer: “A writer once described me as a character actor locked in a leading man’s body, and I’ve always loved that. It’s a nice compliment. I’ve been able to walk the line between television and features.”Tom Skerritt is survived by his third wife, Julie Tokashiki, and five children.

title: Storm Austen hits northwestern France: 161,000 homes lose power
description: The first major autumn storm is sweeping across northwestern France. Named Austen by UK forecasters, it brings violent gusts, disrupts transport and causes power cuts.
content: Storm Austen has caused severe disruption in northwestern France, with 23 departments on orange alert for high winds.Austen intensified rapidly over the Atlantic before heading towards the British Isles and the French coast. Brittany was particularly hard hit overnight from Thursday to Friday, before the violent winds moved on towards Normandy and Hauts-de-France.Gusts were especially strong along the coast, reaching 161 km/h at Pointe du Raz in Finistère. Several weather stations also recorded October wind-speed records.The impact in France is already significant. On Friday, around 161,000 households in the north-west, notably in Brittany, Pays de la Loire and Normandy, were left without electricity.Fallen trees and the difficult conditions are also disrupting rail traffic, and several lines have been suspended as a precaution. Bridges in Seine-Maritime have been closed.Storm will affect more countriesThe UK Met Office issued an amber warning — the second highest — for wind gusts up to 130 km/h in Cornwall and Devon as the storm named Austen by the agency moved into the area early on Friday.According to the National Grid, which distributes electricity around the UK, more than 16,000 homes were without power in the southwest by late morning.Winds up to 100 km/h are forecast across southern and central England throughout the day as the storm moves eastward along the English Channel coast.In Germany, where the storm has been named Luise by the national weather service, gusts of up to 100 km/h are expected in the West and Northwest.Just days earlier, Storm Adam struck southern France and Spain with severe thunderstorms and torrential rain. Flooding hit the departments of Gard, Bouches-du-Rhône and Var particularly hard. Adam left at least six people dead across Spain and southern France, two of them in France, and thousands of households lost power.A second major storm — Boelo — is expected to bring more wind and heavy rains later in the weekend.The Met Office updated its warning for Boelo from yellow to amber for Northern Ireland, Scotland and parts of northern England on Saturday night and throughout Sunday.

title: World Culinary Awards: Which are the best airlines and airports for dining?
description: Where are the best places to eat in the skies or before you board? Airlines, airports and airport lounges were among the winners at this year’s World Culinary Awards.
content: It’s not just restaurants that were crowned at the 2026 World Culinary Awards – airlines, airports and airport lounges also picked up gongs for feeding hungry travellers.Vietnam Airlines took the title of World’s Best Culinary Airline 2026, becoming the first Asian carrier to win the award. It beat fellow nominees including Emirates, Qatar Airways, Singapore Airlines, Air France, Cathay Pacific, and Turkish Airlines.Other aviation sector winners included London’s Heathrow Airport, Turkish Airlines' international lounges, and Clubrooms at Gatwick South Terminal.What’s on the menu with Vietnam Airlines?Designed to “promote Vietnamese cuisine” to international travellers, the carrier’s in-flight menus are adapted to the seasons and routes, so that “each flight gives passengers a different culinary experience”.Economy class cuisine is marked by its “signature dish” – the crispy, layered croissant served for breakfast. Lunches and dinners feature rice and spaghetti dishes with an accompanying sauce, a dessert and bread roll.In addition to Vietnamese cuisine, business class travellers are treated to dishes from around the world, depending on their destination. On flights to South Korea, mixed fried rice, or bibimbap, makes an appearance on the menu, alongside other dishes like ginseng chicken soup (samgyetang) and black bean noodles (jajangmyeon).While on trips to Europe, expect to dine on French, German and British cuisine. Further, business class travellers to European, Australian and American destinations can pre-order their meals.The world’s best airport for diningLondon Heathrow was crowned the World’s Best for Airport Dining 2026, outranking Dubai International, Hamad International Airport in Qatar, Hong Kong International Airport, John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York, Paris Aéroport, and Singapore Changi Airport.Across Heathrow’s four terminals, passengers can choose from a range of casual, café and international dining concepts.Heathrow also offers what it describes as “dining in style”, where the likes of Terminal 2’s Le Café Louis Vuitton features. Guests can choose from sweet treats, such as the hazelnut flower dessert, a morsel of hazelnut ganache, tender praline and fleur de sel, which sports the brand’s iconic monogram flower.While in Terminal 5, celebrity chef Gordan Ramsay’s Plane Food Market serves up all-day breakfast, pizza, sushi, noodles and traditional British favourite, fish and chips.The world’s best airline lounge for diningTurkish Airlines' International Lounges were awarded the World's Best Airline Lounge for Dining. Other nominees included Air France’s La Première First Class Lounge in Paris-Charles de Gaulle, Etihad Airways’ First Class Lounge and Spa at Zayed International Airport, and Lufthansa’s First Class Lounge at Frankfurt Airport.Qatar Airways’ Al Safwa First Class Lounge at Hamad International Airport, SWISS’ First Class Lounge at Zürich Airport, Thai Airways’ Royal Orchid Prestige Lounge at Suvarnabhumi Airport, and Virgin Atlantic’s Clubhouse at London Heathrow Airport were also nominated.At Turkish Airlines’ international lounges, in locations such as Edinburgh International Airport, guests can dine on Turkish and world cuisine, with hot and cold offerings at the buffet.The world's best airport lounge for diningClubrooms at Gatwick South Terminal was awarded the World’s Best Airport Lounge for Dining 2026.Other nominees included Blue Sky Premier Lounge in Terminal 1C at Soekarno-Hatta International Airport in Indonesia, Plaza Premium First Hong Kong, Plaza Premium Lounge in Terminal 3 at Dubai International, SkyTeam Lounge at Sydney Airport in Australia, and the Star Alliance Lounge at Los Angeles International Airport.Gatwick's Clubrooms offers menus that are seasonally updated with a range of hot and cold dishes to choose from, alongside light bites and nibbles. For breakfast, eggs benedict and Belgian waffles feature on the menu.While for evening dining, chicken Caesar salad, gochujang chicken thigh bowl and Moroccan nut roast with green beans in lemon olive oil are just some of the menu items.

title: France slips into contraction as Europe’s growth slows: How bad could it get?
description: France’s private sector contracted this month, dragging eurozone business activity growth to a four-month low amid political uncertainty and high energy costs.
content: France's return to growth lasted just one month. Business activity contracted again in October, while confidence among French companies fell to its lowest level since the first Covid-19 lockdowns in 2020.The drop pulled the wider eurozone down with it.The eurozone's composite purchasing managers' index (PMI), which measures activity across manufacturing and services, fell to 51.9 in October from 53.1 in September.It was the weakest reading in four months, although the index remains above 50, the threshold separating growth from contraction. Economists had expected a smaller decline to 52.7.The services and manufacturing indices also came in lower than expected, albeit still signalling modest expansion.The latest survey suggests Europe's recovery is losing momentum just as inflation is making it harder for the European Central Bank (ECB) to ease borrowing costs.So is this a pause in growth, or the start of something worse?What went wrong in France?France recorded the sharpest deterioration among the eurozone's two largest economies. Its composite PMI dropped to 48.4 from 51.1 in September, well below the 50.5 economists had forecast.The services activity index fell to 48.4, while the manufacturing index slipped to 49.3, its lowest level in 11 months.Companies reported that customers were postponing projects and delaying spending decisions.
