New orders fell at their fastest pace since May, and export business declined for an eleventh consecutive month.Employment fell too.French businesses cut staff for the sixth month running, largely by leaving vacant positions unfilled and allowing temporary contracts to expire.But the figures on business confidence were considerably worse. Expectations for the next 12 months fell to their lowest level since April 2020, when the pandemic had brought much of the French economy to a halt.The survey also recorded negative business expectations for the first time in almost two years.Joe Hayes, senior principal economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence, linked the deterioration to France's political and fiscal problems.The sentiment reading, he said, "reflects firms' concerns about what is shaping up to be a highly uncertain 2027 Presidential Election, compounding pre-existing worries about France's fiscal situation."France's political uncertainty has been accompanied by a sharp increase in government borrowing costs. That matters for businesses because rising interest rates make loans more expensive and can discourage investment, even without further ECB rate increases."Unsurprisingly, the volatile political situation and spike in government borrowing costs meant the downturn in the French composite PMI weighed on the overall picture," said Rory Fennessy, senior economist at Oxford Economics.France had only returned to growth in September after months of contraction. The October numbers suggest that recovery has already run out of steam.Is Germany holding up any better?Germany offered a more encouraging picture, although growth also slowed.The country's composite PMI eased to 52.8 from an 11-month high of 53.8 in September. Economists had expected 53.3.Factories continued to expand. Germany's manufacturing PMI rose to 54.2, its highest reading in two months, supported by export orders and government spending on defence and infrastructure.Services were weaker, with the index falling to 51.7. Companies in that sector reported that customers were delaying decisions and holding back spending as budgets tightened.Phil Smith, economics associate director at S&P Global Market Intelligence, said the slowdown "underscored that the recovery in the eurozone's largest economy remains fragile."Germany's factories also face a problem that could become more serious in the coming months. Manufacturers reported the fastest increase in input costs since May, particularly for oil, raw materials and electronic components.Brent crude was trading near $114 a barrel on Friday, adding to the pressure on energy-intensive industries.Confidence among manufacturers fell to its lowest level since July."A renewed surge in cost pressures has dampened expectations across the sector, with the two likely to remain intrinsically linked in the months ahead," Smith said.Germany is benefiting from stronger factory orders, but companies are increasingly concerned about how much it will cost to fulfil them.Why rising prices are becoming a problem for the ECBThe increase in costs extends beyond Germany. Across the eurozone, manufacturers reported higher prices for energy, fuel and transport, while supplier delivery times lengthened by the most in four months.Chris Williamson, chief business economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence, said the survey still points to quarterly GDP growth of around 0.3%. But "higher interest rates are also starting to take a toll, dampening demand," he said.With inflation remaining stubborn, Williamson said the figures "will likely add to further speculation of more aggressive policy tightening from the ECB."That could mean higher borrowing costs for businesses and households, even as economic growth slows.French stocks and bonds remain under pressureFrance's CAC 40 fell 0.7% on Friday morning to around 7,750 points, more than 11% below its 10 August closing high.Italy's FTSE MIB was broadly flat after Thursday's 2.5% decline, and is also down more than 10% from its August peak.French government bonds have suffered an even sharper sell-off. The 10-year yield reached 5.14% on Thursday, its highest since 2002, before easing to around 5.04% on Friday.The gap with German 10-year yields stood at 170 basis points, more than double the 78 basis points recorded in early August.France now also pays around 45 basis points more than Italy to borrow for ten years. The euro was also under pressure, trading near $1.12, more than 4% below its August high.A weaker euro can make imported energy more expensive, adding another source of inflation at a time when European manufacturers are already paying more for fuel and materials.Is Europe heading for another recession?The October business surveys are disappointing, but they do not yet suggest the eurozone is heading into recession.There are, however, reasons to be cautious.French companies are facing political uncertainty and rising borrowing costs. German manufacturers are struggling with higher energy prices, while businesses across the region are reporting weaker demand.The ECB must now decide how much further it can raise borrowing costs to contain inflation without causing more damage to growth.September's strong business surveys had raised hopes that Europe's recovery was finally gaining ground.The October figures have called that into question, particularly in France, where companies are already cutting jobs and reporting their weakest expectations in more than six years.

title: French kids use AI far more than their parents think, survey finds
description: A new YouGov survey has found parents in France underestimate their children’s use of AI. While 40% of 11- to 12-year-olds report using general-purpose AI services like ChatGPT weekly, only 26% of parents realise their children are engaging with the technology.
content: A new YouGov survey of French teenagers and their parents has shed light on their differing experiences and attitudes to artificial intelligence, revealing that parents significantly underestimate their children’s use of AI and do not feel supported enough to help them understand how to use it appropriately.The survey found that while 40% of 11- to 12-year-olds report using general-purpose AI weekly, just 26% of parents realise their children are doing so — a glaring 14 percentage point gap. It also found that 42% of parents do not feel supported at all in helping their kids understand how to use AI responsibly.Artificial intelligence is becoming embedded in just about every aspect of children’s lives, from helping with homework and research to AI companions and features in social media and gaming.It is unknown yet what the full impact will be on them as they grow up, learn and engage with the world, but the debate over who should bear responsibility for this is shifting.2026 has been a watershed year for Big Tech companies, one that has seen awareness over the impact of their platforms on children’s wellbeing and mental health enter the spotlight.From Australia’s social media bans for children to the litany of lawsuits in the US against tech companies accused of worsening the country’s mental health crisis, and the EU’s latest proposal to rein in platforms — known as the EU Kids Act — people and authorities are growing ever more scrutinising of how digital platforms operate and how best to curb their influence.It also comes at a time when France’s youth is taking to the streets in protest against the deterioration of school infrastructure, severe teacher shortages and an unfair university admission system, while the government is rolling out massive investments in AI infrastructure.Berlin-based NGO Interface commissioned YouGov to carry out an online survey earlier this year exploring these issues in relation to the explosion in the use of artificial intelligence platforms and services among kids and teens in France.The survey took place in France from 24 to 30 June this year. 1138 parents of children aged 11-17 and 970 kids aged 11-17 took part by answering a questionnaire including examples of different AI categories.Categories included general-purpose generative AI such as OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude, AI companions such as Character.AI, generative AI embedded in social media like Snapchat’s My AI and AI voice assistants such as Siri.Respondents were recruited from YouGov’s online panel and with parental consent for the children taking part.Kids are using AI more and starting earlierWhile artificial intelligence has truly entered the mainstream in the last couple of years, the survey reveals just how much it is already a part of children’s lives.Adoption of AI tools start early, with 56% of 11–12-year-old respondents saying they use at least one type of generative AI tool like ChatGPT once a week, with 40% of them using general-purpose AI weekly and 33% using voice assistants like Alexa.A further 23% of 11–12-year-olds reported using AI embedded social media such as Snapchat’s My AI, and 16% — roughly one in six children — use AI companions to chat and converse with.“The AI chatbot is also like having a friend that is available 24/7. It doesn't get tired and it always agrees with you,” says Jessica Galissaire, a senior policy researcher at Interface.The Interface researcher also says that 11-12-year-olds should not even have access to according to the platform’s own terms and conditions, such as Character.AI, which requires children be 16 years old in the EU.Another worrying trend is that the younger the child is, the more their parents underestimate their AI use.56% of 11-12-year-olds reported using generative AI tools regularly, while their parents estimated 44% do. For 13–15-year-olds it is 62%, with their parents estimating 52%. And for 16-17-year-olds, 70% use AI regularly, with the parents believing 61% do — showing the gap narrows with age, however, use consistently increases across the board.This growth in use with age is recognised by teenagers too, with the survey showing they feel that AI is keeping them on platforms longer than they want.“92% of generative AI users say they spend more time than they would like on it also, you know, points to not, I don't want to say addiction, but it's still a widespread feeling of spending too much time with it than intended,” said Galissaire.Among the individual categories, AI companions (59%) and those integrated into social media (57%) scored the highest figures when children were asked if they spent more time with them than they wanted to.Parents want helpThe survey also revealed just how vulnerable parents in France feel in raising their children to deal artificial intelligence and the challenges it raises.“Only 32% of them feel supported enough in helping their children navigate their AI use, 26% feel supported but not enough and 42% of them don't feel supported at all,” said Galissaire, arguing that those who are more vulnerable or use AI the least feel particularly left behind.“For the parents who don't have that knowledge or are less digitally literate or don't have the time, it's even more complex for them to put in place parental control tools and to discuss with their kids,” added the Interface researcher.As to who should help them educate and protect their children when using artificial intelligence services and platforms, it’s a complex picture.A surprising 51% of parents said teachers and schools should bear responsibility, while just 41% felt the platform companies themselves should shoulder the burden, followed by public authorities at 30%, showing that parents feel it should be addressed by both governments and educational institutions as well as by the AI companies responsible for the platforms.What is being doneThe findings of the report raise questions about how effectively the EU’s proposed Kids Act will protect children who are already using AI services at a young age, particularly when many parents say they don’t feel supported enough to help them.The European Commission presented its proposal in September as a way to strengthen platform accountability and shift the burden onto Big Tech companies to make their platforms safer for children.“Today, our children are engaging with the most sophisticated technologies ever created... Our Kids Act is reversing the burden of proof - it is for platforms to show they are safe by design,” said European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in September.The proposal promises age limits, parental controls and a crackdown on the "addictive" features baked into social media, video platforms and AI chatbots alike.It also calls for a total, blanket social media ban for under-13s, while those up to 15 years old would be able to make "mini accounts" — limited, highly supervised profiles linked to a parent's profile.But Galissare believes, based on the survey’s findings, that parental controls and age restrictions won’t be enough.“I'm more in favour of forcing platforms to be safe by design rather than imposing age bans that are tricky to implement for many reasons and also don't seem to work,” she says.She also warns that social media bans “give a false sense of security, as long as it's not properly implemented, because parents may think, okay, there's a ban, so I can give a phone to my kids and not watch what they are doing anymore.”Adding, “Regulation in itself will never be enough. Prevention and empowerment must play a huge role as well.”

title: Pope Leo XIV cancels Assisi trip on doctors' advice as he recovers from surgery
description: The pope's doctors said a follow-up chest X-ray confirmed he was recovering well. However, given the short time that has elapsed since the operation, they recommended as a precaution that he not make the trip to Assisi by helicopter.
content: Pope Leo XIV will miss a planned trip to Assisi next week after doctors advised against the helicopter journey to the Italian town as he recovers from thoracic surgery, the Vatican said Friday.He had been due to attend a gathering on Tuesday marking the 40th anniversary of St. John Paul II’s World Day of Prayer for Peace.In a statement, the Vatican said the pope was advised not to travel “to facilitate his recovery” from the surgery to treat his lung cancer last week. The pope will instead send a message to organisers, Christian and other religious leaders, and guests attending the event, titled “Disarmed and Disarming Peace.”The Assisi meeting commemorates the landmark interfaith peace gathering convened by St. John Paul II in 1986.The Vatican said Pope Leo XIV wanted to express his closeness to participants and reaffirm his belief that the “spirit of Assisi,” dialogue and the search for words and gestures of peace remain valuable resources at a time of conflict.In a separate statement, the pope's doctors said a follow-up chest X-ray confirmed he was recovering well. However, given the short time that has elapsed since the operation, they recommended as a precaution that he not make the trip to Assisi by helicopter.The pope had part of one lung removed last week in the first major health event of his 17-month pontificate. The surgery confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer.The pope will need no further treatment for lung cancer after tests confirmed the disease was localised, the Vatican said.

title: New 007 incoming: James Bond casting down to these actors according to insider reports
description: An official announcement regarding the new actor to portray James Bond is expected soon... And if reports are to be believed, one actor is emerging as the favourite to play the new 007.
content: We're in the final stretch, as Amazon MGM Studios are reportedly setting their final auditions for the casting of the new 007 this weekend and next week.According to various reports, the race to find the next James Bond actor is now down to the final three. Or four.One report from an industry insider revealed that the shortlist only has three names. “A few weeks ago, I was told that the race to become the next James Bond had narrowed to three names: Jacob Elordi, Jack Lowden and an undisclosed third actor,” said World Of Reel’s Jordan Ruimy. “What I’m hearing is that an announcement could come anytime between the last week of October and early November.”Jeff Sneider at The InSneider has claimed that Elordi and Lowden are among the actors who have recently completed screen tests for the role.In contrast, The Hollywood Reporter has revealed that neither Jack O’Connell (Danny Boyle's favourite for 007) nor Elordi will be testing. Elsewhere, sources have told Deadline that four test offers have been given out to Jack Lowden, Callum Turner, Josh O'Connor – with no mention of Elordi. The identity of the fourth actor remains a mystery – even if many are speculating that Jack Barton is still in the running.Josh O'Connor is the wildcard here, as his name has not been mentioned as being amongst the favourites for 007. The star of Challengers, Wake Up Dead Man (in which he shared the screen with former James Bond actor Daniel Craig) and Disclosure Day has proven he has the acting chops, and he could be an interesting left-field turn for 007. Speculation continues, but as we reported earlier this week, considering the shocking cliffhanger ending of the popular Apple TV show Slow Horses, signs look promising when it comes to Jack Lowden – who seems to be the common denominator of all the recent insider reports. The 36-year-old Scottish actor is best known for playing River Cartwright in Slow Horses but has been seen on the big screen in Christopher Nolan's Dunkirk, Mary Queen of Scots (2018) and Benediction (2021). He will appear later this year as Mr Darcy in Netflix's new adaptation of "Pride and Prejudice". Earlier this year, Euronews Culture reported that the official casting for Bond was underway and that Lowden would be an ideal candidate for the 007 mantle. We wrote regarding Lowden: " Spy credentials? Check. Charisma levels? Suit him up. Pre-existing rapport with the casting director? Done. Married to Saoirse Ronan who has previously expressed an interest in being cast as a Bond villain? Make this happen." An exact timeline for finalizing casting is not known. What we do know is that it's happening this year, as Bond 26 producer Amy Pascal revealed in August that "the end of the year is a good bet" for the official announcement. “We are being really, really methodical," said Pascal in August. "Having worked with Barbara Broccoli at the studio, I mean, Daniel Craig is a hard act to follow. And it’s got to be something really different that is stirring, exciting and different.” Bond 26 will be directed by Canadian filmmaker and four-time Oscar nominee Denis Villeneuve and is being written by Peaky Blinders creator Steven Knight. It will be the first Bond film since Amazon took full creative control over the franchise from longtime 007 custodians Barbara Broccoli and Michael G Wilson. Production on the next Bond film is expected to kick off in 2027, with a release planned for 2028.

title: Fitch Ratings: Hungary could meet eurozone entry criteria by 2030
description: According to the credit rating agency, Hungary’s 2027 draft budget supports its aim of meeting the conditions for adopting the euro by the end of the decade.
content: The Hungarian government's draft budget for 2027 and its medium-term deficit targets support its aim of meeting the conditions for joining the eurozone by 2030, Fitch Ratings said in an assessment published on Thursday.According to the 2027 draft budget presented by Prime Minister Péter Magyar on Monday, the government intends to cut the general government deficit to 4.9% of GDP, from the 7.5% expected for this year.The budget includes planned spending cuts worth 1.5% of GDP next year. On top of this, the expiry of temporary and one-off pre-election measures could save a further 1.4%. The budget also counts on lower interest payments of up to 0.2% of GDP, "reflecting declining costs on inflation-linked bonds and lower Hungarian sovereign yields amid improved market sentiment," Fitch said.The government also plans tax increases and other measures to raise additional revenue worth about 1% of GDP.The proposed spending cuts would affect some economic-development subsidies, government communications, public media, and state investment and operating costs. These include a planned reduction of at least 10% in the operating expenditure of ministries and state-owned companies.The government expects tax increases to raise 0.25% of GDP through higher corporate and innovation taxation, 0.2% from a wealth tax, and 0.1% from a levy on energy companies, with smaller amounts coming from increases in mining royalties, company-car tax and advertising tax.However, Fitch warned that putting the overall deficit-reduction plan into practice would be challenging, given the "large number of relatively small measures and the need for sustained consolidation".Some savings remain uncertain, while new spending commitments and tax relief worth about 1.4% of GDP would offset part of the gains.Fitch emphasised the importance of meeting Hungary’s 2027 fiscal target, describing it as "an important measure of the credibility of the government’s frontloaded fiscal consolidation strategy under its plans to meet euro-adoption criteria by 2030". The government's plan sets out a deficit of 4% of GDP in 2028, falling more gradually thereafter, to 3.4% in 2029 and 2.8% in 2030.Fitch's own forecasts put Hungary’s budget deficit on a similar path, narrowing to 5.4% of GDP in 2027, from 7.3% in 2026, and eventually falling below 3% by 2030.According to the agency’s projections, Hungary’s public debt will peak at 77.7% of GDP in 2027–2028, well above the 57.5% median for countries in Fitch’s “BBB” sovereign rating category. The subsequent path of Hungary’s debt will also depend on the forint’s exchange rate and economic growth, Fitch said.Growth has lagged behind that of countries with a similar rating since 2023, Fitch said, putting it down to weak external demand, heightened policy uncertainty, delayed EU funding inflows, and the impact of efforts to reduce the deficit on investment.The Hungarian government expects GDP growth of 2.4% in 2027, accelerating to above 3% by 2030. This could come in part from higher EU-funded investment. The EU recently unfroze €4.2 billion in funding for Hungary, part of a wider €16.4 billion agreement, with access to the remaining funds still subject to approval.The government’s growth outlook is broadly in line with Fitch’s forecasts of real GDP growth of 2.5% in 2027, accelerating to about 3% from 2028, supported by stronger investment and private consumption as EU funds are deployed, and by a recovery in external demand.Meeting the budget targets alone would not qualify Hungary to adopt the euro. Countries must also meet conditions covering inflation, long-term interest rates, exchange-rate stability and national legislation.Political and economic risk consultancy Eurasia Group also considers it possible that Hungary could join the eurozone in 2032, according to a report of its assessment.If Hungary were to enter ERM II, the exchange-rate mechanism that is mandatory before adopting the euro, in 2030, it could potentially join the eurozone in 2032 or later. Countries must spend at least two years in ERM II without severe exchange-rate tensions or devaluing their currency’s central rate against the euro, and meet the other entry conditions.

title: Euronews Culture's Film of the Week: 'Clayface' – Gloopy, gruesome, but not quite great
description: An admirably dark and wince-inducing detour for DC Studios, who get a lot right with 'Clayface' when it comes to horror. However, the script lets it down in the second half, leading to a bold but uneven result.
content: Not many movies have dared to fuse superheroes with horror.Wes Craven dared with Swamp Thing. Sam Raimi followed suit with Darkman. And David Yarovesky also tried the merger with Brightburn, the 2019 horror twist on Superman, which was produced by none other than James Gunn, the current co-CEO of DC Studios.For the third film in the first chapter of their DC Universe, titled "Chapter One: Gods And Monsters", Gunn and co-chief Peter Safran focus on the "monster" part. They bank on a lesser-known Batman villain and orchestrate an admirably dark, more modestly budgeted ($40 million) detour for the studio, following the more bombastic and wholesome adventures of Superman and Supergirl. Clayface stars relatively unknown Welsh actor Tom Rhys Harries as Matt Hagen, a pretty-boy actor whose star is on the rise. From very modest beginnings to award nominations, the chiselled and blue-eyed hunk now has everything going for him. One night, he celebrates by hooking up with a young woman he meets on the dance floor. Snag is she happens to be the girlfriend of a knife-happy Gotham City mobster, Markos Szabo (David Dencik), who retaliates by carving open Matt's face. Repeatedly. Matt's penknifed mouth, slashed cheekbones and destroyed nose mean that his looks are now no longer screen-ready. Desperate to get his heartthrob life and acting prospects back, the disfigured thesp turns to Dr. Caitlyn Corr (the always wonderful Naomi Ackie), a scientist on the cutting edge of nanotechnology who injects him with her experimental serum of stem cells. Powered by artificial intelligence, the unapproved mixture can regenerate dead human tissue and Matt begs Caitlyn to become her first human guinea pig. The initial results seem promising until some unforeseen, face-melty side effects rear their ugly head. This sends Matt into a violent, revenge-fuelled spiral that leads him to inject himself with all of the good doctor's nanocells... Clayface works as a bleak and surprisingly gory origin story, a refreshingly standalone adventure which embraces body-horror with both hands. There's the initial slash attack, with the camera not panning away from all the cutting and peeling; a lot of visceral reconstructive surgery nastiness; and a wince-inducing plane bathroom scene involving Matt trying to keep his fusing eyes open by introducing his peepers to a pair of nail scissors.It's not for the squeamish, but as impressively gory as it is, where Clayface noticeably sags is the (somewhat aptly) skin-deep script, which doesn't live up to the splendid use of practical effects and prosthetics. It stalls in developing its characters, and fails to compellingly explore the narrative's thematic potential or the promise behind Matt's various transformations. From his scarred mug to a nascent ability to alter his face to resemble other people, there was plenty to mine here about the superficiality of beauty standards and the shallow nature of Hollywood. Moreover, when your lead actor sells both the unsettling and heartbreaking toll of his transformations, more could have been achieved regarding the psychological and metaphorical weight inherent to a tragic hero's path to becoming undone by a fatal flaw.No one was expecting an in-depth character study, but some meaningful elaboration regarding the loss of identity was warranted.Instead, director James Watkins (Eden Lake, Speak No Evil) settles for a more generic and predictable second half, in which it becomes tempting to speculate what could have been... You see, the project was originally brought to Gunn and Safran by Mike Flanagan (Midnight Mass, The Haunting of Hill House, Carrie). Due to scheduling conflicts, Flanagan never got to direct Clayface and his script was overhauled by Hossein Amini (Drive, Snow White and the Huntsman). In the film's droopier moments (clunky dialogue, a clumsy backstory regarding Matt's downtrodden origins, a shoehorned romantic subplot between Matt and Caitlyn), it makes you wish that Flanagan had been given the reins and delivered a tighter version of Clayface.It's a damn shame, as the Brian Yuzna aspects and nods to both The Fly and Eyes Without A Face were very promising, and Harries shows he has the acting chops to carry a movie. However, like Milly Alcock in Supergirl, his efforts aren't rewarded by anything particularly new or radical.Congrats to DC Studios for taking a chance and delivering something nastier and gorier than any other blockbuster offering. It's certainly different and a significantly – nay, massively - superior to previous rogue flicks like Morbius, Madame Web or Kraven The Hunter. But as gnarly and queasy as Clayface is, the story and its characters still needed to actually get under your skin to be truly memorable.Clayface is out in cinemas now.

title: 'Music is medicine': RAYE wins Mercury Prize 2026 for her second album 'This Music May Contain Hope'
description: British jazz and soul artist RAYE beat competition from heavyweights including Paul McCartney, Florence + The Machine and favourite Olivia Dean. The Mercury Prize honours the best album released by a British or Irish artist each year.
content: RAYE has been crowned the winner of this year's Mercury Prize, taking home the coveted statue for her second album 'This Music May Contain Hope'.The British artist, born Rachel Keen, beat favourite Olivia Dean, as well as JADE, Florence + The Machine, the War Child 'Help (2)' compilation album and Paul McCartney - who was shortlisted for the first time, aged 84, with his new record, 'The Boys of Dungeon Lane'. The judges praised 'This Music May Contain Hope', which features the hit single 'Where Is My Husband!', for combining old-school Hollywood glamour with kitchen sink realism to tell “a story about a young woman navigating the everyday trials of life and love, on an album that is joyous and indeed hopeful”. “RAYE displays real imagination and scope in showing what an album can be, going beyond any one style or genre to realise her vision,” according to a jury statement. “The judges agreed that RAYE’S’s superb album will serve as a huge inspiration for years to come.” Accepting the award, RAYE said: “I cannot tell you how grateful I am to be holding this. I’m shaking, I’m jetlagged, I’m tired, I’m grateful, it’s all blurry.” “I’ve always banged on about how much I believe in albums,” she continued. “Albums are so important. And not to be bitter, because I feel like I’m mostly at peace with my past, you know? But to come from a place where it’s all about singles and chasing the next thing, I just feel so grateful to be recognised.” RAYE's comments refer to her previously parting ways with her record label after accusing them of refusing to let her release her debut album. She released 'My 21st Century Blues' in 2023 as an independent artist.She also described music as "medicine", saying: “The tears are going to flow now, so I’m just going to say ‘This Music May Contain Hope’. ‘Hope’ is a very cheesy word, especially for us British. We don’t do that kind of deep stuff like that, but hope is just something that we all need. Music is that, music is medicine. I just hope that message comes across to anyone who needs it and thank you so much for this prize.” This was the second time that RAYE was nominated for the Mercury Prize, following 'My 21st Century Blues', which led her to break the BRIT Awards record for the most wins in a single year, with six awards in 2024. RAYE follows in the footsteps of past Mercury winners Sam Fender, Ezra Collective, Michael Kiwanuka, Little Simz, Arlo Parks and Young Fathers, as well as Arctic Monkeys, Pulp, PJ Harvey and Franz Ferdinand. This year's edition of the annual awards, which honours the best album released by a British or Irish artist each year, took place at the Utilita Arena in Newcastle on Thursday evening.

title: Central Park’s horse-drawn carriages face ban as New York votes to end tourist attraction
description: Horse-drawn carriage rides could end in Central Park in June 2028, following years of debate over animal welfare and public safety.
content: One of New York’s longest-running tourist attractions could be reaching the end of the road, after the city council voted to ban horse-drawn carriages in Central Park.Horse-drawn carriages have been part of Central Park since the mid-19th century and the vote on 22 October signals a possible end to a tradition that has sparked years of heated debate. Mayor Zohran Mamdani must still sign the measure into law. He has previously supported a ban but has also raised concerns about protections for workers in the industry. If signed into law, the ban will take effect in June 2028.The lead-up is meant to help the approximately 150 active carriage drivers find new employment, city council speaker Julie Menin told journalists ahead of the vote.The Transport Workers Union, which represents the drivers, has vowed legal action.Legislative battles over the fate of the cultural tradition that's nearly as old as Central Park itself have been ongoing for nearly two decades.Critics say the animals suffer, pointing to deadly collapses and dangerous escapes, while supporters point to the jobs the industry supports and the heritage it preserves.The bill includes a provision for exploring potential compensation for licence holders, Menin said.It mandates that owners of the nearly 200 horses would not be allowed to sell them for slaughter or for the purposes of other horse-carriage businesses.The rides – enshrined in film and television including Robert Redford and Jane Fonda's scene in “Barefoot in the Park”, or a dramatic ride in "Sex and the City" – can cost $150 (€134) for 45 minutes, while for a special occasion such as a marriage proposal it can cost up to several hundred dollars.But after years of wrangling over the issue this past summer season proved decisive in sounding the death knell for the Manhattan carriages.This past June an 18-year-old tourist from India was killed by a horse that got loose and bolted.That followed a series of other incidents with the carriages, including the deaths of several horses.The Central Park Conservancy, which manages the US's most frequented urban park with 42 million annual visits, threw its weight behind the calls for a ban, saying it had become “a matter of public health and safety”.

title: EU and Canada draw closer in Trump’s unpredictable world – with Britain looking on
description: The EU and Canada are hoping to deepen ties at their upcoming Montreal summit, in areas like trade, energy, defence and critical minerals. Meanwhile, the UK is seeking its own reset with Brussels.
content: The European Union has offered Canada something it has never offered another country: associate membership. Quite what that means remains unclear, but Brussels and Ottawa are determined to turn their shared values and increasingly close relationship into a new kind of partnership in a world shaken by Donald Trump's unpredictable foreign policy.The experiment is being watched closely in London, where Prime Minister Andy Burnham is seeking to rebuild Britain's post-Brexit relationship with the EU, raising the question of whether a similar arrangement might eventually be available to the UK.The offer, made by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen last month, has raised questions about whether associate membership is a meaningful new status, an honorary title or something in between.At a summit in Montreal next week, the two sides will begin putting substance behind the idea, seeking closer cooperation on trade, defence, technology and energy without Canada formally joining the bloc.But while Canada is searching for a new framework, Britain is attempting to improve an existing one, with EU and UK leaders set to meet next month to seek a much-needed reset in their relationship."This is a moment to act with clarity and ambition. By aligning more closely - economically, technologically, and strategically - Canada and the EU are building an Alliance for the Future based on trust and shared values," reads the latest draft of the EU-Canada joint statement, discussed by ambassadors on Wednesday.A blank sheetSince European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen invited Canada last month to become the EU’s first “associate member,” Brussels and Ottawa have been exploring what this privileged partnership could look like.Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney prefers to talk about an “Alliance for the Future.” He has sidestepped questions on whether he is comfortable with the “associate membership” label, stressing that substance matters more.The summit in Montreal on 29-30 October is the first real chance to define the partnership in more detail. The latest draft uses “associate membership” interchangeably with “Alliance for the Future.”Crucially, the proposal envisages giving Canada a more regular place at the EU's table, with participation in summits, ministerial meetings and technical discussions.It calls for "early consultations on major policy and regulatory initiatives, with Canada’s participation in these processes as an associate member of the Union."Whether the term survives in the final text is an open question. In any case, “the full scope of this associate membership will be defined by the 2027 Canada-EU Summit,” the conclusions read.From trade to defenceThe document nonetheless tries to put more meat on the bone. It builds on the 2016 Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA), which 10 EU countries have yet to ratify, to remove remaining trade barriers and ensure reciprocal market access.“We will ensure mutually favourable treatment in our respective economic security measures, based on the principle of reciprocity in industrial sectors where both sides have agreed to align their external measures to ensure the same outcome,” the draft statement reads.On energy, the conclusions open the door to “the development of liquefied natural gas exchanges,” notably through a joint long-term feasibility study on LNG exports to Europe.On technology, Canada will join the EU’s supercomputer initiative, a new digital partnership will tackle issues like AI and digital identity, and an agreement to facilitate cross-border data flows is in the making.Critical raw materials, one of Canada’s key assets for the EU, are also on the table. The two sides have agreed that the European Investment Bank will play a role in critical mineral projects, from extraction and processing to manufacturing and recycling.In defence, Canada is already part of several EU projects, including the Permanent Structured Cooperation and the Capability Coalition, and both sides intend to deepen that cooperation on maritime security, crisis management and industrial cooperation.The partners also envisage a cooperation framework to safeguard the information space and protect electoral integrity, with an early warning mechanism and a dialogue dedicated to foreign interference.Other areas under discussion include border security cooperation with EU agency Frontex, criminal justice, climate security, transport and the Arctic.Taken together, the proposals suggest a partnership extending far beyond conventional trade agreements, even if its institutional form remains uncertain.Searching for a resetThe EU's growing closeness to Canada comes as Britain searches for a new relationship with the bloc, a decade after the Brexit referendum.The contrast is striking. While Ottawa is being offered an undefined but potentially far-reaching new status, London is still negotiating improvements to its relationship with Brussels, largely one sector at a time.The next EU-UK summit, postponed from the summer following Keir Starmer's resignation and Burnham's arrival in Downing Street, offers an opportunity to make progress.While the UK government was already searching for amending ties with the bloc, Canada's approach to the EU definitively shattered one of the Brexiteers' key hopes to turn the so-called Anglosphere into a free trade area encompassing the UK, US, Canada, Australia and New Zealand."It is hardly surprising that Brexit has not delivered on that promise, and UK opinion polls have slowly started to shift in favour of rejoining," Charles Tannock, a former Conservative MEP who campaigned for Remain, told Euronews.Since becoming Prime Minister, Burnham has repeatedly signalled that he wants to take the UK closer to the EU. He considers the status quo “not good enough” and has vowed to consider options ranging from following Canada’s example to re-entering the bloc.While Burnham has restarted the domestic debate about rejoining the EU, the post-Brexit relationship between Brussels and London has not always been easy, with some UK officials asking why "associate membership" should not also be available for them.“In an ideal world, with the UK we have even closer ties to the extent that the UK is a European country and if it wishes so, the ambition should not be an associate membership, but full membership,” Tobias Cremer (Germany/S&D), a leading lawmaker on EU-Canada relations, told Euronews.Moving forwardSpeaking during a European Parliament debate on Wednesday, Bernd Lange, the German Socialist who chairs the Trade Committee, welcomed a “new mood” in EU-UK relations. He suggested that Britain could pursue an arrangement resembling Switzerland's relationship with the bloc, alongside closer political and security cooperation and a customs union.But Brussels rejected the Swiss model as a template for Britain during the Brexit negotiations.Switzerland's complex network of bilateral agreements has long frustrated EU officials, who argue that such arrangements are difficult to oversee and enforce, particularly when they provide access to parts of the single market without all the accompanying obligations.Instead, British and EU negotiators are focusing on specific agreements covering agricultural trade, emissions trading and youth mobility.A recent Franco-German proposal to include the UK in the 'Made in Europe' rules removed one sore point, but London is hoping to extend it to other sectors where it sees EU industrial policy becoming increasingly protectionist.In defence, the EU needs the UK as part of a broader European security architecture, but the two sides failed to agree to include Britain in the planned Security Action for Europe (SAFE) for defence procurement.Brussels offered Canada much better terms for SAFE, with a token upfront payment of around €10m. It asked the UK for a whopping €6.5bn, with no guarantee its industry would win any contracts, leading to a breakdown in the negotiations.“Burnham is on a learning curve, to be honest," Tannock said. "He needs to. He’s been the mayor of Manchester for some years. He hasn’t been focused on this issue. He will be trying to get fully up to speed with what’s available."Peggy Corlin contributed to the reporting.

title: Forget the festive rush: Take on Europe’s ‘slowest marathon’ in Vilnius this Christmas
description: Lithuania’s capital city Vilnius will host a slower kind of 'race-cation' this festive season where participants can forget about watching their pace and instead enjoy a leisurely walk among festive settings.
content: Running a marathon is undoubtedly a bucket list ambition for many people – and the rise of “race-cations” has seen active travellers plan holidays around running and endurance events. But what if you could complete a marathon without watching your pace or hitting the dreaded “wall”, and instead enjoy regular stops for cinnamon buns, festive lights and warming drinks? Sounds pretty good, right? That’s exactly what the Go Vilnius tourism development agency is proposing with its new “Europe’s slowest marathon” campaign, which encourages visitors to explore the Lithuanian capital at a leisurely pace this Christmas – rather than battling the usual festive rush and crowds.Open to city residents and visitors with no registration required, the slowest Christmas marathon on 12-13 December 2026 will have routes ranging from 3km to 42.195km, with 10km and 21km options also available. Held alongside Vilnius’ main Christmas attractions, the routes will take visitors through lesser-known corners of the walkable city. Stops will include Senatorių Pasažas (Senators’ Passage), a historic courtyard where visitors can try a popular cinnamon bun, and the Užupis Cat, a sculpture in the bohemian district. Routes will also pass through streets with festive names such as Žiemos (Winter), Šerkšno (Frost), Sniego (Snow), and Elnių (Deer).While taking place on the main weekend of 12-13 December, digital route maps for the "marathon" will be available until 3 January 2027. “Christmas has become a season of rushing from one thing to the next,” said Eglė Girdzijauskaitė, head of communication at Go Vilnius. “We wanted to turn that idea on its head. “In Vilnius, you can take your time – the city is compact, the distances are short, and there is no need to hurry. It offers sparkling lights of its UNESCO-listed Old Town, warm cafés tucked into historic courtyards, and the magical glow of the tree in Cathedral Square. So why not make the slowest marathon possible?” Christmas in Vilnius: Other festive attractionsAs well as the slowest marathon, Vilnius has many other attractions and experiences for visitors to enjoy this winter. The city’s festive season will open on 28 November with the annual Christmas Tree Lighting. Also on the calendar is the Christmas Market in Cathedral Square from 28 November to 27 December, the Christmas Ice Rink at Town Hall Square from 29 November to 25 January, and the Christmas Train around Vilnius’ Old Town from 28 November to 3 January.

title: Look, no hands: Euronews rode driverless in Europe's first robotaxi in Zagreb
description: The US firm’s robotaxi service is up and running in Zagreb in partnership with local company Verne and Chinese AI firm Pony.ai, a partnership that plans to expand across Europe. Euronews got to see how it works firsthand in Croatia.
content: Uber launched a driverless taxi service in Zagreb, Croatia, earlier this year and has now unveiled plans to roll out a fully autonomous vehicle service in a host of European cities with partners across the continent, starting with Manchester.The US tech company deployed driverless robotaxis on the streets of Zagreb in April in partnership with local service operator Verne and Chinese AI firm Pony.ai in a business model they want to scale up across the continent.It is an odd partnership given the divergent philosophies at play in Europe, the US and China, with Europe being particularly cautious compared with the latter two. But the companies believe the partnership works thanks to their shared ambition to deploy autonomous vehicle taxi rides around the world.The partnership is one of more than 30 Uber runs across Europe. Together with Verne and Pony.ai, Uber has begun tests in Manchester, and Pony.ai and Uber plan to launch in London, with many more cities in the pipeline.The Zagreb partnership is the most advanced and was announced in March, in a move that aimed to bring driverless taxis out of testing grounds and onto the market in Europe for the first time.Zagreb was a particularly appealing candidate city for Uber, as it is home to electric hypercar maker Rimac, whose founder Mate Rimac had already branched out into robotaxis through Verne. Verne has its own plans to roll out a “business class” form of autonomous vehicle mobility service.In April, the partnership launched its robotaxi service, giving users in Zagreb the chance to order a driverless vehicle for their journey. These cars still have a human in the driving seat, known as a safety operator, who oversees the trip as a security measure. Safety operators are usually former taxi drivers.The service’s vehicles have since clocked up 200,000 kilometres on Zagreb’s roads.Now the partnership feels confident enough to take the next step and remove the operator from the car, leaving just you, the passenger, alone in the vehicle.Europe’s first fully driverless trips began on 10 September, open to a limited number of invited users on a 22-kilometre route linking Verne’s headquarters with Zagreb’s Franjo Tuđman Airport.‘Look, no hands’Ordering an Uber with the currently available driverless ride service is just as simple as booking any other trip with the platform. Users can choose between human-driven and AI-driven robotaxi rides when requesting UberX or Comfort journeys.Riders can unlock the car with their phone, get in and get comfortable, or as comfortable as possible in a car with no one driving, but with full access to Uber support should anything happen.In Zagreb, riders travel in the BAIC Arcfox Alpha T5, a Chinese electric SUV. A human safety operator sits in the driving seat, and the front passenger seat has been removed to make more space for luggage.Uber and Verne currently run about 30 autonomous vehicles in Zagreb, which return each night to a central hub called a “mothership” for cleaning and maintenance by the Croatian startup.The current setup is what is known as a level 4 driverless car programme, which means the car can drive itself without human interference, but only in strictly controlled areas. Nowhere in the world runs a level 5 programme, which means unrestricted road access.It is a strange feeling seeing a car drive itself for the first time. From the rear passenger seat, you can see the steering wheel spinning as the car makes a turn calmly and methodically, even while negotiating oncoming traffic.The smooth ride puts you at ease, and after a while you forget that it is not a person but an AI driving you to your destination.“We call it a little bit magically boring, meaning, you get in and first you’re like ‘oh, no one’s hands are on the wheel’ and then all of sudden you’re in a car like you normally would be,” said Annie Duvnjak, global head of autonomous mobility operations at Uber.That is not to say the ride is free of interruptions. The car comes to a complete stop at every stop sign, even when the road is empty, and it pulls over to avoid overly aggressive human drivers trying to overtake.It is a learning process for the partnership, which is testing fully driverless vehicles, its end goal, in a limited area of Zagreb.A unique partnershipThe partnership, launched in April, is a unique combination of an American mobility firm, a European startup and a Chinese AI company, with each organisation coming from regions with wildly differing approaches to mobility and AI.Given these divergent approaches and the current geopolitical friction on issues ranging from trade and consumer rules to technological sovereignty and supply chains, it may seem surprising that these companies have joined forces.But Uber says the model works because the three companies share a common goal of bringing autonomous taxis to more markets.“You have Verne, which is an incredible local company in Zagreb, with fleet expertise and vehicle operations and then you Pony.ai, which has world-class AV technology, and you have Uber which helps bring that all together in terms of the mobility platform, rider experience,” said Duvnjak.“So, it’s really everyone’s bringing the best of what they do coming together.”Verne, the European partner in this venture, was co-founded by Mate Rimac and is named after the sci-fi writer Jules Verne. It has been working on robotaxis since 2019 and launched its own service in April.Verne acts as the local service operator and fleet owner, managing the day-to-day operations of the robotaxi service. It also serves as the regulatory lead, talking to local, regional and national authorities to secure legal approval for autonomous vehicles on the road in these areas.This is perhaps the biggest obstacle facing the partnership. Europe’s patchwork legal framework governing driverless cars has left the continent lagging far behind the US and China, where robotaxis have operated commercially for several years.The partnership with Uber gives Verne the opportunity to scale up its operation by offering its services through the app and bring them to other cities across Europe as the roll-out expands.“This is an important milestone not only for Verne, but also for Croatia. A service pioneered here in Zagreb is now available through the world’s largest mobility platform. The experience we are gaining every day in Zagreb will help us bring Verne to other European cities,” said Marko Pejković, the CEO of Verne.In June 2024, the Croatian company unveiled its own autonomous two-seater concept car aimed at business travellers.“We want people to be impressed when you arrive in one of these vehicles,” said Pejković.It is a long, sleek vehicle with enough room for the seats to recline fully while driving. A huge dashboard screen entertains and informs passengers during their ride.Despite its more luxurious appearance, the company says rides will not come at a premium, because removing the driver cuts costs significantly.“We are introducing a completely new vision for the vehicle interior, one designed not as a concept for the distant future, but as something that can work in real service. It will help people use their time in a way that is more productive, more enjoyable, and more relaxing,” said Pejković.The company plans to roll out the vehicle in future but, for now, uses the BAIC Arcfox.A driving school for AI agentsThe third partner in this venture is Chinese AI firm Pony.ai, which provides the artificial intelligence technology that drives the vehicles.The company also brings a lot of experience in the sector. Pony.ai says it was the first autonomous vehicle company to secure a taxi licence in China, and it is one of the few companies globally operating fully driverless commercial vehicles.In Zagreb, the Arcfox vehicles are equipped with Pony.ai’s Gen-7 autonomous driving system, its latest level 4 autonomous driving kit.The kit includes 34 individual sensors. Among them are nine LiDAR sensors, 14 cameras and four millimetre-wave radars, as well as four microphones, two water sensors and one collision sensor. Together they give the vehicle considerable awareness of its surroundings and enough redundancy to reduce the chance of accidents.Driving the car is the Pony.ai Virtual Driver, which treats the vehicle like a physical AI agent. But before an AI agent can hit the road, it must first drive in a virtual environment.“It’s like a virtual training ground, that shows the AI how to drive. It’s like how humans learn to drive is how the AI drivers learn to drive in that environment. Then, after it graduates the ‘virtual driving school’, the AI drivers take control, so we don’t rely on any remote control,” said Dr Ludi Wang, director of global communications at Pony.ai.Next stepsUber announced this week that the partnership’s next city will be Manchester, in the UK. Tests are already under way in the city, and Uber says a service like the one in Zagreb will follow in the coming months.In total, Uber is considering more than 30 cities and has schemes at various stages in London, Madrid, Munich and Zurich.“And we hope to expand this model to other cities as well. So we’ve announced Manchester, where we’ll be coming next with this partnership, and so, more to come from there,” said Duvnjak.But could Brussels be next?“We’re actually talking to Brussels, we’re talking to 30 cities and Brussels is one of those cities. But we don’t want to roll out tests in a city if we don’t see it as an option in the future to fully roll out a driverless service as the end goal. But Brussels is definitely on the map,” said Pejković.

title: Slow travel in the Spanish Pyrenees: Exploring Taüll, Vall de Boí and Val d’Aran
description: From mountain walks and Romanesque churches to glacial lakes and medieval villages, discover a slower side of Spain on a journey through the spectacular Pyrenees.
content: Here’s a confession – this is actually “take two” of this specific travel tale. Originally, I had started writing about how a relaxing week-long outdoorsy holiday in Spain had evolved into a mega summer road trip starting in Barcelona, spending a few days in scenic mountain villages and then taking an “eclipsed-sized detour” to San Sebastian. And back again. Then I realised, just like my itinerary planning and driving skills, that it was all getting a bit too chaotic and veering away from what I really wanted to talk about: and that is the Spanish Pyrenees.Had I continued venturing towards the road trip storyline, you would have read a lot about spending hours behind the wheel as we criss-crossed our way through Catalonia, Aragon, Navarre, and the Basque Country – where we ended up to watch the eclipse on 12 August. Not a bad tale, but that’s one for another day, maybe.While Barcelona and San Sebastian are brilliant cities with so much to see and do, it’s only right that the focus here is on slow travel in a lovely part of Spain that I had never been to before. So, without any more talk of roadworks, dodgy satnavs and drastic searches for petrol stations, here’s how we explored a small section of the Spanish Pyrenees. A coolcation with great views Having flown into Barcelona from London, where it was already warm enough, we had feared that a last-minute trip to Spain in mid-August may have been slightly rash considering the rising temperatures across Europe that week. However, in the Vall de Boí the weather was just perfect. Warm during the day, cool at night, with a few storms thrown in here and there for good measure. It is the mountains after all. After a 297km, near four-hour drive to the Boí valley from Barcelona (sorry, but it’s worth adding in the journey details for context), we found ourselves in Taüll, a small village located on the edge of the Aigüestortes i Estany de Sant Maurici National Park – the only national park in Catalonia.Known for its two UNESCO-listed Romanesque churches, Taüll was to be our base for the trip. Sitting at an altitude of around 1,500 metres, it’s an ideal spot for a summer coolcation and you can enjoy scenic walks to nearby villages – up the valley to Pla de l'Ermita or down the hill to Boí. On the walk back down from Pla de l'Ermita you’ll get some great views of Taüll from above. And if hiking or walking isn’t really your thing, then there’s a few restaurants for relaxed al fresco lunches and dinners. In Taüll, we stayed in a one-bed rental above a selection of eateries – Llesqueria l'Empriu, Tribulosi, and Restaurant El Fai – which all serve local dishes and drinks. The walking is what we were here for though and the views are what make the journey really worth it.In Taüll itself, a must-do is the Santeta Viewpoint. You can walk from the Church of St. Climent through the village to the Church of Santa Maria, where a short 15-minute trail starts to the viewpoint. From here you’ll get panoramic views of the valley below and the villages of Boí and Erill la Vall. There’s plenty more to explore around Taüll, particularly if you want to stay active. The national park has hiking trails past lakes and waterfalls, while the Boí Taüll resort offers adventure activities like e-biking and ziplining during summer and skiing in winter.Further down the valley, around El Pont de Suert, you can enjoy rafting and kayaking.From Vall de Boí to Val d’AranIf you have a car and want to explore the wider area then we’d certainly recommend doing a few day trips to some nearby towns and villages. Around an hour’s drive from Taüll, Val d’Aran offers mountain scenery, glacial lakes and some of the region’s prettiest villages.One of its standout walks is the Circ de Colomèrs, a spectacular glacial basin containing almost 50 lakes. The popular seven-lake circuit covers 5.7 kilometres and takes around five hours, with quite a few short climbs included. Elsewhere, you can explore the town of Arties, known for its Romanesque church, historic houses and lively restaurants, or head higher into the mountains to Bagergue, the highest village in Val d’Aran at 1,419 metres. Both are among the valley’s most picturesque villages, though we really loved Bagergue. Here you can wander around its cobbled streets and see traditional stone houses. There are some nice restaurants that serve local cuisine and there’s also a cheesemaker and museum to visit, too. And further afield to Aínsa… One road trip that we should discuss is the journey from Taüll to Aínsa – which is around 95 kilometres and two hours by car. Although it’s a fair drive, you do get some scenic Pyrenean views and the end destination is just lovely. On our long list of places to see while in Spain, Aínsa is a medieval town in the Aragonese Pyrenees. It has a beautifully preserved old town and the cobbled Plaza Mayor is lined with restaurants, cafés and small shops.Another attraction here is Aínsa Castle, which has an elevated walkway along the top of its walls and offers sweeping views of the surrounding mountains. Slow down and stay a little longerBarcelona and San Sebastian are undoubtedly two of Spain’s great city break destinations, but this trip proved that there’s plenty worth exploring in between.In the Pyrenees, slowing down is pretty much the order of the day. Rather than racing between attractions, you can spend your time walking between villages, stopping for lunch on a sunny terrace or heading into the mountains for a trek.If you have the time to venture away from the cities and explore at a slower pace, this corner of Spain is definitely worth the journey.

title: French government 10-year bond yield tops 5% for first time since 2002
description: The yield on the French government's benchmark 10-year bond surpassed 5% on Wednesday as investors demanded a higher return for holding the country's debt.
content: French yields have been rising for weeks as lawmakers wrangle over a 2027 budget that calls for billions of euros in spending cuts to reduce a debt pile that now stands at around 120% of France's GDP - one of the highest levels in the eurozone and well above the EU limit of 60%.The French Treasury's OAT bond is also used to set interest rates across a wide swath of the economy, meaning borrowing costs could begin rising for businesses and households.The last time it was that high was during the dot-com financial crisis.The spread between the 10-year yield and the German 10-year bond, considered the European benchmark of creditworthiness, also surged to nearly 160 basis points.The bond selloff puts further pressure on the government ahead of a decision Friday by the ratings agency Moody's on France's sovereign credit rating, with most economists expecting a downgrade that would automatically raise the government's borrowing costs.Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu is trying to get a 2027 budget approved in parliament despite not having a political majority for the €43 billion ($48bn) in spending cuts he seeks.Even if approved, the budget would bring France's deficit down to only 5% of GDP next year, well above the 3% limit for EU members.Meanwhile, protests over the weekend calling in part for more spending on schools and other public services, degenerated into the worst street violence seen in years.

title: From ‘sleepmaxxing’ to rising temperatures: getting a good night's sleep is getting harder
description: Climate change, unequal access to healthcare and an ‘always-on’ work culture are undermining sleep across Europe — essential for good health.
content: Sleep allows our bodies to repair tissue, clear brain waste, and consolidate memories — something essential for wellbeing and health. However, rising temperatures, digital technology and round-the-clock working are increasingly disrupting sleep.And it is not for individuals alone to address this, researchers warned in a paper published in the Journal of Sleep Research. They are turning to European governments to address the social and economic conditions that determine whether people can get sufficient, restorative sleep."We're seeing a perfect storm of challenges for sleep health across Europe,” the co-lead author of the paper, Fran Pilkington-Cheney, lecturer in Psychology and Sleep at Nottingham Trent University (NTU), said in a press release.“People are aware that sleep matters, but few recognise how factors such as climate change, technology, shift work, urban environments and misinformation are combining to affect how well we sleep.” Therefore, the authors call for “shifting away from individualised approaches toward coordinated, systems-level action across policy, healthcare, education, industry, and environmental planning” to address the major challenges for getting a good night’s sleep. Those are climate change and urban environments; unequal access to sleep medicine; the rapid expansion of digital health technologies; online misinformation; and a culture of constant connectivity that leaves less time for rest, according to the paper.Climate and inequalityAmong the mix of environmental, technological and societal pressures that are making it harder for people to get sleep, rising temperatures are emerging as a particular concern.Europe is the world's fastest-warming continent, and increasingly hot nights can interfere with the body's ability to cool down, delaying sleep and causing more frequent awakenings.Urban pollution, traffic noise and artificial light at night add to the problem, while climate-related anxiety and extreme weather events can further undermine mental health and sleep.The effects are unlikely to be distributed equally. People living in poorly insulated homes, those unable to afford cooling and people in overcrowded accommodation face greater difficulties maintaining comfortable sleeping conditions. Refugees and displaced people may also be exposed to excessive heat, noise, artificial light and a lack of privacy.Technology presents another challenge. Wearable devices and sleep-tracking applications could help people identify potential problems and allow clinicians to monitor patients remotely, particularly in rural areas with limited access to specialists.But consumer devices are not necessarily accurate enough to diagnose sleep disorders, and their results can cause unnecessary anxiety. The paper highlights “orthosomnia”, a term describing an excessive preoccupation with achieving supposedly perfect sleep measurements. The researchers also warn that social media trends such as “sleepmaxxing” can encourage rigid routines, unproven remedies and excessive self-monitoring.Meanwhile, online influencers and AI tools can spread misleading health advice, making it harder for people to distinguish scientific evidence from commercial promotion.Work is part of the problemEurope's 24-hour economy is also placing pressure on sleep. Shift workers, healthcare staff, transport workers and people in precarious employment may have limited control over their schedules, while remote working and after-hours messages can blur the boundaries between professional and personal life.The report cites estimates that 21% of workers across Europe engage in shift work, with night shifts presenting particular challenges to the body's natural sleep-wake cycle.The researchers advocate stronger protections for workers, more predictable schedules, better fatigue-management systems and workplace practices that protect time for rest.“Without wider co-ordinated action, these pressures are likely to become more significant in the years ahead,” Pilkington-Cheney said.

title: Zelenskyy calls for trilateral talks with Putin and Trump after meeting with US delegation in Oslo
description: Speaking after a meeting with special envoy Steve Witkoff, Zelenskyy added that he was "thankful" that US early warning intelligence "works now."
content: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Tuesday called for a trilateral meeting with US and Russian leaders Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin.Speaking to the media following talks with US special envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo, Zelenskyy said one of the key ideas raised had been the possibility of holding a meeting between the trio "to address the issues that only the leaders can do.""Steve is going to Russia tomorrow, and let's see what Putin has to say," he told reporters.Tuesday's meeting was hosted by Norway and Finland as part of renewed diplomatic efforts to end Russia's war in Ukraine.From Norway, Witkoff is scheduled to travel to Russia for talks with Putin.The Oslo meeting brought together Zelenskyy, Finnish President Alexander Stubb, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, and Witkoff. Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner also joined the talks remotely.US intel warnings working again, Zelenskyy saysZelenskyy also addressed reported restrictions on US intelligence sharing during the press conference, saying he was "thankful" that "intelligence works now.""I'm speaking about early warning, what is very important for our people, for children, adults, civilians, because we can hear when ballistic is coming," he said.In a statement on Tuesday, Støre confirmed that Kyiv had specifically requested the participation of the two American envoys, describing the meeting as an opportunity to put diplomatic efforts towards ending the war on a more constructive footing."Diplomatic efforts have previously taken place in several countries and Norway and Finland are pleased to be able to continue this work," Støre said."The aim is to put diplomatic efforts on a more constructive path."Representatives from the E4 countries - the UK, France, Germany and Poland - as well as the EU and NATO, were also expected to participate.The European Commission confirmed to Euronews that it had been invited by Ukraine to participate in the Oslo discussions but did not specify who would represent Brussels.Witkoff's planned meeting with Putin is also expected to address the possible release of Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old American citizen detained by Russia in 2022 and sentenced to almost seven years in jail for allegedly fighting as a mercenary for Ukraine.Zelenskyy began his trip to Oslo by meeting with Norway's King Haakon VIII on Tuesday.In a post on X, the Ukrainian leader thanked the royal and the Norwegian government and people for their support and said the pair had discussed the return of Ukrainian children abducted by Russia.US-Ukraine relations under strainThe Oslo talks come at a particularly difficult moment in relations between Kyiv and Washington, with the Trump administration pressing Ukraine to halt strikes on Russian oil infrastructure while questions mount over the delivery of urgently needed American air defence weapons.The meeting also follows a telephone conversation on Sunday between Zelenskyy, Witkoff and Kushner, during which they discussed possible next steps towards ending the war.Zelenskyy told Bloomberg at the weekend that he had proposed suspending Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil facilities in exchange for additional US-made Patriot interceptor missiles, which Ukraine urgently needs to defend against Russian ballistic missile attacks.In a separate conversation with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday morning, the Ukrainian president raised three pressing issues: ballistic missile interceptors, early-warning intelligence and restrictions affecting Starlink/Starshield satellite communications."First, ballistic missile interceptors, which are needed to protect lives. Second, early warning of Russian ballistic missile attacks, which is vital. Third, the situation with Starlink/Starshield, which needs to be restored," Zelenskyy wrote on X.The concerns come amid reports that Washington is delaying the delivery of a significant batch of Patriot interceptor missiles already paid for by Ukraine's European allies, with US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth yet to approve their transfer.Ukrainian officials fear the delay is politically motivated and intended to exert pressure on Kyiv. NATO officials, however, maintain that allied-funded deliveries are continuing, while a US government official has disputed the allegations.

title: Australian model and swimwear designer Sahara Ray dies aged 34
description: Her family said she passed away in hospital surrounded by loved ones, just months after she welcomed her first child, daughter Snow.
content: Australian model and swimwear designer Sahara Ray has died aged 34. Her family said in a statement to US celebrity news website TMZ that she died on Sunday night surrounded by family at the hospital.Her cause of death has not been made public.The daughter of Australian surfer Tony Ray, she founded the label Sahara Ray Swim in 2014 and was photographed on holiday with Justin Bieber in 2016.She gave birth to her daughter, Snow, in January this year.

title: EU plans March summit in Rome as Italy eyes early election
description: The EU is preparing to hold its March 2027 summit in Rome to mark the 70th anniversary of the Treaties of Rome, subject to unanimous approval, as Italy faces the prospect of an early spring election.
content: Preparations are under way to hold a European Council summit in Rome in March 2027 to mark the 70th anniversary of the Treaties of Rome, amid speculation over an early election in Italy.It would be the first time an anniversary celebration has been combined with a formal European Council summit held outside Brussels.EU leaders’ summits are normally held in Brussels. In exceptional circumstances, European Council President António Costa can propose another venue, provided all member states agree unanimously.“President Costa has put forward the idea to organise a formal European Council in Rome in the context of the 70th anniversary of the Rome Treaty. Preparations are ongoing,” an EU official told Euronews, speaking on condition of anonymity.The move was first reported by Italian daily La Stampa, which said the summit would give Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni a major international platform shortly before the next general election.Signed on 25 March 1957, the Treaties of Rome established the European Economic Community and the European Atomic Energy Community, laying the foundations for today’s EU.Italy’s next general election is due by the end of 2027, but an early vote in spring is being openly discussed, with April and May the most frequently cited dates.The Italian government has welcomed the move.Costa raised the proposal with Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever during a tour of EU capitals in September, specifically approaching Belgium because Brussels is the usual host of the summits.De Wever said he would not oppose the one-off exception, an official told Euronews, speaking on condition of anonymity.Costa’s current term as European Council president expires on 31 May 2027. He is expected to seek a second two-and-a-half-year term, as his predecessors have done. Reappointment requires the backing of a qualified majority of member states.The change of venue still requires approval from all member states, at ambassadorial or ministerial level. The issue is expected to be discussed in the coming weeks.

title: France arrests man believed to be connected to town hall fire in Limoges
description: The destruction of the building has become a symbol of the violent rioting that erupted on the margins of a day of protests that were called in response to anger about the rising cost of living and conditions in schools.
content: French security forces arrested a man on Tuesday believed to be connected to the ultra-left over the burning down of a historic town hall in central France during rioting at the weekend on the sidelines of nationwide protests.Anti-terror police have also been called in to investigate the suspected arson on the town hall in the central city of Limoges, a building dating back to 1883 whose roof and belfry collapsed when it was engulfed by fire on Saturday.The destruction of the building has become a symbol of the violent rioting that erupted on the margins of a day of protests on Saturday that were called in a show of anger against grievances including the rising cost of living and conditions in schools.The scenes of the building collapsing as it was hit by fire also brought back memories in France of the April 2019 fire that ravaged Notre-Dame cathedral in Paris which investigators believe started by accident but horrified the country.The man, believed to be aged 40, was arrested by officers from the specialised RAID police unit in the nearby town of Val d'Issoire, the office of the Limoges prosecutor said.He had previously been flagged as someone requiring surveillance as a potential threat and is linked to ultra-left movements, a source close to the case said.Meanwhile, France's Counter-Terrorism Sub-Directorate (SDAT), a branch of the judicial police, has been called in to investigate the case further, another source close to the case added, asking not to be named.French Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin said late on Monday that anti-terror prosecutors would soon decide whether to investigate the incident as a suspected terror attack."If they take up the case, it means it is a terrorist act, implying that certain individuals, notably from the far left, clearly organised this destruction of the town hall," Darmanin told French TV channel TF1.The right-wing mayor of Limoges, Guillaume Guerin, has lambasted the response by police, who he said "lacked the necessary resources" and "backed down" in the face of rioters.He called on the government to "inject millions" to rebuild the town hall, adding that "the state has failed." Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu is due to visit Limoges on Friday, his office said.Around 5,000 people, including 700 individuals described by the authorities as "radicalised and extremely violent," took part in the demonstration in Limoges on Saturday.Some 7,000 people then took part in a protest to denounce the violence on Sunday evening.

title: Uzbekistan's $12bn business drive gathers pace during Rubio visit
description: The package covers railways, critical minerals, finance and technology, with major US firms involved. Uzbek President Mirziyoyev outlined measures to attract investors, while business executives told Euronews that commercial activity is growing.
content: Uzbekistan has announced 54 agreements and proposed projects with American partners worth nearly $12bn (€10.7bn), following high-level meetings in Samarkand attended by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.Rubio met President Shavkat Mirziyoyev on Monday, with the two discussing trade, energy, critical minerals, aviation and technology.
