The two countries are seeking to expand their strategic partnership through private investment and joint industrial projects.According to the Uzbek presidency, bilateral trade has increased by 35% since the beginning of the year, although it did not specify the comparison period.New priorities for US investmentSenior officials and American business representatives attended the second meeting of the American-Uzbek Business and Investment Council, where the economic agenda was developed.Mirziyoyev described the council as an important mechanism for developing joint projects, emphasising its distinctive role in Uzbekistan's international economic relations."We do not have this kind of format with any other country of the world," he said during his meeting with Rubio.The Uzbek president announced a package of 54 agreements and prospective initiatives valued at around $12bn and called for a comprehensive action plan to support their implementation.He also proposed a new approach to attracting investors, under which projects would be prepared with land, infrastructure, permits and administrative requirements already addressed.Uzbek companies would be encouraged to participate as partners, while a newly established direct investment fund could help finance eligible projects.Mirziyoyev identified critical minerals, renewable energy, electricity storage, data centres and artificial intelligence as priority areas. He also proposed a joint trade, investment and technology cooperation programme extending to 2035.The council is co-chaired by Head of Uzbekistan's Presidential Administration Saida Mirziyoyeva and US Special Envoy Sergio Gor.Mirziyoyeva encouraged US companies to bring investment proposals and practical problems directly to the council, positioning it as a mechanism for resolving obstacles rather than simply discussing future cooperation.US investors praise growing activityBusiness representatives interviewed by Euronews in Samarkand identified opportunities in mining, agriculture and financial services.Dan Patterson, CEO of Silver Leaf International, pointed to the potential for Uzbek fruit exports to reach US consumers and for US companies to invest in mineral development."So there's also tremendous opportunity for minerals and mining advancements in almost every sector," Patterson told Euronews.Quinn Martin, president of Bluestone, said US investment activity had accelerated after several years of discussions."Just my firm has been involved in three transactions in the last five months regarding US investors," he told Euronews.According to Martin, the transactions involved Uzbekistan's national investment fund, banking and hospitality. He expects US investment to increase further over the coming years.Uzbekistan's Deputy Minister of Investment, Industry and Trade Shokhrukh Gulyamov also described discussions with US financial institutions."Citigroup, one of the leading financial institutions in the United States, is in discussions with our banks about providing financing for various projects," Gulyamov told Euronews.He also highlighted cooperation with Boeing, including aircraft deliveries and the supply of spare parts needed for maintenance.Which companies are involved in the agreements?According to Uzbekistan's Ministry of Investment, Industry and Trade, the agreements and proposed initiatives cover transport, energy, critical minerals, finance, digital technologies, agriculture and healthcare.Railway manufacturer Wabtec is discussing locomotive supplies, maintenance services and local component production.Financial cooperation involving Franklin Templeton, Oppenheimer & Co, Citigroup and BlackRock includes access to international capital markets, institutional investment and infrastructure financing.In critical minerals, projects involving ReElement Technologies, Traxys and Trafigura cover geological exploration, processing technologies and mineral supplies.Other initiatives include satellite communications with Amazon Leo, medical technologies with GE HealthCare and agricultural development with Valmont Industries.

title: Hackers steal 421,000 emails belonging to members of Germany's far-right AfD party
description: It remains unclear who was responsible for the attack and whether additional data has been compromised.
content: Hackers broke into email accounts belonging to members of Germany's far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party and stole large numbers of messages, the party said on Tuesday.More than 421,000 emails were taken in the attack last month, including messages sent by party co-leader Alice Weidel and co-founder Alexander Gauland, the Bild daily reported.A website published what it said were summaries of some of the emails but not the original messages.Bild said the published messages included photos of ID cards of some party members, as well as bank statements, membership applications and membership lists from some local AfD branches.The AfD confirmed to the AFP news agency that an email service provider used by the party had been targeted, and "a small number of email accounts, most of which had not been used for years, were apparently copied unlawfully"."This attack was quickly detected and stopped, and all users were subsequently informed accordingly," said an AfD statement.The party said it was reviewing what had been published online.It remains unclear who was responsible for the attack and whether additional data has been compromised.The anti-immigration, Russia-friendly AfD is topping national opinion polls and came first in two state elections last month, comfortably ahead of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's centre-right CDU.The party scored its biggest win in Saxony-Anhalt, where it hopes to form Germany's first far-right state government since World War II.

title: How planting a 'rain garden' could help protect your home from flooding
description: Flooding is expected to grow more extreme due to climate change. Your garden could be your home's first defence.
content: Heavy rains and flooding hit Spain's Catalonia region last week, claiming at least two lives and submerging homes and roads.Unfortunately, it’s not the first time. And it won’t be the last: scientists predict an increase in extreme weather events globally, fed in part by human-caused climate change.When the deluge subsides, people are left to deal with the devastation, shovelling sludge from streets and pumping floodwater from their living rooms.Gardens may be the last thing people fix, but could they become fortifications against future disasters?As the threat of flooding and droughts strengthens, so too does the argument for planting a 'rain garden'.What exactly is a rain garden?Simply put, a rain garden is a depressed bed planted with native perennials and shrubs selected for their high-water tolerance.It’s strategically situated in a spot where water – from downspouts, driveways, compacted soil and other sources of runoff – flows downward toward it.That runoff waters the plants and filters pollutants as the soil absorbs it. And it means the excess water, as well as the road sediment, debris, pet waste pathogens, fertilisers and chemicals it picks up along the way, is kept out of storm drains, watersheds and wetlands.Rain gardens can also stop water from entering your basement or affecting your foundation.In dry, drought-stricken regions, too, many gardeners are turning to rain gardens and other methods of collecting rainwater.How to create a rain gardenYou can make a rain garden as big or small as you like, but keep it at least three metres from your house, garage or other structures. Don’t plant it over a septic tank or underground utilities, or near a well that provides drinking water. And avoid sloped areas and those that are soggy to begin with.Dig the bed in your preferred size and shape (kidney, crescent, round and teardrop are popular). You can either gradually grade the soil toward the centre so it is 15 centimetres lower than the perimeter, or dig everything but the perimeter 15 centimetres deep so a berm that high surrounds the sunken bed.Direct water toward the bed by installing a gutter extension, creating a downhill slope, digging a trench or connecting a PVC pipe to a distant gutter and running it underground to the rain garden. Slow the flow of water by lining your trench or slope with rocks or small stones.Some gardeners prefer to keep the centre free of plants and cover the soil there with stones, as well.The best plantings for a rain gardenChoose native plants best suited to high-water or, if planting the centre, even swampy conditions. Natives are naturally adapted to your region’s environment, so they’ll be easier to grow, require less maintenance and will also provide a habitat for bees, birds, butterflies and other wildlife.Consider planting flowering perennials alongside sedges and grasses, and incorporating shrubs and small trees, if space allows. Including some evergreens will further help avoid erosion.FloraVeg.EU is a good resource that lets you search for native vegetation by geographical region and other parameters.Put plants with the highest water needs at and around the centre of your rain garden, where water will collect and pool for a bit before seeping into the soil. Plant those with moderate water needs along the elevated perimeter of the bed, which will be somewhat drier.How to care for a rain gardenIn the absence of rain, water the plants as necessary throughout their first year, as their roots grow and anchor into the ground. Keep on top of weeds, too, until the plants grow and fill in the bare spots between them.After you’ve designed, graded and planted your rain garden, there won’t be very much for you to do, except sit back and enjoy your striking natural landscape – and its hidden ecological function.

title: Pope Leo XIV holds call with Zelenskyy, Vatican says
description: Chicago-born Leo, 71, has been calling for a humanitarian truce in Oleshky, a city under Russian siege, to allow food and medical aid to arrive and for civilians to be evacuated safely.
content: Pope Leo XIV held a call with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy late on Monday afternoon, just days after he spoke with Russian leader Vladimir Putin, the Vatican said.During his conversation with Putin, the pontiff had called for a humanitarian truce in Oleshky, a city under Russian siege, to allow food and medical aid to arrive and for civilians to be evacuated safely.According to a statement from the Vatican's Press Office, Oleshky was also the focus of his talks with Zelenskyy."During the conversation, the Holy Father drew attention to the serious situation in the city of Oleshky, in the Kherson region, referring to the request for a humanitarian truce already submitted to the President of the Russian Federation," the statement reads. "The Holy Father expressed the hope that the cooperation of both sides will allow food and medical aid to reach the city and ensure the voluntary and safe evacuation of the civilian population."Ukraine and Russia are in the process of finalising the details of a civilian evacuation in the city and six nearby settlements, the Ukrainian Commissioner for Human Rights, Dmytro Lubinets, has announced.Chicago-born Leo has kept in regular contact with Zelenskyy.In May 2025, Leo held an initial telephone call with the Ukrainian leader, in which Zelenskyy invited him to Kyiv and reiterated his country's readiness for further negotiations.The two met later that month, immediately after the mass marking the beginning of the pope's pontificate in St Peter's Square.They met again on 9 July 2025 for a private audience at Villa Barberini, the papal residence in Castel Gandolfo, where they discussed the possibility of hosting future peace talks at the Vatican.And once again on 9 December, again in Castel Gandolfo, to discuss the need to keep dialogue open, questions surrounding prisoners of war and the return of Ukrainian children deported to Russia.On 3 April this year, the pope again spoke to Zelenskyy as Russian drone and missile attacks ramped up across Ukraine.He expressed his solidarity with the Ukrainian people, underlining the urgency of humanitarian aid, the release of prisoners and a negotiated peace.

title: Cristiano Ronaldo suspended for 30 days after quitting Portugal camp
description: On 30 September, the former Real Madrid and Manchester United star walked out of an international camp before a training session at Parken Stadium in Copenhagen.
content: Portugal legend Cristiano Ronaldo has been given a 30-day suspension by the Portuguese Football Federation (FPF) after leaving an international camp last month.In addition to the ban, Ronaldo will have to pay a fine of €255.According to a ruling by the association's disciplinary committee, part of the player’s suspension has already been served, as he had already been suspended.Ronaldo, who now plays his club football for Saudi side Al-Nassr, began his punishment on 1 October, leaving 11 days left to serve. That means he could be available for the national team’s upcoming matches against Denmark on 14 November and Wales on 17 November.'Mitigating circumstances'The ruling said Ronaldo had asked that "mitigating circumstances be taken into account," in particular his "lack of any disciplinary record in the current season and the previous three seasons, provision of services of relevance to football, commendations for sporting merit and contribution to establishing the material truth.""With regard to the mitigating circumstances of providing services of relevance to football and commendations for sporting merit, the defendant Cristiano Ronaldo submitted his sporting CV, including the awards and recognitions he has received over the course of his career," the document reads.It adds that, in terms of "contribution to establishing the material truth," the player referred to the statement published on his Instagram page on 6 October.The ruling sets out in detail the sequence of events after Ronaldo left the training camp.On 30 September, the former Real Madrid and Manchester United star walked out of a camp before a training session at Parken Stadium in Copenhagen.The player is said to have left without notifying anyone from the FPF or the squad in advance.The document states that the player informed FPF President Pedro Proença of his decision by phone, saying that he did not feel in the right frame of mind to play."During the aforementioned telephone conversation, the defendant player informed the president of the FPF that he was not in an emotional condition to remain with the National Team at the training camp," the disciplinary committee noted.Media coverageIn assessing the case, the committee acknowledged Ronaldo's services to football and his multiple awards. The body also took into account "his conduct after the events, in particular the remorse shown in the statement of 06.10.2026."Even though certain mitigating factors were recognised, there were also aggravating elements in the FPF's view, notably the media coverage of the case and his role as team captain.

title: Mont Blanc: new French measurements, summit 'grows' to 4,807m
description: New measurements from Saint-Gervais-Mont-Blanc show Western Europe's highest peak at 4,807.47 metres, almost two metres higher than in 2023. Experts say the change is due to the thickness of the snow and ice cap.
content: The idea of a mountain growing may sound strange, but that is exactly what happens. Its height can even change in just a few years, as has occurred with Mont Blanc which, according to measurements released in France on Wednesday, now reaches 4,807.47 metres above sea level, almost two metres more than in 2023.The new calculations were carried out on 17 September by experts from the Haute-Savoie Departmental Chamber of Surveyors, whose territory includes part of the mountain shared by France and Italy.The results were officially presented on Wednesday in Saint-Gervais-Mont-Blanc, on the French side of the massif, showing an increase of 1.88 metres in three years, reversing the trend of previous years, when the summit had been lower.Presenting the results, the president of the Chamber of Surveyors, Jean des Garets, recalled that "the summit is in constant motion".Why Mont Blanc's altitude changes over timeThe apparent "growth" is not due to movements of the mountain itself but to variations in the snow and ice cap that covers the top.The height of Europe's second-highest peak changes according to the accumulation and redistribution of snow, influenced by wind, precipitation, temperature, sunshine and seasonal weather conditions.For this reason, the periodic measurement campaigns produce different results. Between 2000 and 2010 the height was repeatedly measured at around 4,810 metres. Afterwards, a gradual decrease was recorded.In 2021 Mont Blanc reached 4,807.81 metres, while in 2023 it dropped to 4,805.59 metres, the lowest figure in recent years. The 2026 measurement, by contrast, puts the mountain back above 4,807 metres.The Alps' highest peak rises back above 4,807 metresThe new survey confirms that Mont Blanc remains a summit in constant evolution. Compared with the historic figure from 1894, its current altitude is around 27 centimetres higher.For experts, the succession of measurements is also a useful tool for monitoring the effects of weather and climate conditions on the Alpine environment.

title: France announces partial curfews after weekend of violence
description: It comes after cost-of-living protests descended into widespread violence and looting across France on Saturday. Clashes with police also continued on Sunday in some parts of the country.
content: Partial curfews are set to come into effect in several French cities following violent protests across France over the weekend.Limited curfews are set to be imposed from 8 pm to 6 am local time in four northern cities on Monday and Tuesday, including Lille, according to the office of Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu.A partial curfew and a ban on demonstrations will also be introduced in parts of the French capital, Paris, on Monday.The curfew is to be in effect from 11 pm on Monday until 6 am on Tuesday in several neighbourhoods, the Paris police prefecture has said.Demonstrations are also to be banned in several areas of the capital from 8 pm on Monday until 6 am on Tuesday.Nice Mayor Eric Ciotti announced that a curfew for minors would begin at 9 pm Monday and last until 6 am Tuesday in the southern French city. It will be limited to streets in the city centre, he said in a video address.Lecornu had announced earlier on Monday that he had instructed regional authorities to bring in "localised and partial" curfews in order to prevent further riots and looting after cost-of-living demonstrations descended into violence on Saturday."On Saturday, despite scenes of extreme violence and major material damage, no one was killed, and that is a miracle," the PM said following a meeting of the government's crisis response team.Lecornu also defended the work of police officers who had confronted groups of rioters.It comes as French President Emmanuel Macron refused to accept the resignation of Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez, citing "the need to ensure the continuity of the command of the security forces given the current situation," the Élysée said in a statement on Monday.The president has tasked the interior minister "with taking all necessary measures to guarantee full transparency on the failures in planning and intelligence that led to this violence," the statement added.Macron has also called for the introduction "of new policing tactics on the ground."Nuñez said that police had "lost control" of the situation in some cities."A number of measures to contain and prevent looters and vandals from acting" will be introduced "from this Monday evening," the interior minister announced on Monday, adding that the number of police and gendarme forces on the ground would be further bolstered going into the weekend.On Sunday evening, some groups again took to the streets to set fire to bins, bicycles, and other objects and looted shops in cities including Paris, Lyon, and Marseille.Around 2,400 people were arrested across France over the weekend in relation to the protests, according to authorities.

title: Protesters block access to Louvre museum in Paris in support of demonstrations
description: Protests initially began last month with students protesting over conditions in lycées across the country but have escalated to cover a broader range of concerns such as the cost of living.
content: Protesters blocked the entrance to the Louvre in Paris on Monday, as French authorities scrambled to stem public discontent fuelling mass cost-of-living demonstrations that over the weekend spilled over into some of the worst street violence in recent years."We are proud to announce that we are blocking the world's largest museum," read a leaflet posted outside the museum, as management and unions said the protest was led by students from Ecole du Louvre.President Emmanuel Macron ordered a security review as the country's interior minister admitted that the police "had lost control" during the weekend's unrest.Undeterred, the Yellow Vests movement which organised the weekend's rallies called for a new round of protests on Saturday.Italy, Spain and Portugal, where anger over rising prices has also led to protests, were keeping a nervous eye on the developments after smaller clashes broke out in Milan over the weekend and protests about housing costs persisted in Spanish cities.Some half a million people turned out across France to protest the surging cost of living, a culmination of four weeks of protests that began with high school students demanding better conditions at their schools.What started as peaceful demonstrations morphed into violence in some places, as masked groups on the sidelines of the protests attacked law enforcement, broke into town halls and other public buildings, setting many of them ablaze, looted shops, and set fire to cars, bicycles and scooters on the streets.Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez offered to resign on Monday after more than 2,500 people were arrested and nearly 1,000 members of the security forces injured.Protesters were also hurt, with one demonstrator's hand blown off by a police crowd-control grenade."On Saturday, in some major cities, you couldn't look shopkeepers in the eye after hundreds of shops had been looted and tell them we hadn't lost control," Nuñez said.Macron refused Nuñez's resignation, even as he acknowledged security and intelligence failures in the government response, despite the some 60,000 law enforcement personnel deployed across the country on Saturday.Nationwide, more than 2,330 people were taken into police custody over the weekend, 70 percent of whom were adults, Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said Monday.More than 2,000 shops were expected to have been affected by the weekend's violence across France, with damage running into "hundreds of millions of euros", according to chamber of commerce president Alain Di Crescenzo.In an address to the nation Sunday evening, Macron slammed the "unbridled" violence and said local authorities would be able to ban "if necessary" certain rallies in coming days.But he stopped short of announcing drastic measures, such as a state of emergency or curfew.Anger across EuropeRising prices have fuelled anger in France, where diesel prices have jumped nearly 40% and petrol by 25% since March and where food prices have risen by 25% since 2021.With costs of living rising across Europe, smaller demonstrations have broken out in other countries.During the weekend, clashes broke out on the sidelines of a cost-of-living demonstration in Milan, with Mayor Giuseppe Sala warning: "I'm very worried because it's a new phenomenon, which also originates from an international scenario and therefore feeds itself."In Spain, hundreds of tents have occupied Madrid's central Puerta del Sol square since September, when the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her lifelong flat sparked nationwide protests in a country with soaring housing costs.Dozens of tents have also sprung up in Portugal's main cities of Lisbon and Porto, with protesters demanding action over rising costs of housing.

title: Macron increasingly isolated amid unrest across France
description: Saturday’s violent protests and looting across France have deepened Macron’s political isolation, raising questions over his authority.
content: With only months left in his presidency, Emmanuel Macron faces mounting social unrest and political criticism that could ultimately shape his legacy.After student protests over living conditions erupted into violence last Saturday, Macron has come under fire from across the political spectrum over his handling of the security situation and his response to grievances over education, the cost of living and inflation.The unrest comes as France grapples with record public debt, soaring fuel prices and escalating international conflicts.The Yellow Vests movement, which has helped coordinate the protests, announced a “second act” on Monday, with further demonstrations planned for next weekend.Addressing the nation, Macron condemned violence and announced new operational procedures for security forces.The Paris prosecutor’s office reported 855 arrests linked to the demonstrations, with 557 people placed in police custody, 433 of whom were adults, representing 78% of those detained.“Looking at these images, we have all asked ourselves: What was going through their minds? How can French people do this to France?” Macron said. “Nothing justifies it, nothing explains it, nothing excuses it. Tonight, we all feel anger and shame.”The response is likely to add to the pressure on Macron, whose performance was viewed unfavourably by 82% of respondents in an Ipsos-BVA poll conducted in October.The French president is currently on a diplomatic trip to the Gulf, which the Élysée says aims to secure energy supplies as prices rise. However, his decision to leave Paris amid the crisis has drawn criticism, with some accusing Macron of evading the situation.Le Pen capitalises on chaosAcross the political spectrum, several potential presidential candidates have argued that Macron has lost authority and that his response came too late.“We have the feeling that the government is collapsing under its own weight, that it is completely overwhelmed,” said Jordan Bardella, president of the far-right National Rally, which is leading in polls ahead of France’s 2027 presidential election.Speaking at a press conference at the party’s headquarters on Monday, Bardella pledged tough measures to restore order if the National Rally came to power. “France is caught in a vice between powerlessness and violence,” he said.Polls put Marine Le Pen ahead of all her potential rivals in the 2027 presidential race. She faced Emmanuel Macron in the 2017 and 2022 run-offs, losing both times.In the aftermath of the looting, Le Pen said France had been “ravaged” by “an alliance of criminals from the banlieues and politicised professional rioters”.Le Pen is expected to focus her campaign on migration and law and order, issues that have traditionally resonated with far-right voters, while playing down foreign policy issues such as the war in Ukraine and wider geopolitical tensions.Macron faces criticism from former alliesMacron has also faced criticism from his former prime ministers, Édouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal, both of whom are running in the 2027 presidential election.Both are seeking to distance themselves from Macron and his political legacy.“Like millions of French people, I would have preferred to see decisions and initiatives aimed at restoring order,” Philippe wrote on X.Attal called on the state to employ all means "so justice is done" including AI facial recognition and deploying the army "if necessary". Macron did not announce extra security measures on Sunday, asking local authorities to coordinate with the police.The divided French left, riven by internal tensions, accused the government of failing to protect citizens.“This is unprecedented in its gravity,” Raphaël Glucksmann, a French MEP and social-democratic contender in the 2027 presidential election, told RTL radio. “I had the feeling that France was dissolving, that the Republic was disintegrating, that the state no longer existed.”Bruno Retailleau, another presidential hopeful representing the conservative Les Républicains party, described Macron as “completely out of his depth, incapable of deploying the full force of the state against the chaos threatening the Republic”.He cited the arson attack on Limoges town hall and vandalism at Marseille’s town hall.Senior members of the government have also acknowledged shortcomings in the response.Police fiascoOn Monday, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez admitted there had been a “lack of anticipation” in preparations. He offered to resign “because I felt responsible for everything that happened”, but Macron rejected his request.Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin likewise acknowledged that the authorities had “undoubtedly failed” in their response, citing “shortcomings in intelligence gathering”.Macron has found few defenders among his former allies, some of whom blame the current political turmoil on his decision to dissolve the National Assembly in June 2024. The move plunged France into political uncertainty, leaving successive governments exposed to the threat of no-confidence votes.Beyond the immediate security crisis, commentators argue that Macron has alienated young people who helped propel him to power in 2017.Some protesters have criticised his 2018 high school reforms, arguing that changes to the organisation of specialist subjects have led to longer school days.In a recent opinion piece, Le Monde described Macron’s relationship with young people as a “major political failure”.The article drew parallels with the Yellow Vests movement, which erupted in December 2018 amid widespread anger over purchasing power and the rising cost of living.“Restoring public order is an essential prerequisite for beginning the talks promised on Sunday with all stakeholders and, in doing so, resuming a social dialogue that has been broken for far too long,” the piece concluded.

title: Trump signs order aimed at boosting women’s health research
description: United States President Donald Trump signed an executive order establishing two bodies to boost women’s health research, address gaps in medical knowledge and improve prevention, diagnosis and treatment.
content: President Donald J. Trump, alongside First Lady Melania Trump, signed an executive order on Monday creating a Women’s Health Division at the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and a White House Women’s Health Task Force to close research gaps and modernise women's care.“My Administration is committed to advancing women’s health and ensuring that medical research, diagnosis, prevention, and treatment reflect the highest quality scientific evidence, with the goal of improving health outcomes in all phases of life,” Trump said.Speaking before the signing, Melania Trump called this “a transformative moment for women in America”. “Previous generations fought for women's rights,” she continued. “Our generation will fight to discover the cure that will ensure that women can live their lives in health and to the fullest.”The task force, which is meeting on the day the order was signed, is led by White House chief of staff Susie Wiles and US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. They are tasked with coordinating women’s health policy across federal agencies. The task force's role is to translate research into evidence-based healthcare, improve prevention and access to care throughout women's lives, and identify policy and regulatory reforms to improve health outcomes.In the meantime, the Women's Health Division will be established within the NIH over the next 90 days.It will coordinate and expand research into understudied women’s health conditions, improve the inclusion of women and girls in clinical trials, and accelerate the development of better diagnostics and treatments. It will also strengthen accountability for researchers to account for sex-based biological differences in their studies.The goal, according to Melania Trump, is to improve women's health outcomes “in all phases of life,” using the advantages of new scientific discoveries, including super intelligence and advanced biotechnology and other therapies.She outlined five priorities: directing research towards diseases that affect women “in a unique way”; using super intelligence to better understand women’s health and develop new treatments; speeding up access to new discoveries from labs to patients; ensuring access to all despite financial situation and addressing previously neglected conditions.

title: EU eyes Arctic cable linking Greenland to Europe amid growing security threats
description: Brussels wants to secure digital infrastructure in the Arctic as melting ice and growing geopolitical tensions turn the polar region into a strategic corridor for trade, communications and security.
content: The European Union is planning a secure submarine cable linking Greenland directly to Europe, with ambitions to extend the network through Canada to Japan and South Korea, according to a draft Arctic strategy seen by Euronews.The project is part of a broader effort to strengthen Europe's digital infrastructure and security in the increasingly contested Arctic region."The EU is working on a Pan-Arctic Cable concept that will connect Europe to Japan and South Korea via Greenland and Canada. In the coming years, the EU will connect Greenland to the European Union with a sovereign and secure submarine cable," the document reads.The plans, outlined in the EU's new Arctic strategy, due to be unveiled on 20 October, reflect growing concerns in Brussels that undersea telecommunications cables have become a matter of strategic security rather than simply commercial infrastructure.The initiative comes amid a deteriorating security environment in the Arctic, where Russia has expanded its military presence and European governments are increasingly concerned about hybrid threats, including interference with satellite navigation and sabotage of undersea infrastructure.Meanwhile, growing US interest in Greenland ,has added another layer of geopolitical tension to the region, underlining Europe's concerns about its dependence on infrastructure controlled by others.The North Atlantic has roughly 17 submarine telecommunications cables, with US technology giants playing a dominant role in the wider infrastructure network.Submarine cables carry the vast majority of international data traffic, underpinning everything from everyday communications to financial transactions. Their vulnerability to accidental damage or deliberate sabotage has become a major concern for European governments.For Brussels, improving Arctic connectivity goes beyond bringing faster internet to remote communities. The EU is looking to create more resilient routes for data and reduce exposure to infrastructure that could be disrupted during a geopolitical crisis.Greenland occupies a particularly sensitive position. Situated between Europe and North America, the autonomous Danish territory has become increasingly important to transatlantic security as competition intensifies over Arctic resources, shipping routes and military access.A more direct digital connection with Europe could strengthen the territory’s links to the EU while giving Brussels a greater stake in the infrastructure underpinning the region’s future."The new submarine cable routes will enhance the access of Arctic communities as well as boost resilience and redundancy in Europe’s digital connectivity. Such connection is a pre-condition for further investments highly relevant for both competitiveness, inclusion, preparedness and defence," reads the document.The proposed extension towards Asia through Canada would add a broader strategic dimension. Rather than treating Greenland as an isolated connectivity challenge, the EU is considering how Arctic infrastructure might form part of a wider network linking European and Asian economies.Whether that vision becomes a viable project will depend on technical feasibility, commercial demand, financing and cooperation with Canada and other partners.Who will pay?The EU has already earmarked €107 million for connectivity projects involving Greenland, meaning the proposed cable would build on existing commitments rather than represent an entirely new area of investment.The Commission had presented the idea of co-financing Far North Fibre, a route planning a subsea cable in the Arctic area, to EU member-state representatives. The project was estimated to cost around $1.15 billion, but the project received around €11 million.The potentially significant development is the prospect of a wider strategic connection between Greenland, Europe and, through Canada, Asian partners.Such a network would raise difficult questions about who pays for construction, who owns and operates the cables, how they would be protected and whether the route would be commercially viable.Any extension towards Japan and South Korea would also require agreement and coordination with partners beyond the EU.However, the strategy does not settle those questions. Nor does it establish a final route, budget or construction schedule for the proposed network.Still, it mentions creating an Arctic Cable Hub for EU countries, Norway and Iceland, to monitor, protect, and support the repair of submarine cables in the North Atlantic-Arctic. The hub will likely require support from an enhanced icebreaker fleet.Expanding the icebreaker fleetThe EU's Arctic ambitions extend beyond digital infrastructure to the ships needed to operate in the region's increasingly contested waters.At the Arctic Summit in September, the EU's special envoy for the region, former Finnish Prime Minister Jyrki Katainen, warned of a critical shortfall in European icebreaker capabilities.“This is not just an issue for Finland, for Norway, for Sweden. This is something for the entire European Union, for the entire European continent. And that's the reason why we are talking about that. And you have my support on that to do that jointly,” German Chancellor Friederik Merz said at the summit’s press conference.Indeed, the strategy goes in this direction, and vows to put in place an EU Industrial Maritime Value Chains Alliance meant to map icebreaking needs, available manufacturing capacity in Europe and the technical specifications required.“The EU, together with member states and like-minded partners, will develop options for joint procurement, pooling and sharing icebreaker capabilities and other capabilities relevant for the Arctic,” reads the strategy.The intent is to pool together funding and technological resources with Nordic countries and examine whether it is possible to facilitate the operational viability of nationally owned assets, while respecting the national command structure.The strategy explicitly mentions “assets with special focus on icebreakers for extreme high North environments utilising advanced, high-endurance propulsion systems, including nuclear.”

title: Istanbul flood death toll rises to eight as rescuers find more bodies, governor says
description: Authorities have received nearly 20,000 reports about property damage as a result of the torrential rainfall and the resulting floods, Governor Davut Gül said.
content: The toll from flooding in and around Istanbul last week rose to eight on Monday as rescuers found more bodies after Turkey's largest city was battered by the heaviest rainfall in over 80 years, officials said.Six died in Istanbul, while the bodies of two more people from a neighbouring province were washed up on the southeastern outskirts of the megacity, Istanbul governor Davut Gül told reporters.Wednesday's historic rainfall, which officials said was the heaviest since records began in 1942, caused chaos and flash flooding, with footage showing cars and people being dragged away by the fast-flowing waters.By Thursday, Gül said three people had died and another five were missing as huge efforts were under way to drain the floodwaters and clear up the damage and destruction caused by the torrential rainfall.One was a 14-year-old boy who was electrocuted when he stepped in a puddle. A fourth body was found on Friday and a fifth on Sunday in the Golden Horn estuary, state media Anadolu said. Both were men.On Monday, Gül's office said the body of another man was found near Ayvansaray ferry pier on the Golden Horn who had been reported missing."In Istanbul, a total of six people have died and one person is missing," Gül told reporters, saying another two people had died outside of Istanbul in the neighbouring province of Kocaeli."Two people who died in Kocaeli and were swept away as far as Pendik were found dead by our search and rescue teams. Therefore, a total of eight bodies have been found," he said, adding that search efforts were continuing for one more missing person.So far, authorities have received nearly 20,000 reports about property damage as a result of the torrential rainfall and the resulting floods, Gül said."We experienced a disaster that generated around 19,300 reports, each with different types of problems. At this point, it has been determined that around 2,000 homes and about 900 businesses...have suffered serious damage," he said.On Friday, authorities paid out 10,000 Turkish lira (€180) to 5,200 affected residents and will pay out the same amount to another 2,500 people on Monday, he said.

title: Amazon deforestation hits record low in Brazil, but El Niño and a tight election threaten progress
description: Deforestation fell almost 42% in a year, but a possible change in president could reverse the trend.
content: Deforestation in the Amazon rainforest has fallen to its lowest level since records began in 1988, Brazil's government has announced.Annual loss between August 2025 to July 2026 stood at 3,335 square kilometres, according to official satellite data – down 41.8 per cent from 5,731 square kilometres a year earlier.It's testament to the success of Brazil’s renewed efforts under President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva to curb Amazon deforestation, reversing a surge under his predecessor, far-right President Jair Bolsonaro.During Jair Bolsonaro’s presidency, from 2019 to 2022, Amazon deforestation surged by around 60 per cent, with more than 45,000 square kilometres cleared, according to official data. Under Lula, deforestation has fallen 71 per cent since 2023, the government said.One of Lula’s first moves after taking office in January 2023 for a third, non-consecutive term was to revive the Action Plan for the Prevention and Control of Deforestation in the Legal Amazon, known by its Portuguese acronym, PPCDAm. Launched in 2004 during his first administration, the plan had been shelved under Bolsonaro.Lula brought back the environmental officials who developed the blueprint two decades earlier, appointing environmental champion Marina Silva – who led the Environment Ministry until she resigned in April to run for Congress – and João Paulo Capobianco, her former deputy and the current minister, to help carry it out.How Brazil's government curbed deforestationThe plan has four pillars: strengthening monitoring and enforcement; promoting a sustainable economy; managing protected areas and determining how undesignated public forests should be used; and using regulations and financial incentives to curb deforestation.Measures included restoring sanctions for illegal forest clearing detected by satellites, a practice seen as the most effective tool to curb deforestation that was halted under Bolsonaro. The government also proposed barring properties with illegal deforestation from receiving bank loans and allocated more funding to priority Amazon municipalities that demonstrated reductions in forest loss. It also funded efforts to fight environmental crime and develop subsidised credit for sustainable businesses in the Amazon.“The formula is always the same, and it works. We saw it work in Brazil years ago and we’re seeing it again now: determination, enforcement on the ground, fighting crime and enforcing the law," says Márcio Astrini, executive secretary of the Climate Observatory, a Brazilian network of environmental groups.Astrini adds that the deforestation rates announced on 16 October show that Brazil's pledge to reach zero deforestation by 2030 is achievable without compromising the country's economy."Agriculture has been setting production and export records while deforestation has fallen. Today’s figures disprove the false narrative that protecting the environment holds back Brazil’s development,” he adds.Deforestation and other land-use changes are Brazil’s largest sources of greenhouse gas emissions, which drive global warming. The stakes are especially high in the Amazon, which stores vast amounts of carbon dioxide and generates atmospheric moisture that helps regulate weather far beyond South America.New president could determine future of the AmazonDespite progress curbing deforestation, the Amazon faces threats from climate change, proposed legislation and a possible change in Brazil’s presidency.Degradation from wildfires, logging and drought affects about 40 per cent of the Amazon and has outpaced clear-cutting in recent years. A strong El Niño, a periodic warming of the equatorial Pacific, could intensify those threats in 2026 and 2027 by bringing hotter, drier conditions that fuel wildfires.Fire counts across the biome were near historic lows this year but have tripled since 4 October, when Brazilians voted in the first round of national elections. Authorities are investigating whether fires were deliberately set for political reasons ahead of this month’s presidential runoff.NASA scientists caution that official satellite counts may understate the damage: around Santarém, a preliminary analysis found about 40 per cent more fires than standard active-fire data shows. Agency satellite observations revealed a sharp increase in fires and smoke emissions across the central and eastern Amazon beginning in September 2026, fuelled by severe drought linked to El Niño.Environment Minister Capobianco said officials flying over protected areas saw fires arranged in a geometric pattern, suggesting they were set deliberately, though it is unclear who is responsible. Smoke has closed schools in Manaus, the largest city in the Brazilian Amazon, and residents were urged to wear face masks.Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, won 47 per cent of the vote, while Lula received 45 per cent. The two face a 25 October runoff.The candidates offer sharply different visions for the rainforest. Climate and conservation experts warn that a Bolsonaro victory could reverse policies to curb deforestation. He has pledged to end illegal deforestation by 2029, a year ahead of Brazil’s current target. Lula’s reelection pledge goes further: zero net deforestation by 2030, with restoration offsetting all forest loss, legal or illegal.'Historic achievement' following 'sweeping dismantling of environmental policies'Cristiane Mazzetti of Greenpeace Brazil says the record low deforestation rate reflects effective policies that could be at risk depending on who wins the presidential election.“Congress has worked to weaken, delay and dismantle laws and regulations that help protect the environment,” she says. “The next legislature will be even more hostile to environmental protection, and depending on the next federal administration, the risk of rollbacks and high deforestation rates will rise sharply.”Former Minister Silva said in a statement on Friday (16 October) that the deforestation reduction was a “historic achievement” for the Brazilian people and that the election outcome would be crucial to sustain it.“Jair Bolsonaro’s administration approached environmental protection and climate change with denial and a sweeping dismantling of environmental policies. Flávio has inherited those views and practices and intends to perpetuate them, as he has indicated on several occasions,” she says.“Those who deny the problem exists will certainly do nothing to address it.”Bolsonaro has denied climate change while portraying himself as an environmental defender, without detailing plans to protect the Amazon or support forest financing. He has called for modernising environmental laws, which many environmentalists interpret as weakening them.“Flávio Bolsonaro is a defender of the environment and of those who preserve standing forests and clean rivers,” his campaign said.

title: Euronews press review: French newspapers dissect weekend of unrest and rioting
description: French newspapers examine the causes of a weekend of unrest, questioning the police response, violence and examining the role of the ultra-left.
content: Euronews reviews France’s leading newspapers after a weekend of unrest, with protests over student living conditions turning violent and riots and looting reported in major cities.Libération: Police fiascoIn its Monday 19 October edition, Libération questions the authorities’ handling of the demonstrations, noting that turnout far exceeded expectations.“There were five times more of them than the 150,000 demonstrators anticipated by Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez,” the newspaper writes.It asks whether the government and security forces took the calls for demonstrations seriously enough, describing the events as “the anatomy of a fiasco”.The paper draws on the analysis of Sébastian Roché, a sociologist specialising in policing practices, who describes how police tactics contributed to the disorder.“It was barely 12.20 pm on Place de la République in Paris when the tear gas began to spread across the sky, accompanied by deafening grenade blasts,” he says, nearly two hours before the march was due to begin.Similar scenes unfolded in Marseille and Bordeaux, where gatherings descended into chaos within minutes. Clashes also broke out in Clermont-Ferrand.Roché argues that police operations split up the marches, scattering demonstrators and making it harder for officers to maintain control — a strategy he says contributed to the damage.Le Figaro: A scathing editorialIn his Monday editorial, Le Figaro deputy editor-in-chief Vincent Trémolet de Villers condemns what he describes as “a state humiliated in its town halls, its préfectures and its police stations”.Trémolet de Villers, also a commentator on Europe 1, owned by billionaire Vincent Bolloré, criticises the judicial system, which he portrays as “indulgent towards criminals but merciless towards law-abiding citizens”.He also attacks what he calls “far-left militias”, “uncontrolled immigration” and the “various forms of socialism that have governed us for the past fifteen years”.In particularly sharp terms, he targets supporters of Jean-Luc Mélenchon, leader of La France Insoumise, calling them “useful idiots” who “not only wear the keffiyeh but also the tie”. He also denounces what he describes as a “technocratic monarchy, drunk on its own power”.Le Monde: Organised ultra-leftLe Monde examines the ultra-left, a movement singled out by several political leaders following the unrest.The newspaper traces its roots to political currents that emerged to the left of communist parties in the 20th century, including council communism, which advocates the direct organisation of workers into councils and rejects political parties.Historian Sylvain Boulouque, a specialist in anarchism and the far left, explains that the ultra-left originally referred to groups that rejected the French Communist Party’s political model, parliamentary politics and elections.The article describes a movement whose actions can follow “a logic of confrontation with the symbols of the state, capitalism or authority”.Historian Gilles Candar, a specialist in the French left, cautions that the term “ultra-left” carries a connotation of excess and is now often used polemically.He argues that some political leaders’ tendency to equate the ultra-left with the ultra-right creates what he calls a “regrettable and harmful false symmetry”.

title: Australian MP Helen Haines 'critically' hurt in car ramming attack, officials say
description: The 43-year-old male driver was detained by civilians, Mason said, and then arrested by police, who found a knife in his car.
content: Australian independent lawmaker Helen Haines was deliberately struck by a car and suffered "critical injuries" on Monday in what Prime Minister Anthony Albanese described as an attack.Haines was hurt outside her office in Wangaratta, just over 200 kilometres northwest of Melbourne, police said.The 65-year-old "suffered what has been described as critical injuries", Victoria Police Acting Superintendent Ashley Mason said, without identifying the victim in line with police custom in Australia.The 43-year-old male driver was detained by civilians, Mason said, and then arrested by police, who found a knife in his car."This wasn't an accident. There was a deliberate act," Albanese told national broadcaster ABC.He also told journalists: "All of our thoughts are with Helen, her family, her friends, her team, and her community at this extremely difficult time. We are praying for her full recovery."The alleged attacker's motive remained unknown, Albanese said, with Australia's counter-terrorism squad activated.The Australian Federal Police has documented a steady rise in threats and abuse directed towards the nation's politicians in recent years.They established a dedicated team last year to investigate groups and individuals targeting lawmakers.Albanese said on Monday that "the temperature has increased in recent times"."I've expressed that concern to people in the media," he said."If you look at anyone's social media feeds and look at the comments, people will say things that they would never say face to face."'Thoroughly decent'Haines entered parliament in 2019 after working as a nurse and midwife, becoming known for stances such as supporting stronger climate action.She was widely praised for her efforts to increase transparency in politics and crack down on corruption."This afternoon, our beloved Helen was involved in an incident outside her Wangaratta Electorate Office, and is receiving medical care," her family said in a statement."We thank the swift assistance of bystanders and the dedicated health workers who assisted her, and police for their response.""Our family, and Helen's staff, will be making no further comment at this time, and ask that their privacy be respected by the public and media," the statement said.Albanese said Haines was "incredibly hardworking"."She is fiercely intelligent but, most importantly, she's just a thoroughly decent human being," he said.

title: Musk pledges SpaceX shares to every US child in potential $10.7bn giveaway
description: Elon Musk says he will give one SpaceX share to every child in America next year, a pledge worth about $10.7bn (€9.5bn) at Friday’s closing price. He has yet to explain who would qualify or how the shares would be distributed.
content: Elon Musk on Monday pledged to give one of his own SpaceX shares to "every kid in America" next year.The offer came a day after artificial intelligence company Anthropic announced in a social media post that it would commit 5% of its shares to a new "public benefit" fund, subject to shareholder approval.In a response to that Sunday post, Musk wrote, "I recommend giving the shares directly to the public."Shares of SpaceX, which will report its quarterly earnings on Tuesday, closed at $146.03 (€130.09) on Friday.With approximately 73 million children under the age of 18 in the United States, that would put the value of Musk's pledge at about $10.66 billion (€9.5 billion), based on Friday's closing price.Anthropic said Sunday that the shares it is committing would go to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, a new entity wholly owned by the company. The fund's value could rise if the shares increase in value.Musk did not provide further details on how his share pledge would be carried out, but added in his post that "This will be the first of many."The announcements by Musk and Anthropic come as Americans grow increasingly wary of AI. A new poll from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research found that 64% of Americans think AI is developing "too fast," while 27% say its development has been "about right" and only 8% say it's moving "too slow."Anthropic's Dario Amodei, OpenAI's Sam Altman, Musk and other prominent industry leaders said last month that AI's development needs to slow down. The consensus came after an Anthropic researcher resigned with a dire warning about the threats the technology poses to humanity. But obstacles including domestic and global competition, the pursuit of profit and pushback from President Donald Trump all stand in the way of a coordinated effort to slow AI's development.Meanwhile, Musk has quietly become the biggest known donor in this year's US midterm elections, giving more than $276 million (€246 million) since July to try to preserve Republican majorities in Congress.Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei and the company's five other co-founders established Anthropic as a public benefit corporation, a designation that for-profit companies can choose to balance financial goals and social impact.Anthropic is planning a major initial public offering (IPO) as soon as November. In June, the company said that it had submitted a confidential filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission for its proposed IPO.That same month, Musk's SpaceX made its Wall Street debut and made Musk the world's first trillionaire. However, SpaceX shares have fallen 35.3% since peaking days after the IPO, reducing Musk's fortune.

title: Visegrad Four urge Brussels to ease Russian energy phase-out rules
description: The group is calling on Brussels for more funding to cope with the end of Russian energy imports in 2027, amid high electricity prices across Europe.
content: Slovakia and Hungary called on Brussels on Monday for greater flexibility in phasing out Russian gas, arguing that their landlocked position and reliance on existing supply routes make diversification more difficult and costly.Bratislava said it had historically served as an entry point for Russian oil and gas but now risks becoming the end of the line, alongside Hungary, as Russian energy supplies to Central Europe are due to end in 2027 under the EU’s plan to phase out imports from Moscow.“We would like to discuss with the European Commission how the next EU funding period and the availability of EU funds can meet our needs, particularly regarding the expansion of oil and gas infrastructure in the Visegrad Four region,” Slovakia’s Deputy Prime Minister Denisa Saková said on the sidelines of a press conference in Bratislava attended by Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen.Central European ministers want Brussels to recognise their specific circumstances and take regional needs into account when allocating EU funds for new oil and gas infrastructure and preparing the next EU budget period — another point of contention among member states at the latest European Council summit.The appeal follows pressure from the Visegrad Group — Hungary, Slovakia, Czechia and Poland — on EU leaders at their 15-16 October summit to reconsider measures to lower electricity bills in the region.Their demands included greater flexibility in the ongoing review of the bloc’s carbon market, the Emissions Trading System (ETS), and delaying its second phase, ETS2, until 2030.Energy Commissioner Jørgensen acknowledged the “serious” situation facing people in Central Europe and reiterated the need for “targeted and temporary measures” that would not undermine the bloc’s goal of reducing its reliance on imported fossil fuels.“We used to be dependent on Russia. We’re moving out of that. Now, that is good. But the current situation shows that we are now dependent on the global market, and events in the Middle East can affect citizens here in Bratislava,” Jørgensen said.The four EU countries, traditionally more reliant on fossil fuels, argue that high energy prices make it difficult for their industries to commit to investments in electrification. Prices have been driven higher by the US-Israeli war against Iran.Central European consumers are facing a significantly heavier financial burden, with wholesale electricity futures more than 60% above pre-crisis levels, according to energy think tank Ember.Ditching Russian energy is raising economic concerns in both countries.Bratislava and Budapest argue that they face particular challenges in meeting the EU’s diversification requirements and want funding to expand oil and gas infrastructure in the region.The Visegrad Group has access to several alternative energy sources and supply routes that bypass Russia, albeit at higher cost, with varying levels of integration across the four countries.“From 2027, we will not be able to import gas from Russia and would like to sign new diversification contracts. Diversification and energy security mean that we have to have prepared rules for the supplies of oil and gas for the V4 region,” Saková added.Under former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, Hungary challenged the EU’s plan to phase out Russian energy imports, taking the case to an EU court.Slovakia backed Budapest’s legal challenge, arguing that phasing out Russian energy would put its industrial competitiveness at a significant disadvantage compared with most other EU countries. A first ruling is expected to take months.

title: Putin seeks Ukraine summit with Trump and Xi but refuses talks with Zelenskyy
description: The proposed talks come as Washington eases economic pressure on Moscow while pressing Ukraine to halt strikes on Russian oil infrastructure, raising concerns in Kyiv that the Kremlin is securing concessions without making any of its own.
content: Russia's President Vladimir Putin has reportedly proposed a three-way summit with US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping next month to negotiate an end to the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, according to US media.Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha warned on Monday that such a meeting would only encourage Putin to continue the war, while the European Commission questioned Moscow's willingness to negotiate an end to the conflict."A trilateral meeting between the leaders of Ukraine, the US, and Russia could help end the war sooner. A trilateral meeting between the leaders of Russia, China, and the US would do only the opposite: encourage Putin to continue this war," Sybiha wrote on X.The proposal was reportedly made during a telephone conversation between Putin and Trump on 9 October, which also produced a controversial agreement involving Russian diesel exports to US and international markets.Citing people familiar with the discussions, the Wall Street Journal reported on Sunday that the Kremlin suggested holding the meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen which takes place on 18–19 November.Kremlin spokesman Dmitri Peskov confirmed to the paper that discussions were under way, although no agreement has been reached yet on the meeting or its agenda.A senior US official told the newspaper that Trump has not agreed to attend but could be receptive to the proposal.There was no indication that Ukraine would participate in the proposed talks.Putin repeatedly declined proposals to meet Zelenskyy on neutral ground, insisting that any direct talks between the two leaders take place in Moscow, a condition Kyiv has rejected.Kyiv and Brussels challenge Putin's proposed summitSybiha argued that offering Putin a place alongside the American and Chinese presidents would reward Moscow without requiring it to take meaningful steps towards peace."Inviting Putin to such a meeting would feed his appetite for self-aggrandisement and give him a stature he does not deserve. He is not a global leader; he is a war criminal. And Russia is not a global power; it is a global problem," he wrote."By any pragmatic or moral measure, Putin has no place at the table with presidents Trump and Xi," Sybiha said.He argued that accepting a ceasefire before any such meeting could demonstrate a genuine willingness to negotiate, rather than continuing attacks on Ukrainian civilians."As long as he continues this terror, there should be no place for him at any table," he added.The European Commission also questioned Moscow's willingness to end the war, pointing to Russia's continued attacks despite the energy ceasefire announced by Trump."If Putin would like to end this war, you can just stop this war today. And the war could be over today," a Commission spokesperson said on Monday.The spokesperson also recalled the conclusions of the latest European Council summit, stressing that Europe had a key role to play in any future settlement and would defend its interests.The prospect of such a meeting comes as Trump seeks to revive negotiations with Moscow, arguing that imposing further economic pressure on Russia could undermine efforts to end the war."My decision on Russia is a very simple one," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform on Sunday."I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don't want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table. Great progress is being made, and that includes current hostage negotiations!"He offered no details of any concessions secured from Moscow.Trump defends Russian diesel deal amid growing criticismTrump's remarks followed his decision on 16 October to waive a series of new sanctions and tariffs targeting Russia and countries trading with it, just days before the measures were due to take effect.The move came a week after his agreement with Putin on Russian diesel exports, as Washington seeks to contain soaring fuel prices exacerbated by the war in Iran.Trump defended the diesel arrangement by arguing that Russia had refrained from providing more substantial assistance to Iran in its conflict with the US."Russia is doing very little, if anything, to help the Islamic Republic of Iran, compared to what they could be doing, and I want to keep it that way, and will, unless stupid people get in the way," he wrote.He also praised Moscow for supplying diesel to global markets at reduced prices, portraying the agreement as a contribution to easing pressure on international energy supplies.At the same time, Washington has increasingly pressed Kyiv to suspend its campaign against Russian oil refineries, which Ukraine considers legitimate military targets because of the revenue they generate for Moscow's war effort.The Trump administration even reportedly threatened to suspend intelligence-sharing and weapons deliveries unless Ukraine halted the strikes.The dispute further strained relations between Washington and Kyiv, particularly as Russia continues to bombard Ukrainian cities and critical infrastructure.Zelenskyy accuses partners of ignoring reality of Russia's warVolodymyr Zelenskyy warned that easing pressure on Moscow risks prolonging the war, accusing Russia of rejecting diplomatic efforts to end the conflict while intensifying its attacks on Ukraine.His latest comments followed another overnight bombardment in which, according to Zelenskyy, Russian forces launched 16 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and the surrounding region, alongside more than 200 drones across the country, including jet-powered variants.More than ten energy facilities were damaged, leaving at least 550,000 households without electricity, he said. A medical clinic, a school, a metro station and residential buildings were also damaged.Zelenskyy also said Ukraine had once again received no advance warning from its partners about the incoming ballistic missiles."Putin not only doesn't want to end this war – he doesn't even want to take any steps toward de-escalation," Zelenskyy wrote on X.He stressed that Ukraine had responded positively to every ceasefire proposal put forward by its partners, while Russia had continued its attacks."When deliveries of missiles for Ukraine's air defence are blocked while Russia is granted relief or delays in sanctions, this is, unfortunately, a denial of reality on the part of our partners," he said."The reality is that the war continues, and it continues solely because of Russian strikes and Russia's desire to drag this war out," Zelenskyy said.

title: Could France’s debt troubles tip Italy into recession?
description: Rising borrowing costs and political uncertainty are putting France’s finances under pressure. Oxford Economics warns that a severe bond-market shock could push both France and Italy into recession in 2027, although a debt crisis remains outside its central forecast.
content: The eurozone’s second-largest economy saw its bond yields rise further on Monday, following violent street demonstrations in the country over the weekend.France’s 10-year government bond yield hovered around 4.9% on Monday, near its highest level in more than two decades, as investors demanded a higher premium for holding French debt. Protesters are demanding action on the rising cost of living and declining public services, including education.The unrest adds to pressure on the government as it battles to get its 2027 budget through a deeply divided National Assembly, the lower house of France’s parliament.The immediate challenge is to pass a credible budget that reassures investors ahead of the presidential election in spring 2027. But restoring confidence will also depend on whether the next administration can commit to improving public finances over several years.What is fuelling investors’ concerns?France is nursing one of the highest public debt ratios in the EU, at 119% of GDP, according to the latest reading from INSEE, the national statistics office. This is coupled with a government forecast for a deficit of 5.4% of GDP in 2026. Public debt stood at €3.596 trillion at the end of June 2026.The cost of servicing that debt has been rising sharply. The government forecasts public debt interest payments of €91 billion in 2027, up from €79.2 billion this year — an increase of almost €12 billion.Accelerating inflation and low growth threaten to weaken tax revenues and raise the deficit and debt further.The current fiscal situation therefore leaves little room for the government to meet protesters’ demands through another large spending package, along the lines of French President Emmanuel Macron’s “whatever it costs” approach when the pandemic hit the country.The government faces pressure to reduce the deficit and commit to lasting savings to calm nerves on the bond market. If borrowing costs keep rising, France’s debt could become increasingly difficult to control.And a spiralling crisis could also hit other major eurozone economies, such as Italy.How France’s debt troubles could hit ItalyModelling the impact of bond turmoil in France, with some contagion to other high-debt eurozone countries, Oxford Economics found that Italy would be particularly vulnerable because it combines slow growth, high debt and investment that is sensitive to tighter financial conditions.A key yardstick for measuring market concerns is the gap between a country’s 10-year government bond yield and Germany’s equivalent. The current spread — the extra return investors want to hold French debt instead of German debt — has risen to around 145 basis points (bps). This is still slightly below the peak reached earlier this month, which was the highest since the eurozone debt crisis of 2011–2012.Oxford Economics sets out a baseline and two adverse scenarios. Its baseline assumes that France’s spread stays below 200bps ahead of the April 2027 presidential election and narrows afterwards. It continues to view a French debt crisis as an unlikely but potentially damaging outcome, rather than its central forecast.The two adverse scenarios combine higher borrowing costs with a hit to business and consumer confidence. In the moderate scenario, the French spread widens to 250bps from around 140bps when the report was published on 15 October. In the severe scenario, it reaches 400bps.France and Italy would enter recession in 2027 under the severe scenario. Belgium would also see a jump in its borrowing costs, while Spain, Portugal and Greece would face higher bond yields but less economic damage, with none of the three economies contracting.Crucially, the eurozone as a whole would avoid recession even under this severe scenario.According to Andrew Kenningham, chief Europe economist at Capital Economics, a widening of France’s spread to 400bps is a “plausible adverse scenario, (…) which would be comparable to Italy’s spreads in 2012”.Kenningham agreed that, in that case, there would certainly be a lot of pressure on other high-debt economies, including Italy.“However, in contrast to the early 2010s, the ECB would be well placed to support countries other than France through its Transmission Protection Instrument,” he said.With this instrument, the ECB can buy government bonds to help keep borrowing costs under control if the country meets certain conditions.Kenningham also said that the risks to the banking sector and the risk of a property crash are much lower than in the 2010s.“So things could get very bad but not as bad as in the 2010s.”According to Oxford Economics, in its severe scenario, France’s 10-year bond yield would reach 7% in the second quarter of 2027, with the public deficit on track to surpass 6% of GDP. The consultancy warns that yields at such levels could trigger a liquidity crisis.But expectations of ECB intervention to help France remain low. ECB President Christine Lagarde said last week that the means to stop the surge in French borrowing costs “must first be found in France”, through budget measures to reassure investors.What France can do to regain investors’ confidenceAccording to Oxford Economics, the measures needed to calm markets could include gradual spending restraint over several years, accompanied by clear legislative commitments, especially on the retirement age.But the consultancy warns that “the current minority government will not be able to credibly commit to sustained fiscal consolidation to soothe markets”. Much of the responsibility for carrying out any painful measures could therefore fall to the next administration.In the meantime, Kenningham said investors are expecting the government to pass a budget that reduces next year’s deficit to around 5% of GDP, “so anything less than that could lead to further loss of confidence in the French bond market”.Ahead of next spring’s presidential election, far-right leader Marine Le Pen is leading in the polls. In an interview with the Financial Times last week, she promised: “massive reductions in public spending, while reviving the economy”.She presented her “counter-budget” on 6 October, targeting €140 billion in net savings by 2032 compared with 2026, a deficit below 3% of GDP by 2030 and a constitutional budget rule. Her party proposes cutting administrative and social security spending, immigration-related expenditure and France’s EU contribution.But economists questioned the figures. Mathieu Plane, deputy director of analysis and forecasting at the French Economic Observatory (OFCE), told Le Monde that more than €80 billion of the proposed savings were questionable, poorly defined and difficult to implement.In the meantime, France is facing the risk of a vicious circle in which higher borrowing costs force further spending cuts or tax rises, weakening growth and making its debt harder to control.“France has been heading towards a debt crisis for many years and that moment is now getting closer,” Kenningham concluded.

title: Protests spread across Europe: Cost-of-living pressures behind the demonstrations
description: From rising food prices and unaffordable housing to stagnant purchasing power and strained public services, demonstrations across Europe highlight growing frustration over living standards.
content: Thousands of people took to the streets across Europe over the weekend to protest against rising living costs, unaffordable housing, low wages and pressure on public services. While the grievances varied from country to country, the demonstrations highlight growing frustration over household budgets.In France, hundreds of thousands of people joined demonstrations involving students and other groups protesting over living costs and public services. Many marched peacefully, but French President Emmanuel Macron vowed to hold accountable those who “sought to bring down the Republic" after some gatherings descended into looting and rioting across major cities, with some 1,500 shops and retailers damaged.The cost to the establishments will run to "several hundreds of millions of euros", Alexandre Bompard, president of the Retail and Trade Federation, told LCI television, adding it was too early to give an exact figure.Limoges city hall went up in flames, as did the iconic tourist office on Place Bellecour in Lyon. Vandals also forced their way into town halls in Marseille, Lille, and Angers, whilst in Bordeaux, the prefect's residence was ransacked."Protesting is a right, and anger deserves to be heard. Yet, no disagreement or grievance can ever justify the destruction of public property," Guillaume Guérin, the mayor of Limoges, said, calling the violence "unacceptable."In Belgium, police clashed with demonstrators in Brussels and Liège during cost-of-living protests. High-school students had also demonstrated in recent weeks against rising education costs, joining students in France protesting over school conditions and teacher shortages.Sharing the same sentiment as the mayor of Limoges and other politicians, Belgian interior minister Bernard Quintin said on Saturday that the situation was "no longer simply a protest," calling it "pure and simple violence."In Portugal, trade unions and housing-rights groups called for higher wages, better pensions, improved public services and action on housing affordability. Organisers pointed to rising rents, mortgage costs and everyday expenses as mounting pressures on household budgets.Italy also saw demonstrations over economic conditions and rising prices. Clashes in Milan, Turin and Bologna left people injured, while dozens were detained in Milan.Why are Europeans angry?Rising food, housing and energy costs have left many households struggling to make their incomes stretch further. Even when inflation slows, prices generally remain higher than they were before, leaving consumers with less room in their budgets.Housing is a particular concern for renters and younger people in many cities. Low-paid workers face pressure from essential expenses, while concerns over education and other public services have added to discontent in some countries.Eurostat data analysed by Euronews Business shows that EU food and non-alcoholic beverage prices rose by 34% between August 2021 and August 2026. The amount of food a gross monthly minimum wage could buy fell by 6% in Malta, 5% in Spain and 4% in France, while it increased in most of the countries studied.
