The comparison excludes taxes, rent and other household expenses, however, and does not capture the full cost-of-living squeeze.The protests do not represent a single Europe-wide movement, and their demands differ. However, they highlight the pressure on household finances and the growing challenge of ensuring wages keep pace with the cost of essentials.How are the markets reacting?European markets, including France's CAC 40, opened lower this morning, as was also noted by Victoria Scholar, head of investment at Interactive Investors."There is a sea of red across European markets today with the CAC and FTSE MIB down over 1.5% on the continent. Demonstrations and protests about the state of public services and rising prices have turned to riots, weighing on financial markets," she told Euronews Business."The risk-off mood has spread to the bond and currency markets too, including French and Italian government debt and the euro which are under pressure. The spread between French and German yields have also widened reflecting the uncertainty in France."It comes at an already unstable time for the French government with markets worrying about the 2027 budget bill, the challenging state of public finances and the looming presidential election next year," she added.

title: German police say two men turned themselves in after smashing car into airport fence
description: In August, an attack with an explosives-laden drone took place at the same airport. German authorities blamed that on Russia, an allegation denied by Moscow.
content: German police said on Monday that two men turned themselves in after a security fence was damaged at the airport in the city of Leipzig, an incident that raised concerns following an attack at the same airport over the summer that German authorities attributed to Russia.The two individuals, aged 20 and 32, turned themselves in on Sunday night, according to a statement issued by the Leipzig police.The younger man said through a lawyer that he lost control of the car while driving in the airport area the previous night and crashed through the fence.He then left the scene of the accident and sent for the car to be towed away. He did not have a driver's licence.The 32-year old admitted he was the owner of the car and gave no further details, the police said. The car has been seized and the investigation was continuing, the statement also said.German authorities had been investigating how a gaping hole was cut into a fence around Leipzig Airport.The damage was discovered at around 2300 CET on Saturday. Police said initial evidence suggested that a vehicle had ploughed through the fence along a publicly accessible road.Emergency teams that searched the airport grounds didn’t find the vehicle or any intruder.In August, an attack with an explosives-laden drone took place at the airport. German authorities blamed that on Russia, an allegation denied by Moscow.

title: Daedalus: Greece unveils new supercomputer as it eyes role in Europe's AI race
description: With a performance of 85.69 petaflops, Daedalus opens up new possibilities for developing advanced AI models in Greece.
content: Greece is entering a new phase in the development of high-performance computing infrastructure with the launch of Daedalus, the most powerful supercomputer ever installed in the country.Backed by an investment of 58.9 million euros and performance figures that, according to available data, place it 31st worldwide, the system inaugurated in Lavrio (Attica) aims to bolster domestic technology production and reduce reliance on overseas computing facilities.The significance of the project goes beyond the power of the equipment. Daedalus creates the conditions for universities, research centres, businesses, public bodies and health organisations to develop and train advanced Artificial Intelligence (AI) models, process large volumes of data and carry out complex computing projects on infrastructure located in Greece.Particularly important is the ability to process sensitive or confidential data within the country, under the prescribed security and personal data protection safeguards.This feature could prove crucial for applications in medical research, public administration and sectors where data handling is subject to strict constraints.Daedalus' position in the European computing infrastructureWith a measured computing power of 85.69 petaflops, that is roughly 85.69 quadrillion floating-point operations per second, Daedalus is capable of supporting demanding AI model training, simulations and advanced data analytics.Its global ranking is an indication of the country's technological upgrade. However, assessing its position relative to other European supercomputers requires a distinction between systems of different scale and purpose.Europe hosts extremely high-performance infrastructures, including exascale-class systems with power exceeding one exaflop, that is 1,000 petaflops.Daedalus is not designed to compete directly with the largest European installations in terms of absolute computing power.Its value lies mainly in giving Greece access to substantial computing resources, supporting specialised applications and integrating into a broader European ecosystem of AI infrastructures.For the domestic research and business community, having such an infrastructure can lower barriers to accessing computing resources, facilitate the development of technology products and strengthen cooperation with European research networks.At the same time, Greece gains greater capacity to set its own priorities in developing Artificial Intelligence applications.The focus on energy efficiency is underscored by the fact that, according to the Green500 ranking of June 2026, Daedalus ranked 23rd worldwide among supercomputers on the basis of their energy performance.Liquid cooling and Nvidia technologyThe system is based on Nvidia Grace Hopper GH200 technology and uses liquid cooling, which helps manage the thermal loads generated by high-performance equipment during operation.It has been installed in the historic building of the former power station at the Lavrio Technology and Cultural Park, which operates under the responsibility of the National Technical University of Athens.The National Infrastructures for Research and Technology (EDYTE – GRNET) has taken on the management and technical operation of the system and is also responsible for delivering the project.Hewlett Packard Enterprise supplied and installed the computing equipment under a budget of 41 million euros, while Mainsys carried out the electromechanical installations and configured the data centre, with a budget of 17.9 million euros. The amounts include VAT.Funding comes from the Recovery and Resilience Facility and the European High-Performance Computing Joint Undertaking (EuroHPC).Pharos AI Factory: bridging the gap to the marketA decisive role in bringing Daedalus to the business community is expected to be played by Pharos AI Factory, the Greek Artificial Intelligence factory, which is among the first seven similar initiatives selected by the European Union.With a capacity of 85.69 petaflops, Daedalus opens up new possibilities for developing advanced Artificial Intelligence models in Greece.Its position within Europe's computing infrastructure, its ability to process sensitive data inside the country and its interconnection with Pharos AI Factory create a new space for research, innovation and entrepreneurship.According to the current planning, broader service provision to businesses is scheduled to begin in March 2027, once the period of technical testing and system configuration has been completed.Access will combine computing resources with advisory support and services that facilitate the transition from research to commercial exploitation.Start-ups and small and medium-sized enterprises are expected to be able to use computing power without charge, within the limits set by European state aid rules.For larger companies, charging based on the time spent using computing resources is being considered. The final access conditions, detailed services and pricing policy have not yet been finalised.The planned service package includes guidance on adopting Artificial Intelligence, support for the commercial exploitation of applications, access to collaboration networks and business acceleration programmes.It also envisages secure testing environments, infrastructure for deploying applications in production, access to AI models, selected datasets and open data.For the commercial exploitation of the initiative, the company Hellenic AI Factory S.A. has been established, in which the Hellenic Corporation of Assets and Participations (the "Superfund") holds a 70% stake, while the remaining 30% belongs to the Ministry of Digital Governance and Artificial Intelligence.Planned actions include a training programme on developing AI agents, in cooperation with Endeavor Greece and Nvidia.The programme, scheduled for 10 November, is expected to host 45 selected participants, who will be trained in creating digital agents, linking them to large language models and using related tools through practical exercises.A second supercomputer in Western MacedoniaIn parallel, planning is advancing for the development of a second supercomputer at the University of Western Macedonia in Kozani.The EDYTE board has approved the launch of a public consultation on the tender for the supply and installation of computing equipment, storage systems and software, with a budget of 21.57 million euros, including VAT.The amount concerns this specific sub-project and not the entire investment. For that reason, a revision of the budget and an update of the timetable are expected to be examined by amending the inclusion decision.The new system is designed to operate in a green data centre, integrated into EDYTE's RE-Cloud network, with an emphasis on Artificial Intelligence, cloud computing services and the analysis of sensitive data.The plan envisages IT infrastructure with power of between 1.2 and 1.5 MW, as well as a photovoltaic installation with capacity of more than 2 MWp.The sub-project is financed by the Just Development Transition Programme, and the planned duration of the contract's implementation is 12 months from the date of signature.

title: Northern Ireland and Scotland schools sent hoax bomb warnings, officials say
description: Meanwhile, Scottish police said "threatening messages" had also been sent to "a number of schools across Scotland".
content: Dozens of schools in Northern Ireland and Scotland received warnings about a bomb threat on Monday, police and authorities said, with some places reportedly evacuated, even though officials said it appeared to be a hoax."This morning 160 schools received a threat...At this stage the advice to schools is that we're not treating this as a viable threat, but it has clearly caused huge alarm," Northern Ireland Education Minister Paul Givan told reporters."It would appear to me (to be) from Islamists threatening that Sharia law will be brought into our country and that there is viable devices within those school settings and it was signed off 'Allah Akbar'," Givan added.Northern Ireland police said they had received reports "of an email sent to a number of schools across Northern Ireland"."As a result of this email, police are conducting urgent enquiries, and liaising with the schools in question," police said in a statement.Local media and Givan said "some schools" had closed as a result.Meanwhile, Scottish police said "threatening messages" had also been sent to "a number of schools across Scotland"."These are being treated as a hoax and officers are investigating," Police Scotland said in a statement.The nature and scale of the messages sent to Scottish schools was unclear.A politician in Belfast's parliament, Deborah Erskine, said emergency evacuation procedures were initiated at "some local schools" in her constituency in the southwest.

title: Polish satellite maker Creotech Instruments plans tenfold capacity boost by 2029
description: CEO Grzegorz Brona warned that Europe could remain reliant on US rockets to launch its satellites into orbit for years.
content: Polish satellite maker Creotech Instruments plans to increase its production capacity tenfold by 2029, CEO Grzegorz Brona said in an interview with Reuters. He also warned that Europe will still need US rockets to launch its satellites into orbit for years.The satellite maker is aiming to open a new factory in 2029 in Mazowieckie, Poland, capable of making 40 satellites a year across different models, or 100 of a single model. This compares with 10 at its current site in Piaseczno, just outside Warsaw.The comments come at a time when Europe is trying to reduce its reliance on US technology.Two days before the interview, reports emerged that Elon Musk’s SpaceX had been ordered to limit Ukraine’s access to Starshield, its military-grade version of the Starlink satellite network, by the White House.Donald Trump has since said: “It wasn’t me, and I don’t think it was Elon. I don’t know if it was anybody. From what I understand, it’s the same as it’s always been.”The lack of clarity over who was responsible for the decision is one concern. But for European leaders, the prospect of the Trump administration using US technology as political leverage against its allies is even more alarming.Europe lags far behind the US in rocket launches, accounting for just eight of the world’s 324 orbital launches last year, compared with 193 by the US. Starlink alone accounts for more than 60% of active satellites, according to European Space Agency data.Asked whether European industry could build an alternative to Starlink, Brona said the continent could produce thousands of satellites and still have no one to launch them.“Launch vehicles are now becoming a means of political pressure on the European Union in the hands of [US President] Donald Trump’s administration,” he said.Creotech, which does not build rockets, has kept US technology out of its satellites to avoid US arms export rules. Under these rules, Washington can block sales of satellites containing even a small American component.Yet the company still relies on US rockets. SpaceX carried all four satellites Creotech built for Poland’s MikroGlob military programme into orbit.Europe seeks to increase launch capacityEurope is trying to expand its launch capacity in several ways.The European Space Agency (ESA) announced in September that it was considering increasing the number of launches of its Ariane 6 and Vega-C rockets in the coming years to overcome a potential bottleneck in satellite deployments.ESA Director General Josef Aschbacher said a decision was needed soon ahead of an expected sharp rise in demand.Arianespace, the operator of the Ariane 6 rocket, is planning nine or 10 launches a year from 2027.Meanwhile, European Commissioner for Defence and Space Andrius Kubilius has said the EU wants to increase the number of government satellites from 80 to 630 and carry out 62 launches annually by 2034 from sites in Europe and Canada.The plans are intended to meet anticipated demand from the EU’s Galileo navigation and Copernicus Earth observation satellite programmes.Aschbacher has also proposed a €10 billion, 10-year plan to develop an independent European crew vehicle and launch recovery system before the International Space Station retires at the end of 2030 or early 2031.In March, the ESA launched the European Launcher Challenge to support private companies and start-ups developing launch services.These efforts include plans for commercial spaceports such as SaxaVord in Scotland and Andøya in Norway, while companies including Isar Aerospace and Rocket Factory Augsburg aim to expand small-to-medium-lift launch options.Creotech plans further expansionCreotech Instruments currently makes small satellites and microsatellites, typically weighing between 10 kg and several dozen kilos, using its proprietary Hypersat modular platform family.Its satellites include the HyperSat Earth observation platform, its Seagull, Eagle 2.0 and Nano 2.0 models, the PIAST Constellation and the MikroGlob Constellation, built for the Polish Armament Agency and launched this month.The company also works with the ESA and has contributed platforms and subsystems to missions including Comet Interceptor, JUICE (Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer), LISA (Laser Interferometer Space Antenna), the Plasma Observatory and the Twardowski lunar mission to map the Moon’s surface.Brona added that Creotech would start opening subsidiaries in France and Germany in the coming weeks and was aiming to build 500 kg satellites by 2032.

title: ‘Bismillah, c’est les ténèbres’: What does the French student protest slogan mean?
description: A Snapchat message, which students believe came from an undercover police officer, has become the rallying cry of a youth movement that has now spread to Belgium and Italy.
content: It has been scrawled on cardboard placards outside blockaded schools, shared in parody videos tens of thousands of times and repeated by Greta Thunberg. In the space of a few weeks, "Bismillah, c’est les ténèbres" has become the unofficial slogan of France’s high school protests.Taken literally, the phrase means very little, and that is the point.What does ‘Bismillah, c’est les ténèbres’ mean?"Bismillah" is Arabic for "in the name of God". Muslims traditionally say it before beginning a task, and in everyday French slang it can mean something closer to "let’s go"."C’est les ténèbres" translates as "it’s the darkness". Among young people it is slang for a situation that is catastrophic or grim.Put together, the phrase is nonsensical - "In the name of God, it’s the darkness". Students say that is exactly why it caught on. They are mocking someone trying, and failing, to sound like them.Where did the slogan come from?The phrase comes from a screenshot of a Snapchat conversation that began circulating in early October, while students were using the app to organise school blockades.In the message, a user named "Mamadou" asks to join a group: “Hi, in the name of God, it’s the darkness. When’s the blockade, wallah, bro?"The message was accompanied by Algerian flag emojis.Other screenshots showed similar accounts asking students where blockades would take place and who was selling fireworks and smoke grenades.To many students, the clumsy mix of Arabic, street slang and national flags gave the game away. They concluded that the messages were written by police officers posing as teenagers to infiltrate private protest groups.Did police really infiltrate student Snapchat groups?This has not been proven. Neither the police nor the interior ministry in France has commented on the screenshots, and nobody has independently verified who was behind the accounts.Some internet users claimed to have traced the accounts to locations near police stations, but those claims have not been verified. Some of the circulating screenshots may themselves be hoaxes or parodies.Why are French students protesting?The movement began in Créteil, south-east of Paris, on 18 September and quickly spread nationwide. A range of student grievances lie at the heart of the movement, including long school days, overcrowded classrooms, run down schools and teacher absences.Many argue that these problems hit working-class suburbs and minority communities hardest. Around 400 schools were closed by blockades on 2 October alone.The student protests fed into the nationwide demonstrations over the cost of living on Saturday 17 October, which ended in some of the worst rioting and looting France has seen in years.Has the slogan spread outside France?Swedish activist Greta Thunberg used it during a visit to striking students in Seine-Saint-Denis, north of Paris, on 13 October, according to the Italian news agency ANSA.On 9 October, it appeared on placards at a union-led demonstration in Brussels against the Belgian government’s budget cuts. There, it was used as a gesture of solidarity with French students rather than a reference to the infiltration claims.In Italy, ANSA reported that the phrase appeared at student demonstrations in Bologna on 15 October. It was heard again in Milan over the weekend of 17 and 18 October, when protests in Piazza del Duomo also turned to looting and students from a french school in Berlin were photographed holding a banner of the slogan.

title: What do travellers want from AI? Room rates, not personalised itineraries, study says
description: Just 44% of travellers feel comfortable letting artificial intelligence plan out their holidays.
content: Conversations around artificial intelligence (AI) and its uses are going on in every industry, from health and transport to banking and art.The travel industry isn’t immune to this, and you’ll no doubt already have encountered it when researching a trip, whether that’s through AI overviews, chatbots or even influencers.But while plenty of us are happy to use the technology, what we’re willing to use it for only goes so far, with just 44% of travellers saying they would let AI plan out their itinerary.That’s according to a survey from Mews, a hospitality management software used by hoteliers, with 3,250 tourists polled across France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Spain, Sweden, the UK and the US.According to the poll, the most common uses for AI are watching hotel rates – with 63% of travellers using it for this purpose – and translating on the spot (56%). Using data for customisationOne of the best uses for AI is letting it pull on various data sources to compile a complete picture without wasting time, and in the ultra-competitive world of travel, this means using it for customisation.But, perhaps unsurprisingly, travellers aren’t a big fan of AI using data collected on them through online behaviour or social media data being used by hotels, with 43% consenting to the former and 34% to the latter.Travellers are, however, happy with AI using stated preferences (61%) and past stay history (56%).How comfortable a traveller is with the use of AI varies from country to country, too, with Italian travellers being the most optimistic about AI's role five years from now (51% vs. 39% on average), with Spain having the most positive attitude towards AI (58%).“Having clever technology is great, but firstly, we should know whether guests want a task done for them or want to be part of it. Get that wrong and even good AI feels intrusive,” Josef Starýchfojtů, Chief Product and Technology Officer (CPTO) of Mews, said.“We're building for human hospitality: technology handles the mundane, repetitive admin, and hotel teams have more time for their guests."

title: Why 2027 is set to be the year for birdwatching holidays – and where to go birding in Europe
description: We’re now heading into the ‘birdwatching era’ with a new generation picking up the binoculars and travelling for birding holidays.
content: What was once seen as a niche hobby among nature lovers, birdwatching is now spreading its wings and becoming a popular reason for travel. In its Hidden Trends List for 2026, published last November, GetYourGuide said that birdwatching is “having a moment” with #BirdTok videos going viral on social media. Last month, the company reported a 65% year-on-year increase in global bookings for birdwatching experiences between 1 January and 27 August 2026.“Birdwatching as a travel experience has flown well beyond being a ‘Hidden Trend’,” said Anne Wallin, GetYourGuide's global trends and experiences expert. “It’s growing in popularity every month as travellers rediscover ways to connect with nature and disconnect from the daily hustle – whether that’s among a flamboyance of flamingos in southern France or spotting rare sightings in your own city.”A trends report by Voyageurs du Monde also said that we’re now “heading into the birdwatching era” and that 2027 is “set to be the year of birdwatching”.The travel company has reported growing demand, saying bookings for birdwatching holidays between July and October 2026 to date were 57% higher than during the first six months of the year.“Rather than asking our clients where they want to go, we ask what fascinates them? And what we’ve increasingly found is a growing interest in birdwatching holidays,” Tom Barber, chief brand officer of Voyageurs du Monde, told Euronews Travel. “In an industry where slow travel is here to stay, and in a world where so much of life happens at speed and through a screen, there’s something wonderfully simple about stepping outside with a pair of binoculars and seeing what you can spot.”Where to go for birdwatching So, where should travellers go to experience birdwatching? The Danube Delta and northern Greece are great choices for a European birding trip, according to Barber. “For beginners who want a taster, spend a day on the Danube Delta in eastern Romania,” he said. “The vast wetlands and waterways here constitute some of the most important wetlands in the world, home to over 300 species of birds, including huge concentrations of breeding and migrating flocks. “Northeast Greece has also been one of our top sellers of European birding holidays this year, as it’s along a key migration flyway and is home to a diverse blend of wetlands and forests. Go in the shoulder season, because it’s quieter overall, but also an excellent time for birdwatching around the lakes.”Writing on GetYourGuide's The Explorer, birder Cindy Brzostowski says Portugal is one of the best places for checking out seabirds. “With its long Atlantic coastline and position along the East Atlantic Flyway, a major bird migration route stretching from the Arctic to Southern Africa, Portugal is a top destination for scouting seabirds,” she said. “The Portuguese islands of the Azores and Madeira are prime birdwatching territory, too.”If seeing puffins is your thing, then there’s no better place than Iceland, Brzostowski said. “The Westman Islands off the south coast are home to the world’s largest colonies.”In a ranking of the world’s 20 best birdwatching destinations by AllClear Travel, just two European destinations featured. The study assessed birdwatching sites using factors including recorded species, weather, airport proximity and daily travel costs.Ranked 19th worldwide and first in Europe in the study, Falsterbo Peninsula on the southwestern tip of Sweden is a “hotspot for birders”. On England’s north Norfolk coast, Titchwell Marsh is one of the UK’s most celebrated birdwatching destinations. Europe’s top 15 birdwatching destinations according to AllClear1. title: Russia woos Asian tourists in attempt to counter European visits collapse
description: EU tourist arrivals fell from 5 million in 2019 to 160,000 in 2025 as sanctions, cancelled flights and other restrictions due to Russia's ongoing war in Ukraine severed Western leisure travel, prompting Moscow to look east.
content: Russia has introduced visa-free entry for Vietnamese citizens as part of a broader effort to deal with the collapse of Western visits since its 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine, with visitors from Asia and the Middle East.The number of tourists from EU countries travelling to Russia fell to around 160,000 in 2025, from just over 5 million in 2019. Cancelled direct flights, payment card restrictions and sanctions have effectively severed leisure travel from Europe and the US, and inbound tourism as a whole declined further in the first half of 2026.The Vietnam visa-free decree signed by Vladimir Putin and taking effect on Thursday covers tourists, businesspeople, members of delegations and transit passengers.Vietnamese nationals seeking long-term residency, employment or study in Russia will still require a visa. For several years, Russian citizens have been able to enter Vietnam visa-free for stays of up to 45 days.Vietnamese visitors to Russia rose 69% in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period in 2025, according to the Association of Tour Operators of Russia, which projects a further 25-30% increase after the visa requirement was removed.Vietnam has become the third most popular foreign destination for Russian travellers. Figures were also rising on the other end: the Vietnam National Administration of Tourism recorded 1,134,000 Russian visitors in the first nine months of 2026, a 160% increase, making Russia its third-largest source market.The visa arrangement followed an early September meeting in Moscow between Putin and Vietnamese President To Lam, who described the Russian leader as "a great friend and close brother of the Vietnamese people."Moscow and Beijing introduced reciprocal visa-free travel in late 2025, with Chinese arrivals growing but falling short of official expectations.The Russian government has projected 4.2 million Chinese visitors by year-end and 5.5 million in 2027. Up to 516,000 Chinese tourists arrived in the first half of 2026, a pace analysts described as well below those targets.Safety concerns have been cited as a factor, with reports of drone incidents over Moscow's airports attracting attention in Chinese media.Vietnam has not joined Western sanctions against Russia over the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and does not supply weapons to Kyiv. Hanoi has called for a ceasefire and negotiations but has avoided publicly criticising the Kremlin. China maintains a similar position of official neutrality.Russian government figures could not be independently verified.

title: Mother leaves children on Poland mountain trail for 'whining', hikes to summit alone
description: Conditions on the trail were poor with a thick fog over the area, prompting shocked tourists to take care of the young boys.
content: A mother left her two children alone on the Bieszczady Mountains hiking trail in southern Poland on Saturday because they were "whining" and she wanted to reach the summit alone."We are near the point where the blue and yellow trails split above Muczne. We are hiking with a group from the PTTK branch in Rzeszow. Suddenly we hear a piercing sob and a child’s scream. We stop, and two boys – a crying eight-year-old and his fourteen-year-old brother – are standing, bewildered, by the side of the trail," the Rzeszow branch of the Polish Tourist and Sightseeing Society (PTTK) wrote on its Facebook profile."We find out that their mother has left them behind and gone on alone to reach the summit (which from this point is about an hour away). She told them that if they were whining and didn’t want to walk, they should wait for fifteen minutes," the post continued.The boys were left waiting on their own for far longer than 15 minutes."No reflection, no sense of guilt"Conditions on the trail were poor; as the author of the PTTK post notes, a thick fog had settled over the area, prompting shocked tourists to take care of the young boys."After about a quarter of an hour, a fit-looking woman appears. The younger son grabs her by the hand and stops crying. When we point out how she could leave underage children alone in high mountains, in such weather conditions, she responds coolly that she was gone only for a moment, that she wanted to go higher, and that they were forcing her to give up on achieving the planned goal," PTTK said.PTTK criticised the women for showing "no sense of guilt.""The forced word 'sorry' comes from her lips only when I say that this could amount to charges from the public prosecutor. My reply, that she should not be apologising to me but to the children, is met with no reaction..." the author of the post wrote.The incident was reported to local authorities and has sparked widespread public outrage in Poland regarding parental responsibility and safety on mountain trails.

title: The big winners you need to know about from the World Travel Awards Europe 2026
description: Now in its 33rd year, the World Travel Awards has named the best destinations, hotels and airlines on the continent for 2026.
content: For the past 33 years, the World Travel Awards has handed out gongs to the very best of the industry, from airlines and airports to hotels and destinations.With such a wide scope, the list of winners can get seriously lengthy – which is why we’ve combed through the Europe awards to narrow it down to the ones you need to know about.Announced on 17 October at a gala ceremony at the Hyatt Regency Kotor Bay Resort in Montenegro, Lisbon took home the biggest prize of the night, being named Europe’s best city, as well as the top cruise destination for 2026.Here are all the other winners you might have missed.Where you should be heading on your next holiday Across its various destination categories, the World Travel Awards has rounded up the different countries and cities you should be visiting depending on the type of holiday you’re after.Beach bum? Then the Portuguese Algarve is the spot for you. Prefer more of a city break? Book your flight to Athens ASAP.If you’re all about culture, then it’s Italy that should be calling your name, while those who are after heritage should be headed to Armenia.For those who like to turn their holiday into an adventure, Spain is the place to be, while those who want to enjoy some time in nature will love Montenegro.While Lisbon was named Europe’s best city, Portugal was also given the title of Europe’s leading destination for 2026.Where you should be stayingLong-time readers will know we’ve already covered many, many, many rankings of the best new hotels for 2026 (from Travel + Leisure, Forbes and Esquire, to name a few), but of course, the World Travel Awards has had its say, too.The Chancery Rosewood in London was crowned the leading new hotel for 2026, while AMOH, a Luxury Collection Resort in Rhodes was named the leading new resort. For a boutique stay like no other, Avali, Mar-Bella Collection in Corfu, is the place to book.Much like its destination categories, World Travel Awards also handed gongs out based on the type of hotel.Unsurprisingly, a hotel in Venice – The Gritti Palace, a Luxury Collection Hotel – took the title of Europe’s most romantic hotel, while those looking to book their honeymoon will want to stay at Domes Noruz Chania, Autograph Collection in Crete.If you want to spend most of your time flopped on the beach, book Elounda Beach Hotel & Villas in Crete, and if you don’t want to leave the resort at all, try the all-inclusive Ikos Odisia in Corfu.If you’re travelling as a family, Sani Resort on Greece’s Halkidiki coast has everything you need, while those with an interest in interior design should be booking 1908 Lisboa Hotel in Portugal.For an island resort, try Inchydoney Island Lodge & Spa in West Cork, and for a boutique stay with a twist, book Fingal Hotel in Edinburgh (the twist being that the hotel is floating).Who you should be flying with – and where fromThe World Travel Awards also crowned Europe’s best airlines and airports.Turkish Airlines was named the continent’s leading airline for 2026, while Volotea took home the title of leading low-cost carrier. As for airports, Switzerland’s Zurich Airport walked away with the top award.The World Travel Awards has already hosted all of its regional ceremonies, with the overall winners set to be crowned on 12 December at a gala in Tanzania.

title: Lula and Bolsonaro trade insults in TV debate ahead of weekend presidential runoff
description: Corruption is a top concern for many Brazilian voters ahead of the weekend runoff vote but experts say its greatest impact may not be on which candidates voters choose, but on whether they decide to sit out of the election altogether.
content: Firing off personal attacks, Brazil's President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and right-wing senator Flávio Bolsonaro held an acrimonious first debate on Sunday, a week before a tight presidential election runoff.A chaotic exchange between the two men, who called each other liars on multiple occasions, accusing each other of corruption and dragging up various scandals, encapsulated the tone of a bitter election campaign in the deeply polarised nation.Bolsonaro, 45, son of the far-right former president Jair Bolsonaro, secured a shock first-round lead over Lula earlier this month and polls predict a close battle for the runoff on 25 October.The two men sparred over the economy, public security, healthcare, corruption and Brazil's ties to the United States."Brazil is going to retire you," fired off Bolsonaro, seeking to unnerve his adversary by pacing up and down behind him throughout the debate in view of the camera, shaking his head, smirking and scoffing while his adversary spoke.Lula called Bolsonaro "a habitual liar, a thug," and said he did not want to stand close to a "militiaman," alluding to his alleged ties to Rio de Janeiro's paramilitary groups.Bolsonaro, who made several jabs about Lula's time jailed for corruption on charges that were later annulled, retorted that it was better he stay at a distance "because my wallet could be stolen."Lula, who at almost 81 is seeking a fourth term in power, battled to control his irritation at times and repeatedly asked viewers to "look it up on Google" to prove his adversary was lying.While Bolsonaro has led in polls since the first round, his edge slightly narrowed in two polls this week which showed him with 51% of voting intentions compared to 49% for Lula.'Subservient' to US interestsBolsonaro hammered away at the primary concerns of Brazilians, such as the cost of living and insecurity, and accused Lula of "reckless spending to get re-elected" due to various social measures he has announced while campaigning.Lula countered by asking Bolsonaro about his plans to emulate the drastic "chainsaw" cuts to public spending implemented by Argentina's libertarian President Javier Milei, which led to higher unemployment and cuts to benefits.Throughout the debate, Bolsonaro dodged the question and pivoted to different topics.Lula questioned the right winger's his ties to US President Donald Trump, an ally of the Bolsonaro family, and plans to "hand over" Brazil's rare earth minerals."It is striking how the Bolsonaro family is subservient to American interests," said Lula.Former president Jair Bolsonaro came up several times, including when his son asked Lula why so many prisoners had supported him in the election.Lula said he wanted all of their votes, including that of Jair Bolsonaro, who is currently serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest for a botched coup bid after his failed 2022 re-election bid."Vote for me, Bolsonaro, you know your son, you know I'm better than him."Top concernCorruption is a top concern for many Brazilian voters ahead of the weekend runoff vote but experts say its greatest impact may not be on which candidates voters choose, but on whether they decide to sit out of the election altogether.In the minds of many Brazilians, both candidates are associated with graft and for those who strongly support either candidate, such alleged ties will do little to curb their enthusiasm.But experts say that a generalised perception of corruption can increase abstention and anti-incumbency sentiment, potentially benefiting Bolsonaro, who received 2.2 million more votes than Lula in the first round.During the first round, many lined up to cast their votes wearing either red hats and T-shirts — signalling support for Lula’s party — or the yellow and green of the Brazilian flag adopted by Bolsonaro’s movement, reflecting the polarisation gripping the country.Supporters of Bolsonaro and Lula are highly distrustful of the other side and view their opponents as a threat. Such voters are less likely to give weight to allegations of corruption, experts say.“We have a great ability to filter information that goes against our beliefs,” said Nara Pavão, a political science professor at the Federal University of Pernambuco. “People don’t want to discover the truth about their candidates, they want to beat the opponent.”Camila Tobji de Aquino, a 19-year-old student of pedagogy and psychology, thinks that corruption is a cross-partisan issue and a significant problem in Brazil.But her main concern is what she sees as the threat Flávio Bolsonaro poses to democracy.“If I were to vote only for a candidate not tied to any corruption, I would vote blank,” she said. “But that’s not the choice Brazil is facing. For me it’s a question of being able to vote in the next election.”

title: High prices and interest rates: Expert advice on managing your money
description: Careful budgeting, managing borrowing costs, protecting cash reserves and limiting financial risks: experts tell Euronews how households and businesses can cope with inflation and high interest rates.
content: Should we go ahead with a major purchase or wait it out? Is now the right time to start a business? What will happen to interest rates, and how much further can the cost of living rise?For millions of Europeans, these decisions have become harder. The surge in the cost of living, swings in energy prices, and higher borrowing costs are creating an environment where planning even a few months ahead feels complicated.The problem is not only that prices have gone up. It is also that consumers are struggling to gauge what will happen next.Euronews spoke to financial risk management experts about the options facing consumers and businesses at the sixth HAT International Treasury Summit in Athens, organised by the Hellenic Association of Treasurers.Should we wait or move ahead?Janet Legge, deputy chief executive of the UK-based Association of Corporate Treasurers, which represents professionals who manage businesses’ money and financial risks, believes that caution is justified when international developments remain so unpredictable.Asked what she would advise someone considering starting a business or making a major purchase, she said: "I think we need to watch developments for a while and be somewhat cautious at the moment."For a household, putting this approach into practice starts with a few basic questions.How essential is this particular expense? Can it be covered without exhausting available savings? Will it require borrowing and, if so, what share of income will the repayments represent? And what happens if income temporarily falls or some essential costs rise?Interest rates: why forecasts remain difficultThe path of interest rates is one of the key sources of uncertainty, especially for those who have loans or are considering taking on new debt.Speaking about the UK, Legge noted that interest rates were expected to ease, but the experience of recent years shows how easily forecasts can be overturned."In recent years we keep hearing that interest rates are about to fall and then they go back up again," she said.In her view, volatility is likely to be a feature of the new normal."They will go up and down, and we will have to adapt," she said.For borrowers, the key question is how their own contract is affected: whether the interest rate is fixed or variable, when it is adjusted and how much the monthly repayment can change.How to protect the household budgetGilles Bonn-Long, an executive in corporate cash management, links pressures on the cost of living to international geopolitical developments.And he warned that living costs could continue to rise in the short term.His main advice to consumers is "careful management of spending".This means tracking monthly outgoings more systematically and planning purchases more carefully. It is also useful to distinguish between essential expenses, such as housing and energy, and those that can be adjusted more easily.What businesses can doFor businesses, uncertainty is not confined to product prices. It affects the cost of financing, the supply of raw materials and their ability to plan future investments.Bonn-Long stressed the importance of strategies to limit risk, commonly known as hedging. This means using financial contracts to limit the impact of changes in interest rates or prices."From a corporate perspective, it is important to have hedging policies in place to limit exposure to rising variable interest rates," he explained.These include interest rate swaps, which can allow businesses to exchange variable interest payments for fixed ones, and similar strategies to limit risks from changes in commodity prices.A more optimistic assessment came from Ralf Kesten of the German company cflox, which specialises in working capital management.As he explained to Euronews, higher interest rates and the successive crises of recent years have pushed up operating costs for businesses, putting pressure on their liquidity. However, he believes there are now more solutions available to help address these challenges."We are seeing prices rise, but there are also solutions that can help companies and prevent consumers from being excessively burdened," he said.Planning for uncertaintyExperts agree on one key point: uncertainty requires preparation.For consumers, this means having a clearer picture of their finances and being more cautious about the commitments they take on. For businesses, it means identifying risks early and planning how to deal with them.Perhaps the most important dilemma is the one posed by Janet Legge: how long can we wait before we feel confident enough to take our next decision?In a period when conditions are constantly changing, she told us, the answer lies neither in rushing nor in postponing everything. It lies in being able to take decisions based on adequate information, realistic planning and enough flexibility to adapt when the facts change.

title: European stocks open in the red as French businesses count the cost of the riots
description: European stock markets opened lower on Monday after a weekend of violent protests and looting in France, as business owners count the cost and accuse the government of failing to protect them.
content: Stocks across Europe fell at the start of trading on Monday as France reeled from one of its most violent weekends in years, with shopkeepers and CEOs alike tallying the damage and accusing the authorities of leaving them exposed.The Euro Stoxx 50 only traded 0.1% lower but the broader pan-European Stoxx 600 was down over 0.6% at the start of Monday’s session.France’s CAC 40 traded 0.5% lower as, for example, shares in retailer Carrefour, which said 50 of its stores were targeted by looters, were down more than 2%.French borrowing costs also rose, as a divided parliament debates the 2027 budget, with the 10-year government bond yield at 4.86% after hitting its highest level since 2002 earlier this month.The gap with German debt, a gauge of investor nerves, stood at 143.5 basis points, having topped 150 in early October, the widest since the euro debt crisis.Ratings agency Moody’s reviews France’s Aa3 credit rating, which carries a negative outlook, on Friday.As for other European indexes, the UK’s FTSE 100, Italy’s FTSE MIB and Spain’s IBEX 35 all traded between 0.4% and 0.6% lower than their Friday close.Germany’s DAX led the decline and dropped over 0.8% while the Netherlands’ AEX was the outlier, and traded more than 0.4% higher.The euro was 0.2% lower against the US dollar at around $1.121 and also dropped 0.2% against the British pound to roughly £0.841.Last week, it sank to its lowest level against the US dollar since mid-May 2025, and against the British pound since early June 2025, with France’s debt troubles and a stronger US dollar outweighing two European Central Bank rate hikes this year.The ECB next meets on 29 October.French business owners count the costAuthorities counted about 550,000 people at Saturday’s nationwide marches against rising living costs and the state of French schools, which descended into rioting and looting in Paris, Lyon, Marseille, Bordeaux and other cities.Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said 2,400 people were arrested, while injured police officers, gendarmes and firefighters reportedly number anywhere between 500 and nearly 1,000.Nuñez, who admitted a lack of anticipation and a loss of control in some cities, offered to resign, but President Emmanuel Macron refused, his office said on Monday, arguing that the security forces needed unbroken command.Carrefour CEO Alexandre Bompard, who heads the French retail federation FCD, said about 1,500 shops were hit, with a bill running into hundreds of millions of euros, and that the Republic must protect its shopkeepers.At Carrefour alone, "the cost of the repairs will run to well over ten million euros," Bompard stated.Thierry Guibert, CEO of fashion brand Lacoste, whose Lacoste and Aigle stores were looted, urged the French state on social media to act without delay to protect businesses and staff.Thierry Cotillard, head of supermarket chain Intermarché, also said on social media he was deeply angry, while Patrick Martin, head of employers’ group Medef, called the looting unacceptable.Smaller traders were blunter.The boss of outdoor retailer Snowleader said he alerted police as looters forced open the door of his Lyon shop, only to be told to wait and follow up on Tuesday if no one came, while the head of Marseille’s city-centre traders’ association said shopkeepers had been abandoned by the authorities.Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu was set to chair a crisis meeting on Monday, and Commerce Minister Serge Papin to meet trade federations, banks and insurers.Meanwhile, unions have called a national strike for 5 November.

title: US is coming to Central Asia with deals to stay, Rubio tells Euronews
description: Replying to Euronews' questions in Uzbekistan's historic city of Samarkand, the US secretary of state outlined plans for new commercial agreements and cooperation on critical minerals.
content: US companies were preparing to announce new agreements in Uzbekistan as Washington seeks to expand its economic presence in Central Asia and diversify critical mineral supplies, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told Euronews on Monday.Speaking to reporters during a visit to Samarkand, Rubio said the deals could mark the start of broader US engagement with a region he believes American policymakers have paid too little attention to.Asked by Euronews what people in Uzbekistan could expect from the visit and the accompanying business delegation, Rubio said, "I think we'll have some concrete deals to announce."He said US companies were keen to do business in Uzbekistan and that announcements would follow the forum's meetings. "This is not the end. This is the beginning," he added.Rubio said nearly 300 American businesses were represented in Samarkand, where they were discussing agreements potentially worth billions of dollars.The US State Department had previously said more than 200 US business leaders were accompanying his trip. No final list of agreements or values had been announced at the time of his remarks.Critical minerals and strategic supply chainsIn response to a second question from Euronews, Rubio identified critical minerals as an area for potential cooperation with Uzbekistan."It's not smart just for the whole world to depend on one place for 100% of anything," he said, stressing that he was not singling out any particular country.He argued that industries and technologies likely to shape the 21st century would increasingly rely on critical minerals, making supply-chain diversification an international priority rather than solely a US concern.He said that for resource-rich countries, developing mineral deposits and processing capacity responsibly could also serve their own economic interests."We're obviously going to explore that and I think we have a chance to do that here," Rubio told Euronews.The subject was also discussed at the C5+1 summit US President Donald Trump hosted in Washington in November 2025. Uzbekistan and its neighbours have been seeking additional investment and technology to develop their mineral resources, while the US and Europe are looking for alternatives to highly concentrated supply chains.Asked separately about China's growing economic influence in Central Asia, Rubio described US involvement as competition, not an attempt to make regional governments choose sides."This is not about coming here to say, stop talking to somebody else or stop working with some other country," he said, describing Uzbekistan as open to economic relationships with different partners and praising its economic growth.Meetings in SamarkandRubio began Monday's programme with a morning tour of Registan Square, Samarkand's historic architectural landmark, alongside Saida Mirziyoyeva, Head of Uzbekistan's Presidential Administration. He called the city a centuries-old crossroads of trade and commerce.His official schedule also includes talks with Uzbek Foreign Minister Bakhtiyor Saidov and a document-signing ceremony, followed by a meeting with Kazakhstan's Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tileuberdi and the C5+1 ministerial meeting involving Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan.On Monday, Rubio is also scheduled to meet President Shavkat Mirziyoyev and attend events involving the Uzbekistan–US Business and Investment Council. The council, co-chaired by Saida Mirziyoyeva and US Special Envoy Sergio Gor, was established to promote commercial partnerships and investment.The visit follows last year's White House C5+1 summit, where more than $25bn (approximately €22bn) in commercial agreements and commitments were announced. Those commitments covered several Central Asian countries and were at different stages of implementation.Rubio disputes Zelenskyy's account of intelligence pauseThe visit also gave Rubio an opportunity to address growing tensions between Washington and Kyiv over Russia's war in Ukraine.Asked about Ukrainian claims that the US had briefly stopped sharing intelligence used to warn of Russian missile attacks, Rubio denied any interruption."There has been no pause," he told reporters.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had said on Sunday that intelligence sharing had resumed after a three-day suspension. The two accounts remain at odds.Rubio urged both Russia and Ukraine to focus on ending the war that began with Russia's all-out invasion, now in its fifth year. "What he should be focused on and what we want to be focused on is bringing an end to this war," he said.Trump had criticised Zelenskyy a day earlier, accusing him of lacking the will to end the conflict and blaming Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries for disruption to global diesel markets.Trump has also defended temporary relief from some sanctions affecting Russian energy exports, saying it could help diplomacy.Rubio acknowledged that US efforts to broker an end to the war had not made the progress Washington wanted, but said the administration would continue exploring opportunities for negotiations.

title: Can Europe beat the cost-of-living crisis? Take our poll
description: From supermarket shelves and energy bills to housing and education, rising prices are putting pressure on households across Europe. But which sectors are being hit hardest by inflation? What is the EU doing to ease the burden on consumers?
content: According to Eurostat, inflation in the eurozone reached 3.8% in September, nearly double the European Central Bank’s target. Energy prices surged 18.8% in a year. The squeeze reaches every key sector in the bloc. A European Central Bank analysis showed that, at supermarket checkouts, 35% of EU consumers worry about affording food. 74% have noticed everyday products shrinking in size without getting cheaper. Soaring energy bills are leaving millions struggling to keep their homes warm, while rising construction costs and housing shortages keep pushing rents and property prices higher. In Portugal alone, house prices jumped 16.5% in a year. Education is also under pressure, as schools face operating costs and families must cover books, transport and supplies. Meanwhile, education's share of EU public spending stood at 9.7% in 2024, down from 10% in 2019. Can the EU protect consumers from these rising costs? Brussels has proposed an expanding list of measures, from the Affordable Energy Action Plan and the Citizens’ Energy Package to the €86.7 billion Social Climate Fund, aimed at reducing energy costs and supporting vulnerable households. But much of this response focuses on long-term reforms, while the latest price shocks are already hitting consumers. The Commission has also presented its European Affordable Housing Plan, proposed an Affordable Housing Act in September and introduced its first Anti-Poverty Strategy. Are these measures enough to tackle soaring global inflation? Should it be the EU’s task? Or are national governments not doing enough? Our poll is anonymous and takes only a few seconds to complete. The results will be featured across XL's EU-wide coverage, including videos, articles and newsletters, and will help shape our reporting as we examine how Europe can secure its position in the age of artificial intelligence.

title: France grapples with the aftermath of a weekend of violence
description: Hello from Brussels. It’s Monday, and I’m Mared Gwyn. Today: France grapples with the aftermath of a weekend of violence and chaos, and Trump berates Zelenskyy once again.
content: France reels: France continues to grapple this morning with the fallout of this weekend’s events, when anti-austerity protests spilled over into violent riots across the country. Around 2000 people were arrested and more than 500 police officers, gendarmes and firefighters were injured, amid scenes of chaos, burning buildings, and violent clashes in cities from Marseille to Paris to Lyon.Saturday’s protests started peacefully, with demonstrators calling for more public spending to repair decrepit schools and improve education standards, as well as measures to tackle the rising cost of living. But the marches were hijacked by groups of masked rioters, who started fires, smashed storefronts and built barricades. Euronews’ France correspondent Estelle Nilsson-Julien was among the journalists targeted by looters on Saturday in central Paris. “The calmer protests earlier in the day descended into complete anarchy,” Estelle told me last night, describing how masked individuals encircled her and attacked her camera operator.‘Honte et colêre’: In an address to the nation last night, French President Emmanuel Macron said the nation felt shame and anger, as he made a plea for unity.Picking up the pieces: The wreckage is on the one hand material: trade bodies estimate the damages to be in the hundreds of millions of euros. But this weekend’s events will also likely leave a deep mark on French society and politics, as the country enters what many see as one of its most consequential periods in history ahead of April’s presidential election.Questions are now being asked about where the political responsibility lies. The government has failed to make sufficient concessions to address the grievances of students, who have been holding demonstrations for weeks. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez handed in his resignation this morning, but his request has been rejected by President Macron.On Sunday, Marine Le Pen of the far-right National Rally (RN), the frontrunner to become the next French President, spoke of a “crisis of confidence” and a “threat to democracy”.Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the leader of the far-left France Unbowed (LFI), has also come under fire from government figures and right-wing leaders, with the centrist presidential candidate Edouard Philippe saying his party carries “considerable responsibility” for the violence of recent days.Contagion: The scenes seem to have awakened an underlying unease in other parts of Europe, with similar demonstrations over the weekend descending into violence, including in Belgium, Italy and Portugal.Magyar’s take: Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar has linked the riots to immigration levels, saying the “shocking scenes” vindicated his government’s tough migration policies. More from my colleague Sándor Zsiros in our top story below.Trump berates Zelenskyy: Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump has said that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy “doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did”, after Kyiv launched a major drone attack on an oil terminal in Saint Petersburg over the weekend.“His (Zelenskyy’s) country is in shambles, a large portion of his land is lost, his oceans and seas are gone, and his male population is low, wounded and/or dead,” Trump also said in a blistering Truth Social post.Ukraine-US talks continue: The escalation came just after a sign of a possible détente. Zelenskyy said on Sunday that he held talks with US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to discuss the next steps in diplomatic efforts to end Russia’s war.Zelenskyy also revealed that Washington had restored intelligence-sharing on incoming Russian ballistic missiles after a three-day interruption. "We are very thankful for this," he told NBC News. "Now it works."But the Ukrainian leader also painted a dire picture of the relationship with the US in a separate interview with Bloomberg, where he said he believed “steps have been taken to convince Ukraine to capitulate" to Russia, and suggested Washington was slowing down Patriot missile deliveries via NATO’s PURL scheme.Russia continues to pound Ukraine: Russia meanwhile launched successive ballistic missile attacks on Kyiv overnight, damaging a metro station and nearby railway infrastructure. This time, unlike during the previous evening's strikes, residents received advance air-raid warnings.Moscow’s relentless attacks have turned Kyiv into a "true frontline city", the EU's ambassador to Ukraine, Katarína Mathernová, exclusively told my colleague Sasha Vakulina in an interview, as she described the growing disruption to everyday life in the capital. Watch.The day after: Meanwhile, Brussels will today begin to reckon with the aftermath of last week’s momentous summit, where EU leaders committed to addressing Ukraine’s request for an additional €70 billion in financial and military support for next year, Jorge Liboreiro, who covered the two-day meeting, writes.The European Commission has been tasked with presenting options to fund the €70 billion gap, which will come on top of the €90 billion loan that leaders agreed to less than a year ago. It’s painful for leaders to reopen the debate, but Russia’s all-out escalation, aimed at collapsing Ukraine’s economy, has radically changed the equation and ballooned wartime costs.“At the time when we planned for the €90 billion (loan), we could not foresee what 2027 would look like, but now it is clear that we have a gap of €70 billion that has to be covered,” Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said.What now? For now, issuing a new round of joint debt looks like the easiest and fastest option, though it will be significantly costlier, both financially and politically. Some countries, like Germany, Spain and the Netherlands, prefer to tap into the €210 billion of immobilised Russian assets. But Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever made clear during the summit that his objections still stand. Other options, such as redeploying EU funds and coordinating bilateral contributions, are much more limited.Brussels insists the EU won’t be left shouldering the €70 billion alone. But Western allies haven’t stepped up enough, deepening Kyiv’s financial shortfall. It seems that this time, the bloc will have to carry the torch. President Zelenskyy told leaders as much: “This is a realistic amount. And I ask you to find this support.”Explosive mix: The effort to find the cash will overlap with the bitter negotiations over the next EU budget. The summit laid bare the enormous differences that still exist among capitals, which are sticking to their red lines. The frugals insist larger cuts are needed, but the Friends of Cohesion oppose further reductions. António Costa, the president of the European Council, has taken charge of the process and will present a new compromise text in the coming weeks. Can the funding for Ukraine be agreed in tandem with the budget? Some say it must, others say it shouldn’t. Magyar links French riots to migration, says ‘shocking scenes’ justify hard lineHungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar has linked the weekend riots in France to immigration levels, saying the “shocking scenes” vindicated his government’s tough migration policies.“Seeing this senseless destruction and unjustified violence, perhaps it is now clear to everyone why Hungary takes the toughest possible stance on migration,” Magyar wrote on social media on Sunday, alongside a video showing buildings on fire.He also said that the "overwhelming majority of European countries" want a tougher approach to migration and have "finally woken up".At a European summit held last week, a group of countries, including Denmark, Italy and Hungary, pushed for stronger language on migration in the conclusions. French President Emmanuel Macron warned against “the stigmatisation” of immigrants and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez praised their positive contribution.Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk shared a similar message on Sunday, saying Poland would “not repeat the mistakes of other European countries” on immigration. My colleague Sándor Zsiros has more.More from our newsroomsWages vs prices: The economic pressures behind Europe's protests. From rising food prices and unaffordable housing to stagnant purchasing power and strained public services, demonstrations across Europe highlight growing frustration over living standards. Angela Barnes has the details.Can Spain afford its pensions? What to know about the funding debate ahead of the election. This year, Spain has set a new record for its monthly pension bill, at almost €14.5 billion. Its Social Security system, which pays pensions and other benefits, reported its smallest deficit since 2011. How could this play into the electoral campaign ahead of the November 29 vote? Cristian Caraballo explains.Trump endorses Netanyahu nine days before Israeli election, breaking months of silence. US President Donald Trump on Sunday endorsed embattled Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the final stretch of his reelection campaign, after the two leaders’ strategies on Iran and Gaza have diverged. Jeremiah Fisayo-Bambi has more.We’re also keeping an eye onEU employment and social affairs ministers gather in Luxembourg.The European Parliament’s plenary session kicks off later this evening.European Commissioner for Migration Magnus Brunner is in London for meetings with government representatives.That’s it for today. Jorge Liboreiro and Sasha Vakulina contributed to this newsletter.

title: Emmanuel Macron rejects resignation of interior minister Laurent Nuñez
description: In a statement issued on Monday morning, the Élysée announced that the French president had refused the interior minister's resignation "given the need for continuous command of the security forces in the current situation".
content: After the serious violence in several major French cities on Saturday 17 October, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez offered his resignation to President Emmanuel Macron, who refused to accept it.In a statement on Monday morning, the Élysée said Macron had asked Nuñez to deploy “new methods of action on the ground as quickly as possible (…) against violent rioters”.The presidency said it had turned down the resignation “in view of the need for continuous command of the security forces in the current context”.Macron also acknowledged “failures in anticipation and intelligence-gathering” that led to riots, destruction and the looting of numerous businesses.Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu is due to chair an interministerial crisis unit from 10:00 CEST.Meanwhile, Macron, who spoke about Saturday’s violence on Sunday evening, is pressing ahead with his diplomatic tour of the Gulf. From today, he will visit Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain and Qatar as part of efforts to secure supplies of oil and diesel and bring down fuel prices.

title: Europe Today: France counts cost of violence as Ukraine hits St Petersburg, Leningrad
description: France is cleaning up after the worst unrest in years, as violent groups hijacked the marches. Also on today's Europe Today: Ukraine hits St. Petersburg in a large-scale drone attack, and the UN’s aid chief, Tom Fletcher, warns that more aid workers are at risk of dying.
content: On today's show:Valerie Gauriat, Euronews correspondent, reports from Paris on the destruction left by the weekend's protests, how it compares with the war zones she usually covers, what the final cost could be, and whether the government has regained control after President Emmanuel Macron vowed in an address to the nation to catch all those responsible.Alberto Alemanno, Professor of EU law at HEC Paris, looks at the cost-of-living and housing protests spreading across Europe, from Albania to Portugal and Italy, and how long they could last.Sasha Vakulina reports on the Ukrainian drone attack on St Petersburg, which Russian officials say hit an oil terminal and a data centre, with reports of a bridge also being targeted, and what it means for Donald Trump's energy ceasefire. She speaks exclusively to Katarina Mathernova, the EU's Ambassador to Ukraine.Tom Fletcher, UN aid chief, discusses how bad the plight of aid workers is, after more than 1,000 were killed in three years. He was in Brussels for an EU conference on the protection of humanitarian aid workers, as a fight unfolds over how development, humanitarian aid and geopolitical priorities will be financed in the EU's 2028–2034 budget.When and where to watch Europe Today?You can join Euronews’ anchors Méabh Mc Mahon and Stefan Grobe live on TV and Euronews' website, as well as digital platforms (YouTube, Facebook, X, and Instagram), every weekday at 8 am Brussels time.In just 20 minutes, we bring you the day's key events plus crucial analysis of all the stories shaping the EU and beyond. Also available as a newsletter and podcast.

title: Albertans vote on path to independence as Carney fights to keep Canada united
description: Alberta has the world's fourth-largest proven oil reserves and separatist momentum has been driven by anger over Ottawa's management of the sector.
content: The province of Alberta will decide on Monday if it wants to pursue a binding referendum on secession from Canada, with Prime Minister Mark Carney warning a separatist win would bring dangerous uncertainty during a trade war with the United States.Polls indicate less than a quarter of people in the western Canadian province support independence.But attention has focused on turnout in the days before the vote and whether a motivated separatist camp could defy the polls, helped by complacent federalists."Don't let anyone tell you this is already decided. Turnout will determine the outcome," Carney said at a rally on Thursday.Carney, who grew up in Alberta, has called the referendum "a dangerous bluff" as US President Donald Trump imposes punishing tariffs and levels annexation threats aimed at breaking Canadian resolve, Carney said."Vote like Canada depends on it, because it does," Carney said.Alberta has the world's fourth-largest proven oil reserves and separatist momentum has been driven by anger over Ottawa's management of the sector.Many Albertans loathed Carney's predecessor, Justin Trudeau, who they accused of trying to suppress oil production to advance his pro-climate agenda."If you want me to pinpoint who is responsible for the separatist sentiment, I think it's Justin Trudeau," Alberta Premier Danielle Smith told the Canadaland podcast this month.At a separatist rally in Edmonton on Saturday, 61-year-old Sandy Martel said people connected to the oil industry feel "robbed, cheated (and) mistreated.""It's time to stand up and say stop," she told the AFP news agency.The vote comes days after a fire at a military base in the province left at least four soldiers dead and wounded dozens, prompting a national outpouring of condolences.'Huge uncertainty'Alberta’s conservative premier says she wants Alberta to remain in Canada but called the referendum to settle the divisive issue.If a majority votes to separate, she has pledged to move forward with a binding referendum.If the federalists win, Smith says the secession question should be considered closed.Analysts have compared Smith's tactics to those of former UK prime minister David Cameron, who had hoped to resolve the debate over Britain's European Union membership with a vote.Carney led the Bank of England through the turmoil that surrounded Brexit and issued a warning to Albertans about that experience on Thursday."It wasn't clear what 'Brexit' meant at the time," he told a Calgary television station."For the next few years, while that was being determined, there was huge uncertainty, investments stopped, the economy started to underperform," he added, cautioning over unintended economic consequences.AI influenceMonday's referendum features 10 questions, including several related to immigration, but focus is on question 10, which asks: "Should Alberta remain a province of Canada?" or should the province take the legal steps required for a definitive independence vote.Alberta's election authority says ballots for question 10 will be counted first, with results expected in the early hours of Tuesday.The pre-referendum period was clouded by avalanches of manipulated AI content.Carney has urged "a decisive result," but experts are concerned about a contested outcome no matter the numbers."A very likely result of this referendum is going to be a community that sees this election as stolen or at least unfair," said Aengus Bridgman, director of the Media Ecosystem Observatory at McGill University.Close Trump allies have also inserted themselves into the discussion, including Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who in January described Alberta as a "natural partner" for the United States.After a separatist party won Quebec's provincial election on 5 October, tech billionaire Elon Musk posted on X that "they would be better off" if they seceded."Alberta and Saskatchewan should separate too," he added.Asked about alleged foreign interference, Carney said on Thursday that foreign governments, including the US, should not "get themselves involved in our elections."

title: Lisbon named Europe's best city and cruise destination for 2026
description: Lisbon has reclaimed its shine on Europe's tourism map, earning two titles at the World Travel Awards Europe 2026, presented on Saturday in Montenegro's Bay of Kotor.
content: Lisbon has been distinguished as the Best City Destination in Europe at the World Travel Awards Europe 2026. The Portuguese capital was also named Best Cruise Destination in Europe. The two accolades were presented on Saturday, 17 October, at a ceremony in Kotor Bay, Montenegro.In a statement, the Lisbon Tourism Association says these awards "recognise Lisbon's international appeal and the diversity of its tourism offer".António Valle, director-general of the Lisbon Tourism Association, quoted in the statement, stresses that "these awards show how Lisbon is a unique and authentic destination"."Lisbon sets itself apart from the main European destinations by valuing its own identity while responding to different travel motivations," he says, underlining that the awards are also "recognition of a collective effort to improve and enhance the tourism offer".For António Valle, these prizes "help boost the local economy and reaffirm the authenticity and identity that sets" the Portuguese capital apart."Lisbon is increasingly setting the trend in the international tourism sector, creating value both for those who visit us and for those who live and work here," he adds.The Lisbon Tourism Association also points out that "the focus on improving the offer, enhancing heritage and culture, and diversifying the experiences available across the entire Lisbon Metropolitan Area remains central to the destination's international competitiveness"."This strategy seeks to attract visitors who stay longer, discover different parts of the region and help generate greater economic and social value," the note sent to newsrooms adds.The World Travel Awards are among the most prestigious international distinctions in the tourism sector and annually reward destinations, hotels, airlines and other industry players.This year the ceremony took place at the Hyatt Regency Kotor Bay Resort, a five-star luxury hotel in Kotor Bay, in south-west Montenegro on the Adriatic Sea, classified as a UNESCO World Heritage site.This was the first time the Balkan country had hosted the awards in the 33-year history of the World Travel Awards.

title: Four Canadian service members killed, dozens injured in fire at Alberta military base
description: Prime Minister Mark Carney described the incident as one of the worst peacetime tragedies for Canada’s military on domestic soil.
content: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Sunday that four service members were killed and dozens more seriously injured in a fire during a military training at a base in Alberta, calling it one of the worst peacetime tragedies for Canada’s military on domestic soil.In a televised address, Carney said the families of those killed had been notified and that the situation was still evolving.He said the victims were taking part in military training when the fire broke out Saturday. Carney ordered flags to fly at half-staff on federal buildings nationwide in their honour.Those affected included reservists and soldiers from Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry, one of the country’s most storied regiments.The personnel had travelled from bases across Canada to train at Wainwright. It was not immediately clear how many people were injured, but Carney said the wounded were being treated in Wainwright, Edmonton, Red Deer and Calgary.Military says cause of incident under investigationFire crews rushed to Canadian Forces Base Wainwright late Saturday as fierce winds pushed flames beyond the base and into the surrounding rural area.The Canadian military said Sunday there were no indications the incident was an act of terrorism, but the cause remains under investigation.A doctor at a hospital in Edmonton, 180 kilometres (112 miles) northwest of the base, told Canada’s national broadcaster that patients were sent to hospitals across the city because healthcare facilities near the base were “completely overwhelmed.”Acute Care Alberta said several hospitals across the province had activated a “Code Orange,” an emergency designation used when multiple severely injured patients need coordinated care.The agency said emergency medical resources were stretched so thin that very few ambulances were available in the Edmonton area. Late Saturday, at least 10 ambulances were parked in and around the Wainwright health centre as paramedics and soldiers rushed about. The town of Wainwright has about 7,000 residents.The fire also disrupted advance voting ahead of Monday’s referendum on whether Alberta should begin a process that could lead to independence from Canada.Elections Alberta said the advance polling location at Wainwright Communiplex closed early Saturday, and ballots and election materials were transported securely. It named polling locations in Lloydminster and Vermilion as alternatives.

title: Can Spain afford its pensions? What to know about the funding debate ahead of the election
