description: Spain’s pension system is not bankrupt, but increasingly relies on state funding. Social Security ended 2025 with a deficit of 0.4% of GDP after €47.8 billion in state transfers. Research institute Fedea puts the underlying deficit, excluding those transfers, at 4.15% of GDP.
content: On 5 October, Pedro Sánchez called a general election for 29 November, and pensions are once again in the spotlight. One of the most common questions is: is the pension system bankrupt?This year, Spain has set a new record for its monthly pension bill, at almost €14.5 billion. Its Social Security system, which pays pensions and other benefits, reported its smallest deficit since 2011. But more than 20% of its income comes from the state, its debt to the Treasury is over €136 billion, and the mass retirement of the baby-boom generation has barely begun.The question is less whether pensions will be paid than who will cover their growing cost.Can a pay-as-you-go pension system go bust?Spain’s pension system is pay-as-you-go: today’s contributions pay today’s pensions. There is no individual account in the name of each worker and no fund that can simply run out. The Constitution requires the state to guarantee adequate pensions and update them regularly. If the system falls short, the gap can be covered through state loans or transfers.Santiago Calvo, professor of quantitative and public economics and deputy director of the Ruth Richardson Centre, says Social Security cannot go bust like a company because behind it stands the state’s ability to raise taxes and issue debt.The problem is that this shifts the risk onto the state itself. In "El elefante en la habitación" ("The elephant in the room"), the book he co-authored with Daniel Fernández, they describe a "Greek-style" default. Calvo describes it as the scenario in which, after years of plugging the hole with debt, a recession or a spike in interest rates drives up borrowing costs until Spain loses the ability to finance itself at a reasonable cost."At that point, the adjustment stops being decided in parliament, with a timetable and gradual steps, and is negotiated with creditors as a condition for a bailout. The biggest budget item is the first to be cut," he warns. In Greece, he recalls, the cuts hit people who were already retired, and the average pension fell from around €1,350 in 2009 to €833 a few years later.Why the deficit figures differIn 2025, Social Security closed the year with a deficit of €7.387 billion, according to Spain’s Ministry for Inclusion, Social Security and Migration.That was 0.4% of GDP, the lowest figure since 2011. Contributions rose by 6.9% in 2025, reaching €176.918 billion. Growth in employment, with the number of registered workers reaching a record high, helped drive the increase.At the end of July 2026, there were more than 22.5 million workers paying into the system, a national record. Foreign workers accounted for 15.6% of all contributors, and in June there were 2.37 workers per pensioner, a key ratio in a pay-as-you-go scheme.But the headline deficit includes substantial state support. Of the €232.782 billion collected by Social Security in 2025, €47.815 billion came in the form of transfers from the state, 11% more than the previous year.Those transfers accounted for 20.5% of income. Some cover benefits intended to be paid through taxes rather than workers’ contributions, including income support and top-ups for minimum pensions.Fedea, a Spanish economic research institute, uses a broader scope to assess the financial situation of the Social Security system. According to its analysis of the accounts from 2005 to 2025, state transfers to the wider system totalled €61.342 billion in 2025.Including those transfers, the overall balance would show a deficit of around €8.4 billion, similar in scale to the ministry’s €7.387 billion. Without them, the underlying deficit comes to €69.783 billion, or 4.15% of GDP – roughly ten times the ministry’s figure as a share of GDP.The two estimates measure different things.The two estimates measure different things. Part of those transfers pays for benefits that are intended to be tax-funded. In 2024, of the €58.301 billion in transfers, €12.951 billion went on non-contributory benefits — paid to people who do not qualify through contributions — and €15.234 billion on pensions for civil servants.The biggest share, €27.505 billion, went to cover contributory benefits — those linked to workers’ and employers’ payments into the system. Fedea’s study counts this as a shortfall in contribution income, whereas the ministry’s accounting treats the state transfer covering it as extra income.The roughly €7 billion deficit is the shortfall left after state transfers under the ministry’s accounting. Fedea’s roughly €70 billion figure excludes transfers and covers a wider system. The debate is over how much spending should be covered by contributions and how much by taxes. Either way, the accounts remain in the red.Calvo agrees that the two figures "are correct, but answer different questions". The ministry’s figure measures the shortfall in Social Security’s accounts after receiving state transfers.Fedea’s number compares what the system raises on its own with what it spends, "which is the relevant question when talking about sustainability".In his view, the official figure also "has a reading problem". In 2025, the accounting deficit fell by about €2.45 billion, while state transfers rose by around €4.86 billion. "Without that extra state contribution, the balance would have worsened." He argues that, as the public sector as a whole remains in deficit, in practice that money comes from new borrowing.Transfers are not the only route. The state also lends money to Social Security.From December 2022 to December 2025, the debt increased by €30.001 billion, topping €136 billion. That is more than twice the amount paid into the pension reserve fund over the same period.Meeting the rules, but facing rising costsOn 29 May, Spain’s independent fiscal watchdog (AIReF) assessed whether pension spending complied with the rule agreed with Brussels~~ (an average of no more than 13.3% of GDP between 2022 and 2050, after deducting new revenue measures)~~. The rule caps average spending between 2022 and 2050 at 13.3% of GDP, after allowing for measures to raise additional revenue. It put the figure at 13.0%, 0.3 percentage points below the threshold.Gross spending was 14.6% of GDP and the revenue measures shaved 1.6 percentage points off that.Spain therefore meets the rule because of additional revenue, rather than lower pension costs.The same study projects that, with no policy changes, public debt would start to rise again from 2035, reaching 123% of GDP in 2050.It forecasts that three out of every four euros of extra pension spending would come from central government, forcing it to cut spending elsewhere or take on more debt. Meeting the rule and keeping debt under control are, on those figures, two separate goals.The government’s own model puts average pension spending at around 14% of GDP until 2050, below AIReF’s 14.6%. The difference reflects assumptions about employment, birth rates and immigration.For Calvo, the country’s vulnerability "increases every year". Spain continues to carry public debt of around 100% of GDP, and pension spending will keep rising with the retirement of the baby-boom generation, reaching 16.4% of GDP in 2050, according to AIReF.He prefers not to put a date on a Greek-style crisis, because it depends on a trigger no one can foresee, but he sees the period of greatest risk as the next two decades. "What currently separates Spain from Greece is the chance to carry out, in good time and by its own decision, a reform that would otherwise be imposed from outside," he argues.How much protection does the reserve fund offer?Spain has introduced an additional payroll contribution to rebuild its pension reserve fund. The levy rises to 1.2% of wages in 2029, and the money cannot be used until 2033.As of 31 March 2026, the Reserve Fund stood at €15.267 billion, its highest level in a decade. In September, the regular monthly payment alone cost €14.498 billion, meaning the fund could cover just over one month of pension payments.At the end of 2011, when it peaked, it reached €66.815 billion, equivalent to 6.22% of GDP. It was gradually run down to help pay pensions in subsequent years.The Reserve Fund was designed to cover temporary mismatches between income and expenditure. Hitting its highest level in ten years says more about how low it fell in the past than about how healthy it is today.The baby-boom generation is already retiringThe strain on the pension system is already clear from the pension bill, and the pressure is set to grow in the coming years. In September, Social Security paid 10.55 million pensions to 9.53 million recipients. The pension bill rose by 6.3% year on year, while the number of pensions increased by just 1.6%.The cost is rising faster than the number of pensions because payments are also increasing. This year, contributory pensions went up by 2.7%, while minimum pensions rose by more than 7%. On top of that comes the substitution effect, as new retirees receive around €500 more per month than those leaving the system.The average retirement pension rose by 4.5% year on year, reaching €1,576.10 in September.The toughest period is still ahead. People born between the late 1950s and the mid‑1970s (the baby‑boom generation) will be retiring over the next 20 years.According to projections published by the National Statistics Institute (INE) in June, the share of the population aged over 65, currently 21.1% of the total, will rise to 30.9% in 2076. These forecasts assume a net migration gain of 6.3 million people by 2040. Without that immigration, the pressure on contributors would be greater.Calvo focuses on what this will mean for people now starting their working lives. The projections, he notes, already show that pensions will cover a smaller share of a final salary, dropping from 77% to 65% in 2050, "and they do so on assumptions that Fedea itself sees as optimistic".Who pays the growing bill?According to early estimates, next year’s rise will be around 3.5%, the highest since 2024. The final figure will depend on the flash inflation rate for November.The new parliament’s first session is scheduled for 23 December, with the timing of a new government depending on the outcome of talks after the election, and the pension rise must take effect from 1 January 2027.The numbers above lead to a political question. Who pays the rising cost of the pension system? The options are limited, and none of them is painless. The first is to raise more revenue.The 2021–2023 reform followed this path with the additional payroll levy and with new contribution rules for the self-employed.The second option is to spend less on each pension. This can be done by delaying the effective retirement age or changing how the initial pension is calculated.The third option is to keep turning to the state for more transfers or more loans, which ultimately means higher taxes or more public debt.The fourth option is to increase the number of people paying into the system through more jobs and a larger working-age population, supported by immigration. Higher productivity and wages could also boost contributions.What would reform mean for future pensioners?Calvo argues for changing the formula. He proposes moving to a system of notional accounts, where pensions are based on each person’s contributions, revalued in line with economic growth, and adding a funded element in which money is invested for retirement.Calculations by Devesa, Doménech and Meneu for Fedea that he cites put the gap between the pension received by new retirees today and the one they would get under that model at between 12% and 25%.The size of the gap depends on the economic growth assumptions used.That difference, he says, measures "the share of the current promise that the system cannot pay out of its own resources, and which someone is already funding through transfers and debt".His proposal leaves existing pensions untouched and applies the change by generation, as Sweden did.Those born in 1970 would have 5% of their pension calculated under the new formula, those born in 1971 would have 10%, and so on up to the 1989 cohort, whose pensions would be calculated entirely using notional accounts.No generation would see a sudden jump compared with the previous one, and each worker would know decades in advance the rules that apply to them. According to Calvo, people with low contribution bases, those with long careers and the self-employed would all gain "with a system that counts every euro contributed".He admits that introducing funded accounts requires more care, because diverting contributions into individual accounts would leave a gap in funding for existing pensions. So he proposes starting with the additional payroll levy, which in 2025 raised almost €5 billion for a Reserve Fund invested in public debt, and redirecting that money into funded accounts with diversified portfolios.Asked who bears the cost of adjustment, he replies that the current system already imposes a cost and that it piles the burden onto young people and future taxpayers "without telling them". The reform, he argues, would make this explicit and share it among all generations still in work.If he had to pick one measure for the government that emerges from the 29 November vote, Calvo would, in its first year, pass a law setting out the move to notional accounts with the generational timetable "fixed from day one".That law would also oblige Social Security to send every contributor an annual statement showing what they have accumulated and an estimate of their future pension.If a 30-year-old wonders whether they will receive a pension, Calvo insists that they will, "because it is the item of spending with the strongest political backing in the country and no government is going to stop paying it". The uncertainty, he adds, lies in how much it will amount to compared with their salary and at what age they will be able to retire.His advice is to start saving independently now, even small sums, to take advantage of any workplace pension scheme on offer, and to follow closely a debate in which their generation has the most at stake. "Their best guarantee is for the system to be reformed while it still has time to adapt."Each option produces different losers and operates on a different timescale, and the clock is ticking. On 27 November, we will learn how much pensions will rise in January. On 29 November, there will be a general election. Pensions will continue to be paid. Whoever wins will face decisions over who has to shoulder the rising cost.

title: Marine Le Pen warns of 'threat to democracy' and blasts 'exhausted Macronist power'
description: The far-right candidate for the 2027 presidential election speaks out the day after a day of riots that left France reeling, just as looting resumed in Paris.
content: "We are experiencing a crisis of confidence," declares presidential candidate Marine Le Pen. She describes it as "a threat to democracy". The National Rally leader lays responsibility at the door of the far left and of Emmanuel Macron, a president who she says is "without credibility or authority."Marine Le Pen spoke less than two hours before Emmanuel Macron’s address, expected at 20:00.For his part, the president of the National Rally believes that "order no longer exists in France today". According to Jordan Bardella, "France was humiliated" on Saturday night. The RN leader made the statement during a visit to a police station in Paris.Violence flares up again in ParisMarine Le Pen and her number two are speaking out just as looting has resumed in Paris, less than 24 hours after a day of chaos that has left France reeling.Fresh scenes of violence erupted in the French capital on Sunday afternoon.CRS-8, the specialist riot police unit that provides rapid response to urban unrest, has been deployed for the second day in a row.Tensions are once again centred in the heart of Paris, particularly around Place de la République.Clashes are pitting several hundred rioters against the forces of law and order.According to the Paris police prefecture, "An undeclared call to assemble at Place de la République today at 14:00 was circulated on social media".Groups of hooded youths have attacked shops and looted them.30,000 looters in Marseille on SaturdayThe latest figures for Saturday’s violence are staggering.For Saturday alone, the Bouches-du-Rhône prefecture counted more than 30,000 looters. A dizzying figure that has left observers specialising in policing and justice dumbfounded.

title: Businesses and shopkeepers pick up the pieces after protests in France spiral into looting
description: On Sunday morning, broken glass and litter filled the streets as Parisians emerged from their apartment blocks after a day of chaos across France.
content: Major businesses and local shop owners are recovering from widespread looting across France on Saturday, after cost-of-living protests spiralled into scenes of violence that saw masked individuals force their way into stores and make off with goods.French authorities say shops were looted across cities including Lyon, Marseille, Bordeaux, Rennes, Strasbourg, Grenoble, Nice, and Limoges, as well as in the French capital, Paris.Among the targets were major supermarket chains including Carrefour, Franprix, and Monoprix, as well as luxury boutiques, bars, and vape shops.Groups of masked individuals, many dressed in black, paraded the streets, smashing windows and pulling at metal shutters until they gave way, before grabbing items from the shelves.On Sunday morning, broken glass and litter filled the streets as Parisians emerged from their apartment blocks to be greeted by the aftermath of the destruction.Alexandre Bompard, the Chairman and CEO of the Carrefour Group, said on Sunday that a "total of 50 shops" had been targeted, "including 19 Carrefour convenience stores and supermarkets."He said the affected locations included premises in Paris, Rennes, Lille, and Bordeaux, among others."My thoughts are also with the 1,500 shops belonging to all the other retail chains and with all the shopkeepers who have suffered the same unacceptable violence," Bompard continued, adding that the destruction would have "considerable human and economic consequences."Dozens of employees at our franchise partners will be forced onto short-time working," he said. "The cost of the repairs will run to well over ten million euros."One store owner near the Place de la République whose shop had been wrecked by rioters told the Brut outlet that he had put all his savings into the business and that he felt like he'd lost everything."I don't know how I'll get by or how I'll live with my family," he said.Brut said a neighbour had decided to set up a fundraiser to help the man get back on his feet.Paris Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire has also pledged to offer his full support to businesses affected in the capital and announced that he had requested the creation of an "emergency task force to support shopkeepers who have been victims of vandalism.""Its role will be to assess the damage, support affected shopkeepers, and assist them with administrative and insurance procedures," he said. "You bring Paris to life every day. Today, it's Paris' turn to stand by your side."Looters assault Euronews crewA Euronews crew were assaulted by looters in Paris on Saturday, near the Place de la République, as they reported on the situation.The crew were making their way to another location when they were confronted by masked individuals looting a nearby Intermarché Express supermarket."We were standing on Boulevard de Magenta, not far from a supermarket that was being looted by young people, young adults, teenagers. When they saw we were filming, they started hitting my cameraman and attempted to take his microphone and they encircled us," Estelle Nilsson-Julien, Euronews’ correspondent in Paris, said."They then pushed him against the wall and started hitting and punching him. They also hit me. They punched him in the face, but because he was wearing goggles and a mask, he was not harmed," she added.A march moving along the Boulevard de Clichy towards the Place de Clichy across the other side of Paris remained peaceful, another Euronews journalist on the ground reported.French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said in an update on Sunday that more than 600 police officers, gendarmes, and firefighters had been injured on Saturday, with more than 2,000 people arrested.

title: Magyar links French riots to migration, says ‘shocking scenes’ justify hard line
description: Hungary’s Péter Magyar said riots in France justified his tough migration stance, echoed by Poland’s Donald Tusk. Left-wing critics accused him of exploiting the unrest, despite most protesters being French nationals.
content: Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar linked the riots in France to immigration, saying the “shocking scenes” vindicated his government’s tough migration policies.Anti-austerity protests turned violent in several French cities on Saturday, with looting reported in Paris, Lyon and Marseille. Several buildings were set on fire, including the historic town hall in Limoges.“Seeing this senseless destruction and unjustified violence, perhaps it is now clear to everyone why Hungary takes the toughest possible stance on migration,” Magyar wrote on social media on Sunday, alongside a video showing buildings on fire.“We will not relax our efforts to protect our external borders or change our immigration policy,” he added.In his post, Magyar also said that the "overwhelming majority of European countries" want a tougher approach to migration and have "finally woken up".“The Europe we all love is in serious trouble today. We also have a responsibility to help preserve our continent as the most wonderful place for our grandchildren," he said.At a European summit held this week, a group of countries, including Denmark, Italy and Hungary, pushed for stronger language on migration in the conclusions.French President Emmanuel Macron warned against “the stigmatisation” of immigrants and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez praised their positive contribution.Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk also commented on Sunday, without explicitly referring to France. He said Poland would “neither repeat nor pay for” other countries’ mistakes, stressing that Warsaw would maintain its strict asylum policy.“We are firmly defending the border against illegal migration; we have our own asylum policy (we do not accept applications); we deport those who break Polish law,” Tusk wrote on X on Sunday.“On security issues, we will be relentless. That is what I told the leaders of Europe in Brussels,” he added.Magyar’s remarks drew criticism in Hungary. András Jámbor, a left-wing activist and Budapest councillor, accused the prime minister of exploiting footage of the French riots for political gain.“It is deeply disturbing that the Hungarian Prime Minister chose not to address the people’s legitimate demands and the unjustified violence, but instead to label them migrants,” Jámbor said.“Although some protesters have an immigrant background, as do some members of the wider population, this demonstration is about more than that,” he added.Macron will deliver an address to the nation at 8pm Sunday.

title: Southern Valencia coast on alert as storm Adam may dump 300 mm of rain in 12 hours
description: The peak of this new DANA will come between Sunday and Monday, bringing heavy rain to Ibiza and Formentera and also to Alicante, Murcia and Almeria.
content: Spain's State Meteorological Agency has issued a special warning for "very heavy and persistent" showers and thunderstorms in Spain's Levante region and parts of the Balearic Islands, from this Sunday and over the next 48 hours.The combination of the DANA Adam, cut off and isolated from the general atmospheric circulation, together with a very humid easterly flow, will bring widespread rainfall to four provinces (southern Valencia, Alicante, the Region of Murcia and the Almería coastline) and up to three of the Balearic Islands, with a particular impact on the Pityusic Islands (Ibiza and Formentera) but also leaving significant totals in Mallorca.Aemet's information note refers to the possibility that the showers could become "torrential", but specifies that it is difficult to calculate exactly where in these regions the highest totals will be recorded. At the time of writing, the agency is maintaining red alerts only along the southern Valencian coast and in the north of Alicante and, in addition to the Mediterranean areas mentioned, orange alerts in the Seville lowlands, Ronda and the Sierra de Grazalema in the province of Cádiz."The most likely scenario indicates that the highest accumulations may occur along the southern coast of Valencia and around Cape La Nao, where amounts in excess of 60-90 millimetres in one hour and up to 200-300 mm in 12 hours are expected, with the possibility that they may extend to adjacent areas; as well as in the Pityusic Islands, where more than 160 mm could accumulate in 12 hours," the agency's statement says."From late in the day, rainfall could also be significant in coastal and pre-coastal areas of Alicante, Murcia and Almería, and across the Balearics spreading to the island of Mallorca, with totals above 50 mm in one hour and 100-140 mm in 12 hours," it adds. The impact on this latter island will be much more pronounced along its southern coast, where the Balearic capital, Palma, is located.Aemet warns that late on Monday the episode could shift towards the north of the Valencia region and even reach Tarragona, before finally losing strength as Tuesday approaches.

title: Check your wallet: some 2-euro coins are worth far more
description: They may say two euros, but collectors sometimes pay many times that amount: rare editions and striking minting errors can turn small change into sought-after treasures.
content: At the bakery, at the parking meter or in the supermarket, coins usually change hands without anyone checking them. Yet it can be worth taking a closer look at your change: some 2-euro pieces have a collector value that far exceeds their face value. What matters, however, are specific features. An unusual design alone does not turn a coin into a rarity.Grace Kelly: From two euros to 3,000One of the best-known treasures is a 2-euro commemorative coin from Monaco issued in 2007. It marks the 25th anniversary of the death of Princess Gracia Patricia, formerly Hollywood actress Grace Kelly. The European Central Bank puts the mintage at just 20,001 copies. The coin can be recognised by the portrait of the princess, the country name "MONACO" and the year 2007. To the right of the effigy is the artist's name, "R.B. BARON".Experts estimate this coin to be worth around 3,100 euros.There is a big catch, though: it was sold directly to collectors and was not released into normal circulation. Finding one in your change would therefore be extremely unlikely. In principle it is a valid 2-euro coin and could be used for payments, but hardly anyone would do so deliberately.When a mistake makes a coin interestingAlongside rare issues, errors can also increase a coin's value, and making such a find would be more realistic. A striking example is the so-called fried-egg strike: the differently coloured inner part of a 1- or 2-euro coin is not seated correctly, so its metal is pressed partly into the outer ring. The irregular shape resembles a fried egg.A pronounced rotation of the two sides of the coin relative to each other or striking on the wrong blank can also be of interest. Business magazine "WirtschaftsWoche" cites possible values of up to 100 euros for fried-egg strikes, up to 200 euros for rotated dies and up to 650 euros for pieces struck on the wrong blanks.When coins are produced, two different metal parts are joined and struck under high pressure. Despite precise technology and careful checks, faulty specimens occasionally make their way into circulation.In this case, the German 2-euro commemorative coin "Saxony-Anhalt" from 2021 was struck on a 1-euro blank. As a result, the colours are reversed compared with a normal 2-euro piece: the outer ring is gold-coloured, the inner part silver-coloured. The specimen also weighs only 7.50 grams instead of the usual 8.50 grams.Coin dealer Münzen Müller values a comparable minting error at 1,200 euros.This tiny "S" won't make you richHow quickly an ordinary coin can turn into an alleged sensation on the internet is illustrated by examples of Greek coins with a small "S" in one of the stars, which are repeatedly offered as valuable minting errors, reports zwei-euro.com.In reality the letter stands for "Suomi", meaning Finland, where part of the Greek coins were produced. According to coin experts, this is a regular variety with a mintage of 70 million pieces. The "S" alone therefore does not justify any exceptional value.Found a valuable coin? Don't polish it!If you spot an unusual coin, you should first identify the issuing country, year and motif. The ECB documents the official 2-euro commemorative issues on its website.If you then believe you have discovered a valuable specimen, you should have it assessed by a specialist coin dealer or auction house. If the find is confirmed, a direct sale or an auction may be possible. Make sure you ask in advance about any fees, and do not clean or polish the coin, as this can reduce its value to collectors. Rubbing or polishing can cause the finest scratches and strip away the original mint lustre.

title: Ukrainian forces strike St Petersburg and Leningrad region
description: It comes as Zelenskyy said Russian forces had targeted Ukraine's energy sector in strikes on four regions on Saturday night. He said attacks on residential buildings had also left two people dead and 12 others reportedly injured.
content: An oil terminal and a data centre belonging to the VK social networking service were reportedly among the targets of a drone attack on St Petersburg and the surrounding Leningrad region overnight into Sunday.The attack is being described by Russian media as one of the largest on the area since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. One person was killed and 15 people were injured in the strikes, local officials said.A total of 144 drones were shot down over the Leningrad region, regional governor Aleksandr Drozdenko said.According to Drozdenko, drone debris fell on houses in Gatchina and other districts, causing fires and damaging 55 vehicles."Emergency power cuts were recorded; specialists are carrying out emergency work and the electricity supply is being promptly restored. At the moment, two transformer substations in Yanino remain switched off, and 50 apartment blocks, home to around 20,000 people, are in the outage zone," he said.The VK press office reported an attack on its data centre in the Leningrad region but said the company's services remained available to users as normal.In St Petersburg, governor Aleksandr Beglov said fires broke out at civilian infrastructure facilities in the Nevsky, Krasnoselsky, Krasnogvardeisky, and Moskovsky districts and on the grounds of the St Petersburg oil terminal.Preliminary information indicated that no one was injured. The oil terminal is located in the Great Port of St Petersburg.The terminal is capable of receiving and shipping 1.1 million tonnes of fuel a month, using four berths for sea-going vessels and tankers. Its 32 storage tanks occupy an area of 442,000 square metres.One of the fires broke out at an Ozon warehouse. According to the company, staff were evacuated. Smoke is rising above the warehouse complex, and several roads have been closed in the area.Due to the attack, flights were suspended at Pulkovo airport for more than seven hours. Rosaviatsia, Russia's aviation authority, lifted the restrictions at 10 am Moscow time.Russian strikes on UkraineIt comes as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Sunday that Russian forces had carried out further strikes against Ukraine's energy sector on Saturday night, targeting substations in the Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Khmelnytskyi, and Odesa regions."Tens of thousands of families remain without power. Energy workers and repair crews are working virtually around the clock to restore electricity supply," he wrote in a post on X.Zelenskyy said attacks on residential buildings had also left two people dead and 12 others reportedly injured.According to the Ukrainian leader, Russia hit Ukraine with close to 2,700 attack drones, 1,700 aerial bombs, and 66 missiles over the last week.

title: France reels after cost-of-living protests see widespread violence
description: The French government has said around 1,200 arrests were made across France in relation to Saturday's events and that 150 police officers and gendarmes were injured over the course of the day.
content: Between 550,000 and 800,000 people took to the streets of France on Saturday, mostly peacefully and often unaware of the unprecedented violence breaking out in some of the country's major cities.Limoges city hall went up in flames, as did the iconic tourist office on Place Bellecour in Lyon. Vandals also forced their way into town halls in Marseille, Lille, and Angers, whilst in Bordeaux, the prefect's residence was ransacked.Widespread destruction"Scenes of insurrection," reads the front page of Le Parisien.In Paris, Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire said "entire streets" had been "systematically devastated" after the French capital saw violent clashes between protesters and police.The French capital quite literally went up in flames on Saturday. By midday, Place de la République was littered with projectiles, police were clashing with rioters in clouds of tear gas, and a thick column of black smoke rose above the city's iconic rooftops as emergency service vehicles burned.After nightfall, in several districts, Parisians watched in fear from restaurants and café terraces as groups of young people continued to rampage through the city.Dressed in black and wearing masks, the groups moved either in their dozens or in small, scattered bands.Each time, they used the same tactic: several would approach a shop and attack its metal shutters until they give way, before people rushed in to loot the premises.They left behind smashed storefronts, charred bicycles, and stolen goods scattered on the ground.Riot police units, who were charged with maintaining public order, followed alongside firefighters as the groups moved on to find more targets ahead.The looters did not spare the Champs-Élysées, and clashes with the police moved closer to the Élysée Palace and the National Assembly.The government has said around 1,200 arrests were made across France and that 150 police officers and gendarmes were injured over the course of the day.Politicians reactAddressing the protests in a post on social media on Saturday evening, French President Emmanuel Macron said there was "no place for violence" in France."Those who have vandalised and attacked prefectures and shops alike, and even looted our town halls, will be prosecuted and punished," he wrote.For his part, the interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, has spoken of "groups of several hundred or even thousands of rioters, very clearly instigated by the far left."Far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen said "legitimate social demands" had been "taken hostage by the far left and by the speeches of Jean-Luc Mélenchon's MPs who, by legitimising violence, by seeing order as oppression and disorder as a right, are trying to plunge the country into chaos."According to Mélenchon, the far-left presidential candidate, the "absurd leadership has opened the door to chaos."The leaders no longer know what to do; the rank and file are afraid and running amok," he wrote on X."I do not know who will hear my voice in such circumstances, but my message is clear: those who share our struggle have no place in looting and vandalism," he added.

title: Euronews' crew assaulted by masked individuals while covering protests in Paris
description: Euronews correspondents in Paris covering the protests reported being targeted by masked individuals on Saturday’s major nationwide demonstrations following calls on social media to target media outlets and professionals to prevent coverage.
content: Euronews’ crew was assaulted by looters and rioters in Paris near the Place de la Republique on Saturday as they were covering the ongoing joint major protests organised by the so-called ‘Yellow Vests’ and student-led groups.The crew was headed to another location from Place de la Republique – where the protests were being staged.Shortly into their journey, they were confronted by masked looters robbing the nearby Intermarché Express supermarket on 14 Place Jacques Bonsergent, which diverges from Place de la Republique, and filmed it.“We were standing on Boulevard de Magenta, where a supermarket was was being looted by young people, young adults, teenagers. When they saw we were filming, they started hitting my cameraman and attempted to take his microphone and they encircled us,” said Estelle Nilsson-Julien, Euronews’ correspondent in Paris.“They then pushed him against the wall and started hitting and punching him. They punched him in the face, but because he was wearing a gas mask, protective eyewear and a helmet, he was not seriously harmed.""He managed to get away with just some bruises on his face," she added.Our correspondent also noted that the looters stole their camera during the scuffles, which was eventually brought back by a group of youngsters who saw what was happening. The returned camera however did not have the SD card, and all footage recorded was lost.Nilsson-Julien reported seeing things on fire in the area in the immediate vicinity of the supermarket, and loud police sirens.“It is to be honest anarchy in the streets. There are many young people who seem like they are ready for a fight and looting going on. So, the calm protests of earlier today, at least in this area, are completely over,” she said.Another Euronews correspondent, Valerie Gauriat, covering the protests at the Place de la Republique also reported a violent incident with a masked individual earlier while conducting an interview with a protester.She noted that a protester slapped the back of her head and mumbled profane words as they walked past, denouncing media presence at the demonstrations.The incidents come after certain groups on social media called on protesters to target media outlets and personnel, to prevent “the spread of misinformation” about the protests and reported violence.

title: Dozens arrested as protesters clash with security forces in Paris
description: The French government stepped up security measures ahead of Saturday’s nationwide protests over the cost-of-living crisis, with student groups also expected to join demonstrations amid fears of potential clashes.
content: Dozens of people have been detained in the French capital, Paris, after protesters clashed with security forces across the city on Saturday.Trade unions and citizens branding themselves as "yellow vests" are protesting against the cost-of-living crisis and rising fuel prices as a result of the US-Israeli war on Iran.A large number of students have also joined in on Saturday's nationwide protests, demanding a revamp of the country's educational system, upgrades to classrooms and facilities and greater access to resources.The French Interior Ministry said around 550,000 people took part in the protests, including roughly 110,000 in Paris.Protesters also broke into the town hall of France's second largest city, Marseille, ramming the door with security barriers.Several then entered, one spray painting an anarchist "A" symbol on a wall before police intervened."We're taking the Bastille," one demonstrator shouted in reference to the 1789 storming of a fortress during the French Revolution.Meanwhile, shops across the country boarded up their storefronts in a bid to avoid potential looting or vandalism. Thousands of police forces and riot units were also deployed across the country to boost security.According to a source close to France's Interior Ministry, 500 actions were anticipated across the country on Saturday, as well as around 90 protests.The protests follow four weeks of student demonstrations over a range of issues, including teacher absences, overcrowded classrooms, and outdated facilities.Most student protests have been peaceful, but there have been clashes involving rioters and widespread criticism of alleged police brutality and violence.The source told Euronews that the far-left movement could seek to provoke confrontations with law enforcement and attempt to breach security perimeters along protest routes. They also warned that blockades of key transportation routes and essential infrastructure would "not be tolerated."Meanwhile, French President Emmanuel Macron said on Friday that whilst the right to protest "is fully respected," it "must be accompanied by respect for people and property.""That is why I call for calm and respect: these rights must be preserved," he said.Mounting scrutiny of police actionsFrench law enforcement authorities have faced increasing scrutiny in recent weeks amid several allegations of police violence.In one case, a 15-year-old schoolboy allegedly lost an eye after being struck by a police rubber bullet. In a separate incident, a 14-year-old reportedly lost his hand after picking up a police stun grenade. The circumstances surrounding both cases remain under investigation.Following the latter case, France suspended the use of certain types of stun grenades.Yet, in an interview on Friday, France's Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said that the use of stun grenades would be allowed on 17 October should "serious urban violence" occur on the sidelines of demonstrations, cautioning that stun grenades were "never used when things are going well."Nuñez told France's Senate on Tuesday that 36 investigations into alleged police violence during student protests had been opened. He said that four of these cases related to mutilating injuries and six to significant injuries, whilst the others were related to alleged blows, insults and reported sexual violence.One man who had flown into Paris from the US on Friday told Euronews he was "supportive" of peaceful protests."Hopefully nobody gets hurt and people's voices are heard," he said.A taxi driver in the capital called the situation "very delicate.""People have the right to protest, but peacefully," he said, adding that the "people in charge need to find some solutions."Yellow vest movementThere has been speculation that the 17 October demonstration could mark the return of the yellow vest grassroots movement, which emerged in 2018 in reaction to a planned government fuel and diesel tax hike.For months, yellow vest protestors gathered every weekend to block roundabouts, motorways, and fuel depots across the country, with tense police clashes also occurring.It comes as the French government also grapples with a major public debt crisis as it attempts to pass a budget containing austerity measures through a hung parliament.Police union lodges complaint against state for 'endangering lives of others'French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said on Thursday that 937 police officers and gendarmes had been injured since the start of the protests. He also reported injuries among 248 students and 149 teaching staff members, which he said was the highest number of injuries ever recorded by France's Education Ministry.Lecornu warned that the “secondary school student movement” was transforming into a “wave of urban violence."Meanwhile, Alliance Police Nationale, one of France's largest police unions, announced in a statement on Tuesday that it would lodge a complaint against the state "for endangering the lives of others."The union denounced what it qualified as "contradictory orders" given to police officers, who have been "exposed to violence and left at the mercy of public hostility" over the course of secondary school protests.“After the president’s [French President Emmanuel Macron] expressions of empathy towards rioters and emphasis on dialogue, we are now faced with vague instructions, contradictory orders and superficial public statements!""The discrepancy between Laurent Nuñez’s public statements and the verbal instructions passed down through the chain of command has become unbearable," the union said.The hard-left France Unbowed party has been accused by the government and political opponents of encouraging violence and stoking unrest through inflammatory language.In a speech delivered on 30 September, the party's leader, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, urged his supporters to "stand up to police brutality," adding that "there will be neither forgetting nor forgiveness for anyone."He later qualified his comments, stating that he backed peaceful protest methods.

title: The world’s biggest fine jewellery factory: How Pandora aims to make more and pollute less in Vietnam
description: Pandora invested $150 million (€132mn) in a Vietnam factory, which it says will operate entirely on renewable electricity. The company also switched to using 100% recycled gold and silver in its jewellery production in 2024.
content: Pandora has opened what it calls the world’s largest fine jewellery crafting facility in Vietnam, expanding production while seeking to reduce its environmental footprint.The factory in Ho Chi Minh City is expected to employ 7,000 people when fully operational.It will produce up to 60 million pieces of jewellery a year, increasing the Danish company’s manufacturing capacity by 50%, according to its opening announcement.The site is Pandora’s fourth factory globally and its first outside Thailand."This gives us flexibility to craft all our collections, our assortments in all our materials and crafting techniques," said Pandora CEO Berta de Pablos-Barbier.The Danish jewellery maker sold 112 million pieces in 2025, equivalent to more than three every second. It describes itself as the world’s largest jewellery brand.Expanding production, reducing emissionsPandora invested $150 million (€132mn) in the Vietnam factory, which it says will operate entirely on renewable electricity. The company also switched to using 100% recycled gold and silver in its jewellery production in 2024.As it increases manufacturing capacity, de Pablos-Barbier said Pandora would continue growing "in a sustainable manner".Gold is particularly suited to repeated reuse, according to experts."In many ways, it is designed for a circular economy. It doesn't oxidise. That's why it's so valuable," said Saleem H. Ali, lead researcher for critical minerals and the inclusive energy transition at the United Nations University."We still have the gold from the ancient Egyptians in pretty good shape."Using recycled metals still requires energy. Refining involves heating and separating metals from other materials to remove impurities.Pandora’s ambition is to extend renewable electricity use beyond its own operations to suppliers involved in producing its jewellery.Challenges in a growing jewellery marketJewellery unit sales are forecast to grow by 4.1% annually between 2025 and 2028 — around four times the rate of clothing, according to The State of Fashion 2026, a report from McKinsey and The Business of Fashion.Pandora’s rise from a small Copenhagen jewellery shop, founded in 1982, was built around manufacturing in Thailand, which began in 1989. Its charm bracelet, launched in 2000, helped drive international expansion before its Copenhagen stock exchange listing in 2010.But the growing jewellery market does not guarantee an easy path for Pandora.Pandora warned in its August 2026 results that US import tariffs would continue to weigh on profitability.The tariffs affect sales to the United States, Pandora’s largest market, where inflation and economic uncertainty are also weighing on demand for its jewellery.Past labour disputes have also drawn scrutiny to conditions behind its production. Danish investigative outlet Danwatch reported in 2020 that a Thai labour court had ruled in May 2019 that union activity had contributed to workers’ dismissals at Pandora’s Bangkok factory.Pandora said the cuts reflected restructuring and employee performance.As Pandora expands in Vietnam, it remains to be seen whether it can increase production while reducing emissions and protecting workers’ rights.

title: Budget, Ukraine, migration: Five takeaways from the EU leaders’ summit
description: EU leaders ended their Brussels summit with no deal on the budget, a new €70bn Ukraine funding gap, open clashes over energy and migration, but fresh resolve to create new trade defence tools to battle China.
content: EU leaders gathered in Brussels on Thursday and Friday with a packed agenda, from the long-term budget and financial support for Ukraine to migration, energy and China.The summit alternated between entrenched positions on the bloc’s budget, a warm welcome for Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and clashes over energy and migration policies.Here are the five highlights.Rallying behind UkraineThe bitter row between Zelenskyy and US President Donald Trump dominated the second day of the summit.Leaders closed ranks behind Zelenskyy and promised to keep sanctions in place for as long as Russia pursues its full-scale invasion. They also condemned the diesel deal struck by Trump with Russian President Vladimir Putin, although the Bulgarian prime minister broke ranks to support it.The reception gave Zelenskyy a moment of diplomatic relief as Trump doubled down, claiming Zelenskyy was “more difficult” to deal with than Putin and demanding new elections in Ukraine. Trump also called Kyiv’s strikes on Russian oil refineries, its main leverage, a “disgrace”.“I defend the interests of Ukraine and the Ukrainian people exclusively,” Zelenskyy said in a defiant tone. “We were attacked, occupied, and our people were killed. It is only logical that we have the right to defend ourselves.”“We will keep living, fighting, and most importantly, living with dignity,” he added.In his address, Zelenskyy asked leaders for an additional €70bn in financial and military support next year to counter Russia’s escalation.The request upends the bloc’s plans, which assumed last year's €90bn loan would cover both 2026 and 2027. EU leaders tasked the Commission to come up with a proposal on how to address Kyiv's financial needs.Filling the gap will be anything but easy. Soaring borrowing costs make joint debt unpalatable. The immobilised Russian assets, which Zelenskyy raised again, remain politically divisive. And bilateral contributions risk leaving the burden on a handful of wealthy countries.EU budgetOn Thursday, leaders debated the next Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) at length but, as expected, made little headway, as the “frugal” net contributors and the southern and eastern “Friends of Cohesion” dug in.One thing is clear: the negotiating box tabled by the Irish presidency just days ago, which proposed slashing €141bn from the overall budget to appease the frugal, is now officially dead.European Council President António Costa will take over the talks. He is due to present a new compromise in the coming weeks, which many expect to come before the special summit he has called for 26 November, just days before the Spanish elections.Costa is expected to pursue three main lines: keep national contributions as low as possible, rework the package of EU-wide taxes, including by drawing on European Parliament proposals, and restore the flexibility instruments the Irish presidency ruthlessly cut.That Costa would sooner or later step in was always on the cards. More worrying is that leaders on both sides now openly say they feel no pressure to close the deal by the end of the year.Seasoned negotiators know that deadlines force concessions. Member states may be playing with fire: a no-deal in December would raise the prospect of talks slipping until after an electoral season that could reshape Europe’s political landscape.MigrationMigration proved once again among the most contentious issues, after the last discussion, in June, descended into a shouting match between Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez on one side and Italy’s Giorgia Meloni and Denmark’s Mette Frederiksen on the other.This time, Rome unexpectedly extended a hand to Madrid just before the dossier reached the table on Friday. Italy and Spain reached what appears to be a first step towards ending their border dispute, after a string of tit-for-tat checks introduced in the wake of the Ceuta crisis.Italy’s temporary border controls were due to expire on Thursday evening. They were extended by a week to align with Spain’s, which expire on 22 October. The two interior ministers are due to agree on replacement measures by then.But while Meloni opened the summit in a conciliatory tone, Sánchez’s other main European nemesis, Frederiksen, did not spare her fellow social democrat over his plan to regularise the status of 600,000 migrants.“I have asked the European Commission to examine what happens when a country does almost the exact opposite of what the rest of us are doing,” Frederiksen said, referring to Spain in all but name.Meloni, Frederiksen and Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten hosted an informal breakfast before the discussion with 17 other EU leaders to explore “innovative solutions” on migration. Support is growing for emergency measures allowing asylum applications to be suspended during crises.Tensions between the migration hard-liners and Spain and France came to the fore as the Italian, Danish and Polish governments pushed to rewrite the conclusions to call for avoiding “measures that could create incentives for illegal migration.”By contrast, the final text merely urges the Commission to coordinate with the member states "on all types of instrumentalisation."ChinaOn “macroeconomic imbalances”, EU jargon for avoiding naming China, leaders held their course despite the deal between the European Commission and Beijing to curb hybrid car imports.Over lunch on Thursday, they pressed the Commission to prepare a toolbox of new trade defence instruments, including safeguards with quotas and tariffs, to shield the chemicals and machinery industries from Chinese competition.China loomed large as the bloc faces a trade deficit of about €360bn with Beijing. Chemicals and machinery, among the sectors hardest hit by cheap Chinese imports, were singled out as the next industries needing urgent protection after the hybrid car quotas.While the car quotas were negotiated with Beijing, leaders called on Thursday for unilateral safeguards to be introduced “without delay”, according to officials.The Commission presented last week’s deal as the first phase of negotiations launched in June. But time is running out: the EU’s trade deficit with China keeps widening month after month, and Chinese customs data show Chinese exports to the EU up 25% over the past year.The EU’s strategy is to keep talking as long as dialogue delivers concrete results, while strengthening its trade defences. France and Germany last week urged the Commission to develop a new instrument to respond swiftly to market disruptions caused by China, which has been accused of unfair trade practices.“The competition must be fair. We will create instruments against leveraging capacities, against high subsidies, against undervalued currencies. And there will be a toolbox for that. The toolbox will be bigger. It will also be applied as necessary,” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said.Commission President Ursula von der Leyen told leaders her institution would begin work on such a tool, though it remains unclear whether it will be ready before the end of the year.Other instruments are in the pipeline, including a diversification tool to encourage EU companies to diversify their suppliers of strategic products such as critical raw materials, and a solidarity mechanism to help member states hit by possible Chinese countermeasures.EnergyOn Thursday, leaders were dragged into an interminable discussion on energy. The Visegrád Group (V4) and Italy asked to amend the summit conclusions to call on the Commission to propose new measures to curb short-term swings in electricity prices and to reassess the proposed Emissions Trading System (ETS).The V4, Italy and, to a lesser extent, Greece led the push because they face some of Europe’s highest energy costs, a concern largely shared by other member states, which ultimately called for a coordinated European response to the ongoing energy crisis.The attempt to reopen the ETS, however, triggered an ideological backlash from Finland, Denmark and Sweden. The system makes companies pay for their emissions and encourages investment in sustainability.Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš, by contrast, lashed out at the carbon tax, accusing it of wrecking Europe’s competitiveness by fuelling soaring energy costs for the benefit of market speculators.“We’ve been engaged in a drafting exercise all day at the leaders’ level about something technical,” an EU official vented at the margins of the summit. “It’s not resulting in any new measures or new policies that actually help EU member states in their problems.”Rome and the V4 know they lack the qualified majority to reopen the EU’s carbon market rules. The aim was rather to signal to domestic audiences that they are doing what they can to contain the surge in energy prices.

title: 'Well, it worked': Elon Musk unveils new Tesla Roadster that can fly
description: Musk said the Roadster has "altitude control thrusters and main thrusters in the rear, so it can basically fly like a rocket."
content: Tech billionaire Elon Musk gave Tesla fans an up-close look at the electric vehicle maker's latest and perhaps most ambitious project on Thursday night - the long-awaited Tesla Roadster."We need an audience to prove that it's not AI or SI," Musk told the crowd at the livestreamed event. "So you guys can tell people that you saw it with your eyes. Because what you see with your eyes, you will not believe."In a dramatic demonstration, the Roadster - Tesla's only manually driven car - then drove up a towering, curved ramp, going upside down before launching off the end, flipping in mid-air, and landing safely back on the ground as the audience cheered."Well, it worked," Musk said.According to Lars Moravy, Tesla's vice president of vehicle engineering, who was presenting alongside Musk, the Roadster uses a "fan suction system" on the underside of the vehicle that he said can "pull up to 2 Gs in order to make the car go upside down.""Then we borrowed some technology from SpaceX to do the rest," he said.Musk added that the Roadster has "altitude control thrusters and main thrusters in the rear, so it can basically fly like a rocket.""It can do rolls, it can do crazy gymnastics," he said, whilst joking that it was "not necessarily a safety optimised car."A second demonstration then put that claim to the test, with the car driving up to a row of other Tesla vehicles before firing into the air and doing a "kickflip" over them.Another display showed the Roadster accelerating from 0 to 60 mph in under one second.Tesla's website shows the company is now taking reservation orders for the car, with three variants available - Performance, Thrust, and Rocket. The Rocket version is listed as invite only.The Roadster has a range of more than 300 miles and a top speed of over 230 mph (Rocket version), per Tesla.

title: Could Tesla’s flying car send sales and shares soaring?
description: Tesla revealed its next-generation Roadster on Thursday in Texas, with one of the three new versions performing a jaw-dropping kickflip and demonstrating flying capabilities. However, analysts contacted by Euronews Business do not expect the model to generate significant revenue.
content: Elon Musk, Tesla’s CEO and co-founder of SpaceX, recreated a “Knight Rider” moment, showing off his companies’ engineering capabilities with a supercar equipped with cold-gas thrusters developed using SpaceX technology.Tesla's share price increased on Friday, largely due to the hype, but while the demonstration impressed, analysts see limited commercial value in the new model.Mamta Valechha, consumer discretionary analyst at Quilter Cheviot, described it as a “headline-grabbing engineering moment” designed “to generate excitement around the brand”.Rico Luman, senior sector economist, transport and logistics, at ING, called the presentation “a publicity stunt which emphasises Tesla’s image as an innovative company, which offers brand value”, adding that cars are still about emotion and lifestyle, so the demonstration makes an impression.Gene Munster, managing partner at Deepwater Asset Management, called the demonstration on X “an engineering flex with no commercial value beyond embarrassing traditional car makers”.Valechha noted that even Elon Musk had previously played down the Roadster’s likely financial impact. “The commercial value is likely to be strengthening Tesla's innovation narrative rather than generating meaningful profits.”Musk said production is expected to start in 2028. Tesla has opened reservations, although the flying Rocket version is available by invitation only. The company has not announced final selling prices.The Roadster was unveiled in 2017, and a year later Musk suggested that thrusters might allow it to fly. This was followed by repeated delays, as the production was originally promised for 2020. "Credibility and execution risks remain high,” summarised Valechha.Could flying cars reach a wider market?The flying features of the Roadster are not approved for public road use, adding another hurdle to any ambitions of a wider roll out of the technology, on top of the high production costs.Luman said the flying car has been designed as a niche sports vehicle, but “larger scale flying car activity won’t be realistic in the foreseeable future as the same airspace rules apply as for aircraft and certification as aircraft by EASA (in Europe) is then required”.Whether the Roadster falls within aviation regulations depends on its design, capabilities and intended operation, the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) told Euronews Business.The agency said it does not comment on “specific certification applications or activities involving individual manufacturers”.However, “any vehicle intended to operate as an aircraft would need to meet the applicable aviation safety requirements”, the agency said. These could include pilot qualifications for the driver.Luman added that, on top of the complex rules that apply, airspace is already rather full, particularly with increasing drone activity.“Large numbers of uncontrolled flying cars won’t likely be allowed by authorities for safety reasons.”Valechha also sees limits to how widely the technology could be used.“Some technologies could filter into other vehicles over time, but flying or thruster-assisted features are unlikely to be economically viable for higher-volume cars in the foreseeable future due to cost, complexity and regulatory hurdles.”Luman agreed, adding that some space technology could be useful in high-end cars.“Flying cars in general may be a cheaper alternative for private jets, but not in this concept”.Pressure to turn technology into profitsLike many big tech companies, Tesla is growing, but faces pressure to turn expensive technology projects into stronger profits.The company is investing heavily in new technology, while profit growth is failing to keep pace with sales.Second-quarter revenue rose 26% year on year to $28.24bn (€25.20bn), but net profit attributable to shareholders fell about 5% to $1.11bn (€990m).First-half capital spending more than doubled to $8.28bn (€7.39bn). Tesla expects capital spending above $25bn (€22.31bn) in 2026, driven by AI and manufacturing investments.Investors have been pricing the company's value gradually lower than at the beginning of the year, when Tesla shares traded at $438, whereas on Thursday they cost more than $362, amounting to a 14.6% fall in 2026 so far.Other analysts also mentioned that Tesla valuation is largely based on its self-driving ambitions, the Optimus model, and SpaceX merger hopes.Merging SpaceX and Tesla? The technology in Tesla's Roadster, borrowed from SpaceX, fuelled expectations that the two companies are going to be merged in the future.Barclays analyst Dan Levy has suggested an announcement could come before Tesla’s annual shareholder meeting, according to Barron’s. However, a deal remains speculative, with no certainty about whether or when it would happen.For now, the Roadster’s clearest appeal may be to wealthy enthusiasts.“This new futuristic model is great for fans and lovers of gadgets who have the ability to spend the money on it. And I’m sure there are quite some around,” added Luman.

title: Portuguese journalist and writer Joaquim Letria dies
description: Joaquim Letria, regarded as one of the leading figures in Portuguese journalism, died this Friday at the age of 82.
content: Journalist and writer Joaquim Letria died this Friday, at the age of 82. The news was reported by the newspaper Observador, citing a close source.The journalist had been in a weakened condition for some time, but was not ill, according to the same source. A family source gave this account to the Lusa news agency.Born in Lisbon in 1943, Joaquim Letria is regarded as one of the leading figures in Portuguese journalism. He founded the weekly newspapers O Jornal and Tal & Qual and also served as deputy news director for Non-Daily Programmes at RTP in the years following the 25 April revolution. He was also elected president of the Journalists' Union.He began his career as a journalist in 1963 at the newspaper Diário de Lisboa and went on to build an international career, first at the news agency The Associated Press and later as a correspondent for Deutsche-Presse Agentur, until 1970. Letria also worked for the BBC in London.He was known for the many facets of his professional life, having been the author and presenter of several radio and television programmes. He received the Press Prize in the Television category in 1974.An author, recognised for his many technical books on journalism and for the title "A Verdade Confiscada", published in 1998, he also taught for more than 20 years at the Higher School of Journalism in Porto, at Universidade Independente and Universidade Autónoma de Lisboa, as well as at the Higher Institute for Information and Administration Sciences (ISCIA) in Aveiro.He was a member of the Portuguese Communist Party until 1968 and later served as spokesperson for the then president of the republic, Ramalho Eanes, until 1986.The Minister for Culture, Youth and Sport, Margarida Balseiro Lopes, expressed her sorrow at the journalist's death, describing him as "one of the most prominent figures in post-25 April journalism".

title: From Samarkand to Paris: Preserving Central Asia's scientific heritage
description: From the scholars of the Silk Roads to new research institutions in Tashkent, Uzbekistan is seeking to make its historical legacy more accessible. Experts meeting at UNESCO headquarters in Paris examined its contribution to world civilisation and the value of shared cultural knowledge.
content: For centuries, Central Asia was a crossroads of scientific discovery, scholarship and cultural exchange. Its historic cities, including Samarkand and Bukhara, developed into important centres of learning, connecting intellectual traditions across the Silk Roads and contributing to advances in mathematics, astronomy, medicine and religious thought.Today, Uzbekistan is seeking to make that legacy more accessible internationally through research institutions, museum collections, digital technologies and academic cooperation.These efforts were explored at an international conference held at UNESCO headquarters in Paris, bringing together more than 300 participants, including scholars, diplomats and representatives of international organisations, according to the organisers.The event was organised by the Islamic Civilization Center in Uzbekistan, alongside the country's Permanent Delegation and National Commission for UNESCO, its foreign ministry and several scientific and cultural institutions.The initiative has its roots in a broader effort outlined by Uzbekistan's President Shavkat Mirziyoyev at the UN General Assembly in 2017, when he called for greater international recognition of Central Asia's intellectual heritage and emphasised the importance of education and religious tolerance.In a further address to the UN in September 2025, he proposed presenting the scientific and spiritual legacy of the region's leading scholars at major international venues. The Paris conference, alongside presentations at UN venues in New York and Geneva, formed part of that programme.Central Asia's intellectual legacyMuch of the discussion focused on Mawarannahr, historically known as Transoxiana, the region between the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers, encompassing much of present-day Uzbekistan and parts of neighbouring Central Asian countries.The region produced or attracted scholars whose work influenced intellectual traditions across the Islamic world and beyond.In an address reported by the Islamic Civilization Center, Mahmud Erol Kılıç, Director General of the Research Centre for Islamic History, Art and Culture (IRCICA), highlighted the contributions of Al-Khwarizmi, Al-Farabi, Ibn Sina and Al-Biruni.Their work reflected a scholarly tradition in which mathematics, medicine, philosophy and religious studies developed through exchanges of knowledge across different regions.Farhan Ahmad Nizami, Director of the Oxford Centre for Islamic Studies, also stressed that the region's historical monuments reflect a broader history of creativity and cultural exchange."Civilisations are not growing in isolation. We cross-fertilise each other, and it is a message that we need to share to see that we have much more in common than elements that separate us," Salima Dalibey, representing the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, told Euronews.Mehrdad Shabahang, head of UNESCO's Silk Roads Programme, highlighted the role of research institutions in documenting that shared history."These centres like the Uzbekistan Islamic Civilisation Center can help us to identify, to document and also to promote our shared past, our shared history," he said.Firdavs Abdukhalikov, director of the Islamic Civilization Center, also emphasised the international significance of this legacy."Cultural heritage and our great ancestors belong to the whole world," he told Euronews.Beyond the museumA central part of this effort is the Islamic Civilization Center in Tashkent, whose museum exhibitions trace more than 3,000 years of history on the territory of present-day Uzbekistan, according to the Center.Its activities include the study of rare manuscripts and historical artefacts, alongside digital technologies designed to support research and make collections accessible to a broader audience.Abdukhalikov emphasised that its purpose extends beyond displaying historical objects."It is not just a beautiful, large building and museum. It is a major platform for scholarship and education," he told Euronews.Frédérique Beaupertuis-Bressand, a specialist in the history and art of the Timurids, described the museum as a valuable resource for researchers and visitors."Finally, culture is being given the prominence it deserves. We can see these objects, touch them, and study them," she said, adding that access to collections offers further opportunities for historical research.The Center is also connected to a wider network of specialised institutions, including international research centres dedicated to Imam Bukhari, Imam Termizi and Imam Maturidi.Sali Shahsivari, managing director of the Al-Furqan Islamic Heritage Foundation, welcomed the expansion of these institutions, saying they were helping to bring greater attention to the region's cultural heritage.The discussions in Paris also explored opportunities for international research cooperation, including joint studies, the digitisation of historical sources and closer collaboration between academic institutions. The Center also highlighted its use of digital technologies and artificial intelligence in researching and presenting cultural heritage.The discussions also considered how a better understanding of shared cultural heritage could contribute to dialogue between different societies."We live in a time where hate speech spreads very fast, so these opportunities to sit, speak, exchange ideas and dialogue help people understand each other and prepare for a culture of peace," Salima Dalibey of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation told Euronews.

title: Inside Qatar’s Geekend where gamers, cosplayers and artists share their love of games, comics and anime
description: From anime costumes to locally designed board games, Geekend brings Qatar’s pop-culture fans together, with artists selling their work and gamers meeting face to face.
content: Organised by Doha Film Institute, Geekend is a gathering for gamers, artists and pop-culture fans. This edition puts a greater focus on art, with stalls where artists can show and sell their work.Geekend is part of the institute’s Geekdom programme. Its founder, Abdulla Al Mosallam, says artists, writers and animators have met at these gatherings and gone on to work together on new projects.In the board-game area, Abdulrahman Al-Homaid, founder of Majlis Shabab, demonstrates his company’s version of Dama, a traditional game given a new design. His team also develops original games, with the aim of getting people talking and playing around the same table.For Khalifa Al-Haroun, founder of gaming retailer Store974, meeting in person gives fans a chance to make friends and discover others who share their interests. He also points to the artists selling everything from posters to small handmade items.Cosplayers arrive dressed as their favourite characters, including figures from Japanese anime. At the Japanese embassy’s booth, visitors try on kimonos and discover more about the culture behind many of the stories and games they enjoy.

title: ‘Subsidising suicide’: UN chief urges governments to stop propping up polluting fossil fuels
description: Fossil fuels are 'boiling our planet', says Guterres. Yet COP31 hosts Türkiye and Australia are expanding them, a new report shows.
content: "Subsidising fossil fuels is subsidising suicide," UN chief Antonio Guterres told leaders today (16 October) ahead of next week's UN biodiversity summit, COP17.At an event in Yerevan, Armenia, Guterres said governments were still "spending money on the wrong things" and singled out incentives for fossil fuels.He urged countries to stop subsidising the production of fossil fuels that are "boiling our planet and are the scourge of biodiversity"."I urge governments everywhere to end these handouts once and for all, and to use the savings for people and planet instead," he said.EU finance ministers earlier this month called for a phaseout of fossil fuel subsidies at the COP31 climate negotiations taking place in November.Slow progress on pulling funding for nature-harming activitiesNations have made little headway since pledging in 2022 to reduce public spending on activities that harm nature such as mining, fossil fuel extraction and intensive farming.Countries have vowed to reduce harmful subsidies by $500 billion (€447b) a year by 2030 but little progress has been made."Nature won't thrive on good intentions," Guterres said.The United Nations says that for every dollar invested in protecting or restoring nature, about $30 (€27) still goes into activities that degrade it.This includes an estimated $2.6 trillion (€2.3t) a year in public subsidies that negatively impact nature and the climate.Nearly 200 nations are participating in the UN biodiversity negotiations in Yerevan starting on 19 October where a lack of finance for nature will be a core focus.Guterres launched a report on 15 October showing that the world was off track to achieving the 2030 biodiversity targets enshrined in a landmark pact dubbed the Paris Agreement for Nature."The war on nature has not yet ended," he said.What is the Paris Agreement for Nature?Signed by nearly 200 countries and territories, the nature pact laid out 23 targets for halting and reversing nature loss by 2030. These included reducing pollution, protecting threatened species and conserving 30 per cent of the world's land and oceans, known as 30x30."It's not all bad news... There is progress, but not enough," Guterres told reporters in Yerevan. "We are far from what is necessary."The report showed that government policies were insufficient to meet the centrepiece 30x30 biodiversity goal. Taken together, government pledges would cover only 27 per cent of land and inland waters by the end of this decade if enacted in full. For oceans, the figure would be just 12 per cent.Other targets were lagging further behind. Guterres said countries must honour their financial pledges to developing countries.The lack of finance has been identified as a particular barrier to achieving the biodiversity goals."Biodiversity is in crisis. Species are disappearing and ecosystems are collapsing," said Sue Lieberman from the Wildlife Conservation Society."Governments and all stakeholders must see that investing in nature is not a luxury, it is the very key to our survival."He also emphasised tackling government spending that harms nature, pointing to the "very strong influence" of some sectors that had "too much power" over government including industrial fishing, fossil fuels and logging operations.COP31 hosts ramp up fossil fuel productionA Global Witness report released this week reveals the power of that influence.Using data from independent energy consultancy Rystad, the environmental NGO's investigation found that the two COP31 hosts Türkiye and Australia are ramping up fossil fuel production ahead of the major international climate negotiations taking place next month.Turkish national oil firm TPAO is set to nearly triple gas production. Two of Australia's biggest fossil fuel firms are also on course to hike oil and gas production: Woodside are set to double liquefied natural gas production by 2032 while Santos is on course to increase crude oil production eight-fold by 2035, according to the report.Türkiye has come under scrutiny for its centrepiece COP31 electrification target. While it aims to raise the global share of energy demand by electricity to 35 per cent, up from around 20 per cent, by 2035, it stops short of specifying how the electricity should be generated.
