This, critics say, could allow governments to count expanded gas-fired generation as progress towards electrification targetsEfforts to reach a global consensus on setting concrete targets or pathways for phasing out fossil fuels have stalled and the contentious issue is not an official item in the COP31 negotiations.Earlier his year, about 60 nations demanding faster action on fossil fuels staged their own breakaway conference outside the United Nations process.Separately from the COP talks, which operate on a consensus-based decision-making process, some countries – including Germany, France and the Netherlands – have released voluntary roadmaps away from fossil fuels. Brazil is expected to follow suit in November.

title: These are the most underrated travel destinations in Europe
description: A little known region in Romania – Bucovina – topped the list for 2027 in a new ranking of underrated travel destinations by Time Out.
content: Major tourist destinations like Venice or Barcelona are popular for a reason, but when our love for certain cities is negatively impacting the locals who made it great in the first place, it’s time for a rethink.The world is a big ol’ place, and there are plenty of lesser-known spots crying out for more visitors. Plus, you’ll have a far better time without having to constantly battle crowds.Which is where Time Out’s list of the world’s most underrated travel destinations comes in. Updated annually, the latest ranking has 41 cities and regions on it – and this year’s number one spot is in Europe.Romania’s Bucovina topped the list for 2027, with Time Out drawing a comparison to the better known Translyvania, saying the region has “the same wild mountain scenery, age-old traditions and mind-boggling architecture”, but without the crowds.Bucovina has been growing in popularity in recent years as the gateway to Via Transilvanica, the 1,400 km-long hiking trail that our writer Rebecca Ann Hughes took on earlier this year.Europe’s most underrated travel destinationsThe next highest-rated underrated travel destinations in Europe are Spain’s Asturian cities, which placed third.Coastal spots here have already proven popular, but Time Out suggests heading to cities like Oviedo, Gijón and Avilés, particularly if you’re a foodie.If you’re looking for a crowd-free beach escape, look no further than Zambujeira do Mar, which ranked sixth overall. The cliffside town in Portugal’s Alentejo region is home to a Blue Flag-listed beach, and with the exception of the weekend of the MEO Sudoeste music festival, you won’t find many other tourists here.Placing ninth overall is Carry-le-Rouet in France. The magazine compared the seaside resort to more popular spots like St. Tropez and Cannes, declaring it to be “just as idyllic with sea-to-cliff landscapes, turquoise waters and fresh seafood at a fraction of the cost”.Just outside of the top 10, The Azores ranked 12th overall. The remote Portuguese archipelago has been attracting more attention in recent years, having been dubbed the “Hawaii of Europe”, but it has been working to ensure its tourism develops sustainably.A destination certified by the Global Sustainable Tourism Council, there are numerous policies in place to protect the nine islands’ cultural, historical and natural assets.The top 10 most underrated spots globallyBucovina, RomaniaSouth Dakota, USAsturian cities, SpainOsa Peninsula, Costa RicaSan Martín, PeruZambujeira do Mar, PortugalBisbee, Arizona, USShenzhen, ChinaCarry-le-Rouet, FranceTioga Pass, California, US

title: These are Europe’s best party cities for a Halloween night out, according to a new ranking
description: From Edinburgh’s fiery Samhuinn festival to Dublin’s Gothic celebrations, Europe has plenty of ways to get into the Halloween spirit.
content: Halloween falling on a Saturday in 2026 means plenty of us will be keen to make the most of the spooky holiday, even travelling abroad to celebrate it. Now, a new ranking has revealed the best party places to experience All Hallows' Eve across the globe. Travel experts at Adventure360 analysed some 113 cities worldwide to uncover where travellers can find the biggest Halloween celebrations this year.Each individual city was scored on the number of Halloween events happening between 30 October and 1 November, as well as the size of its nightlife offering and late-night restaurant scene.The safety of the city was examined, too, and the report noted whether or not the destination hosts a signature Halloween or Day of the Dead event. In the end, each city was given a score out of 100. In first place was New York, with a score of 91.1 out of 100, and it was followed by another US city, Chicago, which got a score of 80.1. In terms of countries, the US had the most showings in the top 10, with New Orleans coming in at number nine but, continent-wise, Europe was revealed to be far and away the best Halloween destination, with five spots on the list. Edinburgh is in third place, thanks in part to its legendary Samhuinn Fire festival, while Dublin follows close behind, partially because of its Bram Stoker festival. Madrid, London and Prague also feature in the top 10, despite none of them actually offering a signature Halloween event; they’re just that spooky!Within the Halloween top 20, other European cities included Rome, Berlin, Amsterdam, Barcelona, Budapest, and LisbonThe world's best Halloween party cities 2026 How the cities rank out of a score of 100, according to the Adventure360 study: 1. New York, USA – 91.1/1002. Chicago, USA – 80.1/1003. Edinburgh, UK – 79.2/1004. Dublin, Ireland – 73.0/1005. Tokyo, Japan – 72.3/1006. Mexico City, Mexico – 71.8/1007. Madrid, Spain – 70.7/1008. London, UK – 69.6/1009. New Orleans, USA – 69.2/10010. Prague, Czechia – 69.0/10011. Rome, Italy – 68.6/10012. Berlin, Germany – 67.4/10013. Amsterdam, Netherlands – 66.7/10014. Osaka, Japan – 66.4/10015. Barcelona, Spain – 65.6/10016. Washington D.C., USA – 65.5/10017. Dubai, UAE – 65.4/10018. Budapest, Hungary – 65.4/10019. Sydney, Australia – 64.3/10020. Lisbon, Portugal – 64.1/100Europe’s top five cities for Halloween partiesFollowing the ranking, these are the five best cities to spend Halloween in Europe this year – and the reasons why. Edinburgh, United KingdomScotland’s capital Edinburgh may only have a relatively small number of nightlife venues and late-night restaurants, but it boasts plenty of Halloween-themed events, not least the Samhuinn Fire festival. The event brings a dramatic twist to Halloween, with Calton Hill transformed by fire, drumming, acrobatics and elaborate costumes. Taking place on 31 October, the event reimagines ancient Celtic traditions marking the end of summer and the arrival of winter, with performers acting out the battle between the Summer King and Winter Queen.Dublin, IrelandDublin has just seven Halloween-themed events – one of the lowest amounts in the top 10 – but it makes up for it with its legendary Bram Stoker festival. This year, the celebration of the city’s Gothic heritage will take place from 23-26 October, with four days of spooky events inspired by the author of Dracula. Expect haunted walking tours, horror theatre, candlelit library visits and a spectacular parade. There’s family-friendly fun, too, including Stokerland, a free gothic-themed park at St Patrick’s Park.Madrid, SpainMadrid may not have one big signature Halloween celebration, but there’s plenty to get stuck into. For a dose of horror, head to MADHORROR at IFEMA Madrid, running from 30 October to 2 November, with haunted houses, horror films, gaming and comic-book events. After dark, join a ghost and legends walking tour through the old town, or head to Malasaña for costume parties and late-night drinks and eats. London, United KingdomAlthough England’s capital doesn’t have a signature Halloween event, it does have some 22 themed happenings, as well as more than 1,000 nightlife venues and 2,600 late-night restaurants, which is the highest number in the top 10. Head to Kew Gardens for its illuminated Halloween trail, featuring Dracula’s Lair, live performers and a Headless Horseman, or explore the capital’s darker history on a Jack the Ripper walking tour. For something quirky, the London Transport Museum is holding a Halloween silent disco among its historic trains and buses.Prague, CzechiaPrague’s Gothic streets make a fitting backdrop for Halloween, with plenty of ways to get into the spooky spirit. While the Czech capital doesn’t have a signature event, Wonderland Halloween takes over the historic Lucerna Great Hall on 30 October for a night of elaborate costumes, live performances, DJs and theatrical decorations. For something more low-key, join a ghost tour through the Old Town’s narrow lanes and medieval underground passages, where guides share tales of murder, alchemy and restless spirits. On 30 October and on Halloween night itself, the legendary five-floor nightclub Karlovy Lázně will play host to its annual Wicked Weekend event.

title: OpenAI tries to solve mathematician backlash problem by pledging $5 million to math foundation
description: “Mathematicians did not ask for this work to be done,” said the Association for Human Mathematics.
content: After causing an uproar among mathematicians, ChatGPT maker OpenAI is donating millions of dollars to a maths foundation. The move comes days after the Association for Human Mathematics (AHM) slammed the artificial intelligence company and alleged plagiarism for solving a decades-old math problem. In September, OpenAI said an unreleased AI model had cracked a major result on the Navier-Stokes equations, which apply Newton’s second law of motion to fluids, a problem that has stumped mathematicians for almost a century.But, according to TechCrunch, two human mathematicians say they were close to a similar result, and they question whether OpenAI’s work drew on theirs. OpenAI denies seeing their work. One of the mathematicians, Levent Alpöge, works at Anthropic and was collaborating in a private capacity.The Sam Altman-led company said on October 6 the model had published more than 700 manuscripts and produced almost 400 other mathematical results, which aimed to tackle some of the most complex questions in maths and computer science, according to OpenAI. AHM said “Mathematicians did not ask for this work to be done,” adding that OpenAI had a “total disregard for the norms of scientific research”.On Thursday, OpenAI announced on social media site X that it would make a $5 million donation to the maths-focused Simons Foundation, intended to “help mathematicians examine, understand, and build on results produced by AI”.“We want to support the mathematics community in turning progress in AI into deeper human understanding and new discoveries,” OpenAI said in a post on X.“To support that goal, we are contributing $5 million (€4.5mn) to a new Simons Foundation initiative to help mathematicians examine, understand, and build on results produced by AI, including the results we recently published.”The money will pay for “workshops, conferences, and special programs,” OpenAI said. “We will also provide access to our models and computing resources to Simons Foundation-supported researchers.”The initiative totals $15 million in combined funding and resources from the Simons Foundation, Anthropic and OpenAI.

title: Fed’s Warsh sees AI boosting productivity but gives no signal on next rate hike
description: US Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh said in Bangkok on Friday that the global economy has proved surprisingly resilient and called AI the most consequential change of his lifetime, but gave no hint on interest rates ahead of the Fed’s meeting this month.
content: The global economy has held up better than Kevin Warsh would have predicted earlier this year, the US central bank chief said on Friday, calling AI the biggest economic shift he had seen.Speaking in Bangkok at the annual meetings of the IMF and the World Bank, Warsh offered no clue on the Federal Reserve’s next rate decision, due on 28 October.Almost everywhere, the economy is showing a resilience "I’m not sure I would have predicted five or six months ago," Warsh said in a discussion on stage with IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva.The Fed chair was most upbeat about the US, stating during the event that a broadening investment surge that "isn’t just AI" had given the economy "plenty of tailwinds", momentum "certainly not found everywhere in the world".Energy prices have soared since the US and Israel went to war with Iran in late February. This, along with an AI investment boom, has fuelled inflation in many economies, forcing central banks to raise rates.The Fed, which has seen inflation run above its 2% target for over five years, raised rates by a quarter point to 3.75-4% in September, its first hike since July 2023."At the Federal Reserve, we made very clear that we would deliver price stability," argued Warsh, who took over as chair in May.He said he had heard the same "resolve" from central bankers in Bangkok, calling the wave of rate hikes, including two by the European Central Bank, a "synchronous tightening" that leaves "no free riders".The IMF on Tuesday nudged up its 2026 global growth forecast to 3.1% but said risks were tilted to the downside. Rich countries also face soaring borrowing costs, with the 10-year US bond yield above 5% and the French bond yield trading around 4.8% at the time of writing.A 'bumpy' road for AIMuch of Friday's discussion focused on AI, which Warsh said was "probably the most consequential change" for the US and global economies in his lifetime.Before taking office, he had argued that an AI-driven productivity boom could curb inflation and make room for lower interest rates. On Friday, he acknowledged that for now, the investment frenzy was pushing prices up by fuelling demand.Minutes of the Fed's September meeting noted that data centre construction had driven up the cost of chips, computer equipment and electrical components.However, over time, Warsh expects AI to boost the economy’s capacity to produce, bringing a "huge benefit" at home and abroad.He also expects it to change central banking as "we torture data with old-fashioned models," he said. "Not so long from now, it won’t be torture."Despite the optimism, the Fed chair also warned that the road ahead was "likely to be a very bumpy one", both in understanding the technology and because "we really don’t know what the market structure is going to be".Eyes on the next Federal Reserve meetingWarsh, who has promised fewer hints about where policy is heading, kept to that pledge."I don’t prejudge meetings," he said, though he noted the world had "broadly conformed" to the Fed’s expectations since September.US consumer price inflation rose to 3.7% in September from 3.4% as petrol prices surged, though core inflation, which excludes food and energy, was 2.6%.Wholesale prices rose 6.3% year on year, the most since 2022, while the economy added just 29,000 jobs last month.Bets on an October hike have swung this week, jumping from about 22% to around 50% after Wednesday’s inflation figures before falling back to about 30%, according to CME FedWatch, a tool that tracks market pricing.Markets currently put the chance of a December hike at around 90%, while the September minutes showed that most Fed officials expect another hike this year.New York Fed President John Williams, vice chair of the Fed’s committee, told Bloomberg on Tuesday that "it may be appropriate to have one more rate hike", but saw no need for more in 2027.On the other hand, Fed Governor Michelle Bowman said at the Bangkok meetings on Wednesday that she felt no urgency to act.The decision comes days before the 3 November US midterm elections.September’s hike defied US President Donald Trump’s demands for lower rates, though he still backs Warsh, his pick for the job.Friday’s remarks were among Warsh’s last before the Fed’s quiet period, which starts on Saturday and bars officials from discussing policy until after the meeting. Investors will next hear from him at his press conference after the decision.

title: Dinosaur fossil hidden in London’s Natural History Museum for 100 years identified as new species
description: The 120-million-year-old skull fragment belongs to Europe’s first known megaraptoran, a predator featuring powerful arms and sharp claws.
content: A dinosaur fossil that spent almost a century in the collections of London’s Natural History Museum has been identified as a new species.The skull fragment belonged to Invictibellatrix amberina, a previously unknown carnivorous dinosaur that lived around 120 million years ago. It’s also the first confirmed evidence of a megaraptoran dinosaur in Europe.The fossil was originally discovered at the foot of a cliff on the southwest coast of the Isle of Wight by amateur fossil hunter Reginald Walter Tooley. After his death in 1924, the Natural History Museum acquired more than 1,000 specimens from his collection, including the fragment.Although scientists knew it belonged to a dinosaur, exactly which one remained a mystery for decades.Now, researchers have taken another look at the fossil using CT scanning technology, allowing them to examine its internal structure and create a 3D model. Their full findings were published in the journal Royal Society Open Science."More dangerous than a T.rex"Professor Paul Barrett, the study’s senior author from the Natural History Museum, says, "Despite over 200 years of collecting, the Isle of Wight continues to surprise us with new dinosaur species, and finds of carnivorous dinosaurs, such as Invictibellatrix, have been particularly elusive.""Work like this shows the exceptional value of working with historical museum collections where there are still many discoveries to be made," he added.Despite their name, megaraptorans were not the small, bird-like dinosaurs we commonly associate with the word "raptor". They were larger predators, more closely related to tyrannosaurs, with "slender heads", "large arms" and "giant curved claws", according to the Natural History Museum.Invictibellatrix amberina is estimated to have measured between 3 and 4 metres (10 and 13 feet) in length and stood around 1.5 metres (5 feet) tall. It lived during the Early Cretaceous period, when dinosaurs dominated terrestrial ecosystems.Researchers have also suggested that it may have had feathers, although its exact appearance still remains uncertain.According to Dr Cassius Morrison, a researcher at the University College London's (UCL) Earth Sciences department, the species would have eaten small dinosaurs, lizards and mammals - similar to the role in the food chain a hyena holds today."It was not the apex predator of its time, but for humans this dinosaur would have been more dangerous than a T. rex. We would have been perfectly sized prey, about a third of their body weight. They definitely would have chased us. A T. rex would not have bothered, as we would have been too small," explains Dr Cassius Morrison, who led the study.The discovery is particularly exciting because megaraptorans have previously been identified in Asia, Australia and South America, but never conclusively in Europe.

title: Grand Voyager | Exploring Berlin beyond the landmarks
description: Berlin is a city filled with history, creativity and energy, from street art on the Berlin Wall to cycling through its leafy streets. In this episode, Lilly Douse discovers what brings Germany’s capital to life.
content: Berlin welcomed over 12 million guests in 2025 and recorded almost 30 million overnight stays. Many visitors come for the famous landmarks, but hidden among them are distinctive areas with plenty to explore.Lilly begins her Berlin journey at the Brandenburg Gate. Built in 1791, it has stood in the heart of some of the most important moments in the city’s history. Together with a local guide, she sets out to discover some of Berlins best know landmarks and the stories behind them.Few have shaped the city recent history more than the Berlin Wall. Constructed in 1961 and brought down in 1989, it divided the city for 28 years. Today, a long stretch of the wall remains, covered in graffiti and street art.Inspired by Berlin's creativity, Lilly joins a graffiti workshop to learn more about the city’s street art culture. There, she meets Hendrik auf der Heidt, founder of Urban Artists, who gives her tips on creating effective street art.In West Berlin, the Wilmina Hotel, a former women’s prison, offers guests the chance to stay in an unusual historic building. With iron window bars and long corridors, the former world war two prison took 10 years to renovate.Cycling with Sascha Möllering of Berlin by Bike, Lilly visits Mauerpark, a green space with a divided history. Their route continues to Zionskirche, a Christian church closely linked to East Germany’s communist past.For visitors wandering through Berlin on foot, by boat or by bike, there is always something unique to experience.

title: Military signals building: Is the US-Iran war about to escalate?
description: Two US aircraft carriers are in the Arabian Sea, tanker sorties over the region are running 50% above September’s rate and Trump has not ruled out intensified strikes after November’s midterm elections.
content: Iran targeted at least 24 commercial vessels near the Strait of Hormuz in a two-week period, the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) said on Thursday, as two US aircraft carriers operate in the Arabian Sea and officials on both sides issue public warnings of a possible return to large-scale hostilities.Britain's Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO), a Royal Navy body that monitors merchant shipping safety, reported at least seven further incidents between Monday and Wednesday.The Washington-based think tank said the attacks show Iran still retains the ability to target shipping despite US strikes on its military infrastructure, and cited a US military official as saying Iranian naval forces have adapted by using small boats and spotters to identify vessels after significant damage to their radar systems.In Tehran, senior military officials have issued warnings in recent days. Major General Mostafa Izadi, deputy commander of the IRGC, said on Thursday that Iran "is advancing with strength and is ready to carry out the most powerful operations."Guards spokesman Hossein Mohibi said on Wednesday that a new war against Iran "would be irrational for the United States" but that "the possibility of such a conflict absolutely exists."Iranian army commander-in-chief Amir Hatami said the armed forces were ready for "any battle" and warned that any attack on Iranian infrastructure would bring proportional strikes on Israeli and allied targets.Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, told Press TV on Sunday that US targets including data centres and AI infrastructure would be "within range" if hostilities resumed, and described Washington's latest diplomatic response as insufficient.Washington increases naval presenceThe US Naval Institute confirmed on Tuesday that the aircraft carriers George Washington and George HW Bush are operating in the Arabian Sea.The HW Bush returned to the region after a port visit to Thailand's Phuket. The George Washington had previously relieved the carrier Abraham Lincoln.Their simultaneous presence is significant, though it does not by itself signal an imminent operation given the regular cycle of carrier rotations.US Central Command (CENTCOM) has published images of an F-15E being refuelled mid-air by a KC-135 over the Middle East, flight operations from the George Washington, and an F-35B taking off from the amphibious assault ship Boxer.CENTCOM also said US forces had altered the routes of 130 commercial vessels under the naval blockade of Iran as of 5 October. That figure comes solely from the US military and has not been independently verified.US President Donald Trump said in an interview earlier this month that intensifying air strikes against Iran after the US midterm elections on 3 November was possible, although he declined to detail any military plans.Asked about reports that his administration was considering renewed use of the GBU-43/B — the Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb, known as the "mother of all bombs" — Trump did not dismiss the idea, saying it "is not nuclear; it is simply a very large bomb."He also said future nuclear disarmament talks with Iran involving Russia and China were a possibility.Specialist flight-tracking account IntelSky reported on Wednesday that US Air Force tanker sorties over the region in the first 14 days of October were running at roughly 50% above the daily rate recorded in September.The account reported a similar increase in transport aircraft activity. IntelSky's figures have not been independently verified as publicly available tracking systems do not capture all military aviation, and changes in radar coverage can affect such comparisons.On 1 October, reports claimed that the US military was sending around 9,000 troops and sailors to the region with the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group and the amphibious ready group centred on the Makin Island.A US official told AP on condition of anonymity that the deployment could bring the total number of American sailors and Marines in the region above 20,000. As of Wednesday, the Theodore Roosevelt had not yet reached the Arabian Sea, according to the Naval Institute.Israel's Channel 12 reported on Thursday citing security sources that Western countries had detected new and unusual military movements inside Iran, but that current events did not necessarily require immediate military action.The channel also reported that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio had spoken about the latest developments.

title: A kite-powered snow sled designed in Spain is gliding across Antarctica in world-first
description: Explorer Ramón Larramendi will lead an 80-day, 3,400 km South Pole expedition in a kite-powered vehicle that can travel up to 80kph.
content: Spanish polar explorer Ramón Larramendi will lead a scientific expedition that will travel around 3,400 kilometres across the interior of Antarctica over roughly 80 days, without using fossil fuels for transport.The Antarctic Wind Sled 2026-2027 project will carry equipment to conduct 16 research projects in some of the most inaccessible regions on the planet, with the aim of expanding knowledge of ice, climate change and polar ecosystems."The wind sled is something completely unique in the world," Larramendi tells Euronews during an interview in Madrid's central Plaza de España. The explorer believes that the vehicle he has designed is an exceptional combination of traditional techniques and advanced technology, conceived to cover long distances without combustion engines or air drops.The expedition will leave Spain on 18 October and is due to return in early February. The route will start near Russia's Novolazarevskaya base, in Queen Maud Land, and end at the French-Italian Concordia station at Dome C, after crossing the Pole of Inaccessibility and passing close to the Pole of Cold.A wind-powered vehicle to cross Antarctica with zero emissionsThe Wind Sled is a polar exploration platform that uses kites to harness the power of the wind and solar energy to fuel scientific equipment. Its design, inspired by Inuit culture, as Larramendi explains, is the result of some 25 years of development and experimentation, during which the explorer has travelled more than 28,000 kilometres over ice on different expeditions."This sled combines Inuit techniques, which can look like old-fashioned and slightly strange bits of technology. That makes it a very, very unusual mix, but hugely efficient," says the explorer, who sees sustainability as one of the fundamental pillars of the project.The vehicle consists of four modules and is 15 metres long. It can carry up to 2,100 kg of cargo, although on this occasion it will initially transport around 250 kg of scientific instruments.The crew will have 20 kites, with sail areas ranging from five to 150 square metres, which they will deploy according to the weather conditions. In favourable conditions, the sled can reach 80 kilometres per hour, with an average speed of around 25 kilometres per hour.The absence of fossil fuels reduces both the environmental impact and the logistical needs of the expedition. By way of comparison, the 2011-2012 Scientific Transantarctic Expedition covered a similar distance using tracked trucks, snowmobiles and sleds, consuming around 170,000 litres of fuel in two months.Larramendi hopes this campaign will showcase the vehicle's potential as a scientific platform for future crossings. "Other systems powered by renewable energy may emerge to cross Antarctica, but none will be more sustainable and have a lower impact than the Wind Sled," he argues.Sixteen projects to study ice, pollutants and microbial lifeThe expedition will carry out 16 scientific projects selected through a call coordinated by the Spanish Polar Committee. The research, involving CSIC, CIEMAT, INTA, six Spanish universities and international bodies, will provide direct measurements in areas where data is scarce, complementing information gathered by satellites and permanent stations.Among the projects is a study by NASA's Ames Research Center, led by Spaniard Alfonso Dávila, which will examine whether conditions favourable to microbial life can exist inside salt rocks exposed to Antarctica's extreme cold. Sensors will measure temperature, relative humidity and electrical conductivity to determine whether liquid water may have formed inside them, despite the low temperatures and the arid environment.Another project, called Dinglac and led by glaciologist Francisco Navarro of the Polytechnic University of Madrid, will use ground-penetrating radar to analyse the top 10 metres of snow. The measurements will help to understand how snow layers accumulate and move and to improve estimates of how Antarctic ice mass is evolving in the context of climate change.The campaign will also study the presence of microplastics, persistent pollutants and possible microorganisms and viruses, as well as investigating the Earth's magnetism and the performance of the European Galileo navigation systems. Some of the experiments will use instrumentation linked to space exploration.For Larramendi, the value of this work also lies in the fact that it will be carried out in territory that is virtually unknown from a scientific point of view. "It is taking place in an area for which there are practically no data," he explains. The system makes it possible to venture into regions where the difficulties and costs of conventional operations mean research campaigns are especially complex.Four people isolated for 85 days: An experiment for future space missionsThe expedition will be made up of four Antarctic veterans: Larramendi himself; Hilo Moreno, polar guide and mountain technician; Mariusz Potocki, a researcher at the University of Maine in the United States; and Javier Selva, photographer, documentary-maker and head of technical image direction. Selva already accompanied Larramendi on an Antarctic expedition between 2011 and 2012.As well as taking part in fieldwork, the four explorers will themselves be study subjects. The WindSled Mind project, led by Gabriel G. de la Torre from the University of Cádiz, will analyse the effects of prolonged isolation on the crew's psychological responses, sleep and social interaction. "We are part of the research project and yes, we do feel a bit like guinea pigs, but we are happy," Larramendi says with a smile.The study aims to generate knowledge applicable to future long-duration space missions, in which astronauts will have to face conditions of confinement, danger and extreme remoteness from Earth. Antarctica is one of the most suitable environments on the planet for studying these factors and testing instruments intended for future planetary exploration."We are the experiment ourselves. Four people isolated for 85 days in the interior of the Antarctic continent," Larramendi notes. The explorer explains that there are two projects in which the members of the expedition themselves are the object of research.Self-sufficiency will be one of the keys to the journey. The team will carry the supplies and equipment needed to remain for weeks without external support, although they have an evacuation plan in place in case of a medical emergency or any other extraordinary situation.An unprecedented route with an eye on future expeditionsThe crossing, which can be followed live on the Trineo de Viento website, is the culmination of decades of development of the Wind Sled and will test its ability to carry a scientific payload unprecedented in Larramendi's Antarctic expeditions. The four members will set up five scientific stations along the route, with extended stops to collect samples, carry out experiments and take measurements.On arrival at Concordia, the explorers will leave the continent by air, while the scientific material will return to Spain with French support. The sled will remain dismantled at the base, ready for a possible future journey in the opposite direction.The aim is for expeditions to be repeated so that data gathered in different campaigns can be compared, something essential for identifying changes in ice and climate. "Repeated data collection is absolutely key to tracking variations," Larramendi stresses.The journey, integrated into the XL Antarctic Research Campaign, which marks the 40th anniversary of the Spanish polar expedition, thus aims to consolidate a low environmental impact route for scientific exploration into the interior of the continent. It offers an alternative that combines research in one of the most extreme regions on Earth with the development of technologies that could contribute to future space missions.

title: Europe's answer to Starlink: Who is building IRIS² and what is Germany's role
description: Who controls the satellites on which armies rely? Reports of Starlink limits in Ukraine highlight the question. The EU is building IRIS², a 348-satellite network with a Bremen manufacturer.
content: This week, the Ukrainian army reported restrictions to the Starlink satellite service. The connection drops as soon as the receivers are travelling at more than 160 kilometres per hour, as is the case with drones.The service was initially partially restored, but an upper limit remained in place. It is unclear who ordered the restriction.SpaceX boss Elon Musk rejected responsibility that the company ordered the shutdown. Starshield is under the direct control of the US government, he wrote on X.It is important to distinguish between the two systems: Starlink and Starshield are both developed by SpaceX but aimed at different customers. Starlink is the service for private and business users, Starshield is designed for governments and the military.Polish foreign minister Radosław Sikorski reacted sharply on X, writing: "Hey, Elon Musk, you big man, are you once again playing politics with your products? As your European customers we are keeping a close eye on you."Poland has paid for a large share of the Ukrainian terminals. This has once again raised the question of how dependent armed forces are on satellite links. Europe has therefore been working for some time on its own solution.The European answer: IRIS²The EU has been developing IRIS², its own satellite network, for around six years. The acronym stands for "Infrastructure for Resilience, Interconnectivity and Security by Satellite".In German this roughly means infrastructure for resilience, connectivity and security via satellites. The system is intended to provide secure connections for governments, companies and citizens and to close mobile coverage gaps in Europe and Africa.For encryption it will rely on quantum technology via the European quantum communication infrastructure EuroQCI.In early August, the European Commission and the SpaceRISE consortium agree on the implementation. The network will grow to 348 satellites, 330 in low Earth orbit and 18 in medium Earth orbit.A further 66 additional satellites are intended specifically to strengthen defence, security and emergency services. According to the Commission’s calculations, this will increase secured capacity for public-sector users by 60 percent in the EU and by 54 percent worldwide.The focus is on states, the military and critical services; later on, private individuals are also to be able to use the network. The first satellites are scheduled to launch in 2029. Initial services are to be introduced gradually from 2029 or 2030.Germany's roleGermany is represented by the Bremen-based space company Orbitale Hochtechnologie Bremen (OHB).On 31 August it signed a contract worth just under €1 billion with satellite operator SES for 18 satellites in medium Earth orbit for IRIS².A single satellite weighs around 2.6 tonnes at launch. OHB chief executive Marco Fuchs sees the programme as an important step towards greater European independence.Germany’s share of the project sparked disputes early on.In December 2023, the Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs sent a strongly worded letter to the companies involved demanding urgent clarification of the German industry’s participation and its share in value creation, as reported by the Frankfurter Rundschau daily.Bundeswehr: Its own satellite network?Independently of IRIS², the Bundeswehr is planning its own satellite network. It is a national project financed by the federal government.Major General Armin Fleischmann, the Bundeswehr’s space commissioner in the Cyber and Information Domain, told regional public broadcaster MDR that the plan is for a constellation similar to Starlink, only smaller.He told the Handelsblatt business newspaper they wanted to have "flying Fritzboxes" in space. The network is initially to cover NATO’s eastern flank, under national control. Individual components will come from Western partners, including the United States.As early as September 2025, defence minister Boris Pistorius announced at the space congress of the Federation of German Industries in Berlin that a total of €35 billion would be invested in military space projects by 2030. In July he visited OHB in Bremen to inspect satellite programmes and ongoing production.The project is called SATCOMBw 4, short for satellite communication of the Bundeswehr. In its final expansion stage, according to the Bundeswehr, it is to comprise a three-digit number of satellites in low Earth orbit and cost between eight and ten billion euros. An initial partial constellation with up to 40 satellites is scheduled to be operational as early as 2029, with full operations planned from 2030.The joint venture "OHB Rheinmetall Space Networks", based in Bremen, is bidding for the contract According to company information, OHB would be responsible for the satellites, Rheinmetall for the ground stations and end devices. No decision has yet been taken.Industry reports suggest that the contract award could come around the turn of the year, though insiders consider early 2027 possible as well. OHB would then be involved in both major projects: in IRIS² as satellite manufacturer and in the Bundeswehr network as part of the joint venture.Up to now, the Bundeswehr has been using two of its own satellites in geostationary orbit at around 36,000 kilometres altitude, COMSATBw-1 and COMSATBw-2, launched in 2009 and 2010.Their successors are being built by Airbus and are scheduled to be handed over in orbit in 2029. The first of the three German radar satellites SARah was launched in 2022 on a Falcon 9 rocket from SpaceX.Young Belgian company helping to build Europe’s satellite networkThe satellites for IRIS² are being built by several companies. The largest share will not be supplied by an established group but by a young company:Aerospacelab, founded in 2018 and based in Charleroi in Belgium, is building 264 satellites for low Earth orbit.The order volume amounts to €2.4 billion, according to the company. The satellites are to be delivered by 2030. They will be produced in a new factory in Charleroi, where up to 500 satellites per year are to be built from 2027.Airbus is building at least 66 satellites in the first layer for military communication, which are due to be ready in 2029. This means the entire low-orbit segment with 330 satellites has been allocated.Together with the 18 OHB satellites for medium orbit, the network will comprise 348 satellites.How realistic is 2029?Whether the timetable can be met remains an open question. The first satellites are scheduled to launch in 2029; according to media reports, the original plan was for them to go up two years earlier.Experts view rocket launches as the bottleneck. Even the best satellites cannot reach space without rockets and those unable to launch them themselves remain dependent on others.Europe is relying on the Ariane 6 launch vehicle, which has been lifting off into space since 2024. Andreas Knopp of the Bundeswehr University Munich points out in the weekly paper Das Parlament that the number of launches is limited, while political scientist Antje Nötzold of TU Chemnitz speaks in MDR of a "launcher problem."So far this year, Ariane 6 has launched four times, three of those flights carrying satellites for Amazon Leo into orbit, the US company’s satellite internet service that is also intended to compete with Starlink.Amazon has booked at least 18 Ariane 6 launches. In early August, the Commission named the procurement of launch services for IRIS² as one of the next steps.

title: Doomsday Glacier will keep melting even if oceans cool. Here’s why cutting emissions still matters
description: The total collapse of Thwaites Glacier, known as the Doomsday Glacier, would contribute an estimated 65cm to global sea level rise.
content: Thwaites Glacier, aka the ‘Doomsday Glacier’, will keep melting even if our turbocharged oceans cool down, scientists have warned.The world’s oceans reached their highest daily temperature on record this summer, with sea surfaces outside the polar regions averaging 21.1°C on 22 August. With El Niño still intensifying in the Pacific, it is unlikely temperatures will drop dramatically in the near future.But even under the “most extreme ocean cooling conditions imagined”, new research led by British Antarctic Survey (BAS) has found that the Doomsday Glacier, located in West Antarctica, will continue losing ice for at least the next 150 years.The total collapse of the ice sheet would contribute an estimated 65cm to global sea level rise. To put that into perspective, for every centimetre of sea level rise around an additional six million people on the planet are exposed to coastal flooding.‘Unavoidable future ice loss’ for Doomsday GlacierResearchers ran a modelling experiment for Thwaites Glacier and its neighbour Pine Island Glacier, which are currently the largest contributors to ice loss from this area of Antarctica.They completely switched off the melting effects of the ocean – driven by climate change – beneath both glaciers in three independent computer models. Published in the science journal Geophysical Research Letters, the study revealed a “striking difference” between how the two glaciers fared over a 150-year period. Pine Island Glacier responded as scientists might have expected. Under the modelling, the ice sheet stopped melting and began thickening – advancing back towards the position it held in the first half of the 20th century.However, Thwaites Glacier continued to lose ice, even without any ocean melting. The rate of ice loss slowed down over time as the glacier thinned. “These results show that past changes in ocean-driven melting have now committed us to unavoidable future ice loss from Thwaites Glacier,” says Dr Rosie Williams, a glaciologist at BAS and lead author of the paper.“This ice loss cannot be undone or prevented by simply cooling the ocean.”Can we stop the Doomsday Glacier melting?A zero-melting scenario would never occur in the real world, as the presence of seawater below glacier ice alone is enough to cause some level of melting.BAS ocean modeller and co-author of the report Professor Paul Holland explains that the Thwaites Glacier started to retreat in the 1940s, with the warming of our oceans becoming a “major factor” driving ice loss.While the simulations show that historical melting of Thwaites Glacier has “committed future generations to the challenges of sea level rise”, the ice loss will be further exacerbated if the world does not reduce and ideally reverse the emissions of greenhouse gases. “We don’t yet know if Antarctica’s other major glaciers are moving into a state of committed change,” Holland says. “We urgently need to take action to modify the human activities that are driving changes in ocean melting of these glaciers.”

title: Risk of electric battery fire: VW recalls thousands of cars again
description: Car maker Volkswagen is recalling more vehicles in Germany, this time electric models. Faulty batteries could, in the worst case, trigger fires.
content: A few weeks ago it was a faulty screw; now a suspected battery defect means VW has to recall thousands of cars once again. In the worst case, there is a risk of fire.Recall campaigns are already reported to be under way in the United States and the United Kingdom, and models in Germany are now also being recalled. According to the authorities, around 22,000 ID.4 electric cars are affected in the US.VW prepares recall in GermanyWith recalls already under way in the US and the UK, VW is planning and rolling out recall campaigns in Germany and other markets.Some battery cells in Volkswagen electric cars are defective. Internal quality checks have revealed the problem, according to Handelsblatt. A Volkswagen spokesperson told the outlet that several thousand vehicles are affected.VW cited production faults at suppliers as the cause of the faulty battery cells. The issue is limited to a specific production period.Because of the defect, the batteries may be exposed to increased thermal stress, according to the information available. In extreme cases, a fire in these electric vehicles cannot be ruled out, VW said.According to Handelsblatt, the VW ID.3, ID.4, ID.7, ID Buzz and Cupra Born models produced between 2023 and 2025 are among those affected. The company has not yet confirmed this list of models.The recall is being prepared in close coordination with the relevant authorities, the spokesperson said. It has not yet appeared in the databases of Germany’s Federal Motor Transport Authority (KBA).VW sets out immediate measuresTo prevent possible damage and incidents, the group is now recommending that potentially affected cars be charged only to a maximum of 80%. The manufacturer plans to recall some of the vehicles to service centres to check the batteries. Once the batteries have been inspected, the charging limit will be lifted for cars in which no fault is found.If a defective battery is identified, the high-voltage battery module would not necessarily have to be replaced and could potentially be brought up to date with a software upgrade.Customers whose vehicles are affected will be contacted by the company, according to the report. Owners will receive a letter informing them of the next steps.A damaged screw led to a recall of around 2.86 million VW and Audi vehicles worldwide in September. The component could have caused the steering to fail, the KBA warned.20% of VW deliveries are electricVW’s electric-car business is strongest in Europe compared with the rest of the world.The share of battery electric vehicles in Volkswagen Group’s European deliveries rose to 20% in the first three quarters of 2026, meaning one in five vehicles delivered was fully electric.Overall, the group is grappling with falling demand worldwide, with business in China in particular slumping. In Germany, VW continues to dominate both the market for new electric car registrations and the used EV market.

title: Extreme weather is decimating Europe’s crops. These farmers have a solution
description: World Food Day: Europe is ‘losing hundreds of farms a day’. Crop diversification and subsidies that pay for outcomes could save them, farmers say.
content: Almonds decimated by frost, tomatoes disrupted by heat, and Halloween pumpkins shrunk by drought: it’s been a punishing year for agriculture in Europe.The hot, dry summer – which would have been “virtually impossible" if it weren’t for climate change – reduced the continent’s forecast grain harvest by an estimated 16.7 million tonnes, costing farmers more than €3 billion, according to the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit (ECIU).“After this summer, many European farmers are on the brink,” says Josefine Herz, managing director of the European Alliance for Regenerative Agriculture (EARA). “One year prices collapse because they grew too much; the next, drought punishes them for growing at all, and each swing hands a bigger share to the same few processors and retailers who are increasing prices on the consumer side.”French vegetable growers’ association Légumes de France warned in July that losses in some sectors could reach 50 per cent. Disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, triggered by the war on Iran, have added to pressure on fuel and fertiliser supplies, while drought has restricted cargo traffic on some European waterways. Together, these supply-chain problems are adding to concerns about the cost of farming and the security of food supplies.But could changing the way we farm pave the way for a more certain future?Diversification of crops helps farmers weather the extremesAt Curly Creek Ranch in Spain’s Basque Country, tomatoes – one of the farm’s highest earners at €7/kg – stopped flowering in the extreme heat. “Imagine the length of the tomato plant and the middle third has a gap without fruit. We never saw that before,” says farmer Meghan Sapp, who is also EARA’s external relations director. Flowering has since resumed, and she hopes a later-than-usual season will make up some of the shortfall. A lack of water has also affected the farm’s Halloween pumpkins, which are smaller than usual this year, while high temperatures left corn with “early signs of burning on the leaves, which we’d never seen before”, says Meghan.The heat also exposed weaknesses in the local water supply, including leaky infrastructure: Curly Creek Ranch repeatedly received less than its expected daily allocation, forcing authorities to deliver 50,000 litres by tanker.But diversification has helped spread the risk.“Many years we don’t get a single aubergine due to lack of heat and yet we plant them anyway, just in case,” Meghan explains. “This year that bet paid off… for the first time ever we had a huge crop.”It’s a tactic that’s also working for farmers further south in Spain.“Historically, our farm depended heavily on cereals,” says Yanniek Schoonhoven, who owns La Junquera farm in Murcia. “We have gradually diversified… looking for systems that are better suited to an increasingly unpredictable climate.” Aromatic plants like rosemary, lavender, sage and oregano are particularly well adapted to dry Mediterranean conditions. They also fetch good prices: around €2,000 per hectare, with costs of about €1,000, according to Yanniek. Pistachios, which also cope well in a dry climate, bring in even more: around €2,350 per hectare with similar costs. But frost during a critical period wiped out La Junquera’s almonds, a “very significant loss” of around €700–€1,050 per hectare.The challenges of branching out from commodity crops Despite the attractive margins on certain drought-resilient crops, it’s not a simple switch.While aromatics can be distilled into essential oils, a higher-value product than grain, “these markets require processing, investment and reliable buyers”, explains Yanniek. Cereals and oilseeds, by contrast, are commodity crops: standardised products sold in bulk, with prices largely dictated by wider markets. Farmers may have established buyers for their harvests, but have little leverage to charge more for climate resilience. At La Junquera, wheat brings in around €600 per hectare against roughly €500 in costs, according to Yanniek.Subsidies tend to favour these crops, though. The EU’s Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) pays basic income support by hectares farmed, not by crop type or output, so more funding naturally flows to large-scale farms which often grow commodities. The EU also steps in if market prices for commodity crops fall below a certain threshold.Yet commodities are not immune to extreme weather. On Gut Weimarschmieden, a 700-hectare organic conservation agriculture farm in Fladungen, Germany, summer barley and winter wheat struggled in the heat, says manager Maximillian Krimm, while the cornfields produced about 17 tonnes instead of the usual 25 to 30. Spelt and canola fared better. Maximillian is also considering emmer, an old wheat variety whose yields are 20 to 30 per cent lower than conventional wheat, for only a slightly higher price. “In general we don’t grow much that’s lower value because the prices don’t justify it,” he says.Restoring soil health can turn things around for Europe’s farmersCommodity farming also favours intensive methods that deplete soil and generate emissions, not least from synthetic fertiliser – and crop choice alone won’t fix that.“A drought-tolerant crop planted into dead, compacted soil in a biodiversity dead zone will still struggle, because there’s nothing left to hold the water when it comes,” says Lily Maxwell-Lwin, head of advocacy at international non-profit Commonland.Her team works with local communities across more than 50 countries to restore degraded landscapes using a holistic approach that blends social impact, biodiversity restoration, financial return and pride in place.“For most arable farms in our region, years of tillage, monoculture and synthetic input use has turned the soil into hard, dry land with low soil organic carbon, limiting the soil’s ability to infiltrate and retain the rain when it does come. Instead it runs off, creating erosion,” explains Meghan.Healthier soil can raise yields, cut the need for costly synthetic fertiliser and hold more water, easing drought and flooding alike. “We’ve watched degraded landscapes turn around in a decade: soil that crusted over starts absorbing rain again, hillsides that shed water start acting like sponges,” says Lily.At La Junquera, ponds, swales, vegetation cover and keyline design slow runoff and increase infiltration. “For us, adapting to drought isn’t about finding more water. It’s about making much better use of every drop of rain that falls,” says Yanniek.That is what gives resilient crops “a fighting chance”, says Lily. “If we want farmers to take the risk of switching to lower-yield, climate-resilient varieties, we have to invest in restoring the land underneath them first, not just hand them a different seed and call it done.”What support do farmers need from governments?The EU’s CAP subsidy scheme does reward regenerative practices like crop rotation, cover cropping and planting nitrogen-fixing crops, which produce natural fertiliser and improve soil health. But farmers still largely bear the costs and responsibility of implementing these measures alone, with little recognition for the benefits they create for food security, biodiversity and human health.“We need policies that make it less risky for farmers to adapt,” says Yanniek, pointing to better insurance against drought and frost, and financial support during the years it takes to establish perennial crops.Meghan wants regional policymakers to move fast and fund the move to regenerative land management, through advisory services, transition insurance and co-investment in new machinery.EARA farmers achieve equal or better harvests with less water and fewer inputs, says Josefine, yet “neither the market nor the CAP pays for the resilience built”. She calls for “a fair market and a CAP that pays for outcomes, not just practices and hectares, so resilience stops being a cost farmers absorb alone”. One of the alliance’s farmers, Gunnar Thelin of Västra Gatugård, a five-hectare holding in Vederslöv, Sweden, sketches how that could work: satellite measurements over the season would check that photosynthesis is above an agreed level for the region, and bare ground and soil temperature below agreed levels. Meet them and you receive CAP money; miss them and you don’t. “That’s the incentive to go regen,” he says.Not everyone is convinced. Maximillian says he’s “not a big fan of subsidies” and believes farmers must simply adapt through regenerative farming. Better prices alone, he says, won’t solve the underlying problem.But for many, a fair market remains the missing piece. “Growing a drought-resistant crop is only half the solution,” says Yanniek. “Farmers also need a market that pays enough to make growing it worthwhile.” Without one, Josefine warns, “Europe loses hundreds of farms a day this way, the very farms holding the solutions to regenerating it.”

title: These are the world’s best destinations for ‘golden hour’, according to a meteorologist
description: Greece dominated the golden hour list, with four destinations making the top 10, including the Lindos Acropolis in Rhodes.
content: Even amateur photographers know that the best time to get snapping is during “golden hour” – but not all are created equal.Some are far longer than an hour, others shorter; clouds can get in the way of the effect, as can rainfall; and light pollution can have an impact, too.Luckily for us, travel company Kuoni has teamed up with meteorologist Jim Dale from British Weather Services to create a ranking for the world's best spots for golden hour.Having analysed 165 destinations against metrics including cloud cover, light pollution, rainfall, artificial brightness, wind speed and average sunset duration, 20 places made the final list.Greece dominated the rankings, with four places making the cut – ahead of Namibia with three, and two each for the US, Australia and Botswana.“There’s something about that soft, warm light of golden hour that makes a destination feel truly unforgettable, whether you're watching the sun dip below the Acropolis in Lindos or over the dunes of the Namib Desert,” Marco Rocha, the product, commercial and operations director at Kuoni, said.“What's interesting is that the best golden hour locations aren't always the most obvious ones – clear skies, low light pollution and a bit of local knowledge often matter more than a destination's reputation.”Golden hour destinations you need to know aboutJordan’s Wadi Rum came out on top overall, with little cloud cover and almost no rain, followed by Sossusvlei in Namibia, the desert landscape with no light pollution and sunsets that last an average of 27.9 minutes.Namibia has three locations in the top six. As well as Sossusvlei, Damaraland placed third, with Etosha National Park in sixth.Chile’s Atacama Desert came fourth, with Kuoni noting that wildlife like flamingos, alpacas and Andean foxes make a visit here even more special, while Wahiba Sands in Oman rounded out the top five.As for Europe, Lindos Acropolis in Rhodes narrowly made it into the top 10, with Kuoni noting that its perch 116 metres above the sea gives you uninterrupted golden hour views most evenings.Next up was Paphos in Cyprus, coming in 16th, followed by Rhodes Town (17th), Cape Sounion in Athens (19th), and Zante’s Navagio Shipwreck Beach (20th).The world’s top 20 destinations for golden hour1. title: Income after rent: How much is left across European cities?
description: One salary is not enough to afford a three-bedroom flat in many European city centres. Euronews Business takes a closer look at how much a working couple has left after paying the rent.
content: Many European countries face a housing crisis, with a shortage of homes and rising prices. Rents also continue to increase, and city centres are particularly expensive. A single salary is no longer enough to cover the rent for a family-sized flat in the heart of a major city for many European households.But what if a couple both work and share the rent? Is that enough? How much money would they have left each month after paying rent? And how do European cities compare globally?The Mapping the World’s Prices 2026 report, published by Deutsche Bank Research Institute, sheds some light on the topic. It looks at two people earning a local net salary and deducts the rent on a three-bedroom apartment in the given city centre. What remains is the household’s disposable income after rent.Among 28 European cities, the disposable income after rent ranges from €253 in Lisbon to €9,140 in Zurich.Swiss cities lead the rankingZurich has the most expensive rent (€5,502) among the 28 cities. But it also has the highest net salary (€7,321). As a result, a couple in Zurich has the most money left after rent (€9,140).In addition to Zurich, Geneva is far ahead of the rest. In Geneva, a couple has €8,783 left each month after rent. This is thanks to the second-highest net salary (€6,516).Luxembourg is third with €5,890. It has the third-highest net salary (€4,548). Its rent is also high (€3,206), but lower than in cities such as London, Dublin and Amsterdam. This leaves couples with more money at the end of the month.Birmingham follows with €5,238, just ahead of Copenhagen with €5,233.Birmingham vs London: Rent makes the differenceA couple in Birmingham has €5,238 left each month after rent. In London, the figure is €3,148. That means couples in Birmingham have €2,090 more each month.Salaries are lower in Birmingham, but rent is much cheaper. A city-centre flat costs €1,949 in Birmingham, compared with €4,362 in London. Couples also have more than €4,000 left after rent in Oslo (€4,936), Frankfurt (€4,786), Munich (€4,575) and Amsterdam (€4,431).Amsterdam’s rent is among the five highest (€3,542), but a high net salary (€3,986) makes up for it.Vienna (€3,709) and Stockholm (€3,674) are very close to this level.Berlin beats Paris thanks to lower rentSalaries in Paris are higher than in Berlin (€3,171 compared with €2,946). Yet couples in Berlin have more left after rent (€3,554 compared with €3,336). The reason is rent. A city-centre flat costs €3,005 in Paris but €2,339 in Berlin.Dublin has a higher net salary (€3,455) than Paris, Berlin, Vienna and Stockholm. But couples there have less left after rent than in all of these cities (€3,038). Rent in Dublin is the fourth-highest in Europe (€3,873), and it is higher than one net salary.Southern Europe is at the bottomCities in southern Europe have the lowest income after rent. Lisbon and Milan are the hardest cities for couples. In Lisbon, just €253 is left after rent. The net salary there is €1,408, but the rent is €2,561. In Milan, only €697 is left. In Madrid, a couple has €1,905 left each month. In Barcelona, they have €1,832. The figure falls to €1,265 in Rome and €1,148 in Athens. In Athens, the rent (€1,164) is slightly higher than one net salary (€1,156).Istanbul follows Lisbon at the bottom of the European list with €353. The net salary there is €1,027, but the rent is €1,701.Central and Eastern Europe do better than the southSome cities in Central and Eastern Europe perform better than those in Southern Europe. In Prague, a couple has €2,054 left after rent. In Warsaw, they have €1,985, and in Budapest €1,548. All three are above Rome and Athens.It is important to note that rent is the only cost included. Couples still need to pay for food, bills and transport.Is one salary enough to pay the rent?The answer is no in many cities. In 11 cities, rent is higher than one net salary. These are Athens, Barcelona, Budapest, Dublin, Istanbul, Lisbon, London, Madrid, Milan, Prague and Rome.Lisbon has the biggest gap. The net salary is €1,408, while rent costs €2,561, which is 82% more than one salary. In Milan, a net salary is €1,940, compared with rent of €3,184.In Prague and Budapest, rent and one net salary are almost the same.How does Europe compare with the rest of the world?Europe performs well in the global ranking. Zurich (€9,140) and Geneva (€8,783) top the list of 69 cities, ahead of San Francisco (€7,992). Seven of the top 10 are in Europe.No European city is in the bottom 10. All of them are in Latin America, Asia and Africa. In six, rent costs more than two net salaries. Manila (-€882) and Bangkok (-€759) are at the bottom.In Moscow, a couple has €313 left after rent. The net salary is €1,570, but the rent is €2,827.Several European cities also do better than New York (€1,921).Younger generations in Europe have lower homeownership rates than earlier generations. In 2026, house prices and rents continue to rise across Europe, outpacing inflation in many countries.

title: Nvidia to open Stockholm AI hub for start-ups tackling health and climate challenges
description: The AI hub will bring selected Swedish start-ups and Nvidia staff under the same roof, alongside a biotechnology demonstration lab.
content: Nvidia is opening an AI hub in Stockholm, Sweden, to help start-ups tackle health and climate challenges.The US chipmaker is partnering with Norrsken, a Swedish non-profit foundation established by Niklas Adalberth, co-founder of Swedish payments company Klarna. The foundation supports start-ups working on social and environmental problems.Called Stockholm AI Lab, the hub is due to open in central Stockholm in 2027, according to Norrsken’s announcement.It will bring selected start-ups and Nvidia staff under the same roof, alongside a biotechnology demonstration lab.Nvidia will contribute computing infrastructure, software tools and connections to its international start-up network. The partners have not disclosed the size of the investment in the project.What will happen inside?The hub in central Stockholm will provide private offices and host events connecting founders with investors, researchers, industry representatives and policymakers.“What these founders need now is what every great movement needs: a place. Somewhere to find each other, their investors, their first customers, and the conviction that they are not building alone,” Adalberth said in the announcement.The demonstration lab will be run by Nvidia and Stockholm-based Root Bio, a start-up using AI to design molecules for biological applications, including reducing greenhouse gas emissions.The partners say it will show how AI can help automate biological discovery. They also plan to select further demonstration partners working in robotics, climate, health and manufacturing.Nvidia’s software tools will support work in robotics, simulation and life sciencesHowever, the announcement does not specify which equipment will be installed, how much computing capacity members will receive or what they will pay to use it.Part of Nvidia’s wider European pushNvidia has announced similar efforts elsewhere in Europe to help businesses and researchers use AI, although the projects take different forms.In the United Kingdom (UK), the company announced a robotics research and development hub with technology trade association techUK in September 2025, working with training company QA to develop AI and robotics skills.In June 2025, Nvidia also announced new or expanded AI technology centres in Germany, Italy, Spain, Finland, Sweden and the UK, supporting research, training and access to AI computing infrastructure.

title: ‘Appalling’: Actor Omar Sy joins public figures criticising French authorities’ response to student protests
description: The student protests have been building since late September, sparked by complaints of staff shortages and dilapidated schools. A major strike action is planned for this Saturday, and more public figures are expressing their support for the students’ demands.
content: Protests in France rage on, as students and teachers continue to raise awareness of staff shortages, poor school infrastructure, defective equipment, and deeper anxieties over diminishing prospects and the cost-of-living crisis. This week, on Tuesday, more than 480,000 protestors took to the streets across France (according to the inter-union of high-school and university group), with placards which read: “Nos lycées tombent en ruines, comme nos espoirs” ("Our schools, like our hopes, are falling into ruin”) and “Diplômés aujourd’hui, précaires demain” ("Graduates today, insecurity tomorrow"). Since the nationwide movement began in September, acts of violence have been reported, with one teenager losing their hand and more than 6,800 youngsters taken into temporary police custody.According to the government, 147 National Education staff members have been injured, and nearly 40 investigations have been launched into alleged acts of violence committed by the police against protesters. Public figures have been expressing their support for the protests, including environmental activist Greta Thunberg, NBA star Victor Wembanyama, singer Louane, and celebrated actor Vincent Lindon, who stars in the recently released Victor Hugo adaptation, Les Misérables. The actor praised the movement in French outlet Le Parisien: “These are young people who want chairs to sit on […] decent, functional sanitary facilities, and the fair distribution of resources – and therefore opportunities.” Lindon added: “I have children who went through middle school, high school, and so on, and it is true that this is one of the first times the younger generation is legitimately asserting demands and rights in the face of a state that currently lacks the funds to buy social peace.” Before a major countrywide mobilisation takes place this Saturday, with more than half a million people expected to take to the streets, further public figures have been speaking out. The latest is French actor Omar Sy. During a guest spot on France Inter, the star of The Intouchables, Jurassic World: Dominion and the hit Netflix show Lupin, criticised the authorities’ handling of the protests and called for the demands of students to be listened to, first and foremost. “These are our kids; it is the future of our country that is speaking out to a nation that is completely adrift,” said Sy.The actor condemned the violence surrounding the protests, adding: “When I see that there’s no response to this, and that the immediate instinct is to stop them from speaking out, or to beat them up, or even to pit them against one another in childish brawls, I find it appalling.”Sy added: “I ask myself: where are the adults in charge? What is our role, as adults, as parents? What are we actually doing to our children? Instead of jumping straight to reprimanding, punishing, or correcting them, or forcing them to face off against one another, we aren’t listening to them at all.""In fact, it’s even worse. We tell them to be quiet, and then we expect them to reach an agreement on their own. We don’t even know what they have to say.” The police response to the protests has also drawn criticism from human rights organisations, with Amnesty International denouncing a "disproportionate" use of force, while the UN Human Rights Office has expressed concern, calling for de-escalation.

title: 'It melts all sides': Slovenia takes drastic measures to stop its last glacier from vanishing
description: Locals say ‘unique ecosystems’ are vanishing and rivers are losing water as Slovenia’s last glacier melts away.
content: Drop by drop, Slovenia is losing its ice. The Skuta Glacier is now the last glacier left in the country. Its other glacier on Mount Triglav, Slovenia’s highest peak, has almost completely melted away.Mountain guide Andrej Slak has watched Slovenia’s glaciers shrink for 35 years. Climbing over rocky terrain toward what remains of Skuta, he says the change has been especially noticeable over the past decade and that its impact on the local community has been devastating."We are standing next to Slovenia's last remaining glacier and just look at what is left of it – nothing but a small patch of ice covered in grit and debris; the change is striking. "These glaciers serve as vital water reservoirs for us in the valley throughout the year. Shepherds used to utilise icy hollows like this to store and preserve meat, but they can no longer do that as such ice pockets are nowhere to be found in the mountains anymore."What remains is a patch of ice on the surface of the mountainside, and the rest buried under stones, with a narrow opening leading into a crevasse.How quickly is Slovenia’s last glacier shrinking?In Ljubljana, scientists have been gathering data on the glaciers.This year marks 80 years since the Anton Melik Geographical Institute at the Research Centre of the Slovenian Academy of Sciences and Arts began monitoring both glaciers."When we started, there were about two and a half to three hectares of ice under Skuta. Now it has shrunk to 1.5 hectares, and ice has mostly thinned out. On Skuta, it has thinned from several tens of metres to just a few metres. Back when we started, the Triglav Glacier covered a little over 14 hectares. Later, five or 10 years ago, we were still talking about half a hectare to one hectare. In recent years, it has been less than 0.2 hectares, but the ice, as I said, has now completely disappeared," explains Miha Pavsek.Pavsek says the change is due to a combination of two factors."The turning point comes when we have a combination of very little snow, meaning a very low maximum seasonal snow depth, followed by a very warm summer,” he says. “And those two factors coincided very well this year.”On Skuta, a marker painted on a rock shows how high the glacier reached in 1994. The ice has pulled back from this point since then.“Skuta is following the same path as the Triglav Glacier. The ice is now protected. We were in the mountains a week ago, and about 80 to 90 per cent of the ice surface is covered by gravel, which provides additional protection, but it melts from all sides," says Pavsek.Glacier melt has knock on effects on rivers and groundwaterGravel gives the ice’s surface some protection from the sun, but inside the cave beneath the ice, water falls from the ceiling.The effects reach well beyond the mountains."The waters from the glaciers feed our great rivers, including the Drava, in Croatia, as well as the Mura, which originates in Austria. There, according to the latest forecasts, all glaciers below 3,500 metres will disappear by 2050. So, these rivers will have much less water. And normally, these rivers feed the groundwater, where we have wells and pumps for drinking water," explains Pavsek.For hikers who still come to the mountain, the loss is easy to see."I am concerned about this from a broader perspective, specifically regarding climate change in general, because glaciers serve as a vital reserve of Earth's water," says Tanja Plavec, a local hiker. "As they disappear, that reserve disappears with them. Furthermore, glaciers host a unique ecosystem that also vanishes as the perennial ice disappears." This year, Europe sweltered under an exceptionally hot and arid summer, the intensity of which scientists say would have been "virtually impossible" without climate change from humans' burning of fossil fuels.The continent is the world’s fastest-warming, with temperatures increasing twice as fast as the global average since the 1980s, according to the European Union’s Copernicus Climate Change Service.

title: Chios airport to close from 15 November to 15 March amid strong local opposition
description: Four-month suspension of runway operations at Chios State Airport "Homer" aims to complete works by 28 February 2027 and boost flight safety.
content: The State Airport of Chios "Homer" will temporarily suspend operations from the evening of Sunday 15 November 2026 until 15 March 2027, as part of works to extend and upgrade the take-off and landing runway, according to an announcement by the Hellenic Civil Aviation Authority (HCAA).The Authority considers the suspension necessary for the safe execution of the works, which include extending the runway to the north and an overall improvement of the airport's operational infrastructure.As the HCAA points out, the planning takes into account the particularities of an airport with a limited runway length, the winter weather conditions and the need to ensure smooth air links to the island during the 2027 tourist season.Shorter timetable for the worksUnder the updated schedule, the works in the second and third phase will be completed in four months, instead of the five months foreseen in the original approved timetable.At the same time, the contractor has pledged to make every effort to speed up the works, with the aim of completing them by 28 February 2027. The HCAA notes that its goal is to limit the runway closure to the shortest possible period.For the duration of the shutdown, a relevant NOTAM has already been issued so that all parties concerned are informed and can adjust their planning in good time.What applies to emergency flightsDuring the works, emergency flights will be able to operate with helicopters, landing and taking off directly to and from the airport apron.This provision covers, among others, air ambulance transfers, search and rescue missions, firefighting operations, humanitarian and state missions, as well as other flights of national character.It is noted that at this stage the airport remains operationally available, as the works are still in their first phase. Flights are being served by turboprop aircraft with a limited number of passengers, due to the temporary reduction in the available runway length.1,799m-long runway once the works are completedThe upgrade provides for the extension of the runway to the north, bringing its total length to 1,799 metres.The aim is to further enhance operational safety and to enable the airport to serve larger types of aircraft, a development expected to strengthen Chios's air connections and bring benefits both to passengers and to the local economy.The HCAA calls on passengers, airlines and all stakeholders to take the planned suspension of operations into account when arranging their travel between 15 November 2026 and 15 March 2027.Reactions from the local community – protests and request for a meeting with the ministerLocal organisations on Chios are warning of protest action, including the possibility of shutting down shops to keep the airport open over the holidays, reacting to the plan for an earlier suspension of the island's airport operations.At the same time, they are requesting a meeting with the Minister of Infrastructure and Transport in order to clarify the timetable for the works and avoid last-minute changes.Representatives of local bodies express their strong opposition to the prospect of the airport closing on 15 November instead of 15 January, as they say was initially agreed.
