They describe such a development as a blow to the economic and social life of Chios and call for the original schedule to be respected.The president of the Chios Chamber of Commerce, Pantelis Legatos, warned of the impact that the interruption of air links will have, especially during the festive period, when many residents have already planned journeys, family visits and medical appointments.He stressed that the geographical position of Chios, about five nautical miles from the Turkish coast, makes the air link with Athens particularly important for residents' access to health services, as well as for their personal and social needs.Doubts over completion of the worksReservations about the timetable were also voiced by the regional governor of the North Aegean, Kostas Moutzouris, who took part via teleconference from Mytilene. He raised questions as to whether the airport will be ready to resume operations before Easter 2027.At the same time, he underlined the need for a substantive upgrade of the airport's infrastructure, noting that he will take part in the decision-making procedures on the issue.'No decision without the local community'The mayor of Chios, Giannis Malafis, stressed the need to maintain the island's air connection during the major festive periods.The mayor asked for the airport to remain in operation at Christmas, New Year and Easter, while also insisting that any decision on the future of the project should be taken in consultation with local bodies and Chios society.The timetable for the works remains at the heart of the reactions, with the island's representatives seeking clear answers on the duration of the shutdown and its impact on residents' daily lives and on the local economy.

title: IMF warns attacks on Saudi Arabia could hurt global economy after strike on Aramco headquarters
description: Aramco's headquarters has been hit, flights are suspended and oil prices are rising. The IMF warns that the economic fallout from attacks on Saudi Arabia could be felt worldwide.
content: The International Monetary Fund warned on Wednesday that attacks on Saudi Arabia could hurt economies worldwide, after a strike damaged oil giant Aramco's headquarters.IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva pointed to Saudi Arabia’s economic importance.“In that sense, these developments have potentially negative spillovers for everybody, everywhere,” she said at the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok.Saudi Arabia's energy ministry said an administrative building at Aramco's headquarters in Dhahran was hit on Tuesday evening, causing a limited fire. It said there were no deaths or injuries.Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis claimed responsibility. The group has also attacked Saudi airports during renewed fighting with a Saudi-led coalition.The building's top three floors, including chief executive Amin Nasser's office, were badly damaged, a person with direct knowledge told Reuters.Two sources said operations at the complex were continuing as normal, although some employees had been told to work from home. Another said some work had moved to offices abroad.Aramco oversees its oil rigs, refineries, export terminals and pipelines from a centre at its headquarters. The company had not responded to the news agency's request for comment.Oil prices rose on Wednesday, with Brent crude trading above $106 a barrel. Aramco's shares fell 0.5% in early trading.Air travel has also been disrupted. Lufthansa has suspended flights to Riyadh up to and including 18 November, according to its latest advisory.Saudi Arabia plans to let executives join its Future Investment Initiative conference online after attacks on Riyadh airport, Reuters reported, citing two people familiar with the plans. The event is due to take place later this month.Recovery depends on shippingSaudi Arabia's economy was already under pressure from the Iran war and disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.The IMF expects it to shrink by 3.3% this year, before growing by 7.9% in 2027.The fund published those forecasts on Tuesday, but had prepared them before Saturday's deadly attack on Riyadh airport.The recovery forecast assumes the Strait of Hormuz will gradually reopen from March 2027, with shipping returning to pre-war conditions by October.Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline carries oil to Yanbu on the Red Sea, allowing exports to avoid the Strait of Hormuz. The IMF said this had reduced the economic damage compared with some neighbouring countries.Georgieva said the kingdom’s efforts to develop businesses outside oil had also helped protect its economy from the war’s impact.She warned that poorer countries that depend on imported energy were among the hardest hit by rising costs. She urged governments to help people facing higher food and energy bills.

title: El Niño vs climate change: Which had more influence over the powerful Hurricane Polo?
description: El Niño turbocharged the Pacific hurricane – but climate change had an even greater impact, scientists find.
content: A new study finds that climate change and El Niño combined to rev up last month's explosively intensifying Hurricane Polo, which was the longest-lasting Category 5 storm ever to churn in the Pacific.Global warming caused by the burning of coal, oil and gas was the bigger of the two culprits, adding nearly 10 kph to its already monstrous strength, according to a joint study published on 14 October by scientists from World Weather Attribution and Climate Central. El Niño contributed a bit less, about 8 kph, a study co-author said.Climate change made the conditions that fuelled the hurricane 23 times more likely, while El Niño – the natural and temporary warming of parts of the Pacific – made it 14 times more likely, the study found. It all has to do with the 31.2°C waters that were as much as 2°C warmer than normal, the study said.This year, with a super strong El Niño, has set records for strength and longevity of Pacific storms. Polo set the record for time spent at Category 5 in the Pacific at two-and-a-half days.'El Niño comes and goes, but climate change only gets worse'“El Niño and climate change both made this hurricane stronger than it would have otherwise been, but the effect of climate change is even bigger than the one of El Niño,” says climate scientist and study co-author Friederike Otto, who coordinates the international science team behind World Weather Attribution.“El Niño comes and goes, but climate change only gets worse. That means that now every hurricane that will occur in the East Pacific has at least this climate change signal making it stronger. And as long as we keep burning fossil fuels, that will only get bigger,” Otto adds.Researchers found that without climate change and El Niño, Polo would have been a monster storm anyway. But every bit of additional wind speed can dramatically increase the damage.Decoding Polo's rapid strengtheningWhile Hurricane Polo ultimately weakened considerably before it hit a sparsely populated part of Mexico, scientists remain fascinated by how it turbocharged from a tropical storm to a top-of-the-chart Category 5 hurricane in about 24 hours.The study puts the different atmospheric dangers in perspective, says Kristina Dahl, a climate scientist and vice president of science at Climate Central, a science and journalism nonprofit out of New Jersey.“It’s a powerful reminder that even though El Niño right now is shifting hazards around the globe and changing where it’s flooding and getting dry, the really dominant signal behind all of this remains climate change,” she says.The study looked at the warm water that fuels storms, using a measure of how strong they can get. But the study didn't focus on the upper level wind shear where El Niño has a huge footprint. El Niño usually increases those storm-decapitating high altitude winds in the Atlantic. However, in the Pacific because of changes in wind patterns, El Niño decreases the winds that weaken storms.The two sets of researchers measured conditions slightly differently and used different techniques but came to the same general conclusion, making them more confident in the result. However, the rapid study has not had time to be peer-reviewed, which is the gold standard of science.To calculate the impact of climate change on Polo, both teams used the scientifically accepted method of comparing what happened in our warmer real world to a hypothetical world that hasn't warmed by 1.4°C since pre-industrial times.How El Niño and climate change interactStudy co-author Daniel Gilford, a Climate Central scientist, says the process they looked at was similar to cars on a road. Wind shear from El Niño can be a red light, as it is in the Atlantic, or a green light, as it is in the Pacific. In the Pacific that green light says go, and then the water warmed by both climate change and El Niño acts like a driver flooring the accelerator.University at Albany atmospheric scientist Brian Tang, who wasn't part of the study, says he was initially surprised that the research found climate change to be the bigger influence on Polo, “given how extreme this El Niño is, but from a long-term standpoint, perhaps the result isn’t as surprising as it might seem.”But three other outside scientists – Jeff Masters of Yale Climate Connections, University of Pennsylvania's Michael Mann and North Carolina State University's Carl Schreck – say they believe the study underestimates how much climate change has added to Polo's strength. Masters points to Gilford's own 2024 study that found climate change added 30 kph to hurricanes in the Atlantic from 2019 to 2023.Gilford acknowledges that Thursday's report could be underestimating climate change's impact a bit, but says he was factoring in other conditions and being conservative.

title: Anthropic revenue jumps 46% to $16.8bn as AI firm eyes record $2 trillion IPO valuation
description: AI developer Anthropic grew its sales by about 46% to $16.8 billion (€15bn) last quarter and turned an adjusted profit, it told investors on Wednesday, weeks before a November stock market debut that could value it at up to $2 trillion (€1.79bn).
content: Anthropic, the San Francisco-based developer of the Claude AI models, generated $16.8 billion (€15bn) in revenue between July and September, up about 46% from $11.5 billion (€10.3bn) in the previous three months, and posted an adjusted profit.It presented the figures to investors at its headquarters on Wednesday, according to Bloomberg citing people familiar with the matter, weeks before a planned initial public offering in November that could value the company at up to $2 trillion (€1.79bn).The company told investors it was profitable for a second straight quarter on an adjusted basis, a measure that strips out certain costs. On the same basis, it had positive free cash flow, meaning it brought in more cash than it spent, and an operating margin of 11%, the share of revenue left after running costs.Each dollar it spent on computing power brought in $1.70 of revenue in the quarter, but growth is slowing.Revenue had more than doubled from the first to the second quarter, and the latest figures fell short of some investors’ hopes cited by the Financial Times.Annualised revenue, which projects recent sales over a full year, is now reportedly expected to end 2026 below $100 billion (€89.5bn), short of the more than $100 billion (€89.5bn) several backers had previously anticipated.For instance, research firm SemiAnalysis puts the current figure at about $74 billion (€66.2bn), compared with some $65 billion (€58.1bn) in late July.Record IPO in sightAnthropic filed confidentially for an IPO with US regulators in June and has yet to publish its full prospectus.It is aiming to list in November, once the US midterm elections are over, at a valuation of as much as $2 trillion (€1.79bn), with US investment banks Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley reportedly leading the deal.That would top the roughly $1.8 trillion (€1.6tn) at which SpaceX, Elon Musk’s rocket and satellite company, priced its record-breaking IPO in June, and be about double the $965 billion (€863bn) valuation at which Anthropic raised $65 billion (€58.1bn) from private investors in May.On standard accounting measures, Anthropic lost $42 billion (€37.5bn) in 2025 on revenue of $4.6 billion (€4.1bn), according to a draft prospectus reported last month, largely because of $34 billion (€30.4bn) in accounting charges linked to past fundraising.Race with OpenAIRival OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, was approaching $50 billion (€44.7bn) in annualised revenue at the end of September, although the two count revenue differently, so the figures are not like for like.OpenAI is not expected to list on public markets before 2027, but competition in the sector remains fierce.Anthropic had appeared to lose ground to OpenAI in recent months due to the release of the Astra model by Sam Altman's firm, while much cheaper Chinese models posed a risk to its revenue.Anthropic could start marketing its shares to investors as soon as the week of 9 November, according to Bloomberg, further citing people familiar with the matter.

title: New J.K. Rowling documentary set to explore ‘polarising’ Harry Potter author
description: The two-part series, commissioned by the BBC, will look at how Rowling's "unflinching personal beliefs have sparked a fraught and divisive dialogue that continues to this day”.
content: A new two-part documentary has been commissioned by the BBC about the career and legacy of “polarising” Harry Potter author J.K. Rowling.The controversial author, who has alienated a sizeable portion of her fanbase and film cast due to her views on gender and the trans community, is not involved in the documentary's creation.The first part of the documentary will look at the author’s “bookish childhood” and the creation of the Harry Potter series.“As the books inspired a generation of outsiders and brought millions of young fans together through the emerging internet, Rowling created a universe with an economic legacy worth billions,” according to the press release.The second episode will explore her post-Harry Potter career.“Amid the rise of social media and intensifying culture wars, her interventions on Scottish independence, feminism, free speech and gender identity place her at the centre of increasingly bitter online exchanges.”The announcement of the documentary, which is set to premiere next year, after the launch of HBO’s new Harry Potter adaptation in December, follows accusations of “trans rights censorship” levelled at the BBC, after they blurred out the pro-trans slogan ‘Protect The Dolls’ from a t-shirt worn by House Of The Dragon’s Bethany Antonia during an episode of the show Strictly Come Dancing. The new HBO Harry Potter series has been the subject of debate and controversy, with many fans speaking out against Rowling – who is executive producer on the series - and calling for the show to be boycotted because of the author’s “transphobia”.In August, actor Nicolas Hoult was criticised for joining the cast of the show. Hoult ended up stepping down and was replaced by Kit Harrington – who has also faced backlash.John Lithgow, who will be playing Albus Dumbledore in the show, recently said that he considered quitting the show over the backlash he received due to Rowling’s anti-trans views. However, he revealed he decided to stay, describing the books as “clearly on the side of the angels, against intolerance and bigotry.”

title: Pan Am-inspired cruise set to launch in 2027 to mark airline’s 100th anniversary
description: The 28-day cruise will trace some of the former airline’s historic routes through the Caribbean and Central America.
content: Ever dreamed of travelling with Pan Am? While flying with the former airline isn’t a possibility, Holland America Line is offering up the next best thing.Next year, the cruise line will be hosting a Pan Am 100th Anniversary Legendary Voyage, complete with talks from aviation historians, Pan Am-inspired dining experiences, and a recreation of the Clipper Club, the private airport lounges the brand was known for.The 28-day cruise will set sail from Miami in Florida on 30 October 2027, and will retrace parts of the Pan Am’s historic routes through the Caribbean and Central America.“Pan Am helped redefine what it meant to travel, turning the journey into an experience filled with discovery, connection and a sense of occasion,” Paul Grigsby, vice president of itinerary planning and deployment for Holland America Line, said. “With this cruise, we’re bringing that era to life while merging elements of Pan Am’s storied history with Holland America Line’s signature experiences, giving guests a chance to see how the legacies of two travel brands come together in ways that feel authentic to both, from the ship to the destinations along the way.”What to expect on boardAirline food today leaves a lot to be desired (at least if you’re in economy class, that is), but the same cannot be said for the plates on Pan Am.Guests on the cruise will be able to try special menus that might once have appeared on board, including cocktail de crevettes, with jumbo shrimp, boiled egg, asparagus and Louis dressing; broiled filet mignon Maître d’Hôtel; and soufflé grand marnier with crème anglaise.Cocktails, too, will be themed, with the Pan Am featuring white rum, Campari, orgeat, lemon juice and egg white, and the Clipper, with rum, Dolin Blanc and grenadine garnished with a lemon twist.The programme will also include talks giving an insight into the airline’s culture and history from people including Linda Freire, the chair and co-founder of the Pan Am Museum Foundation, and David Kliman, a former Pan Am pilot.As for land-based activities, passengers will visit destinations including Cartagena in Colombia, Colón in Panama, St. John’s in Antigua, and Port of Spain in Trinidad & Tobago for Pan Am-inspired excursions.Other Pan Am revivalsLate last year, JP Hospitality announced it would be reviving the Pan Am brand for a collection of airport hotels.The brand plans to open in locations across Europe including Amsterdam, Berlin, Brussels, Copenhagen, Geneva, Lisbon, London, Oslo, Madrid, Milan, Munich, Paris, Stockholm and Vienna, as well as cities around the globe such as Dubai, Bangkok, New York, Tokyo and Sydney.Pan Am Hotels already operates a suite and lounge in Berlin, which have a mid-century design.

title: Deepening tech sell-off drags stocks lower as major markets slide
description: A deepening tech sell-off drags Asian stocks lower as South Korean and Japanese markets sink. European markets open mixed.
content: European markets opened mixed on Thursday morning, while US equity futures fell. Asian shares dropped sharply, with South Korean and Japanese indexes sinking as a technology sell-off deepened following a decline in US stocks on hotter-than-expected inflation data.Germany’s DAX fell 0.13% to 25,272.07 points, while France’s CAC 40 rose 0.42% to 7,905.62 and the broader Stoxx 600 slipped 0.11% to 637.02. In London, the FTSE 100 was up 0.42% to 10,769.21.Markets slide on AI spending concernsAhead of European markets opening, South Korea’s benchmark Kospi index lost 7.7% to 5,548.78. It was well below the 9,000 mark that it crossed in June at its all-time high driven by optimism over the global artificial intelligence frenzy.Samsung Electronics slid 9.5% and South Korean memory chipmaker SK Hynix plunged 11.4%.Japan’s Nikkei 225 tumbled 4.8% to 64,489.06. OpenAI investor SoftBank Group lost 9.4%. Chip equipment maker Tokyo Electron dropped 7.3%, and memory chipmaker Kioxia Holdings lost 11.2%.Taiwan’s Taiex, which also benefited from the AI boom, fell 3%. Its leading chipmaker Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., or TSMC, dropped 2.2% ahead of its earnings report and remained in the red after the company updated investors.Hong Kong’s Hang Seng dropped 1% to 24,071.25. The Shanghai Composite index slipped 1.4% to 3,713.22.Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 edged down 0.1% to 8,715.60.Declines follow Wall Street lossesThe declines followed losses on Wall Street on Wednesday. The S&P 500 dropped 1.1%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average dipped 0.1%, and the technology-heavy Nasdaq composite slipped 1.9% as AI-related stocks fell.Nvidia lost 3.2%, Broadcom gave up 3.1%, and Advanced Micro Devices, or AMD, declined 5.7%.The US reported on Wednesday that the consumer price index rose 3.7% year-on-year in September, up from 3.4% in August and worse than what economists had expected.

title: 'Spain's hallmark in Vatican': The Spanish medical science behind Pope Francis' lung operation
description: Thoracic surgeon Diego González Rivas, based in A Coruña, Spain, developed the Uniportal VATS technique, a minimally invasive procedure using a single incision, which was used in the pontiff's surgery.
content: Pope Leo XIV's lung operation at Rome's Gemelli Hospital has thrown the spotlight on the contribution of Spanish science to thoracic surgery. The procedure, carried out to remove a cancerous tumour from his right lung, used the Uniportal VATS technique developed by Spanish surgeon Diego González Rivas."The Pope has already been operated on; he is on the ward with hardly any pain and recovering very well," the surgeon said in a video released on social media. "The most interesting thing, and the reason why I feel deeply proud, is that he was operated on using our Uniportal VATS technique."González Rivas, who graduated in medicine and surgery from the University of Santiago de Compostela, explained that this is a technique developed in A Coruña in 2010 and that since then "it has been spreading around the globe, reaching 146 countries so far".The doctor expressed his satisfaction at the use of the technique he devised and at the fact that the operation was performed by the Gemelli team, with whose staff he said he has a close relationship. "Spain's hallmark at the Vatican," the physician concluded proudly.The 71-year-old pontiff underwent surgery on Tuesday, in an operation lasting around 90 minutes which, according to the Vatican, went smoothly and as planned. Leo XIV spent a "calm" night and woke up normally, while doctors await test results to determine whether the cancer has spread.What the Uniportal VATS technique involvesUniportal VATS is a minimally invasive thoracic surgery technique that allows surgeons to operate through a single small incision of between 3 and 5 centimetres. A video camera, which guides the operation, and specialised surgical instruments are introduced through this opening.This method makes it possible to carry out complex procedures, such as removing part of a lung, as well as lung or pleural biopsies. Its main advantages include reduced post-operative pain, a shorter hospital stay and faster recovery.However, its use requires thoracic surgeons with experience both in minimally invasive techniques and in conventional surgery, capable of dealing with possible complications during the operation and in the post-operative period.

title: EIB seeks cross-border projects to boost Central Asia’s economic development
description: The European Investment Bank is seeking to expand cross-border investments in Central Asia, while requiring projects to meet environmental standards and offer benefits for both regional economies and European industry.
content: The European Investment Bank (EIB) is looking to expand its financing of cross-border infrastructure projects in Central Asia as it seeks to support economic development across the region.“We would be, of course, very much interested not only in financing the individual country projects, but if there was a cross-country project, it would be even more interesting for us because we would also see a potential for development of the whole region,” EIB Vice-President Marek Mora told Euronews during his visit to Astana.Interstate hydropower plantOne of the most prominent examples of interstate cooperation that the EIB supports in Central Asia is the construction of the Kambar-Ata-1 hydropower plant in the Kyrgyz mountains.The project is being jointly developed by Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, and the EIB allocated €900 million to the three countries for water management projects and the construction of energy grids.The plant, which is expected to be completed around 2035, will be able to generate 5.6 billion kWh of electricity per year. It will greatly contribute to energy security in the region.According to Mora, Europe could also benefit from this project.“We heard some ideas about energy or electricity interconnector between Kazakhstan under the Caspian Sea to Azerbaijan, which could then further continue to Europe,” he said.The water management aspect of this project is important too. The power plant is being built on the biggest river in Kyrgyzstan — the Naryn River. The Naryn merges with the Kara Darya River in Uzbekistan to form the Syr Darya River.The Syr Darya flows through Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan and empties into the Aral Sea. For both countries, it is one of the major rivers supplying water to agricultural land and providing drinking water.The power plant will regulate the seasonal flow of the Naryn River, storing water during periods of snow and glacier melt and releasing it during the dry months. This will provide a more stable and predictable flow of water into the Syr Darya River.Kazakhstan could build industries around transit routesTransport projects are also of great interest to the EIB. The bank recognises the importance of Central Asia’s role as a transport corridor between Asia and Europe.Mora highlighted that Kazakhstan has potential beyond being a transit country.“We have a firm conviction that Kazakhstan does not have only potential as a transit country. We think that around this whole transit industry, there could be its own industry built around it, be it logistics, be it services," Mora said.When it comes to transport investments, there is already a €150 million loan to KazAvtoZhol, Kazakhstan's national road management operator, to improve roads.The project covers key transport routes in Kazakhstan, including access roads to international border crossings, the Caspian route, corridors to China, the southern transit route, and important interregional highways.There is a similar €200mn loan to the Development Bank of Kazakhstan, aimed at both transport and energy."And this was even then enlarged by a letter of intent to increase this amount by €120 million,” Mora added.What does a project need to secure EIB funding?But projects need a lot of preparation to qualify for financing, says the EIB vice-president. They have to be predictable, have clear objectives and methods, and follow transparent procurement rules before the bank is ready to put money on the table.“There are two groups of conditions, which a project would need to fulfil if we were ready to finance it. One is the already mentioned environmental and social standards, to which we put a lot of attention,” said Mora.This means projects linked to the coal industry, coal technologies or gas technologies are excluded from the list of potential investment opportunities. The bank is more interested in green technologies, such as the autonomous truck project, which Mora discussed with Kazakh Minister of Transport Nurlan Sauranbayev during his visit.“We had a very good meeting today with the minister of transport. He mentioned to us one of the possible future projects: that Kazakhstan would build special roads for autonomous trucks, which could cross Kazakhstan. And these trucks could be even electric and maybe of European origin,” Mora explained.The second condition for the EIB to finance a project is a "win-win situation".“A win for Kazakhstan, but also a win for the European economy or the European industry. We would like to see that if we finance a project in Kazakhstan, that, of course, it's there to support the Kazakh industry. But if possible, if there was a European content, it's really something we would be very much interested in,” Mora noted.At the same time, he highlighted that the general development of the region is one of the bank's priorities.“I think water management is, I would say, a global public good. So, the better we do in Kazakhstan, the better we contribute to the world management of this resource, which will become more scarce in future everywhere. And it's already quite scarce in Kazakhstan,” he said.In June, the EIB opened a representative office in Tashkent, Uzbekistan, highlighting the strategic importance of the region.

title: UK economy unexpectedly grows despite fall in consumer spending
description: Britain's economy grew unexpectedly in August, official data showed on Thursday, in a boost to Finance Minister John Healey ahead of the Labour government's budget update this month.
content: Gross domestic product rose 0.1% in August from the previous month, beating analysts' consensus forecast for a 0.1% contraction.The figure still marked a slowdown from the 0.4% expansion recorded in July.Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who has made easing the cost of living a key focus for his Labour government, has set the stage for difficult decisions to be made in the 28 October budget presentation.With inflation rising and government bond yields reaching multi-decade highs, Healey, who will unveil the budget, has pledged to maintain strict fiscal discipline.But he has not been drawn on whether his budget will include new tax rises to help reduce Britain's debt pile.Analysts expect UK inflation to rise towards the end of the year as higher oil and gas prices feed through to household bills, with little sign of an end to the Middle East war."We still expect the coming rise in inflation to dampen growth, but the economy is more robust than we thought," Paul Dales, chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said.GDP in the three months to the end of August grew 0.7%, the ONS noted.Liz McKeown, ONS director of economic statistics, said that "computer programming was once again the largest contributor to growth in the three months to August".The boom in the artificial intelligence sector had also helped drive growth in July."There is a bit of a divergence going on within the economy, with businesses performing well (partly due to AI-related spending) while households are becoming more circumspect," Dales said.Samuel Edwards, head of client portfolio management at financial solutions firm Ebury, sent his comments on the update in a client note to Euronews. He noted how the IMF's gloomier outlook for 2027 suggests the UK is far from out of the woods.“Rising energy prices linked to the ongoing Iran conflict risk reigniting inflation, potentially forcing the Bank of England to raise interest rates further and piling more pressure on households and businesses.“With confidence already fragile, the prospect of further tax rises in the Autumn Budget could see consumers rein in spending and businesses put investment on ice.“Against this backdrop, businesses must strengthen their financial resilience – keeping operations lean, maintaining access to finance and using effective FX hedging to limit exposure to further volatility,” Edwards added.

title: Sally Rooney forced to withdraw sale of books in UK due to support for Palestine Action
description: The best-selling author of “Conversations With Friends” and “Normal People” is being forced to withdraw her books from sale in the UK because of her support for Palestine Action.
content: Sally Rooney, the celebrated and best-selling Irish author behind “Conversations With Friends”, “Normal People” and “Intermezzo”, has said that she can no longer sell books in the UK.Rooney said she is being forced to withdraw her books from sale because of her public support for the organisation Palestine Action, meaning she could no longer receive royalties from UK sales.Rooney’s publisher Faber said: "Current legislation in the UK has led to circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work. To sell a writer's work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher.” "As such, and in full agreement with Sally, we have taken the decision that we can no longer supply her works in the UK in any format," the British publisher said, adding that it would continue to sell her work in other countries and regions.The UK banned Palestine Action last year, with the UK government previously warning Rooney that her support could fall foul of terrorism laws. The "terrorist" organization is not banned in Ireland, where Rooney lives.Thousands of people have protested against the ban and been detained, while rights groups condemning the ban as criminalizing dissent. More than 3,700 people are believed to have been arrested in the UK for alleged support of Palestine Action since it was banned in July 2025.Palestine Action's stated goal on its website is to end "global participation in Israel's genocidal and apartheid regime."In a statement, Rooney said: “‘In July 2025, the direct-action protest group Palestine Action was proscribed as a terrorist organisation in the UK. The following month, I wrote an opinion piece expressing my intention to go on supporting Palestine Action, which is not a proscribed or otherwise prohibited group here in the Republic of Ireland."“As a result, the fulfilment of contracts to publish my work in the UK could now constitute a serious criminal offence. After a process of consultation and deliberation, and with my full agreement, my publisher Faber has therefore determined that it can no longer supply my work within the UK. I have made every effort to be honest with the public about my beliefs and intentions, and I am wholly prepared to accept the consequences.”Huda Ammori, a co-founder of Palestine Action, said: “Sally Rooney being unable to publish her work in the UK marks a new low in the escalating assault on free speech caused by the proscription of Palestine Action … [She] took a brave and principled stand from the moment plans to ban Palestine Action were announced. She has refused to compromise her convictions, even at considerable personal and professional cost.”Ammori added: “Her work should be celebrated and widely available , not driven off the shelves of British bookshops because she refuses to be complicit in the suppression of solidarity with the Palestinian people. No author should have to choose between their principles and their freedom to publish.”

title: ‘They’re not dead yet’: Bleached corals recover in record time after touching healthy clones
description: In the lab, bleached corals recovered within just seven weeks of being put in brief contact with healthy corals.
content: Dying corals may have found an unexpected lifeline: their neighbours.Scientists at Stanford University have discovered a way to bring corals back from the brink of death by placing them in contact with healthy corals for just a few days.Published in Science Advances, the study presents a promising new approach to restoring coral reefs as rising sea temperatures cause more frequent and severe coral bleaching events.When water becomes too hot, corals expel the microscopic algae that provide much of their energy, an event known as bleaching, which leaves them vulnerable to starvation.After bleaching events, it can take months or years for surviving corals to recover – but the scientists contend hope is not lost for them.“While bleached corals may be dying, they are not dead yet,” says lead author Danny Collins, a PhD student at Stanford. “The question we wanted to answer is, once a coral has bleached, what can we do?”How scientists brought bleached corals back to full strengthThe discovery happened by accident in 2025, when Steve Palumbi, a professor of oceans and marine biologist at Stanford’s Doerr School of Sustainability, noticed two pieces of coral that had fallen against each other in a laboratory tank. One was healthy while the other was bleached. But where the two touched, the bleached coral was beginning to regain its colour.Collins then arranged 10 pairs of coral fragments, each containing a healthy and bleached piece from the same colony. Five pairs were placed in contact with one another, and the others were kept a few millimetres apart.Within seven weeks, all five bleached fragments put in contact with their healthy clones had recovered. The ones that were kept apart had died.Under a microscope, the scientists discovered the corals had fused together, creating tiny channels that allowed algae and nutrients to pass from one to the other. Within three days, beneficial algae had begun moving from the healthy corals into the bleached ones. After about a week, some had received enough algae to recover on their own.Once inside the damaged corals, the beneficial algae began multiplying rapidly. “They flood in and start dividing at the fastest rates seen in corals,” says Palumbi.During the second week, the algae doubled in number every four days – about 10 times faster than in wild corals – allowing the damaged corals to continue recovering even after they were separated from the healthy ones. The finding marked a breakthrough in the lab. “Bleached corals are often considered a lost cause because recovery after a heatwave is very slow, if it happens at all,” says Fiorenza Micheli, a Stanford professor and one of Collins’ faculty advisors.But the scientists say the technique isn’t ready for wide-scale application in the oceans.The corals must be genetically identical for their tissues to fuse. In other words, every damaged coral would need a healthy copy of itself – an impractical solution for restoring whole reefs. But the researchers hope to find ways to deliver the beneficial algae without requiring direct contact or identical twins.Coral reefs may be running out of recovery timeThe revelation comes at a crucial time for coral reefs.According to the Global Coral Reef Monitoring Network’s latest assessment, the world's reefs have lost nearly 10 per cent of their living coral over the past four decades. Between 2023 and 2024 alone, it fell almost 9 per cent during a global bleaching event – the largest single-year decline ever recorded.Global bleaching now occurs roughly every five to six years, leaving reefs less time to recover between bouts of extreme heat. The report warns that reefs will continue declining unless man-made emissions fall and threats such as overfishing, water pollution and coastal developments are curbed.And while combining coral to help them recover from bleaching might save some of them, Palumbi stresses that it can’t protect them from rising sea temperatures.“This is a recovery story. It doesn’t blunt heatwaves; it just helps the aftermath. There is still a huge need to reduce heatwaves and protect all of Earth’s life from rapid climate stress,” he says.“Eventually, it can hopefully help the huge effort being put into restoration succeed better by helping those coral gardens survive heatwaves more completely.”

title: 2027 budget: French cinema fears a catastrophic scenario
description: More than 170 figures from France's film industry warn about the impact of the 2027 budget, fearing hundreds of films could vanish if measures like doubling VAT on Canal+ pay-TV offers go through.
content: In an opinion piece published in the newspaper Le Monde, directors and producers denounce the threat posed by the draft 2027 finance bill to the funding of French cinema. The signatories believe that the measures currently being debated in Parliament could lead to the disappearance of 400 films over five years, around 80 productions a year.Among the signatories are several leading figures in French and European cinema, including Jacques Audiard, Costa-Gavras, brothers Luc and Jean-Pierre Dardenne, Claire Denis, Michel Hazanavicius, Agnès Jaoui, Justine Triet, Julia Ducournau, Cédric Klapisch and Alice Winocour."The new finance bill risks wiping French cinema from our screens on a scale never seen before", they write. The authors of the op-ed condemn a build-up of measures likely to weaken the two pillars of funding for the sector: public money and private investment.Budgets for public broadcasting and the CNC cut backOn the public funding side, industry professionals point out that the budget for France Télévisions (which helps finance many films, around 70 a year) is set to fall by 47 million euros by 2027.In addition, the general rapporteur for the budget, Philippe Juvin (Les Républicains), is proposing a 35‑million‑euro levy on the resources of the National Centre for Cinema and the Moving Image (CNC) in 2027. The aim would be to return to the state part of the additional revenue expected from changes to advertising tax rules.The CNC is the beating heart of French cinema: it redistributes money to support writing, shooting, distribution and the screening of films in cinemas. This system has a unique characteristic: it does not cost the state a cent.The CNC is funded by small taxes collected directly on cinema tickets, television and streaming platforms. It is topped up by private copying levies, which apply to devices used to store creative works, such as smartphones, tablets, external hard drives and USB sticks.It is therefore the sector itself that pays for its own creation.The CNC is in fact funded by several earmarked taxes, collected notably on cinema tickets, television channels and streaming platforms. It is topped up by private copying remuneration, which applies to devices that can store works, such as smartphones, tablets, external hard drives and USB sticks.Funding for creation therefore rests to a large extent on contributions collected directly within the sectors concerned and from consumers."French cinema therefore runs without costing taxpayers a single cent", the signatories recall. They also highlight the "major" economic weight of this industry, which generates 260,000 jobs (compared, for example, with 400,000 in the car industry), "brings life to the regions thanks to location shooting and sustains an exceptionally dense network of cinemas across the country".Canal+: fears that a VAT hike could spell the final curtain for hundreds of filmsThe other major threat concerns the private sector, and Canal+ in particular, which is the biggest private contributor to French cinema. In France, Canal+ has a legal obligation to reinvest part of its revenue in funding national film production.The government is considering doubling VAT on pay-TV subscriptions by 2027, raising it from 10% to 20%. To absorb this extra tax, the pay-TV channel could pass the cost directly on to its subscribers or decide to invest far less money in cinema.It is worth remembering, however, that at this stage it is still only a draft budget under examination. There is no guarantee that this VAT hike will be retained in the final version of the 2027 budget.If adopted, the measure could nonetheless have far‑reaching consequences. Filmmakers point out that a cross-industry agreement signed at the end of July stipulates that any increase in VAT for Canal+ would render its investment obligations in cinema null and void. They estimate that such a break would mean a reduction of 750 million euros for film creation between 2028 and 2032."Very concretely, over a five‑year period, this means 400 films simply will not exist", they warn. The most fragile productions could struggle even more to raise finance, with knock‑on effects on shoots, jobs and ultimately the diversity of films available to audiences.Canal+: a love-hate relationshipThe situation is not without irony.In May, during the Cannes Film Festival, several of the signatories to this new op-ed took part in the "Zapper Bolloré" movement, launched by some 600 film professionals to protest against Vincent Bolloré’s growing influence over the sector, notably through Canal+, which belongs to the group controlled by the conservative billionaire.The protest prompted a sharp reaction from Canal+: its CEO, Maxime Saada, then announced that he no longer wished to work with the signatories.A few months on, some of these filmmakers are therefore sounding the alarm about the impact that a VAT hike for Canal+ could have, when its financial contribution remains vital for French production.A paradox that illustrates how dependent French cinema has become on a player whose influence is nevertheless contested by part of the profession.A new law on cinemaBeyond budget measures, the signatories call for a complete overhaul of the sector’s legal framework, still largely governed by the audiovisual law dating back to 1986. They are therefore arguing for a genuine cinema law that would safeguard the "chronologie des médias" – a French rule which sets out how long after a theatrical release a film can be shown on different platforms, from VOD and free-to-air television to Netflix.They also want tighter regulation of artificial intelligence and protection of the remit of the National Centre for Cinema and the Moving Image (CNC).The signatories are urging MPs to back the amendments proposed by professional organisations in support of public broadcasting, the CNC budget and the retention of a 10% VAT rate for Canal+, in return for firm commitments in favour of creation.The filmmakers believe that the stakes go far beyond the sector’s economic balance. Faced with the standardisation of content, which they blame on major US platforms such as Amazon Prime, Disney+ and Netflix, they defend a model which, in their view, helps sustain France’s cultural influence.

title: Flooded homes and rising costs: Why some Thai villages are paying the price to protect Bangkok
description: As climate change causes more frequent and severe flooding, could cities in Europe face the same tough choices?
content: Inside their home, raised more than three metres above the ground in the central province of Ayutthaya in Thailand, Kamonchanok Sathaphonamonwut’s family of three sleeps on makeshift platforms and cannot use the waterlogged toilet.Her village has been flooded six years in a row, pushing some to move away, while others have raised their houses higher."Our area simply cannot cope with this much water anymore," the 34-year-old says as she wades through her soaked home.But while authorities prioritise protecting Bangkok and other business hubs from floods, "when it comes to our residential communities, they neglect us", she says.Flood defences protect cities but leave villages submergedThailand experiences flooding every year during the monsoon season, and scientists say human-made climate change has made heavy rain and floods more frequent and severe.After devastating floods in 2011, the government expanded embankments, water gates and other infrastructure to direct water away from Bangkok, the historic city of Ayutthaya and industrial zones along the Chao Phraya River, which flows through the capital.The defences have largely kept commercial centres safe, but residents of other areas have been left to fend for themselves.Around 20 kilometres from Ayutthaya's centuries-old temple ruins, a UNESCO heritage site, residents say floods that once reached their knees now rise above their heads in some areas and can take several months to recede.Office worker Kamonchanok has been forced to commute by boat and hoist her household appliances and other belongings above the waterline."All we can do is deal with the consequences," she says. "There's only so much we can do to adapt."The 'cruel' cost of flood protectionClimate change, low-lying geography and recently built embankments that have altered the natural flow of the Chao Phraya have contributed to more severe flooding in downstream communities, says Thai irrigation department spokesman Thanet Somboon."Even when water is released from the Chao Phraya Dam at the same rate as before, the impact is greater than it used to be," he explains.And after irrigation channels are completely full of diverted water, he says authorities have "no choice but to discharge the remaining water downstream".But Thanet acknowledges that officials may need to review infrastructure to "ensure floodwater can be kept within the intended limits".Environmental conservationist Sasin Chalermlarp adds the government has done "an excellent job" managing floods across the central plains, but its efforts were "cruel" to those bearing the brunt of the flooding.In low-lying riverside districts that serve as flood retention zones, stretches of villages were left underwater this October, with some homes abandoned and others submerged up to their roofs.Sasin says floodwater that once spread across much of Ayutthaya is now concentrated in just "five to 10 percent" of the province.The rising costs of staying dryAs flooding in hard-hit districts has become more severe, many who remain have paid to lift their stilt houses higher and keep their living space dry.Kamonchanok's family raised their home twice in the 1990s, the second time by 1.5 metres. But floodwater still reached their house in 2011, and again for the past six consecutive years.Raising a house can cost between 100,000 and one million baht (about €2,700-€27,000), depending on its size and height, residents say.Some families have lifted their homes twice in just a few years, exhausting their savings and borrowing to get by.Despite spending more than one million baht (€27,000) to raise her home, Sawong Raksri, 87, has become resigned to the reality she now faces. "It floods like this every year recently. What's the point of complaining?" she says. Could a 'flood-free tax' help?Sasin acknowledges that the area's low-lying land makes it a natural route for floodwater. "But the villagers have no choice. They are being forced to make sacrifices," he says.Sasin, who lives in a protected part of Ayutthaya, has proposed a "flood-free tax" on those who benefit from the defences to help impacted families raise their homes and repair damage.Thanet, meanwhile, says the idea warranted further study to determine "how to support people who sacrifice their land to accommodate floodwater".The government's flagship fix is a €700-million flood diversion canal, designed to carry 1,200 cubic metres of water – around half the volume of an Olympic-size swimming pool – per second around the bottleneck where the Chao Phraya narrows through Ayutthaya.It is expected to be completed by 2030.Until then, Kamonchanok says that her community is not even demanding an end to intentional flooding, but rather a cap on water levels and financial support for those whose homes sit below the flood line."All we're asking for is to be able to live comfortably in our own homes," she says. "Why can't they give us that?"

title: Taiwan chip giant TSMC says net profit hit record in third quarter
description: Taiwanese chip giant TSMC said on Thursday that net profit soared 68.7% to a record high in the third quarter, buoyed by massive global demand for AI hardware.
content: It marked the sixth straight record quarterly net profit for TSMC, the world's biggest contract maker of microchips, including those used in Nvidia AI data centre processors.TSMC's net profit for July to September surged year-on-year to 763.1 billion New Taiwan dollars (€23.6bn), beating analyst estimates of NT$739.5 billion (€22.9bn).The result surpassed its previous quarterly record of NT$706.6 billion (€21.9bn) set in April-June 2026.Quarterly revenue rose 50.9% to NT$1.5 trillion (€46.4bn).TSMC shares were down 2.2% ahead of its earnings report. Following the update, it remained in the red.

title: Europe’s debt map flips: Belgium borrows like Greece as France pays more than Italy
description: Eurozone treasuries are preparing record bond sales for 2027 just as the IMF warns that borrowing costs have hit a two-decade high.
content: Imagine an investor who fell asleep in the summer of 2012, at the height of the euro crisis, and woke up this morning. He would remember a simple map. In the north, a core of countries that borrowed cheaply, with Germany at the centre. In the south, a periphery of debtors – Greece, Portugal, Spain, Italy, Ireland – that paid dearly for the privilege of staying in the single currency. Fourteen years later, that map no longer describes the eurozone.Belgium, home to the European Union institutions, now borrows for ten years at 4.29%. Greece, bailed out three times, pays 4.35%, almost the same rate. Portugal, rescued in 2011, pays less than Spain. Ireland, rescued in 2010, pays almost the same as the Netherlands. And France, which he remembered as part of the core, pays more than Italy.The old periphery has moved north. That is the backdrop against which eurozone governments are about to ask investors for more money than ever before.What moved the borderBond yields are the interest rates a government pays to borrow. They rise when investors think a country will need more money than it can comfortably repay, and they fall when it proves the opposite. Greece has spent a decade proving the opposite.In 2025, Athens ran a budget surplus of 1.7% of gross domestic product (GDP), and its debt, though still the highest in Europe, fell by more than nine percentage points of GDP in a single year.“For years, when markets talked about sovereign risk in Europe, the focus was usually on the periphery,” Ken Egan, head of European sovereign credit at the rating agency KBRA, told Euronews.Over the past decade, he said, those countries have followed more prudent fiscal policy, improved their primary balances, extended debt maturities, collected taxes better through digitalisation and rebuilt their banks.“That has helped smooth refinancing risks and put debt on a much firmer path than 10 or 15 years ago.”Belgium went the other way. Its deficit widened to 5.2% of GDP last year, larger than France’s 5.1% in the same year, and its debt rose above 109% of GDP in the first quarter of 2026, and investors noticed.“The traditional core has changed as well, but in a different direction,” Egan said.“In some cases there is less clarity around the policy path, more political uncertainty, rising structural spending pressures and much higher refinancing costs than governments had become used to during the low-rate period.”France’s position on the map is defined by one figure above all: the state spends 57.2% of everything the economy produces, the highest share in the G20. Debt has reached €3.6 trillion, or 119% of GDP, up from 98.2% before the pandemic.The bill due in 2027On 29 September, the French Treasury set out how much it will need to borrow next year: €340 billion in medium- and long-term bonds, a record, equal to about 11% of GDP and up from €310 billion this year.Much of it is not new spending but old debt coming back for refinancing, as bonds issued during the pandemic and the energy crisis mature.Every euro of that debt is being renewed at a higher price.France has paid an average interest rate of 3.55% on medium- and long-term bonds issued so far this year, up from 3.14% last year. Its annual interest bill is forecast to rise from €62.6 billion in 2026 to €72.9 billion in 2027, roughly a fifth of what the state collected in revenue last year.That last number is the one investors now read first.“Markets are looking much more closely at the fiscal story, and not just at how much governments are borrowing, but what they are borrowing for,” Egan said.“Borrowing that supports investment and future growth is one thing; borrowing mainly to cover a rising interest bill is viewed quite differently.”Germany is issuing a record €512 billion of securities this year, but to pay for defence and infrastructure, which is the kind of borrowing markets forgive.Italy and Spain will each refinance several hundred billion.And the IMF, in its latest World Economic Outlook, pointed to a detail that makes every government more exposed: in the G7 and Spain, nearly 30% of public debt now matures within a year, so a change in interest rates reaches the budget within months rather than decades.Why sovereign yields keep risingBetween February and September, the average 10-year yield across the G7 rose by more than a full percentage point to its highest level in nearly two decades, the IMF’s fiscal chief Rodrigo Valdés and his deputy Era Dabla-Norris wrote this week.The oil shock, persistent inflation and the money pouring into artificial intelligence all played a part. But at the centre, they wrote, are fiscal fundamentals: investors demand more to lend for ten years to governments that keep spending more than they collect.The European Central Bank (ECB) has added to the cost, raising its deposit rate twice this year to 2.50% to contain inflation.The German 10-year yield, the floor for the whole eurozone, has climbed from 2.64% in February to 3.45%. France’s has risen twice as fast and briefly touched 5% in early October, the widest gap with Germany since 2012.The danger, Egan said, is that the market itself becomes part of the problem.“A political headline or weak budget can push the curve higher, refinancing becomes more expensive, fiscal space narrows, and the market then has another reason to demand a higher premium.”That loop turns faster than it used to, because the buyers have changed.For a decade the ECB bought government bonds with newly created money; now it lets them run off.“There is less natural long-duration demand in the market, with central banks stepping back, pension demand changing and more of the marginal buying coming from price-sensitive investors,” Egan said. Higher energy prices, he added, make it worse by “weakening growth while keeping inflation and rates higher”.The IMF describes the result in one sentence: in a growing number of countries, the interest rate on new debt is now higher than the growth rate of the economy.When that happens, debt rises on its own unless the government runs a surplus before interest.Most of Europe does not. “The more countries wait, the more painful the adjustment becomes,” the Fund wrote.Is this 2012 again?Not yet, says Lombard Odier. The Swiss bank’s investment office argues that markets are “pricing uncertainty rather than the conditions for a new sovereign debt crisis”. France’s interest payments remain affordable, at slightly above 2% of GDP, half Italy’s.Its current account deficit is small, and it does not depend on foreign money the way Portugal, Spain and Greece did in 2012, when they imported capital worth 7% to 12% of their economies every year.The bank’s forecast is dull rather than dramatic: French spreads stay wide until a credible budget passes parliament, probably not before the May 2027 presidential election, and the euro drifts lower, to $1.09.Clara Raposo, vice-governor of the Banco de Portugal, offered a different warning this month.Sovereign bond markets, she said, have become more sensitive to inflation, fiscal doubts and geopolitics, and shocks now spread faster from one country to another, amplified by funds that sell first and ask questions later.“Trust may be intangible, but its economic consequences are real,” Raposo said.Your debt, my inflationThe transmission is not only financial.A randomised experiment with German firms in the Bundesbank’s panel, which surveys roughly 7,000 firms, published by the Centre for Economic Policy Research (CEPR) earlier this year, found that half of them think the ECB will hold back on rate rises to protect weaker treasuries.When researchers showed them a pessimistic forecast for the average debt-to-GDP ratio of France, Italy and Spain, the firms raised their expectations for German inflation three years ahead by 1.4 percentage points among those who distrust the ECB.Fiscal stress in one member state, in other words, can raise inflation expectations in another, and the channel is trust.In 2012, the question was whether the periphery could pay. In 2027, the question is who, exactly, the periphery is.

title: Embryo gene editing is getting more precise, but how safe and ethical is the practice? | Euronews Tech Talks
description: The use of a precise gene editing technique to edit human embryos has caught the attention of academics and society, yet doubts over its safety and ethics remain.
content: In the summer of 2026, two studies revived the debate on embryo gene editing, a technique that consists of manipulating the DNA of a human embryo for reasons ranging from better understanding human development to preventing children from developing certain diseases. One study was led by Kathy Niakan at Cambridge University in the United Kingdom, and the other by Dieter Egli at Columbia University in the United States. Both researchers employed base editing, a technique developed in 2016 to alter genetic material with greater precision than earlier methods. Both conducted their research on human embryos instead of mice, and both delivered results which caught the attention of many around the world. Embryo gene editing is not yet a medical reality. Scientifically, modifying the genes of a human embryo is extremely challenging. In addition, no country allows the modification of cells that can be passed on to offspring. With these studies, is society closer to the possibility of safely creating gene-edited babies? What are the ethical concerns surrounding this practice? The studiesUsing base editing, the Cambridge study targeted NANOG, a specific gene which was found to be essential for the formation of future bodies from an embryo. “Base editing represents a significant advance on conventional CRISPR-Cas9 because it carries a far lower risk of causing unintended chromosome errors,” Kathy Niakan said in a press release. On the other side of the Atlantic, Columbia’s research group tried base editing in three genes: one linked to high cholesterol and cardiovascular disease, and the other two related to haemoglobin production. “By introducing such damage using editors, we are starting to understand how human embryos handle damage in their genomes. Long term, we hope to learn how to prevent genetic and developmental abnormalities during IVF to create more efficient, safer, and more affordable fertility treatments,” said Dieter Egli in a press release. According to Robin Lovell-Badge, principal group leader and head of the laboratory of stem cell biology and developmental genetics at the Francis Crick Institute in London, the two studies are on the right path, but there’s room for improvement. “The methods look much safer. But there's still work to do,” he told Euronews Next. “It looks like the levels of mosaicism are low, but not zero. So there's going to have to be more work done there,” he added. Mosaicism is one of the main obstacles of gene editing. It happens when base-editor molecules fail to find and modify certain cells. This phenomenon could potentially cause the development of certain diseases. The ethical debateAlthough research on embryo gene editing might be advancing, several ethical questions remain unanswered. “A question that very often pops up in regard to that is the tension between therapy versus enhancement,” Pascal Borry, professor of bioethics at the University of Leuven, in Belgium, told Euronews Next. “Where do we put the line? What is therapeutic? What is an improvement?” he added. Borry also highlighted other ethical puzzles, ranging from the issue of consent to the problem of stigmatising a community already living with a certain disease. In addition, he underlined that embryo gene editing might not be necessary: “There are many other alternatives to this technology, and I think it’s important to reflect upon that. And I’m thinking about the pre-implantation genetic testing,” he said. Pre-implantation genetic diagnosis is a medical test that takes place during in vitro fertilisation treatment to detect any abnormalities in the embryos. Björn Heindryckx, professor at Ghent University in Belgium and principal investigator coordinating research in the infertility department, agrees with Borry on the non-necessity of using embryo gene editing to prevent certain genetic conditions. Yet, he argues that this technique could still have benefits: “If we understand, and with this tool we can really test it much better, if we can get more insight into embryo development, it will give us more insight into certain forms of infertility.” Badge, on the other hand, is less worried about the ethical implications of this technique. “I don't have a problem with doing it if it's safe and there's a good ethical reason for doing it. I think it's unethical to allow people to have children that have a genetic disorder if you can avoid it,” he explained.According to Badge, countries should regulate the practice; however, they should not adopt a restrictive ban. “Let's say you want to fly to Mars. You're going to be in space for a long time; you're going to have an environment with very high levels of radiation. So you may want to be modified to deal with high levels of radiation,” he told Euronews Next.Euronews Tech Talks is a podcast produced, written, presented and published in English.

title: ‘Plot twist trips’: Why going off-script is the ‘ultimate travel flex’, according to Booking.com
description: In its 2027 predictions report, Booking.com says travellers look set to break out of their comfort zones by taking a trip to do something that’s completely out of character.
content: Fellow travellers, it’s time to forget about that all-too-comfortable beach break and plan to do something that’s, let’s say, not on your usual holiday agenda. That’s the thinking behind the “plot twist trip”, one of nine trends identified in Booking.com’s travel predictions for 2027, which suggest holidaymakers are interested in “going off-script”. Based on research from more than 28,000 travellers worldwide, the report’s findings show that people are rethinking where they are going, who they are travelling with, and how they experience the world. Next year, travellers will “humble everyone who thought they had them figured out” and surprise themselves in the process with “a trip nobody saw coming”, said the online travel platform. And according to the data, 77% are interested in choosing a holiday specifically to do something "completely out of character”.Booking.com said the reaction from others will be “part of the appeal”, with 36% actively wanting to surprise their friends and family with their holiday choices. “These trips are designed to disrupt the status quo, rewrite the story everyone thought they knew, and deliver the twist nobody predicted.” In fact, nearly a third of respondents (29%) have deleted or avoided posting about a holiday “because it felt too predictable or ordinary”.So, will 2027 finally be the year that they have something worth sharing on their socials? As Booking.com puts it: “The best souvenir? The look on everyone else’s face.”From all-exclusives to a hotel in the sky Beyond the plot twist trips, Booking.com’s predictions suggest that travellers want holidays tailored to their lifestyles and budgets. Its “all-exclusive” trend sees 66% of respondents wanting packages that let them remove services they won’t use. "Moving forward, the most appealing travel package isn't the one that includes everything."Meanwhile, “vibe check(in)” finds 81% of travellers would choose a destination primarily based on how they want to feel, rather than where they want to go. Under “social currency”, money could shape the holiday guest list. Half of travellers have reconsidered who to invite on a trip because of spending differences and 38% have removed people from a travel group entirely. The kids may not make the cut either as 61% of parents are keen to travel child-free so they can spend more on themselves. Venturing into the supernatural, 65% are interested in paranormal experiences and a “trip to the beyond”. Nearly half (48%) would seek an experience with the hope of speaking to someone on the “other side”.While back in the working world, the “PTO: powered by AI” trend finds that 64% are interested in having AI cover their work while they’re away.“Hotel in the sky” reflects demand for wellness in the air, with 89% of respondents saying they would take a long-haul journey if it guaranteed they would arrive rested and refreshed.For “sweat synergy”, 66% of respondents who have travelled alone say a shared physical activity or challenge has led to a lasting connection or friendship.Under “trailside therapy”, the new romantic getaway may be more about tough talks with your partner, rather than candlelit dinners. The data found that 47% would consider a trip to resolve conflicts or arguments, with walking and hiking among the activities that help couples tackle difficult conversations.Top trending destinations for 2027 Alongside its predictions report, Booking.com has revealed 10 trending destinations for 2027, including three in Europe: Reims in France, Bratislava in Slovakia, and Pescara in Italy.Reims, France Monterey, California, USA Sendai, Japan Rosario, Argentina Puri, India Christchurch, New Zealand Bratislava, Slovakia Goiânia, Brazil Pescara, Italy Asunción, Paraguay

title: Hidden for 7,000 years: The twisted skeleton baffling German archaeologists
description: Was the Stone Age teenager laid to rest in a twisted pose on purpose, or did the body slip in a sloping grave?
content: Sometimes a dark discolouration in the soil is enough to open a window onto a long-forgotten world. In the Lower Bavarian village of Großköllnbach (Dingolfing-Landau district) just such a clue led to a discovery that is posing new questions for archaeologists: in a pit they uncovered the remains of a person who lived around 7,000 years ago.But it is not just the great age of the find that makes it remarkable. Above all, it is the unusual position of the skeleton: unlike the burials that were customary at the time, the body lies in a striking, twisted posture. The condition of the cervical spine is also puzzling researchers.A burial that breaks the mouldThe discovery came to light during archaeological investigations in the future Steigäcker IV development area. The excavation team had been examining the site for five weeks when what initially appeared to be a nondescript change in soil colour turned out to be a pit containing human bones.For district archaeologist Dr Florian Eibl, it is above all the type of burial that is unusual. The people of the Linear Pottery culture (Linienbandkeramik), one of the earliest farming cultures in Central Europe, often buried their dead in crouched burials. The deceased were laid on their side with their legs drawn up, in a posture resembling a sleeping person.In Großköllnbach, however, the picture is different: the dead person's right leg was bent up extremely sharply, while the left leg was angled outwards. This posture clearly departs from the usual burial practices.The pit itself also raises questions. Its base was uneven and sloping. In the archaeologist's view, the body may have slipped down the incline after being laid to rest. Individual bones could therefore have shifted or been pressed into the soft clay.Was the unusual posture therefore intentional? Or did it only arise because of the conditions in the grave?A young person with striking bonesOne thing is clear from the initial examinations: the dead person was an adolescent, as shown by the growth plates on the bones, which had not yet completely fused.Bones can also provide clues to diseases, injuries and physical strain. The experts are currently paying particular attention to the cervical spine, where a pronounced deformation can be seen. Whether this is due to an illness or a physical peculiarity during life, or only arose because of the position in the grave and after death, still has to be clarified.A detailed anthropological analysis is expected to provide further clues.Discovery among clay ovens and age-old longhousesThe skeleton is not the only remarkable find on the site. The excavations are bringing to light an extensive settlement landscape of the Linear Pottery culture. This culture emerged in the 6th millennium BC and marks the spread of the first farming way of life across large parts of Central Europe.After five weeks of excavation the archaeologists had documented around 150 features. The traces of three large longhouses can be seen in the ground, although at most two of them are likely to have stood at the same time.Particularly revealing are several preserved hearths and cooking areas, including domed clay ovens whose floors were insulated with tightly packed pebbles. This is where food was cooked, grain was processed and, in all likelihood, an important part of communal life was organised.Grinding slabs were also discovered. In the archaeologists' view, the stone used for them may have come from areas beyond the Danube or the Bavarian Forest. If this origin is confirmed, the finds would indicate that even the early farmers were procuring and transporting materials over considerable distances.What happened 7,000 years ago?The excavation site is not open to the public. The skeleton has now been completely recovered and taken to the district archaeology department for further examination. There the bones are to be studied anthropologically. Only then will it be possible to say in more detail what traces this young person’s life has left, and which questions may never be answered.Once the scientific investigations have been completed, the district archaeology service intends to share further findings.Until then Großköllnbach remains a place where the soil reveals not only the traces of an ancient settlement but also the story of a person whose final resting place still poses riddles even after seven millennia.

title: Mont Blanc rises by almost two metres, now standing at 4,807.47 metres
description: An altitude that "is close to the historical value" measured at the end of the 19th century, but still not enough to draw conclusions about the effects of global warming.
content: Mont Blanc has grown higher. The tallest peak in Western Europe now stands at 4,807.47 metres, almost two metres more than in 2023.An altitude that "is close to the historical value" recorded at the end of the 19th century, according to expert surveyors in Haute-Savoie who have been regularly measuring the summit since 2001.However, they are urging caution: this "one-off" reading does not allow any conclusions to be drawn about the effects of global warming. Mont Blanc's elevation varies with the weather, in particular precipitation and winds that shift and redistribute the snow at the summit."Today, the summit is really shaped by the force of the winds and by precipitation, even though this year has been particularly dry," explains Mathieu Dragon, a chartered surveyor in Haute-Savoie.A new technique to study the summitThis year, to refine their observations, the surveyors used ground-penetrating radar to map the ice cap and the rocky peak beneath it.The data collected will help refine their measurements and track how the roof of Western Europe changes over the coming years.

title: FBI arrest Saudi OpenAI employee for allegedly planting recording device in office
description: The ex-OpenAI employee allegedly wrapped a USB device in toilet paper and inserted it into a television located in an "executive conference room".
content: OpenAI said it has alerted the FBI after it found a hidden recording device in an executive conference room in its San Francisco office, which led to the firing of an employee. The suspect was identified as employee Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old Saudi national, who was arrested on October 9, about a week after OpenAI discovered the surveillance device. He made an initial appearance in a US court on Tuesday. He was charged with using or endeavouring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. Alfozan joined OpenAI as an engineer in July 2025. Prosecutors said the device was wrapped in toilet paper and inserted in a USB port on the back of a TV in an executive conference room.He was allegedly spotted near the executive conference room in CCTV footage on multiple dates before the device was discovered, according to the Justice Department.Conversations in the conference room "frequently involved discussions of highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information," the Justice Department said.The allegations come as the US and China race to become the leader in AI, which the Trump administration has pushed to be rebranded as "superintelligence".“We discovered a sophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our offices. We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier,” OpenAI said in a statement posted on X. The ChatGPT maker said it had “no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data”.If convicted, Alfozan faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $250,000 (€200,000) fine, followed by three years of supervised release.

title: Todd Haynes at Lumière Festival: 'It is a time to remember how important it is to protect our freedoms'
description:
"It is a time to remember how important it is to protect our freedoms, and our ability to speak freely."
Euronews Culture sits down with celebrated filmmaker Todd Haynes during this year's Lumière Film Festival.
content: One of the guests of honour this year at Lyon’s Lumière Film Festival is none other than Todd Haynes, one of the most important and singular voices in contemporary American cinema.The celebrated director and screenwriter of Far From Heaven, I’m Not There, Carol, and May December is known for his pioneering work associated with the New Queer Cinema movement of the early 90s. He then gained acclaim for his films exploring the emotional repercussions of social repression and the unspoken desires revealed by marginalized experiences.He attends the Lumière Film Festival to present the restored versions of his directorial debut Poison (1991), a provocative exploration of AIDS-era perceptions. He also presents the Julianne Moore-starring psychological drama Safe (1995), marking the first time that these two films have screened in French cinemas since their initial releases.Euronews Culture sat down with Todd Haynes during the festival to discuss the enduring timeliness of Poison and Safe, his thoughts on the evolving Hollywood ecosystem, as well as his upcoming film De Noche. Euronews Culture: How does it feel to be at the Lumière Film Festival in Lyon, the birthplace of cinema?Todd Haynes: Pretty thrillingly natal! No, really, it's a festival I've been hearing so much about for so long. And it really is such a celebration of movies of all kinds, of every genre, of every era. Restorations are presented, artists are attributed, and it's a really remarkable place and atmosphere, and it's so much about just the filmmaking and the films.There's a retrospective of your films, including two newly restored versions of Poison and Safe. How do you look back on these films, and how do you feel about the fact that there are going to be audiences at this festival who are seeing these two films for the very first time?I was there for the introduction of Poison. People were asked in the theater who were seeing it for the first time and almost every hand went up! And it was a completely full theatre, so that just demonstrates a kind of interest and curiosity about what's being shown in Lyon, and an audience that is very enthusiastic about it.So, it's incredibly meaningful.
