These are my first two features. They are very, very different. Poison came out in the height of the AIDS era and it was among the first couple of films that would join other films in being categorised as the New Queer Cinema. None of which, I don't think, would have been possible outside of that political and socio-economic crisis - the public health crisis of AIDS. In certain times, those kinds of conditions make creating film and documentary, and protest and organised resistance, essential. They drive a kind of urgency that we don't always feel in our medium or our market. That was absolutely true for Poison. And then I made a film [Safe] that also is, in my mind, inconceivable without the AIDS era as a framework. It's a film that takes the place about as far away from the battlefield, if you will, but still engaged. A lot of the themes and issues deal with illness, and the body, and feeling alienated from the world around you... I had the pleasure of re-watching both films, and that sense of isolation in Safe still feels incredibly prescient.That’s always surprising and encouraging to hear. I understand how that might be what people could say about Safe. The film was watched again during Covid. There was a lot of discussion about the film and articles that came out were sent to me. And sadly, these issues remain relevant when we're hit by things that are overwhelming and that challenge every single aspect of the way we lead our lives, and the assumptions about how to live our lives that we take for granted. Both explicitly and implicitly about the AIDS crisis, do you find it heartening or disheartening that Poison and Safe still feel timely? After all, Poison was made at a specific time, and there are many members of the gay, trans, queer communities who continue to feel threatened and continue to express fears...Absolutely. One does feel at times like we’re in a replay, if not crashing backwards in battles we’ve fought. Battles around reproductive rights, around tolerance and acceptance over queer communities and trans communities. Poison in particular addressed very much that sense of vulnerability that the community was feeling under the siege of AIDS and HIV.Jean Genet, who's a writer and thinker and poet and playwright who I've always loved - but also derived a certain energy from his attitude about how important it is to remember that being defined marginal... The goal to that is not necessarily to find your way back to the table and become just like everybody else. For him, his queerness, it came out of a criminal background. He liked that homosexuality had this criminal aspect to it. He used that as a way of weaponising his critique of dominant culture. Poison was made at the very end of the 80s and we needed a voice like that.I'm heartened to see that some of Jean Genet’s books are displayed next to DVDs of your films at the Lumière marketplace...Oh, I didn’t see that. That’s awesome!From a European perspective, when you look at present day Hollywood, it’s hard not to see a sense of regression. For instance, to take a recent example, the Paramount-Warner merger feels like it threatens the financing of films from a plurality of voices. What are your thoughts on the evolution of the studio system and Hollywood at the moment? It's distressing when you see the conglomeration of huge media organizations that one might imagine would provide enough revenue and foundation for risk-taking to still occur. But sadly, that is rarely what you end up seeing. I don't feel it, particularly in the moment, among some of the big streaming companies. There's a sense of wanting to repeat what worked the last time, and keep replicating what the audiences seem to crave. And that's tough. For my last couple films, we've really gone elsewhere. I mean, we did sell May December, my last feature, to Netflix - and they were a fantastic company, full of incredibly smart people who really believed in the film. But the way we made the film was through the limited amount of investment that we absolutely had to have to get it done so we could all retain our creative freedom and identity. That's how we put together the financing for my current film that I'm finishing now, De Noche. And in that case, I really do want a company fully committed to theatrical release.Discourse around film and the creation of film feels in jeopardy at the moment. For example, we saw it this year at the Berlinale with the controversy surrounding Tricia Tuttle and the pro-Palestinian speeches made by invited filmmakers. Do you fear or foresee that cultural institutions will become increasingly threatened by political pressure, like in Berlin? Sure. I think Germany has a unique, specific, and at times contradictory attitudes or laws around how we discuss Israel, for instance. There's this happening on the one hand where speech is kind of being watchdogged and limited, and people have a hard time of just saying that it doesn't have to be about Jewish people to have problems with the policies of Netanyahu, or whoever it may be.But at the same time, the AfD is rising in Germany... So you have that complete sort of disconnect between these two forces - one trying to make remedy after an incredibly horrific past in history, and then all of a sudden, wanting such extreme change to come into place from completely the opposite direction. So, Germany is a unique case, but I think we're feeling similar things about a crackdown on content and what is called ideology or point of view in the United States. It's targeted at the media, it's targeted at the news industries, and it's targeted at universities... So it is a time to remember how important it is to protect our freedoms, and our ability to speak freely.To temporarily move away from the doom and gloom, I wanted to share with you that the first film of yours that I saw was Velvet Goldmine (1998), which had a profound impact on me. I remember seeing the trailer for the first time, watching Brian Slade in his feather outfit on stage, hearing the gunshot followed by the needle drop of T. Rex’s '20th Century Boy', and... it still gives me goosebumps.(Laughs) Awww....The film turns 30 very soon... How do you look back on Velvet Goldmine and please tell me there’ll be a resotration?Oh, it's another film that sort of realised or completed a phase of my creative life that was very profound and deep in that whole era of music and the early 70s. And the very interesting relationship between the UK and the US in how that music came to be. Criterion Collection is working on the release of Poison that will coincide with that 30th anniversary. I'm very, very excited about that.Music plays a big part in your filmography – whether it’s Karen Carpenter, Bob Dylan, The Velvet Underground... I read somewhere that you’re working on a documentary about The Cure... You know, that was news to me! (Laughs) Somebody brought it up... I mean, I love The Cure and they were formative in my life. Their music and evolution as a band from record to record... But no, it's not something I'm doing, and I'm not exactly sure where that came from! (Laughs) Can you blame people for trying to manifest this project into existence? (Laughs) Exactly! Well, glad we got that cleared up! You mentioned your upcoming film, De Noche... You’ve wrapped, right?We've wrapped the film and we're in post-production. We're moving from the picture cut to the sound. The whole production was based in Mexico. And this film was a particular struggle to get to this place, so I'm very proud of it. You mention struggles... Oh well, it began with the relationship with an actor [Joaquin Phoenix] who came to me for it and we moved forward. We got very close to production two years ago, and then he had a very abrupt or unexpected change of heart and walked away. And so De Noche 1 fell apart. But it was remarkable how the financiers and the investors who were there for that version came back, and demonstrated loyalty to the project and a film that means so much to all of us.I’m glad De Noche 2 happened, with Danny Ramirez and Pedro Pascal starring. You also worked with Jon Raymond, who you’d previously collaborated with on the miniseries Mildred Pierce. I’m a huge fan of his work with Kelly Reichardt, especially on Old Joy and First Cow, which is a masterpiece in my book. I couldn't agree more. Jon is a novelist first and has become a screenwriter. I’m so proud to have played even the smallest part in introducing Jon to Kelly when I moved to Portland, Oregon. They met each other, and they really hit it off. Many of his short stories were the first places that she went to in order to resuscitate a career in feature filmmaking that she had kind of put aside. And amazingly, well before she ended up even settling down in the Pacific Northwest, she and Jon really became the chroniclers of that region, its history, of Portland and beyond. So that unexpected move in my life to Portland from New York City... There have been so many rewards from it. And Jon is one of my dearest, closest friends. He's the most fabulous human being.I can't wait to see De Noche. Is there anything else you can tell us about the film? I don't know if I've ever quite seen anything like it before as a concept. It sort of begins as a detective story in the late 30s in a very corrupt Los Angeles, and through circumstances and the corruption that these two characters have become embroiled in, they're forced to leave Los Angeles and flee to Mexico. A very inexplicable, unexpected relationship begins to form between the two of them. To get to that point, a lot of dynamics of divisions between them in terms of power and race are overcome bit by bit, step by step, through the exploration of each other as lovers. It ultimately becomes a love story that that leaves you, I hope, longing and wondering what will happen between these two men.To wrap up, at the opening ceremony of the Lumière Festival, you shared with me that the first film that had a profound impact on you was Mary Poppins. What was it about that film that marked you? For one thing, it was the sort crown jewel of the Disney experiment, in terms of the films that came out of Disney at that time. The score is so exquisite, the two actors who take the leads are just perfection, it's so beautifully produced... I think for a three-year-old's imagination, there’s something about a maternal subject who comes with unique powers, and also discipline. Just a curious combination of various aspects of that character. I think seeing a movie on the big screen for the first time can't be overstated. The sheer power of that... I think all of those things conjoined to make it a sort of escapable moment of introduction to this medium. This year has been a very good one in terms of cinema attendance and that being mirrored at the box office. Still, there are cinemas struggling and many fears expressed about the threat that artificial intelligence represents for the creative arts. As broad a question as this is, are you optimistic about the future of cinema?I have to be optimistic. Because it's a medium I just love. I wasn't able to shoot De Noche on film, as we couldn't afford it, but it will always be my starting point on any film that I make. And what you are seeing among young people is an incredible desire to go out of their houses and leave their home screens and their phones behind and join in the experience of watching a movie on the screen. You know how we all thought vinyl was going to go away with the introduction of CDs and MP3 and there was a sort of counter movement that was like ‘No, I want to hold it in my hand'... The desire to actually experience it and the warm resonance of hearing vinyl play with a needle on... Sometimes the simplest technology remains the best and the most profound. I hope that continues and I hope we can see that still being played out. It is about younger people and exposing them to what that experience means, and what that's like to share communally in a theatre in the dark.On that note, Mr Haynes, thank you very much for your time.The Lumière Film Festival takes place until 18 October in Lyon, France. The restored versions of Todd Haynes' Poison and Safe are being screened, as well as Far From Heaven and I'm Not There. Safe is out now on Criterion 4K UHD Blu-ray.Todd Haynes' new film, De Noche, finished shooting in April 2026. No release date has yet been announced.

title: IEA warns diesel prices in Europe could rise as global crunch lasts into 2027
description: Europe could face renewed wholesale diesel price rises in the coming weeks, the International Energy Agency warned on Wednesday, as disrupted supplies leave markets tight well into 2027 despite recovering Gulf oil output.
content: Diesel markets will remain tight well into 2027, and wholesale diesel prices in Europe could rise again in the coming weeks, the International Energy Agency (IEA) warned on Wednesday.In its monthly report, the Paris-based energy watchdog said recovering Gulf oil supplies had failed to resolve the fuel squeeze, with global output still falling short of consumption.Supply rose by 2.5 million barrels a day (mb/d) to 102.3 mb/d in September on a Saudi-led jump in Gulf crude exports to more than three-quarters of pre-war levels, but remains slightly below global demand of around 103.5 mb/d, the IEA estimated.The war that began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran on 28 February is far from over.Iran has choked the Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world’s oil, and recently stepped up attacks on ships there, while Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels are striking Saudi oil sites."Renewed attacks in the Gulf leave the recovery fragile," the IEA stated.On Tuesday, Britain’s maritime security agency UKMTO said projectiles of unknown origin had hit a tanker and a container ship in the strait.Early on Wednesday, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said a container ship carrying more than 2,500 containers sank south of the strait after hitting a naval mine and catching fire, claiming it took an unauthorised route and warning others of continued dangers in the maritime chokepoint.Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil prices, rose around 1%, spiking above $107 per barrel in early trading on Wednesday, but it later pared gains and is hovering around $106 at the time of writing.Meanwhile, the US benchmark, West Texas Intermediate, has traded flat at roughly $94.75 per barrel.Diesel crunchDiesel prices have retreated from September’s records above $200 a barrel, but benchmarks "remain nearly double the price of crude oil and their pre-crisis levels", the IEA stated.With Middle Eastern fuel exports below half of their pre-war levels and Russian refineries hit by Ukrainian drones, diesel supplies remain under pressure.Rising shipping costs could add to that pressure."As tensions in the crude freight market have spread to other tanker categories, delivered diesel prices in the dominant gasoil importing markets – Europe, Africa and Latin America – could rise again in the coming weeks," the IEA said.The IEA said lost diesel stocks were unlikely to be replenished beyond normal seasonal changes before the second half of 2027.The G7 pledged on 2 October to release up to 100 million barrels of emergency stocks through the IEA, diesel first.However, an internal document seen by Euronews shows this would cover barrels still owed under March’s 400 million pledge, 326 million of which have been released, rather than add to it.Diverging demand viewsThe IEA now expects high prices and weaker growth to cut global oil demand by 2.6 mb/d this year to 102.4 mb/d, slightly more than the 2.5 mb/d drop it forecast last month.It also trimmed next year’s rebound to 2 mb/d from 2.6 mb/d, meaning 2027 demand would stay 0.6% below 2025 levels instead of edging above them.On the other hand, OPEC, the oil exporters’ group, is more upbeat.It lowered its forecast for 2026 demand growth for a sixth month running on Tuesday, to 180,000 barrels a day from 380,000, but raised its 2027 estimate to 2.55 mb/d from 2.36 mb/d, expecting stocks drained by the war to be rebuilt.Crude output from OPEC+, which includes Russia, rose by about 900,000 barrels a day to 39.07 mb/d in September, OPEC said.Seven core members kept November targets unchanged on 4 October, with most pumping below quota due to the war, and will meet again on 1 November. The UAE quit both groups in May.Unless the conflicts in the region are resolved, "oil markets may experience more turmoil in the months ahead before any eventual surplus emerges in 2027", the IEA warned as its board meets on Thursday.

title: Rutte urges allies to send more air defence to Ukraine
description: NATO Secretary General, Mark Rutte said allies need to do more to support Ukraine, especially in air defences. His pleas come amid drastic Russian escalation over the skies in Kyiv.
content: Mark Rutte has urged NATO countries to step up military aid to Ukraine - in particular air defences - as Russia continues to pummel Kyiv with hundreds of drones and ballistic missiles every day.Over 600,000 people across Ukraine were left without electricity on Wednesday after deadly Russian strikes, Ukrainian President Zelenskyy said."With winter coming, and with Russia’s aggression unrelenting, Allies need to do more, especially in support of air defence," Rutte told journalists in a press conference in Tallinn alongside Estonian Prime Minister, Kristan Michal.The NATO chief is meeting the Ukrainian president in Brussels on Thursday, on the margins of an EU summit of European leaders, Euronews can confirm.The two are gathering amid major tensions between the US and Ukraine over Kyiv's targeting of Russian diesel infrastructure.US President Trump threatened to cut off vital intelligence sharing on ballistic missile attacks with Kyiv over Ukraine's continuing targeting of Russian diesel infrastructure. Gas and oil are Russia's most important assets and provide the Kremlin with the capital to keep its war against Ukraine going.'Intelligence helps save lives'And in recent days, Zelenskyy said his country was given no warning ahead of a mass of ballistic missiles which rained down across the capital."A Russian ballistic missile attack on Kyiv. Once again, no early warning from our partners," Zelenskyy said on Tuesday."Our systems detected these missiles only when they were already virtually on approach to Kyiv," he said on "X".“Intelligence on Russian ballistic missile launches helps save lives, and this is one of the most critical issues. This is precisely what helps prevent people from being killed — when there is an early warning about ballistic missiles," said Zelenskyy.Washington rolled back sanctions on Russian diesel and President Donald Trump confirmed the US could buy the stock in a bid to ease surging prices in the US.Trump has demanded Zelenskyy halt the targeting of diesel plants saying it was this - rather than the US-Israel war in Iran - that is responsible for skyrocketing prices.Rutte brushed off the question of the US withdrawing intelligence to Ukraine when asked by reporters. He pointed to a brief response from Trump on Tuesday where the president denied withholding the intel."I think the President was very clear yesterday when he had a short moment with the media leaving the White House for a campaign event, when he said intelligence sharing has not stopped," he told reporters.Both Rutte and the Estonian prime minister said the Kremlin was aiming to deter European allies from helping Ukraine."Russia wants us to focus on our own problems and grow weary of supporting Ukraine. We must not let that happen. Estonia will continue to provide military support to Ukraine," said Michal.

title: Lufthansa beats Air France-KLM to €1.2bn stake in TAP Air Portugal
description: Portugal has chosen Lufthansa to buy a 44.9% stake in TAP, completing the first phase of the airline’s privatisation. The deal still needs regulatory approval.
author_name: Ana Filipa Palma, Ema Gil Pires
content: The Portuguese government announced after Wednesday's cabinet meeting that German carrier Lufthansa had been chosen to buy a 44.9% stake in TAP as part of the Portuguese airline’s privatisation."The government is successfully bringing to a close the first phase of the privatisation of our national airline. A process conducted with strict respect for competition, a stringent approach to negotiations and complete transparency vis-à-vis the Portuguese public," Portuguese prime minister Luís Montenegro said.The prime minister then announced that, after assessing the bids, the government had opted for the Lufthansa Group, "whose financial offer is 16% higher than the rival proposal and carries a lower degree of uncertainty."The transaction will bring in "€1.201 billion in this first phase" and the state will retain a majority stake of 50.1% in the company. "Lufthansa will be responsible for executive and operational management," he said."This is an offer that gives the airline a total valuation of €2.552 billion. A figure far above the independent valuations put forward a few years ago or even just a few months ago," he added.Montenegro also stressed the "ambitious strategy" in the aviation sector, particularly when it comes to airport infrastructure.As a result, "we are ensuring the growth of TAP, the growth of the fleet, the growth in passenger numbers, the growth in destinations and routes, and also the growth in investment, not only in TAP but across the entire aeronautics sector in Portugal," he said.The proposal will support further investments, including €500 million to set up a new pilot training school in Tancos, an innovation centre in Aveiro and a corporate services centre, in addition to the already announced investment by Lufthansa Technik in Santa Maria da Feira.Montenegro also pointed to plans to create jobs. "We are envisaging 3,000 associated jobs linked to TAP's projected growth and a total of 5,500 direct and indirect jobs across all these investment initiatives in our country."Miguel Pinto Luz, minister for infrastructure and housing, set out the offer in detail, highlighting plans to expand the fleet to 117 aircraft by 2035 and 130 after 2035. Up to eight Airbus A350-900s are also due to be transferred to TAP from 2030 onwards.The proposal also includes investment in Francisco Sá Carneiro Airport, the strategic base for the entire operation, as well as in Faro Airport and the airports in Portugal’s autonomous regions.At the end of September, Air France-KLM and Lufthansa submitted their respective final bids to acquire 44.9% of the Portuguese airline's share capital, according to Parpública, the company that manages state holdings.A further 5% of the company’s shares are reserved for employees. However, under the decree-law on TAP's privatisation, published in August and cited by Lusa, the chosen private investor — in this case Lufthansa — may also buy any shares not bought by employees. The state will retain the remaining 50.1%.According to Portugal's business press, TAP posted a loss of €99.2 million in the first half of 2026, 40% higher than a year earlier.The finance minister, Joaquim Miranda Sarmento, said last week that the privatisation process would only be concluded in 18 to 24 months, in 2028, after approval from the European Commission.

title: Russia’s internet shutdowns push state firms back to landline phones
description: State procurement of landline telephones tripled in the first eight months of 2026 as mobile internet outages hit nearly 80% of the country. Rostelecom’s chief urged Russians to keep one at home “like a fire extinguisher".
content: Russian state-owned companies spent more than three times as much on landline telephones in the first eight months this year as in the same period in 2025, as mobile internet shutdowns affecting nearly 80% of the country push ministries and businesses to seek alternatives to disrupted networks.Procurement data cited by the Russian business daily Vedomosti show spending at 118 million roubles (€1.26 million) from January through August, with the number of purchase tenders up 12.5%.Purchases are concentrated in the country’s largest business and infrastructure hubs.Market participants told Vedomosti that the surge was driven by the restrictions, a shift by Russian ministries and companies to domestically produced software-based PBX systems after Western vendors withdrew from the Russian market following the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, and demand for secure communications channels.Russia began systematically shutting down mobile internet access in May 2025, when services went offline in more than 40 regions ahead of Victory Day celebrations. What were initially episodic outages quickly became routine.An independent monitoring project recorded 655 mobile internet outages in June 2025, rising to 2,099 in July, a figure that exceeded the worldwide total for the entire previous year, according to analysts.The disruptions have hit banking, taxi services, food delivery and navigation, particularly in rural areas.The authorities have justified the shutdowns as a defence against Ukrainian drones, which they say are guided via mobile internet signals.Experts have disputed this, saying drones can fly preset routes without a network connection, and the shutdowns have reached regions far from the front line.In March, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the presidential administration “uses landline telephones” when asked how restrictions in central Moscow affect the work of the president’s office.Shortly after, head of state telecoms company Rostelecom Mikhail Oseyevsky urged Russians to return to fixed lines.“Like a fire extinguisher, there should be one in every home," Oseyevsky said.Russia has approximately 12.2 landline telephones per 100 residents. In Moscow, around 2 million households use fixed lines provided by MGTS, the city’s main telephone operator.Across the country, there are about 17.4 million urban household landline connections.The Ministry of Economic Development forecasts that the number of all landlines will fall to between 8.2 and 8.5 per 100 residents by 2029.

title: US inflation rises to 3.7% as fuel costs climb ahead of midterms
description: Higher petrol prices and airfares pushed US inflation to 3.7% in September, adding pressure on households and the Federal Reserve weeks before the midterm elections.
content: US inflation accelerated last month as petrol, clothing and airfares became more expensive, adding pressure on households just a few weeks before the midterm elections.The consumer price index rose 3.7% in September compared with a year earlier, the US Department of Labor said on Wednesday, up from 3.4% in August. On a monthly basis, prices jumped 0.6%, up from 0.4% the previous month.The annual figure was above the 3.6% forecast by economists surveyed by data provider FactSet.The figures underscore the lingering impact of the Iran war on petrol prices and the persistence of inflation, which fell sharply from a 9.1% peak in 2022 but has risen since the war began in late February.Excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core prices rose 2.6% from a year earlier, up from 2.4% in August. Monthly core inflation held at 0.3%.“CPI came in at 3.7%, slightly above expectations, and similarly core inflation was above predictions, suggesting that prices are feeding into the wider economy,” said Richard Carter, head of fixed interest research at Quilter Cheviot.Elevated inflation has posed political problems for Republicans in Congress and complicated the Federal Reserve’s efforts to bring price rises under control.A poll by The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research found that just 17% of US adults approve of President Donald Trump’s handling of the cost of living. Only 26% approve of his handling of the economy overall, a new low.Markets react: Will the Fed raise rates again?Following the higher-than-expected inflation figures, major US stock indices turned negative. Gold fell more than 1.7% to $4,105.50 an ounce, while silver was down more than 4% at $56.91 an ounce.Oil prices were mixed, with international benchmark Brent trading just above $105.70 a barrel, close to its opening level. US benchmark WTI rose 1.4% to $95.50 a barrel.Bond yields jumped following the news. The policy-sensitive two-year US Treasury yield rose 13 basis points to 4.93%, as traders increased bets on further Fed rate rises. The benchmark 10-year yield climbed about eight basis points to around 5.3%.Inflation moving further away from the Federal Reserve’s 2% target was the “last thing” global bond markets needed, according to Robin Brooks, a former Goldman Sachs economist and a senior fellow in economic studies at the Brookings Institution.Carter warned that persistent inflation could push US government borrowing costs higher. “It is not inconceivable that ten-year Treasury yields continue to march higher,” he said.The figures add pressure on the Fed as it weighs whether to raise rates again at its next meeting on 27–28 October.Last month, the central bank raised rates for the first time in three years, to a range of 3.75%–4%. Fed chair Kevin Warsh said inflation was not falling quickly enough towards its target.“The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long,” Warsh said at a news conference last month. He added that summer inflation reports “do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved”.Some Fed officials have since suggested they can wait before raising rates again, although their latest projections point to one more increase this year.Higher borrowing costs can slow spending and growth, helping to ease inflation. But they cannot resolve supply disruptions such as those caused by the Iran war, leaving the Fed trying to prevent higher energy costs from feeding into broader price rises.Higher fuel costs feed through to other pricesWarsh has said his goal is to keep the petrol price spike from spreading to other areas of the economy. Higher fuel costs have already helped push airfares up by about 23% from a year ago.Petrol prices jumped about 9% from August to September, driving much of the overall increase in inflation.Prices at the pump have eased in recent weeks, though they remain higher than a month ago. Petrol averaged $4.34 a gallon nationwide on Tuesday, up a few cents from a month earlier.Higher fuel prices also raise shipping costs for businesses, some of which pass those costs on to consumers. Last week, PepsiCo said it would raise prices for some snacks and soft drinks to offset higher costs for fuel, aluminium and food ingredients.The expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure has also sharply increased the cost of semiconductors, computer equipment and electrical components, feeding through to prices for consumer electronics such as gaming devices, laptops and smartphones.

title: Holidays remain a ‘spending priority’, but ‘cost-conscious’ travel is on the rise, report reveals
description: Travellers are planning on booking cheaper accommodation and eating out less while away, rather than giving up holidays completely.
content: It has been quite the year for the travel industry, with the Middle East conflict and heatwaves causing major disruption for holidaymakers while the cost of living crisis has seen people tightening their belts.But that hasn’t stopped people from prioritising their vacations, with 70% of adults planning to travel abroad in the next 12 months, according to ABTA’s Holiday Habits report 2026/27.Based on polling of more than 2,000 adults based in the UK, the new research shows that holidays are still a “priority”, but that “cost-conscious” travel is on the rise.Just 7% of people said that the cost of living crisis would mean they would not go on holiday at all next year, but 21% said they would book cheaper accommodation, and 19% would eat out less while away.Package holidays are proving popular as a result of the cost of living crisis, with 48% of those booking one saying they were doing so as it was the best value option for the price, up from 43% last year.While the percentage of people who took a cruise in 2026 is stable (13%), the percentage of people planning to do so next year is rising (17%), and the reasons for doing so are reflecting the need for cost-conscious trips.Some of the main reasons cited for booking a cruise are value for money (52%, up from 49%) and being able to pay for everything up front (40%, up from 38%).“We continue to love our holidays and the desire to travel remains strong; this looks set to continue despite the ease of getting away, for some, being affected by geopolitical and economic challenges,” Mark Tanzer, chief executive of ABTA – The Travel Association, said.“When times are uncertain, booking with an expert ABTA member gives holidaymakers added confidence. And, in a ‘value for money’ market, they are excellently placed to find people a fantastic holiday at a budget that works for them.”City breaks overtake beach escapesCity breaks were the most popular holiday type in the last 12 months for UK travellers, with 53% of those polled going on one, up from 48% last year, while 49% of people went on a beach break.Of those surveyed, the third most popular type was a countryside break (23%), followed by a multi-destination trip (16%), adventure holiday (14%), cruise (13%), lake and mountains (10%), and wellness (9%).Europe remained the most popular choice for holidays, with certain destinations seeing an uptick in visitors as people avoided the Middle East or avoided travelling via the region.For Brits, the top country over the past 12 months was Spain, with 36% of those surveyed having visited. Portugal overtook Germany as the sixth most visited destination, behind France (24%), Italy (15%), the US (14%) and Greece (12%), with 11% having visited.The top 10 was rounded out by Türkiye, Australia and Cyprus.

title: Gothic getaways, un-adulting and trip snacking: Expedia ‘unpacks’ its top travel trends for 2027
description: Travellers will be going full Kate Bush, indulging their inner child and taking shorter breaks in between their bigger holidays next year and beyond.
content: ‘Tis the season. No, not that season – there are still 11 weeks until Christmas. Not Halloween, either, or even Gilmore Girls-rewatch time.We’re of course referring to the glorious season when all the industry trends reports are released, and the latest travel company to share its predictions is Expedia Group.Pulling on insights from Expedia, Hotels.com and Vrbo, as well as a survey of 26,000 travellers across 16 countries, plus social media data, Unpack ’27 has identified five key travel trends.“Travel is about creating memories, and Unpack ’27 uncovers the destinations and experiences shaping those moments,” said Ariane Gorin, CEO of Expedia Group. “In 2027, travellers are being more intentional in choosing their next adventure, seeking experiences that are more personal and purposeful to them.”The travel trends to know in 2027According to Expedia Group, indulging your inner child will be the move in 2027, with travellers swapping the mundane facets of day-to-day life for playful getaways involving theme parks, water parks or other nostalgic activities.Some 57% of travellers say they will book a so-called “un-adulting” trip in 2027, rising to 71% among Gen Z and Millennials.Top options for embracing the trend? Disneyland Tokyo, Colour Factory Chicago and Park Xcaret in Mexico.This year was all about “snackpacking”, aka trying crisps, chocolate and other supermarket treats, but in 2027, we’ll be embracing “trip snacking”.Meant to satisfy a different type of appetite, trip snacking involves quick, spontaneous getaways that can ease the break between longer, less-frequent trips.Some 79% of travellers are planning to book a one-night stay in the next year, with searches for one-night stays up 10% on Hotels.com.Wuthering Heights hit screens in 2026, bringing with it a revival in appreciation for all things Gothic.Some 56% of travellers have booked hotels specifically for the atmosphere or aesthetic, with 65% of these interested in booking a Gothic-style hotel, whether that be a historic castle or a destination steeped in folklore or the supernatural.The numbers speak for themselves: The “Gothic Getaways” trend has seen a 20% increase year-on-year in demand for castles, according to Hotels.com.“Skillcations” were a big trend in 2026, and that is set to continue in 2027 with “hobby hubs” – travellers specifically booking holiday homes for crafting weekends, photography retreats, mahjong game nights and antique-hunting breaks.Last but not least, “heartland hideouts”, aka hidden gem destinations that are landlocked, are on the rise, too.

title: Meet the 76-year-old Kazakh traveller on a mission to walk around the world
description: Sarsenbay Kotyrashov began travelling on foot in his 70s. After walking across Kazakhstan and through parts of Asia and Europe, he is now preparing to cross the US.
content: It is hot and noisy inside the blacksmith workshop. Sarsenbay Kotyrashov, a 76-year-old blacksmith, wipes the sweat from his forehead as he works with a piece of hot iron.“There is a Kazakh verse that goes: ‘I’m as soft as iron and as white as coal,’” Kotyrashov says with a laugh.There is something of the iron he works with in his own character. Kotyrashov was introduced to blacksmithing at an early age and has practised the craft ever since. Years of hard physical work seem reflected in the strength and endurance that now take him far beyond his workshop.“I had never travelled far in my life. But it is never too late to travel. Age doesn’t matter,” Kotyrashov says.In 2022, he finally set out on his first long-distance journey. Starting in his native Ulytau region, Kotyrashov crossed Kazakhstan entirely on foot. His route took him through the south of the country, then east and north, before finishing in the west, on the shores of the Caspian Sea in Aktau.The 8,000-kilometre journey took him six months. By the end of it, Kotyrashov realised he could go even further. He decided to push himself beyond Kazakhstan’s borders and, for the first time in his life, set foot in another country.Later, setting off from Atyrau in western Kazakhstan, Kotyrashov crossed into Russia and continued through the Caucasus, eventually reaching Türkiye and Istanbul. Along the way, he met people from different cultures and saw places he had never visited before. The experience only fuelled his appetite for more.By then, Kotyrashov had adopted the nickname Ulytauman, a reference to his native region. His distinctive look — a lean but strong figure in a hat, pulling a suitcase covered with stickers from the places he had visited — became increasingly recognisable. People began posting photos and videos of him on social media and stopping him for selfies along the way.His next destination was China. Setting off from Oskemen in eastern Kazakhstan, Kotyrashov made his way through Russia’s Altai region and Mongolia before reaching Beijing. The journey eventually brought him to one of China’s most famous landmarks, where he posed for a photograph on the Great Wall.On his latest journey, in 2026, Kotyrashov secured funding, obtained a Schengen visa and walked through five European countries. He started in Belgrade, Serbia, then continued through Hungary, Austria and Germany before reaching Paris, France, covering around 3,000 kilometres in 53 days.Kotyrashov recounts the long list of countries he has crossed on foot almost like a tale, moving from one place to another and drawing his listener into the journey.But as he retraces his journeys from memory, he also recalls some of their most difficult moments. “Once, I spent three and a half days out in the wilderness without food or water. It turns out a person can endure it. If you have the will and desire to live, you can endure anything,” he says.Then the conversation takes a lighter turn as Kotyrashov shifts to one of his most recognisable travel companions — his signature leather hat.“I’ve travelled through five European countries wearing this. Now, God willing, I’ll conquer America next,” he says.Now, Kotyrashov is preparing to walk across eight US states in 2027, travelling from the Atlantic to the Pacific coast. The journey is part of a bigger ambition. Kotyrashov says he hopes to enter Guinness World Records by covering more than 40,000 kilometres on foot after the age of 75.With a mischievous smile, Kotyrashov adds: “I don’t consider myself old. Until I complete this plan and make it into the Guinness World Records, I won’t consider myself old.”

title: World’s oldest shipwreck off Turkey: 4,700-year-old amphorae discovered
description: The shipwreck found near Antalya’s Kekova Island, dated to roughly 4,400–4,700 years ago, sheds light on maritime trade in the eastern Mediterranean.
content: Underwater excavations carried out off the island of Kekova in Antalya have brought to light amphorae dating back around 4,400–4,700 years. The finds, which are said to belong to a wreck from the Early Bronze Age, are expected to shed light on Anatolia's maritime history and trade links in the Eastern Mediterranean.Turkey's Minister of Culture and Tourism Mehmet Nuri Ersoy, in a post on his social media account, underlined the importance of the ancient vases recovered during the excavations, saying: "In our 'Blue Homeland', we are bringing to light traces of the world's oldest shipwreck."Clay analyses carried out on the amphorae, which are thought to have been used to transport olive oil or wine, indicate that the jars were probably produced in workshops in the Jordan Valley. The discovery of similar examples in Egypt, Troy and Crete reveals traces of trade and cultural interaction between different regions.Ersoy stated that they would continue to illuminate Anatolia's maritime history with new findings and to preserve the underwater cultural heritage for future generations. The minister also congratulated Associate Professor Hakan Öniz, who's leading the scientific excavations, and the team involved in the work.How was the wreck off Kekova found?Amphora samples taken from the remains of a wreck identified off the island of Kekova during underwater surveys carried out in previous years by Akdeniz University showed that the ship may date back to the Early Bronze Age.Acting on permits from the Ministry of Culture and Tourism, excavations in the area began in 2026 under the leadership of the Antalya Museum Directorate.The fact that similar vessels have been found near the pyramids of Giza, Saqqara and Abusir in Egypt, as well as in Troy and Crete, suggests that the cargo carried by the wreck may have been linked to an extensive trade network. Researchers believe that the ship set sail from a port on the Levantine coast and headed towards Troy or Crete.An amphora marked with nine signs sheds light on sailors' livesOne of the amphorae found in the excavations stands out with two holes in its body and nine distinct marks on it. Initial examinations suggest that the jar may have been a churning amphora used in the production of cheese or butter.This possibility raises the prospect that sailors of the period may have carried goats on long voyages, milked them on board and produced their own dairy products. The finds therefore contribute not only to research into the transport of commercial goods, but also to studies on the everyday conditions of sea journeys and eating habits.

title: Brian Cox awarded 2026 Stephen Hawking Medal for Science Communication
description: British physicist and broadcaster Brian Cox has been awarded the 2026 Stephen Hawking Medal for Science Communication, recognising his work bringing complex scientific ideas to audiences around the world.
content: Cox was presented with the award at a private ceremony at the Royal Astronomical Society in London on 2 October, by co-founders of Starmus, Sir Brian May and astrophysicist Garik Israelian. STARMUS is a global platform for science, art, and human inspiration that brings together some of the most brilliant minds on the planet.The medal, established by Starmus with Stephen Hawking a decade ago, honours outstanding science communicators across disciplines and creative forms – from literature and broadcasting to music, film and art – who are helping bridge the gap between science and society, spark curiosity and make science accessible to all. “It’s a great honour to receive the 2026 Stephen Hawking Medal from Starmus, and particularly poignant for me because I was there with Stephen when the Medal was first announced 10 years ago,” Cox said at the ceremony. “Astronomy is the oldest science, and in today’s fractured world I believe that striving to understand the Universe is more important than ever,” Cox added.“The Stephen Hawking Medal was born from a shared belief that science should inspire people far beyond the scientific community,” May said. He also emphasised this message was particularly important at a time when “truth, evidence, and critical thinking are increasingly challenged”. Stephen Hawking Medal recognises Cox’s accessible science Cox is one of Britain’s best-known science communicators. He has presented television series including Universe and The Planets, written books such as The Quantum Universe and delivered lectures around the world. He currently serves as Professor of Particle Physics and Royal Society Professor for Public Engagement in Science at the University of Manchester. His work attempts to enlighten the public on subjects ranging from the smallest building blocks of matter to the origins and eventual fate of the Universe – ideas that are not always easy to explain while keeping an audience engaged. Alongside Cox, this year’s medal winners are filmmaker Ridley Scott, the Artemis II crew, Nobel Laureate Geoffrey Hinton, and 17-year-old Valeria Corrales, who receives the Stephen Hawking Medal Junior. Christiana Figueres, a key figure in brokering the 2015 Paris climate agreement, will also be awarded the inaugural Jane Goodall Earth Medal. Previous recipients of the Steven Hawking medal include broadcaster David Attenborough, astrophysicist Neil deGrasse Tyson, marine biologist Sylvia Earle, filmmaker Christopher Nolan, composer Hans Zimmer and musician Brian Eno. The NASA communications office has also received the award. The medal’s design reflects the unique mix of science and culture at the heart of Starmus’ vision. One side features a portrait of Hawking by Soviet cosmonaut Alexei Leonov, while the other depicts Leonov during his historic spacewalk, alongside an image of Brian May’s ‘Red Special’ guitar associated with rock band Queen. During the London ceremony, Cox, May and Israelian discussed astronomy, humanity, music, artificial intelligence and Hawking’s enduring legacy. Cox was also presented with an OMEGA Speedmaster Moonwatch crafted in 18K Moonshine Gold. ‘The Search for Truth’ continues at the 8th Starmus Festival The award will be celebrated as part of Starmus VIII Festival, which takes place on the Canary Islands from 17 to 22 October. This year’s festival, themed ‘The Search for Truth’, will bring scientists, astronauts, Nobel Prize winners, artists and musicians together across Tenerife and La Palma. The location is fitting for such a celebration, with both islands recognised for the quality of their night skies and astronomic facilities, the latter protected as a Starlight Reserve. Alongside lectures and discussions, the programme includes music, art, stargazing and a science camp, aiming to take the conversation beyond the lecture hall and inspire real-world curiosity. Music from Andrea Bocelli, Rick Wakeman and Sarah Brightman will set the tone, alongside more than 40 speakers across the week, including Nobel laureates May-Britt Moser, Donna Strickland and Steven Chu, and astronauts Chris Hadfield, Victor Glover, Reid Wiseman and Jeremy Hansen. The festival will close in La Palma with a free public performance of Ilan Eshkeri’s Space Station Earth. This live orchestral work is accompanied by footage from space, exploring how seeing Earth from above can reshape human perspective. Ten years after Hawking helped launch the medal, Starmus is recognising Cox’s embodiment of its original ambition: not only to explain what we know about the Universe, but to inspire us all to look up and wonder.

title: 'Grand odysseys': Why historic travel and legendary journeys are trending for 2027
description: Skyscanner’s 2027 travel trends report points to growing demand for historic trails, ancient ruins and iconic destinations brought to life on screen, as travellers look to the past for a sense of connection in a fast-paced world.
content: It’s the season when travel companies start to reveal their predictions for the following year, and now Skyscanner has launched its 2027 Travel Trends report. Pairing global search insights and research from more than 28,000 travellers, the report uses data from the likes of TikTok, ClassPass, Wise, Universal Music Group for Brands, and AllTrails.Among the new trends for 2027 is history-focussed travel, which follows on from a trend which has already seen significant traction this year thanks, in no small part, to The Odyssey, Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster adaptation of Homer's epic poem. Skyscanner has called this particular trend “Grand Odysseys”, and suggests that its popularity is down to travellers trying to escape a fast-paced world. They’re seeking out history which offers context and grounds them in timeless human stories. Next year will see tourists following sacred walking trails, exploring legendary ruins and turning to the past to enrich their often overwhelming present. Skyscanner’s research found that cinematic releases have been driving real-world bookings, with films and TV shows including The Odyssey and Gladiator proving particularly inspiring. Data from TikTok backs this up, too, showing that video views for cinematic travel content are up +346% year on year, while posts featuring #HeroJourney are up some +452%.The Odyssey reportedly prompted a third of people to plan a trip inspired by the epic, and the data shows that almost half – 43% – of Millennials have been inspired by films and TV set in antiquity, from Troy to the tales of Ancient Greece.And 24% of them have taken it further and travelled in the footsteps of ancient stories, a figure which rises to 30% among Gen Z. The top historic hikes for 2027Among Skyscanner’s partners for the report was the app AllTrails, which revealed its top five walking trails to experience historical travel on foot in 2027. In first place is Corfu’s Cape Drastis Loop. The popular route on the Greek island is said to be ancient author Homer’s mythical land of Phaeacia, where a shipwrecked Odysseus shared the story of his epic 10-year journey home.Next up was the route between Horcones Viewpoint, Horcones Lagoon and Espejo Lagoon in Argentina. Walkers can experience shimmering glacial lakes as they walk in the shadow of Mount Aconcagua, South America’s highest peak. In third place was China’s Xi’an City Wall. Here, visitors can stroll along impressive Ming Dynasty walls where ancient gateways, sweeping views and centuries of history unfold below.In fourth is Monte Santa Caterina in Favignana, Italy. Adventurous travellers can climb to Favignana’s highest point, which is home to a historic castle with a rich history linked to the island, long associated with Odysseus’ legendary voyage.Finally, Rizes Cave, or the Cave of Eumaeus, in Ithaca, Greece continues The Odyssey theme. Here, walkers will pass through olive groves above the Ionian before arriving at a cave where Odysseus sought refuge after returning home in the epic tale.“It’s grounding to visit a trail and realise you’re seeing the same rugged peaks, ancient forests, and horizons that travellers did thousands of years ago,” said Shelby Eagleburger, head of data integrity at AllTrails. “Historic routes remind us that exploring the outdoors is a universal human experience, and it connects us across generations. How we travel evolves, but the pull of natural landscapes stays the same.”Skyscanner’s top trends for 2027Grand Odysseys is one of seven trends featured in the Skyscanner report, all of which show a shift in traveller behaviour. The prediction trends also include “Signal Severance”, which is linked to the fact that one in four Gen Z travellers plan to disconnect in 2027. Many of us are craving a less connected world and are seeking out remote travel spots, or places where it’s possible to switch off entirely. Skyscanner found that digital detox spots in Finland, including Kittilä and Rovaniemi, are seeing rising demand.Most of us like to bring back a keepsake from a trip – whose fridge isn’t covered in magnets? But for 2027, Skyscanner believes that the best souvenirs are the ones you have to travel for, with travellers increasingly building itineraries around unique regional apparel, artisanal crafts and location-exclusive items.One in four travellers have taken a trip specifically for items they couldn't buy online, including the vastly popular Trader Joe's tote from the United States and merchandise from the Ritz Paris. Weddings and travel often go hand-in-hand and, increasingly, couples are choosing to move away from gendered celebrations and are embracing the “sten do”, a combination of stag and hen parties. The report shows that 25% of travellers are opting for these combined celebrations abroad as they’re more fun, less expensive and easier to organise. If you’re into fitness and wellbeing, you may already be an aficionado of the gym-cation, but it’s set to be a huge trend in 2027. The report found that 67% of millennials are more likely to book a hotel which serves a nutritious breakfast, and 40% of Gen Z travellers said they prioritise hotels with gyms. TikTok data also showed a +659% year-on-year increase in video views for "Gym Hotel" content.Increasingly, many travellers are opting to base a trip around seeing live music and experiencing unusual events. Cultural immersion is a priority as traditional carnivals rank highly for both Gen Z (33%) and Millennials (30%), while 25% of those surveyed said the setting of a concert is almost as important as the set list, with fans hoping for gigs held in the likes of ancient caves or pyramids.Finally, the “currency chasers” trend is set to be huge in 2027. Those keen to save cash are plumping for destinations where they can take advantage of positive foreign exchange rates. According to the data, 45% of Gen Z and 40% of Millennial travellers have switched destinations to get more bang for their buck. Vietnam is a particularly popular choice for this trend, as the currency means tourists can spend relatively little while making the most of the beautiful Asian nation.

title: ‘Heartbreaking’ elephants and wily coyotes: Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 – in pictures
description: This year's winners showcase powerful stories from the natural world and the urgent need to protect it.
content: A poignant photo of a female elephant carrying a deceased calf has won the Wildlife Photographer of the Year competition 2026.Titled ‘The Aftermath’, it was taken by Italian wildlife photographer Federico Veronesi while he was tracking elephants in Huab River Valley in Namibia.After noticing an unusual pattern of drag marks in the sand of a dry riverbed, he caught up with a family of elephants, one of whom had the calf wedged between her tusk and trunk.It isn’t the first time possible displays of grief have been witnessed in elephants, with previous behaviours including vocalisations, guarding the dead, and inspecting and handling bones.The black-and-white image has been described by Kathy Moran, Chair of the Wildlife Photographer of the Year Jury, as an emotional “gut punch” and “heartbreakingly poignant” proof of the animals’ consciousness.As well as the Young Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026, a further 19 category winners were selected from a record-breaking 65,403 entries from 121 countries and territories.Who won Young Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026?Oscar Whitfield, who was 14 when he captured his prize-winning photo, took home the main youth award this year for a shot of a dung beetle at work in Zambezi National Park, Zimbabwe.Though small, these powerful insects play their part in curbing the Earth’s greenhouse gases by breaking up and burying dung, preventing it from producing planet-heating methane. This also helps it decompose faster, reducing the number of pests affecting livestock and wildlife. There are more than 5,000 species of dung beetle found around the world. Prize-winning photographers capture urban wildlifeFrom coyotes roaming the hills of San Francisco to giant lizards hunting in Bangkok, this year’s winning photographs also revealed how animals are adapting to life alongside humans. In his award-winning portfolio, ‘Wily Coyotes of San Francisco’, US photographer Loren Elliott documents a resident pack living among the city’s more than 800,000 inhabitants. Around 100 coyotes are thought to live in the city, where attitudes towards the animals are mixed. While they sometimes prey on domestic animals, they also help control populations of disease-carrying rodents. Elliott’s photographs invite viewers to reconsider these often-misunderstood animals and their place in an increasingly urban world. Another urban encounter by UK photographer Seth Forestson won the Urban Wildlife category.Capturing a common monitor lizard carrying its prey through Bangkok’s Lumphini Park, Seth lowered himself onto the muddy ground to frame the creature against the city skyline.Common water monitors have successfully adapted to the Thai capital’s urban environment, taking advantage of readily available food, including catfish and koi in Bangkok’s park lakes. Underwater encounters reveal what’s hidden in the depthsHuman impacts on wildlife are not confined to land. Beneath the surface, photographers are documenting both intimate animal encounters and the growing pressures on marine ecosystems.Animal Portrait-winner Aaron Sanders had been diving off a Cornish beach when he noticed the footprints of octopus suckers through a thin blade of kelp. As a single eye emerged, “We remained perfectly still, watching one another with a seemingly shared curiosity,” he recalls.The encounter is a glimpse of a wider story brewing in the waters off southwest England, where sightings of common octopuses have increased dramatically. While the carnivorous predators are more commonly found in the Mediterranean, above-average spring sea temperatures have expanded their territory, with devastating impacts on local fishing industries.In another show of humans’ impact on marine life, US photographer Alex Lindbloom snapped a whale shark investigating the catch of a ‘bagan’, or mobile net-fishing platform, in the inky waters off Papua, Indonesia.The species has declined sharply over the past 75 years mainly due to ship strikes, fishing gear entanglements and illegal fishing.A watering hole brings wildlife together Some of the winning images reveal the unexpected interactions that take place when different species gather in the same habitat. In ‘The Meeting Place’, UK photographer James Lewin captures a young bull elephant spraying a group of zebras as they congregate around a waterhole in Kenya’s Chyulu Hills. Lewin used an infrared-converted camera to soften the harsh light, giving the scene a dreamlike quality. Waterholes can become vital lifelines during severe droughts, bringing together animals that might otherwise keep their distance. Wildlife Photographer of the Year is developed and produced by the Natural History Museum, London. The winning photographs will be on display at the Natural History Museum from 16 October 2026 until July 2027.

title: IKEA has just launched another second-hand marketplace. But will it stop producing ‘fast furniture’?
description: Sustainability is noticeably absent in IKEA’s latest press statement about its second-hand marketplace.
content: IKEA has launched a second-hand marketplace in the UK, providing customers with a new way to buy and sell pre-loved furniture.The scheme, which is already available in countries like Sweden and Spain, follows the company’s Buyback & Resell service 2021. This allowed shoppers to sell eligible products back to IKEA in exchange for in-store credit.But the new initiative enables “peer-to-peer transactions”, allowing sellers to receive cash for their pre-loved furniture or a digital IKEA refund card.How does IKEA’s second-hand market place work?Customers can list current or previously sold IKEA home furnishing products on the marketplace – with the exception of mattresses, appliances and food. Modified produce, recalled products and furniture not from the IKEA brand are also not permitted. Sellers can scan an eligible item to create a listing, making it easier to pass on IKEA furniture they no longer need. The platform provides recommended pricing, professional product photography and accurate measurements, helping sellers prepare their listings. Each listing also includes product descriptions, assembly instructions and care information, giving prospective buyers useful details before they make contact. Sellers can choose to receive their proceeds as cash or receive a 15 per cent top-up on an IKEA digital refund card.The move follows research commissioned by IKEA that found that more than one in four UK adults said a personal history or story would make pre-owned furniture more desirable to them. Last year, 63 per cent of UK consumers bought products through reselling platforms, marking a 51 per cent increase compared to 2024. More than half (52 per cent) had sold something online in the last 12 months, while 60 per cent say buying second-hand helps stretch their budget.“The way people furnish their homes has changed,” says Greg Lucas, IKEA UK & Ireland’s sustainability manager. “Whether they’re moving, redecorating or looking for a particular piece, more customers are considering pre-owned furniture alongside new and are actively searching for items that can help create a home that feels personal to them.”IKEA’s marketplace is part of the company’s aim to prioritise affordability in a cost-of-living crisis. Prices on the marketplace are on average 60 per cent lower than comparable new products. Sustainability absent from IKEA’s new marketplace launchBuying second-hand furniture is significantly better for the environment as it can help keep bulky items out of landfills and cuts emissions from manufacturing. Opting for pre-loved furniture as opposed to new items also reduces the demand for virgin resources – helping to protect ecosystems such as forests. But each year, IKEA reportedly introduces 2,000 new products. It’s why the Swedish firm is often referred to as a ‘fast furniture’ brand and has garnered heavy criticism from environmentalists.“We see the IKEA second-hand marketplace as complementary alongside our new product offer,” a spokesperson from Ingka Group, the largest IKEA retailer, tells Euronews Earth. “People’s homes, needs and budgets change. Sometimes they choose new, and sometimes a pre-owned product is a better fit.”IKEA products already account for nine per cent of Europe’s second-hand furniture market through other platforms, according to the spokesperson. It seems the firm is looking to expand in this market – without giving up on its ‘fast furniture’ model.A 2024 investigation by Greenpeace found that furniture manufacturers producing for IKEA were sourcing wood from some of Europe’s last remaining old-growth forests in the Romanian Carpathians, including in Natura 2000 protected areas. At the time, IKEA said it remains “committed” to responsible sourcing practices that ensure its products and operations don’t contribute to deforestation or forest degradation.IKEA aims to halve its absolute greenhouse gas emissions across the entire value chain by 2030 compared to 2016 levels. It also wants to only use renewable and recycled materials by 2030, and shift towards 100 per cent renewable electricity and energy efficiency across its operations.

title: Climate change is putting Europe’s brain health at risk
description: Rising temperatures, poor air quality and the spread of infectious diseases could increase the burden of neurological disorders, with the most vulnerable communities facing the greatest risks.
content: Climate change is emerging as a growing threat to brain health, as rising temperatures and other environmental pressures add to the burden of neurological health conditions.Neurological disorders, ranging from migraines to dementia and Parkinson’s disease, affect around one in three people over their lifetime, according to estimates cited by neurologist Ulf Kallweit, who is also a co-chair of the environmental influences task force at the European Academy of Neurology. Combined with mental health conditions, they accounted for an estimated global economic burden of €1.5 trillion in 2019.“Everybody is somehow affected or knows somebody who is affected by a neurological disorder,” Kallweit told Euronews Health on the sidelines of the European Health Forum Gastein.As climate change drives temperatures higher, the situation could deteriorate further, he warned, worsening existing conditions and potentially increasing the risk of developing neurological disorders.But the trajectory is not inevitable. Policymakers can help limit the risks through measures that reduce exposure to heat and pollution and improve the environments in which people live.Heat puts the brain under pressureOne of the clearest concerns is the relationship between high temperatures and stroke.The number of stroke cases rises as temperatures climb above 30°C, Kallweit said, warning that heat-related strokes, which he said currently account for around 1% of all stroke cases, could represent 5 to 8% within the next 20 to 30 years.Heat can also affect brain health indirectly by disrupting sleep.Tropical nights, when temperatures remain above 20°C overnight, make it harder for the body to cool down. This can interfere with deep sleep and prevent people from recovering properly overnight.“Everybody who experienced the last summer knows that sleep gets worse in these kind of heat nights,” Kallweit said.Prolonged sleep disruption may have more serious consequences than a few restless nights.“If you don't sleep well, not maybe one night, but for a longer time, there's a huge increase, let's say, for the risk of getting a stroke or also becoming demented,” he said.Rising temperatures are also changing the geographical range of some infectious diseases, including those transmitted by ticks and mosquitoes. Some of these infections can affect the nervous system. Lyme borreliosis, for example, is transmitted by infected ticks and can cause neurological complications.Malaria, meanwhile, remains a concern in discussions about the future spread of mosquito-borne diseases in Europe.“Malaria is still not fully on yet there, but maybe in five or 10 years it may also affect us in southern parts of Europe,” Kallweit said.Where you live mattersThe risks are not shared equally.Children, pregnant women, older people and those with pre-existing health conditions can be particularly vulnerable to extreme heat and other environmental pressures.If they live in deprived neighbourhoods, their health risks rise further. Recent research has found that people living in socioeconomic deprivation have poorer indicators of brain health, including lower total brain volume and more signs of vascular damage.Climate change could compound these existing inequalities.“If you have heat and you cannot afford an AC, then you are more bothered,” Kallweit said. Access to healthy food, housing conditions and the surrounding environment can also shape people's health, he added.Urban environments are particularly important. Noise, pollution and stressful living conditions can all affect wellbeing, while access to green spaces may offer some protection.Therefore, improving access to green spaces is one potential way to support brain health.“Going out to the forest one hour per week decreases your stroke risk by 3% or dementia risk by 4%,” Kallweit said.Kallweit urged people to spend time in green surroundings and to protect their sleep by limiting exposure to light, noise and other disturbances.But individual measures are only part of the answer. Public policy can help determine whether people have access to cooler homes, quieter neighbourhoods and cleaner air.Kallweit called for safeguards against pollution and toxic substances, as well as changes to the way buildings are designed.“How buildings are constructed should be reconsidered because they're still looking very much to the south, where the sun is entering,” he said, adding that such architecture “may be changed in the future.”

title: A new night train will launch between Hamburg and Munich in March 2027
description: Nox Mobility’s first night train will link Hamburg and Munich via Bremen and Augsburg, with individual private ‘suites’ for all passengers.
content: A new night train in Germany linking Hamburg and Munich is set to launch on 23 March 2027.Berlin-based Nox Mobility says its first service will run three times a week in each direction, with stops in Bremen and Augsburg. With a new generation of night trains designed to make overnight rail “the most obvious alternative” to short-haul flights, Nox Mobility previously revealed that it plans connections between 100 European cities by 2035.Its proposed network includes Paris, Barcelona, Amsterdam, Copenhagen, Warsaw, Budapest and Rome.What will the new night train offer?Passengers will travel in individual “Nox Suites”, each featuring a large seat, a table for working or eating, space for large luggage and power outlets.At night, the seat unfolds into a lounge position, providing two metres of space to stretch out alongside the window.However, travellers expecting the fully private bedrooms outlined in Nox’s original plans will have to wait. Its “Nox Rooms”, designed for one or two people, are scheduled to join the fleet from 2029.As Euronews Travel reported in June 2025, the company initially envisaged launching in 2027 with private sleeping cabins. The latest announcement sets out a phased introduction, starting with the seat-based suites.“With Nox, every passenger has their own space to work and rest in,” said Thibault Constant, Co-Founder of Nox Mobility. “A night on a Nox train should eventually bring together everything that used to take three bookings: getting there, staying the night and the morning at the destination.”What time will the trains depart?One-way fares start at €65. Southbound trains scheduled to leave Hamburg at 9:22 pm, calling at Bremen at 10:30 pm and Augsburg at 7:35 am before reaching Munich at 8:14 am.In the opposite direction, departures from Munich are planned for 9:20 pm, stopping in Augsburg at 9:51 pm and Bremen at 7:20 am, with arrival in Hamburg at 8:27 am.

title: Portuguese parliament backs extension of parental leave: what changes?
description: The new legal framework, arising from a joint proposal by PS and PSD, will give parents a more favourable regime than the one currently in force.
content: On Tuesday, MPs meeting in a parliamentary working group approved a joint proposal by the PS and PSD to extend parental leave. Under the proposal, parents would be entitled to fully paid leave for 180 days (six months) if it is shared, or 150 days (five months) if it is taken by only one of them.In the first of these scenarios, each parent will have to take at least 30 consecutive days or two periods of 15 days in a row, in order to receive a benefit equal to their full reference wage, calculated by Social Security, for the period in which they are away from work. In single-parent families, the lone parent will be entitled to the full 180 days on 100% pay.Alternatively, parents will be covered by a benefit worth 83% of their reference wage for six months (180 days) if the leave is not shared. They may also take up to 210 days of leave, paid at 90% if the father takes at least 60 consecutive days (two months) in addition to his 28-day exclusive parental leave, or at 86% if each parent stays at home with the baby, on an exclusive basis, for one of the last two months of leave.The new legal framework will create more favourable conditions for parents than those currently in force. At present, fully paid leave only covers the first 120 days of the baby's life if there is no sharing, or 150 days if the father takes 30 days of leave on an exclusive basis. In both scenarios, parents can extend that period by a further month, although with a loss of income, as the benefit then corresponds to 80% and 83% of the reference amount respectively.Following approval in the parliamentary working group, the text now moves on to the parliamentary Committee on Labour, Social Security and Inclusion and will then go to a final overall vote in the full chamber.Even so, this extension of parental leave falls short of what was proposed in a citizens' legislative initiative submitted to parliament in 2023, which called for 100% pay during the baby's first 180 days of life, with the possibility of extending that period to 210 or even 240 days if the leave was shared. That initiative formed the basis for the joint amendment put forward by PS and PSD, a less ambitious proposal that has now been approved.However, according to "Negócios" (source in Portuguese), this extension of parental leave will not affect leave that is already under way, as the measure approved by the working group will apply only to leave starting from next year.The proposal also introduces the possibility for private-sector workers, as is already the case in the public sector, to opt for a continuous working day. This would allow employees with children under 12, or with dependants who have a disability or a chronic or oncological illness, to forgo their lunch or dinner break and work their hours in one stretch so that they can leave earlier. They will, however, retain the right to a break of up to 30 minutes.How does Portugal compare with other European countries?Even with the extension of parental leave, Portugal will still have a less generous system than, for example, neighbouring Spain (source in Portuguese). At present, in two-parent families, each parent is entitled to 19 weeks of fully paid leave, rising to 32 weeks in the case of single-parent families.In France, until a few months ago, (source in Portuguese) maternity leave for a first child was just under four months on full pay, while fathers were entitled to 28 days of leave after the birth. New rules in force since July now allow parents to share an additional period of one or two months' leave on top of their existing entitlements. In such cases, they are paid 70% of their net salary in the first month and 60% in the second.In Sweden, often cited as a benchmark in this field, the law provides for a total of 480 days (around 16 months) of paid leave, although the monthly benefit cannot exceed 80% of the recipient's salary. In Finland, (source in Portuguese) parents are entitled to 320 working days of leave per child (about 14 months): each parent has 160 working days, 63 of which can be transferred to the other parent. Parental benefit is calculated on the basis of the worker's income and paid by social security.

title: The world's best 50 bars have been revealed for 2026 – and 18 are in Europe
description: Europe dominates this year’s 50 Best ranking, with 18 bars making the top 50 and Paris overtaking London as the continent’s best-represented city. Hong Kong’s Bar Leone retains the global crown, while Milan’s Moebius Milano and Athens’ Line also break into the top five.
content: The annual ranking of the 50 Best Bars in the world has been revealed, and 18 are in Europe.Following its unveiling of positions 51-100 in September, the prestigious ranking body revealed that Hong Kong’s Bar Leone held on to the top spot for a second year running. The results were announced at a ceremony in Milan on Wednesday, and two European bars – Moebius Milano in Milan and Line in Athens – featured in the top 10. Europe was far and away the most represented continent in the ranking with its 18 spots. It also achieved a further 18 wins in the 51-100 extended list, meaning it takes up more than a third of the positions overall. Italy had plenty to celebrate, with Moebius Milano taking second place and the top spot in Europe, while Italy’s other entry, Locale Firenze in Florence, was at number 33.Paris has overtaken London as the most represented European city on the list for the first time, with four bars making the cut. The Cambridge Public House is number 13, followed by Bar Nouveau at 15, newcomer De Vie at 23 and Danico at 26. That puts Paris level with Hong Kong and New York as the cities with the most bars in the global top 50.London still has a strong showing, led by Connaught Bar at number eight. Satan’s Whiskers is 29, while new entry Waltz comes in at 32.Athens also has three bars on the list. Line leads the way at number five, while The Bar in Front of the Bar climbed 28 places to 19, earning the Nikka Highest Climber Award. Barro Negro rounds out the city’s entries at 40.Spain has three bars in total, with Barcelona’s Sips at 16 and Paradiso at 17, while Madrid’s Angelita makes its debut at 50. Paradiso also picked up the Rémy Martin Legend of the List Award.The top five are very varied, geographically and style-wise, and are all well worth adding to any bar lover’s bucket list. The top five best bars in the worldBar Leone, Hong KongItalian bartender Lorenzo Antinori opened this Hong Kong venue in 2023, bringing the atmosphere of a traditional Roman neighbourhood bar to the city. The focus is on classic Italian aperitivo, with simple, well-made cocktails and a relaxed setting. Although it’s relatively new to the scene, Bar Leone has already cemented itself as something of an institution in the Asian city. Moebius Milano, MilanMilan’s Moebius Milano has made a significant leap up the ranking, climbing from seventh place last year to number two in 2026. The bar is part of a much larger venue housed in a former textile factory, combining cocktails, food, music and design under one roof. Its cocktail offering ranges from classic serves to more experimental creations, while the industrial setting gives it a distinctly contemporary Milanese feel. Alquímico, CartagenaAlquímico in Cartagena has taken third place, making it the highest-ranked bar outside Europe and Asia. Set inside a restored colonial mansion in the heart of the Colombian city, the bar stretches across three floors, each with its own atmosphere and cocktail menu. Drinks draw heavily on Colombian ingredients and landscapes, with the team using local produce and traditional techniques to create a menu that changes with the country’s seasons.Bar Us, BangkokBangkok’s Bar Us has secured fourth place, making it the Thai capital’s highest-ranked bar this year. The intimate venue takes a tasting-menu approach to cocktails, with drinks designed around seasonal ingredients and carefully balanced flavour combinations. Rather than simply ordering from a conventional drinks list, guests are taken through a series of serves that explore different ingredients and techniques.
