It’s part of Bangkok’s growing reputation as one of Asia’s major cocktail destinations.Line, AthensAthens’ Line has climbed to fifth place, making it the second highest-ranked European bar on this year’s list. Housed in one of the Greek city’s most significant former art galleries, it offers cocktails with a strong focus on fermentation. Many of its ingredients are made in-house, including fermented fruit, syrups and other preparations used in the drinks. The result is a menu that puts Greek produce and flavours at the centre of the experience, while the industrial-inspired setting keeps things relaxed and contemporary.The top 50 bars in the world1. title: EU’s AI rules face first enforcement test over lab incidents
description: The EU is investigating OpenAI and Anthropic over AI agents that hacked outside organisations, raising questions about whether the AI Act covers rogue models escaping the testing environment.
content: The European Commission is moving to enforce its new rules on leading AI labs after a string of incidents, EU digital chief Henna Virkkunen said. But applying the rulebook is far from straightforward, and these early cases will set important precedents.The Commission’s AI Office is investigating OpenAI and Anthropic after AI agents autonomously hacked into other organisations, the first test of the limits of the EU’s AI rules.“Our AI Office has started enforcing these rules, and sent requests for information addressing issues such as security, external evaluation and monitoring how models are used,” Commission Executive Vice-President for Technological Sovereignty Henna Virkkunen said at the International AI Summit in Dublin on Wednesday.The investigations concern an “unprecedented” incident in which an OpenAI agent escaped its testing environment to hack rival Hugging Face, and one in which a recent Anthropic model gained “unauthorised access” to three outside organisations.Both incidents happened over the summer. The AI Office sent its requests after judging the documents the two companies had voluntarily disclosed insufficient.Since August, the AI Office has held enforcement powers under the AI Act, the EU’s comprehensive law on artificial intelligence, which also covers the most powerful models and requires their developers to implement risk-mitigation measures.But legal experts are contesting the Commission’s power to investigate. The incidents occurred during testing, before the models were placed on the EU market, so they argue, the AI Act does not apply.“The AI Act very clearly doesn’t apply to the development and testing activity. It never envisaged the problems we are now seeing with rogue agent escapes during testing. It’s a bit of a stretch to say that an agent was put into service if it escapes its testing environment during development,” Barry Scannell, a partner at the law firm William Fry, told Euronews.The law does include an R&D exemption covering research, testing and development. The Commission is pushing a broader interpretation that would let the AI Office police the development phase too under certain circumstances.“We won’t enforce in the testing phase. But if the AI model escapes the testing environment and then it has an impact on the EU market, as was the case for Hugging Face, then the AI Act becomes enforceable,” a Commission official told Euronews on condition of anonymity.Hugging Face has global operations, hosting AI models and datasets that developers use globally. As a result, the OpenAI incident also impacted customers in the EU.The Commission likens it to a virus escaping a lab: the company has clearly failed to put adequate risk-mitigation measures in place and is harming others.Last week, Virkkunen met the Scientific Panel, an advisory group of independent experts, to discuss the technical developments behind the multiplication of such incidents in recent months.The experts flagged worrying trends, Euronews has learned. Leading labs are investing in ever more powerful models with inadequate cybersecurity and safety practices, raising concerns that many incidents may go unreported.Even more troubling, the more capable the models become, the more they tend to drift from their design objectives. Oversight mechanisms grow less effective, and models might even cheat when evaluated.For parts of the AI safety community, the nightmare scenario is that models’ continuous self-improvement turns such temporary losses of control into permanent ones, with rogue agents escaping human control for good.In short, the EU executive is determined to enforce its rules when agents escape their testing environment, in what could be Brussels’ first legal battle to force Silicon Valley’s labs to take safety into account already at the development stage.“The Commission has been loud and clear: AI must remain under human direction, oversight and control and we stand ready to take all necessary steps to ensure that companies follow the AI Act rules,” Virkkunen said.

title: ASML posts record €11.7 billion in sales but warns it can’t keep up with AI demand
description: Dutch equipment supplier ASML warned on Wednesday that its planned supply of machines will not fully meet customers’ AI-driven demand in 2027 and 2028, as it reported record quarterly sales of around €11.7 billion and lifted the lower end of its full-year sales forecast.
content: ASML, the Netherlands-based equipment supplier to the semiconductor industry, said on Wednesday that its current production plans would fall short of customer demand in 2027 and 2028, as AI investment continues to drive up orders.The company also posted its highest-ever quarterly sales, at €11.7 billion in the third quarter, and raised the bottom of its sales forecast for 2026.ASML said customers are still increasing their forecasts for equipment demand, largely based on how big and long-lasting they expect AI investment to be. Some even want to book machines now for 2029 or 2030.In July, the company said it would expand capacity by 30% in 2027 for both its low-NA extreme ultraviolet (EUV) and deep ultraviolet (DUV) immersion machines. ASML is the only company that makes EUV systems, which are used for the most advanced chips. It was also looking at a further 30% rise in 2028."We are investigating ways to increase capacity for 2028 beyond the 30% increase we previously communicated," CEO Christophe Fouquet said in a statement."Customers are asking us every single day to get more tools," Fouquet stated in a video interview released alongside the results.Record quarterThird-quarter sales of €11.66 billion were up 55% from a year earlier, towards the top of ASML’s €11-12 billion forecast and broadly in line with the €11.7 billion average of analysts’ estimates compiled by Bloomberg.Net income more than doubled to €5 billion, helped by a €510 million gain on stakes ASML holds in other companies.Gross margin, the share of sales left after production costs, beat ASML’s forecast at 57.5%, mainly lifted by €3.3 billion in sales from servicing and upgrading customers’ existing machines.ASML now expects 2026 sales of €44-45 billion, up from €43-45 billion, with a gross margin of around 56%, up from 54-56%. It also forecasts fourth-quarter sales of €14.2-15.2 billion."ASML delivered a strong set of numbers, but realistically, they have only caught up to where the market already was with its expectations," explained Ben Barringer, head of technology research at UK wealth manager Quilter Cheviot.A test for the AI tradeThe results follow a jittery week for AI-linked stocks.Last Thursday, chipmakers fell after a Financial Times report suggested ChatGPT maker OpenAI’s annualised revenue was running about $20 billion (€17.8bn) below figures reported late last month, a gap largely down to how they are counted.On Tuesday, Asian chip stocks tumbled after Hock Tan, head of US chipmaker Broadcom, said many AI investors did not understand what they were investing in. This came as reports of progress by Chinese memory chipmaker CXMT towards denser memory chips raised concerns over future competition and pricing pressure.ASML’s Amsterdam-listed shares were up by more than 3% at around 10:00 CEST on Wednesday.Since chipmakers order ASML’s machines well in advance, investors watch its outlook for clues on whether AI spending plans are holding up."Durable growth will continue into 2027 and 2028, however, the market will begin asking the question of whether or not there will be any sign of a downturn from 2029 and what impact that has for ASML," Barringer said.ASML’s investor call is at 15:00 CEST on Wednesday. Taiwan’s TSMC, the world’s biggest contract chipmaker and a major ASML customer, reports on Thursday.

title: Africa records world's fastest gains in disaster resilience, new study shows
description: The World Risk Poll, which surveyed 143,000 people across 140 countries, found North Africa up five points and Southern Africa up four, driven by expanding internet access and household preparedness. Yet 220 million people affected by disasters in the past five years received no warning.
content: Africa has recorded the world's fastest improvements in disaster resilience, a new major global study has revealed.Research from Lloyd's Register Foundation shows that African regions have made the biggest gains in people's ability to withstand and recover from disasters and other major disruptions since 2023.North Africa, for instance, recorded a five-point increase in resilience, followed by Southern Africa with four points. Eastern Africa and Central and Western Africa each improved by three points.Expanding internet access, better household preparedness, and improved financial resilience in countries including Kenya, Egypt, Uganda, Algeria, and Nigeria propelled the gains.The findings, however, expose a significant trial. In Central and West Africa, few disaster-affected adults received any warning, raising questions about whether resilience improvements are translating into better protection for vulnerable communities.What is driving Africa's progress?This is the outcome of the fourth edition of the World Risk Poll, which surveyed more than 143,000 people across 140 countries and territories in the year 2025. Conducted by Gallup, the study examines experiences of safety risks, including in countries where official data is limited.Its Resilience Index measures people's ability to absorb and recover from major shocks on a scale of 0 to 100. The assessment covers four areas: individual resilience, household preparedness, community support and wider societal conditions.Increased internet access can help people obtain information about potential dangers, while household preparedness can improve their ability to respond when emergencies occur.The researchers identified Algeria, Nigeria, Kenya, Egypt, and Uganda as countries contributing to regional improvements, although the factors behind the gains varied. The findings, however, do not mean Africa has become the world's most resilient continent. Rather, its regions have recorded the fastest improvements over the period examined.But why are millions still missing disaster warnings?Despite the progress, the study discloses massive inequalities in access to potentially life-saving information. In Central and Western Africa, for instance, 47% of adults affected by disasters said they had received a warning.Globally, people in low-income countries were almost twice as likely to have experienced a disaster over the previous five years as those in high-income countries.Nearly one in three adults in poorer countries reported being affected, compared with 16% in wealthier nations.Yet only 64% of disaster-affected adults in low-income countries received warnings, compared with 84% in high-income countries. Even when warnings were issued, many people could not respond.Fewer than half of warned adults in low- and lower-middle-income countries took action before disaster struck, compared with 71% in high-income countries.Nancy Hey, director of evidence and insight at Lloyd's Register Foundation's Global Safety Evidence Centre, said the results highlighted the importance of preparedness."A warning is only as good as what people can do with it," she said.Can mobile phones help save more lives?The research identifies mobile technology as a major opportunity to close gaps in disaster warning systems.Worldwide, an estimated 1.1 billion adults experienced a disaster in the previous five years, but almost 220 million received no warning beforehand.Of those not warned, 77% owned a mobile phone, or more than 170 million people.The study also found that people were more likely to act when warnings reached them through several channels.Only 37% of those receiving alerts through one channel took action, compared with 51% reached through two and 64% through three. These channels include text messages, television and social media.Local preparedness is already evident in parts of Africa.In Malawi, volunteers mobilised communities to clear storm drains ahead of extreme rainfall in January, according to the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies.This initiative illustrates how communities can take practical steps before severe weather arrives.Caroline Zastiral, acting global lead for disaster risk reduction and resilience, said effective warnings depended on people's ability to respond."Warnings lead to action when people have the trust, knowledge, time and resources to protect themselves, their loved ones and their assets," she said.Challenge for rich and poor countries alikeWhile the study highlights poorer countries' greater exposure to disasters, especially amid climate change, it also challenges the assumption that national wealth necessarily makes people more resilient.The research also states that societal resilience, including trust in national institutions, rose globally from 63 points in 2021 to a record 66 in 2025. However, individual resilience fell from 46 to 42, its lowest recorded level.Lloyd's Register Foundation is urging governments and disaster management agencies to widen warning coverage and invest more in household preparedness.Dr Andrew Tupper, chief of the Early Warning Services Section at the World Meteorological Organisation, said warnings must be part of a broader system that helps communities to respond."An early warning system is useless if it doesn't empower people to act," he said.

title: Taxes, housing and tuition fees: 2027 budget measures impact family budgets in Portugal
description: From taxes and wages to pensions, housing and tuition fees, the 2027 State Budget contains several measures that will directly affect household incomes.
content: The draft State Budget for 2027 (OE2027) sets out changes that will affect the disposable income of Portuguese households, from taxes on wages to social benefits and spending on housing and education.Key measures include a new update of the IRS brackets, an increase in the national minimum wage and a strengthening of some social benefits. On the other hand, tuition fees in higher education are expected to start rising again from the next academic year.In addition, the evolution of prices for essential goods may swallow up part of the tax savings.The draft must still go through the parliamentary approval process before being promulgated by the President of the Republic.IRS: new update may boost disposable incomeOne of the main measures is the update of the IRS bracket thresholds. The rates planned for 2027 remain, according to the budget proposal, at the levels presented by the Government in September, but the income limits from which each bracket applies will be higher.The IRS table presented sets out nine brackets, with rates between 12.2% and 48%. The first covers annual taxable income of up to 8,666 euros, followed by a rate of 15.2% for the slice between that amount and 13,075 euros. In the next two brackets, which go up to 18,530 euros and 23,985 euros, the rates are 20.7% and 23.6% respectively.From there, the rates rise to 30.6% in the bracket up to 30,538 euros and to 34.6% in the next, up to 44,762 euros. Income between 44,762 and 48,373 euros is taxed at 43.1%, while the slice between 48,373 and 89,995 euros is taxed at 44.6%. The top rate of 48% applies only to the portion of annual taxable income above 89,995 euros.The upper and lower limits for each bracket have been updated by 3.88%, a percentage lower than the reference value set for wage increases in collective bargaining, which in the Tripartite Agreement on Wage Enhancement and Economic Growth, agreed in Social Concertation, aims for an average wage rise of 4.5% next year.Because the brackets are updated by around 3.9%, all taxpayers stand to gain, taking into account the progressive nature of this tax.The Government also plans to update the specific IRS deduction, which excludes a portion of workers’ and pensioners’ income from taxation, but the exact amount is still unknown, as it depends on the update of the Social Support Index (IAS).The IAS is set by a ministerial order that fixes the value in force each year from 1 January, but it is usually calculated a few weeks earlier based on inflation and economic growth.There is also a change targeting higher incomes: the additional solidarity rate of 2.5% will apply only to taxable income above 89,995 euros a year. For income over 250,000 euros, the 5% rate remains in place.The proposal to exempt from IRS productivity bonuses, performance bonuses, profit-sharing and balance-sheet gratuities up to a limit of 6% of a worker’s annual basic pay also remains, provided the company meets the wage enhancement criteria laid down.Minimum wage rises to 970 eurosWorkers earning the national minimum wage are set to move from the current gross 920 euros a month to 970 euros in 2027, an increase of 50 euros per month.This figure is in line with the wage enhancement agreement reached in Social Concertation and represents a boost to the gross income of those on the minimum wage. The net amount will depend, among other factors, on each worker’s tax situation.In the public administration, the proposal provides for a minimum salary update of 2.3% or 60.52 euros, raising the basic pay to 995.51 euros a month.At present, the basic pay in the public administration stands at 934.99 euros.Pensions to rise in 2027, with increases of around 3%Pensioners will in 2027 benefit from the regular indexation of pensions, calculated on the basis of inflation and growth in Gross Domestic Product (GDP). Although the final figure is not yet known, available data point to an increase close to 3% for pensions of just over 1,000 euros a month or less, covering most pensioners.This update is expected to add 824 million euros to public spending next year.Before that, in December, pensioners with pensions of up to 1,611.39 euros a month will receive an extraordinary supplement, paid automatically together with their pension: 200 euros for those receiving up to 537.13 euros, 150 euros for pensions above that amount and up to 1,074.26 euros, and 100 euros for pensions above that level and up to the defined ceiling.The aim is to strengthen pensioners’ incomes, especially those on the lowest pensions, although the regular 2027 increase can only be confirmed once the final inflation and economic growth data are known.Older people to get an extra 50 euros in the Solidarity SupplementPensioners on the lowest incomes are among the beneficiaries of one of the social top-ups planned in the budget. The Solidarity Supplement for Older People (CSI) is expected to increase from 670 to 720 euros, a rise of 50 euros in the monthly reference amount.The measure is designed to bolster the incomes of older people in situations of greater economic vulnerability. The Government is also maintaining its goal of raising this reference value to 870 euros by 2029.Extra 60 million euros in spending on child benefitChild benefit is also expected to see higher public spending, linked to indexation of amounts to inflation and the forecast increase in the number of beneficiaries.The 2027 budget proposal states that spending on child benefit will rise next year by 59.5 million euros, "by comparison with the forecast outturn for 2026".The Government explains the increase in the budget report by pointing to higher spending due, on the one hand, to "an increase in beneficiaries of around 1.1%" and, on the other, to "higher average amounts in line with the projected change in inflation".Housing: benefit for landlords, IMT exemption for young people and public guaranteesOn the rental market, there are changes with different impacts for landlords and tenants.Landlords covered by the moderate rent tax regime will continue to benefit from an IRS rate of 10%, instead of the 25% previously applied.The measure covers income earned up to 31 December 2029, in both new and existing contracts, but applies only to rents of up to 2,300 euros a month, the amount the Government set in September 2025 as a "moderate rent".For tenants, the maximum IRS deduction on rents will increase from 900 to 1,000 euros in 2027. For taxpayers with lower taxable incomes, the ceiling may reach 1,100 euros. This change allows a larger share of spending on permanent housing to be offset against tax, within the applicable legal conditions.Young people up to the age of 35 will continue to benefit from exemption from IMT property transfer tax and stamp duty when buying their first home, with updated exemption thresholds. The maximum value covered by the IMT exemption is expected to rise to 338,141 euros.The Government also plans to reinforce the Porta 65 scheme, which supports young people renting a home, but gives no figures.The continuation of the public guarantee scheme for the purchase of a first home is also described as likely, although, when presenting the budget, the finance minister clarified that a "formal decision" was still pending.Tuition fees to be unfrozenOne of the measures that may mean an additional burden for families is the unfreezing of tuition fees in public higher education from the 2027/2028 academic year.The current maximum fee for bachelor’s degrees and higher professional technical courses, set at 697 euros, is to start being updated in line with inflation.The same rule will apply to certain master’s degrees that are required to work in a given profession or demanded by the relevant professional associations. For other master’s and doctoral programmes, the proposal states that updates should reflect the actual cost of providing the training.This measure could raise annual expenses for households with children in higher education, especially when there are other associated costs, such as accommodation, transport and food.The update of tuition fees had already been proposed by Luís Montenegro’s Government in last year’s State Budget, which envisaged raising the maximum fee for bachelor’s degrees to 710 euros, but the measure was eventually rejected during the detailed vote.Support for parenthoodThe budget provides for higher spending on parental benefits, reflecting expectations that eligibility conditions will be improved. The debate on extending the initial parental leave paid at 100% to 180 days could affect how these measures are implemented and how much they cost.Spending on parental benefits is expected to increase by 349.1 million euros in 2027, reflecting "growth of 31.7% compared with the forecast outturn for 2026". The total budgeted amount comes to 1,452 million euros.Parliament is in the final stage of detailed consideration of a citizens’ initiative that proposes extending initial parental leave paid at 100% to 180 days, or six months.The 2026 State Budget already factored in the financial impact of extending payment of the initial parental benefit by two months.According to the labour minister, Maria do Rosário Palma Ramalho, around 230 million euros had been set aside for this measure. However, that estimate was based on the Government’s proposal, under which payment of parental leave at 100% for six months would depend on a fair sharing of leave between both parents.The group of citizens behind the proposal argue that full payment for the six months should be guaranteed regardless of how the parents split the leave. This solution would mean higher costs for the State, as all parents would be eligible to receive 100% pay while on parental leave.Fuels and cars: no tax cuts announcedFor those who use a car every day, the proposal does not provide for direct changes to taxes on fuel, either increases or decreases. The Government does, however, expect tax revenues from these products to rise by 5.2%, purely through higher consumption. That represents an extra 186 million euros.The budget proposal does not spell out the Government’s plans for the future of the current 23-cent-per-litre tax discount on fuel. Part of this discount results from a mechanism used by the executive to refund, in petroleum tax, the extra VAT revenue generated by rising fuel prices.Finance minister Joaquim Miranda Sarmento has said the Government will maintain its policy of responding to price shocks, with support for specific sectors and a refund of the tax windfall collected by the State.The surcharge on diesel vehicles in the Single Circulation Tax (IUC) also remains. The rates for this tax are not changed in the budget, but the payment schedule will be different in 2027, a transition year to the new model.Under the new schedule, IUC bills of up to 500 euros will fall due in October, with larger amounts paid in two instalments, the first in July. From 2028, IUC will be payable from April.The executive is considering "new incentives for the purchase of zero-emission vehicles", but both the timetable and the budget envelope and conditions remain undefined, making it impossible to calculate how much support each household might receive.The grant scheme for buying electric cars, opened in June, exhausted its budget of ten million euros in just a few hours. At the time, environment and energy minister Maria da Graça Carvalho said that "no further [funding rounds] are likely to open this year"."Regressar" programme extended for another yearThe Government plans to extend for a further year the benefits under the Regressar (Return) Programme, aimed at emigrants who come back to Portugal. The scheme is currently in force until the end of 2026, but the Government has decided to prolong it.Created in 2019, the programme is aimed at former tax residents in Portugal who have spent at least five years abroad and then return to the country.The benefit excludes from taxation 50% of employment income and business and professional income for a period of five years.

title: Hospitality is the key: Porto tops ranking as Europe's friendliest city, with Lisbon close behind
description: Portuguese hospitality has once again won over international travellers. Porto was voted Europe's friendliest city, with Lisbon second in Condé Nast Traveller readers' ranking.
content: Portugal is often considered one of the most welcoming and hospitable countries in the world, with international studies and surveys repeatedly placing the Portuguese people at the top of tourists’ favourites. It is therefore no surprise that Porto has been awarded the title of "Europe's friendliest city".The distinction comes from readers of Condé Nast Traveller in the Readers’ Choice Awards 2026, which also place the city of Lisbon in second position in this category.The vote aims to identify cities where "hospitality is at its warmest" and "you find locals eager to help, whether you’re trying to make sense of a neighbourhood restaurant’s menu or looking confused on the metro".The recognition now given to the Invicta, as Porto is known, "reflects the significant rise in Porto’s popularity as the ideal city-break refuge, both for lovers of good food and for culture enthusiasts", the magazine explains, also highlighting the city’s authenticity and relaxed atmosphere."Unwind in a stunning square lined with azulejo tiles or share petiscos – small portions of local delicacies – with residents in a neighbourhood restaurant," Condé Nast encourages, "and you will quickly realise how generous hospitality has made Porto a destination many of us end up returning to time and time again".Lisbon appears in the next spot. "Few European cities are as picturesque as the sun-drenched Portuguese capital, famous for being built on the seven hills that punctuate the banks of the River Tagus", the magazine notes, describing it as "a wonderful city of winding alleys, soulful fado and creamy pastéis de nata"."But what really ties it all together is the people. A youthful, inclusive atmosphere pulses through its steep neighbourhoods, and there are plenty of opportunities for travellers to get involved too. Experiencing the vibrant café culture is unmissable, where groups gather to savour their ritual morning espressos, or visiting during the Festival of Saint Anthony to see the cobbled streets fill with open-air parties", the publication recommends.In the European ranking, the top five is completed by mentions of Amsterdam in the Netherlands, Stockholm in Sweden and Valletta in Malta.The 15 friendliest cities in EuropeAccording to Condé Nast Traveller’s 2026 Readers’ Choice Awards:1. Porto, Portugal2. Lisbon, Portugal3. Amsterdam, Netherlands4. Stockholm, Sweden5. Valletta, Malta6. Edinburgh, Scotland7. Vienna, Austria8. Krakow, Poland9. Palma, Spain10. Granada, Spain11. Genoa, Italy12. Cork, Ireland13. Paris, France14. Rome, Italy15. Reykjavík, Iceland

title: FIFA proposes €5.5bn football development fund amid Infantino scrutiny
description: The proposal comes as European football leaders seek a candidate to try to unseat Gianni Infantino as FIFA president.
content: FIFA will propose a $6.35 billion (€5.5 billion) four-year development fund, including $25 million (€21.5 million) for each national association, according to news agency Associated Press (AP).On 28 September, FIFA President Gianni Infantino sent the proposal to the heads of football's six continental confederations. The plan is expected to be finalised by the FIFA Council in December and approved at its congress in March, according to a letter reviewed by AP.“Taken together, your submissions confirm broad agreement on the central objective: FIFA’s financial success must serve football and all FIFA’s 211 member associations,” Infantino said in the letter.“I am confident that together we can reach a sustainable and properly supported outcome for FIFA’s member associations and for football in every part of the world.”FIFA plans to reinvest revenue from the latest World Cup into football development across its member associations, confederations and other stakeholders. Each association was initially set to receive $10 million (€8.6 million) over four years.FIFA plans to distribute more than $3.5 billion (€3 billion) from reserves boosted by the success of the 48-team World Cup, according to two officials who spoke anonymously as the proposal has yet to be announced.FIFA expects around $15 billion (€12.9 billion) in revenue for the 2022–2026 cycle, including the men's World Cup hosted by the US, Canada and Mexico, significantly exceeding projections, the officials told AP.Infantino under scrutinyIn August, UEFA announced it was preparing a criminal complaint against Infantino in Switzerland over possible financial mismanagement linked to a World Cup commercial rights deal. It also sought court approval in the US to obtain evidence.UEFA's 55 member associations represent more than a quarter of FIFA's 211 voting members ahead of the presidential election on 18 March in Rabat, Morocco.Last month, Infantino, who has led FIFA since 2016 and is seeking re-election next year, expressed openness to an independent review of FIFA's governance and possible reforms.Candidates seeking to challenge Infantino must enter the race by 18 November.

title: Money laundering failures land Bank of America with a $1.2 billion fine
description: US authorities have imposed a $1.2 billion (€1.07bn) penalty on Bank of America over failures to tackle money laundering. The bank also settled alleged sanctions violations involving Iran and Russia.
content: The US Treasury Department said on Tuesday that it had imposed a $1.2bn (€1.07bn) fine on Bank of America for anti-money laundering failures."When a bank of this size fails to meet its anti-money laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the entire U.S. financial system to significant illicit finance risks," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement. "Today's actions send a clear message that even the biggest financial institutions are not above the law."Treasury said Bank of America, the country’s second-biggest bank, also reached an $11.6 million (€9.9mn) settlement with the department's Office of Foreign Assets Control over "apparent violations of numerous sanctions programs, including on Iran, Russia, narcotics, and global terrorism."In a statement, Treasury said its Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) imposed the $1.2bn penalty for Bank of America's "failure to mitigate and report priority national security risks, including Chinese Money Laundering Networks and illicit finance along the southwest border."Treasury said the bank failed to report more than $5bn (€4.27bn) in suspicious transactions on time, including over $1bn (€853mn) linked to national security and other priority financial crime risks.The penalty includes a $750 million (€640mn) fine imposed by the US Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the largest fine ever imposed by the federal banking regulator.Treasury said that Bank of America "admits that it willfully violated" the 1970 Bank Secrecy Act, which requires banks to help the government detect and prevent money laundering."Financial crime compliance is serious, and we are responsible for getting it right," Bank of America said in a statement. "We worked with regulators to reach these penalty resolutions stemming from violations cited in the previously reported 2024 (Comptroller of the Currency) Consent Order and FinCEN's investigation."We have invested billions of dollars in technology and dedicated thousands of employees to combat financial crime, and our team is far along with and committed to completing the work required to address the issues raised by our regulators."The latest action is the third-largest penalty ever issued by the Treasury Department, behind a roughly $4bn (€3.41bn) settlement in 2023 with Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, and an approximately $3bn (€2.56bn) settlement with Canada-based TD Bank the following year.Both settlements were part of the Biden administration's efforts to combat money laundering. Its broader push also aimed to improve compliance in the cryptocurrency industry.In 2024, Binance founder Changpeng Zhao was sentenced to four months in prison after pleading guilty to failing to prevent money laundering on the platform. Prosecutors said criminals had used it to move money connected to child sex abuse, drug trafficking and terrorism.US President Donald Trump pardoned Zhao in October 2025.

title: France’s emissions are falling as fuel prices soar. Why is it still missing climate targets?
description: Despite using less fossil fuels, France is still far short of the 5 per cent annual reduction in emissions it needs to meet its climate targets.
content: France is getting an unexpected boost in its efforts to cut greenhouse gas emissions, but it comes with a catch consumers are feeling at the fuel pump.Soaring fuel prices caused by the war in Iran have prompted people to buy less diesel and cut down on their gas use at home. That has helped bring emissions down 4.1 per cent in the first half of 2026, according to Citepa, a French organisation that measures air pollution and greenhouse gases to track the country’s environmental impact.France is now on track to cut emissions by 2.8 per cent this year, up from 2.1 per cent in 2025. That would amount to 10 million tonnes fewer emissions than last year.Even so, it’s still falling short of the pace needed to meet its long-term climate targets. France is aiming to halve emissions by 2030 compared to 1990 levels, but meeting that goal will require annual reductions of around 5 per cent.Fuel prices hit French consumersMuch of the emissions reduction boils down to the cost of filling up the car. Fuel prices have surged since the start of the year, with diesel climbing 45 per cent after the war in Iran choked off oil supplies through the Strait of Hormuz.People have simply bought less fuel since then. Diesel sales fell 7.3 per cent in the first six months of 2026. In that same timeframe, transport emissions dropped 4.5 per cent.Emissions from homes and commercial buildings fell even more, dropping 12 per cent in the first half of the year mostly due to less natural gas use for heating, water and cooking.But the downward trajectory is unlikely to last. Citepa expects emissions to fall just 1.3 per cent in the second half of the year, partly because France is using more gas-fired power plants to produce electricity for neighbouring countries.The energy industry’s emissions are expected to rise by 3.6 per cent over the full year, even as transport and other sectors continue to record reductions.France’s Ecological Transition Minister Monique Barbut called the decline “encouraging” but acknowledged it was “not yet enough to meet our climate targets”, according to AFP.Global emissions could fall for first time since 2020Elsewhere in Europe, emissions are on a steady – if slow – decline. Germany’s emissions fell about 2 per cent in the first half of 2026 as demand for oil dropped. However, the think tank Agora Energiewende has warned the country could still exceed its annual emissions limit by around 10 million tonnes – the first time it will have done so since passing its landmark climate law in 2019.High energy costs have also encouraged European households to find more affordable alternatives to fossil fuels. Heat pump sales rose 25 per cent in France, Germany and Poland early in 2026, and EV sales have also spiked since the start of the war. Meanwhile, solar power has saved the EU an estimated €37.4 billion in gas imports since it broke out in February.Outside of Europe, emissions are also going down. In China, oil use fell 9 per cent in the second quarter of 2026, while carbon emissions dropped 1 per cent – the first time a decline in China’s emissions had been linked to oil rather than coal.A recent report by Carbon Brief based on forecasts from the IEA suggests global fossil fuel CO2 emissions could fall about 0.5 per cent this year, which would be the first annual decline since stay-at-home orders caused them to plummet in 2020.While the IEA expects oil demand to climb when the war ends, the widespread embrace of solar and wind power, nuclear energy, electric cars and heat pumps could keep fossil fuel use down even after their prices stabilise. Those technologies helped to prevent an estimated 3 billion tonnes of CO2 emissions worldwide in 2025, the agency reports.

title: Police boost presence and detain 17-year-old after 'Bloody Friday' threat to Polish schools
description: Warnings about an alleged series of attacks on schools planned for 9 October have circulated on social media. Police say they are monitoring the situation and will deploy officers to schools they believe are at risk. In several towns in the Mazovia region, on-site classes have been cancelled.
content: On Thursday, social media were flooded with claims about alleged planned attacks on schools. Among pupils and parents, screenshots and recordings have been circulating, warning of a so-called "bloody Friday", said to fall on Friday 9 October.The reports appeared after a series of serious incidents in schools in the Mazovia region.On Wednesday, a 19-year-old attacked nine people with a knife at a school in Ostrołęka. The following day in Leszczydole-Nowinach, a 15-year-old former pupil attacked three people, where a 37-year-old school employee died from her injuries.Boosted police presence in schoolsIn response to mounting concern, police have announced reinforced preventive measures. National Police Commander-in-Chief Marek Boroń said officers would be present around schools from Friday morning to help combat the threat and ease anxiety."The police will do everything to ensure these schools are secure" – Boroń told Polish media outlets.He added that patrols had already appeared near school premises on Thursday and were in contact with their representatives. On Friday, officers are expected to work with principals, teachers and local authorities.The police chief also appealed to pupils and parents to report any credible suspicions of planned violence to teachers or law enforcement directly.Boroń added that after the attack in Ostrołęka, the number of reports about potential threats has risen sharply. He also urged caution in spreading information about alleged attacks.Social media-induced panicOne of the main reasons behind the growing anxiety was a video that began circulating on social media platforms in the country.According to Polish news outlets, the material referred to alleged plans to attack schools as part of "bloody Friday", after its author had announced a "massacre in Przasnysz".Officers in Przasnysz quickly took up the case. They detained a 17-year-old resident of Przasnysz county, who is believed to be the likely author of the video."Officers detained a 17-year-old resident of Przasnysz county, who is the probable author of the video circulating online. Activities with the man are under way" Mazovian police reported.Schools closed on FridayAlarming reports have also emerged in other localities.In Sierpc, police detained a 17-year-old who had said he intended to hurt someone at school. Two knives were found on the teenager. In this case, pupils and teachers played a key role in his detention by reporting information about his behaviour to the police.On Thursday, there was also a tragic attack in Leszczydole-Nowinach near Wyszków.A 15-year-old former student attacked a caretaker, the principal and a teacher with a sharp tool, likely a knife. The 37-year-old school employee succumbed to their wounds while two other victims were injured.Authorities have decided that primary schools in the Wyszków municipality will not hold classes on Friday as a result of the attacks and further safety-related concerns.The institutions are however still expected to provide care for their pupils. Local media reported that on Friday all secondary schools in Ciechanów will operate remotely. In-person classes will also not take place in schools in the district of Pułtusk.

title: Europe’s satellite sovereignty push faces funding test as EU space budget cycle ends
description: Regulators, EU officials and Spanish satellite operator Sateliot gathered at the European Parliament on Tuesday to debate how spectrum and investment will shape Europe’s networks in orbit, with the EU’s 2021-2027 space funding cycle ending next year.
content: National telecoms authorities, EU policymakers and Barcelona-based satellite company Sateliot met at the European Parliament in Brussels on Tuesday to discuss how radio frequencies and fresh money will decide who controls the communications Europe relies on from orbit, with the bloc’s current seven-year space budget expiring in 2027.Euronews was at the event, organised by Sateliot, whose spacecraft act as mobile phone masts in space, connecting Internet of Things (IoT) devices such as sensors and trackers where ground networks don’t reach.The EU’s €14.8 billion space programme for 2021-2027, which funds Galileo, the bloc’s satellite navigation system, and Copernicus, its Earth observation service, ends next year along with the Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF), the EU’s seven-year budget.For 2028-2034, the European Commission wants space funded from a new European Competitiveness Fund, a single pot for strategic industries that would set aside €131 billion for defence and space.EU leaders are due to discuss the next budget at the European Council meeting on Thursday and Friday.The Commission’s defence industry and space department, DG DEFIS, closed bids on 29 September for a four-year, €55 million framework contract for management and legal support on three fronts: IRIS², the EU’s planned secure satellite constellation, space surveillance and tracking, which monitors objects in orbit, as well as analysis of the space economy.More calls under Horizon Europe, the EU’s research and innovation programme, follow in 2027, while EUSPA, the EU Agency for the Space Programme, and the European Space Agency (ESA), an intergovernmental body separate from the EU, keep running tenders.Spectrum and sovereigntyMuch of the debate centred on spectrum, the radio frequencies that satellites and mobile networks need to transmit.In May, the Commission proposed a single EU-wide licence for mobile satellite services, which link satellites directly to phones and other devices, in the 2 GHz band, whose current rights expire in May 2027. It would specifically reserve part of the band for European operators and a secure system linked to IRIS².European Parliament Vice-President Javier López hosted the meeting and the Commission’s digital department, DG CONNECT, was represented by Gerasimos Sofianatos, head of the radio spectrum policy unit."This discussion could not come at a better moment considering the current geopolitical tensions and the debate surrounding technological competition", said López in his opening statement."A Europe that controls its own network and data is a Europe that can act independently and make its own decisions [...] satellite connectivity is a perfect example of an area where we must achieve strategic control", López added.Speaking to Euronews after the event, the CEO and co-founder of Sateliot Jaume Sanpera stated that "we have to build and support European champions that can compete globally in the space sector," adding that "today half the world wants to work with European companies in defence and space because we are more predictable."In September, the ESA selected Sateliot to contribute to IRIS²’s Low-LEO layer, a testing ground in low orbit where new government services are tried out before any are added to the main system. The ESA plans in-orbit test missions from 2027 to 2029.Through its RESCUE-NET project, Sateliot will also study how 5G connectivity from space can keep public authorities connected when ground networks fail. The ESA signed 18 contracts worth €20 million in total with nearly 80 companies for this phase.From SpaceX to PLD SpaceFor small satellites, reaching orbit still largely means flying American.On 1 October, Sateliot sent five satellites built by Spanish small-satellite maker Alén Space into orbit on Transporter-18, a rideshare mission by Elon Musk’s rocket company SpaceX that carries spacecraft for many customers, taking its total launched to 11.The extra satellites double its daily passes over any given point, the company says.Asked by Euronews whether Europe can expand its fleets without relying on non-European launchers, Sanpera said that he is optimistic and mentioned that there are currently four or five companies in the race to fill that gap.The CEO of Sanpera also explained that the firm's next launch will be in July 2027, again in collaboration with SpaceX, but the one after that will be with PLD Space, a Spanish launch company based in Elche.That launch in late 2027 will not only be entirely European, but it will also feature Sateliot's first two Tritó satellites, a larger next generation designed to offer 5G direct-to-device services to ordinary phones.They will fly on Miura 5, a small orbital rocket built by PLD Space that has yet to fly.Back in August, PLD won a conditional €158.9 million contract under ESA's European Launcher Challenge, which backs new European rockets, and it plans a debut launch from Europe’s spaceport in French Guiana by the end of this year.Meanwhile, Sateliot, which is raising €150 million from investors, comprising €100 million in equity and up to €50 million in debt, aims to grow its constellation to more than 500 satellites.

title: Qatar’s emir vows that country will emerge stronger as he outlines national strategies
description: Qatar's emir outlined in a speech to the nation how the Gulf nation has managed to overcome the consequences of the Iran war and will emerge stronger and better equipped to adapt to global changes by diversifying its economy and focusing on non-carbon industries in addition to existing LNG exports.
content: Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani said on Tuesday that his country "will emerge from this crisis more resilient and better equipped to adapt to global changes," outlining the country's national strategies which now also focus on diversifying the economy towards the "non-hydrocarbon sectors," in addition to the traditional model of liquefied natural gas global supply which Qatar wants to increase.In a speech to the nation at the opening of the Shura Council’s annual session in Doha, Sheikh Tamim made it clear that "Qatar was attacked on its territory by Iran, in a blatant violation of its sovereignty, the provisions of international law, and the principles of good-neighborly relations."“Qatar has always preferred to resolve disputes through negotiation and diplomatic and peaceful means," Sheikh Tamim added."Our commitment to dialogue and peaceful solutions does not mean being complacent about defending our country," he said. "Our right to defend our sovereignty does not conflict with our determination to prevent a wider war."Iran has consistently maintained that it was only targeting US interests among its neighbours during the war.Against the backdrop of widening conflicts across the region, he stressed the need for the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries to cooperate, stating that "the security of the GCC states and the protection of their sovereignty and stability are non-negotiable."Sheikh Tamim urged "to redouble our efforts to secure navigation in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, and to protect energy and water facilities, as well as civil infrastructure."Sheikh Tamim also outlined the country's response during the war and its strategies going forward, based on long-term planning before the crisis and the measures Qatar implemented to adapt to the war's consequences.He addressed "the extraordinary events" that impacted the country and the region, which "demonstrated (...) our ability to respond to crises efficiently and responsibly" and that "resilience isn't born in the moment of crisis; rather, it is the result of the planning that precedes it.""In this crisis, Qatar has shouldered three responsibilities simultaneously: protecting its sovereignty, fulfilling its role in energy security and the global economy, and keeping the doors of diplomacy open," Sheikh Tamim said.Based on these responsibilities, Qatar's Emir outlined "four key elements" that formed the country's strategy in addressing the crisis: "first, defending the homeland firmly without being drawn into war; second, maintaining essential services, supply chains, and economic activity; third, contributing to efforts to secure a ceasefire and reopen waterways; and fourth, urging negotiations and seeking opportunities to return to talks to reach peaceful resolutions to the conflict."Sheikh Tamim acknowledged Qatar's key role in global energy systems, supplying about one-fifth of the world’s liquefied natural gas (LNG), and said that "any disruption affecting it is quickly reflected in markets and consumers everywhere.""The closure of the Strait of Hormuz, together with the direct damage inflicted on some energy facilities in Ras Laffan Industrial City, disrupted a significant portion of the country’s exports," the Qatari emir said.Signalling a key development, Sheikh Tamim said Qatar absorbed the shock by focusing on the "non-hydrocarbon sectors", which "continued to grow with their contribution reaching approximately 80% of real GDP."He explained that the "non-hydrocarbon sectors" alternative "reflects the resilience of the national economy and its ability to sustain growth under exceptional and complex circumstances", and that "the stock of foreign direct investment continued to grow."He revealed that "the total revenues declined by 42% during the first half of the year, while public expenditure fell by 14%, without compromising essential services or development priorities," as "the state did not succumb to panic.""Instead, it continued to look to the future with confidence in the national economy," Sheikh Tamim said."We decided not to reduce essential services and opted to maintain our developmental priorities, in order to sustain Qatar’s ongoing economic momentum," Sheikh Tamim said."The policies adopted by the state prior to the crisis — including strengthening reserves, reducing public debt, budgeting based on conservative oil price assumptions, and developing non-oil revenues — have enabled us to absorb the repercussions of this crisis thus far."Moving forward, Sheikh Tamim said the Gulf country's "aim is not to return to the pre-crisis situation, but rather to use the recovery as a springboard to accelerate economic diversification and strengthen national capabilities.""Our duty is to always strive for the best, but we must also be prepared for the worst-case scenarios, and everyone—institutions and citizens alike—must take responsibility," the emir told the nation.He outlined the country's plans for the energy sector, which include the expansion of the North Field Gas project to increase LNG production capacity, the progress of the Golden Pass project in the US and QatarEnergy's increased investments and international partnerships, "alongside the development of petrochemical industries, solar energy projects, and efforts to strengthen water security."He also outlined the country's focus on food security, agriculture, technology, institutional efficiency, investment in education "to face the challenges of our time" and in digital transformation.Sheikh Tamim said the Palestinian cause remained a priority for Qatar, declaring that "what has happened in the Gaza Strip is undoubtedly a genocide, and those responsible must not escape accountability."He warned of "the dangers" resulting from Israeli settler attacks on Palestinians in the West Bank, "not to mention the repeated raids on the Al-Aqsa Mosque, and countless violations of the provisions of international law, the UN Charter, and international humanitarian law."Sheikh Tamim's criticism in his national speech underlined Qatar's ongoing firm position towards Israel's actions in Gaza and Lebanon. Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has lashed out frequently at Qatar, calling it "a hostile state".Beyond Gaza and the Gulf, the emir reaffirmed Qatar's continuing role in mediating political agreements to resolve the crises in Sudan, Libya, Yemen and Somalia.

title: Netflix secures 2030 World Cup rights in Spain and Andorra
description: The 2030 World Cup is scheduled to take place across Morocco, Portugal, and Spain, with three special centenary celebration matches also set to be held in Argentina, Paraguay, and Uruguay.
content: Netflix has acquired the broadcasting rights for the 2030 FIFA World Cup in Spain and Andorra, the platform announced on Tuesday.Under the deal, the streaming service will show all 104 of the tournament's matches live.The 2030 World Cup is scheduled to take place across Morocco, Portugal, and Spain, with three special centenary celebration matches also set to be held in Argentina, Paraguay, and Uruguay.The move marks a significant step in Netflix's strategy to expand its portfolio of live sports events and to compete with traditional television broadcasters.In Spain, viewers will be able to watch at least one match per matchday free of charge. In addition, a nationwide free-to-air channel will be allowed to broadcast all of Spain's matches, the two semi-finals, and the final."Few events unite people like the World Cup," Bela Bajaria, Netflix's chief content officer, said, per the media company's official companion site Tudum. "I was in the stands this year as Spain lifted the trophy and witnessed the passion, the pride, the stories - they all become part of a nation’s culture and are remembered for generations."Mattias Grafström, the secretary general of world football governing body FIFA, added: "We are pleased to build on our partnership with Netflix as we look ahead to the FIFA World Cup 2030.""Our shared ambition is to bring fans closer to the game and enable as many people as possible to share in the excitement of the competition," he said.

title: Spreading the flow: cruise tourism helps Europe protect local identity
description: Europe’s tourism strategy is shifting to sustainable, year-round travel, promoting lesser-known destinations, local culture and smarter visitor management.
content: Today's travellers want more than a photo. They want a story to tell. They want to immerse themselves in the life of places they visit, however fleeting their stay. When cruise travellers step ashore, they are increasingly looking to connect with a place in a tangible and personal way. From cycling and snorkelling to walking tours to wine tasting, they want to pursue activities that help them to experience the authentic traditions and local culture that give a destination its unique identity. Across Europe, tourism leaders and local communities are considering how destinations can protect their identity, safeguard the natural environment, ensure that tourism creates local value, and respond to growing visitor demand. As the EU develops its vision for sustainable tourism, understanding the importance of well-planned tourism is key to answering this question. Take diversification, for example. Encouraging people to visit less well-known places can help to ease pressure on busier sites. Greece offers a compelling example. This is a country that draws visitors from all over the world to enjoy its historical wonders, and stunning coastlines and islands. At the same time, we see growing potential in some of its less famous islands. Since we added the island of Syros to our itineraries, our guests have praised its authenticity and cultural heritage, brought to life through the insight and knowledge of local guides. Greece is not the only country to offer such potential. Europe is home to countless destinations with unique identities and rich heritage, many of which lie off the beaten track. This winter, for example, we will continue our collaboration with local authorities in the Canary Islands to bring our guests further inland to the villages of Garachico, Betancuria, Teguise and Tejeda. Local traditions, craftsmanship, and gastronomy remain central to everyday life in these villages, where visitors enjoy more meaningful experiences while also creating local value.The key lesson is that these new itineraries were the result of extensive cooperation. Opening new places in the right way does not happen overnight and requires planning and strong local partnerships. These examples also show a link between the growing demand for more personal, authentic experiences and the need to achieve more balanced tourism flows.Tourism management means understanding a destination’s vision, its capacity, and the infrastructure needed to support it. That means looking beyond the port to the roads, public transport, walking routes, cycling options, and visitor information. The city of Dubrovnik’s “Respect the City” programme, for example, features visitor management measures including digital data and street signage to recommend the best times to visit popular attractions and help people move through the historic old town more easily.In fact, when people travel can be just as important as where they travel. Many remarkable destinations have just as much to offer in spring, autumn, or winter as they do at the height of summer. As travellers increasingly spread their trips across the year, there is an opportunity to support local economies beyond the traditional peak season. Off-peak cruise travel is a growing trend, and Europe is seeing the highest increase in share of cruise passengers sailing during off-peak months. This enables destinations to reduce dependence on seasonal peaks and build greater long-term resilience. As travel patterns evolve, policy should help destinations adapt to longer tourism seasons, supporting the infrastructure, services and workforce needed to welcome visitors throughout the year.With careful planning, collaboration and the right systems in place, cruise tourism can provide a steady and controlled flow of guests. Cruise operators plan itineraries up to two years in advance, which gives destinations time to anticipate demand and manage capacity. The island of Mykonos in Greece shows how this works in practice. The implementation of a digital berthing system has shown how cruise traffic can be monitored and managed, helping support a more balanced distribution of visitors.As Europe shapes its future tourism strategy, policy should be directed towards helping destinations to manage tourism more effectively. This includes targeted investment in infrastructure. Better connectivity between transport networks, destinations and visitor experiences helps spread tourism benefits more widely while reducing pressure on the most visited places. Investment should also support development of data tools to support visitor flow management, while clear information at terminals with maps, suggested routes and links to public transport can help travellers discover a region in a more balanced way. There should be greater support for destination management plans that bring together local authorities, transport providers, and tourism businesses around a shared vision for tourism development. Adopting a holistic approach towards coastal and island tourism, considering cruise, ferries and other forms of maritime travel, would help avoid bottlenecks and shape visitor flows in line with local priorities.When visitors can explore throughout the year, discover lesser-known places and engage with local culture, tourism can deliver lasting benefits beyond the places that are most visited. With investment in long-term planning and collaboration between destinations and tourism partners, visitors can be welcomed in ways that support local value while preserving what makes each place special.By Gianni Onorato, CEO MSC Cruises

title: US banks post strong earnings but economic risks cloud the sector’s outlook
description: Wall Street's biggest banks reported another strong quarter on Tuesday, but they warned that higher rates and inflation could bite.
content: Higher profits at four of the biggest US banks offered fresh signs of economic resilience, as consumers continued repaying their debts and businesses kept investing heavily in AI.But even as JPMorgan Chase, Citigroup, Wells Fargo and Goldman Sachs reported higher profits than a year ago, they warned about the long-term impact of higher interest rates and the pressure rising prices could put on consumers if inflation is not brought under control.JPMorgan Chase, the largest US bank by assets, posted a $15.3 billion profit in the third quarter, or $5.57 a share, up from $14.4 billion, or $5.07 a share, in the same period a year earlier. The results missed analysts' expectations, with Wall Street expecting the bank to earn $5.93 a share.It was a rare earnings miss for JPMorgan and its CEO, Jamie Dimon. The last time the bank missed analysts' expectations was nearly three years ago. The bank reported $658 million in investment securities losses and a 12% rise in expenses. Fixed income markets revenue fell 4% from a year earlier, although overall markets revenue rose 15%."The US economy continued to be fueled by strong business investment and ongoing consumer spending," Dimon said in a statement. "However, large fiscal deficits, sticky inflation, elevated asset prices, rising interest rates and geopolitical conditions continue to shift under the surface."The big banks typically open the quarterly earnings season, and this is a key one for the stock market given that strong corporate profits have helped push the S&P 500 to record levels.Analysts expect companies in the S&P 500 to deliver overall growth of nearly 30% in earnings per share from a year earlier, according to data provider FactSet. If they're correct, it would be the third consecutive quarter of growth above 25%.Goldman Sachs, whose third-quarter profits rose sharply as revenue from its equities business jumped 72% from a year earlier, also reported that its fixed income, currencies and commodities revenue fell 24% from the second quarter. The bank posted a profit of $5.29 billion, or $17.01 a share, compared with $4.1 billion, or $12.25 a share, a year earlier.The bond market saw significant volatility this summer, as investors became increasingly worried about government spending and inflation. Yields on 10-year and 30-year US Treasury bonds rose to levels not seen in years. Higher diesel, technology and food prices gave the Federal Reserve reason to raise interest rates last month, despite pressure from the White House against a rise.Citigroup said its third-quarter profits jumped 40% from a year ago, beating Wall Street expectations. The bank posted higher revenue from investment banking and wealth management, while profits in its credit card division were flat.Wells Fargo posted a profit of $5.95 billion, or $1.87 a share, beating Wall Street forecasts. The San Francisco-based bank has seen its profits climb steadily in recent quarters after federal bank regulators removed the asset cap imposed following its sales practices scandal nearly a decade ago.

title: ‘No regret’: The EEA’s six steps to make Europe more competitive without sacrificing sustainability
description: From resource efficiency to education, these six sustainable steps could make Europe more competitive in the long term.
content: Geopolitical instability, technological disruption and climate change are casting a shadow over Europe’s future.Could investing in sustainability make the continent more resilient?A new report by the European Environment Agency (EEA) reveals how Europe could strengthen its long-term competitiveness by nurturing both the economy and nature.Rather than promoting short-term productivity and economic growth based on resource depletion and environmental degradation, the EEA urges a more holistic approach that treats nature restoration and social capital as integral to long-term stability.The report, titled ‘Competitive by nature: Europe’s long-term competitiveness through the lens of sustainability’, released on 13 October, identifies six ‘no-regret’ options that could boost the economy while sustaining life on Earth.6. Investing in climate adaptation and resilienceEurope is warming faster than any other continent, with flooding, heatwaves, droughts and wildfires growing increasingly extreme as a result of climate change.Adapting to this new reality and mitigating its effects is no longer just an environmental necessity but an economic one too, the EEA argues.This includes investing in nature-based solutions, like restoring wetlands and floodplains or adding green space to cities, which can help soak up floodwater and cool urban areas.5. Using resources more efficientlyEurope imports a huge share of its raw materials and energy, and recent supply shocks have shown how risky that is.Disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, triggered by the war on Iran, have put immense pressure on fuel supplies, prompting an accelerated shift to homegrown renewable energy.But the technology behind wind turbines, solar panels and batteries relies on critical minerals, and the grids to carry all that clean power still have to be built.Circularity – repairing, reusing and recycling products – “can reduce demand for primary materials and energy, preserve the value embodied in products and infrastructure, and limit exposure to volatile commodity and energy markets,” the EEA says.Sometimes there are trade-offs, however: for example, while keeping old buildings and infrastructure in use is good for circularity, it can lock in assets that are inefficient or vulnerable to climate impacts.4. Leveraging next-gen techAI can be leveraged to help Europe use its resources more wisely, the EEA says. Digital tools can track materials through supply chains, manage variable renewable energy on the power grid, and monitor environmental damage in real time. Building these capabilities at home also reduces Europe’s reliance on technology developed elsewhere. The EU is already utilising these tools to strengthen accountability: its Digital Product Passport launched in July and will first be a requirement for batteries from February 2027. Consumers will be able to access information, for example through a QR code, on the origin of a product’s materials, its environmental performance, and how it can be repaired or recycled.But the energy- and water-hungry data centres needed to fuel AI are a growing concern in their own right.The EEA also encourages the development of next-gen biotechnology – making materials and fuels from plants and other biological sources, rather than oil and gas. While this can cut fossil fuel use, it also comes with its own footprint: growing biomass takes land and water and can put nature under strain.3. Investing in skills and educationSpreading and developing these new technologies is key to developing a low-carbon economy that sacrifices neither wages nor the environment. While a recent EEA analysis found that clean energy is creating jobs across the EU, it faces major bottlenecks in workforce availability and training.That’s why the agency’s latest report urges investment in skills, education and lifelong learning that will create a resilient workforce capable of adapting to a rapidly changing world. Ensuring these skills are spread across different demographics would foster social cohesion and fairness.2. Building public trustIn several EU countries, climate policy has become politically divisive, with fierce debate over costs, farming rules and red tape. Ensuring the green transition leaves no one behind would also help to build public trust in and support for it. Without this, even well-designed policies risk being watered down, delayed or scrapped.The EEA argues that clear, predictable regulation and effective institutions are integral to this. Companies are more likely to invest in clean technologies if they can rely on clear, stable rules, and the public is more likely to back the transition if it trusts those rules are applied fairly.1. Leading on sustainable standard-settingThe EU’s single market has the power to shape global rules on everything from chemicals to carbon emissions. The EEA says it should keep playing an active role in setting environmental and social standards, including through international institutions. Cooperating with other countries through democratic, international forums like the UN’s COP can help create common rules, diversify trade relationships and make supply chains more resilient.But the system is under strain. Nearly 200 nations pledged to transition away from fossil fuels at COP28 in 2023, yet a new agreement on fossil fuels is considered unlikely at COP31 in Türkiye next month. Meanwhile, fossil fuel-reliant nations are pushing to delay the UN climate science panel’s next major report until after the global climate summit, with the IPCC meeting this week to try to resolve the deadlock.At home, the EU is also under pressure to simplify its own green rules in the name of competitiveness. The EEA maintains that sustainability can reinforce competitiveness.

title: Lake Tuzkan – life and tourism around Jizzakh’s desert lakes
description: Lake Tuzkan brings fishing, tourism and recreation to the dry landscape of Jizzakh, as new transport links are expected to make the area easier to reach.
content: The landscape of Jizzakh region changes quickly. Dry earth and sandy stretches dominate much of the Mirzachul area, until a large body of water appears on the horizon.Lake Tuzkan is part of the Aydar-Arnasay lake system, one of the largest inland water areas in Uzbekistan. Its setting, between the Hungry Steppe and the Kyzylkum Desert, gives the lake a distinctive place in the region.For visitors, the contrast with the surrounding landscape is part of the attraction. For local communities, the lakes have a more practical role, providing livelihoods through fishing, tourism and other activities.A lake in the middle of the steppeTuzkan is one of Uzbekistan’s largest lakes and has long been connected with life in the surrounding communities.Local residents depend on fishing, while tourism has created another source of income. Visitors come for time by the water, fishing and recreation, while some also seek the mineral-rich waters of Tuzkan for what they describe as health and wellness benefits.Tourist Ulugbek Musulmonov says the natural environment was one of the main reasons for his visit.“Our main reason for coming here is the natural environment and the health benefits of Tuzkan lake,” he says, adding that some visitors come with the hope of improving particular health conditions.The lake is also part of the wider Aydar-Arnasay system, where fishing remains an important economic activity for communities living nearby.The surrounding area has gradually developed facilities for visitors, creating a tourism economy alongside traditional activities connected with the lakes.Tourism takes hold by the waterOn the shore of neighbouring Lake Aydarkul, Aydarkul resort has developed accommodation and recreation facilities for visitors.The resort has 225 rooms and can accommodate up to 600 guests. Its facilities include conventional rooms, capsule-style accommodation, restaurants, a beach and shaded outdoor platforms known locally as tapchans, as well as boats and other water activities.Operations manager Jamshid Qarshiboyev says the resort received large numbers of visitors during the summer season, including tourists from Uzbekistan, Russia and Kazakhstan.Weekend events, including festivals and concerts, have become part of the resort's programme. Swimming, boating and time on the beach are among the main activities available to guests.The resort also has a medical centre offering treatments such as massage and hydromassage. Guests staying at the resort can receive one complimentary treatment as part of their accommodation package.The resort's location beside Aydarkul also gives visitors access to Tuzkan, where the waters are saltier and mineral-rich.Fishing remains another attraction. It is restricted during certain periods of the year, but resumes after the closed season.For some guests, a visit that begins as a day trip becomes an overnight stay.A changing destinationThe development of tourism around the lakes is also changing the way visitors reach the area.A new airport has been developed at Arnasoy, near the lakes, while construction of a railway line from Do‘stlik towards the Aydar-Arnasay lake system began in 2026. The projects are intended to improve access for visitors from Uzbekistan and abroad.The development could give the lake area a larger role in regional tourism, particularly for visitors already travelling through Uzbekistan's better-known historic destinations.For Ahmad Jabir Abdullah Mohammed Al Harbi, a visitor from the United Arab Emirates, the new airport could help introduce the area to a wider international audience.He describes the lakeside as a place for quiet and relaxation and says he would recommend it to people from his home country and elsewhere.The area is still developing, however, and some planned facilities have yet to be completed.Keeping visitors safeAs visitor numbers increase, safety has become another part of managing the recreation area.The Aydar-Arnasoy recreation area has operated since November 2025, with safe tourism officers working around the clock.Tourism police officer Meyirbek Amirxanov says the area can receive between 6,000 and 7,000 visitors on a Saturday or Sunday.Surveillance cameras cover the recreation area and are connected to the Ministry of Internal Affairs’ Qalqon security-monitoring system.The most common requests involve children who become separated from their families and visitors who lose personal belongings. Amirxanov says officers receive around five or six such requests on an average day and deal with them as they arise.With more visitors expected as transport links improve, managing large crowds will remain an important part of the area's development.A landscape shaped by waterThe history of Tuzkan goes beyond its growing tourism industry.The lake is a natural feature, but the wider landscape has also been affected by human activity. Irrigation and water-management projects during the 20th century changed the region's hydrology and contributed to the formation of the wider Aydar-Arnasay lake system.Today, the result is an unusual landscape: large expanses of water surrounded by dry steppe and desert.Along the shores, recreation areas have introduced another layer of activity. Families gather for weekends, visitors swim and fish, and resorts provide accommodation and organised entertainment.For local communities, the lakes remain connected to everyday economic life. For visitors, they offer a different experience of Jizzakh, away from the region's more familiar image of open steppe.The planned transport links are expected to bring more visitors to the lakes once completed.The landscape itself remains the main attraction: water stretching towards the horizon, with the dry plains and desert beyond it.

title: Pearls, diamonds and the stories behind Doha’s international jewellery show
description: From family memories to cultural traditions, we meet the people behind the pieces at the Doha Jewellery and Watches Exhibition, bringing together more than 500 brands from 30 countries.
content: There’s no shortage of luxury at the Doha Jewellery and Watches Exhibition. But look beyond the diamonds, gold and pearls, and some of the most interesting stories are about the people behind them.Now in its 22nd edition, the exhibition brings together more than 500 brands from 30 countries.Aadel Haleem meets Qatari businessman and jeweller Hussain Alfardan, who grew up surrounded by the pearl trade and still has a deeply personal connection to it. One of the pieces he shows us took seven years to complete.Indian fashion designer Manish Malhotra explains how traditional jewellery is finding a new audience through contemporary fashion, while Qatari designer Noora Al-Ansari looks closer to home for inspiration, drawing on the country’s colours, architecture and pearl heritage.There’s also a look at the technology being used to tell natural and synthetic diamonds apart.From international names to homegrown designers, this episode of CULT goes inside the Doha Jewellery and Watches Exhibition to discover why the value of a piece isn’t always about its price. Sometimes, it’s about a childhood memory, a family business or a tradition being passed from one generation to the next.

title: The world's best cruise lines and ships have been announced for 2026
