description: At the World Cruise Awards, Norwegian Cruise Line was named the world’s best cruise line for 2026 following a glitzy ceremony in Jamaica.
content: The winners of the World Cruise Awards have just been revealed for 2026 – and Norwegian Cruise Line has taken the top prize.Now in its sixth edition, the winners were announced on 12 October at a gala ceremony in Jamaica.Norwegian Cruise Line was named the world’s best cruise line for 2026, beating out nominees including MSC Cruises, Royal Caribbean International and Silversea.As for where you should be going for your next voyage, the UAE’s capital Abu Dhabi was named the world’s best cruise destination. It should be noted that some cruise lines have revised their 2026/27 schedules to avoid Gulf ports, given the ongoing crisis in the region. Lisbon was the only European destination among the nominees’ list, which also included Auckland Island in New Zealand, Jamaica, Mexico, Morocco, Prince Edward Island in Canada, the Seychelles and Vietnam.For those who have Patagonia on their bucket list, you should be looking to book with Australis, which was named the world’s best expedition cruise line.Thinking about a river cruise? Pandaw, which operates throughout countries in Asia including India, Vietnam, Cambodia, Laos and Myanmar, was named the world’s best river cruise line.Which is handy, because Vietnam was also named the world’s best river cruise destination.Within Europe, DouroAzul was named the best river cruise line, while Lisbon in Portugal was selected as the best river cruise destination.Which cruise ship is right for you?The World Cruise Awards also hand out gongs to individual cruise ships under categories such as dining, families and romance.For foodies, the best cruise ship is Sun Princess, which has seven specialty restaurants. These include American steakhouse Crown Grill, Sabatini's Italian Trattoria, seafood spot The Catch by Rudi (Sodamin, the cruise line’s head of culinary arts), The Butcher's Block by Dario (Cecchini, an eighth generation Italian butcher), show-stopping Umai Teppanyaki, sushi eatery Makoto Ocean, and Umai Hot Pot.If you’re travelling with your little ones, Disney Wish was named the best option for families, for obvious reasons.Expect live shows themed around classics like The Little Mermaid and Aladdin, restaurants that will transport you to Frozen’s Arendelle or the world of Marvel, plus water slides, sports courts and a movie theatre. Big kids won’t miss out on the fun, either, with cocktail bars, pubs, a spa, and an adults-only refuge with an infinity pool.Celebrity Apex was selected as the world’s best cruise for romance. Here, you can relax by the adults-only Solarium pool, catch a live performance with a cocktail at the cantilevered, floating platform The Magic Carpet, or play games together at The Casino.If you want a cruise ship that will keep you entertained even between ports, try Utopia of the Seas.On board, there are five pools, three water slides, 21 restaurants and 23 bars (including a karaoke spot), two casinos and plenty of shows, whether you’re into comedy or live music.

title: A schoolboy, a professor and a designer among winners of Dubai's app championship
description: From a 13-year-old with a YouTube channel to a professor who quit academia, this year's winners show the reach of a competition that drew almost 10,000 entries.
content: Ehsan Adouane started interviewing scientists on YouTube at the age of nine. At 13, he beat thousands of entrants worldwide to win one of Dubai's top tech prizes.His app, Ettan Ehsan turns homework into a game, breaking school subjects into quick, visual challenges. It took the Best Youth-made App award at this year's Create Apps Championship. "I want to now help students just like me to make homework more fun and more fast-paced and more gamified," he says.The win brings money and backing. "I really can now make my mark on the market as I have money to further develop this app and support from Dubai government to help me do this."The competition was fierce. There were 9,754 entries this year, more than the competition's first two editions combined. Launched in 2023 as a local contest, the championship opened to the world in its second year and has now drawn applications from 153 countries. The winners were honoured on 7 October by Mohammed bin Rashid bin Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, at Emirates Towers Boulevard.'A very disconnected world'For almost 20 years, Agnieszka Kocznur designed retail spaces for beauty brands. Then she walked away to back her own idea. "I left my corporate job; I'm completely full-time on Rush, and I really believe we can create an impact on human disconnection," she says.RUSH, which matches travellers with group trips built around shared interests, won the Most Impactful App award. "This reward matters because we are living in a very disconnected world with technology, but we found a way for technology to bring us together." Her message to anyone hesitating is simple. "I think you have to be courageous, believe in your ideas, and apply, see what happens."From lecture hall to fintechAlan Villegas spent years teaching entrepreneurship in Mexico City. Then he decided to put his teaching into practice. He quit academia, and after an earlier fintech venture elsewhere, chose Dubai. "I moved here specifically to do this business because we are in fintech and this is the most active fintech hub in the world probably," he says.His company, LiaPay, took Most Innovative App. "We are a UAE-based company helping UAE employees access their salaries earlier than payday."Part of the draw, he says, is a regulator open to new ideas. "The regulator is friendly; they understand or try to understand the innovation."Built to a deadlineFor the team behind Kwelio, the biggest enemy was perfectionism. "All three of us are perfectionists unfortunately and we kind of dwell on the little details so having set deadlines was a godsend," says co-founder and CEO Mohamed Al Rahma.Then the mentors pushed them further, and they rebuilt the app mid-competition. "The mentors from CreateApps actually told us that it needs to be calmer; it needs to be more of a journaling experience, which is why we actually redid the UI and the UX of the app during the competition," says co-founder and CTO Sumi Mahmud.The pitch they built is now their template. "I think this is the best pitch that we have ever done, and we use this pitch across every other investor pitch or other competitions."The top prize, Dubai's App of the Year, went to POP by Kwelio, a medication-adherence app.Life after the trophyFor past winners, the trophy was just the beginning. Takeem, a winner from the first edition, set out to bring trust to Dubai's rental market. "We won the CreateApps Championships and what it did is what every early-stage startup needs and that's credibility," says co-founder, Rakesh Mavath. "That credibility opened doors to partnerships, to investors."The numbers since speak for themselves. "We're now over 117,000 units, which is about nine billion dirhams in annual rent that Takeem can protect." The support did not stop at the ceremony. "Whenever we've asked them for anything or opened a door, they've immediately done it," he says, pointing to "the real open-door policy to regulators and government officials".Last year's App of the Year, Boom, helps delivery drivers find customers and set their own prices. For co-founder Mariam Mohammed Almarri, the win was the turning point. "Before the championship, the application was still a project in its early stages of ideation and prototyping."This year's finalists and semi-finalists now head straight into a six-month programme with Oraseya Capital, the venture capital arm of Dubai Integrated Economic Zones Authority, built to get young start-ups ready for investors. For anyone still wondering whether to take the leap, Takeem's advice is blunt. "If you're thinking about getting involved, my advice is just do it."

title: Stellantis bets on Chinese partnerships to avoid European plant closures
description: Chief executive Antonio Filosa says sharing factory capacity could help keep plants open, as Stellantis invests in new platforms and European batteries.
content: Stellantis wants to use partnerships with Chinese carmakers to keep its European plants open as it tackles excess production capacity, chief executive Antonio Filosa said in Paris.Speaking at the Paris Automotive Summit, held alongside the Paris Motor Show, Filosa outlined plans to share factory capacity with partners including Leapmotor and Dongfeng."We have excess production capacity, especially in Europe, but we do not want to shut plants," he said.The aim is to make better use of existing factories while matching production to demand, without introducing vehicles that compete directly with the group’s own brands.Stellantis bets on partnerships with Chinese manufacturersThe collaboration with Leapmotor, Filosa explained, makes it possible to combine the Chinese company’s technology with Stellantis’s factories and access to markets. Production in Europe could help serve local customers and expand the range of affordable electric vehicles.Stellantis is pursuing similar partnerships with other Chinese companies and partners in markets such as India. It aims to combine their technology with its manufacturing experience, sales network and knowledge of customers to develop new models faster and make better use of its plants.More battery gigafactories in EuropeThe shift to electric vehicles will also require further investment in battery production. Stellantis already has European gigafactories developed with two partners, but Filosa said more would be needed to support demand and meet “Made in Europe” requirements.He stressed that carmakers need enough time to make these investments, with European battery production a key part of efforts to make the industry more competitive.STLA One platform to launch with PeugeotStellantis is preparing to launch its new global STLA One platform, which will initially be used by Peugeot in France before being rolled out to the group’s other brands in Europe and North America.The project is part of the FaSTLAne 2030 plan, which sets out €60 billion in investment. Of that, 40% will go towards platforms, powertrains and technologies shared across brands and markets.Stellantis also plans to develop shared powertrains for use in several regions. The aim is to avoid duplicate spending and reduce costs by producing at scale. The remaining 60% of investment will go towards individual brands and products.Filosa urges swift agreement on emissions rulesFilosa also called for a swift agreement on changes to European CO2 emissions rules and measures to support production in Europe. He said the industry agreed on most objectives but needed to resolve the remaining differences."We all agree on 90 per cent of the issues," he said, stressing the need to finalise the rules quickly.The talks also involve the diplomatic initiatives of France and Germany and meetings with manufacturers and suppliers promoted by French President Emmanuel Macron.Ahead of the Paris Motor Show, Stellantis unveiled six of the nine concept cars planned for the event at a preview called The Night Before.The models from Alfa Romeo, Citroën, DS Automobiles, Fiat, Opel and Peugeot offer a glimpse of the group’s FaSTLAne 2030 strategic plan, presented in May by Filosa, to accelerate model development and strengthen the group’s competitiveness.

title: Dubai swaps apps for AI agents in its race to lead the next wave of tech
description: The Create Apps Championship, which has drawn more than 15,000 entries from 153 countries, is reinventing itself as a global contest to build autonomous AI agents.
content: One team flew 55 hours from Nicaragua for a shot at the title. They made the journey, says Saeed Al Gergawi, Vice President of Dubai Chamber of Digital Economy, "because they know that Dubai provides them with the right platform to be able to serve global economies".It is a long way to travel for an app competition. But this is no longer just an app competition. Three editions in, the Create Apps Championship is reinventing itself. It returns as the Create AI Agents Championship, a global race to build systems that don't just answer questions but carry out tasks and make decisions on their own.Hamdan bin Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, Crown Prince of Dubai, announced the switch, as this year's winners were honoured on 7 October. The ambition is stated plainly: "making Dubai the first city to lead innovation in this field."From Dubai to 153 countriesThe growth has been rapid. Launched as a local contest in 2023, it has drawn 15,564 applications from 153 countries. This year alone brought 9,754, more than the first two editions combined.It has helped produce 1,700 prototypes and more than 140 live apps. According to Al Gergawi, more than 250 mentors from around the world have been involved. It began as a local competition. The second and third editions opened it to the world, and the third drew entrants from as far as Central America. Now the brief is bigger.Beyond the chatbotThe shift follows technology, and it is a big one. A chatbot answers a question. An AI agent can be given a goal and left to work towards it, checking, booking, filing and following up with limited human input.For a competition built on apps, it is a natural next step. Apps put services on the phone. Agents can use those services on the user's behalf.Founders who have already been through the championship are now building with the technology. For Rakesh Mavath, co-founder of Takeem, a winner from the first edition, the case is simple. "Agentic AI matters for one simple reason. It's ease of use of the consumer." Much of it is invisible. "We also use a lot of agentic AI in the backend to help with administration, content marketing, go-to-market, but that's the part that the public doesn't see."The Dubai Chamber of Digital Economy runs the championship, one of three chambers under Dubai Chambers, set up to attract digital companies, talent, and investment to the emirate. The new format is part of a wider push to accelerate agentic AI use across Dubai's business community.'To serve humanity'Entrants must find a real problem, build an AI agent to solve it, test its impact and show how it could become a business. Al Gergawi wants the championship "to provide the platform for anyone with an idea, any business, to be able to be on the level field with the world". "Ultimately what we want to do is we want to be able to use agentic AI as tools to serve humanity and to serve global economies," he says.The appeal for smaller players is productivity. AI tools, he says, allow companies "to be able to accelerate and increase their productivity, be it small startups, being able to compete with large corporates, thanks to AI tools and agentic AI."But productivity is not the only test. "What we're trying to do here that is unique is to ensure that all of the participants and anyone that applies does so to positively impact humanity as a whole, businesses, and society."Years into monthsSpeed is the selling point. The idea is that innovators prove a concept in Dubai, then take it home. Dubai wants to "become a platform for global innovators, anyone that has just an idea, to be able to test it and then be able to deploy it in their own markets, in their home geographies," says Al Gergawi.The target is to shrink a journey that usually takes years into less than six months.Age is no barrierThere is no minimum age to enter, and no need to write a line of code. Teenagers can go head-to-head with start-ups and established firms, and Al Gergawi believes that gives them an edge, not a handicap.Their advantage, he says, comes "by being young and being able to move much faster". "So, keeping an eye on tomorrow's economy, it's important to foster the right culture and to involve the youth early on."The stakes are high. Each of the four category winners, covering societal, personal, business and youth agents, receives around €128,000 (AED 550,000), and one goes on to be named AI Agent of the Year, with around €232,000 (AED 1 million). The first three editions asked entrants to build an app. The next will ask whether their agents can do the work themselves.

title: The art of haute couture: Valentino Garavani through the eyes of sculptor Joana Vasconcelos
description: Lisbon is hosting an exhibition where works by sculptor Joana Vasconcelos converse with dresses by renowned Italian designer Valentino Garavani, fusing domestic life and haute couture.
content: MAAT – the Museum of Art, Architecture and Technology in Lisbon – is hosting the exhibition "VENUS – Valentino Garavani through the eyes of Joana Vasconcelos" (source in Portuguese), inspired by the world of the renowned Italian fashion designer.The project stems from a partnership between the Valentino Garavani and Giancarlo Giammetti Foundation – Giammetti being the designer's life and business partner – and Portuguese sculptor and artist Joana Vasconcelos, who has devised a visitor journey in which her own work enters into dialogue with the pieces created over the years by the designer."I wanted to show the diversity and the wonder of Valentino's work, the way he worked with embroidery, all the fabrics he used, completely different from one another. But also how, from these materials, he created this idyllic woman, this goddess-like woman," the Portuguese artist told Euronews, recalling how the designer "transformed, through his dresses, women's identities".Drawing on the designer's archive, to which Joana Vasconcelos had access in order to shape this exhibition, the sculptor revealed that she had sought "to choose dresses that weren't the cliché of 'Valentino Red'", a colour strongly associated with the ideals of power, passion and sensuality. Even so, the show includes a particularly emblematic example of what has become one of the Italian creator's trademarks.At the press presentation of "VENUS – Valentino Garavani through the eyes of Joana Vasconcelos", the Portuguese artist explained to Euronews that it was from this "idea of luxury" that Valkyrie Venus emerged, a textile sculpture that occupies the central place in the entire show."And it was from this work that the exhibition was born, in which we play on the paradox between the domestic and luxury. The woman at home, the woman in intimacy, the woman who is not seen; and the woman in public space, the woman who becomes a goddess because she wears a Valentino dress," Joana Vasconcelos explained. The Valkyrie Venus itself incorporates the "textures" and colours of the garments chosen as the source of inspiration for its creation.It was with this apparently contradictory relationship "between the private and the public" in mind that the sculptor has designed, within MAAT's spaces, a route where visitors can see some of her most emblematic works, as well as new creations, in symbiosis with garments bearing the signature of the acclaimed Italian fashion designer.Speaking about the whole process of selecting the dresses to be included in the exhibition and their interconnection with her own sculptures, Joana Vasconcelos confided to Euronews that "it was not a challenge", but rather something "very dynamic and fun". One example is the "Ironing Room", as she calls it, for which she chose "dresses that cannot be ironed", displayed flanking an artistic composition in which that household appliance is the main protagonist."So it was this strange way of life that led me to create this exhibition," a true "game between dresses that are worn only on certain occasions of perfection and luxury" and life "in the domestic sphere, which does not include that kind of elements". This second dimension appears throughout the route through the "presence of feather dusters, pots and cutlery", among other utensils that are highly characteristic of life at home.The show at MAAT is an adapted version of a project originally on display in the Italian city of Rome, more specifically at PM23, the cultural space founded by Valentino and Giancarlo Giammetti, where it ran until 19 July 2026.The exhibition which aims to be a meeting point between art and haute couture, is being held as part of the celebrations marking MAAT's 10th anniversary, at a time when the museum itself is also hosting three other new exhibitions.VENUS - Valentino Garavani through the eyes of Joana Vasconcelos is on at MAAT until 22 February 2027.

title: LVMH sales miss growth forecasts as China luxury demand slows
description: LVMH, the world's leading luxury group, said its sales edged higher in the third quarter despite a slowdown in demand in China hitting its fashion and leather goods segment.
content: The fashion giant, once Europe’s most valuable listed company, reported revenue of €18.5 billion in the three months to the end of September.The firm, whose brands include Louis Vuitton, Dior, Celine and drinks maker Hennessy, saw a revenue increase of 1.2% year on year in the third quarter, after a 0.1% rise in the second quarter and a 5.9% fall in the first.However, organic sales growth, which excludes currency movements and changes to the group's business portfolio, fell short of expectations. Growth slowed to 1% in the third quarter from 3% in the second.Overall, in the first nine months, sales were €57.1 billion, with organic sales up 2%.The company praised its diverse business portfolio in a statement, saying it provided resilience in an uncertain geopolitical and economic environment.LVMH said sales growth was good in the United States, Europe and Japan, but it faced a less favourable environment in China.As a result, the fashion and leather goods segment saw sales drop 5% on an organic basis as weaker demand in the world's second-largest economy weighed on the business. The decline was steeper than the roughly 2% fall expected by analysts, according to Deutsche Bank.Louis Vuitton also saw its public image take a hit in China after suing local tea company Molly Tea for copying its logo. While it won the case, the dispute provoked a wave of indignation on social media and calls to boycott the brand.Overall, the quarter proved to be a setback for the fashion and leather goods segment, as the drop in sales followed the division posting its first organic sales gain in two years in the previous quarter.But LVMH's selective retailing division, which includes the Sephora perfume and cosmetics retail chain, posted an 8% organic sales increase, while the watches and jewellery and wines and spirits segments both managed 6% organic gains.Deutsche Bank analysts said the results could prompt further cuts to earnings forecasts for the second half of 2026 and 2027.“It is hard to see what could change investor sentiment in the short term,” they wrote, although they viewed the weakness as cyclical rather than structural."Overall, recovery is taking longer due to the weaker Chinese demand, but the company do not see it as a structural issue. Brand initiatives are producing results and they expect these bottom-up measures to be more gradual," they wrote.LVMH's share price has dropped nearly 40% since the start of the year. In September, L'Oréal overtook the group as France's most valuable listed company. LVMH’s share price was down more than 1.6% at around 10am CEST in Paris.

title: This French AI stock is up 570% in 2026: Analysts see a further 90% upside
description: Despite its extraordinary rally, Bank of America analysts have upgraded Soitec SA stock to Buy and see potential for a further 90% upside.
content: A little-known French semiconductor company has become one of Europe's biggest artificial intelligence stock market winners in 2026, thanks to a technology few competitors can produce.Shares in Soitec SA have risen almost sevenfold this year, from about €23 at the start of January to roughly €154 on Monday afternoon in Paris.Yet the company reported a 34% decline in annual revenue last year.Now, Bank of America believes the stock could nearly double again.On Friday, the US bank upgraded Soitec from Neutral to Buy and raised its price target from €152 to €300, implying more than 90% upside.So what is driving this rally, and how much of it rests on a single product?The French company behind a critical AI technologySoitec does not make the processors that train artificial intelligence models. It makes the engineered silicon wafers on which other semiconductor companies build their chips.Based in Bernin, near Grenoble, the company was spun out of French research institute CEA-Leti in 1992.It employs more than 2,000 people and holds more than 4,700 patents.Earlier this month, Euronews journalist Valérie Gauriat visited Soitec's production facilities for the Made in Europe series.Inside its clean rooms, silicon wafers undergo dozens of manufacturing stages, allowing the company to manipulate incredibly thin layers of material."Our job is to run faster than the competition," Chief Technology Officer Christophe Maleville told Euronews.That expertise is becoming increasingly valuable as AI data centres need to transfer enormous amounts of information between processors.Silicon photonics offers a faster, more energy-efficient alternative to traditional copper connections by using light instead of electrical signals.Soitec supplies the specialised silicon wafers used to manufacture these optical chips, giving it a critical role in the expanding AI infrastructure market.Wall Street was not the first to make the case.On 11 March, a pseudonymous account on X called Serenity, which then had about 100,000 followers, said it had taken a large position in Soitec, arguing that the company had a near monopoly in wafers for AI optical links and that the shares could triple within two years.Soitec jumped 16% that day and nearly 30% over two sessions, despite no company announcement explaining the rally.Why Bank of America sees a near monopoly in AI photonics"We estimate that Soitec currently holds ~95% market share in supplying Photonics-SOI wafers," Bank of America analyst Oliver Wong and his colleagues said.Rivals, including Taiwan's GlobalWafers, are attempting to enter the market.However, the bank expects Soitec's technological expertise and decades of manufacturing experience to protect its dominant position.That advantage could become increasingly valuable as AI data centres grow larger and require more optical connections between processors.Bank of America estimates that the total wafer area required for photonic chips will expand by approximately 60% annually between 2026 and 2030.In other words, demand for Soitec's materials could grow considerably faster than the number of AI processors themselves.The company's latest forecasts already suggest a major acceleration.In September, Soitec projected that photonics revenue would reach between 2.5 and three times the previous year's level in the financial year ending March 2027.It also forecast approximately 50% growth in total revenue for the September quarter.Meanwhile, Soitec expects to secure multi-year capacity agreements with eight of its roughly ten largest photonics customers.These agreements could make future demand more predictable, supporting investment in additional production capacity.How AI could reshape Soitec profitabilityUntil recently, Soitec depended heavily on the smartphone industry, which accounted for roughly half of its revenue last fiscal year.But in the June quarter, its broader Edge & Cloud AI division generated 57% of sales.Bank of America expects that transformation to accelerate.It projects photonics revenue will climb from €92 million in fiscal 2026 to approximately €680 million in fiscal 2029.That would represent almost half of projected group revenue of €1.43 billion, compared with just 16% last fiscal year.More importantly, profitability could grow even faster than sales.The bank estimates that photonics wafers retain about 80 cents from every euro of sales after raw material costs, compared with 56 cents for Soitec's other products.As photonics becomes a larger part of the business, Bank of America expects the company's gross profit margin to rise from 16% to 44% by fiscal 2029."We believe FY26 gross margin of 16% marked the trough for Soitec," Wong and his colleagues said.That expected recovery underpins their forecast of €10.62 in earnings per share for fiscal 2029, approximately 71% above the Visible Alpha analyst consensus.Why a nearly 600% rally still carries substantial risksSoitec's transformation is far from complete.Annual revenue declined 34% to €592 million in fiscal 2026, while mobile communications sales plunged 43%.The smartphone division contracted another 10% in the June quarter as customers continued reducing inventories.Bank of America expects the mobile business to reach its lowest point this fiscal year, but a recovery is not guaranteed.Meeting growing demand for photonics will also require substantial investment.The bank expects Soitec to announce an extension of its Singapore manufacturing plant in the coming months, potentially costing around €700 million.Valuation presents another challenge.At approximately €154 per share, Soitec trades at nearly 96 times Bank of America's projected earnings for the financial year ending March 2027.Such an elevated valuation leaves investors vulnerable if AI infrastructure spending slows or competing technologies gain ground.Soitec will publish its first-half results on 18 November, offering a fresh test of its ambitious growth outlook.At the beginning of 2026, investors were focused on shrinking smartphone sales and deteriorating profits.Today, Soitec is increasingly being valued as a critical supplier to the global AI industry.The question is whether its photonics business can grow fast enough to justify a share price that may have already anticipated an extraordinary transformation.This article is for informational and educational purposes only and does not constitute financial advice, investment advice, or a recommendation to buy or sell any financial instrument. Readers should conduct their own research and consult a qualified financial adviser before making any investment decisions. Investing involves risk, including the potential loss of capital. Past performance is not indicative of future results.

title: Child marriage in southern Germany: Over 350 cases recorded, some brides as young as 11
description: A written question by two AfD members of the Baden-Württemberg state parliament revealed 358 marriages involving minors, but only eight have so far been annulled with final legal effect.
content: In the southwestern German state of Baden-Württemberg, a total of 358 so-called child marriages have been officially recorded since 2012. Only eight of these forced marriages have so far been legally annulled. According to authorities, the other 350 cases were brought to an end in other ways.This alarming finding comes from a response by the Baden-Württemberg state government to a minor inquiry submitted by AfD state parliament members Nikolaos Boutakoglou and Emely Knorr.The Tübingen regional authority is responsible for recording the data, the answer came from the Ministry of the Interior.11-year-old Iraqi girl married offThe eight final annulments took place between 2018 and 2024. Among the documented cases was the marriage of an 11-year-old girl from Iraq to a 17-year-old Iraqi, which was annulled in 2020.As early as 2018, the marriage of a 14-year-old Afghan girl to a 30-year-old man had been ended. In 2024 two further annulments were added: they concerned a 16-year-old German girl and a 25-year-old Pakistani man and a 16-year-old Syrian girl and a 27-year-old man from the same country.State parliament member Nikolaos Boutakoglou wrote on Facebook that the issue was "really awful" but was being treated as a taboo.According to its own account, the ministry deals exclusively with such marriages entered into abroad.Since summer 2017, the Act to Combat Child Marriages has been in force in Germany. In 2024, the Bundestag adopted new rules to protect minors in marriages concluded abroad.Hundreds of cases without state interventionThe significantly higher number of cases concluded in other ways raises questions about how these marriages continued. For the period from 2015 to 2026, the regional authority lists a total of 350 proceedings under the heading "other disposals."But what became of the other child marriages? The state government cites, among other things, the death of a spouse, reaching adulthood, a decision not to seek annulment or a new marriage concluded abroad. In these cases, there was therefore no legally binding annulment.For 2023, the records include the case of a 12-year-old Afghan girl who was married to a 21-year-old Afghan man. Girls aged 13 and 14 also appear several times in the statistics.The most recent entries in the overview relate to 2026. They include, among other things, marriages of 16- and 17-year-old girls to adult men. The statistics record the age of the spouses at the time of marriage and their respective nationalities.According to the Interior Ministry, at the time the inquiry was answered there were no court proceedings pending to annul child marriages.State parliament member Emely Knorr, who co-initiated the inquiry, demanded on the social media platform Instagram: "Child marriages are incompatible with our values. Children have a right to safety, education and a self-determined future. That is why we need effective protection, early intervention and resolute action against forced marriages."How many pupils are affected?The two MPs wanted to know what impact forced marriages have on their schooling.The Ministry of Education explained that no such data are collected. According to the state government, it also has no information on the countries in which the recorded marriages were contracted.The age and nationality at the time of marriage are recorded, as these are relevant for possible annulment proceedings.Another question from the MPs concerned how often the YASEMIN counselling centre, which is funded by the state, had been called in for cases of forced marriage involving pupils at schools in Baden-Württemberg.In its reply of 9 September 2026, the Interior Ministry wrote that the counselling centre does not break down its cases by the school status of the people it advises or by school year.Instead, cases are recorded by the age of those affected and by calendar year. The precise number of counselling sessions remains unclear.Threat of forced marriage: 80 cases recordedIn the 2025 calendar year, YASEMIN recorded a total of 271 counselling cases. In 80 cases, the people concerned were at risk of being forced into marriage. Of these 80 people, 33 were minors.Four of the minors were under 12 years old, five were 12 and another two were 13. The counselling centre distinguishes between people at risk of forced marriage and other counselling issues; it does not carry out any school-related analysis.According to the MPs, the trigger for the parliamentary inquiry was an emergency checklist by the women's rights organisation Terre des Femmes, published at the end of July 2026 and aimed primarily at teaching staff.In legal terms, people up to the age of 14 are considered children in Germany; from then until the age of 18 they are deemed adolescents.Under the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, everyone up to the age of 18 is regarded as a child. Only once they reach adulthood are people allowed to marry in Germany. Forced marriage is defined as a separate criminal offence in the Penal Code.With a population of around 11.24 million people, Baden-Württemberg accounts for just under 13.5% of the total German population of about 83.5 million inhabitants.

title: Lufthansa Group boosts Japan network with up to 50 flights per week from summer 2027
description: Due to a ‘strong increase in demand’, the group’s airlines will offer up to 50 weekly flights to four Japanese airports next summer.
content: Lufthansa Group is boosting its Japan network for 2027, bringing back its Frankfurt-Nagoya route and adding a daily service between Frankfurt and Tokyo-Narita in response to a “strong increase in demand”.The group’s airlines – including Lufthansa, Austrian Airlines, SWISS and ITA Airways – will offer up to 50 flights per week next summer to four Japanese airports: Tokyo-Haneda, Tokyo-Narita, Osaka and Nagoya.The expansion follows a record year in 2025 for international arrivals in Japan, with the country welcoming 42.7 million overseas visitors, up 15.8% on 2024, according to the Japan National Tourism Organization (JNTO). Visitor arrivals from several European markets have continued to grow in 2026. Japan recorded 27.6 million international visitor arrivals between January and August, down 2.7% compared with the same period in 2025. However, arrivals from Germany rose 5.6% to 281,500, while arrivals from the UK increased 5.8% to 364,800. France, Italy and Spain also recorded growth.Frankfurt-Nagoya flights return in MarchLufthansa’s seasonal Frankfurt-Nagoya service will resume on 29 March 2027, operating three times a week on Mondays, Wednesdays and Saturdays.Outbound flights will leave Frankfurt at 2:10 pm and arrive in Nagoya at 9:35 am the following morning. Return services will depart Nagoya at 11:30 am and land in Frankfurt at 6:30 pm. All times are local.Nagoya, in Aichi Prefecture, is one of Japan’s major industrial centres, with strong links to the automotive sector. For holidaymakers, the city also offers samurai history and a gateway to destinations including Kyoto.Passengers travelling from Nagoya will be able to connect through Frankfurt to destinations across Europe and South America.Daily service to Tokyo-Narita A daily seasonal service between Frankfurt and Tokyo-Narita will begin on 28 March 2027, complementing Lufthansa’s existing daily flights to Tokyo-Haneda from Frankfurt and Munich.The new Narita service will depart Frankfurt at 1:45 pm, arriving at 9:30 am the next day. Return flights will leave Narita at 11:20 am and reach Frankfurt at 6:40 pm.Both the Nagoya and Narita routes will use Boeing 787-9 aircraft equipped with Lufthansa’s Allegris cabins, offering 28 business class seats, 28 premium economy seats and 231 economy seats.“Japan is a key market for the Lufthansa Group, and we are pleased to further strengthen our presence with additional capacity and the resumption of flights to Nagoya,” says Dieter Vranckx, the group’s chief commercial officer.“Together with our expanded Tokyo services, these investments provide our customers with more travel options and support the continued diversification of our intercontinental network.”SWISS will also increase its Japan services, offering up to seven weekly flights between Zurich and Tokyo-Narita during summer 2027.

title: ‘We’re not waiting anymore’: Media mogul Mo Abudu opens a new hub for African cinema in London
description: Nigerian media mogul Mo Abudu has opened EbonyLife Place London, a new cultural hub celebrating African cinema and Black culture. The venue brings together a cinema, restaurant and boutique showcasing designers from Africa and its diaspora.
content: A new cultural hub dedicated to African cinema and Black culture has opened its doors in London, with Nigerian media mogul Mo Abudu hoping to bring stories from Africa and its diaspora to a wider audience.EbonyLife Place London features a cinema, a restaurant and a boutique showcasing designers from Africa and its diaspora. The project aims to create a destination where visitors can experience different aspects of Black culture without having to travel abroad.For Abudu, the centre is the result of a long-held ambition to give African stories a permanent home in the British capital. “The idea has probably been buried in my subconsciousness for the longest time. I know how important it is for stories to travel. I know how important it is for culture to travel. And I just felt that we needed to have a destination point to where this culture could travel to and that's really what got me started on this journey,” she said.A cinema dedicated to Black storytellingAt the heart of EbonyLife Place London is a cinema designed to showcase African films and productions celebrating Black actors and stories.The programme will include Nollywood films from Nigeria, alongside international productions that explore the Black experience. Abudu said the cinema would also screen major American releases featuring Black talent.Abudu believes African culture deserves greater visibility in international markets. Rather than waiting for audiences to discover it elsewhere, she wants to make it more accessible in one of Europe's major cultural capitals.“We have consumed so much of the world. How much of the world has consumed us? And I'm not waiting anymore for anyone to take a six-hour trip from London to understand what it is to watch a Nigerian film, or to see Nigerian fashion, and so on and so forth. It's right here in London,” she said.The initiative also reflects a personal ambition for Abudu, who was born in England and says she grew up without a place to watch Black films.“I think it's important for us to know that if I didn't create this moment, it wouldn't exist. So if it's the moment or if it's not the moment, I mean, I am 62 years old. I was born in England. I lived in England for many years. I could never go anywhere during my youth to go and watch a black movie. No one in my time thought they should have done that. It's taken this long for someone like me to do this."Making African cinema mainstreamAbudu's ambition extends beyond opening a single cultural centre. She wants African and Black cinema to become a familiar part of the entertainment landscape, with more venues offering audiences access to films, art, fashion and food from across the diaspora.“Then years from now, we shouldn't be here saying, this is the first black cinema, which it is. Ten years from now, it should just be, there's another cinema. There should be several others opening. So, cinemas, you know, culture hubs, food, fashion, art, bringing it all together."With EbonyLife Place London, Abudu hopes to help create an environment in which African stories are not treated as a niche interest, but as an integral part of mainstream culture.

title: ‘Outdated and inadequate’: Tefal manufacturer urged to drop ‘forever chemicals’ from non-stick pans
description: The legal notice came from three environmental groups in the midst of fierce discussions over upcoming EU PFAS legislation, expected in 2027.
content: Last week, three environmental organisations gave an ultimatum to French cookware manufacturer Groupe SEB over its use of PFAS, human-made, long-lasting chemical substances also known as forever chemicals. Groupe SEB owns pan brand Tefal, which continues to use PFAS in some of its non-stick cookware.According to ClientEarth, Générations Futures and Notre Affaire à Tous, the company's approach to forever chemicals is “outdated and inadequate” and fails to comply with legal requirements under the French corporate responsibility law. “It's not just for PFAS producers to be sanctioned for what they're doing, but it's also for the companies at the end of the chain who really use those PFAS to show that is possible to have a PFAS free market,” Hélène Duguy, environmental lawyer at ClientEarth, tells Euronews Earth. In response to the accusations, Groupe SEB told Euronews Earth that it will review its contents and respond, if necessary, in accordance with the law. These allegations come at a critical time in the European Union (EU)’s PFAS debate. Brussels is under pressure to ban forever chemicals, but industry groups are seeking as many exemptions as possible to avoid phasing out these substances from their products. But what exactly are the NGOs accusing Groupe SEB of, and how is this relevant for the broader EU PFAS regulation?What do environmental groups want from Tefal’s manufacturer?ClientEarth, Générations Futures and Notre Affaire à Tous put Groupe SEB on notice, a formal legal step that does not necessarily lead to a lawsuit. It could, however, if the company does not publicly commit to transitioning away from PFAS in the next three months, a press release by ClientEarth states. Specifically, the NGOs argue that Groupe SEB’s latest vigilance plan, a legal document required by French law, identifies PTFE (polytetrafluoroethylene) as “safe”, thereby failing to recognise the risks it poses and to consider measures to mitigate them. PTFE is the PFAS used in cookware produced by Tefal, which, according to a statement provided to Euronews Earth by Groupe SEB, “conducts its business in strict compliance with French and European regulations applicable to its industrial activities, under the regular oversight of the relevant authorities.” Are Tefal pans ‘safe’?Known commercially as Teflon, PTFE is a specific type of PFAS used in many products, including cookware, for its water-, stain-, and grease-resistant properties. Unlike other toxic PFAS, like the potentially carcinogenic PFOS and carcinogenic PFOA, PTFE has not been linked to cancer, yet it has already put Groupe SEB under scrutiny. In July 2025, three French environmental groups filed a lawsuit against the multinational for misleading commercial practices. The complaint was linked to an advertising campaign in which Tefal promoted its non-stick coatings as “safe”, thus undermining the risks caused by PTFE according to the environmental organisations. “PTFE is non-toxic,” Hans Peter Arp, professor of environmental chemistry at the Norwegian University of Science, tells Euronews Earth. “But how it's made and how it is disposed of may release toxic PFAS,” he adds. In particular, disposing of products containing PTFE through incineration might release hazardous chemicals into the environment. “If you have these [PTFE] products in your home, which many of us do – I do – I may not be contaminating my home, but I might have been contaminating the area where the PTFE was made or the future area of the landfill where that PTFE is going,” Arp explains. According to Hélène Duguy, the broader context of PFAS’s consequences is what Groupe SEB is failing to recognise. “If you want to understand the risks of a PFAS like PTFE, you need to look at the entire value chain,” she stresses. Is Europe banning PFAS? Over the last few years, PFAS have been highly discussed in the EU, which has vowed to ban forever chemicals in everyday consumer products, while allowing exemptions in sectors considered critical, such as defence and healthcare. Industry lobbyists are currently working to obtain as many exemptions as possible to the regulation. "It is by far the biggest file I've handled in the past five years," lobbyist Simon Terwagne told news agency AFP. The consultancy he works for, Forward Global, represents clients from the chemical industry."Reducing exposure to PFAS is a sensible goal, but it must be done in the most measured and proportionate way possible," he added.The official proposal is expected in early 2027 as the European Commission is waiting for a final report from the European Chemicals Agency, which should arrive in December. However, in March 2026, the agency already said that PFAS "pose growing risks to people and the environment", calling for a broad ban on their use across the bloc with some exceptions when there is no alternative.As far as PTFE is concerned, there are alternatives to it in its cookware application. For instance, cast iron is a PFAS-free material that can be used in pans and other kitchenware. Groupe SEB is already manufacturing some products like this, and that is why, according to Hélène Duguy, the company should already be planning for a transition. “We're not asking SEB to do this tomorrow, but to plan this transition… to make sure that their workforce has a plan B and that there is adaptation,” she says. At the start of 2026, France banned the sale, production or import of any product containing forever chemicals for which an alternative already exists. The first draft of this law originally included prohibiting non-stick saucepans, but this was later removed following reports of “intense lobbying” from French manufacturer Tefal.PFAS: A symbol of a broader environmental crisisThis is not the first legal action ClientEarth has pursued on the topic of PFAS. Earlier this year, the environmental NGO filed a human rights complaint against Belgium over its failure to tackle widespread PFAS pollution across the country. According to Duguy, PFAS is becoming a symbol of the environmental crisis the world is facing. “PFAS is quite emblematic of a general societal reality, which is accepting collateral damage for the benefits of short-term profits,” she says. PFAS were created by the chemical industry in the first half of the 20th century and are now employed in several items, including some raincoats, food packaging and menstrual products. Overall, they are difficult to remove from the environment and can have harmful effects on human health, two characteristics that major corporations like 3M and DuPont knew about but covered up for years. PFAS pollution is particularly widespread in Europe. In 2023, cross-border investigation The Forever Pollution Project estimated that there were around 23,000 PFAS-contaminated sites across the continent. Earlier this year, an EU-wide crackdown on forever chemicals in drinking water came into force, requiring member states to monitor PFAS levels in water and inform the European Commission of their results. If the limit values are exceeded, member states must “take action” to reduce the level of PFAS and protect public health – while also informing the public. While this was viewed as a positive step, experts warned that the approach treats the symptoms, rather than preventing harm at its source by restricting PFAS from being made, marketed or released.

title: Glass igloos, sky villas and boutique suites: New places to stay in Finnish Lapland this winter
description: Finnish Lapland is a winter wonderland with plenty of things to see and do as well as a variety of places to stay. Here we take a look at some of the new accommodation options.
content: A trip to Finnish Lapland is the stuff of travel bucket lists, especially during the winter months. Trust me, this is one of the most magical places I’ve ever been and somewhere I would want to return to time and time again.Snow-covered forests, frozen lakes and possibly seeing the Northern Lights are all part of the appeal. And in Rovaniemi, there’s also the chance to visit the Santa Claus Village and embrace the festive side of this winter wonderland. In terms of accommodation, there’s plenty of choice here. You can watch the glistening sky from a glass igloo or settle into a lakeside villa – often with sauna access included or the chance for an ice-cold dip. Here we pick out some of the new places to stay that are opening across Finnish Lapland for the 2026-2027 winter season.Santa’s Hotel Noelle, Rovaniemi Located within the Arctic Circle, Rovaniemi is the capital of Finnish Lapland and also recognised as the "official hometown of Santa Claus". As well as being home to the iconic Santa Claus Village, there are also a number of Santa-inspired hotels. In time for the winter season, the Santa’s Hotels group will unveil its newest property opening in the centre of Rovaniemi. Santa’s Hotel Noelle will feature 101 rooms, including junior suites with balconies, and a souvenir shop. It will be connected to Santa’s Hotel Santa Claus by a covered pedestrian bridge. Halo Riverside Resort, Vikäköngäs, RovaniemiMid-October is the opening date for the 39 new glass igloos at Halo Riverside Resort, located on the banks of the Vikäköngäs river. The River View and Forest View igloos sleep up to four people, and each comes with a heated panoramic glass roof, a private sauna and an outdoor hot tub.For active travellers, there are plenty of hiking trails on the doorstep, too. Other activities include husky and reindeer safaris, snowmobiling and Northern Lights tours.Aava Glass Igloos, RovaniemiOn Ollerovaara Hill just 10 kilometres outside of Rovaniemi, new family-owned retreat Aava Glass Igloos will open on 13 November 2026 and offer views across the Arctic landscape.Aava will feature 12 glass igloo suites for up to four guests, plus a one-bedroom suite, each with a heated panoramic glass roof and a private Finnish sauna.There will also be real-time aurora alerts while activities include husky and reindeer safaris, snowmobiling, ice karting and snowshoeing.Arcora Boutique Hotel & Villas, Muonio Boutique property Arcora will open on 14 December 2026 in Muonio, on the edge of Pallas-Yllästunturi National Park. It will have a range of luxury suites, sky villas and deluxe villas, two restaurants, an artisan bakery, and a champagne bar.Wellness will also be a major focus with three saunas, a cold plunge, an outdoor hot tub, a rooftop infinity pool, and a gym available for guests to use. Adventures include Northern Lights tours, husky and reindeer safaris, snowmobiling and snowshoeing.Kelo Sky Villas, Raattama Boutique resort Kelo in Raattama officially opened its doors in November 2025 and this December it will bring more accommodation options with the launch of its Sky Villas.Accommodating up to four guests, the Kelo Sky Villas are designed for couples, families, and small groups, and their floor-to-ceiling windows will offer panoramic fell views. Guests can enjoy saunas or dine at the resort’s Restaurant Jäkälä, which offers traditional Lapland-inspired dishes.North Resort, Lake MiekojärviIntimate all-inclusive retreat North Resort opens on 1 December 2026 on the shores of Lake Miekojärvi. The resort’s accommodation options include 14 villas and two spacious suites, which have panoramic windows to view the wilderness of Finnish Lapland.The suites also come with a private sauna, fireplace and jacuzzi. Full-board meals are included and guests can enjoy the spa and sauna, as well as an ice-hole dip. The resort's own Safari House offers Northern Lights tours, snowshoeing, husky safaris and snowmobile safaris. Octola III, Enontekiö, Finnish LaplandOpening on 1 December, Octola III is the latest addition to the Octola Private Wilderness portfolio. It sits 500 metres above sea level on the site of a former radar station within a protected Sámi wilderness area in Finnish Lapland. The exclusive property will accommodate just six guests, but don’t expect to make a simple booking online – access is only granted through a private invitation-only waiting list. Guests have the option of booking one suite, two suites or the entire property. Despite its remote setting, the lodge is just a 20-minute private transfer from Enontekiö Arctic Airport.

title: French navy intercepts and boards 'shadow fleet' ship, Macron says
description: Ukraine's Main Directorate of Intelligence says the DF Peak tanker is involved in the transportation of Russian crude oil and that it is associated with the Sovcomflot shipping firm.
content: French President Emmanuel Macron announced on Monday that the French navy had intercepted and boarded an oil tanker suspected of being involved in illegal fuel-trafficking activities.The operation took place 450 nautical miles south of the island of Réunion in the Indian Ocean, according to Macron."Our French Navy boarded the oil tanker DF Peak, which is suspected of sailing under a false flag and of being involved in illicit fuel-trafficking activities," he wrote in a post on social media, whilst also sharing video footage appearing to show troops rappelling down onto the vessel.He added that France remained "determined to combat the ‘shadow fleet’ wherever it may be in the world."Catherine Vautrin, France's minister for the armed forces, congratulated those who took part in the operation and said the French military was escorting the DF Peak for further checks, under the authority of the prefect of Réunion.Ukraine's Main Directorate of Intelligence (GUR) says the vessel is involved in the transportation of Russian crude oil and that it is associated with the Sovcomflot shipping firm.The ship was built in 2006 and has sailed under multiple flags, per the GUR.In June, French forces also intercepted the Russian shadow fleet tanker "Deliver" as it was sailing off the coast of Sicily "in violation of maritime law," Macron announced at the time.Russia's shadow fleet enables the country to evade Western sanctions on its energy sector, which prevent it from chartering or insuring oil tankers unless it complies with certain restrictions.The shadow fleet bypasses these restrictions by making use of complex ownership structures, flags of convenience, and other tactics designed to conceal the origin of its cargo.A number of other European countries have reported intercepting Russian shadow fleet vessels in recent months.

title: French investigators use DNA and vehicle tracking to solve stolen Renoirs case
description: The arrests were prompted by the "very strong suspicion that another heist was imminent," the Marseille prosecutor said.
content: Investigators in France used DNA evidence and vehicle tracking to help recover two paintings worth millions of euros that were stolen from a Renoir museum last month.Four men have been handed preliminary charges after the impressionist artist's "Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano" and "Young Woman at the Well" works were taken from the Musée Renoir in Cagnes-sur-Mer on the French riviera in a daring September heist.The suspects are believed to have gained entry to the museum after sawing through a fence using an electric saw. They then cut clips securing four paintings before an alarm went off.Marseille prosecutor Nicolas Bessone told reporters on Monday that this caused the suspects to panic and that they abandoned two paintings as they fled. These were apparently later found in a protective cover.Bessone said a breakthrough came when DNA found on an abandoned cover matched that of a 29-year-old who was already being investigated by police in a drug trafficking case, and that the man's vehicle was being tracked as part of the investigation.Tracking data showed that the suspect and a 41-year-old man had visited the home of a third man after the theft took place, per Bessone.Investigators believed a plot to carry out another heist was also in motion, after surveillance found the 29-year-old had visited the Maeght Foundation in Saint-Paul-de-Vence on 3 October. The Maeght Foundation opened in 1964 and is home to works from celebrated artists including Pierre Bonnard, Georges Braque, and Alberto Giacometti.The suspect is then said to have met up with another man who is known to police from art theft and forgery cases in the early 2000s.The arrests were prompted by the "very strong suspicion that another heist was imminent," Bessone said.The third suspect hid the paintings behind a wall under a staircase following the theft, from where investigators recovered the Renoirs, he added.

title: Blindsided again by Trump, Europe puts on a brave face and rallies behind Ukraine
description: European leaders closed ranks and rallied behind Ukraine as news of the diesel deal between Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin continued to send shockwaves across the alliance.
content: Europe is once again trying to save face after US President Donald Trump blindsided the continent by striking a tailored deal with his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, to release thousands of tonnes of diesel that had until now been sanctioned.The news alarmed Ukraine and its European allies, who have long been wary of Trump's unpredictable diplomacy and his understanding of what a just and lasting peace means.Tensions between the two sides of the Atlantic have never fully receded since February last year, when Trump unexpectedly called Putin and launched negotiations to end the war without consulting any European leader in advance.That was the start of a series of unexpected developments that have rattled Europe and upended its long-held assumptions about the post-war international order. These include a hastily organised Trump-Putin summit in Alaska, a leaked 28-point plan heavily favourable to Moscow and a sanctions waiver for Russian crude oil.The diesel deal, announced on Friday on Truth Social, added yet another chapter.Trump then resorted to a familiar pattern: public attacks against Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's legitimacy and calls for fresh elections. Ukraine's constitution bars elections in wartime, a point that Zelenskyy tends to remind Trump."I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals and for some reason he never does," Trump said to Moscow's applause.As in previous episodes, Europe finds itself scrambling to close ranks, rally behind Ukraine and make clear that, regardless of what the White House does and says, this side of the Atlantic will stay the agreed course."I think we need to be collectively serious. Today, I believe, we have no factual reason to change our position," French President Emmanuel Macron said on Monday.German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said emulating the Trump-Putin diesel deal was "out of the question" for Europe, despite rising energy prices."Russia will only negotiate seriously under pressure, and that is why we are sticking to our sanctions against Russia," Merz told reporters.A similar message echoed through Luxembourg as EU foreign ministers met and insisted that the pressure campaign on Moscow would continue unabated. Some openly decried the diesel deal, calling it regrettable and concerning.Foreign ministers also approved a record-breaking addition of 1,600 names to the sanctions list, half of them linked to the production of ballistic missiles that fall on Ukraine. The contrast between the EU and the US could hardly have been starker."We showed unity today on these (1,600) listings," High Representative Kaja Kallas said at the end of the meeting."But, of course, it would be much stronger if we had acted together with the US. Our message to the United States is that only pressure works with Russia."United in strainAlthough the Trump-Putin deal fits a familiar pattern of erratic diplomacy that sidelines European interests, its grim context sets it apart.The diesel deal comes at a time when Russia is rapidly escalating its attacks against Ukraine, killing scores of civilians and wrecking the levers that sustain the local economy, including power stations, data centres, warehouses and railways.Russia's blockade in the Black Sea has left Ukrainian farmers unable to send tonnes of grain to their global clients and deprived the state of an essential revenue source.As economic activity stagnates and material costs pile up, the EU is realising its multibillion-euro lines of support will fall short sometime next year. With the US out of the picture, the burden is set to fall on the European pocket.The prospect of Russia selling diesel that had until now been sanctioned and making extra money to finance the bombs that rain down on Ukraine is particularly difficult to stomach for Kyiv and its allies. It also raises serious questions about how much the US can be trusted to provide security guarantees for the post-war scenario.And yet, Europe's collective assessment remains that there is still more to lose than to gain from breaking away from the Americans."What we need to do is refocus and redouble our efforts in keeping pressure on Russia," Ireland's Foreign Minister Helen McEntee said on Monday."Our priority has to be to maintain that pressure, but also to maintain our channels with the US, because this is not going to be achievable without the support of the US."Just as news of the diesel deal broke, senior officials from Ukraine, France, Germany, the United Kingdom, the European Commission and NATO were in Miami, Florida, for a round of talks hosted by Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Trump's special envoys.The meeting was the first of its kind since the outbreak of the US-Iran war, which has absorbed the White House's foreign policy and relegated Ukraine to the second row."We will continue to engage with our partners and also with the US in bringing this war to a close, and the latest example of this has been the talks on Friday in Miami," the Commission's chief spokesperson said, describing the meeting as a "positive step".Europe initially struggled to secure a seat at the negotiating table as Trump and Putin marched ahead with their private calls. It took months after European countries established the “Coalition of the Willing” for them to be brought into the US-led negotiating process.The statements from Brussels confirm that retaining a seat at the table where Ukraine’s future as a sovereign state and Europe’s security architecture will be decided takes precedence over any diplomatic slight, however pointed or public.Zelenskyy, whose country is already suffering blackouts ahead of a winter expected to be the harshest yet of the war, agrees that the transatlantic alliance must prevail, notwithstanding the deals that might be cut behind its back."An energy ceasefire and other steps to reduce escalation and guarantee security are truly needed here – in reality, not just on Truth Social," Zelenskyy said."We need to end Russia's war. We need to guarantee security. We need to stand together. Europe and the United States."

title: UK PM Burnham says 'status quo' with Brussels 'not good enough' as he details upcoming EU summit
description: Burnham has repeatedly signalled his intention to move the UK closer to the EU since taking office in July and recently said reentering the bloc was one of a number of options for the country moving forward.
content: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the UK's relationship with Brussels needs to change as he spoke to parliament ahead of next month's UK-EU summit.Burnham told MPs that "sticking with the current status quo is not good enough for Britain" and that a conversation over future relations must be had "if we are serious about promoting growth, controlling immigration, upholding our values and security.""Worse, it would be a major dereliction of duty" for the government to "turn away" from exploring options for a closer relationship with the European Union, he continued, adding that his "immediate priority" was to land a "successful outcome at the summit," which is scheduled for 20 November.He stressed that the British public would "be the boss" at "every stage" of the process.Burnham has repeatedly signalled his intention to move the UK closer to the EU since taking office in July and recently said reentering the bloc was one of a number of options for the country moving forward.The PM told an audience at the Labour Party's annual conference in Liverpool last month that Brexit had "done more harm than good" and that the UK needed a clear strategy on its long-term relationship with Brussels."We will not give Britain the clear path we need into the rest of this century until we decide on a long-term relationship with what is still our largest market," he said at the time.On Monday, Burnham said the November summit would focus on boosting growth and controlling illegal immigration, whilst some of the other issues "on the table" would be a food and drink trade deal, linking energy systems, an emissions trading deal, and a youth experience scheme."We should not turn our backs on this opportunity," he added.Right-wing figures in Britain have accused Labour of seeking to reopen the divisive Brexit debate, with Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch on Monday saying Burnham was "unpicking" the withdrawal agreement with the EU and that he would not get a better deal.European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has said she was "really looking forward" to the upcoming summit and that the "EU and the UK have so much to achieve together.""Let's be ambitious and deliver for citizens on both sides of the Channel," she wrote in a post on social media on Monday.RAF Fairford incidentElsewhere in his speech, Burnham said an incident at a UK airbase in September was "almost certainly directed" by Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) as he warned that Britain "will not tolerate these threats."On 27 September, five men were arrested near RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, southwest England, on suspicion of explosives offensives before being further arrested on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act. They were later released on police bail.Police later arrested another man, a 25-year-old dual UK-Iranian national, in London on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts related to the incident. A 22-year-old British man was then arrested on 6 October, also in London and on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts. Both were released on police bail.According to UK Counter Terrorism Policing, all seven men remain on police bail as specialist teams "continue to pursue all lines of enquiry."RAF Fairford is home to the US Air Force's 501st Combat Support Wing headquarters and the 420th Air Base squadron. It has also served as the USAF Global Strike Command's preferred bomber forward operating location in Europe.In July, the IRGC said it was aware that the base was being used by US bombers as part of Washington's military operations against Iran and warned the UK that "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces."The US has now withdrawn its bombers from Fairford.

title: What we know about Pope Leo XIV's upcoming operation to remove lung nodule
description: The Vatican press office has said doctors expect the pope's recovery to take around a week. That would make it possible for him to leave for his visit to Latin America as planned on 6 November.
content: Pope Leo XIV has said he will have an operation to remove a lump on his lung this week, the first time a pope has made a personal medical announcement of this kind.The 71-year-old is otherwise healthy and is known for his love of sport.Here is what we know.When will the operation take place?The pope said the operation was planned "in the coming days" and the Vatican press office said it would be at the beginning of the week, without giving a date.Italian media have speculated that the operation could be on Tuesday, although the pope is due to preside over a Mass in St Peter's Basilica on Wednesday morning with Church leaders from around the world and there have so far been no announced changes in his schedule.The Vatican press office has said doctors expect the pope's recovery to take around a week. That would make it possible for him to leave for his visit to Latin America as planned on 6 November.The 11-day trip will take him to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, a country close to the pope's heart as he worked there as a missionary for two decades and took on Peruvian citizenship.What is a pulmonary nodule?A pulmonary nodule is a small growth of tissue in the lung. Most are benign, meaning they are non-cancerous. But a small percentage can be an early stage of lung cancer.Most small nodules cause no symptoms and are only discovered during checks for other health issues.Larger nodules can cause shortness of breath, chest pain and persistent coughing, sometimes with blood.The operation is normally carried out under general anaesthetic with the patient breathing through a tube.Where will the operation take place?The operation is expected to take place at Rome's Gemelli hospital, where popes are usually treated.Pope Leo XIV's predecessor Francis spent weeks there for treatment before his death last year.John Paul II, head of the Church from 1978 until his death in 2005, was treated nine times at Gemelli, Rome's largest hospital, and spent a total of 153 days there.He quipped that the hospital was like "Vatican number three."The Vatican ultimately created a top-floor apartment at the hospital site, accessed by a long corridor guarded by Italian and Vatican police.Besides the pope's room, the suite reportedly includes a meeting room for medical staff, a kitchen, bathroom and rest areas.There is also a small chapel.

title: When will El Niño peak and end? A full timeline of the weather phenomenon taking the world by storm
description: A ‘Godzilla’ El Niño is still intensifying in the Pacific. When will we see the weather phenomenon peak – and when will it come to an end?
content: 2026 will go down in history for what could become the largest El Niño in living memory, as the world scrambles to prepare for an onslaught of extreme weather. The natural weather phenomenon (Spanish for ‘the boy’) occurs irregularly – roughly every two to seven years – when sea temperatures in the Eastern Pacific Ocean become unusually warm. Experts first started warning that a strong El Niño could form at the beginning of this year, supported by large amounts of heat in the subsurface ocean and the expected weakening of low-level trade winds.In the first week of June, the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) confirmed that El Niño conditions were officially underway. Towards the end of summer, experts warned that the “unprecedented” El Niño could become the largest event since the 19th century – gaining the nickname of a ‘Godzilla’ or ‘Super’ El Niño.Is El Niño getting stronger – and what are the impacts?In its monthly bulletin on 12 October, Copernicus Climate Change Service announced that September's average sea-surface temperature reached 21.05°C – the highest on record for the month – amid strengthening El Niño conditions.According to the WMO, sea-surface temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific are also forecast to reach record levels during October, November and December. Sea-surface temperature anomalies across the central-eastern equatorial Pacific, the region at the heart of El Niño, are measured by the widely used Niño 3.4 index. This increased markedly from an average +1.6 °C above normal in June 2026 to +2.5 °C above normal in August. For October-November-December, the seasonal average Niño 3.4 sea surface temperature anomaly is forecast to reach approximately +3.7°C. This would be the highest since observations began and is stronger than the previous record of +2.6°C in November 2015-January 2016.Previous El Niño events have contributed towards record-breaking heat, fuelling long-standing droughts, flash floods and deadly wildfires across the globe. El Niño’s weather impacts are mainly felt in the tropics, but Europe can experience milder, wetter winters. An El Niño peak can also weaken the polar vortex, increasing the likelihood of a cold snap.South America, the southern US, East Africa and Central Asia have all experienced heightened flood risks during previous El Niño events – while droughts and wildfire risks rise across large parts of Australia, northern parts of South America and in certain Asian countries such as Indonesia.Extreme weather overseas will still have a knock-on effect for Europe. The IHE Delft Institute for Water Education in the Netherlands has been working in areas that are directly impacted by El Niño and warn that many staple foods that Europe imports could be at risk.For example, in Nicaragua, crops such as maize and beans may fail in already fragile areas, leading to food insecurity and income loss in the country. A lack of rain and low flows in rivers also mean that irrigated crops in Colombia, Northeast Brazil and India will face severe restrictions or will need to rely more on groundwater, potentially causing overexploitation in the area – and export shortages.A timeline of El Niño: When will it peak and end?The WMO’s latest statement says that El Niño is forecast to peak in December, and will continue into next year.“El Niño is firmly established and strengthening rapidly,” warns WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo. “WMO forecasts indicate a near-100 per cent likelihood that it will persist through February 2027, potentially being one of the strongest since at least 1950.”The almost-certain figure isn’t from one climate model. The WMO has coordinated ocean buoy, satellite and radiosonde data from 13 national and international centres to make the prediction.El Niño isn’t expected to end until spring 2027, but its impacts will likely stretch further. It’s why experts warn that next year could become the hottest on record.El Niño clashes with climate changeMost El Niño events increase global average temperatures by around 0.2°C. While this is enough to trigger extreme weather conditions across the Global South, it is a fraction of the additional warming caused by climate change.Human-caused global warming from the burning of fossil fuels has pushed global average surface temperatures 1.3°C to 1.4°C above pre-industrial levels. It is this that paved the way for Europe’s scorching summer, long-standing drought and deadly wildfires.Nowadays, El Niño’s impacts are compounded by an already warming world – one that has a much stronger influence on the extreme weather we’re witnessing. 2025, for example, was the third warmest year on record – hotter than the El Niño year of 2016 – despite the naturally-forming cool drag of El Niño’s counterpart, La Niña.Recent research suggests that climate change is turbocharging El Niño events too, by making them 36 per cent stronger than before the industrial era.“El Niño doesn't add new heat to the planet. It releases heat the ocean has already been storing beneath the surface – which is why a strong event so often becomes one of the hottest years measured (as with 2024),” Saulo told the Global Heat Forum in Bangkok in October. “The ocean it’s drawing from is the warmest we’ve ever measured it. There is simply more heat available to release.”

title: EU decries 'concerning' Trump-Putin deal, insists sanctions on Russia will continue
description: The Trump-Putin diesel deal has been badly received by EU foreign ministers, who say it undermines transatlantic unity at a time when Russia intensifies its attacks on Ukraine.
content: The European Union will continue to apply sanctions on Russia despite the diesel deal struck by United States President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin over the weekend, foreign ministers said on Monday.The deal, as announced by Trump on social media, envisages that Moscow will release 300,000 tonnes of diesel to the US and global markets immediately, with an additional 500,000 tonnes in November and one million more after that.To facilitate the arrangement, Washington issued a broad sanctions waiver for Russian diesel until April 2027, raising concerns in Ukraine and among its allies."The US is our biggest ally, but our message is clear: if we want to end this war, the only way we can do this is (by) putting more pressure on Russia," High Representative Kaja Kallas said on Monday morning as foreign ministers gathered in Luxembourg."Russia has started this war. We should not forget about this."Kallas urged the White House to enforce the bill promoted by Senator Lindsey Graham that envisions far-reaching sanctions and tariffs on Moscow.
