But the law, approved in the wake of Graham's sudden death, leaves the decision to the president's discretion."If they would enact the Graham bill, we could really put the pressure so that Russia will finish this war," Kallas said.Ireland's Foreign Minister Helen McEntee said the Trump-Putin diesel deal was "concerning" but insisted the bloc would continue its yearslong strategy.The EU adopted on Monday its largest-ever addition to its sanctions list, targeting more than 1,600 people and entities accused of propping up Russia's war. More than half of them are connected to ballistic missile production."What we need to do is refocus and redouble our efforts in keeping pressure on Russia," McEntee said upon arrival."Our priority has to be to maintain that pressure, but also to maintain our channels with the US, because this is not going to be achievable without the support of the US."Her Swedish counterpart, Maria Malmer Stenergard, criticised the diesel deal and encouraged her European peers to tap into the immobilised Russian assets to ramp up their military and financial support for Ukraine."I very much regret this (deal). I hope it will not go into force," she said."EU countries, regardless of what happens with the US, must stay calm and carry on and increase support by using the frozen assets and increase the pressure on Russia."Her Lithuanian counterpart, Kęstutis Budrys, was also highly critical, saying the diesel deal "doesn't help, neither the prices of the oil products nor the unity within the transatlantic community"."It is not the European way," Budrys told reporters."Our way is to increase pressure because we already see how it works. We are not done here because for Europe, this is the vital interest: to help Ukraine sustain this winter."Estonia's Margus Tsahkna linked the agreement to the "domestic situation" in the US ahead of next month's midterm elections, where Trump's Republicans trail the Democrats, and predicted its material impact would be limited.Trump has struggled to contain the backlash against his war on Iran, which is widely seen as the main reason behind the pronounced rise in fuel prices.Tsahkna also said the energy ceasefire suddenly announced by Trump on Sunday was "not working", pointing to Russia's relentless airstrikes on Ukraine.The truce is reportedly designed to cover oil refineries as a first step, which would make it heavily lopsided. Ukraine has just one plant while Russia has 32 major ones.Kyiv has systematically hit Moscow's oil industry to cripple its war chest and gain leverage. But the strikes have angered Trump, leading to his deal with Putin."Energy is extremely important because the winter is going to be cold," Kallas said."It is important that it does not only apply to the refineries, where Ukraine has one, and Russia has plenty. It is definitely (to) the benefit of the Russians."

title: Americans Hall and Woodford win Nobel Prize in economics for stabilisation models
description: The economics prize is the only Nobel not among the original five created in the will of Swedish scientist Alfred Nobel, who died in 1896.
content: American economists Robert Hall and Michael Woodford were awarded the Nobel economics prize on Monday for their work on how monetary and fiscal policy can help stabilise fluctuations in the economy."The laureates' work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world," the jury at the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said in a statement."With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume," John Hassler, chair of the prize committee, said in the statement.During the oil crises in the 1970s, the existing Keynesian models long used to determine when and how measures should be implemented to tackle recessions or other economic fluctuations no longer worked.That prompted Hall and Woodford to develop new tools for understanding which policy responses could be the most effective."Rather than basing the models on statistical links between macroeconomic variables, such as inflation, production and consumption, they chose to build them on a microeconomic foundation," the academy jury said."This encompasses an understanding for how the total mass of individual households and businesses affect the economy through their actions."The economics prize is the only Nobel not among the original five created in the will of Swedish scientist Alfred Nobel, who died in 1896.It was created instead through a donation from the Swedish central bank in 1968, leading detractors to dub it "a false Nobel."But like the Nobels in chemistry and physics, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences chooses the winner and follows the same selection process.Last year, the award went to American-Israeli Joel Mokyr, France's Philippe Aghion and Canada's Peter Howitt for research into how technology drives and affects growth.Like the other Nobels, the economics prize consists of a diploma, a gold medal and a $1.2 million (€1 million) cheque.The laureates will receive their prizes at formal ceremonies on 10 December, the anniversary of the death in 1896 of scientist Alfred Nobel, who created the prizes in his will.

title: Explore the patterns of Qatar’s visual identity and architectural language
description: Cult explores the visual language of Qatar, where geometry isn’t ornamental. At the Doha Design District, we learn about 15 patterns from the Msheireb Pattern Collection, tracing their cultural and architectural origins, revealing how design can carry memory, identity and a sense of belonging.
content: Look closely around Qatar’s Msheireb district, and you’ll start to see a pattern. It’s etched into buildings, woven into textiles and carved into the details of everyday life. But these shapes are more than decoration, they are clues to a culture, heritage and identity that has evolved over generations. We decode the patterns and ornaments that have come to define Qatar’s visual identity and architectural language, formed by taking elements of the past and giving them new meaning in the present for building a city of the future. Cult dives deeper into what makes the intricate designs specific to Qatar and the region, from the use of colour to the mathematical calculations hidden in seemingly simple shapes.

title: Started planning summer 2027 holidays? Ryanair and easyJet announce 47 new flight routes
description: Ryanair has released its first 29 new flight routes for summer 2027, while easyJet has also confirmed 18 new routes from the UK.
content: It’s not even winter yet in Europe, but airlines are already putting new routes on sale for summer 2027, as holidaymakers start planning next year's sunny escapes. A number of carriers have issued schedule updates, including Ryanair, which has announced its first 29 new routes for next summer, and easyJet, which has put 18 new routes on sale from 10 UK airports. 'Bumper' summer scheduleRyanair says its “bumper” summer schedule for 2027 will cover more than 2,500 routes across 230 destinations in its network.Italy features prominently with new routes including Alicante-Naples, Athens-Turin, Bari-Friedrichshafen, and Bari-Oslo Torp. Sicily gains Catania-Wrocław, alongside Palermo connections to Tirana and Marrakesh. For Greek island holidays, Bratislava-Chania offers access to western Crete, while Leeds Bradford-Corfu and Newcastle-Rhodes provide further options for UK holidaymakers. Croatia also features through a new Dubrovnik-Warsaw Modlin service. Portugal’s Porto gains connections with Bournemouth, Exeter and Friedrichshafen. Spain’s additions include Memmingen-Seville, Norwich-Málaga and Newcastle-Reus.Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast gets new links through Burgas-Wrocław and Memmingen-Varna, while Gdańsk-Stockholm Skavsta adds another connection between Poland and Sweden. Beyond Europe, the carrier expands access to northern Morocco with Tangier gaining services from Alicante, Kraków and Turin. It says it will be the only carrier offering direct flights on 10 of these connections. Spain accounts for six additions, including easyJet’s first flights to Girona from the UK, offering access to the Costa Brava. Services from Liverpool to Girona begin on 28 March, followed by London Gatwick on 3 June. In Scotland, Aberdeen gains flights to Barcelona and Majorca, while Edinburgh adds Bilbao alongside Rome, Hamburg and Tivat.Birmingham will also get a connection to Tivat from 3 May. Corsica features twice, with Manchester-Bastia launching on 29 June and Gatwick-Ajaccio the following day. Bristol-Montpellier follows on 1 July. Other additions include Birmingham-Milan Malpensa, Liverpool-Murcia, Bristol-Burgas and Newcastle-Larnaca. For Greek holidays, Southend-Rhodes begins on 27 April and Luton-Thessaloniki on 1 May. easyJet’s new routes for summer 2027Liverpool to Girona Birmingham to Milan Malpensa Edinburgh to Hamburg Edinburgh to Tivat Liverpool to Murcia Edinburgh to Bilbao Edinburgh to Rome Fiumicino Aberdeen to Barcelona Newcastle to Larnaca London Southend to Rhodes London Luton to Thessaloniki Aberdeen to Palma de Mallorca Birmingham to Tivat Bristol to Burgas London Gatwick to Girona Manchester to Bastia London Gatwick to Ajaccio Bristol to MontpellierOther notable new routes for summer 2027Speaking at the Euronews Travel & Tourism Summit 2026, Florian Sengstschmid, Chief Executive Officer of the Azerbaijan Tourism Board, said that Azerbaijan Airlines will operate four-weekly flights between Brussels and Baku from 8 May 2027. Several US airlines are also adding European routes for next summer. Alaska Airlines will connect Seattle with Athens from 12 May and Paris from 25 May. American Airlines is adding Philadelphia-Porto and Philadelphia-Vienna, alongside New York JFK flights to Amsterdam and Nice, and Charlotte-Barcelona. Delta’s daily Austin-Paris service launches on 27 March. United’s additions include Newark flights to Ljubljana, Ibiza, Valencia, Marseille, Terceira in the Azores, Olbia in Sardinia and Catania in Sicily. It will also connect Washington Dulles with Toulouse.Meanwhile, Air Canada will launch seasonal flights from Toronto to Oslo, Norway; Shannon, Ireland; and Nice, France in June. The Canadian flag carrier will also serve Dubrovnik, Croatia and Basel, Switzerland, from Montréal in May and June next year, respectively.

title: Did Ukrainian strikes on Yandex data centres cause Russian bot activity to plummet?
description: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said social media had become less hostile following Kyiv's strikes on Russian technology giant Yandex's data centres, as web users report plummeting bot activity.
content: Ukrainian strikes on Russian technology giant Yandex's data centres have been followed by a dramatic decline in automated online activity, raising questions about whether the attacks may also have disrupted Moscow's influence operations abroad.The sudden drop fuelled speculation in Europe and the United States about just how much of the political debate on social media might have been driven by Russian bots.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy weighed in on Monday, saying social media platforms had become noticeably less hostile."When we started responding to Russia's operation against our data centres and when our strikes reached Yandex data centres, it suddenly became a little easier to breathe on many social media platforms," Zelenskyy said addressing the Warsaw Security Forum."A lot of people, a lot of people noticed it, and there was less hate, less division and fewer provocations because there were fewer bots.""And it's pretty clear where those bots were coming from," he added."If they disappeared when Yandex went offline, this proves again and again that Europe is not the source of the problems.""Europe is not the one making everything more difficult," he said.Three data centres targetedThree data centres operated by Yandex, often described as Russia's equivalent of Google, were hit by Ukrainian drone strikes over the past few days.The facilities were located in Sasovo, in the Ryazan region, the Kaluga region, south-west of Moscow and the Vladimir region, east of the Russian capital, where the latest strike was reported on Sunday.The attacks damaged the company's infrastructure and disrupted services. Yandex confirmed that operations at its Vladimir facility had been suspended following a drone strike."Following a drone attack, the infrastructure of the Vladimir data centre was damaged," the company said in a statement published on Telegram."Operations at the data centre have been completely suspended. The remaining infrastructure resources are unstable and the platform is down."According to an analysis of Cloudflare Radar data, automated traffic originating from Yandex's network fell by approximately 94% on Sunday compared with its average levels in the second half of September.However, the figures also include legitimate automated traffic, such as search-engine crawlers, and do not establish whether Kremlin-linked social media bots were affected.Political repercussions across Europe and the USIn Germany, claims of a sharp decline in online activity surrounding the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) circulated widely following the attacks, although no independently verified figures have emerged.Czech MEP Tomáš Zdechovský questioned the apparent coincidence between the disruption and the reported decline in activity around the party."If confirmed, this is telling: Russian data centres get hit, and online activity around AfD suddenly plummets," he wrote on X.Similar claims emerged in Britain, where online activity associated with Reform UK was also reported to have declined following the attacks.In the United States, social media users reported fewer apparently automated pro-conservative responses on X, the platform owned by Elon Musk.The speculation has attracted attention from prominent political figures and commentators, including Laura Loomer, a right-wing activist and supporter of Donald Trump, Russian opposition figure and former world chess champion Garry Kasparov, and Michael McFaul, the former US ambassador to Russia.The debate comes just weeks before the US congressional midterm elections in early November, amid longstanding concerns about foreign interference and the influence of automated accounts on political discourse.

title: Thales to open what could be Japan’s first foreign-run defence maintenance base
description: The facility could be the first in Japan set up by a foreign defence company to maintain military equipment and support its operation, according to Nikkei.
content: French defence company Thales SA will establish a maintenance and operational support base in Japan for military equipment, Nikkei reported on Monday, but neither an opening date nor a location has been revealed.Chairman and chief executive Patrice Caine told the Nikkei business daily that the base "will mark a milestone toward Thales's long-term engagement in Japan".The facility could be the first in Japan set up by a foreign defence company to maintain military equipment and support its operation, the newspaper reported.The new maintenance base will check the condition of military equipment and diagnose faults, according to Nikkei. Initially, it will focus on equipment for the Maritime Self-Defence Force, with plans to extend its work to the Ground and Air Self-Defence Forces.Caine cited technologies such as radar and sonar as possible areas for cooperation with Japan, saying that he hoped to "provide support in areas where Thales has an advantage in terms of performance".The facility’s work could also extend to civilian equipment in the future, the newspaper said.The report comes as Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi continues to increase defence spending amid concerns over China's rapid military expansion and North Korea’s weapons programmes.Alongside its maintenance plans, Thales is also expanding local production. It will transfer technology for its 2R2M heavy mortar system to Japan Steel Works, which will begin producing it in Japan in 2027, according to Nikkei.Thales has been supplying Mitsubishi Heavy Industries with sonar for underwater vehicles used by Japan’s Maritime Self-Defence Force to detect mines.Thales has operated in Japan since 1970, with activities spanning defence, aerospace and digital security.The company's share price in Paris was up by about 1.5% around midday on Monday.

title: Zelenskyy says Russia ignored Trump's 'energy ceasefire' and kept attacking Ukraine
description: Zelenskyy addressed the Warsaw Security Forum in one of his first reactions to renewed turmoil with Washington, following Trump's surprise energy ceasefire announcement and controversial diesel deal with Russia.
content: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Russia on Monday of violating an energy ceasefire announced by Donald Trump, saying Kyiv had not even been consulted about the purported agreement and had only learned of it through the media. "We did not know about that. We've learned that from the media as well, that the president of the United States has secured an energy ceasefire," Zelenskyy said.Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum, Zelenskyy questioned whether Moscow had agreed to the proposal at all, saying he had seen neither a public endorsement from Russia nor any let-up in its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure."We have not seen that they support this ceasefire anywhere," he said, pointing to continued Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy facilities.Large parts of Kyiv were without electricity and water when Trump made his announcement, as repair crews struggled to restore power following Russian strikes. Shortly afterwards, Russia launched another targeted attack on a power plant in Kharkiv, Zelenskyy said."It was clear that Putin does not read Truth Social," he remarked, referring to Trump's social media platform.Zelenskyy also accused Russia of striking a Ukrainian gas production facility and a petrol station overnight, while Ukraine had refrained from attacking Russian oil refineries.Despite the continued attacks, he said Kyiv remained willing to observe a reciprocal halt to strikes on energy infrastructure."We are ready to respect an energy ceasefire if Russia is ready to do the same. We agree if they agree," he said.Zelenskyy offered to sign formal guarantees if Washington considered them necessary, but stressed that the US would have to secure Moscow's compliance.Trump-Putin diesel deal sparks backlashZelenskyy's remarks followed several days of mounting tensions with Washington, beginning on Friday when Trump announced a deal with Vladimir Putin to supply Russian diesel to US and global markets, in an attempt to bring down soaring fuel prices ahead of November's US midterm elections.The US Treasury subsequently issued a six-month licence easing sanctions on Russian diesel already loaded onto tankers, allowing deliveries until April 2027 — a sharp reversal of Washington's efforts to restrict Moscow's energy revenues.The move drew criticism from European leaders and US lawmakers, including a bipartisan group of senators who urged Trump to reverse course, warning that the deal could provide Moscow with fresh revenues to finance its war against Ukraine.Trump, meanwhile, blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for rising fuel prices and demanded that Zelenskyy halt them. On Saturday, he went further, suggesting Ukraine needed a new president and accusing its wartime leader of obstructing efforts to end the war.On Sunday, Trump announced on Truth Social that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an immediate energy ceasefire, although neither side had publicly confirmed an agreement.It was not the first such declaration. A similar announcement in September failed to halt the strikes.Against this backdrop, Zelenskyy used his Warsaw address to make a pointed appeal for Washington to change course."We need American pressure on Russia, not sanctions relief, not concessions, but real pressure," he said.He argued that Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil refineries and exports were a response to Moscow's sustained campaign against Ukrainian energy infrastructure, and that both sides would have to halt such attacks for a ceasefire to work.Zelenskyy offers elections if Trump secures 60-day ceasefireResponding to Trump's renewed pressure to hold presidential elections, Zelenskyy said voting remained impossible under current security conditions, with Russian attacks now taking place around the clock."From a security standpoint, that's completely impossible. We have attacks day and night," he said.He also pointed to the logistical challenges of organising a vote for more than a million Ukrainian military personnel, including those serving on the front line.Nevertheless, Zelenskyy signalled that he was prepared to seek changes to Ukraine's legal framework if Washington could secure a comprehensive ceasefire with Moscow."If there is a ceasefire and if the Americans reach such an agreement with the Russians, I'm ready to engage with our Parliament and find difficult solutions," he said.He suggested this could involve changes to legislation and even the constitution, although constitutional amendments are prohibited under martial law.Zelenskyy then turned Trump's own diplomatic engagement with Moscow into a challenge to the US president, arguing that Washington should be able to use its influence over Putin to secure a complete halt to hostilities."And if we have at least a 60 day full ceasefire, then I'll be ready to work on holding elections," he said.Zelenskyy warns of Russian hybrid attacksBeyond the dispute with Washington, Zelenskyy warned that Ukrainian intelligence had uncovered further Russian plans to destabilise European countries."Our intelligence services know that Russia is planning many, many aggressive hybrid operations against Europe, against different countries, against your countries," he told the forum."There is no such thing as a small act of destabilisation," he added, urging European governments to remain vigilant and united.Zelenskyy also appealed for continued military assistance, including ammunition for Ukraine's F-16 fighter jets, air-defence interceptors and funding for domestic weapons and drone production.He called for closer defence-industrial cooperation with Poland, arguing that joint production and technological partnerships could strengthen both countries' security.The Ukrainian president also urged European leaders to prevent further delays in Ukraine's EU accession negotiations, saying progress was essential not only politically but also for the morale of Ukrainians living through another winter of war."Please do not allow any pauses in Ukraine's European integration," he said.Zelenskyy said Kyiv expected to open two negotiating clusters and wanted another two opened by the end of the year."Our people need to feel that despite all the difficulties, Ukraine's European future is close," he said.He concluded by urging European leaders to ensure Washington understood that an energy ceasefire, de-escalation and credible security guarantees were urgently needed in practice, rather than simply being announced on social media."In reality, not just on Truth Social," he said.

title: ‘Critical moment’: World leaders urged to course correct on nature protection ahead of COP17 summit
description: Game-changing global nature pact still has potential – but nations need to speed up progress, conservationists urge.
content: Governments are falling short on their commitments to protect the plants, animals and ecosystems that sustain life on Earth ahead of this month's UN biodiversity summit.The so-called COP17 summit in the Armenian capital, Yerevan, will be a reckoning for the nearly 200 nations that joined the landmark Paris Agreement for Nature in 2022 but have been slow to act on its objectives.It set 23 targets for halting and reversing nature loss by 2030, including reducing pollution, protecting threatened species and conserving 30 per cent of the world's land and oceans.But the world is off-track to meet these goals, according to a draft review by the United Nations Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), which oversees the biennial international negotiations on protecting the natural world."COP17 comes at a critical moment," says An Lambrechts from Greenpeace International."The most important outcome from Yerevan must therefore be a clear course correction. Governments need to move beyond restating promises and agree on concrete actions."Astrid Schomaker, executive director of the UN biodiversity convention, says that progress was being made and the 2030 goals were "still reachable – but only with significant change being made".This includes reducing incentives for politically sensitive industries like agriculture and fossil fuel production, areas where governments have made very little headway to date."Do I think we're moving in the right direction? Yes, but way too slowly," Schomaker says.Around 10 heads of state are expected in Yerevan for a leaders' summit on Friday (16 October) to start proceedings "and tell the negotiators to be ambitious and constructive" when talks formally begin on 19 October, she says.What's holding progress on nature conservation back?The nature summit comes weeks before the annual international climate negotiations (COP31) in neighbouring Türkiye, and is the first time nations have taken stock of progress since the biodiversity pact was adopted.Drawing on national reports and other inputs, a "global review" of collective improvements and pitfalls is being finalised.A draft scorecard published in July painted a mixed picture of progress.Some countries have taken strides toward the '30x30' conservation goal (protecting 30 per cent of Earth's land and waters by 2030), said Campaign for Nature in a September analysis.But taken together, government pledges would cover only 27 per cent of land and inland waters by the end of this decade if enacted in full. For oceans, the figure would be just 12 per cent.Money is a major barrier to the success of the biodiversity goals and an expected source of tension at COP17.Nations are lagging behind a pledge to raise $200 billion (€179b) a year for biodiversity by 2030 from public and private sources, including $30 billion (€27b) a year in international finance for developing countries.Wealthy countries are under pressure to fill the gap but face their own budget challenges, making the issue politically fraught.The United States, which is not a party to the biodiversity convention, is not involved in the talks."The more time you spend talking about funding, the less you talk about objectives," a French government official told news agency AFP.Decision makers must 'unite in fight' for survival of life on EarthAttention at the Yerevan summit is expected to focus on how the private sector can make up the shortfall.Under scrutiny will be the lacklustre performance of the Cali Fund, a milestone UN initiative launched in February 2025.The fund aimed to raise $1 billion (€894m) a year from corporations for conservation in developing countries but so far has attracted just $6,000 (€5,363)."Everyone was hoping... this would be a game changer. And we continue to believe that it absolutely has the potential," although corporate engagement had been "slower" than anticipated, says Schomaker.Subsidy reform has also proved to be a roadblock, with barely any movement toward the 2030 goal of reducing nature-harmful incentives by $500 billion (€447b) a year.For every dollar invested in protecting or restoring nature, about $30 (€27) still goes into activities that degrade it, according to UN figures.In October, more than 130 businesses and financial institutions – including Nestle and H&M Group – called on governments to reform incentives, citing $2.6 trillion (€2.3t) in annual public spending "that rewards practices depleting the soils, water and ecosystems".Guido Broekhoven from nature conservation organisation WWF International says that repurposing subsidies must be "a matter of priority" at COP17."At a time when geopolitical tensions are putting multilateral cooperation under pressure, it's even more important to show the world that our decision-makers can still be united in the fight for the survival of life on Earth," Greenpeace's Lambrechts says.

title: Chinese carmaker BYD considers opening a factory in France
description: France is among the European countries where BYD is considering opening a plant. According to vice-president Stella Li, "France is on the shortlist".
content: BYD wants French drivers to see it as a local company — and a factory in France could be its next step."France is on the shortlist," vice-president Stella Li said at the opening of the Paris Motor Show. "We are looking very closely at the possibility of setting up a plant in France."Li said her objectives were simple: she wants "people in France to think that BYD is a French company. I want them to like it".She added that BYD "will try to open a second and a third plant in Europe".The group's vice-president spoke as BYD prepares to open a plant in Hungary by the end of this year, she said.China agreed on Friday to "moderate" exports of hybrid and plug-in hybrid vehicles to the EU, according to European trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič.According to Li, the Chinese group "has a strong commitment in Europe" and intends "to become a local company in every region of the world".A dealer network gaining ground in FranceBYD is already relying on a well-established distribution network in France. The Chinese manufacturer has forged partnerships with major French automotive groups such as Bymycar, Emil Frey and Bodemer. These dealers handle sales and after-sales service for its vehicles in the country's main cities.In July, BYD said it had around 115 dealerships in France. The brand is continuing to expand through established local dealers. BYD registered 13,935 passenger vehicles in France in the first half of 2026, up 136% from a year earlier, according to the company.BYD’s expansion comes as electric car registrations across the EU rise sharply, against a backdrop of record fuel prices.

title: Oil prices drop as stocks rise after Trump touts 'energy ceasefire'
description: Most stock markets rose early Monday as oil prices fell after Donald Trump announced an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine, which offset a fresh wave of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.
content: Both main crude contracts, Brent and US WTI, sank more than 1% following the US president's declaration, even as it sparked astonishment in Kyiv, which also said Moscow had struck multiple power plants in the country."Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine," Trump said early Sunday on Truth Social. "Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!"His post came after he called on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to halt attacks on Russian refineries and said it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president" who would finally settle the war.Zelensky appeared to express surprise at the announcement, saying he was seeking further details, but added that "Ukraine supports the ceasefire, and it is important that Russia support it as well".Russia has yet to confirm its agreement.While the announcement was welcomed by Ukraine's allies, Trump had come under fire after declaring a temporary easing of US sanctions on Russian diesel, which European leaders and Kyiv said would only embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin.The drop in oil prices reversed an initial spike that came in response to Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia at the weekend.At least a dozen people were killed at Riyadh's international airport Saturday - the deadliest attack on Saudi soil for more than a decade - and another one died following a second strike on Sunday.The assaults marked a sharp escalation in the Yemen war, where Riyadh has long militarily supported the internationally recognised government against the Houthis.The Iran-backed group on Sunday claimed multiple attacks over the past 24 hours and threatened to keep targeting the kingdom's transit hubs, calling them "a theatre of operations for our forces"."The market is no longer paying full geopolitical premium on every headline, and that is probably the most useful signal in the morning price action," wrote SPI Asset Management's Stephen Innes."A strike matters if it threatens real barrels, shipping lanes, refining capacity or insurance costs; otherwise, the market is getting increasingly reluctant to pay up simply because the geopolitical ticker flashes red."The physical market remains tight enough to keep Brent above $100, but futures are refusing to treat every new escalation as the start of another straight-line inflation shock."Markets overview early MondayEuropean markets opened in the green with most regional sectors and major bourses gaining, while US futures were sharply higher.The drop in oil prices provided support to most Asian markets, with Hong Kong, Sydney, Singapore, Wellington and Manila all up in early hours. But Seoul and Taipei were dragged by losses in chipmakers SK hynix, Samsung and TSMC. Tokyo was closed for a holiday.Investors are also gearing up for the release of key US inflation and retail sales data, which could play a big role in the Federal Reserve's decision-making regarding interest rates. The bank is due to meet at the end of October.Also in view is the beginning of earnings season this week, with banking giants JP Morgan, Goldman Sachs and Bank of America due to report.Tech giants will follow later in the month and November, with traders keen to get an idea on the outlook for the AI sector in light of the vast sums of cash pumped into it in recent years.Elsewhere, the dollar index steadied at 102.16 as the escalating Middle East conflict kept investors cautious, while the euro stayed pinned near $1.121 after five straight weekly declines on French fiscal concerns. The yen, meanwhile, held at 158.24 per dollar with Japanese intervention risk deterring speculators.Also early Monday, spot gold rose 0.1% to $4,198 an ounce, supported by a softer dollar and lower oil prices that eased inflation and rate worries, while silver gained 0.4% to $61.02 an ounce.

title: IEA urges additional diesel releases ahead of key meeting
description: Tightening global diesel markets prompted the International Energy Agency to call on its members to accelerate previously agreed releases from strategic oil reserves, prioritising diesel. The IEA also asked member states to assess "whether additional diesel releases are necessary".
content: Ahead of the International Energy Agency's (IEA) governing board meeting this Thursday, its executive director Fatih Birol has written to member governments calling for further action as global diesel markets face tight supplies.Birol suggested that members that have not yet released all the oil they pledged in March, when the IEA agreed to release 400 million barrels, should speed up their remaining releases, prioritising diesel. Some countries have already released more than they initially pledged.All members were also asked to assess whether additional diesel releases are necessary and, if so, explain how much they could release and when.The governing board will review these efforts at its meeting on 15 October.“As we did in March, I believe we can once again demonstrate the IEA’s capacity to act together in support of energy security and economic stability,” Birol said in the statement published on Sunday.The G7 previously announced plans to release up to 100 million barrels of oil to curb soaring energy prices. However, an internal document seen by Euronews showed that these volumes would fulfil outstanding March commitments, rather than add to the original 400-million-barrel pledge."Of its 400 million barrels, 326 million have been released. Because some members over-delivered, the 100 million barrels in the G7 statement can be covered within the existing action if everyone fulfils their commitments," the document states.Diesel prices have been soaring amid global fuel shortages. The Iran war disrupted crude oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, while damage to refineries has also restricted fuel supplies.According to Kpler, crude oil and condensate exports from the Middle East Gulf, excluding Iran, returned to pre-war levels in September. However, much of that oil now travels through alternative routes or is transferred between tankers offshore.The IEA statement comes two days after US President Donald Trump announced a diesel supply deal with Russia. Washington temporarily eased sanctions on Russian diesel, allowing its sale and delivery, including imports into the US, until 7 April 2027.Moscow said it was ready to supply oil and petroleum products to the US and global markets following a telephone conversation between Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin."I am convinced this will have a positive impact on the entire global economy," Putin said, according to the Russian statement.European sanctions remain in place, but additional Russian supply to the global market could help lower diesel prices. The impact will depend on how much fuel Russia can deliver, with damage to its refineries limiting production.Brent crude, the international oil benchmark, remained above $100 a barrel on Monday morning. European diesel futures fell about 3% to around $1,437 a tonne.

title: Narrow-body jets will ‘change the shape of travel’, says Dubai Airports CEO
description: Speaking on the sidelines of the WTTC Global Summit in Malta, Dubai Airports chief Paul Griffiths shared that he believes the expansion of regional airports will be key in the next decade of travel.
content: The CEO of Dubai Airports has said that aircraft technology improvements, with smaller planes able to fly longer distances, will “change the shape of travel”.Talking at a roundtable on the sidelines of the World Travel & Tourism Council’s Global Summit in Malta, Paul Griffiths spoke about the expansion of Al Maktoum International Airport (DWC), noting that there are plans to have direct connections from Dubai to more than 600 cities.“The great thing, of course, is aircraft technology is changing all the time, and with smaller aircraft able to fly longer distances we'll have all of those secondary cities in Europe directly connected to Dubai, so you'll be able to fly from, you know, Exeter or Valencia or Lyon or Marseille or Baden Baden, to Dubai and then on to the world, so it's going to change the shape of travel,” he said.Dubai Airports announced plans to turn DWC into the world’s largest airport back in 2024. Once complete, the airport will have 400 terminal gates and five runways, with capacity for up to 260 million passengers annually.The airport expansion should be completed by 2032.“I think over the next decade or so there will be a fantastic opportunity for regional airports to expand their operations,” Griffiths added. “With narrow-body jets now capable of flying the Atlantic to minor destinations, where you don't need a wide body jet to fill to make it commercially sustainable, there'll be huge opportunities for regional airports.“All they have to do is get their surface transport access sorted out and that will be a good place to invest and it will be great for regional economies.”How aviation can reach net zeroOf course, you can’t talk about expansion without mentioning sustainability.Griffiths highlighted sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) as being “probably the only way” for the industry to eliminate carbon emissions, pointing to Singapore, which has introduced a green fuel tax, as a destination to emulate.He noted that the private sector must be persuaded to invest in SAF’s production, while governments must mandate its use, slowly increasing the required percentage of SAF blended with conventional fuel.“My message is please balance the community impact by mitigating it through taking environmental control seriously, but setting a target and a framework to allow the expansion of the infrastructure to facilitate this increase in income from travel and tourism,” he added.The future of airportsGriffiths said in a panel on digital identity and resetting the border experience that he believes the need for passports could be eliminated within the next five years, but he expanded on his comments in the roundtable.Discussing the new airport, he said: “I can't comment on the technology that you see, because hopefully if you don't see any technology, then we will have done our job incredibly well.“The idea is to make all of the process and the entire customer experience all about human contact.”Facial recognition will be at the heart of the new experience, with no need to show your passport at the border or to present your boarding pass. AI will also be used to scan baggage.“We can do it so much more quickly and less obtrusively,” he said. “I always think that airport security – and particularly in some airports which I won't name and shame – is probably the most intrusive process that any human being could go through outside of a hospital operating theatre, and we don't really want to do that to our customers.”

title: UK’s Burnham says Russia interfered in Brexit vote
description: The prime minister said Germany’s Friedrich Merz had told him the far-right AfD was linked to Russia, as he faces questions at home over Labour’s ties to the UAE.
content: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said Russia interfered in Britain’s 2016 referendum on leaving the European Union, in what is believed to be the first time a British leader has publicly acknowledged such meddling.Burnham told The Rest is Politics podcast that on taking office in July he asked advisers whether Russia had interfered in the Brexit vote."I’ve had the clear answer that yes, there was," he said. "These things are important now to put clearly on the record and I believe help voters in Germany and France understand that some of this politics is instigated via our enemies, namely Russia."Moscow has long denied meddling in other countries’ elections or referendums.Burnham’s remarks come as UK intelligence agencies warn of a growing threat of Russian interference in Britain’s democratic institutions. In 2020, a parliamentary committee found the government had failed to fully assess the possible impact of Russian state media and "troll" accounts on the referendum.Burnham also said he had discussed possible links between Russia and Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party with Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Berlin last week."You know he was saying to me that the AfD are clearly linked to Russia, funded I believe," Burnham said. "There is certainly misinformation, disinformation that is emanating from Russia into German politics."Labour’s links to the UAEAt home, Burnham is under pressure over his ties to Manchester City, the Gulf state-backed Premier League club that was found guilty last month of widespread breaches of financial rules.The former mayor of Greater Manchester was criticised for saying he would be "really concerned" to lose the club’s wealthy arab owners. Labour MPs have accepted around €325,500 in hospitality and foreign trips from the United Arab Emirates, far more than any other party, according to official records analysed by the British newspaper The Sun.On the podcast, Burnham agreed to an opposition request to publish details of his meetings with the club’s owners, saying he had held only one significant meeting, in 2021.This will not include information of Manchester City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak's private meeting with Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds in Downing Street on 14 September, 11 days before the club was found guilty.The timing is suspicious although reports claim talks were held in Al Mubarak's separate role as chief executive of Abu Dhabi’s sovereign wealth fund, Mubadala and focused on defence, security intelligence and trade.Burnham has said the football issues were serious and subject to an independent process, but should be kept separate from questions of investment.

title: Trump turns the screws on Kyiv as EU budget talks hit a wall
description: Good morning. It’s Monday. I’m Mared Gwyn. Today: Europe braces as Trump turns up the heat on Zelenskyy, and Ireland’s EU budget compromise falls dead on arrival.
content: Kyiv under pressure: For Ukraine, the past few days have brought back the distinct taste of the Oval Office showdown: public pressure on President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, accusations that Ukraine is obstructing peace and a growing fear (again) that the aim is not compromise, let alone a just peace, but to force Ukraine to surrender, our correspondent Sasha Vakulina writes this morning.Blindsided: US President Donald Trump made a surprise announcement on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an immediate ceasefire on attacks against energy infrastructure. There was just one rather significant problem: at least one of those parties appeared unaware of the agreement.“If President Trump negotiated it with Putin, please tell us when the ceasefire begins,” Zelenskyy said in response. Ukraine, he added, was ready.It was not entirely clear Moscow got the memo either, Sasha explains. After Trump’s announcement, Russia struck a thermal power plant in Kharkiv, before targeting several other power plants overnight. And that was only Sunday.Diesel deal rattles Europeans: On Friday, Trump had also announced a deal with Vladimir Putin to ease sanctions on Russian diesel exports, without informing Ukrainian or European negotiators who were in Miami for talks. It’s seen as an effort to bring down soaring diesel and gasoline prices, a major issue for American voters, ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.Zelenskyy did not mince his words, branding the deal “weak” and warning it would hand Putin “billions” more to wage war. Trump told him he “better damn well stop” striking Russian refineries, before taking it further and saying Ukraine needed a “new leader”. Putin’s leadership, notably, did not come up for discussion.Rallying around Zelenskyy: There is another irony for Trump: publicly berating Zelenskyy has hardly proven an effective way of weakening him at home - quite the opposite. EU leaders have also been rallying behind the Ukrainian leader – and Zelenskyy is now expected to join leaders when they gather for a summit in Brussels this Thursday and Friday, sources have told Euronews.Hard reckoning: News of the Trump-Putin diesel deal and the subsequent energy ceasefire is also set to dominate the conversation today in Brussels and Luxembourg, where foreign ministers are gathering, Jorge Liboreiro writes.Once again, the EU finds itself scrambling to close ranks behind Zelenskyy and push back, with calculated criticism, against Trump’s Russian-friendly diplomacy. The US Treasury’s sanctions waiver to enable the diesel sales, set to last until April 2027, has particularly enraged Europeans, who see their own sanctions regime undermined by Trump’s out-of-the-blue decisions. It must be noted that the majority of vessels that Russia uses to trade its refined oil products are subject to the G7 price cap ($100 per barrel).Foreign ministers will today make clear their pressure campaign on Moscow will continue unabated by formally blacklisting more than 1,600 people and companies accused of enabling the war, a record number in one go.“We are of course continuing our path,” Kallas said on sanctions upon arriving in Luxembourg this morning. “Our message is clear. If we want to end this war, the only way we can do this is putting more pressure on Russia, and we would call on the US to put the sanctions in place so we can finish this war,” she added.More is needed: Russia’s all-out escalation has forced EU officials and diplomats to admit that their multibillion-euro support for Ukraine will fall short next year. But there are no easy solutions, Jorge writes in his in-depth analysis.Warsaw watches: The mounting tensions have also raised the stakes of the Warsaw Security Conference kicking off this morning, with President Zelenskyy expected to address delegates from Kyiv in around an hour.Our chief EU editor Maria Tadeo, on the ground in the Polish capital, reports that security is tight and the mood tense after Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on Sunday that a man had been arrested on suspicion of plotting to assassinate him and his defence minister. More from our Warsaw colleagues.Dead on arrival: Meanwhile, a new pitch to trim down the EU’s next long-term budget – known as the Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) – tabled by Ireland over the weekend has been met with immediate pushback from the so-called frugal countries, which are demanding a much smaller spending pot.“The size of the new proposal is not a basis for agreement. The EU budget must be affordable for those who bear the brunt of financing it,” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said in a statement on Saturday.Dutch directness: Dutch Finance Minister Eelco Heinen was even more blunt. “The Netherlands cannot accept this proposal. At this rate, there will be no deal by the end of the year,” he said in a statement. Sweden also rejected the proposal, insisting that the “overall volume” needs to come down.Ireland, which currently holds the rotating presidency of the Council of the EU, on Saturday pitched €141 billion in cuts to the previous proposal in an attempt to appease the frugals. The country’s EU affairs minister, Thomas Byrne, described the proposal as a “compromise designed to act as a catalyst” for wrapping up negotiations by the end of this year – a prospect that now looks increasingly remote.Crunch time: EU leaders are set to tackle the budget issue when they gather for talks in Brussels on Thursday and Friday – and European Council President António Costa is pushing for a swift compromise. There has been a political push to wrap up the budget negotiations before the end of 2026 to prevent talks from being torpedoed by elections in major EU economies including France, Italy and Poland next year. My colleague Luca Bertuzzi has more.Oil prices tumble as stocks rise after Trump touts 'energy ceasefire'Most stock markets rose early Monday as oil prices tumbled after US President Donald Trump announced an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine, which offset a fresh wave of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, my colleague Angela Barnes reports.Both main crude contracts sank more than 1% following the announcement, reversing an initial spike that came in response to Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia at the weekend.At least a dozen people were killed at Riyadh's international airport Saturday - the deadliest attack on Saudi soil for more than a decade - and another one died following a second strike on Sunday.The Iran-backed group on Sunday claimed multiple attacks over the past 24 hours and threatened to keep targeting the kingdom's transit hubs, calling them "a theatre of operations for our forces"."The market is no longer paying full geopolitical premium on every headline, and that is probably the most useful signal in the morning price action," wrote SPI Asset Management's Stephen Innes. He added: "The physical market remains tight enough to keep Brent above $100, but futures are refusing to treat every new escalation as the start of another straight-line inflation shock."Angela has the details.More from our newsroomsTens of thousands urge EU for climate action at Brussels demonstration. Ahead of a major UN summit, thousands of protesters marched through the streets of Brussels demanding greater action to combat climate change. Euronews’ Evelyn Ann-Marie Dom was on the ground and spoke to protesters and organisers.Macron's popularity hits lowest level since 2017 as Bardella and Le Pen also lose ground. Some 82% of French people now disapprove of the French President, while the far-right National Rally’s Marine Le Pen and Jordan Bardella’s ratings were also weakened by Mediapart's revelations about antisemitic texts attributed to Bardella. Alexander Kazakevich has more.North Korea fires 'several ballistic missiles' into Sea of Japan, Seoul's military says. North Korea fired multiple ballistic missiles off its east coast, Seoul's military said on Monday, after weeks of mounting friction over a landmine explosion along the heavily fortified border that divides both countries. Gavin Blackburn has the details.We're also keeping an eye onWarsaw Security Conference kicks off. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to give the opening address from Kyiv. Speakers include Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk and European Commissioner for Defence, Andrius Kubilius.EU foreign affairs and environment ministers gather for talks in Luxembourg.European Commission Vice-Presidents Stéphane Séjourné and Roxana Mînzatu to address the European Parliament’s employment committee.That’s it for today. Sasha Vakulina, Jorge Liboreiro and Luca Bertuzzi contributed to this newsletter.

title: 'Energy ceasefire': Confusion in Kyiv, support from allies, silence from Moscow and fresh strikes
description: Trump announced an immediate energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, but Moscow has not confirmed it. Zelenskyy expressed surprise and reported fresh Russian strikes on Ukrainian power plants, causing outages.
content: US President Donald Trump caused confusion on Sunday by announcing an "energy ceasefire" between Ukraine and Russia, drawing astonishment in Kyiv, silence from Moscow and support from Ukraine's Western allies.However, the ceasefire looked unreliable, as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia struck multiple Ukrainian power plants on Sunday, including one in the capital and another in Kharkiv, causing power outages and outrage.Trump's announcement came two days after he declared a temporary easing of US sanctions on Russian diesel, sparking outrage from European allies and Kyiv, who said it would only embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin."Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine," Trump said early Sunday on Truth Social. "Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!"Zelenskyy appeared surprised by the announcement and said he was seeking further details, but added that "Ukraine supports the ceasefire, and it is important that Russia support it as well."Russia has not yet confirmed this agreement.Zelenskyy later said multiple Ukrainian power stations had been hit and that "Ukrainian skies have been infested with Russian 'shaheds' all day," referring to a type of drone originally designed by Iran that Russia now uses extensively.Since launching a full-scale invasion of its neighbour in 2022, Russia has systematically hit Ukrainian energy infrastructure, leading to energy and heating shortages, prompting Ukraine to hit back at Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says, to fund the war.More recently, Trump's war in Iran has caused oil shortages and sharp price spikes, creating major headwinds for his Republican Party ahead of the midterm elections early next month.Zelenskyy: Tell Putin to give us 60 days of ceasefire for electionsThe ceasefire appeared to win support on Sunday from Ukraine's key western allies, including the UK, France, Canada, and the European Commission, as several leaders urged Russia to honour the deal. But this support contrasted with broad criticism of the US-Russia diesel deal earlier in the week, which has fueled growing tensions between Trump and Zelenskyy.Zelenskyy called the diesel deal a "weak decision," while several of Ukraine's European allies expressed outrage and pledged to step up pressure on Moscow.Seven US senators, including four Republicans, released a statement on Sunday blasting the diesel deal with Russia, saying it was illegal.Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney added to the chorus on Sunday after a call with Zelenskyy, saying the diesel deal "is in direct opposition to the efforts of Ukraine, Canada and our allies to create peace and stability in Europe."Asked about the criticism on Saturday, Trump said it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president" who would finally settle the war.Zelenskyy pushed back, telling ABC News that "it's up to our society, up to our people to choose one or another leader.""Tell (Vladimir) Putin, give us two months — 60 days of total ceasefire, 60 days, and we will organise elections," he said.Full support from Brussels, Berlin, Paris and LondonEU chief Ursula von der Leyen also backed the Ukrainian leader "as he leads the fight for his people's freedom."Germany's foreign minister said on Sunday that Berlin continued to "fully support" Zelenskyy."Europe needs stability, and that means that we are very clearly continuing to stay by the side of Ukraine and its government," Johann Wadephul stressed.France also backed a "real energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine, President Emmanuel Macron said on Sunday."Currently, Russia continues to refuse that, by lately intensifying further its strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure," Macron said, adding: "France will continue to stay by the side of Ukraine and President Zelenskyy."UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham echoed this strong support and Trump's call "for a sustained energy ceasefire to start now."

title: Addictive behaviour is falling among Portuguese teens but most vulnerable are still exposed
description: Portuguese teenagers are drinking and using drugs less and facing fewer problems, but risks are increasingly concentrated among those with multiple vulnerabilities, according to a new ICAD study on addictive behaviours.
content: There are fewer problems and lower levels of consumption among Portuguese teenagers, but the highest-risk behaviours are increasingly concentrated among young people who accumulate several vulnerability factors. This is the main conclusion of a new study by the Institute for Addictive Behaviours and Dependencies (ICAD).The Study on Alcohol, Tobacco, Drugs and other Addictive Behaviours (ECATD-CAD 2024) examines the problematic dimension of addictive behaviours among pupils in Portuguese state schools aged between 13 and 18.The findings point to an overall favourable trend compared with the picture observed in the previous edition of the study, carried out in 2019. According to ICAD, there has been "a consistent reduction in the experience of all the problematic situations analysed, including violent conduct, accidents, hospitalisations, risky sexual behaviours and other episodes with potential negative consequences".This trend is unfolding in a context in which pupils report better academic performance, greater parental supervision and going out at night less often, factors which, according to the report, "appear to contribute to an environment that is generally more protective against risk behaviours".Despite this positive development, ICAD warns that "in several indicators there is a growing concentration of the highest-risk behaviours in a relatively small group of adolescents, characterised by profiles of greater individual and social vulnerability, which makes it clear that the reduction in the overall number of consumers does not remove the need for intervention targeting specific groups".Recent consumption of alcohol and, above all, illicit drugs remains one of the main factors associated with involvement in problematic situations. The report notes that, compared with 2019, this trend has become more pronounced."The group of pupils who use psychoactive substances show significantly higher prevalence of risky sexual behaviours, problems with the police, interpersonal violence, accidents and other potentially serious situations", ICAD states, while stressing, however, that most problematic situations do not occur immediately following an episode of consumption.The report also distinguishes between drinking alcohol only and polyconsumption, identifying them as important factors in the likelihood of experiencing problematic situations.Thus, adolescents who combine recent consumption of alcohol and illicit drugs "display substantially higher levels of involvement in accidents, problems with the police, cyberbullying and risky sexual behaviours when compared with those who consume only alcoholic drinks".The analysis of the problematic dimension of the different addictive behaviours also shows that, in alcohol consumption, motivations linked to pleasure, fun and sociability remain predominant.However, ICAD underlines that there is a significant proportion of young people who say they drink alcohol to forget their problems. According to the institute, this is an "indicator frequently associated with the development of harmful patterns of use and dependence".The report also highlights that, in the case of cannabis, although most users do not present indicators of risk of dependency, "there is an increase in the proportion of users classified as high risk, alongside growth in the group without any identified risk".Social media is a major concern among non-substance-related addictive behavioursAmong non-substance-related addictive behaviours, social media continue to emerge as the main concern, with a significant proportion of young people acknowledging that they spend too much time on these platforms.In electronic gaming, including video games played exclusively online, indicators of problematic use remain broadly stable compared with the previous edition of the study. Gambling for money, meanwhile, although still involving only a minority of adolescents, shows an increase in prevalence, albeit accompanied by a slight decrease in indicators linked to the problematic dimension, such as the need to increase the amounts wagered.There are also important differences between boys and girls. Male pupils continue to show greater involvement in problems with the police and in risky electronic gaming and gambling for money. By contrast, girls stand out for their higher prevalence of problematic use of social media and for resorting to alcohol consumption as a strategy for coping with emotional difficulties.Social and family factors also have an impact. The profile most associated with problematic behaviours includes low academic achievement, weaker parental supervision, frequent nights out, and lower physical and emotional wellbeing. Conversely, good school performance, parental supervision and greater wellbeing act as protective factors.Regional analysis also reveals changes compared with the previous study. Alentejo now appears as the region with the highest concentration of unfavourable indicators, followed by the Autonomous Region of the Azores, while Lisbon no longer occupies the position of greatest vulnerability observed in 2019.

title: Rockies, Route 66 and railway hotels: Why 2027 is the year to explore the US by train
description: The United States is marking 200 years of passenger rail travel with scenic long-distance routes, vintage steam trains, historic stations and unusual railway stays. Here’s how to explore the country by train in 2027.
content: The United States is set to celebrate 200 years of commercial rail travel in 2027, and now is the time to plan a trip to see the vast nation from a different perspective.From Rocky Mountain crossings and Route 66 adventures to vintage steam trains and hotels made from restored carriages, the anniversary is putting the spotlight on the many ways to explore the US by rail.Ahead of the anniversary on 28 February next year, Brand USA is not just throwing its weight behind the country’s varied train routes, but also through ways to experience the heritage, including staying in restored railway carriages. When US passenger rail travel began in 1827, it quickly became a key way to cross the huge country. Railways linked cities, opened up new destinations and turned the train journey itself into part of the American travel experience.While many of us now associate the US with driving and flying from state to state, admittedly, its rail network is significantly less comprehensive than we’re used to in Europe, but it does offer some real gems. "Rail is where America's travel story began, and 200 years later, the romance of the rails endures,” said Fred Dixon, President and CEO of Brand USA.“The 2027 bicentennial is a timely invitation for travellers to slow down, look out the window, and take in the unique beauty of the USA mile by mile.”The 200th anniversary will be marked across the US throughout 2027, with museums, historic stations and heritage railways hosting exhibitions, special train rides and other events. The Mid-Atlantic state of Maryland is highlighting its rail heritage, offering visits to its rail-themed museums and scenic train rides across the state.Meanwhile, Branchville, South Carolina, will host its long-running Raylrode Daze Festivul, which began in 1969. The town is home to the oldest railroad junction in the US, making it a fitting place to celebrate two centuries of American rail travel.Here’s everything you need to know to plan a successful rail adventure in the US in 2027.Explore from the rails rather than by road or airThe US has wildly different landscapes, from rugged coastal spots and metropolises to deserts and mountains, and so many of them can be missed if you choose to fly across the country or go by car. Luckily, there are a number of train routes which allow travellers to see some of these geographical phenomena in a unique way. If you’re keen to explore the west of the country in a different way, a trip aboard the Canyon Spirit is an excellent plan.Taking passengers between Denver, Colorado, and Salt Lake City, Utah, the train only runs in daylight, meaning those onboard can take in dramatic canyons, mountains and red-rock landscapes rather than sleeping through them. Guests can see the best of the West in the daytime, before disembarking and sleeping in hotels along the route. You may think that Route 66 – arguably the ultimate American road trip – might only be done by road, but in fact, you don’t necessarily need a car to follow its path. The Amtrak Southwest Chief runs from Chicago towards Los Angeles, passing through communities and landscapes associated with the legendary highway. Stops including Albuquerque and Flagstaff offer a chance to explore the Southwest, with the Grand Canyon also within reach, before continuing west to LA.Other routes can be explored by using Amtrak, the country’s national passenger rail system.The California Zephyr links Chicago and the San Francisco Bay Area via the Rockies and Sierra Nevada, while the Coast Starlight runs from Seattle to Los Angeles. Meanwhile, the Empire Builder travels from Chicago to the Pacific Northwest, passing Glacier National Park and enormous plains and mountains which give travellers an idea of how awe-inspiringly large the US really is. A new wave of American trains – and some heritage optionsAmerica’s rail network is also getting a modern makeover, with new trains and services opening up different corners of the country. In the Pacific Northwest, Amtrak’s soon-to-be-launched Airo trains will serve the Cascades route between cities including Seattle and Portland, linking urban breaks with mountains, forests, wine country and the coast.Down on the Gulf Coast, the Mardi Gras Service connects New Orleans with Mobile, Alabama. That means visitors can extend a stay in New Orleans beyond its jazz, food and historic neighbourhoods, continuing east by rail and discovering lesser-known coastal communities along the way.If you’re keen to experience a taste of America’s railway past, hop aboard one of its many heritage trains. Colorado’s Durango & Silverton Narrow Gauge Railroad winds through the San Juan Mountains, while the Cumbres & Toltec Scenic Railroad crosses into New Mexico, with themed rides including dinner and live music.Elsewhere, Pennsylvania’s Strasburg Rail Road operates in one of the country’s oldest railway regions, while West Virginia’s Cass Scenic Railroad ferries passengers into the Appalachian Mountains on tracks once associated with the logging industry.If you want to see some of the best fall foliage the Northeast has to offer, New York’s Finger Lakes Rail Experience offers scenic journeys through historic landscapes, which boast plenty of reds and oranges in the autumn. Stations and museums offer historical insightRailway history isn’t confined to the tracks, with museums and former stations offering a closer look at how trains shaped the US. Baltimore is a good place to start, with the former B&O Railroad Museum marking the bicentenary with special programming and a new Innovation Hall. The Railroad Museum of Pennsylvania is also opening a new accessible roundhouse in 2027, housing six historic steam locomotives. Elsewhere, historic stations have been given new lives, including Denver Union Station, which houses the Crawford Hotel, where Pullman-style rooms are designed to mimic vintage sleeper cars.In Omaha, Nebraska, the Durham Museum is inside the 1931 Art Deco Union Station. Visitors here can climb aboard restored 1940s passenger train cars and buy a malted milkshake from a working 1931 soda fountain.Los Angeles Union Station is a particular architectural highlight, with tours exploring its design, history and artwork.Sleep in a piece of railroad historyIf you want to fully embrace all things railways-themed, you don’t even have to leave the station to sleep in America’s railway history. In Chattanooga, Tennessee, Hotel Chalet at The Choo Choo lets guests stay in restored Pullman carriages, while the nearby Tennessee Valley Railroad Museum offers historic train rides. In Salt Lake City, the Asher Adams occupies the former Union Pacific Depot, while Minneapolis’ Renaissance Minneapolis Hotel, The Depot retains its railway heritage.For something more unusual, Idaho Train Stays in Deary has restored carriages and a caboose, while Antigua Inn in Madrid, New Mexico offers stays in converted cabooses. Nearby, Lamy’s The Hamilton has a restored 1920s Pullman railcar, while Sky Railway offers themed journeys from Lamy and Santa Fe. From here, travellers can opt to ride the Sky Railway, a railroad dating to 1880 which was revived and restored in part by Game of Thrones author George R.R. Martin. Today, it hosts experiences with themes including stargazing, murder mystery, live jazz and margarita tastings.In Omaha, 10 restored Union Pacific cabooses at Two Rivers State Recreation Area can be booked for overnight stays in warm-weather months.

title: Shakira sets Amazon Music record in Madrid with most-watched live stream by a female artist
description: The global broadcast of the Colombian singer's Madrid concert has become the most-watched live performance by a female artist on Amazon Music. The platform highlights the role of the Spanish capital as a bridge between Latin America and Europe.
content: The global broadcast of Shakira's concert in Madrid has become the most-watched live performance by a female artist on Amazon Music, according to Claire Imoucha, head of Amazon Music in Spain, speaking in an interview with 'RTVE'.The broadcast allowed viewers to follow the show for free from different countries via Amazon Music, Prime Video and Twitch. The performance, held on 3 October, marked a milestone in the Colombian singer's career, as it was the first time one of her full concerts was streamed live worldwide.The production, coordinated over several months between the artist's team, the promoter and Amazon Music, deployed some twenty cameras, drones and even a helicopter to bring the show to millions of viewers."Madrid has become the epicentre of Latin music, the bridge between Latin America and Europe," Imoucha said, defending the choice of the Spanish capital because of Shakira's prominence in the country and the scale of her music residency. The Amazon Music executive added that Latin and Spanish-language music already accounts for 65% of digital consumption in Spain, a share which, she said, continues to grow.Shakira and music residencies in MadridThe performance is part of the Madrid residency of the "Las Mujeres Ya No Lloran World Tour", linked to ES Latina, which has seen the singer give several concerts in the capital since September. The initiative adds to the presence of other major Latin artists in Madrid and strengthens the city's drive to host international-scale shows.Amazon Music also has extensive experience with major music broadcasts: it has spent more than five years streaming the Primavera Sound festival in Barcelona live to audiences around the world.

title: Antarctic penguins emit up to 7 million tonnes of methane a year, study finds
description: A study by CSIC and the University of Granada finds that chinstrap penguin colonies are a previously unmeasured natural source of methane, emitting up to 7 million tonnes a year.
content: Large colonies of chinstrap penguins in Antarctica are a significant natural source of methane, a greenhouse gas whose impact on global warming is greater than that of carbon dioxide (CO₂).This has been demonstrated for the first time by a study carried out by the Institute of Marine Sciences of Andalusia (ICMAN), a research centre of the Spanish National Research Council (CSIC), in collaboration with the University of Granada.The research, published (source in Spanish) in the journal 'Climate and Atmospheric Science', estimates that the guano produced by these birds generates around 490,000 tonnes of methane a year. This amount is comparable to emissions from other recognised natural sources, such as all the world's coastal ocean areas.Until now, most studies on methane emissions have focused on human activities such as the use of fossil fuels, agriculture and waste management, as well as on domesticated animals. However, large concentrations of wildlife can also generate emissions through the accumulation and decomposition of organic matter."The guano that builds up in these bird colonies, which can bring together tens of thousands of individuals, creates extraordinarily intense methane emission hotspots that until now had never been measured or quantified in situ," explains Alejandro Román, a researcher at ICMAN-CSIC and lead author of the study, quoted in a press release (source in Spanish).To obtain these results, the team carried out direct gas measurements in two large penguin colonies on Deception Island, in the South Shetland Islands archipelago. It also used drones equipped with optical sensors to map the surfaces covered in guano and to estimate the size of the populations.If the calculation is extended to all Antarctic land areas influenced by these birds, emissions could reach millions of tonnes. "They could amount to around 7 million tonnes of methane per year, a figure of the same order of magnitude as global estimates for other major methane sources associated with animal activity, such as termites," says Emma Huertas, principal investigator of the DICHOSO project, together with Antonio Tovar.The authors believe that this phenomenon should be included in global emissions inventories and underline the need to study how climate change could alter it by affecting both penguin populations and the soil microorganisms that produce methane as the guano breaks down.

title: Police clear Guano beach camp in Ceuta days before royal visit
description: Spain's National Police have cleared Guano beach in Ceuta, where about 400 migrants were still camped, two days before the King and Queen visit the city. It was the last remaining camp; some migrants fled to the nearby hills.
content: The eviction operations carried out by the state security forces began shortly after 8:00 am on the Guano beach in Ceuta, where around 400 migrants were still present following the wave of illegal immigration from Morocco that brought more than 70,000 people at the end of July.The operation was made up largely of officers from the National Police, the Spanish riot units, immigration staff and members of the Civil Guard and local police. The procedure was similar to the two previous clearances on Tarajal and Trampolín beaches.The migrants were grouped together and taken by bus to the Centro de Atención Temporal de Extranjeros (CATE), where their details will begin to be registered. Afterwards, they will be housed in one of the camps set up by the government, such as the one at the port.On the two previous occasions, not all the migrants cooperated with the procedure, and many fled into the hills, only coming down when food was distributed. This morning, many gathered up their belongings and left the area before the police arrived.Minors separated from adultsDuring the eviction, officers found numerous minors. They were assembled separately and will be transferred apart from the adults.Several of them were carrying signs asking to be taken to a centre for minors. According to local media, many of the children on this beach had already tried to be registered previously but ran away.On 20 August, the transfer of migrants from Trampolín beach to temporary reception centres in Loma Margarita and El Embolsamiento began. Some migrants later returned to the beach, as happened when the camp at the port of Ceuta was opened.Clean-up and assessment of the settlementOnce the site had been emptied, cleaning crews moved in to remove tents, rubbish and all kinds of debris. The work will continue throughout the day, as there is still much to do in a place that has served as a camp for a long time. The ecological damage is significant and will have to be assessed by environmental experts in contact with the Ministry of the Environment.The camp has left behind serious incidents, including the deaths of two people, as well as brawls, thefts and fights. A parallel life also developed there, with street markets and a way of life of its own.The eviction comes ahead of the visit by King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia, scheduled for 13 October. The royal couple will preside in Ceuta over a tribute to those who died at sea during the mass crossing at the Tarajal border. After spending the night in the autonomous city, they will travel on to Melilla. It will be the first time a Spanish monarch has spent the night in Ceuta since the visits by Alfonso XIII in 1904 and 1927.

title: Man who planned to attack Poland's prime minister has been arrested, interior minister says
description: After Poland's police said Sunday they received information about a possible plot to attack Prime Minister Donald Tusk and Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, the Polish interior minister announced the man was arrested.
content: A man who threatened and planned to attack Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk was arrested, the country's interior minister said Sunday.Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński gave no details about the identity of the man nor the type of attack planned.Security services in Poland have been on alert after police received information about a possible attack on Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk and Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz.Poland has been on high alert following a series of school stabbings this week, as well as fears of a possible Russian hybrid attack to weaken Western support for Ukraine in its war against Moscow's full-scale invasion."We take this matter extremely seriously", said Jacek Dobrzyński, spokesperson for the minister overseeing Poland's intelligence services.
