He said authorities considered there was a "high probability" the threats would be carried out.Adam Szłapka, a spokesperson for the Polish government, told Polish media that Tusk learned about the threat first thing on Sunday morning. He said that even if officials do occasionally get threats, this one was "exceptionally concerning".Dobrzyński said that the Polish services were receiving an increasing number of various threats every month.Three attacks at schools in Mazovia province in central Poland took place within four days this week, leaving one dead and many wounded, including children.In September, Tusk warned about likely intensified hybrid attacks by Russia on NATO’s eastern flank.He said Russia was planning strikes with drones or rockets on European countries supporting Ukraine, among them Poland, with the goal of weakening Western support for Kyiv's fight against the Russian invasion. Moscow has denied any such plans.

title: Russian army strikes Sloviansk and Kyiv as Ukrainian drones hit third Yandex data centre
description: Russian forces struck two apartment blocks in Sloviansk, injuring four, and hit warehouses in Kyiv. Overnight, Ukrainian drones targeted Yandex's data centre in Vladimir, causing major service outages but no casualties.
content: On the morning of 11 October, the Russian army struck two blocks of flats in Sloviansk in the Donetsk region."At this point, four people are known to have been injured", said the city's mayor Vadym Liakh. "Everyone is receiving medical treatment".There may be people trapped under the rubble, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.Warehouses are on fire outside Kyiv following an overnight Russian attack. Storage facilities at an industrial plant in the Bucha district of the Ukrainian capital caught fire, and firefighters are still working to extinguish the blaze.A paramedic and a driver were injured when a Russian drone hit an ambulance in the Sumy region. According to the head of the regional military administration, Oleh Hryhorov, the medical workers managed to get out of the damaged vehicle on their own.Emergency power cuts were introduced on Sunday in several regions of Ukraine because of the difficult situation in the energy sector caused by Russian shelling, the press service of the national energy company Ukrenergo said.Previously published schedules for hourly power cuts are currently not in force. The emergency outages will be lifted once the situation in the power system stabilises.Ukrainian drones hit Yandex, third data centre targetedOvernight into Sunday, Ukrainian drones attacked Russian technology giant Yandex's data centre in Vladimir, east of Moscow in the third reported attack on the firm in days.The company said the centre's infrastructure had been damaged and its operations completely halted. According to the latest information, there were no casualties in the attack.Yandex added that it is continuing to assess the state of the infrastructure and cannot yet say how long repairs will take. This is already the company's third data centre to be attacked in October.Yandex, often dubbed "Russia's Google", runs the country's most popular search engine, as well as food-ordering and taxi apps used by tens of millions of people.Governor Aleksandr Avdeyev confirmed (source in Russian) the UAV attack in Vladimir and the ensuing fire. He said residential areas had escaped destruction. Residents of the houses closest to the attack site have begun to be evacuated.In Vladimir, two substations supplying electricity to 5,000 residents were switched off. An hour later, the governor said that 80% of the power supply had been restored and heating and water supplies were back to normal.Preliminary reports suggest that a supercomputer housed at the Vladimir data centre was damaged. An identical machine is located at the Yandex data centre in Ryazan that was also targeted.Taxi and navigation disruptionIn the wake of the attack, users experienced widespread disruptions to the company's services. People were unable to order taxis in Moscow, St. Petersburg, Perm, Krasnoyarsk, Vladivostok, Ulan-Ude, Yekaterinburg and other Russian cities."I can't get anything to work at all", said Yevgeny, a 69-year-old sitting behind the wheel of a Yandex-branded taxi near Moscow."I've never seen anything like this before. It hasn't happened in the last five years. Now I don't know what to do", he said.Similar problems were reported in Serbia, Kazakhstan, Belarus and Armenia. Drivers say they cannot log into the app or are facing navigation failures, while passengers see no available cars. There have also been reports of outages across many of the company's other services.On 9 October, drones attacked (source in Russian) Yandex's data centre in Kaluga. On the morning of 8 October, the Ukrainian armed forces struck (source in Russian) a Yandex data centre near Ryazan. After that, malfunctions began in the internal systems of major Russian companies. Websites of major Russian media outlets also stopped loading.Ukrainian monitoring channels reported strikes on Sunday on a movable railway bridge (source in Russian) in Rostov-on-Don, near the Black Sea. The regional authorities have not yet reported it.In early October, Russia repeatedly carried out (source in Russian) strikes on key bridges in Kyiv. According to The Telegraph, against the backdrop of military setbacks, Putin decided to switch to attacks on Ukraine's critical infrastructure and the bridges in Kyiv.The crisis centre of the Krasnodar region reported that "fragments of drones" had fallen on the grounds of Sochi airport. A fire broke out in one of the administrative buildings, with no casualties. Debris also fell in a residential area.Russia's Defence Ministry said that overnight air defence forces had shot down 479 Ukrainian drones over 17 regions of Russia and the annexed Crimea.

title: Pope Leo XIV to have surgery in 'coming days' to remove nodule in lung
description: "It was detected at a very early stage and is well localised," the pontiff said during an address in St. Peter's Square.
content: Pope Leo XIV announced on Sunday that he was scheduled to have surgery in the "coming days" to remove a nodule in his lung.Speaking during his weekly address in St. Peter's Square, the 71-year-old pontiff said the nodule had been discovered during "recent checkups" and that doctors believed it would be best to intervene."It was detected at a very early stage and is well localised," he said."I have decided to undergo surgery to have it removed," he continued, adding that the procedure was "already scheduled for the coming days."The operation will reportedly take place at Rome's Gemelli University Hospital.The Vatican press office told reporters that the procedure is set to take place early in the week and that the expected recovery time is roughly one week.Chicago-born Leo became pope in 2025 following the death of his predecessor, Francis.According to the American Lung Association, a lung nodule is a "small mass of dense tissue on the lung" that can be spotted on chest X-rays or CT scans.It says that while most lung nodules are benign, some can be cancerous."If the nodule looks cancerous (malignant) or your health history suggests a higher risk for cancer, physicians will order tests to learn more about your nodule(s)," the association says on its website. "These tests often include a combination of imaging scans, nodule and lymph node biopsies, and sometimes blood tests."This is a developing story. Please check back here for further details.

title: Protesters take to the streets in Portugal over rising living costs and housing prices
description: A post from an Instagram account appearing to be linked to the protests that had promoted the demonstrations said people had "been squeezed by rising house prices and the cost of living" for years.
content: Thousands of people gathered in Lisbon and Porto on Saturday to protest rising living costs and housing prices.The protests, which were also planned in Aveiro, Braga, and Funchal, were organised by a platform named "You can't live like this anymore," and saw demonstrators chanting about wages and holding signs with messages such as "this salary isn't enough to live on."Others lifted placards bearing slogans such as "I want to move out of my parents' house before I'm 50."One attendee at the Lisbon march, Teresa Fonseca, told the Lusa news agency that she had taken inspiration from similar recent protests in Spain."I saw on Instagram that this protest was going to take place, so I came. Enough is enough. This country is getting worse and worse, and now we need to leave our homes and take to the streets to make our voices heard, just as the Spanish did," she said.A post from an Instagram account appearing to be linked to the protests that had promoted the demonstrations said people had "been squeezed by rising house prices and the cost of living" for years."We spend our lives working and exhausting ourselves just to make our wages last until the end of the month, to cope with rising fuel prices and basic living costs, and to avoid losing our homes," it said."We can’t go on living like this!" it added.'Let’s do it like they do in Spain'Some protesters, like Fonseca, seemed to be seeking to emulate recent events in Spain, where housing protests broke out following the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal, who later died.One group in Porto - where around 1,500 demonstrators reportedly turned out - stood next to a sign reading "let’s do it like they do in Spain."In Spain, Maricarmen's case served as a launch pad for further demonstrations against the country's housing crisis and heaped pressure on Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's government.The Spanish government proposed new emergency housing legislation as pushback mounted, but it failed to pass, prompting Sánchez to call a snap general election for late November.

title: 12 killed and more than 300 wounded in attack on Riyadh airport
description: Turki Al-Maliki, a spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition forces, said that the attack had been carried out by Yemen's Houthi rebels and that it had targeted a passenger terminal.
content: An attack on Riyadh's international airport left 12 people dead and more than 300 wounded on Saturday, according to Saudi Arabia's General Authority of Civil Aviation.In a statement, the authority said four Saudi nationals were among those killed in the attack on King Khalid International, alongside two Bangladeshis, one American, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian, and one Sudanese."The attack also left 309 others injured, including individuals in critical condition," the statement continued, adding that the wounded were being treated at several hospitals.Turki Al-Maliki, a spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition forces, said that the attack had been carried out by Yemen's Houthi rebels and that it had targeted a passenger terminal. He vowed that the coalition forces would "respond decisively."Al-Maliki reported on Sunday that coalition forces had also intercepted and destroyed a "ballistic missile" in Al-Kharj Governorate launched by the Houthis."A drone was intercepted and destroyed in the Eastern Province," he added later.US President Donald Trump on Saturday suggested that the US could join Saudi strikes against the Houthis following the attack."We may. We're going to look at it," he told reporters. "We just found out about the recent attack, so we'll make a decision. We move very quickly."'Dangerous escalation'European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called the attack a "dangerous escalation" as she warned that such moves by Iran's proxies were "pushing the region into a spiral of violence.""They are destabilizing crucial global transport and energy nodes with shockwave sent through the world," she said, adding: "We stand in solidarity with Saudi Arabia and its people."It comes days after three people were killed in Houthi-claimed attacks on Riyadh's international airport on Thursday.Several witnesses reportedly said people at King Khalid International were being evacuated on Saturday, as the airport called on passengers to check their flight status.One witness reported hearing an explosion while waiting to board, while another said they saw a strike that had wounded people."I was on gate 403," one witness told the AFP news agency. "I saw 401 hit, I saw injured in front of my eyes. Everyone was running."The US, Canadian, German and Spanish embassies in Saudi Arabia warned nationals to avoid the airport following reports of the attack.According to flight-tracking site Flightradar24, all flights to Riyadh have been either diverted or cancelled.Meanwhile, Kuwait Airways said it cancelled two flights in and out of the Saudi capital, citing a "security situation"."Kuwait Airways announces that flight KU775 from Kuwait to Riyadh and flight KU776 from Riyadh to Kuwait have been cancelled today, Saturday, October 10, 2026, due to the closure of the airport as a result of the security situation," read a statement posted online.Several airlines, including Air India, FlyDubai, Lufthansa Group and Pakistan International Airlines had already suspended flights to and from Saudi airports following the attack on Thursday. The Houthis had warned global airlines about facing possible consequences for continuing to operate in Saudi airspace.Saudi Arabia's airports, oil facilities and tankers are often the target of Houthi attacks, as fighting in Yemen between the rebel group and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces continues to escalate.

title: Teen revolt or revolution? The student protests threatening France's presidential race
description: French students' grievances include long school days, overcrowded classrooms, outdated facilities and teacher shortages. Their anger has resonated across Europe, with students in Belgium and Italy also staging protests.
content: Three weeks into France’s student protests, questions are mounting over whether the demonstrations will fizzle out or evolve into a broader social movement.The protests and school blockades began in Paris’s suburbs in mid-September, before rapidly spreading nationwide. Dramatic images of students climbing the iconic column at Paris' Place de la Bastille on Thursday managed to capture audiences worldwide.The scenes carried historical weight given that the square stands on the site of the former Bastille fortress and state prison, stormed by Parisians on 14 July 1789 in a defining moment of the French Revolution.After its demolition, the Bastille became a lasting symbol of the triumph of regular citizens against political oppression. Taking to X on Thursday, hard-left France Unbowed leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon declared that the Bastille had been "retaken."A range of student grievances lie at the heart of the movement, including long school days, overcrowded classrooms, run down schools and teacher absences. Their anger has resonated with young people across Europe, with students in Belgium and Italy also staging protests in recent days.Could the student movement grow into something broader?Another day of protests, backed by student and trade unions, is scheduled for Tuesday, 13 October. Meanwhile, a separate demonstration against the cost of living crisis and rising fuel prices — planned before the student movement erupted — is scheduled for 17 October.There is speculation that the 17 October demonstration could mark the return of the yellow vest grassroots movement, which emerged in 2018 in reaction to a planned government fuel and diesel tax hike. For months, yellow vest protestors gathered every weekend to block roundabouts, motorways, and fuel depots across the country, with tense police clashes also occurring.If student protests converge with wider social unrest, France could potentially face scenes reminiscent of May 1968. In recent weeks, many students have brandished banners referencing these historic demonstrations, which saw student protests escalate into a nationwide general strike.At the time, several million workers joined the demonstrations, bringing the country to a standstill, but also sparking major wage negotiations. The movement also triggered a political crisis, prompting General de Gaulle, then France's president, to dissolve the National Assembly and call snap legislative elections in June 1968, in which his supporters secured a parliamentary majority.Regardless, May 1968 left an indelible mark on France by dismantling rigid post-war social hierarchies. The demonstrations helped advance civil, student and labour rights, permanently embedding a tradition of mass protest into the nation's political identity.France's tense political backdropAt present, France's minority government is struggling to secure parliamentary support for its 2027 budget, as opposition parties resist proposed austerity measures. The country's public finances are squeezed, with the government projecting the public deficit to reach 5.4% of GDP for 2026, among the highest level in the eurozone.The deepening cost-of-living crisis, driven largely by high fuel and energy prices, has intensified public frustration. The economic pressure on households has heightened social tensions across the country, less than six months away from the country's presidential elections — amid a highly fragmented political landscape.According to a poll by public polling firm Ifop, carried out between 25 and 29 September, the far-right National Rally party's Marine Le Pen (35%) is currently leading for the first round, followed by Edouard Philippe (15%) and Jean-Luc Mélenchon (14%). Under these projections, the second round would see a Le Pen-Philippe face off. Other projections have predicted a Le Pen vs Mélenchon scenario for the second round.A movement which shows no sign of abatingDespite Education Minister Édouard Geffray's announcement on Thursday that 3,000 substitute teachers would be deployed nationwide to schools facing teacher shortages, public anger shows little sign of abating. Geffray said the measure would likely cost “tens of millions of euros” for 2026.Unions have criticised the plan as a short-term fix, warning that available substitute teachers may not match schools' needs in terms of specialisms or location. In cases where no replacement is available, classes may still go uncovered, while substitute teachers may be assigned support duties until a matching vacancy arises.“We need to look at the details, because we have to be careful with this figure that has been thrown around," Jean-Rémi Girard, a teacher and president of the national union of schools and higher education (SNALC) told Euronews.From the onset, students have been supported by teaching unions, as Girard pointed to a system in "crisis.""We are increasingly struggling to replace teacher absences, French classrooms are among the most crowded in Europe, classrooms aren't properly equipped during heat waves. These are things we already know.""The starting point is that the school system is in crisis, and it has been for a long time."Major trade union federations in France have also rallied alongside students. Following Thursday's protests, the CGT, one of the country's largest trade unions, highlighted a range of demonstrations, some of which were unrelated to the student movement, declaring: "The struggles are multiplying, and the balance of power is shifting!"Parallels with past student protests in FrancePaolo Stuppia, professor of sociology and politics at Sciences Po Paris, drew parallels between the current demonstrations and past social movements in France, citing a range of movements including May 1968."It’s not new for students from the suburbs to rally around demands that are specific to them, and then for those demands to be taken up by other secondary schools located closer to the city centre."For Stuppia, the fact that students from private schools have also participated in blockades marks a new departure for student protest movements. Many observers were also surprised that students from the Université Paris-Panthéon-Assas, which is viewed as having a conservative student body, staged a blockade on Thursday.Nevertheless, Stuppia warned that the movement's momentum could be impacted by upcoming school half-term holidays in France."When there’s a two-week school break, it becomes harder to get a movement going again afterwards, because everything has been on hold."A movement which has expanded in response to police violenceWhile many demonstrations have been peaceful, others have been marred by sideline riots and clashes with law enforcement authorities. According to figures shared by France's Ministry of Justice on Friday, there have been 6,877 arrests since the beginning of the movement, with 86% involving minors.The scale of arrests is striking compared with those made in the initial weeks of the yellow vest movement in 2018, which saw 4,596 people placed in police custody during its first month.Rights groups have condemned police brutality following a wave of shocking injuries to students.Outrage has grown over cases including a 15-year-old schoolboy who lost his left hand to a police stun grenade, a 16-year-old partially blinded by a rubber bullet, and a 14-year-old who suffered a shattered jaw and lost multiple teeth after being struck by a tear gas canister. The incidents are under internal investigation, with a total of 24 currently being conducted by the French police disciplinary body.A United Nations spokesperson declared on Friday that the organisation was concerned about the situation in France, calling for demonstrations to remain peaceful and for the use of force to be proportionate.Meanwhile, according to authorities, 761 police officers and gendarmes have been injured since the beginning of the protests. Across the country, several schools have been damaged, burned or ransacked. In some cases, rioters have infiltrated the demonstrations.For Stuppia, the level of police repression in recent weeks was "unprecedented" since May 1968 protests.Meanwhile, Valérie Becquet, a sociologist at CY Cergy Paris University and co-author with Paolo Stuppia of "Geopolitics of Youth: Engagement and (e)Mobilisation", said police brutality has helped draw adults into the movement."Adults [trade unions and parents] have been marching alongside students, but have also intervened through contacting lawyers and magistrates, in response to violence and possible human rights violations."However, she said that there was also a portion of the adult population which viewed the protests with "disdain" and "dismissed or discredited" them.Increasingly politicised protestsIn a TV address on Wednesday evening, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu lamented the “violence, students and staff being attacked, police officers and gendarmes injured, schools set on fire or vandalised, thousands of hours of classes lost, not to mention threats and insults.”He took aim at “political leaders who use this anger to conduct their electoral battles.” France goes to the polls for a presidential election in April. “We cannot play with the safety of France’s youth,” Lecornu said.The government, joined by right-wing and far-right opposition parties, has accused Mélenchon and his France Unbowed party of exploiting and manipulating young people for political gain. Mélenchon has maintained that while his party supports the movement, it is not organising the protests and wants them to remain peaceful.Ahead of the protests which took place on 5 October, the hard-left France Unbowed party hailed the fact that “student, secondary school, trade union and professional organisations" were "converging across the country."For Becquet, although certain political leaders have been accused of “instrumentalising” student protests, secondary school students are on the whole able to distinguish between genuine political support and attempts to exploit the movement."There are people who have no particular interest in the movement, as you can see. Some are on the left, while others think 'well, this could be useful to us.'""Because of the way things work, and the way young people are treated — how they are dismissed and criticised — it ultimately creates opportunities for political intermediaries."She warned that the protests could evolve into a broader social movement, given that frustration over school conditions reflect deeper anger about inequality across French society."There are inequalities at all levels, with gaps widening between different social groups.""Given the rising cost of living, and the fact that working-class people already face numerous daily challenges, such as long working hours and commuting distances, in terms of social inequality, we are at a critical point."Students share protests 'firsthand' on social mediaStudent demonstrations have spread rapidly across the country in part because footage of the initial demonstrations staged in the Paris suburbs went viral on social media.According to Olivier Ertzscheid, senior lecturer in Information and Communication Sciences at the University of Nantes, social media allows students to organise themselves, but also to document protests firsthand from the ground."Social media allows them to document reality, to provide firsthand accounts of what is happening, both when things go well and when, unfortunately, they do not. Police investigations are now open, and social media images can be used as evidence, or at least play a part in the legal process."Ertzscheid said that social media is also actively fostering a sense of connection and shared identity among protesters, which drives momentum."It is a way of building a sense of group identity and expressing one’s social connections, including their political awareness or at least civic engagement. This notion of young people's sense of belonging and social interaction is at play here, and these are very important in an age where the use of social media is so widespread."Given that a large proportion of young people in France and across the world rely on social media as their main news source, the medium has also played a role in informing their perception of the protests, as well as the government's response.Ertzscheid said there are no "hard and fast rules" governing how protests might evolve in coming weeks."Whatever happens next with this movement, we know that the media and social networks will act as echo chambers. By itself, no social media platform — however powerful it may be — is strong enough to trigger a movement. But these platforms are certainly helping with visibility and allowing students to get organised very quickly."He described several different "converging" agendas ahead of upcoming protests in France, stating that "it is possible, that all these different starting points for anger or discontent could eventually converge. But equally, it is entirely possible that the student movement will fizzle out.”

title: Farming and solar power are competing for land. Can agrivoltaics solve the problem?
description: Agrivoltaics could help to prevent farmland abandonment by protecting crops and boosting income. But some say the solution ignores the real problems.
content: As the sun moves westward across the sky in Murcia, Spain, solar panels capture its rays while sheltering diverse crops, from bell peppers to wine grapes and dragon fruit.Known for its agriculture and abundant sunshine, this southeastern region is exploring whether, rather than competing for land, farming and solar energy can coexist peacefully.“Agrivoltaics is the integration of food production with renewable energy production,” explains Silvia Tomasi, Senior Researcher at Eurac Research. This entails installing photovoltaic panels above, in between or at the margins of agricultural production, she adds.A 2023 study estimated that Europe has the potential to generate 25 times its current electricity demand via agrivoltaics, also known as agri-PV.Yet solar power is fraught with its own environmental and social costs. Requiring more land than other energy sources to generate the same amount of electricity, it has sparked conflicts over land use, especially in rural areas.“Agrivoltaics has great potential: both economic benefits and environmental ones,” Tomasi says. “But then it’s always a matter of how the technology is implemented and who really benefits.”Governments and Big Tech turn to agrivoltaicsThe idea of turning southern Europe into a solar powerhouse received a high-profile endorsement in January, when Elon Musk said sparsely populated areas of Spain and Sicily could theoretically generate enough solar power for all of Europe.Big Tech has already caught on. In southern Italy, Amazon and Apple have signed contracts to purchase power from large-scale agrivoltaic projects with a combined capacity of over 150 megawatts – enough to meet the yearly needs of roughly 100,000 Italian households. Europe is also funding the shift. The EU-funded AGRISOL project intends to invest €1.9 million in agrivoltaics projects, including in Italy and Spain, while Italy alone has secured €1.7 billion in state aid for the initiative.“For now, [agrivoltaics] is just a minimal contribution,” says Angelo Gentili, national secretary of Legambiente, Italy’s largest environmental organisation. “But if it expands, it will represent a big impulse for decarbonisation goals.”Managing the impact on crops and landEU and national rules increasingly require agriculture to remain a meaningful part of land where solar panels are installed. In France, projects must maintain at least 90 per cent of crop production compared to locally determined reference yields. In Italy, at least 70 per cent of the area must remain dedicated to agriculture.Experts say not just any combination of solar and agriculture should qualify. “More than a definition, what we really need is a classification,” says Pilar Flores, who coordinates an EU-funded agrivoltaics project at the Murcian Institute for Agricultural and Environmental Research and Development (IMIDA). She says protecting agriculture should drive all classifications: “The key is to ensure there’s minimal loss [of arable land].”Why use farmland rather than empty or abandoned land in the first place? Flores says the requirements are similar: relatively flat and near the grid. Unused land may also hold ecological value. “It’s not just a simple calculation of how much free land is left,” she says.How agrivoltaics can benefit farmersIn some cases, agrivoltaics have been found to improve water-use efficiency, protect crops from extreme weather and increase the productivity of land. Solar installations can also help farmers face climate change. “Excessive rainfall and heat have heavily damaged agricultural fields, pushing farmers to abandon farmland,” says Gentili. “Agrivoltaics represent a great instrument to avoid land abandonment and profit gaps for farmers.”Panels cast shade that can reduce evaporation, help soil retain moisture and offer relief to farmworkers and grazing animals. They can also protect crops from hail. Farmers can use the energy to power their own operations and sell any excess to the grid, or rent the space above their fields to energy producers.But the benefits are not guaranteed, Flores warns. “All these opportunities are sometimes discussed as if they always happened, but it depends on the agrivoltaic system used and the specific characteristics of the site.” In Murcia, her team found that water-stressed peppers grew better under solar panels than well-watered ones. “You have to analyse each case and each location,” she says.But who really benefits from agrivoltaics?Not all farmers are convinced. To Fabrizio Garbarino, president of the Italian farmers’ union Associazione Rurale Italiana, agrivoltaics fail to address the root problems farmers face. “Agrivoltaics are taking advantage of the farming sector crisis in Italy while we should actually focus on real solutions for preventing farmland abandonment,” he says. “To me, this just sounds like a shortcut.”Startups representing larger companies, including data centre developers, are hounding farmers for their land, he says. “Even if the energy produced is good, we’re taking away [farmers’] land to support businesses that require a lot of energy.” Big Tech firms say agrivoltaic power-purchase agreements help them reach net-zero targets. But a PPA does not necessarily mean that the electricity from a particular solar farm physically supplies a particular company facility, and the exact carbon footprints of AI data centres remain opaque.A 2025 study co-authored by Tomasi, based on expert interviews across four European regions, found that the benefits of agrivoltaics can favour large-scale farmers, landowners and investors over smaller farmers and local communities. It also found that excluding residents and ecosystems from decision-making can deepen existing power imbalances.High upfront costs and grid connection queues mean large projects backed by multinationals tend to dominate the sector. A 2025 review by the Italian newspaper Today.it found that about 86 per cent of the roughly €775 million in government funds for agrivoltaic projects went to large-scale projects, including ones owned by foreign multinationals.In September, a new agrivoltaics project financed by an Israeli company in Tuscany sparked widespread outrage and raised concerns over who gets to profit.Tomasi says local communities must have a voice to ensure a just transition. “Big investors going into places they really don’t know anything about, with a top-down approach… and getting the economic benefits from the renewable energy generation side of agrivoltaics… shouldn’t be labelled as agrivoltaics, from my point of view.”‘Agriculture should not be a secondary concern’Flores says administrations can help by offering farmers funding and giving agrivoltaic systems priority access to the grid.There is also the question of what kind of agriculture the income supports. To live up to the environmental promise, one study has noted, “the type of agriculture funded by the rental income from agrivoltaics should not be a secondary concern”. Instead, the author argues, this rent could subsidise agroecological practices or help farmers transition away from industrial farming.Agrivoltaics has the potential to be mutually beneficial to farmers and the renewable energy sector. It can help protect farmland, support farmers facing climate change and contribute to Europe’s decarbonisation goals. But it also risks becoming a greenwashing opportunity, a crutch for unsustainable farming practices, or a way of meeting growing corporate energy demand on arable land. On its own, it is not a silver bullet. Much depends on how the systems are designed, who owns them and, ultimately, who benefits.“The goal of agrivoltaics is to protect farmland and the entire ecosystem; that’s the philosophy,” says Flores. “We have to be able to distinguish that from other interests.”Reporting for this story was made possible by the Magma Environmental Reporting Fellowship.

title: Europe's best Christmas markets to visit in 2026, according to travellers
description: Europe is world-famous for its Christmas markets, and more than 1,500 take place every year. Choosing which to visit can be as tricky as putting together your present wish list. Here are the top picks, as voted for by travellers.
content: As we get deeper into autumn, it feels as if we’ll blink and Christmas will be upon us. With the festive season comes new opportunities to book a winter trip away, and a favourite must-do for many travellers is to visit a Christmas market.There are more than 1,500 in Europe alone, and this year more than 800,000 travellers have voted for their favourites via the European Best Destinations platform. A total of 20 were included in the final ranking, and we’re taking a closer look at the top five to give you some inspiration on where to go to shop, drink gleuwein and get into the festive spirit in 2026. European Christmas markets: The top picks by travellers Craiova, RomaniaYou might never have heard of Craiova, but the Romanian city has pipped far more famous Christmas markets to the top spot. It’s an absolutely huge space, with more than 280,000 square meters transformed into a festive wonderland each year. The theme in 2026 is The Nutcracker, and visitors will be able to see giant ornaments and toy-shaped sculptures along with countless sparkling lights. The market, which runs from mid-November to early January, will also boast Eastern Europe’s highest-flying Santa sleigh, as well as an ice rink, a Ferris wheel, and traditional hand-painted chalets.Visitors to the Craiova market also sing the praises of the food on offer here, which celebrates the flavours of Eastern Europe and beyond, serving dishes from the likes of Armenia, Georgia, Greece, Bulgaria and Serbia. Zurich, SwitzerlandZurich may be better known for its chocolate and banking than Christmas markets, but the Swiss city has made a name for itself as one of Europe’s top festive destinations.The main attraction is Wienachtsdorf at Sechseläutenplatz, between the Opera House and Lake Zurich. The market is filled with wooden chalets, twinkling lights and a huge Christmas tree, combining traditional Alpine touches with the city’s more polished feel.There’s plenty more to discover beyond the main market, which was also voted as the most beautiful Christmas market in Europe. Weihnachtsallee near the main station is now in its third year, with around 80 rotating stalls selling international food, design-led crafts and, of course, plenty of fondue.There’s even a dome dedicated to mulled wine, making it a popular spot for locals and visitors looking to warm up.Zurich also puts its own artistic spin on the festive season with the Illuminarium at the Swiss National Museum. The courtyard is transformed with lights, music and immersive displays, adding something a little different to the city’s Christmas celebrations.Riga, LatviaRiga may not have the same name recognition as some of Europe’s bigger Christmas destinations, but Latvia’s capital puts on a seriously atmospheric festive display each winter.The main market takes over Doma Square in the heart of the UNESCO-listed Old Town, with wooden chalets selling Latvian crafts, cosy knitwear and local treats.From late November to early January, the square fills with the smells of mulled wine, roasted almonds and cinnamon, while choirs and folk performers add a distinctly Baltic feel.But Riga’s Christmas appeal goes well beyond the market itself. The city is known for its spectacular lights, with parks, squares and canals transformed into a glowing winter wonderland.Head to places including Opera Square, Bastejkalns and Kronvalda Park to see installations inspired by Latvian fairy tales, with light, music and storytelling bringing the festive season to life.Lisbon, PortugalLisbon offers a slightly different take on the Christmas market, swapping snowy streets for mild temperatures and winter sunshine.Wonderland Lisboa takes over Parque Eduardo VII from late November to early January, with the Portuguese capital’s biggest Christmas market returning for its 11th edition in 2026.This year’s theme, “The Roots of Christmas”, brings together nature, art, food and entertainment, with local artisans, live performances and plenty of family-friendly attractions.There’s also a Ferris wheel offering views across the city, alongside a traditional carousel and plenty of opportunities for Christmas shopping.Food is a big part of the experience too, with the Wonderland Lisboa Food Court serving Portuguese festive favourites, regional specialities and seasonal sweets.More than 1.2 million people visited in 2025, making it a popular choice for anyone who wants their Christmas market with a side of sunshine.Debrecen, HungaryHungary’s second-largest city may be less famous than the capital Budapest, but it certainly knows how to do Christmas properly. In the winter, Debrecen’s main squares and pedestrian streets are transformed with glowing installations and wooden stalls selling handmade crafts, toys, decorations and Christmas ornaments.There’s plenty of food to enjoy too, with classic festive treats including mulled wine, roasted chestnuts and kürtőskalács, the sweet Hungarian chimney cake.More than 100 cultural events are held throughout the season, featuring more than 200 performers, while families can make the most of an ice rink and the Fairytale Town attraction.There are also plenty of special events, including traditional advent candle-lighting ceremonies and a St Nicholas weekend complete with a carriage arrival, concerts and a mini train.The top 20 best European Christmas marketsAccording to traveller votes via European Best Destinations:1. Craiova, Romania2. Zurich, Switzerland3. Riga, Latvia4. Lisbon, Portugal5. Debrecen, Hungary6. Govone & Asti, Italy7. Valkenburg, The Netherlands8. Vienna, Austria9. Montbeliard, France10. title: ESA director general reveals €10bn plan to get to space without NASA
description: The space industry, currently valued at €600 billion, is expected to grow by 10% a year, according to European Space Agency (ESA) director general Josef Aschbacher. He spoke to the Big Question about how Europe can benefit from this booming industry.
content: The European Space Agency received record budget commitments of more than €22 billion from member states at its ministerial council meeting in 2025, a 32% increase on 2022. Member states also gave ESA a historic mandate to use space technology for non-aggressive security and defence, including technologies to monitor external borders. With that backing, ESA director general Josef Aschbacher wants Europe to take its next big step: developing the ability to launch its own astronauts into space.In the latest episode of The Big Question, Josef sat down with Hannah Brown to discuss Europe’s independent future in space. ‘Why don’t we do it ourselves?’Since its founding in 1975 (and its first astronaut mission in 1983), the European Space Agency has relied on international partners, including NASA and Russia, for astronaut launches.And while this arrangement has worked for all this time, geopolitical tensions are pushing Europe to seek an alternative.Only the US, China and Russia have the capability to launch astronauts into space. But political tensions with China and Russia leave ESA reliant on the US. And in recent years, NASA has partnered with SpaceX to launch astronauts into space. One way or another, today, ESA astronauts travel to space aboard a US spacecraft.“SpaceX has already announced that they want to decommission Falcon 9 and Crew Dragon (the crew vehicles that bring the astronauts to space) probably around 2029,” Josef explained.“That means in a few years, we will not have at least this capability available anymore. There may be others coming up, which we do not know today.”This leaves Europe facing uncertainty over how to get its astronauts into space in the future. To ensure reliable access and support investment in European industry, Josef is developing a plan for Europe to strengthen its position as a global space power by gaining the ability to launch its own astronauts.Is space autonomy good for the European economy?Of course, this won’t happen overnight and it needs political approval from ESA’s member states to secure funding.Here’s how it might work. Europe isn’t starting completely from scratch. It already has strong technological capabilities and world-leading programmes like Copernicus (Earth observation) and Galileo (satellite navigation constellation), as well as a talented workforce. But Europe lacks its own crew vehicle and recovery system, in other words the means to get astronauts up there and bring them safely back to Earth. Josef estimated that with a budget of around €10 billion, ESA could develop these independent capabilities in the next 10 years.And yes, €10 billion is an enormous amount of money, but what’s the alternative?ESA is facing the prospect of spending billions of euros in the coming years either way. The question is how to turn that spending into an investment in Europe’s space industry rather than simply a cost. The International Space Station is essentially a floating laboratory where ESA does much of its vital science. After its decommission in 2032, this is likely to be replaced by a commercial space station. Without its independent access to space, Europe will have to continue to rely on buying seats aboard US spacecraft with uncertain availability and then rent facilities aboard commercial space stations for research. Josef estimated that this would come at a cost of around €5 billion over the next 10 years. “But the money is lost, or lost in the sense it's being spent not in Europe. So I'd rather invest this funding in Europe, strengthen our industry, increase the autonomy of Europe in this domain,” Josef explained.But he stressed this would not mean an end to international collaboration for Europe.“[We could] even offer a seat maybe to our friends and colleagues from Japan or Australia or some other countries, and I think this is also something that Europe could consider to build up its own strength, its autonomy, not to isolate, not at all - the opposite, but to be a strong partner internationally to other countries and other agencies.”The Big Question is a series from Euronews Business where we sit down with industry leaders and experts to discuss some of the most important topics on today’s agenda.Watch the video above to see the full discussion with the European Space Agency.

title: Lee Claims World Gold as Tasoev Secures His Third World Title in Baku
description: Hyeonji Lee claimed her first world title at +78kg, defeating former champion Romane Dicko to complete a dominant day. At +100kg, Inal Tasoev delivered a spectacular ippon against home favourite Ushangi Kokauri to secure his third world title and retain the red backpatch.
content: Today closes out the individual competition at the Baku World Judo Championships and it's time for the heavyweights to take centre stage in Azerbaijan.Before the finals, the traditional flag-passing ceremony was held to commemorate the closing of the event, as Azerbaijan passed the IJF flag to Kazakhstan - with Astana set to host the World Championships in 2027.At +78kg, 19 year old Hyeonji LEE was on fire enroute to the final, with ippon in every contest. With a World bronze from last year, she would be feeling confident that this was her moment to claim the red backpatch.Facing her was Romane DICKO, a former World Champion and no stranger to the podium. DICKO would be looking to regain the mantle and become a two time World Champion. Displaying a groundwork masterclass today, could she repeat her former success?In the final, LEE continued her dominant run and bested DICKO with a waza-ari that transitioned into a hold down. The Korean had written her name into history. A composed finish to a remarkable day that sealed the biggest title of her career.IOC Member Ms Yael ARAD awarded the medals.In the +100kg category, reigning double World Champion Inal TASOEV had come to Baku to earn his third title and looked in complete control on his route through the draw. Powerful and assured throughout the day, he arrived in the final with another World gold firmly within reach.His opponent was Azerbaijan’s own Ushangi KOKAURI. With the crowd behind him, he had the chance to turn their energy into the biggest victory of his career. Every roar from the stands added pressure, but also belief that a home World title was possible.In the +100kg final, TASOEV delivered a moment of pure judo feeling to score ippon, and achieve an incredible third World title. TASOEV will wear the red backpatch for another year. A commanding finish underlined his status as the man to beat.Azerbaijan Minister of Youth and Sport Mr Farid GAYIBOV awarded the medals.Join us tomorrow in Baku where the Mixed Team competition kicks off.3 men 3 women, one team, one goal.Don’t miss it!

title: Cristiano Ronaldo suspended by Portuguese FA for leaving training camp
description: As expected, the Disciplinary Board of the Portuguese Football Federation has opened disciplinary proceedings against national team captain Cristiano Ronaldo, who has been temporarily suspended.
content: The Disciplinary Board of the Portuguese Football Federation has opened disciplinary proceedings against Cristiano Ronaldo for walking out of the national team’s training camp in Copenhagen, Denmark.Before the match against Denmark, the captain clashed with coach Jorge Jesus (JJ) after being left on the bench and not brought on in the previous game against Norway, despite what he had been promised. According to Ronaldo, Jorge Jesus had assured him he would play for 30 minutes.Feeling that JJ had gone back on his word, Cristiano Ronaldo walked out on the national team on 30 September, posting a message on his Instagram account announcing his decision and promising that, “in due course”, he would tell “the truth to all Portuguese people” about the reasons behind his sudden departure.Until the captain made that public statement, the football world struggled to ignore the controversy that had erupted within the squad. The players, however, did everything they could to stay out of the affair, avoiding media questions and ultimately delivering the national team’s four best performances in recent years.Under coach Jorge Jesus, Portugal won all four matches, qualified for the next phase of the Nations League and climbed back to fifth place in the world rankings, pushing Brazil down to sixth.In the letter Ronaldo posted on social media to explain why he had left the national team camp, he apologised to the squad, his teammates and the Portuguese people. He also said he was willing to return to the team and took “responsibility” for walking out, adding that he was prepared to face the disciplinary consequences.According to the Disciplinary Board (CD), Cristiano Ronaldo has therefore been provisionally suspended while the case, classified as “urgent”, is processed.“Disciplinary proceedings have been opened against Cristiano Ronaldo dos Santos Aveiro by decision of the Non-Professional Section on 9 October 2026, with the aim of determining whether the facts reported on 7 October 2026 have any disciplinary implications. Without prejudice to the automatic preventive suspension to which he was subject until the proceedings were opened, a non-automatic preventive suspension has been imposed on the player, and the case has been given urgent status,” reads the statement released by the CD.According to sports website MaisFutebol ( source in Portuguese), the disciplinary proceedings began “after two complaints were filed against Ronaldo: one by the Federation’s own board and another by third parties outside the FPF”.Cristiano Ronaldo has been suspended for 20 days under paragraph 2 of Article 40-A of the Federation’s Disciplinary Regulations.The suspension ends on 30 October, which could mean the captain will be available to rejoin the squad in time for the national team’s November fixtures, adds MaisFutebol.Ronaldo could face a severe punishment for leaving the training camp. The federation’s disciplinary regulations stipulate that any player who, without justification, “leaves or fails to attend” a training session, a match, or a national team activity “shall be sanctioned with a suspension of between one and six months”, in addition to a fine.Ronaldo informed the federation that he was leaving, but it remained unclear whether the decision would be deemed justified under the regulations.“I have already apologised, but I know that actions must have consequences. Anyone in the world of football, just like me, knows that, regardless of one’s status, the rules are the same for everyone,” Ronaldo wrote in the letter in question.The federation said on Saturday that the case is before the disciplinary inquiry committee (CD) and that the information gathered will remain confidential until it reaches a conclusion.

title: Electric cars and rising Chinese brands: Paris Motor Show opens Monday
description: As the 91st Paris Motor Show approaches, European carmakers face fierce competition from China, waning consumer confidence and mounting geopolitical pressure.
content: First held in 1898 in the Tuileries Gardens in Paris, the Paris Motor Show has, year after year, attracted crowds of visitors keen to discover the latest models, around a hundred of them for the 2026 edition, which runs from 12 to 18 October 2026."I really think people need to see the cars, touch them, sit in them, try them out", says Serge Gachot, CEO of the Paris Motor Show. This is especially true for electric models.According to the European Automobile Manufacturers' Association (ACEA), fully electric cars accounted for 21.7% of all new vehicle registrations in the EU in the first eight months of 2026, compared with 15.8% over the same period the previous year. France was one of the key markets posting the strongest growth, with registrations of fully electric vehicles up 74.2% year on year.China's rapidly expanding car industry is particularly keen to showcase its vehicles to European buyers. Around twenty Chinese brands are expected in Paris."The outlook is extremely worrying for traditional European carmakers", says Tim Urquhart, principal automotive analyst at Mobility Global. "The progress made by China's car industry in recent years has been extraordinary, particularly over the past decade, but above all this advance has accelerated even further over the past five years."Their arrival comes as European buyers are increasingly turning away from traditional petrol and diesel cars.For European carmakers, a transition in a tough climateAccording to ACEA, hybrid electric vehicles remained the most popular type of powertrain in the EU up to August, with a market share of 36.6%, while plug-in hybrids reached 10%. The combined share of petrol and diesel fell to 29%, from 37.5% a year earlier.High petrol prices, government support and a much wider choice of cheaper electric cars have all contributed to this shift.But carmakers are trying to manage this transition in an exceptionally challenging environment. High oil prices linked to the conflict involving Iran are weighing on the sector's margins. European manufacturers also have to contend with weak consumer confidence, tighter emissions rules and mounting pressures in China, once a major source of growth for German giants such as Volkswagen, BMW and Mercedes-Benz."There was a time when the Chinese market was something of a cash cow for European carmakers. That is no longer the case today", says Mr Urquhart.At the same time, the European Union and China remain bogged down in a trade dispute over state aid, customs duties and the growing influx of Chinese vehicles into Europe."There are huge geopolitical tensions, oil prices are very high, the broader economic environment is under strain, and confidence is being affected in Europe", Mr Urquhart explains.To respond, European manufacturers are opting to look both to the past and the future. Retro-inspired models are expected to be one of the standout themes of the Paris Motor Show, at Renault, Citroën, Peugeot, Opel, Lancia and Fiat.The 91st Paris Motor Show opens with its press day at Paris Expo Porte de Versailles on 12 October, before welcoming the public from 13 to 18 October.

title: Teacher salaries in Europe: Which countries offer the best pay?
description: Teacher salaries vary widely across Europe, and large gaps remain even after adjusting for living costs. Experts call for better pay to attract and retain more teachers.
content: Higher pay for teachers is among the demands of unions behind recent protests in France, alongside more staff and better working conditions.Their concerns reflect a wider challenge across Europe: making teaching financially attractive. Teachers are generally paid less than similarly educated workers, according to the OECD, and experts warn that salaries are not competitive enough to attract and retain staff.So, which countries pay the highest teacher salaries? And how do teacher salaries rank when purchasing power is taken into account?Teacher salaries vary widely across Europe, according to the OECD’s Education at a Glance 2026 report. Among the 28 education systems compared, actual salaries for primary school teachers in 2025 ranged from €18,669 in Turkey to €74,086 in Denmark. Actual salaries refer to the annual average earnings received by full-time teachers aged 25-64 before taxes. They include all work-related payments, such as the base salary, performance-related bonuses, extra pay for holidays, and other payments.Iceland (€73,752), Ireland (€69,747), Germany (€69,453) and Austria (€65,851) complete the top five, all above €65,000.Teachers in Norway (€59,453), Belgium’s Flemish Community (€59,105), Northern Ireland (€57,838), Scotland (€57,619), Belgium’s French Community (€55,689), Wales (€52,894), Finland (€52,272) and England (€50,727) also earn more than €50,000.Major economies: Germany highest, Italy lowestAmong the major European economies, Germany pays teachers the most. The four UK nations follow Germany, all with salaries above €50,000. Teachers earn €41,968 in France, while Italy has the lowest salaries at €32,100. A figure for Spain is not available.Several countries below €25,000 Actual teacher salaries are below €25,000 in seven countries: Czechia (€24,457), Hungary (€23,181), Slovakia (€22,936), Romania (€20,805), Latvia (€20,516), Greece (€18,746) and Turkey (€18,669).“Large differences in European teacher salaries reflect differences in national income levels, salary structures, qualifications and career progression, rather than one single factor,” Daniel Wisniewski, secretary general of the European Federation of Education Employers, told Euronews Business.“Differences in taxation, social benefits and allowances also complicate comparisons between countries.”Teachers at upper secondary schools generally earn more than those at primary schools, except in Turkey and Northern Ireland. Salaries are the same at both levels in Scotland, Lithuania and Estonia.Upper secondary teacher salaries range from €17,615 in Turkey to €93,938 in Iceland. They are also above €80,000 in Denmark (€85,999) and Germany (€80,163).The largest gaps in favour of upper secondary teachers are seen in Iceland, Finland, Belgium, Denmark, Austria and Germany, where they are paid at least €10,000 more than primary school teachers.What can teachers buy with their salaries?Salary figures alone don't tell the whole story. If prices are high in a country, even relatively high teacher salaries could buy less than in another country.To account for differences in living costs, Euronews Business adjusted the OECD’s salary figures in national currencies using Eurostat’s purchasing power parities for household final consumption expenditure.The results are expressed in purchasing power standards (PPS), a common unit that can buy the same amount of goods and services in each country. The PPS measure uses average EU prices as a benchmark, while the OECD expresses its purchasing power comparisons in purchasing-power-adjusted US dollars.On this basis, teachers in Germany have the highest purchasing power — meaning their gross salaries can buy the most goods and services — among the education systems compared.Primary school teachers’ average annual pay after adjusting for price differences is lowest at 21,456 PPS in Greece and highest at 64,143 PPS in Germany.Wisniewski noted that sizeable differences remain after adjusting for purchasing power, showing that living costs cannot by themselves explain the salary variation.“National pay policies, qualification requirements, career scales, experience and the earnings available in alternative graduate professions also contribute significantly to the remaining gap,” he said. Germany is followed by Austria (58,265 PPS), Denmark (53,036 PPS), Ireland (51,226 PPS) and Belgium’s Flemish Community (50,846 PPS), completing the top five education systems where primary school teachers’ salaries buy the most.At the other end of the ranking, Greece is joined by Latvia (24,670 PPS), Slovakia (26,916 PPS), Czechia (27,349 PPS) and Estonia (28,197 PPS), where primary school teachers’ salaries buy the least among the education systems compared.For upper secondary school teachers, Germany also tops the overall purchasing power ranking at 74,034 PPS, while Greece ranks lowest at 23,289 PPS.Among Europe’s largest economies compared, Italy comes last at 36,964 PPS.Three UK nations follow Germany, while England (43,091 PPS) ranks below France (46,058 PPS).Professor Mihails Hazans of the University of Latvia noted that countries at the top of the teacher salary rankings in PPS also have GDP per capita well above the EU average.“The factors behind these differences include traditions and social norms, strength of teachers’ trade unions, as well as actual workload covered by the statutory salaries,” he told Euronews Business. Significant changes in PPS rankingsWhen nominal salary and PPS rankings are compared, some countries change position significantly. For primary school teachers, the biggest risers are Turkey, up six places, and Poland (up five). Belgium’s French Community and Romania both move up four places.This means that these countries rank higher once differences in price levels are taken into account.Iceland records the biggest fall, dropping from second place to 12th. Sweden and Estonia also fall by three places.The OECD’s purchasing power rankings, which are based on US international dollars, differ from Euronews Business’s calculations using Eurostat conversion rates.Turkey ranks significantly higher in the OECD rankings. It is 11th for primary school teachers and 17th for upper secondary school teachers. Pay is not competitive enough to attract and retain teachersDaniel Wisniewski pointed out that across OECD countries, teachers’ actual salaries at primary and general secondary levels average only 87–95% of the earnings of tertiary-educated workers, meaning that similarly qualified people can often earn more outside teaching. “Teacher pay is not consistently competitive enough to attract and retain teachers across Europe,” he said. Jelmer Evers, European director at the European Trade Union Committee for Education, suggested that teachers should be paid at least as much as other workers with comparable qualifications and responsibilities, reflecting the complexity and societal importance of their profession.

title: Historic Gold for Lytvynenko as Sulamanidze Triumphs in Baku
description: Yelyzaveta Lytvynenko made history at -78kg, defeating Kaila Issoufi to become the UAE’s first-ever judo world champion. At -100kg, Georgia’s Ilia Sulamanidze overcame Dota Arai in the final to claim his first world title, turning previous bronze into gold.
content: Welcome back to the Baku World Judo Championships.At -78kg, Kaila ISSOUFI of France was on great form, working her way through the draw with some impressive judo along the way. ISSOUFI looked ready to make the most of her opportunity on the world stage.Facing her was Yelyzaveta LYTVYNENKO of the U.A.E. The world number two’s fantastic judo had carried her all the way to the World Championship final in Baku. With World gold now just one contest away, she stepped onto the tatami knowing this was her chance to produce the biggest result of her career.In the final, LYTVYNENKO wasted little time imposing herself, scoring waza-ari from an impressive o-uchi-gari that caught ISSOUFI off guard and offered an early advantage. She then decisively ended the contest with a second score. Marking not just her first gold medal at the World Championships, but the first judo World Champion ever for the United Arab Emirates.IOC Member Mrs Filomena FORTES awarded the medals.In the -100kg category, Ilia SULAMANIDZE was looking to upgrade his World bronze to gold, and he was in outstanding form on his route to the final. Powerful and decisive throughout the day, the Georgian arrived in the final with real momentum. Now, one more victory would deliver the crowning moment of his career and with it, the red backpatch.ARAI Dota earned World bronze in 2024 and World silver in 2025. Could 2026 finally be the year that the Japanese powerhouse strikes gold and raises himself to the top of the podium? Only the final hurdle remained.In the -100kg final, both athletes were determined but it was a yuko for SULAMANIDZE that crowned the Georgian as World Champion. A fitting finish to a career-defining performance.Georgian National Federation of Aquatic Sports President Mr Dimitri ABDUSHELISHVILI awarded the medals. Tomorrow it’s the heavyweights!

title: Latvia’s border guard seeks greater powers amid increasingly violent border crossings
description: As “armed, masked escorts” lead migrants from Belarus into Latvia, the Latvian Border Guard is seeking greater powers to “protect Latvia’s security.” The interior minister supports the proposal.
content: On 5 October, a group used makeshift stairs to enter Latvia. While the Baltic country of two million has faced irregular migration from Belarus since 2021, the latest incident was particularly aggressive.The group of 20 migrants was led by “armed, masked escorts openly threatening Latvian soldiers,” Latvia’s Interior Minister, Jānis Dombrava, told Euronews. In the following hours, border surveillance equipment was damaged, reducing Latvia’s “ability to detect and respond to further incursions.”“The combination of armed intimidation and targeted sabotage raises the risk of a violent confrontation and tests both our defences and our willingness to respond,” Dombrava said, adding that it’s “a security threat, not simply a migration-management problem.”Latvia completed the fencing of its 173-kilometre border with Belarus this year and installed advanced surveillance systems, making crossings harder. The obstacles are making facilitators increasingly aggressive, according to Guntis Pujāts, head of Latvia’s State Border Guard.“That’s why they are trying to be more aggressive and so to throw stones as well, to show what looks like a weapon and so on,” Pujāts told Euronews, adding that the incident “shows that the situation is not going to decrease but in the opposite way”.More powers to Border GuardThe State Border Guard is now seeking greater powers to protect its personnel and secure the country’s border, as Latvia enters its fifth year of dealing with irregular migration from Belarus. The interior minister supports the move.Currently, border guards already have the right to use firearms in circumstances prescribed by law, including when responding to serious threats and attempted acts of sabotage. Pujāts wants to broaden their powers, as well as those of police and military personnel supporting border operations, to enable them to “protect the security of Latvia”.On Thursday, the Border Guard submitted a proposal to the Interior Ministry seeking changes to the rules.Under the proposed changes, border guards would no longer have to issue a warning before using force in certain circumstances, Pujāts said. They would also be able to use the tools at their disposal to stop and “neutralise” people damaging border infrastructure.“We will not be obliged to warn before, and we will be allowed all tools that we have to stop and so to neutralise persons who are damaging our border infrastructure,” he said.The interior minister confirmed to Euronews that he will propose amendments “to give those protecting our country clearer powers and greater discretion when facing threats of this kind.”“Those who protect Latvia's state border – border guards, soldiers and other officials – must be confident that they will not be unjustifiably subjected to criminal prosecution for the lawful use of firearms or special means,” he said. Pujāts said he did not know how long it would take for the proposal to become law. Asked when he would like the changes to take effect, he replied: “Yesterday, or the day before yesterday.”

title: EU paid €7.9bn for Russian Arctic LNG amid record imports
description: Continued Russian LNG imports undermine the credibility of the EU’s promise to sever its energy ties with Moscow, particularly as Russia continues its war against Ukraine.
content: Europe paid around €7.88 billion for liquefied natural gas (LNG) from Russia’s Arctic energy project in the first nine months of 2026 despite Brussels’ efforts to phase out gas from Moscow, according to the campaign group Urgewald.The figures, compiled by Urgewald using data from the market intelligence firm Kpler, expose just how reliant the EU remains on Russian energy, with a record of 12.18 million tonnes reaching European ports between January and September this year.The EU has been trying to wean itself off Russian energy for a while, and this year introduced a number of measures to end its reliance on Moscow. Brussels introduced a ban on new Russian energy contracts at the beginning of 2026, with a complete ban on Russian LNG taking effect on 1 January 2027.Meanwhile, the Trump administration recently announced the Lindsey Graham Act, giving the US the power to sanction Russian LNG deliveries to Europe before the EU's import ban kicks in.This comes at a time when Europe's gas storage levels are at a record low, and the bloc faces a brutal energy crisis, leaving Brussels increasingly vulnerable to decisions from Washington, the EU's major LNG supplier.European LNG imports from the Russian Yamal project rose 9.5% year-on-year between January and September, with EU ports receiving 85% of Yamal’s recorded deliveries.France received nearly three-quarters of September’s EU deliveries, with the Dunkirk and Montoir ports receiving 571.716 million tonnes of Arctic LNG, according to Kpler.The Netherlands imported 146.461 million tonnes of LNG and Portugal 74.263 million tonnes. No cargoes were recorded in Spain or at Belgium’s Zeebrugge terminal.The persistence of the Arctic LNG trade into Europe shows the difficulty of translating a long-term phase-out commitment into an immediate commercial break.Ineffective short-term bansThe figures also raise questions about the effectiveness of the EU’s initial restrictions on Russian LNG.A ban on imports under existing short-term contracts took effect on 25 April, but September deliveries reached 792,440 tonnes, slightly above the level a year earlier.The EU’s full ban on Russian LNG under eligible existing long-term contracts is scheduled to take effect on 1 January 2027.Until then, continued purchases generate revenue for Russia's war against Ukraine and expose the limits of restrictions that target some contracts without immediately stopping the wider trade."We have always assumed that the impact would not be particularly significant, since most of the export capacity is tied up in long-term contracts anyway," Sebastian Rötters, energy campaigner at Urgewald, told Euronews."In addition, export volumes are generally lower in the summer due to maintenance work at the terminal and LNG shipments to Asia via the Northern Sea Route," Rötters added.The real litmus test for Yamal will be the EU’s phase-out starting in 2027, Rötters said, noting it may lead to noticeable reductions in exports due to the increased logistical challenges.Call to strengthen 22nd sanctions packageThe German-based NGO Urgewald is calling for the upcoming 22nd EU sanctions package to close loopholes, particularly those supporting the specialised Arc7 ice-class tanker fleet needed to transport LNG from the Arctic.Yamal’s reliance on specialised vessels makes its export system vulnerable to restrictions on transport and associated services.European ports are also geographically convenient destinations, allowing tankers to unload and return to the project relatively quickly.Urgewald argues that disrupting those logistics could pile pressure on Russia’s ability to sustain Arctic LNG exports."The EU should not wait passively for the 2027 embargo to take effect. The next sanctions package should close the remaining loopholes, above all those that keep the indispensable Arc7 LNG tanker fleet operating. Washington, meanwhile, now has the power to sanction this trade at any time before then,” reads Urgewald's statement.However, such measures would require political coordination among the EU and its member states and could complicate European gas procurement before the import ban takes effect and ahead of an unpredictable winter season.The data provided does not establish how much of the trade could be redirected to other buyers or what the consequences would be for European gas prices, but any additional trade disruption on top of the loss of LNG from the Middle East would have an impact.Trump gains another lever over the EU’s energy securityUS sanctions under the Lindsey Graham Act could disrupt trade before the EU's ban on Russian LNG takes effect, forcing European governments and buyers to respond.The US administration faces an 18 October deadline for its first review under the law. However, the deadline should not be mistaken for an automatic ban on Yamal deliveries, Urgewald say, as the law’s practical impact depends on how the administration exercises its powers."The US President must compile a list of ships transporting Russian LNG by October 18. These ships will then be subject to sanctions unless Trump issues so-called waivers. This is possible and, given Trump’s track record regarding Russia, not unlikely," Rötters told Euronews.EU imports from Yamal will depend on the goodwill of the US President from 18 October until the final embargo takes effect in 2027, Rötters stressed.US sanctions have already severely restricted Russia’s Arctic LNG 2 project and the Northern Sea Route, while Yamal LNG continues to supply Europe.Data from Kpler shows that 706.473 million tonnes of LNG were destined for China, South Korea and Taiwan in September this year.

title: Sounds of Mexico brings Mexican orchestral music to Doha
description: The Qatar Philharmonic brings the sounds of Mexico to Doha, with musicians from around the world exploring Mexican orchestral traditions.
content: Mexican rhythms and melodies take centre stage in Doha as the Qatar Philharmonic Orchestra performs Sounds of Mexico, part of the Qatar-Mexico 2026 Year of Culture.Led by Mexican conductor Enrique Arturo Diemecke, the programme takes audiences on a musical journey across the country, with works by Arturo Márquez, Carlos Chávez, Blas Galindo and Silvestre Revueltas.For Diemecke, the concert is a chance to show just how varied Mexican music can be, with different rhythms and melodies reflecting different parts of the country. Among the pieces is Huapango, which he says is almost like a second national anthem for Mexicans.But the musicians bringing these sounds to life come from around the world. More than 28 nationalities are represented in the Qatar Philharmonic Orchestra.For Colombian tuba player Richard Alonso Diaz, the music also brings back childhood memories of listening to mariachi with his father.Euronews goes inside rehearsals to see how an international orchestra approaches the sounds and rhythms of Mexico, and how music can introduce audiences to another side of a country’s culture.

title: Helsinki votes in favour of banning fossil fuel adverts – but there could be a 10-year delay
description: “Cities can’t keep working to cut emissions while allowing their own advertising spaces to encourage more flying and fossil fuel consumption.”
content: Helsinki has become the latest European city to vote in favour of banning advertising for fossil fuels and other carbon-intensive products and services.The landmark proposal was brought to the City Council of Helsinki by Councillor Isaac Jyväsjärvi and 27 fellow councillors. It follows previous attempts to introduce restrictions on outdoor advertising from “carbon-intensive industries” that gained momentum in 2021 but failed to reach a majority support.The exact scope of the restriction is to be determined ahead of the next advertising contract period, but campaigners say it could one day rid the streets of billboards promoting industries such as aviation, shipping, tourism and construction – as well as fossil fuels. Existing advertising contracts in the city run until 2035, meaning it may take almost a decade for the ban to come into effect. Helsinki will now investigate the legal possibilities for restricting different types of advertising, as well as the potential impacts on the environment, the city’s finances and the wider media landscape.Helsinki votes to ban fossil fuels ads“Cities can’t keep working to cut emissions while allowing their own advertising spaces to encourage more flying and fossil fuel consumption,” says Niklas Kaskeala, Helsinki-based climate campaigner and Board Member of Protect Our Winters Finland.“Helsinki’s decision won’t make these ads disappear overnight, but it draws an important line – and every city that takes this step makes it easier for others to follow.”Anna Jonsonn, co-founder of NGO New Weather Sweden, also welcomes the ban, adding: “It’s time to stop promoting the industries that are fuelling the climate crisis.“With this decision, Helsinki becomes the second Nordic capital to move towards such a ban, after Stockholm. A ban on fossil fuels ads is not a question of if; it is a question of when.”Europe’s new era of green marketingHelsinki City Council specifically cited other European cities that have moved to restrict fossil advertising when discussing the proposal.Earlier this year, Amsterdam stripped its streets of billboards promoting meat and fossil fuel products as part of its target to reach carbon neutrality by 2050 and halve meat consumption during the same period.The decision to ban fossil fuel advertising... comes at a crucial moment in the fight against climate change,” Femke Sleegers, coordinator of the Reclame Fossielvrij (Fossil Free Advertising) initiative, said when the ban was first proposed in 2020.“Adverts that portray fossil fuels as normal worsen climate disruption and have no place in a city − or a country − that has complied with the Paris Agreement.”Over in the UK, Bristol has recently become the first British city to impose an advertising ban on fast-fashion, SUVs, airlines, cruises and fossil fuels on all council-owned sites.Since the summer of 2026, fossil fuel advertising has also been banned across city-owned billboards and public spaces in Stockholm.

title: Passport-free travel, AI agents and longevity: Key takeaways from the WTTC Global Summit
description: The 26th edition of the World Travel & Tourism Council Global Summit just concluded in Malta – here’s what you may have missed from the ‘Davos of travel’.
