content: Hundreds of the world’s biggest names in travel gathered in Malta this week for the 26th edition of the World Travel & Tourism Council (WTTC) Global Summit to discuss the challenges and opportunities the industry is facing.Covering everything from luxury travel and longevity to the future airport experience and how destinations can grow sustainably, the panels gave an insight into what governments and businesses will be focusing on in the coming years.Euronews Travel was reporting on the ground – here’s what you may have missed.Justin Trudeau: Tourism is the best counter to an increasingly insular worldCanada’s former Prime Minister Justin Trudeau was this year’s main speaker, joining WTTC President and CEO Gloria Guevara on stage to chat about “how to shape the opportunity ahead”.Directly addressing the “Trump Slump”, Trudeau said in recent years “the US hasn’t been very good at making travellers feel welcome”.He said: “There’s a tendency right now in countries around the world, and we’re seeing it to a greater or lesser extent in certain countries or governments, that are encouraging people to look inward, turn inward, to go a little more insular and be mistrustful or in opposition to the rest of the world. That’s not necessarily a productive path for the world, and the best counter to that is tourism.“It’s getting to know people who are different. It’s wanting to travel, being curious about the world, being empathetic. These are the instincts that people need to be developing, and this is something that makes your industry so great.”When pressed on which single destination Trudeau would recommend to visit in Canada, he suggested Montréal, his home city.“Montrealers, we love good restaurants, we love good art. We fill our summers with festivals, in winter, it’s worth coming to see the snow,” he added.You won’t need to use your passport to travel within the next five yearsIn a panel discussing the implementation of digital identity and changing the border experience, Dubai Airports CEO Paul Griffiths said that passports will no longer be a necessity for travel within the next five years.The barrier isn’t the technology, but a lack of coordination between the different systems that must be connected to make this happen, he added.Panellists envisioned a future where travellers won’t need to use their passport when passing through borders, when collecting hire cars, or even checking in to hotels.AI is already being used to plan holidays – the next stage is letting agents book your tripTourists across the globe are becoming “super-empowered travellers” by using AI to plan out their trips, according to Christie Travers-Smith, a director for EMEA Strategic Partnerships at Google Inc.The next big step for AI? Building enough trust for customers to hand over their credit card information and allow AI agents to book for them.While the luxury sector is leading the way, ‘longevity as standard’ is what all hotels should be aiming forBryan Johnson’s antics have brought longevity out of the fringe and into the mainstream in recent years, and luxury hotel groups have been paying attention, introducing things like hyperbaric oxygen therapy and infrared saunas.But Tim Gray, the founder of Health Optimisation, argues that “longevity as standard” is what all hotel groups should be aiming for.What that means is allowing travellers to stick to the basic principles of recovery – eating well, sleeping well, staying hydrated and staying active – even while away from home, and that starts from small things like adding black-out blinds and removing blinking lights, to ensuring that mini bars are stocked with healthier options. All of the fancy tools are just meant to help “turbo charge” the basics. Having tried out HPO.TECH’s hyperbaric oxygen therapy for ourselves at the WTTC summit, we can certainly see how jet-lagged travellers could benefit.Measuring success by value, rather than volumeFor many years, the travel industry’s main measure for success was the number of tourists flowing into a destination.Today, the indicators people are paying attention to are changing – governments are now shifting from “volume to value”, according to Michelle Fridman, Secretary of Tourism of Jalisco, Mexico.“We are looking for those tourists that are better tourists, that stay for a longer period, that spend a bigger amount of money, that consume local products,” Fridman said during a panel on destination stewardship.“More importantly, we are looking for those that respect and are interested in our identity.”She added that Jalisco is “the most Mexican destination, and we want to keep it that way”.It was a sentiment shared across the panellists, with Miguel Sanz, Director-General at Turespaña, saying that his role was now more of a “tourism curator”, with efforts being made to attract a different kind of traveller to Spain.The idea was further explored on the “impact-oriented traveller” panel, with Mark Weingard, CEO & founder of Iniala, noting that it’s important for the industry to not become too focused on bringing in high-value travellers “because then we are almost being elitist” and “saying only the wealthy can travel”.“At the same time, I think it's very important that we position travel that it benefits the cities that it's in, that it doesn't destroy the culture, it doesn't destroy the neighbourhoods and that we are making sure that the work that we are doing in hospitality actually gives back to the community,” he added.

title: What happened to OpenAI’s $20bn? Revenue scare rattles AI trade
description: US tech futures rebounded on Friday, a day after a report that OpenAI’s annualised revenue was $20 billion (€17.8bn) below earlier estimates helped send the Nasdaq down 1.25% and hit chipmakers and cloud giants.
content: Wall Street looks set to recover some ground on Friday morning after confusion over how much money OpenAI, the ChatGPT maker, is actually bringing in shook investor faith in the artificial intelligence boom.Nasdaq 100 futures were around 0.8% higher, and S&P 500 futures were up 0.4% in early trading on Friday.On Thursday, the Financial Times reported that OpenAI’s annualised revenue, which projects recent sales over a full year, was "approaching $50 billion (€44.6bn)" at the end of September, according to figures shared with investors.That is about $20 billion (€17.8bn) less than the company projected last month.The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite fell 1.25% to around 27,193, while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, which tracks major US chip stocks, sank 3.4%. A jump in oil prices added to the pressure.Where did the $20 billion go?In short, nowhere.The gap does not mean OpenAI missed a target or lost sales: the roughly $70 billion (€62.5bn) figure was an estimate, not a company forecast, built on a different way of counting revenue.According to the FT, the higher number came from OpenAI’s backers recalculating its sales to match the method of rival Anthropic, which counts what customers spend on its AI models through cloud platforms such as Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud as revenue, while OpenAI excludes such sales.Taken at face value, OpenAI’s figure trails the $65 billion (€58bn) Anthropic reportedly hit at the end of July, although the different accounting methods make a direct comparison difficult. At the time of writing, OpenAI has not publicly reacted to the reports.The figures matter as OpenAI, valued at $852 billion (€760bn) in March, is reportedly seeking at least $30 billion (€26.7bn) in fresh funding at a $1.4 trillion (€1.25tn) valuation.Shares in firms that have bet big on OpenAI’s growth were among the hardest hit after the news broke on Thursday.Oracle, which has agreed to supply OpenAI with vast computing power, slid 5.5%, while CoreWeave, an AI cloud specialist with multibillion-dollar contracts with the firm, lost nearly 8%.Microsoft, a major OpenAI shareholder, Amazon, Alphabet and Meta all fell by more than 1%. Like Oracle, all four are hyperscalers that are pouring money into AI data centres.Chipmakers slid too, with Nvidia down almost 3%, AMD down around 4% and Broadcom, which is building a custom chip with OpenAI, down 4.35%.In Tokyo on Friday, shares in SoftBank Group, which owns about 13% of OpenAI, fell as much as 7.3% before paring losses.Chip demand still strongDespite the negative news, other signals this week suggest demand for AI hardware remains robust.South Korea’s Samsung estimated on Thursday that its third-quarter operating profit hit a record 107.4 trillion won, or $80.2 billion (€71.5bn).The figure, if confirmed, would be the biggest quarterly operating profit ever reported by a technology company, beating the $63.7 billion (€56.8bn) in operating income that US chip designer Nvidia booked in its latest quarter.Taiwan’s TSMC, the world’s biggest contract chipmaker, said the same day that September sales rose 54.6% year-on-year, taking third-quarter revenue to a record NT$1.49 trillion, or $46.8 billion (€41.8bn).Investors will get a clearer read next week, when Dutch chip equipment maker ASML reports on 14 October and TSMC on 15 October.Potential listings by Anthropic, as soon as November, and OpenAI next year could bring their audited accounts into the open.

title: Inside Kazakhstan’s historic rock-hewn mosques now recognised by UNESCO
description: Five rock-hewn mosques and associated sacred sites dating from the 12th to the 18th centuries make up Kazakhstan’s newest UNESCO World Heritage property. The complexes preserve centuries of Sufi tradition alongside much older beliefs.
content: The World Heritage Committee adopted the decision at its 48th session on 25 July in Busan, South Korea. This follows President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s 2024 instructions to pursue the inscription of these rock-hewn mosques on the World Heritage List.Set amid the otherworldly landscapes of Mangystau, the newly recognised mosques and their associated sites are named after revered Sufi masters: Beket-Ata, Shopan-Ata, Karaman-Ata, Shakpak-Ata and Sultan-Epe.In Central Asian Sufism, ‘Ata’, meaning ‘father’ or ‘ancestor’, is used as an honorific for a revered spiritual figure.Their spiritual lineage traces back to the 12th-century Sufi master Khoja Ahmed Yasawi. His teachings helped spread Islam among the Turkic-speaking peoples of Central Asia, connecting Islamic practices with older Tengri beliefs and local shamanistic traditions.The mosques welcome both pilgrims and visitors seeking to explore Kazakhstan’s spiritual, cultural and architectural heritage.Mangystau – the cradle of nomadic spiritualityAccording to the UNESCO World Heritage Centre, the complexes reflect the evolution of a distinctive spiritual culture.They represent “sacred practices in which Islamic Sufi spirituality organically continued and transformed more ancient practices related to ancestor worship, the sacredness of the landscape and the role of spiritual leaders”.Developed over many centuries, the monuments show how spiritual traditions and practices were adapted to the region’s distinctive natural environment and geological features through local architecture.Speaking at the 48th session in July, Erlan Karin, Chairman of Kazakhstan’s National Commission to UNESCO and ICESCO, highlighted the significance of the inscription for the country.“The inscription of the sacred monuments of Mangystau on the World Heritage List was not only a recognition of their significance for humanity as a whole, but also a tribute to the rich history, spiritual heritage and cultural identity of the Kazakh people.”For local resident Almagul Zhaiman, the sacred sites embody a faith passed down through generations.“These sacred sites have been preserved because of the faith passed down through generations, the knowledge of that heritage, preserving it and passing it on to our future generations. I believe that is what makes all these mosques so meaningful to us,” she said.The Sufi masters of the mosquesKaraman-Ata was a Sufi missionary who came to spread Islam in the region. His mosque is believed to date back to the 12th or 13th century, while its associated necropolis is one of the largest and oldest in Mangystau.For the Kazakhs and Turkmens who lived on the Mangyshlak Peninsula, the necropolis was considered a sacred place. According to local tradition, it was also a site for resolving disputes and negotiating peace. Those who made vows there were expected to honour them, as breaking a vow was believed to bring death and the end of one's lineage.Karaman-Ata is believed to have been the grandson of Shopan-Ata, a 12th-century mystic revered as the spiritual protector of shepherds and their livestock.According to tradition, Shopan-Ata was a disciple of the renowned Sufi master Khoja Ahmed Yasawi. Once part of an ancient caravan route to Khorezm, Shopan-Ata’s site remains an important destination for Sufi pilgrims.Beket-Ata is said to have regarded Shopan-Ata, who lived centuries earlier, as a spiritual mentor.Local traditions attribute extraordinary abilities to the 18th-century scholar, healer and architect, including teleportation and levitation.“He was also regarded as the last and highest-ranking spiritual master among other holy men, which is why he became known as Pir Beket,” said Bakhtiyar Esimbetov, caretaker of Beket-Ata’s mosque.In Sufi tradition, the Persian word ‘Pir’ refers to a spiritual guide or master, often one who has attained a high level of spiritual wisdom.The Shakpak-Ata complex served as one of the region’s principal Sufi centres for centuries. Shakpak-Ata is believed to have lived sometime between the 9th and 14th centuries.Carved into a chalk and limestone cliff, the sanctuary is arranged around a central domed hall with a cross-shaped layout.Local traditions say the scholar taught astrology and astronomy, as well as ideas linked to the cosmos.Inside the mosques’ architectural layoutAccording to local belief, divine signs guided the Sufi masters to the places where they built their mosques.The sanctuaries are scattered across Mangystau, in western Kazakhstan, a region shaped by its nomadic heritage and geological history. Much of the area was once covered by the ancient Tethys Ocean.Locally known as “underground mosques”, the complexes were built in natural caves, carved into steep rock faces or dug into the ground, providing shelter in the semi-desert landscape.Their architectural layouts vary. They include prayer halls, mihrabs, rooms for contemplation and self-reflection, multifunctional spaces and tombs of the Sufi masters, sometimes alongside those of their immediate families.Some underground cells were carved out for silent meditation and ascetic isolation.“These underground mosques were places of retreat from society, where people could withdraw from everyday life and devote themselves fully to spiritual purification,” said Yersultan Islam, a local sacred sites guide.The complexes also feature courtyards, water sources, sacred trees, pathways and cemeteries, some of which date from the 10th to the 20th centuries.PilgrimsFor centuries, Mangystau’s sacred mosques have been important destinations for pilgrims.Visitors are expected to dress modestly, while women are required to cover their heads before entering the underground mosques as a sign of respect for the sacred sites.The sanctuaries attract not only local worshippers but also pilgrims from abroad.Among them is Dinara Farvazova, whose family travels from Bashkortostan, Russia, to visit Mangystau’s sacred sites year after year.“We read the Quran here, pray and make wishes. People come here seeking healing, and many see their dreams come true. They then tell their relatives and friends about the place, who come here too.”Some visitors come in search of a deeper understanding of Islam.Kaahn Ozturk, a traveller from Turkey, stopped at Karaman-Ata’s mosque during a long-distance motorcycle journey across the country.“I have lots of questions in my mind, and I just want to find answers. That’s why I’m trying to discover every mosque, every place, every idea about Islam, to understand it better.”Rinat Aubekerov and his wife, ethnic Kazakhs from Russia, made a pilgrimage to Shopan-Ata, hoping their prayers to have children would be answered.For Davide Passanante, a visitor from Italy, the appeal was different.After experiencing the crowds of summer tourism at home, he found a sense of calm in the remote sanctuaries. Travelling with a group of friends across Mangystau’s Martian-like landscapes, he was struck by the region’s spiritual atmosphere.“I'm very impressed because the religion here is very important. I see how people pray and how they feel, how they think of God every time.”Easing travel for visitors to sacred sitesThe remote sanctuaries are attracting growing numbers of pilgrims from around the world. Kazakhstan is now planning to improve access to the newly listed sites while preserving them for future generations.A five-year comprehensive development plan, due to begin in 2027, is expected to support tourism at the sites, including restoration work and the development of new visitor infrastructure.Each sanctuary already has basic facilities where visitors can sleep and eat free of charge, although donations are welcome to help cover maintenance costs.Plans include building visitor centres at Shopan-Ata, Beket-Ata and Karaman-Ata, complementing the existing centre serving Sultan-Epe and Shakpak-Ata.“An asphalt road will be built to the site as part of the development plan. We also hope that internet connectivity issues will be resolved,” said Baltabai Balapan, director of the Mangystau State Historical and Cultural Reserve.The five rock-hewn mosques and associated sacred sites of Mangystau, now collectively inscribed on UNESCO’s World Heritage List, are bringing the region’s spiritual heritage to a global audience, inviting visitors to discover its sacred landscapes.

title: Ukrainian and European officials fly to Miami for US-led peace talks
description: The US is hosting a round of peace talks in Miami with Ukrainian and European officials. President Zelenskyy aims to secure a targeted ceasefire that can cover either the Black Sea, energy facilities or both.
content: High-level officials from Ukraine and Europe have flown to Miami, Florida, to take part in a new round of peace negotiations to end Russia's full-scale invasion amid a new wave of escalation that has battered Ukrainian cities and killed scores of civilians.The talks, set to take place on Friday and Saturday, will be hosted by Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, the US special envoys, and will discuss several options to break the diplomatic impasse ahead of a winter expected to be the harshest yet of the war.Witkoff and Kushner's recent trips to Moscow and Kyiv will inform the deliberations.Among those options is a targeted ceasefire, covering the Black Sea, a vital trade route for shipping grain to low-cost nations, and/or energy facilities, which Moscow has hit at a relentless pace. Kyiv has responded in kind, striking Russia's oil refineries."I'm not yet ready to say what might be realistic or more realistic. In principle, I understand, but I don't want to say anything, only for Russia, as always, to do the opposite just to be spiteful," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Thursday in a voice note sent to journalists."Let's wait and see. We are seeing an intensification of talks and meetings on the part of the United States," he added."I myself have spoken three times in recent days with the American side and am hopeful for a positive outcome from the meeting between our negotiators."Zelenskyy said his team would comprise Kyrylo Budanov and Sergiy Kyslytsya, head and deputy head of the president's office; Davyd Arakhamia, leader of the ruling party in the Parliament; and Rustem Umerov, head of the Foreign Intelligence Service.They are expected to be back in Kyiv on Monday morning to brief the president."There are things we cannot talk about, but we must remain wise, united, and support our military. Peace is not achieved through grand statements – it's hard, collaborative work, and we’re working on it," Budanov said on social media ahead of the trip.The European side will be represented by the national security advisors of the so-called E3: France, Germany and the United Kingdom. The three countries lead the "Coaltion of the Willing" to provide future security guarantees for Ukraine.The European Commission will also take part, a spokesperson confirmed to Euronews. NATO has sent its chief of staff, Geoffrey van Leeuwen, an official said.Russia will not participate.The Miami meeting comes after several media reports suggested that Washington is exploring business deals with Moscow that could be signed even before a final peace deal is reached. The reports have alarmed Ukrainians and Europeans, who have long feared economic interests would trump diplomacy in the White House's vision.Zelenskyy took exception after US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the war was stuck in a "diplomatic stalemate" with risk of an escalatory spillover."One cannot, on the one hand, negotiate with the Russians about future economic projects, whilst on the other hand say that we find ourselves in some sort of diplomatic stalemate," he said as he visited the site of a Russian attack.Zelenskyy also urged the US to expand the use of Starlink satellite service inside Russian territory to help Ukraine target ballistic-missile launchers.European officials have actively engaged in the US-led process, arguing their security architecture is directly at stake. Following the cut-off of American aid, the continent is now the main provider of financial and military support for Ukraine.However, scepticism over Moscow's intentions runs deep. The Kremlin has once again dismissed the possibility of a trilateral meeting at the leaders' level."We cannot have our vested hopes in (these talks) because we don’t see that Russia is ready at all to negotiate in good faith," a senior EU official said on Friday."But with stronger US pressure, hopefully, on Russia, and European influence over those talks, there is also a track that can lead to a partial ceasefire that Ukraine has been asking for and is ready to commit to."Sasha Vakulina and Shona Murray contributed reporting.

title: EU countries agree to shift oversight of major financial markets to European authority ESMA
description: EU countries struck a deal on Friday to give the EU’s financial markets watchdog more powers, aiming to make cross-border investment easier and help businesses raise more money across the bloc.
content: EU countries have agreed on a package to strengthen the bloc’s financial markets watchdog at a meeting of finance ministers in Luxembourg on Friday.The Market Integration and Supervision Package (MISP) would give the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) direct oversight of major market operators currently supervised by national authorities.While some rules are harmonised across the EU, differences in implementation, supervision and enforcement have contributed to fragmentation in financial markets.The Irish presidency said the package aims to make it easier for savings and investments to flow across borders, helping companies access finance and giving households more opportunities to earn returns on their savings.The package would give ESMA direct oversight of major trading venues, clearing houses and bodies that handle securities settlement, as well as crypto-asset service providers. It would also create a full-time, independent executive board within the watchdog.Market operators could opt into a new framework for operating across the EU. The reforms would make national supervision more consistent and update rules on trading, completing transactions, managing investments and using blockchain technology.However, some trading venues run by Deutsche Börse, which operates the Frankfurt stock exchange, may remain outside ESMA’s direct supervision.Euronews previously learnt that Germany had secured an exemption for Deutsche Börse’s domestically focused trading venues, leaving a key part of the system under regional German supervision. The current announcement did not give details on this matter.Dutch Finance Minister Eelco Heinen welcomed the agreement, saying: "Major step forward today in advancing the Capital Markets Union. We made more progress in 10 months than in 10 years.This marks an important milestone in the Savings and Investments Union (SIU), which aims to channel more of Europeans' savings into investments that support the economy.Supporters of more integrated capital markets argue that they would lower costs and improve access to funding for companies, while giving savers and investors more investment options.

title: US military will livestream the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter, 'torture' for UN
description: Convicted military base shooter Nidal Hasan's execution will take place on 3 December at Fort Hood military base, where he committed the shooting. It will be the first US military execution carried out by a firing squad since World War II.
content: The firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan will be livestreamed, the Pentagon said Thursday, a controversial revelation about plans for the first military execution by firing squad since World War II after Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth had described it as being "public."The UN promptly condemned the US decision as "torture"."The livestreaming of an execution is tantamount to a public execution and would breach the absolute prohibition of torture," said the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights.The UN body said it had made similar statements about public executions in Afghanistan and Iran, saying they "constitute a form of cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment".Nidal Hasan, a US Army psychiatrist, shot and killed 13 people and injured 32 others at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009."We are going to make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public", this is how US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth announced the "public" execution of convicted military base shooter Nidal Hasan."People need to understand that... there's serious consequences for these types of things", said Hegseth.His execution by firing squad will be livestreamed on 3 December; it will be the first execution by the US military in more than 65 years, and the first carried out by firing squad since World War II."I kind of like the mentality we had in World War II, which was win, which was understand when the enemy attacks you, you need to stand your ground", Hegseth said.Officials in the Pentagon clarified Thursday that the execution would be livestreamed and that more details would follow.The revelation from Hegseth about the public nature of the execution has raised further questions about how the death penalty is carried out in the US, especially after the botched lethal injection of Christa Pike in Tennessee.'We'll see him on December 3'"He is going to get a firing squad of soldiers, as it should be", said Hegseth.In an interview with right-wing influencer Jack Posobiec, the Pentagon chief was asked if Hasan had made any final request. "Don't care. We'll see him on December 3", Hegseth said — the day Hasan is slated to die.Hasan could choose to resist execution and file a habeas petition — a legal request to review the legality of a detention — in civilian court, which could significantly delay the execution, experts said."It frankly might outlast the current administration, and who knows if the next one will have the same penchant for executions", said Eugene R. Fidell, a visiting lecturer at Yale Law School specialising in military law.Deborah Denno, a death penalty expert and law professor at Fordham University, said livestreaming an execution could make the process "much more transparent" and inform the public about all that capital punishment entails.Those are benefits that she said would be useful at a time when Pike’s botched execution has raised fresh questions about the manner by which criminal defendants are put to death for their crimes. "I think it could possibly be a good idea because it would be transparent and the public would be fully aware that it’s happening", she said.Firing squad 'less inhumane'When many states have had difficulty carrying out lethal injections due to difficulty accessing drugs or finding medical professionals willing to participate in executions, firing squads are coming to be seen as a less inhumane alternative, said Brenner Fissell, a professor at Villanova Law and vice president of the National Institute of Military Justice."Firing squads can be a quicker, cleaner, more precise way to execute a prisoner", he said. "I don’t think that’s what’s motivating this. There’s a perceived masculinity and military-ness to firing squads that is part of the aura Hegseth is trying to emphasise — the 'lethality culture".Elisabeth Semel, co-director of the Death Penalty Clinic at UC Berkeley Law, said Hegseth’s announcement raises a host of legal and public policy questions, including concerns for the dignity of the defendant, who will be eligible to view the execution and what the Trump administration has in mind in opting for an unusual spectacle.Though there has been a long-running discussion about the idea of televising an execution, "I don’t recall a situation in which it was instigated by the government. I think that also raises serious questions about what the motivation of the government is", she said."This is a president who’s about spectacle and that’s, I think, precisely the message that he intends to deliver", Semel said, adding that she was sceptical that the administration had given a second thought to the legal and social questions being presented by the decision.Media reports state that Trump, who approved Hasan’s execution, has previously been critical of public executions in Iran, at times using the possibility of protesters being killed by the Iranian government as a possible rationale for military action that preceded his ultimate choice to attack Iran on 28 February.US executions scrutinised after failed injectionTexas has carried out the first execution in the US since Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike survived a failed lethal injection last week. Jamaal Howard, 46, has received a lethal injection on Wednesday evening and was shortly after declared dead.Lawyers for Howard asked to pause the execution in spite of Pike's botched lethal injection last week, but the courts denied the request.A further two executions are scheduled to take place in November — death row inmates John Rubio and Reinaldo Dennes.Since the beginning of the year, the US has executed 30 people. In 2025, US executions reached the highest figure since 2009, with 47 people being put to death.

title: Intense diplomatic manoeuvring in Athens over first Russian team in European tournament
description: The Kazan club was the first Russian club to play an official European club match in Greece, after discreet pressure to keep Russian symbols out of the Serafio pool.
content: According to information obtained by Euronews, the presence of the Russian club Sintez Kazan in the qualifying group of the Euro Cup in water polo, hosted by Apollon Smyrnis at the Serafeio Swimming Pool of the City of Athens, was accompanied by intense diplomatic manoeuvring behind the scenes.This tournament marked the official return of Russian teams to European cross-border sports competitions, after their abrupt removal when Russia launched its invasion of Ukraine. The draw carried out by the European confederation meant that this comeback would take place in Greece.This, however, did not go unnoticed by the Greek government, which at the same time is participating in the EU's collective sanctions against Moscow. Because of those sanctions, the Russian team was unable to find a direct flight to Athens or to any destination in the European Union.No national anthems playedThe issue reached the Greek Ministry of Foreign Affairs, which issued guidance both for heightened but discreet security measures and for keeping Russian flags out of the Serafeio Swimming Pool, as well as any playing of the Russian national anthem. This obstacle was overcome by the decision not to play any national anthem at all, not even the Greek one, but only club anthems such as that of the hosts Apollon Smyrnis.No mention of the countries of origin of the teams was made on the tournament poster, a deliberate move, although no one hid that "we are talking about Russia's comeback to aquatics".Inside the pool, behind one of the goals, there was a row of flags (including those of the City of Athens, Apollon Smyrnis and several countries such as Greece, Germany and Israel, but not Russia).The Greek government confirmed to Euronews that it was assured not only that there would be no Russian symbols in the arena, but also that the Kazan team would compete as a neutral side, as had been the case for Russian teams and athletes in aquatics up until last summer.However, that regime has changed, and Russia can now be represented in full, according to European Aquatics. That is why on its official website (source in Greek), Kazan is explicitly listed as representing Russia, with the colours of the Russian flag also displayed.Change of stance towards RussiaLast July, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) itself changed its stance towards Russia and largely relaxed the sporting sanctions against it, while clarifying that the final decision for each sport would be taken by the respective sports federation.Since then, some federations have proceeded to lift sanctions (for example, judo, wrestling and others), while there are also those, such as athletics, that continue to ban Russian athletes from taking part, prompting Moscow to challenge this ban at the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS).The World Aquatics federation, in contrast to the athletics body, was one of the first to move towards lifting sanctions on Russians, as early as 13 April (source in Greek), well before the IOC issued its well-known recommendation.World Aquatics thus became the first major Olympic federation to fully scrap the political exclusion guidelines that had been in place since 2022, following the Russian invasion of Ukraine.Its board decided to fully restore the membership rights of Russia and Belarus, on the grounds that "sport must stay out of political conflicts". The decision provided for a complete return, even allowing the use of national symbols (jerseys, flags, anthems), provided the national federations comply with the regulations.The European Aquatics Federation reacted to the immediate application of this new statute and, at the end of April, officially requested from World Aquatics a postponement or delay (source in Greek) in its implementation. It argued that it wanted to protect the European summer events and avoid upending their planning, which is why athletes who competed then did so under neutral and independent status.It was decided that no Russian athlete or team would return with full national symbols before 1 September 2026. After the extension expired, from 1 September, the new European Aquatics framework came into force, under which at youth level Russian athletes and teams compete without any restrictions, while at senior level Russian clubs are allowed to enter European club competitions but their athletes and staff are required, for the duration of the matches, to retain the status of Approved Neutral Athlete.Sport federations dividedIn this way, on Thursday night, Sintez Kazan became the first club in a team sport to play in an official international competition since the start of the war in Ukraine, openly representing Russia.It was drawn in the group that Apollon Smyrnis is hosting at the Serafeio, and faced Partizan Belgrade, losing 14-13. Over the weekend, it will play German side Duisburg, Italian club Savona and the hosts Apollon Smyrnis.European federations in football (UEFA), basketball (FIBA), handball (EHF), volleyball (CEV) and ice hockey have not taken similar steps to lift restrictions.Only last week, CEV decided to allow Russian national teams back into its competitions in both indoor volleyball and beach volleyball, but it did not take a corresponding decision regarding Russian clubs in European tournaments."We had been absent from the European stage for a long time and that added an extra burden, a responsibility, because we knew we were the first Russian team in such a long time to represent Russia. Unfortunately, we lost our opener against Partizan, but I believe we have the ability to win the next matches and qualify for the next phase", Kazan goalkeeper Pyotr Fedotov told Euronews.From the qualifying group being staged in Athens, three of the five participating teams will advance to the next phase. Hosts Apollon Smyrnis have already laid the foundations to be one of them after their emphatic 16-9 victory over Duisburg in the opening game.

title: Turkmenistan marks 35 years of independence with an eye on the future
description: Turkmenistan celebrated 35 years of independence with a vast parade through Ashgabat, as the country set out its ambitions for the decades ahead.
content: Turkmenistan has marked 35 years of independence with parades across Ashgabat, joined by international partners including the United Nations.Permanent neutrality, recognised by the UN General Assembly in 1995, remains the cornerstone of its foreign policy and has shaped its economy, with growth above 6% and public debt below 2%. Gas is the backbone, led by the vast Galkynyş field, while ports, motorways and education are expanding.Celebrations also honour the ancient Akhal-Teke horse breed, as the country pairs pride in its heritage with ambitions for the next 35 years.

title: Greece is the most popular luxury honeymoon destination for 2027 – with Italy and France also in the top 10
description: Greece tops the ranking of the world’s most popular honeymoon destinations for 2027 in Virtuoso’s latest Luxe Report, ahead of Bali and the Maldives.
content: With its romantic sunset spots and stunning islands that are perfect for lazy beach days, there are plenty of reasons why newlyweds would choose Greece for a luxury honeymoon. Now, Greece has been named the world’s most popular honeymoon destination for 2027 in the latest Virtuoso Luxe Report, ahead of traditional favourites such as Bali and the Maldives, which placed second and third respectively. On the honeymoon hotlist, Italy takes fourth place and France eighth, putting three European countries among the top 10 destinations for affluent couples planning a post-wedding holiday. French Polynesia, Japan, Fiji, Thailand and South Africa make up the top 10. Drawing on insights from Virtuoso's global travel agency members, the annual survey of more than 3,100 advisors across more than 50 countries reveals the destinations and behaviours that are “guiding the choices of affluent travellers worldwide”.Alongside priorities such as celebrating milestones and the excitement of exploring a new destination, honeymoons also ranked sixth among the top 10 motivations for affluent travel in 2027.“Greece took the top spot for 2027, ending Italy’s long-standing lead, while Italy remained in the top five and France also placed in the top 10,” said Misty Belles, Vice President, Global Public Relations at Virtuoso. “Together, the results point to strong demand for destinations that combine romance with culture, cuisine and opportunities to build a more varied itinerary beyond the traditional beach escape.”Why Greece is the leading destination for 2027As well as ranking first in the 2027 honeymoons list, Greece was also number four on the report’s 10 most popular global destinations for luxury travel overall.With its combination of “romance, spectacular scenery, exceptional food, history and culture with an impressive range of luxury hotels”, Greece is “almost tailor-made for honeymoons”, said Kayla Zeigler, Founder and Travel Advisor at Destination Europe, an affiliate of Virtuoso.Speaking to Euronews Travel, Zeigler said that couples are increasingly “looking beyond the traditional Mykonos and Santorini combination”, which have become “much busier and increasingly oriented toward cruise tourism”. She revealed that newlyweds are now looking for a “more relaxed, authentic” Greek island experience “without sacrificing luxury”, with Paros, Milos and Crete emerging as new favourites. Other Greek destinations attracting interest include the “exciting development” along the Athens Riviera, she said, with new luxury hotels giving honeymooners “an attractive alternative” to spending their entire stay in Athens city centre. “Couples can experience the history and energy of Athens and then retreat to the coast before continuing to the islands,” she said. “Overall, affluent honeymooners still want beautiful hotels and exceptional service, but increasingly they're also looking for authenticity, privacy and a genuine sense of place – a trend reflected in Virtuoso's 2027 findings.”What are honeymooners looking for in Europe?Italy and France have long been top choices for honeymoon bookings. Couples making their first trip to Europe still want “iconic destinations” like Rome, Florence and Paris, Zeigler said. But there has been much more interest in combining them with places that feel “more intimate, authentic and less saturated”. “In Italy, we're increasingly recommending Ischia over Capri for couples visiting the Amalfi Coast region,” she added. “Capri will always be iconic, but Ischia offers beautiful hotels, thermal spas, wonderful food and a more relaxed island experience. “We're also selling more Piedmont and Umbria in lieu of Tuscany, alternatives to Lake Como among Italy's other beautiful lakes, and Puglia continues to be an up-and-coming favourite, particularly for its masserias, coastline and food.” The Dolomites are also “having a moment”, offering spectacular scenery, exceptional mountain hotels, wellness and outdoor experiences. “With Venice, this is a wonderful honeymoon combination.” There’s a similar shift happening in France, Zeigler revealed. “Couples are looking beyond Paris and combining it with Provence, where the villages, markets, vineyards and countryside lend themselves beautifully to a honeymoon, or the French Riviera for a Mediterranean coastal experience”. Champagne is a “natural fit” for a celebratory trip, while Burgundy and Bordeaux appeal to couples interested in food and wine. “France makes it very easy to combine a few exciting days in Paris with a completely different, slower-paced experience.” Overall, one of the biggest changes Zeigler is seeing at Destination Europe is the move towards shoulder and off-season travel. “June and July in southern Europe are becoming increasingly hot and crowded, and we're booking more honeymoons in April and May, as well as October and even into November,” she said. “Depending on the destination, couples can enjoy more comfortable weather, fewer crowds and better value. “Overall, luxury honeymooners seem less interested in checking off as many destinations as possible and more interested in slowing down, finding places that still have a strong sense of place, and really experiencing Europe together.”How is the luxury honeymoon evolving?Honeymooners are becoming more selective about where they splurge, according to Zeigler, and are balancing standout hotel stays with personal experiences.“We're seeing couples choose a beautiful suite in a smaller boutique hotel – something charming, full of personality and with a real sense of place – over the grand palace hotel, and then use that portion of their budget for unique, private and personal experiences,” she said. That might mean booking an exceptional suite for a few nights, then choosing more moderately priced boutique properties elsewhere. Private boat trips, cooking classes, wine tastings and guided tours are increasingly part of the appeal, alongside time to relax and explore together. Zeigler estimates honeymoons account for around a quarter of her agency’s bookings, with European trips typically lasting 10-14 nights. Longer journeys spanning several cities, regions or countries have also reshaped budgets. For many experienced travellers, she sees the honeymoon as the start of a lifetime of shared trips, rather than a single grand adventure. “Luxury today is becoming less about extravagance at every turn and more about choosing where to splurge, creating meaningful experiences and having the time and freedom to enjoy them.”Key findings from the 2027 Virtuoso Luxe ReportThe 10 most popular honeymoon destinations in 20271. title: Hungary's 2026 drought is the country's most severe in 126 years, data shows
description: The central European nation has been facing a critical water shortage following a drought that began in the second half of 2025.
content: Hungary has experienced its most severe drought in 126 years in 2026, according to data from its national weather service, HungaroMet.The Central European nation also recorded its driest summer since 1901 this year, as well as its second hottest.Following a winter that saw lower rainfall than usual, Hungary was hit by a heatwave in June, followed by further hot spells in July and August. The unusually dry conditions also led to record low water levels on the Danube.According to a HungaroMet analysis of the summer, average rainfall across the country amounted to just 74.1 millimetres, 36 per cent of the 1991 to 2020 mean.The seasonal mean temperature was 23.43°C on average across the country, 2.59°C above the long-term norm of 20.84°C.What's behind Hungary's drought?HungaroMet said in its analysis that the 2026 drought was the result of prolonged weather patterns and disruptions to the water cycle.Whilst January saw cold and wet weather, the following months were marked by a severe lack of rainfall and higher than normal temperatures. In April, for example, rainfall was just 10 per cent of the usual amount.May saw some wetter periods, but the soil had still not recovered enough moisture by the end of spring, and the summer months then brought further spells of unusually dry weather.By late June, almost the entire country was experiencing a soil moisture deficit of more than 100 millimetres in the top metre of soil. The lack of rainfall, combined with temperatures far above average, increased evaporation losses and caused soil moisture levels to fall sharply.Between 1 April and 2 September, at least 30 per cent of Hungary's territory experienced moderate or more severe drought conditions for nearly 84 per cent of the period. By the end of August, agricultural drought had reached severe levels across half the country.Groundwater shortages in EuropeA report by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) said that water levels below the ground are continuing to fall, with Central and Eastern Europe among the regions most affected by groundwater shortages.Soil moisture was already far below normal levels in 2025, and the situation deteriorated further in 2026.In Hungary, an earlier estimate put the average groundwater level at 1.4 to 1.7 metres below what is considered ideal. Even if autumn brings wetter days, this alone will not be enough to solve the water shortage.Experts have been warning for years that Hungary would only be able to tackle its water crisis by retaining water instead of allowing it to drain away quickly, whether it comes from rainfall or rivers.However, achieving this would require changes in farming practices as well as major structural reforms and investment.

title: QatarEnergy’s LNG expansion targets early 2027 production amid reports of $3bn loan
description: QatarEnergy is advancing its LNG expansion and has reportedly secured a $3 billion (€2.68bn) loan from Chinese banks as war damage and shipping risks constrain exports. Shipments through Hormuz are recovering, but remain far below pre-war levels.
content: QatarEnergy’s first production unit at its North Field East liquefied natural gas (LNG) project is expected to be ready to start up in November, Reuters reported on Wednesday.LNG production is expected to begin in the first quarter of 2027, two people familiar with the plans told the agency.Last month, QatarEnergy chief executive and Minister of State for Energy Affairs Saad Sherida Al-Kaabi said the first unit was expected to come online in the first half of 2027. He warned that disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz could delay equipment deliveries for later units.North Field East includes four large production lines, known as trains, each designed to produce about 8 million tonnes of LNG a year. The project is intended to raise Qatar’s export capacity from 77 million to 110 million tonnes annually.The expansion comes as Qatar works to recover from Iranian attacks on Ras Laffan in March. The attacks damaged two LNG production units, affecting around 17% of the country’s export capacity.Al-Kaabi said last month that repairs to the damaged units could take three years, while undamaged facilities could return to normal operations within weeks of Hormuz reopening.Bloomberg also reported on Wednesday that at least 12 empty LNG carriers owned or chartered by QatarEnergy were waiting near Qatar. LNG shipments through Hormuz rose in September but remained about 75% below February levels.Chinese banks reportedly provide financingSeparately, Bloomberg reported on Wednesday that QatarEnergy had secured a $3 billion (€2.68bn) loan from four Chinese banks, citing people familiar with the agreement.The five-year loan was provided by Bank of China, Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, Agricultural Bank of China and China Construction Bank (Asia), according to the report.The money is intended for general working capital. The loan was priced at 50 basis points, or half a percentage point, above the Secured Overnight Financing Rate, a US dollar lending benchmark.The deal would add to Chinese banks’ lending in the Gulf, which rose more than fivefold to a record $11.5 billion (€10.29bn) in 2025, excluding bilateral loans, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.QatarEnergy had not yet responded to Euronews’ request for comment on the production timetable and reported loan.

title: El Niño could weaken the polar vortex. Does a scorching summer mean a freezing winter?
description: El Niño’s European weather impacts tend to be indirect and less severe than in the tropics. But experts warn it could weaken the polar vortex.
content: Experts have warned that this year’s El Niño event could be the “strongest in living memory” – increasing the likelihood of 2027 becoming the hottest year on record. Sea surface temperatures in the equatorial Pacific Ocean have already surpassed the highest recorded during any previous El Niño events, and the weather phenomenon isn’t expected to peak until late autumn or early winter.Between June 2026 and February 2027, experts estimate that the extreme heat associated with El Niño could contribute to 451,000 additional deaths. The extra warming also paves the way for more extreme weather impacts, such as wildfires and floods.South America, the southern US, East Africa and Central Asia have all experienced heightened flood risks during previous El Niño events – while droughts and wildfire risks rise across large parts of Australia, northern parts of South America and in certain Asian countries such as Indonesia.But in Europe, El Niño’s weather impacts tend to be much more indirect and less severe. The natural phenomenon could increase the chances of more unsettled conditions later in the year, such as a milder, wetter and windier autumn and early winter.So, why are fears growing that Europe will be cast into a deep freeze this winter?What is a Sudden Stratospheric Warming event?Every year in winter, strong westerly winds circle around the pole high up in the stratosphere – which extends from an altitude of about 10 to 50 km above the Earth’s surface.This is referred to as the stratospheric polar vortex (SPV) and it circulates around cold air high over the Arctic. However, following a peak in El Niño, the SPV can become weaker. This can increase the likelihood of a Sudden Stratospheric Warming (SSW) event, which would subsequently increase the potential for cold weather.A SSW is where temperatures rapidly increase (up to about 50C in just a couple of days) in the stratosphere. As the cold air from high up in the stratosphere disperses, it can affect the shape of the jet stream as the cold air sinks from the stratosphere into the troposphere.“Typically this will form over the North Atlantic and Scandinavia,” the UK Met Office says.“This means that northern Europe, including the UK is likely to get a long spell of dry, cold weather, whereas southern Europe will tend to be more mild, wet and windy. On the boundary of these areas, cold easterly winds develop and in some cases the drop in temperatures leads to snow.”Will El Niño trigger a ‘deep freeze’ in Europe?Multiple newspapers have recently warned of a “deep freeze” hitting Europe due to the risk of El Niño peaking and weakening the polar vortex.However, winter weather across the UK and mainland Europe is influenced by a wide range of factors – including human-caused climate change. For example, a 2025 study from Newcastle University found the burning of fossil fuels is accelerating winter rainfall changes in the UK and Europe, almost 25 years sooner than expected.Many of the factors that impact Europe’s weather cannot be predicted so far in advance. In fact, meteorologists can only reliably forecast individual SSW events about a week ahead.“While there is a known teleconnection between El Niño and a colder end to the UK winter, this outcome is by no means guaranteed,” Grahame Madge, a Met Office climate spokesperson, tells Euronews Earth. “There are many other drivers of UK winter weather including El Niño, and it is the balance of these drivers that determines the winter forecast rather than any single one.”

title: Six injured as heavy rains batter Chile's capital, sweeping away cars and flooding homes
description: Authorities have placed 10 other Chilean districts on high alert as risks of potential mudslides and rain-related emergencies threaten to batter the region.
content: Heavy rains battered Chile’s capital Santiago and its surrounding regions on Thursday, triggering mudslides that swept cars through streets, flooded homes, forced residents to evacuate and injured at least six people, according to authorities.Chilean President José Antonio Kast declared a state of emergency in Las Condes, a wealthy suburb east of Santiago, giving government agencies more power to respond as torrential rains turned key roads into impassable waterways.The district's mayor, Catalina San Martín, said 14.4 centimetres of rain had fallen in recent days — about nine times the average October rainfall — leaving the area “totally drenched.”The Mapocho River, which runs through Santiago, overflowed, prompting evacuation orders.Chile’s disaster-response agency put 10 other districts on high alert for more landslides and ordered schools to close on Friday.Rain storms earlier this week had already damaged a few dozen homes across central Chile and left nearly 12,000 customers in Santiago without power, officials said. The downpours were expected to ease on Friday.No deaths were reported on Thursday as a result of the heavy rains. The injured however included a one-year-old child, who suffered broken bones. Firefighters said they'd rescued or evacuated more than 1,000 people.The floods come as a powerful El Niño gains strength.The naturally recurring warming of tropical Pacific waters scrambles rainfall patterns worldwide and often brings wetter springs to the Southern Hemisphere.The World Meteorological Organization said on Thursday that this year’s El Niño was expected to peak in December and could be among the most intense since at least 1950.

title: Tsunoda Claims World Gold as Murao Retains His Title in Baku
description: Ai Tsunoda Roustant claimed her first senior world title at -70kg, defeating Michaela Polleres in golden score. At -90kg, Sanshiro Murao delivered a spectacular ippon against Goki Tajima in an all-Japanese final, defending his title to become a two-time world champion.
content: It’s Day 5 in Baku at the World Judo Championships and the action rolls on.At -70kg, Ai TSUNODA ROUSTANT was entering her first senior World Championships final. After an impressive run through the draw, the former cadet and junior world champion now stood just one contest away from a Senior World title and the red backpatch.Michaela POLLERES had built momentum with every contest. Olympic silver and bronze and also two World Championship bronzes, she was no stranger to judo’s biggest stages. Her wealth of experience could prove crucial with World gold now within reach.The final went into Golden Score, but TSUNODA ROUSTANT emerged as new World Champion after a tactical bout. The Spaniard stayed focused to claim the biggest victory of her career.International Judo Federation Head Referee Director Mr Juan Carlos BARCOS awarded the medals.In the -90kg category, reigning World Champion MURAO Sanshiro displayed his exceptional talent on the tatami. Having defeated double olympic champion Bekauri early on, a huge ippon in the semi final gave him the chance to become a two-time World Champion.TAJIMA Goki would be his opponent in a repeat of last year’s World final. A former World Champion himself, TAJIMA knew exactly what it took to win on this stage. Their rematch set up an all-Japanese showdown, with a second World title on the line for both men.In the -90kg final, MURAO delivered when it mattered most, scoring a huge ippon to bring the contest to a dramatic close. With victory secured, the Japanese star retained his title and became a two-time World Champion in Baku.International Judo Federation Executive Committee Member & Kodokan President Mr Haruki UEMURA awarded the medals. See you tomorrow for more Judo!

title: Taxes account for over 53% of labour costs in Spain, study finds
description: In 2025, Spain's Finance Ministry argued that its tax cuts for middle-income earners had delivered €38 billion in savings
content: More than half of the total cost of employing an average worker in Spain goes to public authorities, according to the Juan de Mariana Institute, a liberal think tank highly critical of the government.The institute estimates the tax burden at €53.60 for every €100 in labour costs. The figure comes from a report the think tank describes as an "economic autopsy" of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's time in office, as reported by The Objective.The report, written by the institute's head of research, Diego Sánchez de la Cruz, estimates that €21,144 of the average employee's €39,481 annual labour cost goes towards taxes and social security contributions — equivalent to a tax burden of €53.60 for every €100 in labour costs.The think tank describes the report as an "economic autopsy" of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's time in office, according to The Objective.The calculation includes social security contributions, income tax, VAT and other taxes, using the employer's total labour cost rather than gross salary as its basis.The institute previously documented 141 tax increases between 2018 and 2026.It also estimates that the average taxpayer pays €460,600 in taxes over their lifetime, equivalent to almost 30 years of Spain's most common salary, or 16.4 years based on the average salary.Higher tax revenues, spending and debtAccording to the report, revenue from taxes and social security contributions has risen by 39.7% since 2018, an increase of around €168.17 billion. The figure is nominal, meaning it also reflects inflation and employment growth. The tax-to-GDP ratio has increased from 34.9% to 37.1%.The report acknowledges that healthcare spending has risen by 43% and education spending by 40%. However, it argues that public services have deteriorated, citing a 28% increase in surgical waiting lists to 853,509 patients, an average wait of 102 days to see a specialist, and the results of the 2025 PISA report.Public debt stands at €1.763 trillion, around €600 billion more than eight years ago. The report also notes that one in every four euros spent on pensions is funded through government contributions.Housing and wagesAccording to the study, median rent (€1,080) now exceeds the median salary of a young worker (€1,048), while only 15.2% of young people live independently, the lowest figure since 2006.The author attributes this to a housing shortage, noting that 1.16 million new households have been formed since 2021, compared with just 465,000 completed homes on the open market.The report also blames rent caps introduced under Spain's housing law, linking them to a 43% drop in new rental contracts in Barcelona, 44% in Navarre and 51% in A Coruña.On employment, the report acknowledges a 66% increase in the minimum wage but describes it as leading to "unprecedented wage compression". It also claims unemployment figures are distorted by inactive workers on permanent seasonal contracts.The institute describes the period as "devastating" and criticises the state's response to crises including Covid-19, the DANA floods and the crisis in Ceuta as "non-existent".The report comes shortly after Sanchez called an early general election following the defeat of his government's decrees.

title: From tigers to turtles: The conservation success stories that prove there’s still hope for wildlife
description: “Biodiversity continues to be degraded at an alarming pace, yet amid these steep declines there are grounds for hope.”
content: Biodiversity continues to be degraded at an “alarming pace” – but experts insist there are still grounds for hope.New research from the WWF and the Zoological Society of London (ZSL) warns that there has been an average 73 per cent drop in the size of monitored wildlife populations over a 52-year period. The Living Planet Index (LPI) tracks how species populations are faring around the world and is based on almost 35,803 population trends and 5,790 species of vertebrates (amphibians, birds, fish, mammals and reptiles).Its latest findings, published in WWF’s Living Planet Report (LPR) 2026, show an average decline of monitored wildlife populations of 2.5 per cent between 1970 and 2022.The LPI uses changes in population sizes to establish whether, on average, the relative abundance of monitored vertebrate species has increased, decreased or stayed the same. It does not mean that there are 73 per cent fewer wild animals in total today than in 1970.What is causing wildlife population declines?The new research warns that habitat loss and degradation are the most frequently reported threats affecting monitored wildlife populations, followed by overexploitation, climate change, pollution, invasive species and disease.“These threats are, in turn, driven by broader systemic failures across the food, energy and finance systems,” the report states. The steepest declines are seen in Latin America and the Caribbean, Africa and Asia and the Pacific. In both Europe and North America, large-scale impacts on nature had already taken place and biodiversity was in a poorer state by the baseline year of 1970, which explains why there is less of a negative trend in these regions.‘Progress is already underway’Despite the stark findings, the report highlights the effectiveness of conservation efforts – arguing that there is still time to buck the trend.Tigers are one of the clearest examples. In 2010, only around 3,200 wild tigers remained and the species seemed to be heading rapidly towards extinction. But by last year, the population had grown to roughly 5,700 – marking a 70 per cent increase. Atlantic bluefin tuna were also destined for a similar fate, with numbers collapsing from decades of overfishing. Now, populations have recovered to the point where neither is considered threatened. Over in South Africa, elephants are stable or growing in many of the places where local communities lead the management of the land they share with them. And last year, the green sea turtle became the first marine turtle ever to be downlisted from Endangered to Least Concern, following decades of conservation efforts.“Biodiversity continues to be degraded at an alarming pace, yet amid these steep declines there are grounds for hope,” says Dr Kirsten Schuijt, director general of WWF International. “The report highlights evidence that many species populations are stable or recovering, alongside inspiring stories that show nature can rebound and change is possible.”Dr Schuijt credits years of “sustained collective conservation” for recoveries in populations of tigers, tigers, bluefin tuna and green turtles.She adds: “To continue and expand these conservation successes, the industries and systems that drive nature loss need to be transformed. “Progress is already underway. Not everywhere, and not yet at the scale required, but enough to demonstrate that change is possible. It's time to accelerate the scale of those systemic changes already underway and work together in harmony with nature to build a more sustainable, equitable and resilient world.”The three systems driving biodiversity lossWhile the report acknowledges the importance of these recoveries, it argues that they sit inside a “much larger set of forces” driving biodiversity loss in the opposite direction. The first: the way the world produces and uses energy.“Burning coal, oil, and gas to power homes, transport and industry generates roughly three-quarters of the greenhouse gas emissions driving climate change, which has now become a driver of biodiversity loss across every ecosystem on Earth,” the report says.The second is the way the world produces and consumes food. Agriculture is the single largest cause of habitat loss and degradation and the leading driver of biodiversity decline.“The third is the financial system,” the report explains. “Capital allocation – the decisions about which industries receive investment and which do not – determines which activities grow and which shrink.”In 2023, around $7.3 trillion (€6.5t) flowed into activities that harm nature, while just $220 billion (€197b) went towards activities that protect or restore it. “Until that ratio shifts, the underlying drivers of biodiversity loss will continue to be funded,” the report says. Positive tipping pointsExperts say that transforming these systems, even if it feels “impossible”, can trigger positive tipping points. This occurs when a threshold is crossed and change accelerates.The clean energy transition is a clear example of this. Decades ago, a technology like solar power was used in pocket calculators and satellites.Now, it is the cheapest source of new electricity generation in most countries – one that is cushioning Europe’s energy price shock from the war on Iran.Last year, solar generated 13.1 per cent of EU electricity, outpacing coal and coming close to competing with gas. Together with wind, solar generated more EU electricity than fossil fuels for the first time in 2025.“Every phase of the transition has produced resistance from industries and political interests whose dominance is threatened by it,” the report says. “In recent years, that resistance has intensified in some parts of the world. The pushback is part of how transformations work, and it indicates that the change has become disruptive enough to matter. Moving through this phase takes resilience, a willingness to adjust and the determination to keep going.”

title: OE2027: youth housing guarantee stays, defence hits 2.15% of GDP, €1m for AI
description: The government on Thursday submitted to parliament the 2027 state budget, projecting 2% growth and a surplus of 0.1–0.2% of GDP. Approval is assured, as the PS will abstain in the key vote.
content: On Thursday afternoon the Government submitted to Parliament the draft State Budget law for 2027, two days before the deadline, after approving it this morning in the Council of Ministers.The document was handed over by the Minister of Finance, Joaquim Miranda Sarmento, to the Speaker of the Assembly of the Republic, José Pedro Aguiar-Branco.The third State Budget of Luís Montenegro's government has its passage once again guaranteed by the Socialist Party (PS).The Socialist leader, José Luís Carneiro, announced last week the intention to abstain in the first overall vote, which takes place on 28 October, after the prime minister, Luís Montenegro, gave assurances on four conditions set by the Socialists: a constitutional review with PS and PSD playing a central role, protection of current and future pensions, funding for investments left unfinished after the RRP, and support for the recovery of municipalities and regions affected by storms.The detailed debate and vote will run between 29 October and 24 November, with the final overall vote scheduled for 24 November.The PCP and the Left Bloc have already announced that they will vote against the Government's proposal. Chega has also threatened to vote against (source in Portuguese)if the prime minister refuses to lower the retirement age, and has put forward an additional demand to cut VAT on fuels and apply zero VAT to a basic basket of essential foodstuffs. These are red lines the Government has already rejected.The remaining parties have not yet announced how they will vote.The President of the Republic, António José Seguro, said on Thursday that he hoped for a "fruitful debate" to improve people's lives "at a very difficult time".Speaking to journalists in Parliament after meetings with the parties on the Budget proposal, the Minister of Finance, Joaquim Miranda Sarmento, declined to say how much room there was for negotiations.The Government estimates that the economic measures already adopted, which will continue to affect the public finances in 2027, will have a impact of 4.8 billion euros next year, still without taking into account any new policies to be included in the next Budget.As for the macroeconomic scenario for next year, the Government is forecasting economic growth of 2%, in line with the pace seen in recent years, but representing a slight slowdown compared with the 2.3% expected for this year.The Government is projecting a budget surplus of 0.1% of gross domestic product (GDP) next year.In the document, the Ministry of Finance raises its inflation forecast for this year to 2.9% and expects a slowdown to 2.3% in 2027.The Government also projects that public debt will fall to 84.5% of GDP in 2027, three percentage points less than the 87.5% estimated for this year.The cost of financing public debt will weigh more heavily on the state's accounts, with the bill for interest rising by 23.2% to 8,217 million euros. That is equivalent to 2.4% of GDP, compared with 2% in 2026 and 2025.Pensions, public-sector wages and debt interest are among the main sources of pressure, alongside tax measures such as the updating of personal income tax brackets, the reduction of the corporate tax rate and housing measures.Measures on personal, corporate and property taxesThe Minister of Finance said that the 2027 Budget provides for a further cut in personal income tax, through the updating of tax brackets, the specific deduction and the minimum subsistence threshold, mechanisms which by law have to be adjusted.The PSD/CDS-PP government has decided to lower personal income tax rates in the first to sixth brackets by between 0.3 and 0.5 percentage points, a measure with an estimated impact of 400 million euros, which will already be reflected in withholding tax in 2026.The reduction will be 0.3 percentage points in the first bracket, 0.5 percentage points from the second to the fifth brackets, and again 0.3 percentage points in the sixth bracket.The rates remain the same as those presented in September 2026, with retroactive effect.The proposal also confirms a 3.88% update of personal income tax brackets next year, below the 4.5% pay rise in the private sector set out in the social concertation agreement.In practice this means there is a risk that the tax burden will increase for taxpayers whose pay rises exceed 3.88%. Anyone earning more may be pushed into a higher tax bracket, paying more tax and seeing all or part of their pay rise eroded.The minimum income exempt from personal income tax in the 2027 State Budget will track the minimum wage. The annual reference value for the minimum subsistence income is 13,580 euros, which divided by 14 months corresponds to 970 euros, the planned minimum wage in 2027.Productivity bonuses, performance bonuses, profit-sharing and year-end bonuses will also be exempt from personal income tax "up to a limit of 6% of the worker's annual basic pay", according to the 2027 State Budget proposal.The Government estimates that corporate tax revenue will fall by 99 million euros in 2027 compared with the projected outturn for 2026, a drop of 1%."This trend reflects the 1 percentage point cut in the corporate tax rate, whose impact on revenue should be partially offset by the expected growth in economic activity," the document states.The revenue impact of the one percentage point cut is 300 million euros.Last year the general corporate tax rate fell from 20% to 19%, which is the rate applied to companies' 2026 profits.In 2027 the general rate will be cut by another point, from 19% to 18%, but this rate will apply only to 2027 profits, with an impact on the public finances in 2028.The Government's goal is to bring the corporate tax rate down to 17% by 2028, cutting it by one percentage point a year. The rate will be 15% on the first 50,000 euros of profit for micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs).The corporate tax break for companies that increase average wages by at least 4.5% will also remain in place next year.The proposal includes a 2.3% increase in the brackets of municipal property transfer tax (IMT) on the purchase of an urban property or autonomous unit used exclusively for housing, whether or not it is a primary residence.The purchase of property up to 108,792 euros in value for use as a primary residence will be exempt from IMT. This represents an increase of 2,446 euros compared with this year's threshold of 106,346 euros.The Government also expects to raise an extra 300 million euros in taxes in 2027 from anti-fraud measures on fuel approved this year.The State Budget proposal also envisages a 5.2% increase in receipts from the tax on petroleum products (ISP), reaching 3,796 million euros. The Government attributes this growth to private consumption. For 2026, ISP revenue is expected to be 3,610 million euros.The Government is also forecasting for 2027 an increase of 139 million euros (8.1%) in revenue from tobacco tax, rising to 1,864 million euros.Revenue from the tax on alcohol, alcoholic beverages and drinks with added sugar or other sweeteners (IABA) is expected to grow by 27 million euros (7.5%), to 392 million euros.Minimum income, minimum wage and civil serviceThe document also confirms a 50-euro increase in the solidarity supplement for the elderly (CSI) in 2027, with the reference amount rising to 720 euros.The Government's programme envisages this reaching 870 euros in 2029, up from the current 670 euros.This strengthening of the CSI will have an impact of 100 million euros entered in next year's Budget.Total social security spending on support for the most vulnerable older people is budgeted at 709 million euros in 2027, 38 million more than the amount budgeted last year.A rise in the minimum wage from 920 to 970 euros is also planned. The tripartite agreement on pay and economic growth for 2025-2028, signed in October 2024 between the Government, the four employers' confederations and the UGT, revised upwards the trajectory of the national minimum wage. The agreement provides for annual increases of 50 euros, with the aim of reaching 1,020 euros in 2028.In the civil service, the multi-annual agreement in force provides for pay rises of 2.30% in 2027, with a minimum increase of 60.52 euros.If the planned rise in the agreement goes ahead, the minimum wage in the public administration should increase to 995.51 euros in 2027.The agreement also provides for an increase in the meal allowance, currently set at 6.15 euros, of 15 cents a year until 2029.State guarantees maintained in 2027The Government has also decided to maintain support for access to first homes, including the public guarantee on mortgage loans and IMT and stamp duty exemptions for young people.The Government foresees the "continuation" of these measures, specifically "the public guarantee on the purchase of a first home, as well as IMT and stamp duty exemptions on the purchase of a first permanent home".According to Government data, these measures "have already benefited almost 120,000 young people", with an average purchase price of 200,000 euros.The public guarantee allows the state to act as guarantor for young people up to the age of 35 when they buy their first home as their main residence. It can cover up to 15% of the initial loan capital, allowing them to obtain 100% financing of the purchase price, without needing an upfront deposit.The IMT, stamp duty and registry fee exemptions on the purchase of a first home by young people up to the age of 35 have been extended to properties worth up to 338,141 euros.The Government also plans to strengthen Porta 65, the programme supporting young tenants, although the report does not say by how much the programme's allocation will increase, nor whether there will be changes to the eligibility criteria.Health budget to fall by 1.5% next yearIn the key policy areas, the health budget will total 17,858 million euros next year, 1.5% less than the total amount the Government expects to spend this year.According to the document, the health programme has a consolidated total expenditure of 17,858.4 million euros for 2027, below the 18,125.9 million euros the Government expects to execute this year, including money from the Recovery and Resilience Plan (PRR).At least 15.5 billion euros will go to funding the National Health Service, 603.4 million euros (4%) more than estimated for this year. On the spending side, the largest share of the budget goes on the purchase of goods and services (8.4 billion euros), a line item the Government wants to cut by around 4.2% compared with this year's estimate.
