More than 30% of the urban population lives in inadequate conditions, according to the housing yearbook produced by CAF and the Lincoln Institute.The crisis also affects people who have built their own homes in neighbourhoods without basic services.In Madrid, aside from exceptions such as the Cañada Real settlement, the problem is mainly one of affordability: there are homes available, but often at prices wages cannot support.Across the cities examined, the common challenge is the gap between housing costs and what people earn. Lower prices alone do not make a home affordable if rent still consumes most of a worker’s income, leaving little for other essentials.

title: Mercedes global sales fall 6% as electric car sales hit record high
description: Mercedes-Benz shares fell after the German carmaker reported a 6% fall in global sales, driven by weakness in China. Sales outside China edged higher, supported by growth in Europe and North America.
content: Mercedes-Benz shares fell by 4% at around 1 pm CEST on Wednesday before paring their losses, after the firm announced sales of 491,700 cars and vans in the third quarter of 2026, 6% fewer than a year earlier.Growth in Europe and North America, alongside record battery-electric vehicle (BEV) sales, was not enough to offset weakness in China“Mercedes-Benz Cars achieved the highest quarterly BEV sales in the company’s history, led by the electric GLC, whose sales more than tripled compared with Q2,” said Mathias Geisen, the Mercedes-Benz board member responsible for sales and customer experience.Global sales in the car segment alone dropped 8% year on year to 407,200 vehicles.In Asia, Mercedes sold 25% fewer cars than a year earlier, a total of 132,300 vehicles. This was dragged down by a 31% decline in the Chinese market, where intense competition and challenging market conditions squeezed Mercedes’ sales, according to the carmaker. The best-performing models in China included the GLC and E-Class; together, these accounted for almost two-thirds of Mercedes-Benz Cars sales in the country.China accounted for almost a quarter of Mercedes-Benz’s global car sales in the second quarter, underlining the importance of the market to the German manufacturer.The latest decline follows a 30% fall in Chinese car sales in the second quarter. Mercedes cut its full-year car sales and group revenue forecasts in July, citing continued weakness in China, where tougher competition, subdued demand and changes to its model range had weighed on performance.Excluding China, group sales increased 2%, while car sales alone rose 1%. “Outside China, car sales increased for the third consecutive quarter in 2026,” Geisen said.Electric car sales reach record highGrowth in Europe and North America helped support sales. This came as interest in EVs grew significantly.Electric car sales rose 61% year on year globally to 68,400 vehicles, up 29% from the second quarter.In Europe, Mercedes-Benz Cars achieved record quarterly battery-electric vehicle (BEV) sales, up 78% year on year and 24% compared with the second quarter.“Our new electric models GLC, CLA, GLB and GLA are sold out in Europe for the rest of the year, with order books extending into 2027,” Geisen said.The company added that its plants in Bremen and Rastatt in Germany, and Kecskemét in Hungary, were operating on three-shift schedules to meet demand.Fully electric vehicles accounted for a record 16.8% of global car sales, up 7.2 percentage points from the prior-year quarter, according to Mercedes.Overall European car sales rose 5% to 168,700 vehicles. This was mainly driven by growth in Germany, where sales increased 13%, and the UK, where they rose 7%.In North America, Mercedes-Benz Cars sales increased 4% to 83,200 vehicles in the third quarter, with US sales rising 6%.In the first nine months of 2026, Mercedes-Benz sold 1,244,400 cars, down 7% from the same period a year earlier, while sales of fully electric cars rose 40% to 165,500 units.

title: Judo 2026 World Championships: Koga and Yusifov Strike Gold on Opening Day in Baku
description: Wakana Koga claimed her first world title at -48kg, defeating Assunta Scutto in the final. At -60kg, home favourite Ahmad Yusifov came from behind to beat Sherzod Davlatov, sending the Baku crowd into celebration on an unforgettable opening day.
content: Welcome to Baku, Azerbaijan, where new legends will rise to claim their red back patches at the Baku World Judo Championships 2026.At -48kg, Italy’s Assunta SCUTTO claimed her place in the final for the third time in a row with impressive judo all morning. Her third time in a World final, but could she take the gold for a second time?Meeting her there was Japan’s KOGA Wakana. The Japanese judoka was in fantastic form, with high quality judo throughout the day. KOGA already has a World bronze and silver, would this be the year to claim the missing gold? With every contest, she looked increasingly assured, carrying real momentum into the final.In the final the two experienced judoka clashed. It was a tightly fought contest, with neither judoka giving much away, before KOGA seized her opportunity on the ground. Calm under pressure, she converted the opportunity decisively to bring the contest to an emphatic close. It was KOGA who walked away crowned the World Champion. A breakthrough moment for the Japanese star.Azerbaijan National Olympic Committee Secretary General Mr Azer ALIYEV awarded the medals.In the -60kg, Ahmad YUSIFOV secured his first time in a World final here in his home nation. An impressive feat for the local favourite who was looking to claim his red backpatch. With the Baku crowd firmly behind him, the stage was set for a huge home final.Facing him was Kazakhstan’s Sherzod DAVLATOV, also in his first World final. Would DAVLATOV secure himself a place in history? The Kazakh had looked composed and dangerous throughout the day.YUSIFOV rose to the occasion in front of a passionate home crowd to claim victory. With the pressure at its highest, YUSIFOV came from a score down, sparking huge celebrations and creating what is sure to be one of the standout moments of this World Championships.International Judo Federation Executive Committee Member Mr Timur KEMELL awarded the medals.What an incredible first day here in Baku. Join us tomorrow in the land of fire.

title: DiscoverEU applications now open: Thousands of free travel passes for young Europeans up for grabs
description: Applications for the scheme are open until 15 October, giving eligible young Europeans the chance to explore the continent by train and other sustainable transport, with discounts on accommodation, culture and more.
content: If you’re 18 years old, living in an EU or Erasmus+ country, and are keen to explore Europe, you may be able to do just that – for no cost.Applications are now open for the European Union’s DiscoverEU scheme, which offers more than 40,000 free travel passes for young Europeans. The application process will close at midday Brussels time (CET) on 15 October 2026 and you can apply at youth.europa.eu.Here’s everything you need to know about the DiscoverEU programme. Thousands of passes for free travel will be awardedIf you were born between 1 January 2008 and 31 December 2008, and are a citizen or resident of the EU, Overseas Countries and Territories associated with the EU or third countries associated with the Erasmus+ programme, including Iceland and Türkiye, you’re able to apply to the schemeIf selected, you’ll receive a travel pass for the most environmentally friendly means of transport, including trains.You'll be able to travel for up to seven days within a one-month period, any time between 1 March 2027 and 31 May 2028. Lucky passholders will also receive a DiscoverEU discount card, which will offer numerous discounts on accommodation, culture, sports, local transport, and other services, making trips significantly more affordable. If you’re keen to travel with friends, that’s doable, too. If a group submits the application together, they may all be given the chance to travel for free.Where could your journey take you?The DiscoverEU Culture Route is a pre-planned itinerary covering destinations across Europe, with stops for everything from architecture, music and fine art to theatre, fashion, folk art and local food.Some of the cities featured have received European Commission recognition, including Cork in Ireland and Valletta in Malta, both named European Capitals of Culture.Others, such as Lyon in France, have been recognised for their efforts to improve accessibility for everyone, regardless of age, ability or mobility.Young travellers can also use DiscoverEU as a starting point for planning their own routes and exploring destinations that interest them.

title: A heavy lift: Thieves steal Dalí's 200kg diamond-studded 'Book of the Apocalypse' in France
description: Police in central France are searching for an art collector's book worth an estimated €1 million that was stolen from an art centre in Issoire in Puy‑de‑Dôme. The "Book of the Apocalypse", a 210‑kilo volume contains works by Salvador Dalí, Jean Cocteau and Bernard Buffet.
content: Another theft in the art world: the "Book of the Apocalypse", described as one of the most expensive (and heaviest) books in the world, was stolen from a private museum in Issoire, in Auvergne, overnight from Sunday to Monday, the Clermont-Ferrand public prosecutor’s office has said.The original and unique copy of this book, conceived by the Auvergne publisher Joseph Forêt, was designed as a total work of art inspired by the Apocalypse of Saint John.Weighing 210 kilos in total, this work made up of 150 parchments was produced between 1958 and 1961 by seven leading writers and seven leading painters of the time, among them Ossip Zadkine, Léonard Foujita, Jean Cocteau and Jean Giono. Salvador Dalí, for his part, sculpted the cover using the lost-wax casting technique.A work that has travelled the worldAfter being shown in nearly 150 exhibitions around the globe between 1961 and 1972, the book disappeared from view for several years. Stored in Switzerland, it was eventually sold to Japanese collectors.As they were preparing to auction it off, piece by piece, it was bought in 2003 by Christian Karoutzos, CEO of an art restoration company in Issoire. He decided to display the cover and several parchments in his contemporary art centre in the town until the autumn."It is a cathedral-like work, a masterpiece, unique in the world", the new owner lamented to ICI Pays d’Auvergne after the theft, adding that"France was murdered last night, French heritage was murdered"."This was a privately owned work kept in a small private contemporary art museum that also housed other, less valuable pieces", said Issoire’s mayor, Bertrand Barraud. He stressed that the loss was "incalculable" and that it was "the work of a lifetime".An investigation has been opened by the Clermont-Ferrand gendarmerie’s research unit. The work is estimated to be worth several million euros.It's the latest in a long line of high-profile art thefts in France which began with the daring broad daylight robbery at the Louvre in Paris on 19 October 2025, when thieves managed to steal royal French jewels valued at €88 million euros.

title: EU-China trade tensions: Five things to know as Brussels and Beijing face crunch talks
description: The next ten days will be critical for EU-China relations. EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič will travel to Beijing later this week for high-level talks aimed at rebalancing the trade relationship and securing “tangible” results ahead of next week’s meeting of EU leaders.
content: After months of tensions, relations between Brussels and Beijing are entering a crucial phase, with the European Commission having set October as a deadline to secure "tangible” results with Beijing to rebalance their trade relationship.The stakes are high for the EU, whose trade deficit with China has now reached a record €1 billion a day.Key talks will take place in Beijing at the end of this week between EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič and his Chinese counterpart, Wang Wentao. They will be followed next week by a meeting of EU leaders, with China set to top the agenda.For European policymakers, the diagnosis is increasingly clear: the situation is unsustainable, with a new wave of Chinese competition putting pressure on the EU’s industrial base two decades after China’s rapid economic expansion began — and putting thousands of jobs at risk.“A massive industrial shock is affecting sectors at the heart of the European industrial model and of systemic relevance [pharmaceuticals, aerospace, automotive, machine tools, chemicals, etc.],” reads a Franco-German document which was sent on Monday to capitals and Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.Ahead of these crucial ten days, Euronews takes a deep dive into the EU-China relationship. Here are five things to know.1. Brussels seeks a breakthrough in BeijingAfter several weeks of discussions held at a technical level between EU and Chinese officials, Šefčovič will travel to Beijing on Thursday and Friday for high-level political discussions with Wentao.Negotiations were launched last June, with the Europeans hoping to secure commitments from Beijing to rebalance the trade relationship. At the heart of the discussions is Chinese access to the EU market of 450 million consumers, with the Europeans seeking to protect EU industry from a wave of low-cost Chinese imports."Today we're losing thousands of jobs every week," EU Industry Commissioner Stéphane Séjourné told Euronews in an exclusive interview three weeks ago, adding that the EU had already lost 250,000 industrial jobs last year.The Europeans also want to secure exports of rare earths from China, which are essential for EU industry, after Beijing blocked them amid a trade war with the US in 2025. Exports eventually resumed, but the truce runs only until 10 January 2027.For the Commission, this week’s talks are essential, as EU leaders expect concrete results from the EU executive for their meeting next week.2. The German shiftEU member states’ approach to China has evolved since Germany came to recognise that its economy — the bloc’s largest — was increasingly exposed to Chinese competition. In 2024, Berlin opposed EU tariffs on low-cost Chinese electric vehicles (EVs). But in recent weeks, Germany has moved closer to France, which has taken a tougher stance and advocated stronger measures towards China.German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron called on Monday, in a letter to Commission President von der Leyen, for “the full use” of the EU’s existing trade defence instruments and for a “comprehensive framework” with new legal instruments.In a document accompanying the letter, they listed proposals, including a new tool that would be in the hands of the Commission to allow a “decisive and systemic reaction,” including measures that could lead to “an immediate cut-off from the internal market if needed.”The Commission would activate the tool unless a qualified majority voted against it. By introducing a reversed qualified majority voting system, the two leaders hope to make EU action easier and faster.However, among member states, Madrid remains one of the most cautious towards China, despite having sought Chinese investment for several years.Spain’s domestic political situation, with Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez calling for new elections, could nevertheless limit Madrid’s opposition to the EU’s strategy towards China.3. Industry is bracing for tougher measuresAcross Europe, European businesses are calling for tough action despite the risk of retaliation.They want the EU not only to protect European industry through trade policy, but also to reduce its dependence on China, given the bloc’s critical vulnerabilities. Beijing demonstrated the risks of these dependencies in 2025, when it restricted exports of rare earths and chips essential to the automotive industry amid a dispute involving Dutch-based Nexperia.The Federation of German Industries, the BDI, published a report on 25 September, saying that “systemic competition with China’s economy is increasingly calling into question the resilience of the open social market economy.”It added: “Even if de-risking entails costs — including in the form of countermeasures — inaction would be significantly more costly economically in the long term and irresponsible from a security policy perspective.”On 29 September, the Commission launched a consultation with EU businesses to help shape new measures, including a diversification tool aimed at addressing situations where reliance on a single supplier country poses a risk to the EU’s security of supply.4. Will China play ball in the negotiations?Since they began last June, negotiations between the Commission and Beijing have made little progress.Beijing wants to maintain access to the EU market, while the Commission is seeking to negotiate import quotas by product. However, China holds important leverage in the talks, as it has a global monopoly on the production and processing of rare earths, which are key to the EU’s green tech, defence and car industries.China already pushed back against a Commission proposal for “voluntary export restrictions” on EVs. On 20 September, a Chinese spokesperson said that such measures were contrary to the “principle of fair competition.”"China's position is consistent. Any solution between China and the EU must ensure a balance of interests, comply with WTO rules and their respective domestic laws, and fully accommodate the interests of industries on both sides," the spokesperson said.5. Is a trade war on the horizon?Tensions are mounting between the two sides, with both refraining from more aggressive moves.Before negotiations started in June, the EU had already proposed the so-called Industrial Accelerator Act and the Cybersecurity Act, restricting access to the EU market for Chinese companies, with Beijing threatening of retaliation.Since June, the Commission has continued to open probes into Chinese products over unfair trade practices, irritating Beijing, which over the summer forbade its companies from cooperating with Brussels on antitrust probes.According to several people familiar with the matter, EU countries are also holding back the launch of an investigation into the chemicals sector that could lead to safeguards — tariffs and quotas.Finally, last Saturday, China put pressure on the Europeans ahead of this week’s critical talks by launching an investigation into EU chemicals, suspecting dumping of EU p-nitrotoluene. The move follows an investigation by the EU, opened in September, into polyvinyl chloride imports from countries including China.

title: Why are Melania Trump staffers gloating about ‘Digger’ and its box office woes?
description: A senior advisor to Melania Trump posted a comparison online that doesn't make much sense...
content: What is it they say about one person’s misfortune...? Well, Melania Trump’s staff seem to be embracing that opportunistic sentiment with regards to Digger ’s woes at the box office. As reported earlier this week, Oscar-winning director Alejandro González Iñárritu’s Digger, starring Tom Cruise as a powerful oil tycoon who has triggered an environmental disaster, made just $8 million in the US and $20 million in total globally in its opening weekend.Considering Digger had a production budget of up to $180m (plus hefty marketing), this means the divisive film is on track to become one of 2026’s biggest flops with estimated losses projected at between $150-200 million. As if that wasn’t bad news enough, some are indulging in schadenfreude and getting their gloat on... Marc Beckman, a senior advisor to Melania Trump, posted a comparison online, stating that the Cruise-led satire had been outperformed by the biographical film Melania released earlier this year. “On a per-theater basis, MELANIA outperformed Tom Cruise’s DIGGER by approximately 67%, despite opening in roughly half as many theaters,” wrote Beckman on X. Granted, Melania was a hit in US cinemas for a non-fiction movie, eventually grossing $16.7 million. However, given that Amzon spent $40 million to acquire the documentary and a reported $35 million to market it, that still makes it a sizeable loss.Following Beckman’s post, many were quick to point out that the comparison between Melania and Digger was not appropriate. Check out some of the reactions below: Regardless of Digger ’s misfortunes, you have to hand it to Iñárritu and Cruise for delivering an ambitious piece of cinema.In Euronews Culture’s review of Digger, we said that the director had made “both the boldest film of 2026 and this year’s wildest misfire.”“It’s hard to write more about Digger without spoiling Iñárritu’s brave but misguided gambit, but safe to say that once he does pull the rug from under the audience, he leaves viewers with a boated folly that’s both hollow and heavy-handed.”We also noted how “high concepts are always to be applauded”, even if they end up feeling like "empty theatrics". Read the full review here.Conversely, when reviewing Melania at the start of the year, we wrote that it was a “self-congratulatory portrait of privilege, one singularly uninterested in mining anything beyond the surface” and that it was both a “despicable” and “soul-crushingly bleak”. Read the full review here. Put simply, compared to Melania, Digger is Citizen Kane. Back-handed compliment though that may be, that comparison feels apt.Euronews Culture interviewed documentary filmmaker Raoul Peck for his 2026 film Orwell: 2+2=5, in which the filmmaker said about the Melania film: “First of all, I wouldn't call that a film. It’s not even propaganda, because propaganda can be more intelligent. This is basically a publicity stunt. It’s a bribe.""This film happened because a network could spend $40 million to make it. I know many other filmmakers who would have loved to have that kind of money to make a more convincing film.”He added: “Ethically speaking, no documentarian would accept to make a film where the subject is the executive producer of the film and basically calling the shots. That's ethically unacceptable. That's why I cannot call it a film.”

title: Can Europe afford its defence boost? MEPs debate in The Ring
description: As security and hybrid threats are on the rise across Europe and the war in Ukraine enters its fifth year, the focus in Brussels is firmly on increasing defence spending. But who should pay, and how?
content: In this special live edition of The Ring from the Euronews Defence & Space Summit, Méabh Mc Mahon is joined by a live audience and leading European lawmakers — Belgian centre-right EPP member Wouter Beke and German social democrat Tobias Cremer.Both MEPs engage in a wide-ranging discussion, covering topics from national control and vetoes to the possibility of a European army and a proposed European Security Council.With defence budgets under the microscope, the debate in The Ring goes straight to the heart of the controversy: is the 5% of GDP target a necessary goal or a misleading obsession? And who ultimately pays the bill for rearmament as national control comes up against the prospect of a European Defence Union?Beke and Cremer discuss if Europe should aim to become capable of defending itself without America, and if so, how European that defence should be.Watch the full debate in the video above to see Europe's political heavyweights go face-to-face on how the continent prepares for an uncertain tomorrow.This special live episode of The Ring is moderated by Méabh Mc Mahon, produced by Luis Albertos Altarejos and Amaia Echevarria, and edited by Vassilis Glynos.

title: Czechia withdraws from Eurovision Song Contest 2027 citing budget pressures
description: Czech Television said in a statement: "We won't see the Czech flag on stage next year,” citing ongoing financial pressures.
content: Czechia will not take part in the upcoming 2027 Eurovision Song Contest in Burgas after its public broadcaster decided to withdraw, citing ongoing budget adjustments."In light of the ongoing budget adjustments, Czech Television has decided not to participate in the 2027 edition," the broadcaster announced on Tuesday."We assess each edition of the competition separately, and therefore do not want to speculate at this point about when Czech Television will participate in the Eurovision Song Contest again," the statement said."We know that Eurovision means a lot to all of us." The broadcaster said on X: "That's why we thank all the Czech representatives and, above all, you, the fans, for every vote, every comment, every cheer, and for being there with us."Czechia's withdrawal comes as Eurovision faces growing pressure and controversy over Israel's participation in the contest. Five countries - Iceland, Ireland, the Netherlands, Slovenia and Spain - withdrew from the 2026 contest over the issue.Ireland has already confirmed it will boycott Eurovision for a second year in 2027, citing the "appalling and ongoing loss of lives in Gaza".Ireland's national broadcaster RTÉ also said that they remain "deeply concerned by the continued denial of independent access to international journalists to the territory".Spain is also considering extending its boycott. RTVE president José Pablo López said that he would recommend that Spain remain out of the 2027 contest, saying it was “deeply painful” that Israel’s public broadcaster would remain eligible to compete "despite everything, and given this situation that is still being experienced in Gaza." A final decision has not been made by RTVE yet.Czech Television has not linked its decision to the controversy surrounding Israel's participation.Next year's Eurovision Song Contest will be held at the Arena Burgas in Burgas, Bulgaria.

title: IMF chief signals austerity is back as global public debt heads for 100% of GDP
description: IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva has urged heavily indebted governments to tighten their belts and central banks to take a hawkish stance, signalling a return to austerity as the energy shock from the Iran war, record public debt and a credit-fuelled AI investment boom weigh on the global economy.
content: The days when governments could lean on cheap money and fast growth to keep their debts in check are over, according to the head of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), who called for spending discipline and tighter monetary policy around the world.Speaking in Singapore on Wednesday, ahead of the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok next week, Kristalina Georgieva said policymakers "can no longer rely on higher growth rates alone to solve fiscal problems".Worldwide public debt is close to levels last seen after World War II and could top 100% of GDP before 2030, the IMF chief warned, singling out developed economies as the "worst offenders"."Yet, we don't see decisive action in the high-debt advanced economies where the need of the hour is for credible medium-term fiscal consolidation plans," Georgieva said, adding that "fiscal space is crying out for replenishment".Borrowing costs are already climbing, she noted, with 10-year government bond yields in the US, Germany and Japan at their highest levels since 2007, 2009 and 1996 respectively.On monetary policy, Georgieva described recent rate hikes by the US Federal Reserve, the European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan as "highly appropriate"."Now may be a good time for a prudently hawkish bias in many countries' monetary policy," she said.The IMF chief also warned that the global economy is being pulled in opposite directions by a negative energy supply shock from the Iran war and a positive demand shock from artificial intelligence, adding that "the combined impact of these two forces is highly uneven across the world".Oil prices remain at about $100 a barrel, she said, well above the $89 the IMF assumed for this year in its July forecasts, which put global growth at 3% in 2026 and 3.4% in 2027."Even if the war in the Gulf were to end soon, the problem of high energy prices will likely persist for some time," Georgieva said.An AI boom with risks attached"Love it, hate it, or fear it, AI is here," the IMF chief said, describing the technology as "rapidly becoming a key driver of countries' relative fortunes in the world economy".If done right, AI could lift global growth by as much as half a percentage point a year, according to IMF estimates.Over a decade, that would be like adding "an economy the size of ASEAN to the world economy", Georgieva said, referring to the Southeast Asian bloc.But she cautioned that "the AI building boom is inflationary", with spending on the technology, relative to the size of the economy, likely to outstrip past investment waves in railways, power grids and telecoms.A letdown for investors could become "a far-reaching shock," she warned.Georgieva also flagged dangers ranging from job losses and cyberattacks to cutting-edge models that could "escape human control and run amok".The IMF is due to publish updated global growth forecasts during next week's meetings in Bangkok.

title: India hikes interest rates for first time in over three years as Iran war fuels inflation
description: The Reserve Bank of India raised borrowing costs for the first time in over three years on Wednesday, as the Middle East war pushes up prices in Asia's third-biggest economy and weighs on an already fragile rupee.
content: India's central bank has switched to tightening, delivering a quarter-percentage-point increase as the fallout from the Iran war lifts prices and drags on the national currency.The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) lifted its benchmark repo rate, the rate it charges commercial banks for loans, by 25 basis points to 5.50%, with all six members of its monetary policy committee voting in favour.The move puts India alongside several other central banks that have tightened policy to rein in inflation or prop up their currencies.The RBI had kept rates on hold since the war erupted in February, as it gauged how swings in oil prices would affect the fastest-growing of the world's biggest economies.Robust economic growth in the last quarter gave policymakers room to turn their attention to rising prices in a country that relies on imports for the bulk of its energy, and where a poor monsoon threatens to push up food costs.Consumer price inflation climbed to 4.82% in August, exceeding the central bank's medium-term target of 4% for a third month in a row, and the data suggested price pressures were no longer confined to food and transport.The RBI is also contending with a sliding rupee, which has hovered close to all-time lows in recent days.To support the currency, it has introduced a series of measures to attract US dollars, among them a deposit scheme aimed at Indians living abroad that drew in about $127 billion (€113bn).Those efforts halted the rupee's slide for a time, but it has come under renewed strain as overseas investors keep selling Indian shares and oil prices hover near $100 per barrel.As the world's third-biggest oil importer, India usually gets around half of its crude via the Strait of Hormuz, a route that has been all but shut since the conflict began.That leaves India among the economies most exposed to a worldwide energy shock, analysts say, with costlier crude and fertiliser inflating its import bill.

title: Eva Marie Saint, ‘North By Northwest’ star and 'On the Waterfront' Oscar winner, dies aged 102
description: The Oscar-winning actress was one of the last stars of the Golden Age of Hollywood and was the oldest living Oscar winner.
content: Hollywood legend and acting royalty Eva Marie Saint has died aged 102.Saint, whose acting work lasted well into her 90s, died of natural causes at her home in Los Angeles on Tuesday, confirmed a family representative.Seen as one of the last stars of the Golden Age of Hollywood, Saint was best known for winning an Oscar for her feature film debut On The Waterfront and for her work on one of Alfred Hitchcock’s greatest films, North By Northwest.Born in Newark, New Jersey, on 4 July 1924, Saint studied acting at Bowling Green State University in Ohio. She started her career in television, making appearances in game shows and advertising segments.Her film career began in 1954, when she was cast opposite Marlon Brando in Elia Kazan’s celebrated drama On The Waterfront, playing Edie Doyle - whose brother's death sets the film's drama in motion. The film was nominated for 12 Academy Awards and ended up winning eight, including Best Picture, Best Actor for Brando, and Best Supporting Actress for Saint. A star was born and following her impressive debut, she starred in a musical adaptation of Thornton Wilder’s Our Town (1955) co-starring Paul Newman and Frank Sinatra; Bob Hope’s That Certain Feeling (1956); opposite Elizabeth Taylor and Montgomery Clift in Raintree County (1957); and in A Hatful of Rain, a pioneering drug-addiction drama which earned Saint further recognition and nominations at the Golden Globes and BAFTA.Then came the role that would go on to define her career: North By Northwest. Alfred Hitchcock’s 1959 masterpiece spy thriller saw her play Eve Kendall, the femme fatale, agent undercover opposite James Mason and love interest of Cary Grant.Even though North By Northwest was a huge hit and propelled her to stardom, Saint decided to limit her film work and spend time with her family. She had married director Jeffrey Hayden in 1951 and had two children.Still, her film career continued with memorable roles opposite Paul Newman in 1960’s Exodus and with Warren Beatty and Angela Lansbury in 1962’s All Fall Down. Other notable acting credits include John Frankenheimer’s hit racing drama Grand Prix, The Sandpiper, 36 Hours, and the comic satire The Russians Are Coming, The Russians Are Coming.In the 70s and 80s, Saint returned to television and recieved Emmy nominations for the 1977 miniseries How The West Was Won and 1978’s Taxi!!!. She also played the mother of Cybill Shepherd’s character in Moonlighting and the mother of Peri Gilpin’s Roz Doyle in Frasier.Later in her career, she played Superman’s mother Martha Kent in Superman Returns (2006) and made her final film appearance in 2014’s Winter’s Tale, starring Colin Farrell, Russell Crowe and Will Smith. In 2021, she played Marisa Tomei's aunt in the brief audio play “The Bus Ride”, part of The Pack Podcast.Saint’s husband Jeffrey Hayden died in 2016. She is survived by her two children, Darrell and Laurette, four grandchildren, Eli, Tyler, Molly, and Stella and two great grandchildren, Arlo and Finley.RIP Eva Marie Saint 1924 - 2026

title: Invasive plant spreads across Portugal and lengthens allergy season
description: Known for its showy plumes and used as an ornamental for decades, pampas grass, also known as Cortaderia selloana, is spreading, threatening biodiversity and raising vegetation management costs. Experts call for urgent action to halt its advance and reduce pollen exposure.
content: For decades, pampas grass, also known as Cortaderia selloana, was seen mainly as an ornamental plant. Its large feathery plumes made it a familiar sight in gardens and, more recently, in decorative arrangements indoors. But what many still regard as a showy plant is, in Portugal, an invasive alien species that can spread rapidly and has potential consequences for health.This invasive plant has already been identified in at least 208 municipalities in mainland Portugal, according to a study published in 2025 (source in Portuguese). The real number may, however, be higher, as existing maps depend on records submitted by people on the ground.The species’ spread is particularly visible along the coast. Areas where there used to be isolated specimens have been turning into zones densely occupied by the species, according to biologist Hélia Marchante, a lecturer at the School of Agriculture of the Polytechnic University of Coimbra and a specialist in invasive plants."It is a very, very fast-spreading species", she told Euronews. Unlike other invasive plants that can benefit from specific triggers such as wildfires, the plant also known as cortaderia has an especially effective advantage for spreading: "It only needs the wind."A plant that has learnt to escape the gardenThe history of the invasion helps explain how serious the problem has now become. Native to South America, cortaderia was introduced in different parts of the world as an ornamental plant. For decades, the fact that only female plants were present in gardens is thought to have limited its ability to reproduce.According to Marchante, that changed at the end of the last century, when hermaphrodite plants were introduced, 'almost certainly by accident', as "pollen donors". Fertilisation of the female plants then allowed the production of large quantities of seed."From then on it only needs the wind," the researcher said.The process repeats itself every year. During flowering, the plants that produce pollen release it into the atmosphere. In female plants, once fertilisation has taken place, each flower can give rise to a seed. The plumes end up acting as a kind of transport system: thousands of tiny seeds can be carried by the wind and colonise new sites.Spread does not depend solely on natural phenomena, however. People who move the plumes to use them as decoration, as well as vehicles, clothing or equipment, can also inadvertently help to carry seeds to other places."It is the movement of the plant itself that has the potential to spread it", warns Marchante, also pointing to cases where plumes are taken indoors.Pampas grass is no longer just an ornamental feature of the landscape. It is also an invasive species capable of altering the ecosystems where it becomes established. Once the species moves from isolated specimens to large stands, it becomes dense enough to exclude other plants, which can no longer survive in those areas.The impact extends to fauna as well, since the plant’s sharp leaves and the high density of the stands can make it harder for animals to move through.There are also less visible effects. According to Marchante, some studies show that the species can also alter nutrient cycles and modify the soil and the microorganisms that live in it.The problem goes beyond the environmentThe environmental dimension of the invasion is only part of the story. Cortaderia also has consequences for human health.Mário Morais de Almeida, an immunoallergology specialist and president of the World Allergy Organisation, explains that pampas grass belongs to the grass family and therefore releases pollen that can trigger symptoms in sensitised people."As this is a grass species, it will indeed release its pollen into the atmosphere, again carried by the wind, and it can cause significant allergic symptoms."The problem is particularly serious because of the time of year when cortaderia flowers. The grasses most familiar to Portuguese people are prominent in spring and early summer. Cortaderia can extend that exposure into late summer and autumn.For people with allergic rhinitis or conjunctivitis, exposure can lead to sneezing, itching, runny nose, congestion, red and watery eyes. In those with asthma, exposure can contribute to respiratory symptoms and more severe attacks."This grass, which can indeed release very, very large amounts of pollen, manages to do so throughout the summer, and even into autumn," says Morais de Almeida.However, the doctor stresses that there is currently no specific epidemiological evidence that would allow a given number of allergy cases in Portugal to be attributed to pampas grass. What exists is knowledge about grass allergies, clinical experience and evidence of the allergenic capacity of this species’ pollen."At the moment we do not have evidence that is directly linked to pampas grass," he notes, adding that there is nonetheless a perception that allergic complaints are lasting longer. According to the specialist, the combination of climate change, different types of pollen and other agents present in the atmosphere makes the picture more complex.Because the seeds are carried by the wind, the impact is not necessarily confined to the immediate vicinity of the plant. Marchante explains that the seeds can travel several kilometres, especially in conditions of strong wind, while the pollen can also be transported over long distances.There is another issue: people can unwittingly help to move the pollen around."People pick the plumes because they are very beautiful, they paint them, they take them home," the biologist explains. In addition to contributing to the spread of seeds, that behaviour can bring potentially allergenic material into homes.Morais de Almeida therefore offers an important piece of advice: do not take the plumes home and avoid handling the plant. On top of its allergenic potential, the leaves themselves are sharp enough to cause injuries."The pleasant appearance the plant may have" should not make people forget the risks associated with exposure to it, the doctor warns.The danger of letting another year passFor Marchante, one of the main challenges is precisely time. The more a plant grows and produces seed, the greater the likelihood that new individuals will emerge nearby and that the invaded area will expand."Each one that is left on its own in a more isolated area is another that will produce thousands of seeds, which will germinate and give rise to new plants next year," she explains, stressing that "if we fail to act now, next year it will be much, much more difficult, much more expensive and much worse to intervene".The strategy does not necessarily have to focus on trying to eliminate all the large stands that are already established in one go. The biologist argues for the identification and priority removal of isolated specimens and small clusters on the edges of the areas currently occupied. The aim is to prevent these hotspots from acting as new starting points for invasion of fresh territory.In some of the areas where the species has been established for longer, complete eradication will be much more difficult, if not practically impossible, the specialist believes. The alternative is control and ongoing intervention."What I think is that we still have a huge amount of work we can do, because there are so many places with small nuclei of individual plants," she says.The timing of intervention is equally important. Removing only the plumes after the seeds have already been shed can mean working without preventing the spread that has already occurred."To be sure of eliminating this plant, there has to be a window of time before May; it is during that period that it should be pulled out," she explains.And she has a clear message: "In fact, I say pull it up, pull it up by the roots, pull everything up, always pull it up; that is what we want."However, during the period when the seeds are being released, any intervention must be carried out in such a way as to avoid the control measures themselves contributing to their dispersal.Prohibited species still widespreadCortaderia has been on the Portuguese national list of invasive species (source in Portuguese) since 2019. The legislation bans, among other actions, its possession, planting, sale and introduction into the wild.In practice, however, it can still be found in private gardens, municipal spaces, industrial areas, roadsides and other locations.Marchante points to a lack of awareness of the law and a lack of enforcement as some of the obstacles to controlling the species.There is also a coordination problem. A municipality may remove plants from a garden under its management, only to find specimens in private plots or in infrastructure managed by other bodies.The invasion also has a socioeconomic dimension, as the presence of large cortaderia plants makes vegetation management more difficult and more expensive, particularly in areas where vegetation has to be cleared for wildfire prevention.There are already projects such as LIFE COOP Cortaderia (source in Portuguese), which brings together institutions in Portugal, Spain and France to fight this invasive species, and municipalities involved in control measures, but the researcher calls for a coordinated strategy.The Institute for Nature Conservation and Forests (ICNF) has drawn up a proposal for a National Action Plan for the Control of Cortaderia under Decree-Law No. 92/2019 (source in Portuguese), although its official publication and implementation have been delayed.The biologist hopes that the forthcoming National Action Plan against invasive alien species will set out priorities, responsibilities and ways of intervening.To make those measures effective, she argues that the plan should be accompanied by funding mechanisms enabling municipalities, non-governmental organisations, parish councils, road management bodies and even private citizens to cover the costs of removal."To remove one of the big cortaderia plants, you often need a mini excavator," she notes, stressing that the size of some specimens makes control operations costly, and not everyone can afford them.What can you do if you come across cortaderia?For citizens, the first recommendation is not to plant or move the species. Anyone who has cortaderia in their garden should seek to remove it, ideally with technical support if it is a large specimen.People who spot specimens in public spaces can also help to build knowledge about the species’ distribution. Hélia Marchante recommends using the iNaturalist (source in Portuguese) platform, where it is possible to photograph a plant and record its location. These data help build maps that can then be used to set priorities for action."That is very important when strategies are being drawn up to eliminate it," she stresses.While the plant has not yet been removed, cutting the plumes before the seeds are released can help to curb dispersal. But that is only a temporary measure. "Removing the plumes does not solve the problem," the biologist stresses. "The aim must always be to remove the whole plant."For people with respiratory allergies, Morais de Almeida also advises reducing exposure during periods of higher pollen concentration. In certain circumstances, wearing a mask and eye protection may be useful, along with sticking to medication prescribed for diagnosed allergic disease."We know that early in the morning and later in the afternoon are the times when pollen levels are highest, so at those times we should avoid airing or ventilating our homes; otherwise we may be contaminating the indoor environment. If we are travelling by car, we should probably keep the windows closed; if we are on a motorbike, we should opt for a full-face helmet and wear goggles," the immunoallergology specialist recommends.The doctor also draws attention to specific weather conditions. During storms, humidity can contribute to the fragmentation of pollen grains, making them easier to inhale, which can worsen respiratory symptoms in sensitised individuals.

title: UBS only European bank in top 10 of AI adoption as JPMorgan Chase leads
description: UBS is now the only European lender among the top 10 banks judged most advanced in adopting artificial intelligence, after HSBC dropped out of the top tier of the Evident AI Index, while JPMorgan Chase widened its lead and North American banks tightened their grip.
content: Switzerland's UBS stands alone for Europe in the top ten of an annual league table measuring how far major banks have gone in putting AI to work, as North American lenders led by JPMorgan Chase pull further ahead.The ranking, published on Tuesday by Evident, a firm that tracks AI adoption in financial services, rates 50 large lenders in North America, Europe and Asia-Pacific using only public data.Banks are deploying the technology to catch fraud, write software, vet loans and help advisers serve clients, and the 50 lenders have made public over 1,100 distinct uses of AI since 2021.They are scored on AI talent, which carries the most weight, as well as innovation such as research and patents, leadership focus and transparency on responsible use.UBS climbed one place to sixth this year, while London-headquartered HSBC, eighth in 2025, slipped to 11th.European banks dominate the next ten places, including British lenders Lloyds Banking Group, unchanged in 15th, NatWest in 17th and Barclays, which rose four places to 19th.JPMorgan Chase, which ranked in the top two in all four categories, widened its lead over second-placed US lender Capital One. Royal Bank of Canada was third and Australia's CommBank fourth, with six US and two Canadian banks in the top ten.Evident found that the banks' AI capabilities improved almost three times as fast over the past year as in the three preceding years on average, the quickest progress since it began measuring in 2023."This was the year AI in banking went industrial," said Alexandra Mousavizadeh, Evident's co-founder and co-CEO.Hiring, not firingEvident also challenged the idea that AI will gut bank workforces, finding that the leaders are still recruiting AI specialists and prioritising growth over job cuts.That contrasts with London-based Standard Chartered, which said in May it would cut around 7,800 back-office jobs by 2030 as it leans on AI and automation.Software implementation roles grew 4.3% across the 50 banks over the past year.US bank Morgan Stanley is reinvesting more than one million developer hours freed up by its DevGen.AI platform rather than trimming IT teams, while UBS's STAAT Insights tool saves its advisers roughly 1,200 hours a week."Roles are changing, and some are not being backfilled, but the banks at the top of our Index are growing, and growing headcount," Mousavizadeh stated.Twelve banks now report a realised or projected return on AI, up from eight, including newcomer Lloyds, which said in January that generative AI delivered around £50 million (€58.8mn) in value in 2025 and should add more than £100 million (€117.6mn) this year."With AI budgets at record levels, the banks that can prove their returns will keep the money flowing to the right places," said Daniel Shackleford Capel, managing director of banking at Evident.Amid growing concern over keeping ever more capable AI under control, 80% of the leading banks have advanced safeguards, such as checks on the data that models use and the answers they give, against 40% of the remaining banks in the index.In the EU, AI used to assess people's creditworthiness is classed as high-risk under the AI Act, though the rules for such systems were pushed back in July to December 2027.Evident plans to add a fifth pillar to the index in 2027, measuring the outcomes banks actually achieve from AI.

title: These are the best wine regions in Europe, with Slovenia claiming top spot above France and Italy
description: Štajerska, praised for its authenticity and centuries of wine culture, beat out more than 90 leading territories for the title.
content: A new ranking has just revealed the best wine regions in Europe, and oenophiles should take note, because number one went to a spot in Slovenia.Crowned by European Best Destinations, Štajerska beat out more than 90 leading wine territories across countries including France, Italy, Spain, Portugal, Germany, Austria, Hungary, Greece and Georgia.Regions were evaluated on things like the diversity of grape varieties and wine styles, the number of cellars, tasting rooms and wine rooms, the beauty of the landscape, sustainability and accessibility, among others.Štajerska – which covers Maribor, Ptuj, Jeruzalem Slovenija, Haloze, Slovenske gorice, Ravno polje and Pohorje – topped the list thanks to its “remarkable wine stories”.“Štajerska represents exactly what today’s travellers in Europe are increasingly looking for: authenticity, exceptional landscapes, centuries of wine culture, outstanding expertise and, above all, a very strong regional identity,” Maximilien Lejeune, director of European Best Destinations, said.“From the World’s Oldest Vine in Maribor to the historic wine cellars of Ptuj, from wine roads and vineyards to the people who keep these traditions alive, wine here is much more than a product.”Other wine regions in Europe making the cutItaly’s Langhe-Roero-Monferrato took second place, with European Best Destinations highlighting its Nebbiolo red wine grape variety and its truffles as reasons to visit, particularly in autumn.Third place went to Ribeira Sacra in Spain, praised as being “one of Europe’s most dramatic wine landscapes” with terraces carved into the canyon walls of the Sil and Miño rivers.For fans of Riesling and Grüner Veltliner, Kamptal in Austria, which came out fourth overall, is the place to be.Rounding out the top five is Chianti Rufina in Tuscany, the “quieter, more intimate sibling of Chianti Classico”. The top 12 wine regions in Europe Štajerska, SloveniaLanghe-Roero-Monferrato, ItalyRibeira Sacra, SpainKamptal, AustriaChianti Rufina, ItalySancerre and Pouilly-Fumé, FranceEtna, ItalySaumur and Anjou, FranceWachau, AustriaValle d'Aosta, ItalyAlentejo, PortugalNaoussa, Greece

title: Judo: Japan crowns two new world champions in Baku
description: Akari Omori claimed her first world title at -57kg, defeating reigning champion Eteri Liparteliani in golden score. At -73kg, Ryuga Tanaka overcame Makhmadbek Makhmadbekov in a tight final to secure gold and complete a double triumph for Japan.
content: It’s day three of the 2026 World Championships here in Baku.International Judo Federation President Mr Marius Vizer and CEO of CBH Bank, Mr Simon Benhamou, signed a sponsorship agreement.And an MOU was signed between the IJF General Treasurer Dr Naser Al Tamimi and the International Police Sports Union Secretary General, Gonzalo LondonoAs the National Gymnastics Arena filled, fans were treated to the chance to meet some of their judo heroes, before settling in for another fantastic day of competition.Current World Champion, Eteri LIPARTELIANI made it to the final once again at -57Kg.LIPARTELIANI provided some of the highlight throws of the day!Trying to take the title was Japan’s Akari OMORI. Throughout the prelims, OMORI showed how dangerous she can be in standing and groundwork. Her toughest fight came from teammate Momo TAMAOKI. A huge victory on the road to the final.In a tense final that entered golden score, OMORI showed her dominance on the ground, successfully turning over and holding down the current world champion to take the title.CBH Bank CEO Mr Simon BENHAMOU, Awarded the medals.At -73KG, TANAKA Ryuga had a tough draw, but after successfully defeating the category’s top seed, a waza-ari score in the semi-final put him in contention for gold.World number 3, Makhmadbek MAKHMADBEKOV of the UAE already has a World bronze, and today he was hoping to finally take the top spot. A fantastic display of skill and power in the preliminaries made that look possible.The final was another close battle, with just a single score enough to take the victory.It was TANAKA who struck the winning blow, an incredible driving ouchi-gari, taking down MAKHMADBEKOV for a yuko score. Two new world champions for Japan, crowned on Day 3!General Treasurer of the International Judo Federation Mr Naser AL TAMIMI awarded the medals.We’ll see you tomorrow for Day 4.

title: UK trial of three Iranians over alleged plot to target Iran dissident journalists
description: In London three Iranians go on trial accused of targeting UK-based journalists opposed to the regime in Tehran
content: Opening the trial the prosecution alleges the three men were Iranian spies, conducting surveillance of journalists at a UK-based Persian news channel critical of the government in Tehran, with the intention of physically harming and intimidating.Mostafa Sepahvand, 41, Farhad Javadi Manesh, 46, and Shapoor Qalehali Khani Noori, 57, went on trial in Woolwich Crown Court on charges of engaging in conduct likely to assist Iran’s foreign intelligence service between August 2024 and March 2025.Prosecutor Bill Emlyn Jones said people criticize Iran “at their peril” and that Iran International, a London-based satellite channel, had “come under particular attack” for its opposition to Tehran. He reminded jurors that former leader Ayatollah Khomeini ordered the death of Salman Rushdie in 1989 for his novel “The Satanic Verses,” and noted the vicious 2022 stabbing of the author in New York.The three men have denied the two charges brought against them under Britain's National Security Act.This new law was passed to give the British authorities additional powers to counter threats posed by foreign states.'Ultimate aim': expose them to 'serious violence'The trial of the three men has opened at a time when tensions between Britain and Iran have been rising. Prosecutors say Iran has repeatedly targeted its critics and opponents both inside the country and abroad.According to reports from the trial the three defendants had investigated at least two journalists working for Iran International, visited addresses linked to them, and taken photographs and video footage in preparation for an attack that Sepehvand was to carry out.The group is accused of spying on journalists Mojtaba Pourmohsen and Kambiz Hosseini, both journalists for Iran International, as well as Jonathan Turner, a founding member of U.K. Lawyers for Israel, crown prosecutor Emlyn Jones said.He added: "Their ultimate aim was that one of these individuals, and perhaps more than one, should be exposed to serious violence, an act which was undoubtedly in retaliation for their criticism of the Iranian government, and also intended to create fear and to try to silence others."He told the court that all three defendants have admitted going to the locations and taking images, but they disagree over why they did so.AP news agency, citing the prosecution case, reports that Javadi-Manesh and Nouri have said they did not know their actions would assist Iranian intelligence, while Sepehvand has admitted he was aware of this but claims he was forced to act "under coercion or threat".

title: Fuel prices in Italy: tax cuts end, diesel rises and hauliers threaten strikes
description: With tax breaks expiring and the decree on flexible excise duties delayed, diesel prices are rising again. The haulage sector warns of a strike as the government summons oil companies that have introduced initial capped prices.
content: Diesel will once again cost €0.61 more per litre from Tuesday, after the expiry at midnight of the latest tax discount on fuel. In the absence of the ministerial decree due to be published in the Official Gazette, the much-heralded mechanism of "accise mobili" remains on hold.Filling up at the pump is officially more expensive, marking the complete end of fuel tax cuts for the first time since last March, when the first decree was adopted in the wake of the outbreak of the conflict between the United States and Iran.Despite assurances in recent days about the activation of the mobile excise duty, the joint decree from the Ministry for the Environment and Energy Security and the Ministry of Economy and Finance did not arrive in time.The mobile excise duty is designed to reuse the extra VAT revenue generated by the previous month’s crude oil price increases. Unlike discounts financed directly from the public purse, this system does not add to the deficit, but it only allows for smaller reductions in prices.The excise rate on diesel therefore returns to its standard level. This is the final step in a phase-out that began on 26 September, when the original discount of €0.122 per litre had already been halved.On the government’s table, the issue of targeted measures for low-income households and haulage operators also remains unresolved, with no political agreement reached so far.Palazzo Chigi had announced its intention to scrap across-the-board fuel cuts, which mainly benefit wealthier people who consume more, in favour of targeted aid for those categories most exposed to rising prices.Hauliers sound the alarmThe end of the subsidies has prompted a backlash from the logistics sector. Assotir has issued a "cry for help", highlighting the dramatic situation facing companies."Road haulage is going through a dramatic time and if it does not come to a halt in protest, it will grind to a halt because of the price of diesel," said Assotir president Anna Vita Manigrasso.The association’s secretary-general, Claudio Donati, has not ruled out a sector-wide strike."It is a last-resort weapon because it means bringing the country to a standstill. We would like to avoid it, but in the absence of answers the government will have to reckon with us," he said.The response from government and businessIn a bid to curb the impact of the international situation, Business and Made in Italy Minister Adolfo Urso and Environment and Energy Security Minister Gilberto Pichetto have summoned the main refining operators, including Eni, IP, Q8, Saras and Isab, to Palazzo Piacentini on Thursday to consider boosting domestic production.At the same time, private companies have begun to move. Since 28 September Eni has introduced a price cap of €2.19 per litre for diesel and €1.99 for petrol, for 30 days across the Enilive network.Similar initiatives to cap prices or apply tiered discounts have also been launched by IP and Q8, covering more than 11,000 service stations, over half of the national network.Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has welcomed the response from the oil groups and thanked "all those who are making an effort at a difficult time".The overall outlook remains uncertain, clouded by warnings from Brussels of a "difficult winter" due to energy costs, which are pushing the European Union to consider postponing until 2028 the rules to curb methane leakage from energy imports.

title: These are the easiest countries for digital nomads, according to a new study
description: Holafly’s Digital Nomad Friction Index 2026 looked at factors such as visa complexity, banking access, healthcare and cost of living.
content: Becoming a digital nomad is a goal for many remote workers, but the hoops you have to jump through to achieve it vary from place to place.Bureaucracy can be a beast in any country, but certain destinations are making it easier for those who want to set up shop abroad.Now, we know exactly which places are doing so thanks to Holafly’s Digital Nomad Friction Index 2026.The eSIM company analysed 17 popular digital nomad destinations, looking at factors such as visa complexity, banking access, healthcare, connectivity, cost of living and disruption risk, in order to create an overall friction score.“Arriving to a country is usually the easy part. The real burnout happens when remote professionals hit a wall of post-landing bureaucracy, lost work hours, and unstable internet,” Metin Kastro, COO at Holafly, said.“We ran this study to shed light on these hidden friction points because long-term mobility only works when everyday logistics stop eating into people’s livelihoods and peace of mind.”The easiest countries to set up in as a digital nomadAfter all the number crunching, one destination came out on top with the lowest friction score: Georgia.The Caucasus nation has no mandatory residence registration, no tax ID requirement, and you can open a bank account with just a passport within hours, making it a bureaucratic breeze.Next up is Peru, which came in second place to its Rentista residency category which allows for indefinite permanent residency with a low income threshold. It was beaten out for the top spot because of its earthquake and El Niño exposure.Third place went to South Africa, which has no mandatory address registration or tax ID for non-residents, but was let down by its below-average healthcare score.Thailand and Malaysia are in fourth and fifth place respectively, with purpose-built digital nomad visa programmes and moderate banking friction as pluses, but natural disaster exposure among the negatives.The only European nations to make the top 10 were Croatia, Hungary and Poland, in seventh, eighth and ninth place respectively. All three have nomad visa programmes, but mandatory registration and tax ID requirements held them back from securing a higher spot.The top 10 countries for pain-free digital nomad set-upGeorgiaPeruSouth AfricaThailandMalaysiaVietnamCroatiaHungaryPortugalUAE

title: Shooting and scoring: Photographer Alex Pantling on capturing the world’s greatest footballers
description: Getty photographer Alex Pantling reported on the FIFA World Cup 2026 and shared with European Lens his reflection on the experience along with some of his favourite shots from the tournament.
content: What does it take to photograph the greatest footballers on the planet, in action, on the world's biggest stage?Getty photographer Alex Pantling has spent more than a decade capturing sport’s biggest moments, from FIFA World Cups and Champions League nights to Formula 1 and the Olympic Games. Along the way, he has photographed some of the most recognisable athletes in the world, including F1 racing driver Max Verstappen, footballers, Lionel Messi, Cristiano Ronaldo, Harry Kane, and 19-year-old superstar Lamine Yamal.This summer’s World Cup gave him some of his most striking football images yet. As he told Euronews Culture, capturing those moments is less about luck than preparation meeting instinct: "You can plan, you can have ideas in your head, but you've got to react when those ideas change in the moment."After this summer's unforgettable World Cup, we caught up with Pantling to discuss his path into photography, the challenges of working at the highest level of sport, and the stories behind some of his favourite images from the 2026 tournament.Could you tell me briefly how you got into photography, and the path that led you to sports photography?Alex Pantling: I always knew I wanted to be involved in sport. Originally it was kind of a fluke, to be honest. At school I actually wanted to do architecture, but the way subjects were bracketed meant I couldn't do architecture and the sport-related subject I wanted at the same time. I also found out architecture was a seven-year course at university, which put me off a little.Someone suggested photography, so I thought, I'll give that a go - which I know isn't the romantic story you're hoping for. But I gave it a go and absolutely loved it. Then I realised there was a job that combined my two passions: sport and photography.So I pushed that further and went to university at Nottingham Trent. At the start of the course I wasn't really photographing sport yet - it was predominantly an art photography course, so I was doing still life, street photography, portraiture, that kind of thing.In my second year, I had a tutor from Italy who'd been at Nottingham Trent in the same year as a colleague of mine, Julian Finney. She put me in touch with Julian, which led to work experience at Getty with another photographer, Michael Regan - one of our best football photographers. And from there, it led into a job with Getty.How much of your work is careful planning, and how much is reacting in the moment?You plan everything, but reacting is more important, because what you plan never actually happens - let's be honest. You might get to a game thinking you want to sit in a certain spot because of the light, or because you want to photograph a particular team attacking your side in the first half. Then the captains do the coin toss, they swap ends, or the rain comes - there are so many variables that change in football.I think that's why I love it. You never work the same day twice as a football photographer, because no game is the same. I might shoot Chelsea versus Tottenham again this year, but it won't be the same as last year or the year before. You can plan, you can have ideas in your head, but you've got to react when those ideas change in the moment.What changes when you're photographing a World Cup game versus a normal Premier League match?It does feel very different. The Premier League is amazing - I might be a little biased being English, but I think it's the greatest football league in the world, and it's incredible that we get access to it weekly working in the UK. But when you get to FIFA, it's something really special.It's not just the Argentinas, the Englands, the Frances - I was lucky enough to being doing Curaçao, smaller countries like this, which were almost as enjoyable because of how much it meant to them to be there, and to their fans. And I love that aspect. So yeah, in terms of how it changes: you're still doing the same job, but the emotion and the felling behind the pictures and games is completely different.Do you still feel nervous before these big games? You're there to capture huge moments and big players - is there a sense of pressure?Yeah, 100%. Take Messi, for example - I'm sure we'll come to that. You know he'll arguably be one of the greatest footballers to have ever lived, and in ten, twenty, thirty, forty years, people will look back on pictures of him playing. You've got the opportunity to take the pictures people are going to look at. I find that really exciting.In terms of nerves - yes, they're always there. Getting the goal picture, the celebration, being in the right place. But it does get easier with time. I was lucky enough to shoot the final of the Qatar World Cup, arguably one of the greatest football matches ever. I was up in the stands, and I remember Messi scoring his first goal - the penalty - on my side of the pitch, and my hands were literally shaking, I was so nervous about missing the shot. I think that was because it was my first World Cup, and there was a lot of pressure on me to do a good job so I could hopefully cover more of these. I don't have that same nervousness now, though there are still elements of it.So, let's take a closer look at some of your images you took from this year's World Cup. Your portrait of Austria's David Alaba in the tunnel is a very cinematic image - most of the frame is actually in darkness. What was the intention behind it?We get such great access from FIFA at these events. We're allowed in the tunnel before the game as the players walk out, and that always makes for iconic pictures - the two teams lined up, the referees, the ball kids, the players locked in, wearing their tracksuits. Those pictures are a little busier, there's a lot going on, and that's good in its own way for documenting the moment.But what I try to do - and I think a lot of my colleagues do too - is use the tunnel at half-time as an opportunity, rather than just before the game. This stadium, Kansas City Stadium, was probably my favourite to work in. The tunnel the players came out of was long and narrow, and at the end, rather than going straight up the stairs, it split: the home team went one way, the away team the other, with a wall in front. At night games, the floodlights cast a shaft of light straight onto the players' faces.You have to be patient - there were plenty of games where I tried this shot and it didn't quite work out. On this occasion, David Alaba was waiting for some of his teammates to come back from the dressing room, and he took a moment, looking out into the light. It worked out as a really nice picture. I think the colours worked well too - the blue branding against the red kit.Talk us through your image of Lionel Messi taking a corner.Absolutely. When I first walked into the stadium, the architecture was fascinating - a lot of the American stadiums are, because they're so different from what we have in the UK, mainly due to their scale. What I loved about the Kansas City stadium specifically was that it had no roof, so a lot more light came in during the day, and the floodlights were more prominent. I knew the wider shots would work really well because of how beautiful the stadium was.When we work for FIFA, we get exclusive access to shoot from behind the bench, right down at pitch level, without an LED board in front of us - unlike the photographers positioned elsewhere, who can't get as low an angle. Going into this game, I knew this was a shot I wanted. A corner isn't the most athletic thing a footballer does, but as a picture, it lets you get close to the player on a wide lens. As he brings his leg back, that's maybe one of the most athletic positions a footballer can be in. I took around 20 frames of him doing it, but the best one is where his leg is fully extended - a really nice body shape, with the lights right above his head.The low angle makes him look almost heroic in the frame - like the technique directors use in film, shooting from below to give someone a sense of authority. Where you going for the same effect?Exactly. The low angle makes a big difference. It was actually quite funny - there's not much space to work in down there. You've got the linesman, the player taking the corner. About 20 minutes before this, Argentina won a corner, and as Messi walked over to take it I thought, this is the moment. But another player joined him and they played it short, so I didn't get the shape I was after. Luckily, the second time, he put it into the box himself. But yes - the low angle makes a real difference. If I'd been standing, it wouldn't have had the same impact.You also captured this striking image of Ronaldo leading Portugal out. What did you see in that scene that made you want to shoot it differently?Yes - again, I'm grateful to FIFA for the access. As with the Messi picture, we're allowed tunnel access before the games. I walked into this tunnel about ten or fifteen minutes before the teams came out to warm up, knowing Ronaldo would lead the team out as captain - that was the shot I wanted.But the light in this tunnel wasn't as good as some others, and there were a lot of stewards around, making it a bit messier for pictures. So I stepped outside and thought about what else I could do. I liked the lettering above the tunnel, and there was a sea of Portugal fans nearby, all clearly about to be on their phones trying to photograph Ronaldo - because that's what everyone was there for. I also noticed the photographers had LED boards pushed back, so they had to stay behind a certain line. I thought if I shot from behind that line, framing the photographers with their cameras and the fans with their phones, it would show that all the focus was on him.There's a certain poignancy to your image of Lamine Yamal walking alone on the pitchYes - I think this was in the Los Angeles Stadium. There's just something about that stadium - I don't think I'd been anywhere quite like it. The architecture is incredible to work in, and the roof is translucent, so you don't get full sun, but you get these shafts of softer light, which can make for really nice pictures.What's also interesting about this one: I think it was a round-of-16 or quarter-final match, and FIFA had just started using pyrotechnics before kick-off. After the anthems, flares or fireworks went off from inside the stadium, which created a kind of misty effect in the air - you can see that smokiness in the picture, and I think it adds a lot.This was just after the anthems - the players had come over for a drink or electrolytes, whatever they take pre-match - and Yamal took a moment to himself. It worked out well that no other player was in frame; it almost looks like everyone's there just to watch him.Spain celebrating with the trophy in the dressing room. What was it like being in the middle of that chaos, and how did you go about finding the picture?I'll never forget this one. I was on the pitch before the players came back to the dressing room, and it was my job to get in there. We were hoping Spain would let us in, and thankfully they did. I tried to time it so I didn't miss too much of the action on the pitch - players with their families and so on - while still getting back in time.I waited outside for ten or fifteen minutes until we got the nod from FIFA to let us inside. And it was absolutely amazing - David Raya and lots of others were spraying champagne all over the players, and me to be honest, the state of the camera was not ideal when I got back, but it was brilliant. There were pictures everywhere - players celebrating separately, then together. Nico Williams grabbed me at one point because he wanted to replicate Michael Jordan's famous shower photo with the trophy, so we went and did that. There was a lot going on. It was almost hard to know what to shoot, because every time you took one picture, you felt like you were missing another happening somewhere else - which is a rare situation for a photographer, to be honest.

title: Euronews Travel & Tourism Summit 2026 – watch again
description: The Euronews Travel & Tourism Summit 2026 in Brussels brought together political leaders, policymakers and industry experts to debate the biggest issues shaping the future of travel.
content: Europe’s travel industry was in the spotlight today at the Euronews Travel & Tourism Summit 2026 at the Albert Hall in Brussels.Throughout the day, Euronews was live from the Belgian capital with interviews, panels and debates exploring how tourism is responding to a year marked by geopolitical disruption, airspace closures and extreme weather. Below are the updates and highlights from the Euronews Travel & Tourism Summit 2026 in BrusselsMichelin Guide offers curation of human-centred hotel stays amid digital algorithms noiseThe Michelin Guide’s expanded role beyond restaurants is helping travellers sort through digital noise with a human-centred curation of stays that doesn’t rely solely on new technologies.At the closing panel of the Euronews Travel & Tourism Summit 2026, Marie-France Perrel, Head of Business Development, Hotels at Michelin Guide, said the hotel selection for the Michelin Keys “is based on real humans travelling the world deciding whether or not a property should be a part of the collection based on the five criteria”.Amid algorithms and endless digital reviews at play, Perrel said that the role of hotel guide is “essential” amid all the online chatter.Hotels can receive one, two or three keys based on their quality and consistency, architecture and interior design, personality and character, value for money, as well as what the property adds to its locale.She also highlighted a growing trend of food and travel being seen as one experience. Data from the Michelin Guide found that in 2026, users looking to book a hotel also searched for dining spots nearby.Perrel also highlighted the changes in luxury travel trends, with a shift towards travellers seeking a sense of place and properties that offer a connection to their surroundings. Luxury travel is now an “ecosystem,” she said, adding that it’s also a “broad spectrum,” with the Guide also offering insights into the wide world of hospitality.Direct links to Europe and easier visa set to boost Central Asian and European travelKyrgyzstan’s Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary to Belgium has revealed that the Central Asian country is planning direct air links to Europe, with routes potentially launching as early as 2027.Aidit Erkin, Kyrgyzstan’s envoy, said that transport connectivity is an “extremely important” priority, alongside strengthening cooperation and partnerships with Europe.
