Currently, travellers in Kyrgyzstan connect to Europe with Turkish Airlines-operated flights via Istanbul.However, now that all Kyrgyzstan-certified carriers have been removed from the EU’s Air Safety List in June, Erkin announced during the Euronews Travel & Tourism Summit 2026 that work is underway for “direct flights from Kyrgyzstan to Europe”, with routes on the horizon to launch next year.Joining Erkin on the panel was Florian Sengstschmid, Chief Executive Officer of the Azerbaijan Tourism Board. He highlighted a growing demand for travel between Azerbaijan and Europe, saying that policymakers should consider ways to facilitate that demand.Sengstschmid pointed to visas as a “bottleneck” in Central Asian-European connectivity. Meanwhile, Erkin added that the Kyrgyz President is promoting a common “Silk Road visa” that would unlock access to all Central Asian countries for travellers with a single visa.EXPO 2027 Belgrade poised as tourism catalyst for Belgrade and Western BalkansAmid preparations for Expo 2027, Dušan Borovčanin, advisor at EXPO 2027 Belgrade, sees the event as a catalyst for tourism and development for Serbia’s capital and beyond, across the wider Western Balkans. Belgrade won the right to host over competing proposals like Spain, the US, Argentina and Thailand.Speaking at the Euronews Travel & Tourism Summit 2026, Borovčanin highlighted that Belgrade’s hosting of the event marks the first time it's being hosted in the region. As well as instilling a sense of “national pride” for Serbians, Borovčanin added that Expo 2027 will be an opportunity to showcase the country’s development over the past 20 years.“We want this to be a catalyst for the further development of our region in economic terms,” he said. “But also in terms of the national branding and national pride, and I think that is the reason why countries are also signing up and participating.”He added that 141 official participants are confirmed, and that there is a need “to shed light on the entire region”.Dubrovnik is open to everyone – but under certain circumstances Mayor of Dubrovnik Mato Franković has highlighted the success of his city in being able to find a “new balance” between welcoming large tourist numbers and protecting the quality of life for residents and the local charm. During his one-to-one discussion in Brussels, he revealed that when he took office as mayor in 2017, Dubrovnik was written off as a city that was dying amid the sheer strain of tourist influxes. In response, Dubrovnik launched the "Respect the City" initiative to tackle unsustainable cruise ship arrivals, as well as manage day and overnight visitor flows. While taking into account that the regulations may have taken a toll on the "magic" of visiting his native Dubrovnik, he argued that it has ultimately been for the better, preventing visitors from long queues and busy crowds, especially in the city's Old Town. Despite the measure, Franković highlighted that the city received 35% more guests compared to 2017, but emphasised that the distribution of visitor numbers throughout the day is “crucial”. He added that Dubrovnik is “a world city, it's a historical world site, and it should be open for everyone. But, under certain circumstances”.‘We have to put our money where our mouth is’ Members of the European Parliament must work to ensure that under-the-radar destinations are able to grow their tourism sectors, while hotspots need "room to breathe”, according to Daniel Attard MEP, S&D.Speaking during the panel “Managing visitor flows and shaping tomorrow’s destinations”, he said that there is no use in encouraging travellers to venture beyond the beaten path, especially if there are no means to be able to connect them to those destinations. As such, “we have to put the money where our mouth is at the European level”, he said, adding that “we have to create better connections, invest in new connections”, as well as bolster aviation services. Attard was joined by Ourania Georgoutsakou, Managing Director of Airlines for Europe (A4E), who added that air connectivity is equally as important. She also noted that the trend over the past few years has seen the shoulder season extend and steadily grow by upwards of 30%. “People are choosing to go longer and that kind of collaboration with the local hospitality sector, with the authorities, allows an offering of an extended season, which is an important way of going forward,” she said. While when it comes to destinations experimenting with tourist taxes to manage demand, Marta Machado, Deputy Director General of HOTREC - Hotels, Restaurants, Bars & Cafés in Europe, highlighted the need for better data, especially on the continent's short-term holiday homes to enact better decisions "on the management of the completion capacity of the visitor flows".Edi Rama speaks exclusively to EuronewsSpeaking exclusively to Maria Tadeo at the Euronews Travel & Tourism Summit, Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama explained that his country is making significant leaps and strides in the tourism world.He explained that Albania used to be the “most isolated country in Europe and the North Korea of Europe” and that, after it had emerged, it was “confronted with very, very disturbing stereotypes”.Rama added that the country plans to target the world in terms of tourism. He admitted that the country’s infrastructure is somewhat lacking, but that it’s improving significantly.He claimed that it has an airport that is “the fastest growing airport of Europe”, and there are plans in place to open a new airport in Vlorë, and another seasonal hub in the country’s south.“We have a fourth up in the mountains, but it’s not yet working as we wish,” he added.‘The South Caucasus is completely underrated’: Azerbaijan calls for more visitorsAzerbaijan is looking to expand its tourism offer beyond Baku, with the country’s tourism chief highlighting its natural diversity, cultural heritage and growing connectivity as it seeks to attract more international visitors.Speaking to moderator Jane Witherspoon, Florian Sengstschmid, CEO of the Azerbaijan Tourism Board, said the wider South Caucasus region remains largely overlooked by international travellers.“The South Caucasus is completely underrated,” he said, adding that Azerbaijan had “much more to come and much more to offer”.He urged visitors to venture beyond the capital and explore the country’s Silk Road heritage, ancient villages, UNESCO sites and mountain landscapes.“It really is to travel beyond Baku, to travel along the Silk Road through side valleys, ancient heritage villages, UNESCO World Heritage sites,” he said.Azerbaijan is also working to improve international connectivity, with Brussels set to gain four weekly flights to Baku from May 2027.Schmid said tourism development should also benefit local communities, pointing to villages where investment had helped create businesses and revive traditional crafts.But he said growth should not simply be measured by visitor numbers.“Is it all about the numbers? No, it’s not all about the numbers,” Sengstschmid said.“It’s about how you really increase the length of stay. How do you make people enjoy more of the country during their journey?”His ambition, he added, was for “a few more travellers, but a higher impact”.Romania invites travellers to explore beyond BucharestDan-Adrian Pop, Romania’s Secretary of State at the Ministry of Economy, Digitalisation, Entrepreneurship and Tourism, spoke to moderator Evi Kiorri about one of the most exciting emerging destinations in Europe. Despite Romania’s proximity to Ukraine and the ongoing conflict, Pop urged visitors to come and see the nation for themselves. “Overall, I would say that we are safe as any other European country. The whole country is very well protected, and from internal security for the citizens and for the travellers, I think we are one of the safest countries in Europe,” he said. Bucharest as a destination has long been popular with European travellers, but Pop explained that Romania has so much more to offer than just the charms of its capital. “We focus very much on rural tourism, spa tourism, and adventure and active tourism,” he said.“They have a lot of options to be out in nature and close to the citizens, to the people who live there, who know the places, and who guide them through this experience.”He also praised the vast amount of walking routes in the country, some “1,000 kilometres from north to south, through the Carpathian Mountains”.While he admitted that infrastructure is lacking in some places, and the summer season isn’t as long as in other European nations, there’s still plenty to experience thanks, in part, to the country’s citizens.“The people of Romania are one of our most valuable promoters, and they know the destinations, the local destinations that would fit for their friends. They are the first ones to invite their friends all over the world to Romania,” Pop said.Cruise industry targeting younger travellers and greener futureGianni Onorato, CEO of MSC Cruises, speaking to Hannah Brown as part of The Big Question, has said the sector is attracting a younger generation of travellers, while diversification and new technology could help it tackle concerns around overtourism and environmental impact.The cruise executive also said the profile of passengers had changed significantly during his 40 years in the industry.“While now there is a much younger demographic. The average age is 35 to 54. A lot of families, a lot of young people, and this is very good because this can ensure the future of this industry,” he said.He also pushed back against the perception that cruise passengers simply arrive in a destination, spend little money and leave again, pointing to the industry's wider economic contribution.“Cruises contribute to the European economy by €65 billion a year and with 445,000 permanent jobs,” he said.He argued that cruise operators could also help spread tourism beyond Europe's busiest destinations by working with local authorities and promoting lesser-known ports.“We are looking very much to diversify our destinations,” he said, highlighting the Greek island of Syros, close to the more famous Santorini and Mykonos.“Syros is becoming more and more on the map of tourism, and we are very happy about it because it is also helping to respond to the [overtourism problem],” he added.The executive also pointed to the potential for cruises to support tourism outside the traditional summer season, noting that ships can move between destinations as weather conditions change.On sustainability, he said the industry was making progress but still had work to do. He said MSC had reduced its emissions by almost 42 per cent against its 2008 baseline, putting it “almost five years ahead of the checkpoint for 2030”.But he said the availability of cleaner fuels remained a major challenge.“The target is there. There is only one issue: the fuel availability. So that needs to be produced at large scale,” he said.Looking ahead, he predicted that cruise holidays would continue to attract new audiences, including solo travellers and multigenerational families.“More and more we will have a younger audience. By the way, we will have new segments: solo travellers. It’s a new segment, very important,” he said.Onorato also suggested the industry could increasingly move away from measuring success simply by passenger numbers.“I believe tourism in general will be much less measured on the quantity, on the volumes, but much more on the quality of the emotions that we are able to give to the travellers and also the quality of the contribution, not only economically, that we can give to the locals and local community,” he said.Sustainability in focusSustainability, affordability and accessibility can work together, but tourism needs to balance environmental, social and economic considerations, panellists told the Euronews Travel & Tourism Summit.Speaking to moderator Mike Starling, Andreea Stăjcu, Deputy Head of Unit, Head of Tourism Sector, DG MOVE at the European Commission, said travellers themselves were increasingly demanding more sustainable options.“The travellers really want to travel in a sustainable way,” she said, pointing to cycling and night trains as examples.MEP and former Croatian tourism minister Nikolina Brnjac said sustainability could not be reduced to environmental measures alone.“It is achievable, but only if we approach it in three pillars: social, environmental and economical,” she said, adding that better rail and public transport connections were needed to reach rural and peripheral areas.Managing visitor numbers was another key theme. “We must not be afraid of the numbers,” Brnjac said. “It’s bad management of the tourist flows.”István Ujhelyi, former MEP and UN Tourism official, similarly stressed that tourism growth cannot simply be stopped.“You can’t stop this growing,” he said, noting that international tourist numbers had risen from 25 million in 1950 to more than 1.5 billion last year.Sven Wiltink of Radisson Hotel Group said sustainability needed to become part of the industry’s core business, rather than an optional extra.“Sustainability is not a bolt-on element,” he said.Central Europe as 'one destination'Olivér Csendes, President, Hungarian Tourism Agency and Sandrine Buffenoir, Director, Netherlands, Belgium & Luxembourg, Atout France, sat down with moderator Mared Gwyn-Jones to talk about looking at Central Europe as one destination and the inextricable link between nature and tourism.Oliver Cndish, representing the Hungarian Tourism Agency, said tourism should be used to promote Central Europe as a single, interconnected destination rather than being constrained by national borders.“I would love to see more international collaborations where we position the way we live and our regions, basically as one destination,” he said.“We don’t have to limit our thinking and the creation of experience spaces to national borders,” he added.Cndish pointed to the relatively short distances between European countries as an opportunity to create multi-country experiences - part of the popular “trip-maxxing” trend, which has gained traction this year especially. “If you look at it from the US or Asian perspective, the distances are very small in Europe. You can travel 100 kilometres, and you have already touched two or three Central European capitals,” he said.He also highlighted the Danube as an example of an attraction that could be promoted across borders.“We have treasures like the Danube, that’s found in a lot of countries in Europe, and has always been a connection, connecting cultures,” he said. “So why not use this as an active part of the experience that people will have, enriching their lives and the way they see and experience Europe.”Cndish also praised cooperation within the EU, saying: “I believe Europe is doing an amazing job collaborating.”He pointed to the European data space for tourism as one example, saying it could help countries work together on issues including visitor flows and extreme weather.“Think about all the discussions we had about visitor flow, protecting visitors, warning them in case there is a danger, whether it’s wildfire, whether it’s whatever different extreme weather conditions. This is only possible if we have the right data at the right places,” he said.He also stressed the importance of protecting the natural environment, saying: “There is no tourism without nature.”“Tourism needs to be a force for good and needs to also support the resilience of the living areas,” he added.Atout France’s Benelux director Sandrine Buffeno also highlighted tourism’s role in bringing Europeans together.“Tourism is a key aspect of connection between all European people. It’s a key factor in knowing each other better, in working together better, living with each other,” she said.“It’s a classroom to learn about each other,” she added.'Climate change the biggest threat to tourism'Eduardo Santander, the CEO of the European Travel Commission, sat down with moderator Mared Gwyn-Jones to speak about the impact of the threat of climate change on global tourism and the role of Europe as a destination.The CEO explained that “climate change is the biggest threat to tourism right now, by far.”He was speaking following a summer of record heat and related travel chaos across the continent.“We see that trains cannot run sometimes because the rails are expanded because of the heat. We saw this at the cruise lines on the European rivers - they couldn’t run because it was too dry,” Santander said.“We have to prepare for that in a much more coordinated and comprehensive way,” he added.“We see resilience becoming one of the engines of European tourism. We have to become even more resilient to whatever is next.”Santander explained that, due to the impact of climate change, travel and tourism is getting less affordable.“Travelling is becoming much more expensive, and you all have travelled this summer, I guess, and you notice it in your pockets.”He also spoke about the trend for “coolcations”, which have gained plenty of traction this year, especially: “We see a lot of people from southern European destinations looking for what we call ‘cool locations’ — places that are cooler in summer and where you can enjoy the weather in a more predictable way.”Santander also emphasised the economic importance of tourism, which makes up some 10% of the European economy, a figure that rises to between 15% and 20% of some nation’s GDP.He also sang the praises of Europe as a tourism destination.“Europe is becoming the playground, some people call it. It’s becoming a museum, an attraction park,” he said, asking, “what’s wrong with that?”“An attraction park or a museum is a perfect place to be. Normally it’s well organised, well managed, they have a nice restaurant, they have clean toilets, so there’s nothing wrong.”US Global Entry for Belgians by end of 2026?Bill White, the Ambassador of the United States of America to the Kingdom of Belgium, sat down with summit host Jane Witherspoon to speak about the special relationship between the two nations.While the Ambassador praised Belgium for having so much more to offer than “waffles, chocolate and beer”, he did criticise the lines at the airport in Brussels, saying they “suck”.“They’re really bad. One of the things we have to do in our transatlantic alliance and relationship is to recognise that if we want people to come to Belgium, we have to fix this problem. It must get better immediately,” he added.Nevertheless, White announced that he has received approval from President Donald Trump to allow Belgian citizens to apply for the US Global Entry programme, which is designed to speed up entry at US airports. Global Entry is a DHS programme for pre-approved international travellers.In practical terms, he explained, that means: “you’ll register, you pay your fee, get vetted, and then you fly to the United States, and you look at the kiosk at JFK or wherever it is, you smile, don’t smile, you get ‘whoop!’ right through, and then you go get your bags and spend money”.He urged Belgian citizens to “write to your congressman or your parliament person, let’s go, get the paperwork done, because when you travel, it’ll be seamless. One, two, three.”

title: From desalination to irrigation: How countries are adapting to water scarcity
description: From desalination in the UAE to modernising irrigation systems in Uzbekistan, countries facing water pressure are finding ways to secure supplies and reduce losses.
content: Roughly half the world's population experiences severe water scarcity for at least part of the year, according to the UN's Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, a figure climate change, population growth and rising demand are expected to push higher.The pressures vary by location. In the UAE, where rainfall is scarce and no permanent rivers exist, most drinking water comes via desalination of seawater. In Uzbekistan, agriculture depends on irrigation networks moving water across dry landscapes. Both countries are turning to technology and infrastructure to stretch limited supplies further.Securing water in an arid climateIn the UAE, limited rainfall and the absence of permanent rivers have long shaped how communities obtain and use water.Efforts to manage scarce resources predate modern desalination by centuries. Traditional falaj irrigation systems channelled water through settlements and agricultural areas allowing communities to sustain local economies.Abdulla Balalaa, the UAE's Assistant Minister of Foreign Affairs for Energy and Sustainability, said such systems were engineered over 1,000 years ago.Today, much of the country's drinking water comes from desalination. Balalaa said the UAE has achieved universal access to water and is also applying newer technologies, including artificial intelligence, to the sector.As populations and cities grow, limiting water use and reusing existing supplies are becoming increasingly important.Few places demonstrate that principle as clearly as the International Space Station.Emirati astronaut Dr Sultan Al Neyadi spent six months aboard the station, where water is needed for drinking, hygiene, food preparation and oxygen production.“Every drop on board the International Space Station is accounted for,” Al Neyadi said. “We recycle about 95% of our water.”Water passes through several stages of filtration before being used again, providing an example of how a limited resource can be repeatedly recovered rather than discarded when there are no other options.The UAE is also seeking to push water higher on the international agenda. It will co-host the 2026 UN Water Conference with Senegal in Abu Dhabi from 8 to 10 December. The event will bring together governments, international organisations, businesses and other stakeholders, with investment, technology and innovation among the areas under discussion.Balalaa said solutions will vary by location. Technology and innovation can help bridge gaps, he said, alongside financing and cooperation needed to turn ideas into active projects.In Uzbekistan, the pressures are different. Much of the country's agriculture relies on moving water over long distances, limiting losses along the way and ensuring it reaches farmland when it is needed.Getting water to Uzbekistan's farmsCanals, reservoirs and pumping stations carry water across Uzbekistan's dry landscapes. In some areas, scarcity is therefore also a question of whether available water can reach agricultural land at the right time.In the Fergana Valley, a World Bank-backed project launched in 2017 has modernised irrigation infrastructure.At one site, water from local springs is collected and pumped around nine kilometres to areas where access has historically been difficult. The pumping station and pipeline are expected to improve irrigation for around 9,740 hectares of farmland.More reliable irrigation has also allowed previously difficult-to-cultivate land to be farmed.At one orchard in the valley, drip irrigation is used to deliver water to peach trees planted in 2024. The farm harvested around 200 tonnes of fruit the following year.Moving water across the desertFarther west, water from the Amu Darya is pumped across the desert through the Amu-Bukhara Machine Canal. The wider network irrigates more than 350,000 hectares across Bukhara and Navoi regions and supplies drinking water to Bukhara and Kogon.The new Amu-Bukhara-1 pumping station replaced older infrastructure as part of a wider modernisation effort. Its digital control system tracks water and electricity use, and the new equipment has cut energy use by up to 15%.Moving water over long distances is only one part of the process; preventing it from disappearing before reaching farms is another.In parts of Bukhara, water losses through seepage previously reached around 37%, according to Sherzod Sharipov, a representative of the regional water delivery service. Canals are now being lined with concrete to reduce losses and provide steadier flows to farmers.Farmer Hikmat Nazrullayev said large amounts of water once disappeared before reaching wheat and cotton fields. Since canals were lined, he said, irrigating crops has become easier.Water beyond the fieldsThe irrigation network also connects agriculture with the wider environment.Drainage and return flows from farmland feed Dengizkul, a wetland of international importance in Bukhara region and an important resting and wintering site for migratory birds.Professor of Water Engineering Malika Ikramova said the lake receives water from precipitation and groundwater as well as drainage returning from irrigation systems. Its water is highly mineralised, but supports fisheries and provides habitat for migratory birds.As populations grow and climate conditions change, Ikramova said reducing losses, improving water accounting and expanding water-saving irrigation will remain important.“We are going to have to adapt,” she said.From desalination in the Gulf to irrigation canals in Central Asia, the methods differ considerably. But the underlying task is similar: reducing losses and making limited water supplies go further.

title: Caves, castles and domes: The countries with the most unusual places to stay
description: France came out top overall, with nearly 3,000 unusual property listings on Airbnb, including more than 1,000 castles.
content: From Airstream caravans and Poké Ball-shaped hotels to Victorian water towers and cosy caves, there are plenty of alternatives to the bog standard bed and breakfast these days.And if you’re looking for unconventional options in Europe, you should be heading to France as it just topped a new ranking of the countries with the most unusual stays around the world.Produced by Holafly, the ranking looked at Airbnb listings around the world across eight property types: Caves, castles, treehouses, houseboats, windmills, lighthouses, earth homes, and domes.The number of each was added up by destination, and with a whopping 2,947 listings, the world’s most-visited country came out on top.France leads the rankings in several stay categories, too, with more than 1,000 castles, 400 houseboats, and 30 windmills you can book.Where else to go in Europe for an unusual stayThird place in the overall ranking went to Italy, thanks to its Tuscan castles, the trulli (aka cone-roofed stone huts) of Puglia, and cave dwellings in Matera.Next up in Europe is the UK, which has 696 listings and places sixth overall. Here, you’ll find nearly 250 castles, almost 150 domes and more than 100 houseboats, alongside 23 lighthouses and 12 windmills.The last European destination to make the cut was Greece, in ninth overall. Unsurprisingly, the country won for the number of cave stays, with 279, and it was also in second place for windmill stays, with 27.The top 10 countries for unusual staysFrance (2,947 listings)US (2,533 listings)Italy (1,050 listings)Brazil (873 listings)Colombia (762 listings)UK (696 listings)Mexico (675 listings)India (604 listings)Greece (599 listings)Chile (548 listings)

title: Trump defers diesel tax for truckers as fuel costs bite weeks before US midterms
description: US President Donald Trump has signed an executive order deferring tax payments on red-dyed diesel used on public roads, as near-record fuel prices linked to the Iran war weigh on the Republican Party weeks before the midterm elections.
content: Truckers, farmers and other diesel users in the US could benefit from deferred tax payments on fuel normally reserved for tractors and other off-road machinery, as the White House moves to ease a fuel squeeze that threatens to hurt the Republican Party in the midterm elections next month.US President Donald Trump signed the order on Monday at a rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, where he was campaigning to fire up Republican voters.Trump told supporters the order would "officially waive the off-road requirement and allow anyone to purchase tax-free red-dyed diesel for any reason."Trump also conceded he was no expert on the fuel. "I don't know what the hell it is, but whatever it is, it's supposed to be very good," he joked.The dyed fuel is almost identical to ordinary diesel but is exempt from highway taxes, and using it on public roads normally carries penalties."The federal diesel tax is 24.4 cents per gallon, or about $60 on a 250-gallon fill," the White House stated in a press release, adding that savings would top $100 per fill where states follow suit. For a large truck taking on 250 gallons, a fill costs about $1,580 including tax at Monday’s average diesel price.However, the order itself is narrower than Trump's pitch to the crowd suggested.It does not abolish the levy but postpones payment on dyed diesel used on roads between 5 October and 31 December, free of interest and penalties, and asks US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to find ways, including legislation, to "eliminate the obligation to pay the amounts deferred," the executive order said.It relies on a law that lets the US Treasury postpone tax deadlines for people affected by disasters or military action, and gives Bessent five days, in consultation with US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, to determine whether those conditions are met and which taxpayers qualify.Unless the Trump administration finds a way to cancel it, the deferred diesel tax will still be owed once the relief period ends on 31 December.While the White House has pitched the measure at truckers and farmers, the order itself does not single them out, in line with Trump's promise that anyone could buy the fuel. In practice, the relief matters mainly to those running diesel trucks and farm vehicles, as most American cars run on petrol.Federal authorities and state governors may also choose to suspend inspections and drop the tax, the White House added.Diesel squeezeThe average price of diesel in the US stood at $6.32 a gallon on Monday, according to motoring group AAA, just below the record $6.53 set on 22 September and more than 70% higher than a year ago.Prices have soared since the Iran war began in February, disrupting shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, while Russia has curbed fuel exports after Ukrainian attacks on several of its refineries.The White House announcement did not mention Iran, instead blaming "the Russia-Ukraine war and a lack of refining capacity around the world", as well as "Democrat-led states that chose to shut down their refineries in the name of 'Green Energy' policies".Trump also pointed to the G7 deal struck last week to release 100 million barrels of refined diesel from strategic stocks over the next four months, after he had threatened to ban US diesel exports.American farmers, who are in the middle of the harvest, welcomed the order."Every cent per gallon matters when you're running a fleet of grain trucks or hauling cattle hundreds of miles," said Zippy Duvall, president of the American Farm Bureau Federation, the country's biggest farm lobby.Oil prices eased further on Tuesday as oil exports from the Gulf excluding Iran recovered towards pre-war levels.Brent crude, the international benchmark, dropped below $100 a barrel in early trading, down roughly 2.5%, while the US benchmark West Texas Intermediate also fell 2.5% to under $88.

title: Far-right AfD gains first-ever state parliament speaker in Germany
description: The AfD's Tobias Rausch was elected speaker of Saxony-Anhalt's state parliament on Tuesday, marking the first time the far-right party has held such a post in Germany.
content: A candidate for Germany's AfD was elected parliament speaker in the state of Saxony Anhalt Tuesday, the first time a far-right party has held such a post in the country since 1945.Lawmakers gathered for the first time since the AfD's landslide election victory in the eastern region last month, with 48 MPs voting for the party's Tobias Rausch as speaker and 29 against.The AfD won the state election on 6 September with 43.8 percent and now holds 39 of the 83 seats. As the largest parliamentary group, it has the right to nominate the president. For the election itself, however, a simple majority of valid votes cast is sufficient.This means Rausch is reliant on votes from other parties. The Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), with five deputies, has announced it will back him. The conservative CDU, the Social Democrats (SPD), the Greens and the Left Party intend to vote against the AfD candidate. If the BSW deputies vote for Rausch, he will have the votes he needs.Why is this election so significant?The AfD's state branch in Saxony-Anhalt is classified as a confirmed right-wing extremist organisation by the state office for the protection of the constitution, the domestic intelligence agency, which is a department within the CDU-led Interior Ministry. Observers therefore see Rausch's possible election as a political watershed.The office of president of the state parliament is not merely ceremonial: the president chairs the plenary sessions and the council of elders and heads the parliamentary administration. Political scientist Nicolas Spohn told the magazine Focus that the president's power lies "above all in procedural issues and powers relating to the rules of the house".Spohn stressed that it remains open how an AfD politician would actually exercise the office. Rausch has offered his own description of his political style. "I am not a hardliner, I am pragmatic," he said, according to the German Press Agency. He wants "to take the interests of everyone into account as far as possible".The culture of debate in parliament, he said, should be "tough on substance but fair to individuals".The election of the speaker of the state parliament does not decide who will lead the future state government. Nevertheless, it is likely to be closely watched.AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund is aiming to be elected minister-president, the head of the state government, in December and needs at least 42 votes to do so.

title: World's tallest wind turbine reaches final height in Germany's former coal mining region
description: Winds are stronger at higher altitudes, allowing for twice as much energy to be produced.
content: A region of Germany once dominated by coal mines has achieved a remarkable pivot to clean energy.After roughly two years of construction, the world's tallest wind turbine now towers over Schipkau, a small town in Brandenburg.At 365 metres from the foundation slab to the rotor tip, the wind turbine is only three metres shorter than the Berlin TV Tower, making it among the tallest structures in Germany.At a time when the Iran war is driving up energy prices for Europeans, the project could not be more needed. "This will help us to become independent of oil and gas from other regions of the world," says Germany's Federal Environment Minister Carsten Schneider.A telescopic device raised the wind turbine up to its full heightAt 365 metres high, the completed turbine is equivalent to a 100-storey building.What's the advantage of such a giant structure? The wind blows more strongly and steadily above 300m, allowing for more wind energy to be produced.You might be wondering how a structure as narrow and free standing as a turbine can possibly be built this high. Conventional cranes are not up to the job, after all. Instead, a patented telescopic device was used.The turbine initially reached a height of 150 metres, then the telescopic device raised it up to 300 metres.The groundbreaking project has not been without its challenges. At the end of 2025, problems were discovered with steel parts meaning work had to be stopped."Safety and quality have absolute priority in this globally unique project," said Jochen Großmann, construction company GICON's CEO and founder, at the time.If all goes to plan, the wind power giant should be connected to the grid in November.How much energy will the wind turbine produce?GICON say they hope for an annual electricity yield of 30-33 gigawatt hours and electricity production costs of less than five cents per kilowatt hour. This is 220 per cent more than conventional turbines nearby and could supply approximately 7,500 four-person households with electricity.High-altitude wind turbines could be a win in less windy European countriesThe higher a wind turbine stands, the stronger and more evenly the wind usually blows. GICON, which says it has been working on the technology since 2010, wanted to scientifically validate this assumption.On behalf of beventum GmbH, a subsidiary of the Federal Agency for Leap Innovations (SPRIND), the company erected a wind-measuring mast in neighbouring Klettwitz. This showed that the wind does in fact blow more steadily and strongly at a height of 300 metres than at the height of conventional wind turbines.Large parts of Europe, from eastern Poland to the Iberian Peninsula, have trouble benefitting from wind power due to weak ground winds. High-altitude wind towers could be the answer. SPRIND emphasises: "Europe needs a strong position in wind turbine construction in order to guarantee its own energy production."Where is the world's tallest wind turbine?Schipkau is located in Lusatia, a region that was characterised by coal for decades before going through remarkable changes. Authorities in the area now incentivise clean energy projects, offering space, infrastructure and political support.In the long term, the site is to be developed into a hybrid power plant, with two levels of wind power and a solar park on the ground.This triple use should quintuple the energy yield compared to pure solar use. The combination of different energy sources should also make it possible to generate electricity year round.Clean energy is wasted all over Europe due to outdated gridsThis ambitious project highlights a problem which is becoming more and more obvious all over Europe: outdated grids can not keep up with the booming growth in renewable infrastructure.In Germany this creates an expensive irony: if more electricity flows into the grid in windy north-east Germany than the lines can transport to the high-consumption south, wind turbines have to be throttled back or switched off. This means fossil gas and other dirty fuels have to fill the gap, driving increases in prices for consumers as well as more carbon emissions.According to analysis by German media Tagesspiegel, around 9.3 terawatt hours of wind power were lost in 2023 alone. The costs for congestion management amounted to almost €3 billion and these are borne by consumers via the grid fees that are added to their electricity bills.GICON and its client SPRIND argue that high-altitude wind towers could alleviate this dilemma in the long term: because high-altitude winds blow more evenly and turbines could also be operated economically where ground winds are too weak, expansion could be more decentralised.Europe favours wind powerAt the end of 2025, around 304 gigawatts of wind power were installed onshore and offshore in Europe, according to the German Wind Energy Association.With around 77.7 gigawatts of installed capacity, Germany was ahead of the UK with 31.6 gigawatts and Spain with 31.2 gigawatts.With 5,735 megawatts of newly installed capacity, Germany added more than any other European country in 2025.Germany is pushing for more renewable energyAt the end of March, German Federal Environment Minister Carsten Schneider presented the Climate Protection Programme 2026 in the Bundestag: 67 measures aimed at saving an additional 25 million tonnes of CO₂ by 2030.2,000 more wind turbines are to be awarded in the upcoming tenders than previously planned. In addition, 12 gigawatts of wind power capacity will be put out to tender to be connected to the grid by 2030.

title: New European ski lodges and hotels opening in winter 2026-2027
description: The winter sports season will see the arrival of many new properties in Europe. Highlights include The First Cortina in Cortina d’Ampezzo and the aptly named Ski Lodge in Verbier, while several properties are also returning after renovations.
content: Winter is coming and that means only one thing – it’s time to dust off the skis and get ready to hit the slopes. In Europe, we’re lucky to have the world’s most developed ski market, with the Alps a traditional favourite alongside resorts in the Dolomites, Pyrenees, Scandinavia, the Balkans, and Central and Eastern Europe. In fact, according to the Skiresort.com database, Europe is home to more than 3,900 resorts, with 37,800 kilometres of marked slopes and more than 16,800 ski lifts.With so many ski destinations to choose from, there’s no shortage of places to stay. Here are some of the hotels and lodges opening or reopening this winter.New ski hotels and lodges in Europe Fahrenheit Seven Les Menuires, FranceFahrenheit Seven will open its Les Menuires hotel on 11 December 2026, adding a third Alpine address to its collection after Val Thorens and Courchevel. Set on the ski front in the Preyerand district, it promises direct access to Les 3 Vallées, along with an in-house ski boutique, bar, restaurants, terrace and indoor pool. The First Cortina, by The Pavilions, ItalyThe First Cortina, by The Pavilions is scheduled to open in early December 2026 on Corso Italia, in the centre of Cortina d’Ampezzo. Its 76 rooms and suites put guests within reach of the Dolomites while offering a base in town. Some suites even have private wellness facilities and terraces with mountain views. Dining options include Zuma (contemporary Japanese) and Velo (Italian) and there will also be a dedicated ski room and REVĪVŌ Spa.The Green Resort, Zillertal, AustriaThe Green Resort is due to welcome guests in Uderns from December 2026, combining a Zillertal ski base with a substantial wellness offering. Its 3,300-square-metre indoor and outdoor spa area includes pools, saunas and steam baths. For snowsports fans, the hotel offers a seven-night winter ski package which includes accommodation, meals, a six-day Zillertal Super Ski Pass per person, plus wellness treatments. The Ski Lodge, Verbier, SwitzerlandOpening in December 2026, The Ski Lodge is a 36-room boutique hotel close to Verbier’s Place Centrale. As well as its location, other highlights include a spa and a bar. The state-of-the-art spa will have an indoor swimming pool, cold plunge, sauna, hammam and a relaxation area. While the hotel’s bar, The Listening Room, will be open for guests and visitors.Schiefergut Family Resort, Flachau, AustriaFamilies heading to Flachau in Austria will have a new option when Schiefergut opens in December 2026. The four-star resort has 28 suites and chalets and is located close to the ski lifts, Snow Space Salzburg, the Achter Jet lift, and cross-country trails.Hôtel Le Tremplin, Morzine, FranceFollowing an extensive three-year renovation, Hôtel Le Tremplin in the heart of Morzine is opening 13 self-contained holiday suites for the 2026-2027 ski season. This marks the full reopening of the property after the bar, restaurant and après-ski terrace returned last winter.Garance Hotel & Spa, Morzine, FranceThe former Les Airelles hotel in Morzine is set to return as Garance Hotel & Spa in December 2026. Close to the ski lifts, and the legendary slopes of the Portes du Soleil ski area, the four-star Mont-Blanc Collection property will have 65 rooms, a brasserie, cocktail bar and spaces for children and teenagers. Its wellness facilities are planned to include a pool, Nordic spa, treatment rooms and areas for yoga and fitness.Also on the horizon Les Gets celebrates 90th year with new snowpark While not a new property, Les Gets resort in Haute-Savoie, France, is celebrating a milestone year – the 90th anniversary of its first ski lift – and will welcome a new snowpark in 2026. Designed for beginners, the snowpark beneath the La Croix chairlift will replace the mini boardercross course.Les Gets plans a partial opening on 12 December 2026, subject to snow conditions, followed by full opening on 19 December 2026. The season is scheduled to run until 11 April 2027.Raffles and One&Only in Courchevel 1850Ok, so these next two luxury properties will not be ready for a few years just yet, but they are certainly worth adding to your winter travel bucket list. Slated to open in 2028, Raffles Hotels & Resorts will debut its first ever-alpine resort in Courchevel 1850, one of skiing’s most iconic addresses which sits at the heart of Les 3 Vallées in the French Alps, the world's largest interconnected ski area.Then a couple of years later in 2030, One&Only Resort and Private Homes will also open in Courchevel 1850, the brand's first resort in the French Alps.

title: George Fenton, British composer behind David Attenborough’s Earth Trilogy, dies aged 76
description: Best known for his award-winning film scores and long-lasting partnership with director Ken Loach, George Fenton also created the music for what became known as David Attenborough's Earth Trilogy: The Blue Planet, Planet Earth and Frozen Planet.
content: Celebrated British composer George Fenton has died aged 76.The five-time Oscar-nominated composer wrote numerous scores for film, television, and theater over a career spanning more than five decades – including scores for Ghandi, Cry Freedom, Dangerous Liaisons, The Fischer King and Groundhog Day.In a statement, Fenton's family said: "We are very sad to announce that George Fenton passed away unexpectedly today (Monday 5 October). He is survived by his loving wife Amanda, ex-wife Jane, children Gemma, Grace and Bridget, and grandchildren Lola, Audrey, Alfred, George, Frank and Beatrice, and a life of music." Some of Fenton’s most notable film work as a composer also includes The Jewel in the Crown, Mary Reilly, The Object of My Affection, You’ve Got Mail, Anna and the King and Bewitched. He also maintained a long-lasting partnership with director Ken Loach, scoring most of the director’s films, with music for My Name Is Joe, Sweet Sixteen, The Wind That Shakes the Barley, The Angels’ Share, I, Daniel Blake, Sorry We Missed You, and The Old Oak. Fenton’s work for television includes several of beloved wildlife broadcaster David Attenborough’s documentary series, including The Blue Planet, Planet Earth, Frozen Planet, as well as the 2023 series Wild Isles. Over his career, Fenton won two Emmys (for The Blue Planet and Planet Earth), three BAFTAs (Bergerac, The Monocled Mutineer, The Blue Planet), five Ivor Novellos (Ghandi, The Jewel in the Crown, The Monocled Mutineer, Cry Freedom, Shadowlands), and earned two Grammy and three Golden Globe nominations. He also wrote many well-known theme tunes British audiences will be familiar with, including the BBC's One O'Clock News, Six O'Clock News, Nine O'Clock News, Newsnight, The Money Programme, and Radio 4's PM Programme. In 2023, Fenton was appointed Commander of the Order of the British Empire for services to music.His final film score was for Trudie Styler’s Up Against It, which premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival last month, on 12 September. RIP George Fenton 1949 - 2026

title: Global oil stocks are alarmingly low and could take two years to rebuild, Aramco warns
description: The CEO of the world's biggest oil company warned at a conference that the global oil supply system is reaching its limit and that replenishing global oil stockpiles could take two years.
content: Saudi Aramco chief executive Amin Nasser has warned that the world’s oil supply cushion is shrinking. The head of the world’s largest oil company said the Iran war has drained stocks that could help offset further supply disruptions.The effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway that typically handles around 20% of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas supplies, led to major supply disruptions and higher prices, hitting the global economy.Seven months into the war, the global oil stockpile system is "already straining," said Nasser, speaking at the Energy Intelligence Forum in London on Monday."And with precious little else the world can turn to, the supply resilience cushion is scarily thin," he told the two-day conference attended by leaders from across the energy sector.G7 countries, in coordination with the International Energy Agency (IEA), agreed on Friday to immediately release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil to ease global energy supply concerns caused by the US-Iran war.But Nasser explained that total oil inventories do not reflect the amount of oil that can actually be supplied to the market. "That's why you find they're struggling with 100 million barrels."But Nasser warned Monday against looking at headline figures for commercial reserves, noting that "less than 10%" were available for use. A large portion of the reserves reported by countries represent the minimum volume required to keep infrastructure operational, he said.According to Nasser, global oil inventories stood at around 10 billion barrels at the start of the crisis. Since then, nearly 3 billion barrels of oil supply have been lost, or roughly half the crude and refined products that would normally pass through the Strait of Hormuz during that time. More than 1 billion barrels have been withdrawn from global inventories to help offset those losses, with most drawn from onshore commercial inventories.Nasser described these inventories as "the last major tool in the box", adding that much of the remaining stock, estimated at less than 6 billion barrels, is “not practically available.”Nasser said tapping reserves buys the market time but does not fix long-term supply and demand imbalances. He added that these volumes could help the world through one winter, but do not amount to a lasting solution.He pointed out that rebuilding inventories after the Strait of Hormuz fully reopens could take up to two years. Regional exports recover as producers use alternative routesDespite attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz, crude oil exports from the Middle East Gulf region, excluding Iran, returned to pre-war levels in September, according to maritime tracking firm Kpler."At least 16.5 mbd (million barrels a day) left the region between 1 and 28 September, matching the pre-war average excluding Iran. That is 10.5 mbd above March's monthly average," said the firm.The recovery followed changes to the region’s export routes.Some 40% of those exports now bypass the Strait of Hormuz, compared with 17% before the war, with pipelines in Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates providing key alternative routes. Most crude crossing the strait changes tankers offshore.Nasser said Aramco was meeting its customers' requirements, citing the company's use of international storage facilities and the speed with which it has repaired infrastructure damaged during the conflict.Aramco is also seeking additional routes for crude exports and new storage facilities abroad, in order to reduce its reliance on a single channel to reach buyers in global markets.Saudi oil facilities have been hit by several attacks launched by the Houthis in Yemen since fighting resumed between the Saudi-led military coalition and the Iran-backed Houthi fighters.

title: How many birds are killed by offshore wind turbines? Scientists use thermal cameras to find out
description: A year-long study has observed millions of birds migrating across the North Sea to measure the threat of offshore wind farms.
content: Europe leads the world in offshore wind energy, with more than 30 gigawatts (GW) of installed capacity across the continent – enough to power more than 26 million homes annually.Earlier this year, Belgium, Denmark, France, Germany, Iceland, Ireland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Norway and the UK committed to deliver 100GW of joint offshore wind projects across shared North Sea waters by 2050. The €9.5 billion plan, known as the Hamburg Declaration, aims to turn the North Sea into the world’s “largest clean energy reservoir” and mobilise €1 trillion of capital in Europe. But is our path to a fossil fuel-free future jeopardising birds that are already plummeting in number due to human-caused climate change? Are offshore wind turbines a threat to birds?Most studies into bird collisions with turbines tend to focus on wind farms located on land. But every year, millions of songbirds cross the North Sea during spring and autumn migration, mostly at night. Capturing collisions at sea can be difficult, due to a lack of light and the remote location.However, a new year-long pilot study has allowed researchers to detect these small birds and bats during hours of darkness, as well as larger birds during daylight hours, using a combination of thermal cameras and artificial intelligence (AI). The study, initiated by the energy company Vattenfall, was carried out at the Hollandse Kust Zuid offshore wind farm in collaboration with Wildlife Imaging Systems (WIS) and Wageningen University & Research (WUR). WIS installed 16 thermal cameras on an offshore wind turbine, covering all angles and operating 24 hours a day. Combined with AI, the system detected and interpreted bird movements day and night, including in poor visibility such as fog or rain.“Safeguarding biodiversity is an important part of the energy transition,” says Karen Krijgsveld, a bird ecology researcher at Wageningen University & Research.“On land, we already know quite a lot about when and why birds collide with turbines, and which species are most at risk. As offshore wind energy continues to expand, we need to develop that same understanding at sea.”Over almost a year of monitoring, covering both a spring and an autumn migration season, 22 possible bird collisions were identified – two of which were confirmed and one considered highly probable.“Until now, estimates of offshore bird collisions were mainly based on theoretical models,” says Jesper Kyed Larsen, a bioscience expert at Vattenfall.“At sea, it’s extremely difficult to verify fatalities because there are no remains to recover. This study demonstrates how we can get the empirical data needed to improve collision estimates and secure efficient mitigation measures.”The study does not claim that collisions are rare or that these initial results from one turbine can be applied everywhere. The primary aim was to test the technology’s performance under real offshore conditions. But a previous study by the German Offshore Wind Energy Association (BWO) also yielded similar results.Researchers analysed more than four million bird movements over one and a half years, using radar and AI-based cameras. They found that more than 99.8 per cent of migratory birds reliably avoided the wind turbines.Vattenfall previously conducted another study on an offshore wind farm near Aberdeen, Scotland. Over a period of 19 months – from June 2023 to December 2024 – video recordings of a wind turbine were made with the help of AI-supported analyses.A total of 2,007 bird flight paths near the monitored turbine were examined and no collisions were found.How can Europe protect its endangered birds?Despite all three studies suggesting a minimal impact of offshore wind farms on birds, conservationists warn that measures must still be put in place to help protect endangered species. Of the 26 seabirds that breed on the UK’s coastlines and islands, 10 are already on the endangered list.Back in 2020, the land-based Smola wind farm in Norway, which consists of 68 turbines, painted one blade on each turbine black to make them stand out to birds. They found the initiative reduced avian fatalities by a staggering 70 per cent, from 11 recorded bird carcasses before painting to six afterwards.Some critics argue that making wind farms more visible could impact birds’ migration patterns, forcing them to fly longer routes around a turbine. This means they will use up more energy, and it will take them longer to get back to their chicks.Other measures include placing turbines far away from sensitive habitats and avoiding migration paths in the first place. Thermal cameras and radar can also be used to further investigate the risk these turbines pose to our flying friends.

title: Trump says US moved their B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford airbase after additional threats were made
description: Trump detailed that additional threats received by Washington prompted their moving of the military aircraft from the UK base they were deployed in.
content: US President Donald Trump said on Monday that the United States had withdrawn all B-1 bombers from a British airbase because of unspecified threats that he believed were linked to Iran.The Pentagon confirmed earlier that the bombers had left the RAF Fairford airbase – used by the United States to launch ‘defensive’ strikes on Tehran – even as the British government insisted the site was safe."There were some threats," Trump told reporters at the White House."And rather than tempting the enemy – we'll capture the enemy and beat the enemy, but why should we leave them there? So we moved them around a little bit, not very far."Speculation has swirled about the incident since police were called to the base in southwest England on 27 September after a local farmer reported a group of men with several vans engaged in "suspicious" activity.Despite a major counter-terrorism probe, five suspects arrested at the time and a British-Iranian national detained afterwards have all since been released on bail.Investigators did not find any explosives in the vans, but "a quantity of petrol was recovered," according to counter-terrorism police.Trump would not comment on a report that the threat involved attack drones, saying: "I can't tell you that but if they did they'll suffer greatly.""We actually know the people that made the threat," said Trump, adding: "They would be linked to Iran."Two US officials told US media outlets that the bombers were moved after commanders received new threats about an Iran-backed plot.One US official said the new information was part of the same threat warnings that surfaced three weeks ago, but the situation became urgent in the past 24 hours.Asked whether the base was safe however, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham's official spokesman replied "yes.""We have tried and tested approaches to defend our bases around the country and throughout the world," he told reporters.Speculation about the motives behind the incident ranged from terror threat to fuel theft, as energy prices in the UK hit record highs this week.Burnham previously said there were "strong indications that Iran played a part" in the incident, a charge rejected by Tehran.Trump had previously rebuked British authorities for releasing the arrested men, all in their mid-20s, on bail – pending further investigation.Iran's embassy in London said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" speculation that Tehran was involved.

title: Climate damage already ‘locked in’ – but these 10 insights show our future is still being decided
description: From rising sea levels to food systems fuelling climate change – experts have laid out 10 insights that require urgent action.
content: Past emissions have already “locked in” future climate impacts – but the scale of this damage still depends on what action we take right now, according to a major new study.The 10 New Insights In Climate Science report is produced by more than 70 scientists from nearly 30 countries and aims to translate complex research into accessible, concise insights to “inform high-stakes decisions”.Published today (6 October) it warns that the overshooting of 1.5°C, as set out in the legally binding Paris Agreement, carries “rapidly escalating risks of irreversible impacts” for our oceans, glaciers and permafrost – and that the economic and social costs of doing so are greater than previously understood. 10 insights to prevent further climate damage“The evidence is unequivocal," says Johan Rockström, director of the PotsdamInstitute for Climate Impact Research, co-chair of The Earth League and a member of the report’s editorial board.“1.5°C is a limit that we cross at our own risk. Beyond it, the risks of cascading and potentially irreversible climate impacts increase, with every additional tenth of a degree making them more severe.”The 10 New Insights highlights, created by Future Earth, The Earth League and the World Climate Research Programme, point to a “narrowing window for action” but one that is still open, showing us what is already locked in, what can still be avoided, and where policy can have the greatest effect.Ocean heat uptake clouds long-term outlookThe ocean continues to absorb record amounts of heat due to human-caused climate change – locking in further warming for years to come. In August, global sea surface temperatures reached 21.1°C – the hottest ever recorded. Experts warned last year that the planet’s ocean acidification - where the water’s pH is lowered due to CO₂ absorption - entered the danger zone for the first time.The new report says deep cuts to greenhouse gas emissions are “urgently needed” to prevent further long-term heat accumulation.“The ocean has been our planet’s shock absorber,” says Wendy Broadgate, Global Hub Director at Future Earth and a member of the report’s editorial board.“Because heat takes decades to penetrate ocean depths, today's emissions effectively lock in further warming and sea level rise. Deep, rapid emissions cuts are the only way to limit these risks.”Sea levels keep risingMelting glaciers and ice sheets are driving rising seas, putting more people at risk of severe flooding.The report warns that some sea-level rise is already irreversible due to the impact of past emissions, but the magnitude of this still depends on how quickly the world acts to cut greenhouse gases.Freshwater sources are getting scarceWater gaps are widening as continental drying – the long-term, large-scale decline in freshwater availability and water storage – accelerates. According to the UN, By 2030, one-in-two people are expected to face severe water shortages.“Climate change and growing water use are causing the rapid loss of freshwater across continents, threatening water security, ecosystems, and food production,” the report says. “The consequences of inaction extend from threats to local livelihoods to cascading impacts across the Earth system.”Governments are being encouraged to develop holistic water management plans, known as Integrated Water Resource Management, that take into account the entire water cycle: from source to distribution, treatment, reuse and return to the environment.Nature-based solutions such as restoring wetlands, rivers and forests can also help capture fresh water that remains on land, rather than letting it dry up or run straight into the ocean.Impacts of overshooting 1.5CA recent report from the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) warned that global temperature rise will exceed 1.5°C, likely within the next few years. This would accelerate much of the environmental degradation the natural world is already experiencing, from shrinking ice sheets to rising sea levels and “unprecedented dieback” of coral reefs and rainforests.The UNEP says that there are “no good outcomes if we remain above 1.5°C” and that governments must focus on making the overshoot as small and short as possible.Food systems still fuel climate changeThe report says that transforming food systems, particularly through more plant-rich diets, can deliver major benefits for climate, biodiversity and health, but they must be done “carefully and fairly”.Globally, food and agriculture contribute one-third of total greenhouse gas emissions, second only to burning fossil fuels – and meat has been identified as the main culprit.In fact, animal-sourced foods make up between 81 and 86 per cent of total greenhouse gas emissions from EU food production, despite only supplying an estimated 32 per cent of calories and 64 per cent of protein.According to the carbon footprint calculator CO2 Everything, one 100g serving of beef is equivalent to 78.7 km of driving, releasing 15.5 kg CO2 equivalent.Understanding the ‘social cost’ of carbonExperts warn that the economic damages caused by carbon emissions are "substantially higher” than previously estimated – adding that every extra tonne of CO2 carries “additional risk”.“Using more realistic, up-to-date climate models reveal a social cost of carbon up to four times higher,” the report says.Strengthening claims for compensationAdvances in science have made it possible to trace climate impacts back to the emissions that caused them. That means scientists can now link a single company or major emitter to warming – and perhaps even to specific losses or damages. Moving forward, this extra evidence could strengthen climate litigation and demands for compensation.‘Climate clubs’ can help industries clean up their act‘Climate clubs’ made up of countries working together on climate and trade policies can create a collective force to cut down on carbon emissions. These so-called clubs can rally behind carbon border taxes that prevent companies from off-shoring to places with weaker climate policies, for example – a problem known as ‘carbon leakage’. But there’s a caveat. While climate clubs can accelerate industrial decarbonisation, they can also have a punitive effect on developing countries that lack the tools, money or technology to cut emissions.That’s why the authors suggest that wealthier nations may need to combine tougher rules with technical or financial support for other economies.Climate obstruction is getting harder to spotProgress is being derailed by more than just denialism. The report says that carbon-heavy industries are holding back effective policy not just by denying climate change exists anymore. Lobbying efforts now also include a bevy of subtler tactics, from greenwashing to the digital spread of disinformation.To combat this more deceptive form of climate obfuscation, the report calls for greater transparency in lobbying and political donations, stronger rules against making misleading environmental claims and coordinated action against disinformation.Conflict creates unequal energy transitionsWars, trade disputes and fierce competition over energy sources are complicating the global push to decarbonise. Energy security concerns, like those caused by the war on Iran and the war in Ukraine, have not been met with one universal response. While many wealthy countries have invested in renewables as a buffer against shocks in the oil and gas markets, others have doubled down on fossil fuel production or sought new sources overseas. The report explains that global instability could make the energy transition more unequal than it already is.Some blocs of nations could wall off neutral or politically unstable nations, ultimately slowing the global efforts to transition away from fossil fuels. And since more often than not, the most vulnerable suffer from price spikes, the authors add that there is valid reason to be concerned about climate justice in the future.

title: France's sovereign debt crisis explained: How dangerous could it be?
description: French borrowing costs hit their highest level since 2002, and the gap with Germany is the widest since 2011. What is driving France's debt crisis and how far could it go?
content: For most of the past decade, lending money to France was considered almost as safe as lending money to Germany.That belief is now breaking down, and it is happening fast.Last week, investors demanded up to 5% a year to lend to the French government for 10 years. France had not faced borrowing costs that high on its 10-year bonds since July 2002.The extra return investors want to hold French debt instead of German debt rose to its highest level since the eurozone debt crisis of 2011-2012.France now pays more to borrow than Italy and Greece, two countries that sat at the centre of that crisis.This matters well beyond the bond market. Government borrowing costs influence the rates on mortgages and business loans and the interest bill that every French taxpayer ends up covering.So how did the eurozone's second-largest economy get here, and how far could it go?France's government debt has skyrocketed to 119% of GDPThe root of the problem is simple.Every year, the French state spends far more than it collects in taxes, and it borrows to cover the difference.This year, the gap, the deficit, is expected to reach 5.4% of the country's annual economic output, its gross domestic product (GDP).EU rules set a deficit limit of 3% of GDP.Year after year, those deficits pile up as debt.French public debt reached €3.6 trillion in the second quarter of 2026. That equals 119% of GDP, up from 115.6% a year earlier, according to INSEE, the national statistics office.The trouble starts when investors begin to doubt the repayment plan.Why markets are losing patience with ParisFrance has a plan. The problem is its track record.Last Thursday, the minority government of Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu presented its 2027 draft budget, which proposes about €54 billion in spending savings and additional revenue.It targets a deficit of 5% of GDP next year, down from 5.4% in 2026.Around two-thirds of the adjustment in the budget would come from spending restraint and one-third from higher taxes and contributions.Proposed measures include €6 billion of savings each in pensions and healthcare.Government spending excluding interest and defence would be frozen in cash terms, squeezing budgets after inflation.Yet, instead of calming investors, it worried them.Lecornu has no majority in parliament, the National Assembly starts debating the text on 13 October, and a presidential election is due in spring 2027.Stéphane Colliac, an economist at BNP Paribas, noted that France had already missed its budget targets in three of the four years between 2023 and 2026.Interest payments and defence spending are both rising, so the government must find savings worth about 1% of GDP just to cut the deficit by 0.4 percentage points, Colliac calculates.Supply adds to the pressure.The French Treasury plans to issue €340 billion of debt in 2027, €20 billion more than this year, as pandemic-era borrowing comes due.Even if everything goes to plan, Colliac expects debt to rise to 121% of GDP in 2027 and to stabilise only at 124% in 2032.Enrique Díaz-Alvarez, chief economist at Ebury, said: “The political deadlock in Paris remains very much unresolved,” adding that the proposals had met with scepticism from the fiscal watchdog.Student protests over underfunded schools have added to the pressure on the government.Why France's sovereign risk is blowing up nowBeyond the rise in France’s 10-year bond yield to 5%, its widening gap with Germany shows investors are increasingly concerned about French debt.Its premium over Germany’s equivalent Bund reached 152 basis points, or 1.52 percentage points, returning to levels associated with the 2011 eurozone crisis.Intesa Sanpaolo strategists, led by Gian Marco Salcioli, argue that the speed of the move matters more than its level.When yields jump this fast, they say, the fear shifts from the price of borrowing to the risk of not being repaid in full, and France is the clearest example."The move tends to transform rate risk into something broader, first and foremost credit risk," Salcioli said in a note to clients.Díaz-Alvarez said this was "the largest weekly widening in said spread in seventeen years."Could the crisis spread across Europe?There are already warning signs.ING strategists Michiel Tukker and Benjamin Schroeder reported that Italian and Greek spreads over German Bunds had widened by almost 15 basis points during the French turmoil.“Debt dynamics are no longer deemed only a French problem,” they wrote.Currency markets are also reacting.Intesa’s currency analysts Luca Cigognini and Fabio Vacchelli noted that the euro touched $1.1161 in Monday’s Asian trading despite weaker US employment figures.They warned that French fiscal concerns could push it towards $1.10.For the ECB, that creates a difficult balancing act.September eurozone inflation rose to 3.8%, strengthening the case for continued tightening. Meanwhile, stress in government bond markets bolsters the case for pausing and considering support.“An ECB pause would weigh on the EUR from a rates-spread perspective, although the stabilisation of debt markets would return flows into the currency,” Ana Munera, BBVA’s director of global markets strategy, said.The ECB does have a targeted bond-purchase tool, the Transmission Protection Instrument, to counter unwarranted market disruption.But support depends on factors including debt sustainability and fiscal-policy compliance.It is not an unconditional guarantee of French borrowing costs.Such purchases can address disruptive differences in borrowing costs between countries without requiring the ECB to cut its main interest rates.So how dangerous is it?The immediate risk is that political deadlock prevents France from passing a budget.BBVA's Munera warns that Lecornu could fail to secure sufficient parliamentary support and be forced from office.Without an approved budget, France would again rely on an emergency law to maintain essential government financing, as it did in 2025 and 2026.Each new delay has a price.BNP Paribas' Colliac estimates that if serious deficit cuts slip to 2028, debt would reach 126% of GDP by 2032.With borrowing needs of €340 billion next year, every extra tenth of a percentage point on France’s borrowing costs adds up quickly.There are also reasons not to panic.France is not a country that has lost access to markets. It is a country whose lenders want to be paid more and want to see a plan they can believe.The first parliamentary test of that credibility begins on 13 October, when the Assembly starts debating the budget.

title: Simpler itineraries, longer stays: How travellers embrace doing less while on holiday
description: From slower, less-planned breaks to AI scepticism and the rise of nearby escapes, travellers are expected to prioritise deeper and more meaningful experiences in 2027.
content: With the arrival of autumn comes a flurry of new travel trend reports and predictions for the coming year. The latest body to make its predictions is UK-based travel and tourism marketing brand Lemongrass, which has revealed its picks of the top trends for 2027.Experts at the company believe that a lot of travel undertaken next year will revolve around the “anti-optimised” holiday, which means that travellers will be choosing to do less and spend longer in a destination, rather than rush about and tick off everything on a perfunctory list. The Lemongrass travel trend report has also revealed that travellers are also moving away from bucket lists, biohacking and AI-generated itineraries and are instead plumping for deeper, slower and more emotional experiences. “For years, travel has been caught up in the language of optimisation – more destinations, more experiences, more personalisation and more efficiency,” said Mirjam Peternek McCartney, CEO and Founder of Lemongrass Marketing. “But our 2027 trends suggest that travellers are beginning to ask a much more human question: how do I want to feel? “This isn’t a rejection of technology, luxury or ambition. It’s a recalibration. People want travel that gives something back – whether that means feeling calmer, understanding a place more deeply, connecting with other people, or simply having the freedom to enjoy a moment without having to maximise it.” Here are some of the findings from the report.The anti-optimised holiday and other insightsLemongrass says "anti-optimised holidays" – that is, cramming every minute of a trip with activities – could be on the way out. Travellers are increasingly looking for trips that feel less like a checklist and more like a proper break – with fewer destinations, simpler itineraries, longer stays and plenty of time to simply see where the day takes them.The new meaning of having a luxurious holiday could just be having nowhere to be.Nervous system designWellness is moving beyond spa treatments, health checks and the latest biohacking trends. Increasingly, hotels and destinations are looking at the whole environment, from lighting and sound levels to access to nature, food, movement and opportunities to connect with other people.Rather than adding more treatments to an itinerary, the focus is shifting towards creating spaces that naturally help guests slow down, rest and recover and, most importantly, leave feeling better. From bucket list to depth listAI can increasingly give travellers a pretty good idea of what to expect before they even set off. As more of the planning process becomes automated, though, there’s growing interest in the things an algorithm can’t quite provide, namely context, curiosity and human insight.Instead of chasing supposedly hidden gems or ticking off must-see sights, travellers are likely to seek out expert-led tours, cultural trails, literature, history, architecture, workshops and conversations with people who actually live there. The appeal is less about discovering somewhere first and more about understanding it properly, rather than just working off a checklist. Epistemic vigilance and the AI trust gapAs AI takes hold of all aspects of travel, knowing what information to trust could become just as important as finding it in the first place.Travellers are increasingly having to navigate AI-generated content, synthetic images and paid-for recommendations, making first-hand experience and local knowledge more valuable.That means they’ll also likely want to trust tour operators or travel agents who can say “we’ve been there and seen it first-hand”, rather than an AI programme which is effectively just winging it.Other travel trends to expect in 2027Alongside the headline findings, the report also identified 10 other trends which we can expect to see play out in the coming year. Shifting conversations around masculinity are, apparently, creating a new travel market for men seeking physical, emotional and mental wellbeing. Fitness, nature, mindfulness and outdoor experiences are no longer being used by men just to improve performance, but also to facilitate connection, resilience and meaningful friendship.Climate change is undoubtedly having an impact on travel, and it’s not just where people go, but how the destinations themselves cope. In 2027, it seems that travellers won’t want to just escape the heat, but also put value on spots which offer resilient infrastructure, flexible experiences, strong local knowledge and tourism businesses able to respond when conditions change.That leads into the next trend: citizen science.Travellers are increasingly moving from observing nature to actively participating in its protection, whether that’s wildlife monitoring, water sampling or recording species. The aim of playing such a role in conservation can mean that tourists achieve a deeper connection with the places they visit.More tourists will also want to leave places better than they found them, and not just in nature terms. The challenge is making meaningful, locally led conservation and community projects accessible without slipping into traditional voluntourism – and that leads into the new "giving journey" trend. It’s similar to another trend: journeys “without sacrifice or sermon”. Sustainable travel is becoming less about compromise and more about the experience. Rail, for example, can offer a more scenic, comfortable and enjoyable way to travel – as well as a lower-impact one.
