Sustainability is often embraced when it delivers a better experience, rather than making people feel less guilty. Next up is “earned travel”, or the rejection of trips that are too easy. Travel has never been more convenient – and that may be exactly why some travellers are starting to seek out the opposite.From remote landscapes to independent adventures, a bit of effort, uncertainty and spontaneity can make a trip more rewarding. Increasingly, getting there is part of the experience.At the same time, travellers will be hunting for the next trend, which is the so-called “joy economy”. With uncertainty and digital overload everywhere, travellers are looking for things that simply make them feel good – from play and surprise to connection and escapism. They're using travel as a form of emotional restoration, and not just something to do. That ties into the mystic outlands trend, which will see folklore, fantasy and atmospheric landscapes drawing travellers looking to step into another world, not just a destination – whether that means dark skies, ancient forests or places steeped in stories.More travellers will be asking “who gets to tell the story?” rather than “where are we going?”.Travellers are increasingly interested in who gets to tell a destination’s story, with female guides, historians, artists, chefs and community leaders bringing different perspectives, especially in areas where the female voice has typically been overlooked. Finally, according to the report, “near is the new far”.In 2027, it predicts that travellers will realise they don’t always need to go far to get away. Short-haul trips, rail journeys, staycations and off-season breaks offer an easier escape, with less time, cost and hassle. Short-haul travel can be cool – and as enjoyable and meaningful as destinations thousands of miles away.

title: Musical residencies: Business is booming, but who pays the most for pop stars playing in Europe?
description: Musical residencies are on the rise in Europe for major pop stars, but costs are increasingly being heaped upon audiences with travel, accommodation and extras pushing up ticket prices, according to Spanish consumer rights group FACUA.
content: For decades, Las Vegas made musical residencies part of its identity. Instead of taking a show from city to city, major artists would stage the same production in a single venue for weeks or even months, and it was the audience who travelled to see it. Europe is now beginning to experiment with a similar formula.Madrid is one of the most visible examples of this transformation. Shakira has headlined a 12-date residency in a temporary venue, the Shakira Stadium, set up at Iberdrola Music in Villaverde. Bad Bunny has concentrated ten concerts at the Riyadh Air Metropolitano as part of his tour, while Dani Martín has become the first artist to develop a residency at Madrid’s Movistar Arena.The phenomenon goes beyond Spanish and Latin American performers. Other international stars such as Céline Dion, Adele and Ariana Grande have also been linked, in different ways, to formats that group several performances in the same European city. The result is a major change in the relationship between artist, city and audience.For Rubén Sánchez, secretary-general of consumer rights group FACUA, this formula "does not benefit the public". He believes that concentrating performances allows the industry to cut costs by using the same venue for longer, while forcing many spectators to take on additional expenses."It is not the same for all the shows to be held in Madrid as for there to be a tour of different cities in Spain," Sánchez explains. On top of the ticket price can come transport, accommodation, food and other costs linked to the trip.More dates, but also more expensesResidencies can increase the number of tickets available by offering several chances to see the same artist. However, for those who live far from the chosen city, the real cost of attending can be considerably higher.Sánchez believes it will be the public’s response that ultimately determines the future of the model. If fans are willing to travel and absorb those extra costs, he thinks it is likely that more residencies will appear. If there is a backlash that translates into lower ticket sales, the industry may reconsider its strategy."The success or failure of the new model will depend on the mass reaction of users," he says.The issue of the final priceFACUA also warns of another problem linked to ticket sales: the lack of clarity over how much consumers end up paying. Sánchez is particularly critical of the so-called "booking fees" added during the purchasing process. For FACUA, the advertised price should include all compulsory costs from the outset."From the very first minute, from the very first screen, from the first advert, they have to say what the ticket price is," he insists. On top of that comes the resale market. FACUA argues that resale should only be allowed on a non-profit basis, for instance when a consumer who cannot go sells their ticket to someone else. The organisation is calling for tighter regulation of resale aimed at making a profit.The consumer will have the final sayThe model emulates Las Vegas because it turns the concert into a destination. For host cities, thousands of fans can generate business for hotels, restaurants, transport and shops. For consumers, however, it means shouldering a larger share of the cost and the logistics.Sánchez believes it is still too early to know whether residencies will become established in Europe. The key will be whether audiences accept this new equation: more chances to see a major artist, but also a greater likelihood of having to travel and spend more to do so.

title: São Paulo stock exchange surges after Flávio Bolsonaro election result
description: The Ibovespa, São Paulo's main stock index, had already closed higher on Friday, but after the first-round election results in Brazil the market opened at a new record.
content: Brazil woke up today not only to a new political reality, with two presidential candidates heading into a second round in which Flávio Bolsonaro has the advantage, but also to a rise on the stock exchange.With Flávio Bolsonaro’s strong showing in Sunday’s vote, taking 47% of ballots cast, the Ibovespa index (IBOV), the main benchmark for shares traded on Brazil’s leading stock exchange (B3), recorded an 8% jump. On Friday it had also closed higher, up 2.46%.According to some specialists, the rally is linked to the unexpectedly wide lead secured by the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, which increases the chances of a victory seen as ushering in a new fiscal and economic outlook for the country.Flávio Bolsonaro’s platform includes scrapping taxes, measures to rein in public debt and the privatisation of dozens of state-owned companies.Analysts at BTG Pactual, Latin America’s largest investment bank, estimate that a Flávio Bolsonaro victory on 25 October could push B3’s shares up by as much as 45%.The Brazilian real also strengthened over the course of the day, trading at 4.98 reais to the dollar, compared with 5.22 at Friday’s close.Although inflation has been brought under control and unemployment has fallen to a historic low during Lula da Silva’s third term, Brazilians complain of a loss of purchasing power.Flávio Bolsonaro, of the far-right Liberal Party, won more than 56 million votes (47.03%), while the left-wing candidate Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva secured the backing of almost 53.9 million voters (45.16%).

title: VAT hike: Canal+ threatens to reduce its support for cinema
description: As the government drafts its 2027 budget, Canal+ is alarmed by a planned doubling of VAT on pay-TV. Boss Maxime Saada may slash film spending, threatening a sector it heavily bankrolls.
content: Tensions are rising between Canal+ and the government. As the executive prepares its 2027 budget, Maxime Saada is openly opposing plans to scrap the reduced VAT rate enjoyed by pay television. The Canal+ boss describes the move as "political" and "absurd", and says it would mean an additional cost of around 200 million euros a year for his group.According to him, raising VAT from 10% to 20% could lead to higher subscription prices, as well as internal savings and job cuts."We cannot absorb 200 million euros", the executive told RTL, warning that Canal+ will have to rein in its spending.Cinema as leverageCanal+ plays a central role in financing French cinema. In 2025, the group invested 155.6 million euros in French films and helped fund 148 productions. It thus accounts for almost half of the investment made by traditional private broadcasters. Any cut in its spending would therefore have a direct impact on production.This is precisely where the threat is being exerted. Canal+ was due to invest 980 million euros in French and European cinema between 2028 and 2032. But Maxime Saada warns that if VAT doubles, these commitments could be scaled back. He even raises the prospect of financing "maybe three quarters fewer films".undefinedThe showdown comes against an already tense backdrop around Canal+. In May, Saada announced that the group no longer wished to work with the signatories of a column criticising the influence of conservative billionaire Vincent Bolloré, who controls Canal+.The Human Rights League and the CGT-Spectacle union have since taken legal action, denouncing discrimination based on opinions.undefinedWith its 2027 budget, the government is seeking to bring the public deficit down from 5.4% to 5% of GDP. The VAT rise for Canal+ is part of this hunt for extra revenue, but it opens up a new front with a group determined to defend its profit margins and its role in French creative industries.

title: This new Japanese walking trail connects six cities across 320 kilometres
description: Japan’s longest loop trail is now fully open. Spread across 320 kilometres, the Hitachinokuni Long Trail takes hikers through mountains, rural villages, waterfalls, beaches and historic ruins.
content: If you’re heading to Japan for an active holiday you should lace up your walking boots and tackle a 320km-long hiking trail that is now fully open.The Hitachinokuni Long Trail, Japan’s longest loop trail, has been in the works for seven years since first announced in 2019 by the Ibaraki Prefecture and the Hitachi Province Trail Club.Now having opened in September, the hiking destination links six cities and towns across the northern Ibaraki Prefecture, less than a two-hour train ride away from Tokyo.Connecting Kitaibaraki, Takahagi, Hitachi, Hitachi Ota, Hitachi Omiya and Daigo, the route takes hikers through landscapes known as “satoyama”, which are rural spaces where communities have lived alongside mountains, meadows, ponds and rice fields.The trail is not high in elevation, nor easily impacted by heavy snowfall due to its geography, making it an experience that can be enjoyed year-round. However, there aren’t many refuelling points, while some areas are rocky and others include steep slopes.Where to start?Due to its design, hikers can choose where to tackle the circular trail, which is roughly divided into five areas.The Central Area is one of the more challenging sections of the trail, featuring continuous steep ascents and descents for especially skilled hikers. Located in the Yazimo mountain range, on the northern edge of the Japanese town of Daigo, the Central Area rewards hikers with views including the Fukuroda Falls, the rocky peaks of Okukuji Nantaiyama as well as the Ryujinkyo Gorge valley.The Northeastern portion of the trail covers mountains, like the high peaks of Eizomuro and Hanazono Yama, as well as coastal destinations, including the Kohama and Sasaki beaches. The area also takes hikers through history, including the Salt Road, which is an ancient trade route, and the Jikkoku Canal, which has been in use dating back to the Edo period from 1603 to 1868.Within the Southeastern area, which first opened in 2024, the hike begins at Hananuki Valley with a climb up Mount Tsuchidake, which offers sweeping views of the surrounding scenery. The area is also marked by waterfalls, historic sites like the Kitadaimon Castle ruins before ending at the Kuji River.The Southwest area is in Hitachiomiya City and takes hikers through mountains that are home to diverse flora and fauna, including Iwauchiwa flowering plants. This area also features a once thriving gold mining region.Mt. Yamizo is just one of the stops along the Northwest area. Here, visitors can explore sacred sites steeped in history, such as the Yamizomine Shrine, which is thought to date as far back as the 1st century. At the summit of the mountain, there is also a castle-shaped observation deck that offers panoramic views of Fukushima and Tochigi's mountains.

title: Extreme heat is raising risks for mothers and babies - but experts say cooling solutions already exist
description: 73 per cent of maternal healthcare workers surveyed say they have seen heat-linked cases rise in the last five years.
content: Extreme heat is making pregnancy and childbirth more dangerous, health experts warn. Nearly three in four doctors, midwives and other maternal health workers say that heat-related cases or complications have increased over the past five years, according to a survey commissioned by global health foundation Wellcome.Simon Stiell, the head of the UN’s climate body, cited the findings today, 5 October, at the pre-COP summit in Nadi, Fiji, as he warned about the less obvious dangers of extreme heat.Higher temperatures have been linked to premature birth, stillbirth and low birth weight, as well as complications for mothers. According to Wellcome, every 1°C rise in temperature correlates with a five per cent increase in premature births and a seven per cent increase in gestational diabetes. But many of these risks can be reduced through better planning, Stiell says, whether it’s improved heat alerts or simply reliable water and electricity in clinics.Health workers want help tackling extreme heatThe Wellcome survey included 1,000 maternal health professionals in Australia, Brazil, India, the UK and Zimbabwe. 98 per cent had cared for a pregnant woman whose health they believed had been affected by extreme heat, and 99 per cent said the same of a baby.The vast majority surveyed also said they need more support. 92 per cent called for more training, guidance and resources to protect pregnant women from heat.Stiell delivered his speech at a Wellcome-organised event on the opening day of pre-COP, which runs from 5 to 8 October. The meeting is the final major gathering before COP31, held from 9 to 20 November in Antalya, Türkiye.This year’s co-hosts – Türkiye and Australia – have billed this as an “Implementation COP” focused on turning pledges into progress. Their priorities include climate finance, building resilient cities and infrastructure, and protecting vulnerable regions. However, both countries have come under scrutiny for embracing coal, which is often referred to as the ‘dirtiest’ form of energy.Stiell argued that governments should make maternal and newborn health part of the climate action, too.Pregnant women who work outdoors, live without adequate cooling at home or have to travel long distances for medical care may have little protection during extreme heat, he said. Clinics can also struggle when water, electricity or cooling are unreliable.“‘Staying cool’ is simply not an option when there is no cool place to go,” Stiell says.From heat alerts to cooling roofs, solutions already existIn his call to action, Stiell said governments should invest in practical solutions such as heat alerts, better trained healthcare workers, water and electricity infrastructure, and clinics better prepared for extreme temperatures.Around the world, some of these ideas are already being tested.In Zimbabwe and South Africa, a Wellcome-funded project involving 1,600 women is testing low-cost protections for extreme heat, including sunhats, water bottles, umbrellas and fans. Some communities are also painting roofs white, broadcasting heat advice on the radio and training health workers to deliver daily warnings through an app.Cities can also reduce the heat pregnant women and children face in their daily lives. Some of the most promising fixes are relatively cheap and can make use of infrastructure that already exists. For example, University of Manchester researchers found that rooftop rainwater systems could help keep cities cool by spraying stored rainwater onto hot roofs.As the water evaporates, it cools the roof, reducing the amount of heat entering the building as well as the need for air conditioning. Using less air conditioning also means less heat is expelled outdoors.In Spain, meanwhile, hundreds of existing public buildings have been designated as climate shelters, giving people somewhere cool to go during dangerous heatwaves. Barcelona alone has around 400 of them, including libraries, museums and municipal markets.The COP31 host city is already searching for solutions to extreme heat. Antalya has mapped neighbourhoods where high temperatures and vulnerable populations overlap, then used the data to direct shade, green space, early-warning systems and health support towards those areas.Paying for measures like these that safeguard society’s most vulnerable will be another test for governments. At COP30, the participating nations agreed to triple climate adaptation financing by 2035. COP31 could test whether their promises translate into real action.“A changing climate must never be accepted as a reason pregnancy and birth become less safe,” Stiell says. “A newborn’s healthy start must never depend on a family’s ability to escape the heat.”

title: Ukraine warns of fake government and media sites tied to Russian intelligence
description: Ukraine's security agency claims that Russia is impersonating official government sites to spread disinformation and collect personal data.
content: Russian intelligence services are creating fake websites, social media pages, and messenger channels to imitate Ukrainian government agencies, security bodies, media outlets and senior officials, Kyiv has said.According to the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU), these fake resources copy official names, logos, photographs and branding in an attempt to appear legitimate.The agency said it had recorded a key increase in such manipulative activities and had already identified and blocked more than 50 resources that copied the SBU’s own branding and appearance.Fake accounts have also been created in the names of senior Ukrainian officials. Previous examples include Telegram accounts impersonating President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, First Lady Olena Zelenska, former presidential office chief Andriy Yermak and former SBU chief Vasyl Maliuk.Ukraine's Center for Countering Disinformation has also warned about fake accounts using the names and photographs of security officials to publish supposed insider or exclusive information.In some cases, operators repurpose older Telegram channels, including cryptocurrency pages, by changing their names and branding to make them appear official.The goal: information and influenceThe SBU says the fake resources are mainly used to spread disinformation and collect personal data.By copying government agencies, officials or media organisations, Russia can present false or misleading information as though it came from a legitimate Ukrainian source.The SBU says these campaigns aim to destabilise the political and social situation inside Ukraine and weaken the country's position internationally.The same resources can also be used to collect information from users. Fake pages and channels may encourage people to follow an account, click on links, send messages or provide personal details.According to the SBU, Russian intelligence services also target users who interact with fake pages and messenger channels and may compromise their accounts to obtain personal data. The agency says this information can later be used in recruitment operations or to gather confidential information.Russian intelligence services are particularly interested in information about the combat and operational activities of Ukraine's defence and security forces, according to the SBU.The fake resources can therefore serve several purposes at the same time. First, they can spread disinformation, attract users by posing as trusted sources and direct them towards links or accounts that can be used to collect information.This tactic often relies on small differences that can be difficult to spot, like different usernames for fake accounts. Meanwhile, a fake website may closely copy the design of a government or media page but use a different web address.Ukrainian authorities are therefore advising users to check account names, web addresses and verification badges carefully, avoid suspicious links and rely on official sources.

title: Schneider Electric shares plunge on record $22.6bn PTC deal
description: French energy technology group Schneider Electric has signed a definitive agreement to acquire Boston-based PTC for $22.6bn (€20.1bn) to expand its industrial AI business. The French company's shares plummeted on Monday following the announcement.
content: Schneider Electric, one of Europe's most valuable companies, saw its shares plunge after confirming an agreement to buy US-based industrial design software company PTC.The deal is expected to be the largest acquisition in Schneider Electric's history, as the company seeks to expand its industrial AI capabilities using product and engineering data.The French energy technology group will pay $205 per share for 100% of PTC's shares in cash, valuing its equity at $22.6bn (€20.1bn) and the business, including debt, at $23.7bn (€21.1bn).The deal "creates a leading, scaled, open and interoperable industrial software and AI franchise", Schneider said in a statement, adding that PTC's board had agreed to the deal. The offer represents a 42.3% premium to PTC's last closing share price.Schneider said the deal would combine industrial software and AI to help customers design, manufacture, operate and maintain products more efficiently, using industrial data to guide decisions and improve performance.Olivier Blum, chief executive of Schneider Electric, said: "The acquisition of PTC represents an important step forward in our ambition to lead the new era of Energy and Industrial Intelligence. Together, we are creating the industry’s most complete Software & AI powerhouse and highest-quality portfolio bridging the physical and digital worlds."The move comes amid concerns that advances in artificial intelligence could undermine software companies' business models by offering cheaper alternatives to their services.PTC’s valuation this year had fallen as low as 13.1 times the next 12 months' earnings, according to MarketWatch, citing FactSet.The publication cited analysts at Jefferies who warned that fears of AI disruption had depressed software valuations, allowing Schneider to buy PTC at a decade-low valuation, but could continue to weigh on Schneider's shares after the deal.PTC's chief executive Neil Barua said: "We gain substantial scale and resources to accelerate innovation, advance our Intelligent Product Lifecycle vision, and expand our business into more geographies and end markets to serve more customers."The Boston-based company has more than 7,000 employees and serves more than 30,000 customers. It generated roughly half of its revenue in the Americas in its 2025 financial year.Schneider expects to issue up to €17bn in debt and up to €6bn in new shares to pay for the deal.The company said it expects annual cost savings of €250m by the third year after completion, alongside approximately €800m in additional revenue from combining the businesses.Schneider also expects to pause share buybacks in 2027 and 2028, before accelerating purchases to complete its existing €2.5bn–€3.5bn programme by the end of 2030.The deal is expected to close by the third quarter of 2027, subject to customary conditions, including approval from PTC shareholders holding at least a majority of its outstanding shares and the required regulatory approvals.Schneider's shares were down more than 9% in morning trading in Paris following the announcement.

title: Musk to follow Trump and rebrand SpaceXAI as SpaceXSI
description: The company will be known as SpaceXSI, its third name this year alone, as Elon Musk follows Donald Trump’s push to rebrand AI into "super intelligence".
content: Elon Musk is changing the name of his combined AI and space company SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI, embracing US President Donald Trump’s executive order renaming artificial intelligence as super intelligence in all government communication.Musk only recently renamed xAI as SpaceXAI, about 90 days ago, after SpaceX's June stock market debut and February takeover of the company. The agreement valued SpaceX at $1 trillion (€892bn) and xAI at $250 billion (€223bn).The South African tech tycoon revealed that the company is making the change yesterday in a reply to a user on his social media platform X, who asked if there was “any possibility of renaming to SpaceXSI?”“Yes, we will make that change,” said Musk.The user asked the tech tycoon following an earlier post where he stated: “No more AI. SI. It’s better.” He later tweeted, “SpaceX is a super intelligence company.”No changes to the company’s websites or social media have been made as of publication, with no indication of when the changes will take effect.SpaceXAI currently operates the AI chatbot Grok, which is built into Musk’s social media platform X, with roughly 117 million active monthly users.Grok is also widely integrated into US government and military operations, as part of a $200 million (€178mn) agreement reached in July 2025.The decision follows US President Donald Trump’s latest executive order to rename something globally recognised to a name more in keeping with his world view, such as changing the Gulf of Mexico to Gulf of America and Lake Ontario to Lake America.The fact that Musk willingly agreed to Trump’s latest rebranding is nothing out of the ordinary, with Google and Apple both following Trump’s demand by renaming the bodies of water on their map platforms for US users.Trump first mentioned his preference for super intelligence over artificial intelligence during a speech at the UN general assembly, where he argued that “artificial” makes it sound fake when it is actually “amazing,” claiming that “super intelligence" is a more accurate description.On the same day Trump issued the executive order he hosted an AI summit with Sundar Pichai (Google), Dario Amodei (Anthropic, Mark Zuckerberg (Meta), Greg Brokman (OpenAI), Jensen Huang (Nvidia) and Musk.The six tech leaders signed a “Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities,” establishing a loose framework for companies to implement and self-regulate their own security controls. It is also legally unenforceable and carries no penalties.It sets a worrying precedent given the escalating number of incidents involving AI agents carrying out “rogue” behaviour that has seen US and Australian government websites attacked, prompting calls for tighter regulation by world leaders and “pacing the frontier” by America’s leading AI companies.Instead, Trump’s agreement allows these companies to regulate themselves without scrutiny or consequences.On Sunday 4 October, Trump announced the creation of a “Super Intelligence Force” to coordinate American efforts and ensure the US stays ahead in the AI race.

title: Anatomy of a flop: ‘Digger’ a disaster at box office and a major misfire for Tom Cruise
description: The Tom Cruise starring black comedy 'Digger' has tanked at the box office and threatens to become one of the biggest box office disasters of recent times.
content: It was a big swing, and it has turned out to be a huge miss.What was supposed to be the awards season heavyweight to finally get Tom Cruise to the Oscar podium has ended up as one of the biggest box office flops of the actor’s career. Worse, early indicators strongly suggest that Digger is on track to lose between $150-200 million. Those are John Carter numbers.The movie, starring Tom Cruise as a powerful oil tycoon who has triggered an environmental disaster, made just $8 million in the US and $20 million globally in its opening weekend. By comparison, Digger had a production budget of up to $180m.On top of Digger ’s huge budget, the trades report that Warner Bros. spent another $100m on marketing, which means that the movie needs to make $300m just to break even.Granted, intake never equates to quality, but when an Oscar-winning director of Alejandro González Iñárritu’s calibre teams up with Tom Cruise, one of the world’s biggest stars and box office magnets, this disastrous performance is notable.Digger was always a gamble as a rare big-budget, star-driven original comedy. The metatextual eco-satire has proven to be audience antagonizing, with its bold twist being both admirable in its ambition and a baffling gambit. In Euronews Culture’s review of Digger, we wrote: “Alejandro González Iñárritu (Birdman, The Revenant, Bardo), a polarising filmmaker to begin with, has made both the boldest film of 2026 and this year’s wildest misfire. Digger is certainly his most pretentious film to date. (...) It’s hard to write more about Digger without spoiling Iñárritu’s brave but misguided gambit, but safe to say that once he does pull the rug from under the audience, he leaves viewers with a boated folly that’s both hollow and heavy-handed.” Read the full, spoiler-free review here. Digger’s dismal box office numbers contribute to an annus horribilis for Warner Bros., as the studio has struggled throughout 2026 to gross more than $100 million domestically for each of its releases so far. Both The Bride and Supergirl produced big losses for the studio. Additionally, the timing of Digger ’s commercial failure couldn’t be worse. Paramount Skydance’s controversial acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery is set to close next week after approval from the US district court for the $110bn deal was received last Wednesday. Warner Bros.'s only hope at salvaging its disastrous year will come in December, with the release of Dune: Part Three, which is projected to open globally to around $200-230 million.

title: The best place to retire abroad is no longer in Europe – but six of the top ten are
description: European destinations scored highly in a new global retirement ranking, with six countries among the top ten, as people looking to retire abroad weigh higher taxes against quality of life.
content: Uruguay has taken the top spot in a new global retirement ranking, overtaking last year’s leader, Portugal. But Europe remains the most represented region, with six countries in the top ten. The Americas hold three places, while Mauritius ranks second.Global Citizen Solutions’ 2026 retirement index compares 46 retirement and passive-income residence programmes, assessing quality of life, travel freedom and routes to citizenship, taxation, application procedures and costs.Europe’s strengths lie in its high living standards, strong passports and routes to citizenship, although higher taxes weigh on its scores. Spain, Portugal, Latvia, Andorra, Italy and Greece all make the top ten, with Portugal slipping to fifth this year.Uruguay leads thanks to solid scores across all five categories, rather than coming first in any one of them. Mauritius follows, combining favourable taxation with good results elsewhere.The report stresses that the right destination depends on each retiree’s priorities. Fewer than four points separate first and tenth place, making the leaders closely matched.What are the major priorities for those retiring abroad?Quality of life carries the most weight in the index, followed by mobility and citizenship, then taxation, application procedures and costs. The weighting reflects the priorities of a typical person retiring abroad, according to the report.Europe performs strongly on quality of life and mobility but scores less well on taxation, with wide differences between its programmes. The Americas stand out for affordability and favourable taxation, while Mauritius leads Africa’s performance. In the Middle East, low taxes and fast processing are the main attractions. The United Arab Emirates, 19th overall, ranks first for preferential tax regimes. Spain, third overall, also scores strongly on mobility and options for moving with family members.Strong passports and clear routes to citizenship help European and many Latin American programmes score highly. Gulf destinations offer favourable taxation and fast processing, but their retirement programmes provide no standard route to citizenship.Europe’s top-performing programmes in the 2026 indexEurope’s ten highest-ranked international retirement programmes are those offered by Spain, Portugal, Latvia, Andorra, Italy, Greece, Austria, Albania, Cyprus and Malta. All ten rank in the top half of the index.European programmes perform particularly well on quality of life and mobility. The trade-off is taxation. Spain, the best country in Europe to live abroad in retirement, ranks fifth in the world for quality of life and offers a smooth application process taking up to eight months. However, the country also ranks last out of 46 on tax, with worldwide taxation, regional wealth taxes and no special regime for visa holders.Portugal ranks second in Europe. The country, which topped the global list in 2025, slipped to fifth place this year. This came as Portugal increased the number of years required for citizenship. In May, the requirement increased from five to ten years for most non-EU applicants.The country has still secured a very high global ranking, helped by its position as one of the most affordable major European routes, with the income requirement set at €920 a month. Portugal also scores highly on mobility, but processing takes up to two years, and its 41st-place tax ranking may make it less attractive to retirees prioritising lower taxes.The programmes that do perform well on tax, notably Malta, Andorra and Cyprus, often have other demanding requirements, including high income thresholds, large investments or slow processing. Several countries also offer opt-in regimes, such as the 7% flat tax on foreign pensions in Greece and southern Italy.Processing times and costs vary widely: Latvia, third in Europe, offers processing times of two to four months and one of the lowest-cost programmes. By contrast, the process in Cyprus can take more than two years, but the country offers a 5% tax rate, subject to specific conditions.Ireland ranks first for quality of life in the index. It combines an English-speaking environment with some of the strongest safety and environmental ratings.Andorra posts the index’s best safety and environmental scores; it ranks third in the world for quality of life and offers low taxes, with income tax capped at 10% and no wealth or inheritance tax. It is also the most expensive programme in the entire index, requiring a €1 million local investment on top of substantial income.Italy and Greece rank first and second globally for mobility and citizenship, respectively. They are also Europe’s fifth- and sixth-highest-ranked retirement destinations. Both offer options for lower taxation, but Greece’s monthly income requirement of €3,500 is one of the highest.How much monthly income do you need to qualify?Monthly income requirements vary widely, from less than €600 in Nicaragua to more than €9,000 in Bahrain. In Europe, a monthly income of less than €800 could be sufficient in Cyprus if other requirements are met, while in Andorra, monthly income has to be more than €4,500. For comparison, the amounts shown in the chart have been converted to euros, so they may fluctuate with exchange rates.The qualifying sources of income are also important. In some cases, applicants must show foreign-sourced passive income or a pension; others accept savings or dividends. And while the income threshold may be relatively low, some routes also require savings, deposits, investments or other substantial upfront payments.Cape Verde, Namibia, Chile, Zambia and Morocco are excluded from the chart because the report does not specify whether their income requirements are monthly. El Salvador is also excluded, as it gives separate thresholds for pensioners and people living on passive income. Income requirements in these countries vary between $825 and $1,800.How quickly can you get a passport?A route to citizenship is common, but not guaranteed. The report says 24 programmes offer naturalisation within five years and 17 within six to ten years. Andorra requires 20 years. Four — Malta, the UAE, Ireland and Bahrain — offer no standard route through retirement or passive-income visas.The shortest timelines are in South America: around two years in Argentina and roughly three in Uruguay, Paraguay and some other countries.However, 11 countries, including Austria, Andorra, the UAE and Malaysia, do not permit dual nationality, according to the report. Applicants may therefore have to give up their original citizenship. For those unwilling to do so, permanent residence may be the limit.What other regions offerThe Americas stand out for affordability and favourable taxation. Brazil, Argentina and Chile also offer strong passports and relatively short routes to citizenship, adding to the region’s appeal.Mauritius is Africa’s strongest performer. In the Middle East, the main attractions are low taxes and fast processing, although retirement routes offer no standard path to citizenship.

title: Middle East oil exports return to pre-war levels, excluding Iran
description: Oil exports from the Middle East, excluding Iran, exceeded their pre-war average last week, Kpler data showed, as pipelines helped bypass the Strait of Hormuz despite continued attacks on shipping.
content: Despite attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz, crude oil exports from the Middle East Gulf region, excluding Iran, returned to pre-war levels in September, according to maritime tracking firm Kpler. The recovery followed changes to the region’s export routes."At least 16.5 mbd (million barrels a day) left the region between 1 and 28 September, matching the pre-war average excluding Iran. That is 10.5 mbd above March's monthly average," said the firm.However, 40% of those exports now bypass the Strait of Hormuz, compared with 17% before the war, with pipelines in Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates providing key alternative routes. Most crude crossing the strait changes tankers offshore.The figures cover crude oil and condensate.The export figures include shipments via the Red Sea, which exporters increasingly use to bypass Iran’s attempted blockade of Hormuz. Around a fifth of the world’s oil supplies passed through the strait before the conflict.Oil prices remain well above their pre-war levels. International benchmark Brent crude futures for December delivery traded at $102.25 a barrel on Monday morning, while US benchmark West Texas Intermediate traded at $90.50 a barrel.Brent futures were around $72 before the war. The disruption to shipping through the strait has sent shock waves through the global economy, prompting countries to scramble for alternatives and sending fuel prices soaring.Iran continues to claim control over the waterway, and ships travelling without its authorisation risk attack. Nevertheless, more vessels are getting through, while alternative routes are operating at full capacity.Despite the recovery in exports, experts warned that conditions remained far from normal. A US blockade of Iranian ports continues to restrict a large share of Iran’s own oil exports.Saudi Arabia has benefited from the reopening of its East–West pipeline, which connects its main oil fields in the east to the Red Sea terminal at Yanbu, bypassing Hormuz.The pipeline shut down on 11 September after strikes launched from Iraq and resumed operations on 22 September, Kpler analyst Amena Bakr said last week.The UAE also has a route around Hormuz through its pipeline linking Abu Dhabi’s oil fields to Fujairah, a terminal on the Gulf of Oman outside the strait.The recovery in exports comes as the seven core members of OPEC+, which comprises the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and its allies, including Russia, agreed on Sunday to leave their production targets unchanged for November, in line with expectations.The seven countries produced about 25 million barrels of crude oil a day in August, up 630,000 barrels a day from July, according to OPEC’s September report.

title: Intelligence Everywhere: Inside Europe’s Next Technology Era
description: AI is moving beyond the screen. Featuring Qualcomm engineers and leaders, this documentary explores how hybrid AI, edge computing, open innovation and 6G could transform smartphones, smart glasses, cars and robots, and what role Europe will play in the next era of AI.
content: Partner Content presented by QualcommIntelligence is moving closer to where data is created. From smartphones and computers to glasses, cars and industrial devices, AI is becoming embedded across the technologies that shape everyday life.As AI expands beyond traditional computing environments, it is increasingly being delivered across devices and the cloud. "Our vision is intelligence everywhere," says Wassim Chourbaji, SVP and President Europe, Middle East and Africa, Qualcomm.“It’s where the data is created at the edge, but also in the data centre,” explains Wassim Chourbaji. “We call it hybrid AI, and it’s really an orchestration between intelligence at the edge and intelligence in the data centre.”Rooted in EuropeFor Qualcomm, this transformation builds on more than 35 years in Europe, with R&D centresacross France, Germany, Sweden, Ireland, Spain and Italy. “Our platforms combine connectivity, high-performance, low-power compute and AI,” says Chourbaji. These technologies are relevant to a wide range of industries, and Qualcomm partners with European industries including automotive, energy, robotics and industrial applications. “We like innovation. We like to drive partnerships, and you will see us very excited about the future and what we’re building in Europe.” Qualcomm’s approach also builds on academic collaboration and open innovation. Amira Alloum, Director of Engineering and R&D Europe, Qualcomm, highlights collaboration with institutions including the Luxembourg Institute of Science and Technology, Politecnico di Milano and the University of Manchester.These collaborations reflect a broader conviction at the heart of Qualcomm's approach where industry, academia and developers can build on each other's work. That philosophy also extends to open-source communities. A prime example is Arduino, the open-source electronics platform now under Qualcomm’s umbrella. Fabio Violante, VP & GM of Arduino, points to the platform’s 36.7 million development environment downloads last year as proof of the power of open communities. “Distributed innovation means having anybody contributing to some form of knowledge,” says Violante. “This is a massive democratisation, lowering the barrier to entry to technology. People who have a problem can now just assemble their solution with a few clicks.” Beyond Connectivity: The Role of 6GAs intelligence spreads across devices and data centres, the networks that connect them must evolve as well. "6G is not just a new generation of connectivity," says Wassim Chourbaji. "It's connectivity, but also distributed computing and sensing." In Cork, Qualcomm’s teams are already working with new spectrum and conducting trials for 6G. “Everything is about bridging the gap between theory and reality,” explains Jarbas Pinheiro,Senior Engineer, QT Technologies Ireland Limited. “We invest a lot in research, simulations, prototypes and field trials.” One of 6G's most promising capabilities is “transforming the network itself into a platform that perceives the physical world in real time,” Alloum explains. By leveraging integrated sensing, the network can create live virtual replicas of physical environments, mapping vehicles, drones, pedestrians, and infrastructure in real time without relying on physical cameras or additional sensors.Defining Europe’s AI FutureAs AI becomes further embedded in daily life, localised implementation and data sovereignty are becoming increasingly important considerations. “I truly believe AI is local by nature,” Chourbaji says. “It understands our dialects, our thinking. So it has to be with the local culture.” This places Europe in a strong position to benefit from the transformation. “Europe is extremely well positioned in this transformation,” he says, pointing to the region’s industrial base, research capabilities and the need for robust AI and telecom infrastructure.The opportunity for Europe is not simply to adopt AI technologies, but to help shape their development and deployment. By combining infrastructure, industrial expertise, talent and open innovation, the region has many of the ingredients needed to play a leading role in the next phase of AI. Watch the full film above to explore how this transformation is taking shape across Europe. title: Hackers access data of 8.8 million people in Denmark in 'extremely serious' breach
description: A major cybersecurity breach has exposed the personal data of 8.8 million people in Denmark.
content: Denmark has suffered a major data breach after hackers broke into the country's national population registry and accessed the personal information of millions of people.The country's digital affairs minister announced the data breach on Monday, calling it "an extremely serious incident" that affected 8.8 million people."Unauthorised individuals obtained illegal access" to the names, addresses and CPR, including those who have died or emigrated, the ministry said in a press release, referring to Denmark’s social security numbers.“This is an extremely serious incident,” Christina Egelund, digital affairs minister, was quoted as saying in the press release.“Together with all the relevant authorities, we are in the process of mapping out the full extent of the incident,” she added.Denmark has a population of around six million, but the national registry has information on 11 million, including data on those deceased and people who have emigrated from the country.An investigation has now been launched into the incident. Authorities said they have no information on who carried out the breach.They broke into the national registry by hacking into a Danish company that legally had access to it, the government said, adding that the access has not been revoked.

title: Euro hits 17-month low as French debt fears mount and Spain heads for snap election
description: The euro slid to its weakest level against the US dollar since May 2025 on Monday, as France's debt troubles and Spain's political turmoil, capped by a snap election call, fuelled fears of a fresh eurozone crisis and of contagion across the bloc's bond markets.
content: The euro fell to a 17-month low against the US dollar at the start of the week, as fiscal and political risks in Paris and Madrid revived memories of the eurozone debt crisis.The euro touched $1.1161 during Asian trading, after four consecutive weekly losses, and stood at around $1.12 at the European open, recovering slightly.Analysts at Dutch bank ING warned in a note on Friday that the market could "easily add another 2% in risk premium to the euro" if the bond sell-off extended.The spread between French and German 10-year bond yields stands at roughly 146 basis points, after the largest weekly increase in 17 years last week, according to data provider LSEG.France's 10-year yield rose to 4.917% in early trading on Monday, close to last week's 24-year high, after closing Friday at around 4.856%.French Finance Minister Roland Lescure insisted last week that France remained a solid borrower, unveiling a 2027 budget that aims to cut the deficit from 5.4% of GDP to 5%, ahead of next spring's presidential election.Spain added to the political uncertainty on Monday, when Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called a snap general election for 29 November, after the parliament rejected two of his minority government's housing decrees on Friday.Spain's 10-year yield was mostly steady between 4.07% and 4.09% on Monday morning, leaving its premium over German debt at around 65 basis points, less than half of France's current gap.Against this backdrop, European stocks were mixed at the open.The Euro Stoxx 50 fell 0.4%, and the broader Stoxx 600 rose 0.6%.France's CAC 40 fell more than 1%, while Spain's IBEX 35, which slipped into the red after Sánchez's announcement, was 0.4% higher.Meanwhile, Germany's DAX, Italy's FTSE MIB, the UK's FTSE 100 and the Netherlands' AEX traded between 0.1% and 0.3% higher.Contagion fears test the ECBLast week's sell-off also hit Italian, Belgian and Greek bonds, while German debt drew safe-haven demand. Italy's premium over Bunds neared 110 basis points on Thursday.Analysts at Belgian bank KBC wrote in a note on Monday that there had been "clear contagion towards the likes of Belgium or Italy" since then.The turmoil leaves the European Central Bank in a bind.It has raised rates twice since June to tame inflation, which hit 3.8% in September, but traders have pared bets on more hikes.Its Transmission Protection Instrument, a bond-buying backstop created in 2022, has never been used.Speaking at a think tank event on Thursday, Joachim Nagel, head of Germany's Bundesbank and a likely candidate for the ECB's next presidency, said the central bank's focus was price stability, not "certain spread levels".Asked about France, ECB President Christine Lagarde told French daily La Croix last week that "when your debt is close to 120% of GDP and not on course to be brought under control, it's a serious matter".However, Lagarde asserted that "it's not 2008 or 2011".Wall Street rallies after weak jobs dataUS stocks climbed on Friday after the American economy added just 29,000 jobs in September, far fewer than expected, prompting traders to pare bets on a Federal Reserve rate hike in October.The S&P 500 rose 0.7%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average 0.5% and the Nasdaq Composite 1.2%.US futures were mostly flat on Monday, except for the Nasdaq-100, which was about 0.5% lower.The minutes from the Fed's September meeting are due on Wednesday.

title: How is Europe tightening borders and speeding up returns? Ask the Euronews AI chatbot
description: The EU is toughening its migration policy, just months after rolling out the Migration and Asylum Pact. But where does it want to invest, and what tools does it plan to use? Ask the Euronews AI chatbot.
content: At last week’s Justice and Home Affairs Council, EU interior ministers and Commissioner Marcus Brunner decided to tighten migration rules, focusing on stricter border controls and faster returns. These priorities echoed those raised by the parties at the Munich Migration Conference on 26 September. Member states introduced a European Return Order, a standardised form on which they would have to enter the key elements of a return decision. They want to give national authorities the information they need to recognise return decisions issued by other member states.For now, mutual recognition of these decisions would remain voluntary, but the arrangement would be reassessed three years after the new rules enter into force. At that point, the Commission could table a legislative proposal to make mutual recognition mandatory.A key part of the discussion was how to improve the EU’s response to sudden mass arrivals, after this summer’s events in Ceuta exposed weaknesses in its emergency systems. A new European Emergency Response Framework will help national authorities react more quickly when migratory pressure is high. Ministers insisted on accelerating repatriations through so-called “return hubs”. These are facilities in non-EU countries where people without the right to remain are transferred until deportation. The “Group of Five”, including Denmark, Germany, Austria, the Netherlands and Greece, is leading efforts to reach agreements with third countries and have the first hubs operational in 2027. Further measures include strengthening “migration diplomacy” with third countries to curb irregular migration before it reaches EU borders, as well as using new technologies to improve border protection. The €250 million Drone Action plan will receive an additional €130 million. Do you want to know more about the EU’s plans to protect its borders? Ask the Euronews AI chatbot!

title: Glastonbury 2027 tickets sell out in 42 minutes – with line-up still unannounced
description: Organisers announced last month that general admission tickets would cost £408 each, including a £5 booking fee – taking the price above £400 for the first time.
content: General admission tickets to Glastonbury, the UK’s biggest music festival, have sold out in 42 minutes, leaving the lucky few now wondering: Who will be playing?Following its traditional fallow year, the event – which will take place between 23 to 27 June 2027 – is a cause of both joy and frustration – the latter especially for fans who spend hours in the virtual queue and who still fail to secure a spot at Worthy Farm. Tickets went on sale yesterday at 10am CET. At 10:42am, See Tickets confirmed that the entire allocation had been snapped up.“Tickets for @Glastonbury Festival 2027 are now SOLD OUT,” it wrote. “Confirmation emails are going out now. Thank you to everyone who bought tickets this morning and sorry to those who missed out.”Organisers announced last month that general admission tickets would cost £408 each, including a £5 booking fee – taking the price above £400 for the first time. That's approx. €480 in total – an increase of nearly £30 (€34) from 2025 and, according to reports from BBC News, part of a steady rise since 2010, when tickets cost £286 (€330). The price hike led to complaints, with some calling the 2027 price tag "unreasonable", "insane" and "a scam", while many feel like they're being priced out.One fan wrote: “The last time I went was 2009. It was £165. It felt affordable, worth every penny. With inflation, sure, it should be £300 now. I get it, it’s a charity event. But £400?? That doesn’t feel right or fair.” Someone else shared: "In 2000 it was £87. That’s an extra £321 in 27 years. The money went up but the music went down. Even accounting for inflation, that should be about £160 today. You pay more money to listen to shit music. How is this fair?"Still, unconditional Glasto fans who missed out this weekend will have another opportunity to secure a spot when unwanted tickets and those for which the remaining balance has not been paid (buyers were required to pay a £100 deposit, with the remaining £308 due between 1 and 7 April next year) are offered in the spring 2027 resale.No acts have yet been officially announced for Glastonbury 2027. Early bookmakers’ favourites have included Sam Fender, Taylor Swift, Rihanna and Little Simz, while there is growing speculation that The Rolling Stones, Radiohead and Fontaines D.C. could be in with a shot. Two major names have effectively been ruled out. Organiser Emily Eavis dismissed speculation around both Madonna and Oasis. However, she did confirm that all of the headliners have been booked: “We’re very excited about it,” she told BBC Radio 4’s PM programme in August. “It’s all coming together really well.” The Glastonbury 2027 line-up is expected to be announced in the coming months. The 2027 edition takes place from 23 to 27 June 2027.

title: Coral reefs are bleaching in extreme heat. Could underwater umbrellas save them?
description: Underwater shades could help corals survive extreme heat, but  researchers stress that they’re not a catch-all solution.
content: Can an umbrella work underwater? The answer appears to be yes, just not for the reason many might imagine.Around the world, marine heatwaves have put coral at risk of excessive heat stress. When ocean temperatures get too hot, stressed corals can expel the microscopic algae that live in their tissues, causing them to turn white and lose their main source of food – a phenomenon known as bleaching that is occurring with alarming frequency.A group of scientists in Florida believes that underwater umbrellas could mitigate the damage.“Heat-related coral bleaching is probably the biggest threat to reefs worldwide,” says Karen Neely of Nova Southeastern University, lead author of a research article published this week in Frontiers in Marine Science. “Solutions like shading can offer temporary protection on small scales.”How underwater umbrellas protected Florida coralsThe study came together after a record-breaking marine heatwave struck the Florida Keys in 2023.At most sites, every kind of coral bleached, and branching corals – species that grow in tree- or antler-like formations, such as the aptly named staghorn and elkhorn corals – were almost wiped out. At one inshore site, more than half of the corals researchers monitored lost some or all their living tissue. “This study stemmed directly from that event: we wanted to provide proof of concept for tools to save targeted corals in similar future events,” says Neely. The following summer, the researchers selected 40 colonies belonging to two species of brain coral in the lower Florida Keys. Half were left exposed and half were fitted with floating shades made from PVC frames and nylon mesh – like underwater parasols suspended about 30 centimetres above the coral.The shades, the researchers stress, were not used to cool the water. Instead, they reduced the intense sunlight and ultraviolet radiation that can make bleaching worse.Divers began monitoring the corals in July 2024 and installed the umbrellas in August, when summer heat intensified. They continued until November, when temperatures cooled, tracking changes in their colour and the algae living inside their tissue.Despite 2024 seeing the second-highest level of heat stress recorded at the site since 1985, some of the shaded corals began to regain their colour after the umbrellas were installed. The exposed corals became paler during the hottest part of the experiment.But the umbrellas are still a temporary fix, the researchers stress.Covering entire reefs would be impractical, so they see it primarily as a way to protect vulnerable corals during extreme heat. Ultimately, though, long-term protection depends on limiting the warming of the seas.“Scaling is the big limitation of this study,” Neely explains. “Shading is not a cure-all.”Marine heatwaves are bleaching reefs worldwideGlobally, ocean temperatures continue to break records. On 22 August, the average global sea surface temperature outside the polar regions reached 21.1°C, the highest daily temperature recorded.Meanwhile, extreme heat is hitting coral reefs more often. In August, the Global Coral Reef Monitoring Network reported that bleaching events now occur roughly every five to six years, compared with about once a decade in the past.Although corals can recover from bleaching when sea temperatures cool, frequent marine heatwaves can leave too little time for damaged reefs to repair themselves.The most recent global bleaching event began in 2023. Between 2023 and 2024, hard coral cover fell by 8.9 per cent globally – the largest one-year decline on record.By March 2025, 84 per cent of the world’s reefs had experienced temperatures hot enough to cause bleaching, while parts of Australia’s Great Barrier Reef recorded their largest annual losses of living coral in almost 40 years of monitoring.Although coral reefs cover less than 0.2 per cent of the ocean floor, they are vital to life, both underwater and on land. They provide food and shelter for at least a quarter of all marine species, including many fish caught for food, and are a natural shield for coastlines.While underwater umbrellas may be able to prevent marine heatwaves, the Florida study suggests they could give these important creatures at least some protection as temperatures rise.

title: The best road trips to spot Europe’s most impressive wildlife
description: Planning a wildlife escape? These European road trips combine spectacular scenery with some of the continent’s best opportunities for spotting animals in the wild.
content: Europe has many charms, and its wide variety of wildlife is certainly among them. Across the continent, travellers can spot everything from flamingos and starlings to deer, seals and golden eagles. Many of them can be spotted from the road, meaning they’re accessible to a majority of tourists.Now, car rental company Avis has ranked Europe’s best wildlife driving routes, taking into consideration the reliability of sightings, proximity to airports, how practical and compact each road trip is, and its popularity online, specifically in terms of Google search volume and appearances on Instagram. Southern England’s New Forest topped the list, followed by Denmark’s part of the Wadden Sea, while Spain appears twice in the top 10. These are the best driving routes for spotting wildlife across Europe. Five European scenic drives where you can spot wildlifeNew Forest wildlife drive, EnglandAt the top of the ranking is the New Forest in the south of England. This beautiful spot scores 93 out of 100 on the Avis wildlife routes index, for various reasons. A 32km drive starting in Lyndhurst and travelling through Bolderwood and Rhinefield Ornamental Drive and finishing up in Brockenhurst takes just 45 minutes to one hour – one of the speediest wildlife drives on the list. This area is particularly famous for its native, free-roaming native New Forest ponies, but visitors can also expect to see the likes of fallow and roe deer and buzzards soaring overhead.Autumn is an ideal time to visit, with October playing host to the deer rut, the annual mating season for the creatures. Wadden Sea (Route 11), DenmarkIn second place is Denmark’s Wadden Sea – or Route 11 – route, which comes in with a score of 80 out of 100. Driving from Ribe via the Gammel Hviding marshes to Skærbæk covers around 65km and takes approximately one to 1 hour and 25 minutes to drive. Expect to see migratory birds, seals and harbour porpoises around the wider Wadden Sea landscape. This route is also the most accessible in the ranking, as Esbjerg Airport is just 30km away. In the autumn, visitors can experience Denmark’s famous Black Sun phenomenon, where starling murmurations flock overhead in shifting patterns before heading to roost. Ebro Delta birding drive, SpainThird on the list is the Ebro Delta birding drive in Spain’s Catalonia, scoring 74 out of 100. The route runs for just 25km, which can take approximately 45 to 60 minutes to drive, although there’s so much to see here that wildlife lovers may want to allow a full day for stops. The route takes in Poblenou del Delta, Pont de Través, Encanyissada, Migjorn and Alfacada and encompasses lagoons, wetlands and rice fields which are variously home to bird species including flamingos, glossy ibis, purple herons, spoonbills, marsh harriers and waders.While the late spring and summer are particularly good for spotting breeding birds, September and October bring spectacular displays of migrating species. Camargue wildlife drive, FranceThe Camargue wildlife drive in France, with a score of 73 out of 100, is in fourth place. The route is approximately 90km long and takes 2.5 hours, although it can take longer if drivers take more stops. It runs from Arles to Étang de Vaccarès and Pont de Gau and on to Saintes-Maries-de-la-Mer. Pink flamingos are the star attraction here, but visitors can also spot herons, the famous white Camargue horses and black bulls. September is the best time to see the flamingos, but all the other creatures can be easily seen all year round. Scotland’s North Coast 500 The iconic North Coast 500 in Scotland ranks in fifth, scoring 71 out of 100 – and it’s by far the longest route in the top five. In fact, the full circuit covers some 830km and requires about 14 to 16 hours of driving, which most people usually choose to spread across several days. The route takes drivers from Inverness through Black Isle, Wester Ross, Durness, Dunnet Head and John O’Groats and to Inverness. Those who take it can see habitats which are home to red deer, pine martens, harbour seals and golden eagles. May to September might provide the most favourable conditions for a road trip, but autumn is a great time to visit for those who want to see the red deer rut. title: “We don't feel a sense of worry” in Europe, says the head of the Muslim World League
description: While in Brussels to meet with political and religious leaders, Sheikh Dr Mohammad bin Abdulkarim Al-Issa stressed the need to deepen dialogue in order to confront the turmoil facing the world and that Europe's "civilised constitutions" will prevent political excesses.
content: Dialogue. That was the word repeated by the Secretary-General of the Muslim World League, Sheikh Dr Mohammad bin Abdulkarim Al-Issa, during his visit to Brussels on Friday.During his stay in the Belgian capital, the Saudi religious leader met political figures and representatives of the country’s religious communities and civil society who gathered for a high-level meeting on dialogue and social cohesion.Al-Issa stressed the importance of dialogue in resolving conflicts, saying it needed sincere intentions and effective leadership.“Of course, we always believe in dialogue and place great faith in it,” he said, adding that “dialogue is the language of reason and wisdom.”Established in 1962, the Muslim World League is a Mecca-based Islamic organisation that describes its mission as promoting Islam, tolerance and friendship among peoples.Europe’s far-right rise and containing its dangersHis visit came after the far-right Alternative for Germany, or AfD, finished first in state elections in both Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania in September.France is due to hold a presidential election in 2027, while parliamentary elections are expected in Italy, Poland and Greece.Despite the rise of the hardline right in some European countries, Al-Issa expressed confidence in national constitutions, European institutions and societal values.“As for talk of a hardline right emerging in some European countries, we are generally not worried. Each European country has a civilised constitution that no one can override. There are also societal values that everyone must respect,” he explained.“Any departure from the constitution and these civilised societal values will prompt society to speak out and put things right,” he said.He also pointed to the possibility of challenging legislation before constitutional courts.Al-Issa said similar questions had arisen in other countries because of certain governments. Things had turned out as he had hoped, he said, where there was constitutional oversight and an active public conscience.Religious freedom is protected by national constitutionsHe also called for respect for religious practices within the framework of national constitutions.The issue comes amid debate over restrictions on religious clothing in Europe. Italy’s government has approved a decree banning face coverings during school activities, with exceptions for certified medical reasons and educational activities.The decree does not explicitly mention the burqa or niqab, although Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni referred to both when announcing the measure, saying that in Italy “no one should force a girl to hide herself”.“We always call for respect for each religion’s distinctive practices, provided they do not conflict with the constitution,” Al-Issa said.“There is no doubt that civilised constitutions, particularly European ones, respect those practices and the observance of religious rituals.”

title: Has plague returned to Siberia? Panic in Russia after death of lab worker
description: A female staff member at an anti-plague institute in the Irkutsk region who died amid rumours of a "black death" outbreak was diagnosed with "pneumonia of unknown origin". Rospotrebnadzor insists that the situation in the region is "stable".
content: Residents of Russia's Irkutsk region are deeply worried by rumours of a possible outbreak of pneumonic plague in this Siberian area. Speculation began to spread rapidly after the death of an employee of the Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute.Darya Shipilova died in the early hours of 2 October in the intensive care unit of the district hospital in the town of Shelekhov. According to local media, she broke a test tube containing the plague pathogen.The incident prompted authorities to introduce quarantine measures: around 200 people have been placed under strict medical observation. The outlet "Baikal People" (source in Russian) reports that several Irkutsk hospitals were immediately closed and placed under quarantine, due to last three weeks. On Saturday, masks were made compulsory as a preventive measure at the Irkutsk aluminium plant in Shelekhov.Residents of Shelekhov have seen people on the streets wearing protective suits, masks and gloves. Local parents also say masks were handed out in kindergartens.Where did the plague come from?The deceased, a 28-year-old laboratory assistant, specialised in research on dangerous pathogens. According to the main account reported by her colleagues and independent media, on 25 September, while working with live biological material in the laboratory, she accidentally smashed a test tube containing the dangerous bacterium Yersinia pestis.Two days later Shipilova's condition suddenly worsened. She was rushed to Shelekhov district hospital. At first doctors, unaware of what had happened, suspected a severe case of coronavirus and admitted her to a specialised Covid unit. However, the rapid deterioration and the clinical picture forced them to carry out rapid tests for highly dangerous infections. The patient was put on a ventilator, but her life could not be saved.The pulmonary form of plague develops extremely fast and, without prompt and targeted antibiotic treatment, is almost invariably fatal.Are the authorities hiding information?The authorities' immediate response underlined how serious the situation was. The head of Rospotrebnadzor, Anna Popova, urgently arrived at Shelekhov hospital and took part in an emergency meeting of the sanitary and anti-epidemic commission chaired by regional governor Igor Kobzev.After the incident, officials initially restricted the information they released. During the first 24 hours, authorities in the Irkutsk region and Governor Igor Kobzev avoided using the word "plague". On 2 October Kobzev spoke of "a particularly dangerous infection" and said that "the situation is under strict control". The next day the authorities in Baikalsk urged residents not to travel to Shelekhov because of plague, but deleted the post a few hours later.The head of Buryatia, Alexey Tsydenov, also commented on the situation. Citing Rospotrebnadzor and the republican government, he said the woman's death was linked to plague infection, but later his statement was amended to a more cautious wording.This lack of clarity has fuelled panic on social networks in Irkutsk and neighbouring regions.Well-known Russian epidemiologist Gennady Onishchenko tried to reassure local residents, saying that plague carriers - rodents and fleas - in Siberia usually go into winter dormancy by early October. But that did not dispel people's fears."Pneumonia of unknown aetiology"On Sunday, Rospotrebnadzor said that the sanitary and epidemiological situation in Irkutsk region was stable, and that the woman had died from "pneumonia of unknown aetiology". The agency insists that further testing of samples taken from the patient did not reveal any micro-organisms related to her professional work."The sanitary and epidemiological situation in Irkutsk region, in the cities of Irkutsk and Shelekhov, is stable," the press service of Rospotrebnadzor said. "A special package of measures has been organised and carried out in connection with the illness of an employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East, diagnosis: 'Pneumonia of unknown aetiology'."Rospotrebnadzor also stated that no incidents involving pathogenic microorganisms had been recorded at the institute and that "no staff member has sought medical help for infectious diseases in the past 10 days".

title: Increasing influence: Italy marks 800 years since death of Saint Francis of Assisi
description: Ceremonies and events are being held in Assisi throughout the day in honour of Italy's patron saint. The festivities form part of the Franciscan Jubilee Year, proclaimed by Pope Leo XIV.
content: This Sunday, 4 October, marks the 800th anniversary of the death of Saint Francis of Assisi, Italy's patron saint. From this year, and for the first time since 1977, 4 October once again becomes a national holiday.To mark the occasion, the city of Assisi is celebrating this historic anniversary by exceptionally bringing together all of Italy's Regions and provincial capital municipalities, with 18 Regions and just as many municipalities already represented.More than 3,000 pilgrims and tourists have arrived in the city to take part in the celebrations, which culminate in an address to the Nation by the President of the Republic, Sergio Mattarella, from the loggia of the Sacred Convent.Events to celebrate the 800th anniversary of Saint FrancisThe day of prayer and festivities follows a tightly scheduled programme that began at midnight on Saturday with the festive ringing of the bells. At 6.00 a.m. mass is celebrated for the community of friars, presided over by the Minister General, Friar Carlos Alberto Trovarelli, followed at 6.50 a.m. by the offering of prayers at the Saint's Tomb.The arrival of President Mattarella is expected by 9.45 a.m. for the solemn mass in the Upper Basilica, presided over by Cardinal Matteo Maria Zuppi. During the celebration, attended also by ambassadors and representatives of accredited countries, Umbria will offer the oil and the mayor of Assisi, Valter Stoppini, will light the votive lamp on behalf of all Italian municipalities. This will be followed, at 11.20 a.m., by official speeches and, at noon, by the live broadcast of Pope Leo XIV's Angelus prayer on the giant screens in the square.Cultural initiatives linked to Saint FrancisAlongside the institutional and religious ceremonies, major cultural initiatives have been organised, starting with the exhibition "Saint Francis at the Porziuncola", open to visitors until 25 October 2026.The exhibition is hosted in the Porziuncola Museum at the Basilica of Santa Maria degli Angeli, which for the occasion has created a new entrance by refurbishing the ancient 15th-century cloister, once a traditional passageway for the friars. This exhibition itinerary, curated by the director Friar Saul Tambini and Donatella Vaccari, offers visitors a profound immersion in Franciscan iconography from its origins in the 13th century.For the first time, the exhibition brings together the breviary of Saint Francis and that of Saint Clare, highlighting the deep bond between these two key figures of the early Franciscan movement. Visitors can admire paintings and relics, such as the famous portrait-relic attributed to Cimabue, which tradition holds was the lid of the Saint's first coffin, and the table on which Francis greeted death in song.Among the works on display is also the Crucifix of the suffering Christ painted by Giunta Pisano around 1236. The entire cycle of exhibitions and celebrations forms part of the Franciscan Jubilee Year, proclaimed by Pope Leo XIV, which began on 10 January 2026 and is due to conclude on 10 January 2027.

title: The eyes have it: Iconic World Cup pictures explored by Getty photographers
description: Whether on or off the pitch, many of the most memorable moments from FIFA  World Cups have been captured by Getty. Here, some of the photographers behind those lenses share their thoughts about taking the best emotive images.
content: Competition by its nature leads to comparison but there is no title to play for in this piece. Instead, we've asked several Getty photographers to pick their favourite shots from the past five World Cup tournaments that best capture the beauty and emotion of effort, grace, victory and defeat.Argentina v France: Final - FIFA World Cup Qatar 2022"This photo was taken at least 30 minutes after the main trophy lift. All the Argentina fans and photographers are waiting for Messi to go over to acknowledge the fans. All the Getty Images photographers had a loose plan of what we’d capture, but luck also kicked in with this picture. This is the first moment he opened his arms with the biggest of smiles two metres in front of me, whilst I was looking up on a 24-70mm lens." Shaun Botterill. France v Croatia: Final - 2018 FIFA World Cup Russia"What makes this image special is not only the celebration itself, but the access and the atmosphere around it. Thanks to FIFA’s exclusive access, I was the only photographer allowed on the pitch after the celebrations, which gave me a very different perspective on the aftermath of the World Cup final. "The fireworks had just finished and the rain had left smoke and haze hanging inside Luzhniki Stadium. As the light came through that haze, it created visible rays above Paul Pogba while he held the World Cup Trophy. The combination of the smoke, rain, light and the space around him helped give the image a stronger sense of atmosphere than a standard trophy celebration. "Technically, I wanted to keep the frame wide enough to show the scale of the stadium, the crowd, the haze and the pitch. The access allowed me to stay low and close, but the wider composition lets the atmosphere become part of the story. For me, it feels less like a standard trophy picture and more like a surreal, emotional moment in the aftermath of France winning the 2018 FIFA World Cup." David Ramos Italy v France: Final - FIFA World Cup 2006 Germany"The picture came following the 2006 final after Italy won on penalties against France, where my colleague Shaun Botterill and I were in prime position for the cup presentation."I was shooting tighter on a 400mm concentrating on the Italian captain Fabio Cannavaro, and as the players went on a lap of honour they suddenly started to reach out and touch the trophy en masse. I quickly balanced on top of a metal barrier near the front row of seats for extra height and took the image. I remember other photographers pulling at my feet trying to reach my position on the barrier, but the moment was over in a flash. The confetti and pyrotechnic smoke also adds to the picture. Trophy presentations can sometimes feel staged, but this felt like a more impulsive and natural way of a team coming together, bonding in their historic moment." Michael SteeleNetherlands v Spain: Final - FIFA World Cup 2010 South Africa"There are moments in every FIFA World Cup that transcend the match itself and become part of football folklore.
