Nigel de Jong's challenge on Xabi Alonso in the 2010 FIFA World Cup Final is unquestionably one of them.Positioned perfectly to capture the incident, this image freezes the exact moment De Jong's outstretched boot meets Alonso's chest, preserving one of the most controversial flashpoints in World Cup history. Shown only a yellow card by referee Howard Webb, the challenge immediately sparked debate, with many believing the Netherlands midfielder was fortunate to remain on the pitch. More than fifteen years later, the photograph remains one of the enduring visual symbols of South Africa 2010, a split second that encapsulated the tension, physicality and controversy of a fiercely contested final." Laurence Griffiths.England v Belgium: Group G - FIFA World Cup 2018 Russia“Occasionally we are allowed to work from the ‘catwalk’ of a stadium, up 80 or 100 metres above the field. Only a small group of people are allowed up there. It comes with a long process of approval, training courses, safety belts, helmets, sometimes even medical certificates, because you need to be able to work at height."The pressure is massive. You are standing above people’s heads, so if you drop even a single small thing, the reality is you could seriously hurt somebody. Everything you take up there has to have a double connection. Every camera, every lens, even your phone, has to be attached. You empty your pockets. You can’t take spare pieces, because everything could fall. But it is a mega opportunity."This was Belgium versus England, and a header with six players involved, which does not happen often and is hard to predict from above. I like it because it is a different football image, an angle you do not see every day. I am a big fan of the green grass and the clean background, but it is also about what goes into getting there. You are lucky if six players jump for one header and you can still see the faces, the action, body language, the white line and the colours. In the end, it all just came together.” Matthias HangstArgentina v France: Final - FIFA World Cup Qatar 2022"The FIFA World Cup Final in Doha was my first World Cup final, and I knew I was witnessing history. Like everyone else on the pitch, I expected the defining image of the night to be Lionel Messi lifting the World Cup trophy. Before that moment, he walked past the trophy as he received the Golden Ball award as the tournament's best player. At this moment he turned and looked toward the photographers, managed to capture this frame. Is just a quiet and simple photo but still powerful." Maja Hitij

title: Where to celebrate Halloween 2026 in Europe: Spooky cities, haunted hotels and scary events
description: Fancy a fright? These European destinations, hotels and Halloween events promise everything from Gothic legends to full-blown horror.
content: Halloween is nearly upon us, and the festival has become so popular that it’s nearly impossible to escape it throughout the entirety of October.The month is peak spooky season, as temperatures drop across much of Europe and things start getting a bit darker and, in some cases, eerier.If you’re a big fan of Halloween, there’s no shortage of things to do across the continent, from the best cities to experience the creepy vibes to haunted hotels and events, which will be over once November comes.These are the best ways to get into the Halloween spirit, European-style this year.DestinationsTransylvania, RomaniaStarting, of course, with the most obvious destination, some might argue that a visit to Romania’s Transylvania region is the ultimate way to do Halloween.It’s forever linked to Dracula and the imposing Bran Castle, but there’s far more to its spooky appeal, with atmospheric villages, medieval citadels, striking churches and more than 100 castles scattered across the region.October is also the perfect time to see the beautiful autumn colours which fill the forests of the Carpathian Mountains and to explore Brașov, a beautiful city with plenty of atmosphere of its own.Bruges, BelgiumBruges may be known for its canals and romantic medieval streets, but come Halloween, the Belgian city takes a much darker turn.Hear the story of the water ghost said to haunt the Lake of Love, or join a night-time tour through the city’s legends, myths and more sinister tales.The Historium gets a spooky makeover too, with pumpkins, cobwebs and bats, and a Halloween Virtual Reality Experience. There’s also the Torture Museum, if you’re feeling brave enough.Paris, FranceParis is more than just romance and lights – and has plenty of spooky sights to go with its usual glamour.Start underground in the Catacombs, where the bones of some six million people line the dimly lit tunnels. Afterwards, wander through Père Lachaise Cemetery, where winding paths and elaborate tombs are the final resting place of figures including Oscar Wilde, Marcel Proust, Molière, and Édith Piaf.There are countless themed parties throughout the city but, if you prefer a bit of light relief rather than gore, head to Disneyland Paris, which extends its park hours until 11 pm on the night itself.Edinburgh, ScotlandEdinburgh’s dark history and atmospheric old town make it a natural fit for Halloween.Each year, the Samhuinn Fire Festival brings the Scottish capital’s ancient Celtic traditions to life, with colourful costumes, fire performers and a lively procession through the cobbled streets.It’s a dramatic way to mark the holiday, with plenty of local folklore thrown in.Derry, Northern IrelandDerry puts a more festive spin on Halloween, making it a good option for families and groups who want plenty of atmosphere without too many scares.Each October, the city hosts Derry Halloween, billed as one of Europe’s biggest Halloween festivals, with light shows, acrobatic banshees and Celtic circus performers taking over the streets.During the day, visitors can pick pumpkins or try a craft workshop, before live music and performances take over after dark.HotelsThe Haunted Bedroom at Talliston, Great Dunmow, EnglandWhat was once a normal house in the Essex market town of Great Dunmow has been transformed into something far stranger.Talliston House and Gardens is a maze of rooms, each designed to transport visitors to a different time and place, with elaborate details that make the property feel more like stepping into a story than visiting a home.For a proper fright, book a stay in the Haunted Bedroom. It recreates the bedroom of a seven-year-old Edwardian child in unsettling detail, complete with old-fashioned toys, books and furniture.Castello Dal Pozzo, Piedmont, ItalyNow a hotel, this Italian estate on the shores of Lake Maggiore has a tragic story that has given it a distinctly spooky reputation.Set in its own hillside grounds, the property is a quick drive from Arona on the lake’s southwestern shore. Its ghostly tale dates back to 1467, when a young woman named Barbara fell in love with an army captain, Matteo.The pair planned to elope, but Barbara’s father discovered their romance and locked her in the estate’s tower, while Matteo was sent into exile in France. Barbara never knew what had happened to him and died waiting for him to return.According to local legend, she never quite left. Guests have reported seeing Barbara at the tower window, still watching and waiting for her lost love.Ballygally Castle Hotel, Northern IrelandBallygally Castle has a ghostly tale dating back to the 1600s, when Lady Isabella Shaw, wife of the castle’s builder, is said to have died after being locked in a tower room.Legend has it she either jumped or was pushed to her death, and her ghost is now said to haunt the castle.Guests have reported knocking sounds, sudden cold spots and sightings of a woman in period dress, particularly around the tower stairs and Room 421, known as the Ghost Room. The four-star hotel embraces the story without overplaying it, with historical exhibits in the tower and Room 421 available to guests brave enough to request it.The Haunted Chamber Apartment, York, EnglandDating back more than 600 years, this atmospheric apartment feels like stepping straight into York’s spookier past. Overlooking York Minster, it is filled with original character, including timber panelling and historic details that give the property a suitably eerie feel.The city itself adds to the spooky setting, with its winding medieval streets, ghost stories and centuries of dark history. Nearby, York Dungeons and the Halloween thrills of Hallowscream at York Maze offer plenty more scares after dark.Hotel U Prince, PragueRight on Prague’s atmospheric Old Town Square, Hotel U Prince combines luxury with centuries of history. The building’s foundations date back to the 12th century, giving it plenty of old-world character – and some suitably spooky stories.Guests have reported unexplained noises, cold spots and shadowy figures in the corridors, while Prague’s Gothic architecture, alchemical legends and long history of ghost stories add to the eerie atmosphere.After dark, the city’s winding streets and medieval buildings make the setting feel even more mysterious.EventsBran Castle Halloween Party, Transylvania, RomaniaOn 31 October, the legendary ‘Dracula's Castle’ in Bran hosts a Halloween party, combining a special night-time tour with interactive characters, horror screenings and a party in the Royal Park. The 2026 event includes DJs, costumes and theatrical touches, with festivities running until 4 am.Bram Stoker Festival, Dublin, IrelandTaking place from 23-26 October, the Bram Stoker Festival brings four days of Gothic-inspired events to venues across Dublin. Expect immersive outdoor theatre, dark storytelling and literary events celebrating the Dracula author, who was born here.Tivoli Gardens Halloween, Copenhagen, DenmarkFrom 2 October to 1 November, Copenhagen’s historic Tivoli Gardens gets a spooky autumn makeover, with more than 20,000 pumpkins, atmospheric decorations and seasonal market stalls.Families can also enjoy Halloween-themed rides and entertainment throughout the parkHalloween Horror Festival at Movie Park Germany, Bottrop, GermanyFrom September 26 to November 8, Movie Park Germany transforms into a full-blown horror experience, with more than 300 roaming monsters, terrifying scare zones and haunted mazes.It’s aimed firmly at thrill-seekers, with plenty of jump scares and creepier attractions after sunset.Halloween at Little Kook, Athens, GreeceOctober and Halloween is the best time of year to visit Little Kook in Athens. The fantasy-themed café goes all out for scary season, transforming its buildings and surrounding streets with elaborate seasonal decorations.Expect giant pumpkins, skeletons, witches, ghosts and cobwebs spilling across colourful façades and balconies, creating theatrical street scenes that feel like a Halloween film set. Visit after dark, when the illuminated displays make this atmospheric corner of central Athens even more dramatic.

title: Ceuta support T-shirt: €10 of its €35 price goes to self-described ‘patriotic’ movement Save Europe Act
description: A T-shirt bearing the slogan “We are all from Ceuta” is being sold as a show of support for Ceuta, but part of the proceeds goes to Save Europe Act, a self-described patriotic movement that advocates remigration.
content: Journalist and social media expert Carmela Ríos posted an investigation into the sale of the garment on X on 27 September. The T-shirt emerged following the mass entry of migrants into Ceuta on 30 and 31 July. Here is what lies behind the sale.The T-shirt is being launched by Terre de France, a brand that sells a "patriotic and solidarity-based" range of products it claims are 100% French. Part of the revenue is used to support other organisations that, according to its website, include groups of farmers, agricultural colleges and an association for wounded French soldiers.In this case, €10 of the garment’s €35 price goes to Save Europe Act. No money is earmarked for directly supporting people or organisations in Ceuta, while almost 28.6% of the purchase price goes directly to Save Europe Act.The company claims that residents of Ceuta, whose nickname and popular demonym is "caballas", "are surviving a migratory invasion that threatens the very existence of their city". One X account, Damien Rieu (@DamienRieu on X), who has 325,000 followers, promoted the sale on 26 September.The promotional image shows a person wearing the T-shirt in front of what appears to be Trampolín beach, but the image is fabricated. The tools Hive Detect, TruthScan and Sight Engine indicate that it was generated using artificial intelligence.On its social networks, Terre de France spreads messages claiming to defend a Catholic and white France, which, according to the brand, is not represented by LGBTQ+ people. It also rejects "crousty", the fried-chicken-based fast food currently in fashion in the country, saying it is not 100% French.Save Europe Act and remigrationSave Europe Act presents itself as a "patriotic" movement. It demands that "the political elite" "put an end to replacement immigration", that borders be protected and that the "ethnocultural identity of European nations" be defended. It proposes halting "non-Western/non-European migration routes" until "social cohesion and cultural continuity" have been restored in the member states.It also advocates "remigration", compulsory or voluntary, of people in an irregular situation, those who have committed crimes and those "who are not integrated or constitute a significant cultural or financial burden".The organisation is collecting signatures across Europe in a bid to reach one million and submit its proposal as a European Citizens' Initiative. That mechanism allows citizens to put forward new rules to the European Commission.The Commission has refused to register it, considering it "manifestly contrary to the values enshrined in the Treaty and in the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the EU". The Commission also says the initiative would be used as “a vehicle for offensive or caricatural messages". According to 'Euronews', its organisers are preparing to challenge the decision in court.Europe's far right in Ceuta and a precedentFollowing Ceuta's migrant crisis, the autonomous city was visited by members of far-right organisations. Activists from Reform UK on 1 August, from Junge Tat in Switzerland on 2 August, and from Reconquista in Portugal on 4 August, as well as from Generation Identity in Germany.Members of the neo-Nazi organisation Núcleo Nacional were expelled on 1 August when they attempted to hold a demonstration and were met with a counter-demonstration by local residents.Among the promoters of Save Europe Act is Martin Sellner, who has almost 200,000 followers on X. On 3 August he shared videos from the city in which he called for "this ethnic replacement" to be stopped through "non-violent civil disobedience".Its co-founder Eva Vlaardingerbroek posted on 31 July a message denouncing the "orchestrated invasion" of Ceuta, which was shared by Elon Musk. She has 1.2 million followers on X and 1.3 million on Instagram.Ríos argues that Europe's far right sees Ceuta as a real stage "to advance its strategy". She outlines a roadmap based on "the massive use of disinformation, artificial intelligence and the whole machinery of bots, trolls and fictitious digital operations". According to the journalist, these movements rely on one another "on the basis of similar talking points and a shared technological framework".There is a precedent. In the Torre Pacheco case in July 2025, when an attack on a local resident by a young man of Moroccan origin triggered a wave of racist unrest, the promoters of Save Europe Act and the organisation itself spread false claims.They claimed that "Moroccan migrants" had assaulted white people for three nights in a row and that "North Africans" were arming themselves "to terrorise Spaniards". In any case, their proposal for that situation was "remigration".

title: Muchas gracias: Woody Allen presents new film in Madrid made with €3m from public purse
description: The 90-year-old American director has unveiled in the Spanish capital his 51st film, that's due to start shooting on 5 October with public funding, as past scandals still shadow his career.
content: Woody Allen is stepping behind the camera once again. The American director presented his next film in Madrid on Thursday, the 51st of his career, which will start shooting on 5 October and will be filmed mainly in the Spanish capital and Aranjuez.At 90, Allen was joined at the launch by the president of the Madrid region, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, and the mayor of the capital, José Luis Martínez-Almeida. The project is being financed by both authorities: the City Council and the regional government will equally share €3 million costs through sponsorship contracts linked to promoting Madrid. The film has a budget of around €12 million, so public support will cover roughly a quarter of the overall cost.The film, still without a final title and provisionally known as Wasp 2026, will be a contemporary comedy blending romance, intrigue and infidelity in a diplomatic atmosphere.The cast includes Alexi Wasser, Jemima Kirke, Peter Vives, Marton Csokas and Jakob Oftebro, while much of the technical crew will be Spanish. Filming will run for around six weeks and will span more than 30 locations in Madrid and Aranjuez.The sponsorship agreement also stipulates that Madrid must appear in the title of the film and that the city should have a clearly recognisable presence on screen. The City Council justifies its contribution as a tool to strengthen Madrid's international profile as a cultural, tourist and film-making destination.Allen steers clear of Spanish housing crisisDuring the presentation, Allen was also asked about the protests linked to the housing crisis taking place in Madrid. The director declined to comment on the situation, saying he has never seen himself as a filmmaker driven by political causes and that his films have focused mainly on human relationships and existential and romantic questions.He did say he is "deeply" concerned about the rise of fascism and stressed that he has always opposed it in all its forms, whether in government or in areas such as theatre, censorship or literature.The new production marks Allen's return to Spain after works such as Vicky Cristina Barcelona and Rifkin's Festival'. The filmmaker again raised the possibility of retiring. During the event he said making films is exhausting and recalled that he had previously expressed his intention to give up cinema, although the chance to shoot this story in Madrid proved too tempting to refuse.The controversies that follow Woody AllenThe director's return to Spain is also bringing renewed attention to the controversies that have defined his public image in recent decades. The main one concerns accusations of sexual abuse made by his adopted daughter Dylan Farrow, who alleges that Allen abused her in 1992, when she was seven. The filmmaker has repeatedly denied the allegation.Allen has never been formally charged or tried over these claims. In 1993, Connecticut state prosecutor Frank Maco said there was probable cause to bring charges, but decided not to do so, arguing that putting Dylan Farrow through a court case could harm her. Meanwhile, a team of specialists at the child sexual abuse clinic of Yale-New Haven Hospital concluded after its assessment that Dylan had not been sexually abused. Allen has maintained ever since that the accusation is false.The controversy flared up again decades later, particularly with the #MeToo movement and following the release in 2021 of the documentary series 'Allen v. Farrow'. Several Hollywood figures publicly distanced themselves from the filmmaker, and his professional relationship with Amazon ended up before the courts. Allen sued the company for around €68 million after it cancelled its agreement to produce several films. The two sides later reached an out-of-court settlement, the terms of which were not made public.Another widely debated episode in his private life has been his relationship with Soon-Yi Previn, the adopted daughter of Mia Farrow and André Previn. The relationship between Allen and Previn became public in 1992, when the filmmaker had long been in a romantic relationship with Farrow. Allen and Previn married in Venice in 1997, when he was 62 and she was 27, a 35-year age gap.

title: Greece will not 'borrow' its own treasures, Mitsotakis says of Parthenon Marbles
description: Bulgaria's Rumen Radev said the two countries had left the shadows of the past behind them, and the 48 artefacts will go on display until 5 November before returning to the places they were taken from.
content: Speaking in Thessaloniki, Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis made special reference to the Parthenon Sculptures on the occasion of the exchange of historic relics between Greece and Bulgaria."Monuments and historic artefacts cannot be treated as spoils of war, nor as victims of circumstances that arose after their creation and their inherent nature as unified works," Mitsotakis said."It is precisely this same principle, the principle of a monument's integrity, that underpins our ongoing effort to reunite the Parthenon Sculptures. Because they are not lifeless objects from the past. They are evidence in a living and unbroken connection with the natural and cultural landscape that gave birth to them," the Greek prime minister added."The Parthenon is a unique and self-contained case. That is why it cannot be 'imprisoned' within the confines of legal or technical issues. It is about restoring the aesthetic and semantic integrity of a truly universal monument which, unfortunately, remains violently dismembered."My country will not accept arrangements that imply recognition of foreign ownership, nor will it borrow, supposedly, its own treasures. On the contrary, it now believes that the time has come for truth, for reason, for justice, but also for morality," Mitsotakis concluded, speaking at the Museum of Byzantine Culture.Radev: We have left the shadows of the past behind us"Our joint efforts have allowed us to leave the shadows of the past behind us and to create a relationship of mutual respect and friendship," Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev stressed in his speech at the event."I am pleased that our two peoples have managed to move beyond confrontation and today we enjoy a very high level of economic, political and cultural co-operation," he said, adding: "I am full of hope that what we have achieved today will further consolidate our strategic partnership, because over the past decades we have managed to create a very strong axis of strategic co-operation between Bulgaria and Greece, an axis of stability, security, prosperity and development."The remains of Tsar SamuelMore than a thousand years after his death, the remains identified as those of Tsar Samuel, one of the most important rulers of the First Bulgarian Empire, are returning to Bulgaria. Their return is part of the agreement on the mutual handover of historic artefacts and anthropological material signed by Greece and Bulgaria, which the Bulgarian side has described as being of historic significance.In exchange, Greece is receiving 48 ecclesiastical artefacts that were removed by Bulgarian troops from churches and monasteries in northern Greece during the First World War. The objects were taken away in 1917 and for more than a century remained in Bulgaria, where they were kept or displayed at the National History Museum in Sofia.Samuel ruled from 997 to 1014 and played a leading role in the military clashes with the Byzantine Empire. Initially, he acted together with his brothers, one of whom he later ordered to be executed. Gradually, he extended his authority over a large part of the Balkans, while the region of the Prespa and Ohrid lakes, mainly in what is now North Macedonia, became the centre of his power.From the early 11th century, however, the situation began to change in favour of the Byzantines. After 1001, the forces of Emperor Basil II intensified their pressure and in 1014 Samuel's army suffered a heavy defeat. According to historical sources, the Byzantine emperor, who became known as "Boulgaroktonos", ordered thousands of Bulgarian prisoners to be blinded. Tradition holds that Samuel suffered a shock when he saw his soldiers returning blind and died shortly afterwards.The Bulgarian state finally came under Byzantine rule four years after his death, in 1018.The remains attributed to Samuel are linked to excavations at the Basilica of Saint Achilleios in Prespa. In 1965, Professor Nikolaos Moutsopoulos uncovered four sarcophagi, together with anthropological material. In recent years, the finds have been kept at the Museum of Byzantine Culture in Thessaloniki and now form part of the exchange agreement with Bulgaria.What Greece is receivingOn the Greek side, the 48 artefacts come from the Holy Monastery of Panagia Eikosifoinissa, the Holy Monastery of Timios Prodromos of Serres and the Holy Metropolis of Serres and Nigrita. Before their final return to the places from which they were removed, they will be on display at the Museum of Byzantine Culture until 5 November 2026.The mutual handover took place on Saturday morning in Thessaloniki, in the presence of Mitsotakis and Radev, with the signing of the relevant delivery and receipt protocols.The procedure marks the implementation of the memorandum of understanding signed by the culture ministers of Greece and Bulgaria, Lina Mendoni and Eftim Miloshev, after many years of negotiations and regular contacts between the two sides.

title: ‘It’s given my mental health a massive boost’: Why everyone should hone their bushcraft skills
description: The Bushcraft Bus is reconnecting Europeans with nature.
content: If you’re not a military green-clad survivalist or a forest-bathing wellness enthusiast, you might feel “a little bit lost” in the great outdoors, says bushcraft instructor and conservationist Jim Todd.It’s a problem the brightly coloured Bushcraft Bus – the mobile home of wilderness and nature education – aims to solve.“We’re trying to fill that gap in the middle, where you don't have to identify with anything. You just need to have a little bit of kit, and just be up for it,” says Jim.Jim, 39, and Bushcraft Bus co-founder Tom Young, 37, met in Dorset five years ago while qualifying to be bushcraft instructors. Now they host foraging walks, wilderness skills workshops and fire-roasted woodland dinners in the south of England and beyond. In the UK – which ranked 55th out of 61 nations in a global study on “nature connectedness” – some of the people who join them have never even set foot in the woods.It doesn’t take long for them to realise what they’ve been missing.“The excitement builds through the day,” Tom tells Euronews Earth from their camp in the Cotswolds’ Voltaires Wood. “Some people are quite timid at the start but they’re often the ones who get the most out of it,” adds Jim. King Alfred’s Cakes or ‘cramp balls’ are a particular crowdpleaser. Resembling round lumps of coal, this fungus is commonly found on fallen ash and beech trees, and can be used as a fire lighter – a discovery that left a recent participant of their woodland cookout “just ecstatic”, recalls Tom.What’s the most essential wilderness skill?Being ‘apocalypse-ready’ isn’t a focus of the Bushcraft Bus – but the skills it teaches feel increasingly important. The UK government recently advised citizens to prepare for threats from the climate crisis and hostile states, including by stocking up on tinned food. It came after a record-hot summer placed swathes of Europe under heat and water stress – compounded by soaring household bills resulting from tensions in the Middle East, not to mention the looming threat of water- and energy-hungry AI. Jim says these factors are a motivating force for some participants who join their courses, and many leave less fearful, more confident and better connected.“When you start thinking through that lens, you realise how little you actually know to defend yourself or survive in that situation,” he says. “We’re so reliant on all of these big systems working. And if any of them collapse, we’re back to basics really quickly… Like, what if there was no heating and it was the middle of winter? Or how do I find water and purify it?”Fire-making is “instrumental” – not only for survival but also for “how much you can enjoy the time that you have in the woods,” says Jim. “Fire ties everything together”, agrees Tom – from “learning about tree identification, so you can burn the right woods, to learning about what to forage and how to cook it”.For this reason, Tom always carries a ferro rod (a metallic fire starter stick) – a tool that was indispensable on his 66-day solo hike through the European Arctic in 2018.But bushcraft skills only go so far – and the biggest lifeline often gets overlooked: community. That could mean curating your friendship group: “Making sure you’ve got a friend who’s a nurse and who would know how to treat an injury, and someone else who’s got a mechanical mind who could help turn a dead car into something useful,” says Tom.‘When you pour energy and curiosity into nature, you get it back’This collaborative spirit is something off-grid living seems to nurture – not only between fellow humans, but with the land itself.“A lot of people don’t learn about the woods anymore. So from a very young age, you’re already disconnected,” says Tom.There are signs that this is slowly starting to change: the UK government recently approved a new Natural History GCSE (an exam subject that can be chosen at 14-years-old) for secondary school students, which it hopes will “grow the next generation of green careers”.“I think if you can teach people and give people some of that knowledge and awareness, they’ll naturally start caring and appreciating more about those spaces,” says Tom.This can look like conserving precious resources: “We’ve wheelbarrowed all of our water up a 15-minute steep, bumpy track,” says Jim, sitting in their woodland camp. “So we’re not splashing it around when we’re up here… Instinctively it does reset your brain to be way more conservative with your usage.”Or being mindful of what you take from the land: “You need to leave some of whatever you’re foraging for the animals,” says Jim – and in the case of mushrooms, for the fungus itself: “The reason they fruit is to spread the spores,” adds Tom.Connecting with nature is “like a relationship”, muses Jim. “You have to build it – you can’t just expect it to give you everything. You have to pour energy and curiosity into it, and then you get it back. That’s when it starts providing real value to you.”‘Exploring the outdoors has given my mental health a massive boost’Both Jim and Tom admit that in their younger years, they were more interested in going to the pub than on long country walks. These days, it’s more often screens that are keeping teenagers indoors.Both also think Europe has a lot to learn from other cultures about connecting with nature. During time spent in New Zealand and Canada, they found outdoor skills are embedded more deeply into everyday life. Vast landscapes make the outdoors harder to ignore, while activities such as kayaking, hiking and camping are familiar from a young age.“The outdoors is all around you all the time,” says Jim, contrasting that with the UK’s denser landscape, where farmland and privately owned woodland can make natural spaces feel surprisingly inaccessible.As a result, “we almost see ourselves as separate from the natural world,” reflects Jim. “But I think if you do get out into it, most people very quickly feel this connection to it. And when you add in skills that you can use outside, you are just building that self-reliance and confidence.”Tom’s experience stands as testament to this: “Exploring the outdoors has given me what feels like a purpose,” he says. “It’s given my mental health that massive boost. In life as well, just talking to people with more confidence, and that’s developed through the years.”

title: From food-led escapes to trip of a lifetime hotels: How luxury travel has evolved and ‘doesn’t look one way’
description: The fusion of food and hospitality is a major driving force in the world of luxury travel. We spoke to Michelin Guide's Marie-France Perrel about how the sector is changing.
content: In years gone by, the luxury travel sector was all about opulent hotels and extravagant surroundings. But for today's travellers, the experience is becoming much harder to define. Speaking at the Euronews Travel & Tourism Summit 2026 in Brussels last week, Marie-France Perrel, Head of Business Development, Hotels at Michelin Guide, said luxury hospitality has evolved to bring together a fusion of food, wellness, service, as well as connection to the destination. “Luxury today is completely different than what it was,” she said. “It’s no longer the sort of standards of opulence that we had in mind. It’s no longer about the amount of marble you have in a bathroom or the number of rooms in one property.” Instead, Perrel said travellers are looking for “properties who are giving you a sense of place” and hotels with a special connection to their surroundings. “It really is a whole ecosystem, and I think that’s what luxury is today,” she added. Part of the same travel experience Food is increasingly central to this changing definition of hospitality. While there’s always been a correlation between eating and travelling, Michelin is seeing evidence that visitors increasingly consider the two as part of the same experience. “Before, they were lived as two separate experiences, whereas now we’re seeing that as one experience,” Perrel said. Michelin's own data shows that users looking to book hotels in Northern Europe were also searching for nearby restaurants during the same session. Perrel also pointed to the rise of “intentional travel around food”, with holidaymakers booking trips specifically to experience a particular dish or cuisine.“They want to go on walking food tours, or they will want to go to a destination because they saw on television this great meal that was being consumed,” she said. “They want to have that same authentic pizza or whatever that may be. So absolutely, food is a huge component of travel these days.” What are Michelin Keys? Michelin's connection with travel stretches back more than a century. The first Michelin Guide was published in France in 1900 to encourage motorists to travel, listing practical information including places to eat and stay. Michelin began awarding stars to restaurants in 1926. Hotels have also featured in the guides for decades, but the company introduced its “Michelin Key” distinction in 2024, applying a dedicated methodology to identifying outstanding hotel experiences. Its 2026 global selection includes 2,832 Michelin Key hotels across 79 destinations: 2,020 with one key, 657 with two keys, and 155 with three keys. Some 470 hotels joined the selection this year, while 18 received three keys for the first time. One key represents a “very special stay”, while two keys signify an “exceptional stay”. Three keys are reserved for the highest level – an extraordinary stay providing the ultimate experience. “This is like the trip of a lifetime type of situation,” Perrel said. But Michelin's selections illustrate how luxury no longer has to fit a single mould. Its hotel portfolio ranges from grand hotels to independent boutiques and retreats. “What I love about it is that it’s not cookie-cutter,” Perrel said. “Luxury doesn’t look one way. It’s a broad spectrum.”At the end of her session at the Euronews summit, Perrel was asked to share one piece of advice to travellers when choosing a hotel for their next holiday. Her response was to look at the trip “backwards”. “Try to think of your next trip in a different way and instead of choosing a destination, choose a hotel first,” she said. “You don't look at the destination, but look at a hotel that speaks to you and then go to that place.”

title: Russia 'tearing Kyiv apart', mayor says, as strikes paralyse traffic
description: Russian attacks on key infrastructure were "tearing Kyiv apart", the city's mayor said Friday, as strikes on a bridge linking the capital's east and west brought traffic to a standstill.
content: President Volodymyr Zelensky accused his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, of ripping up the rulebook of armed conflict by sanctioning massive attacks on civilian areas, an accusation the Kremlin has rejected.The grinding conflict, which began with Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, has largely focused on ground fighting in the east, with Kyiv mostly spared from the devastation wrought near the frontline.But Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko said the city should now be on a war footing."The capital is in a very dramatic situation," he posted on Telegram. "It's no longer possible to pretend that we can live now as we lived in peacetime.""The enemy is tearing Kyiv apart."His message came as the authorities shut one of Kyiv's main bridges and restricted movement on a second after another wave of deadly strikes by fast-moving, jet-powered drones.Traffic heavily disturbedLong lines of stationary cars and buses were gridlocked on main roads as commuters sought alternative routes — or even made their way on foot."I've been travelling for three hours... to get to work," said Tetiana Osypenko, a 49-year-old seamstress whose bus was stuck in a traffic jam."There's just no way to get there. Nothing. It's impossible to cross the bridges today," she said.Traffic built up due to the complete closure to all vehicles going in both directions on the Southern Bridge, one of eight bridges connecting the east and west of Kyiv over the Dnipro river.The cable-stayed bridge has been hit several times since Thursday, with new strikes confirmed by Klitschko on Friday afternoon.The Paton Bridge, further north, was open in one direction only, though there were no reports that it had been struck.On X, Zelensky accused Putin of last month declaring there were "no rules now", citing unnamed intelligence and people around Putin."The Russians couldn't occupy us. So now they are doing massive attacks and massive killings," Zelensky said in remarks first made in a Financial Times interview.The Kremlin made no immediate public response to the claim.Daily bombing fearKyiv has been increasingly under aerial bombardment in recent months, putting the city on near-constant alert and disrupting daily life.Air raid sirens warning of approaching threats in the skies sound almost round the clock, urging the city's estimated three million people to seek shelter.Repeated strikes on trains and petrol stations have already hit the rail and road networks while attacks on energy facilities threaten power and heating as winter approaches.Osypenko, the seamstress, said previous disruptions to subway services during air raids have forced her to spend the night in a metro station near the Southern Bridge.Loss of earnings compounds the financial pressures caused by the war, she added. "You just spend the whole day feeling completely beaten down."The latest Russian attacks killed one person and wounded at least two other people when a 25-storey residential building was hit in southeast Kyiv.Two people were killed and dozens more injured when Russian shelling hit residential areas in the eastern city of Kharkiv, city mayor Igor Terekhov said on Telegram.'Political will'Zelensky urged tougher sanctions to prevent Russia from manufacturing jet-powered drones, which are harder to intercept.Russia's production of the weapons was "critically dependent" on foreign components, he wrote on social media on Friday."Every Russian drone can actually be stopped right at the production line. What is needed is the political will of these countries," he added.Zelensky has repeatedly called on Ukraine's Western allies for more military support, particularly for US-made Patriot missile interceptors.On Thursday, he said Ukraine had used its FP-7 tactical ballistic missile in combat for the first time, without disclosing where or what it had been used against.He also said Ukraine was testing five of its own interceptors against drones.Ukraine's military on Friday said it struck an oil refinery in Volgograd and another facility in Samara, both in southwest Russia, for allegedly supplying fuel to Russian forces.Kyiv also dismissed reports that its F-16 fighter jets — another key tool used against jet-powered drones — could be grounded due to delays in maintenance inspections and the supply of parts.But Zelensky told the Financial Times that around half of Ukraine's fleet was spending lengthy maintenance periods in Europe.

title: French government forecasts 1% growth in 2027: What do experts think?
description: France's High Council for Public Finance calls the government's 1.0% growth forecast for the 2027 budget "optimistic", as economists warn of a possible "slippage" and the executive still has to secure approval.
content: The budget battle is only just beginning, and the growth figure chosen by the government for 2027 is already prompting reservations.In an opinion published on Thursday, the High Council for Public Finance (HCFP) judged that the draft budget and social security financing bills, presented the same day to the Council of Ministers, were based in particular on a 1.0% growth forecast it considers "optimistic".The institution chaired by Amélie de Montchalin, currently First President of the Court of Audit and formerly minister for Public Action and Accounts under Emmanuel Macron, also highlights the "significant uncertainty" surrounding the domestic situation, notably regarding "the very adoption of the budget for 2027".According to the first draft unveiled, the executive aims to bring the public deficit down to 5.0% of GDP in 2027, from 5.4% this year, at the cost of an "effort" totalling €54 billion."That would make it the fifth consecutive year with a deficit equal to or above 5%," notes Hadrien Camatte, senior economist for France, Belgium and the eurozone at Natixis CIB, in a commentary to Euronews."Risk of budget slippage"To reach this target, the government is planning €43 billion in new measures, including €25 billion in spending cuts and €18 billion in additional revenue. On top of that would come €12 billion already decided this year.In detail, the deficit of central government would widen to 5.0% of GDP in 2027, from 4.8% in 2026, mainly "under the impact of higher debt-servicing costs (€10.3 billion), defence spending (€6.5 billion) and the contribution to the EU budget (€2.8 billion)," observes Hadrien Camatte.Most of the measures would focus on the social security system, the expert continues, "with a target surplus of 0.2% of GDP, compared with a deficit of 0.1% in 2026". This would notably involve a partial freeze on pensions, expected to generate around €4 billion in savings, and on family benefits, for €500 million, according to the government.As for the deficit of local authorities, it "would improve slightly", the economist says, narrowing to 0.1% of GDP from 0.2% in 2026.On the revenue side, the plan provides for €17.2 billion in new compulsory levies, notably through an overhaul of cuts to social contributions (€6.6 billion), higher local taxes and shaving down a tax allowance currently enjoyed by retirees.This trajectory rests on several assumptions judged "optimistic", Hadrien Camatte recalls. The government is banking on GDP growth of 1% in 2027, compared with 0.8% for Natixis, the corporate and investment bank of the BPCE group (Caisses d'Épargne and Banques Populaires).The economist also points to "an average rate of 4.3% for 10-year government bonds, a level already far exceeded in recent days, at 4.9%.""Weaker economic growth, the high sensitivity of debt-servicing costs to interest rates – a 100 basis-point increase would mean an additional €3.4 billion in 2027 – and the insufficiently documented nature of certain measures all create a risk of budget slippage in 2027," warns the Natixis expert.For Jérôme Mathis, professor of economics at Paris-Dauphine University, the government is adopting "a stance of deliberate confidence.""By basing its forecasts on the assumption that energy costs will stabilise and household consumption will gradually recover, the executive is seeking to maintain a positive signal for investment and economic activity," he told Euronews.The challenge of the upcoming parliamentary debates, the researcher added, is precisely to "find that point of balance: a responsible budget that credibly reduces the deficit without stalling the engine of growth."Mathis stressed that the review of the 2027 draft budget "highlights a fundamental consensus: the absolute imperative to restore France's public finances in order to preserve our financial sovereignty and our credibility within the eurozone.""The current discussions are not about that objective, which everyone shares, but about the most appropriate calibration for achieving it," he noted."Tomorrow the overseas territories, universities, the health sector"It is "very difficult" to predict what growth will be in 2027, says François Facchini, professor of economics at the University of Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne. He points in particular to the uncertainty surrounding the outcome of the war in the Middle East, which is driving the surge in fuel prices in France, but also stresses political instability.The new government, which will take office after the 2027 presidential election, "will probably pass an amending finance bill that will affect growth", he believes.According to the researcher, it is also "likely" that the election year will be marked by strikes and social movements, with each group seeking to "weigh on candidates' promises". He mentions civil servants and students, but also, potentially, "tomorrow the overseas territories, universities, the health sector, all the sectors that are highly dependent on political choices"."It is likely, moreover, that food prices will rise after the heatwaves and drought of 2026," he adds.François Facchini considers that, between geopolitical and political uncertainty, likely inflationary pressures and the risk of a debt crisis, "the High Council is right: 1% [growth] is optimistic". He does, however, qualify this: "That is generally the rule for budget scenarios."A parliamentary wallBut the current government must first get this budget passed, in a National Assembly that is becoming ever more fragmented as the presidential election approaches.Hadrien Camatte identifies two scenarios for Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu: resorting to article 49.3, which allows adoption without a vote but automatically triggers no-confidence motions, or using ordinances.The first option would, however, mean reducing the planned savings effort in the budget and would require "abstention either by the Socialist Party – an unlikely prospect in light of its recent statements – or by the National Rally, whose stated positions are more open to this possibility but with red lines that could shift, particularly on pensions", according to the Natixis CIB expert.As for ordinances, they would give France a budget "matching the version adopted by the government" in the event of deadlock at the end of the 70 days of debate in the National Assembly.France would then be entering uncharted territory under the Fifth Republic.

title: Beyond K-pop and cinema: Major Korean exhibition brings centuries of art and belief to London
description: The exhibition includes 10 national treasures and official Korean designations recognising their cultural importance, with most exhibits drawn from the collection of late Samsung billionaire Lee Kun-Hee.
content: Long before K-pop filled stadiums and Korean films won global acclaim, the peninsula’s artists were casting temple bells, shaping delicate ceramics and capturing mountains in ink.That older cultural world takes centre stage in ‘Korea’, the British Museum’s first major exhibition on Korean art and history in more than 40 years.Spanning from 300 BC to the present, its 100 exhibits explore the beliefs and traditions that shaped Korean art.The display includes 10 national treasures and 13 other treasures, official Korean designations recognising their cultural and historical importance, according to Samsung, the exhibition’s corporate partner.Among the objects on display are a 900-year-old incense burner crowned with a mythical creature and a huge Buddhist temple bell around 1,000 years old.The exhibition moves from the luminous blue-green ceramics of the Goryeo dynasty to the restrained porcelain of Joseon, shaped by Confucian ideals, according to the British Museum and Samsung.Together, they show how Buddhism and Confucian ideas shaped Korean art over the centuries.For the exhibition’s curator, Yoojin Kwak Choi, the “absolute star exhibit” is Jeong Seon’s Clearing After Rain on Mount Inwang.Jeong Seon is an 18th-century Korean painter of the Joseon dynasty who helped shift landscape painting from idealised Chinese-style scenes towards Korea’s actual scenery, Choi explains.But there are modern examples of Korean craftsmanship too.Yeesookyung’s 2018 vase combines ceramic shards from North and South Korea. In Korean artisanal tradition, imperfect work is destroyed, so the artist has taken broken shards from that destruction and glued them together with gold leaf.Most exhibits come from the collection of the late Samsung chairman Lee Kun-Hee.The billionaire amassed a vast collection over his lifetime, and after his death in 2020, his family donated more than 23,000 works to South Korean national museums.“Some people might think that Korean culture is new, but it is thousands upon thousands of years old,” said Benjamin Braun, Samsung Europe’s chief marketing officer.For visitors drawn to Korea through its music and cinema, the exhibition opens a door onto that longer history.‘Korea’ runs at the British Museum until 31 January 2027.

title: Inside Soitec, the French tech company powering the global semiconductor industry
description: From smartphones to data centres, the French company’s advanced silicon substrates underpin technologies used around the world. Valérie Gauriat went inside its production site in the French Alps.
content: In the Grésivaudan Valley near Grenoble, sometimes dubbed the “Silicon Valley of the Alps”, millions of highly sophisticated silicon wafers are produced every year.They come from Soitec, a French company little known to the general public, but a world leader in advanced substrates for the semiconductor industry.Founded 33 years ago around an invention developed at French technological research institute CEA-Leti, Soitec started with just a dozen or so people. Today, it employs more than 2,000 and holds more than 4,700 active patents worldwide, with production facilities in France and Singapore.“Our roots are French, our reach is global. Our job is to run faster than the competition,” says Christophe Maleville, Soitec’s Chief Technology Officer.The company produces advanced substrates: a high-tech silicon wafer used as the base material to build the world's most powerful microchips. Its technology can be found in mobile phones, connected devices, cars and household appliances, as well as data centres.“Today, we are the world leader in advanced substrates for semiconductors,” says Chief Operations Officer Cyril Menon. He points to Grenoble’s combination of research laboratories, universities and industrial companies as one reason for that success.Inside Soitec’s highly controlled clean rooms, wafers pass through between 30 and 50 processing stages, involving the transfer of extremely thin layers of material from one substrate to another at atomic scale.Several million advanced substrates leave Soitec’s factories each year. Around 60% of its revenue is generated in Asia, 30% in Europe and 10% in the United States.Maintaining a technological lead requires heavy investment: SOITEC devotes 20% of its revenue to research and development.“The speed of innovation becomes absolutely key, because we have to maintain the distance with the competition,” Maleville says.Artificial intelligence is creating another opportunity, and another challenge. Its rapid development is driving demand for increasingly powerful data centres, while raising concerns about their energy and resource consumption.SOITEC’s photonics products are designed to transfer information faster while reducing energy use.They could also help fuel the highly controversial growth of artificial intelligence.“How this AI is used is a debate that is worth having,” acknowledges Cyril Menon. “How we regulate it, how we make the best use of this AI, is an important issue for society. And this AI consumes a lot of energy, a lot of resources. So it is also important to provide products that help address this issue.”For SOITEC’s executives, mastering these technologies is also about Europe’s place in the global industry.“It is also by having these advanced technologies that we can have an impact on Europe’s future,” concludes Cyril Menon. “And have a seat at the table.”

title: From ocean waste to fabric: inside Spain’s sustainable fashion revolution
description: Every year, more than 12 million tonnes of plastic ends up in our oceans. Spanish fashion company Ecoalf transforms marine waste and discarded materials into fabrics and clothing through a circular supply chain. But can sustainable fashion transform an industry built on overproduction?
content: There are almost 5,000 fishermen and one not-for-profit foundation behind Spanish sustainable fashion brand Ecoalf. Every day, the fishermen recover waste caught in their nets, while the Ecoalf Foundation has developed a system to give that waste a second life, turning it into raw material, ultimately, fabric."Plastic alone now accounts for around 80% of everything we bring up. This is our daily reality,” says fisherman Tony Beltrán, while showing the waste that got caught in his nets off the coast of Gandía, south of Valencia. “Even before recycling became popular, we were already collecting it, the only difference was that we didn't separate it." Since 2015, the Upcycling the Oceans project, launched alongside the creation of the Ecoalf Foundation, has recovered more than 2,000 tonnes of marine waste, the equivalent of around 100 truckloads of rubbish. Today, the initiative involves around 80 ports and has expanded to France, Italy, Greece, Egypt and Thailand. Yet, it’s still a drop in the ocean: the Foundation points out that every minute, the equivalent of a truckload of plastic ends up in the world's oceans.“Our goal has always been to bring together 10,000 fishermen across the Mediterranean so that, together, we can help clean up the Mediterranean Sea,” explains Andrea Ruzo, director of the Ecoalf Foundation.Of all the materials recovered from the sea, most of them, like glass and metals, follow conventional recycling routes. But around 5% of this waste are plastic bottles, which are transformed into what Ecoalf calls Ocean Yarn.“The first step, once the waste has been collected, is to shred it and turn it into flakes and then pellets, that’s the stage before spinning,” explains Ángela Pérez, Ecoalf’s expert in textile innovation and sustainability. The beating heart of this supply chain is Ecoalf’s headquarters in Madrid, where ocean yarn and other recycled materials are turned into fabrics. Since its creation in 2009, the company continues to source raw materials from a range of waste well beyond plastic bottles. Some fibres come from discarded fishing nets, others from tyres or recycled natural textiles, such as cotton and wool. The goal, the company says, is to reduce the environmental impact of both production and the finished garment, while maintaining its look and quality.Circularity influences the decisions a fashion designer makes throughout the design process says Julie Sohn, Ecoalf’s creative director.“It changes everything from the very beginning. Everything is designed so that the garment can be completely disassembled, without any additional processing, and re-enter the circular economy,” she says. Among the pioneers of sustainable fashion, Ecoalf was founded with a clear ambition: to prove that a business can succeed while helping transform one of the world’s most polluting industries. 17 years later, the company has grown into a global brand, with annual revenues of around €65 million, 300 employees and dozens of stores worldwide. “The problem we’ve been facing in recent years is mass overconsumption and overproduction. Brands need to move beyond sustainable capsules or focusing on a single material. We need to learn to design with eco-design principles from the very beginning,” explains Carolina Álvarez-Ossorio, Ecoalf’s chief marketing officer. But could sustainable fashion eventually replace fast fashion? There is still a long way to go according to Álvarez-Ossorio, who is also convinced designers have a role to play in finding new ways to work with purpose and ultimately help protect our planet.Ecoalf is a striking example of the circular economy, but it also raises a bigger question: can recycling the waste we already produce ever compensate for new waste we continue to create?

title: South Korea warns of 'further measures' if Ukraine refuses public apology over POW transfer disclosure
description: The POWs were captured by Ukrainian forces early last year after being deployed alongside thousands of North Korean troops to support Russia's war against Ukraine.
content: South Korean President Lee Jae-myung said on Friday that Seoul would take "further measures" if Ukraine refuses to publicly apologise over what he called its unilateral disclosure of North Korean prisoners of war being sent to South Korea.Seoul has taken a hard stance on Ukraine disclosing the transfer of two soldiers captured fighting for Russia, warning that their families could be targeted by Pyongyang.North Korea is known to retaliate against defectors and their families.Both POWs are identifiable as they had been photographed by South Korean media before their arrival to the South.The POWs were captured by Ukrainian forces early last year after being deployed alongside thousands of North Korean troops to support Russia's war against Ukraine, in exchange for economic and military assistance to Pyongyang.Hours after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy disclosed last week the transfer in remarks at the United Nations, Lee expressed his dismay, with Seoul claiming confidentiality was key to protecting the POWs' relatives.Seoul later demanded an official apology from Ukraine, saying that both sides had reached a "clear understanding" during consultations to keep the transfer confidential."If Ukraine continues to refuse to acknowledge the facts and publicly apologise, we will take further measures," the South Korean president said on Friday, accusing Kyiv of making him out to be a "liar.""This is a matter concerning the dignity of the Republic of Korea and its people and cannot be overlooked," Lee posted on X.Analysts say that from South Korea's perspective, keeping the transfer of the POWs confidential may have partly been for Ukraine's sake, as making it public could have complicated Kyiv's own prisoner exchanges with Russia.In domestic South Korean politics, however, Seoul's approach "could prove problematic," Shin Yul, a political science professor at Myongji University, said given the current administration's dovish approach to the nuclear-armed North."The government has acted swiftly in this case involving Ukraine, while exercising extreme caution over the North Korean landmine incident (that injured South Korean soldiers). That contrast could leave the public deeply dissatisfied."Diplomatic misunderstandingLee referred on Friday to an interview with Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha published by RBC-Ukraine and other Ukrainian outlets on Thursday.Sybiha said he would "not like to call it an incident," describing it instead as a "diplomatic misunderstanding.""South Korea is an important country for us. And I very much hope for momentum, continued cooperation, and concrete results that we are indeed achieving with them," he said.Seoul's spy agency said that Zelenskyy may have disclosed the transfer of the North Korean soldiers to boost public support in South Korea for Seoul providing arms to Ukraine, a lawmaker said on Wednesday.South Korea has in recent years emerged as a major arms exporter, particularly since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022, including through a multibillion-dollar arms deal with Poland.But it has refrained from supplying Kyiv with lethal weapons, citing its longstanding policy of not arming countries engaged in active conflicts.

title: Man City lodges 'comprehensive' appeal after being found guilty of financial rule-breaking
description: According to the Premier League, potential sanctions against City could be a reprimand, a fine, a suspension, points deduction or, in the worst case, expulsion from the competition.
content: Manchester City has lodged a “comprehensive” appeal, the club confirmed on Friday, following the publication of a report by an independent commission detailing large-sclae financial rule-breaking by the Premier League giant.“The club’s firm position,” read a short statement from City, “is that, on multiple grounds, the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe.”City has protested its innocence throughout the long-running case, which dates back to 2018, and reached a milestone on Tuesday when the Premier League published a verdict saying the Abu Dhabi-controlled club was “guilty of all charges related to serious breaches” of the competition’s financial rules from 2009-18.Officials said they would lodge an appeal and that was filed on Thursday evening, the club said, ahead of Friday’s deadline.“The club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case,” City said, using language from previous statements on the case.According to the Premier League handbook, the chair of the three-person disciplinary commission that found against City now has to appoint a new appeal board.That should consist of three people, one of whom “shall have held judicial office,” the league’s rules state.The appeal board will then schedule a hearing that should finish within 12 weeks after the appeal is filed and cannot exceed five consecutive days.City has yet to receive a punishment for the violations found. That will be addressed in a separate, confidential hearing with the commission and there has been no word whether sanctions can be imposed before the decision of the appeal is reached.The Premier League has only said its intention is that the process is concluded “as soon as possible.”According to the Premier League, potential sanctions against City could be a reprimand, a fine, a suspension, points deduction or, in the worst case, expulsion from the competition.No team has ever been expelled from English football’s top flight.City's €975m rule-breaking using ‘sham’ commercial dealsCity was found to have systematically broken the Premier League’s financial rules for nearly a decade in what the competition’s chief executive, Richard Masters, described as the most significant disciplinary case in the league’s history.The investigatory panel found that City artificially inflated its revenue, using what the league has called “sham” commercial deals, by more than $1 billion (€975 million) from 2009-18 to circumvent financial fair-play rules that restricted rival clubs, and allowing City to buy some of the best players in the world.That was the foundation of a long and unprecedented period of success in which City changed the landscape of the world’s most popular football league, with the northwest club winning eight league titles from 2012-24.City committed almost all of the 115-plus violations, the commission found: 80 from 2009-18 for alleged financial misdeeds and another 35 from 2018-23 for allegedly not cooperating with the investigation.

title: Fact check: What's going on with Spain's 'Maricarmen' housing protests?
description: Spanish protests against the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen have led to misleading claims about Spain's housing activists and the wider rental crisis.
content: Thousands of people are protesting across Spain after authorities evicted Maricarmen Abascal from her home in Madrid.Maricarmen, who is 87 years old, had been living there for over 70 years. Images of police forcibly removing her from the flat on a stretcher have now turned the legal dispute into a symbolic fight for housing activists.The protesters marched through Madrid, camped out in Puerta del Sol, and organised demonstrations in other Spanish cities.They are using Maricarmen's case to protest the wider housing crisis: rising rents and a shortage of affordable homes, which are fuelling fears that tenants can no longer afford to stay in major cities.The situation has become a very politicised debate, fuelling several false, misleading, and selectively edited claims.A legal decisionOne of the most prominent claims circulating online is that Maricarmen’s eviction was "illegal". This is false: courts authorised the eviction after a years-long dispute over a protected rental contract dating back to the 1950s. It was carried out under a valid court order, despite the backlash it received.Maricarmen's father originally held the lease, which later passed to her mother and then to Maricarmen herself. The courts ruled that this second transfer could continue for only two years unless Maricarmen had a recognised disability above 65%; authorities recognised hers at 50%.Spain's Supreme Court upheld the owner’s position, which meant the old, protected tenancy had legally expired and the company could recover the flat. The eviction was therefore lawful.The goal of the protestsSo, contrary to what some misleading headlines imply, protesters are not arguing whether the eviction was lawful, but whether it was fair. This is partly because, under Francisco Franco’s dictatorship laws, married women could not legally sign financial contracts or property leases independently.Maricarmen's mother could inherit the lease only by subrogation upon her husband's death. Had she been a co-owner or co-signer from the start, Maricarmen's inheritance of the lease would have counted as the first subrogation, legally protecting her right to stay in the home for life.Protesters also point out that Maricarmen is 87, has lived in the property for more than seven decades, and continued paying her protected rent.After the old tenancy ended, property management company Urbagestión proposed a rent of around €1,650 a month, far above the roughly €440 to €500 she had previously paid. This is higher than her monthly pension of around €1,350, therefore forcing a vulnerable long-term tenant out because she cannot afford the new rent.Protesters are asking for stronger protections against evictions of vulnerable tenants, longer or automatically renewed rental contracts, and tighter limits on rent increases.Some groups also want tougher rules on speculative housing practices and greater public intervention in the rental market. They are now pressing parliament to approve new protections for vulnerable tenants and longer lease terms.Other false and misleading claimsAnother disputed claim going around online is that the Sindicato de Inquilinas, Spain's main union for tenants, prevented Maricarmen from reaching an agreement with the owner before the eviction.Urbagestión says the union made it hard to contact Maricarmen directly, while Maricarmen’s lawyer says the opposite: that the company had refused repeated attempts to negotiate.Urbagestión has also accused people involved in the dispute of coercion, extortion and hacking phones and email accounts. However, the company did not provide evidence for these claims in reporting reviewed by fact-checkers like Spain's Maldita.es.Another misleading assertion comes from a shortened video of Maricarmen herself. In the clip, she appears to blame left-wing Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez specifically for her situation, but the full interview adds more names: she also criticises Madrid regional president Isabel Díaz Ayuso, Madrid mayor José Luis Martínez-Almeida (both members of the right-wing Popular Party) and Urbagestión itself. The clip therefore uses a genuine quote but removes the wider context of her answer.A separate false claim involved two protesters called "Irene and Pablo" who spoke to elDiario.es at a protest camp at the Puerta del Sol square in Madrid. Some social-media users suggested they were Pablo Iglesias, former leader of far-left party Podemos, and MEP Irene Montero, from the same party.However, a quick look at the article itself shows us that they are actually a different 28-year-old woman and 37-year-old man, with no indication that they were the politicians in question.The next stepsMaricarmen has now accepted an agreement that will allow her to return to the apartment once she leaves hospital. Under the new arrangement, she will pay roughly the same as her previous rent, around €500 a month, capped at 30% of her income. The agreement creates a new tenancy; it does not overturn the court ruling that ended her old, protected lease.Meanwhile, Spain's government has proposed measures that would extend some eviction protections and lengthen rental contracts, but parliament still needs to approve them. Protesters are therefore continuing their campaign and pushing politicians to adopt those measures while demanding broader reforms to Spain's housing system.

title: Meloni asks Brussels for fiscal leeway as energy shock squeezes Italy
description: Italian prime Minister Giorgia Meloni is urging the European Commission again to relax the EU's fiscal rules, saying that higher inflation due to soaring energy prices is squeezing households and businesses, according to a letter seen by Euronews.
content: Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni is urging Brussels once again to give capitals more room to cushion households and companies from the latest energy-price shock, arguing that European Union fiscal rules are becoming increasingly restrictive as inflation drives up government spending.In a letter addressed to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, seen by Euronews, Meloni said the prolonged Middle East crisis has left European energy markets “extremely tight,” with oil prices up almost 80% and gas up to 156%."Against this backdrop, the agreed net expenditure paths under the European fiscal framework leave limited room to alleviate the impact on households and firms without resorting to tightening measures at a time of significant downside risks for the economy," Meloni added.Italy, which is heading to polls next year, holds one of the highest debt-to-GDP ratios in the EU, trailing only Greece, which has recently sought a similar appeal to relax fiscal rules with the Commission.The Italian leader argues that governments are collecting more tax revenue because prices are higher, but EU fiscal rules make it difficult to recycle that windfall into temporary energy support.Higher inflation automatically increases indirect tax receipts such as VAT, but using that additional revenue to finance measures that reduce energy costs can count as discretionary fiscal action and run into limits imposed by agreed national spending paths, Meloni noted.As a solution, the Italian leader is asking Brussels to recognise that some of the additional spending is not the result of governments choosing to spend more, but of inflation mechanically increasing existing obligations.Meloni wants the Commission to find a way to allow at least part of those additional revenues to be used for "temporary and targeted measures" to reduce the impact of high energy prices — an approach that has been repeatedly recommended by EU officials.EU budget rules put a limit on how much governments can increase spending, based on the amounts agreed in their budget plans. But when inflation rises more than expected, some government costs automatically go up — such as pensions linked to the cost of living — leaving governments with less room to absorb those extra costs.The EU’s fiscal framework sets national spending limits in nominal terms, meaning governments cannot simply raise expenditure when inflation comes in significantly above initial forecasts. At the same time, some areas of public spending automatically increase as prices rise.Meloni said that spending directly affected by inflation exceeding the assumptions underpinning Italy’s budget plan amounts to 20.4% of GDP, while a further 12% of GDP in other expenditure is also expected to come under pressure in 2027."We are mindful of the risk of amending newly introduced fiscal rules that pursue a goal we all share, debt sustainability. We are also fully mindful of Italy's commitments under the ongoing excessive deficit procedure and of the need to comply with the corrective net expenditure path," reads the letter.Meloni called for the issue to be discussed at the upcoming meeting of finance ministers in Brussels on 9 October.

title: What does music look like? This British artist paints what he hears
description: Sounds can sometimes interrupt Andrew’s thoughts, but he sees synaesthesia as an inseparable part of his life.
content: For British artist Jake Andrew, music has colour, shape and texture. His paintings capture what he sees when he hears it.Andrew has synaesthesia, a rare neurological condition in which one sensory experience can trigger another. For him, sounds produce an immediate visual response.His favourite instrument to paint is the cello.“It's dark, but it doesn't feel ominous," he says. "It's got this kind of like... and then edge of.... Does this make any sense? Like the edge of the tube itself, of where the sound comes from has these kind of like almost dust particles that come off it."These responses extend to everyday sounds. A passing motorbike appears dark purple to Andrew, while a friend’s dog’s bark takes on a lime-green colour.In September, he brought that way of experiencing sound to a live performance at the Handbag Factory in Vauxhall, London, United Kingdom.Pianists Camden Stewart and Karim Kamar improvised around their original compositions as Andrew translated the music into paint.The results do not always follow familiar associations between colour and mood. A minor key need not produce a sombre-looking painting.“E minor, that's usually dark blue, slow legato movements where it's kind of like swirling,” he explains.Finding the meeting point between visual and audioExperts say sound-to-colour synaesthesia, known as chromesthesia, can also involve shapes, movement and texture.“It's the shapes, it's the movement, it's texture and all of these things, and how it's organised in space as well,” shares Jamie Ward, professor of cognitive neuroscience at the University of Sussex.Sounds can sometimes interrupt Andrew’s thoughts, but he sees synaesthesia as an inseparable part of his life.“It's not a curse, though. I can't imagine what it would be like to not have it,” says Andrew.For the musicians who are taking part in the live performance, it has been a fascinating process.“That's like asking me 'what does a fourth dimension look like?' I can't even fathom it.”Check out the video above for footage of Jake Andrew's performance.

title: Did Trump order Maduro’s kidnapping based on Grok’s advice?
description: The US president spent hours in the White House asking Musk’s AI chatbot questions, including how Venezuelans would react if the US captured Maduro, Time magazine reports.
content: In December 2025, Elon Musk visited the White House for a secret meeting with the US President, with Trump spending hours asking AI chatbot Grok questions about his presidency and legacy and how Venezuelans would react if US forces captured President Nicolás Maduro, Time magazine reports.According to an official present at the meeting, the chatbot responded that Maduro was a repressive and deeply unpopular dictator and that many Venezuelans would likely celebrate his downfall.Following the US capture of Maduro in January of this year, Venezuelans did indeed celebrate in large numbers all over the country. Trump came away from this experience “thinking Grok was ingenious”.The meeting took place seven months after Musk left his role at the controversial Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), yet how this meeting fits into the timeline of escalations in December is unclear.At the time, tensions between the two countries were at their highest, with the Trump administration waging a war against drug cartels known as Operation Southern Spear, the setting up of a maritime blockade and the US declaration of Maduro’s government as a “Foreign Terrorist Organization”.Behind the scenes, the Trump administration had also been making transition plans should they decide to oust Maduro and seize the country’s oil and mineral resources.The reports in Time magazine suggest that Grok may have convinced Trump to go ahead.The US government has ramped up the use of AI this year, with Google’s Gemini and Musk’s Grok both used in public services such as Medicare, and applying for government jobs as well as for defence purposes, including integration into fighter planes.OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Meta’s Llama and Anthropic’s Claude have all been approved for certain functions in the US government.Musk is back in the foldTime's report lands the same week Musk returned to an official government role for the first time since leaving DOGE in May 2025.On Wednesday, Hegseth named the world's richest man, Anduril founder Palmer Luckey and former Republican House Speaker Newt Gingrich to co-lead a new Pentagon study on the future of warfare.The appointment has raised questions about conflicts of interest, as both Musk and Luckey run companies with substantial defence business. Musk's SpaceX is already building satellite networks for Trump's planned Golden Dome missile defence shield.Musk is also spending millions to help Republicans keep control of Congress in November's midterm elections.

title: Trans-Caspian Corridor: Europe and Central Asia target faster trade
description: Transit along the Trans-Caspian Corridor currently takes around 35 days, with a target of cutting this to between 15 and 20. Officials say customs, digital systems and predictable border procedures are as important as new railways and ports.
content: Countries along the Trans-Caspian Corridor, backed by the European Union, are trying to make the route faster and more predictable, with a target of cutting transit times from around 35 days to between 15 and 20.For cargo moving west from Uzbekistan, the route can run through Kazakhstan to the Caspian Sea, cross by ferry to Azerbaijan, and continue through Georgia and Türkiye towards Europe.
