More than 150 other cinemas in Italy are expected to extend programming. “As long as theatres want to show it, NAZA will continue to be screened,” Andrea Romeo, founder of I Wonder Pictures, the film’s distributor in Italy, told La Repubblica.“We made this film out of a sense of obligation to use our position as Israelis to examine the systems behind the mass killing of Palestinian civilians for which our country is responsible,” explained Abraham and Szor.“While filming over the past three years, we found ourselves asking the very questions that were asked by our grandparents’ generation and throughout the 20th century: how does one group of people allow the total dehumanisation of another? What do the inner workings of such a system look like?” Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has attacked the makers of NAZA, accusing the film of contributing to “global antisemitic incitement”. “It’s shocking. We are fighting global antisemitic incitement and when it comes from within us it is intolerable,” Netanyahu said in a video posted on Telegram. “And now two Israeli directors portraying the IDF (Israel Defense Forces) as war criminals receive applause at the Venice festival.”Netanyahu's comments followed those of Israeli Culture Minister Miki Zohar, who directly equated criticism of Israel's actions to antisemitism and announced that he would “act immediately to revoke the Israeli citizenship” of the Israeli directing duo Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor.NAZA will be released in more than 50 territories in the coming weeks before being made free-to-watch on The Guardian’s website in November.

title: Rogue AI agents tried and failed to hack US and Canadian government websites
description: Researchers cannot confidently say who was responsible, but evidence points to rogue Google and OpenAI agents carrying out a range of aggressive tactics to collect datasets and test their vulnerabilities.
content: Rogue AI agents attempted to hack US and Canadian government websites, according to non-profit research lab Transluce, with evidence suggesting that Google and OpenAI’s agents were responsible.Two incidents in particular demonstrated aggressive techniques being used to access publicly available data from the US Department of Education’s Civil Rights Data Collection, and Library and Archives Canada, a Canadian federal agency, with both ultimately failing to compromise any data.Transluce reports that the incidents are part of a “broader pattern of automated workflows” attributed to AI agents. “These workflows use aggressive or grey-area techniques to retrieve information from government websites, sometimes using sites in unintended ways or violating explicit usage policies,” the organisation’s researchers said.Among the additional targets were the White House, Departments of War, Justice and Commerce, as well as the Centers for Disease Control and the Securities and Exchange Commission, and state agencies in California, Maryland, Illinois, Texas, and New York.In none of these cases, however, did agents gain access to information that was not already publicly available.The latest findings come amid a growing number of reports of unexpected or unauthorised behaviour by AI agents.In September alone, there have been two major incidents involving rogue OpenAI agents — the first involved agents leaking private user images to public websites, and the second with agents attempting to win access to government data in the US and Australia.The company has since decided to delay the rollout of its next-generation Astra model after safety researchers flagged “critical” cybersecurity capabilities and unpredictable, unauthorised behaviour.US and Canadian attemptsAgents attacked the US Department of Education on 17 June while looking up school statistics.Transluce reports that the agents made more than 200,000 requests to the website, including a failed attempt to send deliberately flawed data to test the site’s database vulnerability and consequently bypass the site’s normal filters.The researchers found that data stored on the website appeared to match a web search task in Google’s DeepSearchQA benchmark, which they say suggests the agents were not told to carry out hacking attacks but were “graded on their ability to successfully retrieve specific niche information from the internet”.Transluce disclosed the attempted hack to the US Department of Education in September, with the department responding they had not seen any impact on their services.AI agents made similar attempts on Library and Archives Canada in two separate incidents, on 28 May and later on 9 June.The agents issued 899 “collection-search” requests for data relating to divorce records from 1905-1911, according to data picked up by the official Portuguese web archive Arquivo.pt.Of the 899 requests, 13 carried attack payloads to test the website’s vulnerability. Again, none of the attempts on either occasion were successful.Transluce says it cannot “confidently attribute” the attempts to Open AI, but the tactics were consistent with activity it had previously attributed to the company.The organisation reported these incidents to the Canadian government earlier this week.The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security issued a statement in response, saying “there is no indication that government systems have been compromised at this time.”Transluce published its findings yesterday, after carrying out research using information from Arquivo.pt and urlquery.net, the free web-based security service for URL and domain scanning.

title: Euronews Culture's Film of the Week: 'Digger' – Tom Cruise stuck in postmodernist misfire
description: Oscar-winning director Alejandro González Iñárritu teams up with Tom Cruise for 'Digger', one of the boldest and wildest films of 2026. It may also be one of this year's biggest misfires.
content: NB: Spoiler-free review.A billionaire narcissist’s hunger for power and proclivity for manipulating public narrative for personal gain threatens to unleash a worldwide disaster.If you’re looking for escapism, Digger may not be the way to go. But that’s not the only reason you’ll want to stay away.Digger Rockwell (Tom Cruise) is an aging oil tycoon whose 38-year-old cat is circling the drain. But poor Maggie, who has somewhere between “two weeks and five minutes” left to live, will have to wait as her master's reckless drilling in Greenland has unleashed methane chaos. This results in a massive explosion and a renegade chunk of Arctic glacier to break free. They quickly name the glacier Judy. She’s five times the size of Washington D.C., and she’s headed straight for Europe.“Let’s blow that frozen cunt up!” suggests one general to President Compton (John Goodman). But the typical US reaction – launch first ask questions later – won't work with Judy.“We’re up against the reality of nature,” explains Digger’s top environmental scientist Dr. Ganesh (Riz Ahmed, Digger 's MVP and looking like he just wandered off a Wes Anderson set).Refusing to accept that the fate of the world (naturally, measured more in terms of infrastructure devastation and monetary loss rather than loss of life) could be in the hands of the wind and ocean currents, President Compton decides that the “great big dildo of a pickle” is down to Digger, who needs to avert Armageddon. And hopefully save Maggie.Alejandro González Iñárritu (Birdman, The Revenant, Bardo), a polarising filmmaker to begin with, has made both the boldest film of 2026 and this year’s wildest misfire. Digger is certainly his most pretentious film to date and sees him employing his inarguably impressive knack for staging to tell an eco-satire with Dr. Strangelove on the mind.It kicks off promisingly enough as a heightened farce that pokes fun at bullish American geopolitics and crisis management, the Trump administration (business above all – and the fact the threat comes from American meddling in Greenland couldn’t be timelier), and how arrogant Americans see Europe (“those little boys piss sitting down”). It’s very broad, but it’s never not entertaining... And just when it all seems too exhaustingly cartoonish for comfort comes the metatextual twist to end all metatextual twists.You can’t fault its boldness and the promise it carries, as the reveal – which shan’t be disclosed here – not only explains the caricatured and largely one-note performances from Cruise, Goodman and Sandra Hüller (reduced to playing Digger’s half-sister Emma as someone who enters rooms and shouts), but harks back to Iñárritu’s Oscar-winning Birdman. The director goes full postmodernist once more and sets the stage for Digger to become a satire about the very concept of satire. More specifically, about the importance of lampooning past calamity, in a sort of Twain-esque “tragedy plus time equals comedy”.While initially promising, it sadly goes nowhere, with Iñárritu, Alexander Dinelaris, Nicolás Giacobone and Sabina Berman’s screenplay never getting to the heart of the social criticism, distraction, catharsis and yes, possible narrative rewriting, the genre can offer. The script also lacks the laughs to bolster its mordant aspirations and never - excuse us – digs deep enough to engross, relying instead on Cruise’s OTT efforts to entertain.To his credit, Cruise does pull out all the stops here, dialling it up with his prosthetic belly, terrible comb-over and Foghorn Leghorn delivery. However, this won’t be the vehicle that gets the Best Actor Oscar that has eluded him for so long, as his performances in Digger are both larger-than-life and unrewarding. It’s a shame, as Cruise has proven time and time again that he’s more than Mission: Impossible’s Ethan Hunt; however, he mistakes pantomimic and jowly excess for "serious” acting, and the divisive (by design?) film itself may dissuade Academy voters to give him his fourth acting nomination, following Born on the Fourth of July, Jerry Maguire and Magnolia. As for Iñárritu, it doesn’t look like he’ll be adding a third Best Director Oscar to his shelf, after winning two consecutive awards in a row - Birdman (2015) and The Revenant (2016) - as Digger comes off as far too sanctimonious for its own good. Then again, when has that stopped the Academy? Still, should reason prevail, Digger ’s award chances hang on Emmanuel Lubezki’s impressive cinematography and Dennis Gassner’s flawless production design. Both save the day.It’s hard to write more about Digger without spoiling Iñárritu’s brave but misguided gambit, but safe to say that once he does pull the rug from under the audience, he leaves viewers with a boated folly that’s both hollow and heavy-handed in the way it loudly announces everything via didactic speeches.It’s still uniquely fascinating in the way it means well as a commentary on complicity, knows where it wants to go while breaking every fourth wall in its way, and understands what it’s trying to say as a cautionary tale; it simply can’t get out of its own finger wagging way. One character (again, no spoilers), played by Jesse Plemons, delivers a monologue towards the end of Digger that may as well have been delivered straight-to-camera, essentially telling the audience that if this all feels too on-the-nose, it’s by design, and that if we’re not in awe at what we’ve just witnessed, it’s because we’re not getting it.The only thing to get is that high concepts are always to be applauded. But when they end up as empty theatrics that make Adam McKay's Don’t Look Up feel like a masterclass in allegorical subtlety, conceptual bravado just comes off as self-indulgent. Chances are you won’t dig it.Digger is out in cinemas now.

title: 'They should cast Jack': Danny Boyle names his pick for the next James Bond
description: Jack O’Connell’s name has been mentioned as a possible Bond contender during the audition process, but has not been elevated to frontrunner status like Jack Lowden, Callum Turner, Jacob Elordi and Jack Barton. Now, ex-Bond director Danny Boyle has named O'Connell as his ideal pick for the new 007.
content: Once upon a time, Danny Boyle was set to direct Daniel Craig’s swansong as James Bond. The Oscar-winning British director behind Trainspotting, Slumdog Millionaire and the upcoming Rupert Murdoch biopic Ink, was originally set to direct 2021’s No Time To Die before exiting due to alleged creative differences. He was ultimately replaced by Beasts Of No Nation filmmaker Cary Joji Fukunaga. “When they asked me to do Bond, we came up with the story [with John Hodge] and they lost confidence in it,” he said at the Zurich Film Festival. “It’s a shame, because it could have been really good.”The Bond-helmer-we-never-got also weighed in on who he thinks should be the next 007, naming British actor Jack O’Connell as his choice to replace Daniel Craig. “They should cast Jack O’Connell as Bond,” he said at the festival, per Variety, before praising O’Connell’s performance in the 2024 Amy Winehouse biopic Back To Black and as infamous British tabloid editor Larry Lamb in Ink.“Have you seen Back to Black? It’s a wonderful film. He plays the boyfriend [Blake Fielder-Civil] and that’s an impossible part. It was an incredible performance,” said Boyle.O’Connell’s name has been mentioned as a possible Bond contender during the audition process, but has not been elevated to frontrunner status like Jack Lowden, Callum Turner, Jacob Elordi and Jack Barton. The 36-year-old actor got his big break in the E4 series Skins and is best known for starring in the Oscar-winning film Sinners and Boyle’s 28 Years Later - one of Euronews Culture's Best Movies of 2026... So Far.Boyle also expressed strong support for Bond 26 director Denis Villeneuve. “Villeneuve is amazing. Did you see that beginning of [Dune: Part Three], which they showed before The Odyssey? God, if I was directing The Odyssey, I would have thought everybody would be disappointed in my film following it. But obviously, Chris Nolan has more confidence than I have.” Boyle is not the first to throw his support behind a Bond contender. Jack Lowden’s Slow Horses co-star Gary Oldman recently said that Lowen would be his pick for Bond. “Jack, it’s been rumored that he’s on the shortlist,” said Oldman while appearing on the Canadian talk show The Morning Show. “We’re going to find out pretty soon, aren’t we? Because they have picked him. They have made their choice, but they have not announced it yet. So my fingers are crossed for Jack.”Casting for the seventh James Bond remains unannounced, but not long to find out... Bond 26 producer Amy Pascal recently shared that "the end of the year is a good bet" when it comes to the timing of the new actor's announcement. “I would say the end of the year is a good bet,” said Pascal. “We are being really, really methodical. Having worked with Barbara Broccoli at the studio, I mean, Daniel Craig is a hard act to follow. And it’s got to be something really different that is stirring and exciting and different.”Production on Bond 26 is expected to kick off in 2027, with a release planned for 2028. Danny Boyle’s Ink premiered at this year’s Venice Film Festival. It is releasing in limited theatres on 11 December before streaming on Netflix on 8 January 2027.

title: Is the EU planning to freeze funds to German states that voted for the AfD?
description: Claims circulating online allege that the EU is threatening to block funds intended for the German state of Saxony-Anhalt, after the far-right AfD party won a recent election there. However, there's no evidence that this is the case.
content: Is Brussels trying to freeze EU funds to a German state that voted for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in an election in early September?According to several social media posts amassing thousands of views, likes and shares, and often with a picture of European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen attached, it is.They allege that millions, or even billions, of euros could be withheld from the state of Saxony-Anhalt, located in east-central Germany, after voters handed the AfD a landslide victory on 6 September.However, the 39 seats it won were not enough to command a majority, even though the party secured more than twice as many seats as any other party.The AfD has since struggled to establish a coalition, however, as the other parties have refused to collaborate with it.Von der Leyen herself has repeatedly criticised the AfD in the past, and her own centre-right CDU party suffered a crushing defeat, winning just 17.2% of the vote and falling to 15 seats. This possibly fuelled the suggestions online that she is behind the scheme to freeze the EU funds.However, there's no evidence that that's the case. Instead, the narrative seems to stem from a statement by German Green MEP Daniel Freund, who said after the state election that he would push to freeze EU money flowing to an AfD-led government if it violated any European values or misused funds.Saxony-Anhalt is set to receive €2.95 billion in EU funding as part of the current 2021-2027 budget. This includes €1.3 billion from the European Regional Development Fund, €571 million from the European Social Fund, and €594 million from the European Agricultural Fund for Rural Development.On a per capita basis, Saxony-Anhalt benefits more from EU funding than any other German state, according to Freund, averaging over €650 per citizen over the full EU budget cycle.He also highlighted that the EU had used similar freezing measures in the past in Poland and Hungary.Brussels did indeed block money intended for those countries a few years ago, over rule-of-law and democratic backsliding concerns under previous governments.Some of these funds have since been released following reforms. In Poland, for example, the European Commission formally unlocked €137 billion in cohesion and post-pandemic funds in 2024, after Prime Minister Donald Tusk's government brought in guarantees for judicial independence and the rule of law.For Hungary, meanwhile, it has proposed unlocking a first tranche of €4.2 billion in cohesion funds and restoring access to programmes like Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe.Billions of euros had been frozen over rule-of-law and corruption concerns under former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, but recent legislative actions by Péter Magyar's administration have paved the way for the money to be unfrozen.Nevertheless, for now, the idea that this could happen to Saxony-Anhalt appears to be the opinion of a few MEPs, rather than a concerted effort by Brussels.Under the EU's rule-of-law conditionality mechanism, funding cannot be suspended simply because a particular party takes office. The European Commission says measures can only be proposed where breaches of the rule of law directly affect, or seriously risk affecting, the sound management of the EU budget or the EU's financial interests.Such a measure would have to be proposed by the European Commission, with the Council of the European Union ultimately deciding whether to adopt it.A spokesperson for the government of Saxony-Anhalt also told The Cube, Euronews' fact-checking team, that it was not aware of any plans to freeze the EU funds heading its way."In the current situation, there would be no legal basis for such a course of action," the spokesperson added, noting that a new state government has not yet been formed following the election on 6 September.The European Commission meanwhile confirmed to us that it is not considering blocking EU funds for Saxony-Anhalt."As a matter of general practice, the Commission monitors the situation in all Member States and regions and takes action where necessary, in accordance with the legal frameworks governing EU funding," it said. "The election result itself does not constitute a legal basis for suspending EU funding."In addition to that vote, the AfD also saw success in another election in the state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania in the north a couple of weeks later. The Left meanwhile won in the Berlin state election.- This article was updated to include a comment from the European Commission.

title: ‘Thrilling’: Dutch cattle farmers switch to rice as solution to warmer climate and sinking peatlands
description: Dutch cattle farming dries out peatland and releases CO2. Is switching to Japanese rice-growing a solution?
content: The warming climate is allowing Dutch farmers to grow a grain never before harvested in the Netherlands: rice.For centuries, cows were the country's agricultural staple. But now farmers are experimenting with produce previously unthinkable in such a wet, temperate country.And researchers behind the scheme hope rice cultivation could help address one of the country's most pressing environmental challenges: peat soils that are sinking as they dry out, pushing parts of the low-lying Netherlands ever lower."It's extraordinary," says Philippe Terheggen, chairman of the Land van Ons association that has provided the fields for the rice harvest."We would never have thought maybe 20 years ago that we would be able to grow rice in the Netherlands," says the 68-year-old."But it's also scary because it tells you what is possible... now the climate has changed," he says.For now, the project is a pilot scheme, consisting of just 0.6 hectares, with organisers hoping to produce around three tonnes of short-grain rice suitable for sushi or risotto.The team is working with around 30 different rice cultivars from as far afield as Russia, China, Japan and Uzbekistan, to see which grows best in the Dutch climate.'I just want to show that things can be changed for the benefit of the future'In a soggy field between Amsterdam and The Hague, farmer Sander Roeleveld ploughs his rice crops with a combine harvester, backdropped by windmills and canals.Roeleveld, who describes himself as a "pioneer", says he wants to show other farmers that rice could grow in boggy Dutch soil."My goal is to show that more things are possible on wetland than just grass," the 53-year-old says."Of course, when you have had cows for 600 years, it's really hard to imagine that you want to do something else than having milk from your cow," he laughs."I just want to show that things can be changed for the benefit of the future."How rice farming could cure dried out peatlandsBut the project is about much more than crop diversification. Researchers believe it could help tackle one of the Netherlands' most persistent environmental problems.Roughly one-tenth of the country is peatland, which farmers drain for grass to feed their cattle.As the peat dries out, it releases millions of tonnes of carbon dioxide while causing the land to subside by up to several centimetres a year in the worst-affected areas.According to Wageningen University, greenhouse gas emissions from Dutch peat soils account for around two to three per cent of the country's total emissions.The only way to resolve this vicious cycle is to keep the fields wet – but then farmers would have nothing to grow there... until now."Basically it started with just a crazy idea," explains Julian Helfenstein, a researcher from Wageningen University and Research, who is piloting the project along with colleagues from nearby Leiden University.It is a rare combination of both adapting to climate change and mitigating its effects, says the 36-year-old."Rice is an opportunity for this part of the world to adapt to climate change, so to grow something that previously wasn't possible," he says."But also to mitigate climate change because it stops this peat from degrading and emitting all the CO2 because you can keep it wet."The peat issue affects not just the Netherlands, but much of northern Europe, including Germany, Belgium, even the Baltic states, he says.Helfenstein and his team are closely monitoring the CO2 and methane emissions from cultivating rice compared to maintaining grassland – to ensure the cure is not worse than the illness."So far the results are promising," he says."As an environmental scientist, you're always pointing to the problems. And it can be a bit depressing, like, 'Oh, here's more climate change, here's more pollution'," says Helfenstein."And then here's an opportunity for science to work also towards a solution. So I find that thrilling."'Chewy, but great': Dutch rice could be used to make sushi and sakeLocal restaurants have already voiced an interest in offering premium Dutch-sourced rice, says Guusje van der Vossen from the Wij Land association which helps farmers transition to more sustainable production.She says the rice being harvested now was a grain from northern Japan, which seems the best adapted to Dutch conditions.The 27-year-old is one of the few people ever to have eaten Dutch-grown rice – from an experimental batch grown last year."It tasted delicious, to be honest," she laughs, saying the aim was to make sushi with it – and maybe sake."It was a bit chewy, but also great."

title: Kanye West’s controversial concerts in Russia have finally been cancelled
description: According to the Moscow-based organizer Say Agency, the controversial rapper's two October dates in St Petersburg have been cancelled. Russian media states that the decision was made by the authorities, who are reportedly investigating the organizers for alleged fraud.
content: Most artists have avoided performing in Russia since the start of the war in Ukraine. But Kanye ‘Ye’ West would never stoop to putting himself in that category. The controversial American rapper, who has been barred from several European countries, was due to perform in St Petersburg on 10 and 11 October, thereby becoming the biggest western act to play in the country since 2022. Following earlier reports that St Petersburg’s Gazprom Arena said it would not host the rapper, as no rental agreement has been signed, Ye’s two dates have now officially been cancelled.According to the Moscow-based organizer Say Agency, who confirmed the cancellation, refunds for purchased tickets will be available.The agency, which had previously disputed the venue’s statement regarding rental agreements, did not elaborate further on the reasons behind the cancellation. However, according to the Russian media, the decision was made by the authorities. The organisers had begun selling tickets before obtaining the necessary approval, and the cancellation was decided following “a call from Moscow”. Russian authorities are reportedly investigating the organizers for alleged fraud – as reported by the Kommersant newspaper, citing an anonymous source. St Petersburg outlet Fontanka had previously reported that the concerts had not received all the necessary approvals and were going to be called off following a “call from above” in Moscow. The cancellation follows opposition to West's booking from some Russian politicians wishing to rid the country of any Western influence. These include conservative Russian lawmaker Vitaly Milonov, who released a video statement in which he suggested West should perform traditional Russian songs instead of his planned setlist. “Maybe after that he’ll stop his disgusting antics and become a normal person,” he said. Conversely, some Russian politicians had hailed the announcement of West’s visit as a victory against “anti-Russian hysteria” - despite the rapper’s antisemitic past and comments glorifying Nazi Germany. West’s antisemitic remarks began in 2022, when he made a series of offensive comments on social media which ended up getting him booted off both X and Instagram. The musician was dropped by his talent agency and fashion brands like Adidas and Balenciaga also distanced themselves from West. West went on to post a picture of KKK robes, rescind his previous apology to the Jewish community, declare himself “a Nazi” and assert that he has “dominion over his wife”. In February 2025, West started selling swastika t-shirts, and in May, he released a song titled ‘Heil Hitler’, which praised the Nazi leader. This led him to be stripped of a visa to enter Australia and faced with immediate arrest in Brazil. West apologised for his actions and took out a full-page ad in the Wall Street Journal earlier this year. He addressed his past antisemitic comments, reflecting on a "four-month-long manic episode of psychotic, paranoid and impulsive behaviour" and saying that he “lost touch with reality.” Still, many questioned the timing of his apology, considering it coincided with the release of his new album ‘Bully’ and the start of his world tour.

title: Gimmick or recipe for success? Japan's convenience stores test AI flavours
description: Japanese convenience store chains are turning to AI for dessert ideas. Some are unexpected mashups.
content: A pickle-flavoured lemon tart might seem an unlikely dessert, but Japanese convenience store chains are betting that artificial intelligence (AI) can help them find combinations customers never knew they wanted.Popular convenience store chains FamilyMart and Lawson are using the technology to develop new food products, looking for ideas that go beyond familiar flavours.The experiments come amid wider concerns about AI replacing workers and increasingly powerful systems slipping beyond human control.Here, the technology’s role is more modest — suggesting what might go into your next snack.AI supplied the ideas, but humans still had to turn them into something worth eating. Companies used the technology mainly for brainstorming, with human specialists involved in developing the final products.FamilyMart fed sales data into AI to help develop a French-style canelé made with dough containing sweet potato purée and topped with caramel sauce. The chain said it wanted to create something new but likely to sell.In July, the chain test-launched its first AI experiment with a biscuit sandwich filled with thick milk cream.Rival chain Lawson took a different approach, asking AI for unexpected combinations without feeding it past sales figures or market data to generate ideas “unconstrained by existing ways of thinking or market trends," according to a statement from the company.One suggestion was to pair lemon tart with pickles.For Shingo Shiina, a 64-year-old who works in architecture, the combination came as a surprise.“I was like ‘huh’ at first, but it actually goes pretty well, doesn’t it? The pickles. I’m surprised,” he said after tasting the tart.“It’s a strange flavour, but it’s tasty. It really is delicious.”Shiina was also impressed by the idea itself.“You’d probably never come up with this, right? Pickles and this. I don’t think a human would ever think of that. That’s AI for you,” he said.Lawson’s other AI-inspired products include a bread roll filled with red bean paste, margarine and yoghurt cream, and a Japanese-style salad presented like a parfait.The pickle-flavoured lemon tart is being launched in Tokyo and surrounding regions in September, according to Lawson.

title: Oil falls below $100 after Trump reports talks with Iran
description: Brent crude fell on Wednesday morning after Donald Trump said US and Iranian representatives had held what he called “very productive” talks. Reports that Saudi Arabia is restarting a key oil pipeline also weighed on prices.
content: Oil prices fell on Wednesday after US President Donald Trump said American and Iranian representatives had held talks at the United Nations.Brent crude, the international benchmark, was trading at $98.41 a barrel in the morning in Europe. US benchmark West Texas Intermediate cost $89.21 a barrel for next month delivery.Brent has repeatedly risen above $100 since the Middle East war began in February.The three-hour meeting was “very good” and “very productive”, Trump told reporters during a meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. He said another meeting was planned soon.His comments came hours after he told the UN he faced a “big decision” on whether to reach a deal with Iran or “annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly”.The US and Iran remain at an impasse. Iran has kept the Strait of Hormuz closed, while the US has maintained a blockade of Iranian ports. Fighting involving Saudi-backed government forces and the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen has also disrupted energy exports through the Red Sea.“The three-hour US-Iran meeting matters because it shifts the market from pure escalation pricing toward a genuine diplomatic process, even if a final deal still looks distant,” said Stephen Innes of Quintex Intel.Prices also fell following a report that Saudi Arabia had restarted operations along its East–West Pipeline. The route allows Saudi crude to reach the Red Sea without passing through the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi Arabia said this month that drones launched from Iraq had forced it to close the pipeline.The kingdom hopes to resume exports later this week, Bloomberg reported, citing a source. Saudi Aramco has reportedly told Asian refiners that they may soon be able to collect crude from the Red Sea port of Yanbu. European refiners, however, have reportedly been told they will receive no Saudi crude under their October supply agreements.Global stocks edge higher ahead of Trump–Xi meetingEuropean stock markets had mixed reactions at the open.The Euro Stoxx 50 was about 0.1% lower in early trading while the broader pan-European Stoxx 600 traded over 0.3% higher.The UK's FTSE 100, France's CAC 40, Italy’s FTSE MIB and Switzerland's CH20 all traded around 0.1% higher.However, Germany's DAX 30, Spain's IBEX 35 and the Netherlands' AEX all traded between 0.3% and 0.4% lower than their Tuesday close.Asian shares mostly rose. South Korea’s Kospi gained 1.2%, with Samsung and SK Hynix both up more than 2%. Taiwan’s Taiex rose 0.9%. The MSCI index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan gained 0.5%, its sixth consecutive daily rise. Japan’s stock market was closed for a holiday, although Nikkei futures traded higher.On Wall Street, the Nasdaq rose 0.5% to a record close on Tuesday. The S&P 500 was little changed, while the Dow fell 0.4%.In currency markets, the euro traded at $1.1429, near a two-month low, as investors considered the possibility of another US interest rate rise. The dollar also edged up against the yen to 157.60 yen.Gold traded at $4,379 an ounce. US Treasury futures rose slightly as oil prices eased, keeping the yield on the 10-year government bond below 5%.Investors were also looking ahead to a meeting on Thursday between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping. Trade and competition over AI are expected to be on the agenda.Kyle Rodda, a senior financial market analyst at Capital.com, said the war in the Middle East could prove more consequential for markets, including whether the US could persuade China to use its influence with Iran.

title: Tallinn Defence EXPO: Counter-drone systems and robot soldiers steal the show
description: Drones have changed the face of war in Ukraine. At the Tallinn Defence EXPO, Estonian companies showed the counter-drone systems and battlefield robots they say Europe now needs.
content: Unmanned systems are both a growing threat and an increasingly vital part of the defence arsenal.That theme ran through the Tallinn Defence EXPO, where more than 100 companies showed their latest products.The stakes are high for Estonia, which borders Russia. According to an industry briefing, its defence spending rose from 1.9% of GDP in 2013 to an average of 5.4% through 2029.The EXPO was one of six events in Estonian Defence Week, held in Tallinn over five days in late September.The week drew around 4,500 visitors from 56 countries and featured 133 speakers across 68 sessions, including a NATO innovation conference and a Baltic defence conference.Seeing and stopping dronesEstonian firm Marduk Technologies presented a detection system that uses powerful optics and AI to find and identify flying objects."It's a camera-based drone detection system. It's fully passive, and with this we can see whatever is flying. We can differentiate automatically whether it is a bird, drone, helicopter or any flying object," Leet Rauno Lember, CEO of Marduk Technologies, told Euronews Next."Passive" means this optical system sends out no radio signal, remaining hard to spot — unlike radars.Lember said their optical detection system is not "better" than other technologies but complements them.Acoustic sensors reach only a few hundred metres, he explained, while electric drones can be very quiet. Radar covers long distances but may miss drones made of lightweight foam."All of the layers are complementing each other, and end users are able to make better decisions," he said.Marduk Technologies has been developing the drone-detection devices for more than a decade.The war in Ukraine confirmed the company's early warnings, Lember said. "Back in 2016, everybody said that drones will not be a problem, at least in the near future."Another Estonian company, DefSecIntel, combines optical, radar, acoustic and radio-frequency sensors in one mobile, highly autonomous system called Eirshield."This is a turnkey counter-drone system," Jaanus Tamm, CEO and founder of DefSecIntel Solutions, told Euronews Next.It helps users detect hostile drones, track them, then decide how to intercept them. Its effectors range from jammers to interceptor drones and, if needed, lasers."Eirshield detection sensors will detect the drones, then the operator will select which one to go after, and then they launch the interceptor drone," Tamm said. "Then the hostile drones will be destroyed and they will not hit any infrastructure elements or do any harm for the civilians."Tamm called Eirshield "one of the few" TRL 9 counter-drone systems in Europe that can be bought now, in large numbers. TRL 9 is the top of the technology readiness scale.The design is open, so it can evolve. "If there are new threats coming, we can just add new effectors, or new sensors to detect better," he said.One of those effectors is Blaze, an interceptor drone from Latvia's Origin Robotics. According to the industry briefing, France's defence procurement agency selected it at Eurosatory 2026.Robots instead of soldiersUnmanned vehicles can support, or even replace, soldiers on dangerous missions. Milrem Robotics presented its THeMIS unmanned ground vehicle.The company says the technology enables "an unmanned kill zone," where robotic vehicles would detect and push back invading troops. That would minimise human casualties among the defenders.The vehicles are remotely controlled and partly autonomous. "Instead of sending troops on the battlefield, we can send in these machines and save lives," Raul Rikk, Capability Development Director at Milrem Robotics, told Euronews Next at the company's Tallinn factory.The modular platform can carry a machine gun, an anti-tank system or other weapons. It can also handle reconnaissance, mine clearing, logistics and casualty evacuation.Rikk said the concept is already proven. "Nothing is theoretical anymore. Ukrainians are using them on the battlefield," he said.Rikk said the company's current production capacity is not public. "We are talking about hundreds of vehicles, and different sizes," he said. "We can take the production everywhere, so it's not complicated to set up the production, and we can scale up quite rapidly."For Rikk, the direction is clear. "Tomorrow's war is already in Ukraine," he said.

title: Humanoid robots: China builds them, but Germany could supply the joints and hands
description: Europe has so far built few humanoid robots, yet could profit from each one. German car part suppliers may play a key role in joints, says a Fraunhofer study.
content: At first glance, humanoid robots look like a field dominated by the big tech corporations: artificial intelligence, cameras, sensors, software.But beneath their casing lies a great deal of traditional industry.Every leg, every arm and every hand contains motors, gearboxes, bearings and sensors — components European companies have been producing for decades.German research is still at the starting point in the race to develop humanoid robots, but industrial suppliers are already far ahead when it comes to specialised parts.Researchers are now asking whether Europe even needs to build humanoid robots itself in order to benefit from a potential boom in the technology.Could conventional industrial companies simply become suppliers to a new robotics sector? Or will this value creation also relocate to China or the United States?Europe so far plays hardly any role in finished machinesChina currently dominates deliveries by a clear margin and has overtaken the United States. Europe so far plays hardly any role in finished machines. Yet German companies could still profit from their potential march to victory.An unusual strategy could emerge for Europe: not building the robot itself, but supplying the parts it is made of.According to a specialist report by the Fraunhofer Institute for Manufacturing Engineering and Automation IPA, this component business could be much easier for Germany in particular to capture."In principle, the potential along the German and European supply chain is very large," says the author of the paper, Vincent Bezold, head of the Automated Manufacturing Systems business segment at IPA.Together with consultancy P3, IPA has examined what opportunities this opens up for industrial suppliers.They already have the expertise and production facilities for the components humanoids urgently need — and, according to recent comparisons, a specific advantage over Chinese parts of this kind.IPA expects the market to be worth around 30 billion dollars by 2030.China dominates global deliveries of humanoid robotsAround 19,100 humanoid robots were delivered in the first half of 2026. A huge share of them — 97 percent — came from China, according to data from research company Smart Analytics Global (SAG) published in August 2026.For the whole of 2026, researchers expect around 60,000 robots to be shipped, rising to half a million by 2030.According to SAG, China is currently winning the race to develop AI-powered humanoids. Agibot, a company based in the greater Shanghai area, alone has delivered 8,400 robots. US firms such as Tesla, Figure AI and Agility Robotics are lagging behind.However, the number of humanoid robots in commercially productive use is still low. Mass production off the assembly line has not yet been reached, and despite China’s high shipping volumes the market is far from settled.With government backing, China’s industry is working hard to accelerate the rollout of humanoid robots into widespread use.The goal is clear: humanoid robots in manufacturing, logistics and warehousing. In these areas, robots could perform clearly defined tasks, SAG notes.Their profitability and productivity can be easily compared and optimised here. Even so, the leap from "robots that can put on a show" to "robots that can work reliably" has yet to be made, SAG adds.Humanoid robots need more than 40 jointsBehind every AI robot sits a classic mechanical engineering industry. Before the software can link all the components together, they have to be mechanically and technically sound.Conventional industrial robots manage with seven joints, while humanoid robots need more than 40. Each joint means a motor, gearbox, bearing and sensor.While Chinese companies such as Agibot are already shipping thousands of humanoids, several of the firms producing crucial components for these machines are based in Germany.Gearboxes, motors, sensors and grippers are part of the traditional business of German and European automotive suppliers. These include German companies such as Schaeffler, Bosch, Schunk, Wittenstein and Neugart. They could also sell these parts to robot manufacturers.China is producing these components as well, but so far with significantly shorter lifetimes."They don’t happen to run, as recently in Beijing, a half marathon as a PR stunt by chance. They do it because they wouldn’t withstand a full marathon," explains Sebastian Reitelshöfer, head of robotics research at the University of Erlangen–Nuremberg, in an interview with the ARD-Finanzredaktion.According to Reitelshöfer, some components in these flagship models would only last "one or two weeks".In his assessment, some showcase models developed in China still have durability problems in certain parts: individual components can only be operated for a few weeks under heavy load.By contrast, some European designs from the automotive sector would last far longer.That, however, is precisely where one of the difficulties lies, Bezold tells Euronews. Supply chains are primarily developed locally around the original manufacturers."As a large proportion of humanoids currently comes from China, corresponding supplier structures are likely to form there as well, just as they did in Germany around the automotive industry," Bezold estimates. There are particular gaps in specialised components.Not all components are competitive yetIn August, Schaeffler unveiled a new gearbox developed specifically for humanoid robots. The company’s name also appears in the white paper by the Fraunhofer Institute for Manufacturing Engineering and Automation.The automotive supplier based in Herzogenaurach specialises in motors and drive technology. Its new strain wave gear – a high-precision specialist gearbox for industrial robots – is designed to transmit movements as accurately and powerfully as possible in the smallest installation space. According to the company, the new gearbox meets the core requirements of humanoid robot joints.A new production method could also cut manufacturing costs by more than 25 percent and reduce material consumption by over 75 percent. That makes the strain wave gear competitive."The re-shaped strain wave gear is another example of how we are industrially advancing core robotics components and preparing them for high-volume series production," says Schaeffler’s President Humanoid Robotics, David Kehr. The company is creating solutions "designed for quality, cost-effectiveness and scalability". Series production is expected to start in mid-2027.At the Hannover Messe in April 2026, the company received the Hermes Award for its development of humanoid robot joints. The prize underscores Schaeffler’s key role as a component supplier in the field of humanoid robotics, the company said in a subsequent statement.The award specifically recognised the actuators platform used in shoulder, elbow and knee joints in robots. According to Schaeffler, actuators account for around 50 percent of the total cost of a humanoid. They are therefore a central lever for competitiveness.Schaeffler is thus not simply trying to sell a single part for a robot. The company is looking to define part of the robot’s architecture.Robot hands from GermanyHow far this approach can go is illustrated by a partnership between Bosch and Schunk, two other German firms. Since June 2026, the two companies have been working together on a robot hand that can be integrated into different humanoid robot systems. This moves beyond individual parts such as gearboxes or motors to a complete key component of the humanoid robot.Schunk has spent around 20 years developing robot hands and specialises in gripping technology. Bosch contributes precision mechanics, electronics and software, and is expected to manufacture the hand in series later on."Robot hands are a key component in advancing humanoid robotics in production and enabling more flexible and precise work than with conventional gripping systems," said Mathias Pillin, Chief Technology Officer at Robert Bosch GmbH, when the collaboration was announced.The hand is particularly crucial for industrial use: it has to grip different workpieces, modulate force and operate reliably over long periods. At the same time, it should be compatible with as many robot platforms as possible. Hands are also among the hardware elements that most strongly influence the cost of a humanoid robot.Supplying parts does not mean controlling the whole productionBut a strong components business does not in itself amount to a robotics industry. The key question, therefore, is how much value creation remains in Europe if Chinese or US companies control the robot platforms, the software and access to customers.For Fraunhofer IPA and P3, the crucial issue is not only whether Europe produces its own humanoid robot, but also where the industrial value chain takes shape. This is the core business of many European suppliers, who could reap substantial profits by entering the market.From Bezold’s perspective, "access to manufacturers of humanoid robots" is the biggest shortcoming, because there are relatively few manufacturers in Europe and, as things stand today, only a small number of humanoid robots are actually built there. "That makes it harder for European suppliers to become part of the relevant value chains at an early stage."According to the specialist report, hardware is just as decisive as software development for the economic viability, scalability and industrial impact of humanoid robots. IPA and P3 see an opportunity here for European suppliers and call for coordinated action by industry, policymakers and researchers."Suppliers who engage early with actuators, gearboxes, batteries, dexterous hands and lightweight structures can help shape future reference architectures and secure long-term positions in emerging supply chains," the study says. IPA considers the opportunity tangible if action is taken immediately. The authors criticise funding policies that focus exclusively on artificial intelligence.The humanoid robots that will one day work in factories do not necessarily have to come from a single European plant. Europe may instead be hidden in their joints, hands and drives.The crucial question is who sets the technical standardsWhether this will develop into an industrial strength of its own, or whether Europe will simply become a supplier of parts for robots from China and the US, is still unclear. What is likely to be decisive is who not only delivers individual components, but also helps define the standards and architectures of the next robot generation.In its study "Humanoid Robotics 2040", Germany’s mechanical and plant engineering association VDMA argues that the entire production and supply chain should also be brought to Europe.Over the coming years, VDMA expects a mass market for humanoid robots. Its study (source in German) "Humanoid Robotics 2040", published in April 2026, considers annual sales in the millions to be possible by 2042.If Europe wants to help shape these markets, the study says it will need "far more capital, stronger support for start-ups and bolder industrial steps". Bezold also argues: "We ourselves need more manufacturers of humanoid robots in Europe." The industry association recommends treating humanoid robots as a priority and getting involved in the supply chain as early as possible. "That also means telling users that they should not be afraid to back projects even if the precise outcome is not entirely clear at the beginning," Bezold explains.

title: Israel says pilot tried to crash Tel Aviv-bound plane during cockpit fight before safe emergency landing
description: FlyDubai flight FZ1073 to Israel made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia as passengers describe harrowing scenes of a fight between the pilots, with one of them stabbed. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said a pilot "attempted to crash the plane," as Israeli security services investigate.
content: A commercial plane traveling from the United Arab Emirates to Israel made a safe emergency landing in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday, following harrowing minutes in which the co-pilot stabbed the captain and then tried to crash the jet, but was eventually subdued by passengers.In his first statement on the incident, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said that “one of the pilots stabbed the other and apparently attempted to crash the plane, with everyone on board."In a video statement, Netanyahu said he spoke with one of the passengers who told him that “somehow, he managed to break into the cockpit with one of the crew members, and together they subdued the pilot who had committed the stabbing while he was attempting to sabotage the aircraft's systems" and that "another flight crew member entered the cockpit and managed to stabilise the plane.""I salute these heroes who demonstrated resourcefulness and extraordinary courage. They saved many lives and averted a terrible disaster," the Israeli prime minister said, adding that almost all of the passengers on the flight were Israelis.He also announced that “the pilot who committed the stabbing has been arrested and is currently being interrogated by Saudi authorities."Later on Wednesday, Netanyahu hailed Indian captain Smit Machchaar as “a true hero” for “his extraordinary bravery” in “preventing a catastropic mid-air disaster.”“Despite being stabbed and seriously injured, he fought back, resisted, opened the cockpit door, and enabled passengers and crew to overpower the attacker,” Netanyahu said.The Israeli prime minister did not comment on a possible terror link, while Israel's security agencies continue their investigations.The plane carrying 174 passengers, including 27 children, landed safely in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, a civilian and military base in the kingdom, as passengers described harrowing scenes onboard of fighting and blood in the cockpit followed by a steep dive and erratic manoeuvres.Around two and a half hours after departing from Dubai, the flydubai plane transmitted a 7700 general emergency signal followed by 7500, the international code for unlawful interference or hijacking, according to the Flightradar24 flight tracking portal, prompting Israeli fighter jets to scramble.Flightradar24 showed the Boeing 737 abruptly descending from 33,000 feet to 17,000 feet in under 1 minute, then making an erratic circle back near the Jordanian border before landing in Tabuk.The aircraft’s sudden descent, along with its reported high speed, is consistent with a struggle for control.Israeli media quoted passengers and Israeli officials stating that a fight broke out in the cockpit between the two pilots and one of them was stabbed. The captain was able to open the cockpit door which allowed crew and passengers to enter and subdue the co-pilot.Two off-duty pilots among the passengers took control of the plane and landed it safely, according to multiple Israeli media reports.Passengers told Israel’s Channel 12 that they heard shouts of the altercation between the pilots and the plane dipped steeply.Another passenger told Israel’s Channel 15 that when the cockpit door was opened, passengers saw blood inside and they intervened to stop the fight between the pilots. According to the same passenger, one of the pilots was injured with a folding knife.Others described the chaotic scenes onboard, with passengers shouting in fear for their lives during the steep dive and then as the plane engaged in its emergency landing.Channel 12 Israel interviewed another passenger who said her husband helped “neutralise the terrorist” onboard as he “tried to crash the plane.” “There were stabbings and a lot of blood,” the passenger said.Israeli media published a photo purportedly taken inside the plane appearing to show a passenger in a blood-stained shirt, as well as a video showing the injured pilot on the floor covered in blood as crew and passengers try to help him. Other videos showed passengers stained with blood.Multiple Israeli media outlets reported that sources believe the co-pilot is a national of Oman.A photo of the plane on the tarmac, taken by disembarking passengers, showed damage to the rudder likely caused by the aircraft's rapid descent.According to a statement released by Tabuk airport, both pilots were being treated in hospital.Stranded passengers at Tabuk airport praised the care they received from Saudi authorities. They later boarded a replacement flydubai plane which flew them to Tel Aviv's Ben Gurion airport on Wednesday evening, after Saudi Arabia declined Israel's request to send their own military transport planes. Some passengers initially refused to board the replacement flydubai plane.The passengers posted videos on social media showing them celebrating their arrival in Israel after their ordeal.Netanyahu welcomed them at the airport upon their arrival in Tel Aviv, with passenger Yaniv Hayun, still in his blood-stained clothes, telling the prime minister that the captain was able to open the cockpit door before collapsing, which allowed him and other passengers to enter and subdue the attacking co-pilot.Flydubai confirmed in a statement on Wednesday that "a confrontation occurred in the cockpit of the flight," and that "the crew operating the aircraft managed to take control of the situation, divert the plane and land it safely at the airport in Tabuk.""At this early stage the reasons and motives behind the incident are not known and remain subject to an official investigation. The airline called on all parties to refrain from early speculation while the authorities gather the facts," the airline stated.Netanyahu has warned in recent days of unspecified, escalated security threats and on Wednesday ordered reinforced security over Israeli aviation.Israel has not experienced an aeroplane hijacking in decades but maintains some of the strictest airport security in the world.

title: Can Canada be the EU's answer to 'unreliable' trade partners?
description: Ahead of October's EU-Canada summit, both sides are considering a partnership beyond CETA and €130 billion in annual trade. Nothing is agreed on financial services, and the new "associate member" tier has no legal definition.
content: With tariffs, export controls and politics turning trade into a geopolitical lever, the EU seems to be shopping for partners it can count on. Canada, a like-minded economy already tied to the bloc by a free-trade agreement, is pitching itself as one.Ahead of the EU-Canada summit at the end of October, the two sides are discussing a partnership beyond the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA).Prime Minister Mark Carney proposed exploring an integrated market for financial services, alongside cooperation on payments, strategic minerals, energy, AI, and defence production. Nothing has been agreed on financial passports, mutual recognition of licences, or bank access.Fabian Zuleeg, Chief Executive and Chief Economist at the European Policy Centre, says the summit must deliver more than words. "So by the time we get to the summit, we should really be concrete," he says.A trade order under strainThe EU's problem is dependence. It relies on the US for technology and security, on Chinese supply chains for critical inputs, and on outside suppliers for energy, at a time when trade access is increasingly used as leverage.Canada offers economic gains, Zuleeg says, in areas like financial markets and technologies CETA does not fully cover. "The more important argument is political, and it's geopolitical."The existing EU-Canada partnership is CETA, provisionally applied since 2017. It removed 98% of tariff lines immediately, rising to 99% by 2024. Trade in goods and services reached €130 billion in 2025, up 80% from €72.1 billion in 2016, according to Commission figures.But that model has run its course. Erik van de Merel, chief economist at the European Centre for International Political Economy (ECIPE) and associate professor at the Université Libre de Bruxelles, notes that "tariffs among developed countries and between Canada and the European Union are fairly low."The next gains lie elsewhere, "in the area of services, technology collaboration, all these sort of intangible activities that are important for future growth," he says. Negotiations on a Digital Trade Agreement began in March 2026.What each side wantsFor the EU, the appeal is security of supply. Canada says it holds deposits of more than 34 critical minerals and is a leading producer of 10 considered essential to the energy transition. Europe needs them for batteries, grids and defence."We are very dependent, in particular on China, at the moment," Zuleeg says. Reducing that reliance, he argues, matters less for prices than for keeping European industry running during a dispute. Cheaper energy is possible too, he adds, but not overnight.For Ottawa, the logic is diversification. The US takes roughly seven in ten Canadian exports, while the EU was Canada's second-largest goods-trade partner in 2024 with 7.9% of its global goods trade. Canada also wants easier access to European customers and investors for its clean-energy, mining, AI, and defence firms. Canadian pension funds could co-finance mineral-processing and infrastructure projects.Defence is already a test case. In June 2026, Canada became the first non-European country included in the EU's €150 billion SAFE defence instrument, a possible template for sector-by-sector integration.The rule-taker questionThe hardest issue is regulation. Canada wants better access to European banking, insurance, and professional services such as law, accountancy, and architecture.Van de Merel expects the EU to ask for something in return. "The new rules that we are going to develop, to some extent, you would have to take them over," he says. If Canada wanted to set its own banking and professional rules without European oversight or harmonisation, he argues, it would have to think again because deeper market integration is a core EU goal.Alignment, he says, is the test of whether the project works. He adds that "one has to have regulatory alignment and I think that's going to be really key and a challenge whether this is going to be a success or not." It will not be quick. The EU's single market in services remains unfinished after decades, so a newcomer seeking the same benefits faces a long catch-up.Zuleeg is less worried about Canada becoming a mere rule-taker. Iceland follows single-market rules because it sits in the European Economic Area, he notes, but Canada would not be joining the single market. In his view, it would keep a distinct voice, for example on foreign policy. He doubts the deal would require treaty change and considers "associate membership" a misnomer. A tailored association agreement under Article 217 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU looks the more likely legal route.Practical steps are already under way. In March 2026, a joint EU-Canada committee agreed to pursue regulatory alignment on motor vehicles and conformity assessment and to widen mutual recognition in pharmaceuticals.The politics could still bite. In Ottawa, the question is how much EU regulation Canada can accept without a vote in EU institutions. In Brussels, candidate countries undergoing lengthy reforms may ask why Canada should get privileged access. Van de Merel is also watching the UK, which could object if Canada obtains terms it never had after Brexit.Limits and risksThe idea should not be oversold. Canada cannot replace China's role in manufacturing and mineral processing or the scale of the US economy. Mines, refineries, and ports take years to build, and the Atlantic is a logistical hurdle. Canada's exposure to Washington means a US–Canada crisis could spill into its production and investment.Then there is CETA itself. As of mid-September 2026, ten member states, including France, Italy, Poland, Belgium and Ireland, had still not ratified it, so its investment-protection provisions are not in force. The EU is discussing an unprecedented new tier while its flagship trade deal with Canada remains only partly ratified.Van de Merel warns that without institutions behind it, the initiative could fizzle. "Otherwise it's just an idea that is very symbolic and without any sort of political institutional consequences," he says.

title: Rutte responds to Moscow's nuclear threats, and the UK leader weighs re-joining the EU
description: Good morning, I’m Mared Gwyn. Welcome to your Thursday newsletter. Today: NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte tells Euronews that Russia should stop issuing nuclear threats, and the UK Prime Minister puts EU membership back on the table.
content: Nuclear tensions: In an interview with Euronews, NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte has told Russia to stop issuing nuclear threats, after Moscow sent a letter to the alliance saying it is prepared to deploy its nuclear arsenal if its territory – including the enclave of Kaliningrad – comes under attack.‘Stop’: "We are a defensive alliance. Stop the nuclear threats. This is absolutely not called for and not helpful," Rutte exclusively told the Euronews Defence and Space Summit on Wednesday, at a moment of heightened tension between Russia and the West.Rutte, however, dismissed the immediate threat to the alliance’s members, saying "we will defend every inch of NATO territory”.“That threat is not there, and if anything happens, we are ready to counter it,” he explained. Reuters first reported that Russia had warned NATO in a document that it could resort to nuclear weapons if the alliance attempted to annex the Russian enclave of Kaliningrad, while also threatening strikes on “decision-making centres” in NATO member states from the outset of a conflict.‘Worst-case scenario’: Earlier on Wednesday, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev – also speaking at Euronews’ summit – called for European dialogue with Russia to avert a nuclear attack. While rejecting the Kremlin’s escalatory rhetoric, Radev reminded his European counterparts of the “nuclear card”, noting Russia would be prone to play it if weakened or cornered."We cannot close our eyes (to the fact) that there are nuclear weapons on our continent, there are nuclear weapons in the arsenal of Russia. And this is part of the game calculation,” Radev said.Making Putin feel that ‘war is coming’: The European Commissioner for Defence, Andrius Kubilius, rejected Radev’s call for diplomatic engagement, warning it could embolden President Putin and undermine Ukraine."Russians are standing with their position very clear: Ukraine needs to surrender - that is their diplomacy position," Kubilius told Euronews, adding that Putin needs to “feel that war is coming to Russia itself”.‘Made in Europe’ under fire: A push from Brussels to prioritise domestic European companies in defence contracts was also front and centre of the debate on Wednesday. NATO chief Rutte described the debate as a “luxury”, warning that the initiative ignores a basic problem: Europe's defence industry cannot produce enough.Earlier on Wednesday, the US Ambassador to the EU, Andrew Puzder, slammed the EU’s “Buy European” weapons push as “self-interest”, saying it could disrupt the transatlantic defence industrial base and benefit Europe’s "enemies"."One attack by a powerful adversary on a member state, and we’ll all be glad that we focused on weapon superiority rather than regional economics," Puzder told the summit audience.My colleagues and I have more takeaways from the summit for you in this debrief.Migration talks: Home Affairs Ministers are meeting in Luxembourg with migration top of the agenda. Ministers are expected to discuss proposed measures to tackle irregular arrivals under the European Emergency Response Framework, expected to be unveiled by the Commission next month. EU sources tell my colleague Vincenzo Genovese that the proposal is expected to include a temporary suspension of asylum rights.Italy extends border controls: The meeting comes as tensions between Italy and Spain escalate again, after Rome extended aerial and maritime border checks with Spain by another 15 days in response to the situation in the enclave of Ceuta, where 80,000 migrants entered in an unprecedented mass entry in July.Meanwhile, a delegation of MEPs visited the Spanish exclave on Wednesday, denouncing the attacks and smear campaigns directed against activists and organisations working on the ground by far-right groups.French and Spanish leaders welcome Andy Burnham’s suggestion UK could go ‘all the way’ and rejoin the EUFrench President Emmanuel Macron and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez have welcomed Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s suggestion that the UK could look to rejoin the EU, with Macron saying “welcome back” when asked about the prospect during a press conference in Madrid.“If the British want to come back and if the Prime Minister is moving in that direction, I think that is very good news, both for his country and for the Europeans,” Macron said, speaking alongside Spain’s Pedro Sánchez, who also said the UK would be welcome back in the bloc.UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Wednesday floated going “all the way” and rejoining the EU, as he vowed to scope out options for future EU-UK ties.“We could stay as we are. We could look at what George Osborne has said about a customs union, we could look at what the Liberal Democrats said about the (EU) single market, or we could go all the way," Burnham said. The UK leader also said that the EU-UK summit postponed in July amid Starmer’s resignation would be held in November. Burnham has so far been perceived as much less focused on international and EU affairs than his predecessor Keir Starmer, leaving EU officials second-guessing his intentions for resetting relations with the bloc. But his statements now offer the clearest indication yet that his government is prepared to consider a much more ambitious overhaul of post-Brexit ties with Brussels. More.More from our newsroomsMethane is responsible for 30% of global warming – so why is the EU trying to delay rules to cut it? The EU has proposed to delay new rules to cut planet-warming emissions from methane, saying a delay would “relax” pressure on energy markets and therefore cut oil and gas prices. But will the new regulation really push up oil and gas prices, and how harmful are methane emissions? Ruth Wright explains.Hundreds held, dozens wounded as protests over conditions in French schools escalate. French security forces detained more than 600 people while dozens of police and gendarmes were wounded as protests that have seen blockades of high schools and violent clashes escalated, the interior minister said on Wednesday. Christina Molle and Gavin Blackburn have the details.Israel says pilot tried to crash Tel Aviv-bound plane during cockpit fight, before safe emergency landing. Flydubai flight FZ1073 to Israel made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia as passengers describe harrowing scenes of a fight between the pilots, with one of them stabbed. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said a pilot "attempted to crash the plane," as Israeli security services investigate. More.We're also keeping an eye onEuropean Commission President Ursula von der Leyen continues her Western Balkan tour in Kosovo and Montenegro.European Commissioner for the Economy Valdis Dombrovskis visits Chișinău, Moldova, and delivers a keynote speech at the National Bank of Moldova’s annual conference.EU home affairs ministers gather in Luxembourg.EU health ministers gather for an informal meeting in Dublin, Ireland.That’s it for today. Vincenzo Genovese contributed to this newsletter.

title: Before the Iran war vs now: How much of a worker’s wage is needed to fill a 50-litre tank?
description: A 50-litre diesel tank costs the equivalent of 15.4% of Bulgaria’s gross monthly minimum wage, compared with 3.8% in Luxembourg, as fuel prices have risen since the Iran war began.
content: The cost of filling a 50-litre diesel tank now takes 15.4% of Bulgaria’s gross monthly minimum wage, up from 9.9% before the Iran war began, highlighting the growing pressure on workers in Europe’s lowest-paid countries.Fuel prices have risen significantly since the Israeli-US joint attack on Iran resulted in effectively blocking the Strait of Hormuz, an essential route for one-fifth of global oil to pass through.In the EU, average consumer diesel prices rose by 40% between 23 February, before tensions in the Middle East escalated, and 21 September, according to the EU Weekly Oil Bulletin.Rising fuel prices affect many people both directly and indirectly, particularly low-paid workers and those earning the minimum wage. Asked why lower-income households are particularly affected, Torsten Müller, senior researcher at the European Trade Union Institute, told Euronews Business: “Because they spend a larger proportion of their income on essentials such as housing, food and transport than high-income households.”So, how much of the monthly minimum wage is needed to fill a 50-litre tank across Europe? And how much has that share increased since the war began?On 23 February 2026, the average price per litre in the EU was €1.637 for Euro 95 petrol and €1.594 for diesel. By 21 September, these had risen to €2.092 and €2.226 respectively. This represents increases of 27.8% for petrol and 39.6% for diesel.The table above shows all the details, including minimum wages and fuel prices across 22 EU countries and Turkey, an EU candidate country, for these two periods.The comparison uses gross monthly minimum wages, before tax and social security deductions.Minimum wages remained unchanged in most countries over this period, while Estonia recorded the largest increase in the eurozone at 6.8%, between the first and second halves of 2026. In some countries, the rise in petrol prices exceeded 30%, while diesel prices rose by 50%. Malta was the only country in the comparison where fuel prices remained unchanged.As of 21 September, the percentage of the monthly minimum wage needed to fill a 50-litre petrol tank ranged from 3.3% in Luxembourg to 13.4% in Bulgaria.It was also above 10% in Latvia (12.8%), Turkey (11.5%), Romania (11.5%), Greece (10.2%), Czechia (10.2%), Estonia (10.1%) and Slovakia (10.1%). The percentage was below 5% in Ireland (4.1%) and Belgium (4.4%).Among the major economies, Germany had the lowest figure, as minimum wage earners needed to spend 5% of their monthly minimum wage to fill a 50-litre petrol tank.Torsten Müller noted that the large differences between countries in these shares can largely be explained by the wide differences in minimum wages.“One litre of diesel is only marginally cheaper in Bulgaria while the minimum wage is less than a fourth of the one in Luxembourg,” he said. He underlined that the large differences are still reflected in the value of minimum wages in purchasing power standards (PPS), which take differences in price levels into account. In Luxembourg, the minimum wage in PPS is still twice as high as in Bulgaria.Workers in countries with lower minimum wages face a heavier burden, as they now need to allocate a larger share of their salaries to fuel than before the conflict. In Bulgaria, for example, the share rose by 3.6 percentage points for petrol, followed by Turkey (3.1) and Latvia (3).Filling a tank takes more than 10% of the monthly minimum wageA 50-litre diesel tank takes a bigger share of the monthly minimum wage where diesel costs more per litre than petrol. The share of the monthly minimum wage needed to fill a 50-litre diesel tank ranged from 3.8% in Luxembourg to 15.4% in Bulgaria.“When the average cost of rent is already more than a third of the minimum wage, spending another 15% of your entire wage on fuel is just not possible,” Esther Lynch, general secretary of the European Trade Union Confederation, told Euronews Business. She warned that people would be forced to give up their jobs, particularly in areas where there are no reliable public transport links. She said this would be bad for both workers and companies already facing labour shortages.The country rankings are broadly similar for diesel. Minimum wage earners needed to allocate more than 10% of their monthly minimum wage to fill a 50-litre tank in several countries. The share was 13.9% in Latvia, 13.8% in Turkey, 12.7% in Romania, 11.2% in Czechia and Estonia, 10.8% in Hungary, 10.4% in Greece and 10.3% in Portugal.Workers in Ireland (4.3%), Germany (5.2%), Belgium (5.3%) and the Netherlands (5.5%) needed to spend among the lowest shares of the minimum wage to afford a tank.Where does the minimum wage buy more fuel?The two charts above for petrol and diesel also show how much fuel a monthly minimum wage can buy in each country. A smaller share needed to fill a 50-litre tank means the minimum wage buys more fuel, while a larger share means it buys less.For example, as of 21 September, a minimum wage earner could buy 324 litres of diesel in Bulgaria, compared with 1,311 litres in Luxembourg.Fuel costs hit Central and Eastern European countries hardestCompared with February, the shares needed for a diesel tank rose sharply in Bulgaria (5.5 percentage points) and Turkey (5.3 percentage points). Workers in Latvia, Czechia and Estonia were also hit hard by fuel inflation, as the share of their minimum wage needed for a tank rose by more than 3 percentage points.Pointing to the gap in minimum wages between Western European countries and Central and Eastern European (CEE) countries, Müller said it is mainly in CEE countries that minimum wage earners have to spend the largest share of their salaries on petrol.

title: Explained: How the EU’s new cabin baggage rules will work – and when they start
description: EU travellers could soon get a larger cabin allowance at no extra cost – but UK passengers flying out of UK airports are unlikely to benefit from the new rules.
content: European air passengers travelling within the EU could soon be entitled to more hand luggage without paying extra, under a major overhaul of passenger rights.The European Parliament and EU member states reached a provisional agreement in June on new air passenger rules – the first major revision of the legislation since 2004.Under the new rules, passengers buying a standard ticket would be entitled to two pieces of hand luggage free of charge.This would include one small personal item, such as a handbag or backpack, which must fit under the seat in front. They would also be allowed one larger cabin bag weighing up to 7kg, with combined dimensions of up to 100cm.The changes are expected to come into force from late 2027 at the earliest, with October 2027 currently thought to be the earliest possible start date. However, the rules still need to complete the remaining EU legislative process before they can take effect.The European Parliament says the new provisions give passengers the right to carry a personal item on board “without additional fee”, potentially putting an end to some of the extra charges currently levied by airlines for cabin baggage.The Parliament also decided that airlines will still be able to offer cheaper fares to passengers who choose to travel without hand luggage, although it remains unclear exactly how this pricing system will work once the new rules come into force.The changes are part of a broader overhaul of EU air passenger rights, covering issues including delays, cancellations and compensation.For travellers, the key change is that a standard fare would have to include both an under-seat personal item and a small cabin bag, rather than passengers having to pay extra for the latter.It’s not good news for British passengers, who have not been considered European citizens since Brexit came into force. One of the country’s largest operators, easyJet UK, says passengers on outbound journeys won’t be able to take advantage of the incoming rules, according to a report by Which?.That will apply to all UK-based airlines, including British Airways and Jet2.Passengers flying out of the UK will not benefit from a free item of hand luggage despite new rules in Europe, easyJet has said.The airline said the rules will apply to UK passengers “only on return flights from EU countries”. However, EasyJet says that alongside all other British airlines, it is reviewing its own baggage rules, in preparation for when the EU legislation comes into effect.
